Use $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0$, and $a = -0.3833\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to solve for the distance $s = AB$:\begin{aligned} &v^2 = u^2 + 2as \cr &0 = 8^2 + 2(-0.3833)s \cr &0.7667s = 64 \cr &s = \dfrac{64}{0.7667} \cr &s \approx 83.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) (ii) Immediate Change in Tractor's Motion:

The tractor will immediately accelerate more rapidly. The backward-acting tension force ($T = 320\text{ N}$) is removed, increasing the net forward force on the tractor from $180\text{ N}$ to $500\text{ N}$.

Final Answer: $$R = 230\text{ N},\; T = 320\text{ N}$$
$$AB = 83.5\text{ m}$$
$$\text{Inextensible rope;}$$
$$\text{accelerates more rapidly}$$

pi_options.ans:
$$R = 270\text{ N},\; T = 360\text{ N}$$
$$AB = 75.2\text{ m}$$
$$\text{Smooth road;}$$
$$\text{constant velocity}$$
pi_options.feedback: This represents a calculation slip when applying Newton's Second Law to the combined system, which affects both the resistance $R$ and the tension $T$.

pi_options.ans:
$$R = 230\text{ N},\; T = 320\text{ N}$$
$$AB = 95.5\text{ m}$$
$$\text{Negligible air resistance;}$$
$$\text{tractor decelerates}$$
pi_options.feedback: This indicates a kinematic error when calculating the distance $AB$. Additionally, removing a resistive tension force causes the tractor to accelerate more rapidly, not decelerate.

pi_options.ans:
$$R = 230\text{ N},\; T = 320\text{ N}$$
$$AB = 83.5\text{ m}$$
$$\text{Elastic rope;}$$
$$\text{tractor stops completely}$$
pi_options.feedback: This is conceptually incorrect. In standard mechanics models, ropes are modelled as inextensible, not elastic. If the rope were elastic, the bodies would not share a uniform acceleration.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Internal vs. External Forces
bradley_insight.content: When resolving the tractor and trailer as a single combined system, the tension $T$ becomes an internal force and cancels out. This is a highly powerful trick to find the unknown resistance $R$ directly, without solving simultaneous equations first!

question:
A car is towing a caravan up a rough road inclined at $8^\circ$ to the horizontal by means of a light, inextensible tow-bar.
  • The mass of the car is $1200\text{ kg}$ and the mass of the caravan is $800\text{ kg}$.
  • The car exerts a constant driving force of $D$ Newtons parallel to the slope.
  • The resistance to motion is $150\text{ N}$ on the caravan and $250\text{ N}$ on the car.
  • The car and caravan accelerate uniformly up the plane at $0.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$.


(a) Find the value of $D$, giving your answer to three significant figures.

(b) Find the tension, in Newtons to three significant figures, in the tow-bar as they accelerate up the plane.
steps:
(a) Find the driving force D:

Treat the car and caravan as a single combined system. The total mass is $2000\text{ kg}$, and the total resistance force is $400\text{ N}$.

Calculate the component of total weight acting down the slope:\begin{aligned} &W_x \cr &\quad = m_{\text{total}} g \sin 8^\circ \cr &\quad = 2000(9.8)\sin 8^\circ \cr &\quad \approx 2727.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Apply Newton's Second Law parallel to the inclined plane (taking up the slope as positive):\begin{aligned} &D - R_{\text{total}} - W_x = m_{\text{total}} a \cr &D - 400 - 2727.8 = 2000(0.4) \cr &D - 3127.8 = 800 \cr &D = 3927.8 \cr &D \approx 3930\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the tension T:

Consider the caravan alone. Calculate the component of its weight acting down the slope:\begin{aligned} &W_{\text{caravan}} \cr &\quad = 800(9.8)\sin 8^\circ \cr &\quad \approx 1091.1\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Apply $F = ma$ to the caravan directed up the slope:\begin{aligned} &T - R_{\text{caravan}} - W_{\text{caravan}} \cr &\quad = m_{\text{caravan}} a \cr &T - 150 - 1091.1 = 800(0.4) \cr &T - 1241.1 = 320 \cr &T = 1561.1 \cr &T \approx 1560\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Final Answer: $$D = 3930\text{ N};$$
$$T = 1560\text{ N}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you completely ignored gravity in both steps, forgetting that the vehicles are travelling up an inclined plane. You must resolve the weight component parallel to the slope.
This represents a calculation slip where you used an incorrect trigonometric function (such as $\cos 8^\circ$ instead of $\sin 8^\circ$) when resolving the weight components parallel to the slope.
This indicates an error in part (b). You likely omitted the caravan's weight component when resolving the caravan's forces. Both resistance and gravity oppose the upward tension force.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Inclined Connected Particles
bradley_insight.content: When bodies are moving on an incline, never forget to resolve their weights parallel to the slope ($mg\sin{ \theta }$). This weight component acts as a backward resistive force that must be added to the physical resistance forces in your $F = ma$ equations!

question:
A lift of mass $500\text{ kg}$ contains a passenger of mass $80\text{ kg}$. The lift is pulled vertically upwards by a light, inextensible cable. The lift accelerates uniformly upwards at a rate of $1.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$.


(a) Find the tension in the cable.

(b) Find the normal reaction force exerted by the floor of the lift on the passenger.
steps:
(a) Find the tension in the cable:

Treat the lift and passenger as a combined system of total mass $580\text{ kg}$. Apply Newton's Second Law vertically upwards:\begin{aligned} &T - m_{\text{total}} g = m_{\text{total}} a \cr &T - 580(9.8) = 580(1.2) \cr &T - 5684 = 696 \cr &T = 6380\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the normal reaction R:

Consider only the passenger of mass $80\text{ kg}$ inside the lift. The vertical forces acting on the passenger are:

• Normal reaction $R$ pointing upwards from the floor.

• Weight of the passenger ($80g$) pointing downwards.

Apply Newton's Second Law to the passenger vertically upwards:\begin{aligned} &R - m_{\text{pass}} g = m_{\text{pass}} a \cr &R - 80(9.8) = 80(1.2) \cr &R - 784 = 96 \cr &R = 880\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Final Answer: $$T = 6380\text{ N};$$
$$R = 880\text{ N}$$

pi_options.feedback: This represents a static error. You likely assumed the lift was stationary (or moving at constant speed), setting tension and reaction equal to the weights. Since it is accelerating, the forces must exceed the weights.
This indicates an algebraic error where you set the upward forces equal to $ma$ alone, completely omitting the gravitational weights ($mg$) from the equations.
This is a sign error in part (b). You likely resolved the passenger's equation as $R = m(g - a)$ instead of $R = m(g + a)$. Accelerating upwards increases the normal reaction force.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Apparent Weight
bradley_insight.content: When accelerating vertically upwards, the normal reaction force $R = m(g+a)$ is greater than the passenger's static weight $mg$. This is why you feel heavier when a lift first starts moving upwards—your 'apparent weight' has increased!

question:
Two blocks, of mass $5\text{ kg}$ and $3\text{ kg}$, are connected by a light, inextensible string passing over a smooth, fixed pulley suspended from a ceiling. The blocks are released from rest.


(a) Find the acceleration, in $\text{m s}^{-2}$, of the blocks.

(b) Find the tension in the string.

(c) Find the force exerted by the string on the pulley.
steps:
(a) Find the acceleration:

Let $a$ be the acceleration of the system. The heavier $5\text{ kg}$ mass accelerates downwards and the lighter $3\text{ kg}$ mass accelerates upwards. Set up the equation of motion for each block:

• For the $5\text{ kg}$ block (downwards):
$$5g - T = 5a$$

• For the $3\text{ kg}$ block (upwards):
$$T - 3g = 3a$$
Add the two equations together to eliminate $T$ and solve for $a$:\begin{aligned} &5g - 3g = 8a \cr &2g = 8a \cr &a = \dfrac{2(9.8)}{8} \cr &a = 2.45\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the tension T:

Substitute $a = 2.45\text{ m s}^{-2}$ into the equation of motion for the $3\text{ kg}$ block:\begin{aligned} &T - 3g = 3a \cr &T - 3(9.8) = 3(2.45) \cr &T - 29.4 = 7.35 \cr &T = 36.75\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the force exerted on the pulley:

The string hangs down on both sides of the pulley wheel, pulling downwards with tension $T$ on each side. The total downward force $F$ exerted on the pulley is:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = 2T \cr &\quad = 2(36.75) \cr &\quad = 73.5\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Final Answer: $$a = 2.45\text{ m s}^{-2};$$
$$T = 36.75\text{ N};$$
$$F = 73.5\text{ N}$$

pi_options.feedback: This is a common error in part (c). The string pulls downwards on the pulley from both sides, so the total force exerted on the pulley is $2T$, not $T$.
This represents a major error where the tension $T$ was neglected during acceleration calculations, assuming the heavier mass falls under pure gravity.
This represents a calculation slip in part (b) where you equated the tension $T$ to the static weight of the $3\text{ kg}$ block, ignoring its upward acceleration.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Forces on Pulleys
bradley_insight.content: Students frequently make the mistake of setting the force on the pulley equal to $T$. Because the string wraps over the top and hangs down both sides, it pulls downwards with a tension $T$ on both the left and right, resulting in a total downward force of $2T$ on the pulley wheel!

question:
A block $A$ of mass $8\text{ kg}$ is held on a rough plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between block $A$ and the plane is $0.25$.

Block $A$ is connected by a light, inextensible string passing parallel to the line of greatest slope over a smooth pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block $B$ of mass $M\text{ kg}$.

Given that the system is in limiting equilibrium and block $A$ is on the point of sliding up the plane:


(a) Find the normal reaction force, in Newtons to three significant figures, acting on block $A$.

(b) Find the value of $M$, giving your answer to three significant figures.
steps:
(a) Find the normal reaction force acting on A:

Resolve the forces acting on block $A$ perpendicular to the inclined plane:\begin{aligned} &R_A \cr &\quad = 8g\cos 30^\circ \cr &\quad = 78.4 \times 0.86603 \cr &\quad \approx 67.9\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the value of M:

Calculate the maximum frictional force, $F_{\text{max}}$, acting on block $A$:\begin{aligned} &F_{\text{max}} \cr &\quad = \mu R_A \cr &\quad = 0.25 \times 67.896 \cr &\quad = 16.974\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Because block $A$ is on the point of sliding up the plane, friction opposes this motion and acts down the plane. Therefore, both friction ($F_{\text{max}}$) and the component of weight along the slope ($8g\sin 30^\circ$) pull block $A$ down the incline.

Apply equilibrium to block $A$ parallel to the slope:\begin{aligned} &T \cr &\quad = F_{\text{max}} + 8g\sin 30^\circ \cr &\quad = 16.974 + 8(9.8)\sin 30^\circ \cr &\quad = 16.974 + 39.200 \cr &\quad = 56.174\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Analyze hanging block $B$. In static equilibrium, the tension $T$ is balanced by the weight ($Mg$):\begin{aligned} &T = Mg \cr &56.174 = M(9.8) \end{aligned}
Solve for $M$:\begin{aligned} &M \cr &\quad = \dfrac{56.174}{9.8} \cr &\quad \approx 5.73 \end{aligned}

Final Answer: $$R_A = 67.9\text{ N};$$
$$M = 5.73$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you assumed block A was on the point of sliding down the plane. If it were sliding down, friction would act up the plane ($T = 39.200 - 16.974$, giving $T = 22.226\text{ N}$), but because it is sliding up, friction acts down the plane.
This is a non-inclined error. It occurs if you forgot to resolve forces parallel and perpendicular to the inclined plane, treating the table surface as if it were completely flat.
This represents a calculation slip where the frictional force component was completely omitted from the tension equation in part (b).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Direction of Impending Motion
bradley_insight.content: In limiting equilibrium problems, always verify the direction of impending motion! Because block A is on the point of sliding up the plane, the friction force acts down the slope, opposing the tension. If it were on the point of sliding down, friction would point up the slope.

question:
A girl throws a small stone vertically upwards from a bridge. At the instant the stone leaves her hand, it is $9\text{ m}$ above the water below and is moving with a speed of $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The motion of the stone is modelled as that of a particle moving freely under gravity, and the acceleration due to gravity is modelled as being of constant magnitude $10\text{ m s}^{-2}$. The stone hits the water $T$ seconds after leaving the girl's hand.

Using the model, find the value of $T$.
steps:
Set up the parameters for the motion, taking the vertically upwards direction as positive:

• Initial velocity, $u = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}$

• Displacement, $s = -9\text{ m}$ (since the water is below the starting point)

• Acceleration, $a = -10\text{ m s}^{-2}$

Substitute these values into the constant acceleration displacement formula:\begin{aligned} &s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 \cr &-9 \cr &\quad = 12T + \dfrac{1}{2}(-10)T^2 \cr &\quad = 12T - 5T^2 \end{aligned}
Rearrange the equation to form a standard quadratic equation equal to zero:\begin{aligned} &5T^2 - 12T - 9 = 0 \end{aligned}
Factorise the quadratic expression to solve for $T$:\begin{aligned} &(5T + 3)(T - 3) = 0 \end{aligned}

This gives two possible mathematical solutions:\begin{aligned} &T = 3 \cr &\text{or} \cr &T = -0.6 \end{aligned}

Since time $T$ must be greater than zero, we choose the positive solution. Therefore, $T = 3\text{ seconds}$.
Final Answer: $T = 3$

pi_options.feedback: This occurs if you model the initial velocity as vertically downwards ($u = -12\text{ m s}^{-1}$) instead of vertically upwards. Check the direction of projection specified in the question.
This is the time taken for the stone to reach its maximum height where $v = 0$. The question asks for the total time $T$ until the stone hits the water, not just the ascent time.

This value arises from a sign or factorisation error in the quadratic equation, such as factorising $5T^2 - 12T - 9 = 0$ incorrectly. Always expand your brackets to verify they reconstruct the original quadratic.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Watch the Given Constants
bradley_insight.content: Pay close attention to the value of $g$ specified in the question. While $9.8$ is the standard physical constant, this question explicitly specifies $10\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Using the wrong constant will lead to messy decimals and a loss of accuracy marks.

question:
A boy throws a ball vertically upwards from a balcony that is $14.7\text{ m}$ above the horizontal ground. The ball is thrown with an initial speed of $9.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The motion of the ball is modelled as that of a particle moving freely under gravity, and the acceleration due to gravity is modelled as being of constant magnitude $9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Using the model, find the time, $T$ seconds, from when the ball is thrown to when it hits the ground.
steps:
Set up the motion parameters with the vertically upwards direction defined as positive:

• Initial velocity, $u = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$

• Displacement, $s = -14.7\text{ m}$ (since the ground is below the balcony)

• Acceleration, $a = -9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$

Substitute these parameters into the constant acceleration displacement formula:\begin{aligned} &s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 \cr &-14.7 \cr &\quad = 9.8T + \dfrac{1}{2}(-9.8)T^2 \cr &\quad = 9.8T - 4.9T^2 \end{aligned}
Simplify the quadratic equation by dividing every term by $4.9$:\begin{aligned} &4.9T^2 - 9.8T - 14.7 = 0 \cr &T^2 - 2T - 3 = 0 \end{aligned}
Factorise the simplified quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &(T - 3)(T + 1) = 0 \end{aligned}

Solve for $T$:\begin{aligned} &T = 3 \cr &\text{or} \cr &T = -1 \end{aligned}

Since time $T$ must be positive, we reject the negative solution. Thus, $T = 3\text{ seconds}$.
Final Answer: $T = 3$

pi_options.feedback: This result occurs if you assume the initial velocity is downwards ($u = -9.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$), which alters the quadratic to $T^2 + 2T - 3 = 0$. Remember that the ball is projected upwards.
This is a common error resulting from forgetting to multiply the acceleration term by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in the equation $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$, leading to an incorrect quadratic.

This represents calculating only the ascent time (the time taken to reach maximum height where $v = 0$), plus an incorrect scaling factor. Make sure to solve the full displacement quadratic to find the total time of flight.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Spotting Common Factors
bradley_insight.content: When $u$ and $g$ are multiples of each other (such as $9.8$ and $4.9$), look to simplify the quadratic by dividing through before using your calculator. Here, dividing by $4.9$ turns a messy expression into a simple, factorable GCSE quadratic: $T^2 - 2T - 3 = 0$.

question:
A particle is projected vertically upwards with speed $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from a point $25\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground. The particle moves freely under gravity, with the acceleration due to gravity modelled as being of constant magnitude $10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Find the total distance travelled by the particle from the instant of projection to the instant it hits the ground.
steps: Identify that total distance is different from displacement. To find total distance, we must compute the upward climb to maximum height and the subsequent downward fall to the ground separately.

Calculate the distance travelled upwards to the peak where velocity $v = 0$. Using the formula $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with upwards as positive:\begin{aligned} &0 \cr &\quad = 20^2 + 2(-10)s_1 \cr &\quad = 400 - 20s_1 \cr &20s_1 = 400 \cr &s_1 = 20\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Thus, the particle climbs $20\text{ m}$ upwards from the projection point.
Determine the total height of the peak above the horizontal ground:\begin{aligned} &\text{Peak Height} \cr &\quad = 25 + 20 \cr &\quad = 45\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Calculate the total distance travelled by adding the upward journey and the downward journey:

• Distance up = $20\text{ m}$

• Distance down = $45\text{ m}$ (from peak to ground)\begin{aligned} &\text{Total Distance} \cr &\quad = 20 + 45 \cr &\quad = 65\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $65\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This is the magnitude of the final displacement, which only measures the straight-line distance between the start point and the end point. Total distance must account for the entire path travelled.
This is the maximum height reached above the ground. To find the total distance, you must add the initial $20\text{ m}$ ascent to this downward descent of $45\text{ m}$.

This is the total distance for the round trip back to the point of projection ($20\text{ m}$ up and $20\text{ m}$ down), which neglects the final $25\text{ m}$ fall from the projection level to the ground.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Distance vs. Displacement
bradley_insight.content: Total distance is a scalar representing the actual path length, whereas displacement is a vector representing the change in position. Do not confuse the two! Always sketch or track the physical path: $20\text{ m}$ up, then $45\text{ m}$ down, giving a total of $65\text{ m}$.

question:
A small ball is thrown vertically upwards from a platform that is $15\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground. The ball is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity, and the acceleration due to gravity is modelled as being of constant magnitude $10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Given that the ball hits the ground $3$ seconds after it is released, find the speed with which it was initially thrown.
steps:
Define the SUVAT parameters with vertically upwards as the positive direction:

• Displacement, $s = -15\text{ m}$ (since the ball lands below the platform)

• Time, $t = 3\text{ s}$

• Acceleration, $a = -10\text{ m s}^{-2}$

• Initial velocity, $u$ (to be found)

Substitute these values into the constant acceleration equation $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} &-15 \cr &\quad = u(3) + \dfrac{1}{2}(-10)(3)^2 \cr &\quad = 3u - 5(9) \cr &\quad = 3u - 45 \end{aligned}

Rearrange the equation to isolate $u$:\begin{aligned} &3u = 45 - 15 \cr &3u = 30 \cr &u = 10\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

The initial speed of the ball was $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Final Answer: $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: This is the result of using a positive displacement ($s = +15\text{ m}$). Because the ball lands on the ground below its release point, the displacement must be negative when choosing upwards as the positive direction.
This error occurs if you forget to multiply the acceleration term by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in the formula $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$, leading to the equation $-15 = 3u - 10(3)^2$.

This value often results from dividing the distance directly by time ($15 \div 3 = 5$) and incorrectly adding or adjusting for gravity without using the proper constant acceleration kinematic equations.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Sign Conventions are Key
bradley_insight.content: Since the ball is thrown upwards and lands below its release height, its displacement must be negative ($s = -15\text{ m}$). A very common mistake is using $+15\text{ m}$, which will lead to an incorrect initial velocity of $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Consistency in sign conventions is vital.

question:
A hot-air balloon is rising vertically with a constant speed of $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$. At the instant the balloon is $30\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground, a passenger drops a camera. The camera is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity, and the acceleration due to gravity is modelled as being of constant magnitude $10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Calculate the time, $T$ seconds, from the moment the camera is dropped to the moment it hits the ground.
steps:
Determine the initial velocity of the camera. Because the camera is released from a balloon rising at $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, it inherits this upward velocity at the instant of release:

• Initial velocity, $u = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (vertically upwards)

Set up the remaining SUVAT parameters with vertically upwards defined as the positive direction:

• Displacement, $s = -30\text{ m}$ (since it lands on the ground below)

• Acceleration, $a = -10\text{ m s}^{-2}$
Substitute these parameters into the constant acceleration formula $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} &-30 \cr &\quad = 5T + \dfrac{1}{2}(-10)T^2 \cr &\quad = 5T - 5T^2 \end{aligned}
Rearrange this into standard quadratic form and simplify by dividing every term by $5$:\begin{aligned} &5T^2 - 5T - 30 = 0 \cr &T^2 - T - 6 = 0 \end{aligned}
Factorise the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &(T - 3)(T + 2) = 0 \end{aligned}

Solve for $T$:\begin{aligned} &T = 3 \cr &\text{or} \cr &T = -2 \end{aligned}

Since time $T$ must be positive, we reject the negative solution. Thus, $T = 3\text{ seconds}$.
Final Answer: $T = 3$

pi_options.feedback: This occurs if you assume the initial velocity is $0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ relative to the ground. Objects dropped from a moving platform inherit the velocity of that platform at the instant of release.
This result occurs if you assume the initial velocity of the camera is directed downwards ($u = -5\text{ m s}^{-1}$). Since the balloon is rising, the camera initially continues upwards.
This represents a calculation error, typically from using positive displacement ($s = +30\text{ m}$) or a mistake in applying the quadratic formula to the coefficients.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dropped Objects and Inertia
bradley_insight.content: This is a classic 'relative motion' trap. Any object released from a moving vehicle inherits the vehicle's instantaneous velocity. Even though the passenger 'drops' the camera, relative to the ground it actually travels vertically upwards briefly before gravity slows it down and it begins to fall.

question:
A train travels along a straight horizontal track between two stations, $P$ and $Q$. In a model of the motion, the train starts from rest at $P$ and moves with constant acceleration $0.4\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$ for $50\text{ s }$. The train then moves at a constant velocity before it moves with a constant deceleration of $0.8\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$, coming to rest at $Q$.

(a) For this model of the motion of the train between $P$ and $Q$:
(i) state the value of the constant velocity of the train,
(ii) state the time for which the train is decelerating,
(iii) sketch a velocity-time graph for the motion of the train.

The total distance between the two stations is $3250\text{ m }$.

(b) Using the model, find the total time taken by the train to travel from $P$ to $Q$.

(c) Suggest one improvement that could be made to the model to make it more realistic.
steps:
(a)(i) Constant Velocity ($V$):
The train starts from rest ($u = 0$) and accelerates at $a = 0.4\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$ for $t = 50\text{ s }$. Using $v = u + at$:

\begin{aligned} V &= 0 + 0.4 \times 50 \cr V &= 20\text{ m s}^{ -1 } \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Deceleration time ($t_d$):
The train decelerates from its constant velocity of $20\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ to rest ($v = 0$) at a rate of $0.8\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$. Using $v = u + at$:

\begin{aligned} 0 &= 20 - 0.8t_d \cr 0.8t_d &= 20 \cr t_d &= 25\text{ s } \end{aligned}

(a)(iii) Velocity-time graph sketch:
The graph consists of three phases:
1. Acceleration from $(0,0)$ to $(50, 20)$
2. Constant velocity of $20\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ until deceleration begins
3. Deceleration from $20\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ to rest at the final time $T$, lasting $25\text{ s }$:

(b) Find the total time $T$:
We can find the total distance by calculating the area under the velocity-time graph for each phase:

• Phase 1 (Acceleration): Area of triangle = $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \times 50 \times 20 = 500\text{ m }$
• Phase 3 (Deceleration): Area of triangle = $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \times 25 \times 20 = 250\text{ m }$
• Phase 2 (Constant Velocity): The remaining distance is:

\begin{aligned} 3250 - (500 + 250) = 2500\text{ m } \end{aligned}

The time spent at constant speed ($t_c$) is:

\begin{aligned} t_c &= \dfrac{ 2500 }{ 20 } \cr t_c &= 125\text{ s } \end{aligned}

The total time $T$ is the sum of the durations of all three phases:

\begin{aligned} T &= 50 + 125 + 25 \cr T &= 200\text{ seconds } \end{aligned}

(c) Suggested Improvement:
The model could be made more realistic by smoothing the transitions between phases rather than assuming instantaneous changes in acceleration (i.e. avoiding sharp corners on the velocity-time graph), or by incorporating air resistance and friction.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (a)(ii) $25\text{ s}$, (b) $200\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: This result is based on an arithmetic slip when summing the times of the three phases: $50 + 125 + 25$ is equal to $200\text{ s}$, not $187.5\text{ s}$.

This occurs if you miscalculate the deceleration time as $16\text{ s}$ instead of $25\text{ s}$ by multiplying by $0.8$ instead of dividing. Deceleration time is found by dividing the constant velocity by the rate of deceleration.
This error occurs if you miss one of the journey segments (such as the deceleration phase) when calculating the total travel time.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: End Phases First
bradley_insight.content: For multi-stage journeys represented as a trapezium on a velocity-time graph, always calculate the durations and distances of the two 'end' phases (acceleration and deceleration) first. The middle phase distance is then easily found by subtracting these from the total distance.

question:
A cyclist travels along a straight horizontal road. She starts from rest at point $X$ and accelerates uniformly at $1.2\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$ until she reaches a speed of $18\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$. She maintains this speed for $T$ seconds before decelerating uniformly at $0.6\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$, coming to rest at point $Y$. The entire journey from $X$ to $Y$ takes $120\text{ s }$.

(a) Sketch a velocity-time graph for the cyclist's journey.

(b) Find the value of $T$.

(c) Find the total distance between $X$ and $Y$.

(d) State one physical factor that has been ignored in this model of the cyclist's motion.
steps:
(a) Velocity-time graph sketch:
The journey contains three distinct sections:
1. Uniform acceleration from rest to $18\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ over $15\text{ s }$
2. Constant speed of $18\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ for $T$ seconds (from $15\text{ s }$ to $15 + T$)
3. Uniform deceleration from $18\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ to rest over $30\text{ s }$ to the final time $120\text{ s }$:

(b) Find the value of $T$:
First, calculate the duration of the acceleration phase ($t_a$):

\begin{aligned} t_a &= \dfrac{ v }{ a_1 } \cr t_a &= \dfrac{ 18 }{ 1.2 } \cr t_a &= 15\text{ s } \end{aligned}

Next, calculate the duration of the deceleration phase ($t_d$):

\begin{aligned} t_d &= \dfrac{ v }{ a_2 } \cr t_d &= \dfrac{ 18 }{ 0.6 } \cr t_d &= 30\text{ s } \end{aligned}

Since the total time for the entire journey is $120\text{ s }$, the constant velocity duration $T$ is:

\begin{aligned} T &= 120 - t_a - t_d \cr T &= 120 - 15 - 30 \cr T &= 75\text{ seconds } \end{aligned}

(c) Find the total distance:
The total distance is the area of the trapezium under the velocity-time graph. The formula for the area of a trapezium is $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }(a + b)h$:
• Bottom parallel side, $a = 120$
• Top parallel side, $b = T = 75$
• Height, $h = 18$

\begin{aligned}& \text{ Total Distance }\cr & \qquad= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \times (120 + 75) \times 18 \cr & \qquad= 97.5 \times 18 \cr &\qquad= 1755\text{ m } \end{aligned}

(d) Ignored Factor:
The model treats the bicycle and cyclist as a particle, thereby ignoring air resistance, friction between the tyres and road, and the physical dimensions of the cyclist.
Final Answer: (b) $T = 75\text{ s}$, (c) $1755\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This distance of $1620\text{ m}$ is obtained if you make an arithmetic error during the trapezium area calculation, such as using incorrect parallel side values.

This occurs if you fail to subtract the deceleration phase time of $30\text{ s}$ from the total time when calculating $T$, leading to $T = 90\text{ s}$ and a corresponding overestimate of the distance.

This distance of $1350\text{ m}$ represents only the distance covered during the constant velocity phase ($75 \times 18$). Ensure you include the triangular areas for both the acceleration and deceleration phases.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Trailing Journey Constraints
bradley_insight.content: The entire journey time is given as $120\text{ s }$, so $T$ is simply the total time minus the durations spent changing speed. Always verify that your individual phase durations add up perfectly to the given total before calculating the distance.

question:
Two cars, $A$ and $B$, start from rest at the same point at time $t = 0$ and travel in the same direction along a straight horizontal road.
• Car $A$ accelerates uniformly at $1.5\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$ for $10\text{ s }$ to a speed of $15\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$, and then continues at this constant speed.
• Car $B$ accelerates uniformly at $1.0\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$ for $20\text{ s }$ to a speed of $20\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$, and then continues at this constant speed.

(a) Sketch, on the same axes, the velocity-time graphs for the motion of both cars for $0 \le t \le 30$.

(b) Find the value of $t$ when the two cars are travelling at the same speed.

(c) Find the distance between the two cars at $t = 30\text{ s }$.
steps:
(a) Sketch on the same axes:
• Car $A$ accelerates to $15\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ at $t = 10\text{ s }$ and remains constant.
• Car $B$ accelerates to $20\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ at $t = 20\text{ s }$ and remains constant.
• The two graphs intersect at $t = 15\text{ s }$, where both cars are travelling at $15\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$:

(b) Find $t$ when speeds are equal:
Car $A$ reaches its constant speed of $15\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ at $t = 10\text{ s }$.
Car $B$ is still accelerating at $t = 10\text{ s }$. We want to find the time $t$ when Car $B$ reaches $15\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ during its acceleration phase:

\begin{aligned} v &= u + at \cr 15 &= 0 + 1.0 \times t \cr t &= 15\text{ seconds } \end{aligned}

Since $15\text{ s }$ is within Car $B$'s acceleration phase ($0 \le t \le 20$), this is the correct time.

(c) Find the distance between the cars at $t = 30\text{ s }$:
We calculate the distance travelled by each car by finding the area under their respective velocity-time graphs from $t = 0$ to $t = 30$.

• Distance for Car $A$:
The shape is a trapezium with parallel sides of length $30$ and $20$, and a height of $15$:

\begin{aligned} \text{ Distance }_A &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \times (30 + 20) \times 15 \cr &= 25 \times 15 \cr &= 375\text{ m } \end{aligned}

• Distance for Car $B$:
The shape is a trapezium with parallel sides of length $30$ and $10$, and a height of $20$:

\begin{aligned} \text{ Distance }_B &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \times (30 + 10) \times 20 \cr &= 20 \times 20 \cr &= 400\text{ m } \end{aligned}

• Distance between the two cars:
Subtract Car $A$'s distance from Car $B$'s distance:

\begin{aligned} \text{ Separation } &= 400 - 375 \cr &= 25\text{ m } \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $t = 15\text{ s}$, (c) $25\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This separation of $75\text{ m}$ occurs if you make an error in calculating the trapezoidal areas for the distance of Car $A$ or Car $B$.
The time of equal speed is $15\text{ s}$, because Car $B$ reaches the constant speed of Car $A$ ($15\text{ m s}^{-1}$) at exactly $t = 15\text{ s}$. Avoid equating average speeds to find this point.

Make sure you calculate the entire distance covered by both cars up to $t = 30\text{ s}$, including both the acceleration and constant speed phases, rather than just comparing their acceleration phases.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Visualising Area Separation
bradley_insight.content: On a combined velocity-time graph, the distance between the two vehicles is visually represented by the difference between the areas under their respective lines. Finding equal speeds tells you where the vertical separation is zero, but the physical separation is found by computing the area difference.

question:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight horizontal line. At time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$), the velocity of $P$, $v\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$, is modelled by the formula:
$$v = 6t - t^2 \quad \text{for } 0 \le t \le 6$$
and $v = 0$ for $t > 6$.

(a) Sketch a velocity-time graph for the motion of $P$ for $0 \le t \le 8$.

(b) Find the maximum speed of $P$ during the interval $0 \le t \le 6$, stating the value of $t$ at which it occurs.

(c) Find the total distance travelled by $P$ during the interval $0 \le t \le 6$.
steps:
(a) Sketch of the velocity-time graph:
The graph is a parabola passing through the origin $(0,0)$ and meeting the t-axis again at $t = 6\text{ s }$. For $t > 6$, the velocity is zero (horizontal line on the axis):

(b) Find the maximum speed:
The velocity function is $v = 6t - t^2$. To find the maximum speed, we differentiate $v$ with respect to $t$ and set the derivative to zero:

\begin{aligned} \dfrac{ \mathrm{d}v }{ \mathrm{d}t } &= 6 - 2t \cr 6 - 2t &= 0 \cr t &= 3\text{ seconds } \end{aligned}

Substitute $t = 3$ back into the velocity formula to find the maximum speed:

\begin{aligned} v_{ \text{ max } } &= 6(3) - (3)^2 \cr &= 18 - 9 \cr &= 9\text{ m s}^{ -1 } \end{aligned}

The maximum speed is $9\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$, occurring at $t = 3\text{ s }$.

(c) Find the total distance travelled:
Since $v \ge 0$ during the interval $0 \le t \le 6$, the total distance is found by integrating the velocity function between these limits:

\begin{aligned} \text{ Distance } &= \int_{ 0 }^{ 6 } (6t - t^2) \, \mathrm{d}t \cr &= \left[ 3t^2 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }t^3 \right]_{ 0 }^{ 6 } \cr &= \left( 3(6)^2 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }(6)^3 \right) - 0 \cr &= (108 - 72) \cr &= 36\text{ m } \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 3\text{ s}$, (c) $36\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This distance of $18\text{ m}$ is obtained if you integrate $t^2$ incorrectly as $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }t^3$ or make a division slip during integration. Remember that $\int t^n \, \mathrm{d}t = \dfrac{ t^{n+1} }{ n+1 }$.
To find the maximum speed, substitute $t = 3$ into the original function $v = 6t - t^2$, which yields $18 - 9 = 9\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Ensure you use the correct function.
Make sure you use definite integration limits from $0$ to $6$ to find the exact area under the curved parabola rather than trying to approximate it with a bounding rectangle.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Variable Kinematics Rules
bradley_insight.content: When velocity is a non-linear function of $t$, you must use calculus rather than SUVAT. As a nice pure-maths verification, the area of the 'hump' of this parabola is exactly $\dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 }$ of the bounding box ($6 \times 9$), which is $36\text{ m }$.

question:
A parachutist jumps from a stationary balloon and falls vertically. She falls freely under gravity from rest for $4\text{ s }$. At the instant $t = 4\text{ s }$, her parachute opens, causing her to decelerate uniformly at $12\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$ for $2.5\text{ s }$. She then continues to fall vertically at a constant speed of $V\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ until she reaches the ground. The acceleration due to gravity is modelled as $9.8\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$.

(a) Show that the speed of the parachutist at $t = 4\text{ s }$ is $39.2\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$.

(b) Find the value of $V$.

(c) Sketch a velocity-time graph for the motion of the parachutist from the instant she jumps to the instant she reaches the ground.

Given that the total vertical distance fallen is $230.9\text{ m}$:

(d) Find the total time taken from the instant she jumps to the instant she reaches the ground.
steps:
(a) Show that the speed at $t = 4\text{ s }$ is $39.2\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$:
The parachutist falls freely from rest under gravity ($u = 0$, $a = 9.8\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$) for $4\text{ s }$. Using $v = u + at$:

\begin{aligned} v &= 0 + 9.8 \times 4 \cr v &= 39.2\text{ m s}^{ -1 } \end{aligned}

(b) Find the value of $V$:
At $t = 4\text{ s }$, the parachute opens, decelerating her at $12\text{ m s}^{ -2 }$ for $2.5\text{ s }$. Using $v = u + at$ with initial speed $u = 39.2\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$:

\begin{aligned} V &= 39.2 - 12 \times 2.5 \cr V &= 39.2 - 30 \cr V &= 9.2\text{ m s}^{ -1 } \end{aligned}

(c) Sketch the velocity-time graph:
The graph comprises three segments:
1. Linear acceleration from $(0,0)$ to $(4, 39.2)$
2. Linear deceleration from $(4, 39.2)$ to $(6.5, 9.2)$
3. Horizontal line representing a constant terminal speed of $9.2\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$ until she lands at $T$:

(d) Find the total time of flight $T$:
We split the total distance of $230.9\text{ m }$ into the three phases of the journey:

• Phase 1 (Free Fall): Area of triangle:

\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \times 4 \times 39.2 \cr &= 78.4\text{ m } \end{aligned}

• Phase 2 (Deceleration): Area of trapezium under the graph between $t = 4$ and $t = 6.5$ (duration of $2.5\text{ s }$):

\begin{aligned} s_2 &= \dfrac{ 39.2 + 9.2 }{ 2 } \times 2.5 \cr &= 24.2 \times 2.5 \cr &= 60.5\text{ m } \end{aligned}

• Phase 3 (Constant Speed): Find the remaining distance to the ground:

\begin{aligned} s_3 &= 230.9 - (78.4 + 60.5) \cr s_3 &= 230.9 - 138.9 \cr s_3 &= 92\text{ m } \end{aligned}

Calculate the time spent in Phase 3 ($t_3$) at constant speed $V = 9.2\text{ m s}^{ -1 }$:

\begin{aligned} t_3 &= \dfrac{ s_3 }{ V } \cr &= \dfrac{ 92 }{ 9.2 } \cr &= 10\text{ s } \end{aligned}

• Total Time: Sum the times of all three phases:

\begin{aligned} T_{\text{ total }} &= 4 + 2.5 + 10 \cr &= 16.5\text{ seconds } \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $V = 9.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (d) $16.5\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: This total time of $15.5\text{ s}$ is a common arithmetic slip when summing the phases ($4 + 2.5 + 10$), where $4 + 2.5$ is added incorrectly or one of the values is misread.
Make sure you use the trapezium area formula $\dfrac{ u + v }{ 2 } \times t$ to calculate the distance travelled during the deceleration phase rather than a simple triangle.
Since the parachute causes a deceleration, the acceleration is negative relative to the direction of motion, so $V = 39.2 - 12(2.5)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Mid-Journey Trapeziums
bradley_insight.content: The deceleration phase of this motion is a trapezium on the velocity-time graph. Make sure you use the average velocity $(\dfrac{ u + v }{ 2 })$ to find that middle distance correctly, rather than mistakenly treating it as a simple triangle.

question:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. At time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$), the displacement, $x$ metres, of $P$ from the origin $O$ is given by:$$x = t^2(t^2 - 4t + 4)$$(a) Find the times when $P$ is instantaneously at rest.

(b) Find the total distance travelled by $P$ in the time interval $0 \le t \le 3$.

(c) Show that $P$ will never move along the negative $x$-axis.
steps:
(a) Find when $P$ is instantaneously at rest:

First, expand the expression for displacement $x$ to make differentiation straightforward:\begin{aligned} &x \cr &\quad = t^2(t^2 - 4t + 4) \cr &\quad = t^4 - 4t^3 + 4t^2 \end{aligned}

The velocity $v$ is the derivative of displacement with respect to time:\begin{aligned} &v \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = 4t^3 - 12t^2 + 8t \end{aligned}Set $v = 0$ to find when the particle is instantaneously at rest:\begin{aligned} &4t(t^2 - 3t + 2) = 0 \cr &4t(t - 1)(t - 2) = 0 \end{aligned}The particle is at rest at $t = 0\text{ s}$, $t = 1\text{ s}$, and $t = 2\text{ s}$.

(b) Find the total distance travelled in the interval $0 \le t \le 3$:

Evaluate displacement $x$ at the endpoints and turning points within this interval:

• At $t = 0$:\begin{aligned} &x(0) \cr &\quad = 0^2(0 - 2)^2 \cr &\quad = 0\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 1$:\begin{aligned} &x(1) \cr &\quad = 1^2(1 - 2)^2 \cr &\quad = 1\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 2$:\begin{aligned} &x(2) \cr &\quad = 2^2(2 - 2)^2 \cr &\quad = 0\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 3$:\begin{aligned} &x(3) \cr &\quad = 3^2(3 - 2)^2 \cr &\quad = 9\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Calculate the distance covered during each individual leg where direction is constant:

• From $t = 0$ to $t = 1$:\begin{aligned} &|1 - 0| \cr &\quad = 1\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• From $t = 1$ to $t = 2$:\begin{aligned} &|0 - 1| \cr &\quad = 1\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• From $t = 2$ to $t = 3$:\begin{aligned} &|9 - 0| \cr &\quad = 9\text{ m} \end{aligned}Calculate total distance:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total distance} \cr &\quad = 1 + 1 + 9 \cr &\quad = 11\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Show that $P$ never moves along the negative $x$-axis:

Express the displacement as a squared term:\begin{aligned} &x \cr &\quad = t^2(t - 2)^2 \cr &\quad = (t(t - 2))^2 \end{aligned}Since the square of any real number is always non-negative, $x \ge 0$ for all real values of $t$. Therefore, $P$ can never have a negative displacement along the $x$-axis.
Final Answer: (a) $t = 0, 1, 2$, (b) $11\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This distance represents only the final displacement at $t = 3$. Because the particle changed direction at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, the total distance travelled is greater than the displacement.
Do not forget $t = 0\text{ s}$ when listing times at rest. Setting $4t(t-1)(t-2) = 0$ yields three solutions, including the initial instant of release.

This is a common arithmetic error when calculating the segments. Ensure you calculate the absolute movement for each interval: $0 \to 1$ ($1\text{ m}$), $1 \to 2$ ($1\text{ m}$), and $2 \to 3$ ($9\text{ m}$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Turning Point Traps
bradley_insight.content: Students often confuse distance with displacement and simply calculate $x(3) - x(0) = 9$. When asked for total distance, you must identify every turning point (where $v = 0$) within the time window and calculate the sum of the absolute displacements for each leg.

question:
A particle $Q$ moves along a straight horizontal line. At time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$), the velocity, $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$, of $Q$ is given by:$$v = 3t^2 - 12t + 9$$At $t = 0$, $Q$ is at the origin $O$.

(a) Find the times when $Q$ is instantaneously at rest.

(b) Find an expression for the displacement, $s$ metres, of $Q$ from $O$ in terms of $t$.

(c) Find the total distance travelled by $Q$ in the time interval $0 \le t \le 4$.

(d) Show that $Q$ never has a negative displacement for $t \ge 0$.
steps:
(a) Find when $Q$ is instantaneously at rest:

Set the velocity $v = 0$ and factorise the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 0 \cr &3(t^2 - 4t + 3) = 0 \cr &3(t - 1)(t - 3) = 0 \end{aligned}The particle is instantaneously at rest at $t = 1\text{ s}$ and $t = 3\text{ s}$.

(b) Find an expression for the displacement $s$:

Displacement is found by integrating velocity with respect to time:\begin{aligned} &s \cr &\quad = \int (3t^2 - 12t + 9)\text{d}t \cr &\quad = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t + c \end{aligned}Since the particle starts at the origin, $s = 0$ at $t = 0$, giving $c = 0$.

Therefore, the displacement is:\begin{aligned} &s \cr &\quad = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t \end{aligned}

(c) Find the total distance travelled in the interval $0 \le t \le 4$:

Evaluate displacement at endpoints and turning points within this interval:

• At $t = 0$:\begin{aligned} &s(0) \cr &\quad = 0\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 1$:\begin{aligned} &s(1) \cr &\quad = 1^3 - 6(1)^2 + 9(1) \cr &\quad = 4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 3$:\begin{aligned} &s(3) \cr &\quad = 3^3 - 6(3)^2 + 9(3) \cr &\quad = 27 - 54 + 27 \cr &\quad = 0\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 4$:\begin{aligned} &s(4) \cr &\quad = 4^3 - 6(4)^2 + 9(4) \cr &\quad = 64 - 96 + 36 \cr &\quad = 4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Sum the absolute values of the movements for each section:

• From $t = 0$ to $t = 1$:\begin{aligned} &|4 - 0| \cr &\quad = 4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• From $t = 1$ to $t = 3$:\begin{aligned} &|0 - 4| \cr &\quad = 4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• From $t = 3$ to $t = 4$:\begin{aligned} &|4 - 0| \cr &\quad = 4\text{ m} \end{aligned}Calculate total distance:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total distance} \cr &\quad = 4 + 4 + 4 \cr &\quad = 12\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Show that $Q$ never has a negative displacement for $t \ge 0$:

Factorise the displacement expression:\begin{aligned} &s \cr &\quad = t(t^2 - 6t + 9) \cr &\quad = t(t - 3)^2 \end{aligned}Since $t \ge 0$ and $(t - 3)^2 \ge 0$, their product must be non-negative. Therefore, $s \ge 0$ for all $t \ge 0$.
Final Answer: (b) $s = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$, (c) $12\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This is the net displacement at $t = 4$. Remember that the particle travels $4\text{ m}$ away from $O$, reverses back to $O$ at $t = 3$, and then travels $4\text{ m}$ away again. Total distance is the sum of these absolute path lengths.
This is a common error where the final segment (from $t = 3$ to $t = 4$) is omitted. Make sure to check every single segment between your turning points.

This formula for $s$ results from integrating incorrectly without dividing by the new powers. Always apply the integration rule:\begin{aligned} &\int t^n\text{d}t \cr &\quad = \dfrac{t^{n+1}}{n+1} \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Absolute Movements
bradley_insight.content: Integrating $v$ directly over an interval gives displacement, not distance. For distance, always identify the turning points, evaluate the position at each, and manually add up the absolute movements of each leg: $4\text{ m}$ out, $4\text{ m}$ back, and $4\text{ m}$ out again.

question:
A particle $R$ moves along a straight horizontal line. At time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$), the displacement, $s$ metres, of $R$ from a fixed point $O$ on the line is given by:$$s = \dfrac{1}{3}t^3 - 3t^2 + 8t$$(a) Find the values of $t$ when the particle is instantaneously at rest.

(b) Find the acceleration of the particle at the instant it first comes to rest.

(c) Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the time interval $0 \le t \le 6$.

(d) State the range of times for which the velocity of the particle is decreasing.
steps:
(a) Find when $R$ is instantaneously at rest:

Differentiate displacement with respect to time to find velocity $v$:\begin{aligned} &v \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = t^2 - 6t + 8 \end{aligned}Set $v = 0$ to find the times at rest:\begin{aligned} &t^2 - 6t + 8 = 0 \cr &(t - 2)(t - 4) = 0 \end{aligned}The particle is instantaneously at rest at $t = 2\text{ s}$ and $t = 4\text{ s}$.

(b) Find the acceleration at first rest ($t = 2$):

Differentiate velocity with respect to time to find acceleration $a$:\begin{aligned} &a \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = 2t - 6 \end{aligned}At the first resting instant ($t = 2\text{ s}$):\begin{aligned} &a(2) \cr &\quad = 2(2) - 6 \cr &\quad = -2\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the total distance travelled in the interval $0 \le t \le 6$:

Evaluate displacement at $t = 0$, $t = 2$, $t = 4$, and $t = 6$:

• At $t = 0$:\begin{aligned} &s(0) \cr &\quad = 0\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 2$:\begin{aligned} &s(2) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{3}(2)^3 - 3(2)^2 + 8(2) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{8}{3} - 12 + 16 \cr &\quad = 6\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 4$:\begin{aligned} &s(4) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{3}(4)^3 - 3(4)^2 + 8(4) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{64}{3} - 48 + 32 \cr &\quad = 5\dfrac{1}{3}\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 6$:\begin{aligned} &s(6) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{3}(6)^3 - 3(6)^2 + 8(6) \cr &\quad = 72 - 108 + 48 \cr &\quad = 12\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Sum the absolute values of the movements for each segment:

• From $t = 0$ to $t = 2$:\begin{aligned} &|6\dfrac{2}{3} - 0| \cr &\quad = 6\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• From $t = 2$ to $t = 4$:\begin{aligned} &|5\dfrac{1}{3} - 6\dfrac{2}{3}| \cr &\quad = 1\dfrac{1}{3}\text{ m} \end{aligned}

• From $t = 4$ to $t = 6$:\begin{aligned} &|12 - 5\dfrac{1}{3}| \cr &\quad = 6\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ m} \end{aligned}Calculate total distance:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total distance} \cr &\quad = 6\dfrac{2}{3} + 1\dfrac{1}{3} + 6\dfrac{2}{3} \cr &\quad = 14\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) State the range of times when velocity is decreasing:

Velocity is decreasing when acceleration is negative ($a < 0$):\begin{aligned} &2t - 6 < 0 \cr &t < 3 \end{aligned}Since $t \ge 0$, the range of times is $0 \le t < 3$.
Final Answer: (b) $-2\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $14\dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 }\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This is the displacement of the particle at $t = 6$, not the total distance. Because the particle turned around at $t = 2$ and $t = 4$, you must calculate the path lengths of each leg separately.
In part (b), the acceleration at $t = 2$ is $2(2) - 6 = -2\text{ m s}^{-2}$. A positive acceleration of $+2$ represents an incorrect sign error.

This is a common fraction arithmetic error when summing the segments. Verify each calculation carefully:\begin{aligned} &6\dfrac{2}{3} + 1\dfrac{1}{3} + 6\dfrac{2}{3} \cr &\quad = 14\dfrac{2}{3}\text{ m} \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Pure Calculus Connections
bradley_insight.content: In part (d), 'velocity is decreasing' means the gradient of the velocity function is negative ($a < 0$). This is a direct application of Pure calculus (finding the intervals where a function is decreasing) mapped onto a physical kinematics context.

question:
Two particles, $A$ and $B$, move along the same straight horizontal line. At time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$), the displacements, $s_A$ metres and $s_B$ metres, of the particles from a fixed origin $O$ are modelled by:$$s_A = t^3 - 3t^2 + 5t$$$$s_B = 2t^2 + 2t$$(a) Find the values of $t$ when the two particles are travelling at the same velocity.

(b) Find the distance between the two particles at the instant $t = 2$.

(c) Find the acceleration of particle $A$ at the instant its velocity is at its minimum value.
steps:
(a) Find the values of $t$ when velocities are equal:

Differentiate both displacement expressions with respect to time to find velocity functions $v_A$ and $v_B$:\begin{aligned} &v_A \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}s_A}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = 3t^2 - 6t + 5 \cr &v_B \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}s_B}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = 4t + 2 \end{aligned}

Equate $v_A$ and $v_B$ and solve the resulting quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &3t^2 - 6t + 5 = 4t + 2 \cr &3t^2 - 10t + 3 = 0 \cr &(3t - 1)(t - 3) = 0 \end{aligned}The velocities are equal at $t = \dfrac{1}{3}\text{ s}$ and $t = 3\text{ s}$.

(b) Find the distance between the particles at $t = 2$:

Evaluate the displacement of each particle at $t = 2$:\begin{aligned} &s_A(2) \cr &\quad = (2)^3 - 3(2)^2 + 5(2) \cr &\quad = 8 - 12 + 10 \cr &\quad = 6\text{ m} \cr &s_B(2) \cr &\quad = 2(2)^2 + 2(2) \cr &\quad = 8 + 4 \cr &\quad = 12\text{ m} \end{aligned}

The distance between the two particles is the absolute difference in displacements:\begin{aligned} &\text{Distance} \cr &\quad = |s_B(2) - s_A(2)| \cr &\quad = |12 - 6| \cr &\quad = 6\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the acceleration of $A$ when its velocity is minimum:

Differentiate $v_A$ with respect to time to find acceleration $a_A$:\begin{aligned} &a_A \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}v_A}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = 6t - 6 \end{aligned}Velocity $v_A$ is at a minimum when its rate of change (acceleration) is zero:\begin{aligned} &6t - 6 = 0 \cr &t = 1\text{ s} \end{aligned}At $t = 1\text{ s}$, the acceleration of $A$ is:\begin{aligned} &a_A(1) \cr &\quad = 6(1) - 6 \cr &\quad = 0\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $t = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }, 3$, (b) $6\text{ m}$, (c) $0\text{ m s}^{-2}$

pi_options.feedback: This is a distance error resulting from adding the displacements ($12 + 6 = 18\text{ m}$) instead of finding the difference between them. Since both are on the positive side of $O$, the separation is $12 - 6 = 6\text{ m}$.

This is an acceleration sign error in part (c). The question asks for the acceleration at the instant velocity is minimum, which occurs where acceleration is $0\text{ m s}^{-2}$ (the stationary point of the velocity curve).
This represents an arithmetic slip when evaluating the displacement of particle $A$ or $B$ at $t = 2$. Re-evaluate carefully: $s_A(2) = 6$ and $s_B(2) = 12$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Stationary Point Shortcut
bradley_insight.content: Part (c) contains a classic mathematical trap. The acceleration of a particle at the instant its velocity is at a minimum is always $0\text{ m s}^{-2}$. This is because the minimum of the velocity curve represents a stationary point where the first derivative (acceleration) must be zero.

question:
A car is travelling along a straight horizontal road. At the instant the brakes are applied, the car is at the point $O$. The velocity, $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$, of the car at time $t$ seconds after the brakes are applied is modelled by the formula:$$v = 24 - 1.5t^2 \quad \text{for } 0 \le t \le T$$where $T$ is the time when the car comes to rest.

(a) Find the value of $T$.

(b) Find the distance travelled by the car from the instant the brakes are applied to the instant it comes to rest.

(c) Find the deceleration of the car at the instant it comes to rest.
steps:
(a) Find the value of $T$:

The car comes to rest when velocity $v = 0$. Set $v = 0$ and solve for $T$:\begin{aligned} &24 - 1.5T^2 = 0 \cr &1.5T^2 = 24 \cr &T^2 = 16 \end{aligned}Since $T \ge 0$, we have $T = 4\text{ s}$.

(b) Find the distance travelled to rest:

Integrate the velocity function from braking ($t = 0$) to rest ($t = 4$):\begin{aligned} &s \cr &\quad = \int_{0}^{4} (24 - 1.5t^2)\text{d}t \cr &\quad = \big[ 24t - 0.5t^3 \big]_{0}^{4} \end{aligned}
Evaluate the definite integral limits:\begin{aligned} &s \cr &\quad = (24(4) - 0.5(4)^3) - 0 \cr &\quad = 96 - 32 \cr &\quad = 64\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the deceleration at rest ($t = 4$):

First, find acceleration $a$ by differentiating $v$ with respect to $t$:\begin{aligned} &a \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = -3t \end{aligned}

At the instant the car stops ($t = 4\text{ s}$):\begin{aligned} &a(4) \cr &\quad = -3(4) \cr &\quad = -12\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Acceleration is $-12\text{ m s}^{-2}$, which means the rate of deceleration is $12\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Final Answer: (a) $4\text{ s}$, (b) $64\text{ m}$, (c) $12\text{ m s}^{-2}$

pi_options.feedback: Deceleration is a positive scalar quantity indicating the rate of slowing down. Stating deceleration as a negative value is a double-negative error; the negative sign is already implied by the word 'deceleration'.
This is an integration error in part (b), usually caused by neglecting to subtract the integrated $0.5t^3$ term from $24t$. Always integrate and evaluate both parts of the expression.
In part (a), $T^2 = 16$. Remember to take the square root of $16$ to find the time $T = 4\text{ s}$, rather than leaving it as $16$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Deceleration vs. Acceleration
bradley_insight.content: Always express deceleration as a positive value. Since acceleration $a = -12\text{ m s}^{-2}$ is already negative (indicating a decrease in speed), 'deceleration' is defined as the magnitude of this rate of slowing down, which is $12\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

question:
Two small blocks, $A$ and $B$, have masses $3m$ and $km$ respectively, where $k < 3$. The blocks are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string that passes over a small smooth fixed pulley. The system is held at rest with the string taut and the hanging parts vertical, as shown in the diagram. The system is released from rest and, in the subsequent motion, $A$ moves downwards with an acceleration of magnitude $\dfrac{1}{2}g$. The blocks are modelled as particles.

Using the model,

(a) find, in terms of $m$ and $g$, the tension in the string,

(b) explain why the acceleration of $B$ also has magnitude $\dfrac{1}{2}g$,

(c) find the value of $k$,

(d) state one physical factor of the string that has been ignored in this model.
steps:
(a) Find the tension in the string:

Consider the downward vertical motion of block $A$ (mass $3m$). Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$) in the direction of motion:\begin{aligned} &3mg - T = 3ma \cr &3mg - T = 3m\big(\dfrac{1}{2}g\big) \cr &3mg - T = 1.5mg \end{aligned}
Rearrange to solve for the tension $T$:\begin{aligned} &T \cr &\quad = 3mg - 1.5mg \cr &\quad = 1.5mg \end{aligned}

(b) Explain why the acceleration of $B$ also has magnitude $\dfrac{1}{2}g$:

Because the string is modelled as being inextensible, the displacement, velocity, and magnitude of acceleration of both particles must be identical at any given instant while the string remains taut.

(c) Find the value of $k$:

Consider the upward vertical motion of block $B$ (mass $km$). Applying Newton's second law in the direction of motion:\begin{aligned} &T - kmg = kma \cr &1.5mg - kmg = km\big(\dfrac{1}{2}g\big) \cr &1.5mg - kmg = 0.5kmg \end{aligned}
Add $kmg$ to both sides and solve for $k$:\begin{aligned} &1.5mg = 1.5kmg \cr &1.5 = 1.5k \cr &k = 1 \end{aligned}

(d) Identify one ignored limitation:

The model assumes the string is light, thereby ignoring the mass/weight of the string.
Final Answer: (a) $T = 1.5mg$, (c) $k = 1$

pi_options.feedback: This occurs if you use a mass of $2m$ instead of $3m$ for block $A$. Double check the masses given in the question description.

This is a sign error when applying Newton's second law to the upward motion of $B$. The equation must be $T - kmg = kma$, not $kmg - T = kma$. Since $B$ moves upwards, the tension must exceed its weight.
This tension of $3mg$ is obtained if you assume the system is in static equilibrium ($a = 0$). Since the system is released and accelerates, the tension must be less than the weight of $A$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Inextensible vs. Light
bradley_insight.content: Do not confuse the modeling assumptions. The term 'light' implies we ignore the mass of the string (tension is uniform throughout). The term 'inextensible' is what guarantees that both particles share the exact same magnitude of acceleration.

question:
A block $A$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ lies on a smooth horizontal table. $A$ is connected by a light inextensible string, passing over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table, to a hanging ball $B$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$ which hangs freely, as shown in the diagram. The system is released from rest with the string taut.

Using the model,

(a) find the acceleration of the system,

(b) find the tension in the string,

(c) find the magnitude of the force exerted by the string on the pulley.
steps:
(a) Find the acceleration of the system ($a$):

Write the equations of motion for each particle using Newton's second law ($F = ma$):

• For block $A$ (moving horizontally):\begin{aligned} &T = 3a \end{aligned}

• For hanging ball $B$ (moving vertically downwards):\begin{aligned} &2g - T = 2a \end{aligned}
Add the two equations to eliminate tension $T$:\begin{aligned} &2g = 5a \cr &a \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2g}{5} \cr &\quad = 0.4 \times 9.8 \cr &\quad = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the tension in the string ($T$):

Substitute $a = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$ back into the equation for block $A$:\begin{aligned} &T \cr &\quad = 3 \times 3.92 \cr &\quad = 11.76\text{ N} \end{aligned}To 3 significant figures, $T = 11.8\text{ N}$.

(c) Find the magnitude of the force on the pulley:

The string exerts two perpendicular forces of magnitude $T$ on the pulley: horizontally to the left and vertically downwards. The resultant force $F$ is found using Pythagoras' theorem:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = \sqrt{T^2 + T^2} \cr &\quad = T\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}

Substitute $T = 11.76\text{ N}$ into the formula:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = 11.76 \times \sqrt{2} \cr &\quad \approx 11.76 \times 1.414 \cr &\quad \approx 16.63\text{ N} \end{aligned}To 3 significant figures, the force exerted on the pulley is $16.6\text{ N}$.
Final Answer: (a) $3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $11.8\text{ N}$, (c) $16.6\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: This is a common error where the force on the pulley is calculated as $T + T = 2T$. Because the horizontal and vertical tensions act at right angles, you must use vector addition (Pythagoras) rather than simple addition.
This occurs if you treat the total mass of the system as $10\text{ kg}$ or make a division error when finding $a$. The total accelerating mass is $3 + 2 = 5\text{ kg}$.
This tension of $19.6\text{ N}$ is the static weight of ball $B$ ($2g$). Since the system is accelerating, the tension in the string must be less than the weight of the hanging mass.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Resultant Pulley Forces
bradley_insight.content: When finding the resultant force on a pulley, look at the geometry. If the string goes from horizontal to vertical, the angle between the two tension forces is $90^\circ$, so the resultant is always $T\sqrt{2}$. If the string goes over a vertical pulley with parallel sides, the force is simply $2T$.

question:
A block $P$ of mass $4\text{ kg}$ lies on a rough horizontal table. $P$ is connected by a light inextensible string, passing over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table, to a sphere $Q$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ which hangs freely, as shown in the diagram. The coefficient of friction between $P$ and the table is $\mu$.

The system is released from rest with the string taut and $Q$ at a height of $1.5\text{ m}$ above the floor. In the subsequent motion, $Q$ descends with an acceleration of $2.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Using the model,

(a) find the tension in the string,

(b) find the value of $\mu$,

(c) find the speed with which $Q$ hits the floor.
steps:
(a) Find the tension in the string ($T$):

Consider the vertical downward motion of sphere $Q$ (mass $3\text{ kg}$). Using Newton's second law in the direction of motion:\begin{aligned} &3g - T = 3a \cr &3(9.8) - T = 3(2.8) \cr &29.4 - T = 8.4 \end{aligned}
Solve for tension $T$:\begin{aligned} &T \cr &\quad = 29.4 - 8.4 \cr &\quad = 21\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the value of $\mu$:

Consider the horizontal motion of block $P$ (mass $4\text{ kg}$) to the right. The horizontal forces acting on $P$ are tension $T$ to the right and friction $F$ to the left:\begin{aligned} &T - F = 4a \cr &21 - F = 4(2.8) \cr &21 - F = 11.2 \cr &F = 9.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Since $P$ is in motion, friction is at its maximum limiting value ($F = \mu R$). The normal reaction force $R$ balances the weight of $P$ vertically:\begin{aligned} &R \cr &\quad = 4g \cr &\quad = 4(9.8) \cr &\quad = 39.2\text{ N} \end{aligned}Substitute $F = 9.8\text{ N}$ and $R = 39.2\text{ N}$ into the friction formula:\begin{aligned} &9.8 = \mu(39.2) \cr &\mu \cr &\quad = \dfrac{9.8}{39.2} \cr &\quad = 0.25 \end{aligned}

(c) Find the speed with which $Q$ hits the floor ($v$):

Using constant acceleration with downward parameters:

• Initial speed, $u = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$

• Acceleration, $a = 2.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$

• Distance, $s = 1.5\text{ m}$Apply $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 0 + 2(2.8)(1.5) \cr &\quad = 8.4 \cr &v \cr &\quad = \sqrt{8.4} \cr &\quad \approx 2.898\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}To 2 significant figures, the speed is $2.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Final Answer: (b) $\mu = 0.25$, (c) $2.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: This occurs if you fail to subtract the force of friction correctly, or write $T + F = 4a$ instead of $T - F = 4a$. Remember that friction always opposes the direction of motion.
This speed of $4.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$ represents forgetting to take the square root of $v^2 = 8.4$, or a minor SUVAT arithmetic slip. Make sure to apply $v = \sqrt{ 2as }$.

This is a common reaction force error where the normal reaction is calculated using mass instead of weight (i.e., using $R = 4$ instead of $R = 4g$, which equals $39.2\text{ N}$). Friction is related to the normal contact force in Newtons.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Normal Reaction in Newtons
bradley_insight.content: When computing the coefficient of friction $\mu = \dfrac{F}{R}$, make sure that both friction $F$ and normal reaction $R$ are expressed in Newtons ($R = mg$). A very common mistake is using the mass directly as the normal reaction, which leads to an incorrect value of $\mu > 1$.

question:
A particle $A$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is held at rest on a smooth plane inclined at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. $A$ is attached to one end of a light inextensible string. The string passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the top of the plane. The other end of the string is attached to a particle $B$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ which hangs vertically below the pulley, as shown in the diagram. The system is released from rest with the string taut.

Using the model,

(a) write down an equation of motion for particle $A$ and an equation of motion for particle $B$,

(b) find the acceleration of the system,

(c) find the tension in the string.
steps:
(a) Write the equations of motion for particles $A$ and $B$:

Since the weight of $B$ ($3g = 29.4\text{ N}$) is greater than the component of the weight of $A$ down the plane ($2g\sin(30^\circ) = 9.8\text{ N}$), particle $B$ accelerates downwards and particle $A$ accelerates up the plane.

Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$) in the direction of motion:

• For particle $A$ (moving up the inclined plane):\begin{aligned} &T - 2g\sin(30^\circ) = 2a \cr &T - 9.8 = 2a \end{aligned}

• For particle $B$ (moving vertically downwards):\begin{aligned} &3g - T = 3a \cr &29.4 - T = 3a \end{aligned}

(b) Find the acceleration of the system ($a$):

Add the two equations to eliminate tension $T$:\begin{aligned} &(T - 9.8) + (29.4 - T) = 5a \cr &19.6 = 5a \cr &a \cr &\quad = \dfrac{19.6}{5} \cr &\quad = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the tension in the string ($T$):

Substitute $a = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$ into the equation for particle $A$:\begin{aligned} &T - 9.8 = 2(3.92) \cr &T - 9.8 = 7.84 \cr &T \cr &\quad = 7.84 + 9.8 \cr &\quad = 17.64\text{ N} \end{aligned}To 3 significant figures, the tension is $17.6\text{ N}$.
Final Answer: (b) $3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $17.6\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: This is a common error resulting from resolving the weight of particle $A$ down the plane using cosine instead of sine (i.e., using $2g \cos(30^\circ)$). Remember that the force component pulling down the incline is parallel to the plane, which involves the sine of the inclination angle.

This tension of $29.4\text{ N}$ is the static weight of particle $B$ ($3g$). Because the system is in motion and accelerating downwards, the tension must be strictly less than the weight of the hanging mass.
This represents an error where the total accelerating mass is treated as $10\text{ kg}$ or a division slip is made when calculating $a$. The total mass of both particles is $2 + 3 = 5\text{ kg}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Slopes and Weight Components
bradley_insight.content: For any particle of mass $m$ on an incline of angle $\theta$, the component of weight acting parallel to the slope is always $mg\sin\theta$, and the component acting perpendicular is $mg\cos\theta$. Memorising this standard decomposition will save you valuable time during exam resolution.

question:
Two particles, $X$ and $Y$, have masses $3\text{ kg}$ and $1\text{ kg}$ respectively. The particles are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string that passes over a small smooth fixed pulley. The system is held at rest with the string taut and both particles hanging vertically, as shown in the diagram.

At the instant of release, particle $X$ is at a height of $5\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground. The system is released from rest and, in the subsequent motion, $X$ hits the ground and does not rebound.

Using the model,

(a) find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string before $X$ hits the ground,

(b) find the speed of $X$ at the instant it hits the ground,

(c) find the total maximum height reached by $Y$ above its initial starting position.
steps:
(a) Find acceleration and tension before $X$ hits the ground:

Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$) to both particles:

• For $X$ (moving downwards):\begin{aligned} &3g - T = 3a \end{aligned}

• For $Y$ (moving upwards):\begin{aligned} &T - g = a \end{aligned}
Add the two equations to eliminate $T$ and solve for $a$:\begin{aligned} &2g = 4a \cr &a \cr &\quad = 0.5g \cr &\quad = 0.5 \times 9.8 \cr &\quad = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
Substitute $a = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-2}$ into the equation of motion for particle $Y$:\begin{aligned} &T - 9.8 = 4.9 \cr &T \cr &\quad = 4.9 + 9.8 \cr &\quad = 14.7\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the speed of $X$ when it hits the ground:

Using constant acceleration with downward parameters:

• Initial speed, $u = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$

• Acceleration, $a = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-2}$

• Distance, $s = 5\text{ m}$Apply $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 0 + 2(4.9)(5) \cr &\quad = 49 \cr &v \cr &\quad = \sqrt{49} \cr &\quad = 7\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the total maximum height reached by $Y$ above its starting position:

This is a two-stage motion problem:

• Stage 1 (String Taut): While $X$ falls $5\text{ m}$, particle $Y$ is pulled upwards by $5\text{ m}$. At the end of this stage, $Y$ has an upward speed of $v = 7\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

• Stage 2 (String Slack): The moment $X$ hits the ground, the string goes slack and tension drops to zero. Particle $Y$ moves freely under gravity with initial upward speed $u_2 = 7\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and acceleration $a = -9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ until $v_2 = 0$:\begin{aligned} &v_2^2 = u_2^2 + 2as_2 \cr &0 = (7)^2 + 2(-9.8)s_2 \cr &0 = 49 - 19.6s_2 \cr &19.6s_2 = 49 \cr &s_2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{49}{19.6} \cr &\quad = 2.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Sum the heights from both stages:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total height} \cr &\quad = s_1 + s_2 \cr &\quad = 5 + 2.5 \cr &\quad = 7.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $a = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-2}, T = 14.7\text{ N}$, (b) $7\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (c) $7.5\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This $2.5\text{ m}$ represents only the extra distance travelled by $Y$ after the string goes slack (Stage 2). To find the total height above its starting position, you must add the initial $5\text{ m}$ of ascent from Stage 1.

This $5.0\text{ m}$ is the height reached at the moment $X$ hits the ground. It fails to account for the fact that $Y$ possesses upward momentum and will continue to rise freely under gravity for another $2.5\text{ m}$.
This occurs due to a SUVAT calculation error in part (b), setting the final speed to $4.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ instead of $7\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Ensure you use the formula $v = \sqrt{ 2as }$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: String Slack Dynamics
bradley_insight.content: Multi-body pulley questions involving impact are classics in Mechanics. When the heavier particle hits the floor, the string immediately becomes slack, meaning $T$ instantly drops to zero. The lighter particle behaves as a free-falling projectile under gravity alone ($a = -g$) until its upward velocity hits zero.

question:
At time $t$ seconds, where $t \ge 0$, a particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane in such a way that its velocity, $\mathbf{v}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, is given by:$$\mathbf{v} = t^{-1/2}\mathbf{i} - 2t\mathbf{j}$$When $t = 1$, $P$ is at the point $A$ and when $t = 4$, $P$ is at the point $B$.

Find the exact distance $AB$.
steps: Find the displacement vector by integrating velocity with respect to time ($t$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r} \cr &\quad = \int (t^{-1/2}\mathbf{i} - 2t\mathbf{j})\text{d}t \cr &\quad = 2t^{1/2}\mathbf{i} - t^2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C} \end{aligned}

Calculate the position vector at $t = 1$ and $t = 4$ (the constant $\mathbf{C}$ will cancel upon subtraction):

• At $t = 1$ (point $A$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}(1) \cr &\quad = 2(1)^{1/2}\mathbf{i} - (1)^2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C} \cr &\quad = 2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C} \end{aligned}

• At $t = 4$ (point $B$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}(4) \cr &\quad = 2(4)^{1/2}\mathbf{i} - (4)^2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C} \cr &\quad = 4\mathbf{i} - 16\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C} \end{aligned}

Find the displacement vector $\vec{AB}$ from point $A$ to point $B$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AB} \cr &\quad = \mathbf{r}(4) - \mathbf{r}(1) \cr &\quad = (4\mathbf{i} - 16\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}) \cr &\qquad - (2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}) \cr &\quad = (4 - 2)\mathbf{i} + (-16 + 1)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 2\mathbf{i} - 15\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Calculate the magnitude of $\vec{AB}$ to find the exact distance:\begin{aligned} &|\vec{AB}| \cr &\quad = \sqrt{2^2 + (-15)^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{4 + 225} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{229}\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $\sqrt{ 229 }\text{ m }$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign slip when calculating the $\mathbf{j}$ component of the displacement, such as computing $-16 - 1 = -17$ instead of $-16 - (-1) = -15$. Always write out the subtraction of negative components carefully.

This is obtained if you integrate $t^{-1/2}$ incorrectly as $-0.5 t^{-3/2}$, leading to an incorrect position vector and distance. Ensure you use the integration rule: add one to the power and divide by the new power.

This result comes from forgetting to double the coefficient when integrating $t^{-1/2}$, integrating it as $t^{1/2}$ instead of $2t^{1/2}$. Remember that dividing by $1/2$ is equivalent to multiplying by $2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Cancelling the Integration Constant
bradley_insight.content: In vector kinematics, when finding the displacement vector $\vec{AB}$ between two points $A$ and $B$ at specified times, the constant of integration $\mathbf{C}$ will always cancel out. You do not need to solve for $\mathbf{C}$ unless the absolute coordinates of the origin are required.

question:
At time $t$ seconds, where $t \ge 0$, a particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane with acceleration, $\mathbf{a}\text{ m s}^{-2}$, given by:$$\mathbf{a} = 6t\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}$$At the instant $t = 0$, the velocity of $P$ is $(\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

When $t = 1$, $P$ is at the point $A$ and when $t = 3$, $P$ is at the point $B$.

Find the exact distance $AB$.
steps: First, find the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$ by integrating acceleration with respect to time ($t$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v} \cr &\quad = \int (6t\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{d}t \cr &\quad = 3t^2\mathbf{i} + 2t\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_1 \end{aligned}

Use the initial condition at $t = 0$, where velocity is $\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}$, to solve for $\mathbf{C}_1$:\begin{aligned} &3(0)^2\mathbf{i} + 2(0)\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_1 = \mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} \cr &\mathbf{C}_1 = \mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Therefore, the velocity vector is:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v} \cr &\quad = (3t^2 + 1)\mathbf{i} + (2t - 4)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Find the position vector $\mathbf{r}$ by integrating velocity with respect to time ($t$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r} \cr &\quad = \int \big[(3t^2 + 1)\mathbf{i} + (2t - 4)\mathbf{j}\big]\text{d}t \cr &\quad = (t^3 + t)\mathbf{i} + (t^2 - 4t)\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_2 \end{aligned}

Evaluate the position vector at $t = 1$ and $t = 3$ (the constant $\mathbf{C}_2$ cancels upon subtraction):

• At $t = 1$ (point $A$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}(1) \cr &\quad = (1^3 + 1)\mathbf{i} + (1^2 - 4(1))\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_2 \cr &\quad = 2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_2 \end{aligned}

• At $t = 3$ (point $B$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}(3) \cr &\quad = (3^3 + 3)\mathbf{i} + (3^2 - 4(3))\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_2 \cr &\quad = 30\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_2 \end{aligned}

Find the displacement vector $\vec{AB}$ from point $A$ to point $B$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AB} \cr &\quad = \mathbf{r}(3) - \mathbf{r}(1) \cr &\quad = (30\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_2) \cr &\qquad - (2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}_2) \cr &\quad = (30 - 2)\mathbf{i} + (-3 + 3)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 28\mathbf{i} + 0\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Find the exact distance, which is the magnitude of $\vec{AB}$:\begin{aligned} &|\vec{AB}| \cr &\quad = \sqrt{28^2 + 0^2} \cr &\quad = 28\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $28\text{ m }$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error when subtracting the $\mathbf{j}$ components, resulting in $-3 - (-3) = -6$ instead of $0$. Ensure you track signs carefully:\begin{aligned} &-3 - (-3) \cr &\quad = -3 + 3 \cr &\quad = 0 \end{aligned}

This is obtained if you forget to add the initial velocity components to the velocity integration, integrating $\mathbf{a} = 6t\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}$ directly to position without applying the initial velocity condition at $t = 0$.
This result comes from integrating $3t^2$ to $t^3$ but making a coefficient error on the linear terms during integration. Double check your calculus steps.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Step-by-Step Integration
bradley_insight.content: Do not attempt to integrate directly from acceleration to position. You must always integrate once to find velocity, apply the boundary conditions to find the first constant vector, and then integrate a second time. Skipping this intermediate step will lead to missing linear terms in the position function.

question:
