At time $t$ seconds, where $t \ge 0$, a particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane. The velocity of $P$, $\mathbf{v}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, is modelled by the formula:$$\mathbf{v} = (3t^2 - 12)\mathbf{i} + (4t - 8)\mathbf{j}$$At $t = 0$, $P$ is at the origin $O$.

(a) Find the value of $t$ when $P$ is moving parallel to the vector $\mathbf{j}$.

(b) Find the position vector of $P$ at this instant.

(c) Find the exact distance of $P$ from the origin $O$ at this instant.
steps:
(a) Find when $P$ is moving parallel to $\mathbf{j}$:

Moving parallel to $\mathbf{j}$ means motion is vertical, so the $\mathbf{i}$ component of velocity is zero:\begin{aligned} &3t^2 - 12 = 0 \cr &t^2 = 4 \end{aligned}Since $t \ge 0$, $t = 2\text{ s}$.

(b) Find the position vector of $P$ at $t = 2$:

Integrate velocity with respect to time ($t$) to find position vector $\mathbf{r}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r} \cr &\quad = \int \big[(3t^2 - 12)\mathbf{i} + (4t - 8)\mathbf{j}\big]\text{d}t \cr &\quad = (t^3 - 12t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (2t^2 - 8t)\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C} \end{aligned}

Since $P$ is at the origin at $t = 0$, $\mathbf{r}(0) = \mathbf{0}$, giving $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{0}$. Therefore:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r} \cr &\quad = (t^3 - 12t)\mathbf{i} + (2t^2 - 8t)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Substitute $t = 2$ into the position vector equation:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}(2) \cr &\quad = (2^3 - 12(2))\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (2(2)^2 - 8(2))\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = (8 - 24)\mathbf{i} + (8 - 16)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = -16\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the exact distance of $P$ from the origin at $t = 2$:

The distance is the magnitude of $\mathbf{r}(2)$:\begin{aligned} &|\mathbf{r}(2)| \cr &\quad = \sqrt{(-16)^2 + (-8)^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{256 + 64} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{320} \cr &\quad = 8\sqrt{5}\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $t = 2\text{ s}$, (b) $-16\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j}$, (c) $8\sqrt{ 5 }\text{ m }$

pi_options.feedback: This distance is incorrect due to a minor calculation slip under the square root, such as computing $256 + 256 = 512$ instead of $256 + 64 = 320$. Ensure you substitute the correct coordinates: $x = -16$ and $y = -8$.
This position vector is obtained if you integrated the horizontal component incorrectly or forgot to multiply by $t$ during the integration. Double check that $\int 12\text{d}t = 12t$.
This distance is the simple sum of the component magnitudes ($16 + 8 = 24$). To find the straight-line distance, you must use Pythagoras' theorem ($d = \sqrt{ x^2 + y^2 }$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Parallel to the Axes
bradley_insight.content: When a particle is 'moving parallel to $\mathbf{j}$', its instantaneous motion is purely vertical, which mathematically means $v_x = 0$. Conversely, if it were 'moving parallel to $\mathbf{i}$', its instantaneous motion is purely horizontal, meaning $v_y = 0$.

question:
At time $t$ seconds, a particle $P$ moves in the $x$-$y$ plane in such a way that its position vector, $\mathbf{r}$ metres relative to a fixed origin $O$, is given by:$$\mathbf{r} = (3\cos 2t)\mathbf{i} + (4\sin 2t)\mathbf{j}$$(a) Find the velocity vector of the particle at the instant $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

(b) Find the exact speed of the particle at the instant $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

(c) Show that the acceleration of the particle is always directed towards the origin $O$.
steps:
(a) Find the velocity vector at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$:

Differentiate $\mathbf{r}$ with respect to $t$ using the chain rule:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}\mathbf{r}}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = (-6\sin 2t)\mathbf{i} + (8\cos 2t)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Substitute $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into the velocity equation:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}\big(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\big) \cr &\quad = \big[-6\sin\big(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\big)\big]\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + \big[8\cos\big(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\big)\big]\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = -6(1)\mathbf{i} + 8(0)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = -6\mathbf{i}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the exact speed at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:

First, evaluate the velocity vector at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}\big(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\big) \cr &\quad = \big[-6\sin\big(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\big)\big]\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + \big[8\cos\big(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\big)\big]\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = -6\big(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\big)\mathbf{i} + 8\big(\dfrac{1}{2}\big)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = -3\sqrt{3}\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

The speed is the magnitude of this velocity vector:\begin{aligned} &\text{Speed} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{(-3\sqrt{3})^2 + 4^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{(9 \times 3) + 16} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{27 + 16} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{43}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Show acceleration is directed towards the origin $O$:

Differentiate $\mathbf{v}$ with respect to $t$ to find acceleration $\mathbf{a}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{a} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}\mathbf{v}}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = (-12\cos 2t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (-16\sin 2t)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Factorise out the common scalar $-4$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{a} \cr &\quad = -4\big[(3\cos 2t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (4\sin 2t)\mathbf{j}\big] \cr &\quad = -4\mathbf{r} \end{aligned}Since $\mathbf{a} = -4\mathbf{r}$, acceleration is a negative scalar multiple of position $\mathbf{r}$. Thus, it always points directly towards the origin $O$.
Final Answer: (a) $-6\mathbf{i}$, (b) $\sqrt{ 43 }\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (c) $\mathbf{a} = -4\mathbf{r}$

pi_options.feedback: This is a sign error in part (c). Having $\mathbf{a} = 4\mathbf{r}$ would mean the acceleration acts in the same direction as the position vector, pointing *away* from the origin (repulsive force) rather than *towards* it (attractive force).
This velocity vector at $t = \pi/4$ occurs if you forget to use the chain rule when differentiating the trigonometric functions, leaving the coefficients as $-3$ and $4$ instead of $-6$ and $8$.
This speed of $7$ is an arithmetic slip when squaring $-3\sqrt{3}$. Note that $(-3\sqrt{3})^2 = 27$, so the speed is $\sqrt{27 + 16} = \sqrt{43}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, not $\sqrt{49} = 7$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Proving Acceleration Towards the Origin
bradley_insight.content: This is a classic vector SHM (Simple Harmonic Motion) setup. To prove that acceleration is always directed towards the origin, you must show that $\mathbf{a} = -k\mathbf{r}$, where $k$ is a positive constant. The negative sign guarantees the vector points in the opposite direction of the displacement (i.e., towards the centre).

question:
Two particles, $A$ and $B$, move in the $x$-$y$ plane. At time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$), the position vectors, $\mathbf{r}_A$ metres and $\mathbf{r}_B$ metres relative to a fixed origin $O$, are modelled by:$$\mathbf{r}_A = (t^2 + t)\mathbf{i} + (3t^2 - 2)\mathbf{j}$$$$\mathbf{r}_B = (4t - 2)\mathbf{i} + (t^2 + 3t)\mathbf{j}$$(a) Show that the two particles collide, and find the time of this collision.

(b) Find the velocity vector of each particle at the instant of collision.

(c) Find the exact magnitude of the relative velocity of $A$ with respect to $B$ at the instant of collision.
steps:
(a) Show particles collide and find collision time:

A collision occurs if $\mathbf{r}_A = \mathbf{r}_B$ for $t \ge 0$.

Equate horizontal ($\mathbf{i}$) components:\begin{aligned} &t^2 + t = 4t - 2 \cr &t^2 - 3t + 2 = 0 \cr &(t - 1)(t - 2) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives $t = 1\text{ s}$ and $t = 2\text{ s}$.
Equate vertical ($\mathbf{j}$) components:\begin{aligned} &3t^2 - 2 = t^2 + 3t \cr &2t^2 - 3t - 2 = 0 \cr &(2t + 1)(t - 2) = 0 \end{aligned}Since $t \ge 0$, the valid solution is $t = 2\text{ s}$.
Since $t = 2\text{ s}$ is a common root for both components, a collision occurs at $t = 2\text{ s}$.

(b) Find the velocity of each particle at $t = 2$:

Differentiate both position vectors with respect to time ($t$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}_A \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}\mathbf{r}_A}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = (2t + 1)\mathbf{i} + 6t\mathbf{j} \cr &\mathbf{v}_B \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}\mathbf{r}_B}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = 4\mathbf{i} + (2t + 3)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Substitute $t = 2$ into both velocity functions:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}_A(2) \cr &\quad = (2(2) + 1)\mathbf{i} + 6(2)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 5\mathbf{i} + 12\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-1} \cr &\mathbf{v}_B(2) \cr &\quad = 4\mathbf{i} + (2(2) + 3)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 4\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the magnitude of relative velocity at $t = 2$:

The relative velocity $\mathbf{v}_{A|B} = \mathbf{v}_A - \mathbf{v}_B$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}_{A|B} \cr &\quad = \mathbf{v}_A(2) - \mathbf{v}_B(2) \cr &\quad = (5\mathbf{i} + 12\mathbf{j}) - (4\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = (5 - 4)\mathbf{i} + (12 - 7)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = \mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Calculate the magnitude of relative velocity:\begin{aligned} &|\mathbf{v}_{A|B}| \cr &\quad = \sqrt{1^2 + 5^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{1 + 25} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{26}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $t = 2\text{ s}$, (b) $\mathbf{v}_A = 5\mathbf{i} + 12\mathbf{j}, \mathbf{v}_B = 4\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j}$, (c) $\sqrt{ 26 }\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: This is a critical collision concept error. While $t = 1\text{ s}$ satisfies the horizontal position equation ($x_A = 2$ and $x_B = 2$), the vertical coordinates at this time are different ($y_A = 1$ and $y_B = 4$). A collision requires both coordinates to be identical simultaneously, which only occurs at $t = 2\text{ s}$.

This is a vector arithmetic error in part (c) where relative velocity magnitude is calculated by adding the component differences ($1 + 5 = 6$) rather than applying Pythagoras' theorem to the relative velocity vector $\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}$.

This occurs if you differentiate the position vectors incorrectly, such as forgetting the linear terms during differentiation (e.g., getting $2t$ instead of $2t+1$ for the $\mathbf{i}$ component of $A$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dual Coordinate Equivalence
bradley_insight.content: For a collision to occur in 2D space, both coordinates must be equal at the exact same time ($t$). Finding a time where only one component matches (such as $t = 1$ where the $x$-coordinates are equal but the $y$-coordinates are not) simply means the particles pass across the same vertical line, not that they collide.

question:
A crate of mass $10\text{ kg}$ is pulled in a straight line along a rough horizontal floor using a handle attached to the crate. The handle is inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the floor, as shown in Figure 1, where $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$.



The tension in the handle is $30\text{ N}$. The coefficient of friction between the crate and the floor is $0.2$. The crate is modelled as a particle and the handle is modelled as a light rod.

Using the model,

(a) find the acceleration of the crate.

The crate is now pushed along the same floor using the handle. The handle is inclined at the same angle $\alpha$ to the floor, as shown in Figure 2. The force applied to the handle is a thrust of $30\text{ N}$.



(b) Explain briefly why the acceleration of the crate would now be less than the acceleration of the crate found in part (a).
steps:
(a) Find the acceleration of the crate:

Resolve pulling tension $T = 30\text{ N}$ horizontally and vertically. From $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$:\begin{aligned} &\sin \alpha = 0.6 \cr &\cos \alpha = 0.8 \end{aligned}

Calculate the components of tension:

• Horizontal component:\begin{aligned} &T_x \cr &\quad = T\cos \alpha \cr &\quad = 30 \times 0.8 \cr &\quad = 24\text{ N} \end{aligned}

• Vertical component:\begin{aligned} &T_y \cr &\quad = T\sin \alpha \cr &\quad = 30 \times 0.6 \cr &\quad = 18\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Set up vertical equilibrium for the crate (taking upwards as positive):\begin{aligned} &R + T\sin \alpha - mg = 0 \cr &R + 18 - 10(9.8) = 0 \cr &R + 18 - 98 = 0 \cr &R = 80\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Calculate the maximum friction force $F$:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = \mu R \cr &\quad = 0.2 \times 80 \cr &\quad = 16\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Apply Newton's second law ($F = ma$) horizontally:\begin{aligned} &T_x - F = ma \cr &24 - 16 = 10a \cr &8 = 10a \cr &a \cr &\quad = \dfrac{8}{10} \cr &\quad = 0.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Explain why acceleration is less when pushed:

When pushed by a thrust force of $30\text{ N}$, the vertical component ($18\text{ N}$) acts downwards instead of upwards.

This changes the vertical equilibrium equation to:\begin{aligned} &R - 18 - 98 = 0 \cr &R = 116\text{ N} \end{aligned}Since normal reaction $R$ increases to $116\text{ N}$, friction $F = \mu R$ increases to $23.2\text{ N}$. This larger friction force reduces the net horizontal force ($24 - 23.2 = 0.8\text{ N}$), resulting in a much smaller acceleration ($a = 0.08\text{ m s}^{-2}$).
Final Answer: (a) $a = 0.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Pulling vs. Pushing Friction
bradley_insight.content: This is a classic conceptual and mathematical trap in Dynamics. Pulling 'lifts' the object (reducing the normal reaction and decreasing friction); pushing 'pins' the object (increasing the normal reaction and increasing friction). This explains why it is physically easier to pull a heavy object than to push it at an angle.

question:
A heavy box of mass $22\text{ kg}$ lies on a rough horizontal floor. The box is pulled by a handle inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the floor, as shown in the diagram, where $\tan \theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

The tension in the handle is $T\text{ N}$. The coefficient of friction between the box and the floor is $0.5$. The box is modelled as a particle and is on the point of slipping.

Using the model, find the value of $T$.
steps: From $\tan \theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$, using a $3$-$4$-$5$ right-angled triangle:\begin{aligned} &\sin \theta = 0.6 \cr &\cos \theta = 0.8 \end{aligned}

Set up vertical equilibrium for the box (taking upwards as positive):\begin{aligned} &R + T\sin \theta - Mg = 0 \cr &R + 0.6T - 22(9.8) = 0 \cr &R + 0.6T - 215.6 = 0 \cr &R = 215.6 - 0.6T \end{aligned}
At limiting equilibrium, friction is at its maximum value ($F = \mu R$):\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = 0.5R \cr &\quad = 0.5(215.6 - 0.6T) \cr &\quad = 107.8 - 0.3T \end{aligned}
Set up horizontal equilibrium ($T\cos \theta - F = 0$):\begin{aligned} &0.8T = 107.8 - 0.3T \end{aligned}
Solve for $T$:\begin{aligned} &0.8T + 0.3T = 107.8 \cr &1.1T = 107.8 \cr &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{107.8}{1.1} \cr &\quad = 98\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $98\text{ N }$

This is the approximate weight of the box ($Mg$). Remember that $T$ is the pulling force required to overcome friction horizontally, which is much smaller than the physical weight of the box.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Point of Slipping
bradley_insight.content: The phrase 'on the point of slipping' is a key indicator of limiting equilibrium. This allows you to write the maximum friction equation $F = \mu R$. Always solve the vertical forces first to write $R$ in terms of $T$ before setting up your horizontal balance.

question:
A block of mass $5\text{ kg}$ lies on a rough plane inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, as shown in the diagram, where $\tan \theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $0.25$.

A force of magnitude $P\text{ N}$ acts parallel to the plane, pulling the block up the plane at a constant acceleration of $2\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Using the model, find the value of $P$.
steps: From $\tan \theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$, using a right-angled triangle:\begin{aligned} &\sin \theta = 0.6 \cr &\cos \theta = 0.8 \end{aligned}
Resolve forces perpendicular to the plane:\begin{aligned} &R - mg\cos \theta = 0 \cr &R \cr &\quad = 5(9.8)(0.8) \cr &\quad = 39.2\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Calculate the maximum friction force $F$ acting down the plane:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = \mu R \cr &\quad = 0.25 \times 39.2 \cr &\quad = 9.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Calculate the component of weight acting down the plane:\begin{aligned} &mg\sin \theta \cr &\quad = 5(9.8)(0.6) \cr &\quad = 29.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Apply Newton's second law ($F = ma$) parallel to the incline:\begin{aligned} &P - F - mg\sin \theta = ma \cr &P - 9.8 - 29.4 = 5(2) \cr &P - 39.2 = 10 \cr &P = 49.2\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $49.2\text{ N }$

pi_options.feedback: This occurs if you neglect to include the $ma = 10\text{ N}$ acceleration term, writing $P - F - mg \sin \theta = 0$. Since the block is accelerating, the pulling force must exceed the static forces.

This is a sign error where the gravity component $mg \sin \theta$ is added instead of subtracted in the equation, as if gravity were pulling the block up. Gravity always opposes upward motion along a slope.

This occurs if you resolve the weight component parallel to the plane using cosine instead of sine (using $mg \cos \theta$ parallel to the slope). Double check your slope components: parallel is always $mg \sin \theta$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Incline Gravity Component
bradley_insight.content: Do not forget the parallel component of weight ($mg \sin \theta$) acting down the slope. Even though you are pulling up the plane, gravity is still fighting you along with friction. This means $P$ must overcome both forces in addition to providing the mass with acceleration.

question:
A block of mass $10\text{ kg}$ is on a rough plane inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, as shown in the diagram, where $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $0.3$.

The block is held in limiting equilibrium, on the point of slipping down the plane, by a horizontal force of magnitude $H\text{ N}$.

Using the model, find the value of $H$.
steps: From $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$:\begin{aligned} &\sin \alpha = 0.6 \cr &\cos \alpha = 0.8 \end{aligned}

Resolve the forces perpendicular and parallel to the inclined plane:

• Component parallel to slope (acting up the slope): $H\cos \alpha = 0.8H$

• Component perpendicular to slope (acting into the slope): $H\sin \alpha = 0.6H$
Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane:\begin{aligned} &R - mg\cos \alpha - H\sin \alpha = 0 \cr &R \cr &\quad = 10(9.8)(0.8) + 0.6H \cr &\quad = 78.4 + 0.6H \end{aligned}
Limiting friction $F$ acts up the plane to oppose slipping downwards:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = \mu R \cr &\quad = 0.3(78.4 + 0.6H) \cr &\quad = 23.52 + 0.18H \end{aligned}
Resolve forces parallel to the inclined plane:\begin{aligned} &H\cos \alpha + F = mg\sin \alpha \cr &0.8H + (23.52 + 0.18H) \cr &\qquad = 10(9.8)(0.6) \cr &0.98H + 23.52 = 58.8 \end{aligned}
Solve for $H$:\begin{aligned} &0.98H = 58.8 - 23.52 \cr &0.98H = 35.28 \cr &H \cr &\quad = \dfrac{35.28}{0.98} \cr &\quad = 36\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $36\text{ N }$

pi_options.feedback: This is a common calculation error where the normal reaction $R$ is resolved incorrectly, or a decimal rounding slip is made. Ensure you perform the algebraic substitutions with exact decimals.

This occurs if you treat the normal reaction $R$ as simply equal to $mg \cos \alpha = 78.4\text{ N}$, neglecting the fact that the horizontal force $H$ pushes the block into the slope and increases $R$.

This is the magnitude of the parallel gravitational force component ($mg \sin \alpha$). Remember that $H$ and friction both assist in holding the block from sliding down, so $H$ is smaller than $58.8\text{ N}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Horizontal Forces on Inclines
bradley_insight.content: This is a notoriously tricky question. A horizontal force $H$ does not act parallel to the slope. It must be resolved into two components: $H \cos \alpha$ parallel to the plane (assisting in holding it up), and $H \sin \alpha$ perpendicular to the plane, which pushes the block into the incline and actually increases the normal reaction $R$.

question:
A block of mass $10\text{ kg}$ is on a rough plane inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, as shown in the diagram, where $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $0.5$.

A force of magnitude $P\text{ N}$ acts parallel to the plane, directed up the plane.

Using the model, find the range of values of $P$ for which the block remains in equilibrium.
steps: From $\tan \alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$:\begin{aligned} &\sin \alpha = 0.6 \cr &\cos \alpha = 0.8 \end{aligned}

Calculate the components of weight:

• Perpendicular to plane:\begin{aligned} &mg\cos \alpha \cr &\quad = 10(9.8)(0.8) \cr &\quad = 78.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}

• Parallel to plane:\begin{aligned} &mg\sin \alpha \cr &\quad = 10(9.8)(0.6) \cr &\quad = 58.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Normal reaction is $R = 78.4\text{ N}$. Calculate maximum limiting friction $F_{\text{max}}$:\begin{aligned} &F_{\text{max}} \cr &\quad = \mu R \cr &\quad = 0.5 \times 78.4 \cr &\quad = 39.2\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Case 1: Point of slipping down (Minimum $P$):

When $P$ is at its minimum, friction $F_{\text{max}}$ acts up the plane:\begin{aligned} &P_{\text{min}} + F_{\text{max}} = mg\sin \alpha \cr &P_{\text{min}} + 39.2 = 58.8 \cr &P_{\text{min}} = 19.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Case 2: Point of slipping up (Maximum $P$):

When $P$ is at its maximum, friction $F_{\text{max}}$ acts down the plane:\begin{aligned} &P_{\text{max}} - F_{\text{max}} = mg\sin \alpha \cr &P_{\text{max}} - 39.2 = 58.8 \cr &P_{\text{max}} = 98\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Combine both extremes for equilibrium:$$19.6 \le P \le 98$$
Final Answer: $19.6 \le P \le 98$

pi_options.feedback: This occurs if you neglect to find the lower limit $P_{\text{min}}$. If $P = 0$, the maximum friction force ($39.2\text{ N}$) is smaller than the gravitational pull down the slope ($58.8\text{ N}$), meaning the block will slide down without at least $19.6\text{ N}$ of support force.

This represents a misunderstanding of the upper limit, setting $P_{\text{max}} = 58.8\text{ N}$ (equal to the parallel weight component). This would only be true if there was no friction; with friction, you can pull with up to $98\text{ N}$ before the block moves up.
This range is obtained if you confuse the friction force magnitude ($39.2\text{ N}$) and reaction force magnitude ($78.4\text{ N}$) with the equilibrium thresholds of the pulling force.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Friction as a Variable Friend
bradley_insight.content: In a 'range of values for equilibrium' problem, friction is variable and adaptive. It can act up the plane (to prevent sliding down under low tension) or down the plane (to prevent being pulled up under high tension). Find the two limiting friction extremes to bound the range.

question:
In this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors due east and due north respectively, and position vectors are given relative to a fixed origin $O$.

A particle $P$ moves with constant acceleration. At time $t = 0$, the particle is at $O$ and is moving with velocity $(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$. At time $t = 2\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the point $A$ with position vector $(8\mathbf{i} - 12\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$.

(a) Show that the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ is $5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

At the instant when $P$ leaves the point $A$, the acceleration of $P$ changes so that $P$ now moves with constant acceleration $(2\mathbf{i} + 5.4\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$. At the instant $t = T$ seconds, $P$ is moving in a direction due north-east.

(b) Find the value of $T$.
steps:
(a) Show acceleration magnitude is $5\text{ m s}^{-2}$:

Using $\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}$, $t = 2\text{ s}$, and $\mathbf{s} = 8\mathbf{i} - 12\mathbf{j}$:\begin{aligned} &8\mathbf{i} - 12\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = (\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})(2) + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}_1(2)^2 \cr &\quad = 2\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{a}_1 \end{aligned}

Isolate and solve for $\mathbf{a}_1$:\begin{aligned} &2\mathbf{a}_1 \cr &\quad = (8 - 2)\mathbf{i} + (-12 + 4)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 6\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j} \cr &\mathbf{a}_1 \cr &\quad = 3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Calculate magnitude $|\mathbf{a}_1|$:\begin{aligned} &|\mathbf{a}_1| \cr &\quad = \sqrt{3^2 + (-4)^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{9 + 16} \cr &\quad = 5\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the value of $T$:

Find velocity at point $A$ ($t = 2\text{ s}$) using $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}_A \cr &\quad = (\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) + (3\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})(2) \cr &\quad = 7\mathbf{i} - 10\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

With acceleration $\mathbf{a}_2 = 2\mathbf{i} + 5.4\mathbf{j}$, the velocity at time $T > 2$ is:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}(T) \cr &\quad = \mathbf{v}_A + \mathbf{a}_2(T - 2) \cr &\quad = (7\mathbf{i} - 10\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + (T - 2)(2\mathbf{i} + 5.4\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = \big[7 + 2(T - 2)\big]\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + \big[-10 + 5.4(T - 2)\big]\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = (2T + 3)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (5.4T - 20.8)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Moving due north-east requires equal, positive components ($v_x = v_y > 0$):\begin{aligned} &2T + 3 = 5.4T - 20.8 \cr &3.4T = 23.8 \cr &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{23.8}{3.4} \cr &\quad = 7\text{ s} \end{aligned}Check positivity at $T = 7$: $v_x = 17 > 0$. Thus, $T = 7\text{ s}$.
Final Answer: (a) $|\mathbf{a}_1| = 5\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $T = 7\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: This value of $T$ is the elapsed duration of the second motion phase ($T - 2 = 5$). Remember that the question asks for the total time $T$ from the start of the entire motion ($t = 0$), which requires adding the initial $2\text{ s}$ phase.
This occurs if you make a sign error when expanding the vertical component of velocity, such as writing $-10 + 5.4T + 10.8$ instead of $-10 + 5.4T - 10.8$, leading to an incorrect algebraic equation.
This represents a calculation error when solving the linear equation $3.4T = 23.8$. Double-check your decimal division carefully: $23.8 \div 3.4 = 7$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Elapsed vs. Total Time
bradley_insight.content: For multi-stage constant acceleration questions, make sure to distinguish between the elapsed time during the second phase (often written as $\tau = T - 2$) and the total time $T$ from the origin. Forgetting to add back the initial time is a very common source of lost marks.

question:
In this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors due east and due north respectively, and position vectors are given relative to a fixed origin $O$.

A particle $P$ moves with constant acceleration. At time $t = 0$, the particle is at $O$ and is moving with velocity $(\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$. At time $t = 3\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the point $A$ with position vector $(12\mathbf{i} - 27\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$.

(a) Show that the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ is $2\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

At the instant when $P$ leaves the point $A$, the acceleration of $P$ changes so that $P$ now moves with constant acceleration $(3\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$. At the instant $t = T$ seconds, $P$ is moving in a direction due south-east.

(b) Find the value of $T$.
steps:
(a) Show acceleration magnitude is $2\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-2}$:

Using $\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}$, $t = 3\text{ s}$, and $\mathbf{s} = 12\mathbf{i} - 27\mathbf{j}$:\begin{aligned} &12\mathbf{i} - 27\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = (\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})(3) + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}_1(3)^2 \cr &\quad = 3\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j} + 4.5\mathbf{a}_1 \end{aligned}

Isolate and solve for $\mathbf{a}_1$:\begin{aligned} &4.5\mathbf{a}_1 \cr &\quad = (12 - 3)\mathbf{i} + (-27 + 9)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 9\mathbf{i} - 18\mathbf{j} \cr &\mathbf{a}_1 \cr &\quad = 2\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Calculate magnitude $|\mathbf{a}_1|$:\begin{aligned} &|\mathbf{a}_1| \cr &\quad = \sqrt{2^2 + (-4)^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{4 + 16} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{20} \cr &\quad = 2\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the value of $T$:

Find velocity at $A$ ($t = 3\text{ s}$) using $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}_A \cr &\quad = (\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}) + (2\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})(3) \cr &\quad = 7\mathbf{i} - 15\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

With acceleration $\mathbf{a}_2 = 3\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}$, the velocity at time $T > 3$ is:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}(T) \cr &\quad = \mathbf{v}_A + \mathbf{a}_2(T - 3) \cr &\quad = (7\mathbf{i} - 15\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + (T - 3)(3\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = \big[7 + 3(T - 3)\big]\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + \big[-15 + 5(T - 3)\big]\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = (3T - 2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (5T - 30)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Moving due south-east requires $v_x = -v_y > 0$:\begin{aligned} &3T - 2 = -(5T - 30) \cr &3T - 2 = -5T + 30 \cr &8T = 32 \cr &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{32}{8} \cr &\quad = 4\text{ s} \end{aligned}Check conditions at $T = 4$: $v_x = 10 > 0$ and $v_y = -10 < 0$. Thus, $T = 4\text{ s}$.
Final Answer: (a) $|\mathbf{a}_1| = 2\sqrt{ 5 }\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $T = 4\text{ s}$

Since the variable $T$ in the equation $(3T - 2)$ already represents the total time from the origin, $T = 4\text{ s}$ is the final total time.
This occurs if you use a direction of north-east ($v_x = v_y$) instead of south-east ($v_x = -v_y$) to set up your components equation. Always identify the correct quadrant for the target bearing.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: South-East Vector Constraints
bradley_insight.content: Due south-east represents a direction of $135^\circ$ from North. In vector terms, this means the velocity vector points to the right and downwards, requiring the $\mathbf{i}$ component to be positive and the $\mathbf{j}$ component to be negative, with equal magnitudes ($v_x = -v_y > 0$).

question:
In this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors due east and due north respectively, and position vectors are given relative to a fixed origin $O$.

A particle $P$ moves with constant acceleration $(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$. At time $t = 0$, $P$ is moving with velocity $(-10\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Find the position vector of $P$ at the instant $t = 4\text{ s}$.

(b) Find the time, $T$ seconds, when $P$ is moving due north.
steps:
(a) Find the position vector at $t = 4\text{ s}$:

Using $\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{s} \cr &\quad = (-10\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})(4) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{1}{2}(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})(4)^2 \cr &\quad = (-40\mathbf{i} - 32\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + 8(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = -40\mathbf{i} - 32\mathbf{j} \cr &\qquad + 16\mathbf{i} + 24\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = -24\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}The position vector is $(-24\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$.

(b) Find the time $T$ when $P$ moves due north:

Find velocity at time $t$ using $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v} \cr &\quad = (-10\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j}) + t(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = (-10 + 2t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (-8 + 3t)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Moving due north requires $v_x = 0$ and $v_y > 0$:\begin{aligned} &-10 + 2T = 0 \cr &2T = 10 \cr &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{10}{2} \cr &\quad = 5\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Verify the vertical component at $T = 5$:\begin{aligned} &v_y \cr &\quad = -8 + 3(5) \cr &\quad = 7\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Since $7 > 0$, the particle is moving due north at $T = 5\text{ s}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Directional Kinematics
bradley_insight.content: For directional motion, look at the bearings: 'due North' means $v_x = 0$ and $v_y > 0$; 'due East' means $v_y = 0$ and $v_x > 0$. Always check that the non-zero component is positive to avoid accidentally solving for due South or due West.

question:
In this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors due east and due north respectively, and position vectors are given relative to a fixed origin $O$.

A particle $P$ moves with constant acceleration $(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$. At time $t = 0$, $P$ is at the point with position vector $(4\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$ and is moving with velocity $(2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Find the position vector of $P$ at the instant $t = 3\text{ s}$.

(b) Find the bearing on which the particle is moving at the instant $t = 4\text{ s}$, giving your answer to the nearest degree.
steps:
(a) Find the position vector at $t = 3\text{ s}$:

Using $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r} \cr &\quad = (4\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + (2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})(3) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})(3)^2 \cr &\quad = (4\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + (6\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + 4.5(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = 10\mathbf{i} + 13\mathbf{j} \cr &\qquad + 4.5\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 14.5\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}The position vector is $(14.5\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$.

(b) Find the bearing at $t = 4\text{ s}$:

Find velocity at $t = 4\text{ s}$ using $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v} \cr &\quad = (2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}) + 4(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = 6\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

The vector $6\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j}$ points East and South (4th quadrant). Find the angle $\phi$ East of South:\begin{aligned} &\tan \phi \cr &\quad = \dfrac{6}{7} \cr &\phi \cr &\quad \approx 40.6^{\circ} \end{aligned}

Measure clockwise from North ($0^{\circ}$):\begin{aligned} &\text{Bearing} \cr &\quad = 180^{\circ} - 40.6^{\circ} \cr &\quad = 139.4^{\circ} \end{aligned}To the nearest degree, the bearing is $139^{\circ}$.
Final Answer: (a) $14.5\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$, (b) $139^{\circ}$

This position vector is obtained if you neglect the acceleration term $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }\mathbf{a}t^2$ in the position formula. Make sure to include all components of the SUVAT position vector.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Sketching Bearings First
bradley_insight.content: Always sketch the velocity vector first before calculating any angle. A velocity of $6\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j}$ has an East component of $6$ and a South component of $7$ (putting it in the 4th quadrant). This immediately tells you the bearing must lie between $90^{\circ}$ and $180^{\circ}$.

question:
In this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors due east and due north respectively, and position vectors are given relative to a fixed origin $O$.

Two particles, $P$ and $Q$, move with constant acceleration:

• At $t = 0$, $P$ is at $(2\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$, moving with velocity $(4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$, under acceleration $(\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

• At $t = 0$, $Q$ starts from $O$, moving with velocity $(6\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$, under acceleration $(2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the position vector of $P$ and the position vector of $Q$ at time $t$ seconds.

(b) Find the exact distance between $P$ and $Q$ at the instant $t = 2\text{ s}$.
steps:
(a) Find the position vector of each particle:

Using $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$:

• For particle $P$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}_P \cr &\quad = (2\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + t(4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{1}{2}t^2(\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = (2 + 4t + 0.5t^2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (5 - t + t^2)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

• For particle $Q$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}_Q \cr &\quad = t(6\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{1}{2}t^2(2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = (6t + t^2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (3t + 0.5t^2)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the distance between them at $t = 2\text{ s}$:

Evaluate the position of $P$ at $t = 2$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}_P(2) \cr &\quad = (2 + 4(2) + 0.5(2)^2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (5 - 2 + 2^2)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = (2 + 8 + 2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (5 - 2 + 4)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 12\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Evaluate the position of $Q$ at $t = 2$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}_Q(2) \cr &\quad = (6(2) + 2^2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (3(2) + 0.5(2)^2)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = (12 + 4)\mathbf{i} + (6 + 2)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 16\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Find the separation vector $\vec{PQ}$ at $t = 2\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{PQ} \cr &\quad = \mathbf{r}_Q(2) - \mathbf{r}_P(2) \cr &\quad = (16\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}) - (12\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = 4\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Calculate the exact distance:\begin{aligned} &|\vec{PQ}| \cr &\quad = \sqrt{4^2 + 1^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{16 + 1} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{17}\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\mathbf{r}_P$, $\mathbf{r}_Q$, (b) $\sqrt{ 17 }\text{ m }$

pi_options.feedback: This distance $\sqrt{26}\text{ m}$ is obtained if you make a component subtraction error when calculating the separation vector, such as evaluating the difference as $5\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$ or similar.
This represents a calculation error where the component differences are simply added ($4 + 1 = 5$) instead of applying Pythagoras' theorem to find the true magnitude.
This is a subtraction error under the square root, such as computing $16 - 1 = 15$ instead of $16 + 1 = 17$. Always write out the sum of the squared components carefully.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Absolute Separation
bradley_insight.content: To find the distance between any two particles in 2D space, first find their individual position vectors at the specified time, subtract one from the other to get the relative displacement vector, and then apply Pythagoras' theorem to find the absolute separation distance.

question:
A uniform horizontal beam $AB$, of mass $M$ and length $3a$, rests with its end $A$ against a rough vertical wall. The beam is held in a horizontal position by a rope. One end of the rope is attached to the beam at $B$ and the other end is attached to the wall at the point $C$, which is vertically above $A$. A small block of mass $2M$ is placed on the beam at the point $P$, where $AP = x$. The beam is in equilibrium in a vertical plane which is perpendicular to the wall. The angle between the rope and the beam is $\alpha$, where $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{5}{12}$.

The beam is modelled as a uniform rod, the block as a particle, and the rope as a light inextensible string.

(a) Show that the tension, $T$, in the rope is given by:$$T = \dfrac{13Mg(4x + 3a)}{30a}$$The magnitude of the horizontal component of the force exerted on the beam at $A$ by the wall is $2.4Mg$.

(b) Find $x$ in terms of $a$.

The force exerted on the beam at $A$ by the wall acts in a direction which makes an angle $\beta$ with the horizontal.

(c) Find the value of $\tan\beta$.

The rope will break if the tension in it exceeds $4Mg$.

(d) Find the range of possible positions of $P$ such that the rope does not break, justifying your answer carefully.
steps:
(a) Show the formula for tension $T$:

Equate clockwise and anticlockwise moments about hinge $A$:\begin{aligned} &(Mg \times 1.5a) + 2Mgx \cr &\qquad = T\sin\alpha \times 3a \cr &1.5Mga + 2Mgx \cr &\qquad = 3aT\sin\alpha \end{aligned}From $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{5}{12}$:\begin{aligned} &\sin\alpha = \dfrac{5}{13} \cr &\cos\alpha = \dfrac{12}{13} \end{aligned}Substitute $\sin\alpha$ into the moments equation:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{Mg(3a + 4x)}{2} = 3aT\big(\dfrac{5}{13}\big) \cr &\dfrac{Mg(3a + 4x)}{2} = \dfrac{15a}{13}T \cr &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{13}{15a} \times \dfrac{Mg(3a + 4x)}{2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{13Mg(4x + 3a)}{30a} \end{aligned}

(b) Find $x$ in terms of $a$:

For horizontal equilibrium at $A$:\begin{aligned} &H_A = T\cos\alpha \end{aligned}Substitute $H_A = 2.4Mg$, $T$, and $\cos\alpha = \dfrac{12}{13}$:\begin{aligned} &2.4Mg \cr &\quad = \dfrac{13Mg(4x + 3a)}{30a} \times \dfrac{12}{13} \cr &2.4Mg = \dfrac{12Mg(4x + 3a)}{30a} \cr &2.4 = \dfrac{2(4x + 3a)}{5a} \cr &12a = 8x + 6a \cr &8x = 6a \cr &x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{6}{8}a \cr &\quad = \dfrac{3}{4}a \end{aligned}

(c) Find $\tan\beta$:

For vertical equilibrium ($V_A$ upwards):\begin{aligned} &V_A + T\sin\alpha = 3Mg \end{aligned}Calculate $T$ when $x = \dfrac{3}{4}a$:\begin{aligned} &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{13Mg(4(\frac{3}{4}a) + 3a)}{30a} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{13Mg(6a)}{30a} \cr &\quad = 2.6Mg \end{aligned}Substitute $T$ into vertical equilibrium:\begin{aligned} &V_A + 2.6Mg\big(\dfrac{5}{13}\big) = 3Mg \cr &V_A + 1.0Mg = 3Mg \cr &V_A = 2Mg \end{aligned}Find $\tan\beta$:\begin{aligned} &\tan\beta \cr &\quad = \dfrac{V_A}{H_A} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2Mg}{2.4Mg} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}

(d) Find the range of positions of $P$:

For the rope not to break, $T \le 4Mg$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{13Mg(4x + 3a)}{30a} \le 4Mg \cr &13(4x + 3a) \le 120a \cr &52x + 39a \le 120a \cr &52x \le 81a \cr &x \le \dfrac{81}{52}a \end{aligned}Since $P$ is on the beam, $x \ge 0$. Thus, $0 \le x \le \dfrac{81}{52}a$.
Final Answer: $$\tan\beta = \dfrac{ 5 }{ 6 }, \quad 0 \le x \le \dfrac{ 81 }{ 52 }a$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you use an incorrect horizontal force $H_A = T$ instead of $T\cos\alpha$, or if you make an algebraic mistake in the inequality for the maximum tension limit.
This slip arises from using $\tan\alpha$ instead of $\sin\alpha$ in the moments equation, which corrupts the expression for tension and all subsequent values of the reaction components.
This error is caused by inverting the expression for $\tan\beta$ as $\dfrac{H_A}{V_A}$ instead of $\dfrac{V_A}{H_A}$, and making a sign error while expanding the bracket in the inequality.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Don't Confuse Horizontal & Vertical Reactions
bradley_insight.content: When resolving forces at a rough vertical wall hinge $A$, never assume the vertical reaction $V_A$ is equal to the total weight of the system. The tension in the rope has a significant vertical component ($T \sin\alpha$) that helps support the weight, meaning $V_A$ is always less than $(Mg + 2Mg)$. Always write a separate vertical equilibrium equation ($V_A + T \sin\alpha = 3Mg$) to avoid dropping these marks.

question:
A uniform beam $AB$, of mass $M$ and length $2a$, is smoothly hinged at $A$ to a vertical wall. The beam is held inclined at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal by a horizontal light rope. One end of the rope is attached to the beam at $B$ and the other end is attached to the wall at a point $C$ vertically above $A$. A block of mass $kM$ is placed on the beam at a point $P$, where $AP = x$. The beam is in equilibrium in a vertical plane.

The beam is modelled as a uniform rod, the block as a particle, and the rope as a light inextensible string.

(a) Show that the tension, $T$, in the rope is given by:$$T = \dfrac{Mg\cot\theta(a + kx)}{2a}$$For the remaining parts of this question, let $k = 3$ and $\theta = 45^{\circ}$.

(b) Given that the rope can withstand a maximum tension of $3Mg$, find the maximum possible value of $x$ in terms of $a$.

(c) For $x = a$, find the horizontal and vertical components of the reaction force exerted on the beam by the hinge at $A$, in terms of $M$ and $g$.

(d) Hence, find the angle the resultant reaction force at $A$ makes with the horizontal, giving your answer to the nearest $0.1^{\circ}$.
steps:
(a) Derive the formula for tension $T$:

Equate moments about hinge $A$:\begin{aligned} &T \times 2a\sin\theta \cr &\quad = (Mg \times a\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad + (kMg \times x\cos\theta) \cr &2aT\sin\theta \cr &\quad = Mg\cos\theta(a + kx) \cr &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg\cos\theta(a + kx)}{2a\sin\theta} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg\cot\theta(a + kx)}{2a} \end{aligned}

(b) Find maximum value of $x$:

With $k = 3$ and $\theta = 45^{\circ}$ (so $\cot 45^{\circ} = 1$):\begin{aligned} &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg(a + 3x)}{2a} \end{aligned}Since $T \le 3Mg$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{Mg(a + 3x)}{2a} \le 3Mg \cr &a + 3x \le 6a \cr &3x \le 5a \cr &x \le \dfrac{5}{3}a \end{aligned}The maximum possible value is $x_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{5}{3}a$.

(c) Find reaction components for $x = a$:

Calculate tension $T$ when $x = a$:\begin{aligned} &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg(a + 3a)}{2a} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4aMg}{2a} \cr &\quad = 2Mg \end{aligned}For horizontal equilibrium ($H_A = T$):\begin{aligned} &H_A = 2Mg \end{aligned}For vertical equilibrium ($V_A = Mg + 3Mg$):\begin{aligned} &V_A = 4Mg \end{aligned}

(d) Find angle with the horizontal:

Using $H_A = 2Mg$ and $V_A = 4Mg$:\begin{aligned} &\tan\phi \cr &\quad = \dfrac{V_A}{H_A} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4Mg}{2Mg} \cr &\quad = 2 \cr &\phi \cr &\quad = \arctan(2) \cr &\quad \approx 63.43^{\circ} \end{aligned}To the nearest $0.1^{\circ}$, the angle is $63.4^{\circ}$.
Final Answer: $$\phi = 63.4^{\circ}, \quad x_{\text{max}} = \dfrac{ 5 }{ 3 }a$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you invert the definition of the reaction angle, calculating $\tan\phi = \dfrac{H_A}{V_A}$ instead of $\dfrac{V_A}{H_A}$, and make an arithmetic slip in the tension inequality.
This error is made if you assume the horizontal and vertical components of the reaction force at the hinge must be equal, or if you neglect the weight of the block in the forces resolution.
This mistake arises if you assume the maximum distance is equal to the length of the beam ($2a$) without checking the tension limit, or if you calculate the tension incorrectly.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Look Out for Trig Simplifications
bradley_insight.content: When dealing with inclined rods, always check the orientation of your tension force. In this question, because the rope is horizontal, its perpendicular distance to the hinge $A$ is simply $2a\sin\theta$. Do not accidentally use the distance along the rod ($2a$) as the perpendicular distance. Spotting this right away prevents messy calculations!

question:
A uniform horizontal beam $AB$, of mass $10\text{ kg}$ and length $4\text{ m}$, is smoothly hinged to a vertical wall at $A$. The beam is supported in a horizontal position by a light cable. One end of the cable is attached to the beam at a point $C$, where $AC = 3\text{ m}$, and the other end is attached to the wall at a point $D$ vertically above $A$, where $AD = 4\text{ m}$. A sign of mass $M\text{ kg}$ is suspended from the end $B$ of the beam. The beam is in equilibrium in a vertical plane perpendicular to the wall.

The beam is modelled as a uniform rod, the cable as a light inextensible string, and the sign as a particle.

(a) Show that the tension, $T$, in the cable is given by:$$T = \dfrac{5}{3}(M + 5)g$$(b) Find, in terms of $M$ and $g$, the horizontal and vertical components of the reaction force exerted on the beam by the hinge at $A$.

(c) Given that the vertical component of the hinge reaction is zero, find the value of $M$.

(d) The hinge at $A$ can withstand a maximum horizontal force of $250\text{ N}$. Taking $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$, find the maximum allowable mass of the sign to the nearest $0.1\text{ kg}$.
steps:
(a) Show tension $T = \dfrac{5}{3}(M + 5)g$:

Cable length $CD$:\begin{aligned} &CD \cr &\quad = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} \cr &\quad = 5\text{ m} \end{aligned}Angle $\alpha$ with the horizontal:\begin{aligned} &\sin\alpha = \dfrac{4}{5} \cr &\cos\alpha = \dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}Equate moments about $A$:\begin{aligned} &(10g \times 2) + 4Mg = 3T\sin\alpha \cr &20g + 4Mg = 3T\big(\dfrac{4}{5}\big) \cr &4g(M + 5) = \dfrac{12}{5}T \cr &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5}{12} \times 4g(M + 5) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5}{3}(M + 5)g \end{aligned}

(b) Find reaction components at $A$:

For horizontal equilibrium ($H_A = T\cos\alpha$):\begin{aligned} &H_A \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5}{3}(M + 5)g \times \dfrac{3}{5} \cr &\quad = (M + 5)g \end{aligned}For vertical equilibrium ($V_A + T\sin\alpha = (M + 10)g$):\begin{aligned} &V_A + \dfrac{5}{3}(M + 5)g\big(\dfrac{4}{5}\big) = (M + 10)g \cr &V_A + \dfrac{4}{3}(M + 5)g = (M + 10)g \cr &V_A \cr &\quad = (M + 10)g - \big(\dfrac{4}{3}M + \dfrac{20}{3}\big)g \cr &\quad = \big(\dfrac{10}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}M\big)g \end{aligned}

(c) Find $M$ when $V_A = 0$:

Set $V_A = 0$:\begin{aligned} &\big(\dfrac{10}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}M\big)g = 0 \cr &\dfrac{10}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}M \cr &M = 10 \end{aligned}Thus, $M = 10\text{ kg}$.

(d) Find maximum allowable mass of the sign:

With $H_A \le 250\text{ N}$ and $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} &(M + 5)g \le 250 \cr &(M + 5)(9.8) \le 250 \cr &M + 5 \le 25.510 \cr &M \le 20.510 \end{aligned}To the nearest $0.1\text{ kg}$, $M_{\text{max}} = 20.5\text{ kg}$.
Final Answer: $$M = 10\text{ kg}, \quad M_{\text{max}} = 20.5\text{ kg}$$

pi_options.feedback: This mistake occurs if you miscalculate the vertical component of the tension as $T\sin\alpha = \frac{3}{5}T$ (using $\cos$ instead of $\sin$), and make an error in the horizontal force equilibrium.
This error is made if you forget to subtract $5\text{ kg}$ from the final inequality $M+5 \le 25.5$ for part (d), and miscount the coefficients in the vertical forces resolution.
This arises from a sign error when expanding and solving the vertical equilibrium equation, leading to an incorrect zero vertical reaction point and subsequent limit.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Visualising Hinge Reactions
bradley_insight.content: It is fascinating to see that for a light sign of mass $M < 10\text{ kg}$, the hinge force at $A$ must push vertically upwards ($V_A > 0$) to support the beam. However, as the mass $M$ of the sign increases beyond $10\text{ kg}$, the downward pull of the cable increases so much that the hinge must actually pull downwards ($V_A < 0$) to maintain equilibrium. This physical transition is why $V_A$ can be exactly zero at $M=10\text{ kg}$.

question:
A non-uniform rod $AB$, of mass $12\text{ kg}$ and length $4\text{ m}$, rests horizontally in equilibrium on two smooth pivots at $C$ and $D$, where $AC = 0.5\text{ m}$ and $BD = 1.0\text{ m}$. The centre of mass of the rod is at a distance $d$ from $A$.

The rod is modelled as a non-uniform rod and the pivots are modelled as simple supports.

(a) Show that when no additional masses are placed on the rod, the reaction forces at $C$ and $D$, denoted by $R_C$ and $R_D$ respectively, are given by:$$R_C = 4.8(3-d)g \quad \text{and} \quad R_D = 4.8(d-0.5)g$$(b) When a particle of mass $8\text{ kg}$ is placed at $A$, the rod is on the point of tilting about $C$. Find the value of $d$.

(c) Using this value of $d$, find the reaction forces at $C$ and $D$ when a mass of $5\text{ kg}$ is placed at $B$ instead of $A$, taking $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(d) Determine the range of masses that can be placed at $B$ without the rod tilting, justifying your answer carefully.
steps:
(a) Show formulas for $R_C$ and $R_D$:

Distance between pivots is $CD = 2.5\text{ m}$.

Take moments about $C$:\begin{aligned} &R_D \times 2.5 = 12g(d - 0.5) \cr &R_D \cr &\quad = \dfrac{12}{2.5}(d - 0.5)g \cr &\quad = 4.8(d - 0.5)g \end{aligned}From vertical equilibrium ($R_C + R_D = 12g$):\begin{aligned} &R_C \cr &\quad = 12g - 4.8(d - 0.5)g \cr &\quad = 12g - 4.8dg + 2.4g \cr &\quad = 14.4g - 4.8dg \cr &\quad = 4.8(3 - d)g \end{aligned}

(b) Find $d$ when tilting about $C$:

At tilting about $C$, $R_D = 0$. Take moments about $C$:\begin{aligned} &8g \times 0.5 = 12g(d - 0.5) \cr &4g = 12g(d - 0.5) \cr &4 = 12d - 6 \cr &12d = 10 \cr &d \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5}{6}\text{ m} \cr &\quad \approx 0.833\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Find $R_C$ and $R_D$ with $5\text{ kg}$ at $B$:

Distance from $C$ to $B$ is $3.5\text{ m}$. Take moments about $C$ with $d = \dfrac{5}{6}\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &R_D \times 2.5 \cr &\quad = 12g\big(\dfrac{5}{6} - 0.5\big) + 5g(3.5) \cr &\quad = 12g\big(\dfrac{1}{3}\big) + 17.5g \cr &\quad = 4g + 17.5g \cr &\quad = 21.5g \cr &R_D \cr &\quad = \dfrac{21.5g}{2.5} \cr &\quad = 8.6g \cr &\quad = 8.6(9.8) \cr &\quad = 84.28\text{ N} \cr &\quad \approx 84.3\text{ N} \end{aligned}Using vertical equilibrium ($R_C + R_D = 17g$):\begin{aligned} &R_C \cr &\quad = 17g - 8.6g \cr &\quad = 8.4g \cr &\quad = 8.4(9.8) \cr &\quad = 82.32\text{ N} \cr &\quad \approx 82.3\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(d) Determine allowable mass range at $B$:

Tilting about $D$ occurs when $R_C = 0$. Take moments about $D$ with $d = \dfrac{5}{6}\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &12g(3.0 - d) = mg(1.0) \cr &12\big(3 - \dfrac{5}{6}\big) = m \cr &12\big(\dfrac{13}{6}\big) = m \cr &m = 26\text{ kg} \end{aligned}Placing mass at $B$ decreases $R_C$, so tilting about $C$ cannot occur. Thus, the range of masses is:$$0 \le m \le 26\text{ kg}$$
Final Answer: $$d = 0.833\text{ m}, \quad 0 \le m \le 26\text{ kg}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error is identical to resolving the moment equation for tilting about $C$ incorrectly by writing $8g(0.5) = 12g(d + 0.5)$, which leads to a center of mass outside the support pivots, and miscalculating the pivot range.
This mistake occurs if you assume the centre of mass is at the pivot $C$ ($d=0.5\text{ m}$) and calculate the mass range by setting the pivot distance incorrectly.
This error is caused by neglecting the pivot distances from the ends of the rod, using $AC = 1\text{ m}$ and $BD = 1\text{ m}$ in your moments instead of the actual dimensions.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Tilting Means Zero Reaction
bradley_insight.content: Whenever a question mentions that a body is 'on the point of tilting' about a pivot, translate this immediately into a mathematical statement: the normal reaction force at any other pivot must equal zero ($R = 0$). This simple trick allows you to instantly simplify your moments equations by eliminating the other unknown reaction forces.

question:
A uniform ladder $AB$, of mass $M$ and length $2L$, rests in equilibrium with its end $A$ on a rough horizontal ground and its end $B$ against a smooth vertical wall. The ladder makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal ground, where $\tan\theta = 2$. A man of mass $3M$ climbs up the ladder.

The ladder is modelled as a uniform rod and the man is modelled as a particle.

(a) Show that when the man has climbed a distance $y$ from $A$, the magnitude of the frictional force, $F$, between the ladder and the ground is given by:$$F = \dfrac{Mg(L + 3y)}{4L}$$The coefficient of friction between the ladder and the ground is $\mu = 0.4$.

(b) Find the maximum distance the man can climb before the ladder slips, expressing your answer in terms of $L$.

(c) Now suppose the ground is smooth and slipping is prevented by a light horizontal rope attached to the ladder at $A$ and to the base of the wall. Find the tension in this rope when the man is at the top of the ladder (i.e., $y = 2L$), in terms of $M$ and $g$.

(d) Explain how the safety of the ladder would be affected if the ladder was placed at a steeper angle (i.e., $\tan\theta > 2$).
steps:
(a) Show friction $F = \dfrac{Mg(L + 3y)}{4L}$:

Resolving vertically ($R_A = Mg + 3Mg$):\begin{aligned} &R_A = 4Mg \end{aligned}Resolving horizontally:\begin{aligned} &F = R_B \end{aligned}Take moments about $A$:\begin{aligned} &(Mg \times L\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad + 3Mgy\cos\theta \cr &\quad = R_B \times 2L\sin\theta \cr &Mg\cos\theta(L + 3y) \cr &\quad = 2LR_B\sin\theta \cr &R_B \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg\cos\theta(L + 3y)}{2L\sin\theta} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg(L + 3y)}{2L\tan\theta} \end{aligned}Since $F = R_B$ and $\tan\theta = 2$:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg(L + 3y)}{4L} \end{aligned}

(b) Find maximum climbing distance:

At slipping, $F \le \mu R_A$ with $\mu = 0.4$ and $R_A = 4Mg$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{Mg(L + 3y)}{4L} \le 0.4(4Mg) \cr &\dfrac{Mg(L + 3y)}{4L} \le 1.6Mg \cr &L + 3y \le 6.4L \cr &3y \le 5.4L \cr &y \le 1.8L \end{aligned}The maximum distance is $y_{\text{max}} = 1.8L$.

(c) Find rope tension when $y = 2L$:

On smooth ground, tension $T$ replaces friction $F$:\begin{aligned} &T \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg(L + 3(2L))}{4L} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{7MgL}{4L} \cr &\quad = 1.75Mg \end{aligned}Thus, $T = 1.75Mg$.

(d) Effect of a steeper angle:

The required frictional force is:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = \dfrac{Mg(L + 3y)}{2L\tan\theta} \end{aligned}If $\theta$ increases, $\tan\theta$ increases.

Since $\tan\theta$ is in the denominator, required friction $F$ decreases for any climber position $y$.

This reduces the likelihood of exceeding the friction limit $F \le \mu R_A$, making the ladder safer.
Final Answer: $$y_{\text{max}} = 1.8L, \quad T = 1.75Mg$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you use $\mu = 0.05$ instead of $0.4$, or if you incorrectly resolve the vertical equilibrium reaction $R_A$ as $Mg$ instead of $4Mg$.
This mistake is caused by omitting the factor of 3 in the man's weight ($3M$), treating him as having mass $M$, which leads to an incorrect moment equation and slipping distance.
This assumes the man can climb to the very top of the ladder ($2.0L$) without it slipping, which violates the friction limit under the given coefficient of friction.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Why Smooth Walls Make Things Simple
bradley_insight.content: In mechanics, leaning against a 'smooth' vertical wall means there is absolutely no vertical friction force acting at the top of the ladder. This is a massive blessing for your equations because it ensures the normal reaction from the wall ($R_B$) is purely horizontal. Always check the wording carefully: if the wall were 'rough', you would have to introduce a vertical friction force at $B$, which drastically increases the algebra!

question:
A ball is thrown from a point $A$, which is $2\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground. The ball is projected with speed $U\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal. The highest point of the trajectory of the ball is $4\text{ m}$ above the ground.

The ball is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity.



(a) Show that:$$U^2 = \dfrac{4g}{\sin^2\alpha}$$The ball hits a target $T$ which is at a horizontal distance of $16\text{ m}$ from $A$ and is at a height of $0.875\text{ m}$ above the ground, as shown in the diagram.

(b) Show that $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{9}{16}$.

(c) Find the value of $U$.

(d) Find the time it takes for the ball to travel from $A$ to $T$.
steps:
(a) Show $U^2 = \dfrac{4g}{\sin^2\alpha}$:

Vertical displacement to the peak is $s_y = 2\text{ m}$ (from $4 - 2$). At the peak, $v_y = 0$.

Using $v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2gs_y$:\begin{aligned} &0 = (U\sin\alpha)^2 - 2g(2) \cr &0 = U^2\sin^2\alpha - 4g \cr &U^2\sin^2\alpha = 4g \cr &U^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4g}{\sin^2\alpha} \end{aligned}

(b) Show $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{9}{16}$:

From horizontal motion ($x = 16\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &t \cr &\quad = \dfrac{16}{U\cos\alpha} \end{aligned}Vertical displacement is $y = -1.125\text{ m}$. Using $y = Ut\sin\alpha - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$:\begin{aligned} &-1.125 \cr &\quad = U\sin\alpha\big(\dfrac{16}{U\cos\alpha}\big) \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{1}{2}g\big(\dfrac{16}{U\cos\alpha}\big)^2 \cr &\quad = 16\tan\alpha - \dfrac{128g}{U^2\cos^2\alpha} \end{aligned}Substitute $U^2 = \dfrac{4g}{\sin^2\alpha}$:\begin{aligned} &-1.125 \cr &\quad = 16\tan\alpha \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{128g\sin^2\alpha}{4g\cos^2\alpha} \cr &\quad = 16\tan\alpha - 32\tan^2\alpha \end{aligned}Rearrange into quadratic form:\begin{aligned} &32\tan^2\alpha - 16\tan\alpha \cr &\qquad - 1.125 = 0 \end{aligned}Multiply by $8$ to clear decimals:\begin{aligned} &256\tan^2\alpha - 128\tan\alpha \cr &\qquad - 9 = 0 \end{aligned}Apply the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} &\tan\alpha \cr &\quad = \dfrac{128 \pm \sqrt{128^2 - 4(256)(-9)}}{512} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{128 \pm \sqrt{16384 + 9216}}{512} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{128 \pm \sqrt{25600}}{512} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{128 \pm 160}{512} \end{aligned}Since projected upwards, $\tan\alpha > 0$:\begin{aligned} &\tan\alpha \cr &\quad = \dfrac{288}{512} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{9}{16} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the value of $U$:

From $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{9}{16}$:\begin{aligned} &\sin\alpha \cr &\quad = \dfrac{9}{\sqrt{9^2 + 16^2}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{9}{\sqrt{337}} \end{aligned}Substitute into $U^2 = \dfrac{4g}{\sin^2\alpha}$ with $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} &U^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4(9.8)}{\big(\frac{9}{\sqrt{337}}\big)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{39.2}{\frac{81}{337}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{39.2 \times 337}{81} \cr &\quad \approx 163.09 \cr &U \cr &\quad = \sqrt{163.09} \cr &\quad \approx 12.8\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(d) Find the time from $A$ to $T$:

Using $\cos\alpha$:\begin{aligned} &\cos\alpha \cr &\quad = \dfrac{16}{\sqrt{337}} \cr &\quad \approx 0.87158 \end{aligned}From horizontal motion $t = \dfrac{16}{U\cos\alpha}$:\begin{aligned} &t \cr &\quad = \dfrac{16}{12.771 \times 0.87158} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{16}{11.131} \cr &\quad \approx 1.44\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$U \approx 12.8\text{ m s}^{-1}, \quad t \approx 1.44\text{ s}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error is identical to failing to evaluate the square root of $163.26$ correctly (mistaking $\sqrt{163}$ for $15.8$), which subsequent corrupts the horizontal velocity component and time of flight.

This mistake arises if you use a maximum height of $4\text{ m}$ relative to the launch point instead of the ground, leading to a wrong vertical displacement of $s_y = 4$ in the initial moments equation.
This slip occurs if you make a sign error when resolving the vertical quadratic equation, setting $y = +1.125$ instead of $-1.125$, which shifts the launch angle and initial velocity.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Track Your Reference Levels
bradley_insight.content: Always be extremely careful with vertical heights in projectile motion. The maximum height of $4\text{ m}$ is given relative to the horizontal ground, not the launch point $A$. Since $A$ is $2\text{ m}$ above the ground, the vertical displacement used in your kinematics equations to the peak must be $s_y = 4 - 2 = 2\text{ m}$. Missing this subtraction is one of the most common ways students lose easy marks on trajectory questions.

question:
A tennis ball is projected from ground level with speed $V\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $45^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The ball just clears a vertical net of height $1\text{ m}$ which is at a horizontal distance of $12\text{ m}$ from the point of projection.

The ball is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity, taking $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Show that:$$V^2 = \dfrac{144g}{11}$$(b) Calculate the value of $V$.

(c) Find the speed of the ball as it clears the net.

(d) State one limitation of the model of the ball's motion.
steps:
(a) Show $V^2 = \dfrac{144g}{11}$:

At the net, $x = 12\text{ m}$ and $y = 1\text{ m}$.

From horizontal motion ($x = Vt\cos 45^{\circ}$):\begin{aligned} &12 = V\big(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\big)t \cr &t \cr &\quad = \dfrac{24}{V\sqrt{2}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{12\sqrt{2}}{V} \end{aligned}Substitute $t$ into $y = Vt\sin 45^{\circ} - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$:\begin{aligned} &1 \cr &\quad = V\big(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\big)\big(\dfrac{12\sqrt{2}}{V}\big) \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{1}{2}g\big(\dfrac{12\sqrt{2}}{V}\big)^2 \cr &\quad = 12 - \dfrac{1}{2}g\big(\dfrac{288}{V^2}\big) \cr &\quad = 12 - \dfrac{144g}{V^2} \end{aligned}Rearrange for $V^2$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{144g}{V^2} = 11 \cr &V^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{144g}{11} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate $V$:

Substitute $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ into $V^2 = \dfrac{144g}{11}$:\begin{aligned} &V^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{144 \times 9.8}{11} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1411.2}{11} \cr &\quad \approx 128.29 \cr &V \cr &\quad = \sqrt{128.29} \cr &\quad \approx 11.3\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the speed clearing the net:

Horizontal component ($v_x = V\cos 45^{\circ}$):\begin{aligned} &v_x \cr &\quad = 11.326 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cr &\quad \approx 8.009\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Vertical component ($v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2gy$):\begin{aligned} &v_y^2 \cr &\quad = (8.009)^2 - 2(9.8)(1) \cr &\quad = 64.144 - 19.6 \cr &\quad = 44.544 \end{aligned}Resultant speed:\begin{aligned} &\text{Speed} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{64.144 + 44.544} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{108.69} \cr &\quad \approx 10.4\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(d) Model limitations:

Any of the following is valid:

• Ignores air resistance, which opposes horizontal and vertical motion.

• Models the ball as a particle, ignoring dimensions and shape.

• Ignores spin (e.g. topspin), which produces aerodynamic forces.
Final Answer: $$V \approx 11.3\text{ m s}^{-1}, \text{ Speed} = 10.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you correctly calculate the initial velocity $V$ but mistake the horizontal velocity component $v_x$ as the final speed clearing the net, neglecting the vertical motion component.
This mistake arises if you use $10$ for the gravity constant $g$ instead of $9.8\text{ ms}^{-2}$, leading to slightly inflated values for both $V$ and the impact speed.

This error is caused by setting up the vertical displacement equation with a height of $0\text{ m}$ instead of $1\text{ m}$ (assuming the ball lands on the ground at $12\text{ m}$ instead of clearing the net).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Energy Conservation as a Kinematic Hack
bradley_insight.content: Finding the final speed of a projectile usually requires resolving $v_x$ and $v_y$ separately and combining them. However, if you only need the speed (not the direction), you can use Conservation of Mechanical Energy! The equation $\frac{1}{2}mV^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 + mgy$ simplifies directly to $v^2 = V^2 - 2gy$. This will save you precious minutes on a timed exam paper.

question:
A stone is projected with speed $U\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from a point $O$ at the top of a vertical cliff of height $25\text{ m}$. The stone is projected at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal, where $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$. The stone lands in the sea at a point $S$ which is at a horizontal distance of $60\text{ m}$ from the base of the cliff, as shown in the diagram.

The stone is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity, taking $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.



(a) Show that:$$U^2 = \dfrac{1125g}{28}$$(b) Calculate the value of $U$.

(c) Find the speed of the stone at the instant it hits the sea.

(d) Find the angle the velocity vector of the stone makes with the horizontal sea surface at the instant of impact.
steps:
(a) Show $U^2 = \dfrac{1125g}{28}$:

From $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$:\begin{aligned} &\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5} \cr &\cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}From horizontal motion ($x = 60\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &60 = U\big(\dfrac{4}{5}\big)t \cr &t \cr &\quad = \dfrac{300}{4U} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{75}{U} \end{aligned}Substitute $t$ into $y = Ut\sin\theta - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ with $y = -25\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &-25 \cr &\quad = U\big(\dfrac{3}{5}\big)\big(\dfrac{75}{U}\big) \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{1}{2}g\big(\dfrac{75}{U}\big)^2 \cr &\quad = 45 - \dfrac{5625g}{2U^2} \end{aligned}Rearrange for $U^2$:\begin{aligned} &-70 = -\dfrac{2812.5g}{U^2} \cr &70 = \dfrac{2812.5g}{U^2} \cr &U^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2812.5g}{70} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1125g}{28} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate $U$:

Substitute $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ into $U^2 = \dfrac{1125g}{28}$:\begin{aligned} &U^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1125 \times 9.8}{28} \cr &\quad = 393.75 \cr &U \cr &\quad = \sqrt{393.75} \cr &\quad \approx 19.8\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Find the speed hitting the sea:

Using conservation of energy:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{2}mU^2 + mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \cr &v^2 = U^2 + 2gh \end{aligned}Substitute $U^2 = 393.75$, $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $h = 25\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 393.75 + 2(9.8)(25) \cr &\quad = 393.75 + 490 \cr &\quad = 883.75 \cr &v \cr &\quad = \sqrt{883.75} \cr &\quad \approx 29.7\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(d) Find angle with horizontal at impact:

Horizontal component remains constant:\begin{aligned} &v_x \cr &\quad = U\cos\theta \cr &\quad = 19.843 \times \dfrac{4}{5} \cr &\quad \approx 15.874\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Angle of impact $\phi$ satisfies $\cos\phi = \dfrac{v_x}{v}$:\begin{aligned} &\cos\phi \cr &\quad = \dfrac{15.874}{29.728} \cr &\quad \approx 0.5340 \cr &\phi \cr &\quad = \arccos(0.5340) \cr &\quad \approx 57.7^{\circ} \end{aligned}The angle with the horizontal is $57.7^{\circ}$.
Final Answer: $$U \approx 19.8\text{ m s}^{-1}, \text{ Speed} = 29.7\text{ m s}^{-1}, \quad \phi = 57.7^{\circ}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you resolve the vertical displacement as $y = -20\text{ m}$ instead of $-25\text{ m}$, leading to a slightly lower velocity and impact angle.
This mistake is caused by setting the vertical displacement to $y = +25\text{ m}$ (treating the cliff as a wall the stone has to clear upwards) which corrupts the sign structure of the quadratic.
This error arises from using $\sin\theta$ in the horizontal motion equation instead of $\cos\theta$ when setting up the initial time-of-flight equation.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Symmetry of Projectiles
bradley_insight.content: For any projectile launched and landing at a lower level (like off a cliff), the horizontal speed stays constant, while the vertical speed increases. If you want to check your calculations, notice that the angle of impact $\phi$ ($57.7^{\circ}$) is significantly steeper than the launch angle $\theta$ ($36.9^{\circ}$), which makes perfect physical sense as gravity has had more time to accelerate the object downwards.

question:
A basketball is shot from a point $A$ which is at a height of $2.1\text{ m}$ above the court. The ball is thrown with speed $U\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The ball enters the hoop $T$, which is at a horizontal distance of $6.0\text{ m}$ and a height of $3.05\text{ m}$ above the court, as shown in the diagram.



The basketball is modelled as a particle moving freely under gravity, taking $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Show that:$$U^2$$ $$= \dfrac{360g}{120\sin\theta\cos\theta - 19\cos^2\theta}$$(b) Given that the ball is thrown at an angle of $\theta = 50^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, calculate the value of $U$.

(c) Find the maximum height above the court reached by the basketball during its flight.

(d) State the effect of modelling the basketball as a particle rather than a sphere with a finite radius on the likelihood of it scoring.
steps:
(a) Show formula for $U^2$:

Vertical displacement to the hoop is $y = 0.95\text{ m}$ (from $3.05 - 2.1$).

From horizontal motion ($x = 6.0\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &6 = Ut\cos\theta \cr &t \cr &\quad = \dfrac{6}{U\cos\theta} \end{aligned}Substitute $t$ into $y = Ut\sin\theta - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$:\begin{aligned} &0.95 \cr &\quad = U\sin\theta\big(\dfrac{6}{U\cos\theta}\big) \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{1}{2}g\big(\dfrac{6}{U\cos\theta}\big)^2 \cr &\quad = 6\tan\theta - \dfrac{18g}{U^2\cos^2\theta} \end{aligned}Multiply by $100$ and rearrange:\begin{aligned} &95 = 600\tan\theta - \dfrac{1800g}{U^2\cos^2\theta} \cr &\dfrac{1800g}{U^2\cos^2\theta} = 600\tan\theta - 95 \end{aligned}Divide by $5$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{360g}{U^2\cos^2\theta} = 120\tan\theta - 19 \cr &\dfrac{360g}{U^2} \cr &\quad = \cos^2\theta(120\tan\theta - 19) \cr &\quad = 120\sin\theta\cos\theta \cr &\qquad - 19\cos^2\theta \cr &U^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{360g}{120\sin\theta\cos\theta - 19\cos^2\theta} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate $U$ for $\theta = 50^{\circ}$:

Evaluate the denominator:\begin{aligned} &120\sin 50^{\circ}\cos 50^{\circ} - 19\cos^2 50^{\circ} \cr &\quad = 120(0.76604)(0.64279) \cr &\qquad - 19(0.41318) \cr &\quad = 59.094 - 7.850 \cr &\quad = 51.244 \end{aligned}Substitute into formula for $U^2$:\begin{aligned} &U^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{360(9.8)}{51.244} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{3528}{51.244} \cr &\quad \approx 68.847 \cr &U \cr &\quad = \sqrt{68.847} \cr &\quad \approx 8.30\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Find maximum height above court:

Using $v_y^2 = u_y^2 - 2gH_{\text{rel}}$ with $v_y = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = (U\sin 50^{\circ})^2 - 2gH_{\text{rel}} \cr &H_{\text{rel}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{U^2\sin^2 50^{\circ}}{2g} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{68.847(0.76604)^2}{19.6} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{68.847(0.58682)}{19.6} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{40.401}{19.6} \cr &\quad \approx 2.06\text{ m} \end{aligned}Add the launch height $2.1\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &H_{\text{max}} \cr &\quad = 2.1 + 2.06 \cr &\quad = 4.16\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Model limitations:

Modelling the basketball as a particle makes scoring more likely in the model than in reality.

A real basketball has a finite radius (approx $12\text{ cm}$); if it passes close to the rim, it may bounce out. A particle has zero size and passes through cleanly as long as its coordinates clear the rim.
Final Answer: $$U \approx 8.30\text{ m s}^{-1},  \text{ }H_{\text{max}} = 4.16\text{ m}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make an algebraic error in part (a) by flipping a trigonometric term to the numerator when resolving the reciprocal, resulting in an incorrect formula of $U^2 = \frac{360g}{120\tan\theta - 19}$.

This mistake is caused by using the incorrect formula $U^2 = \frac{360g}{120\tan\theta - 19}$ but correctly evaluating the square root, which reveals a physical impossibility (the max height is below the hoop height).
This error is caused by neglecting the initial vertical height offset of $2.1\text{ m}$ and setting the displacement equal to the full hoop height $y = 3.05\text{ m}$ in the moments calculations.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Spotting Physical Inconsistencies
bradley_insight.content: Always sanity-check your intermediate mechanics answers! In part (c), if you calculated a maximum height that was less than the target height of $3.05\text{ m}$, your projectile would never have been able to pass downwards through the hoop. Spotting such physical contradictions immediately alerts you to a formula rearrangement or arithmetic error.

question:
A particle is projected from a point $O$ on horizontal ground with speed $14\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of projection $\theta$ to the horizontal. The particle strikes a target on the ground at a horizontal distance of $10\text{ m}$ from $O$.

The particle is modelled as moving freely under gravity, taking $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Show that there are two possible angles of projection, and find these two values of $\theta$.

(b) Find the time of flight of the particle for each of these two angles.

(c) Calculate the difference between these two times of flight, giving your answer to $2$ decimal places.

(d) Describe how the trajectory would change if air resistance were included in the model.
steps:
(a) Find the two projection angles:

Using the horizontal range formula $R = \dfrac{U^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$:\begin{aligned} &10 = \dfrac{14^2\sin 2\theta}{9.8} \cr &10 = \dfrac{196\sin 2\theta}{9.8} \cr &10 = 20\sin 2\theta \cr &\sin 2\theta = 0.5 \end{aligned}Since $0^{\circ} < 2\theta < 180^{\circ}$:\begin{aligned} &2\theta = 30^{\circ} \quad \text{or} \quad 2\theta = 150^{\circ} \cr &\theta = 15^{\circ} \quad \text{or} \quad \theta = 75^{\circ} \end{aligned}

(b) Find times of flight:

Using $T = \dfrac{2U\sin\theta}{g}$:

• For $\theta = 15^{\circ}$:\begin{aligned} &T_1 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2(14)\sin 15^{\circ}}{9.8} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{28(0.25882)}{9.8} \cr &\quad \approx 0.74\text{ s} \end{aligned}

• For $\theta = 75^{\circ}$:\begin{aligned} &T_2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2(14)\sin 75^{\circ}}{9.8} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{28(0.96593)}{9.8} \cr &\quad \approx 2.76\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculate difference in flight times:

Subtract the times using full precision:\begin{aligned} &T_2 - T_1 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{28\sin 75^{\circ}}{9.8} - \dfrac{28\sin 15^{\circ}}{9.8} \cr &\quad = 2.7598 - 0.7395 \cr &\quad = 2.0203 \cr &\quad \approx 2.02\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(d) Effect of air resistance:

• Horizontal speed would decrease continuously, shortening range.

• Maximum height would decrease.

• Trajectory would become asymmetric, with a steeper descent than ascent.
Final Answer: $$\Delta T = 2.02\text{ s}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you use $\sin\theta$ instead of $\sin 2\theta$ in the initial range formula, leading to an incorrect projection angle and corrupted times of flight.
This mistake is caused by using $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$ but failing to calculate the angle change, resulting in a mismatched set of projection times.
This slip occurs if you divide the correct times of flight by $2$ (effectively calculating the difference in the times taken to reach the maximum heights instead of the landing target).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Complementary Launch Angles
bradley_insight.content: For any target distance on flat ground, there are always two complementary launch angles that sum to $90^{\circ}$ (in this case, $15^{\circ} + 75^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$). The high-trajectory launch ($75^{\circ}$) spends much more time in the air ($2.76\text{ s}$) because its initial vertical velocity is much greater, whereas the low-trajectory launch ($15^{\circ}$) relies on horizontal speed to cover the same distance in just $0.74\text{ s}$.

question:
In this question, the horizontal unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are in the directions East and North respectively.

A model ship of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is moving in a horizontal plane so that its acceleration vector $\mathbf{a}\text{ m s}^{-2}$ at time $t$ seconds is given by:$$\mathbf{a} = 2(3t - 7)\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}$$When $t = T$, the magnitude of the resultant horizontal force acting on the ship is $20\text{ N}$.

Find the possible values of $T$.
steps: Express force $\mathbf{F}$ using Newton's second law $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ ($m = 2\text{ kg}$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{F} \cr &\quad = 2\big[2(3t - 7)\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}\big] \cr &\quad = 4(3t - 7)\mathbf{i} + 16\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Solve for $T$ taking the square root:\begin{aligned} &3T - 7 = 3 \cr &3T = 10 \cr &T = \dfrac{10}{3} \end{aligned}Or:\begin{aligned} &3T - 7 = -3 \cr &3T = 4 \cr &T = \dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}So, the possible values of $T$ are $\dfrac{4}{3}$ and $\dfrac{10}{3}$.
Final Answer: $$T = \dfrac{ 4 }{ 3 }, \quad T = \dfrac{ 10 }{ 3 }$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you neglect to multiply the acceleration vector by the mass $m = 2$ in Newton's Second Law, equating the magnitude of the acceleration vector directly to $20$ instead of $10$.
This mistake is caused by a sign error when taking the square root, resolving $3T - 7 = -4$ instead of $-3$, or making an arithmetic slip when simplifying the squared term.
This slip arises if you accidentally calculate the magnitude of the force using only the horizontal component, neglecting the vertical component $16\mathbf{j}$ in Pythagoras' theorem.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Don't Forget the Mass
bradley_insight.content: A very common student error in vector mechanics is confusing the acceleration vector with the force vector. When a question provides a force magnitude, always ensure you multiply the acceleration vector by the mass ($2\text{ kg}$ in this case) before taking the magnitude. Forgetting this step will lead to incorrect quadratic solutions.

question:
A toy boat of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is moving in a horizontal pool under the action of a constant horizontal force $\mathbf{F} = (4\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$.

At time $t = 0\text{ s}$, the boat has velocity $\mathbf{u} = (-2\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
