(a) Show that the acceleration of the boat is given by $(8\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(b) Find an expression for the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$ of the boat at time $t$ seconds.

(c) Find the value of $t$ at which the boat is moving due East.

(d) Find the speed of the boat at this instant.
steps:
(a) Show $\mathbf{a} = (8\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$:

Apply Newton's second law $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{a} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\mathbf{F}}{m} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}}{0.5} \cr &\quad = (8\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$:

Using $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v} \cr &\quad = (-2\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + t(8\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = (8t - 2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (6 - 6t)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(c) Find $t$ when moving due East:

Moving due East requires $v_y = 0$ and $v_x > 0$:\begin{aligned} &6 - 6t = 0 \cr &6t = 6 \cr &t = 1\text{ s} \end{aligned}At $t = 1\text{ s}$, $v_x = 6 > 0$, confirming motion due East.

(d) Find speed at $t = 1\text{ s}$:

Substitute $t = 1$ into velocity $\mathbf{v}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v} \cr &\quad = (8(1) - 2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (6 - 6(1))\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 6\mathbf{i} + 0\mathbf{j} \cr &\text{Speed} \cr &\quad = |6\mathbf{i}| \cr &\quad = 6\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$t = 1\text{ s}, \text{ Speed} = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you correctly calculate the time but miscalculate the horizontal velocity component at $t = 1$ as $10\mathbf{i}$ instead of $6\mathbf{i}$, perhaps by adding the components incorrectly.
This mistake is caused by setting the horizontal component of the velocity to zero ($8t - 2 = 0$) instead of the vertical component, representing the time when the boat is moving due North or South.
This slip arises from a sign error when solving the vertical velocity component equation, leading to $6 + 4t = 0$ or similar incorrect equations.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Interpreting Directions with Vectors
bradley_insight.content: When a mechanics question specifies a direction of motion like 'due East' or 'due North', it is giving you a mathematical constraint. 'Due East' means the vertical component ($\mathbf{j}$) of the velocity must be exactly zero, and the horizontal component ($\mathbf{i}$) must be positive. Translate these directional words into algebraic boundary conditions immediately to simplify your equations.

question:
At time $t = 0$ hours, a yacht $A$ has position vector $(2\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})\text{ km}$ and is moving with a constant velocity $(4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})\text{ km h}^{-1}$.

At the same instant, a yacht $B$ has position vector $(10\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})\text{ km}$ and is moving with a constant velocity $(2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})\text{ km h}^{-1}$.

The horizontal unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ represent $1\text{ km}$ East and $1\text{ km}$ North respectively.

(a) Find the position vector of yacht $A$ and yacht $B$ at time $t$ hours.

(b) Show that the displacement vector from $A$ to $B$, denoted by $\mathbf{r}_{AB}$, at time $t$ hours is given by:$$\mathbf{r}_{AB} = (8 - 2t)\mathbf{i} + (3t - 6)\mathbf{j}$$(c) Find the distance between the two yachts at $t = 2$ hours.

(d) Find the time $t$ at which the two yachts are closest to each other.
steps:
(a) Find position vectors of $A$ and $B$:

Using $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{v}t$:

• For yacht $A$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}_A \cr &\quad = (2\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + t(4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = (2 + 4t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (5 - 2t)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

• For yacht $B$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}_B \cr &\quad = (10\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + t(2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = (10 + 2t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (t - 1)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(b) Show displacement $\mathbf{r}_{AB}$:

Subtract $\mathbf{r}_A$ from $\mathbf{r}_B$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}_{AB} \cr &\quad = \mathbf{r}_B - \mathbf{r}_A \cr &\quad = \big[(10 + 2t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (t - 1)\mathbf{j}\big] \cr &\qquad - \big[(2 + 4t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (5 - 2t)\mathbf{j}\big] \cr &\quad = (10 - 2 + 2t - 4t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (t + 2t - 1 - 5)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = (8 - 2t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (3t - 6)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(c) Find distance at $t = 2\text{ hours}$:

Evaluate $\mathbf{r}_{AB}$ at $t = 2$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r}_{AB}(2) \cr &\quad = (8 - 2(2))\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (3(2) - 6)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 4\mathbf{i} + 0\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Calculate distance:\begin{aligned} &\text{Distance} \cr &\quad = |4\mathbf{i}| \cr &\quad = 4\text{ km} \end{aligned}

(d) Find time of closest approach:

Minimize distance squared $d^2 = |\mathbf{r}_{AB}|^2$:\begin{aligned} &d^2 \cr &\quad = (8 - 2t)^2 + (3t - 6)^2 \cr &\quad = (64 - 32t + 4t^2) \cr &\qquad + (9t^2 - 36t + 36) \cr &\quad = 13t^2 - 68t + 100 \end{aligned}Differentiate with respect to $t$ and set to zero:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}(d^2)}{\text{d}t} = 0 \cr &26t - 68 = 0 \cr &26t = 68 \cr &t \cr &\quad = \dfrac{68}{26} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{34}{13}\text{ hours} \cr &\quad \approx 2.62\text{ hours} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$\text{Distance} = 4\text{ km}, \quad t \approx 2.62\text{ hours}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you assume that the yachts are closest at the specific evaluation time $t = 2$ instead of differentiating the distance squared expression to find the global minimum vertex.
This mistake arises from a sign error when expanding $(3t - 6)^2$, leading to an incorrect quadratic function for distance squared and subsequent differentiation errors.
This slip is caused by subtracting the position vectors in the wrong order ($A - B$) and then making an arithmetic error in the quadratic coefficients.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Closest Approach Trick
bradley_insight.content: To find the time of closest approach, you can always write down the expression for distance squared ($d^2$) and find its minimum. Minimizing $d^2$ is mathematically identical to minimizing the distance $d$, but it has the massive advantage of avoiding messy square roots in your derivatives. Always look to differentiate $d^2$ first!

question:
A small metal ring of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is resting on a smooth horizontal table and is in static equilibrium under the action of three coplanar horizontal forces:$$\mathbf{F}_1 = (3a\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_2 = (-6\mathbf{i} + 2b\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_3 = (15\mathbf{i} - 12\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

(a) Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$.

The force $\mathbf{F}_1$ is suddenly removed.

(b) Write down the resultant force acting on the ring.

(c) Find the acceleration vector $\mathbf{a}\text{ m s}^{-2}$ of the ring after $\mathbf{F}_1$ has been removed.

(d) Calculate the magnitude of this acceleration, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Find $a$ and $b$:

In static equilibrium, $\Sigma\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 = \mathbf{0} \cr &(3a - 6 + 15)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (4 + 2b - 12)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 0\mathbf{i} + 0\mathbf{j} \cr &(3a + 9)\mathbf{i} + (2b - 8)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 0\mathbf{i} + 0\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Equate components to zero:\begin{aligned} &3a + 9 = 0 \cr &a = -3 \cr &2b - 8 = 0 \cr &b = 4 \end{aligned}

(b) Resultant force when $\mathbf{F}_1$ is removed:

Since $\mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 = \mathbf{0}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{R} \cr &\quad = -\mathbf{F}_1 \cr &\quad = -(-9\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = (9\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Find acceleration vector $\mathbf{a}$:

Using $\mathbf{R} = m\mathbf{a}$ with $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{a} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\mathbf{R}}{m} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{9\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}}{0.5} \cr &\quad = (18\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(d) Calculate magnitude $|\mathbf{a}|$:

Using Pythagoras' theorem:\begin{aligned} &|\mathbf{a}| \cr &\quad = \sqrt{18^2 + (-8)^2} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{324 + 64} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{388} \cr &\quad \approx 19.7\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$a = -3, \quad b = 4, \quad |\mathbf{a}| = 19.7\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign slip when setting up the static equilibrium equations, resolving $3a - 9 = 0$ and $2b + 8 = 0$, leading to wrong sign values for $a$ and $b$.
This mistake is caused by neglecting to divide the resultant force vector by the mass $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ when calculating the acceleration, effectively setting $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{R}$.
This slip arises from multiplying the resultant force vector by the mass $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ instead of dividing by it, leading to an incorrect acceleration vector.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Equilibrium Removal Shortcut
bradley_insight.content: When a system is in equilibrium under several forces, the sum of those forces is zero. If you remove one force, say $\mathbf{F}_1$, you do not need to recalculate the sum of the remaining forces from scratch. The remaining forces must sum exactly to $-\mathbf{F}_1$. Recognizing this shortcut will keep your steps clean and prevent algebraic transcription errors.

question:
A particle $P$ of mass $0.2\text{ kg}$ moves in a horizontal plane. At time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$), its position vector $\mathbf{r}$ metres relative to a fixed origin $O$ is given by:$$\mathbf{r} = (t^3 - 3t^2)\mathbf{i} + (2t^2 - 4t)\mathbf{j}$$(a) Find an expression for the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ of $P$ at time $t$.

(b) Find the value of $t$ for which the particle is momentarily moving parallel to the vector $\mathbf{j}$.

(c) Find the kinetic energy of the particle at $t = 3\text{ s}$.

(d) Find the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the particle at $t = 1\text{ s}$.
steps:
(a) Find velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$:

Differentiate $\mathbf{r}$ with respect to time $t$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}\mathbf{r}}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = (3t^2 - 6t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (4t - 4)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(b) Find $t$ when moving parallel to $\mathbf{j}$:

Moving parallel to $\mathbf{j}$ requires $v_x = 0$ and $v_y \ne 0$:\begin{aligned} &3t^2 - 6t = 0 \cr &3t(t - 2) = 0 \end{aligned}Since $t \ge 0$, $t = 0\text{ s}$ or $t = 2\text{ s}$. At $t = 2\text{ s}$, $v_y = 4 \ne 0$, so $t = 2\text{ s}$.

(c) Find kinetic energy at $t = 3\text{ s}$:

Velocity at $t = 3\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{v}(3) \cr &\quad = (3(3)^2 - 6(3))\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (4(3) - 4)\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 9\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Calculate speed squared $v^2$:\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 9^2 + 8^2 \cr &\quad = 81 + 64 \cr &\quad = 145 \end{aligned}Calculate kinetic energy ($m = 0.2\text{ kg}$):\begin{aligned} &\text{KE} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2}(0.2)(145) \cr &\quad = 14.5\text{ J} \end{aligned}

(d) Find resultant force at $t = 1\text{ s}$:

Differentiate velocity to find acceleration:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{a} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{d}\mathbf{v}}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = (6t - 6)\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}At $t = 1\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{a}(1) \cr &\quad = (6(1) - 6)\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j} \cr &\quad = 4\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Using $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ ($m = 0.2\text{ kg}$):\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{F} \cr &\quad = 0.2(4\mathbf{j}) \cr &\quad = 0.8\mathbf{j}\text{ N} \cr &|\mathbf{F}| \cr &\quad = 0.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$t = 2\text{ s}, \quad \text{KE} = 14.5\text{ J},\text{ }\mathbf{F}| = 0.8\text{ N}$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you double the kinetic energy and force value, which typically happens when you use $m = 0.4\text{ kg}$ instead of the correct mass $0.2\text{ kg}$ in your dynamic equations.

This mistake is caused by setting the vertical component of the velocity to zero ($4t - 4 = 0$) in part (b), representing the time when the particle is momentarily moving parallel to $\mathbf{i}$ instead of $\mathbf{j}$.
This slip arises from an integration error or differentiating the position vector components incorrectly, yielding a slightly skewed set of values for velocity and force.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Vector Calculus Directions
bradley_insight.content: Be extremely precise when translating calculus-based kinematics with vectors. Displacement $\mathbf{r}$ to velocity $\mathbf{v}$ to acceleration $\mathbf{a}$ is always done by differentiating with respect to $t$. If you need to go the opposite way, integrate. Remember, component directions $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are independent, so treat them as separate variables during calculus operations.

question:
Particles $P$ and $Q$, of masses $3\text{ kg}$ and $7\text{ kg}$ respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string. The string passes over a smooth fixed pulley. The system is held at rest with the string taut and the hanging parts vertical. Both $P$ and $Q$ are above a horizontal plane. The system is released from rest.

(i) Find the tension in the string immediately after the particles are released.

After descending $2\text{ m}$, $Q$ strikes the horizontal plane and is immediately brought to rest. It is given that $P$ does not reach the pulley in the subsequent motion.

(ii) Find the total distance travelled by $P$ between the instant when $Q$ strikes the plane and the instant when the string becomes taut again.
steps:
(i) Find tension after release:

Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$):

• For $P$ (upwards):\begin{aligned} &T - 3g = 3a \end{aligned}

• For $Q$ (downwards):\begin{aligned} &7g - T = 7a \end{aligned}Add equations to eliminate $T$:\begin{aligned} &4g = 10a \cr &a \cr &\quad = 0.4g \cr &\quad = 0.4 \times 9.8 \cr &\quad = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Substitute $a$ into equation for $P$:\begin{aligned} &T - 3(9.8) = 3(3.92) \cr &T - 29.4 = 11.76 \cr &T \cr &\quad = 11.76 + 29.4 \cr &\quad = 41.16\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Speed $v$ when $Q$ descends $2\text{ m}$ ($a = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$):\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 0^2 + 2(3.92)(2) \cr &\quad = 15.68 \cr &v \cr &\quad = \sqrt{15.68} \cr &\quad \approx 3.96\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(ii) Find distance while string is slack:

When $Q$ stops, the string goes slack. Particle $P$ moves under gravity ($a = -9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$) until $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = v^2 - 2gs_{\text{up}} \cr &0 = 15.68 - 2(9.8)s_{\text{up}} \cr &19.6s_{\text{up}} = 15.68 \cr &s_{\text{up}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{15.68}{19.6} \cr &\quad = 0.8\text{ m} \end{aligned}

The string remains slack until $P$ falls back to the impact height ($s_{\text{down}} = 0.8\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &\text{Total distance} \cr &\quad = s_{\text{up}} + s_{\text{down}} \cr &\quad = 0.8 + 0.8 \cr &\quad = 1.6\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $T = 41.16\text{ N}, \text{distance} = 1.6\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: The tension of $41.16\text{ N}$ is correct, but $0.8\text{ m}$ is only the upward distance $P$ travels after the string goes slack. Since the string only becomes taut when $P$ returns to its height at the moment of impact, you must also add the downward descent of $0.8\text{ m}$.

This error occurs if you assume the tension is equal to the weight of the lighter mass ($3g = 29.4\text{ N}$), neglecting the acceleration of the system. Additionally, $1.6\text{ m}$ is the correct total distance travelled during the slack phase.

This tension is correct, but the distance of $2.8\text{ m}$ is found by adding the initial $2\text{ m}$ ascent of $P$ to the $0.8\text{ m}$ slack upward motion. The question only asks for the distance travelled between the instant $Q$ strikes the plane and when the string becomes taut again.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Don't Forget the Return Journey
bradley_insight.content: A very common mistake in slack-string questions is to calculate only the additional upward distance $s_{up}$ that the rising particle travels before stopping. Remember, the string remains slack as the particle falls back down, only becoming taut again when it returns to the level it was at when the other mass struck the floor. Thus, you must double the upward distance: $\text{Total Distance} = 2 s_{up}$.

question:
Particles $P$ and $Q$, of masses $2\text{ kg}$ and $3\text{ kg}$ respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string. The string passes over a smooth fixed pulley. The system is held at rest with the string taut and the hanging parts vertical. Both particles are above a horizontal plane. The system is released from rest.

(i) Find the tension in the string immediately after the particles are released.

After descending $6.125\text{ m}$, $Q$ strikes the plane and is immediately brought to rest. It is given that $P$ does not reach the pulley in the subsequent motion.

(ii) Find the total time that elapses between the instant when $Q$ strikes the plane and the instant when the string becomes taut again.
steps:
(i) Find tension after release:

Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$):

• For $P$ (upwards):\begin{aligned} &T - 2g = 2a \end{aligned}

• For $Q$ (downwards):\begin{aligned} &3g - T = 3a \end{aligned}Add equations to eliminate $T$:\begin{aligned} &g = 5a \cr &a \cr &\quad = 0.2g \cr &\quad = 0.2 \times 9.8 \cr &\quad = 1.96\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Substitute $a$ into equation for $P$:\begin{aligned} &T - 2(9.8) = 2(1.96) \cr &T - 19.6 = 3.92 \cr &T \cr &\quad = 3.92 + 19.6 \cr &\quad = 23.52\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Speed $v$ when $Q$ descends $6.125\text{ m}$ ($a = 1.96\text{ m s}^{-2}$):\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 0^2 + 2(1.96)(6.125) \cr &\quad = 24.01 \cr &v \cr &\quad = \sqrt{24.01} \cr &\quad = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(ii) Find time until string is taut again:

When $Q$ stops, the string goes slack. Particle $P$ ascends under gravity ($a = -9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$) with $u = 4.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ until $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = u - gt_{\text{up}} \cr &0 = 4.9 - 9.8t_{\text{up}} \cr &9.8t_{\text{up}} = 4.9 \cr &t_{\text{up}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4.9}{9.8} \cr &\quad = 0.5\text{ s} \end{aligned}

By symmetry, time falling back to the impact height equals $t_{\text{up}}$:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total time} \cr &\quad = t_{\text{up}} + t_{\text{down}} \cr &\quad = 0.5 + 0.5 \cr &\quad = 1\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $T = 23.52\text{ N}, \text{time} = 1.00\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: The tension is correct, but $0.50\text{ s}$ is only the time taken for $P$ to reach its maximum height. You must also include the time taken for $P$ to fall back down to the level where the string becomes taut again, which doubles the time.

This tension is incorrect because it assumes $T = 2g = 19.6\text{ N}$ (as if the system were in static equilibrium). Since the system is accelerating upwards, the tension must exceed the stationary weight ($T = 2(g + a)$, which is $23.52\text{ N}$).

This tension is correct, but the time of $1.25\text{ s}$ is incorrect. This error may occur if you use an incorrect deceleration value instead of gravity ($g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$) for the projectile stage of the motion.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Symmetry of Projectile Motion
bradley_insight.content: When a string goes slack, the rising particle acts as a simple vertical projectile. Due to the symmetry of free-fall motion under gravity, the time taken for the particle to rise to its peak is exactly equal to the time it takes to return to its launch height: $t_{\text{total}} = 2 t_{\text{up}}$. This symmetry makes finding the total time very direct.

question:
A block $P$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is held at rest on a smooth plane inclined at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. Block $P$ is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block $Q$ of mass $6\text{ kg}$, which hangs vertically. The system is released from rest with the string taut.

(i) Find the tension in the string immediately after the blocks are released.

After descending $1.6\text{ m}$, $Q$ strikes a horizontal floor and is immediately brought to rest. It is given that $P$ does not reach the pulley.

(ii) Find the total distance travelled by $P$ from the instant $Q$ strikes the floor to the instant the string becomes taut again.
steps:
(i) Find tension after release:

Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$):

• For $Q$ (downwards):\begin{aligned} &6g - T = 6a \end{aligned}

• For $P$ (up the incline, $\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.5$):\begin{aligned} &T - 2g\sin 30^{\circ} = 2a \cr &T - g = 2a \end{aligned}Add equations to eliminate $T$:\begin{aligned} &5g = 8a \cr &a \cr &\quad = 0.625g \cr &\quad = 0.625 \times 9.8 \cr &\quad = 6.125\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Substitute $a$ into equation for $P$:\begin{aligned} &T - 9.8 = 2(6.125) \cr &T - 9.8 = 12.25 \cr &T \cr &\quad = 12.25 + 9.8 \cr &\quad = 22.05\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Speed $v$ when $Q$ descends $1.6\text{ m}$ ($a = 6.125\text{ m s}^{-2}$):\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 0^2 + 2(6.125)(1.6) \cr &\quad = 19.6 \cr &v \cr &\quad = \sqrt{19.6}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(ii) Find distance while string is slack:

When $Q$ stops, the string goes slack. Acceleration along the plane is:\begin{aligned} &a_{\text{slack}} \cr &\quad = -g\sin 30^{\circ} \cr &\quad = -9.8 \times 0.5 \cr &\quad = -4.9\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Distance $s_{\text{up}}$ until $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 19.6 + 2(-4.9)s_{\text{up}} \cr &9.8s_{\text{up}} = 19.6 \cr &s_{\text{up}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{19.6}{9.8} \cr &\quad = 2\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Block $P$ slides back down $2\text{ m}$ until the string is taut again:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total distance} \cr &\quad = s_{\text{up}} + s_{\text{down}} \cr &\quad = 2 + 2 \cr &\quad = 4\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $T = 22.05\text{ N}, \text{distance} = 4.00\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: The tension is correct, but $2.00\text{ m}$ is only the distance $P$ travels up the incline after the string becomes slack. Since the string is slack during both the ascent and the return descent, you must double this value to find the total distance of $4.00\text{ m}$.

A tension of $39.20\text{ N}$ is incorrect; this error arises if you fail to resolve the gravity component of block $P$ on the inclined plane (using $2g = 19.6\text{ N}$ instead of $2g\sin 30^\circ = 9.8\text{ N}$).

The tension is correct, but the distance of $3.60\text{ m}$ is incorrect. This error can happen if you add the initial $1.6\text{ m}$ of motion to the $2.0\text{ m}$ of slack upward motion. The question asks for the distance travelled only after the instant $Q$ strikes the floor.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Deceleration on an Incline
bradley_insight.content: Notice that once the string goes slack, the rising block $P$ is no longer connected to $Q$, so its acceleration is determined solely by the forces acting on $P$. On a smooth inclined plane of angle $\theta$, this acceleration is always $-g \sin \theta$ regardless of $P$'s mass, because mass cancels out on both sides of $F = ma$ ($m a_{\text{slack}} = -m g \sin\theta$).

question:
A block $P$ of mass $5\text{ kg}$ lies on a rough plane inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, where $\sin\theta = 0.6$ and $\cos\theta = 0.8$. The coefficient of friction between $P$ and the plane is $0.25$. Block $P$ is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block $Q$ of mass $5\text{ kg}$. The system is released from rest with the string taut and $Q$ hanging vertically.

(i) Find the tension in the string immediately after the blocks are released.

After descending $10\text{ m}$, $Q$ strikes a horizontal platform and is immediately brought to rest. It is given that $P$ does not reach the pulley.

(ii) Find the total distance travelled by $P$ between the instant $Q$ strikes the platform and the instant the string becomes taut again.
steps: Normal reaction $R$ on $P$ perpendicular to incline:\begin{aligned} &R \cr &\quad = m_P g\cos\theta \cr &\quad = 5(9.8)(0.8) \cr &\quad = 39.2\text{ N} \end{aligned}Maximum friction $F$ opposing motion:\begin{aligned} &F \cr &\quad = \mu R \cr &\quad = 0.25 \times 39.2 \cr &\quad = 9.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(i) Find tension after release:

Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$):

• For $Q$ (downwards):\begin{aligned} &5g - T = 5a \end{aligned}

• For $P$ (upwards, friction acts down):\begin{aligned} &T - 5g\sin\theta - F = 5a \cr &T - 5(9.8)(0.6) - 9.8 = 5a \cr &T - 39.2 = 5a \end{aligned}Add equations to eliminate $T$:\begin{aligned} &49 - 39.2 = 10a \cr &9.8 = 10a \cr &a = 0.98\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Substitute $a$ into equation for $Q$:\begin{aligned} &49 - T = 5(0.98) \cr &49 - T = 4.9 \cr &T \cr &\quad = 49 - 4.9 \cr &\quad = 44.1\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Speed $v$ when $Q$ descends $10\text{ m}$ ($a = 0.98\text{ m s}^{-2}$):\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 0^2 + 2(0.98)(10) \cr &\quad = 19.6 \cr &v \cr &\quad = \sqrt{19.6}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(ii) Find distance while string is slack:

When $Q$ stops, the string goes slack. Gravity component and friction oppose upward motion:\begin{aligned} &-5g\sin\theta - F = 5a_{\text{slack}} \cr &-29.4 - 9.8 = 5a_{\text{slack}} \cr &a_{\text{slack}} \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{39.2}{5} \cr &\quad = -7.84\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Distance $s_{\text{up}}$ until $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 19.6 + 2(-7.84)s_{\text{up}} \cr &15.68s_{\text{up}} = 19.6 \cr &s_{\text{up}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{19.6}{15.68} \cr &\quad = 1.25\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Since $5g\sin\theta = 29.4\text{ N} > 9.8\text{ N}$, $P$ slides back down $1.25\text{ m}$ until the string is taut again:\begin{aligned} &\text{Total distance} \cr &\quad = s_{\text{up}} + s_{\text{down}} \cr &\quad = 1.25 + 1.25 \cr &\quad = 2.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $T = 44.10\text{ N}, \text{distance} = 2.50\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: The tension is correct, but $1.25\text{ m}$ is only the upward distance $P$ slides after the string becomes slack. Since the block must slide back down to the same reference height before the string becomes taut again, you must double this value to find the total distance of $2.5\text{ m}$.

A tension of $49.00\text{ N}$ is incorrect; this is equal to the weight of $Q$ ($5g$), which would only be true if the system were static. Because the system is accelerating, you must calculate the tension using $T = 5(g - a)$, giving $44.10\text{ N}$.

The tension is correct, but a total distance of $1.00\text{ m}$ is incorrect. This error may arise if you incorrectly calculate the deceleration during the slack phase, perhaps by forgetting to include either the friction force or the component of gravity down the plane.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Friction Reversal
bradley_insight.content: Always verify that the particle actually slides back down! On a rough slope, friction always opposes the direction of motion. While moving up, friction acts down the slope. When the block stops and tries to slide back down, friction acts up the slope. The block will only slide back down if the gravitational component down the slope is strictly greater than the maximum static friction: $m g \sin\theta > \mu m g \cos\theta$ (which simplifies to $\tan\theta > \mu$).

question:
A scale pan $P$ of mass $1\text{ kg}$ contains a block $B$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$. The scale pan is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley to a hanging mass $Q$ of mass $6\text{ kg}$. The system is held at rest with the string taut and the hanging parts vertical. The system is released from rest.

(i) Find the magnitude of the force exerted by the block $B$ on the scale pan $P$ immediately after release.

After descending $2.5\text{ m}$, $Q$ strikes a horizontal floor and is immediately brought to rest. It is given that $P$ does not reach the pulley in the subsequent motion.

(ii) Find the total distance travelled by the scale pan $P$ between the instant $Q$ strikes the floor and the instant the string becomes taut again.
steps:
Total mass on left is $m_{\text{left}} = 4\text{ kg}$ ($1 + 3$). Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$):

• For pan and block ($4\text{ kg}$, upwards):\begin{aligned} &T - 4g = 4a \end{aligned}

• For $Q$ ($6\text{ kg}$, downwards):\begin{aligned} &6g - T = 6a \end{aligned}Add equations to eliminate $T$:\begin{aligned} &2g = 10a \cr &a \cr &\quad = 0.2g \cr &\quad = 0.2 \times 9.8 \cr &\quad = 1.96\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(i) Find force exerted by $B$ on $P$:

Consider forces on block $B$ ($3\text{ kg}$) accelerating upwards at $a = 1.96\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} &R - m_B g = m_B a \cr &R - 3(9.8) = 3(1.96) \cr &R - 29.4 = 5.88 \cr &R \cr &\quad = 5.88 + 29.4 \cr &\quad = 35.28\text{ N} \end{aligned}By Newton's third law, the force exerted on the pan is $35.28\text{ N}$.
Speed squared $v^2$ when $Q$ descends $2.5\text{ m}$ ($a = 1.96\text{ m s}^{-2}$):\begin{aligned} &v^2 \cr &\quad = 0^2 + 2(1.96)(2.5) \cr &\quad = 9.8 \end{aligned}

(ii) Find distance while string is slack:

When $Q$ stops, the string goes slack. The pan and block move under gravity ($a = -9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$) until $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = v^2 - 2gs_{\text{up}} \cr &0 = 9.8 - 2(9.8)s_{\text{up}} \cr &19.6s_{\text{up}} = 9.8 \cr &s_{\text{up}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{9.8}{19.6} \cr &\quad = 0.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}

The string remains slack until the scale pan falls back to the impact height ($s_{\text{down}} = 0.5\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &\text{Total distance} \cr &\quad = s_{\text{up}} + s_{\text{down}} \cr &\quad = 0.5 + 0.5 \cr &\quad = 1\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $R = 35.28\text{ N}, \text{distance} = 1.00\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: The contact force of $35.28\text{ N}$ is correct, but $0.50\text{ m}$ is only the upward distance the scale pan travels after the string goes slack. Since the string remains slack until the scale pan returns to the level of impact, you must also include the downward return journey of $0.50\text{ m}$ to find the total distance of $1.00\text{ m}$.

A contact force of $29.40\text{ N}$ is incorrect because it is simply the stationary weight of the block ($3g = 29.4\text{ N}$). Since the block is accelerating upwards, the normal reaction force must exceed its stationary weight ($R = m_B(g+a)$, which equals $35.28\text{ N}$).

The reaction force is correct, but the distance of $3.00\text{ m}$ is incorrect. This error may occur if you add the initial $2.5\text{ m}$ ascent of the scale pan to the $0.5\text{ m}$ slack upward motion. The question asks only for the distance travelled after $Q$ strikes the floor.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Internal vs. External Forces
bradley_insight.content: When analyzing connected systems with composite masses (such as a scale pan containing a block), remember: to find the acceleration of the entire system, treat the scale pan and block as a single external mass ($1 + 3 = 4\text{ kg}$). Only treat them as separate bodies (using a free-body diagram for just the block) when you need to calculate the internal reaction/contact force $R$ between them.

question:
A particle $P$ moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. At time $t = 0\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the origin $O$. After $t = 8\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the point $A$, where $OA = 16\text{ m}$ in the positive direction. The velocity of $P$ at $A$ is $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in the direction $OA$.

(i) (a) Show that the initial speed of $P$ is $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(i) (b) Find the acceleration of $P$.

(ii) $B$ is a point on the line such that $OB = 5\text{ m}$ to the left of $O$. Show that $P$ is never at $B$.

(iii) A second particle $Q$ starts from $O$ at $t = 0\text{ s}$ and moves along the same straight line with variable acceleration. The displacement of $Q$ from $O$ is given by $x_Q(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct$. Initially ($t = 0\text{ s}$), $Q$ has the same velocity and acceleration as $P$ has initially. $Q$ reaches $A$ when $t = 4\text{ s}$. Find the velocity of $Q$ at $A$.
steps:
(i) (a) Show initial speed is $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$:

Using $s = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ with $s = 16\text{ m}$, $t = 8\text{ s}$, and $v = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$:\begin{aligned} &16 = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + 6)(8) \cr &16 = 4(u + 6) \cr &4 = u + 6 \cr &u = -2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Initial speed is $|u| = 2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(i) (b) Find acceleration of $P$:

Using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} &6 = -2 + 8a \cr &8 = 8a \cr &a = 1\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Show $P$ is never at $B$:

At point $B$, displacement $s = -5\text{ m}$. Using $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} &-5 = -2t + 0.5t^2 \cr &0.5t^2 - 2t + 5 = 0 \cr &t^2 - 4t + 10 = 0 \end{aligned}Check the discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$:\begin{aligned} &\Delta \cr &\quad = (-4)^2 - 4(1)(10) \cr &\quad = 16 - 40 \cr &\quad = -24 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta < 0$, no real solutions for $t$ exist. Therefore, $P$ is never at $B$.

(iii) Find velocity of $Q$ at $A$:

Differentiate $x_Q(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(t) = 3at^2 + 2bt + c \cr &a_Q(t) = 6at + 2b \end{aligned}Match initial conditions ($t = 0\text{ s}$) with $P$:\begin{aligned} &c = -2 \cr &2b = 1 \cr &b = 0.5 \end{aligned}So $x_Q(t) = at^3 + 0.5t^2 - 2t$. At $A$ ($t = 4\text{ s}$, $x_Q = 16\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &16 = a(4)^3 + 0.5(4)^2 - 2(4) \cr &16 = 64a + 8 - 8 \cr &16 = 64a \cr &a = 0.25 \end{aligned}

Velocity equation for $Q$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(t) \cr &\quad = 3(0.25)t^2 + 2(0.5)t - 2 \cr &\quad = 0.75t^2 + t - 2 \end{aligned}At $t = 4\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(4) \cr &\quad = 0.75(4)^2 + 4 - 2 \cr &\quad = 0.75(16) + 2 \cr &\quad = 12 + 2 \cr &\quad = 14\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $a = 1\text{ m s}^{-2}, \text{velocity} = 14\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you miss the negative sign for initial velocity, incorrectly using $u = 2\text{ m s}^{-1}$ instead of $u = -2\text{ m s}^{-1}$, leading to incorrect calculations for both the constant acceleration $a$ and the subsequent variable acceleration parameters.

The constant acceleration is correct, but a velocity of $16\text{ m s}^{-1}$ for $Q$ occurs if you incorrectly calculate the coefficient $b$ as $1.0$ (by forgetting to divide the initial acceleration by $2$ when setting up $2b = 1$).

The constant acceleration is correct, but a velocity of $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ represents a slip in evaluating $v_Q(4) = 0.75(16) + 4 - 2$, possibly by subtracting $4$ instead of adding it, or incorrectly determining the value of $a$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Direction and Signs
bradley_insight.content: Always pay close attention to direction when interpreting initial values. Since the displacement $OA = 16$ is in the positive direction and the final velocity is also positive ($+6$), the negative initial velocity $u = -2\text{ m s}^{-1}$ means the particle starts by moving to the left (towards $B$) before turning around and accelerating to the right. Correct signs are crucial for setting up the subsequent quadratic discriminant and variable acceleration integration constants.

question:
A particle $P$ moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. At time $t = 0\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the origin $O$. After $t = 5\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the point $A$, where $OA = 20\text{ m}$ in the positive direction. The velocity of $P$ at $A$ is $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in the direction $OA$.

(i) (a) Show that the initial speed of $P$ is $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(i) (b) Find the acceleration of $P$.

(ii) $B$ is a point on the line such that $OB = 2\text{ m}$ to the left of $O$. Show that $P$ is never at $B$.

(iii) A second particle $Q$ starts from $O$ at $t = 0\text{ s}$ and moves along the same straight line with velocity given by $v_Q(t) = 3kt^2 + 2.4t - 2$, where $k$ is a constant. $Q$ reaches $A$ when $t = 2\text{ s}$. Find the velocity of $Q$ at $A$.
steps:
(i) (a) Show initial speed is $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$:

Using $s = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ with $s = 20\text{ m}$, $t = 5\text{ s}$, and $v = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$:\begin{aligned} &20 = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + 10)(5) \cr &20 = 2.5(u + 10) \cr &8 = u + 10 \cr &u = -2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Initial speed is $|u| = 2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(i) (b) Find acceleration of $P$:

Using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} &10 = -2 + 5a \cr &12 = 5a \cr &a \cr &\quad = \dfrac{12}{5} \cr &\quad = 2.4\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Show $P$ is never at $B$:

At point $B$, $s = -2\text{ m}$. Using $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} &-2 = -2t + 1.2t^2 \cr &1.2t^2 - 2t + 2 = 0 \end{aligned}Check discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$:\begin{aligned} &\Delta \cr &\quad = (-2)^2 - 4(1.2)(2) \cr &\quad = 4 - 9.6 \cr &\quad = -5.6 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta < 0$, no real solutions for $t$ exist. Therefore, $P$ is never at $B$.

(iii) Find velocity of $Q$ at $A$:

Integrate $v_Q(t) = 3kt^2 + 2.4t - 2$:\begin{aligned} &x_Q(t) \cr &\quad = \int (3kt^2 + 2.4t - 2)\text{d}t \cr &\quad = kt^3 + 1.2t^2 - 2t + D \end{aligned}Since $x_Q(0) = 0$, $D = 0$.

At $A$ ($t = 2\text{ s}$, $x_Q = 20\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &20 = k(2)^3 + 1.2(2)^2 - 2(2) \cr &20 = 8k + 4.8 - 4 \cr &20 = 8k + 0.8 \cr &19.2 = 8k \cr &k \cr &\quad = \dfrac{19.2}{8} \cr &\quad = 2.4 \end{aligned}

Substitute $k = 2.4$ into $v_Q(t)$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(t) \cr &\quad = 3(2.4)t^2 + 2.4t - 2 \cr &\quad = 7.2t^2 + 2.4t - 2 \end{aligned}At $t = 2\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(2) \cr &\quad = 7.2(2)^2 + 2.4(2) - 2 \cr &\quad = 7.2(4) + 4.8 - 2 \cr &\quad = 28.8 + 2.8 \cr &\quad = 31.6\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $a = 2.4\text{ m s}^{-2}, \text{velocity} = 31.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: The constant acceleration is correct, but a velocity of $28.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ occurs if you forget to add the $2.4t$ linear velocity term when evaluating $v_Q(2)$.

This error occurs if you use an incorrect formula for $s$ (such as omitting the $\frac{1}{2}$ coefficient), leading to an incorrect acceleration for $P$, though the subsequent math for $Q$ is carried out correctly.
The constant acceleration is correct, but a velocity of $24.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$ occurs if you incorrectly determine $k = 1.8$ during the integration evaluation stage.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Calculus vs. SUVAT
bradley_insight.content: Always remember that SUVAT equations (such as $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$) are only valid for constant acceleration. Since particle $Q$ has variable acceleration, you must use integration to find displacement from velocity, and you cannot use any SUVAT equations for $Q$. Integrating $v_Q(t) = 3kt^2 + 2.4t - 2$ to find the displacement $x_Q(t) = kt^3 + 1.2t^2 - 2t$ is the only valid mathematical pathway.

question:
A car $P$ travels along a straight track with constant acceleration. Initially ($t = 0\text{ s}$), the car is at the starting line $O$. After $6\text{ s}$, $P$ passes a timing gate $A$, where $OA = 24\text{ m}$, with a speed of $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in the direction $OA$.

(i) (a) Show that the initial velocity of $P$ is $-2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(i) (b) Find the acceleration of $P$.

(ii) A marker post $B$ is placed such that $OB = 3\text{ m}$ to the left of $O$. Show that the car $P$ never reaches the marker post $B$.

(iii) A second vehicle $Q$ (a motorcycle) starts from $O$ at $t = 0\text{ s}$ and moves along the same track with variable acceleration. The displacement of $Q$ from $O$ is given by $x_Q(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct$. Initially ($t = 0\text{ s}$), $Q$ has the same velocity and acceleration as $P$ has initially. $Q$ reaches the timing gate $A$ when $t = 4\text{ s}$. Find the velocity of $Q$ at $A$.
steps:
(i) (a) Show initial velocity is $-2\text{ m s}^{-1}$:

Using $s = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ with $s = 24\text{ m}$, $t = 6\text{ s}$, and $v = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$:\begin{aligned} &24 = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + 10)(6) \cr &24 = 3(u + 10) \cr &8 = u + 10 \cr &u = -2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}(i) (b) Find acceleration of $P$:

Using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} &10 = -2 + 6a \cr &12 = 6a \cr &a = 2\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Show car $P$ never reaches $B$:

At marker $B$, $s = -3\text{ m}$. Using $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} &-3 = -2t + t^2 \cr &t^2 - 2t + 3 = 0 \end{aligned}Check discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$:\begin{aligned} &\Delta \cr &\quad = (-2)^2 - 4(1)(3) \cr &\quad = 4 - 12 \cr &\quad = -8 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta < 0$, no real solutions for $t$ exist. Therefore, $P$ never reaches $B$.

(iii) Find velocity of $Q$ at $A$:

Differentiate $x_Q(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(t) = 3at^2 + 2bt + c \cr &a_Q(t) = 6at + 2b \end{aligned}Match initial conditions with $P$ at $t = 0\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &c = -2 \cr &2b = 2 \cr &b = 1 \end{aligned}So $x_Q(t) = at^3 + t^2 - 2t$. At $A$ ($t = 4\text{ s}$, $x_Q = 24\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &24 = a(4)^3 + 4^2 - 2(4) \cr &24 = 64a + 16 - 8 \cr &24 = 64a + 8 \cr &16 = 64a \cr &a = 0.25 \end{aligned}

Velocity equation for $Q$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(t) \cr &\quad = 3(0.25)t^2 + 2(1)t - 2 \cr &\quad = 0.75t^2 + 2t - 2 \end{aligned}At $t = 4\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(4) \cr &\quad = 0.75(4)^2 + 2(4) - 2 \cr &\quad = 0.75(16) + 8 - 2 \cr &\quad = 12 + 6 \cr &\quad = 18\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $a = 2\text{ m s}^{-2}, \text{velocity} = 18\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: The constant acceleration is correct, but a velocity of $14\text{ m s}^{-1}$ occurs if you incorrectly calculate $b = 0.5$ (by setting $2b = 2$, which gives $b = 1$, not $0.5$).

This error occurs if you make an arithmetic slip when calculating the constant acceleration of $P$ (using $a = 1.5$ instead of $2$), but calculate the motorcycle's velocity correctly with your values.
The constant acceleration is correct, but a velocity of $22\text{ m s}^{-1}$ represents a sign slip when evaluating $v_Q(4) = 0.75(16) + 8 - 2$, perhaps by adding the $2$ instead of subtracting it.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Turning Point of the Motion
bradley_insight.content: Since the car starts with a negative velocity ($u = -2\text{ m s}^{-1}$) and accelerates forward ($a = 2\text{ m s}^{-2}$), it must stop and change direction. The turning point occurs when velocity $v_P = 0$, giving $-2 + 2t = 0$, so $t = 1\text{ s}$. The minimum position of the car is $s(1) = -1\text{ m}$ (from $-2(1) + 1^2$). Since marker $B$ is at $s = -3\text{ m}$, the car turns back to the right before it ever reaches $B$.

question:
A particle $P$ moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. At time $t = 0\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the origin $O$. After $t = 10\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the point $A$, where $OA = 40\text{ m}$ in the positive direction. The velocity of $P$ at $A$ is $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in the direction $OA$.

Therefore, $P$ never reaches $B$.

question:
A particle $P$ moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. At time $t = 0\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the origin $O$. After $t = 6\text{ s}$, $P$ is at the point $A$, where $OA = 36\text{ m}$ in the positive direction. The velocity of $P$ at $A$ is $14\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in the direction $OA$.

(i) (a) Show that the initial speed of $P$ is $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(i) (b) Find the acceleration of $P$.

(ii) $B$ is a point on the line such that $OB = 3\text{ m}$ to the left of $O$. Show that $P$ is never at point $B$.

(iii) A second particle $Q$ starts from $O$ at $t = 0\text{ s}$ and moves along the same track with variable acceleration $a_Q(t) = 12kt + \dfrac{8}{3}$, where $k$ is a constant. Initially ($t = 0\text{ s}$), $Q$ has the same velocity as $P$ has initially. $Q$ reaches $A$ when $t = 3\text{ s}$. Find the velocity of $Q$ at $A$.
steps:
(i) (a) Show initial speed is $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$:

Using $s = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ with $s = 36\text{ m}$, $t = 6\text{ s}$, and $v = 14\text{ m s}^{-1}$:\begin{aligned} &36 = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + 14)(6) \cr &36 = 3(u + 14) \cr &12 = u + 14 \cr &u = -2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Initial speed is $|u| = 2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(i) (b) Find acceleration of $P$:

Using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} &14 = -2 + 6a \cr &16 = 6a \cr &a \cr &\quad = \dfrac{16}{6} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{8}{3}\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Show $P$ is never at $B$:

At point $B$, $s = -3\text{ m}$. Using $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} &-3 = -2t + \dfrac{4}{3}t^2 \cr &\dfrac{4}{3}t^2 - 2t + 3 = 0 \cr &4t^2 - 6t + 9 = 0 \end{aligned}Check discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$:\begin{aligned} &\Delta \cr &\quad = (-6)^2 - 4(4)(9) \cr &\quad = 36 - 144 \cr &\quad = -108 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta < 0$, no real solutions for $t$ exist. Therefore, $P$ is never at $B$.

(iii) Find velocity of $Q$ at $A$:

Integrate $a_Q(t) = 12kt + \dfrac{8}{3}$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(t) \cr &\quad = \int \big(12kt + \dfrac{8}{3}\big)\text{d}t \cr &\quad = 6kt^2 + \dfrac{8}{3}t + C \end{aligned}Since $v_Q(0) = -2$, $C = -2$.

Integrate again for displacement $x_Q(t)$:\begin{aligned} &x_Q(t) \cr &\quad = \int \big(6kt^2 + \dfrac{8}{3}t - 2\big)\text{d}t \cr &\quad = 2kt^3 + \dfrac{4}{3}t^2 - 2t + D \end{aligned}Since $x_Q(0) = 0$, $D = 0$.

At $A$ ($t = 3\text{ s}$, $x_Q = 36\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &36 = 2k(3)^3 + \dfrac{4}{3}(3)^2 - 2(3) \cr &36 = 54k + 12 - 6 \cr &36 = 54k + 6 \cr &30 = 54k \cr &k \cr &\quad = \dfrac{30}{54} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5}{9} \end{aligned}Substitute $k = \dfrac{5}{9}$ into $v_Q(t)$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(t) \cr &\quad = 6\big(\dfrac{5}{9}\big)t^2 + \dfrac{8}{3}t - 2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{10}{3}t^2 + \dfrac{8}{3}t - 2 \end{aligned}At $t = 3\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &v_Q(3) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{10}{3}(3)^2 + \dfrac{8}{3}(3) - 2 \cr &\quad = 30 + 8 - 2 \cr &\quad = 36\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $a = \dfrac{8}{3}\text{ m s}^{-2}, \text{velocity} = 36\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: The constant acceleration is correct, but a velocity of $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$ represents a sign slip when evaluating $v_Q(3) = 30 + 8 - 2$, perhaps by subtracting $8$ instead of adding it.

The constant acceleration is correct, but a velocity of $22\text{ m s}^{-1}$ occurs if you fail to integrate correctly, perhaps by setting $v_Q(t) = 12kt^2 + \frac{8}{3}t - 2$ (failing to divide the first term by $2$).

This error occurs if you make an arithmetic slip when calculating the constant acceleration of $P$ (obtaining $2.4$ instead of $\frac{8}{3}$), although the calculus and velocity calculations for $Q$ are carried out correctly.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Rationalizing Fractions
bradley_insight.content: When dealing with fractional accelerations (such as $a = \dfrac{8}{3}\text{ m s}^{-2}$), avoid rounding to decimals like $2.67\text{ m s}^{-2}$ early in your working. Keeping terms in exact fractional form prevents rounding propagation errors and ensures that subsequent integrations and constants resolve to beautifully clean, exact integer results (like $k = \dfrac{5}{9}$ and $v_Q(3) = 36\text{ m s}^{-1}$).

question:
In this question, the unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are directed horizontally due east and vertically upwards respectively.

A particle $P$ of mass $5\text{ kg}$ is initially at rest at the point with position vector $(3\mathbf{i} + 40\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$ relative to a fixed origin $O$. The particle moves under the action of its weight (taking $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$) and two constant applied forces:$$\mathbf{F}_1 = (18\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_2 = (-8\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$(a) Find the acceleration vector of the particle.

(b) Find the position vector of the particle at time $t = 6\text{ s}$.

(c) Find the speed of the particle at the instant it reaches the horizontal level of the origin.
steps:
(a) Find the acceleration vector:

The weight acts vertically downwards ($W = mg$):\begin{aligned} \mathbf{W} &= -5(9.8)\mathbf{j} \cr &= -49\mathbf{j}\text{ N} \end{aligned}Sum all forces acting on $P$:\begin{aligned} \Sigma\mathbf{F} &= \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{W} \cr &= (18 - 8)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (-6 + 10 - 49)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (10\mathbf{i} - 45\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}Using $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ with $m = 5\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= \dfrac{10\mathbf{i} - 45\mathbf{j}}{5} \cr &= (2\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find position vector at $t = 6\text{ s}$:

Using $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}(6) &= (3\mathbf{i} + 40\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{1}{2}(2\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j})(6^2) \cr &= (3\mathbf{i} + 40\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + 18(2\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (3 + 36)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (40 - 162)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (39\mathbf{i} - 122\mathbf{j})\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Find speed at horizontal level of the origin:

The particle reaches the level of the origin when the vertical displacement is zero ($y = 0$):\begin{aligned} &40 - 4.5t^2 = 0 \cr &4.5t^2 = 40 \cr &t^2 = \dfrac{80}{9} \cr &t = \dfrac{\sqrt{80}}{3}\text{ s} \end{aligned}The velocity vector at this time is $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{a}t$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v} &= t(2\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j}) \end{aligned}Calculate speed $|\mathbf{v}|$:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{v}| &= t\sqrt{2^2 + (-9)^2} \cr &= \dfrac{\sqrt{80}}{3}\sqrt{85} \cr &= \dfrac{\sqrt{6800}}{3} \cr &= \dfrac{20\sqrt{17}}{3} \cr &\approx 27.5\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $(2\mathbf{i} - 9\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $(39\mathbf{i} - 122\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$, (c) $27.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you forget to include the weight of the particle ($-mg\mathbf{j}$) when resolving vertical forces. Always include gravity when motion takes place in a vertical plane.
This speed error occurs if you only evaluate the vertical velocity component ($v_y$) instead of finding the full magnitude $\sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$ using both components.
This acceleration error arises from subtracting $54$ instead of $49$ when combining vertical force components. Ensure you compute $mg = 5(9.8) = 49\text{ N}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Vertical Planes and Weight
bradley_insight.content: When a question specifies that unit vector $\mathbf{j}$ is directed 'vertically upwards', gravity acts in the negative $\mathbf{j}$ direction as $-mg\mathbf{j}$. Forgetting to include this weight vector in the resultant force $\Sigma\mathbf{F}$ is one of the most common pitfalls in 2D mechanics.

question:
In this question, the unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are directed horizontally due east and vertically upwards respectively.

A small drone of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is launched from the origin $O$ with an initial velocity $\mathbf{u} = (4\mathbf{i} + 25\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The drone moves under the action of gravity (taking $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$) and a constant engine thrust force $\mathbf{F} = (6\mathbf{i} + 9.6\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$.

(a) Show that the acceleration vector of the drone is $(3\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(b) Find the time $T$ seconds at which the drone is momentarily travelling in a purely horizontal direction.

(c) Find the position vector of the drone at time $t = T\text{ s}$.

(d) Calculate the bearing on which the drone is travelling at time $t = 7\text{ s}$, giving your answer to the nearest degree.
steps:
(a) Show acceleration is $(3\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$:

The forces acting on the drone are thrust $\mathbf{F}$ and weight $\mathbf{W} = -mg\mathbf{j}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{W} &= -2(9.8)\mathbf{j} \cr &= -19.6\mathbf{j}\text{ N} \end{aligned}Sum of forces:\begin{aligned} \Sigma\mathbf{F} &= (6\mathbf{i} + 9.6\mathbf{j}) - 19.6\mathbf{j} \cr &= (6\mathbf{i} - 10\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}Using $\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\Sigma\mathbf{F}}{m}$ with $m = 2\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= \dfrac{6\mathbf{i} - 10\mathbf{j}}{2} \cr &= (3\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find time $T$ when travelling horizontally:

Purely horizontal motion requires vertical velocity $v_y = 0$:\begin{aligned} &25 - 5T = 0 \cr &5T = 25 \cr &T = 5\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Find position vector at $t = 5\text{ s}$:

Using $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $t = 5\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}(5) &= (4\mathbf{i} + 25\mathbf{j})(5) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{1}{2}(3\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})(5^2) \cr &= (20\mathbf{i} + 125\mathbf{j}) \cr &\qquad + 12.5(3\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (20 + 37.5)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (125 - 62.5)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (57.5\mathbf{i} + 62.5\mathbf{j})\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Calculate bearing at $t = 7\text{ s}$:

Find the velocity vector at $t = 7\text{ s}$ using $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}(7) &= (4\mathbf{i} + 25\mathbf{j}) + 7(3\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (4 + 21)\mathbf{i} + (25 - 35)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (25\mathbf{i} - 10\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}The velocity vector has positive East component ($25$) and negative North component (South component $10$).

Find angle $\alpha$ East of South:\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \dfrac{25}{10} \cr &= 2.5 \cr \alpha &= \arctan(2.5) \cr &\approx 68.2^{\circ} \end{aligned}Calculate bearing clockwise from North:\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 180^{\circ} - 68.2^{\circ} \cr &= 111.8^{\circ} \cr &\approx 112^{\circ} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $T = 5\text{ s}$, (c) $(57.5\mathbf{i} + 62.5\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$, (d) $112^{\circ}$

pi_options.feedback: This bearing error occurs if you measure the angle directly from North rather than identifying that the velocity vector points into the south-east quadrant (East $25$, South $10$).

This time error occurs if you set the horizontal velocity component to zero ($4 - 3t = 0$) instead of the vertical component ($25 - 5t = 0$). Purely horizontal motion means the vertical velocity is zero.
This position vector is missing the acceleration displacement term $\dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$, calculating only the linear motion $\mathbf{u}t$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Bearings from Vector Components
bradley_insight.content: Always sketch the velocity components before calculating a bearing. With velocity $\mathbf{v} = 25\mathbf{i} - 10\mathbf{j}$, the motion is East and South (4th quadrant). Calculating $\arctan(25/10) \approx 68.2^{\circ}$ gives the angle measured East from the South axis, meaning the true bearing from North is $180^{\circ} - 68.2^{\circ} = 111.8^{\circ} \approx 112^{\circ}$.

question:
In this question, the horizontal unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are directed due east and due north respectively.

A sledge of mass $8\text{ kg}$ moves on a smooth horizontal sheet of ice. The sledge is acted on by three horizontal forces:$$\mathbf{F}_1 = (p\mathbf{i} + 14\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_2 = (6\mathbf{i} + q\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_3 = (-2\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$where $p$ and $q$ are constants.

The resultant force acting on the sledge causes it to accelerate from rest in the direction of the vector $3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$ with an acceleration of magnitude $2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the resultant force vector acting on the sledge.

(b) Hence, determine the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.

(c) Find the exact distance travelled by the sledge during the first $6\text{ seconds}$ of motion.
steps:
(a) Find the resultant force vector:

Find the unit vector in the direction of $3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$:\begin{aligned} |3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}| &= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} \cr &= 5 \cr \hat{\mathbf{a}} &= \dfrac{3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}}{5} \cr &= 0.6\mathbf{i} + 0.8\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Acceleration vector has magnitude $2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= 2.5(0.6\mathbf{i} + 0.8\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (1.5\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}Resultant force $\mathbf{R} = m\mathbf{a}$ with $m = 8\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R} &= 8(1.5\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (12\mathbf{i} + 16\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Determine the values of $p$ and $q$:

Sum the three applied forces:\begin{aligned} \Sigma\mathbf{F} &= \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 \cr &= (p + 6 - 2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (14 + q - 5)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (p + 4)\mathbf{i} + (q + 9)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Equate components to resultant $\mathbf{R} = 12\mathbf{i} + 16\mathbf{j}$:\begin{aligned} &p + 4 = 12 \cr &p = 8 \end{aligned}For vertical components:\begin{aligned} &q + 9 = 16 \cr &q = 7 \end{aligned}

(c) Find the distance travelled in $6\text{ s}$:

Since the sledge accelerates from rest ($u = 0$) with constant acceleration magnitude $a = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} s &= ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 \cr &= 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}(2.5)(6^2) \cr &= 1.25 \times 36 \cr &= 45\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $(12\mathbf{i} + 16\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$, (b) $p = 8, q = 7$, (c) $45\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make an algebraic sign slip when combining the component forces, adding rather than subtracting the components of $\mathbf{F}_3 = -2\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j}$.
This mistake occurs if you forget to multiply the acceleration vector by the mass ($m = 8\text{ kg}$), equating the force vector directly to the acceleration vector.
This distance error arises from omitting the factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in the SUVAT distance formula, calculating $at^2$ instead of $\dfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Direction Vectors and Unit Scaling
bradley_insight.content: When given a direction as an un-normalized vector like $3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$ along with a magnitude ($2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$), you must convert the direction vector into a unit vector first by dividing by its magnitude ($\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$). Multiplying the magnitude directly by the raw direction vector would scale your acceleration by a factor of 5.

question:
A particle of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ moves in a horizontal plane. At time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$), the particle is acted upon by a single resultant horizontal force $\mathbf{F}\text{ N}$ given by:$$\mathbf{F} = (6t - 4)\mathbf{i} + (12 - 9t^2)\mathbf{j}$$At time $t = 0$, the particle has velocity $\mathbf{u} = (2\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and is located at the origin $O$.

(a) Find the acceleration vector of the particle at time $t$ seconds.

(b) Find an expression for the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}\text{ m s}^{-1}$ of the particle at time $t$ seconds.

(c) Find the kinetic energy of the particle at the instant $t = 2\text{ s}$.

(d) Find the position vector of the particle when $t = 3\text{ s}$.
steps:
(a) Find the acceleration vector:

Using Newton's second law $\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\mathbf{F}}{m}$ with $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a}(t) &= \dfrac{(6t - 4)\mathbf{i} + (12 - 9t^2)\mathbf{j}}{0.5} \cr &= (12t - 8)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (24 - 18t^2)\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}(t)$:

Integrate acceleration with respect to time $t$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}(t) &= \int \mathbf{a}\text{d}t \cr &= (6t^2 - 8t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (24t - 6t^3)\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C} \end{aligned}Since $\mathbf{v}(0) = 2\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j}$, we have $\mathbf{C} = 2\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}(t) &= (6t^2 - 8t + 2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (24t - 6t^3 - 6)\mathbf{j}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Find kinetic energy at $t = 2\text{ s}$:

Evaluate velocity at $t = 2\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}(2) &= (6(2^2) - 8(2) + 2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (24(2) - 6(2^3) - 6)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (10\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Calculate speed squared $v^2$:\begin{aligned} v^2 &= 10^2 + (-6)^2 \cr &= 100 + 36 \cr &= 136 \end{aligned}Calculate kinetic energy ($\text{KE} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$):\begin{aligned} \text{KE} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(0.5)(136) \cr &= 34\text{ J} \end{aligned}

(d) Find position vector at $t = 3\text{ s}$:

Integrate velocity to find position $\mathbf{r}(t)$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}(t) &= \int \mathbf{v}\text{d}t \cr &= (2t^3 - 4t^2 + 2t)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (12t^2 - 1.5t^4 - 6t)\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{D} \end{aligned}Since $P$ starts at the origin $O$, $\mathbf{r}(0) = \mathbf{0}$, giving $\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{0}$.

At $t = 3\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}(3) &= (2(27) - 4(9) + 2(3))\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (12(9) - 1.5(81) - 6(3))\mathbf{j} \cr &= (54 - 36 + 6)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (108 - 121.5 - 18)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (24\mathbf{i} - 31.5\mathbf{j})\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $(12t - 8)\mathbf{i} + (24 - 18t^2)\mathbf{j}$, (b) $(6t^2 - 8t + 2)\mathbf{i} + (24t - 6t^3 - 6)\mathbf{j}$, (c) $34\text{ J}$, (d) $(24\mathbf{i} - 31.5\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This kinetic energy error occurs if you forget the factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in $\text{KE} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, calculating $mv^2$ instead.

This error occurs if you multiply by the mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ instead of dividing by it when calculating acceleration from force, using $\mathbf{a} = m\mathbf{F}$ instead of $\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\mathbf{F}}{m}$.
This occurs if you omit the constant of integration $\mathbf{u} = 2\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j}$ when integrating acceleration to find velocity, neglecting the initial velocity condition at $t = 0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Tracking Constants of Integration
bradley_insight.content: When integrating vector acceleration $\mathbf{a}(t)$ to find velocity, never omit the constant vector $\mathbf{C}$. The initial velocity condition at $t = 0$ provides this constant: $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{u} = 2\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j}$. Dropping this term will propagate errors into both the kinetic energy and displacement evaluations.

question:
In this question, the horizontal unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ represent displacements of $1\text{ m}$ due east and $1\text{ m}$ due north respectively.

Two radio-controlled cars, $A$ and $B$, move on a flat horizontal playground:

• Car $A$ has a mass of $2\text{ kg}$ and starts from the point with position vector $(15\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$ at $t = 0$. It moves with a constant velocity $(2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

• Car $B$ has a mass of $3\text{ kg}$ and starts from rest at the origin $O$ at $t = 0$. It is propelled by a constant horizontal resultant force $\mathbf{F} = (6\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$.

(a) Show that the acceleration vector of car $B$ is $(2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(b) Find expressions for the position vectors $\mathbf{r}_A$ and $\mathbf{r}_B$ of each car at time $t$ seconds.

(c) Show that the displacement vector from $B$ to $A$ at time $t$ seconds is:$$\mathbf{r}_{BA} = (15 + 2t - t^2)\mathbf{i} + (5 + 4t - t^2)\mathbf{j}$$(d) Show that the two cars collide, and find the coordinates of the collision point.
steps:
(a) Show acceleration of $B$ is $(2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$:

Using $\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\mathbf{F}}{m}$ with $\mathbf{F} = 6\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}$ and $m = 3\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a}_B &= \dfrac{6\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}}{3} \cr &= (2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Find position vectors $\mathbf{r}_A$ and $\mathbf{r}_B$:

Car $A$ moves with constant velocity from $(15\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}_A &= (15\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}) + t(2\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (15 + 2t)\mathbf{i} + (5 + 4t)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Car $B$ starts from rest at the origin with constant acceleration:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}_B &= \dfrac{1}{2}(2\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})t^2 \cr &= t^2\mathbf{i} + t^2\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(c) Show displacement vector $\mathbf{r}_{BA}$:

Displacement from $B$ to $A$ is $\mathbf{r}_A - \mathbf{r}_B$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}_{BA} &= \mathbf{r}_A - \mathbf{r}_B \cr &= \big[(15 + 2t)\mathbf{i} + (5 + 4t)\mathbf{j}\big] \cr &\qquad - (t^2\mathbf{i} + t^2\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (15 + 2t - t^2)\mathbf{i} \cr &\qquad + (5 + 4t - t^2)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(d) Show cars collide and find collision coordinates:

A collision occurs when $\mathbf{r}_{BA} = \mathbf{0}$, meaning both components are simultaneously zero.

For the horizontal component:\begin{aligned} &15 + 2t - t^2 = 0 \cr &t^2 - 2t - 15 = 0 \cr &(t - 5)(t + 3) = 0 \end{aligned}Since $t \ge 0$, the valid root is $t = 5\text{ s}$.

For the vertical component:\begin{aligned} &5 + 4t - t^2 = 0 \cr &t^2 - 4t - 5 = 0 \cr &(t - 5)(t + 1) = 0 \end{aligned}Since $t \ge 0$, the valid root is $t = 5\text{ s}$.

Since $t = 5\text{ s}$ satisfies both equations simultaneously, the cars collide at $t = 5\text{ s}$.

Find collision coordinates at $t = 5\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}(5) &= 5^2\mathbf{i} + 5^2\mathbf{j} \cr &= (25\mathbf{i} + 25\mathbf{j})\text{ m} \end{aligned}The coordinates of the collision point are $(25, 25)$.
Final Answer: (d) $t = 5\text{ s}$, coordinates $(25, 25)$

pi_options.feedback: This coordinates error arises if you evaluate the position vector of Car $A$ using the wrong initial position or miscalculating $15 + 2(5) = 25$ as $20$.
This occurs if you take the extraneous root from the horizontal equation ($t = -3$) and treat it as positive $3\text{ s}$, which does not satisfy the vertical position equation.
This mistake occurs if you take the negative root from the vertical quadratic factor $(t + 1)$ and treat it as $t = 1\text{ s}$, where the positions of the two cars are not equal.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: True Collisions Require Simultaneous Equivalence
bradley_insight.content: To prove that two moving bodies collide in 2D, finding a value of $t$ that makes the horizontal distance zero is not enough. You must show that the exact same value of $t$ also reduces the vertical separation to zero simultaneously. If they match at different times, their paths cross, but they do not collide.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform wooden plank $AB$ of weight $120\text{ N}$ and length $6\text{ m}$. The plank rests horizontally in equilibrium on two smooth supports at $C$ and $D$, where $AC = x\text{ m}$ and $CD = 1.5\text{ m}$. The support at $C$ lies between $A$ and the centre of the plank, and the support at $D$ lies between the centre of the plank and $B$.

The magnitude of the normal reaction exerted by the support on the plank at $C$ is $80\text{ N}$.

The plank is modelled as a uniform rigid rod.

(a) Find the magnitude of the normal reaction exerted by the support on the plank at $D$.

(b) Find the value of $x$.

A concrete block, modelled as a particle, is now placed on the plank at end $B$. The plank is on the point of tilting about $D$.

(c) Calculate the weight of the concrete block.

(d)(i) State one assumption made when modelling the concrete block as a particle.
(ii) Explain how this assumption was used in your calculation in part (c).
steps:
(a) Reaction at $D$:

Since the plank is in vertical equilibrium, the sum of the upward normal reactions equals the total downward weight:\begin{aligned} &R_C + R_D = 120 \cr &80 + R_D = 120 \cr &R_D = 40\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Finding the distance $x$:

The plank is uniform, so its weight of $120\text{ N}$ acts at its midpoint, $3\text{ m}$ from $A$.

Support $C$ is at distance $x$ from $A$, and support $D$ is at distance $(x + 1.5)\text{ m}$ from $A$.

Taking moments about $A$:\begin{aligned} &R_C(x) + R_D(x + 1.5) = 120(3) \cr &80x + 40(x + 1.5) = 360 \cr &80x + 40x + 60 = 360 \cr &120x + 60 = 360 \cr &120x = 300 \cr &x = 2.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Tilting about support $D$:

When the plank is on the point of tilting about $D$, it begins to lift off support $C$. Therefore, the normal reaction at $C$ is zero:\begin{aligned} R_C = 0\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Support $D$ is at distance $x + 1.5 = 2.5 + 1.5 = 4\text{ m}$ from $A$.

The distance from $D$ to the midpoint is:\begin{aligned} 4 - 3 = 1\text{ m} \end{aligned}

The distance from $D$ to end $B$ is:\begin{aligned} 6 - 4 = 2\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Taking moments about $D$ for rotational equilibrium:\begin{aligned} &120(1) = W_{\text{block}}(2) \cr &2W_{\text{block}} = 120 \cr &W_{\text{block}} = 60\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(d) Modelling assumption and application:

(i) Modelling the concrete block as a particle assumes that its dimensions are negligible and that its entire weight acts at a single point exactly at end $B$.

(ii) In the calculation in part (c), this allowed the perpendicular distance from the pivot $D$ to the line of action of the block's weight to be taken as exactly $6 - 4 = 2\text{ m}$.
Final Answer: (a) $40\text{ N}$, (b) $x = 2.5$, (c) $60\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect value for $x$. Check the moment equation about $A$; remember that support $D$ is at $(x + 1.5)\text{ m}$ from $A$, so $40(x + 1.5)$ expands to $40x + 60$.
Incorrect weight for the block. In part (c), the pivot is at $D$ ($4\text{ m}$ from $A$). The distance to the midpoint is $1\text{ m}$ and the distance to $B$ is $2\text{ m}$, giving $2W = 120(1)$.
Incorrect reaction at $D$. Total weight is $120\text{ N}$, so $R_D = 120 - 80 = 40\text{ N}$, not $80\text{ N}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Identifying the Tilting Pivot
bradley_insight.content: When a rigid body is on the point of tilting about a support, always immediately set the reaction at every other support to zero. A common exam error is continuing to include $R_C = 80\text{ N}$ in the moment equation for part (c), which causes an algebraic contradiction. Also, remember that modelling a mass as a particle means its weight acts at a single point, fixing the moment arm without having to consider the block's width.

question:
The diagram shows a non-uniform metal girder $AB$ of length $6\text{ m}$ and weight $W\text{ N}$. The girder rests horizontally in equilibrium on two smooth supports at $C$ and $D$, where $AC = 1\text{ m}$ and $DB = 1\text{ m}$.

When a vertical load of $90\text{ N}$ is suspended from end $A$, the girder is on the point of tilting about $C$.

When instead the load of $90\text{ N}$ is removed and a vertical load of $150\text{ N}$ is suspended from end $B$, the girder is on the point of tilting about $D$.

The girder is modelled as a rigid rod.

(a) Find the weight $W$ of the girder.

(b) Find the distance of the centre of mass of the girder from end $A$.

(c) When no additional loads are attached, find the magnitude of the normal reaction exerted by support $C$ on the girder.
steps:
(a) & (b) Setting up dual tilting equations:

Let the centre of mass of the girder be at distance $\bar{x}\text{ m}$ from $A$.

The supports are located at $C$ ($1\text{ m}$ from $A$) and $D$ ($6 - 1 = 5\text{ m}$ from $A$).

Condition 1: When $90\text{ N}$ is at $A$, the girder tilts about $C$, so $R_D = 0$. Taking moments about $C$:\begin{aligned} &90(1) = W(\bar{x} - 1) \cr &W\bar{x} - W = 90 \quad \text{--- [Eq 1]} \end{aligned}

Condition 2 and solving simultaneously:

When $150\text{ N}$ is at $B$, the girder tilts about $D$, so $R_C = 0$. Taking moments about $D$:\begin{aligned} &W(5 - \bar{x}) = 150(1) \cr &5W - W\bar{x} = 150 \quad \text{--- [Eq 2]} \end{aligned}

Adding [Eq 1] and [Eq 2] eliminates the non-linear product $W\bar{x}$:\begin{aligned} &(W\bar{x} - W) + (5W - W\bar{x}) \cr &\qquad = 90 + 150 \cr &4W = 240 \cr &W = 60\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Substituting $W = 60$ into [Eq 1]:\begin{aligned} &60(\bar{x} - 1) = 90 \cr &\bar{x} - 1 = 1.5 \cr &\bar{x} = 2.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Reaction at $C$ with no additional loads:

With no extra loads, the girder of weight $60\text{ N}$ acts at $\bar{x} = 2.5\text{ m}$.

Taking moments about $D$ ($5\text{ m}$ from $A$):\begin{aligned} &R_C(5 - 1) = W(5 - 2.5) \cr &4R_C = 60(2.5) \cr &4R_C = 150 \cr &R_C = 37.5\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $60\text{ N}$, (b) $2.5\text{ m}$, (c) $37.5\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect centre of mass. You have assumed the girder is uniform with centre of mass at $3.0\text{ m}$, but the question explicitly states it is non-uniform.
Incorrect girder weight. Check the elimination step when adding the two moment equations: $5W - W = 4W$, giving $4W = 240 \implies W = 60\text{ N}$.

Incorrect centre of mass position. $\bar{x} = 3.5\text{ m}$ would mean the centre of mass is closer to $B$ than $A$, but the smaller tipping force at $A$ ($90\text{ N}$ vs $150\text{ N}$) indicates it must lie closer to $A$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Eliminating Non-Linear Products
bradley_insight.content: In non-uniform beam problems with unknown weight $W$ and unknown centre of mass $\bar{x}$, the moment equations contain the product $W\bar{x}$. Rather than dividing equations or substituting messy fractions, notice that taking moments about the two supports yields $+W\bar{x}$ in one equation and $-W\bar{x}$ in the other. Adding the two equations immediately eliminates the product term, giving $W$ directly in one clean step.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform scaffolding plank $AB$ of mass $50\text{ kg}$ and length $10\text{ m}$. The plank rests horizontally on two smooth trestles at $C$ and $D$, where $AC = 2\text{ m}$ and $DB = 3\text{ m}$.

A construction worker of mass $80\text{ kg}$ stands on the plank at a distance of $x\text{ metres}$ from end $A$. The plank is modelled as a uniform rigid rod and the worker is modelled as a particle.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the normal reaction at each trestle when the worker stands at the midpoint of the plank.

(b) Find the minimum distance from $A$ to which the worker can walk towards end $A$ without the plank tilting.

(c) Find the maximum distance from $A$ to which the worker can walk towards end $B$ without the plank tilting.

(d) Hence state the complete range of values of $x$ for which the plank remains in horizontal equilibrium.
steps:
(a) Worker at the midpoint ($x = 5\text{ m}$):

The weight of the plank acts at its midpoint, $5\text{ m}$ from $A$. When the worker is also at $x = 5\text{ m}$, both weights act at the same point:

Total downward weight:\begin{aligned} W_{\text{tot}} &= (50 + 80)g \cr &= 130(9.8) \cr &= 1274\text{ N} \end{aligned}

The distance between the trestles is $CD = (10 - 3) - 2 = 5\text{ m}$.

Taking moments about $C$:\begin{aligned} &R_D(5) = 1274(5 - 2) \cr &5R_D = 1274(3) \cr &5R_D = 3822 \cr &R_D = 764.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Resolving vertically:\begin{aligned} R_C &= 1274 - 764.4 \cr &= 509.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}

To 3 significant figures, $R_C = 510\text{ N}$ and $R_D = 764\text{ N}$.

(b) Tilting about trestle $C$:

As the worker walks towards end $A$ ($x < 2$), the plank tends to tilt about $C$, so $R_D = 0$.

Taking moments about $C$:\begin{aligned} &80g(2 - x) = 50g(5 - 2) \cr &80(2 - x) = 50(3) \cr &80(2 - x) = 150 \cr &2 - x = 1.875 \cr &x = 0.125\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Tilting about trestle $D$:

As the worker walks past trestle $D$ towards end $B$ ($x > 7$), the plank tends to tilt about $D$, so $R_C = 0$.

Taking moments about $D$ ($7\text{ m}$ from $A$):\begin{aligned} &80g(x - 7) = 50g(7 - 5) \cr &80(x - 7) = 50(2) \cr &80(x - 7) = 100 \cr &x - 7 = 1.25 \cr &x = 8.25\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Range of equilibrium:

For the plank to remain in horizontal equilibrium without tilting about either support, $x$ must satisfy:\begin{aligned} 0.125 \le x \le 8.25 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $R_C = 510\text{ N}, R_D = 764\text{ N}$, (b) $0.125\text{ m}$, (c) $8.25\text{ m}$, (d) $0.125 \le x \le 8.25$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect reactions in part (a). The midpoint ($5\text{ m}$) is closer to $D$ ($7\text{ m}$) than to $C$ ($2\text{ m}$), so the reaction at $D$ must be larger than at $C$ ($R_D = 764\text{ N}, R_C = 510\text{ N}$).

Incorrect limits of motion. In parts (b) and (c), remember that the midpoint of the plank is at $5\text{ m}$, so the distance from $C$ to the centre is $3\text{ m}$ (giving moment $150g$) and from $D$ to the centre is $2\text{ m}$ (giving moment $100g$).
Incorrect range of equilibrium. The worker cannot walk the entire length of the plank ($0 \le x \le 10$) without it tilting because of the overhangs beyond both trestles.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dividing Through by Gravity
bradley_insight.content: Notice that in parts (b) and (c), the factor of $g$ appears on both sides of the moment equations. Always divide through by $g$ immediately rather than multiplying out $80 \times 9.8 = 784$ and $50 \times 9.8 = 490$. This keeps the arithmetic simple, exact, and completely free from premature rounding errors.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform steel girder $AB$ of length $6\text{ m}$ and mass $120\text{ kg}$. The girder is suspended horizontally by two vertical, light, inextensible cables. One cable is attached to the girder at end $A$ and the second cable is attached at a point $C$, where $AC = 4\text{ m}$.

A machine of mass $M\text{ kg}$, modelled as a particle, is placed on the girder at end $B$.

Each cable has a maximum safe working tension of $1800\text{ N}$ without snapping. The cables cannot support compressive forces (they become slack if tension reaches zero).

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) When $M = 0$, calculate the tension in the cable at $A$ and the tension in the cable at $C$.

(b) Find the tension in the cable at $C$ at the instant when the cable at $A$ becomes slack.

(c) Determine the greatest mass $M$ that can be placed at $B$ such that the girder remains in horizontal equilibrium with neither cable breaking nor becoming slack.
steps:
(a) Tensions when $M = 0$:

Weight of the girder acts at its midpoint ($3\text{ m}$ from $A$):\begin{aligned} W &= 120(9.8) \cr &= 1176\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Taking moments about $A$:\begin{aligned} &T_C(4) = 1176(3) \cr &4T_C = 3528 \cr &T_C = 882\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Resolving vertically:\begin{aligned} T_A &= 1176 - 882 \cr &= 294\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Tension in cable $C$ when cable $A$ is slack:

When cable $A$ becomes slack, $T_A = 0\text{ N}$. The girder is on the point of tilting about $C$.

Taking moments about $C$:\begin{aligned} &120g(4 - 3) = Mg(6 - 4) \cr &120(1) = 2M \cr &M = 60\text{ kg} \end{aligned}

Resolving vertically to find $T_C$ at this instant:\begin{aligned} T_C &= (120 + M)g \cr &= (120 + 60)(9.8) \cr &= 180(9.8) \cr &= 1764\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Greatest safe mass $M$:

There are two physical constraints on the system:

1. Breaking constraint: Cable $C$ snaps if $T_C > 1800\text{ N}$:\begin{aligned} &(120 + M)(9.8) \le 1800 \cr &120 + M \le 183.67 \cr &M \le 63.7\text{ kg} \end{aligned}

2. Slackness constraint: Cable $A$ goes slack if $T_A < 0\text{ N}$, causing the girder to tilt:\begin{aligned} M \le 60\text{ kg} \end{aligned}

At $M = 60\text{ kg}$, $T_C = 1764\text{ N} < 1800\text{ N}$, so cable $C$ has not snapped. If $M > 60\text{ kg}$, cable $A$ goes slack and equilibrium is broken before cable $C$ reaches its $1800\text{ N}$ limit.

Therefore, the greatest allowable mass is $M = 60\text{ kg}$.
Final Answer: (a) $T_A = 294\text{ N}, T_C = 882\text{ N}$, (b) $1764\text{ N}$, (c) $60\text{ kg}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect limiting factor in part (c). Equating $T_C = 1800\text{ N}$ gives $M = 63.7\text{ kg}$, but at that mass $T_A$ would be negative. Cable $A$ becomes slack at $M = 60\text{ kg}$, which breaks equilibrium first.
