Incorrect initial tensions in part (a). The centre of mass ($3\text{ m}$) is closer to $C$ ($4\text{ m}$) than to $A$ ($0\text{ m}$), so cable $C$ carries the larger tension ($882\text{ N}$).

Incorrect tension in part (b). At the instant cable $A$ becomes slack, cable $C$ must support both the weight of the girder ($120g$) and the machine ($60g$), so $T_C = 180g = 1764\text{ N}$, not $1176\text{ N}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Cables Cannot Push
bradley_insight.content: A very frequent trap in suspended beam questions is assuming a cable breaks first. Many students simply equate $T_C = 1800\text{ N}$ to find $M \approx 63.7\text{ kg}$. However, a cable is not a rigid strut; it cannot support a compressive (downward) thrust. Once $M$ exceeds $60\text{ kg}$, $T_A$ would need to be negative to maintain balance, meaning cable $A$ goes slack and the girder tilts about $C$ immediately.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform beam $AB$ of length $3\text{ m}$ and mass $20\text{ kg}$. End $A$ is attached to a vertical wall by a smooth hinge. The beam is held horizontally in equilibrium by a light inextensible wire attached to end $B$ and to a point $C$ on the wall vertically above $A$. The wire makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal beam.

A load of mass $15\text{ kg}$, modelled as a particle, is suspended from the beam at a point $D$, where $AD = 2\text{ m}$.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) By taking moments about $A$, calculate the tension in the wire.

(b) Find the horizontal and vertical components of the reaction force exerted by the hinge on the beam at $A$.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of the resultant reaction force exerted by the hinge at $A$, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

(d) Find the angle that the resultant reaction force at $A$ makes with the horizontal, giving your answer correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$.
steps:
(a) Calculating the tension in the wire:

The weight of the beam is $20g = 196\text{ N}$ acting at its midpoint ($1.5\text{ m}$ from $A$).

The load has weight $15g = 147\text{ N}$ acting at $D$ ($2\text{ m}$ from $A$).

The tension $T$ acts at $B$ ($3\text{ m}$ from $A$) at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. The perpendicular component of tension is $T\sin 30^\circ$.

Taking moments about hinge $A$:\begin{aligned} &T\sin 30^\circ(3) = 20g(1.5) + 15g(2) \cr &1.5T = 30g + 30g \cr &1.5T = 60g \cr &1.5T = 60(9.8) \cr &1.5T = 588 \cr &T = 392\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Resolving forces at hinge $A$:

Let $H_A$ be the horizontal component of the reaction at $A$ (acting away from the wall) and $V_A$ be the vertical component (acting upwards).

Resolving horizontally ($\rightarrow$):\begin{aligned} H_A - T\cos 30^\circ &= 0 \cr H_A &= 392\cos 30^\circ \cr &= 392\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \cr &= 196\sqrt{3} \cr &\approx 339.48\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Resolving vertically ($\uparrow$):\begin{aligned} &V_A + T\sin 30^\circ - (20 + 15)g = 0 \cr &V_A + 392(0.5) - 35(9.8) = 0 \cr &V_A + 196 - 343 = 0 \cr &V_A = 147\text{ N} \end{aligned}

To 3 significant figures, $H_A = 339\text{ N}$ and $V_A = 147\text{ N}$.

(c) Magnitude of resultant reaction force:

Using Pythagoras' theorem:\begin{aligned} R_A &= \sqrt{H_A^2 + V_A^2} \cr &= \sqrt{(196\sqrt{3})^2 + 147^2} \cr &= \sqrt{115248 + 21609} \cr &= \sqrt{136857} \cr &\approx 370\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(d) Direction of resultant reaction force:

Let $\phi$ be the angle the resultant makes above the horizontal:\begin{aligned} \tan\phi &= \dfrac{V_A}{H_A} \cr &= \dfrac{147}{339.48} \cr &\approx 0.4330 \cr \phi &= \arctan(0.4330) \cr &\approx 23.4^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $392\text{ N}$, (b) $H_A = 339\text{ N}, V_A = 147\text{ N}$, (c) $370\text{ N}$, (d) $23.4^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect components at the hinge. You have swapped sine and cosine when resolving: the horizontal component is $T\cos 30^\circ \approx 339\text{ N}$ and the vertical component of tension is $T\sin 30^\circ = 196\text{ N}$, giving $V_A = 147\text{ N}$.
Incorrect resultant magnitude. Check your Pythagoras calculation: \begin{aligned}R_A &= \sqrt{339.48^2 + 147^2}\cr & = \sqrt{136857} \approx 370\text{ N}\end{aligned} not $339.48 + 147$.
Incorrect tension calculation in part (a). Remember that the perpendicular component of the tension to the beam is $T\sin 30^\circ$, not $T\cos 30^\circ$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Pivot at the Unknown Hinge
bradley_insight.content: A smooth hinge can exert a reaction force in any direction within the vertical plane, meaning it introduces two unknowns ($H_A$ and $V_A$). By taking moments about the hinge $A$ first, both of these unknown forces have zero moment arm, allowing you to find the tension $T$ in a single equation without having to set up simultaneous equations.

question:
The diagram shows three coplanar forces of magnitudes $5\text{ N}$, $8\text{ N}$, and $Q\text{ N}$ acting at a point. The force of magnitude $Q\text{ N}$ acts vertically downwards. The forces of magnitude $5\text{ N}$ and $8\text{ N}$ act upwards at angles of $2\theta$ and $\theta$ to the upward vertical, respectively.

The forces are in equilibrium.

(a) Show that $\theta = 36.9^\circ$, correct to 3 significant figures.

(b) Hence find the value of $Q$.

The force of magnitude $5\text{ N}$ is now removed, and the force of magnitude $8\text{ N}$ is replaced by a force of magnitude $5\text{ N}$ acting in the same direction.

(c) Find:
(i) the magnitude of the resultant of the two remaining forces, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures,
(ii) the direction of the resultant of the two remaining forces, giving the angle correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$ below the horizontal.
steps:
(a) Finding the angle $\theta$:

Resolving horizontally ($\rightarrow$):\begin{aligned} &5\sin 2\theta = 8\sin\theta \cr &5(2\sin\theta\cos\theta) = 8\sin\theta \cr &10\sin\theta\cos\theta = 8\sin\theta \end{aligned}

Since $\theta \ne 0^\circ$, we divide by $\sin\theta$:\begin{aligned} 10\cos\theta &= 8 \cr \cos\theta &= 0.8 \cr \theta &= \arccos(0.8) \cr &\approx 36.87^\circ \cr &= 36.9^\circ\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(b) Finding the vertical force $Q$:

Using the double angle identity for cosine:\begin{aligned} \cos 2\theta &= 2\cos^2\theta - 1 \cr &= 2(0.8)^2 - 1 \cr &= 2(0.64) - 1 \cr &= 0.28 \end{aligned}

Resolving vertically for equilibrium ($\uparrow$):\begin{aligned} Q &= 5\cos 2\theta + 8\cos\theta \cr &= 5(0.28) + 8(0.8) \cr &= 1.4 + 6.4 \cr &= 7.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Resultant of remaining forces:

The $5\text{ N}$ force is removed and the $8\text{ N}$ force is replaced by a $5\text{ N}$ force acting at $\theta = 36.87^\circ$ to the upward vertical.

Horizontal component of resultant ($\rightarrow$):\begin{aligned} R_x &= 5\sin\theta \cr &= 5(0.6) \cr &= 3\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Vertical component of resultant ($\downarrow$):\begin{aligned} R_y &= Q - 5\cos\theta \cr &= 7.8 - 5(0.8) \cr &= 7.8 - 4 \cr &= 3.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Magnitude and direction:

(i) Magnitude:\begin{aligned} R &= \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2} \cr &= \sqrt{3^2 + 3.8^2} \cr &= \sqrt{9 + 14.44} \cr &= \sqrt{23.44} \cr &\approx 4.84\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(ii) Direction:

Let $\phi$ be the angle below the horizontal:\begin{aligned} \tan\phi &= \dfrac{R_y}{R_x} \cr &= \dfrac{3.8}{3} \cr &\approx 1.2667 \cr \phi &= \arctan(1.2667) \cr &\approx 51.7^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $Q = 7.8\text{ N}$, (c)(i) $4.84\text{ N}$, (c)(ii) $51.7^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect direction in part (c)(ii). The angle was calculated with respect to the vertical ($90^\circ - 51.7^\circ = 38.3^\circ$) rather than below the horizontal ($\tan\phi = R_y / R_x = 3.8 / 3$).

Incorrect value for $Q$. Check the double angle expansion for $\cos 2\theta$:\begin{aligned} \cos 2\theta &= 2\cos^2\theta - 1 \cr &= 2(0.64) - 1 \cr &= 0.28 \end{aligned}giving $Q = 5(0.28) + 8(0.8) = 7.8\text{ N}$.

Incorrect resultant magnitude. In part (c), the remaining $5\text{ N}$ force has an upward component of $4\text{ N}$ while $Q$ acts downwards, so the net vertical component is $7.8 - 4 = 3.8\text{ N}$, not $7.8 + 4$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Exact Pythagorean Ratios
bradley_insight.content: When resolving forces involving $\theta$ where $\cos\theta = 0.8 = \dfrac{4}{5}$, recognise immediately that $\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$. Using these exact rational values avoids rounding discrepancies entirely when finding $\cos 2\theta = 2(0.8)^2 - 1 = 0.28$ and calculating the horizontal and vertical components of the resultant.

question:
The diagram shows three coplanar forces acting at a point $O$:
A force of magnitude $10\text{ N}$ acting along the positive $x$-axis.
A force of magnitude $12\text{ N}$ acting at an angle of $60^\circ$ above the negative $x$-axis.
A force of magnitude $P\text{ N}$ acting at an angle of $\theta$ below the negative $x$-axis.

The forces are in equilibrium.

(a) Show that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}$, and hence find the value of $\theta$ correct to 3 significant figures.

(b) Find the exact value of $P$ in the form $k\sqrt{m}$, where $k$ and $m$ are integers.

The force of magnitude $10\text{ N}$ is now removed, and the force of magnitude $12\text{ N}$ is replaced by a force of magnitude $24\text{ N}$ acting in the same direction.

(c) Find:
(i) the magnitude of the resultant of the two remaining forces, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures,
(ii) the acute angle that this resultant makes with the negative $x$-axis, giving your answer correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$.
steps:
(a) Resolving for equilibrium:

Resolving vertically ($\uparrow$):\begin{aligned} &12\sin 60^\circ \cr & \qquad- P\sin\theta = 0 \cr& \qquad P\sin\theta = 12\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \cr & \qquad P\sin\theta = 6\sqrt{3} \quad \text{--- [Eq 1]} \end{aligned}

Resolving horizontally ($\rightarrow$):\begin{aligned} &10 - 12\cos 60^\circ - P\cos\theta = 0 \cr & 10 - 12(0.5) = P\cos\theta \cr & P\cos\theta = 4 \quad \text{--- [Eq 2]} \end{aligned}

Dividing [Eq 1] by [Eq 2]:\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \cr \theta &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \cr &\approx 68.9^\circ \end{aligned}

(b) Finding the exact value of $P$:

Squaring and adding [Eq 1] and [Eq 2]:\begin{aligned} P^2 &= (P\cos\theta)^2 + (P\sin\theta)^2 \cr &= 4^2 + (6\sqrt{3})^2 \cr &= 16 + 108 \cr &= 124 \cr P &= \sqrt{124} \cr &= 2\sqrt{31}\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) New resultant force:

The $10\text{ N}$ force is removed and the $12\text{ N}$ force is replaced by $24\text{ N}$.

Resolving in the $x$-direction ($\rightarrow$):\begin{aligned} R_x &= -24\cos 60^\circ - P\cos\theta \cr &= -24(0.5) - 4 \cr &= -12 - 4 \cr &= -16\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Resolving in the $y$-direction ($\uparrow$):\begin{aligned} R_y &= 24\sin 60^\circ - P\sin\theta \cr &= 24\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - 6\sqrt{3} \cr &= 12\sqrt{3} - 6\sqrt{3} \cr &= 6\sqrt{3}\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Magnitude and angle:

(i) Magnitude:\begin{aligned} R &= \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2} \cr &= \sqrt{(-16)^2 + (6\sqrt{3})^2} \cr &= \sqrt{256 + 108} \cr &= \sqrt{364} \cr &\approx 19.1\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(ii) Direction:

Let $\alpha$ be the angle above the negative $x$-axis:\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \dfrac{|R_y|}{|R_x|} \cr &= \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{16} \cr &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{8} \cr &\approx 0.6495 \cr \alpha &= \arctan(0.6495) \cr &\approx 33.0^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $68.9^\circ$, (b) $2\sqrt{31}\text{ N}$, (c)(i) $19.1\text{ N}$, (c)(ii) $33.0^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect angle in part (c)(ii). The angle was measured to the vertical rather than the negative $x$-axis ($90^\circ - 33.0^\circ = 57.0^\circ$). The required angle satisfies $\tan\alpha = 6\sqrt{3} / 16$.
Incorrect surd simplification in part (b). $\sqrt{124} = \sqrt{4 \times 31} = 2\sqrt{31}\text{ N}$, not $4\sqrt{31}\text{ N}$.
Incorrect angle in part (a). The tangent ratio was inverted as $4 / (6\sqrt{3})$ instead of $P\sin\theta / P\cos\theta = 6\sqrt{3} / 4$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Vector Linearity in Resultants
bradley_insight.content: In part (c), recognise that the original forces satisfied $\mathbf{F}_{10} + \mathbf{F}_{12} + \mathbf{F}_P = \mathbf{0}$, meaning $\mathbf{F}_{12} + \mathbf{F}_P = -\mathbf{F}_{10}$. When $\mathbf{F}_{10}$ is removed and $\mathbf{F}_{12}$ is doubled to $2\mathbf{F}_{12}$, the new resultant is simply $2\mathbf{F}_{12} + \mathbf{F}_P = \mathbf{F}_{12} + (\mathbf{F}_{12} + \mathbf{F}_P) = \mathbf{F}_{12} - \mathbf{F}_{10}$. This vector insight verifies your resolved components immediately.

question:
The diagram shows a parcel of weight $65\text{ N}$ resting in equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, where $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

A horizontal pushing force of magnitude $P\text{ N}$ is applied to the parcel. The force acts towards the plane in a vertical plane containing a line of greatest slope. The coefficient of friction between the parcel and the plane is $\mu = 0.25$.

(a) When the parcel is on the point of sliding up the plane:
(i) show that the normal reaction $R\text{ N}$ between the plane and the parcel satisfies $R = 52 + 0.6P$,
(ii) calculate the value of $P$.

(b) The magnitude of $P$ is now gradually reduced until the parcel is on the point of sliding down the plane. Calculate this minimum value of $P$, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a)(i) Normal reaction $R$:

Since $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$, by trigonometry:\begin{aligned} \sin\alpha &= 0.6 \cr \cos\alpha &= 0.8 \end{aligned}

Resolving perpendicular to the plane ($\nwarrow$):\begin{aligned} R &= 65\cos\alpha + P\sin\alpha \cr &= 65(0.8) + P(0.6) \cr &= 52 + 0.6P \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) On the point of sliding up the plane:

When sliding up the plane is impending, friction $F$ acts down the plane at its maximum value:\begin{aligned} F &= \mu R \cr &= 0.25(52 + 0.6P) \cr &= 13 + 0.15P \end{aligned}

Resolving parallel to the plane ($\nearrow$):\begin{aligned} &P\cos\alpha = 65\sin\alpha + F \cr &0.8P = 65(0.6) + (13 + 0.15P) \cr &0.8P = 39 + 13 + 0.15P \cr &0.8P = 52 + 0.15P \cr &0.65P = 52 \cr &P = \dfrac{52}{0.65} \cr &P = 80\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) On the point of sliding down the plane:

When sliding down the plane is impending, friction $F$ acts up the plane:\begin{aligned} F = \mu R = 13 + 0.15P \end{aligned}

Resolving parallel to the plane ($\nearrow$):\begin{aligned} &P\cos\alpha + F = 65\sin\alpha \cr &0.8P + (13 + 0.15P) = 65(0.6) \cr &0.95P + 13 = 39 \cr &0.95P = 26 \cr &P = \dfrac{26}{0.95} \cr &P \approx 27.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a)(ii) $80\text{ N}$, (b) $27.4\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect value in part (b). You likely assumed $R = 65\cos\alpha = 52\text{ N}$, forgetting that the horizontal force $P$ contributes a component $P\sin\alpha = 0.6P$ pressing the parcel into the plane.
Incorrect value for $P$ in part (a)(ii). Check the resolution parallel to the slope: $P\cos\alpha = 65\sin\alpha + \mu R$, which gives $0.65P = 52 \implies P = 80\text{ N}$.
Incorrect direction of friction in part (b). When impending motion is down the plane, friction acts up the plane, so $P\cos\alpha + F = 65\sin\alpha$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Horizontal Force Normal Component
bradley_insight.content: A horizontal force $P$ acting on an inclined plane has two perpendicular components: $P\cos\alpha$ parallel to the slope, and $P\sin\alpha$ perpendicular to the slope. Students frequently forget the perpendicular component and write $R = mg\cos\alpha$. Because $P$ presses into the slope, it increases $R$ to $mg\cos\alpha + P\sin\alpha$, which directly increases the maximum frictional force.

question:
The diagram shows a particle $P$ of weight $50\text{ N}$ suspended in equilibrium by two light inextensible strings $PA$ and $PB$. The ends $A$ and $B$ are attached to a horizontal ceiling.

The string $PA$ is inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the vertical, where $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
The string $PB$ is inclined at an angle $\beta$ to the vertical.

The tension in string $PB$ is twice the tension in string $PA$.

(a) By resolving horizontally, show that $\sin\beta = \dfrac{3}{10}$.

(b) Find the value of $\beta$ in degrees, correct to 1 decimal place.

(c) Calculate:
(i) the tension in string $PA$, correct to 3 significant figures,
(ii) the tension in string $PB$, correct to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Resolving horizontally:

From $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$, we have $\sin\alpha = 0.6$ and $\cos\alpha = 0.8$.

Given that $T_B = 2T_A$, resolving horizontally ($\rightarrow$):\begin{aligned} &T_B\sin\beta = T_A\sin\alpha \cr &2T_A\sin\beta = T_A(0.6) \cr &2\sin\beta = 0.6 \cr &\sin\beta = 0.3 \cr &\sin\beta = \dfrac{3}{10} \end{aligned}

(b) Finding angle $\beta$:

Evaluating $\beta$:\begin{aligned} \beta &= \arcsin(0.3) \cr &\approx 17.4576^\circ \cr &= 17.5^\circ\text{ (1 d.p.)} \end{aligned}

(c) Resolving vertically for tensions:

Using $\cos\beta = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\beta}$:\begin{aligned} \cos\beta &= \sqrt{1 - (0.3)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{0.91} \cr &\approx 0.95394 \end{aligned}

Resolving vertically for equilibrium ($\uparrow$):\begin{aligned} &T_A\cos\alpha + T_B\cos\beta = 50 \cr &T_A(0.8) + 2T_A(\sqrt{0.91}) = 50 \cr &T_A(0.8 + 2\times 0.95394) = 50 \cr &T_A(0.8 + 1.90788) = 50 \cr &2.70788 T_A = 50 \cr &T_A = \dfrac{50}{2.70788} \cr &T_A \approx 18.5\text{ N} \end{aligned}

For string $PB$:\begin{aligned} T_B &= 2T_A \cr &= 2(18.4647) \cr &\approx 36.9\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $17.5^\circ$, (c)(i) $18.5\text{ N}$, (c)(ii) $36.9\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect assignment of tensions. The tension in string $PB$ is twice the tension in string $PA$, so $T_B = 36.9\text{ N}$ and $T_A = 18.5\text{ N}$.
Incorrect angle $\beta$. Check part (a): $2\sin\beta = 0.6 \implies \sin\beta = 0.3$. $\arcsin(0.3) \approx 17.5^\circ$, whereas $\arcsin(0.5) = 30.0^\circ$.
Premature rounding error. When evaluating $\cos\beta$, use $\sqrt{0.91} \approx 0.9539$ rather than approximating it to $1$, which significantly distorts the tension.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: String Inclination Angles
bradley_insight.content: Be vigilant about how angles are defined in suspended particle questions. Here, both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are given with respect to the vertical. This means the horizontal components use $\sin$ and the vertical components use $\cos$. If angles are defined with respect to the ceiling, the roles of sine and cosine are reversed.

question:
The diagram shows a particle $P$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ held in equilibrium on a smooth horizontal surface by three horizontal coplanar forces:
A force $\mathbf{F}_1$ of magnitude $25\text{ N}$ acting at an acute angle $\theta$ to the positive $x$-axis.
A force $\mathbf{F}_2$ of magnitude $15\text{ N}$ acting along the negative $y$-axis.
A force $\mathbf{F}_3$ of magnitude $H\text{ N}$ acting along the negative $x$-axis.

(a) Find:
(i) the value of $\theta$, correct to 3 significant figures,
(ii) the value of $H$.

The force $\mathbf{F}_3$ is suddenly removed while $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ remain unchanged. The particle starts from rest at the origin.

(b)
(i) Write down the magnitude and direction of the resultant force acting on the particle immediately after $\mathbf{F}_3$ is removed.
(ii) Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle.
(iii) Calculate the distance travelled by the particle in the first $3\text{ seconds}$ of its motion.

(c) In a different scenario starting from the original three-force equilibrium state, instead of removing $\mathbf{F}_3$, the force $\mathbf{F}_2$ is reversed in direction. State the magnitude and direction of the resulting net force acting on the particle.
steps:
(a) Equilibrium conditions:

Resolving along the $y$-axis ($\uparrow$):\begin{aligned} 25\sin\theta - 15 &= 0 \cr 25\sin\theta &= 15 \cr \sin\theta &= 0.6 \cr \theta &= \arcsin(0.6) \cr &\approx 36.9^\circ \end{aligned}

Since $\sin\theta = 0.6$, $\cos\theta = 0.8$.

Resolving along the $x$-axis ($\rightarrow$):\begin{aligned} 25\cos\theta - H &= 0 \cr H &= 25(0.8) \cr &= 20\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Resultant when $\mathbf{F}_3$ is removed:

In the original equilibrium state:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 = \mathbf{0} \end{aligned}

Therefore, the resultant of $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ is equal and opposite to $\mathbf{F}_3$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 &= -\mathbf{F}_3 \cr &= -(-20\mathbf{i}) \cr &= 20\mathbf{i}\text{ N} \end{aligned}

The resultant force has magnitude $20\text{ N}$ directed in the positive $x$-direction (due East).

(b)(ii) & (b)(iii) Acceleration and displacement:

Using Newton's second law ($F = ma$):\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{F}{m} \cr &= \dfrac{20}{3} \cr &\approx 6.67\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Since the particle starts from rest ($u = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$), using $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} s &= 0(3) + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{20}{3}\right)(3)^2 \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{20}{3}\right)(9) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(60) \cr &= 30\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Reversing the direction of $\mathbf{F}_2$:

Reversing $\mathbf{F}_2$ replaces $-\mathbf{F}_2$ with $+\mathbf{F}_2$. The new net force is:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_{\text{net}} &= \mathbf{F}_1 + (-\mathbf{F}_2) + \mathbf{F}_3 \cr &= (\mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3) - 2\mathbf{F}_2 \cr &= \mathbf{0} - 2(-15\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 30\mathbf{j}\text{ N} \end{aligned}

The resulting net force has magnitude $30\text{ N}$ directed in the positive $y$-direction (due North).
Final Answer: (a)(i) $36.9^\circ$, (a)(ii) $H = 20\text{ N}$, (b)(i) $20\text{ N}$ due East, (b)(ii) $6.67\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b)(iii) $30\text{ m}$, (c) $30\text{ N}$ due North

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $36.9^\circ$, (a)(ii) $H = 20\text{ N}$, (b)(i) $20\text{ N}$ due West, (b)(ii) $6.67\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b)(iii) $30\text{ m}$, (c) $30\text{ N}$ due North
pi_options.feedback: Incorrect direction in part (b)(i). Since $\mathbf{F}_3$ acted to the West (negative $x$-direction) to maintain balance, the resultant of the remaining forces must act to the East (positive $x$-direction).

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $36.9^\circ$, (a)(ii) $H = 20\text{ N}$, (b)(i) $20\text{ N}$ due East, (b)(ii) $6.67\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b)(iii) $60\text{ m}$, (c) $30\text{ N}$ due North
pi_options.feedback: Incorrect displacement in part (b)(iii). You omitted the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in the constant acceleration formula $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, giving $60\text{ m}$ instead of $30\text{ m}$.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $53.1^\circ$, (a)(ii) $H = 15\text{ N}$, (b)(i) $20\text{ N}$ due East, (b)(ii) $6.67\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b)(iii) $30\text{ m}$, (c) $15\text{ N}$ due North
pi_options.feedback: Incorrect angle $\theta$ and value of $H$. Resolving vertically gives \begin{aligned}25\sin\theta &= 15 \cr\implies \sin\theta &= 0.6 \cr\implies \theta &= 36.9^\circ\end{aligned} Confusing sine and cosine results in $\theta = 53.1^\circ$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Removal Equilibrium Principle
bradley_insight.content: Whenever a system of forces is in equilibrium ($\Sigma \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}$) and one force is suddenly removed, the resultant of all remaining forces is always exactly equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the removed force ($-\mathbf{F}_{\text{removed}}$). Recognising this vector identity saves minutes of unnecessary trigonometry in exam conditions.

question:
A motorcycle moves along a straight horizontal road. The velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ of the motorcycle at time $t\text{ s}$, during the first $10\text{ s}$ of its journey ($0 \le t \le 10$), is modelled by:$$v = ct + 0.06t^2$$where $c$ is a constant.

When $t = 10$, the acceleration of the motorcycle is $1.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

For $t \ge 10$, the motorcycle continues its journey with constant acceleration $1.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ until its speed reaches $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Find the value of $c$.

(b) Find the speed of the motorcycle when $t = 10$.

(c) Find the total distance the motorcycle has travelled from $t = 0$ until its speed reaches $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
steps:
(a) Finding the constant $c$:

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &= c + 0.12t \end{aligned}

Given that $a = 1.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ when $t = 10$:\begin{aligned} &c + 0.12(10) = 1.8 \cr &c + 1.2 = 1.8 \cr &c = 0.6 \end{aligned}

(b) Speed at $t = 10$:

Substitute $c = 0.6$ and $t = 10$ into the velocity model:\begin{aligned} v(10) &= 0.6(10) + 0.06(10)^2 \cr &= 6 + 0.06(100) \cr &= 6 + 6 \cr &= 12\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Stage 1 distance ($0 \le t \le 10$):

Integrating velocity gives displacement:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \int_0^{10} (0.6t + 0.06t^2)\text{d}t \cr &= \left[ 0.3t^2 + 0.02t^3 \right]_0^{10} \cr &= 0.3(100) + 0.02(1000) \cr &= 30 + 20 \cr &= 50\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Stage 2 distance ($t \ge 10$):

The motorcycle moves with constant acceleration $a = 1.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ from initial speed $u = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to final speed $v = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:\begin{aligned} &30^2 = 12^2 + 2(1.8)s_2 \cr &900 = 144 + 3.6s_2 \cr &3.6s_2 = 756 \cr &s_2 = 210\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Total distance travelled:\begin{aligned} s &= s_1 + s_2 \cr &= 50 + 210 \cr &= 260\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $c = 0.6$, (b) $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (c) $260\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect total distance in part (c). $210\text{ m}$ is only the distance travelled during Stage 2 under constant acceleration. You must add the $50\text{ m}$ covered during Stage 1 ($50 + 210 = 260\text{ m}$).
Incorrect derivative in part (a). Differentiating $0.06t^2$ yields $2(0.06)t = 0.12t$, not $0.06t$.
Incorrect integration in part (c). When integrating $0.6t$, remember to divide by the new power: $\int 0.6t\text{d}t = 0.3t^2$, not $0.6t^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Blending Calculus and SUVAT
bradley_insight.content: Never apply constant acceleration formulae ($v^2 = u^2 + 2as$) during Stage 1 where acceleration depends on time ($a = 0.6 + 0.12t$). Conversely, do not attempt to integrate the Stage 1 velocity model beyond $t = 10$, as the model changes explicitly to constant acceleration. Always treat piecewise journeys in distinct phases and sum the distances.

question:
A train departs from rest at station $A$ along a straight horizontal track. For the first $20\text{ s}$ of its journey ($0 \le t \le 20$), its acceleration $a\text{ m s}^{-2}$ at time $t\text{ s}$ is modelled by:$$a = 1.8 - 0.06t$$At $t = 20$, the power is cut and the brakes are applied, producing a constant deceleration of $0.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$ until the train comes to rest at a signal.

(a) Find the speed of the train when $t = 20$.

(b) Find the distance travelled by the train during the first $20\text{ seconds}$.

(c) Find the total time taken from the start of the journey until the train comes to rest at the signal.

(d) Find the total distance travelled by the train from station $A$ to the signal.
steps:
(a) Speed at $t = 20$:

Since the train starts from rest, $v = 0$ when $t = 0$:\begin{aligned} v &= \int (1.8 - 0.06t)\text{d}t \cr &= 1.8t - 0.03t^2 \end{aligned}

At $t = 20$:\begin{aligned} v(20) &= 1.8(20) - 0.03(20)^2 \cr &= 36 - 0.03(400) \cr &= 36 - 12 \cr &= 24\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Distance during the first $20\text{ seconds}$:

Integrating velocity gives displacement:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \int_0^{20} (1.8t - 0.03t^2)\text{d}t \cr &= \left[ 0.9t^2 - 0.01t^3 \right]_0^{20} \cr &= 0.9(400) - 0.01(8000) \cr &= 360 - 80 \cr &= 280\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Total time to come to rest:

For the braking phase, $u = 24\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $a = -0.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 24 - 0.5t_2 \cr &0.5t_2 = 24 \cr &t_2 = 48\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Total time from departure:\begin{aligned} T &= 20 + t_2 \cr &= 20 + 48 \cr &= 68\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(d) Total distance to the signal:

Braking distance using $s = \left(\dfrac{u + v}{2}\right)t$:\begin{aligned} s_2 &= \left(\dfrac{24 + 0}{2}\right)(48) \cr &= 12(48) \cr &= 576\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Total distance:\begin{aligned} s &= s_1 + s_2 \cr &= 280 + 576 \cr &= 856\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $24\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b) $280\text{ m}$, (c) $68\text{ s}$, (d) $856\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect total time in part (c). $48\text{ s}$ is solely the duration of the braking stage; the total journey time is $20 + 48 = 68\text{ s}$.
Incorrect total distance in part (d). $576\text{ m}$ is the braking distance alone. You must add the $280\text{ m}$ travelled during the first $20\text{ s}$ to obtain $856\text{ m}$.
Incorrect velocity in part (a). Integrating $a = 1.8 - 0.06t$ gives $v = 1.8t - 0.03t^2$. Omitting the quadratic term leads to an incorrect speed of $36\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Choosing the Quickest SUVAT Formula
bradley_insight.content: In part (d), once you have found the braking time $t_2 = 48\text{ s}$, using $s = \left(\dfrac{u + v}{2}\right)t$ calculates the braking distance in a single mental multiplication ($12 \times 48 = 576$). This avoids squaring $24$ and dividing by $2a$, keeping the arithmetic fast and error-free.

question:
A test car moves from rest along a straight horizontal track. Between $t = 0$ and $t = 10\text{ s}$, the velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ of the car is given by:$$v = 0.75t^2 - 0.05t^3$$(a) Using calculus, show that the car attains its maximum velocity when $t = 10$, and find this maximum velocity.

(b) Calculate the distance travelled by the car during the first $10\text{ seconds}$.

For the next $15\text{ seconds}$ (from $t = 10$ to $t = 25$), the car continues at this constant maximum speed.
At $t = 25$, the car decelerates uniformly to rest in a distance of $100\text{ m}$.

(c) Find the distance travelled by the car while travelling at constant speed.

(d) Find the magnitude of the deceleration in the final stage.

(e) Calculate the total time taken for the entire journey from start to rest.
steps:
(a) Maximum velocity:

Differentiating velocity gives acceleration:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &= 1.5t - 0.15t^2 \cr &= 0.15t(10 - t) \end{aligned}

Setting $a = 0$ for $t > 0$:\begin{aligned} &10 - t = 0 \cr &t = 10\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Confirming maximum using the second derivative:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2v}{\text{d}t^2} &= 1.5 - 0.3t \cr &= 1.5 - 0.3(10) \cr &= -1.5 < 0 \end{aligned}

Evaluating maximum velocity:\begin{aligned} v_{\text{max}} &= 0.75(10)^2 - 0.05(10)^3 \cr &= 75 - 50 \cr &= 25\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Distance during first $10\text{ seconds}$:

Integrating velocity:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \int_0^{10} (0.75t^2 - 0.05t^3)\text{d}t \cr &= \left[ 0.25t^3 - 0.0125t^4 \right]_0^{10} \cr &= 0.25(1000) - 0.0125(10000) \cr &= 250 - 125 \cr &= 125\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Constant speed distance:

Cruising at $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ for $15\text{ seconds}$:\begin{aligned} s_2 &= 25 \times 15 \cr &= 375\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) & (e) Final braking stage:

For the final stage, $u = 25\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $s_3 = 100\text{ m}$.

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with deceleration $d$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 25^2 - 2d(100) \cr &200d = 625 \cr &d = 3.125\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Finding braking duration using $s_3 = \left(\dfrac{u + v}{2}\right)t_3$:\begin{aligned} &100 = \left(\dfrac{25 + 0}{2}\right)t_3 \cr &12.5t_3 = 100 \cr &t_3 = 8\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Total journey time:\begin{aligned} T &= 10 + 15 + 8 \cr &= 33\text{ s} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect total time in part (e). You omitted the initial $10\text{ s}$ acceleration stage: $10 + 15 + 8 = 33\text{ s}$, not $15 + 8 = 23\text{ s}$.
Incorrect deceleration in part (d). In $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, the denominator is $2s = 200$, giving $d = 625 / 200 = 3.125\text{ m s}^{-2}$, not $625 / 100$.
Incorrect integration in part (b). Integrating $0.75t^2$ gives $\dfrac{0.75}{3}t^3 = 0.25t^3$, which evaluates to $250 - 125 = 125\text{ m}$, not $250\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Justifying the Maximum
bradley_insight.content: In questions asking you to 'show that velocity attains its maximum', setting $\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 0$ is only half the proof. You must explicitly verify that it is a maximum, either by evaluating the second derivative $\dfrac{\text{d}^2v}{\text{d}t^2} = -1.5 < 0$ or by demonstrating that acceleration changes sign from positive to negative through $t = 10$.

question:
A particle moves in a straight line such that its velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at time $t\text{ s}$ is given by:$$v(t) = \begin{cases} kt^2 & 0 \le t \le 4 \ A - 2t & 4 < t \le 10 \end{cases}$$where $k$ and $A$ are constants.

The velocity function $v(t)$ is continuous at $t = 4$, and the particle comes to instantaneous rest at $t = 10$.

(a) Find the values of the constants $A$ and $k$.

(b) By finding the acceleration of the particle immediately before and immediately after $t = 4$, explain why the acceleration is discontinuous at $t = 4$.

(c) Calculate the total distance travelled by the particle over the interval $0 \le t \le 10$.

(d) Hence calculate the average speed of the particle during the $10\text{ seconds}$.
steps:
(a) Finding constants $A$ and $k$:

At $t = 10$, the particle is at instantaneous rest ($v = 0$):\begin{aligned} &A - 2(10) = 0 \cr &A - 20 = 0 \cr &A = 20 \end{aligned}

Since $v(t)$ is continuous at $t = 4$:\begin{aligned} &k(4^2) = A - 2(4) \cr &16k = 20 - 8 \cr &16k = 12 \cr &k = 0.75 \end{aligned}

(b) Acceleration discontinuity:

For $0 \le t < 4$:\begin{aligned} a(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0.75t^2) \cr &= 1.5t \end{aligned}

Immediately before $t = 4$:\begin{aligned} a(4^-) &= 1.5(4) \cr &= 6\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

For $4 < t \le 10$:\begin{aligned} a(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(20 - 2t) \cr &= -2\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Since $a(4^-) = 6 \ne a(4^+) = -2$, the acceleration has an abrupt jump discontinuity of $8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ at $t = 4$.

(c) Total distance travelled:

Stage 1 distance ($0 \le t \le 4$):\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \int_0^4 0.75t^2\text{d}t \cr &= \left[ 0.25t^3 \right]_0^4 \cr &= 0.25(64) \cr &= 16\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Stage 2 distance ($4 < t \le 10$):\begin{aligned} s_2 &= \int_4^{10} (20 - 2t)\text{d}t \cr &= \left[ 20t - t^2 \right]_4^{10} \cr &= (200 - 100) - (80 - 16) \cr &= 100 - 64 \cr &= 36\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Total distance:\begin{aligned} s &= s_1 + s_2 \cr &= 16 + 36 \cr &= 52\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Average speed:

Average speed is total distance divided by total time:\begin{aligned} \text{Average speed} &= \dfrac{s_{\text{total}}}{t_{\text{total}}} \cr &= \dfrac{52}{10} \cr &= 5.2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $A = 20, k = 0.75$, (c) $52\text{ m}$, (d) $5.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect average speed in part (d). You averaged the peak speed ($12\text{ m s}^{-1}$) and initial speed ($0\text{ m s}^{-1}$). Average speed is defined strictly as total distance divided by total time ($52 / 10 = 5.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$).
Incorrect value for $k$ in part (a). Setting $16k = 20 - 2(4)$ gives $16k = 12 \implies k = 0.75$, not $1.25$.
Incorrect distance in part (c). $36\text{ m}$ accounts only for Stage 2. You must include the $16\text{ m}$ covered during Stage 1 to obtain $52\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Continuity vs Differentiability
bradley_insight.content: A common theoretical misconception is believing that if velocity is continuous, acceleration must also be continuous. As shown here, a piecewise velocity function can join without gaps, yet have a sharp corner where the gradient jumps abruptly ($a$ jumps from $+6\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to $-2\text{ m s}^{-2}$). Velocity is continuous, but not differentiable at $t = 4$.

question:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$ move along the same straight horizontal line. At time $t = 0$, both particles pass through a fixed point $O$ on the line, travelling in the same direction.

The velocity $v_P\text{ m s}^{-1}$ of particle $P$ at time $t\text{ s}$ ($t \ge 0$) is given by:$$v_P = 6t - 0.5t^2$$Particle $Q$ starts from $O$ at $t = 0$ with an initial velocity of $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and moves with constant acceleration $a\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the time at which particle $P$ attains its maximum velocity, and calculate this maximum velocity.

(b) Find an expression in terms of $t$ for the displacement $s_P$ of particle $P$ from $O$.

Particle $Q$ catches up with particle $P$ at the exact instant when particle $P$ attains its maximum velocity.

(c) Find the distance of both particles from $O$ at this instant.

(d) Calculate the value of the constant acceleration $a$ of particle $Q$.

(e) Find the difference in speeds between particle $Q$ and particle $P$ at the moment they collide.
steps:
(a) Maximum velocity of $P$:

Differentiating $v_P$ with respect to time:\begin{aligned} a_P &= \dfrac{\text{d}v_P}{\text{d}t} \cr &= 6 - t \end{aligned}

Maximum velocity occurs when $a_P = 0$:\begin{aligned} &6 - t = 0 \cr &t = 6\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Maximum velocity value:\begin{aligned} v_P(6) &= 6(6) - 0.5(6)^2 \cr &= 36 - 0.5(36) \cr &= 36 - 18 \cr &= 18\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Displacement expression for $P$:

Since $s_P = 0$ when $t = 0$:\begin{aligned} s_P &= \int (6t - 0.5t^2)\text{d}t \cr &= 3t^2 - \dfrac{1}{6}t^3 \end{aligned}

(c) Distance at collision ($t = 6\text{ s}$):

Substitute $t = 6$ into the displacement expression for $P$:\begin{aligned} s_P(6) &= 3(6)^2 - \dfrac{1}{6}(6)^3 \cr &= 3(36) - 36 \cr &= 108 - 36 \cr &= 72\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) & (e) Acceleration of $Q$ and speed difference:

For particle $Q$, $u_Q = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $s_Q = 72\text{ m}$ at $t = 6\text{ s}$.

Using $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} &72 = 3(6) + \dfrac{1}{2}a(6)^2 \cr &72 = 18 + 18a \cr &18a = 54 \cr &a = 3\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Speed of $Q$ at $t = 6\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} v_Q &= u + at \cr &= 3 + 3(6) \cr &= 21\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Difference in speeds:\begin{aligned} |v_Q - v_P| &= 21 - 18 \cr &= 3\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $6\text{ s}, 18\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (c) $72\text{ m}$, (d) $3\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (e) $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect acceleration for $Q$. You assumed particle $Q$ started from rest ($u_Q = 0$). With $u_Q = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$, \begin{aligned}72 &= 3(6) + 18a \cr \implies 18a & = 54 \cr \implies a & = 3\text{ m s}^{-2}\end{aligned}

Incorrect distance in part (c). Evaluating displacement requires subtracting the cubic term: \begin{aligned}s_P(6) & = 108 - \frac{1}{6}(216)\cr & = 108 - 36 \cr &= 72\text{ m}\end{aligned} not $108\text{ m}.
Incorrect time for maximum velocity. Setting $v_P = 0$ gives $t = 12\text{ s}$ (instantaneous rest), whereas maximum velocity occurs when acceleration $a_P = 0$, giving $t = 6\text{ s}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dual Particle Collision Conditions
bradley_insight.content: When two particles collide or one catches up with another, their displacements from the origin must be identical ($s_P = s_Q$). However, their speeds are rarely the same. For one particle to catch up with another from behind, its speed must actually exceed the other particle's speed at that instant ($v_Q > v_P$), which is why $Q$ is travelling at $21\text{ m s}^{-1}$ while $P$ is travelling at $18\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

question:
The diagram shows a particle $A$ of mass $m\text{ kg}$ held in contact with a rough plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. One end of a light inextensible string is attached to particle $A$. The string passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the top of the plane. The section of string from $A$ to the pulley is parallel to a line of greatest slope of the plane. A second particle $B$, of mass $M\text{ kg}$, is attached to the other end of the string and hangs freely vertically below the pulley.

The coefficient of friction between particle $A$ and the plane is $\mu$.

(a) When $M = \dfrac{1}{5}m$, particle $A$ is on the point of slipping down the plane. Find the exact value of $\mu$, giving your answer in the form $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{k}$, where $k$ is an integer.

Particle $B$ is now removed and replaced by a particle of mass $\dfrac{3}{2}m\text{ kg}$. The system is released from rest with the string taut.

(b) Find the acceleration of the particles in terms of $g$.

(c) State two modelling assumptions made about the string, and explain how each assumption is used in your calculations.
steps:
(a) Finding the coefficient of friction $\mu$:

For particle $B$, vertical equilibrium gives:\begin{aligned} T &= Mg \cr &= \dfrac{1}{5}mg \end{aligned}

For particle $A$, resolving perpendicular to the plane ($\nwarrow$):\begin{aligned} R &= mg\cos 30^\circ \cr &= mg\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \end{aligned}

When $A$ is on the point of slipping down the plane, friction $F$ acts up the plane at maximum value $F = \mu R$. Resolving parallel to the plane ($\nearrow$):\begin{aligned} &T + F - mg\sin 30^\circ = 0 \cr &\dfrac{1}{5}mg + \mu mg\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}mg = 0 \end{aligned}

Dividing through by $mg$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\mu = \dfrac{1}{2} \cr &\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\mu = \dfrac{3}{10} \cr &\mu = \dfrac{6}{10\sqrt{3}} \cr &\mu = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{5} \end{aligned}

Thus $k = 5$.

(b) Acceleration when $M = \dfrac{3}{2}m$:

Since $1.5m > m$, particle $B$ accelerates downwards and particle $A$ moves up the plane. Friction on $A$ now acts down the plane:\begin{aligned} F &= \mu R \cr &= \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{5}\right)mg\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{3}{10}mg \cr &= 0.3mg \end{aligned}

Equation of motion for $B$ (downwards):\begin{aligned} 1.5mg - T = 1.5ma \quad \text{--- [Eq 1]} \end{aligned}

Equation of motion for $A$ (up the slope):\begin{aligned} &T - mg\sin 30^\circ - F = ma \cr &T - 0.5mg - 0.3mg = ma \cr &T - 0.8mg = ma \quad \text{--- [Eq 2]} \end{aligned}

Adding [Eq 1] and [Eq 2]:\begin{aligned} &1.5mg - 0.8mg = 1.5ma + ma \cr &0.7mg = 2.5ma \cr &a = \dfrac{0.7}{2.5}g \cr &a = 0.28g \text{ (or } \dfrac{7}{25}g\text{)} \end{aligned}

(c) Modelling assumptions about the string:

1. Light string: The string has negligible mass, meaning the tension $T$ is uniform throughout the entire length of the string.

2. Inextensible string: The string does not stretch, meaning particle $A$ and particle $B$ have the same magnitude of acceleration $a$.
Final Answer: (a) $k = 5$, (b) $0.28g$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect acceleration in part (b). Remember that friction opposes motion up the slope: $T - 0.5mg - 0.3mg = ma$. Omitting the friction term gives $a = 0.40g$.
Incorrect value for $k$. Solving the equation gives $\mu = \dfrac{6}{10\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{5}$, so $k = 5$, not $3$.
Incorrect direction of friction in part (b). When particle $A$ accelerates up the plane, friction acts down the plane, so the total opposing force is $0.8mg$, not $0.2mg$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Friction Reversal
bradley_insight.content: In connected particle problems on an incline, always re-evaluate the direction of friction whenever the masses change. In part (a), impending motion was down the slope, so friction acted up the slope. In part (b), the heavier hanging mass pulled $A$ up the slope, reversing friction so that it acted down the slope. Forgetting this reversal is one of the most frequent errors on exam scripts.

question:
The diagram shows a block $A$ of mass $4\text{ kg}$ on a rough plane inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, where $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$. Block $A$ is connected to a particle $B$ of mass $6\text{ kg}$ by a light inextensible string. The string passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the top of the plane, and particle $B$ hangs freely vertically below the pulley. The part of the string between $A$ and the pulley lies along a line of greatest slope of the plane.

The coefficient of friction between block $A$ and the plane is $\mu = 0.25$.

The system is released from rest with the string taut.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Show that particle $B$ accelerates downwards, and calculate the magnitude of this acceleration.

(b) Calculate the tension in the string during the motion, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force exerted by the string on the pulley, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Direction of motion and acceleration:

From $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$, we have $\sin\alpha = 0.6$ and $\cos\alpha = 0.8$.

For block $A$, resolving perpendicular to the plane ($\nwarrow$):\begin{aligned} R &= 4g\cos\alpha \cr &= 4(9.8)(0.8) \cr &= 31.36\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Maximum friction:\begin{aligned} F &= \mu R \cr &= 0.25(31.36) \cr &= 7.84\text{ N} \cr &= 0.8g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Component of weight down the plane:\begin{aligned} W_{\parallel} &= 4g\sin\alpha \cr &= 4g(0.6) \cr &= 2.4g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Total resistance for $A$ moving up the slope is $2.4g + 0.8g = 3.2g\text{ N}$. Since the downward weight of $B$ is $6g\text{ N} > 3.2g\text{ N}$, particle $B$ accelerates downwards.

Equations of motion:\begin{aligned} &6g - T = 6a \cr &T - 3.2g = 4a \end{aligned}

Adding equations:\begin{aligned} &2.8g = 10a \cr &a = 0.28g \cr &a = 0.28(9.8) \cr &a = 2.744\text{ m s}^{-2} \cr &a \approx 2.74\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Tension in the string:

Using the equation for $B$:\begin{aligned} T &= 6(g - a) \cr &= 6(9.8 - 2.744) \cr &= 6(7.056) \cr &= 42.336\text{ N} \cr &\approx 42.3\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Resultant force on the pulley:

The string exerts two forces of magnitude $T = 42.336\text{ N}$ on the pulley: one directed down the incline at angle $\alpha$ below horizontal, and one directed vertically downwards.

Resolving horizontally ($\leftarrow$):\begin{aligned} F_x &= T\cos\alpha \cr &= 42.336(0.8) \cr &= 33.869\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Resolving vertically ($\downarrow$):\begin{aligned} F_y &= T + T\sin\alpha \cr &= 42.336(1 + 0.6) \cr &= 42.336(1.6) \cr &= 67.738\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Resultant force:\begin{aligned} R_{\text{pulley}} &= \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} \cr &= \sqrt{33.869^2 + 67.738^2} \cr &= \sqrt{1147.1 + 4588.4} \cr &= \sqrt{5735.5} \cr &\approx 75.7\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $2.74\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $42.3\text{ N}$, (c) $75.7\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect pulley force in part (c). The two tensions are not parallel; you cannot simply add them as $2T = 84.7\text{ N}$. You must resolve vectorially or use $R = \sqrt{2T^2(1 + \sin\alpha)}$.
Incorrect acceleration in part (a). The friction force on block $A$ was neglected, giving $6g - 2.4g = 10a$ which leads to $a = 0.36g = 3.53\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Incorrect tension in part (b). $T = 58.8\text{ N}$ assumes static equilibrium ($T = 6g$). Because $B$ is accelerating downwards, $T = 6(g - a) \approx 42.3\text{ N}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Resultant Force on a Pulley
bradley_insight.content: To find the force on a pulley without resolving into $x$ and $y$ components, note that the angle between the two string segments is $90^\circ - \alpha$. The angle between the tension vectors is $180^\circ - (90^\circ - \alpha) = 90^\circ + \alpha$. Using the cosine rule of vectors gives \begin{aligned}R &= \sqrt{2T^2(1 + \sin\alpha)}\cr & = T\sqrt{3.2}\cr & \approx 1.789T\end{aligned}.

question:
The diagram shows a block $A$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal table. Block $A$ is connected to a particle $B$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$ by a light inextensible string that passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table. Particle $B$ hangs freely vertically below the pulley. The coefficient of friction between block $A$ and the table is $0.4$.

The system is released from rest from a position where block $A$ is a sufficient distance from the pulley.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string.

After the system has been moving for $1.5\text{ seconds}$, particle $B$ reaches the floor and does not rebound.

(b)
(i) Find the speed of block $A$ at the instant particle $B$ hits the floor.
(ii) Calculate the further distance block $A$ travels along the table before coming to rest, assuming it does not reach the pulley.
steps:
(a) Acceleration and tension:

For block $A$, vertical equilibrium gives $R = 3g = 29.4\text{ N}$.

Frictional force:\begin{aligned} F &= \mu R \cr &= 0.4(29.4) \cr &= 11.76\text{ N} \cr &= 1.2g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Equations of motion for $A$ and $B$:\begin{aligned} &T - 1.2g = 3a \cr &2g - T = 2a \end{aligned}

Adding the equations:\begin{aligned} &0.8g = 5a \cr &a = 0.16g \cr &a = 0.16(9.8) \cr &a = 1.568\text{ m s}^{-2} \cr &a \approx 1.57\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Finding tension:\begin{aligned} T &= 2(g - a) \cr &= 2(9.8 - 1.568) \cr &= 2(8.232) \cr &= 16.464\text{ N} \cr &\approx 16.5\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Speed when $B$ hits the floor:

Using $v = u + at$ with $u = 0$ and $t = 1.5\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} v &= 0 + 1.568(1.5) \cr &= 2.352\text{ m s}^{-1} \cr &\approx 2.35\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Further distance travelled by $A$:

After $B$ hits the floor, the string becomes slack ($T = 0$).

Block $A$ decelerates under friction alone:\begin{aligned} -F &= m_A a' \cr -11.76 &= 3a' \cr a' &= -3.92\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2a's$ to find distance to rest ($v = 0$):\begin{aligned} &0 = (2.352)^2 + 2(-3.92)s \cr &7.84s = 5.5319 \cr &s = \dfrac{5.5319}{7.84} \cr &s = 0.7056\text{ m} \cr &s \approx 0.706\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $a = 1.57\text{ m s}^{-2}, T = 16.5\text{ N}$, (b)(i) $2.35\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b)(ii) $0.706\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect deceleration in part (b)(ii). Once $B$ hits the floor, the mass being decelerated is only block $A$ ($3\text{ kg}$), so $a' = -\mu g = -3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$, not the original system acceleration.
Incorrect system acceleration in part (a). The mass term in Newton's second law is the total mass $m_A + m_B = 5\text{ kg}$, not $2\text{ kg}$.
Calculation slip in part (b)(ii). In $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, the denominator is $2a' = 7.84$, giving $s = 5.5319 / 7.84 \approx 0.706\text{ m}$, not $5.5319 / 3.92$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: String Slackness Post-Impact
bradley_insight.content: When a hanging particle hits the ground, students frequently make the error of using the connected system's acceleration to model the subsequent motion. The moment $B$ hits the floor, the string goes slack and tension vanishes ($T = 0$). Block $A$ becomes an independent particle moving solely under its own friction, so its deceleration changes immediately from $a = 1.57\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to $a' = \mu g = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

question:
The diagram shows two particles $A$ and $B$, of masses $5\text{ kg}$ and $3\text{ kg}$ respectively, connected by a light inextensible string that passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the apex of a fixed wedge.

Particle $A$ rests on a smooth face of the wedge inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, where $\sin\alpha = 0.6$.
Particle $B$ rests on a rough face of the wedge inclined at an angle $\beta$ to the horizontal, where $\sin\beta = 0.8$.
The coefficient of friction between particle $B$ and its face is $\mu = 0.2$.

Both sections of the string are taut and parallel to the lines of greatest slope of their respective faces. The system is released from rest.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Determine whether the system moves, and if so, state whether particle $A$ moves up or down its slope, fully justifying your answer.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of the particles.

(c) Calculate the tension in the string during the motion.
steps:
(a) Determining the direction of motion:

From the given values, $\cos\beta = \sqrt{1 - 0.8^2} = 0.6$.

Gravitational driving force of $A$ down the left face:\begin{aligned} W_{A\parallel} &= 5g\sin\alpha \cr &= 5g(0.6) \cr &= 3g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Gravitational force of $B$ down the right face:\begin{aligned} W_{B\parallel} &= 3g\sin\beta \cr &= 3g(0.8) \cr &= 2.4g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Normal reaction on $B$:\begin{aligned} R_B &= 3g\cos\beta \cr &= 3g(0.6) \cr &= 1.8g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Maximum friction on $B$:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{max}} &= \mu R_B \cr &= 0.2(1.8g) \cr &= 0.36g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

If $A$ moves down its slope, $B$ must move up its slope, so friction opposes motion up the right face. The net driving force is:\begin{aligned} W_{A\parallel} - W_{B\parallel} &= 3g - 2.4g \cr &= 0.6g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Since $0.6g > F_{\text{max}} = 0.36g$, the driving force overcomes friction. The system moves, and particle $A$ moves down its slope.

(b) Acceleration of the particles:

Equations of motion for $A$ and $B$:\begin{aligned} &5g\sin\alpha - T = 5a \cr &3g - T = 5a \quad \text{--- [Eq 1]} \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} &T - 3g\sin\beta - F = 3a \cr &T - 2.4g - 0.36g = 3a \cr &T - 2.76g = 3a \quad \text{--- [Eq 2]} \end{aligned}

Adding [Eq 1] and [Eq 2]:\begin{aligned} &3g - 2.76g = 8a \cr &0.24g = 8a \cr &a = 0.03g \cr &a = 0.03(9.8) \cr &a = 0.294\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Tension in the string:

Using [Eq 1]:\begin{aligned} T &= 3g - 5a \cr &= 3(9.8) - 5(0.294) \cr &= 29.4 - 1.47 \cr &= 27.93\text{ N} \cr &\approx 27.9\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Moves, $A$ moves down, (b) $0.294\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $27.9\text{ N}$

pi_options.ans: (a) Moves, $A$ moves down, (b) $0.294\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $47.5\text{ N}$
pi_options.feedback: Incorrect tension in part (c). In the equation of motion for particle $A$, the gravitational component is $5g\sin\alpha = 3g = 29.4\text{ N}$, not $5g$. This gives $T = 3g - 5a = 27.9\text{ N}$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Remains at rest, (b) $0\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $23.5\text{ N}$
pi_options.feedback: Incorrect conclusion in part (a). The gravitational difference between the two slopes is $3g - 2.4g = 0.6g = 5.88\text{ N}$, which strictly exceeds the maximum friction $F_{\text{max}} = 0.36g = 3.53\text{ N}$, so motion does occur.

pi_options.ans: (a) Moves, $A$ moves down, (b) $0.735\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $27.9\text{ N}$
pi_options.feedback: Incorrect acceleration in part (b). The total mass in Newton's second law is $m_A + m_B = 8\text{ kg}$, not $5 - 3 = 2\text{ kg}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Testing Equilibrium on Double Wedges
bradley_insight.content: To determine whether a system on a double wedge moves, never guess the direction. First, calculate the gravitational pull along the slope for each particle: $m_A g\sin\alpha$ and $m_B g\sin\beta$. The larger pull determines the potential direction of motion. Motion only occurs if the difference between these two pulls strictly exceeds the maximum available friction force on the rough plane ($|m_A g\sin\alpha - m_B g\sin\beta| > \mu R$).

question:
The diagram shows a particle $A$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$ held at rest on a smooth plane inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. Particle $A$ is connected to a particle $B$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ by a light inextensible string that passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the top of the plane. The section of string between $A$ and the pulley lies along a line of greatest slope of the plane.

Particle $B$ hangs freely vertically below the pulley at a height of $h = 1.0\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground.

The system is released from rest with the string taut. When particle $B$ hits the ground, it does not rebound, and the string immediately becomes slack.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the system while particle $B$ is descending.

(b) Find the speed of particle $B$ at the instant it hits the ground.

(c) Calculate the further distance particle $A$ travels up the plane before coming to instantaneous rest, assuming $A$ does not reach the pulley.

(d) Find the total time elapsed from the release of the system until particle $A$ first comes to instantaneous rest.
steps:
(a) Acceleration while $B$ descends:

Component of weight of $A$ down the smooth plane:\begin{aligned} W_{A\parallel} &= 2g\sin 30^\circ \cr &= 2(9.8)(0.5) \cr &= 9.8\text{ N} \cr &= 1g\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Equations of motion for $B$ (downwards) and $A$ (upwards):\begin{aligned} &3g - T = 3a \cr &T - 1g = 2a \end{aligned}

Adding the equations:\begin{aligned} &2g = 5a \cr &a = 0.4g \cr &a = 0.4(9.8) \cr &a = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Speed at impact:

Particle $B$ descends from rest ($u = 0$) through $h = 1.0\text{ m}$ under acceleration $a = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2ah$:\begin{aligned} v^2 &= 0 + 2(3.92)(1.0) \cr &= 7.84 \cr v &= \sqrt{7.84} \cr &= 2.8\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Further distance travelled by $A$:

When $B$ hits the ground, the string goes slack ($T = 0$).

Particle $A$ moves up the smooth plane with initial speed $u = 2.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, retarded only by gravity:\begin{aligned} -2g\sin 30^\circ &= 2a' \cr a' &= -g\sin 30^\circ \cr &= -4.9\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2a's$ to find distance until instantaneous rest ($v = 0$):\begin{aligned} &0 = (2.8)^2 + 2(-4.9)s \cr &9.8s = 7.84 \cr &s = \dfrac{7.84}{9.8} \cr &s = 0.8\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Total time to rest:

Time for Stage 1 ($B$ descending):\begin{aligned} v &= at_1 \cr 2.8 &= 3.92t_1 \cr t_1 &= \dfrac{2.8}{3.92} \cr &= \dfrac{5}{7}\text{ s} \cr &\approx 0.714\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Time for Stage 2 ($A$ coasting to rest):\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2.8 - 4.9t_2 \cr 4.9t_2 &= 2.8 \cr t_2 &= \dfrac{2.8}{4.9} \cr &= \dfrac{4}{7}\text{ s} \cr &\approx 0.571\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Total time:\begin{aligned} T &= t_1 + t_2 \cr &= \dfrac{5}{7} + \dfrac{4}{7} \cr &= \dfrac{9}{7}\text{ s} \cr &\approx 1.29\text{ s} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect total time in part (d). $0.714\text{ s}$ is only the duration of the first stage while $B$ descends. You must add the second stage coasting duration ($t_2 = 0.571\text{ s}$) to obtain $1.29\text{ s}$.
Incorrect acceleration in part (a). The total mass accelerating is $m_A + m_B = 5\text{ kg}$, not $3\text{ kg}$, giving $a = 2g / 5 = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Incorrect distance in part (c). $1.8\text{ m}$ is the total distance travelled by $A$ from release ($1.0 + 0.8\text{ m}$); the question specifically asks for the further distance travelled after $B$ hits the ground ($0.8\text{ m}$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Energy Conservation for Coasting
bradley_insight.content: In part (c), because the plane is smooth, energy is conserved during the coasting phase after $B$ hits the ground. All kinetic energy of particle $A$ converts directly into gravitational potential energy: \begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{2}m v^2 &= m g \Delta h\cr & = m g (s \sin 30^\circ)\end{aligned} Thus \begin{aligned}s &= \dfrac{v^2}{2g\sin 30^\circ}\cr & = \dfrac{7.84}{9.8} \cr & = 0.8\text{ m}\end{aligned} avoiding kinematic equations entirely.

question:
A particle is in equilibrium under the action of three coplanar forces, given in newtons by:$$\mathbf{F}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 12 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{F}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 3p \ -4p \end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{F}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ q \end{pmatrix}$$where $p$ and $q$ are constants.

(a) Find the values of $p$ and $q$.

(b) The force $\mathbf{F}_1$ is suddenly removed. State the magnitude and direction of the resultant of the two remaining forces.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{F}_2$ and the acute angle it makes with the positive $x$-axis, giving the angle correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$.
steps:
(a) Equilibrium conditions:

Since the particle is in equilibrium, the vector sum of all forces is zero:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 = \mathbf{0} \cr &\begin{pmatrix} 12 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 3p \ -4p \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ q \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Equating top ($x$) components:\begin{aligned} &12 + 3p = 0 \cr &3p = -12 \cr &p = -4 \end{aligned}

Equating bottom ($y$) components:\begin{aligned} &0 - 4p + q = 0 \cr &-4(-4) + q = 0 \cr &16 + q = 0 \cr &q = -16 \end{aligned}

(b) Resultant of remaining forces:

From the equilibrium condition:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 = -\mathbf{F}_1 \end{aligned}

Therefore, the resultant force $\mathbf{R}$ is:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R} &= -\begin{pmatrix} 12 \ 0 \end{pmatrix} \cr &= \begin{pmatrix} -12 \ 0 \end{pmatrix}\text{ N} \end{aligned}

The resultant has magnitude $12\text{ N}$ and acts in the negative $x$-direction (due West / bearing $270^\circ$).

(c) Magnitude and angle of $\mathbf{F}_2$:

Substituting $p = -4$ into $\mathbf{F}_2$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_2 &= \begin{pmatrix} 3(-4) \ -4(-4) \end{pmatrix} \cr &= \begin{pmatrix} -12 \ 16 \end{pmatrix}\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Calculating magnitude:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{F}_2| &= \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 16^2} \cr &= \sqrt{144 + 256} \cr &= \sqrt{400} \cr &= 20\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Let $\alpha$ be the acute angle with the positive $x$-axis:\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \left|\dfrac{16}{-12}\right| \cr &= \dfrac{4}{3} \cr &\approx 1.3333 \cr \alpha &= \arctan(1.3333) \cr &\approx 53.1^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $p = -4, q = -16$, (b) $12\text{ N}$ due West, (c) $20\text{ N}, 53.1^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect sign for $q$. In vertical equilibrium, $-4(-4) + q = 0$ gives $16 + q = 0$, so $q = -16$.
Incorrect direction in part (b). The resultant of the remaining forces is equal and opposite to $\mathbf{F}_1$. Since $\mathbf{F}_1$ acts due East, the resultant must act due West.

Incorrect angle in part (c). The angle with the horizontal satisfies $\tan\alpha = \frac{16}{12} = \frac{4}{3}$, giving $\alpha \approx 53.1^\circ$. The value $36.9^\circ$ is measured from the vertical.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Equilibrium Removal Trick
bradley_insight.content: When a particle is in equilibrium under three forces, the resultant of any two forces is always exactly equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the third force: $\mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 = -\mathbf{F}_1$. Recognising this means part (b) requires zero calculation.

question:
A particle of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is initially in equilibrium under the action of three coplanar forces:$$\mathbf{F}_1 = (p\mathbf{i} + 2q\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_2 = \big((2p - 1)\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j}\big)\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_3 = \big(-8\mathbf{i} + (q - 7)\mathbf{j}\big)\text{ N}$$where $p$ and $q$ are constants, and $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are perpendicular horizontal unit vectors.

(a) By considering components in the $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ directions, find the values of $p$ and $q$.

The force $\mathbf{F}_3$ is now removed, while $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ continue to act unchanged.

(b) Find the acceleration vector of the particle.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of this acceleration and the angle its direction makes with the unit vector $\mathbf{i}$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Finding $p$ and $q$:

In equilibrium, $\Sigma \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}$.

Summing components in the $\mathbf{i}$ direction:\begin{aligned} &p + (2p - 1) - 8 = 0 \cr &3p - 9 = 0 \cr &3p = 9 \cr &p = 3 \end{aligned}

Summing components in the $\mathbf{j}$ direction:\begin{aligned} &2q - 5 + (q - 7) = 0 \cr &3q - 12 = 0 \cr &3q = 12 \cr &q = 4 \end{aligned}

(b) Acceleration vector:

When $\mathbf{F}_3$ is removed, the resultant force $\mathbf{R}$ is:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R} &= -\mathbf{F}_3 \cr &= -\big(-8\mathbf{i} + (4 - 7)\mathbf{j}\big) \cr &= -(-8\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (8\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Using Newton's second law ($\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$):\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{R}}{m} \cr &= \dfrac{8\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}}{2} \cr &= (4\mathbf{i} + 1.5\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Magnitude and angle of acceleration:

Calculating magnitude:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{a}| &= \sqrt{4^2 + 1.5^2} \cr &= \sqrt{16 + 2.25} \cr &= \sqrt{18.25} \cr &\approx 4.27\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Let $\theta$ be the angle with $\mathbf{i}$:\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{1.5}{4} \cr &= 0.375 \cr \theta &= \arctan(0.375) \cr &\approx 20.6^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $p = 3, q = 4$, (b) $(4\mathbf{i} + 1.5\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $4.27\text{ m s}^{-2}, 20.6^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: Forgot to divide by mass in part (b). Newton's second law is $\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{F}}{m}$. With $m = 2\text{ kg}$, the resultant force must be divided by $2$.
Incorrect angle reference in part (c). The angle with $\mathbf{i}$ satisfies $\tan\theta = 1.5 / 4$, giving $20.6^\circ$. The value $69.4^\circ$ is measured from $\mathbf{j}$.
Algebraic slip in part (a). Summing $\mathbf{i}$ components gives $p + 2p - 1 - 8 = 0$, which leads to $3p = 9$ and $p = 3$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Component Independence
bradley_insight.content: In Cartesian vector mechanics, motion in the $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ directions is completely independent. Equilibrium must hold separately in both axes. Never attempt to combine coefficients from $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ into a single equation.

topic: Newton's Second Law and Vector Kinematics
question:
A particle of mass $1.5\text{ kg}$ is initially at rest at the origin. It is acted upon by three constant coplanar forces:$$\mathbf{F}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \ -1 \end{pmatrix}\text{ N}$$ $$ \mathbf{F}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -3 \ 5 \end{pmatrix}\text{ N}$$ $$\text{and} \quad \mathbf{F}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} k \ -4 \end{pmatrix}\text{ N}$$ where $k$ is a constant.

(a) Given that the particle remains at rest in equilibrium, find the value of $k$.

In a different scenario, the force $\mathbf{F}_3$ is replaced by a force $\mathbf{F}_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{pmatrix}\text{ N}$, while $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ remain unchanged. The particle starts from rest at $t = 0$.

(b) Find the acceleration vector of the particle.

(c) Find the speed of the particle at time $t = 3\text{ seconds}$, giving your answer in exact surd form.

(d) Find the position vector of the particle at time $t = 3\text{ seconds}$, and calculate its distance from the origin.
steps:
(a) Finding $k$ for equilibrium:

Equating the sum of $x$-components to zero:\begin{aligned} &5 + (-3) + k = 0 \cr &2 + k = 0 \cr &k = -2 \end{aligned}

(Checking $y$-components: $-1 + 5 - 4 = 0$, which is consistent).

(b) Acceleration vector with $\mathbf{F}_4$:

The new resultant force $\mathbf{R}$ is:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R} &= \begin{pmatrix} 5 \ -1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} -3 \ 5 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{pmatrix} \cr &= \begin{pmatrix} 5 - 3 + 1 \ -1 + 5 + 2 \end{pmatrix} \cr &= \begin{pmatrix} 3 \ 6 \end{pmatrix}\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Using $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$ with $m = 1.5\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= \dfrac{1}{1.5}\begin{pmatrix} 3 \ 6 \end{pmatrix} \cr &= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \ 4 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Speed at $t = 3\text{ seconds}$:

Using $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$ with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v} &= \mathbf{0} + 3\begin{pmatrix} 2 \ 4 \end{pmatrix} \cr &= \begin{pmatrix} 6 \ 12 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Calculating speed:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{v}| &= \sqrt{6^2 + 12^2} \cr &= \sqrt{36 + 144} \cr &= \sqrt{180} \cr &= 6\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(d) Position vector and distance:

Using $\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \ 4 \end{pmatrix}(3^2) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \ 4 \end{pmatrix}(9) \cr &= \begin{pmatrix} 9 \ 18 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Distance from origin:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{r}| &= \sqrt{9^2 + 18^2} \cr &= \sqrt{81 + 324} \cr &= \sqrt{405} \cr &= 9\sqrt{5}\text{ m} \cr &\approx 20.1\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $k = -2$, (b) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \ 4 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $6\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (d) $\begin{pmatrix} 9 \ 18 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m}, 9\sqrt{5}\text{ m}$

pi_options.ans: (a) $k = -2$, (b) $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \ 6 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $9\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (d) $\begin{pmatrix} 13.5 \ 27 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m}, 13.5\sqrt{5}\text{ m}$
pi_options.feedback: Forgot to divide by mass $m = 1.5\text{ kg}$ in part (b). Acceleration is $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{F} / m$, so each component of the resultant force must be divided by $1.5$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $k = 2$, (b) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \ 4 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $6\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (d) $\begin{pmatrix} 9 \ 18 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m}, 9\sqrt{5}\text{ m}$
pi_options.feedback: Sign error in part (a). Setting $5 - 3 + k = 0$ gives $2 + k = 0$, so $k = -2$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $k = -2$, (b) $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \ 4 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $6\sqrt{5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (d) $\begin{pmatrix} 18 \ 36 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m}, 18\sqrt{5}\text{ m}$
pi_options.feedback: Omitted the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in the displacement formula $\mathbf{s} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$, which doubled the correct position vector.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Collinear Vectors in Kinematics
bradley_insight.content: When a particle starts from rest under a constant resultant force, its acceleration, velocity, and displacement vectors are always collinear. Notice that $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{v}$, and $\mathbf{r}$ are all positive multiples of the base vector $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

question:
A particle $P$ is held in equilibrium by three coplanar horizontal forces $\mathbf{F}_1$, $\mathbf{F}_2$, and $\mathbf{F}_3$:
$\mathbf{F}_1$ has magnitude $12\text{ N}$ and acts on a bearing of $090^\circ$ (due East).
$\mathbf{F}_2$ has magnitude $F\text{ N}$ and acts on a bearing of $330^\circ$.
$\mathbf{F}_3$ has magnitude $G\text{ N}$ and acts on a bearing of $210^\circ$.

Let $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ denote unit vectors directed due East and due North, respectively.

(a) Express each of the three forces in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$, using exact trigonometric values.

(b) By setting up and solving two linear equations for equilibrium, find the exact values of $F$ and $G$.

(c) State the geometrical name of the vector polygon formed by these three forces, fully justifying your answer.
steps:
(a) Resolving into unit vectors:

For $\mathbf{F}_1$ (bearing $090^\circ$, due East):\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_1 = 12\mathbf{i} \end{aligned}

For $\mathbf{F}_2$ (bearing $330^\circ$, which is $30^\circ$ West of North):\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_2 &= -F\sin 30^\circ\mathbf{i} + F\cos 30^\circ\mathbf{j} \cr &= -\dfrac{1}{2}F\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}F\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

For $\mathbf{F}_3$ (bearing $210^\circ$, which is $30^\circ$ West of South):\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_3 &= -G\sin 30^\circ\mathbf{i} - G\cos 30^\circ\mathbf{j} \cr &= -\dfrac{1}{2}G\mathbf{i} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}G\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

(b) Solving equilibrium equations:

In equilibrium, $\Sigma \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}$.

Summing North-South components ($\mathbf{j}$ direction):\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}F - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}G = 0 \cr &\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}F = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}G \cr &F = G \end{aligned}

Summing East-West components ($\mathbf{i}$ direction):\begin{aligned} &12 - \dfrac{1}{2}F - \dfrac{1}{2}G = 0 \end{aligned}

Substituting $G = F$:\begin{aligned} &12 - \dfrac{1}{2}F - \dfrac{1}{2}F = 0 \cr &12 - F = 0 \cr &F = 12\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Since $G = F$, $G = 12\text{ N}$.

(c) Vector polygon:

The forces form a closed equilateral triangle.

Justification: The three forces are in equilibrium, so they form a closed triangle of vectors. Since all three forces have equal magnitude ($12\text{ N}$), the triangle has three sides of equal length.
Final Answer: (b) $F = 12\text{ N}, G = 12\text{ N}$, (c) Equilateral triangle

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect polygon classification in part (c). All three forces have identical magnitude ($12\text{ N}$), so the closed vector triangle has three equal sides, making it an equilateral triangle.
Incorrect force magnitudes in part (b). In horizontal equilibrium, $12 - 0.5F - 0.5G = 0$ simplifies with $F = G$ to $12 - F = 0$, giving $F = 12\text{ N}$, not $6\text{ N}$.
Incorrect values in part (b). Resolving in the $\mathbf{j}$ direction gives $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}F - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}G = 0$, which strictly requires $F = G$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Symmetry in Three-Force Equilibrium
bradley_insight.content: The three bearings are $090^\circ$, $210^\circ$, and $330^\circ$. The angular separation between consecutive vectors is exactly $120^\circ$. By symmetry, three coplanar forces separated by $120^\circ$ must have equal magnitudes to remain in equilibrium.

question:
A particle of mass $2.5\text{ kg}$ is acted upon by three constant coplanar forces:$$\mathbf{F}_1 = (5\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_2 = (-2\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$$$\mathbf{F}_3 = (p\mathbf{i} + q\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$$where $p$ and $q$ are constants.

(a) Find the values of $p$ and $q$ for which the particle is in equilibrium.

In a second situation, $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ act as before, but $\mathbf{F}_3$ is replaced by $\mathbf{F}_4 = (7\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$.
At time $t = 0$, the particle is released from rest at the point with position vector $\mathbf{r}_0 = (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$.

(b) Find the resultant force acting on the particle, and hence determine its acceleration vector.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration and the angle its direction makes with the unit vector $\mathbf{i}$, correct to the nearest $0.1^\circ$.

(d) Find the velocity vector and speed of the particle when $t = 4\text{ seconds}$.

(e) Find the position vector of the particle when $t = 4\text{ seconds}$.
steps:
(a) Values for equilibrium:

In equilibrium, $\Sigma \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}$.

Equating $\mathbf{i}$ components:\begin{aligned} &5 - 2 + p = 0 \cr &3 + p = 0 \cr &p = -3 \end{aligned}

Equating $\mathbf{j}$ components:\begin{aligned} &3 + 7 + q = 0 \cr &10 + q = 0 \cr &q = -10 \end{aligned}

(b) Resultant force and acceleration:

Summing the three forces with $\mathbf{F}_4$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R} &= (5 - 2 + 7)\mathbf{i} + (3 + 7 - 5)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (10\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Using Newton's second law with $m = 2.5\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{R}}{m} \cr &= \dfrac{10\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}}{2.5} \cr &= (4\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Magnitude and angle of acceleration:

Calculating magnitude:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{a}| &= \sqrt{4^2 + 2^2} \cr &= \sqrt{16 + 4} \cr &= \sqrt{20} \cr &= 2\sqrt{5} \cr &\approx 4.47\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Angle $\theta$ with unit vector $\mathbf{i}$:\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{2}{4} \cr &= 0.5 \cr \theta &= \arctan(0.5) \cr &\approx 26.6^\circ \end{aligned}

(d) Velocity and speed at $t = 4\text{ seconds}$:

Using $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{a}t$ with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v} &= 4(4\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (16\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Calculating speed:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{v}| &= \sqrt{16^2 + 8^2} \cr &= \sqrt{256 + 64} \cr &= \sqrt{320} \cr &= 8\sqrt{5} \cr &\approx 17.9\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(e) Position vector at $t = 4\text{ seconds}$:

Using $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{u}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r} &= (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) + \mathbf{0} + \dfrac{1}{2}(4\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})(4^2) \cr &= (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) + 8(4\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) + (32\mathbf{i} + 16\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (36\mathbf{i} + 14\mathbf{j})\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (a) $p = -3, q = -10$, (b) $\mathbf{a} = (4\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $4.47\text{ m s}^{-2}, 26.6^\circ$, (d) $17.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (e) $(36\mathbf{i} + 14\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$

pi_options.ans: (a) $p = -3, q = -10$, (b) $\mathbf{a} = (4\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $4.47\text{ m s}^{-2}, 26.6^\circ$, (d) $17.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (e) $(32\mathbf{i} + 16\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$
pi_options.feedback: Forgot the initial position vector $\mathbf{r}_0 = (4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$. Position is $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{s}$, which gives $(4\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) + (32\mathbf{i} + 16\mathbf{j}) = (36\mathbf{i} + 14\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $p = 3, q = 10$, (b) $\mathbf{a} = (4\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $4.47\text{ m s}^{-2}, 26.6^\circ$, (d) $17.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (e) $(36\mathbf{i} + 14\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$
pi_options.feedback: Sign errors in part (a). In equilibrium, $5 - 2 + p = 0$ gives $p = -3$, and $3 + 7 + q = 0$ gives $q = -10$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $p = -3, q = -10$, (b) $\mathbf{a} = (4\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $4.47\text{ m s}^{-2}, 63.4^\circ$, (d) $17.9\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (e) $(36\mathbf{i} + 14\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$
pi_options.feedback: Angle measured from $\mathbf{j}$ instead of $\mathbf{i}$ in part (c). The angle with $\mathbf{i}$ satisfies $\tan\theta = 2 / 4 = 0.5$, which yields $\theta \approx 26.6^\circ$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Displacement vs Position Vector
bradley_insight.content: Remember the distinction between displacement $\mathbf{s}$ and position vector $\mathbf{r}$. The SUVAT formula evaluates displacement from the starting point: $\mathbf{s} = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$. When the particle does not start at the origin, you must add the initial position vector: $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}_0 + \mathbf{s}$.

question:
The diagram shows a block of mass $3m\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal table and a particle of mass $m\text{ kg}$ hanging freely. The two bodies are connected by a light inextensible string which passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table. The section of string between the block and the pulley is horizontal.

The system is released from rest with the string taut. During the subsequent motion, the friction force between the table and the block has magnitude $\dfrac{1}{4}mg\text{ N}$.

(a) Find an expression in terms of $g$ for the acceleration of the system.

(b) Find an expression in terms of $m$ and $g$ for the tension in the string.

(c) State how the assumption that the pulley is smooth has been used in your calculations.
steps:
(a) Finding acceleration $a$:

Let $a$ be the acceleration of the system and $T$ be the tension in the string.

Equation of motion for the hanging particle (downwards):\begin{aligned} mg - T = ma \quad \text{--- [Eq 1]} \end{aligned}

Equation of motion for the block on the table (towards pulley):\begin{aligned} &T - F = 3ma \cr &T - \dfrac{1}{4}mg = 3ma \quad \text{--- [Eq 2]} \end{aligned}

Adding [Eq 1] and [Eq 2]:\begin{aligned} &mg - \dfrac{1}{4}mg = 4ma \cr &\dfrac{3}{4}mg = 4ma \cr &a = \dfrac{3}{16}g \end{aligned}

(b) Finding tension $T$:
