Substituting $a = \dfrac{3}{16}g$ into [Eq 1]:\begin{aligned} T &= mg - ma \cr &= mg - m\left(\dfrac{3}{16}g\right) \cr &= mg\left(1 - \dfrac{3}{16}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{13}{16}mg \end{aligned}

(c) Assumption about the pulley:

The assumption that the pulley is smooth means there is no friction at the pulley axle. Consequently, the tension $T$ is uniform throughout both sections of the string (the horizontal part and the vertical part).
Final Answer: (a) $\dfrac{3}{16}g$, (b) $\dfrac{13}{16}mg$

pi_options.feedback: Forgot the friction term when finding tension. From the block's equation, \begin{aligned}T &= 3ma + F \cr &= 3m\left(\frac{3}{16}g\right) + \frac{1}{4}mg \cr &= \frac{13}{16}mg\end{aligned}, not just $3ma$.
Forgot to include the hanging particle's mass in the total system mass. The total accelerating mass is $3m + m = 4m$, giving $\frac{3}{4}mg = 4ma$ and $a = \frac{3}{16}g$.
Incorrect sign in Newton's second law for the hanging mass. Since the particle accelerates downwards, $mg - T = ma$, so $T = m(g - a) = \frac{13}{16}mg$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Modelling Assumptions
bradley_insight.content: Exam boards frequently test modelling assumptions. Remember the distinct roles: a light string means tension is uniform along its length; an inextensible string means both particles share the same magnitude of acceleration; a smooth pulley ensures tension does not change across the pulley.

question:
The diagram shows a block $A$ of mass $M_1 = 5\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal table. Block $A$ is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a small smooth pulley at the edge of the table to a hanging particle $B$ of mass $M_2 = 3\text{ kg}$. The string from $A$ to the pulley is horizontal. The coefficient of friction between block $A$ and the table is $\mu = 0.2$.

An external horizontal force of magnitude $P\text{ N}$ acts on block $A$, directed away from the pulley.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the range of values of $P$ for which the system remains in static equilibrium with the string taut.

In a second scenario, the force $P$ is set to $10\text{ N}$ and the system is released from rest.

(b) Explain why block $A$ accelerates towards the pulley.

(c) Calculate:
(i) the magnitude of the acceleration of the system,
(ii) the tension in the string during this motion.
steps:
(a) Range of $P$ for static equilibrium:

For particle $B$ in equilibrium:\begin{aligned} T &= M_2 g \cr &= 3(9.8) \cr &= 29.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Normal reaction on block $A$:\begin{aligned} R &= 5g \cr &= 5(9.8) \cr &= 49\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Maximum frictional force:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{max}} &= \mu R \cr &= 0.2(49) \cr &= 9.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Case 1 (impending motion towards pulley): Friction acts away from the pulley:\begin{aligned} &P + F_{\text{max}} \ge T \cr &P + 9.8 \ge 29.4 \cr &P \ge 19.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Case 2 (impending motion away from pulley): Friction acts towards the pulley:\begin{aligned} &P \le T + F_{\text{max}} \cr &P \le 29.4 + 9.8 \cr &P \le 39.2\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Range for equilibrium: $19.6 \le P \le 39.2$.

(b) Justifying acceleration towards pulley:

When $P = 10\text{ N}$, the net force pulling away from the pulley (excluding friction) is $P = 10\text{ N}$.

The string tension attempting to pull $A$ towards the pulley is $29.4\text{ N}$.

The net driving force towards the pulley is:\begin{aligned} 29.4 - 10 = 19.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Since $19.4\text{ N} > F_{\text{max}} = 9.8\text{ N}$, friction is completely overcome, and block $A$ accelerates towards the pulley.

(c)(i) Magnitude of acceleration:

Since motion is towards the pulley, friction $F = 9.8\text{ N}$ acts away from the pulley.

Equations of motion:\begin{aligned} &B: 29.4 - T = 3a \cr &A: T - 10 - 9.8 = 5a \cr &A: T - 19.8 = 5a \end{aligned}

Adding the equations:\begin{aligned} &29.4 - 19.8 = 8a \cr &9.6 = 8a \cr &a = 1.2\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Tension in the string:

Using the equation for $B$:\begin{aligned} T &= 29.4 - 3a \cr &= 29.4 - 3(1.2) \cr &= 29.4 - 3.6 \cr &= 25.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $19.6 \le P \le 39.2$, (c)(i) $1.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c)(ii) $25.8\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Incorrect equilibrium range in part (a). The tension is $29.4\text{ N}$ and maximum friction is $9.8\text{ N}$, so equilibrium requires $29.4 - 9.8 \le P \le 29.4 + 9.8$, giving $19.6 \le P \le 39.2$.
Assumed static tension in part (c)(ii). Because the system accelerates downwards, $T = 3(g - a) = 25.8\text{ N}$, not $3g = 29.4\text{ N}$.
Divided the net force by the mass of block $A$ alone ($5\text{ kg}$) instead of the total system mass ($5 + 3 = 8\text{ kg}$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dual Direction Friction Limits
bradley_insight.content: Whenever an external force can vary, friction can act in either direction depending on which way motion impends. If $P$ is small, the hanging weight pulls the block right, so friction acts left ($P \ge T - F_{\text{max}}$). If $P$ is large, it pulls the block left, so friction acts right ($P \le T + F_{\text{max}}$).

question:
The diagram shows a block $B$ of mass $6\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal table. Light inextensible strings are attached to each side of block $B$:
One string passes over a small smooth pulley at the left edge of the table and supports a hanging particle $A$ of mass $1\text{ kg}$.
The second string passes over a small smooth pulley at the right edge of the table and supports a hanging particle $C$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$.

Both sections of string on the table are horizontal. The coefficient of friction between block $B$ and the table is $\mu = 0.2$. The system is released from rest with all sections of string taut.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Determine whether the system moves, and if so, state the direction of motion of block $B$, fully justifying your answer.

(b) Calculate the acceleration of the system.

(c) Calculate:
(i) the tension in the string connected to particle $A$,
(ii) the tension in the string connected to particle $C$.
steps:
(a) Determining motion and direction:

Normal reaction on block $B$:\begin{aligned} R_B &= 6g \cr &= 6(9.8) \cr &= 58.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Maximum friction on $B$:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{max}} &= \mu R_B \cr &= 0.2(58.8) \cr &= 11.76\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Pull to the right from $C$ is $3g = 29.4\text{ N}$.
Pull to the left from $A$ is $1g = 9.8\text{ N}$.

Net external driving force to the right:\begin{aligned} 29.4 - 9.8 = 19.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Since $19.6\text{ N} > F_{\text{max}} = 11.76\text{ N}$, the system moves. Block $B$ accelerates to the right (towards pulley $C$).

(b) Calculating acceleration:

Total mass of the system:\begin{aligned} m_{\text{tot}} &= 1 + 6 + 3 \cr &= 10\text{ kg} \end{aligned}

Net resultant force driving the system:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{net}} &= 29.4 - 9.8 - 11.76 \cr &= 7.84\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Using Newton's second law:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{F_{\text{net}}}{m_{\text{tot}}} \cr &= \dfrac{7.84}{10} \cr &= 0.784\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculating tensions:

(i) Tension $T_A$: Particle $A$ accelerates upwards at $a = 0.784\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} T_A - 1g &= 1a \cr T_A &= 9.8 + 1(0.784) \cr &= 10.584\text{ N} \cr &\approx 10.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(ii) Tension $T_C$: Particle $C$ accelerates downwards at $a = 0.784\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} 3g - T_C &= 3a \cr T_C &= 3(9.8) - 3(0.784) \cr &= 29.4 - 2.352 \cr &= 27.048\text{ N} \cr &\approx 27.0\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Moves to the right, (b) $0.784\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c)(i) $10.6\text{ N}$, (c)(ii) $27.0\text{ N}$

pi_options.ans: (a) Remains at rest, (b) $0\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c)(i) $9.8\text{ N}$, (c)(ii) $29.4\text{ N}$
pi_options.feedback: Incorrect conclusion in part (a). The difference between the hanging weights is $29.4 - 9.8 = 19.6\text{ N}$, which strictly exceeds the maximum friction $11.76\text{ N}$, so motion must occur.

pi_options.ans: (a) Moves to the right, (b) $0.784\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c)(i) $27.0\text{ N}$, (c)(ii) $10.6\text{ N}$
pi_options.feedback: Swapped the two tensions in part (c). $T_C$ must exceed $T_A$ to accelerate block $B$ to the right, so $T_C \approx 27.0\text{ N}$ and $T_A \approx 10.6\text{ N}$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Moves to the right, (b) $1.31\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c)(i) $11.1\text{ N}$, (c)(ii) $25.5\text{ N}$
pi_options.feedback: Omitted the friction force on block $B$ when applying Newton's second law, dividing $19.6\text{ N}$ by $10\text{ kg}$ instead of $7.84\text{ N}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Two Separate Strings
bradley_insight.content: Never assume tension is equal across two separate strings. The string on the left has tension $T_A = 10.6\text{ N}$, while the string on the right has tension $T_C = 27.0\text{ N}$. They are completely distinct physical entities connected to opposite sides of block $B$.

question:
The diagram shows a block $A$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ on a rough horizontal table connected by a light inextensible string to a particle $B$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$. The string passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table. The coefficient of friction between block $A$ and the table is $\mu = 0.25$.

Particle $B$ is initially held at a height of $h = 0.9\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground.

The system is released from rest with the string taut. When particle $B$ hits the ground, it does not rebound, and the string immediately becomes slack. Block $A$ continues to slide along the table without reaching the pulley.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the system while particle $B$ is descending.

(b) Find the speed of particle $B$ at the instant it hits the ground.

(c) Calculate the deceleration of block $A$ after the string becomes slack.

(d) Calculate the total distance travelled by block $A$ from the instant of release until it first comes to rest.
steps:
(a) Acceleration during Stage 1:

Normal reaction on block $A$ is $R = 3g = 29.4\text{ N}$.

Frictional force on block $A$:\begin{aligned} F &= \mu R \cr &= 0.25(29.4) \cr &= 7.35\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Equations of motion for $B$ (downwards) and $A$ (towards pulley):\begin{aligned} &2g - T = 2a \cr &T - 7.35 = 3a \end{aligned}

Adding the equations:\begin{aligned} &2(9.8) - 7.35 = 5a \cr &19.6 - 7.35 = 5a \cr &12.25 = 5a \cr &a = 2.45\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Speed at impact:

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$ and $s = 0.9\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} v^2 &= 0 + 2(2.45)(0.9) \cr &= 4.41 \cr v &= \sqrt{4.41} \cr &= 2.1\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Deceleration during Stage 2:

When $B$ hits the floor, the string goes slack ($T = 0$).

Block $A$ is retarded solely by its own friction:\begin{aligned} -F &= m_A a' \cr -7.35 &= 3a' \cr a' &= -2.45\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

The deceleration is $2.45\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(d) Total distance travelled by $A$:

Distance in Stage 1 is $s_1 = 0.9\text{ m}$.

For Stage 2, $u = 2.1\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0$, and $a' = -2.45\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} v^2 &= u^2 + 2a's_2 \cr 0 &= (2.1)^2 + 2(-2.45)s_2 \cr 4.9s_2 &= 4.41 \cr s_2 &= \dfrac{4.41}{4.9} \cr &= 0.9\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Total distance travelled:\begin{aligned} s_{\text{tot}} &= s_1 + s_2 \cr &= 0.9 + 0.9 \cr &= 1.8\text{ m} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Gave only the second stage coasting distance in part (d). The question asks for the total distance travelled from the moment of release: $s_{\text{tot}} = 0.9 + 0.9 = 1.8\text{ m}$.
Omitted the mass of block $A$ when finding acceleration in part (a), using mass $2\text{ kg}$ instead of total system mass $5\text{ kg}$.
Incorrect mass in Stage 2. Once $B$ hits the floor, only block $A$ ($3\text{ kg}$) is decelerated by friction, so $a' = -7.35 / 3 = -2.45\text{ m s}^{-2}$, not $-7.35 / 5$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Work-Energy Check on Flat Surfaces
bradley_insight.content: For this entire journey, the work done by gravity on particle $B$ must equal the total work done against friction by block $A$: $m_B g h = F s_{\text{tot}}$. Rearranging gives $s_{\text{tot}} = \dfrac{m_B g h}{\mu m_A g} = \dfrac{2(0.9)}{0.25(3)} = 1.8\text{ m}$, verifying your multi-stage kinematics in a single line.

question:
The diagram shows a block $P$ of mass $5\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal table where the coefficient of friction is $\mu = 0.3$. Block $P$ is connected by a light inextensible string passing over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table to a scale pan $Q$ of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$. A block $R$ of mass $2.5\text{ kg}$ rests on top of the scale pan $Q$.

The section of string between block $P$ and the pulley is horizontal. The system is released from rest with the string taut.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the acceleration of the system.

(b) Find the tension in the string during the motion.

(c) By considering the vertical forces acting on block $R$ alone, calculate the magnitude of the normal reaction force exerted by the scale pan $Q$ on block $R$.

(d) Explain physically why the normal reaction force found in part (c) is strictly less than the weight of block $R$.
steps:
(a) Finding system acceleration:

Normal reaction on block $P$ is $R_P = 5g = 49\text{ N}$.

Frictional force on block $P$:\begin{aligned} F &= \mu R_P \cr &= 0.3(49) \cr &= 14.7\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Total mass hanging vertically:\begin{aligned} m_{\text{hang}} &= m_Q + m_R \cr &= 0.5 + 2.5 \cr &= 3.0\text{ kg} \end{aligned}

Equations of motion for hanging system and block $P$:\begin{aligned} &3g - T = 3a \cr &T - 14.7 = 5a \end{aligned}

Adding the equations:\begin{aligned} &3(9.8) - 14.7 = 8a \cr &29.4 - 14.7 = 8a \cr &14.7 = 8a \cr &a = 1.8375\text{ m s}^{-2} \cr &\approx 1.84\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Finding tension $T$:

Using the equation for block $P$:\begin{aligned} T &= 14.7 + 5a \cr &= 14.7 + 5(1.8375) \cr &= 14.7 + 9.1875 \cr &= 23.8875\text{ N} \cr &\approx 23.9\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Normal reaction on block $R$:

Consider vertical forces on block $R$ ($m_R = 2.5\text{ kg}$) accelerating downwards at $a = 1.8375\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} &m_R g - R_N = m_R a \cr &2.5(9.8) - R_N = 2.5(1.8375) \cr &24.5 - R_N = 4.59375 \cr &R_N = 24.5 - 4.59375 \cr &R_N = 19.90625\text{ N} \cr &R_N \approx 19.9\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(d) Physical explanation:

The scale pan $Q$ is accelerating downwards. For block $R$ to accelerate downwards at the same rate, there must be a non-zero resultant force downwards. Therefore, the downward gravitational force (its weight) must be strictly greater than the upward contact force exerted by the scale pan ($W_R - R_N = m_R a > 0$).
Final Answer: (a) $1.84\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $23.9\text{ N}$, (c) $19.9\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Assumed the normal reaction equals the static weight of $R$ ($2.5g = 24.5\text{ N}$). Because the scale pan is accelerating downwards, the contact force is reduced: $R_N = m_R(g - a) \approx 19.9\text{ N}$.
Added the acceleration term instead of subtracting it. Downward acceleration requires $m_R g - R_N = m_R a$, which gives $R_N = m_R(g - a)$, not $m_R(g + a)$.
Omitted the mass of the scale pan $Q$ ($0.5\text{ kg}$) from the hanging system, using $2.5\text{ kg}$ instead of $3.0\text{ kg}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Contact Forces in Accelerating Frames
bradley_insight.content: Always isolate the body when finding internal contact forces. A common exam mistake is trying to evaluate $R_N$ from the tension $T$. By drawing a separate free-body diagram for block $R$ alone, you see only two vertical forces: downward gravity $m_R g$ and upward normal reaction $R_N$, giving $m_R g - R_N = m_R a$ directly.

topic: Newton's Second Law and Motion in a Straight Line
question:
A model boat of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is propelled across a pond, starting from rest, for $3\text{ seconds}$. During this time, the boat moves in a straight line with a constant acceleration of $2\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Subsequently, the propeller stops, and the only horizontal force acting on the boat is a constant resistance to motion. The boat travels a further $12\text{ m}$ before coming to rest.

(a) Find the speed of the boat at the instant the propeller stops.

(b) Find the distance travelled by the boat during the $3\text{ seconds}$ of propulsion.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of the constant resistance to motion.

(d) Find the total distance travelled by the boat from rest until it comes to rest again.
steps:
(a) Speed at end of propulsion phase:

Using $v = u + at$ with $u = 0$, $a = 2\text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $t = 3\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} v &= 0 + 2(3) \cr &= 6\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Distance during propulsion phase:

Using $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= 0(3) + \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(3^2) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(9) \cr &= 9\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Magnitude of resistance to motion:

For the second phase, $u = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $s_2 = 12\text{ m}$.

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 6^2 + 2a(12) \cr &0 = 36 + 24a \cr &24a = -36 \cr &a = -1.5\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Using Newton's second law ($F = ma$) with $m = 2\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} -R &= 2(-1.5) \cr -R &= -3 \cr R &= 3\text{ N} \end{aligned}

The magnitude of the resistance is $3\text{ N}$.

(d) Total distance travelled:

Adding the distances from both phases:\begin{aligned} s_{\text{tot}} &= s_1 + s_2 \cr &= 9 + 12 \cr &= 21\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b) $9\text{ m}$, (c) $3\text{ N}$, (d) $21\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: You gave only the distance travelled during the coasting phase. The question asks for the total distance from rest until the boat stops again, which is $9 + 12 = 21\text{ m}$.

You forgot the factor of $2$ in the denominator of $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$. The deceleration is\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{6^2}{2(12)} \cr &= 1.5\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}giving $R = 2(1.5) = 3\text{ N}$, not $6\text{ N}$.
You halved the acceleration during the propulsion phase. The acceleration is $2\text{ m s}^{-2}$ for $3\text{ seconds}$, so the speed reached is $v = 2(3) = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Work-Energy Alternative
bradley_insight.content: In part (c), you can bypass calculating acceleration by applying the work-energy principle. The kinetic energy lost during the second phase equals the work done against the resistance force:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}m v^2 &= R s_2 \cr \dfrac{1}{2}(2)(6^2) &= R(12) \cr 36 &= 12R \cr R &= 3\text{ N} \end{aligned}This method is fast, clean, and avoids sign errors entirely.

topic: Newton's Second Law and Motion in a Straight Line
question:
A sledge of mass $20\text{ kg}$ is pushed from rest along a horizontal surface by a constant horizontal driving force of magnitude $48\text{ N}$. A constant frictional resistance of $12\text{ N}$ opposes the motion.

The sledge is pushed for $4\text{ seconds}$, after which the driving force is removed. The sledge continues to slide in the same straight line against the same constant resistance of $12\text{ N}$ until it comes to rest.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the sledge during the first $4\text{ seconds}$.

(b) Find the speed of the sledge at the instant the driving force is removed.

(c) Calculate the deceleration of the sledge after the driving force is removed.

(d) Calculate the total distance travelled by the sledge from rest to rest.

(e) Find the total time elapsed for the entire motion.
steps:
(a) Acceleration during Phase 1:

Net driving force acting on the sledge:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{net}} &= 48 - 12 \cr &= 36\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Using $F = ma$ with $m = 20\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} a_1 &= \dfrac{36}{20} \cr &= 1.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Speed when driving force is removed:

Using $v = u + at$ with $u = 0$:\begin{aligned} v &= 0 + 1.8(4) \cr &= 7.2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Deceleration during Phase 2:

When the driving force is removed, the only horizontal force is the $12\text{ N}$ resistance opposing motion:\begin{aligned} -12 &= 20a_2 \cr a_2 &= -0.6\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

The deceleration is $0.6\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(d) Total distance travelled:

Distance for Phase 1 ($0 \le t \le 4$):\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1.8)(4^2) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1.8)(16) \cr &= 14.4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Distance for Phase 2 using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 7.2^2 + 2(-0.6)s_2 \cr &0 = 51.84 - 1.2s_2 \cr &1.2s_2 = 51.84 \cr &s_2 = 43.2\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Total distance:\begin{aligned} s_{\text{tot}} &= s_1 + s_2 \cr &= 14.4 + 43.2 \cr &= 57.6\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(e) Total time elapsed:

Duration of Phase 1 is $t_1 = 4\text{ s}$.

For Phase 2, using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 7.2 - 0.6t_2 \cr &0.6t_2 = 7.2 \cr &t_2 = 12\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Total time:\begin{aligned} T &= t_1 + t_2 \cr &= 4 + 12 \cr &= 16\text{ s} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You calculated the distance and time for the coasting phase only. You must include the first phase ($14.4\text{ m}$ and $4\text{ s}$) to give $57.6\text{ m}$ and $16\text{ s}$.
You forgot to subtract the friction force when finding the acceleration in part (a). The resultant driving force is $48 - 12 = 36\text{ N}$, giving $a = 36 / 20 = 1.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
You found the time for the second stage ($12\text{ s}$) but forgot to add the $4\text{ seconds}$ from the first stage, giving a total time of $16\text{ s}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Acceleration Ratio and Time
bradley_insight.content: Notice the relationship between the accelerations and times in the two phases. The acceleration in Phase 1 is $1.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$, which is exactly $3$ times the deceleration in Phase 2 ($0.6\text{ m s}^{-2}$). Because the change in speed is identical, the time taken to stop must be exactly $3$ times the accelerating time: $t_2 = 3 \times 4 = 12\text{ s}$.

topic: Newton's Second Law and Motion in a Straight Line
question:
A small electric car of mass $1200\text{ kg}$ moves along a straight horizontal test track in three stages:
Stage 1: It accelerates uniformly from rest to a speed of $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ over a distance of $75\text{ m}$.
Stage 2: It continues at this constant speed of $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ for a distance of $225\text{ m}$.
Stage 3: The brakes are applied, providing a constant total retarding force of $3600\text{ N}$ until the car comes to rest.

(a) Find the acceleration of the car and the net driving force acting on it during Stage 1.

(b) Find the time taken to complete Stage 2.

(c) Calculate the distance travelled by the car during Stage 3 while braking to rest.

(d) Calculate the total time taken for the car to complete the entire journey from start to rest.
steps:
(a) Stage 1 acceleration and driving force:

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$, $v = 15\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $s_1 = 75\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &15^2 = 0 + 2a_1(75) \cr &225 = 150a_1 \cr &a_1 = 1.5\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Net driving force using $F = ma$:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{net}} &= 1200(1.5) \cr &= 1800\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Time for Stage 2:

Travelling at constant speed $v = 15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ for $s_2 = 225\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} t_2 &= \dfrac{s_2}{v} \cr &= \dfrac{225}{15} \cr &= 15\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Distance travelled during Stage 3:

Using Newton's second law for braking with $F = -3600\text{ N}$:\begin{aligned} a_3 &= \dfrac{-3600}{1200} \cr &= -3\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 15\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 15^2 + 2(-3)s_3 \cr &0 = 225 - 6s_3 \cr &6s_3 = 225 \cr &s_3 = 37.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Total journey time:

Time for Stage 1:\begin{aligned} t_1 &= \dfrac{v - u}{a_1} \cr &= \dfrac{15 - 0}{1.5} \cr &= 10\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Time for Stage 3:\begin{aligned} t_3 &= \dfrac{0 - 15}{-3} \cr &= 5\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Total time:\begin{aligned} T &= t_1 + t_2 + t_3 \cr &= 10 + 15 + 5 \cr &= 30\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}, 1800\text{ N}$, (b) $15\text{ s}$, (c) $37.5\text{ m}$, (d) $30\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: You omitted the $10\text{ seconds}$ from Stage 1 when calculating the total journey time. The total time is $10 + 15 + 5 = 30\text{ s}$.
You omitted the factor of $2$ in $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ during Stage 3. The braking distance is\begin{aligned} s_3 &= \dfrac{15^2}{2(3)} \cr &= 37.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}
You calculated acceleration in Stage 1 as $v^2 / s$ instead of $v^2 / (2s)$. The acceleration is $225 / 150 = 1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Checking via Area under the Graph
bradley_insight.content: A velocity-time graph for this journey forms a trapezium with parallel sides of length $30\text{ s}$ and $15\text{ s}$ and height $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$. You can check the total distance in a single step using the trapezium area formula:\begin{aligned} s_{\text{tot}} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(30 + 15)(15) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(45)(15) \cr &= 337.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}This matches $75 + 225 + 37.5 = 337.5\text{ m}$.

topic: Motion under Gravity and Newton's Second Law
question:
A model rocket of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is launched vertically upwards from rest from the ground. Its engine produces a constant upward thrust of $9.8\text{ N}$. The engine burns for $2\text{ seconds}$ and then cuts out. Air resistance is assumed to be negligible throughout the flight.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the rocket while the engine is burning.

(b) Find the height of the rocket above the ground and its speed at the instant of engine burnout.

(c) Calculate the maximum height above the ground reached by the rocket.

(d) Find the total time elapsed from launch until the rocket returns to the ground, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Acceleration during powered ascent:

Weight of the rocket:\begin{aligned} W &= mg \cr &= 0.5(9.8) \cr &= 4.9\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Net upward force while engine fires:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{net}} &= T - mg \cr &= 9.8 - 4.9 \cr &= 4.9\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Using $F = ma$:\begin{aligned} a_1 &= \dfrac{4.9}{0.5} \cr &= 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Height and speed at burnout:

Burnout occurs at $t = 2\text{ s}$. Speed attained:\begin{aligned} v_1 &= 0 + 9.8(2) \cr &= 19.6\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Height reached during powered burn:\begin{aligned} h_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(2^2) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(9.8)(4) \cr &= 19.6\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Maximum height reached:

After burnout, the rocket moves freely under gravity with acceleration $a = -g = -9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 19.6^2 + 2(-9.8)h_2 \cr &0 = 384.16 - 19.6h_2 \cr &19.6h_2 = 384.16 \cr &h_2 = 19.6\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Maximum height above the ground:\begin{aligned} H_{\text{max}} &= h_1 + h_2 \cr &= 19.6 + 19.6 \cr &= 39.2\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Total flight time:

Time for powered phase is $t_1 = 2\text{ s}$.

For free flight after burnout, the rocket starts at height $19.6\text{ m}$ with upward velocity $u = 19.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and returns to the ground ($s = -19.6\text{ m}$):\begin{aligned} &s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 \cr &-19.6 = 19.6t_2 - 4.9t_2^2 \cr &4.9t_2^2 - 19.6t_2 - 19.6 = 0 \end{aligned}

Dividing through by $4.9$:\begin{aligned} &t_2^2 - 4t_2 - 4 = 0 \cr &t_2 = \dfrac{4 + \sqrt{(-4)^2 - 4(1)(-4)}}{2} \cr &t_2 = \dfrac{4 + \sqrt{32}}{2} \cr &t_2 = 2 + 2\sqrt{2} \cr &t_2 \approx 4.828\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Total flight time:\begin{aligned} T &= t_1 + t_2 \cr &= 2 + 4.828 \cr &\approx 6.83\text{ s} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You forgot to subtract the rocket's weight from the upward thrust. The resultant upward force during the burn is $9.8 - 4.9 = 4.9\text{ N}$, giving $a = 4.9 / 0.5 = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

You assumed the rocket reaches its maximum height at the instant of engine burnout. The rocket is still travelling upwards at $19.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ when the engine cuts out, gaining a further $19.6\text{ m}$ to reach $39.2\text{ m}$.
You omitted the initial $2\text{ seconds}$ of powered flight from your total time calculation: the total elapsed time from launch is $2 + 4.83 = 6.83\text{ s}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Thrust vs Resultant Force
bradley_insight.content: A very common error in vertical rocket problems is equating thrust directly to mass times acceleration ($T = ma$). Gravity never turns off: the upward thrust must both overcome the downward weight and provide the net force to accelerate the rocket ($T - mg = ma$).

topic: Newton's Second Law and Stopping Distances
question:
A car of mass $1000\text{ kg}$ is travelling along a straight horizontal road at a constant speed of $24\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The driver suddenly sees a hazard ahead and, after a reaction time of $0.6\text{ seconds}$, applies the brakes firmly. The brakes produce a constant retarding force of $4800\text{ N}$ until the car comes to rest.

(a) Calculate the thinking distance (the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time).

(b) Calculate the deceleration of the car while braking.

(c) Calculate the braking distance.

(d) State the total stopping distance of the car.

In an alternative scenario, the same car with the same driver is travelling at $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Assuming the driver's reaction time and the braking force remain unchanged:

(e) Calculate the new total stopping distance, and find the percentage increase in the stopping distance compared with your answer to part (d), correct to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Thinking distance:

During the reaction time, the car continues at constant speed $u = 24\text{ m s}^{-1}$:\begin{aligned} s_{\text{think}} &= u \times t_{\text{react}} \cr &= 24(0.6) \cr &= 14.4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(b) Deceleration while braking:

Using Newton's second law with retarding force $F = -4800\text{ N}$ and $m = 1000\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{-4800}{1000} \cr &= -4.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

The deceleration is $4.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(c) Braking distance:

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 24\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 24^2 + 2(-4.8)s_{\text{brake}} \cr &0 = 576 - 9.6s_{\text{brake}} \cr &9.6s_{\text{brake}} = 576 \cr &s_{\text{brake}} = 60\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Total stopping distance:

Adding thinking and braking distances:\begin{aligned} s_{\text{stop}} &= s_{\text{think}} + s_{\text{brake}} \cr &= 14.4 + 60 \cr &= 74.4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(e) New stopping distance and percentage increase:

At initial speed $u = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$:\begin{aligned} s'_{\text{think}} &= 30(0.6) \cr &= 18\text{ m} \end{aligned}

New braking distance:\begin{aligned} s'_{\text{brake}} &= \dfrac{30^2}{2(4.8)} \cr &= \dfrac{900}{9.6} \cr &= 93.75\text{ m} \end{aligned}

New total stopping distance:\begin{aligned} s'_{\text{stop}} &= 18 + 93.75 \cr &= 111.75\text{ m} \cr &\approx 112\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Percentage increase:\begin{aligned} \text{\PI} &= \dfrac{111.75 - 74.4}{74.4} \times 100 \cr &= \dfrac{37.35}{74.4} \times 100 \cr &\approx 50.2\% \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You forgot to include the thinking distance for the second scenario. At $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$, the thinking distance is $30(0.6) = 18\text{ m}$, giving a total stopping distance of $18 + 93.75 = 111.75\text{ m}$.
You omitted the thinking distance when finding total stopping distance in part (d). Stopping distance is thinking distance plus braking distance: $14.4 + 60 = 74.4\text{ m}$.

You assumed stopping distance scales directly with speed ($30 / 24 = 1.25$). While thinking distance is proportional to speed, braking distance is proportional to speed squared, resulting in a $50.2\%$ increase.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Non-Linear Stopping Scaling
bradley_insight.content: Notice why a modest $25\%$ speed increase (from $24\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$) causes a dramatic $50.2\%$ increase in stopping distance. Thinking distance scales linearly with speed ($s \propto u$), but braking distance scales quadratically ($s \propto u^2$) because braking distance depends on dissipating kinetic energy: $\dfrac{1}{2}m u^2 = F s$.

question:
Callum runs a distance of $60\text{ m}$ in $15\text{ s}$. He starts from rest and accelerates to a speed of $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$. He runs the remaining distance at a constant speed of $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Callum proposes a model in which his acceleration is constant until time $T\text{ seconds}$.

(a) Sketch the velocity-time graph for Callum's run using this model.

(b) Calculate the value of $T$.

(c) Find an expression for Callum's displacement $s\text{ metres}$ at time $t\text{ seconds}$ for $0 \le t \le T$.

(d) Use this model to find the time taken for Callum to run the first $15\text{ m}$.

Callum proposes a refined model in which his velocity during the acceleration phase is a quadratic function of $t$. The graph of this quadratic goes through $(0, 0)$ and has its maximum point (vertex) at $(S, 5)$. In this model, the acceleration phase lasts until time $S\text{ seconds}$, after which the velocity remains constant at $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(e) Sketch a velocity-time graph that represents Callum's run using this refined model.

(f) State, with a clear reason, whether $S$ is greater than $T$ or less than $T$.
steps:
(a) Velocity-time graph (Linear Model):

The graph increases linearly from $(0, 0)$ to $(T, 5)$ and then remains horizontal at $v = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ until $t = 15\text{ s}$.

(b) Calculating $T$:

The total distance of $60\text{ m}$ equals the area of the trapezium under the graph:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{2}\big(15 + (15 - T)\big)(5) = 60 \cr &\dfrac{1}{2}(30 - T)(5) = 60 \cr &(30 - T)(2.5) = 60 \cr &30 - T = 24 \cr &T = 6\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Expression for displacement $s(t)$:

The constant acceleration during the first $6\text{ seconds}$ is:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{5 - 0}{6} \cr &= \dfrac{5}{6}\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Using $s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$ with $u = 0$:\begin{aligned} s &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{5}{6}\right)t^2 \cr &= \dfrac{5}{12}t^2 \end{aligned}

(d) Time to run the first $15\text{ m}$:

Setting $s = 15$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{5}{12}t^2 = 15 \cr &5t^2 = 180 \cr &t^2 = 36 \cr &t = 6\text{ s} \end{aligned}

This occurs exactly at the end of the acceleration phase.

(e) & (f) Refined model and comparison:

The refined quadratic graph starts at the origin and curves smoothly with decreasing gradient, reaching a horizontal tangent at $(S, 5)$ before continuing horizontally.

In the linear model, the average speed while accelerating is $\dfrac{0 + 5}{2} = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$. In the quadratic model, the curve bulges upwards towards the top speed, giving a higher average speed during acceleration (specifically $\dfrac{2}{3} \times 5 \approx 3.33\text{ m s}^{-1}$).

However, replacing constant-speed running ($5\text{ m s}^{-1}$) with an accelerating phase lowers the distance covered per second. To maintain the same total area of $60\text{ m}$ over $15\text{ s}$, the duration of the acceleration phase must be longer. Therefore, $S > T$.
Final Answer: (b) $T = 6\text{ s}$, (c) $s = \dfrac{5}{12}t^2$, (d) $6\text{ s}$, (f) $S > T$

pi_options.feedback: You concluded that $S < T$. Because the average speed while accelerating ($\frac{10}{3}\text{ m s}^{-1}$) is less than the cruising speed ($5\text{ m s}^{-1}$), having a fuller quadratic acceleration curve means the acceleration phase must last longer ($S > T$) to balance the total area at $60\text{ m}$.

You made an error setting up the trapezium area. The parallel sides have lengths $15$ and $15 - T$, giving\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}(30 - T)(5) = 60 \end{aligned}which solves to $30 - T = 24$, so $T = 6\text{ s}$, not $3\text{ s}$.
You omitted the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in the displacement formula $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$. With $a = \frac{5}{6}\text{ m s}^{-2}$, the displacement expression is $s = \frac{5}{12}t^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Area Under Parabolic Profiles
bradley_insight.content: For a quadratic velocity curve that starts at the origin and levels off with zero gradient at its vertex $(S, v_{\text{max}})$, the area underneath is always exactly two-thirds of the enclosing rectangle:\begin{aligned} \text{Area} = \dfrac{2}{3} S v_{\text{max}} \end{aligned}Comparing this to the triangle area $\dfrac{1}{2} T v_{\text{max}}$ for constant acceleration confirms algebraically that $S$ must exceed $T$ to maintain the same total distance.

question:
A cyclist travels along a straight cycle path, covering a total distance of $102\text{ m}$ in $20\text{ s}$. The cyclist starts from rest, accelerates to a cruising speed of $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and maintains this speed for the remainder of the journey.

Model A: The acceleration is assumed to be constant from $t = 0$ to $t = T\text{ seconds}$.

(a) Calculate the value of $T$.

(b) Calculate the acceleration of the cyclist during this initial phase.

(c) Calculate the distance travelled by the cyclist during the first $4\text{ seconds}$.

Model B: A sports scientist proposes that the acceleration decreases continuously as speed builds. In this refined model, the acceleration phase lasts until time $S\text{ seconds}$, during which the velocity curve passes through $(0, 0)$ and has a horizontal tangent at $(S, 6)$, followed by constant velocity of $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(d) Sketch the velocity-time graph representing Model B.

(e) Given that the area under the velocity curve during the acceleration phase ($0 \le t \le S$) is $\dfrac{2}{3}(6S)$, determine whether $S > T$ or $S < T$, giving a full mathematical justification.
steps:
(a) Calculating $T$ in Model A:

The total area under the trapezium is $102\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{2}\big(20 + (20 - T)\big)(6) = 102 \cr &3(40 - T) = 102 \cr &40 - T = 34 \cr &T = 6\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Initial acceleration:

Using $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{6 - 0}{6} \cr &= 1\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Distance during first $4\text{ seconds}$:

Since $4 < T$, the cyclist is still accelerating uniformly:\begin{aligned} s &= \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1)(4^2) \cr &= 8\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Velocity-time graph for Model B:

The graph starts at the origin, curves upwards with decreasing gradient to a horizontal tangent at $(S, 6)$, and continues horizontally at $v = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ until $t = 20\text{ s}$.

(e) Comparing $S$ and $T$:

In Model B, the total distance is the sum of the acceleration area and the cruising area:\begin{aligned} &102 = \dfrac{2}{3}(6S) + 6(20 - S) \cr &102 = 4S + 120 - 6S \cr &102 = 120 - 2S \cr &2S = 18 \cr &S = 9\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Comparing the two values:\begin{aligned} 9 > 6 \implies S > T \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $T = 6\text{ s}$, (b) $1\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $8\text{ m}$, (e) $S > T$

pi_options.feedback: You concluded $S < T$. Solving the area equation for Model B gives\begin{aligned} 4S + 6(20 - S) = 102 \end{aligned}which yields $2S = 18$, so $S = 9\text{ s}$. Since $9 > 6$, $S$ is strictly greater than $T$.

You miscalculated the trapezium equation in part (a). The parallel sides are $20$ and $20 - T$, which gives \begin{aligned}3(40 - T) &= 102 \cr \implies 40 - T & = 34 \cr\implies T & = 6\text{ s}\end{aligned}
You calculated the distance using constant speed $s = vt = 6(2)$ or omitted the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in part (c). Under constant acceleration from rest, $s = \frac{1}{2}(1)(4^2) = 8\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Area Deficit Principle
bradley_insight.content: Notice why $S$ must exceed $T$. Every second spent accelerating rather than cruising at $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ creates a distance deficit. In Model B, the average speed during acceleration is $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$, which is closer to $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ than the linear average of $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$. To accumulate the required total distance, the curved phase must persist longer.

question:
A sprinter runs a $100\text{ m}$ race in $12\text{ s}$. The sprinter starts from rest, accelerates to a top speed of $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and maintains this top speed until crossing the finish line.

Model 1: The sprinter's acceleration is assumed to be constant until time $T\text{ seconds}$.

(a) Sketch the velocity-time graph for Model 1.

(b) Calculate the value of $T$.

(c) Calculate the distance run by the sprinter during the acceleration phase.

Model 2: A coach suggests that the sprinter's velocity during the acceleration phase $0 \le t \le S$ is better represented by a parabolic curve passing through $(0, 0)$ with vertex at $(S, 10)$, after which the speed remains constant at $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(d) Sketch the velocity-time graph for Model 2 on a separate set of axes.

(e) Explain, by considering the average speed during the acceleration phase or the area under the graph, whether $S$ must be greater than or less than $T$.
steps:
(a) Velocity-time graph for Model 1:

A straight line from $(0, 0)$ to $(T, 10)$, followed by a horizontal line from $(T, 10)$ to $(12, 10)$.

(b) Calculating $T$:

Using the trapezium area formula for total distance of $100\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{2}\big(12 + (12 - T)\big)(10) = 100 \cr &5(24 - T) = 100 \cr &24 - T = 20 \cr &T = 4\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Distance during acceleration:

The distance is the area of the initial triangle:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(4)(10) \cr &= 20\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Velocity-time graph for Model 2:

A concave-down curve from $(0, 0)$ reaching $(S, 10)$ with zero gradient, followed by a horizontal line at $v = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ until $t = 12\text{ s}$.

(e) Comparing $S$ and $T$:

In Model 1, the average speed during acceleration is $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$. In Model 2, the parabolic curve gives an average speed of $\dfrac{2}{3}(10) \approx 6.67\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Because the sprinter accelerates more efficiently under Model 2, running at this higher average speed rather than the constant top speed ($10\text{ m s}^{-1}$) reduces the total distance by $3.33\text{ m}$ for every second of acceleration.

Equating total distance to $100\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{20}{3}S + 10(12 - S) = 100 \cr &120 - \dfrac{10}{3}S = 100 \cr &\dfrac{10}{3}S = 20 \cr &S = 6\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Since $6 > 4$, $S > T$.
Final Answer: (b) $T = 4\text{ s}$, (c) $20\text{ m}$, (e) $S > T$

pi_options.feedback: You reasoned that because Model 2 is faster initially, the phase must be shorter. However, cruising at $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ covers more distance per second than accelerating. Setting up the area equation yields\begin{aligned} 120 - \dfrac{10}{3}S = 100 \end{aligned}which gives $S = 6\text{ s}$, meaning $S > T$.

You miscalculated the trapezium equation in part (b). The parallel sides are $12$ and $12 - T$, which gives \begin{aligned}5(24 - T) &= 100 \cr \implies 24 - T &= 20 \cr\implies T &= 4\text{ s}\ebd{aligned
You omitted the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ when finding the area of the acceleration triangle in part (c): $s_1 = \frac{1}{2}(4)(10) = 20\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Qualitative Comparison Traps
bradley_insight.content: Students often intuitively guess that a more rapid acceleration curve should lead to a shorter duration ($S < T$). Always test your intuition against the total area constraint: replacing top speed ($10\text{ m s}^{-1}$) with acceleration always creates an area deficit. A higher average acceleration speed means each second loses less area, so more seconds are required to balance the equation.

question:
A rowing boat travels a distance of $78.75\text{ m}$ across a calm lake in $20\text{ s}$. Starting from rest, the boat accelerates to its top cruising speed of $4.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and covers the remainder of the distance at this steady speed.

An initial model assumes the acceleration is constant until time $T\text{ seconds}$.

(a) Sketch the velocity-time graph for the boat using this model.

(b) Calculate the value of $T$.

(c) Find an expression in terms of $t$ for the displacement $s\text{ metres}$ of the boat for $0 \le t \le T$.

(d) Find the time taken for the boat to travel the first $11.25\text{ m}$.

An alternative model assumes the velocity during the acceleration phase ($0 \le t \le S$) is quadratic, passing through the origin and joining smoothly to the horizontal line $v = 4.5$ at $t = S$ with zero gradient.

(e) Sketch the velocity-time graph for this alternative model.

(f) State, with clear mathematical reasoning, whether $S$ is greater than or less than $T$.
steps:
(a) Velocity-time graph for initial model:

The graph increases linearly from $(0, 0)$ to $(T, 4.5)$, then remains horizontal at $v = 4.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ until $t = 20\text{ s}$.

(b) Calculating $T$:

Equating the area of the trapezium to $78.75\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{2}\big(20 + (20 - T)\big)(4.5) = 78.75 \cr &2.25(40 - T) = 78.75 \cr &40 - T = 35 \cr &T = 5\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Expression for displacement $s(t)$:

The constant acceleration is:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{4.5}{5} \cr &= 0.9\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Using $s = \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$:\begin{aligned} s &= \dfrac{1}{2}(0.9)t^2 \cr &= 0.45t^2 \end{aligned}

(d) Time to travel the first $11.25\text{ m}$:

Setting $s = 11.25$:\begin{aligned} &0.45t^2 = 11.25 \cr &t^2 = \dfrac{11.25}{0.45} \cr &t^2 = 25 \cr &t = 5\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(e) & (f) Alternative model and comparison:

The alternative graph curves smoothly from $(0, 0)$ to a vertex at $(S, 4.5)$, followed by a horizontal line.

In the quadratic model, the area under the acceleration curve is $\dfrac{2}{3}(4.5S) = 3S$.

Equating total distance to $78.75\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &3S + 4.5(20 - S) = 78.75 \cr &3S + 90 - 4.5S = 78.75 \cr &90 - 1.5S = 78.75 \cr &1.5S = 11.25 \cr &S = 7.5\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Comparing values:\begin{aligned} 7.5 > 5 \implies S > T \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $T = 5\text{ s}$, (c) $s = 0.45t^2$, (d) $5\text{ s}$, (f) $S > T$

pi_options.feedback: You concluded $S < T$. Solving the area equation for the quadratic model gives\begin{aligned} 90 - 1.5S = 78.75 \end{aligned}which yields $S = 7.5\text{ s}$. Since $7.5 > 5$, $S$ is strictly greater than $T$.
You miscalculated the trapezium equation in part (b). Setting $2.25(40 - T) = 78.75$ gives $40 - T = 35$, so $T = 5\text{ s}$.
You omitted the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in the displacement formula $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$. With $a = 0.9\text{ m s}^{-2}$, the displacement expression is $s = 0.45t^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Boundary Point Verification
bradley_insight.content: Notice in part (d) that the time to reach $11.25\text{ m}$ is exactly $t = 5\text{ s}$. This is the exact boundary where the acceleration phase ends ($T = 5\text{ s}$). If the question had asked for the time to reach $20\text{ m}$, using $s = 0.45t^2$ would be mathematically invalid because the model transitions to constant speed after $t = 5\text{ s}$.

question:
An ice skater travels along a straight track, covering a total distance of $120\text{ m}$ in $20\text{ s}$. The skater starts from rest, accelerates uniformly at $2\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to a maximum speed of $8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, glides at this constant speed for a period of time, and finally decelerates uniformly to rest. The deceleration phase takes $6\text{ seconds}$.

(a) Calculate the duration of the acceleration phase.

(b) Calculate the distance travelled by the skater during the acceleration phase.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration during the final phase, and find the distance travelled while decelerating.

(d) Find the time spent gliding at constant speed, and calculate the distance covered during this phase.

(e) Sketch the velocity-time graph for the skater's entire $20\text{ second}$ journey, clearly indicating the values of $t$ and $v$ at all transition points.
steps:
(a) Duration of acceleration phase:

Using $v = u + at$ with $u = 0$, $v = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $a = 2\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} 8 &= 0 + 2t_1 \cr t_1 &= 4\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Distance during acceleration:

Using $s_1 = \dfrac{u + v}{2}t_1$:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \left(\dfrac{0 + 8}{2}\right)(4) \cr &= 4(4) \cr &= 16\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Deceleration and distance during final phase:

For the final phase, $u = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $t_3 = 6\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} a_3 &= \dfrac{0 - 8}{6} \cr &= -\dfrac{4}{3}\text{ m s}^{-2} \cr &\approx -1.33\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

The magnitude of the deceleration is $1.33\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Distance decelerating:\begin{aligned} s_3 &= \left(\dfrac{8 + 0}{2}\right)(6) \cr &= 4(6) \cr &= 24\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(d) Gliding phase:

The distance covered during the gliding phase is:\begin{aligned} s_2 &= 120 - (s_1 + s_3) \cr &= 120 - (16 + 24) \cr &= 120 - 40 \cr &= 80\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Time spent gliding at constant speed $v = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$:\begin{aligned} t_2 &= \dfrac{s_2}{v} \cr &= \dfrac{80}{8} \cr &= 10\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(Checking total time: $t_1 + t_2 + t_3 = 4 + 10 + 6 = 20\text{ s}$).

(e) Velocity-time graph:

The graph consists of three line segments with transition coordinates $(0, 0)$, $(4, 8)$, $(14, 8)$, and $(20, 0)$.
Final Answer: (a) $4\text{ s}$, (b) $16\text{ m}$, (c) $1.33\text{ m s}^{-2}, 24\text{ m}$, (d) $10\text{ s}, 80\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: You subtracted the acceleration and deceleration distances incorrectly in part (d). The distance while gliding is $120 - (16 + 24) = 80\text{ m}$, not $40\text{ m}$.
You omitted the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ when evaluating the distances for the acceleration and deceleration stages, using $s = vt$ instead of $s = \frac{u + v}{2}t$.
You inverted the division when finding deceleration in part (c). The deceleration is\begin{aligned} a = \dfrac{8 - 0}{6} = 1.33\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}not $6 / 8 = 0.75\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Total Time Self-Consistency
bradley_insight.content: In multi-stage kinematics questions, always perform a self-consistency check on the times. Here, the three distinct stages take $4\text{ s}$, $10\text{ s}$, and $6\text{ s}$. Adding them confirms $4 + 10 + 6 = 20\text{ s}$, verifying your gliding calculations before you move on.

question:
The intensity of solar radiation, $y\text{ watts per square metre}$, and the average distance from the Sun, $x\text{ astronomical units (AU)}$, are given in the table below for the planets Mercury and Jupiter:
QuantityMercuryJupiter
$x\text{ (AU)}$$0.3075$$4.950$
$y\text{ (W m}^{-2}\text{)}$$14\,400$$55.8$
$\ln x$
$\ln y$
The intensity $y$ is modelled as being proportional to a power of the distance $x$.

(a) Write down an equation for $y$ in terms of $x$ and two constants, $k$ and $n$.

(b) Show that this equation can be written in the form $\ln y = a + b \ln x$, stating $a$ and $b$ in terms of $k$ and $n$.

(c) Calculate the values of $\ln x$ and $\ln y$ to complete the table, giving each value correct to 4 significant figures.

(d) Use your values from part (c) to calculate the values of the constants $a$ and $b$, giving each correct to 3 significant figures.

(e) Hence rewrite your equation from part (a) for $y$ in terms of $x$, using appropriate numerical values for the constants.

(f) Sketch a graph of the equation found in part (e) for $x > 0$.

(g) Earth is at an average distance of $1.0\text{ AU}$ from the Sun. Use your model to estimate the intensity of solar radiation reaching Earth.
steps:
(a) Power law equation:

Since $y$ is proportional to a power of $x$:\begin{aligned} y = kx^n \end{aligned}

(b) Showing linear form:

Taking natural logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} \ln y &= \ln(kx^n) \cr &= \ln k + \ln(x^n) \cr &= \ln k + n\ln x \end{aligned}

This is in the linear form $\ln y = a + b\ln x$, where $a = \ln k$ and $b = n$.

(c) Completing the table:

For Mercury ($x = 0.3075$, $y = 14\,400$):\begin{aligned} \ln x &= \ln(0.3075) \cr &\approx -1.179 \cr \ln y &= \ln(14\,400) \cr &\approx 9.575 \end{aligned}

For Jupiter ($x = 4.950$, $y = 55.8$):\begin{aligned} \ln x &= \ln(4.950) \cr &\approx 1.599 \cr \ln y &= \ln(55.8) \cr &\approx 4.022 \end{aligned}

(d) Calculating $a$ and $b$:

Finding gradient $b$ using unrounded values:\begin{aligned} b &= \dfrac{4.0218 - 9.5750}{1.5994 - (-1.1793)} \cr &= \dfrac{-5.5532}{2.7787} \cr &\approx -1.998 \cr &\approx -2.00\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

Finding intercept $a$:\begin{aligned} a &= \ln y - b\ln x \cr &= 9.5750 - (-1.998)(-1.1793) \cr &= 9.5750 - 2.3562 \cr &\approx 7.22\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(e) Rewriting the power equation:

Finding $k$ from $a = \ln k$:\begin{aligned} k &= \text{e}^{7.2188} \cr &\approx 1360 \end{aligned}

Since $n = b = -2$, the equation is:\begin{aligned} y = 1360x^{-2} \quad \text{or} \quad y = \dfrac{1360}{x^2} \end{aligned}

(f) Sketching the curve:

The graph of $y = \dfrac{1360}{x^2}$ is an inverse-square curve in the first quadrant, decreasing smoothly with both axes as asymptotes.

(g) Solar intensity for Earth:

Substituting $x = 1.0\text{ AU}$ into the model:\begin{aligned} y &= 1360(1.0)^{-2} \cr &= 1360\text{ W m}^{-2} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You made a sign error when finding the gradient $b$. Since $y$ decreases as $x$ increases, the gradient is negative:\begin{aligned} b &= \dfrac{4.022 - 9.575}{1.599 - (-1.179)} \cr &= -2.00 \end{aligned}
You forgot to take the exponential of $a$ to find $k$. In the linearised equation, $a = \ln k$, so\begin{aligned} k &= \text{e}^{7.2188} \cr &\approx 1360 \end{aligned}
You assumed $a$ was the value of $\ln y$ at Mercury. To find the intercept $a$, you must evaluate $a = \ln y - b\ln x$, which gives $a \approx 7.22$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Physics Sanity Check
bradley_insight.content: This question models the inverse-square law of radiation. When your gradient evaluates to $b \approx -1.998$, recognise immediately that the underlying physical exponent is exactly $-2$ ($y \propto \dfrac{1}{x^2}$). Furthermore, $k \approx 1360\text{ W m}^{-2}$ represents the solar constant reaching Earth at $x = 1\text{ AU}$.

question:
The orbital period of a planet, $T\text{ years}$, and its mean distance from the Sun, $R\text{ astronomical units (AU)}$, are recorded in the table below for Mars and Saturn:
QuantityMarsSaturn
$R\text{ (AU)}$$1.524$$9.537$
$T\text{ (years)}$$1.881$$29.46$
$\ln R$
$\ln T$
It is suggested that $T$ and $R$ are related by a power law of the form $T = k R^n$, where $k$ and $n$ are constants.

(a) Express $\ln T$ in the form $a + b \ln R$, stating $a$ and $b$ in terms of $k$ and $n$.

(b) Complete the table by finding the values of $\ln R$ and $\ln T$, giving each value correct to 4 significant figures.

(c) Use your values from part (b) to find the constants $a$ and $b$, correct to 3 significant figures.

(d) Hence express $T$ in terms of $R$, giving the numerical values of $k$ and $n$.

(e) Sketch the graph of $T$ against $R$ for $R \ge 0$.

(f) An asteroid orbits the Sun at an average distance of $4.0\text{ AU}$. Use the model to estimate its orbital period in years.
steps:
(a) Linearising the power model:

Taking natural logarithms of $T = kR^n$:\begin{aligned} \ln T &= \ln(kR^n) \cr &= \ln k + n\ln R \end{aligned}

In the form $\ln T = a + b\ln R$, $a = \ln k$ and $b = n$.

(b) Completing the table:

For Mars ($R = 1.524$, $T = 1.881$):\begin{aligned} \ln R &= \ln(1.524) \cr &\approx 0.4213 \cr \ln T &= \ln(1.881) \cr &\approx 0.6318 \end{aligned}

For Saturn ($R = 9.537$, $T = 29.46$):\begin{aligned} \ln R &= \ln(9.537) \cr &\approx 2.255 \cr \ln T &= \ln(29.46) \cr &\approx 3.383 \end{aligned}

(c) Finding constants $a$ and $b$:

Gradient $b$:\begin{aligned} b &= \dfrac{3.3830 - 0.6318}{2.2552 - 0.4213} \cr &= \dfrac{2.7512}{1.8339} \cr &\approx 1.5002 \cr &\approx 1.50\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

Intercept $a$:\begin{aligned} a &= \ln T - b\ln R \cr &= 0.6318 - 1.5002(0.4213) \cr &= 0.6318 - 0.6320 \cr &\approx 0.00\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(d) Final equation for $T$:

Finding $k$:\begin{aligned} k &= \text{e}^a \cr &= \text{e}^0 \cr &= 1.00 \end{aligned}

Since $n = 1.5$, the relationship is:\begin{aligned} T = R^{1.5} \quad \text{or} \quad T = R^{\frac{3}{2}} \end{aligned}

(e) Sketching the graph:

The graph of $T = R^{1.5}$ passes through the origin $(0, 0)$ and curves upwards with increasing gradient in the first quadrant.

(f) Estimating period for asteroid:

Substituting $R = 4.0\text{ AU}$:\begin{aligned} T &= (4.0)^{1.5} \cr &= (\sqrt{4.0})^3 \cr &= 2^3 \cr &= 8\text{ years} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (c) $a = 0.00, b = 1.50$, (d) $T = R^{1.5}$, (f) $8\text{ years}$

pi_options.feedback: You inverted the gradient formula as $\Delta \ln R / \Delta \ln T$. The gradient is\begin{aligned} b &= \dfrac{\Delta \ln T}{\Delta \ln R} \cr &= \dfrac{3.383 - 0.6318}{2.255 - 0.4213} \cr &= 1.50 \end{aligned}
You took $a = 1.00$ instead of $a = 0.00$. The intercept is $a \approx 0$, which gives $k = \text{e}^0 = 1$, so $T = R^{1.5}$.
You calculated $4 \times 1.5 = 6$ instead of raising $4$ to the power of $1.5$. Evaluating the power gives\begin{aligned} 4^{1.5} &= (\sqrt{4})^3 \cr &= 2^3 \cr &= 8\text{ years} \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Kepler's Harmonic Law
bradley_insight.content: This problem illustrates Kepler's Third Law ($T^2 = R^3$). In logarithmic form, squaring both sides yields $2\ln T = 3\ln R$, which leads directly to $\ln T = 1.5\ln R$. Finding an intercept of $a = 0$ confirms that $k = 1$ when periods are measured in Earth years and distances in astronomical units.

question:
A laboratory culture of bacteria is monitored over time. The population, $N\text{ (in thousands)}$, after $t\text{ hours}$ is recorded at two intervals in the table below:
$t\text{ (h)}$$N\text{ (k)}$$\ln N$
$2.0$$45.0$
$5.0$$360$
The population is modelled by the exponential relationship $N = A \mathrm{e}^{kt}$, where $A$ and $k$ are constants.

(a) Show that $\ln N$ can be written in the form $c + mt$, stating $c$ and $m$ in terms of $A$ and $k$.

(b) Complete the table by calculating the missing values of $\ln N$, giving each value correct to 4 significant figures.

(c) Use the completed table to calculate the values of $c$ and $m$, giving each correct to 3 significant figures.

(d) Hence determine the values of $A$ and $k$, giving $A$ correct to 3 significant figures and $k$ correct to 3 decimal places.

(e) Sketch the graph of $N$ against $t$ for $t \ge 0$.

(f) Use the model to predict the bacterial population after $8.0\text{ hours}$.
steps:
(a) Linearising the exponential model:

Taking natural logarithms of $N = A\text{e}^{kt}$:\begin{aligned} \ln N &= \ln(A\text{e}^{kt}) \cr &= \ln A + \ln(\text{e}^{kt}) \cr &= \ln A + kt \end{aligned}

In the linear form $\ln N = c + mt$, $c = \ln A$ and $m = k$.

(b) Completing the table:

For Observation 1 ($N = 45.0$):\begin{aligned} \ln N &= \ln(45.0) \cr &\approx 3.807 \end{aligned}

For Observation 2 ($N = 360$):\begin{aligned} \ln N &= \ln(360) \cr &\approx 5.886 \end{aligned}

(c) Calculating $c$ and $m$:

Gradient $m$:\begin{aligned} m &= \dfrac{5.8861 - 3.8067}{5.0 - 2.0} \cr &= \dfrac{2.0794}{3} \cr &\approx 0.6931 \cr &\approx 0.693\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

Intercept $c$:\begin{aligned} c &= \ln N - mt \cr &= 3.8067 - 0.6931(2.0) \cr &= 3.8067 - 1.3862 \cr &\approx 2.42\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(d) Evaluating $A$ and $k$:

Since $k = m$:\begin{aligned} k = 0.693\text{ (3 d.p.)} \end{aligned}

Finding $A = \text{e}^c$:\begin{aligned} A &= \text{e}^{2.4205} \cr &\approx 11.25 \cr &\approx 11.3\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(e) Sketching the exponential curve:

The graph starts at vertical intercept $(0, 11.3)$ and displays exponential growth with increasing gradient as $t$ increases.

(f) Population after $8.0\text{ hours}$:

Evaluating $N$ at $t = 8.0$:\begin{aligned} N &= 11.25\text{e}^{0.6931(8.0)} \cr &= 11.25\text{e}^{5.5448} \cr &\approx 2880\text{ (thousands)} \end{aligned}

This represents approximately $2\,880\,000$ bacteria.

pi_options.feedback: You forgot to take the exponential of $c$ to find $A$. In this semi-log model, $c = \ln A$, so\begin{aligned} A &= \text{e}^{2.4205} \cr &\approx 11.3 \end{aligned}
You took $c$ as the value of $\ln N$ at $t = 2.0$. To find the vertical intercept $c$, you must subtract $mt$:\begin{aligned} c &= 3.8067 - 0.6931(2.0) \cr &= 2.42 \end{aligned}
You calculated the population at $t = 7\text{ hours}$ rather than $t = 8\text{ hours}$. At $t = 8$, the population doubles again from $t = 7$, reaching $2880\text{ thousands}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Doubling Time Shortcut
bradley_insight.content: Notice that between $t = 2$ and $t = 5$, the population increased by a factor of $\dfrac{360}{45} = 8 = 2^3$. This indicates that the population doubled 3 times in 3 hours, so the doubling time is exactly 1 hour. This confirms that $k = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$.

question:
The atmospheric pressure, $P\text{ kilopascals (kPa)}$, was measured at sea level and at high altitude on a mountain plateau at height $h\text{ kilometres (km)}$, as shown in the table:
QuantitySea LevelPlateau
$h\text{ (km)}$$0$$5.5$
$P\text{ (kPa)}$$101.3$$50.4$
$\ln P$
Pressure is modelled by the formula $P = P_0 \mathrm{e}^{-kh}$, where $P_0$ and $k$ are constants.

(a) Express $\ln P$ in the form $c - mh$, stating $c$ and $m$ in terms of $P_0$ and $k$.

(b) Complete the table by calculating the values of $\ln P$, giving each value correct to 4 significant figures.

(c) State the value of $P_0$, and calculate the value of $k$ correct to 3 significant figures.

(d) Rewrite the formula for $P$ in terms of $h$ using these numerical values.

(e) Sketch the graph of $P$ against $h$ for $h \ge 0$, clearly showing the intercept on the vertical axis.

(f) A commercial passenger aircraft cruises at an altitude of $11.0\text{ km}$. Use the model to estimate the atmospheric pressure outside the aircraft at this altitude.
steps:
(a) Linearising exponential decay:

Taking natural logarithms of $P = P_0\text{e}^{-kh}$:\begin{aligned} \ln P &= \ln(P_0\text{e}^{-kh}) \cr &= \ln P_0 - kh \end{aligned}

In the form $\ln P = c - mh$, $c = \ln P_0$ and $m = k$.

(b) Completing the table:

For Sea Level ($P = 101.3$):\begin{aligned} \ln P &= \ln(101.3) \cr &\approx 4.618 \end{aligned}

For the Plateau ($P = 50.4$):\begin{aligned} \ln P &= \ln(50.4) \cr &\approx 3.920 \end{aligned}

(c) Finding $P_0$ and $k$:

At $h = 0$, $P = P_0$ directly:\begin{aligned} P_0 = 101.3\text{ kPa} \end{aligned}

Finding the decay constant $k$:\begin{aligned} -k &= \dfrac{3.9199 - 4.6181}{5.5 - 0} \cr -k &= \dfrac{-0.6982}{5.5} \cr -k &\approx -0.1269 \cr k &\approx 0.127\text{ km}^{-1}\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(d) Numerical formula:

Substituting $P_0$ and $k$:\begin{aligned} P = 101.3\text{e}^{-0.127h} \end{aligned}

(e) Sketching the decay curve:

The graph starts at vertical intercept $(0, 101.3)$ and decreases asymptotically towards the horizontal axis $P = 0$ as $h \to \infty$.

(f) Pressure at cruising altitude:

At $h = 11.0\text{ km}$:\begin{aligned} P &= 101.3\text{e}^{-0.1269(11.0)} \cr &= 101.3\text{e}^{-1.3959} \cr &\approx 25.1\text{ kPa} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You included a double negative in the decay formula. The gradient of the line is $-k = -0.127$, so the constant $k$ is positive ($0.127\text{ km}^{-1}$), and the equation is $P = 101.3\text{e}^{-0.127h}$.
You used $\ln P_0 = 4.618$ directly as $P_0$. The pressure at sea level is $P_0 = \text{e}^{4.618} = 101.3\text{ kPa}$.
You evaluated the pressure at $5.5\text{ km}$ instead of $11.0\text{ km}$. At $11.0\text{ km}$, the pressure is approximately $25.1\text{ kPa}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Power Law vs Exponential Decay
bradley_insight.content: Pay careful attention to the horizontal variable in logarithmic modelling. When the original equation is $P = P_0\text{e}^{-kh}$, taking logs yields $\ln P = \ln P_0 - kh$. Plotting $\ln P$ against $h$ produces a straight line. If you mistakenly plot $\ln P$ against $\ln h$, you will not get a linear graph.

question:
In biology, Kleiber's law states that the basal metabolic rate, $B\text{ watts}$, of a mammal is related to its body mass, $M\text{ kilograms}$, by a power law of the form $B = k M^n$, where $k$ and $n$ are constants. Data for a rabbit and a horse are given in the table below:
QuantityRabbitHorse
$M\text{ (kg)}$$2.50$$450$
$B\text{ (W)}$$8.16$$405$
$\ln M$
$\ln B$
(a) Show that $\ln B = a + b \ln M$, stating $a$ and $b$ in terms of $k$ and $n$.

(b) Complete the table by finding the values of $\ln M$ and $\ln B$, giving each value correct to 4 significant figures.

(c) Use the completed table to calculate the values of $a$ and $b$, giving each correct to 3 significant figures.

(d) Hence determine the value of $k$ correct to 3 significant figures, and show that $n \approx 0.75$.

(e) Sketch the graph of $B$ against $M$ for $M \ge 0$.

(f) Use the model $B = k M^{0.75}$ to estimate the basal metabolic rate of a human with a body mass of $81.0\text{ kg}$.
steps:
(a) Linearising Kleiber's law:

Taking natural logarithms of $B = kM^n$:\begin{aligned} \ln B &= \ln(kM^n) \cr &= \ln k + n\ln M \end{aligned}

In the form $\ln B = a + b\ln M$, $a = \ln k$ and $b = n$.

(b) Completing the table:

For the Rabbit ($M = 2.50$, $B = 8.16$):\begin{aligned} \ln M &= \ln(2.50) \cr &\approx 0.9163 \cr \ln B &= \ln(8.16) \cr &\approx 2.100 \end{aligned}

For the Horse ($M = 450$, $B = 405$):\begin{aligned} \ln M &= \ln(450) \cr &\approx 6.109 \cr \ln B &= \ln(405) \cr &\approx 6.004 \end{aligned}

(c) Calculating $a$ and $b$:

Gradient $b$:\begin{aligned} b &= \dfrac{6.0039 - 2.0992}{6.1092 - 0.9163} \cr &= \dfrac{3.9047}{5.1929} \cr &\approx 0.7519 \cr &\approx 0.752\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

Intercept $a$:\begin{aligned} a &= \ln B - b\ln M \cr &= 2.0992 - 0.7519(0.9163) \cr &= 2.0992 - 0.6890 \cr &\approx 1.41\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(d) Determining $k$ and verifying $n$:

Finding constant $k$:\begin{aligned} k &= \text{e}^a \cr &= \text{e}^{1.4102} \cr &\approx 4.097 \cr &\approx 4.10\text{ (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

Since $b = n$, $n = 0.752 \approx 0.75 = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

(e) Sketching the power curve:

Since the exponent $n = 0.75$ lies between $0$ and $1$, the graph of $B = 4.10M^{0.75}$ passes through the origin $(0, 0)$ and curves upwards with decreasing gradient (concave down).

(f) Metabolic rate of human:

Substituting $M = 81.0\text{ kg}$ into $B = 4.097M^{0.75}$:\begin{aligned} B &= 4.097(81.0)^{0.75} \cr &= 4.097(\sqrt[4]{81.0})^3 \cr &= 4.097(3^3) \cr &= 4.097(27) \cr &\approx 111\text{ W} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You used the intercept $a = 1.41$ directly as $k$. In the linearized equation, $a = \ln k$, so\begin{aligned} k &= \text{e}^{1.4102} \cr &\approx 4.10 \end{aligned}
You inverted the gradient formula as $\Delta \ln M / \Delta \ln B$. The gradient is\begin{aligned} b &= \dfrac{6.004 - 2.100}{6.109 - 0.9163} \cr &\approx 0.752 \end{aligned}

You calculated $81.0 \times 0.75 = 60.75$ instead of evaluating the power $81.0^{0.75}$. Notice that\begin{aligned} 81.0^{0.75} &= (\sqrt[4]{81})^3 \cr &= 3^3 \cr &= 27 \end{aligned}giving $B = 4.10 \times 27 \approx 111\text{ W}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Fractional Power Mental Maths
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating terms like $81.0^{0.75}$, remember that $0.75 = \dfrac{3}{4}$. Take the fourth root first before cubing: $(\sqrt[4]{81})^3 = 3^3 = 27$. This avoids dealing with massive numbers and provides an instant check on your calculation.

question:
A box of mass $2.5\text{ kg}$ is pushed across a rough horizontal floor against a constant resistance of $14.7\text{ N}$. A person applies a constant horizontal pushing force of magnitude $P\text{ N}$.

The box accelerates from rest to a speed of $1.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ as it travels a distance of $3.2\text{ m}$.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the box.

(b) Calculate the time taken for the box to travel the first $3.2\text{ m}$.

(c) Find the magnitude of the horizontal pushing force $P$.

(d) Given that the resistance force is entirely due to friction between the box and the floor, calculate the coefficient of friction $\mu$ between the box and the floor.
steps:
(a) Acceleration of the box:

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$, $v = 1.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $s = 3.2\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &1.6^2 = 0^2 + 2a(3.2) \cr &2.56 = 6.4a \cr &a = \dfrac{2.56}{6.4} \cr &a = 0.4\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Time taken:

Using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} &1.6 = 0 + 0.4t \cr &0.4t = 1.6 \cr &t = 4\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Pushing force $P$:

Using Newton's second law ($F = ma$) with $m = 2.5\text{ kg}$ and resistance $R = 14.7\text{ N}$:\begin{aligned} &P - 14.7 = 2.5(0.4) \cr &P - 14.7 = 1.0 \cr &P = 15.7\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(d) Coefficient of friction $\mu$:

On a horizontal floor, the normal reaction is:\begin{aligned} R &= mg \cr &= 2.5(9.8) \cr &= 24.5\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Using $F = \mu R$:\begin{aligned} &14.7 = \mu(24.5) \cr &\mu = \dfrac{14.7}{24.5} \cr &\mu = 0.6 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $0.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $4\text{ s}$, (c) $15.7\text{ N}$, (d) $\mu = 0.6$

question:
A crate of mass $12\text{ kg}$ is pushed along a rough horizontal floor by a constant force of magnitude $P\text{ N}$ directed downwards at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.

The coefficient of friction between the crate and the floor is $\mu = 0.25$. The crate accelerates from rest to a speed of $2.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$ over a distance of $3.6\text{ m}$.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the crate.

(b) Show that the normal reaction $R\text{ N}$ between the crate and the floor is given by $R = 117.6 + 0.5P$.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of the pushing force $P$, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

(d) If the crate were instead pulled by a force of the same magnitude $P$ directed upwards at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal, explain with mathematical reasoning whether its acceleration would be greater than, equal to, or less than the value found in part (a).
steps:
(a) Acceleration of the crate:

Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$, $v = 2.4\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $s = 3.6\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} &2.4^2 = 0^2 + 2a(3.6) \cr &5.76 = 7.2a \cr &a = 0.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Normal reaction $R$:

Resolving vertically for equilibrium ($\uparrow$):\begin{aligned} &R - mg - P\sin 30^\circ = 0 \cr &R = 12(9.8) + P(0.5) \cr &R = 117.6 + 0.5P \end{aligned}

(c) Calculating pushing force $P$:

Resolving horizontally ($\rightarrow$):\begin{aligned} P\cos 30^\circ - F_r = ma \end{aligned}

Substitute $F_r = \mu R = 0.25(117.6 + 0.5P)$:\begin{aligned} &P\cos 30^\circ - 0.25(117.6 + 0.5P) \cr& \qquad \qquad= 12(0.8) \cr &P\cos 30^\circ - 29.4 - 0.125P = 9.6 \cr &P(\cos 30^\circ - 0.125) = 39.0 \end{aligned}

Evaluating $P$:\begin{aligned} &P(0.8660 - 0.125) = 39.0 \cr &0.7410P = 39.0 \cr &P = \dfrac{39.0}{0.7410} \cr &P \approx 52.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(d) Comparison if pulled upwards:

When pulled at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal, the vertical equation becomes:\begin{aligned} R = mg - P\sin 30^\circ \end{aligned}

This reduces the normal reaction $R$, which in turn decreases the frictional resistance ($F_r = \mu R$).

Since the forward horizontal driving component $P\cos 30^\circ$ remains unchanged, the net horizontal force is larger, so the acceleration is Greater.
Final Answer: (a) $0.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $52.6\text{ N}$, (d) Greater

You used $R = mg = 117.6\text{ N}$, forgetting that the downward component of the push increases the normal reaction to $R = 117.6 + 0.5P$.
You omitted the factor of $2$ in $v^2 = 2as$, calculating acceleration as $2.4^2 / 3.6 = 1.6\text{ m s}^{-2}$ instead of $2.4^2 / 7.2 = 0.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Pushing vs Pulling Normal Reaction
bradley_insight.content: Always draw clear vertical resolution arrows when a force is applied at an angle. Pushing downwards adds a vertical component $P\sin\theta$ that presses the object harder into the ground, increasing $R$ and therefore increasing friction. Pulling upwards subtracts $P\sin\theta$, reducing friction. This is why pulling a heavy lawn roller is physically easier than pushing it.

topic: Newton's Second Law and Multi-Stage Motion
question:
A worker pushes a storage box of mass $8\text{ kg}$ across a rough horizontal warehouse floor by applying a constant horizontal force of magnitude $38\text{ N}$. The coefficient of friction between the box and the floor is $\mu = 0.35$.

The box starts from rest and is pushed for $5\text{ seconds}$. The worker then lets go, and the box slides to rest under friction alone.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the box while it is being pushed.

(b) Find the speed of the box and the distance travelled during the first $5\text{ seconds}$.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of the deceleration of the box after the worker stops pushing.

(d) Calculate the total distance travelled by the box from the instant it starts moving until it comes to rest again, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

(e) Find the total time elapsed for the entire journey.
steps:
(a) Acceleration while being pushed:

Frictional force on the box:\begin{aligned} F_r &= \mu mg \cr &= 0.35(8)(9.8) \cr &= 27.44\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Net forward force:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{net}} &= 38 - 27.44 \cr &= 10.56\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Acceleration:\begin{aligned} a_1 &= \dfrac{10.56}{8} \cr &= 1.32\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Speed and distance at $t = 5\text{ s}$:

Speed achieved:\begin{aligned} v_1 &= 0 + 1.32(5) \cr &= 6.6\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Distance travelled in Phase 1:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1.32)(5^2) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1.32)(25) \cr &= 16.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Deceleration during coasting:

When the push is removed, friction alone opposes motion:\begin{aligned} -27.44 &= 8a_2 \cr a_2 &= -3.43\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

The deceleration is $3.43\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(d) Total distance travelled:

For Phase 2, using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 6.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 6.6^2 + 2(-3.43)s_2 \cr &0 = 43.56 - 6.86s_2 \cr &6.86s_2 = 43.56 \cr &s_2 \approx 6.3499\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Total distance:\begin{aligned} s_{\text{tot}} &= 16.5 + 6.3499 \cr &\approx 22.8\text{ m (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(e) Total journey time:

Duration of Phase 2 using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 6.6 - 3.43t_2 \cr &3.43t_2 = 6.6 \cr &t_2 \approx 1.924\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Total time:\begin{aligned} T &= 5 + 1.924 \cr &\approx 6.92\text{ s} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You gave the distance and time for the coasting phase only. You must add the first phase ($16.5\text{ m}$ and $5\text{ s}$) to find total distance ($22.8\text{ m}$) and total time ($6.92\text{ s}$).
You forgot to subtract friction during the pushing phase. The net force while pushing is $38 - 27.44 = 10.56\text{ N}$, giving $a = 1.32\text{ m s}^{-2}$, not $38 / 8 = 4.75\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
You omitted the coasting time from the total time. The box takes an additional $1.92\text{ seconds}$ to slide to rest, giving a total time of $5 + 1.92 = 6.92\text{ s}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Work-Energy Check for Multi-Stage Motion
bradley_insight.content: For multi-stage horizontal sliding, the work done by the pushing force equals the total work done against friction over the entire journey: $P s_1 = F_r s_{\text{tot}}$. Checking this yields:\begin{aligned} s_{\text{tot}} &= \dfrac{38(16.5)}{27.44} \cr &\approx 22.8\text{ m} \end{aligned}This confirms your two-stage kinematic calculations in a single line.

topic: Connected Bodies and Newton's Third Law
question:
A constant horizontal force of magnitude $P\text{ N}$ is applied to push two boxes, $A$ and $B$, across a rough horizontal floor. Box $A$ has mass $5\text{ kg}$ and Box $B$ has mass $3\text{ kg}$. Box $A$ is in direct contact with Box $B$, and the force $P$ is applied directly to Box $A$, pushing it towards Box $B$.

The coefficient of friction between each box and the floor is $\mu = 0.2$. The boxes accelerate together from rest to a speed of $1.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in a time of $3\text{ seconds}$.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the acceleration of the boxes.

(b) Calculate the total frictional force opposing the motion.

(c) Find the magnitude of the pushing force $P$.

(d) Calculate the magnitude of the contact force exerted by Box $A$ on Box $B$.

(e) State which of Newton's laws of motion implies that the force exerted by Box $B$ on Box $A$ has the same magnitude as the force calculated in part (d).
steps:
(a) Acceleration of the boxes:

Using $v = u + at$ with $u = 0$, $v = 1.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and $t = 3\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} &1.8 = 0 + 3a \cr &a = 0.6\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Total frictional force:

Total mass is $M = 5 + 3 = 8\text{ kg}$.

Total normal reaction:\begin{aligned} R_{\text{tot}} &= 8(9.8) \cr &= 78.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}

Total friction:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{tot}} &= 0.2(78.4) \cr &= 15.68\text{ N} \cr &\approx 15.7\text{ N (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(c) Pushing force $P$:

Applying Newton's second law to the combined system:\begin{aligned} &P - F_{\text{tot}} = M a \cr &P - 15.68 = 8(0.6) \cr &P - 15.68 = 4.8 \cr &P = 20.48\text{ N} \cr &P \approx 20.5\text{ N (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

(d) Contact force between boxes:

Let $C$ be the normal contact force exerted by $A$ on $B$.

Considering Box $B$ alone ($m_B = 3\text{ kg}$):
Friction on $B$ is $F_B = 0.2(3)(9.8) = 5.88\text{ N}$.

Equation of motion for Box $B$:\begin{aligned} &C - F_B = m_B a \cr &C - 5.88 = 3(0.6) \cr &C - 5.88 = 1.8 \cr &C = 7.68\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(e) Newton's law:

Newton's Third Law of motion states that when body $A$ exerts a force on body $B$, body $B$ exerts an equal and opposite force on body $A$.
Final Answer: (a) $0.6\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $15.7\text{ N}$, (c) $20.5\text{ N}$, (d) $7.68\text{ N}$, (e) Newton's Third Law

pi_options.ans: (a) $0.6\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $15.7\text{ N}$, (c) $20.5\text{ N}$, (d) $1.80\text{ N}$, (e) Newton's Third Law
