A particle $P$ moves along a horizontal straight line such that its velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$) is given by:$$v = 9t^2 - 4t - 7$$At time $t = 2\text{ s}$, the displacement of the particle from a fixed point $O$ on the line is $10\text{ m}$.

Find an expression for the displacement $s$ of the particle from $O$ at time $t$ seconds.
steps:
Integrate velocity to find displacement:

Displacement is the integral of velocity with respect to time:\begin{aligned} s &= \int v\,\text{d}t \cr &= \int (9t^2 - 4t - 7)\,\text{d}t \cr &= 3t^3 - 2t^2 - 7t + c \end{aligned}

Apply the boundary condition:

Substitute $t = 2$ and $s = 10$ into the expression:\begin{aligned} &10 = 3(2^3) - 2(2^2) - 7(2) + c \cr &10 = 24 - 8 - 14 + c \cr &10 = 2 + c \cr &c = 8 \end{aligned}
Therefore, the displacement is:\begin{aligned} s = 3t^3 - 2t^2 - 7t + 8 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $s = 3t^3 - 2t^2 - 7t + 8$

pi_options.feedback: Do not assume that the constant of integration $c$ equals the given displacement $s = 10\text{ m}$. That shortcut only works when $t = 0$; for $t = 2$, you must substitute $t$ into all integrated terms to solve for $c$.
Check your rearrangement when solving $10 = 2 + c$. Subtracting $2$ from both sides gives $c = 10 - 2 = +8$, not $-8$.
You have differentiated the velocity expression instead of integrating it. To find displacement from velocity, integrate $v$ with respect to $t$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Never Assume $c$ Equals the Given Position
bradley_insight.content: Students often assume the constant of integration $c$ equals the value of $s$ given in the question. While $c = s_0$ holds when initial conditions are given at $t = 0$, for any non-zero time such as $t = 2\text{ s}$, you must substitute $t$ into all integrated terms before solving for $c$.

question:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$) is given by:$$v = 12t^2 - 6t - 4$$When $t = 1\text{ s}$, the displacement of the particle from a fixed origin $O$ is $3\text{ m}$.

(a) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ of the particle from $O$ at time $t$ seconds.

(b) Find the acceleration of the particle when $t = 3\text{ s}$.
steps:
(a) Find displacement $s$:

Integrating velocity with respect to time:\begin{aligned} s &= \int (12t^2 - 6t - 4)\,\text{d}t \cr &= 4t^3 - 3t^2 - 4t + c \end{aligned}
Substitute $t = 1$ and $s = 3$:\begin{aligned} &3 = 4(1^3) - 3(1^2) - 4(1) + c \cr &3 = 4 - 3 - 4 + c \cr &3 = -3 + c \cr &c = 6 \end{aligned}
Hence:\begin{aligned} s = 4t^3 - 3t^2 - 4t + 6 \end{aligned}

(b) Find acceleration when $t = 3\text{ s}$:

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(12t^2 - 6t - 4) \cr &= 24t - 6 \end{aligned}
When $t = 3\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} a(3) &= 24(3) - 6 \cr &= 72 - 6 \cr &= 66\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $s = 4t^3 - 3t^2 - 4t + 6$, (b) $66\text{ m s}^{-2}$

pi_options.feedback: Remember to include the constant of integration $c$ and evaluate it using the condition $s(1) = 3$. Omitting $c$ implies the particle starts at the origin when $t = 0$.
Check the sign in the derivative: $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-6t) = -6$, not $+6$. When $t = 3$, $a = 72 - 6 = 66\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Check your algebra when finding $c$: $3 = -3 + c \implies c = 3 + 3 = +6$, not $-6$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Choose the Right Calculus Tool
bradley_insight.content: Keep your calculus operations distinct: finding displacement requires integration ($s = \int v\,\text{d}t$), which introduces an unknown constant $c$. Finding acceleration requires differentiation ($a = \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$), which eliminates the constant term.

question:
A particle moves in a straight line such that its velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$) is given by:$$v = 6\sqrt{t} - 2t$$Initially, when $t = 0$, the particle is at a fixed origin $O$.

(a) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ of the particle from $O$ at time $t$ seconds.

(b) Find the non-zero value of $t$ when the particle is momentarily at rest, and calculate the displacement of the particle from $O$ at this instant.
steps:
(a) Find displacement $s$:

Rewrite using index notation: $v = 6t^{1/2} - 2t$.\begin{aligned} s &= \int (6t^{1/2} - 2t)\,\text{d}t \cr &= \dfrac{6t^{3/2}}{3/2} - t^2 + c \cr &= 4t^{3/2} - t^2 + c \end{aligned}
Since $s = 0$ when $t = 0$, $c = 0$:\begin{aligned} s &= 4t^{3/2} - t^2 \cr &= 4t\sqrt{t} - t^2 \end{aligned}

(b) Instant of momentary rest:

Set $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &6\sqrt{t} - 2t = 0 \cr &2\sqrt{t}(3 - \sqrt{t}) = 0 \end{aligned}
For non-zero $t$:\begin{aligned} \sqrt{t} &= 3 \cr t &= 9\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Displacement at $t = 9\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} s(9) &= 4(9^{3/2}) - 9^2 \cr &= 4(27) - 81 \cr &= 108 - 81 \cr &= 27\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $s = 4t\sqrt{t} - t^2$, (b) $t = 9\text{ s}$, $s = 27\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: From $\sqrt{t} = 3$, square both sides to find $t$: $t = 3^2 = 9\text{ s}$, not $3\text{ s}$.
When integrating $6t^{1/2}$, divide by the new index $3/2$ (multiply by $2/3$) to get $4t^{3/2}$. Multiplying by $3/2$ gives an incorrect coefficient of $9$.
Check the sign of $s(9)$: $4(27) - 81 = 108 - 81 = +27\text{ m}$, not $-27\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Fractional Indices in Integration
bradley_insight.content: When integrating $t^{1/2}$, divide by the new power $\frac{3}{2}$, which is equivalent to multiplying by $\frac{2}{3}$: $6 \times \frac{2}{3} = 4$. Also, note that $\sqrt{t} = 3$ gives $t = 3^2 = 9\text{ s}$, a step where students often accidentally write $t = 3$.

question:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight line with acceleration $a\text{ m s}^{-2}$ at time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$) given by:$$a = 6t - 10$$At time $t = 0$, the velocity of $P$ is $8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and its displacement from a fixed origin $O$ is $-4\text{ m}$.

(a) Find an expression for the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ seconds.

(b) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ of the particle from $O$ at time $t$ seconds.

(c) Find the values of $t$ when the particle passes through the origin $O$.
steps:
(a) Velocity expression:

Integrating acceleration:\begin{aligned} v &= \int (6t - 10)\,\text{d}t \cr &= 3t^2 - 10t + c_1 \end{aligned}
Using initial condition $v(0) = 8$:\begin{aligned} c_1 = 8 \end{aligned}
Hence:\begin{aligned} v = 3t^2 - 10t + 8 \end{aligned}

(b) Displacement expression:

Integrating velocity:\begin{aligned} s &= \int (3t^2 - 10t + 8)\,\text{d}t \cr &= t^3 - 5t^2 + 8t + c_2 \end{aligned}
Using initial condition $s(0) = -4$:\begin{aligned} c_2 = -4 \end{aligned}
Hence:\begin{aligned} s = t^3 - 5t^2 + 8t - 4 \end{aligned}

(c) Times passing through origin ($s = 0$):

Set displacement to zero:\begin{aligned} &t^3 - 5t^2 + 8t - 4 = 0 \end{aligned}
Testing integer factors of $-4$, for $t = 1$:\begin{aligned} 1^3 - 5(1^2) + 8(1) - 4 = 0 \end{aligned}
Thus, $(t - 1)$ is a factor. Factorising the cubic:\begin{aligned} &(t - 1)(t^2 - 4t + 4) = 0 \cr &(t - 1)(t - 2)^2 = 0 \end{aligned}
Therefore, the particle passes through the origin at $t = 1\text{ s}$ and $t = 2\text{ s}$.
Final Answer: (a) $v = 3t^2 - 10t + 8$, (b) $s = t^3 - 5t^2 + 8t - 4$, (c) $t = 1\text{ s}$, $t = 2\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: Check your factorisation of the quadratic factor $t^2 - 4t + 4$. It factors as $(t - 2)^2$, yielding the repeated root $t = 2\text{ s}$, not $t = 4\text{ s}$.
Remember to include the initial displacement of $-4\text{ m}$. Omitting $c_2 = -4$ alters the roots of the displacement function.
When integrating $6t$, remember to divide by $2$: $\int 6t\,\text{d}t = 3t^2$, not $6t^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Interpreting Repeated Roots
bradley_insight.content: At $t = 1\text{ s}$, the particle crosses the origin with non-zero velocity. At $t = 2\text{ s}$, we have a repeated root $(t - 2)^2 = 0$, meaning $s = 0$ and $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} = v = 0$ simultaneously. The particle touches the origin and instantaneously reverses direction without crossing it.

question:
A particle moves in a horizontal straight line such that its velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds ($t \ge 0$) is given by:$$v = 3t^2 - 12t + 9$$At time $t = 0$, the particle is at the origin $O$.

(a) Find an expression for the displacement $s$ of the particle from $O$ at time $t$ seconds.

(b) Find the two values of $t$ at which the particle is momentarily at rest.

(c) Calculate the total distance travelled by the particle in the first $3$ seconds of its motion.
steps:
(a) Displacement expression:

Integrating velocity:\begin{aligned} s &= \int (3t^2 - 12t + 9)\,\text{d}t \cr &= t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t + c \end{aligned}
Since $s(0) = 0$, $c = 0$:\begin{aligned} s = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t \end{aligned}

(b) Times when momentarily at rest:

Set $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 0 \cr &3(t^2 - 4t + 3) = 0 \cr &3(t - 1)(t - 3) = 0 \end{aligned}
The particle is momentarily at rest at $t = 1\text{ s}$ and $t = 3\text{ s}$.

(c) Total distance in first $3$ seconds:

Evaluate displacement at key times:
• At $t = 0\text{ s}$: $s(0) = 0\text{ m}$
• At $t = 1\text{ s}$: $s(1) = 1^3 - 6(1^2) + 9(1) = 4\text{ m}$
• At $t = 3\text{ s}$: $s(3) = 3^3 - 6(3^2) + 9(3) = 27 - 54 + 27 = 0\text{ m}$

Calculate distance for each direction of motion:
• Forward motion ($0 \le t \le 1$): $|4 - 0| = 4\text{ m}$
• Backward motion ($1 \le t \le 3$): $|0 - 4| = 4\text{ m}$

Total distance travelled:\begin{aligned} d &= 4 + 4 \cr &= 8\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $s = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$, (b) $t = 1\text{ s}$, $t = 3\text{ s}$, (c) $8\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: A value of $0\text{ m}$ is the net displacement ($s(3) - s(0) = 0$). Distance is a scalar quantity measuring the total path length travelled, which is $4 + 4 = 8\text{ m}$.

The value $4\text{ m}$ only accounts for the forward travel up to the turning point at $t = 1\text{ s}$. You must also add the distance travelled as the particle returns to the origin between $t = 1$ and $t = 3$.
Check your factorisation of $t^2 - 4t + 3$. The roots are $t = 1\text{ s}$ and $t = 3\text{ s}$, not $t = 2\text{ s}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Distance is Not Equal to Displacement
bradley_insight.content: At $t = 3\text{ s}$, the particle is back at the origin, so its displacement is $0\text{ m}$. However, the question asks for total distance travelled. You must split the journey at each turning point where $v = 0$ (here, $t = 1\text{ s}$) and sum the absolute distances travelled in each direction: $4\text{ m} + 4\text{ m} = 8\text{ m}$.

question:
The diagram shows two objects, $A$ and $B$, of mass $4\text{ kg}$ and $6\text{ kg}$ respectively, connected by a light inextensible string passing over a small, light, smooth pulley fixed at the edge of a smooth horizontal table. Object $A$ rests on the horizontal table and object $B$ hangs freely vertically below the pulley.

Initially, the objects are held at rest with the string taut. The system is then released.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of object $A$ and the tension in the string.

(b) State briefly what effect a rough pulley would have on the tension in the two parts of the string.
steps:
(a) Acceleration and tension:

Applying Newton's second law ($F = ma$) to each object:
• For hanging object $B$ downwards:\begin{aligned} &6g - T = 6a \cr &6(9.8) - T = 6a \cr &58.8 - T = 6a \end{aligned}
• For object $A$ along the smooth table:\begin{aligned} T = 4a \end{aligned}
Adding the two equations eliminates $T$:\begin{aligned} &58.8 = 10a \cr &a = \dfrac{58.8}{10} \cr &a = 5.88\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
Substitute $a = 5.88\text{ m s}^{-2}$ to find tension $T$:\begin{aligned} T &= 4(5.88) \cr &= 23.52\text{ N} \cr &\approx 23.5\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Effect of a rough pulley:

If the pulley were rough, friction would oppose the motion of the string over the pulley.

Consequently, the tension would not be uniform throughout the string: the tension in the vertical section supporting $B$ would be greater than the tension in the horizontal section pulling $A$.
Final Answer: (a) $a = 5.88\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $T = 23.5\text{ N}$, (b) Tensions would differ ($T_{\text{vertical}} > T_{\text{horizontal}}$)

pi_options.ans: (a) $a = 5.88\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $T = 58.8\text{ N}$, (b) Tensions would differ ($T_{\text{vertical}} > T_{\text{horizontal}}$)
pi_options.feedback: Because block $B$ is accelerating downwards, the tension is strictly less than its static weight ($T = m_B(g - a) = 23.5\text{ N}$). Using $T = m_B g = 58.8\text{ N}$ only applies if the system is in stationary equilibrium.

pi_options.ans: (a) $a = 9.80\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $T = 23.5\text{ N}$, (b) Tensions would differ ($T_{\text{vertical}} > T_{\text{horizontal}}$)
pi_options.feedback: Block $B$ is not in free fall. The tension in the string pulls upward on $B$ while pulling $A$ along the table, reducing the system acceleration to below $g$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $a = 5.88\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $T = 23.5\text{ N}$, (b) Tension would remain identical throughout
pi_options.feedback: A smooth pulley allows tension to be transmitted equally across both sides. If the pulley is rough, friction creates a tension difference between the two sections.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Why 'Smooth' Matters
bradley_insight.content: The assumption that the pulley is 'smooth' allows us to model tension as identical throughout the continuous string. If the pulley is rough, friction creates a tension gradient, meaning the tension in the vertical section must exceed the tension in the horizontal section to rotate the pulley.

question:
The diagram shows a block $P$ of mass $5\text{ kg}$ resting on a rough horizontal table. Block $P$ is connected to a block $Q$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ by a light inextensible string passing over a small, smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table. Block $Q$ hangs freely vertically below the pulley.

The coefficient of friction between block $P$ and the table is $\mu = 0.25$. The system is released from rest with the string taut.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Show that the system moves, and calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.

(b) Find the tension in the string during the motion, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Verification of motion and acceleration:

Normal reaction on block $P$:\begin{aligned} R_P &= 5(9.8) \cr &= 49\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Maximum available friction:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{max}} &= \mu R_P \cr &= 0.25(49) \cr &= 12.25\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Downward weight of hanging block $Q$:\begin{aligned} W_Q &= 3(9.8) \cr &= 29.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Since $W_Q > F_{\text{max}}$ ($29.4\text{ N} > 12.25\text{ N}$), the driving force overcomes static friction and the system moves.

Equation of motion for the system:\begin{aligned} &W_Q - F_{\text{max}} = (m_P + m_Q)a \cr &29.4 - 12.25 = 8a \cr &17.15 = 8a \cr &a = \dfrac{17.15}{8} \cr &a \approx 2.14\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Tension in the string:

Applying Newton's second law to hanging block $Q$:\begin{aligned} &3(9.8) - T = 3a \cr &29.4 - T = 3(2.14375) \cr &29.4 - T = 6.43125 \cr &T = 29.4 - 6.43125 \cr &T \approx 23.0\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $a = 2.14\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $T = 23.0\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Remember to subtract the friction force ($12.25\text{ N}$) from the net driving force. Neglecting friction gives $a = 29.4 / 8 = 3.68\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Tension is not equal to the full weight of block $Q$ while it accelerates downwards. Use $29.4 - T = m_Q a$ to find $T = 23.0\text{ N}$.
For block $P$ on the rough surface, $T - F = m_P a$. Therefore, \begin{aligned}T &= m_P a + F \cr &= 5(2.14) + 12.25 \cr &= 23.0\text{ N}\end{aligned} You must add friction to $m_P a$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Check Impending Motion First
bradley_insight.content: Whenever friction is present, always compare the driving force ($m_Q g$) against the maximum available static friction ($F_{\text{max}} = \mu m_P g$) before writing down dynamic equations. If $m_Q g \le F_{\text{max}}$, the system remains stationary ($a = 0$), and static friction simply balances tension.

question:
The diagram shows a block $M_1$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ on a smooth horizontal table, connected by a light inextensible string passing over a small, smooth pulley at the edge of the table to a block $M_2$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$ hanging freely.

Block $M_2$ is initially held at rest at a height of $h = 1.5\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground. The system is released from rest with the string taut. Block $M_2$ descends and strikes the ground without rebounding.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Assume block $M_1$ does not reach the pulley.]

(a) Find the speed of block $M_2$ immediately before it strikes the ground, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.

(b) Find the time taken for block $M_2$ to reach the ground from release, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Acceleration and impact speed:

Applying Newton's second law to the system before impact:\begin{aligned} &m_2 g = (m_1 + m_2)a \cr &2(9.8) = (3 + 2)a \cr &19.6 = 5a \cr &a = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $u = 0$ and $s = 1.5\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} v^2 &= 0 + 2(3.92)(1.5) \cr &= 11.76 \cr v &= \sqrt{11.76} \cr &\approx 3.43\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Time of descent:

Using $v = u + at$:\begin{aligned} 3.4293 &= 0 + 3.92t \cr t &= \dfrac{3.4293}{3.92} \cr &\approx 0.875\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $3.43\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b) $0.875\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: Block $M_2$ does not fall freely under gravity. Its downward pull accelerates both masses ($M_1 + M_2$), so $a = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-2}$, not $9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Do not divide distance by final velocity ($1.5 / 3.43$). Because the block accelerates uniformly from rest, the average speed is $\frac{v}{2}$, giving $t = 1.5 / 1.715 = 0.875\text{ s}$.
Check the kinematic formula $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$. Omitting the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ doubles the calculated value of $t^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Connected Inertia Reduces Acceleration
bradley_insight.content: A hanging mass connected to another block never falls with free-fall acceleration $g$. The downward gravitational force $m_2 g$ must accelerate the entire system mass ($m_1 + m_2$). Always find the combined system acceleration before applying constant acceleration formulae.

question:
The diagram shows a block $A$ of mass $2\text{ kg}$ resting on a smooth horizontal table. Block $A$ is connected to a block $B$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ by a light inextensible string passing over a small, light, smooth pulley fixed at the corner of the table. Block $B$ hangs freely vertically downwards.

The system is released from rest with the string taut.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Find the tension in the string during the motion.

(b) State the direction and calculate the magnitude of the resultant force exerted by the string on the pulley, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Tension in the string:

Applying Newton's second law to the system:\begin{aligned} &m_B g = (m_A + m_B)a \cr &3(9.8) = (2 + 3)a \cr &29.4 = 5a \cr &a = 5.88\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
For block $A$ on the smooth table:\begin{aligned} T &= m_A a \cr &= 2(5.88) \cr &= 11.76\text{ N} \cr &\approx 11.8\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Resultant force on the pulley:

The two segments of string pull away from the pulley at $90^\circ$ to each other:
• A horizontal pull of magnitude $T$ to the left
• A vertical pull of magnitude $T$ downwards

Magnitude of the resultant force $R$:\begin{aligned} R &= \sqrt{T^2 + T^2} \cr &= T\sqrt{2} \cr &= 11.76\sqrt{2} \cr &\approx 16.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Direction: By symmetry, the resultant acts at $45^\circ$ below the horizontal, pointing directly into the corner of the table.
Final Answer: (a) $T = 11.8\text{ N}$, (b) $16.6\text{ N}$ at $45^\circ$ below the horizontal

pi_options.ans: (a) $T = 11.8\text{ N}$, (b) $23.5\text{ N}$ at $45^\circ$ below the horizontal
pi_options.feedback: Forces are vector quantities. You cannot add the two perpendicular tension forces linearly ($11.76 + 11.76 = 23.52\text{ N}$); combine them using Pythagoras ($R = \sqrt{T^2 + T^2} = T\sqrt{2}$).

pi_options.ans: (a) $T = 29.4\text{ N}$, (b) $16.6\text{ N}$ at $45^\circ$ below the horizontal
pi_options.feedback: The tension is not equal to the static weight of block $B$. Because block $B$ accelerates downwards, $T = m_B(g - a) = 11.76\text{ N}$.
The pulley experiences forces from both segments of the string. You must include the horizontal pull as well as the vertical pull.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Right-Angled Pulley Resultants
bradley_insight.content: When a string turns through a right angle ($90^\circ$) over a smooth pulley, the two tension forces are equal in magnitude and perpendicular. The resultant force is always $R = T\sqrt{2}$, directed along the angle bisector at $45^\circ$ to both string segments.

question:
The diagram shows a block $C$ of mass $5\text{ kg}$ resting on a smooth horizontal table. Block $C$ is connected by two separate light inextensible strings passing over smooth pulleys at opposite edges of the table to two hanging blocks, $A$ and $B$, of mass $2\text{ kg}$ and $7\text{ kg}$ respectively. Both blocks $A$ and $B$ hang freely vertically downwards.

The system is released from rest with both strings taut.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the system.

(b) Find the tension in the string attached to block $A$ and the tension in the string attached to block $B$.
steps:
(a) Acceleration of the system:

Block $B$ ($7\text{ kg}$) is heavier than block $A$ ($2\text{ kg}$), so block $B$ accelerates downwards, block $C$ moves to the right, and block $A$ accelerates upwards.

Applying Newton's second law to each block:
• For block $B$ (downwards): $7g - T_B = 7a$
• For block $C$ (rightwards): $T_B - T_A = 5a$
• For block $A$ (upwards): $T_A - 2g = 2a$

Summing all three equations eliminates both internal tensions:\begin{aligned} &7g - 2g = (7 + 5 + 2)a \cr &5g = 14a \cr &5(9.8) = 14a \cr &49 = 14a \cr &a = \dfrac{49}{14} \cr &a = 3.5\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Tensions in the strings:

For string $A$ ($T_A - 2g = 2a$):\begin{aligned} T_A &= 2(9.8) + 2(3.5) \cr &= 19.6 + 7 \cr &= 26.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}
For string $B$ ($7g - T_B = 7a$):\begin{aligned} T_B &= 7(9.8) - 7(3.5) \cr &= 68.6 - 24.5 \cr &= 44.1\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $a = 3.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $T_A = 26.6\text{ N}$, $T_B = 44.1\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: The tensions have been swapped. Because block $B$ ($7\text{ kg}$) accelerates downwards, $T_B = 44.1\text{ N}$ is pulling it, while block $A$ ($2\text{ kg}$) is lifted by $T_A = 26.6\text{ N}$.
Remember to include the mass of table block $C$ ($5\text{ kg}$) in the total system inertia ($2 + 5 + 7 = 14\text{ kg}$). Dividing $49\text{ N}$ by $10\text{ kg}$ omits block $C$.
Because the system is accelerating, neither tension equals the static weight ($mg$) of the hanging blocks. Apply $F = ma$ to each block individually.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Two Separate Strings Mean Two Different Tensions
bradley_insight.content: Because block $C$ is pulled by two independent strings, never assume the tension is the same across the table. Always assign distinct variables $T_A$ and $T_B$. Adding all three equations together eliminates both tensions in one step, letting you find the system acceleration $a$ instantly.

question:
Three forces $\mathbf{F}_1$, $\mathbf{F}_2$, and $\mathbf{F}_3$ act on a particle, where:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_1 &= (3\mathbf{i} - 11\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \cr \mathbf{F}_2 &= (-7\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \cr \mathbf{F}_3 &= (16\mathbf{i} + k\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}
and $k$ is a constant. The resultant of the three forces is $\mathbf{R}$, and the magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$ is $13\text{ N}$.

(a) Find the two possible values of the constant $k$.

(b) For the larger of the two values of $k$, calculate the acute angle that $\mathbf{R}$ makes with the unit vector $\mathbf{i}$, giving your answer to the nearest $0.1^\circ$.
steps:
(a) Find the two possible values of $k$:

Add the three forces component-wise to find the resultant $\mathbf{R}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R} &= (3 - 7 + 16)\mathbf{i} \cr &\quad + (-11 + 6 + k)\mathbf{j} \cr &= 12\mathbf{i} + (k - 5)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
The magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$ is given as $13\text{ N}$:\begin{aligned} &|\mathbf{R}|^2 = 12^2 + (k - 5)^2 \cr &13^2 = 144 + (k - 5)^2 \cr &169 = 144 + (k - 5)^2 \cr &(k - 5)^2 = 25 \cr &k - 5 = \pm 5 \end{aligned}
Solving for $k$:\begin{aligned} k = 10 \quad\text{or}\quad k = 0 \end{aligned}

(b) Angle with unit vector $\mathbf{i}$:

For the larger value $k = 10$, the resultant is $\mathbf{R} = 12\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}$.

Let $\theta$ be the angle $\mathbf{R}$ makes with $\mathbf{i}$:\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{5}{12} \cr \theta &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right) \cr &\approx 22.6^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $k = 10$ or $k = 0$, (b) $22.6^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: This angle is measured relative to the vertical unit vector $\mathbf{j}$ ($\arctan(12/5) \approx 67.4^\circ$). The question asks for the angle with the unit vector $\mathbf{i}$, which is $\arctan(5/12) \approx 22.6^\circ$.
Remember to include both square roots when solving $(k - 5)^2 = 25$: $k - 5 = \pm 5$, which gives $k = 10$ or $k = 0$.
Check the sum of the $\mathbf{j}$-components: $-11 + 6 + k = k - 5$, not $k - 3$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Remember Both Roots
bradley_insight.content: When solving quadratic vector equations like $(k - 5)^2 = 25$, always take both square roots ($k - 5 = \pm 5$). Forgetting the negative root loses marks. Also check whether the angle is requested with vector $\mathbf{i}$ (horizontal) or $\mathbf{j}$ (vertical).

subtopic: Newton's second law in vector form
question:
A particle of mass $4\text{ kg}$ moves under the action of three constant coplanar forces:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_1 &= (8\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \cr \mathbf{F}_2 &= (-2\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \cr \mathbf{F}_3 &= (p\mathbf{i} + q\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}
where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Under the action of these three forces, the particle accelerates with acceleration $\mathbf{a} = (3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the values of the constants $p$ and $q$.

(b) A fourth constant force $\mathbf{F}_4$ is now added so that the particle moves with constant velocity. Find $\mathbf{F}_4$ in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$, and calculate its magnitude, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Find $p$ and $q$:

The resultant force is given by Newton's second law $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F} &= 4(3\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 12\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Summing the three forces:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 + \mathbf{F}_3 &= (8 - 2 + p)\mathbf{i} \cr &\quad + (-5 + 9 + q)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (6 + p)\mathbf{i} + (4 + q)\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Equating components:\begin{aligned} 6 + p &= 12 \implies p = 6 \cr 4 + q &= 8 \implies q = 4 \end{aligned}

(b) Find $\mathbf{F}_4$ and its magnitude:

For constant velocity, the acceleration is zero, so the resultant force must be zero:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{F} + \mathbf{F}_4 = \mathbf{0} \cr &(12\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}) + \mathbf{F}_4 = \mathbf{0} \cr &\mathbf{F}_4 = (-12\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Magnitude of $\mathbf{F}_4$:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{F}_4| &= \sqrt{(-12)^2 + (-8)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{144 + 64} \cr &= \sqrt{208} \cr &\approx 14.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $p = 6$, $q = 4$, (b) $\mathbf{F}_4 = (-12\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$, $|\mathbf{F}_4| = 14.4\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: To bring the resultant force to zero, the balancing force must oppose the resultant: $\mathbf{F}_4 = -\mathbf{R} = (-12\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$.
Remember to multiply acceleration by the mass ($m = 4\text{ kg}$) when applying $\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$. Equating the forces directly to $\mathbf{a}$ neglects the mass.

To find the magnitude of a vector, use Pythagoras \begin{aligned}|\mathbf{F}_4|&= \sqrt{(-12)^2 + (-8)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{208} \cr & \approx 14.4\text{ N}\end{aligned} Do not add the component magnitudes linearly.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Constant Velocity Means Zero Net Force
bradley_insight.content: A classic exam keyword is 'constant velocity'. By Newton's first law, constant velocity means zero acceleration ($\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}$), which in turn means the vector sum of all forces must be zero ($\sum \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}$). The added force $\mathbf{F}_4$ is simply the exact negative of the existing resultant.

question:
Two forces, $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$, act on a body of mass $2.5\text{ kg}$ on a smooth horizontal plane, where:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_1 &= (14\mathbf{i} - 6\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \cr \mathbf{F}_2 &= (-6\mathbf{i} + 21\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}
The unit vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ point due East and due North respectively.

(a) Find the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the body, and hence find the magnitude of the acceleration of the body.

(b) Calculate the direction of the resultant force as a three-figure bearing, giving your answer to the nearest degree.
steps:
(a) Resultant force and acceleration:

Resultant force $\mathbf{R}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R} &= \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 \cr &= (14 - 6)\mathbf{i} + (-6 + 21)\mathbf{j} \cr &= 8\mathbf{i} + 15\mathbf{j}\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{R}| &= \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} \cr &= \sqrt{64 + 225} \cr &= \sqrt{289} \cr &= 17\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Acceleration magnitude:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{|\mathbf{R}|}{m} \cr &= \dfrac{17}{2.5} \cr &= 6.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Bearing of the resultant force:

Since the East component is $+8$ and the North component is $+15$, the force points into the North-East quadrant.

Angle $\theta$ clockwise from North:\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{\text{East component}}{\text{North component}} \cr &= \dfrac{8}{15} \cr \theta &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{8}{15}\right) \cr &\approx 28.1^\circ \end{aligned}
Expressed as a three-figure bearing to the nearest degree: $028^\circ$.
Final Answer: (a) $|\mathbf{R}| = 17\text{ N}$, $a = 6.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $028^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: This angle is measured North of East ($\arctan(15/8) \approx 62^\circ$). Bearings are measured clockwise from North, giving $90^\circ - 62^\circ = 028^\circ$.
Use Pythagoras to calculate the magnitude of perpendicular vector components: $\sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = 17\text{ N}$, rather than adding $8 + 15 = 23\text{ N}$.
To find acceleration from force, divide by mass ($a = F/m = 17 / 2.5 = 6.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$). Multiplying by mass gives $42.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Bearings are Measured from North
bradley_insight.content: A common error on vector mechanics questions is calculating $\arctan(y/x) = \arctan(15/8) = 61.9^\circ$, which gives the angle measured from East. Bearings must always be measured clockwise from North ($y$-axis), so the angle is $\arctan(x/y) = \arctan(8/15) \approx 28^\circ$, written with three figures as $028^\circ$.

question:
Three forces act on a particle:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F}_1 &= (5\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \cr \mathbf{F}_2 &= (-8\mathbf{i} + 7\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \cr \mathbf{F}_3 &= (p\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}
where $p$ is a constant. The resultant of these three forces is denoted by $\mathbf{R}$.

(a) Given that $\mathbf{R}$ acts parallel to the vector $(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$, find the value of $p$.

(b) Given instead that the magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$ is $10\text{ N}$ and the $\mathbf{i}$-component of $\mathbf{R}$ is strictly positive, find the value of $p$.
steps:
(a) Parallel resultant:

Sum the forces to find $\mathbf{R}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{R} &= (5 - 8 + p)\mathbf{i} \cr &\quad + (2 + 7 - 3)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (p - 3)\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
If $\mathbf{R}$ is parallel to $(2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})$, the ratio of components must be equal:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{p - 3}{6} &= \dfrac{2}{3} \cr 3(p - 3) &= 12 \cr p - 3 &= 4 \cr p &= 7 \end{aligned}

(b) Magnitude condition:

The magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$ is $10\text{ N}$:\begin{aligned} &|\mathbf{R}|^2 = (p - 3)^2 + 6^2 \cr &10^2 = (p - 3)^2 + 36 \cr &100 = (p - 3)^2 + 36 \cr &(p - 3)^2 = 64 \cr &p - 3 = \pm 8 \end{aligned}
Since the $\mathbf{i}$-component ($p - 3$) is strictly positive, we take $+8$:\begin{aligned} &p - 3 = 8 \cr &p = 11 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $p = 7$, (b) $p = 11$

pi_options.feedback: Note the condition that the $\mathbf{i}$-component must be strictly positive. Choosing $p = -5$ gives $\mathbf{i}$-component $-5 - 3 = -8$, which violates this constraint.
Remember to include the constant term in the $\mathbf{i}$-component ($5 - 8 + p = p - 3$). Solving $p / 6 = 2/3$ ignores the $-3$.
Check your calculation when subtracting $36$ from $100$: $100 - 36 = 64$, giving $p - 3 = \pm 8 \implies p = 11$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Parallel Vectors and Component Ratios
bradley_insight.content: When two 2D vectors are parallel, their components are in direct proportion: $\frac{R_x}{V_x} = \frac{R_y}{V_y}$. Cross-multiplying gives a simple linear equation that eliminates the need for vector scaling parameters.

question:
A particle $P$ of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ is initially at rest at the origin $O$. Two constant forces, $\mathbf{F}_1 = (6\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$ and $\mathbf{F}_2 = (-2\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j})\text{ N}$, act simultaneously on $P$.

(a) Find the acceleration vector $\mathbf{a}$ of the particle.

(b) Find the speed of the particle when $t = 3\text{ s}$.

(c) Find the position vector $\mathbf{r}$ of the particle from $O$ when $t = 4\text{ s}$.
steps:
(a) Acceleration vector $\mathbf{a}$:

Calculate the resultant force $\mathbf{F}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{F} &= \mathbf{F}_1 + \mathbf{F}_2 \cr &= (6 - 2)\mathbf{i} + (-2 + 5)\mathbf{j} \cr &= (4\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j})\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Applying $\mathbf{a} = \dfrac{\mathbf{F}}{m}$ with $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{a} &= \dfrac{4\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}}{0.5} \cr &= (8\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Speed when $t = 3\text{ s}$:

Velocity vector with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}(3) &= \mathbf{a}t \cr &= (8\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}) \times 3 \cr &= (24\mathbf{i} + 18\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Speed is the magnitude of velocity:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{v}| &= \sqrt{24^2 + 18^2} \cr &= \sqrt{576 + 324} \cr &= \sqrt{900} \cr &= 30\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Position vector $\mathbf{r}$ when $t = 4\text{ s}$:

Using $\mathbf{r} = \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $t = 4\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r}(4) &= \dfrac{1}{2}(8\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})(4^2) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(8\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})(16) \cr &= 8(8\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (64\mathbf{i} + 48\mathbf{j})\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\mathbf{a} = (8\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (c) $\mathbf{r} = (64\mathbf{i} + 48\mathbf{j})\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: Dividing by $m = 0.5\text{ kg}$ doubles the components: $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{F} / 0.5 = 2\mathbf{F}$. Multiplying by $0.5$ halves the acceleration.
Speed is the scalar magnitude of the velocity vector: $\sqrt{24^2 + 18^2} = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Do not add the vector components linearly ($24 + 18 = 42$).
Remember the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in $\mathbf{r} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$. Neglecting this factor gives twice the correct displacement.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dividing by Fractional Mass
bradley_insight.content: Dividing by a mass of $0.5\text{ kg}$ is equivalent to doubling the force: $\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{F}}{0.5} = 2\mathbf{F}$. Also remember that 'speed' is a scalar quantity; never leave your answer as a vector $(24\mathbf{i} + 18\mathbf{j})$ when asked for speed.

question:
A person of mass $70\text{ kg}$ stands on the horizontal floor of a lift of mass $730\text{ kg}$. The lift is suspended by a single light vertical cable and is moving upwards with constant acceleration. The tension in the cable is $8800\text{ N}$.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Determine the acceleration of the lift, giving your answer correct to two decimal places.

(b) State whether the lift is speeding up, travelling at a constant speed, or slowing down.

(c) Calculate the magnitude of the normal reaction force exerted by the floor of the lift on the person.
steps:
(a) Acceleration of the lift:

Total mass of the system:\begin{aligned} M &= 730 + 70 \cr &= 800\text{ kg} \end{aligned}
Applying Newton's second law upwards:\begin{aligned} &T - Mg = Ma \cr &8800 - 800(9.8) = 800a \cr &8800 - 7840 = 800a \cr &960 = 800a \cr &a = \dfrac{960}{800} \cr &a = 1.20\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Motion status:

Because the lift is moving upwards and the acceleration is positive (directed upwards), the lift is speeding up.

(c) Normal reaction on the person:

Applying Newton's second law to the person ($m = 70\text{ kg}$):\begin{aligned} &R - mg = ma \cr &R - 70(9.8) = 70(1.20) \cr &R - 686 = 84 \cr &R = 686 + 84 \cr &R = 770\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $a = 1.20\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) Speeding up, (c) $R = 770\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: The normal reaction equals $mg$ only when the lift is stationary or at constant speed. Here, upward acceleration adds an inertial force: $R = m(g + a) = 770\text{ N}$.
Remember to include the passenger mass in the total system inertia ($M = 800\text{ kg}$). Using only the lift mass ($730\text{ kg}$) overestimates acceleration.
Because the acceleration acts in the same direction as the upward motion, the speed increases.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: System First, Individual Body Second
bradley_insight.content: To find the cable tension or overall acceleration, treat the lift and passenger as a single combined body of mass $M = m_1 + m_2$. The normal reaction $R$ between the floor and passenger is an internal force that cancels out. Once you have $a$, isolate the passenger to find $R$.

question:
A lift of mass $650\text{ kg}$ carries a crate of mass $150\text{ kg}$ resting on its horizontal floor. The lift is descending vertically and is brought to rest with a constant deceleration of magnitude $1.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Calculate the tension in the lift cable while the lift is decelerating.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the normal reaction force exerted by the floor of the lift on the crate.

(c) Explain briefly why the normal reaction force exerted by the floor on the crate is greater than the weight of the crate during this deceleration.
steps:
(a) Cable tension:

Total mass of the system:\begin{aligned} M &= 650 + 150 \cr &= 800\text{ kg} \end{aligned}
A downward deceleration of $1.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$ corresponds to an upward resultant acceleration of $a = 1.4\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

Applying Newton's second law upwards:\begin{aligned} &T - Mg = Ma \cr &T - 800(9.8) = 800(1.4) \cr &T - 7840 = 1120 \cr &T = 7840 + 1120 \cr &T = 8960\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Normal reaction on the crate:

Applying Newton's second law upwards to the crate ($m = 150\text{ kg}$):\begin{aligned} &R - mg = ma \cr &R - 150(9.8) = 150(1.4) \cr &R - 1470 = 210 \cr &R = 1470 + 210 \cr &R = 1680\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Physical explanation:

To decelerate while moving downwards, the net force must be directed upwards. Therefore, the upward normal reaction force from the floor must exceed the downward gravitational force (weight) of the crate ($R > mg$).
Final Answer: (a) $T = 8960\text{ N}$, (b) $R = 1680\text{ N}$, (c) Upward resultant force required to decelerate

pi_options.ans: (a) $T = 6720\text{ N}$, (b) $R = 1260\text{ N}$, (c) Upward resultant force required to decelerate
pi_options.feedback: Decelerating while descending means the acceleration points upwards. The upward forces must exceed the weight, so you add $ma$ to $mg$, not subtract it.

pi_options.ans: (a) $T = 8960\text{ N}$, (b) $R = 1470\text{ N}$, (c) Upward resultant force required to decelerate
pi_options.feedback: The normal reaction is not equal to static weight ($1470\text{ N}$). During upward acceleration, $R = m(g + a) = 1680\text{ N}$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $T = 7840\text{ N}$, (b) $R = 1680\text{ N}$, (c) Upward resultant force required to decelerate
pi_options.feedback: The cable tension must exceed the total weight to produce upward deceleration: $T = 800(9.8 + 1.4) = 8960\text{ N}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Direction of Deceleration
bradley_insight.content: Always identify the direction of the acceleration vector independently of the direction of motion. A descending object that is slowing down has an acceleration pointing upwards. This means upward forces ($T$ and $R$) must exceed the downward gravitational forces.

question:
A lift of mass $500\text{ kg}$ is descending with a constant downward acceleration of $2.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Two parcels, $A$ and $B$, of mass $4\text{ kg}$ and $6\text{ kg}$ respectively, are placed on the horizontal floor of the lift such that parcel $A$ rests directly on top of parcel $B$.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Find the tension in the lift cable.

(b) Find the magnitude of the contact force exerted by parcel $B$ on parcel $A$.

(c) Find the magnitude of the normal reaction force exerted by the floor of the lift on parcel $B$.
steps:
(a) Cable tension:

Total mass of the system:\begin{aligned} M &= 500 + 4 + 6 \cr &= 510\text{ kg} \end{aligned}
Applying Newton's second law downwards ($a = 2.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$):\begin{aligned} &Mg - T = Ma \cr &510(9.8) - T = 510(2.2) \cr &4998 - T = 1122 \cr &T = 4998 - 1122 \cr &T = 3876\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Contact force on parcel $A$:

Considering parcel $A$ ($m = 4\text{ kg}$) accelerating downwards:\begin{aligned} &m_A g - C = m_A a \cr &4(9.8) - C = 4(2.2) \cr &39.2 - C = 8.8 \cr &C = 39.2 - 8.8 \cr &C = 30.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Reaction of the floor on parcel $B$:

Considering the combined stack ($A + B$, mass $10\text{ kg}$) accelerating downwards:\begin{aligned} &m_{\text{stack}}g - R = m_{\text{stack}}a \cr &10(9.8) - R = 10(2.2) \cr &98 - R = 22 \cr &R = 98 - 22 \cr &R = 76\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $T = 3876\text{ N}$, (b) $C = 30.4\text{ N}$, (c) $R = 76\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: Contact force $C$ is not equal to the static weight ($39.2\text{ N}$). During downward acceleration, $C = m_A(g - a) = 30.4\text{ N}$.
The floor must support both parcel $B$ and parcel $A$. Using only the mass of parcel $B$ ($6\text{ kg}$) ignores the load of parcel $A$.
For downward acceleration, tension is less than weight: $T = M(g - a) = 3876\text{ N}$, not $M(g + a)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Stacked Objects Share Acceleration
bradley_insight.content: For stacked objects inside a lift, every sub-system accelerates at the exact same rate. To find the contact force on the top object, isolate the top object alone ($C = m_A(g - a)$). To find the floor reaction, treat the combined stack as a single object of mass $m_A + m_B$.

question:
A person of mass $80\text{ kg}$ stands on a set of bathroom scales (calibrated in Newtons) on the floor of a lift of mass $720\text{ kg}$. The lift is moving vertically upwards with a constant speed of $4.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ when the supporting cable suddenly snaps.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Air resistance may be neglected.]

(a) Describe the immediate motion of the lift and person immediately after the cable breaks.

(b) State the reading on the bathroom scales immediately after the cable has snapped, and justify your answer.

(c) Calculate the time taken for the lift to reach its maximum height after the cable breaks, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Motion immediately after cable break:

Due to inertia, the lift and person continue to move upwards with decreasing speed, decelerating at $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ under gravity alone (free fall).

(b) Reading on the scales:

The reading on the scales is $0\text{ N}$.

Because both the person and the scales accelerate downwards at $g$, there is no normal reaction force between them ($R = m(g - g) = 0\text{ N}$), producing apparent weightlessness.

(c) Time to reach maximum height:

Using $v = u + at$ with upwards as positive ($u = 4.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0$, $a = -9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$):\begin{aligned} 0 &= 4.0 - 9.8t \cr 9.8t &= 4.0 \cr t &= \dfrac{4.0}{9.8} \cr t &\approx 0.408\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Continues upwards under gravity, (b) $0\text{ N}$ (free fall), (c) $0.408\text{ s}$

pi_options.ans: (a) Immediately falls downwards, (b) $0\text{ N}$ (free fall), (c) $0.408\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: Objects in motion maintain their velocity unless acted on by an impulse. The lift had an upward speed of $4.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, so it continues upwards while decelerating before falling.

pi_options.ans: (a) Continues upwards under gravity, (b) $784\text{ N}$ (free fall), (c) $0.408\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: Scales measure normal reaction force, not gravitational pull. In free fall, both the scale and the person accelerate at $g$, so the contact force is $0\text{ N}$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Continues upwards under gravity, (b) $0\text{ N}$ (free fall), (c) $0.816\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: Check the time calculation: $t = u / g = 4.0 / 9.8 \approx 0.408\text{ s}$. The value $0.816\text{ s}$ is the total time to rise and return to the break point.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: What Scales Actually Measure
bradley_insight.content: Weighing scales never measure mass or gravitational force directly; they measure the normal reaction force $R$ pushing up on your feet. When an enclosure is in free fall ($a = g$ downwards), $R = m(g - g) = 0$, giving the sensation of apparent weightlessness.

question:
A lift of mass $900\text{ kg}$ carries a passenger of mass $75\text{ kg}$. The lift makes an upward journey from rest to rest in three successive stages:

• Stage 1: Accelerates uniformly upwards from rest to a speed of $3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in $2.5\text{ s}$.
• Stage 2: Travels upwards at a constant speed of $3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ for $8.0\text{ s}$.
• Stage 3: Decelerates uniformly to rest in $2.0\text{ s}$.

[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Find the tension in the lift cable during Stage 1.

(b) Find the magnitude of the force exerted by the passenger on the floor of the lift during Stage 3.

(c) Calculate the total vertical height gained by the lift during the entire journey.
steps:
(a) Stage 1 cable tension:

Total mass of system:\begin{aligned} M &= 900 + 75 \cr &= 975\text{ kg} \end{aligned}
Acceleration in Stage 1:\begin{aligned} a_1 &= \dfrac{3.0 - 0}{2.5} \cr &= 1.2\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
Applying Newton's second law upwards:\begin{aligned} &T_1 - Mg = Ma_1 \cr &T_1 = 975(9.8 + 1.2) \cr &T_1 = 975(11) \cr &T_1 = 10725\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Stage 3 floor force:

Deceleration in Stage 3:\begin{aligned} a_3 &= \dfrac{0 - 3.0}{2.0} \cr &= -1.5\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}
For the passenger ($m = 75\text{ kg}$) with upward acceleration $-1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} &R_3 - mg = ma_3 \cr &R_3 = 75(9.8 - 1.5) \cr &R_3 = 75(8.3) \cr &R_3 = 622.5\text{ N} \end{aligned}
By Newton's third law, the force on the floor equals $622.5\text{ N}$.

(c) Total vertical height gained:

The height corresponds to the area of the $v$-$t$ graph (trapezium):
• Base $T = 2.5 + 8.0 + 2.0 = 12.5\text{ s}$
• Top $t_{\text{cruise}} = 8.0\text{ s}$
• Height $v = 3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Area of trapezium:\begin{aligned} H &= \dfrac{1}{2}(8.0 + 12.5) \times 3.0 \cr &= 1.5 \times 20.5 \cr &= 30.75\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $T_1 = 10725\text{ N}$, (b) $622.5\text{ N}$, (c) $30.75\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: During Stage 3, the lift decelerates while moving upwards, so $a_3 = -1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$. The normal reaction decreases: $R = 75(9.8 - 1.5) = 622.5\text{ N}$, not $847.5\text{ N}$.
Remember to include the passenger mass in Stage 1 ($M = 975\text{ kg}$). Using only $900\text{ kg}$ underestimates the cable tension.
The lift does not travel at $3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ throughout. Account for the acceleration and deceleration ramps using the trapezium area rule.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Trapezium Rule for Multi-Stage Travel
bradley_insight.content: Rather than calculating the distance for each stage separately using SUVAT, sketch the velocity-time graph. A journey from rest to rest with a cruise phase forms a trapezium: $\text{Distance} = \frac{1}{2}(t_{\text{cruise}} + t_{\text{total}}) \times v_{\max}$, saving time and algebraic steps.

question:
A car travels along a straight horizontal road. Points $A$ and $B$ lie on the road.

As the car passes point $A$, it is travelling with a constant speed of $18\text{ m s}^{-1}$. It continues at this constant speed for $2.5\text{ minutes}$ before a uniform deceleration is applied for $15\text{ seconds}$, bringing the car to rest at point $B$.

(a) Find the distance $AB$.

The car then reverses from rest with a constant acceleration of $2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$ for $6\text{ seconds}$, followed immediately by a constant deceleration of $1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$, coming to rest at point $C$, which lies between $A$ and $B$.

(b) Calculate the total time taken for the car to reverse from $B$ to $C$.

(c) Find the distance $AC$.
steps:
(a) Distance $AB$:

Convert cruising time to seconds: $2.5\text{ min} = 150\text{ s}$.

Distance while cruising:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= 18 \times 150 \cr &= 2700\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Distance while decelerating ($u = 18$, $v = 0$, $t = 15$):\begin{aligned} s_2 &= \dfrac{18 + 0}{2} \times 15 \cr &= 9 \times 15 \cr &= 135\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Total distance:\begin{aligned} AB &= s_1 + s_2 \cr &= 2700 + 135 \cr &= 2835\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(b) Time to reverse from $B$ to $C$:

Stage 1 of reverse ($u = 0$, $a = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $t_1 = 6\text{ s}$):\begin{aligned} v_1 &= 0 + 2.5(6) \cr &= 15\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Stage 2 of reverse ($u = 15\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v = 0$, $a = -1.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$):\begin{aligned} 0 &= 15 - 1.5t_2 \cr 1.5t_2 &= 15 \cr t_2 &= 10\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Total reverse time:\begin{aligned} t_{\text{total}} &= 6 + 10 \cr &= 16\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Distance $AC$:

Reverse distance in Stage 1:\begin{aligned} s_3 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(2.5)(6^2) \cr &= 45\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Reverse distance in Stage 2:\begin{aligned} s_4 &= \dfrac{15 + 0}{2} \times 10 \cr &= 75\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Total reverse distance $BC$:\begin{aligned} BC &= 45 + 75 \cr &= 120\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Distance $AC$:\begin{aligned} AC &= AB - BC \cr &= 2835 - 120 \cr &= 2715\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $AB = 2835\text{ m}$, (b) $16\text{ s}$, (c) $AC = 2715\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: Because point $C$ lies between $A$ and $B$, the car has reversed back towards $A$. You must subtract the reverse distance: \begin{aligned}AC & = AB - BC \cr &= 2835 - 120 \cr &= 2715\text{ m}\end{aligned}
Remember to convert $2.5\text{ minutes}$ into seconds ($150\text{ s}$). Multiplying $18$ by $2.5$ gives only $45\text{ m}$ for the cruising distance.
The reverse journey consists of two stages: $6\text{ s}$ of acceleration plus $10\text{ s}$ of deceleration, giving a total reverse time of $16\text{ s}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Convert Minutes to Seconds Immediately
bradley_insight.content: Always convert time units into standard SI seconds before beginning calculations ($2.5\text{ min} = 150\text{ s}$). Mixing minutes with speeds given in $\text{m s}^{-1}$ is one of the most common early calculation errors in Kinematics.

question:
A lorry $P$ travels along a straight horizontal road at a constant speed of $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$. At the instant lorry $P$ passes a stationary police car $Q$ at point $A$, the police car immediately sets off in pursuit.

Police car $Q$ accelerates uniformly from rest at $2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$ until it reaches its maximum speed of $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$, which it then maintains.

(a) Find the time taken for police car $Q$ to reach its maximum speed, and calculate the distance it travels during this acceleration phase.

(b) Calculate the total time taken from the instant $P$ passes $A$ for police car $Q$ to draw level with lorry $P$.

(c) Find the distance from $A$ at which the police car draws level with the lorry.
steps:
(a) Acceleration phase of police car $Q$:

Using $v = u + at$ with $u = 0$, $v = 30\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $a = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$:\begin{aligned} 30 &= 0 + 2.5t_1 \cr t_1 &= \dfrac{30}{2.5} \cr t_1 &= 12\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Distance travelled during acceleration:\begin{aligned} s_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(2.5)(12^2) \cr &= 180\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(b) Total pursuit time:

Let $t$ be the total time elapsed from the start ($t > 12\text{ s}$).

Distance travelled by lorry $P$:\begin{aligned} s_P = 20t \end{aligned}
Distance travelled by police car $Q$:\begin{aligned} s_Q &= 180 + 30(t - 12) \cr &= 180 + 30t - 360 \cr &= 30t - 180 \end{aligned}
When $Q$ catches $P$, $s_Q = s_P$:\begin{aligned} &30t - 180 = 20t \cr &10t = 180 \cr &t = 18\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(c) Distance from $A$:

Using the distance equation for lorry $P$:\begin{aligned} s &= 20(18) \cr &= 360\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $t = 12\text{ s}$, $s = 180\text{ m}$, (b) $18\text{ s}$, (c) $360\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: Check the pursuit equation. The police car only travels at top speed for $(t - 12)$ seconds. Equating $20t = 30t - 180$ gives $t = 18\text{ s}$, not $16\text{ s}$.
Remember the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$. During the acceleration phase, distance is $\frac{1}{2}(2.5)(144) = 180\text{ m}$, not $360\text{ m}$.
The value $6\text{ s}$ is only the time spent cruising at top speed after accelerating. You must add the initial $12\text{ s}$ of acceleration to find the total time ($18\text{ s}$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Relative Motion During the Cruise Phase
bradley_insight.content: At $t = 12\text{ s}$, the lorry is at $240\text{ m}$ and the police car is at $180\text{ m}$—a gap of $60\text{ m}$. With the police car moving at $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the lorry at $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$, the relative closing speed is $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Closing the $60\text{ m}$ gap takes $60 / 10 = 6\text{ s}$, giving total time $12 + 6 = 18\text{ s}$.

question:
A passenger train travels between two stations, $X$ and $Y$, which are situated $4.2\text{ km}$ apart on a straight horizontal track.

The train accelerates uniformly from rest at $0.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ until it reaches its cruising speed of $24\text{ m s}^{-1}$. It maintains this cruising speed for $T$ seconds before decelerating uniformly to rest at $1.2\text{ m s}^{-2}$ as it arrives at station $Y$.

(a) Find the time taken for the acceleration phase and the time taken for the deceleration phase.

(b) Calculate the distance travelled by the train while accelerating and the distance travelled while decelerating.

(c) Find the cruising time $T$, and hence find the total time taken for the journey from $X$ to $Y$.
steps:
(a) Acceleration and deceleration times:

Acceleration phase ($u = 0$, $v = 24$, $a = 0.8$):\begin{aligned} t_a &= \dfrac{24}{0.8} \cr &= 30\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Deceleration phase ($u = 24$, $v = 0$, $a = -1.2$):\begin{aligned} t_d &= \dfrac{24}{1.2} \cr &= 20\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Distances while accelerating and decelerating:

Distance while accelerating:\begin{aligned} s_a &= \dfrac{1}{2}(24)(30) \cr &= 360\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Distance while decelerating:\begin{aligned} s_d &= \dfrac{1}{2}(24)(20) \cr &= 240\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Cruising time $T$ and total time:

Convert total distance: $4.2\text{ km} = 4200\text{ m}$.

Distance travelled while cruising:\begin{aligned} s_c &= 4200 - (360 + 240) \cr &= 4200 - 600 \cr &= 3600\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Cruising time $T$ at constant speed $24\text{ m s}^{-1}$:\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{3600}{24} \cr &= 150\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Total journey time:\begin{aligned} t_{\text{total}} &= 30 + 150 + 20 \cr &= 200\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $t_a = 30\text{ s}$, $t_d = 20\text{ s}$, (b) $s_a = 360\text{ m}$, $s_d = 240\text{ m}$, (c) $T = 150\text{ s}$, $t_{\text{total}} = 200\text{ s}$

pi_options.ans: (a) $t_a = 30\text{ s}$, $t_d = 20\text{ s}$, (b) $s_a = 360\text{ m}$, $s_d = 240\text{ m}$, (c) $T = 175\text{ s}$, $t_{\text{total}} = 225\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: Remember to subtract the acceleration and deceleration distances from the total distance before finding $T$. Dividing $4200\text{ m}$ directly by $24$ yields an incorrect cruising time.

pi_options.ans: (a) $t_a = 19.2\text{ s}$, $t_d = 28.8\text{ s}$, (b) $s_a = 360\text{ m}$, $s_d = 240\text{ m}$, (c) $T = 150\text{ s}$, $t_{\text{total}} = 200\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: To find time from acceleration, divide speed by acceleration: $t = v / a = 24 / 0.8 = 30\text{ s}$. Multiplying speed by acceleration gives incorrect times.

pi_options.ans: (a) $t_a = 30\text{ s}$, $t_d = 20\text{ s}$, (b) $s_a = 720\text{ m}$, $s_d = 480\text{ m}$, (c) $T = 150\text{ s}$, $t_{\text{total}} = 200\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: Average speed during uniform acceleration from rest is $\frac{v}{2} = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Using the full peak speed of $24\text{ m s}^{-1}$ doubles the distance.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Trapezium Geometry for Three-Stage Journeys
bradley_insight.content: For journeys consisting of uniform acceleration, constant cruise, and uniform braking, sketching a velocity-time trapezium gives an immediate overview. The area of the two end triangles is simply $\frac{1}{2}v(t_a + t_d)$, leaving the rectangular core for the cruise phase.

question:
A particle moves along a straight line with constant acceleration $a\text{ m s}^{-2}$. The particle passes three consecutive points, $P$, $Q$, and $R$, on the line, where $PQ = 24\text{ m}$ and $QR = 40\text{ m}$.

The time taken for the particle to travel from $P$ to $Q$ is $2\text{ seconds}$, and the time taken to travel from $Q$ to $R$ is also $2\text{ seconds}$.

(a) Show that the acceleration $a$ of the particle is $4\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(b) Find the speed of the particle as it passes point $P$.

(c) Given that the particle started from rest at a point $O$ on the line upstream of $P$, find the distance $OP$.
steps:
(a) Show that $a = 4\text{ m s}^{-2}$:

Let $u$ be the velocity at point $P$.

For interval $P \to Q$ ($s = 24\text{ m}$, $t = 2\text{ s}$):\begin{aligned} &s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 \cr &24 = 2u + \dfrac{1}{2}a(2^2) \cr &24 = 2u + 2a \cr &12 = u + a \quad \text{--- (1)} \end{aligned}
For total interval $P \to R$ ($s = 24 + 40 = 64\text{ m}$, $t = 2 + 2 = 4\text{ s}$):\begin{aligned} &64 = 4u + \dfrac{1}{2}a(4^2) \cr &64 = 4u + 8a \cr &16 = u + 2a \quad \text{--- (2)} \end{aligned}
Subtracting (1) from (2):\begin{aligned} a = 4\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(b) Velocity at $P$:

Substitute $a = 4\text{ m s}^{-2}$ into equation (1):\begin{aligned} u &= 12 - 4 \cr &= 8\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Distance $OP$:

For motion from rest at $O$ ($u_0 = 0$) to point $P$ ($v = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$):\begin{aligned} &v^2 = u_0^2 + 2as \cr &8^2 = 0 + 2(4)(OP) \cr &64 = 8(OP) \cr &OP = \dfrac{64}{8} \cr &OP = 8\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $a = 4\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (b) $8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (c) $OP = 8\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, $8^2 = 2(4)(OP) \implies 64 = 8(OP)$, which gives $OP = 8\text{ m}$, not $16\text{ m}$.
Equation (1) gives $u + a = 12$. With $a = 4\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $u = 12 - 4 = 8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, not $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Check the denominator when solving for distance: divide $64$ by $2a = 8$, giving $OP = 8\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Measure from a Common Start Point
bradley_insight.content: When dealing with consecutive intervals, setting up equations for $P \to Q$ and then $P \to R$ is much cleaner than doing $Q \to R$. Measuring from the common origin $P$ ensures both equations share the exact same initial velocity $u$.

question:
A model rocket is launched vertically upwards from rest from the ground. Its engine produces a constant upward acceleration of $6.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$ for $5.0\text{ seconds}$, at which point the engine cuts out.

The rocket continues to move vertically upwards under gravity alone until it reaches its highest point, after which it falls freely back to the ground.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Air resistance may be neglected.]

(a) Find the speed of the rocket and its height above the ground at the instant the engine cuts out.

(b) Calculate the maximum height reached by the rocket above the ground, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.

(c) Calculate the total time elapsed from launch until the rocket returns to the ground, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Engine burn phase ($0 \le t \le 5\text{ s}$):

Speed at engine cut out:\begin{aligned} v_1 &= 0 + 6.0(5.0) \cr &= 30\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}
Height at cut out:\begin{aligned} h_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(6.0)(5.0^2) \cr &= 75\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(b) Maximum height:

During free flight to highest point ($u = 30$, $v = 0$, $a = -9.8$):\begin{aligned} &v^2 = u^2 + 2as_2 \cr &0 = 30^2 - 2(9.8)s_2 \cr &19.6s_2 = 900 \cr &s_2 = \dfrac{900}{19.6} \cr &s_2 \approx 45.918\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Maximum height above ground:\begin{aligned} H_{\max} &= 75 + 45.918 \cr &= 120.918 \cr &\approx 121\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Total flight time:

Time from cut out to highest point:\begin{aligned} t_2 &= \dfrac{30}{9.8} \cr &\approx 3.061\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Time to fall from highest point ($120.918\text{ m}$) to ground:\begin{aligned} &H_{\max} = \dfrac{1}{2}gt_3^2 \cr &120.918 = 4.9t_3^2 \cr &t_3^2 = \dfrac{120.918}{4.9} \cr &t_3 = \sqrt{24.677} \cr &t_3 \approx 4.968\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Total time:\begin{aligned} t_{\text{total}} &= 5.0 + 3.061 + 4.968 \cr &= 13.029 \cr &\approx 13.0\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $75\text{ m}$, (b) $121\text{ m}$, (c) $13.0\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: The value $45.9\text{ m}$ is only the height gained after the engine cuts out. You must add the initial $75\text{ m}$ gained during powered flight to get the maximum height ($121\text{ m}$).
The value $8.06\text{ s}$ is only the time to reach maximum height ($5.0 + 3.06\text{ s}$). You must also add the time taken to fall back to the ground ($4.97\text{ s}$).
Remember the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in $s = \frac{1}{2}at^2$. During powered flight, distance is $\frac{1}{2}(6)(25) = 75\text{ m}$, not $150\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Acceleration Changes Abruptly at Burnout
bradley_insight.content: Engine burnout divides the problem into two completely distinct physical regimes. During the first $5\text{ s}$, the rocket accelerates upwards under its motor ($+6.0\text{ m s}^{-2}$). The moment fuel runs out, acceleration instantly becomes $-9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$ downwards, even though the rocket continues climbing upwards due to its inertia.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform plank $AB$ of length $5\text{ m}$ supported in horizontal equilibrium by means of a central pivot.

On the plank there are three objects of masses $10\text{ kg}$, $4\text{ kg}$, and $18\text{ kg}$ placed in positions $C$, $D$, and $E$ respectively. The distance $AC$ is $0.8\text{ m}$ and the distance $AE$ is $3.5\text{ m}$.

Find the distance $AD$.
steps:
Locate distances from the central pivot:

The plank is uniform and has length $5\text{ m}$, so the central pivot $P$ is at the midpoint, $2.5\text{ m}$ from $A$.

The weight of the plank acts directly through this pivot and exerts zero moment.

Distances from the pivot $P$ ($2.5\text{ m}$ from $A$):
• Distance $CP = 2.5 - 0.8 = 1.7\text{ m}$ (left)
• Distance $EP = 3.5 - 2.5 = 1.0\text{ m}$ (right)

Take moments about the pivot:

Let $d$ be the distance of mass $D$ from end $A$, so its distance from the pivot is $(2.5 - d)$ to the left.

Equating anticlockwise and clockwise moments about $P$:\begin{aligned} &10g(1.7) + 4g(2.5 - d) = 18g(1.0) \cr &17g + 10g - 4gd = 18g \cr &27 - 4d = 18 \cr &4d = 9 \cr &d = 2.25\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Therefore, the distance $AD = 2.25\text{ m}$.
Final Answer: $AD = 2.25\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: Mass $D$ must lie to the left of the pivot ($2.25\text{ m}$ from $A$) to assist mass $C$. Placing it $0.25\text{ m}$ to the right gives $2.75\text{ m}$, unbalancing the clockwise side.
The value $0.25\text{ m}$ is the distance from the central pivot to $D$. The question asks for the distance from end $A$, which is $2.5 - 0.25 = 2.25\text{ m}$.
Check your moment equation: \begin{aligned}17 + 4(2.5 - d) &= 18\cr \implies 4(2.5 - d)& = 1\end{aligned} giving $2.5 - d = 0.25 \implies d = 2.25\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Pivot at Centre of Mass
bradley_insight.content: Placing the pivot at the midpoint of a uniform plank is an examiner's gift: the weight of the plank acts directly through the pivot line, producing zero turning effect. You only need to balance the moments of the external loads.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform beam $AB$ of length $6\text{ m}$ and mass $20\text{ kg}$ resting horizontally in equilibrium on a smooth pivot at $P$, where $AP = 2\text{ m}$.

An object of mass $M\text{ kg}$ is attached to end $A$ and an object of mass $15\text{ kg}$ is attached to end $B$.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) State the distance from end $A$ to the centre of mass $G$ of the beam.

(b) Calculate the mass $M$ required for the beam to rest in horizontal equilibrium.
steps:
(a) Centre of mass:

Because the beam is uniform, its centre of mass $G$ lies at its geometric midpoint:\begin{aligned} AG &= \dfrac{6}{2} \cr &= 3\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate mass $M$:

Distances from the pivot $P$ (located $2\text{ m}$ from $A$):
• Distance to $A$: $2\text{ m}$ (left)
• Distance to $G$: $3 - 2 = 1\text{ m}$ (right)
• Distance to $B$: $6 - 2 = 4\text{ m}$ (right)

Taking moments about the pivot $P$:\begin{aligned} &Mg(2) = 20g(1) + 15g(4) \cr &2Mg = 20g + 60g \cr &2M = 80 \cr &M = 40\text{ kg} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $3\text{ m}$, (b) $M = 40\text{ kg}$

pi_options.feedback: Remember to include the beam's own weight ($20g\text{ N}$) acting at its midpoint. Omitting the beam weight gives $2M = 60 \implies M = 30\text{ kg}$.
The centre of mass is at $3\text{ m}$ from $A$, which is to the right of the pivot ($2\text{ m}$ from $A$). Its moment acts clockwise with the $15\text{ kg}$ mass, not anticlockwise.
The centre of mass of a uniform $6\text{ m}$ beam is at its midpoint ($3\text{ m}$ from $A$), not at the pivot point $P$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Non-Central Pivots Include Beam Weight
bradley_insight.content: Whenever the pivot is not at the midpoint of a beam, the weight of the beam produces a non-zero turning moment. Always mark the centre of mass $G$ clearly and measure its distance from your chosen pivot point.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform plank $AB$ of length $6\text{ m}$ and mass $30\text{ kg}$ resting horizontally on two smooth supports at $C$ and $D$, where $AC = 1.0\text{ m}$ and $AD = 5.0\text{ m}$.

Two loads of masses $18\text{ kg}$ and $10\text{ kg}$ are placed on the plank at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively, where $AP = 2.0\text{ m}$ and $AQ = 5.2\text{ m}$.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Calculate the magnitude of the normal reaction force exerted on the plank by the support at $D$.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the normal reaction force exerted on the plank by the support at $C$.
steps:
(a) Normal reaction at support $D$:

The plank is uniform, so its weight $30g\text{ N}$ acts at its midpoint, $3.0\text{ m}$ from $A$.

Measure distances from support $C$ ($1.0\text{ m}$ from $A$):
• Distance to load $P$: $2.0 - 1.0 = 1.0\text{ m}$
• Distance to midpoint: $3.0 - 1.0 = 2.0\text{ m}$
• Distance to support $D$: $5.0 - 1.0 = 4.0\text{ m}$
• Distance to load $Q$: $5.2 - 1.0 = 4.2\text{ m}$

Taking moments about $C$:\begin{aligned} &4.0 R_D = 18g(1.0) + 30g(2.0) \cr &\qquad + 10g(4.2) \cr &4.0 R_D = 18g + 60g + 42g \cr &4.0 R_D = 120g \cr &R_D = 30g \cr &R_D = 30(9.8) \cr &R_D = 294\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Normal reaction at support $C$:

Resolving forces vertically for equilibrium:\begin{aligned} &R_C + R_D = (18 + 30 + 10)g \cr &R_C + 294 = 58(9.8) \cr &R_C + 294 = 568.4 \cr &R_C = 568.4 - 294 \cr &R_C = 274.4\text{ N} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $R_D = 294\text{ N}$, (b) $R_C = 274.4\text{ N}$

pi_options.feedback: The reactions have been reversed. Support $D$ carries the larger load ($294\text{ N}$) because the $30\text{ kg}$ plank weight and $10\text{ kg}$ mass lie closer to it.
Remember to include the plank's weight ($30g\text{ N}$) at the midpoint. Omitting the plank weight underestimates the reaction at $D$.
Check the vertical resolution: total weight is $(18 + 30 + 10)(9.8) = 568.4\text{ N}$. Subtracting $294\text{ N}$ gives $R_C = 274.4\text{ N}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Vertical Resolution for the Second Reaction
bradley_insight.content: Once you find one support reaction by taking moments about the other, never set up a second moment equation. Resolving vertically ($R_C + R_D = \sum W$) gives the remaining reaction in one simple subtraction.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform beam $AB$ of mass $40\text{ kg}$ and length $6\text{ m}$ resting horizontally on two smooth supports at $C$ and $D$, where $AC = 1.5\text{ m}$ and $DB = 1.5\text{ m}$.

A person of mass $60\text{ kg}$ walks along the overhang $DB$ towards end $B$. When the person reaches point $X$, at a distance of $x\text{ m}$ from support $D$, the beam is on the point of tilting about $D$.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) State the magnitude of the normal reaction force exerted by the support at $C$ when the beam is on the point of tilting about $D$.

(b) Calculate the distance $x$.

(c) State, with a reason, whether the person can safely reach end $B$ without the beam tipping.
steps:
(a) Reaction at support $C$:

When the beam is on the point of tilting about support $D$, it breaks contact with support $C$.

Therefore, the normal reaction at $C$ is:\begin{aligned} R_C = 0\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate distance $x$:

The beam is uniform, so its centre of mass lies at its midpoint, $3.0\text{ m}$ from $A$.

Distance from support $D$ ($4.5\text{ m}$ from $A$) to the centre of mass:\begin{aligned} 4.5 - 3.0 = 1.5\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Taking moments about $D$ with $R_C = 0$:\begin{aligned} &40g(1.5) = 60g(x) \cr &60g = 60gx \cr &x = 1.0\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Safety check for end $B$:

The overhang distance $DB$ is $1.5\text{ m}$.

Because tilting occurs when the person is $1.0\text{ m}$ from $D$, walking past $1.0\text{ m}$ tips the beam. Therefore, the person cannot safely reach end $B$.
Final Answer: (a) $R_C = 0\text{ N}$, (b) $x = 1.0\text{ m}$, (c) No, tilts at $1.0\text{ m}$ before reaching $1.5\text{ m}$

pi_options.ans: (a) $R_C = 0\text{ N}$, (b) $x = 1.5\text{ m}$, (c) Yes, reaches end $B$ exactly as it tilts
pi_options.feedback: The beam tilts before the person reaches end $B$. Equating moments about $D$ gives $60x = 40(1.5) = 60 \implies x = 1.0\text{ m}$, which is short of the $1.5\text{ m}$ overhang.

pi_options.ans: (a) $R_C = 392\text{ N}$, (b) $x = 1.0\text{ m}$, (c) No, tilts at $1.0\text{ m}$ before reaching $1.5\text{ m}$
pi_options.feedback: At the point of tilting about $D$, contact with support $C$ is broken, so $R_C = 0\text{ N}$, not $392\text{ N}$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $R_C = 0\text{ N}$, (b) $x = 0.67\text{ m}$, (c) No, tilts at $0.67\text{ m}$ before reaching $1.5\text{ m}$
pi_options.feedback: Check your moment equation: $60x = 40 \times 1.5 = 60$, which yields $x = 1.0\text{ m}$, not $40 / 60 = 0.67\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Definition of Tilting
bradley_insight.content: The condition 'on the point of tilting about a support' means the beam is just about to pivot off the other support. Immediately set the normal reaction at the non-tilting support to zero ($R_C = 0$).

question:
The diagram shows a non-uniform rod $AB$ of length $4\text{ m}$ and weight $120\text{ N}$ suspended horizontally in equilibrium by two light vertical strings attached to its ends $A$ and $B$.

Two point loads of weights $40\text{ N}$ and $60\text{ N}$ are attached to the rod at points $C$ and $D$ respectively, where $AC = 1.0\text{ m}$ and $AD = 3.0\text{ m}$. The tension in the vertical string attached at end $B$ is measured to be $105\text{ N}$.

(a) Find the tension in the vertical string attached at end $A$.

(b) Calculate the distance of the centre of mass of the rod from end $A$.
steps:
(a) Tension in string at $A$:

For vertical equilibrium, total upward tensions balance total downward weights:\begin{aligned} &T_A + T_B = 120 + 40 + 60 \cr &T_A + 105 = 220 \cr &T_A = 220 - 105 \cr &T_A = 115\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Centre of mass distance from $A$:

Let $\bar{x}$ be the distance of the centre of mass from end $A$.

Taking moments about end $A$:\begin{aligned} &40(1.0) + 120\bar{x} + 60(3.0) \cr &\quad = 105(4.0) \cr &40 + 120\bar{x} + 180 = 420 \cr &120\bar{x} + 220 = 420 \cr &120\bar{x} = 200 \cr &\bar{x} = \dfrac{200}{120} \cr &\bar{x} = \dfrac{5}{3} \approx 1.67\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $T_A = 115\text{ N}$, (b) $\bar{x} = 1.67\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: This distance is measured from end $B$ ($4 - 1.67 = 2.33\text{ m}$). The question asks for the distance of the centre of mass from end $A$.
The rod is non-uniform, so its centre of mass is not at the geometric midpoint ($2.00\text{ m}$), and the tensions at $A$ and $B$ are not equal.
Remember to include the moment of the $40\text{ N}$ load at $C$. Omitting it gives $120\bar{x} + 180 = 420 \implies \bar{x} = 2.0\text{ m}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Non-Uniform Rod Verification
bradley_insight.content: For a uniform rod of length $4\text{ m}$, the centre of mass would be at $2.0\text{ m}$. Our result $\bar{x} = 1.67\text{ m}$ shows that the rod's mass is concentrated more towards end $A$, which explains why the string at $A$ carries more tension ($115\text{ N}$) than the string at $B$ ($105\text{ N}$).

question:
An object of mass $0.4\text{ kg}$ is projected vertically upwards with an initial speed of $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The velocity of the object at time $t$ seconds is $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$. During the upward motion, the object experiences a resistance to motion of magnitude $R\text{ N}$, where $R$ is directly proportional to $v$.

When the velocity of the object is $0.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, the resistance to motion is $0.1\text{ N}$.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Show that the upward motion of the object satisfies the differential equation:
$$\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = -9.8 - 0.5v$$
(b) Solve this differential equation to find an expression for $v$ in terms of $t$.

(c) Determine the value of $t$ when the object reaches its highest point, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Form the differential equation:

Resistance is proportional to velocity: $R = kv$.

Using $R = 0.1$ when $v = 0.5$:\begin{aligned} 0.1 &= 0.5k \cr k &= \dfrac{0.1}{0.5} \cr &= 0.2 \end{aligned}
Taking upwards as positive, both gravity and resistance act downwards:\begin{aligned} &m\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = -mg - R \cr &0.4\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = -0.4(9.8) - 0.2v \cr &0.4\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = -3.92 - 0.2v \end{aligned}
Dividing through by $0.4$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} &= -9.8 - 0.5v \end{aligned}

(b) Solve the differential equation:

Separating variables:\begin{aligned} &\int \dfrac{1}{9.8 + 0.5v}\,\text{d}v = \int -1\,\text{d}t \cr &\dfrac{1}{0.5}\ln(9.8 + 0.5v) = -t + C \cr &2\ln(9.8 + 0.5v) = -t + C \end{aligned}
Substitute initial condition $t = 0$, $v = 20$:\begin{aligned} C &= 2\ln(9.8 + 10) \cr &= 2\ln(19.8) \end{aligned}
Rearranging for $v$:\begin{aligned} &2\ln(9.8 + 0.5v) - 2\ln(19.8) = -t \cr &\ln\left(\dfrac{9.8 + 0.5v}{19.8}\right) = -0.5t \cr &\dfrac{9.8 + 0.5v}{19.8} = \text{e}^{-0.5t} \cr &9.8 + 0.5v = 19.8\text{e}^{-0.5t} \cr &0.5v = 19.8\text{e}^{-0.5t} - 9.8 \cr &v = 39.6\text{e}^{-0.5t} - 19.6 \end{aligned}

(c) Time at highest point ($v = 0$):

At the maximum height, $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &39.6\text{e}^{-0.5t} - 19.6 = 0 \cr &39.6\text{e}^{-0.5t} = 19.6 \cr &\text{e}^{-0.5t} = \dfrac{19.6}{39.6} \cr &\text{e}^{-0.5t} = \dfrac{49}{99} \cr &-0.5t = \ln\left(\dfrac{49}{99}\right) \cr &t = 2\ln\left(\dfrac{99}{49}\right) \cr &t \approx 1.41\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = -9.8 - 0.5v$, (b) $v = 39.6\text{e}^{-0.5t} - 19.6$, (c) $1.41\text{ s}$

pi_options.feedback: A time of $2.04\text{ s}$ ignores air resistance ($t = 20 / 9.8$). Resistance acts downwards with gravity, shortening the ascent time to $1.41\text{ s}$.
Remember the constant term $-9.8$ in the differential equation. Integrating does not give a single exponential decay term.
Check the factor of $2$: $-0.5t = \ln(49/99)$ gives $t = 2\ln(99/49) \approx 1.41\text{ s}$, rather than dividing by $2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Air Resistance Shortens Ascent Time
bradley_insight.content: Under gravity alone, time to peak is $t = u/g = 20/9.8 \approx 2.04\text{ s}$. When air resistance opposes the upward motion, the total retarding force increases, so the object decelerates faster. Your calculated time must always be less than $u/g$.

question:
A skydiver of mass $80\text{ kg}$ falls vertically from rest from an aircraft. At time $t$ seconds after release, the downward velocity of the skydiver is $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The air resistance opposing the motion is modelled as $16v\text{ N}$.
[Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.]

(a) Show that the motion satisfies the differential equation:
$$\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 0.2(49 - v)$$
and state the terminal velocity of the skydiver.

(b) Find an expression for $v$ in terms of $t$.

(c) Calculate the time taken for the skydiver to reach $50\%$ of their terminal velocity, giving your answer to $3$ significant figures.
steps:
(a) Differential equation and terminal velocity:

Taking downwards as positive:\begin{aligned} &m\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = mg - R \cr &80\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 80(9.8) - 16v \cr &80\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 784 - 16v \cr &\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 9.8 - 0.2v \cr &\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 0.2(49 - v) \end{aligned}
Terminal velocity occurs when acceleration is zero ($\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 0$):\begin{aligned} 49 - v &= 0 \cr v &= 49\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Find velocity expression:
