bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Direction of Hinge Reactions
bradley_insight.content: Never assume the reaction force at a hinge acts parallel to an attached wire or perpendicular to the wall. A hinge can exert a force in any direction within the vertical plane. Always represent the hinge reaction as two independent orthogonal components ($H_A$ and $V_A$), solve for them using $\Sigma F_x = 0$ and $\Sigma F_y = 0$, and find the resultant magnitude and direction using Pythagoras and $\arctan$.

question:
The diagram shows a uniform ladder $AB$ of mass $20\text{ kg}$ and length $5\text{ m}$ resting in equilibrium with its upper end $B$ against a smooth vertical wall and its lower end $A$ on rough horizontal ground.

The ladder rests in a vertical plane perpendicular to the wall and is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal ground.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the normal reaction exerted by the ground on the ladder at $A$.

(b) Given that the ladder is on the point of slipping when $\theta = 60^\circ$, calculate:
(i) the magnitude of the normal reaction exerted by the wall on the ladder at $B$,
(ii) the coefficient of friction $\mu$ between the ladder and the ground, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Resolve vertically to find normal reaction R_A:

Because the vertical wall is smooth, there is no vertical friction force at $B$. The only vertical forces are the upward normal reaction $R_A$ and the downward weight $20g$:\begin{aligned} R_A &= 20g \cr &= 20(9.8) \cr &= 196\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Calculate wall reaction R_B by taking moments:

The weight of the uniform ladder ($20g$) acts at the midpoint ($2.5\text{ m}$ from $A$).

Taking moments about $A$ at the base:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma M_A = 0 \cr &(20g)(2.5\cos 60^\circ) \cr &\qquad - R_B(5\sin 60^\circ) = 0 \cr &20g(2.5)(0.5) - R_B(5)\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 0 \cr &25g = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}R_B \cr &R_B = \dfrac{10g}{\sqrt{3}} \cr &R_B = \dfrac{10(9.8)}{\sqrt{3}} \cr &R_B \approx 56.6\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Calculate coefficient of friction μ:

For horizontal equilibrium, the frictional force $F_A$ at the ground balances $R_B$:\begin{aligned} F_A &= R_B \cr &= \dfrac{10g}{\sqrt{3}} \cr &\approx 56.58\text{ N} \end{aligned}Since the ladder is in limiting equilibrium (on the verge of slipping), friction is maximal ($F_A = \mu R_A$):\begin{aligned} \mu &= \dfrac{F_A}{R_A} \cr &= \dfrac{10g/\sqrt{3}}{20g} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \cr &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6} \cr &\approx 0.289 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $196\text{ N}$, (b)(i) $56.6\text{ N}$, (ii) $0.289$

pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(i), you swapped sine and cosine when calculating perpendicular distances, using $\sin 60^\circ$ for the weight and $\cos 60^\circ$ for the wall reaction.
In part (b)(ii), you forgot the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ from the centre of mass position, evaluating $\mu = 1/\sqrt{3} = \tan 30^\circ \approx 0.577$ instead of $\frac{1}{2}\tan 30^\circ$.
In part (a), you calculated $R_A = 20g\cos 60^\circ$, resolving along the ladder rather than resolving vertically.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Standard Ladder Limiting Friction Identity
bradley_insight.content: For any uniform ladder resting against a smooth vertical wall on the verge of slipping, taking moments about the base and resolving horizontally and vertically always yields the classic relation: $\mu = \frac{1}{2\tan\theta} = \frac{1}{2}\cot\theta$. Here, $\mu = \frac{1}{2\tan 60^\circ} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.289$. Memorising this identity lets you verify your calculated coefficient in seconds.

question:
Two particles, $A$ and $B$, are travelling in the same direction along the same straight horizontal line on a smooth surface.

Particle $A$ has mass $4\text{ kg}$ and is moving with a speed of $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Particle $B$ has mass $2\text{ kg}$ and is moving with a speed of $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Particle $A$ collides directly with particle $B$.

(a) Given that the two particles coalesce upon impact to form a single combined body $C$, find the speed of $C$ immediately after the collision.

(b) Find the magnitude and direction of the impulse exerted on $A$ by $B$ during the collision.
steps:
(a) Calculate common speed after coalescing:

By the principle of conservation of linear momentum:\begin{aligned} &m_A u_A + m_B u_B = (m_A + m_B)v \cr &(4)(6) + (2)(3) = (4 + 2)v \cr &24 + 6 = 6v \cr &30 = 6v \cr &v = 5\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate impulse exerted on A by B:

The impulse exerted on $A$ is given by the change in momentum of $A$:\begin{aligned} I_A &= m_A(v - u_A) \cr &= 4(5 - 6) \cr &= 4(-1) \cr &= -4\text{ N s} \end{aligned}The negative sign indicates that the impulse acts in the direction opposing $A$'s initial motion.

Magnitude: $4\text{ N s}$.
Direction: Opposite to the direction of motion.
Final Answer: (a) $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b) $4\text{ N s}$ opposite to motion

pi_options.ans: (a) $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b) $4\text{ N s}$ in direction of motion
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you identified the correct magnitude but reversed the direction: body $B$ slows body $A$ down from $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, so the impulse on $A$ must oppose its forward motion.

pi_options.ans: (a) $4.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b) $6\text{ N s}$ opposite to motion

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Newton's Third Law in Impulse
bradley_insight.content: To verify the impulse on $A$, calculate the impulse on $B$: \begin{aligned}I_B &= m_B(v - u_B)\cr & = 2(5 - 3) \cr &= +4\text{ N s}\end{aligned} By Newton's Third Law, the impulse exerted on $A$ by $B$ must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction: $I_A = -I_B = -4\text{ N s}$. This quick check eliminates sign errors.

question:
Two railway trucks, $P$ and $Q$, move towards each other along the same straight horizontal track.

Truck $P$ has a mass of $1200\text{ kg}$ and is moving at a speed of $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Truck $Q$ has a mass of $800\text{ kg}$ and is moving at a speed of $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The trucks collide directly, and their automatic couplers engage so that they move together as a single unit after the impact.

(a) Determine the speed and direction of motion of the coupled trucks immediately after the collision.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the impulse exerted by truck $P$ on truck $Q$ during the impact.

(c) Calculate the loss in kinetic energy of the system caused by the collision.
steps:
(a) Find velocity of the coupled trucks:

Taking the initial direction of truck $P$ as positive, $u_P = +4\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $u_Q = -3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Applying conservation of linear momentum:\begin{aligned} &m_P u_P + m_Q u_Q = (m_P + m_Q)v \cr &1200(4) + 800(-3)\cr & \qquad \quad = (1200 + 800)v \cr &4800 - 2400 = 2000v \cr &2400 = 2000v \cr &v = 1.2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Because $v > 0$, the coupled trucks move in the original direction of truck $P$ with speed $1.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(b) Calculate magnitude of impulse on truck Q:

Impulse on $Q$ is its change in momentum:\begin{aligned} I_Q &= m_Q(v - u_Q) \cr &= 800(1.2 - (-3)) \cr &= 800(4.2) \cr &= 3360\text{ N s} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculate loss in kinetic energy:

Initial kinetic energy:\begin{aligned} E_{k1} &= \dfrac{1}{2}m_P u_P^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}m_Q u_Q^2 \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1200)(4^2) + \dfrac{1}{2}(800)(3^2) \cr &= 600(16) + 400(9) \cr &= 9600 + 3600 \cr &= 13200\text{ J} \end{aligned}Final kinetic energy:\begin{aligned} E_{k2} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(m_P + m_Q)v^2 \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(2000)(1.2^2) \cr &= 1000(1.44) \cr &= 1440\text{ J} \end{aligned}Loss in kinetic energy:\begin{aligned} \Delta E_k &= 13200 - 1440 \cr &= 11760\text{ J} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $1.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in direction of P, (b) $3360\text{ N s}$, (c) $11760\text{ J}$

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Signs in Head-On Collisions
bradley_insight.content: In head-on collisions, establish a positive reference direction immediately. Because velocity is a vector, $u_Q = -3\text{ m s}^{-1}$. When calculating impulse, subtracting a negative velocity results in addition: \begin{aligned}v - u_Q &= 1.2 - (-3)\cr & = 4.2\text{ m s}^{-1}\end{aligned} Conversely, kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ is a positive scalar—never assign negative kinetic energy to an opposing body.

question:
Two smooth spheres, $X$ and $Y$, of masses $0.5\text{ kg}$ and $0.8\text{ kg}$ respectively, move along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal table.

Sphere $X$ has an initial velocity of $8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and collides directly with sphere $Y$, which is moving in the same direction with an initial velocity of $2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

During the collision, the magnitude of the impulse exerted by sphere $X$ on sphere $Y$ is $2.4\text{ N s}$.

(a) Find the velocity of sphere $Y$ immediately after the collision.

(b) Find the velocity of sphere $X$ immediately after the collision.

(c) Determine whether sphere $X$ and sphere $Y$ will collide again, giving a clear mathematical reason for your answer.
steps:
(a) Velocity of sphere Y:

The impulse exerted by $X$ on $Y$ acts in the positive forward direction ($I = +2.4\text{ N s}$):\begin{aligned} &I = m_Y(v_Y - u_Y) \cr &2.4 = 0.8(v_Y - 2) \cr &v_Y - 2 = \dfrac{2.4}{0.8} \cr &v_Y - 2 = 3 \cr &v_Y = 5\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Velocity of sphere X:

By Newton's Third Law, the impulse exerted on $X$ by $Y$ is equal and opposite ($I = -2.4\text{ N s}$):\begin{aligned} &-2.4 = m_X(v_X - u_X) \cr &-2.4 = 0.5(v_X - 8) \cr &v_X - 8 = -\dfrac{2.4}{0.5} \cr &v_X - 8 = -4.8 \cr &v_X = 3.2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(c) Check for subsequent collision:

Immediately after the collision, both spheres continue moving in the positive direction along the same line.

Because sphere $Y$ is ahead of sphere $X$ and its speed is greater ($v_Y = 5\text{ m s}^{-1} > v_X = 3.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$), the distance between them increases continuously. Therefore, they will not collide again.
Final Answer: (a) $5\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b) $3.2\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (c) No ($v_Y > v_X$)

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you added the impulse to sphere $X$ instead of subtracting it ($v_X = 8 + 4.8 = 12.8$), violating Newton's Third Law.
In part (a), you calculated the change in velocity $\Delta v = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ but forgot to add the initial velocity $u_Y = 2\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
In part (c), you misidentified the overtaking condition: when the leading sphere travels faster ($v_Y > v_X$), the gap widens, preventing any subsequent collision.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Kinematics of Separation
bradley_insight.content: For particles constrained to a line, a second collision occurs only if the trailing body travels faster than the leading body ($v_{\text{trailing}} > v_{\text{leading}}$) or rebounds off a fixed boundary. Here, $X$ trails $Y$, and \begin{aligned}v_X &= 3.2\text{ m s}^{-1} \cr < v_Y &= 5.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\emd{aligned} meaning the separation speed is $1.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and no further collision can occur.

question:
A particle $P$ of mass $3\text{ kg}$ moves across a smooth horizontal floor with a speed of $6\text{ m s}^{-1}$ towards a stationary particle $Q$ of mass $5\text{ kg}$.

The two particles collide directly. The coefficient of restitution between $P$ and $Q$ is $e = 0.6$.

(a) Calculate the speed of $P$ and the speed of $Q$ immediately after the collision.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the impulse exerted by $P$ on $Q$.

(c) Calculate the percentage of the initial kinetic energy that is lost during the collision.
steps:
(a) Form equations to find post-collision speeds:

Let $v_P$ and $v_Q$ be the post-collision velocities in the direction of $P$'s initial motion.

Conservation of linear momentum:\begin{aligned} &m_P u_P + m_Q u_Q = m_P v_P + m_Q v_Q \cr &3(6) + 5(0) = 3v_P + 5v_Q \cr &3v_P + 5v_Q = 18 \end{aligned}Newton's Law of Restitution ($v_Q - v_P = e(u_P - u_Q)$):\begin{aligned} &v_Q - v_P = 0.6(6 - 0) \cr &v_Q - v_P = 3.6 \end{aligned}Multiplying by $3$ gives $3v_Q - 3v_P = 10.8$. Adding this to the momentum equation:\begin{aligned} &8v_Q = 28.8 \cr &v_Q = 3.6\text{ m s}^{-1} \cr &v_P = 3.6 - 3.6 = 0\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate magnitude of impulse on Q:

The impulse exerted on $Q$ is its change in momentum:\begin{aligned} I_Q &= m_Q(v_Q - u_Q) \cr &= 5(3.6 - 0) \cr &= 18\text{ N s} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculate percentage loss in kinetic energy:

Initial kinetic energy:\begin{aligned} E_{k1} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(3)(6^2) \cr &= 1.5(36) \cr &= 54\text{ J} \end{aligned}Final kinetic energy ($v_P = 0$):\begin{aligned} E_{k2} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(5)(3.6^2) \cr &= 2.5(12.96) \cr &= 32.4\text{ J} \end{aligned}Percentage loss:\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage loss} &= \dfrac{54 - 32.4}{54} \times 100 \cr &= \dfrac{21.6}{54} \times 100 \cr &= 40\% \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $v_P = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, $v_Q = 3.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (b) $18\text{ N s}$, (c) $40\%$

pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you swapped the final velocities: the impacting body $P$ is brought to rest, transferring its momentum to the target body $Q$.
In part (c), you calculated the percentage of kinetic energy *retained* ($32.4/54 = 60\%$) rather than the percentage *lost* ($21.6/54 = 40\%$).
In part (a), an algebraic error occurred when setting up Newton's Law of Restitution: you wrote $v_P - v_Q = 3.6$ instead of $v_Q - v_P = 3.6$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Complete Transfer of Momentum
bradley_insight.content: Notice that particle $P$ is brought completely to rest ($v_P = 0$). This occurs whenever $e = \frac{m_P}{m_Q}$. Here, $\frac{m_P}{m_Q} = \frac{3}{5} = 0.6$, exactly matching $e$. Recognizing this relationship allows you to deduce immediately that $v_P = 0$ and $v_Q = e u_P + v_P = 3.6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

question:
A tennis ball of mass $0.06\text{ kg}$ travels horizontally with a speed of $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and strikes a smooth, fixed vertical wall perpendicularly.

The ball rebounds horizontally along its original line of approach with a speed of $15\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The duration of the impact between the ball and the wall is $0.008\text{ seconds}$.

(a) Calculate the coefficient of restitution $e$ between the ball and the wall.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the impulse exerted by the wall on the ball during the impact.

(c) Calculate the average normal force exerted by the wall on the ball during the collision.

(d) Calculate the loss in kinetic energy of the ball during the impact.
steps:
(a) Calculate coefficient of restitution:

For impact with a fixed barrier:\begin{aligned} e &= \dfrac{\text{Speed of rebound}}{\text{Speed of approach}} \cr &= \dfrac{15}{25} \cr &= 0.6 \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate magnitude of impulse:

Taking the direction away from the wall as positive, the initial velocity is $u = -25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the final velocity is $v = +15\text{ m s}^{-1}$.\begin{aligned} I &= m(v - u) \cr &= 0.06(15 - (-25)) \cr &= 0.06(40) \cr &= 2.4\text{ N s} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculate average normal force:

Using the impulse-force relationship $I = F_{\text{avg}} \Delta t$:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{avg}} &= \dfrac{I}{\Delta t} \cr &= \dfrac{2.4}{0.008} \cr &= 300\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(d) Calculate loss in kinetic energy:

Loss in kinetic energy:\begin{aligned} \Delta E_k &= \dfrac{1}{2}m(u^2 - v^2) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(0.06)(25^2 - 15^2) \cr &= 0.03(625 - 225) \cr &= 0.03(400) \cr &= 12\text{ J} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $0.6$, (b) $2.4\text{ N s}$, (c) $300\text{ N}$, (d) $12\text{ J}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you evaluated $0.06(25 - 15)$ by subtracting speeds rather than velocities, ignoring the sign change on rebound.
In part (a), you inverted the restitution ratio, calculating approach speed over separation speed ($25/15$). The coefficient $e$ cannot exceed $1$.
In part (c), you multiplied impulse by time ($2.4 \times 0.008$) instead of dividing impulse by time ($F = I / \Delta t$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Energy Loss via Restitution Formula
bradley_insight.content: For a collision with a fixed barrier, the fractional loss of kinetic energy is always $1 - e^2$. Here, $1 - 0.6^2 = 1 - 0.36 = 0.64$. Since the initial energy is $E_{k1} = \frac{1}{2}(0.06)(25^2) = 18.75\text{ J}$, the energy lost is simply $0.64 \times 18.75 = 12\text{ J}$.

question:
The velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ of a particle travelling along a straight line at time $t\text{ seconds}$ ($t \ge 0$) is given by:$$v = 3t^2 - 12t + 9$$The particle is instantaneously at rest on two different occasions.

(a) Find the two times when the particle is instantaneously at rest.

(b) Find the acceleration of the particle when $t = 4\text{ s}$.

(c) Find the total distance covered by the particle in the first $5\text{ seconds}$ of motion.
steps:
(a) Find the times when the particle is at rest:

The particle is instantaneously at rest when $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 0 \cr &3(t^2 - 4t + 3) = 0 \cr &3(t - 1)(t - 3) = 0 \cr &t = 1\text{ s},\ t = 3\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Find the acceleration when t = 4 s:

Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity:\begin{aligned} a(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &= 6t - 12 \end{aligned}Evaluating at $t = 4\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} a(4) &= 6(4) - 12 \cr &= 24 - 12 \cr &= 12\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculate the total distance covered in the first 5 s:

Because the velocity changes sign at $t = 1\text{ s}$ and $t = 3\text{ s}$, distance must be evaluated across three separate intervals.

Indefinite integral for displacement:\begin{aligned} s(t) &= \int (3t^2 - 12t + 9)\text{ d}t \cr &= t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t + c \end{aligned}Taking $s(0) = 0$ gives $c = 0$:\begin{aligned} s(0) &= 0\text{ m} \cr s(1) &= 1^3 - 6(1^2) + 9(1) = 4\text{ m} \cr s(3) &= 3^3 - 6(3^2) + 9(3) \cr &= 27 - 54 + 27 = 0\text{ m} \cr s(5) &= 5^3 - 6(5^2) + 9(5) \cr &= 125 - 150 + 45 = 20\text{ m} \end{aligned}Summing the absolute displacements over each interval:\begin{aligned} d_1 &= |s(1) - s(0)|\cr &= |4 - 0| \cr &= 4\text{ m} \cr d_2 &= |s(3) - s(1)|\cr & = |0 - 4|\cr & = 4\text{ m} \cr d_3 &= |s(5) - s(3)| \cr &= |20 - 0|\cr & = 20\text{ m} \cr d_{\text{total}} &= 4 + 4 + 20 \cr &= 28\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $t = 1\text{ s},\ t = 3\text{ s}$, (b) $12\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $28\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you evaluated the net displacement $\int_0^5 v\text{ d}t = s(5) - s(0) = 20\text{ m}$ rather than the total distance travelled, ignoring the reversal of motion between $t = 1$ and $t = 3$.
In part (b), you evaluated the velocity $v(4)$ rather than differentiating to find the acceleration $a(4) = 6(4) - 12$.
In part (a), you made an algebraic error factorising the quadratic equation $t^2 - 4t + 3 = 0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Displacement vs Distance with Turning Points
bradley_insight.content: Integrating $\int_0^5 v\text{ d}t$ gives net displacement> ($20\text{ m}$), which cancels out opposing motion. Whenever you are asked for total distance, you must identify all times where $v = 0$ within the interval, evaluate the position at each boundary, and sum the absolute values of the changes in position: \begin{aligned}|4 - 0| + |0 - 4| &+ |20 - 0| \cr &= 28\text{ m}\end{aligned}

question:
A particle moves in a straight line such that its displacement $s\text{ metres}$ from a fixed origin $O$ at time $t\text{ seconds}$ ($t \ge 0$) is given by:$$s = 2t^3 - 15t^2 + 24t + 10$$(a) Find the times when the particle is instantaneously at rest.

(b) Find the minimum velocity of the particle and the time at which this minimum occurs.

(c) Calculate the total distance travelled by the particle during the first $6\text{ seconds}$ of motion.
steps:
(a) Find times when particle is at rest:

Differentiate displacement to obtain velocity:\begin{aligned} v(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \cr &= 6t^2 - 30t + 24 \end{aligned}Setting $v = 0$ for instantaneous rest:\begin{aligned} &6(t^2 - 5t + 4) = 0 \cr &6(t - 1)(t - 4) = 0 \cr &t = 1\text{ s},\ t = 4\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Find minimum velocity:

To find the stationary value of velocity, differentiate to obtain acceleration and set to zero:\begin{aligned} a(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &= 12t - 30 \end{aligned}Setting $a = 0$:\begin{aligned} &12t = 30 \cr &t = 2.5\text{ s} \end{aligned}Evaluating the minimum velocity:\begin{aligned} v(2.5) &= 6(2.5^2) - 30(2.5) + 24 \cr &= 37.5 - 75 + 24 \cr &= -13.5\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}Since $\frac{\text{d}^2v}{\text{d}t^2} = 12 > 0$, this is a local minimum.

(c) Calculate total distance in the first 6 s:

The particle reverses direction at $t = 1\text{ s}$ and $t = 4\text{ s}$.

Evaluating position at key times:\begin{aligned} s(0) &= 10\text{ m} \cr s(1) &= 21\text{ m} \cr s(4) &= -6\text{ m} \cr s(6) &= 46\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Calculating path lengths:\begin{aligned} d_1 &= |21 - 10| \cr &= 11\text{ m} \cr d_2 &= |-6 - 21| \cr &= 27\text{ m} \cr d_3 &= |46 - (-6)| \cr &= 52\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Total distance:\begin{aligned} d_{\text{total}} &= 11 + 27 + 52 \cr &= 90\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $t = 1\text{ s},\ t = 4\text{ s}$, (b) $-13.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 2.5\text{ s}$, (c) $90\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you calculated the net displacement $s(6) - s(0) = 46 - 10 = 36\text{ m}$ rather than summing the individual segments between turning points.

pi_options.ans: (a) $t = 1\text{ s},\ t = 4\text{ s}$, (b) $0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 1\text{ s}$, (c) $90\text{ m}$

In part (a), you solved $t^2 - 5t + 6 = 0$ instead of $t^2 - 5t + 4 = 0$, miscalculating the roots.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Tracking the Origin Offset
bradley_insight.content: Notice that at $t = 0$, $s(0) = 10\text{ m}$, not zero. When finding the first segment length, you must calculate $|s(1) - s(0)| = |21 - 10| = 11\text{ m}$. A frequent blunder is using the coordinate $s(1) = 21\text{ m}$ directly as the distance travelled, forgetting that the particle began $10\text{ m}$ ahead of the origin.

question:
A particle moves along a straight line with variable acceleration $a\text{ m s}^{-2}$ given at time $t\text{ seconds}$ by:$$a = 6t - 18$$At time $t = 0\text{ s}$, the particle passes through a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $24\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(a) Find an expression for the velocity of the particle at time $t$, and determine the values of $t$ for which the particle is instantaneously at rest.

(b) Find the maximum speed of the particle while it is travelling in the negative direction.

(c) Calculate the total distance travelled by the particle in the time interval $0 \le t \le 6\text{ s}$.
steps:
(a) Find velocity expression and times at rest:

Integrating acceleration with respect to time:\begin{aligned} v(t) &= \int (6t - 18)\text{ d}t \cr &= 3t^2 - 18t + c \end{aligned}Applying the initial condition $v(0) = 24$ gives $c = 24$:\begin{aligned} v(t) &= 3t^2 - 18t + 24 \end{aligned}Setting $v = 0$ for instantaneous rest:\begin{aligned} &3(t^2 - 6t + 8) = 0 \cr &3(t - 2)(t - 4) = 0 \cr &t = 2\text{ s},\ t = 4\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Find maximum negative speed:

The vertex of the parabolic velocity curve occurs when $a = 0$:\begin{aligned} &6t - 18 = 0 \cr &t = 3\text{ s} \end{aligned}Evaluating velocity at $t = 3\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} v(3) &= 3(3^2) - 18(3) + 24 \cr &= 27 - 54 + 24 \cr &= -3\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}The maximum speed in the negative direction is $|-3| = 3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

(c) Calculate total distance in 0 ≤ t ≤ 6 s:

Integrating velocity for displacement with $s(0) = 0$:\begin{aligned} s(t) &= \int (3t^2 - 18t + 24)\text{ d}t \cr &= t^3 - 9t^2 + 24t \end{aligned}

Evaluating position at key times:\begin{aligned} s(0) &= 0\text{ m} \cr s(2) &= 20\text{ m} \cr s(4) &= 16\text{ m} \cr s(6) &= 36\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Calculating path lengths:\begin{aligned} d_1 &= |20 - 0| \cr &= 20\text{ m} \cr d_2 &= |16 - 20| \cr &= 4\text{ m} \cr d_3 &= |36 - 16| \cr &= 20\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Total distance:\begin{aligned} d_{\text{total}} &= 20 + 4 + 20 \cr &= 44\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $v = 3t^2 - 18t + 24$, $t = 2\text{ s},\ t = 4\text{ s}$, (b) $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$, (c) $44\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you calculated the net displacement $s(6) = 36\text{ m}$ rather than the total distance $44\text{ m}$, neglecting the $4\text{ m}$ of reverse travel between $t = 2$ and $t = 4$.
In part (a), you omitted the constant of integration $c = 24$ when integrating acceleration, setting $v = 3t^2 - 18t$.
In part (b), speed is a scalar magnitude and must be stated as positive ($3\text{ m s}^{-1}$), not negative.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Velocity vs Speed in Extrema Questions
bradley_insight.content: Always read question wording carefully: velocity has a sign, whereas speed is strictly the magnitude $|v|$. In part (b), the velocity reaches a local minimum of $-3\text{ m s}^{-1}$. Stating the speed as $-3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is a contradictory statement that will be penalised—the speed is simply $3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

question:
A particle moves along a straight line. At time $t\text{ seconds}$ ($t \ge 0$), its velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is modelled by:$$v = 6\cos(2t) - 3$$(a) Find the two smallest values of $t$ for which the particle is instantaneously at rest, giving your answers in terms of $\pi$.

(b) Calculate the acceleration of the particle at time $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\text{ s}$.

(c) Given that the particle is at the origin $O$ when $t = 0\text{ s}$, calculate the total distance travelled by the particle between $t = 0\text{ s}$ and $t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s}$, giving your answer in exact form and to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Find smallest times at rest:

Setting $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &6\cos(2t) - 3 = 0 \cr &\cos(2t) = \dfrac{1}{2} \cr &2t = \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \cr &t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ s},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate acceleration at t = π/4 s:

Differentiate velocity with respect to time:\begin{aligned} a(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &= -12\sin(2t) \end{aligned}At $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} a\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= -12\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \cr &= -12(1) \cr &= -12\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculate total distance in 0 ≤ t ≤ π/2:

Integrate velocity to find displacement with $s(0) = 0$:\begin{aligned} s(t) &= \int (6\cos(2t) - 3)\text{ d}t \cr &= 3\sin(2t) - 3t \end{aligned}Within the interval $[0, \frac{\pi}{2}]$, velocity crosses zero at $t = \frac{\pi}{6}$:\begin{aligned} s(0) &= 0\text{ m} \cr s\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) &= 3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - 3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.0262\text{ m} \cr s\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) &= 3\sin(\pi) - 3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \cr &= -\dfrac{3\pi}{2} \approx -4.7124\text{ m} \end{aligned}Summing the absolute segment lengths:\begin{aligned} d_1 &= \left|\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right| \approx 1.0262\text{ m} \cr d_2 &= \left|-\dfrac{3\pi}{2} - \left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right| \cr &= \pi + \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 5.7397\text{ m} \cr d_{\text{total}} &= 3\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \cr &\approx 6.77\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ s},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\text{ s}$, (b) $-12\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $3\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 6.77\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you calculated the net displacement $s(\pi/2) = -3\pi/2$ rather than summing the forward and backward paths as positive scalar distances.
In part (a), you forgot to divide the angle by $2$ when solving $\cos(2t) = 0.5$, giving $t = \pi/3$ instead of $t = \pi/6$.
In part (b), you lost the negative sign when differentiating cosine: $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\cos(2t)) = -2\sin(2t)$, not $+2\sin(2t)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Exact Surd Integration in Trigonometric Kinematics
bradley_insight.content: When integrating trigonometric velocities, keep exact values in terms of $\sqrt{3}$ and $\pi$ until the final line. Notice that the subtraction $\frac{-\pi}{2}$ in the first stage and the $-\pi$ in the second stage combine with the initial $-\frac{3\pi}{2}$ boundary to collapse into the elegant exact closed form $3\sqrt{3} + \frac{\pi}{2} \approx 6.77\text{ m}$.

question:
A particle moves along a straight line through a medium offering resistance. At time $t\text{ seconds}$ ($t \ge 0$), its velocity $v\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is given by:$$v = 16e^{-0.5t} - 4$$(a) Find the value of $t$ when the particle comes instantaneously to rest, giving your answer in exact logarithmic form and to 3 significant figures.

(b) Find the acceleration of the particle when $t = 0\text{ s}$, and when the particle is instantaneously at rest.

(c) Calculate the total distance travelled by the particle during the time interval from $t = 0\text{ s}$ to $t = 4\text{ s}$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Find time of instantaneous rest:

Setting $v = 0$:\begin{aligned} &16e^{-0.5t} - 4 = 0 \cr &e^{-0.5t} = \dfrac{4}{16} = 0.25 \cr &e^{0.5t} = 4 \cr &0.5t = \ln 4 \cr &t = 2\ln 4 = \ln 16 \cr &\approx 2.77\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Find acceleration at t = 0 s and at rest:

Differentiate velocity with respect to time:\begin{aligned} a(t) &= \dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \cr &= 16(-0.5)e^{-0.5t} \cr &= -8e^{-0.5t} \end{aligned}At $t = 0\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} a(0) &= -8e^0 \cr &= -8\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}When the particle is at rest ($e^{-0.5t} = 0.25$):\begin{aligned} a(2.77) &= -8(0.25) \cr &= -2\text{ m s}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculate total distance in 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 s:

Integrate velocity to obtain displacement:\begin{aligned} s(t) &= \int (16e^{-0.5t} - 4)\text{ d}t \cr &= -32e^{-0.5t} - 4t \end{aligned}Evaluating position at boundaries $t = 0$, $t = \ln 16 \approx 2.7726$, and $t = 4$:\begin{aligned} s(0) &= -32\text{ m} \cr s(2.7726) &= -32(0.25) - 4(2.7726) \cr &= -8 - 11.0904 \cr &= -19.0904\text{ m} \cr s(4) &= -32e^{-2} - 4(4) \cr &= -32(0.135335) - 16 \cr &= -4.3307 - 16 \cr &= -20.3307\text{ m} \end{aligned}Summing the absolute segment distances:\begin{aligned} d_1 &= |s(2.7726) - s(0)| \cr &= |-19.0904 - (-32)| \cr &= 12.9096\text{ m} \cr d_2 &= |s(4) - s(2.7726)| \cr &= |-20.3307 - (-19.0904)| \cr &= 1.2403\text{ m} \cr d_{\text{total}} &= 12.9096 + 1.2403 \cr &= 14.1499\text{ m} \cr &\approx 14.2\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\ln 16 \approx 2.77\text{ s}$, (b) $-8\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $-2\text{ m s}^{-2}$, (c) $14.2\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you calculated the net displacement $s(4) - s(0) \approx 11.7\text{ m}$ rather than summing the separate path segments before and after the turning point.
In part (a), you solved $0.5t = \ln 4$ as $t = \ln 4$ instead of multiplying by $2$ to give $t = 2\ln 4 = \ln 16$.
In part (b), you forgot to multiply by the derivative of the exponent ($-0.5$) when differentiating $e^{-0.5t}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Natural Logarithms in Exponential Models
bradley_insight.content: When solving $e^{-kt} = c$, taking the reciprocal $e^{kt} = \frac{1}{c}$ first eliminates negative signs before taking logarithms. For $e^{0.5t} = 4$, taking logs gives $0.5t = \ln 4$, which simplifies directly to $t = \ln 16$.

question:
The diagram shows a ball struck from a point $O$ on horizontal ground with an initial speed of $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $60^\circ$ above the horizontal.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the magnitude and direction of the velocity of the ball after $2\text{ seconds}$ of flight, giving the speed and the angle with the horizontal to 3 significant figures.

(b) In the plane of projection, a tree of height $24\text{ m}$ stands at a horizontal distance of $60\text{ m}$ from $O$.

Determine whether the ball will clear the top of the tree, stating clearly its vertical height above the ground at this horizontal distance.
steps:
(a) Calculate velocity vector after 2 s:

Resolve initial velocity into components:\begin{aligned} u_x &= 30\cos 60^\circ \cr &= 15\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Vertical component:\begin{aligned} u_y &= 30\sin 60^\circ \cr &= 15\sqrt{3}\text{ m s}^{-1} \cr &\approx 25.981\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

At $t = 2\text{ s}$, horizontal velocity remains constant:\begin{aligned} v_x &= 15\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Vertical velocity at $t = 2\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} v_y &= u_y - gt \cr &= 25.981 - 9.8(2) \cr &= 25.981 - 19.6 \cr &= 6.381\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Speed is the resultant magnitude:\begin{aligned} v &= \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} \cr &= \sqrt{15^2 + 6.381^2} \cr &= \sqrt{225 + 40.717} \cr &= \sqrt{265.717} \cr &\approx 16.3\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Direction above the horizontal:\begin{aligned} \theta &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{6.381}{15}\right) \cr &\approx 23.0^\circ \end{aligned}

(b) Determine whether the ball clears the tree:

Time taken to travel $60\text{ m}$ horizontally:\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{60}{u_x} \cr &= \dfrac{60}{15} \cr &= 4\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Vertical height at $t = 4\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} y &= u_y t - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \cr &= (15\sqrt{3})(4) \cr &\qquad - 4.9(4^2) \cr &= 60\sqrt{3} - 78.4 \cr &= 103.923 - 78.4 \cr &= 25.52\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Because $25.52\text{ m} > 24\text{ m}$, the ball clears the tree by $1.52\text{ m}$.
Final Answer: (a) $16.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $23.0^\circ$ above horizontal, (b) Clears (height $25.5\text{ m} > 24\text{ m}$)

pi_options.ans: (a) $16.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $23.0^\circ$ above horizontal, (b) Does not clear (height $15.5\text{ m} < 24\text{ m}$)
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you evaluated $y = u_y t - gt^2$ without the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$, calculating $103.9 - 9.8(16) = -52.9\text{ m}$ or an incorrect intermediate drop.

pi_options.ans: (a) $20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $45.0^\circ$ above horizontal, (b) Clears (height $25.5\text{ m} > 24\text{ m}$)
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you calculated vertical velocity using $v_y = u_y - \frac{1}{2}gt$ instead of $v_y = u_y - gt$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $16.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $67.0^\circ$ above horizontal, (b) Clears (height $25.5\text{ m} > 24\text{ m}$)
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you evaluated the angle with the vertical $\arctan(v_x/v_y)$ rather than the angle with the horizontal $\arctan(v_y/v_x)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Horizontal Uniformity Principle
bradley_insight.content: In projectile motion under gravity without air resistance, the horizontal velocity component $u_x = u\cos\theta$ is strictly constant. When solving clearance questions, always calculate the flight time to the obstacle position directly using $t = \frac{x}{u_x}$. Once $t$ is known, vertical height is delivered by $y = u_y t - 4.9t^2$.

question:
The diagram shows a projectile fired from a point $O$ at the edge of a vertical cliff of height $20\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground. The initial speed of projection is $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of elevation of $30^\circ$ above the horizontal.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the speed and angle of inclination to the horizontal of the projectile after $1.5\text{ seconds}$ of flight, giving your answers to 3 significant figures.

(b) A vertical radio mast of height $12\text{ m}$ stands on the ground at a horizontal distance of $40\text{ m}$ from the base of the cliff.

Determine whether the projectile clears the top of the mast, and calculate its vertical clearance above the top of the mast to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Calculate velocity after 1.5 s:

Resolve initial velocity:\begin{aligned} u_x &= 25\cos 30^\circ \cr &= 12.5\sqrt{3} \cr &\approx 21.651\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Vertical component:\begin{aligned} u_y &= 25\sin 30^\circ \cr &= 12.5\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

At $t = 1.5\text{ s}$, horizontal component is unchanged:\begin{aligned} v_x &= 21.651\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Vertical component:\begin{aligned} v_y &= u_y - gt \cr &= 12.5 - 9.8(1.5) \cr &= 12.5 - 14.7 \cr &= -2.2\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Speed is the magnitude:\begin{aligned} v &= \sqrt{21.651^2 + (-2.2)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{468.75 + 4.84} \cr &= \sqrt{473.59} \cr &\approx 21.8\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Direction below the horizontal:\begin{aligned} \theta &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{2.2}{21.651}\right) \cr &\approx 5.80^\circ \end{aligned}

(b) Determine clearance over the mast:

Time to reach $x = 40\text{ m}$ horizontally:\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{40}{u_x} \cr &= \dfrac{40}{21.651} \cr &\approx 1.8475\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Height above the ground datum ($y = 0$):\begin{aligned} y &= 20 + u_y t - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \cr &= 20 + 12.5(1.8475) \cr &\qquad - 4.9(1.8475^2) \cr &= 20 + 23.094 - 16.726 \cr &= 26.368\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Vertical clearance above the $12\text{ m}$ mast:\begin{aligned} \text{Clearance} &= 26.368 - 12 \cr &= 14.368\text{ m} \cr &\approx 14.4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Since $26.4\text{ m} > 12\text{ m}$, the projectile clears the mast by $14.4\text{ m}$.
Final Answer: (a) $21.8\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $5.80^\circ$ below horizontal, (b) Clears (clearance $14.4\text{ m}$)

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Tracking the Ground Datum
bradley_insight.content: When a projectile is launched from an elevated cliff, always define your vertical origin clearly. If taking the cliff top as $y = 0$, the mast top is at position $y = 12 - 20 = -8\text{ m}$. If taking the ground as datum, include the $+20\text{ m}$ initial displacement in your position formula: $y = 20 + u_y t - 4.9t^2$.

question:
The diagram shows a stone thrown horizontally with an initial speed of $14\text{ m s}^{-1}$ from a point $O$ at the top of a vertical tower of height $35\text{ m}$ above horizontal ground.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the speed and direction of motion of the stone after $1.5\text{ seconds}$, giving your answers to 3 significant figures.

(b) A vertical boundary wall of height $10\text{ m}$ stands on the ground at a horizontal distance of $28\text{ m}$ from the base of the tower.

Determine whether the stone clears the wall, and calculate its height above the top of the wall as it passes directly over it.
steps:
(a) Calculate velocity after 1.5 s:

Because the stone is thrown horizontally, $u_x = 14\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $u_y = 0$.

At $t = 1.5\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} v_x &= 14\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Vertical velocity:\begin{aligned} v_y &= 0 - gt \cr &= -9.8(1.5) \cr &= -14.7\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Speed is the resultant magnitude:\begin{aligned} v &= \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} \cr &= \sqrt{14^2 + (-14.7)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{196 + 216.09} \cr &= \sqrt{412.09} \cr &\approx 20.3\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Direction below the horizontal:\begin{aligned} \theta &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{14.7}{14}\right) \cr &\approx 46.4^\circ \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate wall clearance:

Time to travel $28\text{ m}$ horizontally:\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{28}{u_x} \cr &= \dfrac{28}{14} \cr &= 2\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Vertical drop during these $2\text{ seconds}$:\begin{aligned} h_{\text{drop}} &= \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \cr &= 4.9(2^2) \cr &= 19.6\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Height of the stone above the ground:\begin{aligned} y &= 35 - 19.6 \cr &= 15.4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Clearance above the $10\text{ m}$ wall:\begin{aligned} \text{Clearance} &= 15.4 - 10 \cr &= 5.4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Since $15.4\text{ m} > 10\text{ m}$, the stone clears the wall by $5.4\text{ m}$.
Final Answer: (a) $20.3\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $46.4^\circ$ below horizontal, (b) Clears (height $15.4\text{ m}$, clearance $5.4\text{ m}$)

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Pure Horizontal Launches
bradley_insight.content: A purely horizontal projection ($u_y = 0$) means the horizontal and vertical problems decouple immediately into standard SUVAT formulas. The vertical motion is identical to dropping an object from rest ($h_{\text{drop}} = 4.9t^2$). Always compute the vertical drop first, then subtract it from the launch elevation to determine ground clearance.

question:
The diagram shows a tennis player serving a ball from a height of $2.5\text{ m}$ above the court with an initial horizontal speed of $30\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The net stands at a horizontal distance of $12\text{ m}$ from the server and has a height of $0.9\text{ m}$. The service line marks the boundary of the service box at a horizontal distance of $18\text{ m}$ from the server.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Determine whether the serve clears the net, and calculate the vertical clearance between the ball and the top of the net.

(b) Determine whether the ball lands within the service court (that is, whether it strikes the court surface before reaching the service line at $18\text{ m}$).
steps:
(a) Calculate net clearance:

Time taken to reach the net at $x = 12\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} t_{\text{net}} &= \dfrac{12}{30} \cr &= 0.4\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Vertical drop during this time:\begin{aligned} h_{\text{drop}} &= \dfrac{1}{2}gt_{\text{net}}^2 \cr &= 4.9(0.4^2) \cr &= 4.9(0.16) \cr &= 0.784\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Height of ball above the court at the net:\begin{aligned} y_{\text{net}} &= 2.5 - 0.784 \cr &= 1.716\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Vertical clearance above the $0.9\text{ m}$ net:\begin{aligned} \text{Clearance} &= 1.716 - 0.9 \cr &= 0.816\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Since $1.716\text{ m} > 0.9\text{ m}$, the serve clears the net by $0.816\text{ m}$.

(b) Check landing position:

The ball strikes the ground when $y = 0$, meaning the total drop is $2.5\text{ m}$:\begin{aligned} 4.9t^2 &= 2.5 \cr t^2 &= \dfrac{2.5}{4.9} \cr &= \dfrac{25}{49} \cr t &= \dfrac{5}{7}\text{ s} \cr &\approx 0.7143\text{ s} \end{aligned}

Horizontal distance travelled before striking the court:\begin{aligned} x &= 30\left(\dfrac{5}{7}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{150}{7} \cr &\approx 21.4\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Because $21.4\text{ m} > 18\text{ m}$, the ball lands beyond the service line (out).
Final Answer: (a) Clears net (clearance $0.816\text{ m}$), (b) No (lands at $21.4\text{ m} > 18\text{ m}$)

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Exact Fractions in Flight Time
bradley_insight.content: Notice how cleanly the numbers simplify when solving $2.5 = 4.9t^2$. Multiplying top and bottom by $10$ gives $t^2 = \frac{25}{49}$, leading directly to the exact rational flight time $t = \frac{5}{7}\text{ s}$. Using the exact fraction $\frac{5}{7}$ delivers $x = \frac{150}{7} \approx 21.4\text{ m}$ without any rounding error.

question:
The diagram shows a rugby ball kicked from a point $O$ on horizontal ground with an initial speed of $28\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of elevation of $48^\circ$ towards the goalposts.

The goalposts are situated at a horizontal distance of $35\text{ m}$ from $O$, and the horizontal crossbar is at a height of $3\text{ m}$ above the ground.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Calculate the time taken for the ball to reach the plane of the goalposts, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

(b) Determine whether the kick is successful by passing above the crossbar, calculating the height of the ball as it reaches the posts.

(c) For a kick taken from the same point with the same initial speed of $28\text{ m s}^{-1}$, use the Cartesian equation of the trajectory to find the minimum angle of elevation $\alpha$ required for the ball to clear the crossbar, giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.
steps:
(a) Calculate time to reach goalposts:

Horizontal component of velocity:\begin{aligned} u_x &= 28\cos 48^\circ \cr &\approx 18.736\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Time to travel $35\text{ m}$ horizontally:\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{35}{u_x} \cr &= \dfrac{35}{18.736} \cr &\approx 1.868\text{ s} \cr &\approx 1.87\text{ s} \end{aligned}

(b) Determine whether kick is successful:

Vertical component of velocity:\begin{aligned} u_y &= 28\sin 48^\circ \cr &\approx 20.808\text{ m s}^{-1} \end{aligned}

Vertical height at $t = 1.868\text{ s}$:\begin{aligned} y &= u_y t - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2 \cr &= 20.808(1.868) \cr &\qquad - 4.9(1.868^2) \cr &= 38.87 - 17.09 \cr &= 21.78\text{ m} \end{aligned}

Because $21.78\text{ m} > 3\text{ m}$, the ball passes well above the crossbar, so the kick is successful.

(c) Find minimum angle of elevation using trajectory equation:

The Cartesian equation of trajectory is:\begin{aligned} &y = x\tan\alpha \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2}(1 + \tan^2\alpha) \end{aligned}

Evaluating the coefficient with $x = 35$, $u = 28$, and $g = 9.8$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2} &= \dfrac{9.8(35^2)}{2(28^2)} \cr &= \dfrac{12005}{1568} \cr &= 7.65625 \end{aligned}

At the crossbar boundary, $y = 3\text{ m}$. Setting $T = \tan\alpha$:\begin{aligned} &3 = 35T - 7.65625(1 + T^2) \cr &7.65625T^2 - 35T \cr &\qquad + 10.65625 = 0 \end{aligned}

Evaluating the discriminant:\begin{aligned} \Delta &= 35^2 \cr &\qquad - 4(7.65625)(10.65625) \cr &= 1225 - 326.336 \cr &= 898.664 \cr \sqrt{\Delta} &\approx 29.978 \end{aligned}

Applying the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{35 \pm 29.978}{2(7.65625)} \cr &= \dfrac{35 \pm 29.978}{15.3125} \end{aligned}

Smaller root for minimum elevation:\begin{aligned} T &= \dfrac{5.022}{15.3125} \cr &\approx 0.3280 \cr \alpha &= \arctan(0.3280) \cr &\approx 18.2^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $1.87\text{ s}$, (b) Successful (height $21.8\text{ m} > 3\text{ m}$), (c) $18.2^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you stated the larger angle root $\arctan(4.243) \approx 76.7^\circ$ (the high-lob trajectory) rather than the minimum angle of elevation.
In part (b), an arithmetic slip in place value occurred: $21.78\text{ m}$ was miscalculated as $2.18\text{ m}$.
In part (a), you used $u_y$ instead of $u_x$ to find the horizontal transit time ($35 / 20.808$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Two-Angle Trajectory Theorem
bradley_insight.content: For any obstacle $(X, Y)$ within maximum range, the trajectory quadratic in $\tan\alpha$ yields two distinct angles: a low-angle direct drive (here $18.2^\circ$) and a high-arching lob (here $76.7^\circ$). Both paths pass through the exact same point in space. Always verify which angle the question asks for (minimum vs maximum elevation).

question:
A uniform ladder of mass $m_1\text{ kg}$ and length $6\text{ m}$ rests with its lower end $A$ on rough horizontal ground and its upper end $B$ against a smooth vertical wall. The ladder is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal ground, where $\sin\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}$.

A window cleaner of mass $m_2\text{ kg}$ stands on the ladder at a distance of $x\text{ metres}$ from the base $A$. The coefficient of friction between the ladder and the ground is $\mu$.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Show that the normal reaction $R_A$ exerted by the ground on the ladder is $(m_1 + m_2)g$.

(b) By taking moments about $A$, show that when the ladder is on the point of slipping:$$x = \dfrac{72\mu(m_1 + m_2) - 15m_1}{5m_2}$$(c) Given that $m_1 = 20\text{ kg}$, $m_2 = 60\text{ kg}$, and the ladder is on the point of slipping when the cleaner has climbed a distance of $x = 4.5\text{ m}$ from $A$, calculate the value of $\mu$, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.

(d) State one modelling assumption you have made about the window cleaner, and explain how it affects your equations.
steps:
(a) Show normal reaction is (m₁ + m₂)g:

Because the vertical wall is smooth, there is no vertical friction at $B$.

Resolving vertically for equilibrium:\begin{aligned} R_A &= m_1 g + m_2 g \cr &= (m_1 + m_2)g \end{aligned}

(b) Prove expression for x:

From $\sin\theta = \frac{12}{13}$, we have $\cos\theta = \frac{5}{13}$, so $\tan\theta = \frac{12}{5} = 2.4$.

At the point of slipping, horizontal friction is limiting ($F_A = \mu R_A$).

Resolving horizontally gives $R_B = F_A$:\begin{aligned} R_B &= \mu(m_1 + m_2)g \end{aligned}

Taking moments about the base $A$:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma M_A = 0 \cr &(m_1 g)(3\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad + (m_2 g)(x\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad - R_B(6\sin\theta) = 0 \end{aligned}

Dividing through by $g\cos\theta$:\begin{aligned} &3m_1 + m_2 x \cr &\qquad - 6\mu(m_1 + m_2)\tan\theta = 0 \cr &3m_1 + m_2 x \cr &\qquad - 6\mu(m_1 + m_2)(2.4) = 0 \cr &3m_1 + m_2 x \cr &\qquad - 14.4\mu(m_1 + m_2) = 0 \cr &m_2 x = 14.4\mu(m_1 + m_2) - 3m_1 \end{aligned}

Multiplying numerator and denominator by $5$:\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{14.4\mu(m_1 + m_2) - 3m_1}{m_2} \cr &= \dfrac{72\mu(m_1 + m_2) - 15m_1}{5m_2} \end{aligned}

(c) Calculate coefficient of friction μ:

Substitute $m_1 = 20$, $m_2 = 60$, and $x = 4.5$:\begin{aligned} &4.5 = \dfrac{72\mu(80) - 15(20)}{5(60)} \cr &4.5 = \dfrac{5760\mu - 300}{300} \cr &1350 = 5760\mu - 300 \cr &5760\mu = 1650 \cr &\mu = \dfrac{1650}{5760} \cr &\mu = \dfrac{55}{192} \cr &\mu \approx 0.286 \end{aligned}

(d) Modelling assumption for cleaner:

The window cleaner is modelled as a particle. This assumes their entire mass acts at a single point on the ladder, ignoring the physical distribution of their body weight across the rungs.
Final Answer: (a) Proof complete, (b) Proof complete, (c) $\mu = \dfrac{55}{192} \approx 0.286$, (d) Particle: mass acts at a point

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dividing Through by Trig Factors
bradley_insight.content: In ladder equilibrium, the moments equation contains factors of $g\cos\theta$ on the gravity side and $g\sin\theta$ on the wall reaction side. Always divide through immediately by $g\cos\theta$. This collapses the trigonometric terms into a single $\tan\theta$ on the reaction side, saving multiple lines of algebra.

question:
A uniform ladder $AB$ of mass $24\text{ kg}$ and length $5\text{ m}$ rests with end $A$ on rough horizontal ground and end $B$ against a smooth vertical wall. The coefficient of friction between the ladder and the ground is $\mu = 0.4$.

A roofer of mass $72\text{ kg}$ ascends the ladder.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) When the ladder is inclined at an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, where $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{4}{3}$, find how far up the ladder the roofer can climb before the ladder begins to slip.

(b) The roofer wishes to be able to reach the very top of the ladder ($5\text{ m}$ from $A$) without the ladder slipping.

Find the minimum angle of inclination $\theta_{\text{min}}$ of the ladder to the horizontal ground that will allow the roofer to safely reach end $B$, giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.
steps:
(a) Find distance climbed before slipping:

From $\tan\alpha = \frac{4}{3}$, we have $\cos\alpha = 0.6$ and $\sin\alpha = 0.8$.

Vertical equilibrium gives:\begin{aligned} R_A &= (24 + 72)g \cr &= 96g \end{aligned}At the point of slipping, limiting friction is:\begin{aligned} F_A &= \mu R_A \cr &= 0.4(96g) \cr &= 38.4g \end{aligned}Horizontal equilibrium gives $R_B = F_A = 38.4g$.

Taking moments about $A$:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma M_A = 0 \cr &(24g)(2.5\cos\alpha) \cr &\qquad + (72g)(x\cos\alpha) \cr &\qquad - R_B(5\sin\alpha) = 0 \end{aligned}

Substituting the values and dividing by $g$:\begin{aligned} &24(2.5)(0.6) \cr &\qquad + 72(0.6x) \cr &\qquad - 38.4(5)(0.8) = 0 \cr &36 + 43.2x - 153.6 = 0 \cr &43.2x = 117.6 \cr &x = \dfrac{117.6}{43.2} \cr &x = \dfrac{49}{18} \cr &x \approx 2.72\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(b) Find minimum angle to reach the top:

At the top of the ladder, $x = 5\text{ m}$.

Taking moments about $A$ with unknown angle $\theta$:\begin{aligned} &(24g)(2.5\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad + (72g)(5\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad - R_B(5\sin\theta) = 0 \end{aligned}

Since $R_B = 38.4g$:\begin{aligned} &60g\cos\theta + 360g\cos\theta \cr &\qquad - 38.4g(5\sin\theta) = 0 \cr &420\cos\theta = 192\sin\theta \cr &\tan\theta = \dfrac{420}{192} \cr &\tan\theta = 2.1875 \cr &\theta = \arctan(2.1875) \cr &\theta \approx 65.4^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $2.72\text{ m}$, (b) $65.4^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you swapped sine and cosine when resolving perpendicular distances for moments about $A$.
In part (b), you evaluated $\arctan(192/420)$, finding the complementary angle to the vertical wall rather than the angle to the ground.
In part (b), you calculated the minimum angle without the person on the ladder, using $\tan\theta = 1/(2\mu)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Critical Ascent Thresholds
bradley_insight.content: As a person climbs a ladder, their weight creates an increasing overturning moment, demanding greater friction at the base. The most dangerous position is always the very top ($x = L$). If the ladder does not slip when the person reaches the top rung, it is stable at every lower rung.

question:
A non-uniform ladder $AB$ of mass $30\text{ kg}$ and length $6\text{ m}$ rests with end $A$ on rough horizontal ground and end $B$ against a smooth vertical wall. The centre of mass of the ladder is located at a distance of $2\text{ m}$ from the base $A$.

The ladder is inclined at an angle of $60^\circ$ to the horizontal ground. The coefficient of friction between the ground and the ladder is $\mu = 0.35$.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) When no person is on the ladder, determine whether the ladder remains in equilibrium or slips.

(b) A decorator of mass $70\text{ kg}$ steps onto the ladder and climbs upwards from $A$.

Calculate the distance $d$ the decorator climbs along the ladder before the ladder is on the point of slipping, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
steps:
(a) Equilibrium check without person:

For the ladder alone, vertical equilibrium gives:\begin{aligned} R_A &= 30g \cr &= 294\text{ N} \end{aligned}Maximum available friction at the ground:\begin{aligned} F_{\text{max}} &= \mu R_A \cr &= 0.35(294) \cr &= 102.9\text{ N} \end{aligned}Taking moments about $A$ to find required wall reaction $R_B$:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma M_A = 0 \cr &(30g)(2\cos 60^\circ) \cr &\qquad - R_B(6\sin 60^\circ) = 0 \cr &30g(1) = 6R_B\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \cr &30g = 3\sqrt{3}R_B \cr &R_B = \dfrac{10g}{\sqrt{3}} \cr &R_B \approx 56.58\text{ N} \end{aligned}Since $R_B = 56.58\text{ N} < F_{\text{max}} = 102.9\text{ N}$, friction is sufficient to prevent slipping, so the ladder remains in equilibrium.

(b) Calculate distance d climbed by decorator:

With the decorator on the ladder, total vertical reaction is:\begin{aligned} R_A &= (30 + 70)g \cr &= 100g \cr &= 980\text{ N} \end{aligned}At the point of slipping, limiting friction is:\begin{aligned} F_A &= 0.35(980) \cr &= 343\text{ N} \cr &= 35g \end{aligned}Horizontal equilibrium gives $R_B = F_A = 35g$.

Taking moments about $A$:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma M_A = 0 \cr &(30g)(2\cos 60^\circ) \cr &\qquad + (70g)(d\cos 60^\circ) \cr &\qquad - (35g)(6\sin 60^\circ) = 0 \end{aligned}

Dividing through by $g\cos 60^\circ$:\begin{aligned} &60 + 70d \cr &\qquad - 210\tan 60^\circ = 0 \cr &70d = 210\sqrt{3} - 60 \cr &70d = 363.73 - 60 \cr &70d = 303.73 \cr &d = \dfrac{303.73}{70} \cr &d \approx 4.34\text{ m} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Equilibrium ($56.6\text{ N} < 103\text{ N}$), (b) $4.34\text{ m}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you calculated maximum friction using the wrong coefficient or normal reaction.
In part (b), you treated the ladder as uniform with its centre of mass at $3\text{ m}$ rather than using the non-uniform position at $2\text{ m}$.
In part (b), you forgot to divide by $\cos 60^\circ$ on the weight terms when simplifying the moments equation.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Non-Uniform Centre of Mass Placement
bradley_insight.content: When a problem specifies a non-uniform body, never place the weight at the geometric midpoint. Here, the centre of mass is located at $2\text{ m}$ from the base, giving a weight moment of $30g(2\cos 60^\circ)$. Using the midpoint distance of $3\text{ m}$ would distort all subsequent moments.

question:
A uniform ladder $AB$ of mass $25\text{ kg}$ and length $6\text{ m}$ rests with end $B$ against a smooth vertical wall. End $A$ rests on smooth horizontal ground, but is prevented from slipping by a light, inextensible horizontal rope attached from $A$ to the base of the wall.

The ladder is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal, where $\cos\theta = 0.6$ and $\sin\theta = 0.8$.

A firefighter of mass $75\text{ kg}$ climbs to the top of the ladder at $B$.

Take $g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}$.

(a) Find the normal reaction exerted by the ground on the ladder at $A$.

(b) By taking moments about $A$, calculate the tension $T$ in the horizontal rope while the firefighter is at $B$.

(c) The rope has a maximum breaking tension of $600\text{ N}$. Determine whether the rope will break when the firefighter reaches the top of the ladder.
steps:
(a) Calculate normal reaction at ground:

Because both the ground and the wall are smooth, there is no vertical friction force at either contact point.

Resolving vertically for equilibrium:\begin{aligned} R_A &= (25 + 75)g \cr &= 100(9.8) \cr &= 980\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(b) Calculate tension in horizontal rope:

The weight of the ladder acts at the midpoint ($3\text{ m}$ from $A$), and the firefighter stands at $B$ ($6\text{ m}$ from $A$).

Taking moments about $A$:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma M_A = 0 \cr &(25g)(3\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad + (75g)(6\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad - R_B(6\sin\theta) = 0 \end{aligned}

Substituting $\cos\theta = 0.6$ and $\sin\theta = 0.8$:\begin{aligned} &(25g)(1.8) + (75g)(3.6) \cr &\qquad - 4.8R_B = 0 \cr &45g + 270g - 4.8R_B = 0 \cr &4.8R_B = 315g \cr &R_B = \dfrac{315(9.8)}{4.8} \cr &R_B = 643.125\text{ N} \end{aligned}Since the ground is smooth, the tension $T$ in the horizontal rope balances the wall reaction $R_B$:\begin{aligned} T &= R_B \cr &= 643.125\text{ N} \cr &\approx 643\text{ N} \end{aligned}

(c) Check rope breaking condition:

The tension required to maintain equilibrium is $T = 643.125\text{ N}$.

Because $643.125\text{ N} > 600\text{ N}$, the tension exceeds the breaking limit, so the rope will break.
Final Answer: (a) $980\text{ N}$, (b) $643\text{ N}$, (c) Rope will break ($643\text{ N} > 600\text{ N}$)

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Horizontal Restraints on Smooth Surfaces
bradley_insight.content: On a completely smooth floor, friction is zero. Equilibrium is possible only if an external horizontal force—such as a peg or tie-rope—restrains the base. By horizontal equilibrium $\Sigma F_x = 0$, the rope tension must equal the normal reaction at the wall ($T = R_B$). Taking moments about the base isolates this tension cleanly.

question:
A uniform rod $AB$ of mass $M\text{ kg}$ and length $2a$ rests in a vertical plane with end $A$ on rough horizontal ground and end $B$ against a rough vertical wall.

The coefficient of friction between the rod and the ground is $\mu_1 = 0.5$, and the coefficient of friction between the rod and the wall is $\mu_2 = 0.25$.

The rod is inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal ground and is in limiting equilibrium, with end $A$ on the point of slipping away from the wall and end $B$ on the point of slipping down the wall.

(a) Draw a clear list of all forces acting on the rod, stating their directions.

(b) Show that the normal reaction $R_B$ at the wall is related to the normal reaction $R_A$ at the ground by:$$R_B = 0.5R_A$$(c) Show that $R_A = \dfrac{8}{9}Mg$.

(d) By taking moments about $A$, calculate the exact value of $\tan\theta$, and hence find $\theta$ to the nearest $0.1^\circ$.
steps:
(a) Forces acting on the rod:

The five forces acting on the rod are:
• At ground $A$: normal reaction $R_A$ vertically upwards
• At ground $A$: friction force $F_A = \mu_1 R_A$ horizontally towards the wall
• At wall $B$: normal reaction $R_B$ horizontally away from the wall
• At wall $B$: friction force $F_B = \mu_2 R_B$ vertically upwards
• At midpoint of rod: weight $Mg$ vertically downwards

(b) Relate R_B to R_A:

Because end $A$ is on the point of slipping away from the wall, friction at $A$ is limiting ($F_A = \mu_1 R_A = 0.5R_A$).

Resolving horizontally for equilibrium:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma F_x = 0 \cr &F_A - R_B = 0 \cr &R_B = F_A \cr &R_B = 0.5R_A \end{aligned}

(c) Show R_A = (8/9)Mg:

Because end $B$ tends to slip downwards, friction at $B$ acts upwards and is limiting ($F_B = \mu_2 R_B = 0.25R_B$).

Resolving vertically for equilibrium:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma F_y = 0 \cr &R_A + F_B - Mg = 0 \cr &R_A + 0.25R_B = Mg \end{aligned}Substitute $R_B = 0.5R_A$:\begin{aligned} &R_A + 0.25(0.5R_A) = Mg \cr &R_A + 0.125R_A = Mg \cr &1.125R_A = Mg \cr &\dfrac{9}{8}R_A = Mg \cr &R_A = \dfrac{8}{9}Mg \end{aligned}

(d) Determine tan θ and θ by moments:

Evaluate $R_B$ and $F_B$ in terms of $Mg$:\begin{aligned} R_B &= 0.5\left(\dfrac{8}{9}Mg\right) \cr &= \dfrac{4}{9}Mg \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} F_B &= 0.25\left(\dfrac{4}{9}Mg\right) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{9}Mg \end{aligned}Taking moments about base $A$ for rod of length $2a$:\begin{aligned} &\Sigma M_A = 0 \cr &(Mg)(a\cos\theta) \cr &\qquad - R_B(2a\sin\theta) \cr &\qquad - F_B(2a\cos\theta) = 0 \end{aligned}

Substitute expressions and divide by $Mga$:\begin{aligned} &\cos\theta \cr &\qquad - \left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right)(2\sin\theta) \cr &\qquad - \left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right)(2\cos\theta) = 0 \cr &\cos\theta - \dfrac{8}{9}\sin\theta - \dfrac{2}{9}\cos\theta = 0 \cr &\dfrac{7}{9}\cos\theta = \dfrac{8}{9}\sin\theta \cr &7\cos\theta = 8\sin\theta \cr &\tan\theta = \dfrac{7}{8} = 0.875 \cr &\theta = \arctan(0.875) \cr &\theta \approx 41.2^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Listed correctly, (b) Proof complete, (c) Proof complete, (d) $\tan\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}$, $\theta = 41.2^\circ$

question:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 - kx^2 + 5x + 3k$.
Given that (x - 2) is a factor of $f(x)$, find the value of the constant k.
steps: According to the Factor Theorem, if (x - 2) is a factor of $f(x)$, then evaluating the polynomial at $x = 2$ must equal zero: $f(2) = 0$.

We substitute $x = 2$ into the expression fo $f(x)$:
$$f(2) = 2(2)^3 - k(2)^2 + 5(2) + 3k$$

Evaluating the powers and simplifying each term gives:
$$f(2) = 2(8) - 4k + 10 + 3k$$
$$f(2) = 16 - 4k + 10 + 3k$$

Combining the numerical terms and the k terms yields:
$$(16 + 10) + (-4k + 3k) = 0$$
$$26 - k = 0$$

Solving this linear equation gives our final value for k:
$$k = 26$$
Final Answer: $$k = 26$$

pi_options.feedback: You evaluated $f(-2) = 0$ instead of $f(2) = 0$. Since the linear factor is (x - 2), the corresponding root to substitute is $x = 2$, not $x = -2$.
You forgot to square the x-value when multiplying by k, evaluating the $-kx^2$ term as simply -k. Remember that at $x=2$, $-kx^2$ becomes $-k(2)^2 = -4k$.
It appears you set $f(2) = 2$ instead of $f(2) = 0$. Since (x - 2) is a *factor*, the remainder must be exactly zero according to the Factor Theorem.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Root Sign Rule
bradley_insight.content: Always double-check your root's sign before substituting. If (x - c) is the factor, you substitute $x = c$. If it is (x + c), you substitute $x = -c$. A tiny sign error here will instantly derail all of your subsequent algebra.

question:
Let $f(x) = 4x^3 + ax^2 - 7x + 2a$.
Given that (x + 2) is a factor of $f(x)$, find the value of the constant a.
steps: According to the Factor Theorem, if (x + 2) is a factor of $f(x)$, then evaluating the polynomial at $x = -2$ must equal zero: $f(-2) = 0$.
We substitute $x = -2$ into the expression for $f(x)$:\begin{aligned}f(-2) & = 4(-2)^3 + a(-2)^2\cr & \qquad- 7(-2) + 2a\end{aligned}

Evaluating the powers and simplifying each term (keeping close track of negative signs) gives:
$$f(-2) = 4(-8) + a(4) + 14 + 2a$$
$$f(-2) = -32 + 4a + 14 + 2a$$

Combining the numerical terms and the a terms yields:
$$(-32 + 14) + (4a + 2a) = 0$$
$$-18 + 6a = 0$$

Solving this linear equation gives our final value for a:
\begin{aligned}6a &= 18 \cr a &= 3\end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$a = 3$$

pi_options.feedback: You evaluated $f(2) = 0$ instead of $f(-2) = 0$. Since the linear factor is (x + 2), the corresponding root to substitute is $x = -2$, not $x = 2$.
Check your signs during substitution. You likely evaluated the term -7(-2) as -14 instead of +14. Multiplying two negative numbers yields a positive product.
Be careful when squaring negative numbers. $(-2)^2 = +4$, not -4. Any real number squared is always positive.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Negative Bases
bradley_insight.content: When cubing and squaring negative numbers like -2, always write them inside brackets on your calculator: $(-2)^3 = -8$ and $(-2)^2 = 4$. Leaving brackets out can cause your calculator to evaluate $-2^2$ as -4, introducing a fatal sign error.

question:
Let $f(x) = 3x^3 - 2kx^2 + 5x + 4k$.
Given that (x - 1) is a factor of $f(x)$, find the value of the constant k.
steps: According to the Factor Theorem, if (x - 1) is a factor of $f(x)$, then evaluating the polynomial at $x = 1$ must equal zero: $f(1) = 0$.

We substitute $x = 1$ into the expression fo $f(x)$:
$$f(1) = 3(1)^3 - 2k(1)^2 + 5(1) + 4k$$

Simplifying the powers and combining terms gives:
$$f(1) = 3 - 2k + 5 + 4k$$

Combining the constant terms and the k terms yields:
$$(3 + 5) + (-2k + 4k) = 0$$
$$8 + 2k = 0$$

Solving this linear equation gives our final value for k:
\begin{aligned}2k &= -8 \cr k &= -4\end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$k = -4$$

Be careful with order of operations. The term $-2kx^2$ evaluated at $x=1$ becomes $-2k(1)^2 = -2k$. The negative sign belongs to the coefficient and is not squared.
Double-check your basic arithmetic. Combining the constant terms 3 and 5 yields 8, not 2.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Simplification First
bradley_insight.content: When $x = 1$, calculations become incredibly fast because $1^3 = 1$ and $1^2 = 1$. The expression simply collapses to the sum of its coefficients: $3 - 2k + 5 + 4k = 0$. Use this shortcut to save precious exam time!

question:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 - ax^2 - 8x + 3a$.
Given that (x - 3) is a factor of $f(x)$, find the value of the constant a.
steps: According to the Factor Theorem, if (x - 3) is a factor of $f(x)$, then evaluating the polynomial at $x = 3$ must equal zero: $f(3) = 0$.

We substitute $x = 3$ into the expression fo $f(x)$:
$$f(3) = 2(3)^3 - a(3)^2 - 8(3) + 3a$$

Evaluating the powers and simplifying each term gives:
$$f(3) = 2(27) - 9a - 24 + 3a$$
$$f(3) = 54 - 9a - 24 + 3a$$

Combining the constant terms and the a terms yields:
$$(54 - 24) + (-9a + 3a) = 0$$
$$30 - 6a = 0$$

Solving this linear equation gives our final value for a:
\begin{aligned}6a &= 30 \cr a &= 5\end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$a = 5$$

Be mindful of BIDMAS/indices. The term $2x^3$ means $2 \times (x^3)$, not $(2x)^3$. You must cube 3 first to get 27, then multiply by 2 to get 54.
Check your algebraic collection of a terms. We have -9a + 3a, which simplifies to -6a, not -12a.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Order of Operations
bradley_insight.content: Remember that index powers always have priority over multiplication. In the term $2x^3$, the exponent only applies to the x. You must evaluate $x^3$ first before doubling the result.

question:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 + 3px^2 - 2x - 3p$.
Given that (x + 3) is a factor of $f(x)$, find the value of the constant p.
steps: According to the Factor Theorem, if (x + 3) is a farctor of $f(x)$, then evaluating the polynomial at $x = -3$ must equal zero: $f(-3) = 0$.

We substitute $x = -3$ into the expression for $f(x)$:
$$ f(-3)= 2(-3)^3 + 3p(-3)^2 - 2(-3) - 3p$$

Evaluating the powers and simplifying each term (taking close care with negative signs) gives:
$$f(-3) = 2(-27) + 3p(9) + 6 - 3p$$
$$f(-3) = -54 + 27p + 6 - 3p$$

Combining the numerical terms and the p terms yields:
$$(-54 + 6) + (27p - 3p) = 0$$
$$-48 + 24p = 0$$

Solving this linear equation gives our final value for p:
\begin{aligned}24p &= 48 \cr p &= 2\end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$p = 2$$

question:
A curve has the equation:
$$y = \dfrac{ 3x^2 + 12x }{ (x+2)^2 }, \quad x \ne -2$$
(a) Show that $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{A}{ (x+2)^n }$, where $A$ and $n$ are constants to be found.
(b) Hence, deduce the range of values for x for which $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} < 0$.
steps: Part (a): We begin by identifying the numerator as $u = 3x^2 + 12x$ and the denominator as $v = (x+2)^2$.

Differentiating both terms with respect to x gives:
\begin{aligned}u' &= 6x + 12 \cr&= 6(x+2)\end{aligned}
$$v' = 2(x+2)$$

Using the Quotient Rule, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{ u'v - uv' }{ v^2 }$:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}&=\dfrac{ (6x+12)(x+2)^2}{ (x+2)^4 } \cr &\quad - \dfrac{(3x^2+12x) \cdot 2(x+2) }{ (x+2)^4 }\end{aligned}

We can factorise out a common term of (x+2) from the numerator to simplify:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (x+2) [ (6x+12)(x+2)]}{ (x+2)^4 }\cr &\quad - \dfrac{ ( x+2 )[ 2(3x^2+12x) ] }{ (x+2)^4 }\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (6x+12)(x+2)}{ (x+2)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ 2(3x^2+12x) }{ (x+2)^3 }\end{aligned}

Expanding and simplifying the remaining terms in the numerator:
\begin{aligned}(6x+12)(x+2)\cr \quad= 6x^2 + 24x + 24\end{aligned}
$$2(3x^2+12x) = 6x^2 + 24x$$
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (6x^2 + 24x + 24) }{ (x+2)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ (6x^2 + 24x) }{ (x+2)^3 }\end{aligned}
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{24}{ (x+2)^3 }$$
Therefore, the constants are $A = 24$ and $n = 3$.

Part (b): For $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} < 0$:
$$\dfrac{24}{ (x+2)^3 } < 0$$

Since the numerator is a positive constant ($24 > 0$), the sign of the fraction is determined entirely by the denominator. Therefore, we require the denominator to be negative:
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^3 &< 0 \cr\implies x + 2 &< 0 \cr\implies x &< -2\end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{24}{ (x+2)^3 }$$ (b) $$x < -2$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably made an inequality error in Part (b). For the fraction to be negative, the denominator $(x+2)^3$ must be negative. Since an odd power preserves the negative sign, this requires $x + 2 < 0$, which simplifies to $x < -2$.
You probably used the Product Rule formula (adding the two terms in your numerator) instead of the Quotient Rule formula (subtracting them). Check your formula sheet: the numerator must be u'v - uv'.
You forgot to decrease the power of the denominator when cancelling out the common factor of (x + 2) from your numerator. The denominator should be $(x+2)^3$, not $(x+2)^4$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Quotient Rule Cancelling
bradley_insight.content: When applying the Quotient Rule to functions with a squared denominator like $(x+a)^2$, both terms in your numerator will always contain a common factor of (x+a). Always factorise and cancel this term out first before expanding the rest of the numerator. It saves significant time and prevents algebraic errors.

question:
A curve has the equation:
$$y = \dfrac{ -4x^2 - 8x }{ (x+1)^2 }, \quad x \ne -1$$
(a) Show that $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{A}{ (x+1)^n }$, where $A$ and $n$ are constants to be found.
(b) Hence, deduce the range of values for x for which $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} < 0$.
steps: Part (a): Let $u = -4x^2 - 8x$ and $v = (x+1)^2$.

Differentiating both terms with respect to x gives:
\begin{aligned} u' &= -8x - 8 \cr &= -8(x+1) \end{aligned}
$$v' = 2(x+1)$$

Using the Quotient Rule, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{ u'v - uv' }{ v^2 }$:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (-8x-8)(x+1)^2}{ (x+1)^4 } \cr &\quad - \dfrac{(-4x^2-8x) \cdot 2(x+1) }{ (x+1)^4 }\end{aligned}

We can factorise out a common term of (x+1) from the numerator to simplify:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (x+1) [ (-8x-8)(x+1)]}{ (x+1)^4 }\cr &\quad - \dfrac{ ( x+1 )[ 2(-4x^2-8x) ] }{ (x+1)^4 }\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (-8x-8)(x+1)}{ (x+1)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ 2(-4x^2-8x) }{ (x+1)^3 }\end{aligned}

Expanding and simplifying the remaining terms in the numerator:
\begin{aligned}(-8x-8)(x+1)\cr \quad= -8x^2 - 16x - 8\end{aligned}
$$2(-4x^2-8x) = -8x^2 - 16x$$
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (-8x^2 - 16x - 8) }{ (x+1)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ (-8x^2 - 16x) }{ (x+1)^3 }\end{aligned}
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{-8}{ (x+1)^3 }$$
Therefore, the constants are $A = -8$ and $n = 3$.

Part (b): For $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} < 0$:
$$\dfrac{-8}{ (x+1)^3 } < 0$$

Since the numerator is a negative constant ($-8 < 0$), the fraction is only negative when the denominator is positive:
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^3 &> 0 \cr\implies x + 1 &> 0 \cr\implies x &> -1\end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{-8}{ (x+1)^3 }$$ (b) $$x > -1$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably forgot to account for the negative sign in your numerator when setting up your inequality in Part (b). Because -8 is negative, the fraction is only negative when the denominator is positive: $(x+1)^3 > 0$, which yields $x > -1$.
Check your expanding and signs. When expanding $- (-8x^2 - 16x)$ in the numerator, the double negative turns both terms positive, which cancels out your quadratic and linear terms perfectly.
Check your differentiation of $u = -4x^2 - 8x$. The derivative must be $u' = -8x - 8$, not +8x + 8. This sign error changed the sign of your constant A from negative to positive.
