bradley_insight.content: In Part (b), be exceptionally careful when the numerator is negative. A fraction $\frac{\text{numerator}}{\text{denominator}} < 0$ means the numerator and denominator must have opposite signs. Since the numerator is -8 (negative), the denominator must be positive to ensure the overall value is negative.

question:
A curve has the equation:
$$y = \dfrac{ 2x^2 + 12x }{ (x+3)^2 }, \quad x \ne -3$$
(a) Show that $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{A}{ (x+3)^n }$, where $A$ and $n$ are constants to be found.
(b) Hence, deduce the range of values for x for which $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} > 0$.
steps: Part (a): Let $u = 2x^2 + 12x$ and $v = (x+3)^2$.

Differentiating both terms with respect to x gives:
\begin{aligned} u' &= 4x + 12 \cr &= 4(x+3) \end{aligned}
$$v' = 2(x+3)$$

Using the Quotient Rule, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{ u'v - uv' }{ v^2 }$:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (4x+12)(x+3)^2}{ (x+3)^4 } \cr &\quad - \dfrac{(2x^2+12x) \cdot 2(x+3) }{ (x+3)^4 }\end{aligned}

We can factorise out a common term of (x+3) from the numerator to simplify:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (x+3) [ (4x+12)(x+3)]}{ (x+3)^4 }\cr &\quad - \dfrac{ ( x+3 )[ 2(2x^2+12x) ] }{ (x+3)^4 }\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (4x+12)(x+3)}{ (x+3)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ 2(2x^2+12x) }{ (x+3)^3 }\end{aligned}

Expanding and simplifying the remaining terms in the numerator:
\begin{aligned}(4x+12)(x+3)\cr \quad= 4x^2 + 24x + 36\end{aligned}
$$2(2x^2+12x) = 4x^2 + 24x$$
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (4x^2 + 24x + 36) }{ (x+3)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ (4x^2 + 24x) }{ (x+3)^3 }\end{aligned}
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{36}{ (x+3)^3 }$$
Therefore, the constants are $A = 36$ and $n = 3$.

Part (b): For $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} > 0$:
$$\dfrac{36}{ (x+3)^3 } > 0$$

Since the numerator is a positive constant ($36 > 0$), the fraction will only be positive when the denominator is positive:
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^3 &> 0 \cr\implies x + 3 &> 0 \cr\implies x &> -3\end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{36}{ (x+3)^3 }$$ (b) $$x > -3$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably set up your inequality incorrectly in Part (b). For the fraction to be positive ($> 0$), both the numerator and the denominator must have the same sign. Since $36 > 0$, the denominator must be positive: $x + 3 > 0$, which yields $x > -3$.
Check your expansion of (4x+12)(x+3). The constant term is $12 \times 3 = 36$, not 18. Remember to multiply the constants together during your expansion.
You forgot to decrease the power of the denominator when cancelling out the common factor of (x + 3) from your numerator. The denominator should be $(x+3)^3$, not $(x+3)^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Odd vs Even Powers in Inequalities
bradley_insight.content: Unlike squared denominators like $(x+3)^2$ which are always positive, cubed denominators like $(x+3)^3$ preserve the sign of their base. This means $(x+3)^3$ will be positive when $x > -3$, and negative when $x < -3$. Always look at the exponent first!

question:
A curve has the equation:
$$y = \dfrac{ -3x^2 - 12x }{ (x+2)^2 }, \quad x \ne -2$$
(a) Show that $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{A}{ (x+2)^n }$, where $A$ and $n$ are constants to be found.
(b) Hence, deduce the range of values for x for which $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} > 0$.
steps: Part (a): Let $u = -3x^2 - 12x$ and $v = (x+2)^2$.

Differentiating both terms with respect to x gives:
\begin{aligned} u' &= -6x - 12 \cr &= -6(x+2) \end{aligned}
$$v' = 2(x+2)$$

Using the Quotient Rule, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{ u'v - uv' }{ v^2 }$:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (-6x-12)(x+2)^2}{ (x+2)^4 } \cr &\quad - \dfrac{(-3x^2-12x) \cdot 2(x+2) }{ (x+2)^4 }\end{aligned}

We can factorise out a common term of (x+2) from the numerator to simplify:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (x+2) [ (-6x-12)(x+2)]}{ (x+2)^4 }\cr &\quad - \dfrac{ ( x+2 )[ 2(-3x^2-12x) ] }{ (x+2)^4 }\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (-6x-12)(x+2)}{ (x+2)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ 2(-3x^2-12x) }{ (x+2)^3 }\end{aligned}

Expanding and simplifying the remaining terms in the numerator:
\begin{aligned}(-6x-12)(x+2)\cr \quad= -6x^2 - 24x - 24\end{aligned}
$$2(-3x^2-12x) = -6x^2 - 24x$$
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (-6x^2 - 24x - 24) }{ (x+2)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ (-6x^2 - 24x) }{ (x+2)^3 }\end{aligned}
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{-24}{ (x+2)^3 }$$
Therefore, the constants are $A = -24$ and $n = 3$.

Part (b): For $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} > 0$:
$$\dfrac{-24}{ (x+2)^3 } > 0$$

Since the numerator is a negative constant ($-24 < 0$), the fraction will only be positive when the denominator is negative:
\begin{aligned}(x+2)^3 &< 0 \cr\implies x + 2 &< 0 \cr\implies x &< -2\end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{-24}{ (x+2)^3 }$$ (b) $$x < -2$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably made a sign error in Part (b). Because your numerator -24 is negative, the fraction is only positive when the denominator is negative (since a negative divided by a negative yields a positive quotient). Therefore, $(x+2)^3 < 0$, which yields $x < -2$.
Check your differentiation of $u = -3x^2 - 12x$. The derivative is $u' = -6x - 12$, not +6x + 12. This sign error changed the sign of your constant A from negative to positive.
Check your expansion of (-6x-12)(x+2). The constant term is $-12 \times 2 = -24$. Make sure you multiply all components of your binomial brackets correctly.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Positive Fraction Logic
bradley_insight.content: For a fraction to be strictly positive ($> 0$), both the numerator and the denominator must have the same sign. If you find your numerator is negative (like -24), your denominator must also be negative. Remembering this basic algebraic sign rule prevents simple mistakes in part (b).

question:
A curve has the equation:
$$y = \dfrac{ 4x^2 + 8x }{ (x+1)^2 }, \quad x \ne -1$$
(a) Show that $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{A}{ (x+1)^n }$, where $A$ and $n$ are constants to be found.
(b) Hence, deduce the range of values for x for which $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} < 0$.
steps: Part (a): Let $u = 4x^2 + 8x$ and $v = (x+1)^2$.

Differentiating both terms with respect to x gives:
\begin{aligned} u' &= 8x + 8 \cr &= 8(x+1) \end{aligned}
$$v' = 2(x+1)$$

Using the Quotient Rule, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{ u'v - uv' }{ v^2 }$:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (8x+8)(x+1)^2}{ (x+1)^4 } \cr &\quad - \dfrac{(4x^2+8x) \cdot 2(x+1) }{ (x+1)^4 }\end{aligned}

We can factorise out a common term of (x+1) from the numerator to simplify:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (x+1) [ (8x+8)(x+1)]}{ (x+1)^4 }\cr &\quad - \dfrac{ ( x+1 )[ 2(4x^2+8x) ] }{ (x+1)^4 }\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (8x+8)(x+1)}{ (x+1)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ 2(4x^2+8x) }{ (x+1)^3 }\end{aligned}

Expanding and simplifying the remaining terms in the numerator:
\begin{aligned}(8x+8)(x+1)\cr \quad= 8x^2 + 16x + 8\end{aligned}
$$2(4x^2+8x) = 8x^2 + 16x$$
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{ (8x^2 + 16x + 8) }{ (x+1)^3 }\cr & \quad-\dfrac{ (8x^2 + 16x) }{ (x+1)^3 }\end{aligned}
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{8}{ (x+1)^3 }$$
Therefore, the constants are $A = 8$ and $n = 3$.

Part (b): For $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} < 0$:
$$\dfrac{8}{ (x+1)^3 } < 0$$

Since the numerator is a positive constant ($8 > 0$), the fraction will only be negative when the denominator is negative:
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^3 &< 0 \cr\implies x + 1 &< 0 \cr\implies x &< -1\end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{8}{ (x+1)^3 }$$ (b) $$x < -1$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably made an inequality boundary error in Part (b). For the fraction to be negative ($< 0$), the denominator $(x+1)^3$ must be negative. Since an odd power preserves the negative sign, this requires $x + 1 < 0$, which yields $x < -1$.

Check your expanding and term cancellations. When subtracting $2(4x^2 + 8x)$ from your left term expansion ($8x^2 + 16x + 8$), both the $8x^2$ and 16x cancel out completely, leaving only the constant 8.
You forgot to decrease the power of the denominator when cancelling out the common factor of (x + 1) from your numerator. The denominator should be $(x+1)^3$, not $(x+1)^4$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Spotting algebraic cancellations
bradley_insight.content: In problems like this, the quadratic and linear terms in your numerator will always cancel out perfectly during expansion, leaving only the constant integer A. If you find yourself left with an x or $x^2$ term in the numerator, go back and check your expansion signs immediately!

question:
A function is defined by:
$$f(x) = \dfrac{1}{ \sqrt{9 - 2x }}.$$
(a) Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of $f(x)$, giving each coefficient in its simplest form.
The expansion can be used to approximate $\sqrt{3}$. Possible values of $x$ that could be substituted into this expansion are:
$$x = -6, \quad x = 3, \quad x = -\tfrac{1}{2}.$$
(b)(i) Without evaluating your expansion, state, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ should not be used.
(b)(ii) State, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ would lead to an approximation of $\sqrt{3}$.
steps:
Part (a): Rewrite f(x) in binomial form by factorising the constant inside the square root:
\begin{aligned}f(x) &= (9 - 2x)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \left[9\left(1 - \tfrac{2}{9}x\right)\right]^{ -1/2 } \cr&= 9^{ -1/2 }\left(1 - \tfrac{2}{9}x\right)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \tfrac{1}{3}\left(1 - \tfrac{2}{9}x\right)^{ -1/2 }.\end{aligned}

Use the binomial expansion $(1 + y)^{ -1/2 } = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}y + \tfrac{3}{8}y^2 + \dots$ with $y = -\tfrac{2}{9}x$:
\begin{aligned} &\left(1 - \tfrac{2}{9}x\right)^{-1/2} \cr &= 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(-\tfrac{2}{9}x\right) + \tfrac{3}{8}\left(-\tfrac{2}{9}x\right)^2 + \dots \cr &= 1 + \tfrac{1}{9}x + \tfrac{1}{54}x^2 + \dots \end{aligned}

Multiply by the factor $\tfrac{1}{3}$:
\begin{aligned}f(x) &\approx \tfrac{1}{3}\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{9}x + \tfrac{1}{54}x^2\right)\cr &= \tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{27}x + \tfrac{1}{162}x^2.\end{aligned}
So the first three terms are $$\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{27}x + \dfrac{1}{162}x^2.$$
Part (b)(i): The binomial expansion for $(1 - \tfrac{2}{9}x)^{ -1/2 }$ is valid when $$\left|\tfrac{2}{9}x\right| < 1 \implies |x| < 4.5.$$
Among the given values, $x = -6$ has $|-6| = 6 > 4.5$, so it lies outside the interval of validity. Therefore, $x = -6$ should not be used.

Part (b)(ii): To approximate $\sqrt{3}$, we need \begin{aligned}f(x) &= \dfrac{1}{ \sqrt{9 - 2x }} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned} This occurs when $9 - 2x = 3$, so $2x = 6$ and $x = 3$. Thus $x = 3$ is the value that leads to an approximation of $\sqrt{3}$.
Final Answer: (a) $$f(x) \approx \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{27}x + \dfrac{1}{162}x^2.$$ (b)(i) $x = -6$ should not be used. (b)(ii) $x = 3$ gives an approximation of $\sqrt{3}$.

pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(i), the restriction $|x| < 4.5$ rules out $x = -6$, not $x = 3$. In part (b)(ii), $x = 3$ is the value that makes $9 - 2x = 3$, so it is the one that approximates $\sqrt{3}$.
Your linear coefficient is incorrect. When expanding $(1 - \tfrac{2}{9}x)^{ -1/2 }$, the first-order term is $+\tfrac{1}{9}x$, which becomes $+\tfrac{1}{27}x$ after multiplying by $\tfrac{1}{3}$.
The quadratic coefficient is too large. Carefully square $-\tfrac{2}{9}x$ and multiply by $\tfrac{3}{8}$, then apply the factor $\tfrac{1}{3}$ to obtain $\tfrac{1}{162}x^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Interval of validity versus target value
bradley_insight.content: Two separate ideas are at work here: the interval of validity, which controls whether the binomial series converges, and the choice of $x$ that actually produces the number you want to approximate. First check |x| against the convergence condition, then solve the algebraic equation that links your function value to the target number.

question:
Consider the function:
$$g(x) = (5 - x)^{ -1/2 }.$$
(a) Rewrite g(x) in the form $k(1 + mx)^n$ and hence find the first three terms of its binomial expansion in ascending powers of $x$.
This expansion can be used to approximate $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5.2}}$. Possible values of $x$ that could be substituted are:
$$x = -0.2, \quad x = 1, \quad x = -6.$$
(b)(i) Without evaluating your expansion, state, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ is outside the interval of validity.
(b)(ii) State, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ would lead to the most accurate approximation to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5.2}}$.
steps:
Part (a): Factorise the constant from the bracket:
\begin{aligned}g(x) &= (5 - x)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \left[5\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}x\right)\right]^{ -1/2 } \cr&= 5^{ -1/2 }\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}x\right)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}x\right)^{ -1/2 }.\end{aligned}

Use the binomial expansion $(1 + y)^{ -1/2 } = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}y + \tfrac{3}{8}y^2 + \dots$ with $y = -\tfrac{1}{5}x$:
\begin{aligned} &\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}x\right)^{ -1/2 }\cr &= 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(-\tfrac{1}{5}x\right) + \tfrac{3}{8}\left(-\tfrac{1}{5}x\right)^2 + \dots\end{aligned}
$$= 1 + \tfrac{1}{10}x + \tfrac{3}{200}x^2 + \dots$$

Multiply by $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5}$:
\begin{aligned}g(x) &\approx \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{10}x + \tfrac{3}{200}x^2\right)\cr &= \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5} + \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{50}x + \dfrac{3\sqrt{5}}{1000}x^2.\end{aligned}
Part (b)(i): The binomial expansion for $(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}x)^{ -1/2 }$ is valid when $$\left|\tfrac{1}{5}x\right| < 1 \implies |x| < 5.$$
Among the given values, $x = -6$ has $|-6| = 6 > 5$, so it lies outside the interval of validity. Therefore, $x = -6$ is not valid for the expansion.

Part (b)(ii): To approximate $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5.2}}$, we need \begin{aligned}g(x) &= \dfrac{1}{ \sqrt{5 - x }} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5.2}}.\end{aligned} This occurs when $5 - x = 5.2$, so $x = -0.2$. Also, |-0.2| is small, so the series converges rapidly. Thus $x = -0.2$ gives the most accurate approximation.

Final Answer: (a) $$g(x) \approx \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5} + \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{50}x + \dfrac{3\sqrt{5}}{1000}x^2.$$ (b)(i) $x = -6$ is outside the interval of validity. (b)(ii) $x = -0.2$ gives the most accurate approximation to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5.2}}$.

pi_options.feedback: For the interval of validity, the condition is $|x| < 5$, so $x = 1$ is valid but $x = -6$ is not. For the approximation, $x = -0.2$ is the value that actually produces $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5.2}}$ and is closest to zero.
Your linear coefficient is too large. The first-order term from $(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}x)^{ -1/2 }$ is $+\tfrac{1}{10}x$, which becomes $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{50}x$ after multiplying by $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5}$.
The quadratic coefficient is incorrect. Carefully square $-\tfrac{1}{5}x$, multiply by $\tfrac{3}{8}$, and then apply the factor $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5}$ to obtain $\dfrac{3\sqrt{5}}{1000}x^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Matching the function to the target number
bradley_insight.content: When a question links a binomial expansion to a numerical approximation, always solve the simple equation that makes the inside of the bracket equal to the target value. Only then worry about which of the candidate x values lies closest to zero for the best accuracy.

question:
A function is defined by:
$$h(x) = \dfrac{1}{ (3 + x)^{1/2 }}.$$
(a) Express h(x) in the form $A(1 + Bx)^n$ and find the first three terms of its binomial expansion in ascending powers of $x$.
This expansion can be used to approximate $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2.7}}$. Possible values of $x$ are:
$$x = -0.3, \quad x = 3, \quad x = -6.$$
(b)(i) Without evaluating your expansion, state, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ should not be used.
(b)(ii) State, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ would lead to the most accurate approximation to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2.7}}$.
steps:
Part (a): Rewrite h(x) in binomial form by factorising the constant:
\begin{aligned}h(x) &= (3 + x)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \left[3\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{3}x\right)\right]^{ -1/2 } \cr&= 3^{ -1/2 }\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{3}x\right)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{3}x\right)^{ -1/2 }.\end{aligned}

Use the binomial expansion $(1 + y)^{ -1/2 } = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}y + \tfrac{3}{8}y^2 + \dots$ with $y = \tfrac{1}{3}x$:
\begin{aligned} &\left(1 + \tfrac{1}{3}x\right)^{ -1/2 }\cr&= 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{1}{3}x\right) + \tfrac{3}{8}\left(\tfrac{1}{3}x\right)^2 + \dots\end{aligned}
$$= 1 - \tfrac{1}{6}x + \tfrac{1}{24}x^2 + \dots$$

Multiply by $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$:
\begin{aligned}h(x) &\approx \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{6}x + \tfrac{1}{24}x^2\right)\cr &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{18}x + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{72}x^2.\end{aligned}
Part (b)(i): The binomial expansion for $(1 + \tfrac{1}{3}x)^{ -1/2 }$ is valid when $$\left|\tfrac{1}{3}x\right| < 1 \implies |x| < 3.$$

Among the given values, $x = -6$ has $|-6| = 6 > 3$, so it lies outside the interval of validity. The boundary value $x = 3$ also does not satisfy $|x| < 3$. Thus $x = -6$ (and $x = 3$) should not be used.

Part (b)(ii): To approximate $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2.7}}$, we need \begin{aligned}h(x) &= \dfrac{1}{ \sqrt{3 + x }} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2.7}}.\end{aligned} This occurs when $3 + x = 2.7$, so $x = -0.3$. Also, |-0.3| is small, so the series converges quickly. Therefore, $x = -0.3$ gives the most accurate approximation.

Final Answer: (a) $$h(x) \approx \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{18}x + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{72}x^2.$$ (b)(i) $x = -6$ is outside the interval of validity. (b)(ii) $x = -0.3$ gives the most accurate approximation to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2.7}}$.

pi_options.feedback: For the interval of validity, the strict inequality $|x| < 3$ rules out $x = -6$ and also excludes the boundary $x = 3$. For the approximation, $x = -0.3$ is the value that actually produces $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2.7}}$ and is closest to zero.

Your linear coefficient is too large in magnitude. The first-order term from $(1 + \tfrac{1}{3}x)^{ -1/2 }$ is $-\tfrac{1}{6}x$, which becomes $-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{18}x$ after multiplying by $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$.
The quadratic coefficient is incorrect. Carefully square $\tfrac{1}{3}x$, multiply by $\tfrac{3}{8}$, and then apply the factor $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$ to obtain $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{72}x^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Boundary points and strict inequalities
bradley_insight.content: When you see a condition like $|x| < a$, remember that the endpoints $x = \pm a$ are excluded. It is common for exam questions to include a boundary value as a tempting but invalid option, so always check whether the inequality is strict or not.

question:
A function is defined by:
$$y = (4 + 3x)^{ -1/2 }.$$
(a) Rewrite y in the form $C(1 + Dx)^n$ and hence find the first three terms of the binomial expansion in ascending powers of $x$.
This expansion can be used to approximate $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3.1}}$. Possible values of $x$ are:
$$x = -0.3, \quad x = 1, \quad x = -2.$$
(b)(i) Without evaluating your expansion, state, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ is invalid for the expansion.
(b)(ii) State, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ would lead to the most accurate approximation to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3.1}}$.
steps:
Part (a): Factorise the constant from the bracket:
\begin{aligned}y &= (4 + 3x)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \left[4\left(1 + \tfrac{3}{4}x\right)\right]^{ -1/2 } \cr&= 4^{ -1/2 }\left(1 + \tfrac{3}{4}x\right)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 + \tfrac{3}{4}x\right)^{ -1/2 }.\end{aligned}

Use the binomial expansion $(1 + y)^{ -1/2 } = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}y + \tfrac{3}{8}y^2 + \dots$ with $y = \tfrac{3}{4}x$:
\begin{aligned} &\left(1 + \tfrac{3}{4}x\right)^{ -1/2 }\cr &= 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\tfrac{3}{4}x\right) + \tfrac{3}{8}\left(\tfrac{3}{4}x\right)^2 + \dots\end{aligned}
$$= 1 - \tfrac{3}{8}x + \tfrac{27}{128}x^2 + \dots$$

Multiply by $\dfrac{1}{2}$:
\begin{aligned}y &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - \tfrac{3}{8}x + \tfrac{27}{128}x^2\right)\cr &= \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{3}{16}x + \dfrac{27}{256}x^2.\end{aligned}
Part (b)(i): The binomial expansion for $(1 + \tfrac{3}{4}x)^{ -1/2 }$ is valid when $$\left|\tfrac{3}{4}x\right| < 1 \implies |x| < \dfrac{4}{3}.$$
Among the given values, $x = -2$ has $|-2| = 2 > \dfrac{4}{3}$, so it lies outside the interval of validity. Therefore, $x = -2$ is invalid for the expansion.

Part (b)(ii): To approximate $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3.1}}$, we need \begin{aligned}y &= \dfrac{1}{ \sqrt{4 + 3x }} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3.1}}.\end{aligned} This occurs when $4 + 3x = 3.1$, so $3x = -0.9$ and $x = -0.3$. Also, |-0.3| is smaller than |1|, so the series converges more rapidly. Thus $x = -0.3$ gives the most accurate approximation.
Final Answer: (a) $$y \approx \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{3}{16}x + \dfrac{27}{256}x^2.$$ (b)(i) $x = -2$ is invalid. (b)(ii) $x = -0.3$ gives the most accurate approximation to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3.1}}$.

pi_options.feedback: For the interval of validity, the condition $|x| < \dfrac{4}{3}$ excludes $x = -2$, not $x = 1$. For the approximation, $x = -0.3$ is the value that actually produces $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3.1}}$ and is closer to zero than $x = 1$.
Your linear coefficient is too large in magnitude. The first-order term from $(1 + \tfrac{3}{4}x)^{ -1/2 }$ is $-\tfrac{3}{8}x$, which becomes $-\dfrac{3}{16}x$ after multiplying by $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
The quadratic coefficient is incorrect. Carefully square $\tfrac{3}{4}x$, multiply by $\tfrac{3}{8}$, and then apply the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ to obtain $\dfrac{27}{256}x^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Scaling before expanding
bradley_insight.content: Always factor out the constant from the bracket before applying the binomial expansion. This keeps the expression in the clean form $(1 + kx)^n$ and makes it much easier to see both the interval of validity and the structure of the coefficients.

question:
A function is defined by:
$$F(x) = \dfrac{1}{ \sqrt{16 - x }}.$$
(a) Find the first three terms of the binomial expansion of $f(x)$ in ascending powers of $x$.
This expansion can be used to approximate $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{15.5}}$. Possible values of $x$ are:
$$x = 0.5, \quad x = -18, \quad x = 3.$$
(b)(i) Without evaluating your expansion, state, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ should not be used.
(b)(ii) State, giving a reason, which of these values of $x$ would lead to the most accurate approximation to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{15.5}}$.
steps:
Part (a): Rewrite F(x) in binomial form by factorising the constant inside the square root:
\begin{aligned}F(x) &= (16 - x)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \left[16\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{16}x\right)\right]^{ -1/2 } \cr&= 16^{ -1/2 }\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{16}x\right)^{ -1/2 } \cr&= \dfrac{1}{4}\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{16}x\right)^{ -1/2 }.\end{aligned}

Use the binomial expansion $(1 + y)^{ -1/2 } = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}y + \tfrac{3}{8}y^2 + \dots$ with $y = -\tfrac{1}{16}x$:
\begin{aligned}&\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{16}x\right)^{ -1/2 }\cr &= 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\left(-\tfrac{1}{16}x\right) + \tfrac{3}{8}\left(-\tfrac{1}{16}x\right)^2 + \dots\end{aligned}

Your linear coefficient is too large. The first-order term from $(1 - \tfrac{1}{16}x)^{ -1/2 }$ is $+\tfrac{1}{32}x$, which becomes $\dfrac{1}{128}x$ after multiplying by $\dfrac{1}{4}$.

question:
(a) Solve, for $$-180^\circ \le \theta \le 180^\circ,$$ the equation:
$$4\sin 2\theta = 7\cos\theta.$$Give your answers, where necessary, to one decimal place. Solutions based entirely on graphical or numerical methods are not acceptable.

(b) Hence deduce the smallest positive solution of:
\begin{aligned}4 & \sin(2x + 20^\circ)\cr & \quad \quad \quad = 7\cos(x + 10^\circ).\end{aligned}

$$4(2\sin\theta\cos\theta) = 7\cos\theta$$
$$8\sin\theta\cos\theta - 7\cos\theta = 0$$
Factorise:
$$\cos\theta(8\sin\theta - 7) = 0.$$
This gives two branches:
Branch 1: \begin{aligned}\cos\theta &= 0 \cr \Rightarrow \theta &= -90^\circ\text{} 90^\circ.\end{aligned}

Part (b): Note that $$2x + 20^\circ = 2(x + 10^\circ).$$ Let $$\theta = x + 10^\circ.$$ Then the equation becomes the same as in Part (a).
Thus the smallest positive solution is:

bradley_insight.title: Factorisation First
bradley_insight.content: When both sides contain products of trig functions, factorising early often reveals clean solution branches and prevents unnecessary algebra.

question:
(a) Solve, for $$-180^\circ \le \theta \le 180^\circ,$$ the equation:
$$3\tan\theta = 2\sin 2\theta.$$Give answers to one decimal place where necessary.

(b) Deduce the smallest positive solution of:
\begin{aligned} &3\tan(x - 15^\circ)\cr & \quad \quad \quad = 2\sin(2x - 30^\circ).\end{aligned}
steps:
Part (a): Use \begin{aligned}&\tan\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}, \cr & \sin 2\theta \cr&= 2\sin\theta\cos\theta.\end{aligned}
Substitute:
$$3\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = 4\sin\theta\cos\theta$$
Multiply by cosθ:
$$3\sin\theta = 4\sin\theta\cos^2\theta$$
Factorise:
$$\sin\theta(3 - 4\cos^2\theta) = 0.$$
Solutions:
• \begin{aligned}\sin\theta &= 0\cr \Rightarrow \theta &= -180^\circ\text{}0^\circ\text{} 180^\circ.\end{aligned}
• \begin{aligned}\cos^2\theta &= \frac{3}{4}\cr \Rightarrow \theta &= \pm 30^\circ\text{}\pm 150^\circ.\end{aligned}

Part (b): Note that $$2x - 30^\circ = 2(x - 15^\circ).$$ Let $$\theta = x - 15^\circ.$$
Smallest positive solution:
\begin{aligned}x &= 0^\circ + 15^\circ \cr&= 15^\circ.\end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned}\theta &= -180^\circ, -150^\circ, -30^\circ,\cr &\quad \quad 0^\circ, 30^\circ, 150^\circ, 180^\circ; \cr\quad x &= 15^\circ.\end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This corresponds to $\theta = 30^\circ$, but it is not the smallest positive solution.
This comes from the negative $\theta$ branch. It is positive, but not the smallest positive solution.
Remember to add $15^\circ$ because $\theta = x - 15^\circ$.

bradley_insight.title: Watch for Restricted Domains
bradley_insight.content: When tanθ appears, always check for excluded angles such as ±90°. They cannot be solutions even if they appear algebraically.

question:

bradley_insight.content: Whenever you see cos2θ or sin2θ, try rewriting everything in terms of sinθ or cosθ. It often collapses into a clean quadratic.

question:
In a simple model, the value, £V, of a motorcycle depends on its age, t, in years.
The following information is available for motorcycle A:
  • its value when new is £15,000
  • its value after one year is £12,000
(a) Use an exponential model to form, for motorcycle A, a possible equation linking V with t.
The value of motorcycle A is monitored over an 8-year period. Its value after 8 years is £2,500.
(b) Evaluate the reliability of your model in light of this information.
The following information is available for motorcycle B:
  • it has the same value, when new, as motorcycle A
  • its value depreciates more slowly than that of motorcycle A
(c) Explain how you would adapt the equation found in (a) so that it could be used to model the value of motorcycle B.
steps: Part (a): We define our exponential model in the standard form $V = A b^t$, where A is the initial value and b is the annual multiplier.

Using the initial condition when the motorcycle is new ($t = 0$):
\begin{aligned}15000 &= A b^0 \cr a &= 15000\end{aligned}

Using the value after one year ($t = 1$):
\begin{aligned}12000 &= 15000 b^1 \cr b &= \dfrac{12000}{15000} = 0.8\end{aligned}

This gives our final exponential equation linking V with t:
$$V = 15000(0.8)^t$$

Part (b): We substitute $t = 8$ into our model to find the predicted value:
\begin{aligned}V &= 15000(0.8)^8\cr &\approx 15000 \times 0.16777\cr &\approx £2,517\end{aligned}
The actual monitored value after 8 years is £2,500. Since our model's prediction of £2,517 is extremely close to the actual value, the model is highly reliable over this period.

Part (c): For motorcycle B, which depreciates more slowly, the value must decrease at a slower rate than $20\%$ per year.
Therefore, the base of the exponent (currently 0.8) must be increased to a value closer to 1 (for example, 0.85 or some multiplier $r > 0.8$). The initial value remains at 15000.
Final Answer: (a) $V = 15000(0.8)^t$ (b) Model is highly reliable ($\approx$ £2,517 vs £2,500) (c) Increase the base (e.g. $V = 15000(r)^t$ where $r > 0.8$)

pi_options.ans: (a) $$V = 15000 - 3000t$$ (b) \begin{aligned} & \text{Model is highly reliable }\cr & \quad(\approx £2,517\text{ vs } £2,500)\end{aligned} (c) \begin{aligned} & \text{Increase the base} \cr \text{(e.g. }V = & 15000(r)^t\text{ where } r > 0.8\text{)}\end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: You formed a linear depreciation model ($V = 15000 - 3000t$) instead of an exponential model in Part (a). Exponential models must be of the form $V = A b^t$ or $V = A \text{e}^{ -kt }$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $$V = 15000(0.8)^t$$ (b) \begin{aligned} & \text{Model is highly reliable }\cr & \quad(\approx £2,517\text{ vs } £2,500)\end{aligned} (c) \begin{aligned} & \text{Decrease the base} \cr \text{ (e.g. } V = & 15000(r)^t \text{ where } r < 0.8\text{)}\end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: Check your reasoning for Part (c). If motorcycle B depreciates more slowly, it retains more of its value each year. Therefore, its base multiplier r must be larger (closer to 1) than 0.8, not smaller.

pi_options.ans: (a) $$V = 15000(0.2)^t$$ (b)$$\text{Model is completely unreliable}$$ (c) \begin{aligned} & \text{Increase the base} \cr \text{ (e.g. }V = & 15000(r)^t \text{ where } r > 0.8\text{)}\end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: When calculating the exponential base in Part (a), you probably used the rate of depreciation ($20\\% = 0.2$) instead of the remaining value multiplier ($1 - 0.2 = 0.8$). This sign error caused your model to predict the motorcycle's value as almost zero after 8 years.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Base Multipliers
bradley_insight.content: In GCE exponential modeling, the base of the exponent (b in $A b^t$) always represents the proportion of value retained each year. If an asset depreciates by $20\%$, it retains $80\%$ of its value, so $b = 0.8$. If it depreciates more slowly, it retains more value, so b must increase closer to 1.

question:
The diagram shows a sketch of part of the curve with equation:
$$y = x(x+1)(x-2)$$
The region $R_1$, shown shaded in the diagram, is bounded by the curve and the negative x-axis.
(a) Show that the exact area of $R_1$ is $\dfrac{5}{12}$.

The region $R_2$, also shown shaded in the diagram, is bounded by the curve, the positive x-axis, and the line with equation $x = b$, where b is a positive constant and $0 < b < 2$.
Given that the area of $R_1$ is equal to the area of $R_2$:
(b) Verify that b satisfies the equation:
$$(b+1)^2(3b^2 - 10b + 5) = 0$$
The roots of the equation $3b^2 - 10b + 5 = 0$ are 0.613 and 2.721 to 3 decimal places. The value of b is therefore 0.613 to 3 decimal places.
(c) Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the significance of the root 2.721.
steps:
Part (a): First, we expand the cubic equation to make it easy to integrate:
\begin{aligned}y &= x(x+1)(x-2) \cr&= x(x^2 - x - 2) \cr&= x^3 - x^2 - 2x\end{aligned}

Since the region $R_1$ lies entirely above the x-axis between the roots $x = -1$ and $x = 0$, its exact area is given by the definite integral:
$$\text{Area } R_1 = \int_{ -1 }^{0} (x^3 - x^2 - 2x) \text{ d}x$$
$$\text{Area } R_1 = \left[ \frac{ x^4 }{4} - \frac{ x^3 }{3} - x^2 \right]_{ -1 }^{0}$$

Evaluating this at the limits 0 and -1:
\begin{aligned} & \text{Area } R_1\cr & \quad = 0 - \left( \frac{ (-1)^4 }{4} - \frac{ (-1)^3 }{3} - (-1)^2 \right)\cr & \quad = - \left( \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{3} - 1 \right) \cr & \quad = - \left( -\frac{5}{12} \right) \cr & \quad= \frac{5}{12}\end{aligned}

Part (b): Since $R_2$ lies entirely below the x-axis in the interval $0 < b < 2$, its area is given by the negative integral:
\begin{aligned} & \text{Area } R_2\cr & \quad = -\int_{0}^{b} (x^3 - x^2 - 2x) \text{ d}x \cr & \quad = -\left[ \frac{ x^4 }{4} - \frac{ x^3 }{3} - x^2 \right]_{0}^{b}\cr & \quad = -\left( \frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ b^3 }{3} - b^2 \right)\end{aligned}

Setting $\text{Area } R_1 = \text{Area } R_2$ gives:
\begin{aligned}&\frac{5}{12} = -\left( \frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ b^3 }{3} - b^2 \right) \cr & \Rightarrow\frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ b^3 }{3} - b^2 + \frac{5}{12} = 0\end{aligned}
Multiplying the entire equation by 12 to clear the fractions:
$$3b^4 - 4b^3 - 12b^2 + 5 = 0$$

We can verify that this factorises to $(b+1)^2(3b^2 - 10b + 5) = 0$ by expanding the brackets:
\begin{aligned} & (b^2 + 2b + 1)(3b^2 - 10b + 5)\cr & \quad = b^2(3b^2 - 10b + 5)\cr & \quad \quad + 2b(3b^2 - 10b + 5)\cr & \quad \quad \quad + 1(3b^2 - 10b + 5) \cr & \quad = 3b^4 - 10b^3 + 5b^2 + 6b^3 - 20b^2\cr & \quad \quad + 10b + 3b^2 - 10b + 5$$ \cr & \quad = 3b^4 - 4b^3 - 12b^2 + 5 \cr & \quad = 0 \quad \text{(verified)}\end{aligned}

Part (c): The root $b \approx 2.721$ lies to the right of the root $x = 2$, which is outside our interval of validity $0 < b < 2$.
Geometrically, this value represents an upper limit where the total net signed area from 0 to 2.721 integrates to $-\frac{5}{12}$. This occurs because the negative area of the lower lobe (between 0 and 2) is partially cancelled out by the positive area of the upper lobe (between 2 and 2.721).

Here is the diagram showing this relationship:
Final Answer: (a) $$\text{Area } R_1 = \dfrac{5}{12}$$ (b) $$(b+1)^2(3b^2 - 10b + 5) = 0 \text{ verified}$$ (c) $$b \approx 2.721$$ $$\text{ point of signed area cancellation}$$

pi_options.feedback: Check your integration signs in Part (a). Because the region $R_1$ lies strictly above the x-axis, its area must be a positive value: $\frac{5}{12}$, not $-\frac{5}{12}$. Area is a physical quantity and cannot be negative.
You probably made a sign error in the double-root factor in Part (b). Since the double root originates from the negative root of the cubic ($x = -1$), the factor must be $(b + 1)^2$, not $(b - 1)^2$.

Check your explanation in Part (c). The value 2.721 is a root of our quartic area equation; it has no relation to the turning points of the curve. It represents the point where the positive area above the axis cancels the excess negative area below the axis.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Net Area Cancellation
bradley_insight.content: When integrating past a root (like $x = 2$ in this question), the curve changes sign. Definite integration calculates signed area, meaning regions above the axis are positive, and regions below are negative. The root 2.721 is simply the algebraic point where these positive and negative lobes balance out.

Setting $\text{Area } R_1 = \text{Area } R_2$ gives:

Part (c): The root $b \approx 4.097$ lies to the right of the root $x = 3$, which is outside our interval of validity $0 < b < 3$.
Geometrically, this value represents an upper limit where the total net signed area from 0 to 4.097 integrates to $-\frac{7}{12}$. This occurs because the negative area of the lower lobe (between 0 and 3) is partially cancelled out by the positive area of the upper lobe (between 3 and 4.097).

question:
The diagram shows a sketch of part of the curve with equation:
$$y = x(x+2)(x-3)$$
The region $R_1$, shown shaded in the diagram, is bounded by the curve and the negative x-axis.
(a) Show that the exact area of $R_1$ is $\dfrac{16}{3}$.

The region $R_2$, also shown shaded in the diagram, is bounded by the curve, the positive x-axis, and the line with equation $x = b$, where b is a positive constant and $0 < b < 3$.
Given that the area of $R_1$ is equal to the area of $R_2$:
(b) Verify that b satisfies the equation:
$$(b+2)^2(3b^2 - 16b + 16) = 0$$
The roots of the equation $3b^2 - 16b + 16 = 0$ are $\dfrac{4}{3}$ and 4. The value of b is therefore $\dfrac{4}{3}$.
(c) Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the significance of the root 4.
steps:
Part (a): First, we expand the cubic equation to make it easy to integrate:
\begin{aligned}y &= x(x+2)(x-3) \cr&= x(x^2 - x - 6) \cr&= x^3 - x^2 - 6x\end{aligned}

Since the region $R_1$ lies entirely above the x-axis between $x = -2$ and $x = 0$, its exact area is given by the definite integral:
$$\text{Area } R_1 = \int_{ -2 }^{0} (x^3 - x^2 - 6x) \text{ d}x$$
$$\text{Area } R_1 = \left[ \frac{ x^4 }{4} - \frac{ x^3 }{3} - 3x^2 \right]_{ -2 }^{0}$$

Evaluating this at the limits 0 and -2:
\begin{aligned} & \text{Area } R_1\cr & \quad = 0 - \bigg( \frac{ (-2)^4 }{4} - \frac{ (-2)^3 }{3}\cr &\qquad \qquad - 3(-2)^2 \bigg)\cr & \quad = - \left( 4 + \frac{8}{3} - 12 \right) \cr & \quad = - \left( -\frac{16}{3} \right) \cr & \quad = \frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}

Part (b): Since $R_2$ lies entirely below the x-axis in the interval $0 < b < 3$, its area is given by the negative integral:\begin{aligned}\text{Area } R_2 &= -\int_{0}^{b} (x^3 - x^2 - 6x) \text{ d}x \cr & \quad = -\left[ \frac{ x^4 }{4} - \frac{ x^3 }{3} - 3x^2 \right]_{0}^{b}\cr & \quad = -\left( \frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ b^3 }{3} - 3b^2 \right)\end{aligned}

Setting $\text{Area } R_1 = \text{Area } R_2$ gives:\begin{aligned} & \frac{16}{3} = -\left( \frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ b^3 }{3} - 3b^2 \right) \cr & \Rightarrow \frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ b^3 }{3} - 3b^2 + \frac{16}{3} = 0\end{aligned}
Multiplying the entire equation by 12 to clear the fractions:
$$3b^4 - 4b^3 - 36b^2 + 64 = 0$$

We can verify that this factorises to $(b+2)^2(3b^2 - 16b + 16) = 0$ by expanding the brackets:\begin{aligned} & (b^2 + 4b + 4)(3b^2 - 16b + 16)\cr & \quad  = b^2(3b^2 - 16b + 16)\cr & \quad \quad + 4b(3b^2 - 16b + 16)\cr & \quad \quad \quad + 4(3b^2 - 16b + 16)\cr & \quad = 3b^4 - 16b^3 + 16b^2 + 12b^3\cr & \quad \quad - 64b^2 + 64b + 12b^2 - 64b + 64\cr & \quad = 3b^4 - 4b^3 - 36b^2 + 64 \cr & \quad = 0 \text{(verified)}\end{aligned}

Part (c): The root $b = 4$ lies to the right of the root $x = 3$, which is outside our interval of validity $0 < b < 3$.
Geometrically, this value represents an upper limit where the total net signed area from 0 to 4 integrates to $-\frac{16}{3}$. This occurs because the negative area of the lower lobe (between 0 and 3) is partially cancelled out by the positive area of the upper lobe (between 3 and 4).

Here is the diagram showing this relationship:
Final Answer: (a) $$\text{Area } R_1 = \dfrac{16}{3}$$ (b) $$(b+2)^2(3b^2 - 16b + 16) = 0 \text{ verified}$$ (c) $$b = 4 \text{ signed area cancellation}$$

You probably made a sign error in the double-root factor in Part (b). Since the double root originates from the negative root of the cubic ($x = -2$), the factor must be $(b + 2)^2$, not $(b - 2)^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Beautiful Exact Roots
bradley_insight.content: Notice how this question resolves to perfectly exact rational and integer roots ($\frac{4}{3}$ and 4). In exam conditions, when your calculations collapse into clean integers rather than long decimals, you can have high confidence that your algebraic working is correct.

question:
The diagram shows a sketch of part of the curve with equation:
$$y = x(x+3)(x-3)$$
The region $R_1$, shown shaded in the diagram, is bounded by the curve and the negative x-axis.
(a) Show that the exact area of $R_1$ is $\dfrac{81}{4}$.

The region $R_2$, also shown shaded in the diagram, is bounded by the curve, the positive x-axis, and the line with equation $x = b$, where b is a positive constant and $0 < b < 3$.
Given that the area of $R_1$ is equal to the area of $R_2$:
(b) Verify that b satisfies the equation:
$$(b+3)^2(b-3)^2 = 0$$
The root of the equation $(b-3)^2 = 0$ is 3. The value of b is therefore 3.
(c) Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the significance of this root.
steps:
Part (a): First, we expand the cubic equation to make it easy to integrate:
\begin{aligned}y &= x(x+3)(x-3) \cr&= x(x^2 - 9) \cr&= x^3 - 9x\end{aligned}

Since the region $R_1$ lies entirely above the x-axis between $x = -3$ and $x = 0$, its exact area is given by the definite integral:
$$\text{Area } R_1 = \int_{ -3 }^{0} (x^3 - 9x) \text{ d}x$$
$$\text{Area } R_1 = \left[ \frac{ x^4 }{4} - \frac{ 9x^2 }{2} \right]_{ -3 }^{0}$$

Evaluating this at the limits 0 and -3:\begin{aligned} & \text{Area } R_1 \cr & \quad = 0 - \left( \frac{ (-3)^4 }{4} - \frac{ 9(-3)^2 }{2} \right)\cr & \quad = - \left( \frac{81}{4} - \frac{81}{2} \right) \cr & \quad = - \left( -\frac{81}{4} \right) \cr & \quad = \frac{81}{4}\end{aligned}

Part (b): Since $R_2$ lies entirely below the x-axis in the interval $0 < b < 3$, its area is given by the negative integral:\begin{aligned}\text{Area } R_2 &= -\int_{0}^{b} (x^3 - 9x) \text{ d}x \cr & = -\left[ \frac{ x^4 }{4} - \frac{ 9x^2 }{2} \right]_{0}^{b}\cr & = -\left( \frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ 9b^2 }{2} \right)\end{aligned}

Setting $\text{Area } R_1 = \text{Area } R_2$ gives:\begin{aligned} & \frac{81}{4} = -\left( \frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ 9b^2 }{2} \right) \cr & \Rightarrow \frac{ b^4 }{4} - \frac{ 9b^2 }{2} + \frac{81}{4} = 0\end{aligned}
Multiplying the entire equation by 4 to clear the fractions:
$$b^4 - 18b^2 + 81 = 0$$

We can verify that this factorises to $(b+3)^2(b-3)^2 = 0$ (which is $(b^2 - 9)^2 = 0$) by expanding the brackets:
\begin{aligned}(b^2 - 9)^2 &= (b^2)^2 - 2(9)(b^2) + 81 \cr&= b^4 - 18b^2 + 81 \cr&= 0 \quad \text{(verified)}\end{aligned}

Part (c): The root $b = 3$ is exactly the second positive root of the cubic equation.
Geometrically, choosing $b = 3$ means that $R_2$ is the entire negative lobe of the curve between 0 and 3. Because $y = x^3 - 9x$ is an odd function, it is perfectly symmetric about the origin, meaning the area of the positive lobe $R_1$ is identical to the area of the negative lobe $R_2$.

Here is the diagram showing this symmetry:
Final Answer: (a) $$\text{Area } R_1 = \dfrac{81}{4}$$ (b) $$(b+3)^2(b-3)^2 = 0 \text{ verified}$$ (c) $$b = 3$$ $$ \text{ symmetric opposite lobe boundary}$$

pi_options.feedback: Check your integration signs in Part (a). Because the region $R_1$ lies strictly above the x-axis, its area must be positive: $\frac{81}{4}$, not $-\frac{81}{4}$.
You probably made an expansion error in Part (b). $b^4 - 18b^2 + 81$ is a quadratic in $b^2$, which factorises to $(b^2 - 9)^2 = (b+3)^2(b-3)^2 = 0$, not $(b-3)^4$.
Check your explanation in Part (c). The value 3 is the x-int of the cubic, not its turning point. It represents the boundary where the two identical lobes are symmetric.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Exploiting Symmetry
bradley_insight.content: When a curve is symmetric about the origin (an odd function), the integral over symmetric intervals has equal magnitudes. Here, the positive lobe from -3 to 0 is identical in shape and area to the negative lobe from 0 to 3. Keeping an eye out for odd and even functions is a great way to double-check your areas.

question:
Given that $a > 0$ and $b > 0$, and that a and b satisfy the equation:
$$\log a + \log b = \log(a + b)$$
(a) Show that:
$$a = \dfrac{b}{ b - 1 }$$
(b) Write down the full restriction on the value of b, explaining the reason for this restriction.
steps:
Part (a): We begin by applying the logarithm addition law, $\log(x) + \log(y) = \log(xy)$, to the left-hand side of our equation:
$$\log(ab) = \log(a + b)$$,

question:
(i) Prove that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $n^2 + 1$ is not divisible by 3.

(ii) "Given $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the value of |2x - 12| is greater than or equal to the value of (x - 5)."
State, giving a reason, if the above statement is always true, sometimes true, or never true.
steps: Part (i): We use proof by exhaustion by splitting the natural numbers into three cases based on their divisibility by 3. Any natural number n can be written as 3k, 3k+1, or 3k+2 for some non-negative integer k.

Case 1: $n = 3k$ (multiples of 3)
\begin{aligned}n^2 + 1 &= (3k)^2 + 1 \cr&= 9k^2 + 1 \cr&= 3(3k^2) + 1\end{aligned}
Since $3(3k^2)$ is divisible by 3, $n^2+1$ leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 3, so it is not divisible.

Case 2: $n = 3k + 1$
\begin{aligned}n^2 + 1 &= (3k+1)^2 + 1 \cr&= 9k^2 + 6k + 1 + 1 \cr&= 3(3k^2 + 2k) + 2\end{aligned}
This leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 3, so it is not divisible.

Case 3: $n = 3k + 2$
\begin{aligned}n^2 + 1 &= (3k+2)^2 + 1 \cr&= 9k^2 + 12k + 4 + 1 \cr&= 9k^2 + 12k + 5 \cr&= 3(3k^2 + 4k + 1) + 2\end{aligned}
This also leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 3, so it is not divisible.
Therefore, since all possible cases have been exhausted, $n^2 + 1$ is never divisible by 3 for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Part (ii): To determine the validity of the statement $|2x - 12| \ge x - 5$, we analyze the critical values by splitting the absolute value into two intervals at the boundary $x = 6$:

Case A: For $x \ge 6$, the term inside the absolute value is positive, so $|2x - 12| = 2x - 12$. Our inequality becomes:\begin{aligned}2x - 12 &\ge x - 5 \cr\implies x &\ge 7\end{aligned}
This means that in the interval $6 \le x < 7$, the inequality is false (for example, at $x = 6$, we get $0 \ge 1$, which is false).

Case B: For $x < 6$, the term inside the absolute value is negative, so \begin{aligned}|2x - 12| &= -(2x - 12) \cr &= 12 - 2x\end{aligned}. Our inequality becomes:\begin{aligned}12 - 2x &\ge x - 5\cr \implies 17 &\ge 3x \cr \implies x &\le 5.67\end{aligned}
This means the inequality is true for $x \le 5.67$ and $x \ge 7$, but fails in the gap $5.67 < x < 7$.

Therefore, the statement is sometimes true, as it holds for most real values (such as $x=0$, giving $12 \ge -5$), but fails for a small range of values (with a counterexample of $x = 6$, where $|2(6)-12| = 0$ is not greater than or equal to $6-5 = 1$).
Final Answer: (i) $$\text{Proof by cases is completed}$$ (ii) $$\text{Sometimes true}$$ $$\text{fails in the interval }5.67 < x < 7\text{)}$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably assumed the inequality is always true because absolute values are always positive. However, you must test the critical interval. In the region $5.67 < x < 7$, the value of the linear expression x-5 is actually larger than the absolute value |2x-12|, making the statement false in this range.
The statement is not 'never true'. It holds for the vast majority of real numbers. For example, substituting $x = 0$ yields $|-12| \ge -5 \implies 12 \ge -5$, which is a true statement.

Part (i) is a proof by exhaustion (cases), not mathematical induction. Induction is used when a statement depends on n and n+1 sequences, whereas here we exhaust all possible algebraic remainders of n directly.

Case B: For $x < 5.5$, the term inside the absolute value is negative, so $|4x - 22| = 22 - 4x$. Our inequality becomes:\begin{aligned}22 - 4x &\ge x - 5 \cr \implies 27 &\ge 5x \cr \implies x &\le 5.4\end{aligned} This means the inequality is true for $x \le 5.4$ and $x \ge 5.67$, but fails in the gap $5.4 < x < 5.67$.

Therefore, the statement is sometimes true, as it holds for most real values (such as $x=0$, giving $22 \ge -5$), but fails for a small range of values (with a counterexample of $x = 5.55$, where $|4(5.55)-22| = 0.2$ is not greater than or equal to $5.55-5 = 0.55$).
Final Answer: (i) $$\text{Proof by cases is completed}$$ (ii) $$\text{Sometimes true}$$ $$\text {(fails in the interval } 5.4 < x < 5.67\text{)}$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably assumed the inequality is always true because absolute values are always positive. However, you must test the critical interval. In the region $5.4 < x < 5.67$, the value of the linear expression x-5 is actually larger than the absolute value |4x-22|, making the statement false in this range.
The statement is not 'never true'. It holds for the vast majority of real numbers. For example, substituting $x = 0$ yields $|-22| \ge -5 \implies 22 \ge -5$, which is a true statement.

Part (i) requires a general proof for all n, which must be handled by exhaustion (testing all possible remainder cases). A simple algebraic deduction is not enough because n is discrete and can have various remainder properties.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Modulo 5 Groupings

question:
(i) Prove that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $n^2 + 3$ is not divisible by 5.

(ii) "Given $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the value of |3x - 17| is greater than or equal to the value of (x - 5)."
State, giving a reason, if the above statement is always true, sometimes true, or never true.
steps: Part (i): We use proof by exhaustion by splitting the natural numbers into five cases based on their divisibility by 5. Any natural number n can be written as 5k, $5k \pm 1$, or $5k \pm 2$ for some non-negative integer k.

Case 1: $n = 5k$ (multiples of 5)
\begin{aligned}n^2 + 3 &= (5k)^2 + 3 \cr&= 25k^2 + 3 \cr&= 5(5k^2) + 3\end{aligned}
This leaves a remainder of 3 when divided by 5, so it is not divisible.

Case 2: $n = 5k \pm 1$
\begin{aligned}n^2 + 3 &= (5k \pm 1)^2 + 3 \cr&= 25k^2 \pm 10k + 1 + 3 \cr&= 5(5k^2 \pm 2k) + 4\end{aligned}
This leaves a remainder of 4 when divided by 5, so it is not divisible.

Case 3: $n = 5k \pm 2$
\begin{aligned}n^2 + 3 &= (5k \pm 2)^2 + 3 \cr&= 25k^2 \pm 20k + 4 + 3 \cr&= 25k^2 \pm 20k + 7 \cr&= 5(5k^2 \pm 4k + 1) + 2\end{aligned}
This leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 5, so it is not divisible.
Therefore, since all possible cases have been exhausted, $n^2 + 3$ is never divisible by 5 for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Part (ii): To determine the validity of the statement $|3x - 17| \ge x - 5$, we analyze the critical values by splitting the absolute value into two intervals at the boundary $x = 5.67$:

Case A: For $x \ge 5.67$, the term inside the absolute value is positive, so $|3x - 17| = 3x - 17$. Our inequality becomes:\begin{aligned}3x - 17 & \ge x - 5 \cr \implies 2x & \ge 12 \cr \implies x & \ge 6\end{aligned} This means that in the interval $5.67 \le x < 6$, the inequality is false (for example, at $x = 5.8$, we get $0.4 \ge 0.8$, which is false).

Case B: For $x < 5.67$, the term inside the absolute value is negative, so $|3x - 17| = 17 - 3x$. Our inequality becomes:\begin{aligned}17 - 3x & \ge x - 5 \cr \implies 22 & \ge 4x \cr \implies x &\le 5.5\end{aligned} This means the inequality is true for $x \le 5.5$ and $x \ge 6$, but fails in the gap $5.5 < x < 6$.

Therefore, the statement is sometimes true, as it holds for most real values (such as $x=0$, giving $17 \ge -5$), but fails for a small range of values (with a counterexample of $x = 5.8$, where $|3(5.8)-17| = 0.4$ is not greater than or equal to $5.8-5 = 0.8$).
Final Answer: (i) $$\text{Proof by cases is completed}$$ (ii) $$\text{Sometimes true}$$ $$\text{(fails in the interval } 5.5 < x < 6\text{)}$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably assumed the inequality is always true because absolute values are always positive. However, you must test the critical interval. In the region $5.5 < x < 6$, the value of the linear expression x-5 is actually larger than the absolute value |3x-17|, making the statement false in this range.
The statement is not 'never true'. It holds for the vast majority of real numbers. For example, substituting $x = 0$ yields $|-17| \ge -5 \implies 17 \ge -5$, which is a true statement.

pi_options.ans: (a) $$\text{Proof by exhaustion of bounds}$$ $$\text{is completed}$$ (b) $$\text{Sometimes true}$$
pi_options.feedback: The standard mathematical name for testing integer remainder cases is a proof by exhaustion (or proof by cases). Avoid using non-standard terms like 'exhaustion of bounds' on your exam script.

question:
The equation $3x^3 + x^2 - 2 = 0$ has exactly one real root.

(a) Show that, for this equation, the Newton-Raphson formula can be written as:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{6x_n^3 + x_n^2 + 2}{9x_n^2 + 2x_n} \end{aligned} [3]

(b) Using the formula given in part (a) with $x_1 = 1$, find the values of $x_2$ and $x_3$, giving your answers to 3 decimal places. [2]

(c) Explain why, for this equation, the Newton-Raphson method cannot be used with $x_1 = 0$. [1]
steps:
Step 1: Define the function and find its derivative for part (a)
Let $f(x) = 3x^3 + x^2 - 2$. To apply the Newton-Raphson method, first differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$:\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x^3 + x^2 - 2) \cr &= 9x^2 + 2x \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the Newton-Raphson recurrence relation
The general Newton-Raphson formula is $x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. Substitute our expressions for $f(x_n)$ and $f'(x_n)$:\begin{aligned} &x_{n+1} \cr &\quad = x_n - \dfrac{3x_n^3 + x_n^2 - 2}{9x_n^2 + 2x_n} \end{aligned}

Step 3: Combine into a single algebraic fraction to complete part (a)
Combine the terms over a common denominator.

The numerator expands to:\begin{aligned} &x_n(9x_n^2 + 2x_n) \cr &\quad - (3x_n^3 + x_n^2 - 2) \cr &\quad = 9x_n^3 + 2x_n^2 - 3x_n^3 \cr &\qquad - x_n^2 + 2 \cr &\quad = 6x_n^3 + x_n^2 + 2 \end{aligned}Placing this over the common denominator gives:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{6x_n^3 + x_n^2 + 2}{9x_n^2 + 2x_n} \end{aligned}This matches the required formula.

Step 4: Perform the iterations for part (b)
Substitute $x_1 = 1$ into the formula to calculate $x_2$:\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \dfrac{6(1)^3 + 1^2 + 2}{9(1)^2 + 2(1)} \cr &= \dfrac{9}{11} \cr &\approx 0.818 \end{aligned}Now, substitute $x_2 = \dfrac{9}{11}$ back into the formula to find $x_3$:\begin{aligned} x_3 &= \dfrac{6\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^3 + \left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^2 + 2}{9\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)^2 + 2\left(\dfrac{9}{11}\right)} \cr &= \dfrac{7927}{10197} \cr &\approx 0.777 \end{aligned}

Step 5: Formulate the explanation for part (c)
Evaluate the derivative $f'(x)$ at our starting value $x_1 = 0$:\begin{aligned} f'(0) &= 9(0)^2 + 2(0) \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}The Newton-Raphson formula involves dividing by the value of the derivative, $f'(x_n)$. Because $f'(0) = 0$, starting with $x_1 = 0$ results in division by zero, which is undefined. Geometrically, this means the tangent to the curve at $x = 0$ is completely horizontal and does not intersect the $x$-axis to provide a next approximation.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(b) } x_2 \approx 0.818, \; x_3 \approx 0.777 \cr &\text{(c) } f'(0) = 0 \cr &\quad\implies \text{division by zero} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(b) } x_2 \approx 0.818, \; x_3 \approx 0.777 \cr &\text{(c) }\text{Curve not defined at } x = 0 \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: You may have correctly calculated the values, but your explanation in part (c) is incorrect. The original cubic polynomial $f(x) = 3x^3 + x^2 - 2$ is fully defined at $x = 0$ (yielding $f(0) = -2$). The method fails because the derivative $f'(0) = 0$, leading to an undefined division by zero.

While Newton-Raphson can fail or diverge if a starting value is too far from the root, a starting value of $x_1 = 0$ fails immediately and strictly because the derivative $f'(0) = 0$, causing division by zero.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Identifying Singular Points
bradley_insight.content: Always remember that the Newton-Raphson method strictly breaks down at any point $x$ where $f'(x) = 0$. Geometrically, this corresponds to stationary points (local maximums, minimums, or stationary points of inflection) where the tangent is horizontal. Since a horizontal tangent has a gradient of 0, it runs parallel to the $x$-axis and can never cross it to find a new approximation.

question:
The equation $x - \cos x = 0$ has exactly one real root in the interval $[0, \pi]$.

(a) Show that, for this equation, the Newton-Raphson formula can be written as:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{x_n \sin x_n + \cos x_n}{1 + \sin x_n} \end{aligned} [3]

Let $f(x) = x - \cos x$. Differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$:\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x - \cos x) \cr &= 1 - (-\sin x) \cr &= 1 + \sin x \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the Newton-Raphson recurrence relation
The general Newton-Raphson formula is $x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. Substitute our expressions for $f(x_n)$ and $f'(x_n)$:\begin{aligned} &x_{n+1} \cr &\quad = x_n - \dfrac{x_n - \cos x_n}{1 + \sin x_n} \end{aligned}

Combine the terms over a common denominator.

The numerator expands to:\begin{aligned} &x_n(1 + \sin x_n) \cr &\quad - (x_n - \cos x_n) \cr &\quad = x_n + x_n \sin x_n \cr &\qquad - x_n + \cos x_n \cr &\quad = x_n \sin x_n + \cos x_n \end{aligned}Placing this over the common denominator yields:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{x_n \sin x_n + \cos x_n}{1 + \sin x_n} \end{aligned}This matches the required formula.

Evaluate the derivative $f'(x) = 1 + \sin x$ at our starting value $x_1 = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:\begin{aligned} &f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \cr &\quad = 1 + \sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \cr &\quad = 1 + (-1) \cr &\quad = 0 \end{aligned}Because the derivative is $0$ at this starting point, the Newton-Raphson formula would require division by zero, which is mathematically undefined. Therefore, the method cannot be used.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(b) } x_2 = 1.000, \; x_3 \approx 0.750 \cr &\text{(c) } f'\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0 \cr &\quad\implies \text{division by zero} \end{aligned}

question:
The equation $x^2 - \ln x - 3 = 0$, where $x > 0$, has a real root in the interval $[1, 2]$.

(a) Show that, for this equation, the Newton-Raphson formula can be written as:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{x_n^3 + x_n \ln x_n + 2x_n}{2x_n^2 - 1} \end{aligned} [3]

(b) Using the formula given in part (a) with a starting value of $x_1 = 2$, find the values of $x_2$ and $x_3$, giving your answers to three significant figures. [2]

steps:
Step 1: Define the function and find its derivative for part (a)
Let $f(x) = x^2 - \ln x - 3$. Differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$ using the power and logarithmic rules:\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x^2 - \ln x - 3) \cr &= 2x - \dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the Newton-Raphson recurrence relation
The general Newton-Raphson formula is $x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. Substitute our expressions:\begin{aligned} &x_{n+1} \cr &\quad = x_n - \dfrac{x_n^2 - \ln x_n - 3}{2x_n - \dfrac{1}{x_n}} \end{aligned}

Step 3: Combine into a single algebraic fraction to complete part (a)
Express the fraction with a common denominator in the derivative:

First, write the denominator as $\dfrac{2x_n^2 - 1}{x_n}$, which gives:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= x_n - \dfrac{x_n(x_n^2 - \ln x_n - 3)}{2x_n^2 - 1} \end{aligned}Now combine over the common denominator $2x_n^2 - 1$. The numerator expands to:\begin{aligned} &x_n(2x_n^2 - 1) \cr &\quad - (x_n^3 - x_n \ln x_n - 3x_n) \cr &\quad = 2x_n^3 - x_n - x_n^3 \cr &\qquad + x_n \ln x_n + 3x_n \cr &\quad = x_n^3 + x_n \ln x_n + 2x_n \end{aligned}Placing this over the common denominator yields:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{x_n^3 + x_n \ln x_n + 2x_n}{2x_n^2 - 1} \end{aligned}This matches the required formula.

Step 4: Perform the iterations for part (b)
Substitute $x_1 = 2$ into the formula to calculate $x_2$:\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \dfrac{2^3 + 2\ln 2 + 2(2)}{2(2)^2 - 1} \cr &= \dfrac{8 + 2\ln 2 + 4}{7} \cr &= \dfrac{12 + 2\ln 2}{7} \cr &\approx 1.912 \cr &\approx 1.91 \text{ (to 3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}Now, substitute $x_2 \approx 1.912$ back into the formula to find $x_3$:\begin{aligned} x_3 &\approx \dfrac{6.990 + 1.239 + 3.824}{6.311} \cr &\approx \dfrac{12.053}{6.311} \cr &\approx 1.91 \text{ (to 3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

Step 5: Formulate the explanation for part (c)
Evaluate the derivative $f'(x) = 2x - \dfrac{1}{x}$ at our starting value $x_1 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$:\begin{aligned} &f'\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \cr &\quad = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} \cr &\quad = 0 \end{aligned}Because the derivative $f'(x_n)$ is $0$, the Newton-Raphson formula is undefined due to division by zero. Thus, the method cannot be used.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(b) } x_2 \approx 1.91, \; x_3 \approx 1.91 \cr &\text{(c) } f'\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 0 \cr &\quad\implies \text{division by zero} \end{aligned}

question:
The equation $\mathrm{e}^x + 3x - 4 = 0$ has exactly one real root.

(a) Show that, for this equation, the Newton-Raphson formula can be written as:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{(x_n - 1)\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 4}{\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 3} \end{aligned} [3]

(b) Using the formula given in part (a) with a starting value of $x_1 = 0$, find the values of $x_2$ and $x_3$, giving your answers to three significant figures. [2]

Step 1: Define the function and find its derivative for part (a)
Let $f(x) = \mathrm{e}^x + 3x - 4$. Differentiate $f(x)$ with respect to $x$:\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\mathrm{e}^x + 3x - 4) \cr &= \mathrm{e}^x + 3 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the Newton-Raphson recurrence relation
The general Newton-Raphson formula is $x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$. Substitute our expressions:\begin{aligned} &x_{n+1} \cr &\quad = x_n - \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 3x_n - 4}{\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 3} \end{aligned}

Step 3: Combine into a single algebraic fraction to complete part (a)
Combine over a common denominator.

The numerator expands to:\begin{aligned} &x_n(\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 3) \cr &\quad - (\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 3x_n - 4) \cr &\quad = x_n \mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 3x_n - \mathrm{e}^{x_n} \cr &\qquad - 3x_n + 4 \cr &\quad = x_n \mathrm{e}^{x_n} - \mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 4 \cr &\quad = (x_n - 1)\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 4 \end{aligned}Placing this over the common denominator yields:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{(x_n - 1)\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 4}{\mathrm{e}^{x_n} + 3} \end{aligned}This matches the required formula.

Step 4: Perform the iterations for part (b)
Substitute $x_1 = 0$ into the formula to calculate $x_2$:\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \dfrac{(0 - 1)\mathrm{e}^0 + 4}{\mathrm{e}^0 + 3} \cr &= \dfrac{(-1)(1) + 4}{1 + 3} \cr &= \dfrac{3}{4} \cr &= 0.750 \quad \text{(to 3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}Now, substitute $x_2 = 0.75$ back into the formula to find $x_3$:\begin{aligned} x_3 &= \dfrac{(0.75 - 1)\mathrm{e}^{0.75} + 4}{\mathrm{e}^{0.75} + 3} \cr &\approx \dfrac{(-0.25)(2.1170) + 4}{2.1170 + 3} \cr &\approx \dfrac{3.47075}{5.1170} \cr &\approx 0.678 \quad \text{(to 3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

Step 5: Formulate the explanation for part (c)
For the Newton-Raphson method to fail due to division by zero, the derivative $f'(x)$ must be equal to zero at some starting value $x_1$.

Our derivative is $f'(x) = \mathrm{e}^x + 3$.

Since $\mathrm{e}^x > 0$ for all real values of $x$, it follows that:\begin{aligned} &f'(x) \ge 3 > 0 \cr &\text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R} \end{aligned}Since the derivative is strictly positive and can never be zero, the Newton-Raphson method cannot fail due to division by zero for any real starting value.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(b) } x_2 = 0.750, \; x_3 \approx 0.678 \cr &\text{(c) } f'(x) \ge 3 > 0 \text{ for all } x \cr &\quad\implies \text{cannot divide by zero} \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the Newton-Raphson recurrence relation

The numerator expands to:\begin{aligned} &x_n(3x_n^2 - 3) \cr &\quad - (x_n^3 - 3x_n - 1) \cr &\quad = 3x_n^3 - 3x_n - x_n^3 \cr &\qquad + 3x_n + 1 \cr &\quad = 2x_n^3 + 1 \end{aligned}Placing this over the common denominator yields:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} &= \dfrac{2x_n^3 + 1}{3x_n^2 - 3} \end{aligned}This matches the required formula.

Step 4: Perform the iterations for part (b)
Substitute $x_1 = 2$ into the formula to calculate $x_2$:\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \dfrac{2(2)^3 + 1}{3(2)^2 - 3} \cr &= \dfrac{16 + 1}{12 - 3} \cr &= \dfrac{17}{9} \cr &\approx 1.89 \quad \text{(to 3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}Now, substitute $x_2 = \dfrac{17}{9}$ back into the formula to find $x_3$:\begin{aligned} x_3 &= \dfrac{2\left(\dfrac{17}{9}\right)^3 + 1}{3\left(\dfrac{17}{9}\right)^2 - 3} \cr &= \dfrac{10555}{5616} \cr &\approx 1.88 \quad \text{(to 3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}

Step 5: Formulate the explanation for part (c)
Evaluate the derivative $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3$ at our starting value $x_1 = 1$:\begin{aligned} f'(1) &= 3(1)^2 - 3 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}The Newton-Raphson formula involves dividing by the value of the derivative, $f'(x_n)$. Because $f'(1) = 0$, starting with $x_1 = 1$ results in division by zero, which is undefined. Geometrically, this means the tangent to the curve at $x = 1$ is horizontal and does not intersect the $x$-axis to provide a next approximation.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(b) } x_2 \approx 1.89, \; x_3 \approx 1.88 \cr &\text{(c) } f'(1) = 0 \cr &\quad\implies \text{division by zero} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(b) }x_2 \approx 1.89, \; x_3 \approx 1.88 \cr &\text{(c) }1 \text{ is too close to the root} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: You may have correctly calculated the values, but your explanation in part (c) is incorrect. The proximity of a starting value to the root does not cause the method to break down. The failure is strictly caused by the derivative equaling zero ($f'(1) = 0$), causing division by zero.

Your numerical approximations are correct, but your explanation is incorrect. The polynomial $f(x) = x^3 - 3x - 1$ is continuous for all real $x$ and has no asymptotes. The method fails because $f'(1) = 0$, resulting in an undefined division by zero.

Your explanation in part (c) is correct, but you made an error when calculating $x_3$, perhaps by using $x_2$ directly or making a rounding slip. Check that you worked with the exact fraction $17/9$ on your calculator to maintain numerical accuracy before rounding to 3 significant figures.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Identifying Singular Points
bradley_insight.content: The Newton-Raphson method strictly breaks down at any point $x$ where $f'(x) = 0$. Geometrically, this corresponds to stationary points (local maximums, minimums, or stationary points of inflection) where the tangent is horizontal. Since a horizontal tangent has a gradient of 0, it runs parallel to the $x$-axis and can never cross it to find a new approximation.

question:
\begin{aligned} &f(x) = -2x^3 + 8x^2 - 9x + 9 \cr &x \in \mathbb{R} \end{aligned}(a) (i) Calculate $f(3)$.

(ii) Write $f(x)$ as a product of two algebraic factors.

Using the answer to (a)(ii):

(b) Prove that there are exactly two real solutions to the equation $-2y^6 + 8y^4 - 9y^2 + 9 = 0$.

(c) Deduce the number of real solutions, for $5\pi \le \theta < 9\pi$, to the equation:\begin{aligned} &2\tan^3\theta - 8\tan^2\theta \cr &\quad + 9\tan\theta - 9 = 0 \end{aligned}State the real solutions to the equation in (b) and the number of solutions in (c).
steps:
Part (a)(i):
Substitute $x = 3$ into the expression for $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} &f(3) = -2(3)^3 + 8(3)^2 \cr &\qquad - 9(3) + 9 \cr &\quad = -54 + 72 - 27 + 9 \cr &\quad = 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(3) = 0$, $x = 3$ is a root, which means $(x - 3)$ is a linear factor of $f(x)$.

Part (a)(ii):
Divide $-2x^3 + 8x^2 - 9x + 9$ by $(x - 3)$ using equating coefficients:\begin{aligned} &f(x) \cr &\quad = (x - 3)(-2x^2 + px + q) \cr &\quad = -2x^3 + (p + 6)x^2 \cr &\qquad + (q - 3p)x - 3q \end{aligned}Equating coefficients gives:\begin{aligned} p + 6 &= 8 \cr p &= 2 \cr -3q &= 9 \cr q &= -3 \end{aligned}Thus, the factored expression is:\begin{aligned} f(x) &= (x - 3)(-2x^2 + 2x - 3) \cr &= (3 - x)(2x^2 - 2x + 3) \end{aligned}We check the discriminant of the quadratic factor $2x^2 - 2x + 3$:\begin{aligned} \Delta &= (-2)^2 - 4(2)(3) \cr &= 4 - 24 \cr &= -20 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta = -20 < 0$, the quadratic factor has no real roots. Therefore, $x = 3$ is the unique real root of $f(x) = 0$.

Part (b):
We want to find the real solutions to:$$-2y^6 + 8y^4 - 9y^2 + 9 = 0$$Let $x = y^2$. This transforms the equation into:$$-2x^3 + 8x^2 - 9x + 9 = 0$$Which is exactly $f(x) = 0$. Since we showed in part (a)(ii) that the only real root is $x = 3$, we have:\begin{aligned} y^2 &= 3 \cr y &= \pm\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}The other factor yields $-2(y^2)^2 + 2(y^2) - 3 = 0$, which has no real solutions because its discriminant is negative. Thus, there are exactly two real solutions:$$y = \pm\sqrt{3}$$

Part (c):
The equation is:\begin{aligned} &2\tan^3\theta - 8\tan^2\theta \cr &\quad + 9\tan\theta - 9 = 0 \end{aligned}Multiplying the entire equation by $-1$, we get:\begin{aligned} &-2\tan^3\theta + 8\tan^2\theta \cr &\quad - 9\tan\theta + 9 = 0 \end{aligned}Let $x = \tan\theta$. This equation becomes $f(x) = 0$, which has only one real root, $x = 3$. Therefore:$$\tan\theta = 3$$We need to find the number of solutions in the interval $5\pi \le \theta < 9\pi$.

The width of the interval is $9\pi - 5\pi = 4\pi$. Since the tangent function $\tan\theta$ has a period of $\pi$, it completes exactly $4$ full cycles over this interval.

In each period, the equation $\tan\theta = 3$ has exactly one unique solution. Thus, there are exactly $4$ real solutions.

Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(3) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (3 - x)(2x^2 - 2x + 3) \cr &\text{(b) } y = \pm\sqrt{3} \cr &\text{(c) } 4 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(3) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (3 - x)(2x^2 - 2x + 3) \cr &\text{(b) } y = \pm 3 \cr &\text{(c) } 8 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: This error in parts (b) and (c) occurs if you mistakenly solve $y^2 = 9$ (perhaps by misidentifying the root of $f(x) = 0$ as $9$ instead of $3$) and double the number of trig solutions by assuming a period of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ instead of $\pi$ for $\tan\theta$.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(3) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (3 - x)(2x^2 - 2x + 3) \cr &\text{(b) } y = \sqrt{3} \cr &\text{(c) } 2 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(3) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (3 - x)(2x^2 - 2x + 3) \cr &\text{(b) } y = \pm\sqrt{3} \cr &\text{(c) } 2 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: Substitution Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: When making algebraic substitutions like $x = y^2$ or $x = e^y$, always check the domain restrictions of the new variable. For example, $y^2 \ge 0$ and $e^y > 0$ mean that any negative roots of the original cubic $f(x) = 0$ will not yield real values for $y$.

question:
\begin{aligned} &f(x) = 2x^3 + x^2 + x - 4 \cr &x \in \mathbb{R} \end{aligned}(a) (i) Calculate $f(1)$.

(ii) Write $f(x)$ as a product of two algebraic factors.

Using the answer to (a)(ii):

(b) Prove that there are exactly two real solutions to the equation $2y^{12} + y^8 + y^4 - 4 = 0$.

(c) Deduce the number of real solutions, for $0 \le \theta < 4\pi$, to the equation:\begin{aligned} &2\sin^3\theta + \sin^2\theta \cr &\quad + \sin\theta - 4 = 0 \end{aligned}State the real solutions to the equation in (b) and the number of solutions in (c).
steps:
Part (a)(i):
Substitute $x = 1$ into the expression for $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 2(1)^3 + 1^2 + 1 - 4 \cr &= 2 + 1 + 1 - 4 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(1) = 0$, $x = 1$ is a root, meaning $(x - 1)$ is a linear factor of $f(x)$.

Part (a)(ii):
Divide $2x^3 + x^2 + x - 4$ by $(x - 1)$:\begin{aligned} &2x^3 + x^2 + x - 4 \cr &\quad = (x - 1)(2x^2 + 3x + 4) \end{aligned}We check the discriminant of the quadratic factor $2x^2 + 3x + 4$:\begin{aligned} \Delta &= 3^2 - 4(2)(4) \cr &= 9 - 32 \cr &= -23 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta = -23 < 0$, the quadratic factor has no real roots. Thus, $x = 1$ is the unique real root of $f(x) = 0$.

Part (b):
We solve:$$2y^{12} + y^8 + y^4 - 4 = 0$$Let $x = y^4$. The equation becomes:$$2x^3 + x^2 + x - 4 = 0$$This is exactly $f(x) = 0$. Since $x = 1$ is the unique real root, we have:\begin{aligned} y^4 &= 1 \cr y^2 &= 1 \cr y &= \pm 1 \end{aligned}The other branch $y^4 < 0$ has no real roots. Thus, there are exactly two real solutions: $y = \pm 1$.

Part (c):
The equation is:\begin{aligned} &2\sin^3\theta + \sin^2\theta \cr &\quad + \sin\theta - 4 = 0 \end{aligned}Let $x = \sin\theta$. This yields $f(x) = 0 \implies \sin\theta = 1$.

We look for solutions in the interval $0 \le \theta < 4\pi$, which represents two complete periods of the sine function.

The sine function equals $1$ exactly once per period (at the maximum point of each cycle):\begin{aligned} \theta &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \cr \theta &= \dfrac{5\pi}{2} \end{aligned}Thus, there are exactly $2$ real solutions.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(1) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (x - 1)(2x^2 + 3x + 4) \cr &\text{(b) } y = \pm 1 \cr &\text{(c) } 2 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error in parts (b) and (c) occurs if you forget that $y^4 = 1$ has two real solutions ($y = \pm 1$) and also miscalculate the number of solutions to $\sin\theta = 1$ in the interval $[0, 4\pi)$, which has only 2 peaks.

This mistake in part (c) arises from correctly identifying the roots of $y^4 = 1$ but miscounting the number of real solutions to $\sin\theta = 1$ in the interval $0 \le \theta < 4\pi$. Over two full cycles, the peak value is only reached twice, not four times.
This version correctly solves the algebraic parts but incorrectly concludes that $\sin\theta = 1$ has no real solutions, perhaps by confusing the required range with values outside $[-1, 1]$.

bradley_insight.title: Sine Wave Maxima Counting
bradley_insight.content: Unlike general values of $k$ where $\sin\theta = k$ has two solutions per cycle, the boundary values $k = \pm 1$ only occur at the single peak or trough of each cycle. Therefore, $\sin\theta = 1$ yields exactly one solution per $2\pi$ period.

question:
\begin{aligned} &f(x) = x^3 + x^2 + x + 6 \cr &x \in \mathbb{R} \end{aligned}(a) (i) Calculate $f(-2)$.

(ii) Write $f(x)$ as a product of two algebraic factors.

Using the answer to (a)(ii):

(b) Prove that there is exactly one real solution to the equation $y^9 + y^6 + y^3 + 6 = 0$.

(c) Deduce the number of real solutions, for $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$, to the equation:\begin{aligned} &\cos^3\theta + \cos^2\theta \cr &\quad + \cos\theta + 6 = 0 \end{aligned}State the real solutions to the equation in (b) and the number of solutions in (c).
steps:
Part (a)(i):
Substitute $x = -2$ into $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} f(-2) &= (-2)^3 + (-2)^2 - 2 + 6 \cr &= -8 + 4 - 2 + 6 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(-2) = 0$, $x = -2$ is a root, meaning $(x + 2)$ is a linear factor of $f(x)$.

Part (a)(ii):
Divide $x^3 + x^2 + x + 6$ by $(x + 2)$:\begin{aligned} &x^3 + x^2 + x + 6 \cr &\quad = (x + 2)(x^2 - x + 3) \end{aligned}We check the discriminant of the quadratic factor $x^2 - x + 3$:\begin{aligned} \Delta &= (-1)^2 - 4(1)(3) \cr &= 1 - 12 \cr &= -11 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta = -11 < 0$, there are no real roots from this quadratic factor. Thus, $x = -2$ is the unique real root of $f(x) = 0$.

Part (b):
We solve:$$y^9 + y^6 + y^3 + 6 = 0$$Let $x = y^3$. The equation becomes:$$x^3 + x^2 + x + 6 = 0$$This is $f(x) = 0$. Since $x = -2$ is the only real root, we have:\begin{aligned} y^3 &= -2 \cr y &= -\sqrt[3]{2} \end{aligned}Unlike even powers, a real number has exactly one real cube root. Hence, there is exactly one real solution: $y = -\sqrt[3]{2}$.

Part (c):
The equation is:\begin{aligned} &\cos^3\theta + \cos^2\theta \cr &\quad + \cos\theta + 6 = 0 \end{aligned}Let $x = \cos\theta$. This equation becomes $f(x) = 0$, which requires:$$\cos\theta = -2$$However, the cosine function has a strict range of $[-1, 1]$. Since $-2$ is outside this range, there are no real values of $\theta$ that satisfy this equation. Thus, there are $0$ real solutions.

Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(-2) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (x + 2)(x^2 - x + 3) \cr &\text{(b) } y = -\sqrt[3]{2} \cr &\text{(c) } 0 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}
