bradley_insight.title: Range Constraints in Trigonometry
bradley_insight.content: Always check whether algebraic solutions are physically possible when substituting transcendental functions like $\cos\theta$ or $\sin\theta$. Any intermediate root outside of $[-1, 1]$ is rejected immediately.

question:
\begin{aligned} &f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x - 2 \cr &x \in \mathbb{R} \end{aligned}(a) (i) Calculate $f(0.5)$.

(ii) Write $f(x)$ as a product of two algebraic factors.

Using the answer to (a)(ii):

(b) Prove that there are exactly two real solutions to the equation $2y^6 + 3y^4 + 2y^2 - 2 = 0$.

(c) Deduce the number of real solutions, for $0 \le \theta < 4\pi$, to the equation:\begin{aligned} &2\cos^3\theta + 3\cos^2\theta \cr &\quad + 2\cos\theta - 2 = 0 \end{aligned}State the real solutions to the equation in (b) and the number of solutions in (c).
steps:
Part (a)(i):
Substitute $x = 0.5$ (or $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$) into $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} &f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \cr &\quad = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 + 3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 \cr &\qquad + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - 2 \cr &\quad = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right) + 3\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right) + 1 - 2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} + 1 - 2 \cr &\quad = 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(0.5) = 0$, $x = 0.5$ is a root, meaning $(2x - 1)$ is a linear factor of $f(x)$.

Part (a)(ii):
Divide $2x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x - 2$ by $(2x - 1)$:\begin{aligned} &2x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x - 2 \cr &\quad = (2x - 1)(x^2 + 2x + 2) \end{aligned}We check the discriminant of the quadratic factor $x^2 + 2x + 2$:\begin{aligned} \Delta &= 2^2 - 4(1)(2) \cr &= 4 - 8 \cr &= -4 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta = -4 < 0$, the quadratic factor has no real roots. Thus, $x = 0.5$ is the only real root of $f(x) = 0$.

Part (b):
We solve:$$2y^6 + 3y^4 + 2y^2 - 2 = 0$$Let $x = y^2$. The equation transforms to $f(x) = 0$, which has the unique real solution $x = 0.5$. Therefore:\begin{aligned} y^2 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \cr y &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cr &= \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{aligned}Since the other factor has a negative discriminant, no further real solutions exist. There are exactly two real solutions: $y = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

Part (c):
The equation is:\begin{aligned} &2\cos^3\theta + 3\cos^2\theta \cr &\quad + 2\cos\theta - 2 = 0 \end{aligned}Let $x = \cos\theta$. This equation becomes $f(x) = 0$, which has only one real solution, $x = 0.5$. Thus:\begin{aligned} \cos\theta &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}We seek solutions in the interval $0 \le \theta < 4\pi$, representing two complete periods of the cosine function.

In each period $[0, 2\pi)$, the equation $\cos\theta = 0.5$ has exactly 2 solutions (at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$).

Therefore, over two full periods, there are exactly $4$ real solutions.

Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(0.5) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (2x - 1)(x^2 + 2x + 2) \cr &\text{(b) } y = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \cr &\text{(c) } 4 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error in parts (b) and (c) occurs if you resolve $y^2 = 0.5$ as $y = \pm 0.5$ (mistaking the square root for a square) and incorrectly assume there is only one solution to $\cos\theta = 0.5$ per period.

This mistake in part (c) arises from miscounting the number of solutions to $\cos\theta = 0.5$ in $0 \le \theta < 4\pi$. Since the interval covers two complete cycles and each cycle has two solutions, there must be 4 in total.
This error in part (b) occurs if you neglect the negative square root of $y^2 = 0.5$, which yields the valid real solution $-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$.

bradley_insight.title: Exact Value Rationalisation
bradley_insight.content: Always rationalise denominators for exact value answers (e.g. write $y = \pm\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ instead of $y = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$). This helps when matching option choices on standard examinations.

question:
\begin{aligned} &f(x) = 4x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 3 \cr &x \in \mathbb{R} \end{aligned}(a) (i) Calculate $f(1)$.

(ii) Write $f(x)$ as a product of two algebraic factors.

Using the answer to (a)(ii):

(b) Prove that there is exactly one real solution to the equation $4\mathrm{e}^{3y} - 2\mathrm{e}^{2y} + \mathrm{e}^y - 3 = 0$.

(c) Deduce the number of real solutions, for $0 \le \theta < \pi$, to the equation:\begin{aligned} &4\tan^3(2\theta) - 2\tan^2(2\theta) \cr &\quad + \tan(2\theta) - 3 = 0 \end{aligned}State the real solutions to the equation in (b) and the number of solutions in (c).
steps:
Part (a)(i):
Substitute $x = 1$ into $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 4(1)^3 - 2(1)^2 + 1 - 3 \cr &= 4 - 2 + 1 - 3 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(1) = 0$, $x = 1$ is a root, meaning $(x - 1)$ is a linear factor of $f(x)$.

Part (a)(ii):
Divide $4x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 3$ by $(x - 1)$:\begin{aligned} &4x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 3 \cr &\quad = (x - 1)(4x^2 + 2x + 3) \end{aligned}We check the discriminant of the quadratic factor $4x^2 + 2x + 3$:\begin{aligned} \Delta &= 2^2 - 4(4)(3) \cr &= 4 - 48 \cr &= -44 \end{aligned}Since $\Delta = -44 < 0$, the quadratic factor has no real roots. Thus, $x = 1$ is the unique real root of $f(x) = 0$.

Part (b):
We solve:$$4\mathrm{e}^{3y} - 2\mathrm{e}^{2y} + \mathrm{e}^y - 3 = 0$$Let $x = \mathrm{e}^y$ (where $x > 0$). The equation becomes $f(x) = 0$.

Since the unique real root is $x = 1$, we have:\begin{aligned} \mathrm{e}^y &= 1 \cr y &= \ln(1) \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}Since the quadratic factor yields no real roots, $y = 0$ is the single unique real solution.

Part (c):
The equation is:\begin{aligned} &4\tan^3(2\theta) - 2\tan^2(2\theta) \cr &\quad + \tan(2\theta) - 3 = 0 \end{aligned}Let $u = \tan(2\theta)$. This equation becomes $f(u) = 0$, which has only one real solution, $u = 1$. Thus:$$\tan(2\theta) = 1$$We search for solutions in the interval $0 \le \theta < \pi$. Since the argument of the tangent function is $2\theta$, we must scale the domain:$$0 \le 2\theta < 2\pi$$The tangent function $\tan(2\theta)$ has a period of $\pi$. Therefore, in the interval $[0, 2\pi)$, the equation $\tan(2\theta) = 1$ has exactly two solutions (at $2\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $2\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}$).

Thus, there are exactly $2$ real solutions for $\theta$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(1) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (x - 1)(4x^2 + 2x + 3) \cr &\text{(b) } y = 0 \cr &\text{(c) } 2 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error in parts (b) and (c) occurs if you solve $e^y = 1$ to get $y = 1$ instead of $y = 0$, and if you fail to scale the domain for the double angle, leading to a count for four cycles instead of two.

This mistake in part (c) arises from forgetting that the argument is $2\theta$. In the interval $0 \le \theta < \pi$, the argument $2\theta$ spans $0$ to $2\pi$, containing two periods and thus 2 solutions.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a)(i) } f(1) = 0 \cr &\text{(a)(ii) } f(x) \cr &\quad = (x - 1)(4x^2 + 2x + 3) \cr &\text{(b) } \text{No real solutions for } y \cr &\text{(c) } 2 \text{ real solutions} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: This occurs in part (b) if you mistakenly believe the exponential equation $e^y = 1$ has no real solutions, whereas $y = \ln(1) = 0$ is a valid unique real solution.

bradley_insight.title: Double-Angle Domain Scaling
bradley_insight.content: When solving trigonometric equations with scaled arguments like $\tan(2\theta)$, always multiply the domain boundaries by the coefficient (e.g., $0 \le 2\theta < 2\pi$) before counting solutions. Failing to do this often results in missing half of the valid solutions.

question:
(a) Solve, for $0 \le x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, the equation $4\cos x = \csc x$, giving your answers in terms of $\pi$.

(b) Solve, for $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, the equation $3\sin\theta - 3\cos\theta = 2$, giving your answers to one decimal place.

steps:
Part (a):
We solve the equation $4\cos x = \csc x$ in the interval $0 \le x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:\begin{aligned} 4\cos x &= \dfrac{1}{\sin x} \cr 4\sin x\cos x &= 1 \cr 2(2\sin x\cos x) &= 1 \cr 2\sin(2x) &= 1 \cr \sin(2x) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}Since $0 \le x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, we have $0 \le 2x < \pi$. Thus:\begin{aligned} 2x &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \quad \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \cr x &= \dfrac{\pi}{12}, \quad \dfrac{5\pi}{12} \end{aligned}

Part (b):
We solve $3\sin\theta - 3\cos\theta = 2$ using the harmonic form $R\sin(\theta - \alpha)$:\begin{aligned} R\cos\alpha &= 3 \cr R\sin\alpha &= 3 \end{aligned}This gives:\begin{aligned} R &= \sqrt{3^2 + 3^2} \cr &= \sqrt{18} \cr &= 3\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \dfrac{3}{3} \cr &= 1 \cr \alpha &= 45^\circ \end{aligned}So the equation becomes:\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{2}\sin(\theta - 45^\circ) &= 2 \cr \sin(\theta - 45^\circ) &= \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{2}} \cr &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \end{aligned}We find the principal angle using a calculator:\begin{aligned} \theta - 45^\circ &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\right) \cr &\approx 28.13^\circ \end{aligned}For $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, we have $-45^\circ \le \theta - 45^\circ < 315^\circ$. The valid solutions for $\theta - 45^\circ$ are:\begin{aligned} \theta - 45^\circ &\approx 28.13^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 28.13^\circ + 45^\circ \cr &\approx 73.1^\circ \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \theta - 45^\circ &\approx 180^\circ - 28.13^\circ \cr &\approx 151.87^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 151.87^\circ + 45^\circ \cr &\approx 196.9^\circ \end{aligned}Thus, the solutions to 1 decimal place are $\theta = 73.1^\circ$ and $\theta = 196.9^\circ$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } x = \dfrac{\pi}{12}, \; \dfrac{5\pi}{12} \cr &\text{(b) } \theta \approx 73.1^\circ, \; 196.9^\circ \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: Shifted Trigonometric Domains
bradley_insight.content: When substituting a compound angle like $\theta - \alpha$ inside a trigonometric function, always adjust your domain limits before finding solutions (e.g., transform $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$ into $-\alpha \le \theta - \alpha < 360^\circ - \alpha$). This prevents you from missing valid solutions or including ones outside the correct range.

question:
(a) Solve, for $0 \le x < \pi$, the equation $2\cos^2 x + 3\sin x = 3$, giving your answers in terms of $\pi$.

(b) Solve, for $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, the equation $4\sin\theta + 3\cos\theta = 2$, giving your answers to one decimal place.

Solutions based entirely on graphical or numerical methods are not acceptable.
steps:
Part (a):
We use the fundamental identity $\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$ to rewrite the equation in terms of $\sin x$:\begin{aligned} 2(1 - \sin^2 x) + 3\sin x &= 3 \cr 2 - 2\sin^2 x + 3\sin x &= 3 \cr 2\sin^2 x - 3\sin x + 1 &= 0 \end{aligned}Let $y = \sin x$. This yields a quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} 2y^2 - 3y + 1 &= 0 \cr (2y - 1)(y - 1) &= 0 \end{aligned}So we solve:\begin{aligned} &\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2} \cr &\quad \implies x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \; \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \cr &\sin x = 1 \cr &\quad \implies x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}Thus, the three exact solutions in the interval $0 \le x < \pi$ are $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \; \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \; \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

Part (b):
We write $4\sin\theta + 3\cos\theta = 2$ in the harmonic form $R\sin(\theta + \alpha)$:\begin{aligned} R\cos\alpha &= 4 \cr R\sin\alpha &= 3 \end{aligned}This gives:\begin{aligned} R &= \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} \cr &= 5 \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \dfrac{3}{4} \cr \alpha &\approx 36.87^\circ \end{aligned}So the equation becomes:\begin{aligned} 5\sin(\theta + 36.87^\circ) &= 2 \cr \sin(\theta + 36.87^\circ) &= 0.4 \end{aligned}We find the principal angle using a calculator:\begin{aligned} \theta + 36.87^\circ &= \arcsin(0.4) \cr &\approx 23.58^\circ \end{aligned}For $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, we have $36.87^\circ \le \theta + 36.87^\circ < 396.87^\circ$. The valid solutions for $\theta + 36.87^\circ$ are:\begin{aligned} \theta + 36.87^\circ &\approx 180^\circ - 23.58^\circ \cr &\approx 156.42^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 156.42^\circ - 36.87^\circ \cr &\approx 119.6^\circ \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \theta + 36.87^\circ &\approx 360^\circ + 23.58^\circ \cr &\approx 383.58^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 383.58^\circ - 36.87^\circ \cr &\approx 346.7^\circ \end{aligned}Note that $23.58^\circ - 36.87^\circ = -13.29^\circ$, which falls outside the required range of $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$. Thus, the solutions to 1 decimal place are $\theta = 119.6^\circ$ and $\theta = 346.7^\circ$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \; \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \; \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \cr &\text{(b) } \theta \approx 119.6^\circ, \; 346.7^\circ \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: Quadratic Factor Domain Scans
bradley_insight.content: When solving quadratic equations in trigonometric functions like $a\sin^2 x + b\sin x + c = 0$, you must always scan both linear branches. Always confirm which branch boundaries contain valid values within the restricted interval, particularly at crucial endpoints like $\sin x = 1$ which yields a single boundary solution.

question:
(a) Solve, for $0 \le x < \pi$, the equation $\sin(2x) = \sqrt{3}\cos(2x)$, giving your answers in terms of $\pi$.

(b) Solve, for $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, the equation $12\cos\theta - 5\sin\theta = 4$, giving your answers to one decimal place.

Solutions based entirely on graphical or numerical methods are not acceptable.
steps:
Part (a):
We divide both sides of the equation by $\cos(2x)$ (noting that $\cos(2x) \neq 0$) to express the equation in terms of $\tan(2x)$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin(2x)}{\cos(2x)} &= \sqrt{3} \cr \tan(2x) &= \sqrt{3} \end{aligned}Since $0 \le x < \pi$, we must scale the domain for $2x$:$$0 \le 2x < 2\pi$$The solutions for $2x$ are:\begin{aligned} 2x &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \quad \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \cr x &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \quad \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \end{aligned}

Part (b):
We write $12\cos\theta - 5\sin\theta = 4$ in the harmonic form $R\cos(\theta + \alpha)$:\begin{aligned} R\cos\alpha &= 12 \cr R\sin\alpha &= 5 \end{aligned}This gives:\begin{aligned} R &= \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} \cr &= 13 \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \dfrac{5}{12} \cr \alpha &\approx 22.62^\circ \end{aligned}So the equation becomes:\begin{aligned} 13\cos(\theta + 22.62^\circ) &= 4 \cr \cos(\theta + 22.62^\circ) &= \dfrac{4}{13} \end{aligned}We find the principal angle using a calculator:\begin{aligned} \theta + 22.62^\circ &= \arccos\left(\dfrac{4}{13}\right) \cr &\approx 72.08^\circ \end{aligned}For $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, we have $22.62^\circ \le \theta + 22.62^\circ < 382.62^\circ$. The valid solutions for $\theta + 22.62^\circ$ are:\begin{aligned} \theta + 22.62^\circ &\approx 72.08^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 72.08^\circ - 22.62^\circ \cr &\approx 49.5^\circ \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \theta + 22.62^\circ &\approx 360^\circ - 72.08^\circ \cr &\approx 287.92^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 287.92^\circ - 22.62^\circ \cr &\approx 265.3^\circ \end{aligned}Thus, the solutions to 1 decimal place are $\theta = 49.5^\circ$ and $\theta = 265.3^\circ$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \; \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \cr &\text{(b) } \theta \approx 49.5^\circ, \; 265.3^\circ \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: Double Angle Domain Expansion
bradley_insight.content: Whenever solving a trigonometric equation with a compound multiple angle like $\sin(2x) = k$, always expand the domain first (e.g. convert $0 \le x < \pi$ to $0 \le 2x < 2\pi$). Solve for all possible values of $2x$ in this wider window, and only divide by 2 as the absolute final step.

question:
(a) Solve, for $0 \le x < 2\pi$, the equation $2\sin x\tan x = 3$, giving your answers in terms of $\pi$.

(b) Solve, for $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, the equation $2\sin\theta + 5\cos\theta = 3$, giving your answers to one decimal place.

Solutions based entirely on graphical or numerical methods are not acceptable.
steps:
Part (a):
We use the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to rewrite the equation (noting that $\cos x \neq 0$):\begin{aligned} 2\sin x\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right) &= 3 \cr 2\sin^2 x &= 3\cos x \end{aligned}Now, substitute the identity $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$ to get a quadratic in terms of $\cos x$:\begin{aligned} 2(1 - \cos^2 x) &= 3\cos x \cr 2 - 2\cos^2 x &= 3\cos x \cr 2\cos^2 x + 3\cos x - 2 &= 0 \end{aligned}Let $y = \cos x$. Factor the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} 2y^2 + 3y - 2 &= 0 \cr (2y - 1)(y + 2) &= 0 \end{aligned}So we solve:\begin{aligned} &\cos x = \dfrac{1}{2} \cr &\quad \implies x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \; \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \cr &\cos x = -2 \cr &\quad \implies \text{No real solutions} \end{aligned}Thus, the solutions in the interval $0 \le x < 2\pi$ are $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ and $x = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

Part (b):
We write $2\sin\theta + 5\cos\theta = 3$ in the harmonic form $R\sin(\theta + \alpha)$:\begin{aligned} R\cos\alpha &= 2 \cr R\sin\alpha &= 5 \end{aligned}This gives:\begin{aligned} R &= \sqrt{2^2 + 5^2} \cr &= \sqrt{29} \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \dfrac{5}{2} \cr \alpha &\approx 68.20^\circ \end{aligned}So the equation becomes:\begin{aligned} \sqrt{29}\sin(\theta + 68.20^\circ) &= 3 \cr \sin(\theta + 68.20^\circ) &= \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{29}} \end{aligned}We find the principal angle using a calculator:\begin{aligned} \theta + 68.20^\circ &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{29}}\right) \cr &\approx 33.86^\circ \end{aligned}For $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, we have $68.20^\circ \le \theta + 68.20^\circ < 428.20^\circ$. The valid solutions for $\theta + 68.20^\circ$ are:\begin{aligned} \theta + 68.20^\circ &\approx 180^\circ - 33.86^\circ \cr &\approx 146.14^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 146.14^\circ - 68.20^\circ \cr &\approx 77.9^\circ \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \theta + 68.20^\circ &\approx 360^\circ + 33.86^\circ \cr &\approx 393.86^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 393.86^\circ - 68.20^\circ \cr &\approx 325.7^\circ \end{aligned}Note that $33.86^\circ - 68.20^\circ = -34.34^\circ$, which is outside the range $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$. Thus, the solutions to 1 decimal place are $\theta = 77.9^\circ$ and $\theta = 325.7^\circ$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \; \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \cr &\text{(b) } \theta \approx 77.9^\circ, \; 325.7^\circ \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: Identifying Spurious Roots
bradley_insight.content: When solving algebraic equations in trigonometry that produce quadratic terms, you will often find multiple branches (e.g., $\cos x = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\cos x = -2$). Always check the physical constraints of the trigonometric functions. Since $-1 \le \cos x \le 1$ for all real $x$, any branch outside this range is a spurious root and must be immediately discarded.

question:
(a) Solve, for $0 \le x < \pi$, the equation $2\sin(2x)\tan x = 3$, giving your answers in terms of $\pi$.

(b) Solve, for $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, the equation $2\sin\theta - 3\cos\theta = 1$, giving your answers to one decimal place.

Solutions based entirely on graphical or numerical methods are not acceptable.
steps:
Part (a):
We apply the double angle identity $\sin(2x) = 2\sin x\cos x$ and the identity $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ (noting that $\cos x \neq 0$):\begin{aligned} &2(2\sin x\cos x) \cr &\qquad \cdot \left(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\right) = 3 \cr &\quad 4\sin^2 x = 3 \cr &\quad \sin^2 x = \dfrac{3}{4} \cr &\quad \sin x = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}Since we are solving in the interval $0 \le x < \pi$, the sine function must be strictly non-negative. Thus, we discard the negative root:\begin{aligned} \sin x &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}Solving this in the interval yields:\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \quad \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \end{aligned}

Part (b):
We write $2\sin\theta - 3\cos\theta = 1$ in the harmonic form $R\sin(\theta - \alpha)$:\begin{aligned} R\cos\alpha &= 2 \cr R\sin\alpha &= 3 \end{aligned}This gives:\begin{aligned} R &= \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2} \cr &= \sqrt{13} \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \tan\alpha &= \dfrac{3}{2} \cr \alpha &\approx 56.31^\circ \end{aligned}So the equation becomes:\begin{aligned} \sqrt{13}\sin(\theta - 56.31^\circ) &= 1 \cr \sin(\theta - 56.31^\circ) &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \end{aligned}We find the principal angle using a calculator:\begin{aligned} \theta - 56.31^\circ &= \arcsin\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}}\right) \cr &\approx 16.10^\circ \end{aligned}For $0 \le \theta < 360^\circ$, we have $-56.31^\circ \le \theta - 56.31^\circ < 303.69^\circ$. The valid solutions for $\theta - 56.31^\circ$ are:\begin{aligned} \theta - 56.31^\circ &\approx 16.10^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 16.10^\circ + 56.31^\circ \cr &\approx 72.4^\circ \end{aligned}and:\begin{aligned} \theta - 56.31^\circ &\approx 180^\circ - 16.10^\circ \cr &\approx 163.90^\circ \cr \theta &\approx 163.90^\circ + 56.31^\circ \cr &\approx 220.2^\circ \end{aligned}Thus, the solutions to 1 decimal place are $\theta = 72.4^\circ$ and $\theta = 220.2^\circ$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}, \; \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \cr &\text{(b) } \theta \approx 72.4^\circ, \; 220.2^\circ \end{aligned}

This error occurs in part (b) if you find the correct shifted values for $\theta - 56.3^\circ$ (which are approximately $16.1^\circ$ and $163.9^\circ$) but forget to add $56.3^\circ$ to solve for $\theta$.

bradley_insight.title: Double Angle Cancellation
bradley_insight.content: When expanding and simplifying expressions like $2\sin(2x)\tan x = 3$, remember that the division by $\cos x$ relies on the assumption that $\cos x \neq 0$. If any of your final answers include values where $\cos x = 0$ (such as $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$), they must be discarded immediately because the original expression would be undefined.

question:
The diagram shows a graph representing the trajectory of a Gaelic football.

The height above the ground, $H$ metres, has been plotted against the horizontal distance, $x$ metres, measured from the point $O$ where the ball was kicked. The ball travels in a vertical plane. The ball reaches a maximum height of $16$ metres and hits the ground $48$ metres from where it was kicked.

(a) Find a quadratic equation linking $H$ with $x$ that models this situation.

The ball passes over the horizontal crossbar of a set of goal posts that is perpendicular to the path of the ball. The crossbar is $3$ metres above the ground.

(b) Use your equation to find the greatest horizontal distance of the crossbar from $O$.

(c) Give one limitation of the model.
steps:
(a) Finding the quadratic model:
The trajectory starts at the origin $O(0,0)$ and lands at the point $(48,0)$, which means the roots of the quadratic function are $x = 0$ and $x = 48$. We can express the model in factored form:$$H = kx(48 - x)$$where $k$ is a constant. The maximum height of $16$ metres occurs at the midpoint of the flight, which is $x = 24$. Therefore, the vertex of the parabola is at the point $(24, 16)$.

Substituting the vertex coordinates $x = 24$ and $H = 16$ into our factored model allows us to solve for $k$:\begin{aligned} 16 &= k(24)(48 - 24) \cr 16 &= 576k \cr k &= \dfrac{16}{576} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{36} \end{aligned}Therefore, the quadratic equation modeling the trajectory is:$$H = -\dfrac{1}{36}x^2 + \dfrac{4}{3}x$$

(b) Finding the greatest horizontal distance:
The horizontal crossbar is $3$ metres above the ground, so we set $H = 3$ and solve for $x$:$$-\dfrac{1}{36}x^2 + \dfrac{4}{3}x = 3$$Multiplying the entire equation by $-36$ to clear the fractions and rearranging into standard quadratic form gives:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 48x &= -108 \cr x^2 - 48x + 108 &= 0 \end{aligned}

We can solve this quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{48 \pm \sqrt{2304 - 432}}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{48 \pm \sqrt{1872}}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{48 \pm 12\sqrt{13}}{2} \cr &= 24 \pm 6\sqrt{13} \end{aligned}

Evaluating both roots gives:\begin{aligned} x &= 24 - 6\sqrt{13} \cr &\approx 2.37\text{ m} \cr x &= 24 + 6\sqrt{13} \cr &\approx 45.63\text{ m} \end{aligned}The question asks for the greatest horizontal distance where the ball is at crossbar height. This corresponds to the larger root where the ball is on its downward trajectory:\begin{aligned} x &= 24 + 6\sqrt{13} \cr &\approx 45.6\text{ m} \end{aligned}

(c) Identifying a limitation:
In reality, the model ignores external forces such as air resistance, wind, and any spin on the ball. These physical factors would cause the actual trajectory to deviate from a perfect parabolic path.

Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } H = -\dfrac{1}{36}x^2 + \dfrac{4}{3}x \cr &\text{(b) } x = 24 + 6\sqrt{13} \cr &\quad \approx 45.6\text{ m} \cr &\text{(c) Ignores air resistance} \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Selecting the Correct Root
bradley_insight.content: Always read the wording of the question carefully. Setting the height $H = 3$ yields two valid mathematical solutions because the ball reaches this height twice: once on the way up ($x \approx 2.37\text{ m}$) and once on the way down ($x \approx 45.6\text{ m}$). question:
The diagram shows a graph representing the trajectory of a golf ball.

The height above the ground, $H$ metres, has been plotted against the horizontal distance, $x$ metres, measured from the point $O$ where the ball was hit. The ball travels in a vertical plane. The ball reaches a maximum height of $25$ metres and hits the fairway $200$ metres from where it was struck.

(a) Find a quadratic equation linking $H$ with $x$ that models this situation.

The ball passes over the top of a tall tree that is perpendicular to the path of the ball. The tree is $16$ metres high.

(b) Use your equation to find the greatest horizontal distance of the tree from $O$.

(c) Give one limitation of the model.
steps:
(a) Finding the quadratic model:
The golf ball starts at the origin $O(0,0)$ and lands at the point $(200,0)$, which means the roots of the quadratic function are $x = 0$ and $x = 200$. We can express the model in factored form:$$H = kx(200 - x)$$where $k$ is a constant. The maximum height of $25$ metres occurs at the midpoint of the flight, which is $x = 100$. Therefore, the vertex of the parabola is at $(100, 25)$.

Substituting $x = 100$ and $H = 25$ into our factored model allows us to solve for $k$:\begin{aligned} 25 &= k(100)(200 - 100) \cr 25 &= 10000k \cr k &= \dfrac{25}{10000} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{400} \end{aligned}Therefore, the quadratic equation modeling the trajectory is:$$H = -\dfrac{1}{400}x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x$$

(b) Finding the greatest horizontal distance:
The tree is $16$ metres high, so we set $H = 16$ and solve for $x$:$$-\dfrac{1}{400}x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x = 16$$Multiplying the entire equation by $-400$ to clear the fractions and rearranging into standard quadratic form gives:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 200x &= -6400 \cr x^2 - 200x + 6400 &= 0 \end{aligned}
We can solve this quadratic equation by factoring:\begin{aligned} (x - 40)(x - 160) &= 0 \cr x &= 40\text{ m} \cr x &= 160\text{ m} \end{aligned}

The question asks for the greatest horizontal distance where the ball is at tree height ($16$ metres). This corresponds to the larger root where the ball is on its downward trajectory:$$x = 160\text{ m}$$

(c) Identifying a limitation:
The model assumes a constant gravitational field and completely ignores air resistance. Over a large horizontal distance of $200$ metres, air resistance (drag) would significantly alter the shape of the flight path, making it asymmetrical.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } H = -\dfrac{1}{400}x^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}x \cr &\text{(b) } x = 160\text{ m} \cr &\text{(c) Ignores air resistance} \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Factoring Large Quadratics
bradley_insight.content: When faced with large constant terms like $6400$ in a quadratic equation, do not panic. Try to scale down the numbers by dividing the coefficients of $x$ and the constant by a power of $10$. Here, $x^2 - 200x + 6400 = 0$ behaves like $u^2 - 20u + 64 = 0$ if we let $x = 10u$. Factoring the scaled version gives $( u - 4 )( u - 16 ) = 0$, which scales back directly to $( x - 40 )( x - 160 ) = 0$.

question:
The diagram shows a graph representing the trajectory of an arrow shot from the ground.

The height above the ground, $H$ metres, has been plotted against the horizontal distance, $x$ metres, measured from the point $O$ where the arrow was released. The arrow travels in a vertical plane. The arrow reaches a maximum height of $18$ metres and hits the ground $120$ metres from where it was shot.

(a) Find a quadratic equation linking $H$ with $x$ that models this situation.

The arrow passes over a high boundary wall that is perpendicular to the path of the arrow. The top of the wall is $10$ metres above the ground.

(b) Use your equation to find the greatest horizontal distance of the wall from $O$.

(c) Give one limitation of the model.
steps:
(a) Finding the quadratic model:
The arrow is shot from the origin $O(0,0)$ and lands at $(120,0)$, which means the roots of the quadratic function are $x = 0$ and $x = 120$. We can express the model in factored form:$$H = kx(120 - x)$$where $k$ is a constant. The maximum height of $18$ metres occurs at the midpoint of the flight, which is $x = 60$. Therefore, the vertex of the parabola is at $(60, 18)$.

Substituting $x = 60$ and $H = 18$ into our factored model allows us to solve for $k$:\begin{aligned} 18 &= k(60)(120 - 60) \cr 18 &= 3600k \cr k &= \dfrac{18}{3600} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{200} \end{aligned}Therefore, the quadratic equation modeling the trajectory is:$$H = -\dfrac{1}{200}x^2 + \dfrac{3}{5}x$$

(b) Finding the greatest horizontal distance:
The wall is $10$ metres tall, so we set $H = 10$ and solve for $x$:$$-\dfrac{1}{200}x^2 + \dfrac{3}{5}x = 10$$Multiplying the entire equation by $-200$ to clear the fractions and rearranging into standard quadratic form gives:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 120x &= -2000 \cr x^2 - 120x + 2000 &= 0 \end{aligned}
We can solve this quadratic equation by factoring:\begin{aligned} (x - 20)(x - 100) &= 0 \cr x &= 20\text{ m} \cr x &= 100\text{ m} \end{aligned}

The question asks for the greatest horizontal distance where the arrow is at wall height ($10$ metres). This corresponds to the larger root where the arrow is on its downward trajectory:$$x = 100\text{ m}$$

(c) Identifying a limitation:
The model ignores physical factors such as air resistance, arrow spin, and wind currents. Over a distance of $120$ metres, wind drift and drag would reduce the range and skew the perfect parabolic path.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } H = -\dfrac{1}{200}x^2 + \dfrac{3}{5}x \cr &\text{(b) } x = 100\text{ m} \cr &\text{(c) Ignores air resistance} \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Symmetry of Parabolas
bradley_insight.content: A key property of quadratic curves is their perfect line of symmetry. Since the axis of symmetry is at $x = 60$, any specific height $H$ (less than the maximum height of $18\text{ m}$) must occur at two horizontal distances that are equidistant from $x = 60$. Notice that the roots $x = 20$ and $x = 100$ are both exactly $40$ units away from $x = 60$. Knowing this symmetry helps you quickly double-check your arithmetic!

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Standard Form Scaling
bradley_insight.content: Using exact fractions instead of decimals (such as $-\dfrac{ 1 }{ 100 }$ rather than $-0.01$) keeps the coefficients clean and makes algebra much easier to solve. Decimal forms often hide simple factorizations that become immediately obvious once the fractions are cleared.

question: Given that $\theta$ is measured in radians, we prove from first principles that $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta}(\sin\theta) = \cos\theta$ by considering the limit of the difference quotient:$$\dfrac{\sin(\theta + h) - \sin\theta}{h}$$Which of the following shows the correct algebraic rearrangement of this expression before the limit is taken as $h \to 0$?
steps:
Step 1: Set up the limit of the difference quotient:
By definition, the derivative of $\sin\theta$ with respect to $\theta$ is given by the limit:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta}(\sin\theta) \cr &\quad = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\sin(\theta + h) - \sin\theta}{h} \end{aligned}

Step 2: Expand the compound angle term:
Using the compound angle identity for $\sin(A + B)$, we expand the numerator:\begin{aligned} &\sin(\theta + h) \cr &\quad = \sin\theta\cos h \cr &\qquad + \cos\theta\sin h \end{aligned}Substituting this expansion back into our difference quotient gives:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{h} \big( \sin\theta\cos h \cr &\qquad + \cos\theta\sin h - \sin\theta \big) \end{aligned}

Step 3: Group the terms:
We group the terms in the numerator and split into two separate fractions:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\sin\theta(\cos h - 1)}{h} \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{\cos\theta\sin h}{h} \cr &\quad = \sin\theta\left(\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\qquad + \cos\theta\left(\dfrac{\sin h}{h}\right) \end{aligned}This is the required algebraic rearrangement before taking limits.

Step 4: Take the limit as $h \to 0$:
Using the standard limit results that as $h \to 0$, $\dfrac{\sin h}{h} \to 1$ and $\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} \to 0$, we evaluate:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta}(\sin\theta) \cr &\quad = \sin\theta(0) + \cos\theta(1) \cr &\quad = \cos\theta \end{aligned}
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\sin\theta\left(\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\quad + \cos\theta\left(\dfrac{\sin h}{h}\right) \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Limit Identification
bradley_insight.content: When proving trig derivatives from first principles, do not skip the intermediate step of splitting the fraction. The limit results $\dfrac{\sin h}{h} \to 1$ and $\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} \to 0$ as $h \to 0$ must be applied separately to each of the distinct algebraic components.

question: Given that $x$ is measured in radians, we prove from first principles that $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\cos(2x)) = -2\sin(2x)$ by considering the limit of the difference quotient:$$\dfrac{\cos(2x + 2h) - \cos(2x)}{h}$$Which of the following shows the correct algebraic rearrangement of this expression before the limit is taken as $h \to 0$?
steps:
Step 1: Set up the limit of the difference quotient:
By definition, the derivative of $\cos(2x)$ with respect to $x$ is given by the limit:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\cos(2x)) \cr &\quad = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\cos(2(x + h)) - \cos(2x)}{h} \cr &\quad = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\cos(2x + 2h) - \cos(2x)}{h} \end{aligned}

Step 2: Expand the compound angle term:
Using the compound angle identity for $\cos(A + B)$, we expand $\cos(2x + 2h)$:\begin{aligned} &\cos(2x + 2h) \cr &\quad = \cos(2x)\cos(2h) \cr &\qquad - \sin(2x)\sin(2h) \end{aligned}Substituting this expansion back into our difference quotient gives:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{h} \big( \cos(2x)\cos(2h) \cr &\qquad - \sin(2x)\sin(2h) \cr &\qquad - \cos(2x) \big) \end{aligned}

Step 3: Group the terms:
We group the terms in the numerator and split into two separate fractions:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\cos(2x)(\cos(2h) - 1)}{h} \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{\sin(2x)\sin(2h)}{h} \cr &\quad = \cos(2x)\left(\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\qquad - \sin(2x)\left(\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h}\right) \end{aligned}This is the required algebraic rearrangement before taking limits.

Step 4: Take the limit as $h \to 0$:
To evaluate the limits, we scale the fractions to match our standard limit forms:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{h} \cr &\quad = 2\left(\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{2h}\right) \cr &\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h} \cr &\quad = 2\left(\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{2h}\right) \end{aligned}As $h \to 0$, we have $2h \to 0$. Therefore:\begin{aligned} &\lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\quad = 2(0) \cr &\quad = 0 \cr &\lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h}\right) \cr &\quad = 2(1) \cr &\quad = 2 \end{aligned}Applying these limits gives:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\cos(2x)) \cr &\quad = \cos(2x)(0) \cr &\qquad - \sin(2x)(2) \cr &\quad = -2\sin(2x) \end{aligned}
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\cos(2x)\left(\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\quad - \sin(2x)\left(\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h}\right) \end{aligned}

question: Given that $x$ is measured in radians, we prove from first principles that $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sin(2x)) = 2\cos(2x)$ by considering the limit of the difference quotient:$$\dfrac{\sin(2x + 2h) - \sin(2x)}{h}$$Which of the following shows the correct algebraic rearrangement of this expression before the limit is taken as $h \to 0$?

Step 1: Set up the limit of the difference quotient:
By definition, the derivative of $\sin(2x)$ with respect to $x$ is given by the limit:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sin(2x)) \cr &\quad = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\sin(2(x + h)) - \sin(2x)}{h} \cr &\quad = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\sin(2x + 2h) - \sin(2x)}{h} \end{aligned}

Step 3: Group the terms:
We group the terms in the numerator and split into two separate fractions:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\sin(2x)(\cos(2h) - 1)}{h} \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{\cos(2x)\sin(2h)}{h} \cr &\quad = \sin(2x)\left(\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\qquad + \cos(2x)\left(\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h}\right) \end{aligned}This is the required algebraic rearrangement before taking limits.

Step 4: Take the limit as $h \to 0$:
To evaluate the limits, we scale the fractions to match our standard limit forms:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{h} \cr &\quad = 2\left(\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{2h}\right) \cr &\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h} \cr &\quad = 2\left(\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{2h}\right) \end{aligned}As $h \to 0$, we have $2h \to 0$. Therefore:\begin{aligned} &\lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{\cos(2h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\quad = 2(0) \cr &\quad = 0 \cr &\lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{\sin(2h)}{h}\right) \cr &\quad = 2(1) \cr &\quad = 2 \end{aligned}Applying these limits gives:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sin(2x)) \cr &\quad = \sin(2x)(0) \cr &\qquad + \cos(2x)(2) \cr &\quad = 2\cos(2x) \end{aligned}

question: Given that $\theta$ is measured in radians, we prove from first principles that $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta}(\cos(3\theta)) = -3\sin(3\theta)$ by considering the limit of the difference quotient:$$\dfrac{\cos(3\theta + 3h) - \cos(3\theta)}{h}$$Which of the following shows the correct algebraic rearrangement of this expression before the limit is taken as $h \to 0$?

Therefore:\begin{aligned} &\lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{\cos(3h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\quad = 3(0) \cr &\quad = 0 \cr &\lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{\sin(3h)}{h}\right) \cr &\quad = 3(1) \cr &\quad = 3 \end{aligned}Applying these limits gives:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta}(\cos(3\theta)) \cr &\quad = \cos(3\theta)(0) \cr &\qquad - \sin(3\theta)(3) \cr &\quad = -3\sin(3\theta) \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.content: Always ensure the arguments inside your sines and cosines remain consistent throughout the proof. For example, do not confuse $\cos(3\theta)$ with $3\cos\theta$; the parameter $3$ is bound within the angle, which is why we must use the compound angle identity with $3\theta$ and $3h$.

question: Given that $\theta$ is measured in radians, we prove from first principles that $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta}(\sin(3\theta)) = 3\cos(3\theta)$ by considering the limit of the difference quotient:$$\dfrac{\sin(3\theta + 3h) - \sin(3\theta)}{h}$$Which of the following shows the correct algebraic rearrangement of this expression before the limit is taken as $h \to 0$?
steps:
Step 1: Set up the limit of the difference quotient:
By definition, the derivative of $\sin(3\theta)$ with respect to $\theta$ is given by the limit:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta}(\sin(3\theta)) \cr &\quad = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\sin(3(\theta + h)) - \sin(3\theta)}{h} \cr &\quad = \lim_{h \to 0} \dfrac{\sin(3\theta + 3h) - \sin(3\theta)}{h} \end{aligned}

Step 2: Expand the compound angle term:
Using the compound angle identity for $\sin(A + B)$, we expand $\sin(3\theta + 3h)$:\begin{aligned} &\sin(3\theta + 3h) \cr &\quad = \sin(3\theta)\cos(3h) \cr &\qquad + \cos(3\theta)\sin(3h) \end{aligned}Substituting this expansion back into our difference quotient gives:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{h} \big( \sin(3\theta)\cos(3h) \cr &\qquad + \cos(3\theta)\sin(3h) \cr &\qquad - \sin(3\theta) \big) \end{aligned}

Step 3: Group the terms:
We group the terms in the numerator and split into two separate fractions:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\sin(3\theta)(\cos(3h) - 1)}{h} \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{\cos(3\theta)\sin(3h)}{h} \cr &\quad = \sin(3\theta)\left(\dfrac{\cos(3h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\qquad + \cos(3\theta)\left(\dfrac{\sin(3h)}{h}\right) \end{aligned}This is the required algebraic rearrangement before taking limits.

Step 4: Take the limit as $h \to 0$:
To evaluate the limits, we scale the fractions to match our standard limit forms:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\cos(3h) - 1}{h} \cr &\quad = 3\left(\dfrac{\cos(3h) - 1}{3h}\right) \cr &\dfrac{\sin(3h)}{h} \cr &\quad = 3\left(\dfrac{\sin(3h)}{3h}\right) \end{aligned}As $h \to 0$, we have $3h \to 0$. Therefore:\begin{aligned} &\lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{\cos(3h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\quad = 3(0) \cr &\quad = 0 \cr &\lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{\sin(3h)}{h}\right) \cr &\quad = 3(1) \cr &\quad = 3 \end{aligned}Applying these limits gives:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta}(\sin(3\theta)) \cr &\quad = \sin(3\theta)(0) \cr &\qquad + \cos(3\theta)(3) \cr &\quad = 3\cos(3\theta) \end{aligned}
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &\sin(3\theta)\left(\dfrac{\cos(3h) - 1}{h}\right) \cr &\quad + \cos(3\theta)\left(\dfrac{\sin(3h)}{h}\right) \end{aligned}

This error occurs if you incorrectly swap the sine and cosine functions in the compound angle identity expansion.
This option fails to divide the first factored term by the denominator $h$, violating the rules of algebraic fractions.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Limit Parameters
bradley_insight.content: Remember that the standard limits $\dfrac{\sin x}{x} \to 1$ and $\dfrac{\cos x - 1}{x} \to 0$ as $x \to 0$ hold true for any variable parameter $x$. By substituting $x = 3h$, we can see that as $h \to 0$, $3h \to 0$, allowing us to evaluate the limits of scaled functions easily.

question:
A spherical sugar candy of radius $6\text{ mm}$ is placed in water and dissolves. Three minutes later, the radius of the candy is $3\text{ mm}$.

In a simple model, the rate of decrease of the radius of the candy is inversely proportional to the square of the radius.

Using this model, find the total time taken for the candy to completely dissolve (to the nearest second).
steps:
Step 1: Formulate the differential equation:
Let $r$ represent the radius of the candy (in mm) at time $t$ (in minutes). Since the rate of decrease of the radius is inversely proportional to $r^2$, we write:$$\dfrac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} = -\dfrac{k}{r^2}$$where $k$ is a positive constant of proportionality.

Step 2: Separate variables and integrate:
We separate the variables and integrate both sides of the equation:\begin{aligned} r^2 \text{d}r &= -k \text{d}t \cr \int r^2 \text{d}r &= \int -k \text{d}t \cr \dfrac{1}{3}r^3 &= -kt + C \cr r^3 &= -3kt + 3C \end{aligned}Let $K = 3k$ and $c = 3C$ to simplify the equation:$$r^3 = -Kt + c$$

Step 3: Apply the initial and boundary conditions:
At $t = 0$, the initial radius is $r = 6$:\begin{aligned} 6^3 &= -K(0) + c \cr c &= 216 \end{aligned}This gives the equation:$$r^3 = 216 - Kt$$Three minutes later, at $t = 3$, the radius is $r = 3$:\begin{aligned} 3^3 &= 216 - K(3) \cr 27 &= 216 - 3K \cr 3K &= 189 \cr K &= 63 \end{aligned}Thus, the equation linking the radius and time is:$$r^3 = 216 - 63t$$

Step 4: Find the total time taken to dissolve:
The candy completely dissolves when $r = 0$:\begin{aligned} 0 &= 216 - 63t \cr 63t &= 216 \cr t &= \dfrac{216}{63} \cr &= \dfrac{24}{7}\text{ minutes} \cr &\approx 3.43\text{ minutes} \end{aligned}

Step 5: Convert the time into minutes and seconds:
We convert $\dfrac{24}{7}$ minutes into minutes and seconds:\begin{aligned} &t = 3\text{ min} + \dfrac{3}{7}\text{ min} \cr &\quad = 3\text{ min} + 25.7\text{ s} \cr &\quad \approx 3\text{ min } 26\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &3\text{ minutes and } 26\text{ seconds} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you misinterpret the decimal output of $3.43$ minutes directly as $3$ minutes and $43$ seconds. Remember that $0.43$ minutes must be multiplied by $60$ to convert it into seconds.
This error occurs if you use a linear model where the radius decreases by a constant $1\text{ mm}$ per minute, which violates the inverse square law of the model.
This is a rounding error or arithmetic slip in solving for the constant of integration $c$ or the constant $K$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Decimal Time Conversion
bradley_insight.content: Always be careful when converting decimal times. A common trap is to write a time of $3.43\text{ minutes}$ as $3\text{ minutes and } 43\text{ seconds}$. Always isolate the decimal fraction of the minute and multiply it by $60$ to get the correct number of seconds ($0.43 \times 60 \approx 26\text{ seconds}$).

question:
The mass of a radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to its mass at that time. The initial mass of the substance is $80\text{ g}$. Ten hours later, the mass is found to be $40\text{ g}$.

In a simple model, the rate of decrease of the mass of the substance is proportional to its mass.

Using this model, find the time taken for the mass of the substance to decay to $5\text{ g}$ (to the nearest hour).
steps:
Step 1: Formulate the differential equation:
Let $M$ represent the mass of the radioactive substance (in g) at time $t$ (in hours). Since the rate of decrease of the mass is proportional to the mass itself, we write:$$\dfrac{\text{d}M}{\text{d}t} = -kM$$where $k$ is a positive constant.

Step 2: Separate variables and integrate:
Separating the variables and integrating both sides of the equation gives:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{M} \text{d}M &= -k \text{d}t \cr \int \dfrac{1}{M} \text{d}M &= \int -k \text{d}t \cr \ln M &= -kt + C \cr M &= A\mathrm{e}^{-kt} \end{aligned}where $A = \mathrm{e}^C$ is a constant.

Step 3: Apply the initial and boundary conditions:
At $t = 0$, the initial mass is $M = 80$:\begin{aligned} 80 &= A\mathrm{e}^{-k(0)} \cr A &= 80 \end{aligned}This gives the equation:$$M = 80\mathrm{e}^{-kt}$$Ten hours later, at $t = 10$, the mass is $M = 40$:\begin{aligned} 40 &= 80\mathrm{e}^{-10k} \cr \mathrm{e}^{-10k} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \cr -10k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \cr &= -\ln 2 \cr k &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{10} \end{aligned}Thus, the equation linking the mass and time is:$$M = 80\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\frac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t}$$

Step 4: Find the time taken to decay to $5\text{ g}$:
Setting $M = 5$, we solve for $t$:\begin{aligned} 5 &= 80\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\frac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t} \cr \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\frac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t} &= \dfrac{5}{80} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{16} \cr -\left(\dfrac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{16}\right) \cr &= -\ln 16 \cr &= -4\ln 2 \cr \left(\dfrac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t &= 4\ln 2 \cr t &= 40\text{ hours} \end{aligned}
Final Answer\begin{aligned} t = 40\text{ hours} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you incorrectly calculate the decay factor or make an arithmetic error when solving for the time constant.
This is a common mistake resulting from dividing the initial mass directly by the mass difference without applying the exponential decay formula.
This is a calculation slip in evaluating the power of $2$ when equating $\frac{1}{16}$ to $\mathrm{e}^{-kt}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Half-Life Constant
bradley_insight.content: Notice that since the substance halves every $10\text{ hours}$ (from $80\text{ g}$ to $40\text{ g}$), the half-life is exactly $10\text{ hours}$. To decay from $80\text{ g}$ to $5\text{ g}$, the substance must halve $4$ times ($80$, $40$, $20$, $10$, $5\text{ g}$). Therefore, the total time is simply $4 \times 10 = 40\text{ hours}$. Recognizing half-lives is a great shortcut to verify your algebraic results!

question:
A circular puddle of water on a flat concrete surface is evaporating in the sun. The initial radius of the puddle is $10\text{ cm}$. After $5$ hours of evaporation, the radius of the puddle has reduced to $8\text{ cm}$.

In a simple model, the rate of decrease of the radius of the puddle is inversely proportional to the radius.

Using this model, find the total time taken for the puddle to dry up completely (to the nearest minute).
steps:
Step 1: Formulate the differential equation:
Let $r$ represent the radius of the puddle (in cm) at time $t$ (in hours). Since the rate of decrease of the radius is inversely proportional to the radius itself, we write:$$\dfrac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} = -\dfrac{k}{r}$$where $k$ is a positive constant.

Step 2: Separate variables and integrate:
Separating the variables and integrating both sides of the equation gives:\begin{aligned} r \text{d}r &= -k \text{d}t \cr \int r \text{d}r &= \int -k \text{d}t \cr \dfrac{1}{2}r^2 &= -kt + C \cr r^2 &= -2kt + 2C \end{aligned}Let $K = 2k$ and $c = 2C$ to simplify the equation:$$r^2 = -Kt + c$$

Step 3: Apply the initial and boundary conditions:
At $t = 0$, the initial radius is $r = 10$:\begin{aligned} 10^2 &= -K(0) + c \cr c &= 100 \end{aligned}This gives the equation:$$r^2 = 100 - Kt$$After $5$ hours, at $t = 5$, the radius is $r = 8$:\begin{aligned} 8^2 &= 100 - K(5) \cr 64 &= 100 - 5K \cr 5K &= 36 \cr K &= 7.2 \end{aligned}Thus, the equation linking the radius and time is:$$r^2 = 100 - 7.2t$$

Step 4: Find the total time taken to dry up:
The puddle dries up completely when $r = 0$:\begin{aligned} 0 &= 100 - 7.2t \cr 7.2t &= 100 \cr t &= \dfrac{100}{7.2} \cr &= \dfrac{125}{9}\text{ hours} \cr &\approx 13.89\text{ hours} \end{aligned}

Step 5: Convert the time into hours and minutes:
We convert $\dfrac{125}{9}$ hours into hours and minutes:\begin{aligned} &t = 13\text{ hours} + \dfrac{8}{9}\text{ hours} \cr &\quad = 13\text{ hours} + 53.3\text{ mins} \cr &\quad \approx 13\text{ hours } 53\text{ mins} \end{aligned}
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &13\text{ hours and } 53\text{ minutes} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you misinterpret the decimal output of $13.89$ hours directly as $13$ hours and $89$ minutes. Remember that $0.89$ hours must be converted to minutes by multiplying by $60$.
This is a rounding error or incorrect approximation made early in the calculations.
This is a calculation slip resulting from an incorrect constant of integration or a sign error during integration.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Early Rounding
bradley_insight.content: Avoid rounding values too early in your calculations. If you round $K = 7.2$ or $t \approx 13.89\text{ hours}$ too aggressively, you may introduce a cumulative rounding error when converting to minutes. Always keep exact fractions (like $\dfrac{125}{9}$) until the very final conversion step.

question:
Water is leaking from a hole at the bottom of a cylindrical water tank. The depth of the water in the tank is $h$ metres at time $t$ minutes. Initially, the depth of the water is $9\text{ m}$. After $12$ minutes, the depth of the water has reduced to $4\text{ m}$.

In a simple model, the rate of decrease of the depth of the water is proportional to the square root of the depth.

Using this model, find the total time taken for the water tank to empty completely (to the nearest minute).
steps:
Step 1: Formulate the differential equation:
Since the rate of decrease of the depth $h$ is proportional to the square root of $h$, we write:$$\dfrac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = -k\sqrt{h}$$where $k$ is a positive constant.

Step 2: Separate variables and integrate:
Separating the variables and integrating both sides of the equation gives:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{h}} \text{d}h &= -k \text{d}t \cr \int h^{-1/2} \text{d}h &= \int -k \text{d}t \cr 2\sqrt{h} &= -kt + C \cr \sqrt{h} &= -\dfrac{k}{2}t + \dfrac{C}{2} \end{aligned}

Step 3: Apply the initial and boundary conditions:
At $t = 0$, the initial depth is $h = 9$:\begin{aligned} 2\sqrt{9} &= -k(0) + C \cr C &= 6 \end{aligned}This gives the equation:\begin{aligned} 2\sqrt{h} &= 6 - kt \cr \sqrt{h} &= 3 - \dfrac{k}{2}t \end{aligned}After $12$ minutes, at $t = 12$, the depth is $h = 4$:\begin{aligned} \sqrt{4} &= 3 - \dfrac{k}{2}(12) \cr 2 &= 3 - 6k \cr 6k &= 1 \cr k &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}Thus, the equation linking the depth and time is:\begin{aligned} \sqrt{h} &= 3 - \dfrac{t}{12} \cr h &= \left(3 - \dfrac{t}{12}\right)^2 \end{aligned}

Step 4: Find the total time taken to empty:
The water tank is completely empty when $h = 0$:\begin{aligned} 3 - \dfrac{t}{12} &= 0 \cr \dfrac{t}{12} &= 3 \cr t &= 36\text{ minutes} \end{aligned}
Final Answer\begin{aligned} t = 36\text{ minutes} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you use a linear model where the depth decreases at a constant rate, rather than using a model with a rate of decrease proportional to $\sqrt{h}$.
This is a calculation slip in integration, such as forgetting the factor of $2$ when integrating $h^{-1/2}$.
This is a sign error or arithmetic slip when solving for the constants $C$ and $k$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Fractional Powers Integration
bradley_insight.content: Remember the power rule for integration: $\int h^{-1/2}\text{d}h = \dfrac{h^{1/2}}{1/2}$, which simplifies to $2\sqrt{h}$. A common trap is to forget the division by $1/2$ and write it as just $\sqrt{h}$, which changes the final constants and yields incorrect empty times.

question:
A spherical raindrop is falling through a cloud and evaporating. The initial radius of the raindrop is $4\text{ mm}$. Ten minutes later, the radius has reduced to $2\text{ mm}$.

In a simple model, the rate of decrease of the radius of the raindrop is proportional to the radius.

Using this model, find the time taken for the radius of the raindrop to decrease to $0.5\text{ mm}$ (to the nearest minute).
steps:
Step 1: Formulate the differential equation:
Let $r$ represent the radius of the raindrop (in mm) at time $t$ (in minutes). Since the rate of decrease of the radius is proportional to the radius itself, we write:$$\dfrac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} = -kr$$where $k$ is a positive constant.

Step 2: Separate variables and integrate:
Separating the variables and integrating both sides of the equation gives:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{r} \text{d}r &= -k \text{d}t \cr \int \dfrac{1}{r} \text{d}r &= \int -k \text{d}t \cr \ln r &= -kt + C \cr r &= A\mathrm{e}^{-kt} \end{aligned}where $A = \mathrm{e}^C$ is a constant.

Step 3: Apply the initial and boundary conditions:
At $t = 0$, the initial radius is $r = 4$:\begin{aligned} 4 &= A\mathrm{e}^{-k(0)} \cr A &= 4 \end{aligned}This gives the equation:$$r = 4\mathrm{e}^{-kt}$$Ten minutes later, at $t = 10$, the radius is $r = 2$:\begin{aligned} 2 &= 4\mathrm{e}^{-10k} \cr \mathrm{e}^{-10k} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \cr -10k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \cr &= -\ln 2 \cr k &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{10} \end{aligned}Thus, the equation linking the radius and time is:$$r = 4\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\frac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t}$$

Step 4: Find the time taken to decrease to $0.5\text{ mm}$:
Setting $r = 0.5$, we solve for $t$:\begin{aligned} 0.5 &= 4\mathrm{e}^{-\left(\frac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t} \cr \mathrm{e}^{-\left(\frac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t} &= \dfrac{0.5}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{8} \cr -\left(\dfrac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right) \cr &= -\ln 8 \cr &= -3\ln 2 \cr \left(\dfrac{\ln 2}{10}\right)t &= 3\ln 2 \cr t &= 30\text{ minutes} \end{aligned}
Final Answer\begin{aligned} t = 30\text{ minutes} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you use a linear model where the radius decreases by a constant $2\text{ mm}$ every $10$ minutes (so it would reach $0\text{ mm}$ at $20$ minutes). Exponential decay does not proceed at a constant rate.
This is a rounding error or calculation slip when resolving the logarithms in Step 4.
This is a sign error or algebraic slip when solving for the constants of integration $A$ or the constant $k$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Half-Life Properties
bradley_insight.content: Since the radius halves every $10\text{ minutes}$ (from $4\text{ mm}$ to $2\text{ mm}$), the half-life of the radius is exactly $10\text{ minutes}$. To decrease from $4\text{ mm}$ to $0.5\text{ mm}$, the radius must halve $3$ times ($4$, $2$, $1$, $0.5\text{ mm}$). The total time is simply $3 \times 10 = 30\text{ minutes}$. Understanding half-life shortcuts can save you precious time under exam pressure!

question: Given that:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{6x^2 + 11x + 1}{(x + 2)(2x + 1)} \cr &\quad \equiv A + \dfrac{B}{x + 2} + \dfrac{C}{2x + 1} \end{aligned}Find the values of the constants $A$, $B$, and $C$.
steps:
Step 1: Set up the algebraic identity:
To express the improper fraction as partial fractions, we first multiply both sides of the identity by the common denominator $(x + 2)(2x + 1)$ to clear the fractions:\begin{aligned} &6x^2 + 11x + 1 \cr &\quad \equiv A(x + 2)(2x + 1) \cr &\qquad + B(2x + 1) + C(x + 2) \end{aligned}

Step 2: Find the constant $A$ by comparing coefficients of $x^2$:
Expanding the quadratic product gives $(x + 2)(2x + 1) = 2x^2 + 5x + 2$. Substituting this back into the identity:\begin{aligned} &6x^2 + 11x + 1 \cr &\quad \equiv A(2x^2 + 5x + 2) \cr &\qquad + B(2x + 1) + C(x + 2) \end{aligned}By equating the coefficients of $x^2$ on both sides:\begin{aligned} 2A &= 6 \cr A &= 3 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Collect coefficients to solve for $B$ and $C$:
Now we expand and group the terms on the right-hand side by powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &6x^2 + 11x + 1 \cr &\quad \equiv 3(2x^2 + 5x + 2) \cr &\qquad + B(2x + 1) + C(x + 2) \cr &\quad \equiv 6x^2 + 15x + 6 \cr &\qquad + 2Bx + B + Cx + 2C \end{aligned}Grouping like powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &11x + 1 \cr &\quad \equiv (15 + 2B + C)x \cr &\qquad + (6 + B + 2C) \end{aligned}Equating the coefficients of $x$ and the constant terms yields two simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} 15 + 2B + C &= 11 \cr 2B + C &= -4 \cr 6 + B + 2C &= 1 \cr B + 2C &= -5 \end{aligned}

Step 4: Solve the simultaneous equations:
From the first equation, express $C$ in terms of $B$:$$C = -4 - 2B$$Substituting this into the second equation:\begin{aligned} B + 2(-4 - 2B) &= -5 \cr B - 8 - 4B &= -5 \cr -3B &= 3 \cr B &= -1 \end{aligned}Substituting $B = -1$ back to find $C$:\begin{aligned} C &= -4 - 2(-1) \cr &= -2 \end{aligned}Therefore, the constants are $A = 3$, $B = -1$, and $C = -2$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} A &= 3 \cr B &= -1 \cr C &= -2 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error when expanding or grouping coefficients, yielding $+1$ for $B$ instead of $-1$.
This error is the result of a sign slip when substituting $B = -1$ back into the simultaneous equations to find $C$.
This occurs if you equate $A$ directly to the leading coefficient of the numerator ($6$), forgetting that the leading term of the denominator is $2x^2$ (meaning $2A = 6$, so $A = 3$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Leading Coefficients in Improper Fractions
bradley_insight.content: When dealing with improper fractions where the numerator and denominator have the same degree, the constant term $A$ is simply the ratio of the leading coefficients. Here, the leading term of the numerator is $6x^2$ and the expanded leading term of the denominator is $2x^2$. Thus, $A = \dfrac{6}{2}$, so $A = 3$. Checking this ratio first is an incredibly fast way to eliminate incorrect options under pressure!

question: Given that:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{2x^2 - x + 5}{(x - 1)(x + 2)} \cr &\quad \equiv A + \dfrac{B}{x - 1} + \dfrac{C}{x + 2} \end{aligned}Find the values of the constants $A$, $B$, and $C$.
steps:
Step 1: Set up the algebraic identity:
Multiply both sides of the identity by the common denominator $(x - 1)(x + 2)$ to clear the fractions:\begin{aligned} &2x^2 - x + 5 \cr &\quad \equiv A(x - 1)(x + 2) \cr &\qquad + B(x + 2) + C(x - 1) \end{aligned}

Step 2: Find the constant $A$ by comparing coefficients of $x^2$:
Expanding the quadratic product gives $(x - 1)(x + 2) = x^2 + x - 2$. Substituting this back into the identity:\begin{aligned} &2x^2 - x + 5 \cr &\quad \equiv A(x^2 + x - 2) \cr &\qquad + B(x + 2) + C(x - 1) \end{aligned}By equating the coefficients of $x^2$ on both sides:$$A = 2$$

Step 3: Collect coefficients to solve for $B$ and $C$:
Now expand and group the terms on the right-hand side by powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &2x^2 - x + 5 \cr &\quad \equiv 2(x^2 + x - 2) \cr &\qquad + B(x + 2) + C(x - 1) \cr &\quad \equiv 2x^2 + 2x - 4 \cr &\qquad + Bx + 2B + Cx - C \end{aligned}Grouping like powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &-x + 5 \cr &\quad \equiv (2 + B + C)x \cr &\qquad + (-4 + 2B - C) \end{aligned}Equating the coefficients of $x$ and the constant terms yields two simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} 2 + B + C &= -1 \cr B + C &= -3 \cr -4 + 2B - C &= 5 \cr 2B - C &= 9 \end{aligned}

Step 4: Solve the simultaneous equations:
From the first equation, express $C$ in terms of $B$:$$C = -3 - B$$Substituting this into the second equation:\begin{aligned} 2B - (-3 - B) &= 9 \cr 2B + 3 + B &= 9 \cr 3B &= 6 \cr B &= 2 \end{aligned}Substituting $B = 2$ back to find $C$:\begin{aligned} C &= -3 - 2 \cr &= -5 \end{aligned}Therefore, the constants are $A = 2$, $B = 2$, and $C = -5$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} A &= 2 \cr B &= 2 \cr C &= -5 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error when solving the simultaneous equations, yielding $B = -2$ instead of $B = 2$.
This is a sign slip in finding $C$ after solving for $B = 2$ (e.g., writing $C = -3 + 2 = -1$ or dropping the minus sign on $-5$).
This occurs if you assume the quotient constant $A$ is $1$ because there are no explicit multipliers on $(x-1)(x+2)$, forgetting that the numerator's leading term is $2x^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Substitution Method
bradley_insight.content: While equating coefficients is robust, you can also solve for $B$ and $C$ extremely quickly by substituting the roots of the denominator. Once you find $A = 2$, let $x = 1$ to get $6 = 3B$, which gives $B = 2$. Then let $x = -2$ to get $15 = -3C$, which gives $C = -5$. This is a great way to save time and double-check your simultaneous equation work!

question: Given that:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{4x^2 + 6x - 1}{(2x - 1)(x + 1)} \cr &\quad \equiv A + \dfrac{B}{2x - 1} + \dfrac{C}{x + 1} \end{aligned}Find the values of the constants $A$, $B$, and $C$.
steps:
Step 1: Set up the algebraic identity:
Multiply both sides of the identity by the common denominator $(2x - 1)(x + 1)$ to clear the fractions:\begin{aligned} &4x^2 + 6x - 1 \cr &\quad \equiv A(2x - 1)(x + 1) \cr &\qquad + B(x + 1) + C(2x - 1) \end{aligned}

Step 2: Find the constant $A$ by comparing coefficients of $x^2$:
Expanding the quadratic product gives $(2x - 1)(x + 1) = 2x^2 + x - 1$. Substituting this back into the identity:\begin{aligned} &4x^2 + 6x - 1 \cr &\quad \equiv A(2x^2 + x - 1) \cr &\qquad + B(x + 1) + C(2x - 1) \end{aligned}By equating the coefficients of $x^2$ on both sides:\begin{aligned} 2A &= 4 \cr A &= 2 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Collect coefficients to solve for $B$ and $C$:
Now expand and group the terms on the right-hand side by powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &4x^2 + 6x - 1 \cr &\quad \equiv 2(2x^2 + x - 1) \cr &\qquad + B(x + 1) + C(2x - 1) \cr &\quad \equiv 4x^2 + 2x - 2 \cr &\qquad + Bx + B + 2Cx - C \end{aligned}Grouping like powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &6x - 1 \cr &\quad \equiv (2 + B + 2C)x \cr &\qquad + (-2 + B - C) \end{aligned}Equating the coefficients of $x$ and the constant terms yields two simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} 2 + B + 2C &= 6 \cr B + 2C &= 4 \cr -2 + B - C &= -1 \cr B - C &= 1 \end{aligned}

Step 4: Solve the simultaneous equations:
From the second equation, express $B$ in terms of $C$:$$B = 1 + C$$Substituting this into the first equation:\begin{aligned} (1 + C) + 2C &= 4 \cr 1 + 3C &= 4 \cr 3C &= 3 \cr C &= 1 \end{aligned}Substituting $C = 1$ back to find $B$:\begin{aligned} B &= 1 + 1 \cr &= 2 \end{aligned}Therefore, the constants are $A = 2$, $B = 2$, and $C = 1$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} A &= 2 \cr B &= 2 \cr C &= 1 \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Spotting Simple Eliminations
bradley_insight.content: When solving the simultaneous equations $B + 2C = 4$ and $B - C = 1$, you can eliminate $B$ immediately by subtracting the second equation from the first. This yields $3C = 3$, giving $C = 1$. This direct subtraction eliminates the need to substitute, reducing the risk of a sign error!

question: Given that:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{3x^2 - 6x + 2}{(x - 4)(3x + 1)} \cr &\quad \equiv A + \dfrac{B}{x - 4} + \dfrac{C}{3x + 1} \end{aligned}Find the values of the constants $A$, $B$, and $C$.
steps:
Step 1: Set up the algebraic identity:
Multiply both sides of the identity by the common denominator $(x - 4)(3x + 1)$ to clear the fractions:\begin{aligned} &3x^2 - 6x + 2 \cr &\quad \equiv A(x - 4)(3x + 1) \cr &\qquad + B(3x + 1) + C(x - 4) \end{aligned}

Step 2: Find the constant $A$ by comparing coefficients of $x^2$:
Expanding the quadratic product gives $(x - 4)(3x + 1) = 3x^2 - 11x - 4$. Substituting this back into the identity:\begin{aligned} &3x^2 - 6x + 2 \cr &\quad \equiv A(3x^2 - 11x - 4) \cr &\qquad + B(3x + 1) + C(x - 4) \end{aligned}By equating the coefficients of $x^2$ on both sides:\begin{aligned} 3A &= 3 \cr A &= 1 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Collect coefficients to solve for $B$ and $C$:
Now expand and group the terms on the right-hand side by powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &3x^2 - 6x + 2 \cr &\quad \equiv 1(3x^2 - 11x - 4) \cr &\qquad + B(3x + 1) + C(x - 4) \cr &\quad \equiv 3x^2 - 11x - 4 \cr &\qquad + 3Bx + B + Cx - 4C \end{aligned}Grouping like powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &-6x + 2 \cr &\quad \equiv (-11 + 3B + C)x \cr &\qquad + (-4 + B - 4C) \end{aligned}Equating the coefficients of $x$ and the constant terms yields two simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} -11 + 3B + C &= -6 \cr 3B + C &= 5 \cr -4 + B - 4C &= 2 \cr B - 4C &= 6 \end{aligned}

Step 4: Solve the simultaneous equations:
From the first equation, express $C$ in terms of $B$:$$C = 5 - 3B$$Substituting this into the second equation:\begin{aligned} B - 4(5 - 3B) &= 6 \cr B - 20 + 12B &= 6 \cr 13B &= 26 \cr B &= 2 \end{aligned}Substituting $B = 2$ back to find $C$:\begin{aligned} C &= 5 - 3(2) \cr &= -1 \end{aligned}Therefore, the constants are $A = 1$, $B = 2$, and $C = -1$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} A &= 1 \cr B &= 2 \cr C &= -1 \end{aligned}

This error occurs if you make a sign error when substituting $B = 2$ back to find $C$ (such as writing $C = 5 + 6 = 11$ or $C = 1$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Fractional Roots Substitution
bradley_insight.content: While substituting $x = 4$ is very straightforward and yields $B = 2$ directly, substituting $x = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ requires careful fraction arithmetic. To avoid fractional errors, once you have solved for $B = 2$ using $x = 4$, you can simply substitute $x = 0$ as a very easy test value to find $C$: $2 = -4 + B - 4C$. Since $B = 2$, this simplifies to $4 = -4C$, which gives $C = -1$.

question: Given that:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{6x^2 - 16x + 12}{(x - 2)(3x - 2)} \cr &\quad \equiv A + \dfrac{B}{x - 2} + \dfrac{C}{3x - 2} \end{aligned}Find the values of the constants $A$, $B$, and $C$.
steps:
Step 1: Set up the algebraic identity:
Multiply both sides of the identity by the common denominator $(x - 2)(3x - 2)$ to clear the fractions:\begin{aligned} &6x^2 - 16x + 12 \cr &\quad \equiv A(x - 2)(3x - 2) \cr &\qquad + B(3x - 2) + C(x - 2) \end{aligned}

Step 2: Find the constant $A$ by comparing coefficients of $x^2$:
Expanding the quadratic product gives $(x - 2)(3x - 2) = 3x^2 - 8x + 4$. Substituting this back into the identity:\begin{aligned} &6x^2 - 16x + 12 \cr &\quad \equiv A(3x^2 - 8x + 4) \cr &\qquad + B(3x - 2) + C(x - 2) \end{aligned}By equating the coefficients of $x^2$ on both sides:\begin{aligned} 3A &= 6 \cr A &= 2 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Collect coefficients to solve for $B$ and $C$:
Now expand and group the terms on the right-hand side by powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &6x^2 - 16x + 12 \cr &\quad \equiv 2(3x^2 - 8x + 4) \cr &\qquad + B(3x - 2) + C(x - 2) \cr &\quad \equiv 6x^2 - 16x + 8 \cr &\qquad + 3Bx - 2B + Cx - 2C \end{aligned}Grouping like powers of $x$:\begin{aligned} &-16x + 12 \cr &\quad \equiv (-16 + 3B + C)x \cr &\qquad + (8 - 2B - 2C) \end{aligned}Equating the coefficients of $x$ and the constant terms yields two simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} -16 + 3B + C &= -16 \cr 3B + C &= 0 \cr 8 - 2B - 2C &= 12 \cr -2B - 2C &= 4 \cr B + C &= -2 \end{aligned}

Step 4: Solve the simultaneous equations:
From the first equation, express $C$ in terms of $B$:$$C = -3B$$Substituting this into the simplified second equation:\begin{aligned} B + (-3B) &= -2 \cr -2B &= -2 \cr B &= 1 \end{aligned}Substituting $B = 1$ back to find $C$:\begin{aligned} C &= -3(1) \cr &= -3 \end{aligned}Therefore, the constants are $A = 2$, $B = 1$, and $C = -3$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} A &= 2 \cr B &= 1 \cr C &= -3 \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Simplifying Simultaneous Equations
bradley_insight.content: Notice how the equation $-2B - 2C = 4$ was simplified to $B + C = -2$ by dividing all terms by $-2$. Simplifying coefficients first prevents trivial arithmetic errors and makes substitution or elimination significantly easier.

question: (a) Prove that:$$1 + \cos 2\theta \equiv \cot \theta \sin 2\theta$$(b) Hence solve, for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ where $x \neq 0$, the equation:\begin{aligned} &(\csc^2 x - 4)(1 + \cos 2x) \cr &\quad = 2\cot^2 x \sin 2x \end{aligned}Give your answers to 3 decimal places where appropriate.
steps:
(a) Proving the identity:
We start by expanding the right-hand side (RHS) of the identity using the definitions $\cot \theta = \dfrac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}$ and $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin \theta \cos \theta$:\begin{aligned} &\cot \theta \sin 2\theta \cr &\quad = \left(\dfrac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}\right)(2\sin \theta \cos \theta) \cr &\quad = 2\cos^2 \theta \end{aligned}Now we expand the left-hand side (LHS) of the identity using the double angle identity $\cos 2\theta = \cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta$ and the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 \theta = 1 - \cos^2 \theta$:\begin{aligned} 1 + \cos 2\theta &= 1 + (\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) \cr &= 1 + \cos^2 \theta -\cr& \quad (1 - \cos^2 \theta) \cr &= 2\cos^2 \theta \end{aligned}Since LHS = RHS, the identity is proven: $1 + \cos 2\theta \equiv \cot \theta \sin 2\theta$.

(b) Solving the equation:
We substitute our proven identity $1 + \cos 2x = \cot x \sin 2x$ into the given equation: egin{aligned} &(\csc^2 x - 4)(1 + \cos 2x) \cr &\quad = 2\cot^2 x \sin 2x \cr &(\csc^2 x - 4)\cot x \sin 2x \cr &\quad = 2\cot^2 x \sin 2x \end{aligned}Since $x eq 0$ and $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, we know that $\sin 2x eq 0$ and $\cot x eq 0$. Therefore, we can safely divide both sides of the equation by $\cot x \sin 2x$:$$\csc^2 x - 4 = 2\cot x$$

Using the trigonometric identity $\csc^2 x = 1 + \cot^2 x$, we rewrite the equation in terms of $\cot x$:\begin{aligned} 1 + \cot^2 x - 4 &= 2\cot x \cr \cot^2 x - 2\cot x - 3 &= 0 \end{aligned}Factorising this quadratic equation gives:\begin{aligned} (\cot x - 3)(\cot x + 1) &= 0 \cr \cot x &= 3 \cr \cot x &= -1 \end{aligned}

Solving for $x$ by rewriting in terms of $\tan x$:

For $\cot x = 3$:\begin{aligned} \tan x &= \dfrac{1}{3} \cr x &= \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \cr &\approx 0.322\text{ rad} \end{aligned}For $\cot x = -1$:\begin{aligned} \tan x &= -1 \cr x &= \arctan(-1) \cr &= -\dfrac{\pi}{4} \cr &\approx -0.785\text{ rad} \end{aligned}Therefore, the solutions are $x \approx 0.322\text{ radians}$ and $x \approx -0.785\text{ radians}$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &x \approx 0.322\text{ rad} \cr &x \approx -0.785\text{ rad} \end{aligned}

This error is the result of failing to identify that $x = 0$ must be strictly excluded from the domain because the original function contains the term $\csc^2 x$, which is undefined at $x = 0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Excluded Domain Values
bradley_insight.content: Always pay close attention to any restriction statements like $x \neq 0$ or open intervals. Since the original equation features the term $\csc^2 x$, the function is undefined at $x = 0$ ($1 / \sin^2(0)$ is undefined). Even if $x = 0$ appears as a potential algebraic solution during factoring, it must be strictly excluded from the final solution set.

question: (a) Prove that:$$1 - \cos 2\theta \equiv \tan \theta \sin 2\theta$$(b) Hence solve, for $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, the equation:\begin{aligned} &(\sec^2 x - 3)(1 - \cos 2x) \cr &\quad = 3\tan^2 x \sin 2x \end{aligned}Give your answers to 3 decimal places where appropriate.
steps:
(a) Proving the identity:
We start by expanding the right-hand side (RHS) of the identity using the definitions $\tan \theta = \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}$ and $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin \theta \cos \theta$:\begin{aligned} &\tan \theta \sin 2\theta \cr &\quad = \left(\dfrac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}\right)(2\sin \theta \cos \theta) \cr &\quad = 2\sin^2 \theta \end{aligned}Now we expand the left-hand side (LHS) using the double angle identity $\cos 2\theta = \cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta$ and the Pythagorean identity $\cos^2 \theta = 1 - \sin^2 \theta$:\begin{aligned} 1 - \cos 2\theta &= 1 - (\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) \cr &= 1 - \cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta \cr &= (1 - \cos^2 \theta) + \sin^2 \theta \cr &= \sin^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta \cr &= 2\sin^2 \theta \end{aligned}Since LHS = RHS, the identity is proven: $1 - \cos 2\theta \equiv \tan \theta \sin 2\theta$.

(b) Solving the equation:
We substitute our proven identity $1 - \cos 2x = \tan x \sin 2x$ into the given equation:\begin{aligned} &(\sec^2 x - 3)(1 - \cos 2x) \cr &\quad = 3\tan^2 x \sin 2x \cr &(\sec^2 x - 3)\tan x \sin 2x \cr &\quad = 3\tan^2 x \sin 2x \cr &(\sec^2 x - 3)\tan x \sin 2x \cr &\qquad - 3\tan^2 x \sin 2x = 0 \cr &\tan x \sin 2x \big[ (\sec^2 x - 3) \cr &\qquad - 3\tan x \big] = 0 \end{aligned}

This gives two possible cases to solve:

Case 1: $\tan x \sin 2x = 0$
Since $\sin 2x = 2\sin x \cos x$, this simplifies to $2\sin^2 x = 0 \implies \sin x = 0$, which yields:$$x = 0\text{ radians}$$This solution lies within our given interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Case 2: $(\sec^2 x - 3) - 3\tan x = 0$
Using the identity $\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x$, we rewrite this in terms of $\tan x$:\begin{aligned} 1 + \tan^2 x - 3 - 3\tan x &= 0 \cr \tan^2 x - 3\tan x - 2 &= 0 \end{aligned}Solving this quadratic in $\tan x$ using the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} \tan x &= \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{(-3)^2 - 4(1)(-2)}}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2} \end{aligned}

Calculating the numerical values for $x$ in the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$:

For $\tan x = \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}$:\begin{aligned} \tan x &\approx 3.562 \cr x &= \arctan(3.562) \cr &\approx 1.297\text{ rad} \end{aligned}For $\tan x = \dfrac{3 - \sqrt{17}}{2}$:\begin{aligned} \tan x &\approx -0.562 \cr x &= \arctan(-0.562) \cr &\approx -0.512\text{ rad} \end{aligned}Therefore, the solutions are $x = 0\text{ radians}$, $x \approx 1.297\text{ radians}$, and $x \approx -0.512\text{ radians}$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &x = 0\text{ rad} \cr &x \approx 1.297\text{ rad} \cr &x \approx -0.512\text{ rad} \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Retaining Null Factor Solutions
bradley_insight.content: A very common trap when solving equations like $A \cdot B = C \cdot B$ is dividing both sides directly by $B$ without consideration. Dividing by $B$ completely deletes the solution branch where $B = 0$. Instead, always factorise the equation to the form $B(A - C) = 0$ to ensure you retain the null solution branch (here, $\tan x \sin 2x = 0 \implies x = 0$).

We expand the right-hand side (RHS) of the identity using the definitions $\cot \theta = \dfrac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}$ and $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin \theta \cos \theta$:\begin{aligned} &\cot \theta \sin 2\theta \cr &\quad = \left(\dfrac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta}\right)(2\sin \theta \cos \theta) \cr &\quad = 2\cos^2 \theta \end{aligned}Now we expand the left-hand side (LHS) of the identity using the double angle identity $\cos 2\theta = \cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta$ and the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 \theta = 1 - \cos^2 \theta$:\begin{aligned} 1 + \cos 2\theta &= 1 + (\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) \cr &= 1 + \cos^2 \theta \cr & \quad - (1 - \cos^2 \theta) \cr &= 2\cos^2 \theta \end{aligned}Since LHS = RHS, the identity is proven: $1 + \cos 2\theta \equiv \cot \theta \sin 2\theta$.

(b) Solving the equation:
We substitute our proven identity $1 + \cos 2x = \cot x \sin 2x$ into the given equation: egin{aligned} &(\csc^2 x - 3)(1 + \cos 2x) \cr &\quad = 3\cot^2 x \sin 2x \cr &(\csc^2 x - 3)\cot x \sin 2x \cr &\quad = 3\cot^2 x \sin 2x \end{aligned}Since $x eq 0$ and $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, we know that $\sin 2x eq 0$ and $\cot x eq 0$. Therefore, we can safely divide both sides of the equation by $\cot x \sin 2x$:$$\csc^2 x - 3 = 3\cot x$$

Using the trigonometric identity $\csc^2 x = 1 + \cot^2 x$, we rewrite the equation in terms of $\cot x$:\begin{aligned} 1 + \cot^2 x - 3 &= 3\cot x \cr \cot^2 x - 3\cot x - 2 &= 0 \end{aligned}Solving this quadratic in $\cot x$ using the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} \cot x &= \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{(-3)^2 - 4(1)(-2)}}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2} \end{aligned}

Solving for $x$ by rewriting in terms of $\tan x$:

For $\cot x = \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}$:\begin{aligned} \cot x &\approx 3.562 \cr \tan x &\approx 0.281 \cr x &= \arctan(0.281) \cr &\approx 0.274\text{ rad} \end{aligned}For $\cot x = \dfrac{3 - \sqrt{17}}{2}$:\begin{aligned} \cot x &\approx -0.562 \cr \tan x &\approx -1.781 \cr x &= \arctan(-1.781) \cr &\approx -1.059\text{ rad} \end{aligned}Therefore, the solutions are $x \approx 0.274\text{ radians}$ and $x \approx -1.059\text{ radians}$.
Final Answer\begin{aligned} &x \approx 0.274\text{ rad} \cr &x \approx -1.059\text{ rad} \end{aligned}
