bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Restricted Domain Stationary Points
bradley_insight.content: When solving trigonometric stationary points like $\tan x = -1$, always pay extreme attention to the interval constraints (here $0 \le x \le \pi$). While tangent has infinitely many solutions, only $x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ lies in Quadrant II of this restricted domain. Always check your boundaries first!

question:
A circle with centre $C$ has equation $x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 10y - 2 = 0$.

Find:
(i) the coordinates of $C$,
(ii) the radius of the circle.
steps: To find the centre and radius of the circle, complete the square for both the $x$ and $y$ terms:$$x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 10y - 2 = 0$$
Group the $x$ terms and $y$ terms together:$$(x^2 + 6x) + (y^2 - 10y) - 2 = 0$$

Complete the square for each variable:

For $x^2 + 6x$:\begin{aligned} (x + 3)^2 - 9 \end{aligned}

For $y^2 - 10y$:\begin{aligned} (y - 5)^2 - 25 \end{aligned}
Substitute these back into the equation:\begin{aligned} &(x + 3)^2 - 9 \cr &\qquad + (y - 5)^2 - 25 - 2 = 0 \cr &(x + 3)^2 + (y - 5)^2 - 36 = 0 \cr &(x + 3)^2 + (y - 5)^2 = 36 \end{aligned}

(i) Compare to $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2$, where $(a, b)$ is the centre and $r$ is the radius.

Here, $a = -3$ and $b = 5$, giving centre $C(-3, 5)$.
(ii) From the completed square equation, $r^2 = 36$:\begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt{36} \cr &= 6 \end{aligned}So the radius of the circle is $6$.

Final Answer: (i) $(-3, 5)$
(ii) $6$

pi_options.feedback: Ensure you use the correct signs when stating the centre from the completed square form. For $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2$, the centre is $(a, b)$. Since we have $(x + 3)^2$ and $(y - 5)^2$, the centre must be $(-3, 5)$.
You have correctly identified the coordinates of the centre, but the right-hand side of the standard equation represents $r^2$, not $r$. Remember to take the square root of $36$ to find the radius.
Check your arithmetic when completing the square. Ensure you subtract $3^2$ and $5^2$ during the process, then correctly transpose all constants to the right-hand side of the equation.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Don't Slip on Sign Conventions
bradley_insight.content: Always double-check your signs when stating the centre of a circle. A common mistake is to write the centre as $(a, b)$ directly from $(x + a)^2 + (y + b)^2 = r^2$. Remember that the standard form is $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2$, so $(x + 3)^2$ corresponds to $a = -3$ and $(y - 5)^2$ corresponds to $b = 5$.

question:
A circle has equation $x^2 + y^2 - 4x + 12y + k = 0$, where $k$ is a constant. Given that the radius of the circle is $7$,

find:
(i) the value of $k$,
(ii) the coordinates of the centre of this circle.
steps: Group the terms to prepare for completing the square:$$(x^2 - 4x) + (y^2 + 12y) + k = 0$$

Complete the square for each variable:

For $x^2 - 4x$:\begin{aligned} (x - 2)^2 - 4 \end{aligned}

For $y^2 + 12y$:\begin{aligned} (y + 6)^2 - 36 \end{aligned}
Substitute these back into the equation:\begin{aligned} &(x - 2)^2 - 4 \cr &\qquad + (y + 6)^2 - 36 + k = 0 \cr &(x - 2)^2 + (y + 6)^2 - 40 + k = 0 \cr &(x - 2)^2 + (y + 6)^2 = 40 - k \end{aligned}
(i) With radius $r = 7$, $r^2 = 49$:\begin{aligned} 40 - k &= 49 \cr -k &= 9 \cr k &= -9 \end{aligned}
(ii) Comparing $(x - 2)^2 + (y + 6)^2 = 49$ to $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2$, the centre is $(2, -6)$.

Final Answer: (i) $k = -9$
(ii) $(2, -6)$

pi_options.feedback: Ensure you use the square of the radius, $r^2 = 49$, on the right-hand side instead of the radius itself, $r = 7$. Also, check your signs for the centre coordinates.

You found the correct value of $k = -9$, but remember that the centre coordinates $(a, b)$ are derived from $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2$. Since we have $(x - 2)^2$ and $(y + 6)^2$, the centre must be $(2, -6)$.
The coordinates of the centre are correct, but when setting up the equation to solve for $k$, you must equate the constant term to $r^2 = 49$ rather than the radius $r = 7$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Radius and Constant Relationships
bradley_insight.content: For any circle represented in general form $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$, the radius is given by $r = \sqrt{ g^2 + f^2 - c }$. This implies $r^2 = g^2 + f^2 - c$. In this question, $g = -2$, $f = 6$, and $c = k$. Substituting these values in gives \begin{aligned}7^2 $= (-2)^2 + 6^2 - k \cr &\implies 49 = 4 + 36 - k \cr &\implies k = -9\end{aligned}. This formula is a very useful shortcut to remember!

question:
A circle has equation $x^2 + y^2 - 10x - 4y + 11 = 0$.

(i) Show that the point $P(8, 5)$ lies on the circle.
(ii) Find the equation of the tangent to the circle at $P$, giving your answer in the form $ax + by + c = 0$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are integers.
steps: (i) Substitute $x = 8$ and $y = 5$ into the left-hand side of the circle equation:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= 8^2 + 5^2 \cr &\qquad - 10(8) - 4(5) + 11 \cr &= 64 + 25 - 80 - 20 + 11 \cr &= 100 - 100 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}Since $\text{LHS} = \text{RHS} = 0$, $P(8, 5)$ lies on the circle.

(ii) Find the centre by completing the square:\begin{aligned} &(x^2 - 10x) + (y^2 - 4y) + 11 = 0 \cr &(x - 5)^2 - 25 \cr &\qquad + (y - 2)^2 - 4 + 11 = 0 \cr &(x - 5)^2 + (y - 2)^2 = 18 \end{aligned}Thus, the centre of the circle is $C(5, 2)$.
Calculate the gradient of the radius line $CP$:\begin{aligned} m_{\text{radius}} &= \dfrac{5 - 2}{8 - 5} \cr &= \dfrac{3}{3} \cr &= 1 \end{aligned}
The tangent gradient is the negative reciprocal of the radius gradient:\begin{aligned} m_{\text{tangent}} &= -\dfrac{1}{m_{\text{radius}}} \cr &= -1 \end{aligned}
Using $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ at $P(8, 5)$:\begin{aligned} y - 5 &= -1(x - 8) \cr y - 5 &= -x + 8 \cr x + y - 13 &= 0 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $x + y - 13 = 0$

pi_options.feedback: You used a gradient of $1$ for your tangent. Remember that the tangent is perpendicular to the radius line $CP$. Since $m_{\text{radius}} = 1$, the tangent gradient must be $-1$.
Check your final algebraic transposition. Rearranging $y - 5 = -x + 8$ by adding $x$ and subtracting $8$ from both sides should lead to $x + y - 13 = 0$.

The tangent line touches the circle specifically at the point $P(8, 5)$, not at the centre $C(5, 2)$. Ensure you use the coordinates of $P$ when setting up the straight line equation $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Perpendicularity is Key
bradley_insight.content: A tangent and a radius are always perpendicular at the point of contact. This geometrical property is the core link that allows us to find the tangent's gradient. Always compute the radius gradient first, then find its negative reciprocal: $m_{\text{tangent}} \cdot m_{\text{radius}} = -1$.

question:
The line $L$ has equation $y = x + 1$ and the circle $C$ has equation $x^2 + y^2 - 6x - 2y + 5 = 0$.

(i) Find the coordinates of the points of intersection, $A$ and $B$, of the line $L$ and the circle $C$.
(ii) Find the exact length of the chord $AB$, writing your answer as a simplified surd.
steps: (i) Substitute $y = x + 1$ into the circle equation:\begin{aligned} &x^2 + (x + 1)^2 \cr &\qquad - 6x - 2(x + 1) + 5 = 0 \end{aligned}
Expand and simplify the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &x^2 + (x^2 + 2x + 1) \cr &\qquad - 6x - 2x - 2 + 5 = 0 \cr &2x^2 - 6x + 4 = 0 \end{aligned}
Divide by $2$ and factorise:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 3x + 2 &= 0 \cr (x - 1)(x - 2) &= 0 \end{aligned}This yields $x = 1$ and $x = 2$.

Substitute back into $y = x + 1$:

For $x = 1$:\begin{aligned} y &= 1 + 1 \cr &= 2 \implies A(1, 2) \end{aligned}

For $x = 2$:\begin{aligned} y &= 2 + 1 \cr &= 3 \implies B(2, 3) \end{aligned}Thus, the points of intersection are $A(1, 2)$ and $B(2, 3)$.
(ii) Apply the distance formula between $A(1, 2)$ and $B(2, 3)$:\begin{aligned} AB &= \sqrt{(2 - 1)^2 + (3 - 2)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} \cr &= \sqrt{2} \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (i) $A(1, 2)$ and $B(2, 3)$
(ii) $\sqrt{2}$

pi_options.feedback: The points of intersection are correct, but verify your distance formula. The distance between $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ is $\sqrt{ (x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 }$, not the sum of the differences.
Check your factorisation of $x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0$. Since the middle coefficient is negative and the constant is positive, both factors must have negative signs: $(x - 1)(x - 2) = 0$.
The coordinates of $A$ and $B$ are correct, but verify your substitution into the distance formula. Make sure you calculate $(2 - 1)^2 + (3 - 2)^2$ under the square root.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Choose the Simpler Equation
bradley_insight.content: Once you have found the $x$-coordinates of the intersection points, always substitute them back into the linear equation ($y = x + 1$) rather than the quadratic circle equation to find the $y$-coordinates. This is faster and reduces the risk of algebraic errors.

question:
The points $A(-2, 7)$ and $B(6, 1)$ are the endpoints of a diameter of a circle $C$.

Find:
(i) the coordinates of the centre of the circle $C$,
(ii) Show that the equation of the circle $C$ can be written in the form $x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 8y - 5 = 0$.
steps: (i) The centre is the midpoint of the diameter $AB$:\begin{aligned} \text{Centre} &= \left( \dfrac{-2 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{7 + 1}{2} \right) \cr &= \left( \dfrac{4}{2}, \dfrac{8}{2} \right) \cr &= (2, 4) \end{aligned}
(ii) Find $r^2$ from the centre $(2, 4)$ to endpoint $B(6, 1)$:\begin{aligned} r^2 &= (6 - 2)^2 + (1 - 4)^2 \cr &= 4^2 + (-3)^2 \cr &= 16 + 9 \cr &= 25 \end{aligned}
Write the standard equation with centre $(2, 4)$ and $r^2 = 25$:$$ (x - 2)^2 + (y - 4)^2 = 25 $$
Expand and simplify:\begin{aligned} &(x^2 - 4x + 4) \cr &\qquad + (y^2 - 8y + 16) = 25 \cr &x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 8y + 20 = 25 \cr &x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 8y - 5 = 0 \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (i) $(2, 4)$
(ii) $x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 8y - 5 = 0$

pi_options.feedback: You have the correct centre and radius, but remember to subtract $25$ from the left-hand side when transposing to get $0$ on the RHS: $+20 - 25 = -5$.
The midpoint formula is $\left( \dfrac{ x_1 + x_2 }{ 2 }, \dfrac{ y_1 + y_2 }{ 2 } \right)$. Make sure you divide the sum of the coordinates by $2$ to find the correct coordinates of the centre.
The diameter is $10$, which means the radius is $5$, so $r^2 = 5^2 = 25$. Make sure you use the radius squared, not the diameter squared, in the standard circle equation.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Diameter vs. Radius
bradley_insight.content: Be extremely vigilant when dealing with diameter endpoints. A common slip is to use the full distance $AB$ as the radius instead of halving it, or to use $r^2 = (AB)^2$ directly. Always write down the midpoint as the centre, compute the radius $r = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } AB$, and then square it to obtain $r^2$.

question: Solve the equation $|3x - 2| = |x + 4|$.
steps:
To solve an equation of the form $|f(x)| = |g(x)|$, split it into two cases:

Case 1: $3x - 2 = x + 4$

Case 2: $3x - 2 = -(x + 4)$
Solve Case 1:\begin{aligned} 3x - 2 &= x + 4 \cr 2x &= 6 \cr x &= 3 \end{aligned}
Solve Case 2:\begin{aligned} 3x - 2 &= -(x + 4) \cr 3x - 2 &= -x - 4 \cr 4x &= -2 \cr x &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}
Both values satisfy the original equation, giving the solutions $x = 3$ or $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Final Answer: $x = 3$ or $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$

pi_options.feedback: Check your signs in the negative case. Setting $3x - 2 = -(x + 4)$ gives $3x - 2 = -x - 4$. Rearranging this correctly should give $4x = -2$, which yields $x = -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }$, not $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }$.
Verify your algebraic rearrangement for both cases. For $3x - 2 = x + 4$, subtracting $x$ and adding $2$ to both sides gives $2x = 6 \implies x = 3$.
When solving $|f(x)| = |g(x)|$, remember that there are two valid cases to consider: $f(x) = g(x)$ and $f(x) = -g(x)$. Both cases yield valid solutions for this equation.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Squaring vs. Signs
bradley_insight.content: While you can solve $|f(x)| = |g(x)|$ by squaring both sides, this often leads to larger quadratic expressions that are more prone to algebraic errors. Simply splitting the equation into $f(x) = \pm g(x)$ is much faster, cleaner, and avoids squaring numbers like $3^2$ or $4^2$.

question: Solve the equation $|2x - 5| = 3x - 1$.
steps:
To solve $|2x - 5| = 3x - 1$, find the values of $x$ that satisfy both branches, then check for extraneous solutions:

Case 1 (Positive branch): $2x - 5 = 3x - 1$

Case 2 (Negative branch): $2x - 5 = -(3x - 1)$
Solve Case 1:\begin{aligned} 2x - 5 &= 3x - 1 \cr -x &= 4 \cr x &= -4 \end{aligned}
Solve Case 2:\begin{aligned} 2x - 5 &= -(3x - 1) \cr 2x - 5 &= -3x + 1 \cr 5x &= 6 \cr x &= \dfrac{6}{5} \end{aligned}

Check both solutions because the right-hand side must be non-negative:

For $x = -4$, the right-hand side is $3(-4) - 1 = -13$, which is negative. Since a modulus cannot equal a negative number, $x = -4$ is an extraneous solution and must be rejected.

For $x = \dfrac{6}{5}$, the right-hand side is $3\left(\dfrac{6}{5}\right) - 1 = \dfrac{13}{5} \ge 0$, which is valid.
Therefore, the only valid solution is $x = \dfrac{6}{5}$ (or $1.2$).
Final Answer: $x = \dfrac{6}{5}$

pi_options.feedback: An absolute value can never be equal to a negative quantity. If you substitute $x = -4$ into the right-hand side, $3x - 1$ becomes $-13$. Since $|2x - 5|$ cannot equal $-13$, $x = -4$ is an extraneous solution and must be rejected.

Be careful! Substituting $x = -4$ into the original equation yields $|-13| = -13$, which is false. You must always solve the negative branch $2x - 5 = -(3x - 1)$ and reject any solutions that make the RHS negative.
Verify your expansion of the negative branch. Setting $2x - 5 = -(3x - 1)$ gives $2x - 5 = -3x + 1$. Adding $3x$ and adding $5$ to both sides yields $5x = 6$, so $x = \dfrac{ 6 }{ 5 }$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Beware of Extraneous Solutions
bradley_insight.content: When solving an equation of the form $|f(x)| = g(x)$, where $g(x)$ is not inside a modulus, you MUST check your final answers by substituting them back into the original equation (or verifying that $g(x) \ge 0$). Failing to filter out extraneous solutions is a major source of lost marks in Year 2 A Level exams.

question: Solve the inequality $|2x - 3| < |x + 2|$.
steps: Since both sides are non-negative, square both sides to eliminate the absolute value brackets:$$(2x - 3)^2 < (x + 2)^2$$
Expand and rearrange the terms:\begin{aligned} &4x^2 - 12x + 9 < x^2 + 4x + 4 \cr &4x^2 - 12x + 9 \cr &\qquad - (x^2 + 4x + 4) < 0 \cr &3x^2 - 16x + 5 < 0 \end{aligned}
Find the critical values by solving $3x^2 - 16x + 5 = 0$:\begin{aligned} (3x - 1)(x - 5) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives critical values $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $x = 5$.
Since $y = 3x^2 - 16x + 5$ is an upward-opening parabola, the inequality is satisfied where the curve lies strictly below the $x$-axis:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3} < x < 5 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3} < x < 5$

pi_options.feedback: The quadratic inequality is $3x^2 - 16x + 5 < 0$. For a positive $x^2$ coefficient, the quadratic expression is negative (less than zero) between the roots, not outside them.
Check your factorisation. The factored form is $(3x - 1)(x - 5) = 0$. Setting $3x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }$, not $-\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }$.

Pay close attention to the inequality sign in the question. The original inequality uses strict inequality ($<$), so your final answer must also use strict inequalities ($<$) rather than weak inequalities ($\le$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Why Squaring Works
bradley_insight.content: Squaring is highly effective for inequalities of the form $|f(x)| < |g(x)|$ because both sides are guaranteed to be non-negative. It completely avoids having to consider multiple boundary cases for each modulus. Always remember to collect all terms onto one side, find the critical values, and sketch the quadratic curve to identify the correct interval.

question: Solve the equation $x^2 - 3|x| - 10 = 0$.
steps: Use the identity $x^2 = |x|^2$ to rewrite the equation entirely in terms of $|x|$:$$|x|^2 - 3|x| - 10 = 0$$
Factorise the quadratic:\begin{aligned} (y - 5)(y + 2) = 0 \end{aligned}So $y = 5$ or $y = -2$.
Since $y = |x| \ge 0$, reject $y = -2$, leaving $|x| = 5$.
Solve $|x| = 5$:\begin{aligned} x = 5 \text{ or } x = -5 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $x = 5$ or $x = -5$

pi_options.feedback: Remember that $|x|$ represents the absolute value of $x$, which can never be negative. Therefore, $|x| = -2$ has no real solutions, and you must reject this branch.
While you correctly rejected the negative root for $|x|$, remember that $|x| = 5$ has two solutions: $x = 5$ and $x = -5$, as both have an absolute value of $5$.
Check your factorisation of $y^2 - 3y - 10 = 0$. Since the middle term is $-3$, the factors must be $(y - 5)(y + 2) = 0$, giving $y = 5$ as the valid positive root.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: $x^2$ and $|x|^2$
bradley_insight.content: The substitution $x^2 = |x|^2$ is an extremely powerful technique for solving equations that mix standard algebraic terms with modulus terms. This allows you to treat the equation as a standard quadratic in terms of $|x|$. Always remember to apply the condition $|x| \ge 0$ to eliminate any invalid negative roots before solving for $x$.

question: Solve the inequality $|2x - 1| \ge 5 - x$.
steps: Find the critical intersection points by solving the corresponding equation:$$|2x - 1| = 5 - x$$

Split into positive and negative cases:

Case 1: $2x - 1 = 5 - x$

Case 2: $2x - 1 = -(5 - x)$
Solve Case 1:\begin{aligned} 2x - 1 &= 5 - x \cr 3x &= 6 \cr x &= 2 \end{aligned}
Solve Case 2:\begin{aligned} 2x - 1 &= -5 + x \cr x &= -4 \end{aligned}The critical values are $x = -4$ and $x = 2$.

Test values in each region defined by $x = -4$ and $x = 2$:

Region 1 ($x \le -4$): Test $x = -5$.
$|2(-5) - 1| = 11$ and $5 - (-5) = 10$. Since $11 \ge 10$, this region is part of the solution.

Region 2 ($-4 < x < 2$): Test $x = 0$.
$|2(0) - 1| = 1$ and $5 - 0 = 5$. Since $1 \ge 5$ is false, this region is not part of the solution.

Region 3 ($x \ge 2$): Test $x = 3$.
$|2(3) - 1| = 5$ and $5 - 3 = 2$. Since $5 \ge 2$, this region is part of the solution.

Combining these results gives $x \le -4$ or $x \ge 2$.
Final Answer: $x \le -4$ or $x \ge 2$

pi_options.feedback: The inequality $|2x - 1| \ge 5 - x$ is satisfied in the outer regions. If you test a value in the inner region, like $x = 0$, you get $1 \ge 5$, which is clearly false.
You have only identified one of the boundaries. When solving a modulus equation or inequality, you must consider both positive and negative branches to find all critical points.
Check your algebra when finding the critical values. For $2x - 1 = 5 - x$, adding $x$ to both sides gives $3x = 6 \implies x = 2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Visualising Modulus Inequalities
bradley_insight.content: Visualising this graphically is incredibly helpful. The graph of $y = |2x - 1|$ is a V-shape with its vertex at $x = 0.5$. The graph of $y = 5 - x$ is a straight line sloping downwards. The two graphs intersect at $x = -4$ and $x = 2$. Looking at the graphs, the V-shape lies on or above the line for $x \le -4$ and for $x \ge 2$. This perfectly matches our algebraic test results!

question:
A rectangular courtyard is being planned. The requirements for the design are:

• the length of the courtyard is to be $4\text{ m}$ longer than its width,
• the length of the courtyard must be at least $10\text{ m}$,
• the area of the courtyard must be less than $96\text{ m}^2$.

Find the set of possible values for the width, $w$, of the courtyard.
steps:
Let $w$ be the width of the courtyard in metres. Since the length is $4\text{ m}$ longer than the width, we can write the length $L$ as:
$L = w + 4$

We are given that the length must be at least $10\text{ m}$. This gives our first linear inequality:
\begin{aligned} w + 4 &\ge 10 \cr w &\ge 6 \end{aligned}

Next, the area of the courtyard must be less than $96\text{ m}^2$. Since $\text{Area} = \text{width} \times \text{length}$, we set up a quadratic inequality:
\begin{aligned} w(w + 4) &< 96 \cr w^2 + 4w - 96 &< 0 \end{aligned}

To solve $w^2 + 4w - 96 < 0$, find the critical values by factorising the corresponding quadratic equation $w^2 + 4w - 96 = 0$:
\begin{aligned} (w + 12)(w - 8) &= 0 \end{aligned}
This gives critical values of $w = -12$ and $w = 8$.

The inequality $w^2 + 4w - 96 < 0$ is satisfied where the quadratic expression is negative. Since the $w^2$ coefficient is positive, the curve is a U-shaped parabola, which lies below the $x$-axis between its roots:
$-12 < w < 8$

Finally, combine our constraints. We have $w \ge 6$ and $-12 < w < 8$ (and physical width $w$ must be positive, which is already satisfied by $w \ge 6$):
The overlapping region gives the final set of possible values for the width:
$6 \le w < 8$

pi_options.feedback: You have only solved the area inequality. You must also consider the requirement that the length of the courtyard must be at least $10\text{ m}$, which yields $w \ge 6$.

Check your inequality signs carefully. The area must be strictly less than $96\text{ m}^2$, which means $w^2 + 4w - 96 < 0$. Therefore, the upper boundary must be a strict inequality: $w < 8$, not $w \le 8$.
Check the inequality for the length requirement. The length must be at least $10\text{ m}$, which is a weak inequality ($\ge$). Therefore, the lower boundary must be $w \ge 6$, not $w > 6$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Combining Inequality Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: Always list out your boundaries carefully before combining them. A common slip is to write $w < 8$ and forget that the physical width must be positive, or to ignore the other linear constraint. Draw a quick number line to find where all inequalities overlap: here, $w \ge 6$ and $w < 8$ overlap to give $6 \le w < 8$.

question:
A right-angled triangle has a base of $x\text{ cm}$ and a height that is $5\text{ cm}$ shorter than the base. The requirements are:

• the height must be at least $4\text{ cm}$,
• the area of the triangle must be less than $42\text{ cm}^2$.

Find the set of possible values for $x$.
steps:
Let the base of the triangle be $x\text{ cm}$. The height $h$ is $5\text{ cm}$ shorter than the base, so:
$h = x - 5$

We are given that the height must be at least $4\text{ cm}$. This gives our first inequality:
\begin{aligned} x - 5 &\ge 4 \cr x &\ge 9 \end{aligned}

The area of the triangle must be less than $42\text{ cm}^2$. Using the formula $\text{Area} = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$:
\begin{aligned} \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } x (x - 5) &< 42 \cr x(x - 5) &< 84 \cr x^2 - 5x - 84 &< 0 \end{aligned}

Solve $x^2 - 5x - 84 < 0$ by finding the critical values. Factorise the quadratic equation:
\begin{aligned} (x - 12)(x + 7) &= 0 \end{aligned}
This gives critical values of $x = 12$ and $x = -7$.

The quadratic expression is negative between its roots, which gives the interval:
$-7 < x < 12$

Now, combine the conditions $x \ge 9$ and $-7 < x < 12$. The overlap of these regions gives the final set of possible values for $x$:
$9 \le x < 12$

pi_options.feedback: The height must be at least $4\text{ cm}$, which gives $x - 5 \ge 4 \implies x \ge 9$. This is a stronger condition than simply requiring the height to be positive ($x > 5$).
The requirement is that the height must be at least $4\text{ cm}$, which includes the possibility of it being exactly $4\text{ cm}$. Therefore, the lower bound must be a weak inequality ($x \ge 9$).
The area must be strictly less than $42\text{ cm}^2$, which means the upper boundary must be a strict inequality ($x < 12$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Don't Forget the Half
bradley_insight.content: A very common slip in triangle questions is forgetting the $\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }$ in the area formula, which would lead to $x(x - 5) < 42$ and messy non-integer roots. Always write out the full geometric formula $\text{Area} = \frac{ 1 }{ 2 } b h$ first before substituting algebraic expressions.

question:
A cardboard box is designed with a square base of side length $y\text{ cm}$ and a height of $8\text{ cm}$. The requirements are:

• the volume of the box must be greater than $128\text{ cm}^3$,
• the total surface area of the box must be at most $450\text{ cm}^2$.

Find the set of possible values for $y$.
steps:
The base of the box is a square with side length $y\text{ cm}$, and the height is $8\text{ cm}$. The volume $V$ of the box is:
\begin{aligned} V &= y^2 \times 8 \cr V &= 8y^2 \end{aligned}

Since the volume must be greater than $128\text{ cm}^3$, we write:
\begin{aligned} 8y^2 &> 128 \cr y^2 &> 16 \end{aligned}
Since $y$ must be positive, this gives:
$y > 4$

The total surface area $SA$ of a closed box with a square base of side $y$ and height $8$ consists of the top and bottom squares ($2y^2$) plus the four vertical side faces ($4 \times 8y$):
\begin{aligned} SA &= 2y^2 + 32y \end{aligned}

Since the total surface area must be at most $450\text{ cm}^2$, we set up the quadratic inequality:
\begin{aligned} 2y^2 + 32y &\le 450 \cr 2y^2 + 32y - 450 &\le 0 \cr y^2 + 16y - 225 &\le 0 \end{aligned}

Solve $y^2 + 16y - 225 \le 0$ by finding the critical values. Factorise the quadratic equation:
\begin{aligned} (y + 25)(y - 9) &= 0 \end{aligned}
This gives critical values of $y = -25$ and $y = 9$.

The quadratic expression is non-positive between its roots, which gives:
$-25 \le y \le 9$

Now, combine our constraints: $y > 4$ and $-25 \le y \le 9$. The overlapping region gives our final set of possible values:
$4 < y \le 9$

pi_options.feedback: The volume must be strictly greater than $128\text{ cm}^3$, which yields $y^2 > 16 \implies y > 4$. This requires a strict inequality ($>$) for the lower boundary.
Make sure to incorporate all constraints. While the side length must be positive, the volume requirement that $V > 128\text{ cm}^3$ restricts $y$ to be strictly greater than $4$.
The total surface area must be at most $450\text{ cm}^2$, which allows the surface area to be exactly $450\text{ cm}^2$. Therefore, the upper boundary must be a weak inequality ($y \le 9$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Identifying Total Surface Area
bradley_insight.content: A closed cuboid has six faces. For a box with a square base of side $y$ and height $h$, the top and bottom faces are squares of area $y^2$, and the four sides are rectangles of area $y h$. Always read carefully to see if a box is 'closed' or 'open'—if it were open-topped, the surface area would only include one square base: $y^2 + 4yh$.

question:
A rectangular paddock is to be enclosed by a fence. The width of the paddock is $x\text{ m}$ and the length is $2x - 5\text{ m}$. The requirements are:

• the total length of fencing used (the perimeter) must be at least $50\text{ m}$,
• the area of the paddock must be at most $300\text{ m}^2$.

Find the set of possible values for $x$.
steps:
The width of the paddock is $x$ and the length is $2x - 5$. The perimeter $P$ is the total sum of all four sides:
\begin{aligned} P &= 2(x + 2x - 5) \cr P &= 2(3x - 5) \cr P &= 6x - 10 \end{aligned}

We are given that the perimeter must be at least $50\text{ m}$. This gives our first linear inequality:
\begin{aligned} 6x - 10 &\ge 50 \cr 6x &\ge 60 \cr x &\ge 10 \end{aligned}

The area of the paddock must be at most $300\text{ m}^2$. Using the formula $\text{Area} = \text{width} \times \text{length}$:
\begin{aligned} x(2x - 5) &\le 300 \cr 2x^2 - 5x - 300 &\le 0 \end{aligned}

Solve $2x^2 - 5x - 300 \le 0$ by finding the critical values. We can factorise this quadratic expression by splitting the middle term:
\begin{aligned} 2x^2 - 25x + 24x - 300 &= 0 \cr x(2x - 25) + 12(2x - 25) &= 0 \cr (x + 12)(2x - 25) &= 0 \end{aligned}
This gives critical values of $x = -12$ and $x = 12.5$ (or $\dfrac{ 25 }{ 2 }$).

Since the quadratic expression is non-positive between its roots, the interval is:
$-12 \le x \le 12.5$

Finally, combine the two constraints $x \ge 10$ and $-12 \le x \le 12.5$. The overlapping region gives the final set of possible values for $x$:
$10 \le x \le 12.5$

pi_options.feedback: The area must be at most $300\text{ m}^2$, which means it can be exactly $300\text{ m}^2$. Thus, the upper boundary must be a weak inequality ($x \le 12.5$).
The perimeter must be at least $50\text{ m}$, which means it can be exactly $50\text{ m}$. Thus, the lower boundary must be a weak inequality ($x \ge 10$).
Remember to apply the perimeter constraint. While the width must be positive, requiring the perimeter to be at least $50\text{ m}$ restricts $x$ to be at least $10$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Splitting the Middle Term
bradley_insight.content: To factorise $2x^2 - 5x - 300$, look for two numbers that multiply to $2 \times (-300) = -600$ and add to $-5$. Since $24 \times (-25) = -600$ and $24 + (-25) = -5$, we split the middle term as $-25x + 24x$. Grouping terms then makes factorising straightforward.

question:
A small company's weekly profit, $P$ (in hundreds of pounds), from producing $x$ units of a product is modelled by $P = 14x - x^2 - 24$. The company wants to ensure that:

• the weekly profit is at least $16$ hundred pounds,
• the number of units produced is strictly greater than $5$.

Find the set of possible values for $x$.
steps:
The profit equation is $P = 14x - x^2 - 24$. We require the profit to be at least $16$ (since $P$ is already defined in hundreds of pounds):
$14x - x^2 - 24 \ge 16$

Rearrange this into standard quadratic inequality form with a positive $x^2$ coefficient:
\begin{aligned} -x^2 + 14x - 40 &\ge 0 \cr x^2 - 14x + 40 &\le 0 \end{aligned}

Solve $x^2 - 14x + 40 \le 0$ by finding the critical values. Factorise the quadratic expression:
\begin{aligned} (x - 4)(x - 10) &= 0 \end{aligned}
This gives critical values of $x = 4$ and $x = 10$.

The quadratic expression is non-positive between its roots, which gives:
$4 \le x \le 10$

Now, combine this with the constraint that the number of units produced is strictly greater than $5$ ($x > 5$):
The overlapping region between $4 \le x \le 10$ and $x > 5$ is:
$5 < x \le 10$
Final Answer: $5 < x \le 10$

pi_options.feedback: You have correctly solved the profit inequality, but you must also incorporate the requirement that the number of units produced must be strictly greater than $5$ ($x > 5$).
The question specifies that the number of units produced must be strictly greater than $5$, which excludes $5$ itself. Therefore, the lower boundary must be a strict inequality ($x > 5$).
The profit must be at least $16$ hundred pounds, which allows it to be exactly $16$. Therefore, the upper boundary must be a weak inequality ($x \le 10$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Reversing the Inequality Sign
bradley_insight.content: When rearranging $-x^2 + 14x - 40 \ge 0$ by multiplying the entire inequality by $-1$, you MUST reverse the inequality sign. Multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number flips the direction of the sign: $\ge$ becomes $\le$.

question:
The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined for all real values of $x$ by $f(x) = x^3$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 3$.

(i) Write down expressions for:
(a) $fg(x)$,
(b) $gf(x)$.

(ii) Hence find the real values of $x$ for which $fg(x) - gf(x) = 60$.
steps: (i)(a) Substitute $g(x)$ into $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} &fg(x) \cr &\quad = f(x^2 + 3) \cr &\quad = (x^2 + 3)^3 \end{aligned}
(i)(b) Substitute $f(x)$ into $g(x)$:\begin{aligned} &gf(x) \cr &\quad = g(x^3) \cr &\quad = (x^3)^2 + 3 \cr &\quad = x^6 + 3 \end{aligned}
(ii) Set up the equation $fg(x) - gf(x) = 60$:\begin{aligned} &(x^2 + 3)^3 \cr &\qquad - (x^6 + 3) = 60 \end{aligned}

Expand $(x^2 + 3)^3$ using binomial expansion:\begin{aligned} &(x^2 + 3)^3 \cr &\quad = (x^2)^3 \cr &\qquad + 3(x^2)^2(3) \cr &\qquad + 3(x^2)(3)^2 \cr &\qquad + 3^3 \cr &\quad = x^6 + 9x^4 \cr &\qquad + 27x^2 + 27 \end{aligned}
Substitute back and simplify:\begin{aligned} &x^6 + 9x^4 + 27x^2 + 27 \cr &\qquad - (x^6 + 3) = 60 \cr &9x^4 + 27x^2 + 24 = 60 \cr &9x^4 + 27x^2 - 36 = 0 \end{aligned}
Divide the equation by $9$:\begin{aligned} &x^4 + 3x^2 - 4 = 0 \end{aligned}
Let $u = x^2$, where $u \ge 0$:\begin{aligned} &u^2 + 3u - 4 = 0 \cr &(u + 4)(u - 1) = 0 \cr &u = -4 \text{ or } u = 1 \end{aligned}

Since $u = x^2 \ge 0$, reject $u = -4$:\begin{aligned} &x^2 = 1 \cr &x = \pm 1 \end{aligned}

Thus, the real values are $x = 1$ or $x = -1$.
Final Answer: $x = 1$ or $x = -1$

pi_options.feedback: Remember that $x^2$ cannot be negative for real values of $x$. When solving for $u = -4$, $x^2 = -4$ has no real solutions, so you must reject this root.
While you correctly identified $x = 1$, remember that $x^2 = 1$ has two real solutions: $x = 1$ and $x = -1$.
Verify your division by $9$ and your subsequent factorisation. The simplified equation should be $x^4 + 3x^2 - 4 = 0$, leading to $u = 1$, which gives $x = \pm 1$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Spotting Hidden Quadratics
bradley_insight.content: Equations of the form $ax^4 + bx^2 + c = 0$ are 'equations in quadratic form'. By using the substitution $u = x^2$, you can solve them using standard quadratic methods. Always remember to filter your final $u$ values, as $u = x^2$ means any negative values of $u$ will yield no real solutions for $x$.

question:
The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined for all real values of $x$ by $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ and $g(x) = 3x - 2$.

(i) Write down expressions for:
(a) $fg(x)$,
(b) $gf(x)$.

(ii) Hence find the values of $x$ for which $fg(x) - gf(x) = 52$.
steps: (i)(a) Substitute $g(x) = 3x - 2$ into $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} &fg(x) \cr &\quad = f(3x - 2) \cr &\quad = (3x - 2)^2 + 1 \cr &\quad = 9x^2 - 12x + 4 + 1 \cr &\quad = 9x^2 - 12x + 5 \end{aligned}
(i)(b) Substitute $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ into $g(x)$:\begin{aligned} &gf(x) \cr &\quad = g(x^2 + 1) \cr &\quad = 3(x^2 + 1) - 2 \cr &\quad = 3x^2 + 3 - 2 \cr &\quad = 3x^2 + 1 \end{aligned}
(ii) Set up the equation $fg(x) - gf(x) = 52$:\begin{aligned} &(9x^2 - 12x + 5) \cr &\qquad - (3x^2 + 1) = 52 \end{aligned}
Simplify the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &6x^2 - 12x + 4 = 52 \cr &6x^2 - 12x - 48 = 0 \end{aligned}
Divide by $6$ and factorise:\begin{aligned} &x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0 \cr &(x - 4)(x + 2) = 0 \cr &x = 4 \text{ or } x = -2 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $x = 4$ or $x = -2$

pi_options.feedback: A quadratic equation $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$ factorises into $(x-4)(x+2) = 0$, which yields two solutions. Make sure you don't lose the negative solution: $x = -2$.
Check your factorisation of $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$. Since the middle term is $-2x$, the factors must be $(x - 4)(x + 2) = 0$, which yields solutions of $x = 4$ and $x = -2$, not the other way around.
Make sure you divide all terms of the equation $6x^2 - 12x - 48 = 0$ by $6$ correctly. This should simplify to $x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Order of Composition Matters
bradley_insight.content: Always remember that composite functions are generally non-commutative, meaning $fg(x) \neq gf(x)$. In this question, $fg(x) = 9x^2 - 12x + 5$ and $gf(x) = 3x^2 + 1$ are completely different functions. Always apply the inner function first, then substitute that entire result into the outer function.

question:
The function $f$ is defined for $x \ge 1$ by $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1} + 3$.

(i) Find an expression for $f^{-1}(x)$, stating its domain.
(ii) Solve the equation $f(x) = f^{-1}(x)$.
steps: (i) Set $y = f(x)$ and rearrange for $x$:\begin{aligned} &y = \sqrt{x - 1} + 3 \cr &y - 3 = \sqrt{x - 1} \end{aligned}
Square both sides and isolate $x$:\begin{aligned} &(y - 3)^2 = x - 1 \cr &x = (y - 3)^2 + 1 \end{aligned}
Swap variables to write the inverse function:\begin{aligned} &f^{-1}(x) = (x - 3)^2 + 1 \end{aligned}
The domain of $f^{-1}(x)$ is the range of $f(x)$. Since $\sqrt{x - 1} \ge 0$, we have $f(x) \ge 3$. Thus, the domain is $x \ge 3$.
(ii) Solve $f(x) = f^{-1}(x)$ along the line $y = x$ by solving $f(x) = x$:\begin{aligned} &\sqrt{x - 1} + 3 = x \cr &\sqrt{x - 1} = x - 3 \end{aligned}
Square both sides for $x \ge 3$:\begin{aligned} &x - 1 = (x - 3)^2 \cr &x - 1 = x^2 - 6x + 9 \cr &x^2 - 7x + 10 = 0 \cr &(x - 2)(x - 5) = 0 \cr &x = 2 \text{ or } x = 5 \end{aligned}
Since the domain requires $x \ge 3$, reject $x = 2$, leaving $x = 5$.

Final Answer: (i) $f^{-1}(x) = (x - 3)^2 + 1$ with domain $x \ge 3$
(ii) $x = 5$

pi_options.feedback: The domain of the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ is equal to the range of the original function $f(x)$, not its domain. Since $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1} + 3$ and $\sqrt{x - 1} \ge 0$, the range is $f(x) \ge 3$, so the domain of $f^{-1}(x)$ must be $x \ge 3$.
You must check your solutions against the domain restriction. Since the domain of $f^{-1}(x)$ is $x \ge 3$, the value $x = 2$ lies outside the domain and must be rejected as an extraneous solution.
Check your algebra when finding the inverse function. Rearranging $y = \sqrt{x - 1} + 3$ starts by subtracting $3$ from both sides, yielding $y - 3 = \sqrt{x - 1}$, not adding $3$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The y = x Intersection Trick
bradley_insight.content: For any strictly increasing function $f(x)$, the curves $y = f(x)$ and $y = f^{-1}(x)$ only intersect along the line of symmetry $y = x$. This is an incredibly powerful shortcut: instead of equating $f(x) = f^{-1}(x)$ (which often leads to a complex quartic equation), simply solve $f(x) = x$.

question:
The function $f$ is defined for $x > 2$ by $f(x) = \ln(x - 2)$, and the function $g$ is defined for all real values of $x$ by $g(x) = \mathrm{e}^{3x} + 2$.

(i) Write down expressions for:
(a) $fg(x)$,
(b) $gf(x)$,
simplifying your answers as far as possible.

(ii) Solve the equation $gf(x) - fg(x) = 10 - 3x$.
steps: (i)(a) Substitute $g(x) = \mathrm{e}^{3x} + 2$ into $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} &fg(x) \cr &\quad = f(\mathrm{e}^{3x} + 2) \cr &\quad = \ln((\mathrm{e}^{3x} + 2) - 2) \cr &\quad = \ln(\mathrm{e}^{3x}) \cr &\quad = 3x \end{aligned}

(i)(b) Substitute $f(x) = \ln(x - 2)$ into $g(x)$:\begin{aligned} &gf(x) \cr &\quad = g(\ln(x - 2)) \cr &\quad = \mathrm{e}^{3\ln(x - 2)} + 2 \cr &\quad = \mathrm{e}^{\ln((x - 2)^3)} + 2 \cr &\quad = (x - 2)^3 + 2 \end{aligned}
(ii) Set up $gf(x) - fg(x) = 10 - 3x$:\begin{aligned} &(x - 2)^3 + 2 - 3x \cr &\quad = 10 - 3x \end{aligned}
Add $3x$ to both sides and isolate the cubed term:\begin{aligned} &(x - 2)^3 + 2 = 10 \cr &(x - 2)^3 = 8 \end{aligned}

Take the cube root of both sides:\begin{aligned} &x - 2 = 2 \cr &x = 4 \end{aligned}

Since $x = 4$ satisfies $x > 2$, it is the valid real solution.

Final Answer: (i) $fg(x) = 3x$, $gf(x) = (x - 2)^3 + 2$
(ii) $x = 4$

pi_options.feedback: Remember the log power law: $3\ln(x - 2) = \ln((x - 2)^3)$. Thus, $\mathrm{e}^{3\ln(x - 2)} = (x - 2)^3$, not $3(x - 2)$.
The domain of $f(x)$ is $x > 2$, which means $x = 2$ is outside the domain and would make $\ln(x - 2)$ undefined. Solving $(x - 2)^3 = 8$ leads to $x - 2 = 2$, which gives $x = 4$.
To solve $(x - 2)^3 = 8$, you need to take the cube root of both sides of the equation, which gives $x - 2 = 2$, not a square root.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Simplifying Log exponentials
bradley_insight.content: A crucial algebraic identity to master is $\mathrm{e}^{\ln(A)} = A$. When simplifying expressions like $\mathrm{e}^{k\ln(A)}$, you must first use the power law of logarithms to write it as $\mathrm{e}^{\ln(A^k)}$, which simplifies directly to $A^k$. Never write $\mathrm{e}^{k\ln(A)} = kA$.

question:
The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined for all real values of $x$ by $f(x) = 2x - 3$ and $g(x) = x^2 - 4x$.

(i) Find the range of $g(x)$.
(ii) Show that the composite function $gf(x)$ can be written in the form $gf(x) = 4(x - a)(x - b)$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants to be found.
(iii) Find the range of the composite function $fg(x)$.
steps: (i) Complete the square for $g(x) = x^2 - 4x$:\begin{aligned} &g(x) \cr &\quad = (x - 2)^2 - 2^2 \cr &\quad = (x - 2)^2 - 4 \end{aligned}
Since $(x - 2)^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$, the minimum value is $-4$. Thus, the range is $g(x) \ge -4$.
(ii) Substitute $f(x) = 2x - 3$ into $g(x)$:\begin{aligned} &gf(x) \cr &\quad = g(2x - 3) \cr &\quad = (2x - 3)^2 \cr &\qquad - 4(2x - 3) \end{aligned}
Expand and simplify:\begin{aligned} &gf(x) \cr &\quad = (4x^2 - 12x + 9) \cr &\qquad - (8x - 12) \cr &\quad = 4x^2 - 20x + 21 \end{aligned}
Factorise the quadratic expression:\begin{aligned} &4x^2 - 20x + 21 \cr &\quad = (2x - 3)(2x - 7) \end{aligned}

Factorise out $2$ from each bracket:\begin{aligned} &(2x - 3)(2x - 7) \cr &\quad = 2(x - 1.5) \cr &\qquad \times 2(x - 3.5) \cr &\quad = 4(x - 1.5)(x - 3.5) \end{aligned}

Thus, $a = 1.5$ and $b = 3.5$.
(iii) Write the composite function $fg(x)$:\begin{aligned} &fg(x) \cr &\quad = f(g(x)) \cr &\quad = 2(g(x)) - 3 \end{aligned}

Since $g(x) \ge -4$:\begin{aligned} &fg(x) \cr &\quad \ge 2(-4) - 3 \cr &\quad \ge -11 \end{aligned}

So the range is $fg(x) \ge -11$.

Final Answer: (i) $g(x) \ge -4$
(ii) $a = 1.5$, $b = 3.5$
(iii) $fg(x) \ge -11$

pi_options.feedback: Check your factorisation of $4x^2 - 20x + 21$. Expanding $4(x - 3)(x - 1.75)$ gives $4x^2 - 19x + 21$, which is incorrect. Factorising $(2x-3)(2x-7)$ gives $4(x - 1.5)(x - 3.5)$, so $a = 1.5$ and $b = 3.5$.
When finding the range of $fg(x) = 2(g(x)) - 3$, you must use the range of $g(x)$, which is $g(x) \ge -4$. Substituting the minimum value of $-4$ gives $2(-4) - 3 = -11$, not $-3$.
Check the range of $g(x) = x^2 - 4x$. Completing the square gives $(x-2)^2 - 4$. Since $(x-2)^2 \ge 0$, the minimum value is $-4$, so the range of $g(x)$ is $g(x) \ge -4$, not $g(x) \ge 0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Finding the Range of Composites
bradley_insight.content: To find the range of a composite function $fg(x) = f(g(x))$, you must trace the output of the inner function $g(x)$ and use it as the domain for the outer function $f(x)$. Since the inner range is $g(x) \ge -4$ and the outer function $f(x) = 2x - 3$ is strictly increasing, applying $f$ to the minimum boundary yields $2(-4) - 3 = -11$, which determines the final range boundary.

question:
Consider the definite integral $I = \int_{0}^{4} \dfrac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}}\text{d}x$.

(i) Use the trapezium rule, with two strips of equal width, to show that:

\begin{aligned} &I \approx 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}

(ii) Use the substitution $x = u^2$ to find the exact value of $I$.

(iii) Using your answers to parts (i) and (ii), show that $\ln(3) \approx k - \sqrt{2}$, where $k$ is a rational number to be determined.
steps: (i) The interval is $[0, 4]$. With $2$ strips of equal width, the width of each strip $h$ is:\begin{aligned} &h = \dfrac{4 - 0}{2} \cr &\quad = 2 \end{aligned}

The $x$-coordinates are $x_0 = 0$, $x_1 = 2$, and $x_2 = 4$. Evaluate $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 + \sqrt{x}}$ at each coordinate:

• $f(0) = 1$

• $f(2) = \dfrac{1}{1 + \sqrt{2}}$

• $f(4) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Apply the trapezium rule formula:\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(0) + f(4) + 2f(2)\big] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{2}{2}\left[1 + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{2}{1 + \sqrt{2}}\right] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{2}{1 + \sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}

Rationalise the denominator of the fractional term:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{2}{1 + \sqrt{2}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2(1 - \sqrt{2})}{(1 + \sqrt{2})(1 - \sqrt{2})} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2 - 2\sqrt{2}}{1 - 2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2 - 2\sqrt{2}}{-1} \cr &\quad = 2\sqrt{2} - 2 \end{aligned}
Substitute this back into the approximation to complete part (i):\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{4}{3} + 2\sqrt{2} - 2 \cr &\quad \approx 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}

(ii) Use the substitution $x = u^2$, which gives $\text{d}x = 2u\text{d}u$ and $\sqrt{x} = u$.

Find the new integration limits:

• When $x = 0$, $u = 0$

• When $x = 4$, $u = 2$
Substitute these into the integral:\begin{aligned} &I = \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{1}{1 + u}(2u)\text{d}u \cr &\quad = \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{2u}{1 + u}\text{d}u \end{aligned}

Rewrite the integrand by splitting $2u = 2(1 + u) - 2$:\begin{aligned} &I = \int_{0}^{2} \left(2 - \dfrac{2}{1 + u}\right)\text{d}u \cr &\quad = \big[2u - 2\ln(1 + u)\big]_{0}^{2} \cr &\quad = (4 - 2\ln(3)) \cr &\qquad - (0 - 2\ln(1)) \cr &\quad = 4 - 2\ln(3) \end{aligned}

(iii) Equate the exact value of $I$ and the trapezium rule approximation:\begin{aligned} &4 - 2\ln(3) \cr &\quad \approx 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{2}{3} \cr &-2\ln(3) \cr &\quad \approx 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{14}{3} \cr &2\ln(3) \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{14}{3} - 2\sqrt{2} \cr &\ln(3) \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{7}{3} - \sqrt{2} \end{aligned}

Thus, the rational number is $k = \dfrac{7}{3}$.

Final Answer: (i) $I \approx 2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{2}{3}$
(ii) $I = 4 - 2\ln(3)$
(iii) $k = \dfrac{7}{3}$

pi_options.feedback: Check your algebra when transposing the equation to isolate $\ln(3)$. Adding $\dfrac{2}{3}$ to $4$ yields $\dfrac{14}{3}$, and dividing this by $2$ gives $k = \dfrac{7}{3}$, not $\dfrac{5}{3}$.
Check your integration steps in part (ii). Evaluating $[2u]_0^2$ yields $2(2) - 0 = 4$, not $2$.
Check your rationalisation in part (i). The term $\dfrac{2}{1 + \sqrt{2}}$ rationalises to $2\sqrt{2} - 2$. Adding this to $\dfrac{4}{3}$ yields $2\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{2}{3}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Splitting Integrands
bradley_insight.content: When integrating an algebraic fraction where the numerator and denominator have the same degree (like $\dfrac{2u}{u + 1}$), always use algebraic long division or a clever manipulation like $2u = 2(u + 1) - 2$ first. This allows you to split the fraction into $2 - \dfrac{2}{u + 1}$, which is instantly integrable.

question:
Consider the definite integral $I = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}\text{d}x$.

(i) Use the trapezium rule, with two strips of equal width, to show that:

\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{31}{40} \end{aligned}

(ii) Find the exact value of $I$ in terms of $\pi$.

(iii) Using your answers to parts (i) and (ii), show that $\pi \approx k$, where $k$ is a rational number to be determined.
steps: (i) The interval is $[0, 1]$. With $2$ strips of equal width, the width of each strip $h$ is:\begin{aligned} &h = \dfrac{1 - 0}{2} \cr &\quad = 0.5 \end{aligned}

The $x$-coordinates are $x_0 = 0$, $x_1 = 0.5$, and $x_2 = 1$. Evaluate $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$ at each coordinate:

• $f(0) = 1$

• $f(0.5) = \dfrac{4}{5}$

• $f(1) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Apply the trapezium rule formula:\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(0) + f(1) + 2f(0.5)\big] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{0.5}{2}\left[1 + \dfrac{1}{2} + 2\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)\right] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{8}{5}\right] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{1}{4}\left[\dfrac{31}{10}\right] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{31}{40} \end{aligned}

(ii) Integrate $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$ analytically:\begin{aligned} &I = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}\text{d}x \cr &\quad = \big[\arctan(x)\big]_{0}^{1} \cr &\quad = \arctan(1) - \arctan(0) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \end{aligned}

(iii) Equate the analytical value of $I$ and the numerical approximation:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx \dfrac{31}{40} \cr &\pi \approx \dfrac{124}{40} \cr &\pi \approx \dfrac{31}{10} \end{aligned}

Thus, the rational number is $k = \dfrac{31}{10}$ (or $3.1$).

Final Answer: (i) $I \approx \dfrac{31}{40}$
(ii) $I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$
(iii) $k = \dfrac{31}{10}$

pi_options.feedback: Check your analytical integration. The integral of $\dfrac{1}{1 + x^2}$ is $\arctan(x)$. Since $\arctan(1) = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the exact value is $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, not $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Verify your trapezium rule calculations. The value of the function at the midpoint $x = 0.5$ is $\dfrac{4}{5} = 0.8$. Ensure you substitute this correct value into the formula.
When solving for $\pi$ in part (iii), remember to multiply both sides of the approximation $\dfrac{\pi}{4} \approx \dfrac{31}{40}$ by $4$ to isolate $\pi$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Historical Approximations of Pi

question:
Consider the definite integral $I = \int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{x}\text{d}x$.

(i) Use the trapezium rule, with two strips of equal width, to show that:

\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{7}{6} \end{aligned}

(ii) Find the exact value of $I$ in terms of natural logarithms.

(iii) Using your answers to parts (i) and (ii), state an approximate rational value for $\ln(3)$.
steps: (i) The interval is $[1, 3]$. With $2$ strips of equal width, the width of each strip $h$ is:\begin{aligned} &h = \dfrac{3 - 1}{2} \cr &\quad = 1 \end{aligned}

The $x$-coordinates are $x_0 = 1$, $x_1 = 2$, and $x_2 = 3$. Evaluate $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ at each coordinate:

• $f(1) = 1$

• $f(2) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

• $f(3) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Apply the trapezium rule formula:\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(1) + f(3) + 2f(2)\big] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left[1 + \dfrac{1}{3} + 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left[2 + \dfrac{1}{3}\right] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{7}{3}\right] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{7}{6} \end{aligned}
(ii) Integrate $\dfrac{1}{x}$ analytically:\begin{aligned} &I = \int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{1}{x}\text{d}x \cr &\quad = \big[\ln(x)\big]_{1}^{3} \cr &\quad = \ln(3) - \ln(1) \cr &\quad = \ln(3) \end{aligned}
(iii) Directly equate the analytical value and the numerical approximation:\begin{aligned} &\ln(3) \approx \dfrac{7}{6} \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (i) $I \approx \dfrac{7}{6}$
(ii) $I = \ln(3)$
(iii) $\ln(3) \approx \dfrac{7}{6}$

pi_options.feedback: Check your limits when integrating in part (ii). Evaluating $[\ln(x)]_1^3$ gives $\ln(3) - \ln(1) = \ln(3)$, not $\ln(2)$.
Verify your trapezium rule sum. Ensure you only double the middle ordinate $f(2) = 0.5$ and do not double the endpoint ordinates.
Check your arithmetic in part (i). The sum inside the brackets is $\dfrac{7}{3}$. Multiplying by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ yields $\dfrac{7}{6}$, not $\dfrac{5}{6}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Overestimates vs. Underestimates
bradley_insight.content: Since the graph of $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$ is concave up over the interval $[1, 3]$, the straight chord segments of the trapeziums lie entirely above the curve. Therefore, the trapezium rule will always produce an overestimate. This explains why $\dfrac{7}{6} \approx 1.167$ is slightly larger than the actual value of $\ln(3) \approx 1.099$.

question:
Consider the definite integral $I = \int_{0}^{2} x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{d}x$.

(i) Use the trapezium rule, with two strips of equal width, to find an approximation for $I$ in terms of the constant $\mathrm{e}$.

(ii) Use integration by parts to find the exact value of $I$ in terms of the constant $\mathrm{e}$.

(iii) Using your answers to parts (i) and (ii), show that $\mathrm{e}^2 - \mathrm{e} \approx k$, where $k$ is an integer to be found.
steps: (i) The interval is $[0, 2]$. With $2$ strips of equal width, the width of each strip $h$ is:\begin{aligned} &h = \dfrac{2 - 0}{2} \cr &\quad = 1 \end{aligned}

The $x$-coordinates are $x_0 = 0$, $x_1 = 1$, and $x_2 = 2$. Evaluate $f(x) = x\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ at each coordinate:

• $f(0) = 0$

• $f(1) = \mathrm{e}^{-1}$

• $f(2) = 2\mathrm{e}^{-2}$

Apply the trapezium rule formula:\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(0) + f(2) + 2f(1)\big] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\big[0 + 2\mathrm{e}^{-2} + 2\mathrm{e}^{-1}\big] \cr &\quad \approx \mathrm{e}^{-1} + \mathrm{e}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Integrate $x\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ analytically using integration by parts, $\int u\text{d}v = uv - \int v\text{d}u$.

Let $u = x \implies \text{d}u = \text{d}x$, and let $\text{d}v = \mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{d}x \implies v = -\mathrm{e}^{-x}$.

Substitute these into the integration by parts formula:\begin{aligned} &I = \big[-x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\big]_{0}^{2} - \int_{0}^{2} -\mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{d}x \cr &\quad = -2\mathrm{e}^{-2} + \int_{0}^{2} \mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{d}x \cr &\quad = -2\mathrm{e}^{-2} + \big[-\mathrm{e}^{-x}\big]_{0}^{2} \cr &\quad = -2\mathrm{e}^{-2} + (-\mathrm{e}^{-2} + \mathrm{e}^{0}) \cr &\quad = 1 - 3\mathrm{e}^{-2} \end{aligned}

(iii) Equate the numerical approximation and the analytical exact value:\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{e}^{-1} + \mathrm{e}^{-2} \approx 1 - 3\mathrm{e}^{-2} \cr &\mathrm{e}^{-1} \approx 1 - 4\mathrm{e}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Multiply the entire equation by $\mathrm{e}^2$ to eliminate negative powers:\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{e} \approx \mathrm{e}^2 - 4 \cr &\mathrm{e}^2 - \mathrm{e} \approx 4 \end{aligned}

Thus, the integer is $k = 4$.

Final Answer: (i) $I \approx \mathrm{e}^{-1} + \mathrm{e}^{-2}$
(ii) $I = 1 - 3\mathrm{e}^{-2}$
(iii) $k = 4$

pi_options.feedback: Check your algebra in part (iii). Transposing $\mathrm{e}^{-1} + \mathrm{e}^{-2} \approx 1 - 3\mathrm{e}^{-2}$ gives $\mathrm{e}^{-1} \approx 1 - 4\mathrm{e}^{-2}$. Multiplying by $\mathrm{e}^2$ yields $\mathrm{e} \approx \mathrm{e}^2 - 4$, which leads to $k = 4$, not $3$.

Check your trapezium ordinate values. The formula is $\dfrac{h}{2}[y_0 + y_n + 2y_1]$. Since $y_1 = \mathrm{e}^{-1}$, we double this to get $2\mathrm{e}^{-1}$. Multiplying the whole bracket by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ yields $\mathrm{e}^{-1} + \mathrm{e}^{-2}$.

Verify your integration by parts. The term $v\text{d}u = -\mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{d}x$. Integrating this over the limits yields another negative term, resulting in the correct analytical expression $1 - 3\mathrm{e}^{-2}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Choosing u in Parts
bradley_insight.content: When using integration by parts for $\int x\mathrm{e}^{-x}\text{d}x$, always use the LATE rule to choose $u$. Since $x$ is algebraic (A) and $\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ is exponential (E), we choose $u = x$. This ensures that differentiating $u$ reduces its degree to $1$, making the remaining integral straightforward to compute.

question:
Consider the definite integral $I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^2(x)\text{d}x$.

(i) Use the trapezium rule, with two strips of equal width, to show that:

\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Use a suitable double-angle trigonometric identity to find the exact value of $I$.

(iii) Explain why the trapezium rule approximation is unusually accurate in this specific case.
steps: (i) The interval is $[0, \pi]$. With $2$ strips of equal width, the width of each strip $h$ is:\begin{aligned} &h = \dfrac{\pi - 0}{2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}

The $x$-coordinates are $x_0 = 0$, $x_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and $x_2 = \pi$. Evaluate $f(x) = \sin^2(x)$ at each coordinate:

• $f(0) = 0$

• $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1$

• $f(\pi) = 0$

Apply the trapezium rule formula:\begin{aligned} &I \approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left[f(0) + f(\pi) + 2f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{\pi / 2}{2}[0 + 0 + 2(1)] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{\pi}{4}[2] \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Integrate $\sin^2(x)$ analytically using $\sin^2(x) = \dfrac{1 - \cos(2x)}{2}$:\begin{aligned} &I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{1 - \cos(2x)}{2}\text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[x - \dfrac{\sin(2x)}{2}\right]_{0}^{\pi} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(\pi - \dfrac{\sin(2\pi)}{2}\right) - 0\right] \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}

(iii) The trapezium rule approximation is exact in this case due to the symmetry of the curve:

The curve $y = \sin^2(x)$ is symmetric about $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$. On the interval $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, the curve is concave down, so the trapezium underestimates the area.

On the interval $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]$, the curve is concave up, so the trapezium overestimates the area.

Because of this symmetry, the underestimate and overestimate cancel each other out exactly.

Final Answer: (i) $I \approx \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
(ii) $I = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
(iii) The trapezium rule is exact because symmetric errors cancel out.

(iii) The trapezium rule is exact because $\sin^2(x)$ is a linear function.
