question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The mass, $M$ (in grams), of a radioactive isotope remaining after $t$ years is modelled by $M = M_0 \mathrm{e}^{-kt}$, where $M_0$ and $k$ are positive constants.

(i) Show that, according to the model, the graph of $\ln M$ against $t$ is a straight line.
(ii) A plot of $\ln M$ against $t$ yields a straight line of best fit which passes through the points $(0, 4.6)$ and $(100, 3.1)$. Find estimates of the values of $M_0$ and $k$.
(iii) Use the model to find the half-life of the isotope (the time taken for the mass of the isotope to reduce to half of its initial mass), giving your answer to the nearest year.
(iv) State a limitation of using a continuous exponential model to represent radioactive decay in the long run.
steps:
(i) Linearising using natural logarithms:
Start with the decay model:\begin{aligned} &M = M_0 \mathrm{e}^{-kt} \end{aligned}
Take natural logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} &\ln M = \ln(M_0 \mathrm{e}^{-kt}) \cr &\quad = \ln M_0 + \ln(\mathrm{e}^{-kt}) \cr &\quad = -kt + \ln M_0 \end{aligned}

Rearrange into linear form $y = mx + c$:\begin{aligned} &\ln M = (-k)t + \ln M_0 \end{aligned}

Since $-k$ and $\ln M_0$ are constants, the graph of $\ln M$ against $t$ is a straight line.

(ii) Finding estimates of $M_0$ and $k$:
Using $(0, 4.6)$ and $(100, 3.1)$:\begin{aligned} &c = 4.6 \cr &m = \dfrac{3.1 - 4.6}{100 - 0} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{-1.5}{100} \cr &\quad = -0.015 \end{aligned}
Find $M_0$ and $k$:\begin{aligned} &\ln M_0 = 4.6 \cr &M_0 = \mathrm{e}^{4.6} \cr &\quad \approx 99.5\text{ g} \end{aligned}

For $k$:\begin{aligned} &-k = -0.015 \cr &k = 0.015 \end{aligned}

Thus, $M_0 = 99.5\text{ g}$ and $k = 0.015$.

(iii) Determining the half-life:
Let $T$ be the half-life when $M = \dfrac{1}{2}M_0$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{2}M_0 = M_0 \mathrm{e}^{-0.015T} \cr &\dfrac{1}{2} = \mathrm{e}^{-0.015T} \end{aligned}

Take natural logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} &\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = -0.015T \cr &-\ln 2 = -0.015T \cr &T = \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.015} \cr &\quad \approx 46.2\text{ years} \end{aligned}

To the nearest year, the half-life is $46\text{ years}$.

(iv) Identifying limitations in the long run:
A continuous exponential decay model predicts remaining mass asymptotically approaches zero without ever reaching it. In reality, radioactive decay is a discrete process of individual nuclei. When few atoms remain, a continuous deterministic model breaks down.
Final Answer: $M_0 = 99.5\text{ g}$, $k = 0.015$, Half-life $\approx 46\text{ years}$

pi_options.feedback: This option fails to take the inverse natural log of the vertical intercept. Since $\ln M_0 = 4.6$, you must calculate $M_0 = \mathrm{e}^{4.6} \approx 99.5\text{ g}$.

The decay constant $k$ must be a positive parameter. Since the gradient of the log plot is $-0.015$, we have $-k = -0.015 \implies k = 0.015$. A negative value for $k$ would represent exponential growth instead of decay.
The half-life calculation is incorrect. Setting up the equation as $\mathrm{e}^{-kT} = 0.5$ yields $T = \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.015} \approx 46\text{ years}$, rather than dividing by a different factor.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Half-Life Constant
bradley_insight.content: For any simple exponential decay model of the form $y = y_0 \mathrm{e}^{-kt}$, the half-life $T$ is completely independent of the starting amount $y_0$. It will always simplify down to the clean relation $T = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}$. Memorising this relation can save you valuable steps during exams!

subtopic: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions and Graphs
question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A scientist monitors the population, $P$, of a bacteria culture in a laboratory experiment. The relationship between $P$ and the time, $t$ (in hours) since the start of the experiment, is modelled by $P = A b^t$, where $A$ and $b$ are constants.

(i) Show that, according to the model, the graph of $\log_{10} P$ against $t$ is a straight line.
(ii) A plot of $\log_{10} P$ against $t$ yields a straight line of best fit which passes through the points $(1, 2.5)$ and $(5, 3.7)$. Find estimates of the values of $A$ and $b$, giving your answers to $3$ significant figures.
(iii) Estimate the population of the bacteria culture after $10$ hours, giving your answer to the nearest thousand.
(iv) Suggest a biological reason why this model will eventually fail for large values of $t$.
steps:
(i) Showing linearisation:
Start with the population model:\begin{aligned} &P = A b^t \end{aligned}

Take the base-$10$ logarithm of both sides:\begin{aligned} &\log_{10} P \cr &\quad = \log_{10}(A b^t) \cr &\quad = \log_{10} A + \log_{10}(b^t) \cr &\quad = (\log_{10} b)t + \log_{10} A \end{aligned}

This is in linear form $y = mx + c$, where $y = \log_{10} P$ and $x = t$. Gradient is $m = \log_{10} b$ and vertical intercept is $c = \log_{10} A$. Thus, the graph is a straight line.

(ii) Finding estimates for $A$ and $b$:
Calculate gradient $m$ from $(1, 2.5)$ and $(5, 3.7)$:\begin{aligned} &m = \dfrac{3.7 - 2.5}{5 - 1} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1.2}{4} \cr &\quad = 0.3 \end{aligned}
Find $b$:\begin{aligned} &\log_{10} b = 0.3 \cr &b = 10^{0.3} \cr &\quad \approx 2.00 \end{aligned}

Find $A$ using $(1, 2.5)$:\begin{aligned} &\log_{10} P = 0.3t + \log_{10} A \cr &2.5 = 0.3(1) + \log_{10} A \cr &\log_{10} A = 2.2 \cr &A = 10^{2.2} \cr &\quad \approx 158 \end{aligned}

Thus, $A = 158$ and $b = 2.00$ to $3$ significant figures.

(iii) Estimating population after $10$ hours:
Substitute $t = 10$ into $\log_{10} P = 0.3t + 2.2$:\begin{aligned} &\log_{10} P = 0.3(10) + 2.2 \cr &\quad = 3 + 2.2 \cr &\quad = 5.2 \end{aligned}

Solve for $P$:\begin{aligned} &P = 10^{5.2} \cr &\quad \approx 158,489 \end{aligned}

Rounding to the nearest thousand, the population is $158,000$.

(iv) Describing biological failures:
An exponential growth model assumes infinite resources. As bacteria multiply, nutrients and space deplete, and waste products accumulate, halting growth for large $t$.
Final Answer: $A = 158$, $b = 2.00$, $P \approx 158,000$

This option incorrectly computes $P$ after $10$ hours as $A \times b \times t$ (i.e. $158 \times 2 \times 10 = 3160$) instead of applying the exponent: $P = Ab^t$, which gives $158 \times 2^{10} \approx 162,000$.
This calculation is off by a factor of 100, which usually stems from a decimal placement error when taking the inverse log of $5.2$. Ensure you evaluate $10^{5.2} \approx 158,000$ carefully.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Early Rounding Cascades
bradley_insight.content: When a question has multiple sequential parts, avoid using rounded parameters ($A \approx 158$ and $b \approx 2.00$) for calculations in later parts unless explicitly instructed. Working directly with the exact linear equation $\log_{10} P = 0.3t + 2.2$ keeps your calculations exact and prevents rounding errors from compounding!

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The temperature, $\theta$ (in $^\circ\text{C})$, of a hot metal component cooling in a laboratory where the ambient room temperature is $20^\circ\text{C}$ is modelled by $\theta = 20 + A \mathrm{e}^{-kt}$, where $t$ is the time in minutes after cooling begins, and $A$ and $k$ are constants.

(i) Show that the relationship can be written in the form $\ln(\theta - 20) = mt + c$, where $m$ and $c$ are constants to be stated in terms of $A$ and $k$.
(ii) A plot of $\ln(\theta - 20)$ against $t$ yields a straight line of best fit with a vertical intercept of $4.0$ and a gradient of $-0.08$. Find the exact value of $k$ and the value of $A$ to $3$ significant figures.
(iii) Estimate the temperature of the metal component after $15$ minutes of cooling, giving your answer to the nearest degree.
(iv) State the long-term temperature predicted by this model, and comment on whether this prediction is realistic in a physical context.
steps:
(i) Rearranging and taking logarithms:
Start with the cooling equation:\begin{aligned} &\theta = 20 + A \mathrm{e}^{-kt} \cr &\theta - 20 = A \mathrm{e}^{-kt} \end{aligned}

Take natural logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} &\ln(\theta - 20) \cr &\quad = \ln(A \mathrm{e}^{-kt}) \cr &\quad = \ln A + \ln(\mathrm{e}^{-kt}) \cr &\quad = -kt + \ln A \end{aligned}

This is in the form $\ln(\theta - 20) = mt + c$, with $m = -k$ and $c = \ln A$.

(ii) Determining $A$ and $k$:
Using gradient $m = -0.08$ and intercept $c = 4.0$:\begin{aligned} &-k = -0.08 \cr &k = 0.08 \end{aligned}

Find $A$ from the intercept:\begin{aligned} &\ln A = 4.0 \cr &A = \mathrm{e}^{4.0} \cr &\quad \approx 54.6 \end{aligned}

Thus, $k = 0.08$ and $A = 54.6$.

(iii) Estimating temperature after $15$ minutes:
Substitute $t = 15$ into the cooling model:\begin{aligned} &\theta \cr &\quad = 20 + 54.598 \mathrm{e}^{-0.08(15)} \cr &\quad = 20 + 54.598 \mathrm{e}^{-1.2} \cr &\quad \approx 20 + 16.44 \cr &\quad \approx 36.4^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}

Rounding to the nearest degree, the temperature is $36^\circ\text{C}$.

(iv) Analyzing long-term predictions:
As $t \to \infty$, $\mathrm{e}^{-0.08t} \to 0$, so $\theta \to 20^\circ\text{C}$.

This prediction is physically realistic because the object reaches thermal equilibrium with the ambient room temperature.
Final Answer: $A = 54.6$, $k = 0.08$, $\text{Temperature} \approx 36^\circ\text{C}$

pi_options.feedback: This option fails to take the inverse natural log of the vertical intercept. Since $\ln A = 4.0$, you must calculate $A = \mathrm{e}^{4.0} \approx 54.6$, rather than equating $A$ directly to the intercept.

This option incorrectly sets $k$ as a negative value. Because the gradient of the log plot is negative ($m = -0.08$), the constant $k$ is positive ($k = 0.08$). A negative value of $k$ would model unbounded growth instead of cooling.

This option computes the cooled portion of the temperature $\theta - 20 \approx 16.44^\circ\text{C}$ but forgets to add the constant ambient temperature of $20^\circ\text{C}$ back onto the final result.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Shifted Log Pitfalls
bradley_insight.content: When dealing with models that have an added vertical displacement constant (like Newton's Law of Cooling, $\theta = 20 + A \mathrm{e}^{-kt}$), never take logarithms before isolating the exponential term first. Attempting to write $\ln \theta = \ln(20 + A \mathrm{e}^{-kt})$ creates an expression that cannot be simplified or linearised. Always subtract the constant first!

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Find the constant term in the binomial expansion of $\left(x^3 + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{12}$.
steps:
Step 1: Write down the general term of the expansion:
The general term in the binomial expansion of $(a + b)^n$ is $T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$.

Substitute $a = x^3$, $b = x^{-1}$, and $n = 12$:\begin{aligned} &T_{r+1} \cr &\quad = \binom{12}{r} (x^3)^{12 - r} \left(x^{-1}\right)^r \cr &\quad = \binom{12}{r} x^{3(12 - r)} x^{-r} \cr &\quad = \binom{12}{r} x^{36 - 3r - r} \cr &\quad = \binom{12}{r} x^{36 - 4r} \end{aligned}

Step 2: Solve for $r$ to find the constant term:
The constant term corresponds to setting the exponent of $x$ to $0$:\begin{aligned} &36 - 4r = 0 \cr &4r = 36 \cr &r = 9 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Calculate the constant term:
Substitute $r = 9$ into the general term formula:\begin{aligned} &T_{10} = \binom{12}{9} x^0 \cr &\quad = \binom{12}{3} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{12 \times 11 \times 10}{3 \times 2 \times 1} \cr &\quad = 220 \end{aligned}

Thus, the constant term in the expansion is $220$.
Final Answer: $220$

pi_options.feedback: This option results from using the wrong value of $r$. If you incorrectly simplified the exponent as $36 - 2r = 0$, you would get $r = 18$ (which is outside the range $0 \le r \le 12$), or if you used $r = 4$, which gives $\binom{12}{4} = 495$.
This option is equal to $\binom{12}{5}$ or $\binom{12}{7}$, which corresponds to setting $r = 5$ or $r = 7$. Check your exponent equation $36 - 4r = 0$ to ensure you solve for $r = 9$.
This option is equal to $\binom{12}{1}$ or $\binom{12}{11}$, which occurs if you incorrectly simplify the exponent of $x$ or guess the index.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Power Laws and Fractions
bradley_insight.content: When expanding expressions like $\left(x^3 + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)^{12}$, don't forget to write $\dfrac{1}{x}$ as $x^{-1}$. If you make a mistake with index laws and write $\dfrac{1}{x}$ as $x$ or $x^1$, you will get the incorrect exponent equation for the constant term.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Find the constant term in the binomial expansion of $\left(2x^2 - \dfrac{3}{x}\right)^9$.
steps:
Step 1: Write down the general term of the expansion:
Using the binomial general term formula $T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$ with $a = 2x^2$, $b = -3x^{-1}$, and $n = 9$:\begin{aligned} &T_{r+1} \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{r} (2x^2)^{9 - r} (-3x^{-1})^r \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{r} 2^{9 - r} (x^2)^{9 - r} \cr &\qquad \times (-3)^r (x^{-1})^r \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{r} 2^{9 - r} (-3)^r \cr &\qquad \times x^{2(9 - r)} x^{-r} \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{r} 2^{9 - r} (-3)^r x^{18 - 3r} \end{aligned}

Step 2: Solve for $r$ to isolate the constant term:
The constant term corresponds to setting the exponent of $x$ to $0$:\begin{aligned} &18 - 3r = 0 \cr &3r = 18 \cr &r = 6 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Calculate the constant term:
Substitute $r = 6$ into the general term:\begin{aligned} &T_7 = \binom{9}{6} 2^{9 - 6} (-3)^6 x^0 \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{3} 2^3 (-3)^6 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{9 \times 8 \times 7}{3 \times 2 \times 1} \times 8 \times 729 \cr &\quad = 84 \times 8 \times 729 \cr &\quad = 672 \times 729 \cr &\quad = 489,888 \end{aligned}

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Find the coefficient of $x^3$ in the binomial expansion of $\left(2x - \dfrac{1}{x^2}\right)^9$.

Using the binomial general term formula $T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$ with $a = 2x$, $b = -x^{-2}$, and $n = 9$:\begin{aligned} &T_{r+1} \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{r} (2x)^{9 - r} (-x^{-2})^r \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{r} 2^{9 - r} x^{9 - r} \cr &\qquad \times (-1)^r (x^{-2})^r \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{r} 2^{9 - r} (-1)^r x^{9 - 3r} \end{aligned}

Step 2: Solve for $r$ to find the term in $x^3$:
Set the exponent of $x$ to $3$:\begin{aligned} &9 - 3r = 3 \cr &3r = 6 \cr &r = 2 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Calculate the coefficient:
Substitute $r = 2$ into the general term:\begin{aligned} &T_3 = \binom{9}{2} 2^{9 - 2} (-1)^2 x^3 \cr &\quad = \binom{9}{2} 2^7 (1) x^3 \cr &\quad = 36 \times 128 \times x^3 \cr &\quad = 4608x^3 \end{aligned}

Thus, the coefficient of $x^3$ is $4608$.

question:

Thus, the coefficient of $x^2$ in the expansion is $-336$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

In the binomial expansion of $(1 + kx)^n$, where $n$ is a positive integer and $k$ is a non-zero constant, the coefficient of $x$ is $-30$ and the coefficient of $x^2$ is $400$.

Determine the value of $n$ and the value of $k$.
steps:
Step 1: Express the coefficients in terms of $n$ and $k$:
Using the binomial expansion of $(1 + kx)^n$:\begin{aligned} &(1 + kx)^n \cr &\quad = 1 + \binom{n}{1}(kx) \cr &\qquad + \binom{n}{2}(kx)^2 + \dots \cr &\quad = 1 + nkx \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}k^2 x^2 + \dots \end{aligned}

Equating coefficients gives:

1) Coefficient of $x$ is $-30$:\begin{aligned} &nk = -30 \end{aligned}

2) Coefficient of $x^2$ is $400$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{n(n - 1)k^2}{2} = 400 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up a simultaneous equation:
From the first equation, express $k$ in terms of $n$:\begin{aligned} &k = -\dfrac{30}{n} \end{aligned}

Substitute this into the second equation:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2} \left(-\dfrac{30}{n}\right)^2 = 400 \cr &\dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2} \left(\dfrac{900}{n^2}\right) = 400 \cr &\dfrac{900n(n - 1)}{2n^2} = 400 \cr &\dfrac{450(n - 1)}{n} = 400 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve for $n$:
Multiply both sides by $n$ and solve the linear equation:\begin{aligned} &450(n - 1) = 400n \cr &450n - 450 = 400n \cr &50n = 450 \cr &n = 9 \end{aligned}

Step 4: Solve for $k$:
Substitute $n = 9$ into the expression for $k$:\begin{aligned} &k = -\dfrac{30}{9} \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{10}{3} \end{aligned}

Thus, the values are $n = 9$ and $k = -\dfrac{10}{3}$.
Final Answer: $n = 9$, $k = -\dfrac{10}{3}$

bradley_insight.content: When expanding $(1 + kx)^n$, the coefficient of $x^2$ is $\dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}k^2$, not $\dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}k$. question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The line $y = 3 - kx$ crosses the curve $y = 4x - x^2$ on the $x$-axis and at one other point.

Determine the value of the constant $k$ and the coordinates of this other point.
steps:
Step 1: Find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis:
The curve crosses the $x$-axis where $y = 0$:\begin{aligned} &4x - x^2 = 0 \cr &x(4 - x) = 0 \end{aligned}

This gives crossing points at $(0, 0)$ and $(4, 0)$.

Step 2: Determine which crossing point the line passes through:
If the line passes through $(0, 0)$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 3 - k(0) \cr &0 = 3 \end{aligned}
This is impossible, so the line cannot pass through $(0, 0)$.

Therefore, the line passes through $(4, 0)$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 3 - 4k \cr &4k = 3 \cr &k = \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve for the other point of intersection:
Equate the line and the curve:\begin{aligned} &4x - x^2 = 3 - \dfrac{3}{4}x \cr &16x - 4x^2 = 12 - 3x \cr &4x^2 - 19x + 12 = 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise the quadratic:\begin{aligned} &(x - 4)(4x - 3) = 0 \end{aligned}

The roots are $x = 4$ and $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$, so the other point has $x$-coordinate $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

Step 4: Find the $y$-coordinate of the other point:
Substitute $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$ into the line equation:\begin{aligned} &y = 3 - \dfrac{3}{4}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) \cr &\quad = 3 - \dfrac{9}{16} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{39}{16} \end{aligned}

Thus, the other point of intersection is $\left(\dfrac{3}{4}, \dfrac{39}{16}\right)$.
Final Answer: $k = \dfrac{3}{4}$, other point $\left(\dfrac{3}{4}, \dfrac{39}{16}\right)$

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The line $y = kx - 6$ crosses the curve $y = x^2 - 3x$ on the $x$-axis and at one other point.

Determine the value of the constant $k$ and the coordinates of this other point.
steps:
Step 1: Find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis:
Set $y = 0$ in the curve equation:\begin{aligned} &x^2 - 3x = 0 \cr &x(x - 3) = 0 \end{aligned}

This gives crossing points at $(0, 0)$ and $(3, 0)$.

Step 2: Determine which crossing point the line passes through:
If the line passes through $(0, 0)$:\begin{aligned} &0 = k(0) - 6 \cr &0 = -6 \end{aligned}
This is impossible, so the line cannot pass through $(0, 0)$.

Therefore, the line passes through $(3, 0)$:\begin{aligned} &0 = 3k - 6 \cr &3k = 6 \cr &k = 2 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve for the other point of intersection:
Equate the line and the curve:\begin{aligned} &x^2 - 3x = 2x - 6 \cr &x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise the quadratic:\begin{aligned} &(x - 3)(x - 2) = 0 \end{aligned}

The roots are $x = 3$ and $x = 2$, so the other point has $x$-coordinate $x = 2$.

Step 4: Find the $y$-coordinate of the other point:
Substitute $x = 2$ into the line equation:\begin{aligned} &y = 2(2) - 6 \cr &\quad = -2 \end{aligned}

Thus, the other point of intersection is $(2, -2)$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The line $y = kx + 6$ is a tangent to the curve $y = \dfrac{8}{x}$.

Given that $k \neq 0$, determine the value of the constant $k$ and the coordinates of the point of contact.
steps:
Step 1: Set up the intersection equation:
Equate the line and the curve:\begin{aligned} &kx + 6 = \dfrac{8}{x} \end{aligned}
Multiply through by $x$ (for $x \neq 0$):\begin{aligned} &kx^2 + 6x = 8 \cr &kx^2 + 6x - 8 = 0 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Apply the tangency condition (discriminant $\Delta = 0$):
A tangent touches the curve at exactly one point, so the quadratic has a single repeated real root:\begin{aligned} &\Delta = 6^2 - 4(k)(-8) \cr &\quad = 36 + 32k \end{aligned}
Set $\Delta = 0$ and solve for $k$:\begin{aligned} &36 + 32k = 0 \cr &32k = -36 \cr &k = -\dfrac{9}{8} \end{aligned}

Step 3: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point of contact:
Substitute $k = -\dfrac{9}{8}$ into the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &-\dfrac{9}{8}x^2 + 6x - 8 = 0 \cr &-9x^2 + 48x - 64 = 0 \cr &9x^2 - 48x + 64 = 0 \cr &(3x - 8)^2 = 0 \end{aligned}

This gives the repeated root $x = \dfrac{8}{3}$.

Step 4: Find the $y$-coordinate of the point of contact:
Substitute $x = \dfrac{8}{3}$ into the curve equation:\begin{aligned} &y = \dfrac{8}{\left(\dfrac{8}{3}\right)} \cr &\quad = 8 \times \dfrac{3}{8} \cr &\quad = 3 \end{aligned}

Thus, $k = -\dfrac{9}{8}$ and the point of contact is $\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 3\right)$.
Final Answer: $k = -\dfrac{9}{8}$, point of contact $\left(\dfrac{8}{3}, 3\right)$

bradley_insight.title: The Discriminant and Tangency
bradley_insight.content: A line is a tangent to a curve if and only if they intersect at exactly one point (or point of contact). Algebraically, this means that the quadratic intersection equation has a single repeated real root, which corresponds to setting the discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac = 0$. This powerful technique is a cornerstone of A Level curve sketching and coordinate geometry.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The line $y = 3x - k$ is a tangent to the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 10$.

Given that $k$ is a positive constant, determine the value of $k$ and the coordinates of the point of contact.

Step 1: Set up the intersection equation:
Substitute $y = 3x - k$ into the circle equation $x^2 + y^2 = 10$:\begin{aligned} &x^2 + (3x - k)^2 = 10 \cr &x^2 + 9x^2 - 6kx + k^2 = 10 \cr &10x^2 - 6kx + (k^2 - 10) = 0 \end{aligned}

The line is tangent to the circle when there is a single repeated root:\begin{aligned} &\Delta = (-6k)^2 \cr &\qquad - 4(10)(k^2 - 10) \cr &\quad = 36k^2 - 40(k^2 - 10) \cr &\quad = 36k^2 - 40k^2 + 400 \cr &\quad = -4k^2 + 400 \end{aligned}

Set $\Delta = 0$ and solve for positive $k$:\begin{aligned} &-4k^2 + 400 = 0 \cr &4k^2 = 400 \cr &k^2 = 100 \cr &k = \pm 10 \end{aligned}

Since $k$ is positive, choose $k = 10$.

Step 3: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point of contact:
Substitute $k = 10$ into the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &10x^2 - 60x + 90 = 0 \cr &x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0 \cr &(x - 3)^2 = 0 \cr &x = 3 \end{aligned}

Step 4: Find the $y$-coordinate of the point of contact:
Substitute $x = 3$ and $k = 10$ into the line equation:\begin{aligned} &y = 3(3) - 10 \cr &\quad = -1 \end{aligned}

Thus, $k = 10$ and the point of contact is $(3, -1)$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A curve has parametric equations $x = \dfrac{t}{1 + t^2}$, $y = \dfrac{t^2}{1 + t^2}$, defined for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

(i) Determine the gradient of the curve at the point where $t = 3$.
(ii) Verify that the cartesian equation of the curve is $x^2 + y^2 = y$.
steps:
(i) Finding the gradient at $t = 3$:
Differentiate $x$ with respect to $t$ using the quotient rule:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{(1 + t^2)(1) - t(2t)}{(1 + t^2)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1 + t^2 - 2t^2}{(1 + t^2)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1 - t^2}{(1 + t^2)^2} \end{aligned}

Differentiate $y$ with respect to $t$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{(1 + t^2)(2t) - t^2(2t)}{(1 + t^2)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2t + 2t^3 - 2t^3}{(1 + t^2)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2t}{(1 + t^2)^2} \end{aligned}

Use the chain rule to find $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{\text{d}y/\text{d}t}{\text{d}x/\text{d}t} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2t}{(1 + t^2)^2}}{\dfrac{1 - t^2}{(1 + t^2)^2}} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{2t}{1 - t^2} \end{aligned}

Substitute $t = 3$ to evaluate the gradient:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{2(3)}{1 - 3^2} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{6}{-8} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = -\dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}

(ii) Verifying the Cartesian equation $x^2 + y^2 = y$:
Substitute $x$ and $y$ into the left-hand side:\begin{aligned} &x^2 + y^2 \cr &\quad = \left(\dfrac{t}{1 + t^2}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{t^2}{1 + t^2}\right)^2 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{t^2}{(1 + t^2)^2} + \dfrac{t^4}{(1 + t^2)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{t^2(1 + t^2)}{(1 + t^2)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{t^2}{1 + t^2} \cr &\quad = y \end{aligned}

Thus, the Cartesian equation $x^2 + y^2 = y$ is verified.
Final Answer: $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = -\dfrac{3}{4}$, Cartesian: $x^2 + y^2 = y$

bradley_insight.title: Simplification Safety
bradley_insight.content: When differentiating rational parametric equations, always simplify your derivatives $\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ and $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ completely before dividing them to find $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$. Leaving common denominators un-cancelled leads to algebraic chaos and makes evaluating the gradient much more difficult.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A curve has parametric equations $x = 3\cos\theta$, $y = 4\sin\theta$, defined for $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$.

(i) Determine the exact gradient of the curve at the point where $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
(ii) Verify that the cartesian equation of the curve is $\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1$.
steps:
(i) Finding the gradient at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
Differentiate both equations with respect to $\theta$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}\theta} = -3\sin\theta \cr &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}\theta} = 4\cos\theta \end{aligned}

Use the chain rule to find $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{\text{d}y/\text{d}\theta}{\text{d}x/\text{d}\theta} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{4\cos\theta}{-3\sin\theta} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = -\dfrac{4}{3}\cot\theta \end{aligned}

Evaluate the gradient at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = -\dfrac{4}{3}\cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = -\dfrac{4}{3}(\sqrt{3}) \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = -\dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3} \end{aligned}

(ii) Verifying the Cartesian equation:
Substitute $x = 3\cos\theta$ and $y = 4\sin\theta$ into the left-hand side:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{(3\cos\theta)^2}{9} + \dfrac{(4\sin\theta)^2}{16} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{9\cos^2\theta}{9} + \dfrac{16\sin^2\theta}{16} \cr &\quad = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta \cr &\quad = 1 \end{aligned}

Thus, the Cartesian equation $\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1$ is verified.
Final Answer: $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = -\dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}$, Cartesian: $\dfrac{x^2}{9} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1$

This option lists an incorrect Cartesian equation. When you square $x = 3\cos\theta$, you obtain $x^2 = 9\cos^2\theta$. To eliminate the coefficient, you must divide by $9$ (not $3$), so the term is $\dfrac{x^2}{9}$.

bradley_insight.title: Cotangent Conversions
bradley_insight.content: When dealing with ellipse parametrics $x = a\cos\theta$ and $y = b\sin\theta$, your gradient $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ will always simplify into a form involving $\cot\theta$. Converting $\dfrac{\cos\theta}{-\sin\theta}$ directly to $-\cot\theta$ makes it quick to evaluate the gradient, since $\cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \sqrt{3}$ is a standard exact value.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A curve has parametric equations $x = \mathrm{e}^{2t}$, $y = t\mathrm{e}^{-t}$, defined for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

(i) Determine the gradient of the curve at the point where $t = 0$.
(ii) Verify that the cartesian equation of the curve is $4y^2x = (\ln x)^2$, for $x > 0$.
steps:
(i) Finding the gradient at $t = 0$:
Differentiate $x = \mathrm{e}^{2t}$ with respect to $t$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} = 2\mathrm{e}^{2t} \end{aligned}

Differentiate $y = t\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ using the product rule:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \cr &\quad = (1)\mathrm{e}^{-t} + t(-\mathrm{e}^{-t}) \cr &\quad = \mathrm{e}^{-t}(1 - t) \end{aligned}

Use the chain rule to find $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{\text{d}y/\text{d}t}{\text{d}x/\text{d}t} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{-t}(1 - t)}{2\mathrm{e}^{2t}} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{1 - t}{2\mathrm{e}^{3t}} \end{aligned}
Evaluate the gradient at $t = 0$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{1 - 0}{2\mathrm{e}^0} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Verifying the Cartesian equation $4y^2x = (\ln x)^2$:
From the equation for $x$, isolate $t$:\begin{aligned} &x = \mathrm{e}^{2t} \cr &\ln x = 2t \cr &(\ln x)^2 = 4t^2 \end{aligned}

Substitute $x$ and $y$ into the left-hand side of the Cartesian equation:\begin{aligned} &4y^2x \cr &\quad = 4\left(t\mathrm{e}^{-t}\right)^2 \left(\mathrm{e}^{2t}\right) \cr &\quad = 4\left(t^2\mathrm{e}^{-2t}\right) \left(\mathrm{e}^{2t}\right) \cr &\quad = 4t^2 \mathrm{e}^{-2t + 2t} \cr &\quad = 4t^2 \mathrm{e}^0 \cr &\quad = 4t^2 \end{aligned}

Since both sides simplify to $4t^2$, the Cartesian equation $4y^2x = (\ln x)^2$ is verified.
Final Answer: $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, Cartesian: $4y^2x = (\ln x)^2$

pi_options.feedback: This option has a sign error on the gradient. Differentiating $y = t\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ yields $\mathrm{e}^{-t}(1 - t)$. Substituting $t = 0$ into this expression gives $+1$ in the numerator, leading to a positive gradient of $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

This option contains an incorrect coefficient in the Cartesian equation. Squaring $y = t\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ gives $y^2 = t^2\mathrm{e}^{-2t}$. When multiplied by $x = \mathrm{e}^{2t}$, you get $y^2x = t^2$. Therefore, you need a factor of $4$ to match $(\ln x)^2 = 4t^2$, making the equation $4y^2x = (\ln x)^2$.
This option arises if you forget the factor of $2$ when differentiating $x = \mathrm{e}^{2t}$ (failing to apply the chain rule), which leads to an incorrect gradient of $1$.

bradley_insight.title: The Product Rule Trap
bradley_insight.content: Be extremely careful when differentiating $y = t\mathrm{e}^{-t}$. A common student slip is to differentiate it term-by-term as if it were a simple sum, obtaining $\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ or $-\mathrm{e}^{-t}$. Remember that this is a product of two functions, so you must strictly apply the product rule: $u'v + uv'$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A curve has parametric equations $x = t + \dfrac{2}{t}$, $y = t - \dfrac{2}{t}$, defined for $t \neq 0$.

(i) Determine the gradient of the curve at the point where $t = 2$.
(ii) Verify that the cartesian equation of the curve is $x^2 - y^2 = 8$.
steps:
(i) Finding the gradient at $t = 2$:
Differentiate both parametric equations with respect to $t$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} = 1 - \dfrac{2}{t^2} \cr &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} = 1 + \dfrac{2}{t^2} \end{aligned}

Use the chain rule to obtain the gradient function $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{\text{d}y/\text{d}t}{\text{d}x/\text{d}t} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{2}{t^2}}{1 - \dfrac{2}{t^2}} \end{aligned}

Substitute $t = 2$ into the gradient function:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{2}{2^2}}{1 - \dfrac{2}{2^2}} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{1 + 0.5}{1 - 0.5} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{1.5}{0.5} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = 3 \end{aligned}

(ii) Verifying the Cartesian equation $x^2 - y^2 = 8$:
Substitute $x$ and $y$ into the left-hand side of the Cartesian equation:\begin{aligned} &x^2 - y^2 \cr &\quad = \left(t + \dfrac{2}{t}\right)^2 - \left(t - \dfrac{2}{t}\right)^2 \cr &\quad = \left(t^2 + 4 + \dfrac{4}{t^2}\right) \cr &\qquad - \left(t^2 - 4 + \dfrac{4}{t^2}\right) \cr &\quad = t^2 + 4 + \dfrac{4}{t^2} - t^2 + 4 - \dfrac{4}{t^2} \cr &\quad = 8 \end{aligned}

Thus, the Cartesian equation of the curve is verified.
Final Answer: $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 3$, Cartesian: $x^2 - y^2 = 8$

pi_options.feedback: This option has an incorrect sign for the gradient. In the first quadrant (where $t = 2$), both parametric derivatives are positive, resulting in a positive gradient of $3$.
This option has an incorrect constant on the Cartesian equation. When you expand the squared brackets, the middle terms are $+4$ and $-4$, so their difference is $4 - (-4) = 8$, not $4$.
This option results from a differentiation error, such as forgetting to apply the power rule to the $\dfrac{2}{t}$ terms, obtaining $1$ for both derivatives.

bradley_insight.title: Difference of Two Squares
bradley_insight.content: Verifying the Cartesian equation $x^2 - y^2 = 8$ is a classic application of algebraic identities. Instead of expanding the squares term-by-term, you can also view it as a difference of two squares: $(x - y)(x + y)$. Since $x - y = \dfrac{4}{t}$ and $x + y = 2t$, multiplying them gives $\left(\dfrac{4}{t}\right)(2t) = 8$ instantly. Spotting these algebraic structures is an excellent mathematical superpower!

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A curve has parametric equations $x = \sin\theta$, $y = \cos 2\theta$, defined for $0 \le \theta < 2\pi$.

(i) Determine the exact gradient of the curve at the point where $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
(ii) Verify that the cartesian equation of the curve is $y = 1 - 2x^2$.
steps:
(i) Finding the gradient at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
Differentiate with respect to $\theta$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}\theta} = \cos\theta \cr &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}\theta} = -2\sin 2\theta \end{aligned}

Use the chain rule to obtain $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{\text{d}y/\text{d}\theta}{\text{d}x/\text{d}\theta} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{-2\sin 2\theta}{\cos\theta} \end{aligned}
Evaluate the trigonometric terms at $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$:\begin{aligned} &\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \cr &\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}

Substitute these exact values into the gradient function:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{-2\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{\dfrac{1}{2}} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = \dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{\dfrac{1}{2}} \cr &\hphantom{\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}} = -2\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}

(ii) Verifying the Cartesian equation $y = 1 - 2x^2$:
Recall the cosine double-angle identity:\begin{aligned} &\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta \end{aligned}

Substitute $x = \sin\theta$ and $y = \cos 2\theta$ into the identity:\begin{aligned} &y = 1 - 2x^2 \end{aligned}

Thus, the Cartesian equation of the curve is verified.
Final Answer: $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = -2\sqrt{3}$, Cartesian: $y = 1 - 2x^2$

pi_options.feedback: This option results from failing to divide by the denominator term $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Remember to divide the $y$-derivative by the $x$-derivative to find the gradient.
This option has the wrong sign order for the double-angle identity. The correct identity is $\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta$, which maps to $y = 1 - 2x^2$, not $y = 2x^2 - 1$.
This option has a sign error on the gradient. Differentiating $y = \cos 2\theta$ yields $-2\sin 2\theta$. In the first quadrant, $\sin(2\pi/3) > 0$, so the gradient must be negative.

bradley_insight.title: Double Angle Identities
bradley_insight.content: When eliminating the parameter $\theta$ from trigonometric equations, always select the correct form of the double-angle identity. Since $x = \sin\theta$, using the form $\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta$ is by far the cleanest choice as it immediately allows you to substitute $x^2$ for $\sin^2\theta$. Choosing the other forms ($\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta$ or $2\cos^2\theta - 1$) requires extra, unnecessary algebraic manipulation.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The function $f(x) = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^x}{2 - \mathrm{e}^x}$ is defined on the domain $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq \ln 2$.

(i) Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
(ii) Write down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$.
steps:
(i) Finding the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$:
Set $y = f(x)$ and rearrange to solve for $x$:\begin{aligned} &y = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^x}{2 - \mathrm{e}^x} \cr &y(2 - \mathrm{e}^x) = \mathrm{e}^x \cr &2y - y\mathrm{e}^x = \mathrm{e}^x \cr &2y = \mathrm{e}^x + y\mathrm{e}^x \cr &2y = \mathrm{e}^x(1 + y) \cr &\mathrm{e}^x = \dfrac{2y}{1 + y} \cr &x = \ln\left(\dfrac{2y}{1 + y}\right) \end{aligned}
Interchanging variables gives the inverse function:\begin{aligned} &f^{-1}(x) = \ln\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x}\right) \end{aligned}

(ii) Writing down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$:
The range of $f^{-1}(x)$ is equal to the domain of $f(x)$.

Since the domain of $f(x)$ is $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq \ln 2$, the range of $f^{-1}(x)$ is:\begin{aligned} &y \in \mathbb{R}, \; y \neq \ln 2 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $f^{-1}(x) = \ln\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x}\right)$, Range: $y \in \mathbb{R}, \; y \neq \ln 2$

pi_options.feedback: This option contains an algebraic error. When solving $2y = \mathrm{e}^x(1 + y)$, you must divide $2y$ by $(1+y)$ to get $\mathrm{e}^x = \dfrac{2y}{1+y}$. This option represents dividing by $2$ instead.

The inverse formula is correct, but the range of $f^{-1}(x)$ is incomplete. Since $f(x)$ is not defined at $x = \ln 2$, its inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ can never output the value $\ln 2$. You must state that $y \neq \ln 2$.

This option has a sign error in the denominator of the log term, changing $1+x$ to $1-x$. When factorising $\mathrm{e}^x + y\mathrm{e}^x$, the correct term is $\mathrm{e}^x(1+y)$, which gives a denominator of $1+x$ in the inverse.

bradley_insight.title: The Domain-Range Mirror
bradley_insight.content: Always remember the golden rule of inverse functions: the domain of $f(x)$ is exactly equal to the range of $f^{-1}(x)$, and the range of $f(x)$ is exactly equal to the domain of $f^{-1}(x)$. Instead of trying to calculate the range of $f^{-1}(x)$ from its formula, simply read the domain of the original function $f(x)$ directly from the question!

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The function $f(x) = \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{1 - x}\right)$ is defined on the domain $0 < x < 1$.

(i) Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
(ii) Write down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$.
steps:
(i) Finding the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$:
Set $y = f(x)$ and rearrange to express $x$ in terms of $y$:\begin{aligned} &y = \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{1 - x}\right) \cr &\mathrm{e}^y = \dfrac{x}{1 - x} \cr &\mathrm{e}^y(1 - x) = x \cr &\mathrm{e}^y - x\mathrm{e}^y = x \cr &\mathrm{e}^y = x + x\mathrm{e}^y \cr &\mathrm{e}^y = x(1 + \mathrm{e}^y) \cr &x = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^y}{1 + \mathrm{e}^y} \end{aligned}
Interchanging variables gives the inverse function:\begin{aligned} &f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^x}{1 + \mathrm{e}^x} \end{aligned}

(ii) Writing down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$:
The range of the inverse function is equal to the domain of the original function $f(x)$.

Since the domain of $f(x)$ is $0 < x < 1$, the range of $f^{-1}(x)$ is:\begin{aligned} &0 < y < 1 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^x}{1 + \mathrm{e}^x}$, Range: $0 < y < 1$

pi_options.feedback: This option is the reciprocal of the correct inverse function. When isolating $x$ from $\mathrm{e}^y = x(1 + \mathrm{e}^y)$, dividing both sides by $(1 + \mathrm{e}^y)$ yields $x = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^y}{1 + \mathrm{e}^y}$.

The formula for the inverse function is correct, but the range is incorrect. The range of the inverse function must match the domain of the original function, which is restricted to the open interval $(0, 1)$.

bradley_insight.title: Exponentiating Fractions
bradley_insight.content: When solving $y = \ln\left(\dfrac{x}{1 - x}\right)$, once you exponentiate to get $\mathrm{e}^y = \dfrac{x}{1 - x}$, clear the fraction immediately by multiplying both sides by $(1 - x)$. Grouping the $x$ terms and factoring is a highly reliable algebraic algorithm for isolating the variable.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The function $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$ is defined on the domain $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq 3$.

(i) Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
(ii) Write down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$.
steps:
(i) Finding the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$:
Set $y = f(x)$ and rearrange to make $x$ the subject:\begin{aligned} &y = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3} \cr &y(x - 3) = 2x + 1 \cr &xy - 3y = 2x + 1 \cr &xy - 2x = 3y + 1 \cr &x(y - 2) = 3y + 1 \cr &x = \dfrac{3y + 1}{y - 2} \end{aligned}
Interchanging variables gives the inverse function:\begin{aligned} &f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2} \end{aligned}

(ii) Writing down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$:
The range of the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ is equal to the domain of the original function $f(x)$.

Since the domain of $f(x)$ is $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $x \neq 3$, the range of $f^{-1}(x)$ is:\begin{aligned} &y \in \mathbb{R}, \; y \neq 3 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2}$, Range: $y \in \mathbb{R}, \; y \neq 3$

pi_options.feedback: This option confuses the domain of the inverse function ($x \neq 2$) with its range. The range of the inverse function is equal to the domain of the original function $f(x)$, which is restricted by $x \neq 3$.
This option contains a sign error in the numerator, writing $3x - 1$ instead of $3x + 1$. Moving $-3y$ to the right side of the equation $xy - 3y = 2x + 1$ yields a positive $+3y$ term.

This option contains a sign error in the denominator, writing $x + 2$ instead of $x - 2$. Moving $+2x$ to the left side of the equation $xy - 3y = 2x + 1$ yields a negative term: $xy - 2x = x(y - 2)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Linear Fractional Transformation Pattern
bradley_insight.content: A linear fractional transformation $f(x) = \dfrac{ax + b}{cx + d}$ has a highly symmetric inverse $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{-dx + b}{cx - a}$. Spotting this pattern can act as an instant verification check: for $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$, swapping the coefficients $2$ and $-3$ with sign changes gives $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2}$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The function $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 7$ is defined on the restricted domain $x \ge 2$.

(i) Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
(ii) Write down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$.
steps:
(i) Finding the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$:
Complete the square for $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} &f(x) = (x - 2)^2 - 4 + 7 \cr &\hphantom{f(x)} = (x - 2)^2 + 3 \end{aligned}
Set $y = f(x)$ and solve for $x$ in terms of $y$:\begin{aligned} &y = (x - 2)^2 + 3 \cr &y - 3 = (x - 2)^2 \end{aligned}
Since the domain is $x \ge 2$, $x - 2 \ge 0$, so select the positive square root:\begin{aligned} &x - 2 = \sqrt{y - 3} \cr &x = 2 + \sqrt{y - 3} \end{aligned}
Interchanging variables gives the inverse function:\begin{aligned} &f^{-1}(x) = 2 + \sqrt{x - 3} \end{aligned}

(ii) Writing down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$:
The range of the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ is equal to the domain of the original function $f(x)$.

Since the domain is $x \ge 2$, the range of $f^{-1}(x)$ is:\begin{aligned} &y \ge 2 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $f^{-1}(x) = 2 + \sqrt{x - 3}$, Range: $y \ge 2$

pi_options.feedback: This option arises if you select the negative square root when rearranging. Since the domain of the original function is $x \ge 2$, the term $x - 2$ is non-negative, meaning you must choose the positive root: $+\sqrt{y - 3}$.
The inverse function is correct, but this option confuses the domain of the inverse function ($x \ge 3$) with its range. The range is the domain of the original function, which is $y \ge 2$.
This option is caused by a mistake in completing the square, such as adding $7$ to the square root term directly without subtracting the squared half-coefficient ($-4$).

bradley_insight.title: Choosing Square Root Signs
bradley_insight.content: When taking the square root to solve $y - 3 = (x - 2)^2$, you mathematically have two roots: $x - 2 = \pm\sqrt{y - 3}$. You must look at the restricted domain $x \ge 2$ to make a choice. Since $x \ge 2 \implies x - 2 \ge 0$, you must select the positive root. Omitting this check can lose you serious marks!

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The function $f(x) = 3 - \sqrt{x - 1}$ is defined on the domain $x \ge 1$.

(i) Find $f^{-1}(x)$.
(ii) Write down the range of $f^{-1}(x)$.
(iii) State the domain of $f^{-1}(x)$.
steps:
(i) Finding the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$:
Set $y = f(x)$ and isolate the radical term:\begin{aligned} &y = 3 - \sqrt{x - 1} \cr &\sqrt{x - 1} = 3 - y \end{aligned}
Square both sides of the equation:\begin{aligned} &x - 1 = (3 - y)^2 \cr &x = 1 + (3 - y)^2 \end{aligned}
Interchanging variables gives the inverse function:\begin{aligned} &f^{-1}(x) = 1 + (3 - x)^2 \end{aligned}

(ii) Finding the range of $f^{-1}(x)$:
The range of the inverse function $f^{-1}(x)$ is equal to the domain of the original function $f(x)$.

Since the domain of $f(x)$ is $x \ge 1$, the range is:\begin{aligned} &y \ge 1 \end{aligned}

(iii) Stating the domain of $f^{-1}(x)$:
The domain of $f^{-1}(x)$ is equal to the range of the original function $f(x)$.

For $x \ge 1$:\begin{aligned} &x \ge 1 \cr &x - 1 \ge 0 \cr &\sqrt{x - 1} \ge 0 \cr &-\sqrt{x - 1} \le 0 \cr &3 - \sqrt{x - 1} \le 3 \end{aligned}

Therefore, the range of $f(x)$ is $f(x) \le 3$, which means the domain of $f^{-1}(x)$ is:\begin{aligned} &x \le 3 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $f^{-1}(x) = 1 + (3 - x)^2$, Range: $y \ge 1$, Domain: $x \le 3$

pi_options.feedback: The inverse function and range are correct, but the domain limit is reversed. Since $f(x) = 3 - \sqrt{x-1}$, the output of $f(x)$ is at most $3$ because we are subtracting a non-negative root from $3$. Hence, the domain of $f^{-1}(x)$ must be $x \le 3$.
This option contains a sign error when solving for $x$. Adding $1$ to both sides of $x - 1 = (3-y)^2$ yields $x = 1 + (3-y)^2$, not a subtraction of $1$.

While the inverse function formula resembles an unrestricted quadratic, its domain is strictly constrained to the range of the original square-root function. You must restrict the domain of $f^{-1}(x)$ to $x \le 3$.

bradley_insight.title: Domain Constraints on the Inverse
bradley_insight.content: For functions involving square roots like $f(x) = 3 - \sqrt{x - 1}$, the inverse function formula $f^{-1}(x) = 1 + (3 - x)^2$ looks like an unrestricted quadratic. However, it is only defined where $f(x)$ exists and produces outputs. You must explicitly state the domain restriction $x \le 3$ for the inverse function to be mathematically complete.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Point $A$ has position vector $\begin{pmatrix} a \cr b \cr 0 \end{pmatrix}$, where $a$ and $b$ can vary. Point $B$ has position vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 1 \cr 0 \end{pmatrix}$ and point $C$ has position vector $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 3 \cr 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

The triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AC = AB$.

(i) Show that $a - b + 1 = 0$.
(ii) Determine the position vector of $A$ such that triangle $ABC$ has minimum area.
steps:
(i) Showing that $a - b + 1 = 0$:
Find $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 - a \cr 1 - b \cr 0 \end{pmatrix} \cr &\vec{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - a \cr 3 - b \cr 2 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Equate the squared magnitudes $|\vec{AB}|^2 = |\vec{AC}|^2$:\begin{aligned} &(3 - a)^2 + (1 - b)^2 + 0^2 \cr &\quad = (1 - a)^2 + (3 - b)^2 + 2^2 \cr &(9 - 6a + a^2) + (1 - 2b + b^2) \cr &\quad = (1 - 2a + a^2) \cr &\qquad + (9 - 6b + b^2) + 4 \cr &-6a - 2b + 10 \cr &\quad = -2a - 6b + 14 \cr &-4a + 4b - 4 = 0 \cr &a - b + 1 = 0 \end{aligned}

(ii) Finding the position vector of $A$ for minimum area:
From part (i), $b = a + 1$, so:\begin{aligned} &\vec{OA} = \begin{pmatrix} a \cr a + 1 \cr 0 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}
The base is $BC$. The midpoint $D$ of $BC$ is:\begin{aligned} &D = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \cr 2 \cr 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

The height vector $\vec{AD}$ is:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AD} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \cr 2 \cr 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} a \cr a + 1 \cr 0 \end{pmatrix} \cr &\hphantom{\vec{AD}} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 - a \cr 1 - a \cr 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Calculate the squared height $|\vec{AD}|^2$:\begin{aligned} &|\vec{AD}|^2 \cr &\quad = (2 - a)^2 + (1 - a)^2 + 1^2 \cr &\quad = (4 - 4a + a^2) \cr &\qquad + (1 - 2a + a^2) + 1 \cr &\quad = 2a^2 - 6a + 6 \end{aligned}
Minimise by setting the derivative to zero:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}a}(2a^2 - 6a + 6) = 0 \cr &4a - 6 = 0 \cr &a = \dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}

Substitute $a = \dfrac{3}{2}$ into $b = a + 1$:\begin{aligned} &b = \dfrac{3}{2} + 1 \cr &\hphantom{b} = \dfrac{5}{2} \end{aligned}

Thus, the position vector of $A$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 1.5 \cr 2.5 \cr 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
Final Answer: $\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.5 \cr 2.5 \cr 0 \end{pmatrix}$

This option arises if the midpoint of the base $BC$ is incorrectly calculated as $D(3, 3, 1)$ instead of $D(2, 2, 1)$. Setting up the height vector with this incorrect midpoint yields the squared height $2a^2 - 10a + 14$, which is minimised at $a = 2.5$ and $b = 3.5$.

This option occurs if you make an error in setting up the quadratic height equation, such as failing to sum the $a^2$ terms or incorrectly expanding the squared brackets, leading to an incorrect minimum value.

bradley_insight.title: Spec-Compliant Area Methods
bradley_insight.content: Many Further Maths students immediately default to using the 3D vector cross product to find the area of triangle $ABC$. While mathematically sound, the cross product is not on the standard A Level Maths syllabus. A much cleaner, spec-compliant method is to find the midpoint $D$ of the base $BC$ and minimise the height vector $\vec{AD}$, which is simple, elegant, and fully accepted in all mark schemes!

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Point $A$ has position vector $\begin{pmatrix} a \cr b \cr 0 \end{pmatrix}$, where $a$ and $b$ can vary. Point $B$ has position vector $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 5 \cr 1 \end{pmatrix}$ and point $C$ has position vector $\begin{pmatrix} 5 \cr 1 \cr 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

The triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $AC = AB$.

(i) Show that $a - b = 0$.
(ii) Determine the position vector of $A$ such that triangle $ABC$ has minimum area.
steps:
(i) Showing that $a - b = 0$:
Find $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - a \cr 5 - b \cr 1 \end{pmatrix} \cr &\vec{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 - a \cr 1 - b \cr 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

(ii) Finding the position vector of $A$ for minimum area:
From part (i), $b = a$. The coordinates of $A$ are $\begin{pmatrix} a \cr a \cr 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
The midpoint $D$ of $BC$ is:\begin{aligned} &D = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 3 \cr 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}
The height vector $\vec{AD}$ is:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AD} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 - a \cr 3 - a \cr 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}
The squared height is:\begin{aligned} &|\vec{AD}|^2 = (3 - a)^2 + (3 - a)^2 + 1^2 \cr &\hphantom{|\vec{AD}|^2} = 2(3 - a)^2 + 1 \end{aligned}

The minimum occurs when $(3 - a)^2 = 0$, giving $a = 3$.

Since $b = a$, $b = 3$. Thus, the position vector of $A$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 3 \cr 0 \end{pmatrix}$.
Final Answer: $\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 3 \cr 0 \end{pmatrix}$

pi_options.feedback: This option is incorrect. Although the coordinates satisfy the relation $a=b$, they do not minimise the height of the triangle. Evaluating the squared height at $a=1$ gives $2(2)^2 + 1 = 9$, which is larger than the minimum squared height of $1$ achieved at $a=3$.
This option contains a sign error on the $b$-coordinate, violating the condition $a - b = 0 \implies b = a$. The two coordinates must be identical.
This option is a non-minimal point on the line $a=b$. The height vector is minimised at the midpoint of the base's projection, which is $a = 3$.

bradley_insight.title: Simplification is Key
bradley_insight.content: When setting up the isosceles condition $|\vec{AB}|^2 = |\vec{AC}|^2$, expanding the squared binomials fully before trying to simplify can look daunting. However, notice that the quadratic terms $a^2$ and $b^2$ appear on both sides and cancel out completely, reducing the equation to a simple linear form $a - b = 0$. Don't get intimidated by the quadratics!

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The points $P$, $Q$, and $R$ have position vectors $\mathbf{p} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr -2 \cr 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $\mathbf{q} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 1 \cr 2 \end{pmatrix}$, and $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} k \cr 2 \cr -1 \end{pmatrix}$ respectively, where $k$ is a constant.

(i) Given that the vector $\vec{PQ}$ is perpendicular to the vector $\vec{PR}$, determine the value of the constant $k$.
(ii) Using the value of $k$ found in part (i), calculate the size of the angle $PQR$, giving your answer to the nearest $0.1^\circ$.
steps:
(i) Finding the value of $k$:
Find $\vec{PQ}$ and $\vec{PR}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{PQ} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \cr 3 \cr -1 \end{pmatrix} \cr &\vec{PR} = \begin{pmatrix} k - 1 \cr 4 \cr -4 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Since the vectors are perpendicular, their scalar product is zero:\begin{aligned} &\vec{PQ} \cdot \vec{PR} = 0 \cr &2(k - 1) + 3(4) + (-1)(-4) = 0 \cr &2k - 2 + 12 + 4 = 0 \cr &2k + 14 = 0 \cr &k = -7 \end{aligned}

(ii) Calculating the angle $PQR$ with $k = -7$:
The vectors starting at vertex $Q$ are $\vec{QP}$ and $\vec{QR}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{QP} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 \cr -3 \cr 1 \end{pmatrix} \cr &\vec{QR} = \begin{pmatrix} -10 \cr 1 \cr -3 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}
Compute the scalar product:\begin{aligned} &\vec{QP} \cdot \vec{QR} \cr &\quad = (-2)(-10) + (-3)(1) + (1)(-3) \cr &\quad = 20 - 3 - 3 \cr &\quad = 14 \end{aligned}
Calculate magnitudes:\begin{aligned} &|\vec{QP}| = \sqrt{(-2)^2 + (-3)^2 + 1^2}\cr & \qquad = \sqrt{14} \cr &|\vec{QR}| = \sqrt{(-10)^2 + 1^2 + (-3)^2}\cr & \qquad = \sqrt{110} \end{aligned}
Calculate $\cos(PQR)$:\begin{aligned} &\cos(PQR) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{14}{\sqrt{14}\sqrt{110}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{14}{\sqrt{1540}} \cr &\quad \approx 0.35675 \end{aligned}
Take the inverse cosine:\begin{aligned} &PQR = \arccos(0.35675) \cr &\hphantom{PQR} \approx 69.1^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $k = -7$, Angle $\approx 69.1^\circ$

This option has the correct value of $k$ but incorrectly calculates the angle because you used vectors starting at different vertices (such as $\vec{PQ}$ and $\vec{QR}$), which yields the obtuse supplement angle $180^\circ - 69.1^\circ = 110.9^\circ$. Ensure both vectors start at $Q$.

This option arises from an arithmetic slip in evaluating the fraction $\dfrac{14}{\sqrt{1540}}$, such as evaluating the square root incorrectly or introducing an intermediate rounding error before taking the inverse cosine.

bradley_insight.title: Choosing the Correct Vertex
bradley_insight.content: When calculating the angle $PQR$, the angle is subtended at the vertex $Q$. This means both vectors must start at the vertex $Q$, which are $\vec{QP}$ and $\vec{QR}$. A very common student error is using the vectors $\vec{PQ}$ and $\vec{QR}$ or $\vec{QP}$ and $\vec{RQ}$, which will calculate the exterior angle ($180^\circ - \theta$) instead. Always check your vector directions!

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A straight line $L$ passes through the points $B(1, 2, 3)$ and $C(2, 4, 1)$.

(i) Find a vector equation for the line $L$ in the form $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{u} + \lambda \mathbf{v}$.
(ii) A point $A$ has position vector $\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 4 \cr -4 \end{pmatrix}$. Determine the coordinates of the point on the line $L$ that is closest to $A$.
steps:
(i) Finding a vector equation for the line $L$:
Find the direction vector $\vec{BC}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{BC} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 - 1 \cr 4 - 2 \cr 1 - 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 2 \cr -2 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}
The equation of the line is:\begin{aligned} &\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 2 \cr 3 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 2 \cr -2 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

(ii) Finding the point on the line $L$ closest to $A$:
A general point $R$ on $L$ is:\begin{aligned} &R = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + \lambda \cr 2 + 2\lambda \cr 3 - 2\lambda \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

The vector $\vec{AR}$ is:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AR} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + \lambda - 1 \cr 2 + 2\lambda - 4 \cr 3 - 2\lambda - (-4) \end{pmatrix}\cr & \qquad = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda \cr 2\lambda - 2 \cr 7 - 2\lambda \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Set $\vec{AR} \cdot \vec{BC} = 0$ for minimum distance:\begin{aligned} &\lambda(1) + (2\lambda - 2)(2) \cr &\qquad + (7 - 2\lambda)(-2) = 0 \cr &\lambda + 4\lambda - 4 - 14 + 4\lambda = 0 \cr &9\lambda - 18 = 0 \cr &\lambda = 2 \end{aligned}

Substitute $\lambda = 2$ into $R$:\begin{aligned} &R = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + 2 \cr 2 + 2(2) \cr 3 - 2(2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 6 \cr -1 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Thus, the closest point on the line is $(3, 6, -1)$.
Final Answer: $\mathbf{r} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 2 \cr 3 \end{pmatrix} + \lambda \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 2 \cr -2 \end{pmatrix}$, Closest point $(3, 6, -1)$

pi_options.feedback: This option is incorrect because $(2, 4, 1)$ is simply point $C$. While $C$ is on the line (at $\lambda = 1$), the closest point to $A$ occurs at $\lambda = 2$, which gives the coordinates $(3, 6, -1)$.
This option has a sign error in the $z$-coordinate. Substituting $\lambda = 2$ into the $z$-component $3 - 2\lambda$ yields $3 - 4 = -1$, not $+1$.
This option lists an incorrect direction vector for the line $L$. The direction vector must be $C - B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cr 2 \cr -2 \end{pmatrix}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Perpendicular Closest Point
bradley_insight.content: The shortest distance from a point to a line occurs when the line connecting them is perpendicular to the line itself. Therefore, the scalar product of the vector $\vec{AR}$ and the line's direction vector must equal $0$. This elegant geometric fact completely bypasses the need for complex calculus and differentiation to find minimum distances.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The points $A$, $B$, and $C$ have coordinates $A(2, -1, 5)$, $B(5, 1, 1)$, and $C(11, 5, -7)$ respectively.

(i) Show that the points $A$, $B$, and $C$ are collinear.
(ii) State the ratio of lengths $AB : BC$.
(iii) Find the coordinates of the point $D$ on the line segment $AC$ produced such that $AC : CD = 3 : 1$.
steps:
(i) Showing that the points are collinear:
Find $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 - 2 \cr 1 - (-1) \cr 1 - 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 2 \cr -4 \end{pmatrix} \cr &\vec{AC} = \begin{pmatrix} 11 - 2 \cr 5 - (-1) \cr -7 - 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9 \cr 6 \cr -12 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Notice that $\vec{AC}$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec{AB}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{AC} = 3\vec{AB} \end{aligned}

Since $\vec{AC}$ and $\vec{AB}$ are parallel and share the common point $A$, the points $A$, $B$, and $C$ are collinear.

(ii) Finding the ratio of lengths $AB : BC$:
Find $\vec{BC}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{BC} = \begin{pmatrix} 11 - 5 \cr 5 - 1 \cr -7 - 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 \cr 4 \cr -8 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Since $\vec{BC} = 2\vec{AB}$:\begin{aligned} &AB : BC = 1 : 2 \end{aligned}

(iii) Finding the coordinates of $D$:
Since $AC : CD = 3 : 1$ and $D$ lies on $AC$ produced, $\vec{CD} = \dfrac{1}{3}\vec{AC}$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{CD} = \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix} 9 \cr 6 \cr -12 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 2 \cr -4 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Add this to the position vector of $C$:\begin{aligned} &\vec{OD} = \begin{pmatrix} 11 \cr 5 \cr -7 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 3 \cr 2 \cr -4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 14 \cr 7 \cr -11 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Thus, the coordinates of $D$ are $(14, 7, -11)$.
Final Answer: $AB : BC = 1 : 2$, $D(14, 7, -11)$

This option lists an incorrect ratio. Because $\vec{BC} = 2\vec{AB}$, the ratio of the lengths $AB : BC$ is $1 : 2$, not $1 : 3$.
This option results from subtracting the vector $\vec{CD}$ from $C$ instead of adding it, which would find a point that lies between $A$ and $C$ rather than on $AC$ produced.

bradley_insight.title: Proving Collinearity
bradley_insight.content: To prove that three points $A$, $B$, and $C$ are collinear, showing that $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ are parallel is only half the battle. You must explicitly state that they also share a common point (such as $A$) to guarantee they lie on the exact same line, rather than on two parallel lines.

question: Solve the equation: $5|3x - 1| = 10|x + 4|$
steps: Divide both sides of the equation by $5$:\begin{aligned} &|3x - 1| = 2|x + 4| \end{aligned}
Square both sides to eliminate the absolute values:\begin{aligned} &(3x - 1)^2 = (2(x + 4))^2 \cr &(3x - 1)^2 = 4(x + 4)^2 \end{aligned}
Expand and simplify the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &9x^2 - 6x + 1 \cr &\quad = 4(x^2 + 8x + 16) \cr &\quad = 4x^2 + 32x + 64 \cr &5x^2 - 38x - 63 = 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise the quadratic:\begin{aligned} &(5x + 7)(x - 9) = 0 \end{aligned}

This yields two solutions:\begin{aligned} &x = 9 \text{ or } x = -\dfrac{7}{5} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $x = 9$ and $x = -\dfrac{7}{5}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you invert the fraction when solving the linear component $5x + 7 = 0$, leading to $x = -\dfrac{5}{7}$ instead of the correct value of $-\dfrac{7}{5}$.
This mistake arises from a sign error when factoring the simplified quadratic equation, which results in the factored form $(5x - 7)(x + 9) = 0$ instead of $(5x + 7)(x - 9) = 0$.
This happens if you only solve the positive linear case $3x - 1 = 2(x + 4)$ and completely omit the negative case $3x - 1 = -2(x + 4)$, which is a critical step in absolute value equations.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Expanding Coefficients
bradley_insight.content: When squaring both sides of an equation like $|3x - 1| = 2|x + 4|$, a very common student mistake is to forget to square the constant multiplier on the right-hand side. Remember that $(2|x + 4|)^2$ becomes $4(x + 4)^2$. Forgetting to square this coefficient will lead to an incorrect quadratic equation.

question: Solve the inequality: $|2x - 3| \ge |x + 3|$
steps: Square both sides since both expressions are non-negative:\begin{aligned} &(2x - 3)^2 \ge (x + 3)^2 \end{aligned}
Expand both quadratic terms and collect terms:\begin{aligned} &4x^2 - 12x + 9 \ge x^2 + 6x + 9 \cr &3x^2 - 18x \ge 0 \end{aligned}
Factorise the quadratic expression:\begin{aligned} &3x(x - 6) \ge 0 \end{aligned}
The critical values are $x = 0$ and $x = 6$. For the product to be non-negative, $x$ must lie outside or on the critical values:\begin{aligned} &x \le 0 \text{ or } x \ge 6 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $x \le 0$ or $x \ge 6$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you correctly determine the critical values of $x = 0$ and $x = 6$ but choose the region between them rather than the regions outside of them.
This is a common error resulting from a miscalculation of the boundary points, sometimes caused by incorrectly handling the absolute value bounds under interval testing.
This happens if you only solve the linear inequality $2x - 3 \ge x + 3$ without considering the other case where the signs of the absolute values differ.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Squaring Inequalities
bradley_insight.content: Squaring both sides of an inequality is only safe when both sides are guaranteed to be non-negative, which is always true for absolute value expressions like $|A| \ge |B|$. It is a highly efficient way to find the boundary points without having to solve multiple separate linear inequalities.

question: Solve the equation: $|x^2 - 3| = 2x$
steps: Establish the domain constraint. Since $|x^2 - 3| \ge 0$, the right-hand side must also be non-negative:\begin{aligned} &2x \ge 0 \cr &x \ge 0 \end{aligned}

Case 1: $x^2 - 3 \ge 0$\begin{aligned} &x^2 - 3 = 2x \cr &x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0 \cr &(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0 \end{aligned}

This gives $x = 3$ or $x = -1$. Since $x \ge 0$, reject $x = -1$, leaving $x = 3$.

Case 2: $x^2 - 3 < 0$\begin{aligned} &-(x^2 - 3) = 2x \cr &3 - x^2 = 2x \cr &x^2 + 2x - 3 = 0 \cr &(x + 3)(x - 1) = 0 \end{aligned}

This gives $x = 1$ or $x = -3$. Since $x \ge 0$, reject $x = -3$, leaving $x = 1$.
Combining the valid solutions from both cases gives $x = 1$ or $x = 3$.
Final Answer: $x = 1$ and $x = 3$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you fail to check the domain condition $x \ge 0$ and incorrectly include the negative root $x = -1$ while rejecting only $x = -3$.
This happens if you do not check for extraneous solutions at all. In absolute value equations where the variable is outside the modulus, negative values can create invalid mathematical statements.
This occurs if you only consider the positive case $x^2 - 3 = 2x$ and completely omit the negative case $-(x^2 - 3) = 2x$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Extraneous Solution Trap
bradley_insight.content: Always check your solutions against the original equation. Since the right-hand side is $2x$, any negative solution is automatically extraneous because $|x^2 - 3|$ cannot equal a negative number.

question: Find the exact real solutions to the equation: $|\mathrm{e}^x - 3| = 2\mathrm{e}^{-x}$
steps: Let $t = \mathrm{e}^x$. Since $\mathrm{e}^x > 0$ for all real $x$, we require $t > 0$:\begin{aligned} &|t - 3| = \dfrac{2}{t} \end{aligned}
Case 1: $t \ge 3$\begin{aligned} &t - 3 = \dfrac{2}{t} \cr &t^2 - 3t - 2 = 0 \end{aligned}
Using the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} &t = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{(-3)^2 - 4(1)(-2)}}{2} \cr &\hphantom{t} = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2} \end{aligned}
Since $t \ge 3$, the positive root is valid:\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{e}^x = \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2} \cr &x = \ln\left(\dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}\right) \end{aligned}

Case 2: $0 < t < 3$\begin{aligned} &-(t - 3) = \dfrac{2}{t} \cr &3 - t = \dfrac{2}{t} \cr &3t - t^2 = 2 \cr &t^2 - 3t + 2 = 0 \cr &(t - 1)(t - 2) = 0 \end{aligned}

This yields $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, both satisfying $0 < t < 3$.

Convert these values back to $x$:\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{e}^x = 1 \implies x = 0 \cr &\mathrm{e}^x = 2 \implies x = \ln 2 \end{aligned}

Thus, the complete set of exact real solutions is $x = 0$, $x = \ln 2$, and $x = \ln\left(\dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}\right)$.
Final Answer: $x = 0$, $x = \ln 2$, and $x = \ln\left(\dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}\right)$

pi_options.feedback: This error is common if you solve Case 2 correctly but fail to identify the valid solution from the Case 1 quadratic equation.
This error occurs from mistakenly substituting the boundary value $t = 3$ as a solution instead of using the actual root $t = \dfrac{3 + \sqrt{17}}{2}$ from the quadratic formula.
This results from a combination of algebraic slips, incorrectly solving the quadratic for $t$, and confusing the boundaries of the absolute value function.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Exponential Substitutions
bradley_insight.content: Substituting $t = \mathrm{e}^x$ is a powerful tool to reduce transcendental equations to algebraic ones. Always remember that because $\mathrm{e}^x > 0$, any negative values of $t$ must be discarded immediately before converting back to $x$.

question: Solve the equation: $|2x - 1| = |x + 5| - 3$
steps:
Identify the critical points where the expressions inside the modulus equal zero: $x = -5$ and $x = 0.5$. These divide the real line into three intervals:

• Interval 1: $x < -5$

• Interval 2: $-5 \le x < 0.5$

• Interval 3: $x \ge 0.5$

In Interval 1 ($x < -5$), $|2x - 1| = 1 - 2x$ and $|x + 5| = -x - 5$:\begin{aligned} &1 - 2x = -x - 5 - 3 \cr &1 - 2x = -x - 8 \cr &x = 9 \end{aligned}

Since $x = 9$ is not in $x < -5$, reject this solution.

In Interval 2 ($-5 \le x < 0.5$), $|2x - 1| = 1 - 2x$ and $|x + 5| = x + 5$:\begin{aligned} &1 - 2x = x + 5 - 3 \cr &1 - 2x = x + 2 \cr &-3x = 1 \cr &x = -\dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}

Since $-\dfrac{1}{3}$ lies in $[-5, 0.5)$, this is a valid solution.

In Interval 3 ($x \ge 0.5$), $|2x - 1| = 2x - 1$ and $|x + 5| = x + 5$:\begin{aligned} &2x - 1 = x + 5 - 3 \cr &2x - 1 = x + 2 \cr &x = 3 \end{aligned}

Since $3 \ge 0.5$, this is a valid solution.
Final Answer: $x = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $x = 3$

pi_options.feedback: This represents an error caused by incorrect interval boundary setup and sign slips during linear algebraic consolidation.
This happens if you solve the algebraic casework but forget to verify whether each solution actually lies within its corresponding interval domain.
This occurs if you only consider the case where both absolute value expressions are positive, neglecting the interval where one is positive and the other is negative.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Interval Casework Verification
bradley_insight.content: When solving equations with multiple moduli, the interval (or critical point) method is the safest route. However, you must always verify that your final algebraic solutions fall inside the specific interval they were derived from.

question:
A circle has centre $O$ and radius $6\text{ cm}$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on the circumference of the circle such that the arc length $PQ$ is $9\text{ cm}$.

(a) Calculate the angle, in radians, subtended at $O$ by the arc $PQ$.

(b) Determine the area of the sector $OPQ$.
steps:
To find the angle $\theta$ (in radians) subtended at the centre by an arc of length $s$, use:\begin{aligned} &s = r\theta \end{aligned}

where $r$ is the radius of the circle.
Substitute $s = 9$ and $r = 6$ into the formula:\begin{aligned} &9 = 6\theta \cr &\theta = \dfrac{9}{6} \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 1.5\text{ radians} \end{aligned}
To find the area $A$ of sector $OPQ$, use the sector area formula:\begin{aligned} &A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta \end{aligned}
Substitute $r = 6$ and $\theta = 1.5$ into the area formula:\begin{aligned} &A = \dfrac{1}{2}(6)^2(1.5) \cr &\hphantom{A} = \dfrac{1}{2}(36)(1.5) \cr &\hphantom{A} = 27\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\theta = 1.5$ rad, (b) $A = 27\text{ cm}^2$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you forget the factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in the sector area formula $A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, calculating $r^2\theta$ instead.

This mistake arises from incorrectly dividing the radius by the arc length to find the angle, writing $\theta = \dfrac{r}{s} = \dfrac{6}{9}$, giving $\dfrac{2}{3}$, instead of $\theta = \dfrac{s}{r}$.
This mistake is caused by incorrectly applying the formula $A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$, such as failing to square the radius and using a linear calculation instead.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Radians Simplicity
bradley_insight.content: Using radians makes circular measure calculations incredibly clean. The simple formula $s = r\theta$ only holds true when $\theta$ is measured in radians. If the angle were in degrees, you would have to carry around the factor $\dfrac{\pi}{180}$.

question:
A sector of a circle of radius $r\text{ cm}$ has an angle of $\theta$ radians at its centre.

Given that the perimeter of the sector is $20\text{ cm}$ and its area is $24\text{ cm}^2$, find the possible values of $r$ and the corresponding values of $\theta$.
steps:
The perimeter $P$ of a sector is given by:\begin{aligned} &P = 2r + r\theta \cr &2r + r\theta = 20 \end{aligned}

The area $A$ of the sector is given by:\begin{aligned} &A = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta \cr &\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta = 24 \end{aligned}
Express $\theta$ in terms of $r$ using the area equation:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta = 24 \cr &r^2\theta = 48 \cr &\theta = \dfrac{48}{r^2} \end{aligned}
Substitute this expression for $\theta$ into the perimeter equation:\begin{aligned} &2r + r\left(\dfrac{48}{r^2}\right) = 20 \cr &2r + \dfrac{48}{r} = 20 \end{aligned}
Multiply through by $r$ and rearrange into standard quadratic form:\begin{aligned} &2r^2 + 48 = 20r \cr &2r^2 - 20r + 48 = 0 \cr &r^2 - 10r + 24 = 0 \end{aligned}

Solve the quadratic equation by factorisation:\begin{aligned} &(r - 6)(r - 4) = 0 \end{aligned}

This yields two possible values for the radius:\begin{aligned} &r = 4 \text{ or } r = 6 \end{aligned}

Find the corresponding values of $\theta$ for each radius:

• For $r = 4$:\begin{aligned} &\theta = \dfrac{48}{4^2} \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 3\text{ radians} \end{aligned}

• For $r = 6$:\begin{aligned} &\theta = \dfrac{48}{6^2} \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = \dfrac{4}{3}\text{ radians} \end{aligned}

Thus, the possible pairs are $(r = 4\text{ cm}, \theta = 3\text{ rad})$ or $(r = 6\text{ cm}, \theta = \dfrac{4}{3}\text{ rad})$.
Final Answer: $r = 4\text{ cm}, \theta = 3\text{ rad}$ or $r = 6\text{ cm}, \theta = \dfrac{4}{3}\text{ rad}$

pi_options.feedback: This mistake occurs if you forget to double the area in the first step when expressing $\theta$, writing $\theta = \dfrac{24}{r^2}$ instead of $\theta = \dfrac{48}{r^2}$.
This error occurs if you express the perimeter as $r + r\theta = 20$ (forgetting that a sector has two radial boundaries, not one), which alters the quadratic coefficient when solving.
This arises from a factorisation error of the quadratic equation, such as misidentifying the factors of $24$ that sum to $-10$ (e.g. using $-8$ and $-3$ incorrectly instead of $-6$ and $-4$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Boundaries of a Sector
bradley_insight.content: A very frequent student error is writing the perimeter of a sector as $P = r + r\theta$ or $P = r\theta$. Remember that a sector is a closed slice of a circle bounded by two straight radii and one curved arc, so its perimeter must always be $P = 2r + r\theta$.

question:
A sector of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $8\text{ cm}$ has a central angle of $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ radians. Let $A$ and $B$ be the points on the circumference bounding the sector.

(a) Find the exact length of the chord $AB$.

(b) Determine the exact area of the segment bounded by the chord $AB$ and the arc $AB$.
steps: Split the isosceles triangle $OAB$ into two right-angled triangles with half-angle $\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ radians:\begin{aligned} &AB = 2r \sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) \end{aligned}

Substitute $r = 8$ and $\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into the chord formula:\begin{aligned} &AB = 2(8)\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \cr &\hphantom{AB} = 16\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \cr &\hphantom{AB} = 8\sqrt{3}\text{ cm} \end{aligned}
The area of the segment is the sector area minus the triangle area:\begin{aligned} &A_{\text{segment}} = A_{\text{sector}} - A_{\text{triangle}} \end{aligned}

Calculate the area of the sector:\begin{aligned} &A_{\text{sector}} = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta \cr &\hphantom{A_{\text{sector}}} = \dfrac{1}{2}(8)^2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \cr &\hphantom{A_{\text{sector}}} = \dfrac{64\pi}{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}

Calculate the area of the triangle:\begin{aligned} &A_{\text{triangle}} = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta \cr &\hphantom{A_{\text{triangle}}} = \dfrac{1}{2}(8)^2\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \cr &\hphantom{A_{\text{triangle}}} = 32\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \cr &\hphantom{A_{\text{triangle}}} = 16\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}
Subtract the triangle area from the sector area:\begin{aligned} &A_{\text{segment}} = \dfrac{64\pi}{3} - 16\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $8\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}$, (b) $\dfrac{64\pi}{3} - 16\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (a) if you assume the triangle $OAB$ is equilateral because of the presence of $\pi/3$ components, leading to a chord length equal to the radius ($8\text{ cm}$).
This error arises in part (b) if you forget the factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in the triangle area formula $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta$, subtracting $32\sqrt{3}$ instead of $16\sqrt{3}$.
This mistake occurs if you use a radius of $4\text{ cm}$ instead of $8\text{ cm}$ in your calculations, perhaps from confusing the radius with half of its value.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Chord Length Shortcut
bradley_insight.content: For any isosceles triangle formed by a sector, the chord length formula $2r\sin\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ is a massive timesaver. It bypasses the need to write out the full Cosine Rule $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$, although both methods yield the exact same simplified result.

question:
A sector of a circle of radius $12\text{ cm}$ with sector angle $\theta = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$ radians is bent to form the curved surface of a right circular cone.

(a) Find the radius of the base of the cone.

(b) Determine the height of the cone, giving your answer in exact surd form.
steps: The arc length $s$ of the sector becomes the circumference of the circular base of the cone (with radius $r$):\begin{aligned} &s = 2\pi r \end{aligned}

Calculate the arc length $s$ using $R = 12\text{ cm}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$:\begin{aligned} &s = R\theta \cr &\hphantom{s} = 12\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) \cr &\hphantom{s} = 16\pi\text{ cm} \end{aligned}
Set the base circumference equal to $s$ and solve for $r$:\begin{aligned} &2\pi r = 16\pi \cr &r = 8\text{ cm} \end{aligned}
The radius of the original sector ($R = 12\text{ cm}$) becomes the slant height of the cone. By Pythagoras' theorem:\begin{aligned} &h^2 + r^2 = R^2 \cr &h = \sqrt{R^2 - r^2} \end{aligned}

Substitute $R = 12$ and $r = 8$ to find the exact vertical height:\begin{aligned} &h = \sqrt{12^2 - 8^2} \cr &\hphantom{h} = \sqrt{144 - 64} \cr &\hphantom{h} = \sqrt{80} \cr &\hphantom{h} = 4\sqrt{5}\text{ cm} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $8\text{ cm}$, (b) $4\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b) if you mistakenly assume a $3-4-5$ Pythagorean triple structure, resulting in a height of $10\text{ cm}$ from a base radius of $8\text{ cm}$ and a slant height of $12\text{ cm}$ (which is mathematically invalid since $8^2 + 10^2 \neq 12^2$).
This mistake occurs in part (a) if you forget the factor of $2\pi$ in the circumference formula, writing $r = \dfrac{s}{\pi} = 16$ or making an arithmetic division slip.

This error occurs in part (b) if you add the squares of the base radius and slant height instead of subtracting them, calculating $h = \sqrt{12^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{208}$, which simplifies to $4\sqrt{13}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Sector-to-Cone Mapping
bradley_insight.content:
Visualizing 3D transformations is a key skill. Always remember the two fundamental rules of sector-to-cone mapping:

1. The arc length of the sector becomes the base circumference of the cone ($s = 2\pi r$).

2. The radius of the sector becomes the slant height of the cone ($l = R$).

question:
Two identical circles, each of radius $6\text{ cm}$, have their centres at $O_1$ and $O_2$. The distance between the centres is also $6\text{ cm}$, so that the circumference of each circle passes through the centre of the other.

Find the exact area of the region common to both circles.
steps:
Let $A$ and $B$ be the intersection points of the two circumferences. Since the distance between centres equals the radius ($6\text{ cm}$):\begin{aligned} &O_1 O_2 = 6 \cr &O_1 A = O_2 A = 6 \end{aligned}

Therefore, triangle $O_1 A O_2$ is equilateral, and $\angle A O_1 O_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ radians.
