By symmetry, the total angle $\theta$ of sector $A O_1 B$ is double $\angle A O_1 O_2$:\begin{aligned} &\theta = 2 \times \angle A O_1 O_2 \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\text{ radians} \end{aligned}

The common region consists of two identical circular segments separated by the common chord $AB$. The area of one segment in circle $O_1$ is:\begin{aligned} &A_{\text{segment}} = A_{\text{sector}} - A_{\text{triangle}} \cr &\hphantom{A_{\text{segment}}} = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta - \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta \end{aligned}

Substitute $r = 6$ and $\theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ into the segment formula:\begin{aligned} &A_{\text{segment}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2}(6)^2\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\cr & \qquad - \dfrac{1}{2}(6)^2\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) \cr &\quad = 12\pi - 18\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \cr &\quad = 12\pi - 9\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}

Double the area of this single segment to find the total common area:\begin{aligned} &A_{\text{total}} = 2 \times A_{\text{segment}} \cr &\hphantom{A_{\text{total}}} = 2(12\pi - 9\sqrt{3}) \cr &\hphantom{A_{\text{total}}} = 24\pi - 18\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $24\pi - 18\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}^2$

pi_options.feedback: This represents the area of only one segment. You must double this result because the overlapping region consists of two identical segments joined along the common chord.
This error occurs if you only subtract the area of one triangle instead of two when combining the sector areas, or make a scaling slip when doubling.
This represents an algebraic simplification error where the coefficients are miscalculated during the expansion of the segment subtraction.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Overlapping Circles Symmetry
bradley_insight.content: When two identical circles of radius $r$ intersect such that each passes through the other's centre, they form a symmetric lens shape. This shape is exactly double the area of a segment of a circle with a sector angle of $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ radians.

question:
The curve $y = f(x)$ passes through the points $(-2, 0)$, $(0, 8)$, and $(4, 0)$, and has a local maximum at $(1, 9)$.

(a) Find the coordinates of the local maximum and the $x$-intercepts of the transformed curve $y = 2f(x + 3)$.

(b) Find the coordinates of the local minimum and the $y$-intercept of the transformed curve $y = 5 - f(x)$.
steps:
To find the transformed coordinates under $y = 2f(x + 3)$:

• Horizontal shift: $x + 3$ shifts the curve left by $3$ units, so $x \to x - 3$.

• Vertical stretch: scale factor $2$, so $y \to 2y$.

Any point $(x, y)$ transforms to:\begin{aligned} &(x - 3, 2y) \end{aligned}

Apply this to the maximum and the $x$-intercepts:

• Maximum $(1, 9)$:\begin{aligned} &(1 - 3, 2 \times 9) = (-2, 18) \end{aligned}

• Intercept $(-2, 0)$:\begin{aligned} &(-2 - 3, 2 \times 0) = (-5, 0) \end{aligned}

• Intercept $(4, 0)$:\begin{aligned} &(4 - 3, 2 \times 0) = (1, 0) \end{aligned}

The new maximum is $(-2, 18)$ and the $x$-intercepts are $(-5, 0)$ and $(1, 0)$.

For $y = 5 - f(x) = -f(x) + 5$:

• Reflection in the $x$-axis: $y \to -y$.

• Upward vertical shift: $y \to -y + 5$.

Any point $(x, y)$ transforms to:\begin{aligned} &(x, -y + 5) \end{aligned}

Apply this to the maximum and $y$-intercept $(0, 8)$. The maximum becomes a minimum:\begin{aligned} &(1, -9 + 5) = (1, -4) \end{aligned}

For the $y$-intercept $(0, 8)$:\begin{aligned} &(0, -8 + 5) = (0, -3) \end{aligned}

The local minimum is $(1, -4)$ and the new $y$-intercept is $(0, -3)$.
Final Answer: (a) Max: $(-2, 18)$, $x$-intercepts: $(-5, 0)$, $(1, 0)$; (b) Min: $(1, -4)$, $y$-intercept: $(0, -3)$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you shift the graph to the right by $3$ units ($x \to x + 3$) instead of to the left by $3$ units ($x \to x - 3$) when evaluating $y = 2f(x + 3)$.
This mistake occurs in part (b) if you forget to reflect the $y$-coordinates before translating them upwards, calculating $y \to y + 5$ instead of $y \to -y + 5$.
This error occurs if you correctly identify the horizontal translation in part (a) but fail to apply the vertical scale factor of $2$ to the maximum point's $y$-coordinate.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Horizontal Shift Sign Rules
bradley_insight.content: A classic mistake is translating the graph in the wrong direction. The transformation $f(x + a)$ shifts the graph horizontally by $-a$ units. Always think of it as solving the equation inside the bracket for $x$: $x + 3 = 0 \implies x = -3$, which means moving $3$ units left.

question:
The curve $y = g(x)$ has a local minimum at $(3, -6)$ and crosses the axes at $(-1, 0)$, $(5, 0)$, and $(0, -5)$.

(a) State the coordinates of the local maximum and the $y$-intercept of the curve $y = |g(x)|$.

(b) State the coordinates of the two local minima of the curve $y = g(|x|)$.
steps:
The transformation $y = |g(x)|$ reflects negative $y$-values across the $x$-axis:

• If $y \ge 0$, $(x, y)$ is unchanged.

• If $y < 0$, $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$.

Apply $y = |g(x)|$ to the minimum and $y$-intercept:

• Minimum $(3, -6) \to (3, 6)$, which becomes a local maximum.

• $y$-intercept $(0, -5) \to (0, 5)$.

On $y = |g(x)|$, the local maximum is $(3, 6)$ and the $y$-intercept is $(0, 5)$.
The transformation $y = g(|x|)$ discards the portion for $x < 0$ and reflects the portion for $x \ge 0$ across the $y$-axis.

The point $(3, -6)$ has $x \ge 0$, so it is retained. Reflecting across the $y$-axis produces $(-3, -6)$.

Thus, the two local minima of $y = g(|x|)$ are $(3, -6)$ and $(-3, -6)$.
Final Answer: (a) Max: $(3, 6)$, $y$-intercept: $(0, 5)$; (b) Minima: $(3, -6)$ and $(-3, -6)$

pi_options.feedback: This mistake occurs if you correctly reflect the local minimum for $y = |g(x)|$ but forget to apply the modulus to the $y$-intercept $(0, -5)$, leaving it negative.
This error arises from confusing the vertical modulus transformation $y = |g(x)|$ with the horizontal modulus transformation $y = g(|x|)$, swapping their behaviors.
This error occurs in part (b) if you mistakenly reflect the $y$-coordinate of the mirrored minimum, writing $(-3, 6)$ instead of $(-3, -6)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Modulus Differences
bradley_insight.content: It is crucial to distinguish between $|f(x)|$ and $f(|x|)$. The transformation $y = |f(x)|$ folds all negative outputs vertically upwards ($y \to -y$ for $y < 0$). The transformation $y = f(|x|)$ mirrors the right-hand side of the graph onto the left-hand side, creating perfect symmetry about the $y$-axis.

question:
The curve $y = f(x)$ has a local maximum at the point $(6, 4)$.

Determine the coordinates of the corresponding stationary point on the transformed curve $y = 3f(2x - 8) + 5$ and state whether this new point is a local maximum or a local minimum.
steps: Set the argument $2x - 8$ equal to the original $x$-coordinate $6$:\begin{aligned} &2x - 8 = 6 \cr &2x = 14 \cr &x = 7 \end{aligned}

Apply the vertical transformation $3y + 5$ to the original $y$-coordinate $4$:\begin{aligned} &y = 3(4) + 5 \cr &\hphantom{y} = 17 \end{aligned}

This gives the coordinates $(7, 17)$.
The vertical scale factor is $+3$, which does not reflect the curve across the $x$-axis. Therefore, the concavity is unchanged and the point remains a local maximum.
Final Answer: $(7, 17)$, which is a local maximum

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you mistakenly think that scaling or translating a graph vertically reverses its concavity, causing a maximum to become a minimum.

This common error occurs if you incorrectly apply the horizontal operations in the order they are written (such as dividing by $2$ to get $3$, then subtracting $8$). The correct sequence is to set $2x - 8 = 6$ and solve for $x$.
This mistake occurs if you solve the horizontal transformation in the wrong direction, calculating $2(6) + 8 = 20$ instead of setting $2x - 8 = 6$ and isolating $x$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Horizontal Mapping Trick
bradley_insight.content: When combining horizontal transformations, the safest mathematical trick to avoid order-of-operation slips is to set the new argument equal to the old coordinate (e.g. $2x - 8 = x_{\text{old}}$) and solve for $x$. This automatically handles the reverse order of operations correctly!

question:
The curve $y = \cos x$ (for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$) has a minimum point at $(\pi, -1)$.

Determine the coordinates of the corresponding minimum point on the transformed curve $y = 4\cos\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - 2$ that lies within the interval $0 \le x \le \pi$.
steps: Set the argument $2x - \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ equal to $\pi$:\begin{aligned} &2x - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \pi \end{aligned}

Solve for $x$ algebraically:\begin{aligned} &2x = \pi + \dfrac{\pi}{3} \cr &2x = \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \cr &x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \end{aligned}

This value satisfies $0 \le x \le \pi$.

Apply the vertical transformation $4y - 2$ to $y = -1$:\begin{aligned} &y = 4(-1) - 2 \cr &\hphantom{y} = -4 - 2 \cr &\hphantom{y} = -6 \end{aligned}

Thus, the coordinates of the corresponding minimum point are $\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}, -6\right)$.
Final Answer: $\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}, -6\right)$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you calculate the vertical transformation incorrectly, such as ignoring the scale factor of $4$ and only applying the vertical translation: $-1 - 2 = -3$, or making other vertical arithmetic slips.
This mistake arises from subtracting $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ instead of adding it when solving for $x$, calculating $2x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$, which gives $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
This mistake occurs if you forget to divide by $2$ when isolating $x$, leaving $x = \dfrac{4\pi}{3}$, which also lies outside the specified interval $0 \le x \le \pi$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Trig Period Stretches
bradley_insight.content: A horizontal stretch of scale factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ (caused by the $2x$ term) compresses the trigonometric wave, meaning key points occur twice as frequently. Always verify that your transformed $x$-coordinate lies within the interval specified in the question.

question:
The curve $y = \mathrm{e}^x - 4$ has a $y$-intercept at $(0, -3)$ and a horizontal asymptote with equation $y = -4$.

The curve is transformed to $y = -3(\mathrm{e}^{x-2} - 4) + 1$. Determine:

(a) the exact coordinates of the new $y$-intercept,

(b) the equation of the new horizontal asymptote.
steps: To find the new $y$-intercept, set $x = 0$ in the transformed curve equation:\begin{aligned} &y = -3(\mathrm{e}^{0-2} - 4) + 1 \end{aligned}

Simplify to find the exact vertical coordinate:\begin{aligned} &y = -3(\mathrm{e}^{-2} - 4) + 1 \cr &\hphantom{y} = -3\mathrm{e}^{-2} + 12 + 1 \cr &\hphantom{y} = 13 - 3\mathrm{e}^{-2} \end{aligned}

Thus, the new $y$-intercept is $\left(0, 13 - 3\mathrm{e}^{-2}\right)$.
For $y = \mathrm{e}^x - 4$, as $x \to -\infty$, $\mathrm{e}^x \to 0$, giving the horizontal asymptote $y = -4$.

As $x \to -\infty$, the exponential term $\mathrm{e}^{x-2} \to 0$ in the transformed curve:\begin{aligned} &y \to -3(0 - 4) + 1 \cr &y \to 12 + 1 \cr &y \to 13 \end{aligned}

Thus, the equation of the new horizontal asymptote is $y = 13$.
Final Answer: (a) $\left(0, 13 - 3\mathrm{e}^{-2}\right)$, (b) $y = 13$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b) if you fail to reflect the original asymptote, calculating $-3(4) + 1 = -11$ instead of $-3(-4) + 1 = 13$ due to a sign error.

This mistake occurs in part (a) if you incorrectly evaluate $\mathrm{e}^{-2}$ as $0$ when calculating the $y$-intercept, which is only its limiting behavior as $x \to -\infty$, not its actual value at $x = 0$.
This arises if you do not distribute the factor of $-3$ across the entire parenthetical expression, or assume that horizontal asymptote equations are unaffected by vertical stretches.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Asymptote Transformation Rules
bradley_insight.content: Horizontal asymptotes are horizontal lines of the form $y = c$. Because they are completely independent of horizontal coordinates, they are completely unaffected by horizontal transformations like shifts ($x \to x-2$) or stretches. They only scale and translate under vertical transformations.

question:
Solve the equation:

\begin{aligned} &2\tan^2\theta - \tan\theta - \sec^2\theta = 1 \end{aligned}

for values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$. Give your answers to two decimal places where appropriate.
steps: Use the identity $\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta$ to write the equation in terms of $\tan\theta$:\begin{aligned} &2\tan^2\theta - \tan\theta \cr &\qquad - (1 + \tan^2\theta) = 1 \end{aligned}
Expand and simplify into a quadratic in $\tan\theta$:\begin{aligned} &2\tan^2\theta - \tan\theta \cr &\qquad - 1 - \tan^2\theta = 1 \cr &\tan^2\theta - \tan\theta - 2 = 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &(\tan\theta - 2)(\tan\theta + 1) = 0 \end{aligned}

This gives two branches:\begin{aligned} &\tan\theta = 2 \text{ or } \tan\theta = -1 \end{aligned}

Solve each branch in $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:

• Branch 1: $\tan\theta = 2$\begin{aligned} &\theta = \arctan(2) \approx 63.43^\circ \cr &\theta = 63.43^\circ + 180^\circ \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 243.43^\circ \end{aligned}

• Branch 2: $\tan\theta = -1$\begin{aligned} &\theta = 180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135^\circ \cr &\theta = 360^\circ - 45^\circ = 315^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $\theta \approx 63.43^\circ$, $135^\circ$, $243.43^\circ$, $315^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error when solving the quadratic branch $\tan\theta = -1$, solving $\tan\theta = 1$ instead and finding the quadrant solutions $45^\circ$ and $225^\circ$.

This mistake occurs if you forget that the tangent function is periodic with a period of $180^\circ$, completely omitting the second-quadrant and fourth-quadrant solutions that lie between $180^\circ$ and $360^\circ$.

This error is caused by a calculator division slip or inverting the tangent value when evaluating the principal value, writing $\tan\theta = 0.5$ (which yields $26.57^\circ$) instead of $\tan\theta = 2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Pythagorean Identity Sign Traps
bradley_insight.content: When substituting $\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta$ into a term preceded by a negative sign, always place the identity inside parentheses first: $-(\sec^2\theta) = -(1 + \tan^2\theta) = -1 - \tan^2\theta$. Forgetting to distribute the negative sign is a very common source of algebraic errors.

question:
Solve the equation:

\begin{aligned} &2\cot^2\theta - \cot\theta - \csc^2\theta = 5 \end{aligned}

for values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$. Give your answers to two decimal places where appropriate.
steps: Use the identity $\csc^2\theta = 1 + \cot^2\theta$ to write the equation in terms of $\cot\theta$:\begin{aligned} &2\cot^2\theta - \cot\theta \cr &\qquad - (1 + \cot^2\theta) = 5 \end{aligned}
Expand and simplify to form a standard quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &2\cot^2\theta - \cot\theta \cr &\qquad - 1 - \cot^2\theta = 5 \cr &\cot^2\theta - \cot\theta - 6 = 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &(\cot\theta - 3)(\cot\theta + 2) = 0 \end{aligned}

Convert to primary reciprocal functions:\begin{aligned} &\cot\theta = 3 \implies \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{3} \cr &\cot\theta = -2 \implies \tan\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}

Solve for $\theta$ in $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:

• Branch 1: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}$\begin{aligned} &\theta = \arctan\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \approx 18.43^\circ \cr &\theta = 18.43^\circ + 180^\circ \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 198.43^\circ \end{aligned}

• Branch 2: $\tan\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$\begin{aligned} &\theta = 180^\circ - 26.57^\circ \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 153.43^\circ \cr &\theta = 360^\circ - 26.57^\circ \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 333.43^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $\theta \approx 18.43^\circ$, $153.43^\circ$, $198.43^\circ$, $333.43^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you mistakenly think $\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}$ implies you should invert the angle rather than the ratio, calculating $\theta = \arctan(3)$ and $\theta = \arctan(-2)$.
This mistake occurs if you solve the first quadratic branch correctly but discard the second branch, perhaps thinking that a negative cotangent ratio has no valid solutions.
This arises from a quadrant mapping error in Branch 1, using $180^\circ - 18.43^\circ = 161.57^\circ$ instead of the correct third-quadrant angle $180^\circ + 18.43^\circ = 198.43^\circ$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Reciprocal Trigonometric Conversions
bradley_insight.content: When solving equations with reciprocal trigonometric functions like $\cot\theta$, $\sec\theta$, or $\csc\theta$, the safest first step is always to isolate the function and then convert it to its primary counterpart (e.g., $\cot\theta = k \implies \tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{k}$). This allows you to safely use your calculator's standard inverse trigonometric functions.

question:
Solve the equation:

\begin{aligned} &3\cos 2\theta + 8\sin\theta = 5 \end{aligned}

for values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$. Give your answers to two decimal places where appropriate.
steps: Use the double-angle identity $\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta$:\begin{aligned} &3(1 - 2\sin^2\theta) + 8\sin\theta = 5 \end{aligned}

Expand and collect terms on one side:\begin{aligned} &3 - 6\sin^2\theta + 8\sin\theta = 5 \cr &6\sin^2\theta - 8\sin\theta + 2 = 0 \end{aligned}

Divide all terms by $2$:\begin{aligned} &3\sin^2\theta - 4\sin\theta + 1 = 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &(3\sin\theta - 1)(\sin\theta - 1) = 0 \end{aligned}

This yields two linear branches:\begin{aligned} &\sin\theta = 1 \text{ or } \sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}

Solve for $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:

• Branch 1: $\sin\theta = 1$\begin{aligned} &\theta = 90^\circ \end{aligned}

• Branch 2: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}$\begin{aligned} &\theta = \arcsin\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \approx 19.47^\circ \cr &\theta = 180^\circ - 19.47^\circ \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 160.53^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $\theta = 90^\circ$, $\theta \approx 19.47^\circ$, $160.53^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a quadrant error when solving the $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}$ branch, mapping the second solution to the fourth quadrant ($360^\circ - 19.47^\circ = 340.53^\circ$) instead of the second quadrant ($180^\circ - \theta$).
This happens if you mistakenly solve for both positive and negative values of $\sin\theta = \pm \dfrac{1}{3}$, generating extraneous third-quadrant and fourth-quadrant solutions.
This error occurs if you fail to solve the branch $\sin\theta = 1$, or discard its solution $\theta = 90^\circ$ because it is an axis angle.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Choosing the Right Double-Angle Identity
bradley_insight.content: The double-angle identity for cosine has three equivalent forms: $\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta$, $2\cos^2\theta - 1$, and $1 - 2\sin^2\theta$. Always look at the other terms in the equation to decide which form to use. Since the other term is $8\sin\theta$, choosing $1 - 2\sin^2\theta$ is the only path that results in a solvable single-variable quadratic.

question:
(a) Express $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta$ in the form $R\sin(\theta + \alpha)$, where $R > 0$ and $0^\circ < \alpha < 90^\circ$. Give the value of $\alpha$ to two decimal places.

(b) Hence, solve the equation $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta = 2.5$ for values of $\theta$ in the interval $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$. Give your answers to two decimal places.
steps:
Expand $R\sin(\theta + \alpha)$ using the compound angle identity:\begin{aligned} &R\sin(\theta + \alpha) \cr &\quad = R\sin\theta\cos\alpha \cr &\qquad + R\cos\theta\sin\alpha \end{aligned}

Equate coefficients with $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta$:\begin{aligned} &R\cos\alpha = 3 \cr &R\sin\alpha = 4 \end{aligned}

Find $R$ by squaring and adding:\begin{aligned} &R^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 \cr &R^2 = 25 \cr &R = 5 \end{aligned}

Find $\alpha$ by dividing the equations:\begin{aligned} &\tan\alpha = \dfrac{4}{3} \cr &\alpha = \arctan\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right) \cr &\hphantom{\alpha} \approx 53.13^\circ \end{aligned}

Thus, $3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta = 5\sin(\theta + 53.13^\circ)$.
Substitute the harmonic form into the equation:\begin{aligned} &5\sin(\theta + 53.13^\circ) = 2.5 \cr &\sin(\theta + 53.13^\circ) = 0.5 \end{aligned}

Solve for $(\theta + 53.13^\circ)$ in the shifted interval $[53.13^\circ, 413.13^\circ]$:\begin{aligned} &\theta + 53.13^\circ = 150^\circ \cr &\theta + 53.13^\circ = 390^\circ \end{aligned}

Subtract $53.13^\circ$ to find $\theta$:\begin{aligned} &\theta = 150^\circ - 53.13^\circ \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 96.87^\circ \cr &\theta = 390^\circ - 53.13^\circ \cr &\hphantom{\theta} = 336.87^\circ \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $5\sin(\theta + 53.13^\circ)$, (b) $\theta \approx 96.87^\circ$, $336.87^\circ$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b) if you subtract $53.13^\circ$ from the incorrect quadrant angle $256.26^\circ$ or make an arithmetic slip when mapping standard principal values.
This mistake occurs if you swap the definitions of the coefficients, writing $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{3}{4}$ to get $\alpha \approx 36.87^\circ$.

This error occurs if you forget to adjust the boundary range of the intermediate angle $\theta + 53.13^\circ$, resulting in keeping the negative angle $-23.13^\circ$ instead of adding $360^\circ$ to find its co-terminal solution in the interval.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Shifting the Interval Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: When solving compound equations like $\sin(\theta + \alpha) = k$, always write down the shifted interval boundary first: if $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$, then $\alpha \le \theta + \alpha \le 360^\circ + \alpha$. This ensures that you don't miss solutions that overflow past $360^\circ$ (like $390^\circ - \alpha$) or keep invalid negative solutions.

question:
Given that $\theta$ is small and measured in radians:

(a) Show that the equation:

\begin{aligned} &\cos\theta - \sin\theta + 2\theta^2 = 1.25 \end{aligned}

can be approximated by the quadratic equation:

\begin{aligned} &3\theta^2 - 2\theta - 0.5 = 0 \end{aligned}

(b) Solve this quadratic equation to find the possible values of $\theta$, giving your answers to three decimal places.
steps: Apply the standard small-angle approximations for small $\theta$ in radians:\begin{aligned} &\cos\theta \approx 1 - \dfrac{\theta^2}{2} \cr &\sin\theta \approx \theta \end{aligned}
Substitute these approximations into the original equation:\begin{aligned} &\left(1 - \dfrac{\theta^2}{2}\right) - \theta + 2\theta^2 \approx 1.25 \end{aligned}

Collect like terms and simplify:\begin{aligned} &1 - \theta + 1.5\theta^2 = 1.25 \cr &1.5\theta^2 - \theta - 0.25 = 0 \end{aligned}

Multiply through by $2$ to clear decimals:\begin{aligned} &3\theta^2 - 2\theta - 0.5 = 0 \end{aligned}

Apply the quadratic formula to solve part (b):\begin{aligned} &\theta \cr &= \dfrac{-(-2) \pm \sqrt{(-2)^2 - 4(3)(-0.5)}}{2(3)} \cr & = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 6}}{6} \cr & = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{10}}{6} \end{aligned}

Evaluate the roots numerically with $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.16228$:\begin{aligned} &\theta_1 \approx \dfrac{2 + 3.16228}{6} \approx 0.860 \cr &\theta_2 \approx \dfrac{2 - 3.16228}{6} \approx -0.194 \end{aligned}

Thus, to three decimal places, the solutions are $\theta \approx 0.860$ and $\theta \approx -0.194$ radians.
Final Answer: (b) $\theta \approx 0.860$, $-0.194$ radians

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you forget to multiply by the factor of $2$ in the denominator when evaluating the quadratic formula, dividing by $12$ instead of $6$.
This mistake arises from a sign error under the discriminant, calculating $4 - 6 = -2$ instead of $4 + 6 = 10$.
This mistake occurs if you discard the negative root $\theta \approx -0.194$ because you assume that small angles must be strictly positive, whereas negative values in radians are fully valid.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Small-Angle Limits
bradley_insight.content: Small-angle approximations are extremely powerful but only hold true when $\theta$ is small (generally, $-0.5 < \theta < 0.5$ radians is highly accurate). While our positive solution $\theta \approx 0.860$ mathematically satisfies the quadratic approximation, it is slightly outside this highly accurate physical bound, whereas $\theta \approx -0.194$ represents a highly accurate, physically realistic small angle.

question:
A function $f$ is defined for $x > 3$ by:

\begin{aligned} &f(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{(x - 1)(x - 3)^2} \end{aligned}

(a) Express $f(x)$ in terms of partial fractions.

(b) Evaluate the definite integral:

\begin{aligned} &\int_{4}^{5} f(x) \text{d}x \end{aligned}

giving your answer to three decimal places.
steps: To express $f(x)$ in terms of partial fractions, set up the decomposition template for a repeated linear factor:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{x + 3}{(x - 1)(x - 3)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{A}{x - 1} + \dfrac{B}{x - 3} + \dfrac{C}{(x - 3)^2} \end{aligned}
Multiply both sides by $(x - 1)(x - 3)^2$:\begin{aligned} &x + 3 \cr &\quad = A(x - 3)^2 \cr &\qquad + B(x - 1)(x - 3) \cr &\qquad + C(x - 1) \end{aligned}

Solve for constants $A$, $B$, and $C$:

• For $x = 3$, $6 = 2C \implies C = 3$

• For $x = 1$, $4 = 4A \implies A = 1$

• Comparing $x^2$ coefficients: $0 = A + B \implies B = -1$

Thus, the partial fractions decomposition is:\begin{aligned} &f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 1} - \dfrac{1}{x - 3} + \dfrac{3}{(x - 3)^2} \end{aligned}
Integrate term-by-term from $4$ to $5$:\begin{aligned} &\int_{4}^{5} f(x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \big[\ln|x - 1| - \ln|x - 3| \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{3}{x - 3}\big]_{4}^{5} \end{aligned}

Evaluate at the limits:

• Upper limit $x = 5$:\begin{aligned} &\ln 4 - \ln 2 - 1.5 \cr &\quad = \ln 2 - 1.5 \end{aligned}

• Lower limit $x = 4$:\begin{aligned} &\ln 3 - \ln 1 - 3 \cr &\quad = \ln 3 - 3 \end{aligned}

Subtract the lower limit evaluation from the upper limit evaluation:\begin{aligned} &\int_{4}^{5} f(x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = (\ln 2 - 1.5) - (\ln 3 - 3) \cr &\quad = \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) + 1.5 \cr &\quad \approx 1.095 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $1.095$

pi_options.feedback: This mistake occurs if you evaluate $\ln\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$ incorrectly as $0$, or omit the logarithmic terms completely during integration.
This error is caused by a sign slip during limit subtraction, calculating $1.5 + \ln 2 + \ln 3$ instead of $1.5 + \ln 2 - \ln 3$.
This arises if you make an integration error with the repeated linear factor, evaluating $\int \dfrac{3}{(x - 3)^2}\text{d}x = 3\ln(x - 3)^2$ instead of $-\dfrac{3}{x - 3}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Repeated Linear Integrals
bradley_insight.content: A very common student trap is integrating a repeated linear factor like $\dfrac{C}{(x-a)^2}$ as if it were a simple reciprocal function, writing $C\ln(x-a)^2$. Always remember that reciprocal terms with exponents greater than $1$ must be integrated using the power rule: $\int (x-a)^{-2}\text{d}x = -(x-a)^{-1}$.

question:
A function $f$ is defined for $x > 0$ by:

\begin{aligned} &f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 3}{(x + 1)(2x + 1)} \end{aligned}

(a) Express $f(x)$ in terms of partial fractions.

(b) Evaluate the definite integral:

\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{1} f(x) \text{d}x \end{aligned}

giving your answer as a single logarithm in exact form.
steps: Decompose the algebraic fraction into two linear terms:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{2x + 3}{(x + 1)(2x + 1)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{A}{x + 1} + \dfrac{B}{2x + 1} \end{aligned}
Multiply both sides by $(x + 1)(2x + 1)$:\begin{aligned} &2x + 3 = A(2x + 1) + B(x + 1) \end{aligned}

Solve for $A$ and $B$:

• For $x = -1$, $1 = -A \implies A = -1$

• For $x = -0.5$, $2 = 0.5B \implies B = 4$

Thus, the partial fractions decomposition is:\begin{aligned} &f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{x + 1} + \dfrac{4}{2x + 1} \end{aligned}
Integrate term-by-term over $[0, 1]$:\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{1} f(x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \big[-\ln|x + 1| \cr &\qquad + 2\ln|2x + 1|\big]_{0}^{1} \end{aligned}

Evaluate at the limits:

• At $x = 1$:\begin{aligned} &-\ln 2 + 2\ln 3 \cr &\quad = \ln 9 - \ln 2 \cr &\quad = \ln\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right) \end{aligned}

• At $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} &-\ln 1 + 2\ln 1 = 0 \end{aligned}

Thus, the exact value of the definite integral is $\ln\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right)$.
Final Answer: $\ln\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right)$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you fail to divide by $2$ when integrating $\dfrac{4}{2x + 1}$, leading to an incorrect coefficient of $4\ln|2x + 1|$ instead of $2\ln|2x + 1|$.
This mistake arises from a sign error when solving the partial fractions for $A$, finding $A = 1$ instead of $A = -1$.
This happens if you evaluate the lower limit $x = 0$ incorrectly, forgetting that subtracting $-\ln(1) + 2\ln(1)$ equals $0$ and instead subtracting another value.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Reciprocal Integration Coefficients
bradley_insight.content: When integrating terms of the form $\dfrac{B}{ax + b}$, a very common student mistake is forgetting to divide by the coefficient $a$ of the $x$ term. Always verify that $\int \dfrac{4}{2x + 1}\text{d}x = \dfrac{4}{2}\ln|2x + 1| = 2\ln|2x + 1|$.

question:
A function $f$ is defined for $x > -1$ by the improper fraction:

\begin{aligned} &f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + 5x + 7}{(x + 1)(x + 2)} \end{aligned}

(a) Express $f(x)$ in the form $P + \dfrac{Q}{x + 1} + \dfrac{R}{x + 2}$, where $P$, $Q$, and $R$ are real constants.

(b) Find the exact value of the definite integral:

\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{1} f(x) \text{d}x \end{aligned}

giving your answer in the form $a + \ln b$.
steps: Expand the denominator:\begin{aligned} &(x + 1)(x + 2) = x^2 + 3x + 2 \end{aligned}

Perform algebraic division to separate the constant term:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{x^2 + 5x + 7}{x^2 + 3x + 2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{(x^2 + 3x + 2) + 2x + 5}{x^2 + 3x + 2} \cr &\quad = 1 + \dfrac{2x + 5}{(x + 1)(x + 2)} \end{aligned}

This gives $P = 1$.
Decompose the remaining proper fraction into partial fractions:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{2x + 5}{(x + 1)(x + 2)} = \dfrac{Q}{x + 1} + \dfrac{R}{x + 2} \cr &2x + 5 = Q(x + 2) + R(x + 1) \end{aligned}

Substitute values of $x$ to solve for $Q$ and $R$:

• For $x = -1$, $3 = Q$

• For $x = -2$, $1 = -R \implies R = -1$

Thus, the complete decomposition is:\begin{aligned} &f(x) = 1 + \dfrac{3}{x + 1} - \dfrac{1}{x + 2} \end{aligned}
Integrate $f(x)$ over $[0, 1]$:\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{1} f(x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \big[x + 3\ln|x + 1| \cr &\qquad - \ln|x + 2|\big]_{0}^{1} \end{aligned}

Evaluate the limits:

• At $x = 1$:\begin{aligned} &1 + 3\ln 2 - \ln 3 \end{aligned}

• At $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} &0 + 3\ln 1 - \ln 2 = -\ln 2 \end{aligned}

Subtracting the lower limit from the upper limit:\begin{aligned} &\int_{0}^{1} f(x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = (1 + 3\ln 2 - \ln 3) - (-\ln 2) \cr &\quad = 1 + 4\ln 2 - \ln 3 \cr &\quad = 1 + \ln 16 - \ln 3 \cr &\quad = 1 + \ln\left(\dfrac{16}{3}\right) \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $1 + \ln\left(\dfrac{16}{3}\right)$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you evaluate the lower limit of the integration as $0$ instead of $-\ln 2$, failing to subtract the lower limit correctly.
This mistake happens if you completely forget to integrate the constant term $P = 1$ over the interval $[0, 1]$, which should yield $1$.
This results from a sign error when determining the partial fraction constants $Q$ or $R$, leading to incorrect logarithmic combinations.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Improper Algebraic Fractions
bradley_insight.content: Before attempting partial fractions, always compare the highest degree of the numerator and the denominator. If the degree of the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator, the fraction is improper, and you must perform algebraic division first to extract the polynomial/constant terms.

question:
Consider the definite integral:

\begin{aligned} &I = \int_{0}^{\ln 2} \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^x}{\mathrm{e}^{2x} + 3\mathrm{e}^x + 2} \text{d}x \end{aligned}

(a) Use the substitution $u = \mathrm{e}^x$ to show that $I$ can be written as:

\begin{aligned} &\int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{1}{(u + 1)(u + 2)} \text{d}u \end{aligned}

(b) Express the integrand $\dfrac{1}{(u + 1)(u + 2)}$ in terms of partial fractions.

(c) Hence, evaluate the exact value of $I$, giving your answer in the form $\ln\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers.
steps:
Apply the substitution $u = \mathrm{e}^x$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} = \mathrm{e}^x \implies \text{d}x = \dfrac{\text{d}u}{u} \end{aligned}

Transform the integration limits:

• When $x = 0$, $u = \mathrm{e}^0 = 1$

• When $x = \ln 2$, $u = \mathrm{e}^{\ln 2} = 2$

Substitute into the integral:\begin{aligned} &I = \int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{u}{u^2 + 3u + 2}\left(\dfrac{\text{d}u}{u}\right) \cr &\hphantom{I} = \int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{1}{u^2 + 3u + 2}\text{d}u \cr &\hphantom{I} = \int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{1}{(u + 1)(u + 2)}\text{d}u \end{aligned}

Decompose the integrand into partial fractions:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{(u + 1)(u + 2)} = \dfrac{A}{u + 1} + \dfrac{B}{u + 2} \cr &1 = A(u + 2) + B(u + 1) \end{aligned}

Substituting $u = -1$ gives $A = 1$. Substituting $u = -2$ gives $B = -1$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{(u + 1)(u + 2)} = \dfrac{1}{u + 1} - \dfrac{1}{u + 2} \end{aligned}

Integrate the decomposed fractions:\begin{aligned} &I = \int_{1}^{2} \left(\dfrac{1}{u + 1} - \dfrac{1}{u + 2}\right)\text{d}u \cr &\hphantom{I} = \big[\ln|u + 1| - \ln|u + 2|\big]_{1}^{2} \end{aligned}

Evaluate at the limits:

• At $u = 2$:\begin{aligned} &\ln 3 - \ln 4 = \ln\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) \end{aligned}

• At $u = 1$:\begin{aligned} &\ln 2 - \ln 3 = \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \end{aligned}

Subtracting the limit evaluations:\begin{aligned} &I = \ln\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) - \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \cr &\hphantom{I} = \ln\left(\dfrac{3/4}{2/3}\right) \cr &\hphantom{I} = \ln\left(\dfrac{9}{8}\right) \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $\ln\left(\dfrac{9}{8}\right)$

pi_options.feedback: This occurs if you only evaluate the upper limit at $u = 2$ and forget to subtract the lower limit evaluated at $u = 1$.
This error is caused by a sign error when evaluating the limits, adding the lower limit evaluation instead of subtracting it.
This happens if you forget to apply the substitution to the integration limits, incorrectly integrating over the original limits $[0, \ln 2]$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Substitution and Limit Transformations
bradley_insight.content: A crucial step in definite integration by substitution is transforming the limits. Changing the limits to match the substitution variable ($u = \mathrm{e}^x$) means you do not need to convert back to the original variable ($x$) after integrating, allowing you to evaluate the integral directly.

question:
The curve $C$ has the equation:

\begin{aligned} &y = \dfrac{3x + 1}{(x + 1)(3x + 2)^2} \end{aligned}

(a) Express $y$ in terms of partial fractions.

(b) Find the exact area of the finite region bounded by the curve $C$, the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines $x = 0$ and $x = 1$.
steps: Set up the template for a repeated linear factor:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{3x + 1}{(x + 1)(3x + 2)^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{A}{x + 1} + \dfrac{B}{3x + 2} + \dfrac{C}{(3x + 2)^2} \end{aligned}
Multiply both sides by $(x + 1)(3x + 2)^2$:\begin{aligned} &3x + 1 \cr &\quad = A(3x + 2)^2 \cr &\qquad + B(x + 1)(3x + 2) \cr &\qquad + C(x + 1) \end{aligned}

Solve for the constants:

• For $x = -1$, $-2 = A(-1)^2 \implies A = -2$

• For $x = -\dfrac{2}{3}$, $-1 = \dfrac{1}{3}C \implies C = -3$

• Comparing $x^2$ coefficients: $0 = 9A + 3B \implies B = 6$

Thus, the partial fractions decomposition is:\begin{aligned} &y = -\dfrac{2}{x + 1} + \dfrac{6}{3x + 2} - \dfrac{3}{(3x + 2)^2} \end{aligned}

Integrate $y$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 1$:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \int_{0}^{1} \big(-\dfrac{2}{x + 1} + \dfrac{6}{3x + 2} \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{3}{(3x + 2)^2}\big)\text{d}x \cr &\quad = \big[-2\ln|x + 1| + 2\ln|3x + 2| \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{1}{3x + 2}\big]_{0}^{1} \end{aligned}

Evaluate at the limits:

• Upper limit $x = 1$:\begin{aligned} &-2\ln 2 + 2\ln 5 + \dfrac{1}{5} \end{aligned}

• Lower limit $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} &-2\ln 1 + 2\ln 2 + \dfrac{1}{2} = 2\ln 2 + \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}

Subtracting the lower limit from the upper limit:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \left(-2\ln 2 + 2\ln 5 + \dfrac{1}{5}\right) \cr &\qquad - \left(2\ln 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \cr &\quad = 2\ln 5 - 4\ln 2 - \dfrac{3}{10} \cr &\quad = \ln 25 - \ln 16 - \dfrac{3}{10} \cr &\quad = \ln\left(\dfrac{25}{16}\right) - \dfrac{3}{10} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $\ln\left(\dfrac{25}{16}\right) - \dfrac{3}{10}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs due to an arithmetic sign slip when evaluating the limits of the repeated linear term, calculating $\dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{7}{10}$ instead of $\dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{2} = -\dfrac{3}{10}$.
This mistake happens if you lose the factor of $2$ on the logarithmic terms during integration, evaluating $-2\ln|x+1| + 2\ln|3x+2|$ as $-\ln|x+1| + \ln|3x+2|$ instead.
This occurs if you omit the integration of the repeated quadratic factor term, completely leaving out the fractional constants.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Combining Logarithms for Exact Areas
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating definite integrals that yield multiple logarithmic terms, always simplify your answer into a single logarithm using the laws of logarithms: $a\ln x - b\ln y = \ln\left(\dfrac{x^a}{y^b}\right)$. This is not only standard practice in A-Level examinations, but it is also essential to prove that a calculated area is positive.

question:
(a) Find the first three terms in the binomial expansion of $(1 - 8x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ in ascending powers of $x$.

(b) State the range of values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid.

(c) By substituting $x = \dfrac{1}{100}$ into your expansion, find an approximate value for $\sqrt{23}$ in the form $\dfrac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.
steps: To find the binomial expansion of $(1 - 8x)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$, we apply the binomial series with $u = -8x$ and $n = -\dfrac{1}{2}$: \begin{aligned} &(1 - 8x)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \cr &\quad = 1 + nu + \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}u^2 + \dots \cr &\quad \approx 1 + \Big(-\dfrac{1}{2}\Big)(-8x) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{\big(-\frac{1}{2}\big)\big(-\frac{3}{2}\big)}{2}(-8x)^2 \end{aligned}

We simplify each term of the expansion: \begin{aligned} &\text{Term 1} = 1 \cr &\text{Term 2} = 4x \cr &\text{Term 3} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{3}{8}(64x^2) \cr &\quad = 24x^2 \end{aligned} Combining these gives the first three terms: \begin{aligned} &1 + 4x + 24x^2 \end{aligned}
For part (b), the range of validity requires the variable term to satisfy: \begin{aligned} &|-8x| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies 8|x| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies |x| < \dfrac{1}{8} \end{aligned}

For part (c), we substitute $x = \dfrac{1}{100}$ into the left-hand side expression: \begin{aligned} &\Big(1 - 8\Big(\dfrac{1}{100}\Big)\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \cr &\quad = \Big(1 - \dfrac{8}{100}\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \cr &\quad = \Big(\dfrac{92}{100}\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{92}} \cr &\quad = \sqrt{\dfrac{25}{23}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{23}} \end{aligned}

Next, we substitute $x = 0.01$ into our expansion from part (a): \begin{aligned} &1 + 4(0.01) + 24(0.01)^2 \cr &\quad = 1 + 0.04 + 0.0024 \cr &\quad = 1.0424 \end{aligned} Converting $1.0424$ into an exact simplified fraction: \begin{aligned} &1.0424 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{10424}{10000} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1303}{1250} \end{aligned}

We equate the two expressions to approximate $\sqrt{23}$: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{23}} \approx \dfrac{1303}{1250} \cr &\quad \implies \sqrt{23} \approx \dfrac{5 \times 1250}{1303} \cr &\quad \implies \sqrt{23} \approx \dfrac{6250}{1303} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (c) $\dfrac{ 6250 }{ 1303 }$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs from assuming that substituting $x = 0.01$ yields $\sqrt{23}$ directly rather than $\dfrac{5}{\sqrt{23}}$, throwing the approximation off by a factor of nearly five.
This mistake occurs if you solve the algebraic relationship between the expansion and $\sqrt{23}$ correctly but omit the factor of $5$, evaluating $\dfrac{1250}{1303}$ instead.
This error occurs if you invert the final fractional relationship, evaluating $\sqrt{23}$ as $\dfrac{1303}{6250}$ instead of $\dfrac{6250}{1303}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Approximation Conversion Trap
bradley_insight.content: When using binomial expansions to approximate roots, students often assume that substituting $x$ yields the root directly (e.g. assuming $(1-8x)^{-1/2}$ equals $\sqrt{23}$). Always write out the left-hand side calculation in full, find its exact relation to the required root, and then rearrange the final fraction carefully.

question:
(a) Find the first three terms in the binomial expansion of $(8 - 3x)^{\frac{1}{3}}$ in ascending powers of $x$, giving each coefficient as a simplified fraction.

(b) State the range of values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid.
steps: To expand a binomial expression of the form $(a + bx)^n$ where the leading term is not $1$, we first factorise the leading constant: \begin{aligned} &(8 - 3x)^{\frac{1}{3}} \cr &\quad = \Big[8\Big(1 - \dfrac{3}{8}x\Big)\Big]^{\frac{1}{3}} \cr &\quad = 8^{\frac{1}{3}}\Big(1 - \dfrac{3}{8}x\Big)^{\frac{1}{3}} \cr &\quad = 2\Big(1 - \dfrac{3}{8}x\Big)^{\frac{1}{3}} \end{aligned}

We apply the binomial expansion to the bracketed expression with $u = -\dfrac{3}{8}x$ and $n = \dfrac{1}{3}$: \begin{aligned} &\Big(1 - \dfrac{3}{8}x\Big)^{\frac{1}{3}} \cr &\quad \approx 1 + \Big(\dfrac{1}{3}\Big)\Big(-\dfrac{3}{8}x\Big) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{\big(\frac{1}{3}\big)\big(-\frac{2}{3}\big)}{2}\Big(-\dfrac{3}{8}x\Big)^2 \end{aligned}

We simplify each term inside the bracket: \begin{aligned} &\text{Term 1} = 1 \cr &\text{Term 2} = -\dfrac{1}{8}x \cr &\text{Term 3} \cr &\quad = \Big(-\dfrac{1}{9}\Big)\Big(\dfrac{9}{64}x^2\Big) \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{1}{64}x^2 \end{aligned} Substituting these terms back gives: \begin{aligned} &2\Big(1 - \dfrac{1}{8}x - \dfrac{1}{64}x^2\Big) \end{aligned}
We multiply through by the factor of $2$: \begin{aligned} &2 - \dfrac{1}{4}x - \dfrac{1}{32}x^2 \end{aligned}

For part (b), the range of validity requires the absolute value of the variable term to be strictly less than $1$: \begin{aligned} &\Big|-\dfrac{3}{8}x\Big| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies \dfrac{3}{8}|x| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies |x| < \dfrac{8}{3} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $2 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } x - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 32 } x^2$, (b) $|x| < \dfrac{ 8 }{ 3 }$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you forget to multiply the final terms of the binomial expansion by the factor of $2$ that was extracted from the leading constant $8^{1/3}$.
This error occurs in part (b) if you assume the range of validity is always $|x| < 1$ regardless of the horizontal coefficients, neglecting the scale factor of the variable.
This mistake is caused by a sign error in evaluating Term 3, failing to recognise that $\frac{1}{3}\big(-\frac{2}{3}\big)$ is negative, which produces a negative quadratic term.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Leading Term Factorisation
bradley_insight.content: For any binomial expansion where the index $n$ is not a positive integer, the first term inside the bracket *must* be exactly $1$ to apply the standard binomial formula. Always extract the leading constant first, making sure to apply the index $n$ to the extracted constant (e.g. $8^{1/3} = 2$).

question:
(a) Find the binomial expansion of: \begin{aligned} &f(x) = \dfrac{3 + x}{(1 - 2x)^2} \end{aligned} in ascending powers of $x$, up to and including the term in $x^2$.

(b) State the range of values of $x$ for which this expansion is valid.
steps: We rewrite the rational function as a product with a negative index: \begin{aligned} &f(x) = (3 + x)(1 - 2x)^{-2} \end{aligned}

We expand $(1 - 2x)^{-2}$ using the binomial theorem with $u = -2x$ and $n = -2$: \begin{aligned} &(1 - 2x)^{-2} \cr &\quad \approx 1 + (-2)(-2x) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{(-2)(-3)}{2}(-2x)^2 \end{aligned}

We simplify each term of this expansion: \begin{aligned} &\text{Term 1} = 1 \cr &\text{Term 2} = 4x \cr &\text{Term 3} \cr &\quad = 3(4x^2) \cr &\quad = 12x^2 \end{aligned} Thus, the expansion of the denominator term is: \begin{aligned} &(1 - 2x)^{-2} \approx 1 + 4x + 12x^2 \end{aligned}

We multiply by $(3 + x)$, ignoring terms of degree $3$ or higher: \begin{aligned} &f(x) \cr &\quad \approx (3 + x)(1 + 4x + 12x^2) \cr &\quad = 3(1 + 4x + 12x^2) \cr &\qquad + x(1 + 4x) \cr &\quad = 3 + 12x + 36x^2 \cr &\qquad + x + 4x^2 \cr &\quad = 3 + 13x + 40x^2 \end{aligned}
For part (b), the range of validity depends on the bracketed term: \begin{aligned} &|-2x| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies 2|x| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies |x| < \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $3 + 13x + 40x^2$, (b) $|x| < \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you forget to include the term $x \times 4x = 4x^2$ when distributing the multiplication of $(3 + x)$ across the quadratic term.
This mistake is caused by using an incorrect expansion for $(1 - 2x)^{-2}$, evaluating the quadratic coefficient as $4$ instead of $12$ due to an index division slip.
This arises from a sign slip when evaluating Term 2 of the binomial expansion, calculating $-4x$ instead of $+4x$, which leads to an incorrect linear coefficient of $11$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Limit Polynomial Multiplication
bradley_insight.content: When multiplying a linear polynomial like $(3 + x)$ by an infinite series expansion, there is no need to calculate every term. Only compute the product terms that contribute up to the required power (in this case, $x^2$). Any higher-order products (like $x \times 12x^2 = 12x^3$) can be immediately ignored.

question:
A function $f$ is defined by: \begin{aligned} &f(x) = \dfrac{3x - 5}{(1 - x)(1 - 2x)} \end{aligned} (a) Express $f(x)$ in terms of partial fractions.

(b) Find the binomial expansion of $f(x)$ in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in $x^2$.

(c) State the set of values of $x$ for which this combined expansion is valid.
steps: To express $f(x)$ in partial fractions, we write the decomposition: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{3x - 5}{(1 - x)(1 - 2x)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{A}{1 - x} + \dfrac{B}{1 - 2x} \end{aligned}

We clear fractions by multiplying by the common denominator: \begin{aligned} &3x - 5 = A(1 - 2x) + B(1 - x) \end{aligned} Substitute $x = 1$: \begin{aligned} &3(1) - 5 = A(1 - 2) \cr &\quad \implies -2 = -A \cr &\quad \implies A = 2 \end{aligned} Substitute $x = 0.5$: \begin{aligned} &3(0.5) - 5 = B(1 - 0.5) \cr &\quad \implies -3.5 = 0.5B \cr &\quad \implies B = -7 \end{aligned} Thus, the partial fractions decomposition is: \begin{aligned} &f(x) = \dfrac{2}{1 - x} - \dfrac{7}{1 - 2x} \end{aligned}
For part (b), we express the partial fractions using negative indices: \begin{aligned} &f(x) = 2(1 - x)^{-1} - 7(1 - 2x)^{-1} \end{aligned}

We expand each term up to $x^2$: \begin{aligned} &2(1 - x)^{-1} \cr &\quad \approx 2(1 + x + x^2) \cr &\quad = 2 + 2x + 2x^2 \end{aligned} And for the second term: \begin{aligned} &-7(1 - 2x)^{-1} \cr &\quad \approx -7\big(1 + 2x + (2x)^2\big) \cr &\quad = -7(1 + 2x + 4x^2) \cr &\quad = -7 - 14x - 28x^2 \end{aligned}
We combine these expansions together: \begin{aligned} &f(x) \cr &\quad \approx (2 - 7) + (2 - 14)x \cr &\qquad + (2 - 28)x^2 \cr &\quad = -5 - 12x - 26x^2 \end{aligned}

For part (c), we find the range of validity for each individual expansion. For $(1 - x)^{-1}$: \begin{aligned} &|x| < 1 \end{aligned} For $(1 - 2x)^{-1}$: \begin{aligned} &|2x| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies |x| < \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned} For both series to converge, we take the stricter interval: \begin{aligned} &|x| < \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $-5 - 12x - 26x^2$, (c) $|x| < \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you use incorrect partial fractions constants ($A = 1, B = -2$), leading to an incorrect binomial expansion.
This mistake occurs in part (c) if you choose the larger interval $|x| < 1$ instead of the stricter overlapping convergence interval $|x| < \dfrac{1}{2}$.
This mistake is caused by evaluating the quadratic term as $-14x^2$ instead of $-28x^2$ by failing to square the $2$ inside $(2x)^2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Overlapping Validity Sets
bradley_insight.content: When expanding multiple binomial brackets in a single expression, each bracket has its own independent range of validity. For the combined final expansion to be valid, both expansions must converge simultaneously. Therefore, the overall range of validity is always the *strictest* (smallest) of the individual intervals.

question:
In the binomial expansion of $(1 + ax)^n$, where $n$ is a negative integer and $a$ is a real constant, the first three non-zero terms in ascending powers of $x$ are: \begin{aligned} &1 - 12x + 78x^2 \end{aligned} (a) Find the values of the constants $a$ and $n$.

(b) State the range of values of $x$ for which the expansion is valid.
steps: We write the general binomial expansion of $(1 + ax)^n$: \begin{aligned} &(1 + ax)^n \cr &\quad \approx 1 + n(ax) \cr &\qquad + \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}(ax)^2 \cr &\quad = 1 + anx + \dfrac{n(n - 1)a^2}{2}x^2 \end{aligned}
We equate coefficients with $1 - 12x + 78x^2$. For the $x$ term: \begin{aligned} &an = -12 \end{aligned} For the $x^2$ term: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{n(n - 1)a^2}{2} = 78 \end{aligned}
From the linear equation, we express $a$ in terms of $n$: \begin{aligned} &a = -\dfrac{12}{n} \end{aligned}

We substitute our expression for $a$ into the quadratic equation: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}\Big(-\dfrac{12}{n}\Big)^2 = 78 \cr &\quad \implies \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}\Big(\dfrac{144}{n^2}\Big) = 78 \cr &\quad \implies \dfrac{72(n - 1)}{n} = 78 \end{aligned}
We solve this equation for $n$: \begin{aligned} &72(n - 1) = 78n \cr &\quad \implies 72n - 72 = 78n \cr &\quad \implies -72 = 6n \cr &\quad \implies n = -12 \end{aligned}
Now, we substitute $n = -12$ back to find $a$: \begin{aligned} &a = -\dfrac{12}{-12} \cr &\quad = 1 \end{aligned} Thus, the constants are $a = 1$ and $n = -12$.
For part (b), we find the range of validity for $(1 + x)^{-12}$: \begin{aligned} &|ax| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies |(1)x| < 1 \cr &\quad \implies |x| < 1 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $a = 1$, $n = -12$, (b) $|x| < 1$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error when solving for $n$, concluding that $n$ is positive ($12$) instead of a negative integer ($-12$), which violates the premise of the question.
This mistake is caused by an arithmetic division error when simplifying the quadratic substitution equation, leading to incorrect values of $a$ and $n$.
This error occurs in part (b) if you mistakenly use the coefficient of the linear term ($12$) instead of the value of $a$ ($1$) to determine the range of validity.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Systems of Binomial Equations
bradley_insight.content: Reverse-engineering a binomial expansion by equating coefficients always results in a system of non-linear equations. Isolating the linear scale factor $a = -\dfrac{k}{n}$ and substituting it into the quadratic term is the most reliable way to eliminate $a$ and solve for $n$ directly.

question: Use small-angle approximations to find the small positive root of the equation: \begin{aligned} &\sin x + \cos x = 1.2 \end{aligned} giving your answer to three decimal places.
steps: For small values of $x$ measured in radians, we apply the standard approximations: \begin{aligned} &\sin x \approx x \cr &\cos x \approx 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2} \end{aligned}
We substitute these approximations into the equation: \begin{aligned} &x + \Big(1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\Big) = 1.2 \end{aligned}

We rearrange the terms into standard quadratic form: \begin{aligned} &1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2} + x - 1.2 = 0 \cr &\quad \implies -\dfrac{1}{2}x^2 + x - 0.2 = 0 \cr &\quad \implies x^2 - 2x + 0.4 = 0 \end{aligned}

We apply the quadratic formula to solve for $x$: \begin{aligned} &x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{-(-2) \pm \sqrt{(-2)^2 - 4(1)(0.4)}}{2(1)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 1.6}}{2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{2.4}}{2} \cr &\quad = 1 \pm \dfrac{\sqrt{2.4}}{2} \end{aligned}

We evaluate the roots using $\sqrt{2.4} \approx 1.5492$: \begin{aligned} &x \approx 1 \pm 0.7746 \cr &\quad \implies x \approx 1.775 \cr &\quad \text{or } x \approx 0.225 \end{aligned} For the approximation to remain valid, $x$ must be close to zero. We reject $x \approx 1.775$ as it is too large, leaving the small positive root: \begin{aligned} &x \approx 0.225 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $0.225$

pi_options.feedback: This is the incorrect algebraic root of the quadratic equation. While mathematically valid for the quadratic model, it is too large to satisfy the fundamental assumption of small-angle approximations ($x \approx 0$).
This error occurs if you forget to divide the discriminant by $2$ when evaluating the quadratic formula, leading to $2 - \sqrt{2.4} \approx 0.451$.
This arises from a sign error when solving the quadratic equation or interpreting the required interval, resulting in a negative root instead of the positive root.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Root Validation in Approximations
bradley_insight.content: Solving algebraic approximations of trigonometric equations often yields multiple quadratic roots. You must always check your solutions against the physical bounds of the approximation: a 'small' angle in radians should generally lie within the interval $[-0.5, 0.5]$ to maintain accuracy. Any roots outside this range must be rejected as extraneous.

question: Show that, for small values of $x$ measured in radians: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{2\cos x - 2 + 5x\sin x}{3x\tan 2x} \approx k \end{aligned} where $k$ is a rational constant to be determined.
steps: For small values of $x$ measured in radians, we apply the standard small-angle approximations: \begin{aligned} &\cos x \approx 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2} \cr &\sin x \approx x \cr &\tan 2x \approx 2x \end{aligned}

We substitute these approximations into the numerator: \begin{aligned} &2\cos x - 2 + 5x\sin x \cr &\quad \approx 2\Big(1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\Big) - 2 + 5x(x) \cr &\quad = 2 - x^2 - 2 + 5x^2 \cr &\quad = 4x^2 \end{aligned}
Next, we substitute into the denominator: \begin{aligned} &3x\tan 2x \cr &\quad \approx 3x(2x) \cr &\quad = 6x^2 \end{aligned}

We divide the numerator by the denominator to determine $k$: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{4x^2}{6x^2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4}{6} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned} Thus, the rational constant is $k = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
Final Answer: $k = \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 }$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make an expansion error in the numerator, evaluating it as $3x^2$ instead of $4x^2$.
This mistake occurs if you forget to substitute $\tan 2x \approx 2x$ in the denominator, using $\tan 2x \approx x$ instead, which results in a denominator of $3x^2$ instead of $6x^2$.
This arises if you make a combined simplification error, such as assuming that the $x^2$ terms cancel out with a coefficient of $1$ without evaluating the multiplier coefficients.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Limit Approximations of Trig Quotients
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating rational quotients of trigonometric functions for small $x$, the powers of the variable $x$ in the numerator and denominator must balance out (in this case, both are of degree $2$). This allows the $x$ terms to cancel, leaving a constant limit that approximates the behavior of the function near $x = 0$.

question: Using small-angle approximations, solve the equation: \begin{aligned} &\cos\theta + 4\sin\theta = 0.8 \end{aligned} Explain clearly why only one of the algebraic roots is valid as a small-angle approximation, and state this valid root to three decimal places.
steps: For small values of $\theta$ measured in radians, we apply the standard approximations: \begin{aligned} &\cos\theta \approx 1 - \dfrac{\theta^2}{2} \cr &\sin\theta \approx \theta \end{aligned}

We substitute these approximations into the equation: \begin{aligned} &\Big(1 - \dfrac{\theta^2}{2}\Big) + 4\theta = 0.8 \cr &\quad \implies -\dfrac{1}{2}\theta^2 + 4\theta + 0.2 = 0 \cr &\quad \implies \theta^2 - 8\theta - 0.4 = 0 \end{aligned}

We solve this quadratic equation using the quadratic formula: \begin{aligned} &\theta \cr &\quad = \dfrac{-(-8) \pm \sqrt{(-8)^2 - 4(1)(-0.4)}}{2(1)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{8 \pm \sqrt{64 + 1.6}}{2} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{8 \pm \sqrt{65.6}}{2} \cr &\quad = 4 \pm \sqrt{16.4} \end{aligned}
We evaluate the roots using $\sqrt{16.4} \approx 4.050$: \begin{aligned} &\theta \approx 4 \pm 4.050 \cr &\quad \implies \theta \approx 8.050 \cr &\quad \text{or } \theta \approx -0.050 \end{aligned}

Small-angle approximations require the angle to be very close to zero radians. Because $\theta \approx 8.050$ radians violates this assumption, it must be rejected. The only valid root is: \begin{aligned} &\theta \approx -0.050 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $-0.050$

pi_options.feedback: This is the positive root of the quadratic equation. While algebraically correct, a value of $8.050$ radians (approximately $461^\circ$) is far too large to be valid as a small-angle approximation.
This mistake occurs if you forget to divide by $2$ when evaluating the quadratic formula, calculating $8 - \sqrt{65.6} \approx -0.100$.
This answer is incorrect because it fails to perform the required validation step. In small-angle approximation problems, you must always evaluate and reject any extraneous non-small roots.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Physical Meaning of Roots
bradley_insight.content: In applied mathematics and physics, solving quadratic models almost always yields a secondary mathematical root. Always relate the mathematics back to the physical model: since the Taylor series expansions are centered at $x = 0$, only the root closest to $0$ represents a physically meaningful solution.

question:
A student uses the small-angle approximation: \begin{aligned} &\cos x \approx 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2} \end{aligned} to estimate the value of $\cos(0.3)$.

(a) Calculate the percentage error in this approximation, giving your answer to four decimal places.

(b) State whether this approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate, justifying your answer.
steps: We calculate the approximated value of $\cos(0.3)$: \begin{aligned} &\cos(0.3) \cr &\quad \approx 1 - \dfrac{0.3^2}{2} \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.045 \cr &\quad = 0.955 \end{aligned}
Next, we determine the exact value of $\cos(0.3)$ using radian mode: \begin{aligned} &\cos(0.3) \approx 0.955336 \end{aligned}

We calculate the percentage error using the standard formula: \begin{aligned} &\text{Percentage Error} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{|\text{Approx} - \text{Exact}|}{\text{Exact}} \times 100 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{|0.955 - 0.955336|}{0.955336} \times 100 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{0.000336}{0.955336} \times 100 \cr &\quad \approx 0.0352\% \end{aligned}
For part (b), because the approximated value ($0.955$) is strictly less than the exact value ($0.955336$), the approximation is an underestimate.
Final Answer: (a) $0.0352\%$, (b) Underestimate

pi_options.feedback: This is incorrect. The approximated value ($0.955$) is smaller than the true value ($0.955336...$), which means it is an underestimate, not an overestimate.
This arises from a rounding error or truncation slip when dividing the difference by the approximate value instead of the exact value in the denominator of the percentage error formula.
This is a decimal placement error caused by multiplying or dividing by $10$ incorrectly when converting the fractional error to a percentage.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Alternating Series and Bounds
bradley_insight.content: The Taylor series expansion for $\cos x$ is an alternating series. Truncating at $1$ is an overestimate, truncating at $1 - \dfrac{x^2}{2}$ is an underestimate, and truncating after degree $4$ is an overestimate, continually bounding the true value.

question:
An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of length $L$ and an included angle of $\theta$ radians, where $\theta$ is small.

By using the small-angle approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta - \dfrac{\theta^3}{6}$, show that the difference between the area of the sector of radius $L$ with angle $\theta$ and the area of this triangle is approximately: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{12}L^2\theta^3 \end{aligned}
steps: We write down the formula for the area of a circular sector of radius $L$ and angle $\theta$: \begin{aligned} &A_{\text{sector}} = \dfrac{1}{2}L^2\theta \end{aligned}
Next, we write down the formula for the area of the triangle: \begin{aligned} &A_{\text{triangle}} = \dfrac{1}{2}L^2\sin\theta \end{aligned}

We express the difference $D$ between the two areas: \begin{aligned} &D \cr &\quad = A_{\text{sector}} - A_{\text{triangle}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2}L^2\theta - \dfrac{1}{2}L^2\sin\theta \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2}L^2(\theta - \sin\theta) \end{aligned}

We substitute $\sin\theta \approx \theta - \dfrac{\theta^3}{6}$ into our expression: \begin{aligned} &D \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{1}{2}L^2\Big[\theta - \Big(\theta - \dfrac{\theta^3}{6}\Big)\Big] \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2}L^2\Big(\dfrac{\theta^3}{6}\Big) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{12}L^2\theta^3 \end{aligned} as required.
Final Answer: $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 12 } L^2 \theta^3$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you forget to multiply by the factor of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ from the area formulas when expanding the final expression.
This is a dimensional error. Area must have dimensions of length squared ($L^2$). This mistake arises from incorrectly using the arc length formula or writing $L$ instead of $L^2$.
This arises from an arithmetic division error, such as multiplying the denominators $2$ and $6$ incorrectly to get $24$ instead of $12$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Higher-Order Approximations
bradley_insight.content: While the first-order approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ is standard, it is sometimes insufficient. If we had used $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ here, the difference between the sector and triangle area would simplify to $0$. We must use the higher-order cubic term $-\dfrac{\theta^3}{6}$ to capture the tiny non-zero gap between the curved arc and the straight chord.

question: Find five numbers which are in arithmetic progression such that the last term is $43$ and the sum of all of the numbers is $135$.
steps: Let the progression have first term $a$, common difference $d$, and $n = 5$ terms. We are given the last term $L = 43$, with $L = a + 4d$, and sum $S_5 = 135$.

We use the sum formula $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + L)$ to find the first term $a$: \begin{aligned} &135 = \dfrac{5}{2}(a + 43) \cr &\quad \implies 270 = 5(a + 43) \cr &\quad \implies 54 = a + 43 \cr &\quad \implies a = 11 \end{aligned}
We substitute $a = 11$ into the expression for the last term to find $d$: \begin{aligned} &11 + 4d = 43 \cr &\quad \implies 4d = 32 \cr &\quad \implies d = 8 \end{aligned}

We generate the five terms starting with $a = 11$ and adding $d = 8$: \begin{aligned} &u_1 = 11 \cr &u_2 = 19 \cr &u_3 = 27 \cr &u_4 = 35 \cr &u_5 = 43 \end{aligned} Thus, the five numbers are $11$, $19$, $27$, $35$, $43$.

This mistake arises if you set up the last term incorrectly as $a + 5d = 43$ instead of $a + 4d = 43$, which alters the calculations for both $a$ and $d$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Choosing the Right Sum Formula
bradley_insight.content: There are two standard sum formulas for an arithmetic series: \begin{aligned} &S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a + (n - 1)d\big] \cr &S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + L) \end{aligned} When given the last term $L$ directly, always use the second formula first to solve for $a$ immediately in one clean algebraic step, bypassing a system of simultaneous equations.

question:
The first three terms of an arithmetic progression are given by $2k + 1$, $4k - 3$, and $5k - 2$ respectively, where $k$ is a constant.

(a) Find the value of $k$.

(b) Hence, find the sum of the first $20$ terms of this progression.
steps: For any arithmetic progression, the difference between consecutive terms is constant: \begin{aligned} &u_2 - u_1 = u_3 - u_2 \end{aligned}

We substitute our terms into this relationship to solve for $k$: \begin{aligned} &(4k - 3) - (2k + 1) \cr &\quad = (5k - 2) - (4k - 3) \cr &\quad \implies 2k - 4 = k + 1 \cr &\quad \implies k = 5 \end{aligned}

For part (b), we substitute $k = 5$ to determine the parameters of the progression: \begin{aligned} &a = 2(5) + 1 \cr &\quad = 11 \cr &u_2 = 4(5) - 3 \cr &\quad = 17 \cr &d = 17 - 11 \cr &\quad = 6 \end{aligned}

We use the arithmetic sum formula $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a + (n - 1)d\big]$ to find the sum: \begin{aligned} &S_{20} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{20}{2}\big[2(11) + (19)(6)\big] \cr &\quad = 10(22 + 114) \cr &\quad = 10(136) \cr &\quad = 1360 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $k = 5$, (b) Sum = $1360$

This mistake is caused by using an incorrect common difference $d = 5$ instead of $d = 6$ when calculating the sum of the first $20$ terms.
This arises if you forget to divide by $2$ in the outer coefficient of the sum formula, evaluating the multiplier as $20$ instead of $10$, which doubles your final answer.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Defining Common Differences Algebraically
bradley_insight.content: Whenever you are given three terms of an arithmetic progression in terms of an unknown variable, always set up the difference equation $u_2 - u_1 = u_3 - u_2$. This is a highly reliable way to construct a single linear equation and solve for the unknown constant immediately.

question:
An arithmetic progression has its 5th term equal to $18$ and the sum of its first $10$ terms equal to $210$.

(a) Find the first term $a$ and the common difference $d$ of this progression.

(b) Determine the value of $n$ for which the sum of the first $n$ terms of this progression is equal to $540$.
steps: For part (a), using $u_n = a + (n - 1)d$, the 5th term gives: \begin{aligned} &a + 4d = 18 \end{aligned}
Using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a + (n - 1)d\big]$ for $S_{10} = 210$: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{10}{2}(2a + 9d) = 210 \cr &\quad \implies 5(2a + 9d) = 210 \cr &\quad \implies 2a + 9d = 42 \end{aligned}

From the first equation, $a = 18 - 4d$. We substitute this into the second equation: \begin{aligned} &2(18 - 4d) + 9d = 42 \cr &\quad \implies 36 - 8d + 9d = 42 \cr &\quad \implies d = 6 \end{aligned}
We substitute $d = 6$ back to find $a$: \begin{aligned} &a + 4(6) = 18 \cr &\quad \implies a + 24 = 18 \cr &\quad \implies a = -6 \end{aligned} Thus, $a = -6$ and $d = 6$.

For part (b), we set up the sum equation $S_n = 540$: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{n}{2}\big[2(-6) + 6(n - 1)\big] = 540 \cr &\quad \implies n(-12 + 6n - 6) = 1080 \cr &\quad \implies n(6n - 18) = 1080 \cr &\quad \implies 6n^2 - 18n - 1080 = 0 \cr &\quad \implies n^2 - 3n - 180 = 0 \cr &\quad \implies (n - 15)(n + 12) = 0 \end{aligned} Since $n$ must be a positive integer ($n > 0$), we reject $n = -12$, giving $n = 15$.
Final Answer: (a) $a = -6$, $d = 6$, (b) $n = 15$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b) if you incorrectly keep the negative algebraic root of the quadratic factorisation, neglecting the boundary condition that the number of terms $n$ must be strictly positive.
This mistake arises from an algebraic error when solving the simultaneous equations in part (a), resulting in incorrect values of $a$ and $d$.
This is caused by a quadratic coefficient division slip or a factorisation mistake when solving the quadratic equation $n^2 - 3n - 180 = 0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Validating Quadratic Term Values
bradley_insight.content: When solving for the number of terms $n$ in an arithmetic series, you will often obtain a quadratic equation with both a positive and a negative root. Always remember that because the term index $n$ represents a physical count of elements, it *must* be a positive integer ($n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$). You must explicitly reject any negative roots as mathematically extraneous.

question:
A woman starts a new job with an initial annual salary of £$24,000$. Under her contract, her annual salary increases by a fixed amount of £$1,200$ at the start of each subsequent year.

(a) Find her annual salary in her 10th year of employment.

(b) Calculate the total amount of money she earns from this job during her first 15 years of employment.
steps: We model her salary increases as an arithmetic progression with first term $a = 24000$ and common difference $d = 1200$.

For part (a), her salary in year $10$ is calculated using $u_n = a + (n - 1)d$: \begin{aligned} &T_{10} \cr &\quad = a + 9d \cr &\quad = 24000 + 9(1200) \cr &\quad = 24000 + 10800 \cr &\quad = 34800 \end{aligned} Thus, her salary in year $10$ is £$34,800$.

For part (b), her total cumulative earnings over the first $15$ years are found using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big[2a + (n - 1)d\big]$: \begin{aligned} &S_{15} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{15}{2}\big[2(24000) + 14(1200)\big] \cr &\quad = 7.5(48000 + 16800) \cr &\quad = 7.5(64800) \cr &\quad = 486000 \end{aligned} Thus, her total earnings are £$486,000$.
Final Answer: (a) £$34,800$, (b) £$486,000$

This mistake is caused by using an incorrect number of terms $n = 14$ instead of $n = 15$ when calculating her total earnings over the 15-year period.
This error arises in part (b) if you apply the sum formula using $T_{10}$ instead of the 15th year's salary.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Starting Value Modeling
bradley_insight.content: When modeling real-world progression problems (such as salaries, rents, or savings), always remember that the initial state is represented by the first term $a$ ($n = 1$). No increase is applied in the first interval. Therefore, the salary in the 10th year must be calculated using $u_{10} = a + 9d$, not $a + 10d$.

question: Evaluate the arithmetic series: \begin{aligned} &\sum_{r = 5}^{35} (4r + 7) \end{aligned} showing all of your working.
steps: The terms of the series are generated by the linear expression $f(r) = 4r + 7$, forming an arithmetic progression.
We find the first term by substituting the lower limit $r = 5$: \begin{aligned} &a = 4(5) + 7 \cr &\quad = 27 \end{aligned}
We find the last term by substituting the upper limit $r = 35$: \begin{aligned} &L = 4(35) + 7 \cr &\quad = 147 \end{aligned}
We determine the number of terms $n$: \begin{aligned} &n = (35 - 5) + 1 \cr &\quad = 31 \end{aligned}

We apply the arithmetic sum formula $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + L)$: \begin{aligned} &S_{31} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{31}{2}(27 + 147) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{31}{2}(174) \cr &\quad = 31 \times 87 \cr &\quad = 2697 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $2697$

This mistake is caused by using $n = 32$ terms, perhaps from a boundary counting error or arithmetic slip.
This error arises if you forget to divide by $2$ when evaluating the arithmetic series sum formula, resulting in a sum that is exactly double the correct value.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Inclusive Sigma Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating series defined in sigma notation $\sum_{r = a}^{b} f(r)$, always remember that the number of terms $n$ is calculated using the inclusive formula $n = (b - a) + 1$. Simply subtracting the boundaries ($b - a$) is a very common student mistake that will omit the first term of the series, leading to an incorrect sum.

question:
(a) Explain why the sum to infinity of a geometric series with first term $a \neq 0$ and common ratio $r$ only exists when $|r| < 1$.

(b) A geometric progression $V$ has first term $3$ and common ratio $r$. Another progression $W$ is formed by squaring each term in $V$.

(i) Show that $W$ is also a geometric progression, stating its first term and common ratio in terms of $r$.

(ii) Given that the sum to infinity of $W$ is twice the sum to infinity of $V$, find the value of $r$.
steps: For part (a), the sum of the first $n$ terms is given by: \begin{aligned} &S_n = \dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r} \end{aligned}

The sum to infinity is the limit as $n \to \infty$: \begin{aligned} &S_{\infty} \cr &\quad = \lim_{n \to \infty} S_n \cr &\quad = \lim_{n \to \infty} \dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r} \end{aligned} This limit exists only if $r^n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, which requires $|r| < 1$. If $|r| \ge 1$, $r^n$ does not converge to $0$, so the series diverges.
For part (b)(i), the terms of $V$ are: \begin{aligned} &V_1 = 3 \cr &V_2 = 3r \cr &V_3 = 3r^2 \end{aligned}
Progression $W$ is formed by squaring each term of $V$: \begin{aligned} &W_1 = 3^2 \cr &\quad = 9 \cr &W_2 = (3r)^2 \cr &\quad = 9r^2 \cr &W_3 = (3r^2)^2 \cr &\quad = 9r^4 \end{aligned}

We calculate the ratio between consecutive terms of $W$: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{W_2}{W_1} = \dfrac{9r^2}{9} \cr &\quad = r^2 \cr &\dfrac{W_{k+1}}{W_k} = \dfrac{9r^{2k}}{9r^{2k-2}} \cr &\quad = r^2 \end{aligned} Since the ratio is constant, $W$ is a geometric progression with first term $9$ and common ratio $r^2$.
For part (b)(ii), the sums to infinity are: \begin{aligned} &S_{\infty}(V) = \dfrac{3}{1 - r} \cr &S_{\infty}(W) = \dfrac{9}{1 - r^2} \end{aligned}

We set up $S_{\infty}(W) = 2S_{\infty}(V)$ and solve for $r$: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{9}{1 - r^2} = 2\Big(\dfrac{3}{1 - r}\Big) \cr &\quad \implies \dfrac{9}{(1 - r)(1 + r)} = \dfrac{6}{1 - r} \cr &\quad \implies \dfrac{9}{1 + r} = 6 \cr &\quad \implies 9 = 6(1 + r) \cr &\quad \implies 9 = 6 + 6r \cr &\quad \implies 6r = 3 \cr &\quad \implies r = 0.5 \end{aligned} Since $|0.5| < 1$, the common ratio is valid.
Final Answer: (b)(i) First term: $9$, Ratio: $r^2$, (b)(ii) $r = 0.5$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b)(i) if you assume the common ratio of the squared progression $W$ remains $r$ instead of squaring it to $r^2$, which corrupts the subsequent calculations.
This mistake arises from a sign slip when solving the linear equation $9 = 6(1+r)$, calculating $r = -0.5$ instead of $r = 0.5$.
This error occurs in part (b)(i) if you double the first term of $V$ ($2 \times 3 = 6$) instead of squaring it ($3^2 = 9$) when defining the first term of $W$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Squaring Series Terms
bradley_insight.content: When squaring every individual term of a geometric series, you create a new geometric series whose first term is the square of the original first term ($A = a^2$) and whose common ratio is the square of the original common ratio ($R = r^2$).

question:
The first three terms of a geometric progression are $x + 2$, $x$, and $x - 1$ respectively, where $x$ is a real constant.

(a) Show that $x = 2$.

(b) Find the common ratio of this progression.

(c) Determine the sum to infinity of this progression.
steps: For any geometric progression, the ratio between consecutive terms is constant: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{u_2}{u_1} = \dfrac{u_3}{u_2} \end{aligned}

We substitute the terms into this relationship to solve for $x$: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{x}{x + 2} = \dfrac{x - 1}{x} \cr &\quad \implies x^2 = (x - 1)(x + 2) \cr &\quad \implies x^2 = x^2 + x - 2 \cr &\quad \implies 0 = x - 2 \cr &\quad \implies x = 2 \end{aligned} as required.
For part (b), we substitute $x = 2$ back into the terms: \begin{aligned} &u_1 = 2 + 2 \cr &\quad = 4 \cr &u_2 = 2 \cr &u_3 = 2 - 1 \cr &\quad = 1 \end{aligned}
We calculate the common ratio $r$: \begin{aligned} &r = \dfrac{u_2}{u_1} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2}{4} \cr &\quad = 0.5 \end{aligned}
For part (c), we use the sum to infinity formula $S_{\infty} = \dfrac{a}{1 - r}$: \begin{aligned} &S_{\infty} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4}{1 - 0.5} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4}{0.5} \cr &\quad = 8 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $r = 0.5$, (c) $S_{\infty} = 8$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you invert the common ratio definition, calculating $r = \dfrac{u_1}{u_2} = 2$ instead of $0.5$.
This mistake is caused by using the first term of the progression as $a = 2$ instead of $a = 4$ when calculating the sum to infinity.

pi_options.ans: (b) $r = 0.5$, (c) The sum to infinity does not exist
pi_options.feedback: This arises if you mistakenly think that the progression diverges because terms decrease, failing to recognise that since $|r| < 1$ (as $r = 0.5$), the sum to infinity converges.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Defining Common Ratios Algebraically
bradley_insight.content: Whenever you are given three terms of a geometric progression in terms of an unknown variable, always set up the ratio equation $\dfrac{u_2}{u_1} = \dfrac{u_3}{u_2}$. Cross-multiplying this equation will construct a solvable polynomial equation that isolates the unknown constant directly.

question:
A geometric progression has a sum to infinity equal to $16$. The sum of the first three terms of this progression is equal to $14$.

(a) Find the common ratio $r$ of this progression, giving your answer in exact fractional form.

(b) Find the first term $a$ of the progression.
steps: For part (a), using the sum to infinity formula: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{a}{1 - r} = 16 \cr &\quad \implies a = 16(1 - r) \end{aligned}
Using the formula for the sum of the first three terms: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{a(1 - r^3)}{1 - r} = 14 \end{aligned}

We substitute $a = 16(1 - r)$ into the sum equation: \begin{aligned} &\dfrac{16(1 - r)(1 - r^3)}{1 - r} = 14 \cr &\quad \implies 16(1 - r^3) = 14 \cr &\quad \implies 1 - r^3 = \dfrac{7}{8} \cr &\quad \implies r^3 = \dfrac{1}{8} \cr &\quad \implies r = \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}
For part (b), we substitute $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$ back to find $a$: \begin{aligned} &a = 16\Big(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\Big) \cr &\quad = 16\Big(\dfrac{1}{2}\Big) \cr &\quad = 8 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $r = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }$, (b) $a = 8$
