While $k$ is correct, this population coefficient is wrong. It occurs if you assumed the term $\left( \dfrac{ 2t + 3 }{ 3 } \right)^{ k/2 }$ simplified directly to $(2t + 3)/3 = 11$, forgetting to apply the exponent of $k/2$.
This occurs if you inverted the constant factor when solving, setting $\dfrac{ k }{ 2 } = \dfrac{ \ln 5 }{ \ln 3 }$ when solving the exponential equation in part (ii).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Integrating Rational Functions
bradley_insight.content: Never forget the reverse chain rule factor when integrating fractions like $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2t + 3 }$. The integral is $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \ln(2t + 3) + C$, not $\ln(2t + 3) + C$. Forgetting this constant factor is one of the most common ways to lose derivation marks.

question:
A curve has the equation:$$y = (x - 4) \ln x$$(i) Show that:$$\dfrac{ \text{d}y }{ \text{d}x } = 1 - \dfrac{ 4 }{ x } + \ln x$$(ii) Show that the curve has a turning point between $x = 2$ and $x = 3$.

(iii) By taking $2.3$ as a first approximation to the x-coordinate of this turning point, use the Newton-Raphson method once to find a better approximation. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
steps:
Part (i): We differentiate $y = (x - 4) \ln x$ using the product rule. Let $u = x - 4$ and $v = \ln x$.

The derivatives are $u' = 1$ and $v' = \dfrac{ 1 }{ x }$.

Applying the product rule:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ \text{d}y }{ \text{d}x } \cr &\quad = u'v + uv' \cr &\quad = \ln x + (x - 4)\left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ x } \right) \cr &\quad = \ln x + 1 - \dfrac{ 4 }{ x } \cr &\quad = 1 - \dfrac{ 4 }{ x } + \ln x \end{aligned}

Part (ii): A turning point on a curve occurs where the first derivative is equal to zero ($y' = 0$).

Let $g(x) = \dfrac{ \text{d}y }{ \text{d}x } = 1 - \dfrac{ 4 }{ x } + \ln x$.

Evaluate $g(x)$ at the interval boundaries $x = 2$ and $x = 3$:

• For $x = 2$:\begin{aligned} &g(2) = 1 - \dfrac{ 4 }{ 2 } + \ln 2 \cr &\quad = -1 + \ln 2 \cr &\quad \approx -0.307 \end{aligned}So $g(2) < 0$.

• For $x = 3$:\begin{aligned} &g(3) = 1 - \dfrac{ 4 }{ 3 } + \ln 3 \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } + \ln 3 \cr &\quad \approx 0.765 \end{aligned}So $g(3) > 0$.

Since there is a change of sign and $g(x)$ is continuous on the interval, a root of $g(x) = 0$ (and thus a turning point of the curve) must lie in $[2, 3]$.

Part (iii): Since we are finding the root of the derivative $g(x) = 0$, our Newton-Raphson formula is:$$x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{ g(x_n) }{ g'(x_n) }$$We first differentiate $g(x) = 1 - 4x^{ -1 } + \ln x$ to find $g'(x)$:$$g'(x) = \dfrac{ 4 }{ x^2 } + \dfrac{ 1 }{ x }$$

Evaluate $g(2.3)$ and $g'(2.3)$ for our first iteration ($x_0 = 2.3$):\begin{aligned} &g(2.3) = 1 - \dfrac{ 4 }{ 2.3 } + \ln(2.3) \cr &\quad \approx 0.0938 \cr &g'(2.3) = \dfrac{ 4 }{ 2.3^2 } + \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2.3 } \cr &\quad \approx 1.1909 \end{aligned}Substitute these values into the Newton-Raphson formula:\begin{aligned} &x_1 = 2.3 - \dfrac{ 0.0938 }{ 1.1909 } \cr &\quad \approx 2.3 - 0.0787 \cr &\quad = 2.221 \end{aligned}Thus, the improved approximation to the x-coordinate of the turning point is $2.221$ (to 3 decimal places).
Final Answer: $$2.221$$

pi_options.ans: $$2.221$$ but you apply Newton-Raphson directly to the original curve $y = 0$
pi_options.feedback: Your numerical calculation of $2.221$ is correct. However, always remember that a turning point occurs where the first derivative is zero, meaning Newton-Raphson must be applied to $g(x) = 0$ (where $g(x) = y'$), which requires using $g'(x) = y''$ as the denominator. Applying it to the original equation $y = 0$ is a major conceptual error.
This error occurs if you make a sign error in the Newton-Raphson formula, incorrectly adding the correction term instead of subtracting it, which yields $x_1 = 2.3 + 0.0787$, giving $2.379$.

This error occurs if you correctly evaluate $g'(x)$ but make an arithmetic slip when evaluating the function value $g(2.3)$, such as incorrectly subtracting the logarithms or using degree mode on your calculator.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Turning Points via Newton-Raphson
bradley_insight.content: When applying the Newton-Raphson method to locate a stationary point, you must perform the iterations on the derivative of the function, $f'(x) = 0$, not on the original function $f(x) = 0$. This means the denominator of your correction term is the second derivative, $f''(x)$.

question:
Let $f(x) = x^2 \mathrm{e}^x - 5$.

(i) Show that:$$f'(x) = (x^2 + 2x)\mathrm{e}^x$$(ii) Show that the equation $f(x) = 0$ has a root in the interval $[1.2, 1.3]$.

(iii) By taking $1.2$ as a first approximation to this root, use the Newton-Raphson method once to find a better approximation. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
steps:
Part (i): We differentiate $f(x) = x^2 \mathrm{e}^x - 5$ using the product rule. Let $u = x^2$ and $v = \mathrm{e}^x$.

The derivatives are $u' = 2x$ and $v' = \mathrm{e}^x$.

Applying the product rule:\begin{aligned} &f'(x) \cr &\quad = u'v + uv' \cr &\quad = (2x)(\mathrm{e}^x) + (x^2)(\mathrm{e}^x) \cr &\quad = (x^2 + 2x)\mathrm{e}^x \end{aligned}

Part (ii): Evaluate $f(x)$ at the interval boundaries $x = 1.2$ and $x = 1.3$:

• For $x = 1.2$:\begin{aligned} &f(1.2) = (1.2)^2 \mathrm{e}^{ 1.2 } - 5 \cr &\quad \approx 1.44(3.3201) - 5 \cr &\quad \approx -0.219 \end{aligned}So $f(1.2) < 0$.

• For $x = 1.3$:\begin{aligned} &f(1.3) = (1.3)^2 \mathrm{e}^{ 1.3 } - 5 \cr &\quad \approx 1.69(3.6693) - 5 \cr &\quad \approx 1.201 \end{aligned}So $f(1.3) > 0$.

Since there is a change of sign and $f(x)$ is continuous on the interval, a root of $f(x) = 0$ must lie in $[1.2, 1.3]$.

Part (iii): We apply the Newton-Raphson formula to find our improved root approximation:$$x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{ f(x_n) }{ f'(x_n) }$$Using $x_0 = 1.2$, evaluate $f(1.2)$ and $f'(1.2)$:\begin{aligned} &f(1.2) \approx -0.2185 \cr &f'(1.2) = ((1.2)^2 + 2(1.2))\mathrm{e}^{ 1.2 } \cr &\quad = 3.84 \mathrm{e}^{ 1.2 } \cr &\quad \approx 3.84(3.3201) \cr &\quad \approx 12.7492 \end{aligned}

Substitute these values into the Newton-Raphson formula:\begin{aligned} &x_1 = 1.2 - \dfrac{ -0.2185 }{ 12.7492 } \cr &\quad \approx 1.2 + 0.0171 \cr &\quad = 1.217 \end{aligned}Thus, the improved approximation to the root is $1.217$ (to 3 decimal places).
Final Answer: $$1.217$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error in the Newton-Raphson step, subtracting a positive term or adding a negative term incorrectly, which leads to $1.2 - 0.0171 = 1.183$.

Since this function only contains algebraic and exponential terms, degree mode will not affect the calculations. However, always ensure your calculator is set to the correct mode when moving between function families.

This error occurs if you make an arithmetic mistake when evaluating $f'(1.2)$, such as forgetting the factor of $2x$ in the product rule and using $f'(1.2) = 1.2^2 \mathrm{e}^{ 1.2 }$ (approximately $4.781$), which yields a larger correction factor.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Product Rule Factoring
bradley_insight.content: When differentiating expressions containing exponential terms like $\mathrm{e}^x$, always factor out the $\mathrm{e}^x$ term immediately. This keeps your derivative $f'(x)$ clean and drastically reduces the chance of manual calculator slips during evaluations.

question:
Let $g(x) = x \sin x - 1$, where $x$ is measured in radians.

(i) Show that:$$g'(x) = \sin x + x \cos x$$(ii) Show that the equation $g(x) = 0$ has a root in the interval $[1.1, 1.2]$.

(iii) By taking $1.1$ as a first approximation to this root, use the Newton-Raphson method once to find a better approximation. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
steps:
Part (i): We differentiate $g(x) = x \sin x - 1$ using the product rule. Let $u = x$ and $v = \sin x$.

The derivatives are $u' = 1$ and $v' = \cos x$.

Applying the product rule:\begin{aligned} &g'(x) \cr &\quad = u'v + uv' \cr &\quad = (1)(\sin x) + x \cos x \cr &\quad = \sin x + x \cos x \end{aligned}

Part (ii): Ensure your calculator is set to Radian mode. Evaluate $g(x)$ at the interval boundaries $x = 1.1$ and $x = 1.2$:

• For $x = 1.1$:\begin{aligned} &g(1.1) = 1.1 \sin(1.1) - 1 \cr &\quad \approx 1.1(0.8912) - 1 \cr &\quad \approx -0.0197 \end{aligned}So $g(1.1) < 0$.

• For $x = 1.2$:\begin{aligned} &g(1.2) = 1.2 \sin(1.2) - 1 \cr &\quad \approx 1.2(0.9320) - 1 \cr &\quad \approx 0.1184 \end{aligned}So $g(1.2) > 0$.

Since there is a change of sign and $g(x)$ is continuous on the interval, a root of $g(x) = 0$ must lie in $[1.1, 1.2]$.

Part (iii): We apply the Newton-Raphson formula to find our improved root approximation:$$x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{ g(x_n) }{ g'(x_n) }$$Using $x_0 = 1.1$ in Radian mode, evaluate $g(1.1)$ and $g'(1.1)$:\begin{aligned} &g(1.1) \approx -0.0197 \cr &g'(1.1) = \sin(1.1) + 1.1 \cos(1.1) \cr &\quad \approx 0.8912 + 1.1(0.4536) \cr &\quad \approx 0.8912 + 0.4990 \cr &\quad = 1.3902 \end{aligned}

Substitute these values into the Newton-Raphson formula:\begin{aligned} &x_1 = 1.1 - \dfrac{ -0.0197 }{ 1.3902 } \cr &\quad \approx 1.1 + 0.0142 \cr &\quad = 1.114 \end{aligned}Thus, the improved approximation to the root is $1.114$ (to 3 decimal places).
Final Answer: $$1.114$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error in the Newton-Raphson step, incorrectly subtracting the correction term when $g(1.1)$ is already negative, resulting in $1.1 - 0.0142 = 1.086$.

This error occurs if you perform the calculations with your calculator set to Degree mode instead of Radian mode. In degree mode, $\sin(1.1^\circ) \approx 0.0192$ and $\cos(1.1^\circ) \approx 0.9998$, which leads to completely incorrect intermediate values and a failed approximation.

This mistake occurs if you make a product rule error when differentiating $x \sin x$, such as forgetting to include the first term ($\sin x$) and using $g'(1.1) \approx 1.1 \cos(1.1)$, which gives approximately $0.4990$, overestimating the step adjustment.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Radian Mode Check
bradley_insight.content: Any calculus-based numerical method involving trigonometric functions (including the sign change rule and Newton-Raphson) must always be performed in Radian mode. Working in Degree mode is one of the most common ways students lose entire question marks on exam papers.

question:
Let $h(x) = \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^x }{ x } - 4$.

(i) Show that:$$h'(x) = \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^x(x - 1) }{ x^2 }$$(ii) Show that the equation $h(x) = 0$ has a root in the interval $[2.1, 2.2]$.

(iii) By taking $2.1$ as a first approximation to this root, use the Newton-Raphson method once to find a better approximation. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
steps:
Part (i): We differentiate $h(x) = \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^x }{ x } - 4$ using the quotient rule. Let $u = \mathrm{e}^x$ and $v = x$.

The derivatives are $u' = \mathrm{e}^x$ and $v' = 1$.

Applying the quotient rule:\begin{aligned} &h'(x) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ u'v - uv' }{ v^2 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ (\mathrm{e}^x)(x) - (\mathrm{e}^x)(1) }{ x^2 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^x(x - 1) }{ x^2 } \end{aligned}

Part (ii): Evaluate $h(x)$ at the interval boundaries $x = 2.1$ and $x = 2.2$:

• For $x = 2.1$:\begin{aligned} &h(2.1) = \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^{ 2.1 } }{ 2.1 } - 4 \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{ 8.1662 }{ 2.1 } - 4 \cr &\quad \approx -0.1114 \end{aligned}So $h(2.1) < 0$.

• For $x = 2.2$:\begin{aligned} &h(2.2) = \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^{ 2.2 } }{ 2.2 } - 4 \cr &\quad \approx \dfrac{ 9.0250 }{ 2.2 } - 4 \cr &\quad \approx 0.1023 \end{aligned}So $h(2.2) > 0$.

Since there is a change of sign and $h(x)$ is continuous on the interval, a root of $h(x) = 0$ must lie in $[2.1, 2.2]$.

Part (iii): We apply the Newton-Raphson formula to find our improved root approximation:$$x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{ h(x_n) }{ h'(x_n) }$$Using $x_0 = 2.1$, evaluate $h(2.1)$ and $h'(2.1)$:\begin{aligned} &h(2.1) \approx -0.1114 \cr &h'(2.1) = \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^{ 2.1 }(2.1 - 1) }{ 2.1^2 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 8.1662(1.1) }{ 4.41 } \cr &\quad \approx 2.0369 \end{aligned}

Substitute these values into the Newton-Raphson formula:\begin{aligned} &x_1 = 2.1 - \dfrac{ -0.1114 }{ 2.0369 } \cr &\quad \approx 2.1 + 0.0547 \cr &\quad = 2.155 \end{aligned}Thus, the improved approximation to the root is $2.155$ (to 3 decimal places).
Final Answer: $$2.155$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error in the Newton-Raphson step, subtracting a positive value instead of adding the double negative, which yields $2.1 - 0.0547 = 2.045$.

Your numerical value of $2.155$ is correct. However, make sure you correctly set up the quotient rule derivative. Using a product rule expansion on a quotient by mistake (which would yield $\dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^x(x + 1) }{ x^2 }$) is a major algebraic error that would usually prevent you from obtaining the correct root on an exam.

This error occurs if you make an algebra mistake in the numerator of the quotient rule, such as writing $u'v + uv'$ by mistake, which leads to $h'(2.1) = \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^{ 2.1 }(3.1) }{ 4.41 }$ (approximately $5.740$), reducing the size of the step adjustment.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Quotient Rule Sign Distribution
bradley_insight.content: The numerator of the quotient rule is $u'v - uv'$. A very common exam error is to write a plus sign by mistake (confusing it with the product rule) or to swap the order of the terms. Since division order is critical, swapping terms or signs will completely change your derivative $f'(x)$.

question:
The curves $y = 3 - x^2$ and $y = \ln(x + 1)$ intersect at a single point in the first quadrant.

(i) Show that finding the x-coordinate of this point of intersection is equivalent to solving the equation:$$\ln(x + 1) + x^2 - 3 = 0$$(ii) Show that the x-coordinate of this point of intersection lies in the interval $[1.4, 1.5]$.

(iii) By taking $1.4$ as a first approximation, use the Newton-Raphson method once to find a better approximation to this x-coordinate. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
steps: Part (i): At the point of intersection of the two curves, their $y$-values must be equal:\begin{aligned} &\ln(x + 1) = 3 - x^2 \cr &\ln(x + 1) + x^2 - 3 = 0 \end{aligned}

Part (ii): Let $f(x) = \ln(x + 1) + x^2 - 3$. Evaluate $f(x)$ at the interval boundaries $x = 1.4$ and $x = 1.5$:

• For $x = 1.4$:\begin{aligned} &f(1.4) = \ln(2.4) + 1.4^2 - 3 \cr &\quad \approx 0.8755 + 1.96 - 3 \cr &\quad \approx -0.1645 \end{aligned}So $f(1.4) < 0$.

• For $x = 1.5$:\begin{aligned} &f(1.5) = \ln(2.5) + 1.5^2 - 3 \cr &\quad \approx 0.9163 + 2.25 - 3 \cr &\quad \approx 0.1663 \end{aligned}So $f(1.5) > 0$.

Since there is a change of sign and $f(x)$ is continuous on the interval, the curves must intersect at a point with an x-coordinate in $[1.4, 1.5]$.

Part (iii): We apply the Newton-Raphson formula to find our improved root approximation:$$x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{ f(x_n) }{ f'(x_n) }$$We differentiate $f(x) = \ln(x + 1) + x^2 - 3$ to find $f'(x)$:$$f'(x) = \dfrac{ 1 }{ x + 1 } + 2x$$

Using our starting approximation $x_0 = 1.4$, evaluate $f(1.4)$ and $f'(1.4)$:\begin{aligned} &f(1.4) \approx -0.1645 \cr &f'(1.4) = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2.4 } + 2(1.4) \cr &\quad \approx 0.4167 + 2.8 \cr &\quad = 3.2167 \end{aligned}Substitute these values into the Newton-Raphson formula:\begin{aligned} &x_1 = 1.4 - \dfrac{ -0.1645 }{ 3.2167 } \cr &\quad \approx 1.4 + 0.0511 \cr &\quad = 1.451 \end{aligned}Thus, the improved approximation to the x-coordinate of the point of intersection is $1.451$ (to 3 decimal places).
Final Answer: $$1.451$$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error in the Newton-Raphson step, subtracting the correction term instead of adding the double negative, which yields $1.4 - 0.0511 = 1.349$.

While this function contains algebraic and logarithmic terms, always make sure you are in Radian mode when applying calculus-based numerical methods, as other families of equations (such as trigonometric ones) will fail completely in degree mode.

This error occurs if you make a differentiation error when finding $f'(x)$, such as writing $f'(x) = \dfrac{ 1 }{ x } + 2x$, which leads to $f'(1.4) \approx 0.7143 + 2.8$, giving $3.5143$ and resulting in a smaller correction step.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Intersections as $f(x) = 0$
bradley_insight.content: When asked to find the intersection of two curves, always equate them and rearrange to form a single function $f(x) = 0$. Trying to apply numerical methods to both equations separately is mathematically impossible. This single-function setup is the fundamental gateway to applying the Newton-Raphson method.

question: (a) Find:$$\int x^{-1/3} \ln x \text{d}x$$(b) Using the substitution $u^2 = x^2 + 9$, or otherwise, find the exact value of:$$\int_{ 0 }^{ 4 } \dfrac{ x^3 }{ \sqrt{x^2 + 9} } \text{d}x$$
steps:
Part (a): We find the indefinite integral using integration by parts:$$\int u \text{d}v = uv - \int v \text{d}u$$Let $u = \ln x$ and $\text{d}v = x^{-1/3} \text{d}x$.

The derivatives and integrals are:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = \dfrac{ 1 }{ x } \text{d}x \cr &v = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^{ 2/3 } \end{aligned}

Substitute these into our integration by parts formula:\begin{aligned} &\int x^{-1/3} \ln x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^{ 2/3 } \ln x \cr &\qquad - \int \left( \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^{ 2/3 } \right)\left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ x } \right) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^{ 2/3 } \ln x - \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } \int x^{-1/3} \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^{ 2/3 } \ln x \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } \left( \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^{ 2/3 } \right) + C \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^{ 2/3 } \ln x - \dfrac{ 9 }{ 4 } x^{ 2/3 } + C \end{aligned}

Part (b): Evaluate using the substitution $u^2 = x^2 + 9$.

Differentiating both sides gives:\begin{aligned} &2u \text{d}u = 2x \text{d}x \cr &u \text{d}u = x \text{d}x \end{aligned}Express the numerator as:\begin{aligned} &x^3 \text{d}x = x^2(x \text{d}x) \cr &\phantom{x^3 \text{d}x} = (u^2 - 9)u \text{d}u \end{aligned}Determine the new limits of integration:

• When $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} &u^2 = 9 \cr &u = 3 \end{aligned}
• When $x = 4$:\begin{aligned} &u^2 = 16 + 9 \cr &u^2 = 25 \cr &u = 5 \end{aligned}

Substitute the terms and the new limits into our integral:\begin{aligned} &\int_{ 0 }^{ 4 } \dfrac{ x^3 }{ \sqrt{x^2 + 9} } \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int_{ 3 }^{ 5 } \dfrac{ (u^2 - 9)u \text{d}u }{ u } \cr &\quad = \int_{ 3 }^{ 5 } (u^2 - 9) \text{d}u \cr &\quad = \left[ \dfrac{ u^3 }{ 3 } - 9u \right]_{ 3 }^{ 5 } \end{aligned}

Evaluate at the upper and lower limits:

• At $u = 5$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 125 }{ 3 } - 9(5) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 125 }{ 3 } - 45 \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{ 10 }{ 3 } \end{aligned}
• At $u = 3$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 27 }{ 3 } - 9(3) \cr &\quad = 9 - 27 \cr &\quad = -18 \end{aligned}Subtract the lower limit value from the upper limit value:\begin{aligned} &-\dfrac{ 10 }{ 3 } - (-18) \cr &\quad = 18 - \dfrac{ 10 }{ 3 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 44 }{ 3 } \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (a) $\dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^{ 2/3 } \ln x - \dfrac{ 9 }{ 4 } x^{ 2/3 } + C$
(b) $\dfrac{ 44 }{ 3 }$

pi_options.feedback: This error in part (a) occurs if you forget to divide by the new exponent when integrating the remaining term $\int \frac{3}{2} x^{-1/3} \text{d}x$, writing $\frac{3}{2}x^{2/3}$ instead of $\frac{9}{4}x^{2/3}$. In part (b), $\frac{10}{3}$ is the result of neglecting the lower integration boundary or making a sign error at $u = 5$.

Your integration in part (a) is correct. In part (b), this error occurs if you make an arithmetic error when evaluating $u^3/3 - 9u$ at the lower limit $u = 3$, such as evaluating $3^3/3 - 9(3)$ as $-6$ instead of $-18$.
Your calculation in part (b) is correct. However, in part (a), this occurs if you integrated $x^{-1/3}$ incorrectly as $\frac{2}{3}x^{2/3}$ instead of $\frac{3}{2}x^{2/3}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Choosing $u$ and $v$ in Parts
bradley_insight.content: When integrating products involving logarithm terms like $\int x^n \ln x \text{d}x$, always choose $u = \ln x$ and $\text{d}v = x^n \text{d}x$. Since we cannot directly integrate $\ln x$ without using parts itself, this selection simplifies the integral immediately because the derivative of $\ln x$ is a simple rational power $\dfrac{ 1 }{ x }$.

question: (a) Find:$$\int 3x \cos 2x \text{d}x$$(b) Using the substitution $u = \cos x$, or otherwise, find the exact value of:$$\int_{ 0 }^{ \pi/2 } \sin^3 x \cos^2 x \text{d}x$$
steps:
Part (a): We find the indefinite integral using integration by parts:$$\int u \text{d}v = uv - \int v \text{d}u$$Let $u = 3x$ and $\text{d}v = \cos 2x \text{d}x$.

The derivatives and integrals are:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = 3 \text{d}x \cr &v = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \sin 2x \end{aligned}

Substitute these into our integration by parts formula:\begin{aligned} &\int 3x \cos 2x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x \sin 2x - \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } \int \sin 2x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x \sin 2x \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } \left( -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \cos 2x \right) + C \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x \sin 2x + \dfrac{ 3 }{ 4 } \cos 2x + C \end{aligned}

Part (b): We evaluate using the substitution $u = \cos x$.

Differentiating both sides gives:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = -\sin x \text{d}x \cr &-\text{d}u = \sin x \text{d}x \end{aligned}Rewrite the integrand in terms of $u$:\begin{aligned} &\sin^3 x \cos^2 x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = (\sin^2 x)(\cos^2 x)(\sin x \text{d}x) \cr &\quad = (1 - u^2)(u^2)(-\text{d}u) \end{aligned}Determine the new integration limits:

• When $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} &u = \cos 0 \cr &u = 1 \end{aligned}
• When $x = \pi/2$:\begin{aligned} &u = \cos(\pi/2) \cr &u = 0 \end{aligned}

Substitute the terms and the new limits into our integral:\begin{aligned} &\int_{ 0 }^{ \pi/2 } \sin^3 x \cos^2 x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int_{ 1 }^{ 0 } (1 - u^2)(u^2)(-\text{d}u) \cr &\quad = \int_{ 0 }^{ 1 } (1 - u^2)u^2 \text{d}u \cr &\quad = \int_{ 0 }^{ 1 } (u^2 - u^4) \text{d}u \end{aligned}Note that the negative sign from the substitution reverses the limits of integration.

Now integrate and evaluate the expression:\begin{aligned} &\int_{ 0 }^{ 1 } (u^2 - u^4) \text{d}u \cr &\quad = \left[ \dfrac{ u^3 }{ 3 } - \dfrac{ u^5 }{ 5 } \right]_{ 0 }^{ 1 } \cr &\quad = \left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 5 } \right) - 0 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 2 }{ 15 } \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (a) $\dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x \sin 2x + \dfrac{ 3 }{ 4 } \cos 2x + C$
(b) $\dfrac{ 2 }{ 15 }$

pi_options.feedback: Your part (b) calculation is correct. However, in part (a), this error occurs if you make a sign error when integrating $\sin 2x$, forgetting that $\int \sin 2x \text{d}x = -\frac{1}{2}\cos 2x$, which results in a negative sign instead of a positive sign for the cosine term.

Your integration in part (a) is correct. In part (b), this occurs if you evaluate the boundaries backwards or fail to handle the negative sign from $\text{d}u = -\sin x \text{d}x$, resulting in $\int_0^1 (u^2 + u^4) \text{d}u = \dfrac{ 8 }{ 15 }$.

Your part (b) calculation is correct. In part (a), this occurs if you forget to divide by the coefficients of $x$ when integrating $\cos 2x$ and $\sin 2x$ (failing to apply the reverse chain rule, which divides by $2$ at each stage).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Limit Boundary Flips
bradley_insight.content: When substituting $u = \cos x$ over the interval $[0, \pi/2]$, the lower limit $x = 0$ becomes $u = 1$, and the upper limit $x = \pi/2$ becomes $u = 0$. Since $1 > 0$, the limits appear 'upside down' ($\int_1^0$). Do not manually flip them! The negative sign from $\text{d}u = -\sin x \text{d}x$ will naturally reverse the limits back to a standard $\int_0^1$ order.

question: (a) Find:$$\int x^2 \ln 2x \text{d}x$$(b) Using the substitution $u = 2x + 1$, or otherwise, find the exact value of:$$\int_{ 0 }^{ 4 } x \sqrt{2x + 1} \text{d}x$$
steps:
Part (a): We find the indefinite integral using integration by parts:$$\int u \text{d}v = uv - \int v \text{d}u$$Let $u = \ln 2x$ and $\text{d}v = x^2 \text{d}x$.

The derivatives and integrals are:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = \dfrac{ 1 }{ x } \text{d}x \cr &v = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } x^3 \end{aligned}

Substitute these into our integration by parts formula:\begin{aligned} &\int x^2 \ln 2x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } x^3 \ln 2x - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } \int x^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } x^3 \ln 2x \cr &\qquad - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } \left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } x^3 \right) + C \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } x^3 \ln 2x - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 9 } x^3 + C \end{aligned}

Part (b): We evaluate using the substitution $u = 2x + 1$.

Rearranging gives $x = \dfrac{ u - 1 }{ 2 }$. Differentiating gives:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = 2 \text{d}x \cr &\text{d}x = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \text{d}u \end{aligned}Determine the new limits of integration:

• When $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} &u = 2(0) + 1 \cr &u = 1 \end{aligned}
• When $x = 4$:\begin{aligned} &u = 2(4) + 1 \cr &u = 9 \end{aligned}

Substitute the terms and the new limits into our integral:\begin{aligned} &\int_{ 0 }^{ 4 } x \sqrt{2x + 1} \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int_{ 1 }^{ 9 } \left( \dfrac{ u - 1 }{ 2 } \right) \sqrt{u} \left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \text{d}u \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } \int_{ 1 }^{ 9 } (u^{ 3/2 } - u^{ 1/2 }) \text{d}u \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } \left[ \dfrac{ 2 }{ 5 } u^{ 5/2 } - \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 } u^{ 3/2 } \right]_{ 1 }^{ 9 } \end{aligned}

Evaluate at the limits:

• At $u = 9$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 2 }{ 5 }(9^{ 5/2 }) - \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 }(9^{ 3/2 }) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 2 }{ 5 }(243) - \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 }(27) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 486 }{ 5 } - 18 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 396 }{ 5 } \end{aligned}
• At $u = 1$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 2 }{ 5 }(1^{ 5/2 }) - \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 }(1^{ 3/2 }) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 2 }{ 5 } - \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 } \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{ 4 }{ 15 } \end{aligned}Subtract the limits and apply the outer factor $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 }$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } \left[ \dfrac{ 396 }{ 5 } - \left( -\dfrac{ 4 }{ 15 } \right) \right] \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } \left( \dfrac{ 1192 }{ 15 } \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 298 }{ 15 } \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (a) $\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } x^3 \ln 2x - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 9 } x^3 + C$
(b) $\dfrac{ 298 }{ 15 }$

pi_options.feedback: Your integration in part (a) is correct. In part (b), this error occurs if you forgot to multiply the bracket's value by the outer coefficient $\frac{1}{4}$ at the very end of the calculation.

Your exact value in part (b) is correct. In part (a), this error occurs if you forgot to divide by the new power $3$ when integrating the remaining term $\int \frac{1}{3}x^2 \text{d}x$, writing $\frac{1}{3}x^3$ instead of $\frac{1}{9}x^3$.

Your integration in part (a) is correct. However, in part (b), always ensure you substitute the upper limit first and subtract the lower limit. Reversing them yields a negative result, which is invalid for an area under a positive curve.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Keep Fractions in Fractions
bradley_insight.content: When solving definite integration problems, avoid converting intermediate fractions into decimals on your calculator. Keeping values like $\dfrac{ 1192 }{ 15 }$ in exact fraction form prevents rounding issues and ensures you get the exact value required by high-mark questions.

question: (a) Find:$$\int x^2 \sin x \text{d}x$$(b) Using the substitution $u = \mathrm{e}^x + 1$, or otherwise, find the exact value of:$$\int_{ 0 }^{ \ln 2 } \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^{2x} }{ \mathrm{e}^x + 1 } \text{d}x$$
steps:
Part (a): We find the indefinite integral using integration by parts. Let $u = x^2$ and $\text{d}v = \sin x \text{d}x$.

The derivatives and integrals are:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = 2x \text{d}x \cr &v = -\cos x \end{aligned}Substitute these into the integration by parts formula:\begin{aligned} &\int x^2 \sin x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = -x^2 \cos x - \int -2x \cos x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = -x^2 \cos x + \int 2x \cos x \text{d}x \end{aligned}

Apply integration by parts a second time on $\int 2x \cos x \text{d}x$. Let $u = 2x$ and $\text{d}v = \cos x \text{d}x$.

The derivatives and integrals are:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = 2 \text{d}x \cr &v = \sin x \end{aligned}Substitute these into the formula:\begin{aligned} &\int 2x \cos x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = 2x \sin x - \int 2 \sin x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = 2x \sin x - 2(-\cos x) \cr &\quad = 2x \sin x + 2 \cos x \end{aligned}
Combine the results to find our final indefinite integral:\begin{aligned} &\int x^2 \sin x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = -x^2 \cos x + 2x \sin x \cr &\qquad + 2 \cos x + C \end{aligned}

Part (b): We evaluate using the substitution $u = \mathrm{e}^x + 1$, which gives $\mathrm{e}^x = u - 1$.

Differentiating gives:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = \mathrm{e}^x \text{d}x \cr &\text{d}x = \dfrac{ 1 }{ u - 1 } \text{d}u \end{aligned}Rewrite the integrand in terms of $u$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^{2x} }{ \mathrm{e}^x + 1 } \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ (u - 1)^2 }{ u } \cdot \dfrac{ 1 }{ u - 1 } \text{d}u \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ u - 1 }{ u } \text{d}u \end{aligned}Determine the new limits of integration:

• When $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} &u = \mathrm{e}^0 + 1 \cr &u = 2 \end{aligned}
• When $x = \ln 2$:\begin{aligned} &u = \mathrm{e}^{ \ln 2 } + 1 \cr &u = 2 + 1 \cr &u = 3 \end{aligned}

Substitute the terms and new limits into our integral and evaluate:\begin{aligned} &\int_{ 0 }^{ \ln 2 } \dfrac{ \mathrm{e}^{2x} }{ \mathrm{e}^x + 1 } \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int_{ 2 }^{ 3 } \left( 1 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ u } \right) \text{d}u \cr &\quad = \left[ u - \ln u \right]_{ 2 }^{ 3 } \cr &\quad = (3 - \ln 3) - (2 - \ln 2) \cr &\quad = 1 - (\ln 3 - \ln 2) \cr &\quad = 1 - \ln\left( \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } \right) \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (a) $-x^2 \cos x + 2x \sin x + 2 \cos x + C$
(b) $1 - \ln\left( \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } \right)$

pi_options.feedback: Your exact value in part (b) is correct. In part (a), this error occurs if you make a sign error during the second integration by parts, incorrectly evaluating the integral of $-2\sin x$ as $-2\cos x$ instead of $+2\cos x$.

Your part (a) integration is correct. In part (b), this error occurs if you make a sign error when handling the limits, writing $(3 - \ln 3) - (2 - \ln 2)$ incorrectly as $1 + \ln 3 - \ln 2$, which gives $1 + \ln(3/2)$.

Your exact value in part (b) is correct. However, in part (a), this is a common error if you fail to distribute the double negative sign when evaluating the first integration by parts subtraction step, leading to sign errors in all subsequent terms.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Iterated Integration by Parts
bradley_insight.content: For integrals of the form $\int x^2 \sin x \text{d}x$, you must apply integration by parts twice. Be extremely careful with sign distribution on the second pass. The entire second integral is subtracted, so you must wrap it in brackets and distribute the negative sign carefully to avoid losing algebraic marks.

question: (a) Find:$$\int (\ln x)^2 \text{d}x$$(b) Using the substitution $u = \mathrm{e}^x$, or otherwise, find the exact value of:$$\int_{ 0 }^{ \ln 3 } \dfrac{ 1 }{ \mathrm{e}^x + \mathrm{e}^{-x} } \text{d}x$$
steps:
Part (a): We find the indefinite integral using integration by parts. Let $u = (\ln x)^2$ and $\text{d}v = \text{d}x$.

The derivatives and integrals are:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = \dfrac{ 2\ln x }{ x } \text{d}x \cr &v = x \end{aligned}Substitute these into the integration by parts formula:\begin{aligned} &\int (\ln x)^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = x(\ln x)^2 - \int x \left( \dfrac{ 2\ln x }{ x } \right) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = x(\ln x)^2 - \int 2\ln x \text{d}x \end{aligned}

Apply integration by parts a second time on $\int 2\ln x \text{d}x$. Let $u = \ln x$ and $\text{d}v = 2\text{d}x$.

The derivatives and integrals are:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = \dfrac{ 1 }{ x } \text{d}x \cr &v = 2x \end{aligned}Substitute these into the formula:\begin{aligned} &\int 2\ln x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = 2x\ln x - \int (2x)\left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ x } \text{d}x \right) \cr &\quad = 2x\ln x - \int 2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = 2x\ln x - 2x \end{aligned}

Combine the results to find our final indefinite integral:\begin{aligned} &\int (\ln x)^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = x(\ln x)^2 - (2x\ln x - 2x) + C \cr &\quad = x(\ln x)^2 - 2x\ln x + 2x + C \end{aligned}

Part (b): We evaluate using the substitution $u = \mathrm{e}^x$.

Differentiating gives:\begin{aligned} &\text{d}u = \mathrm{e}^x \text{d}x \cr &\text{d}x = \dfrac{ 1 }{ u } \text{d}u \end{aligned}Rewrite the integrand in terms of $u$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 1 }{ \mathrm{e}^x + \mathrm{e}^{-x} } \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ u + u^{-1} } \cdot \dfrac{ 1 }{ u } \text{d}u \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ u^2 + 1 } \text{d}u \end{aligned}Determine the new limits of integration:

• When $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} &u = \mathrm{e}^0 \cr &u = 1 \end{aligned}
• When $x = \ln 3$:\begin{aligned} &u = \mathrm{e}^{ \ln 3 } \cr &u = 3 \end{aligned}

Substitute the terms and new limits into our integral and evaluate:\begin{aligned} &\int_{ 0 }^{ \ln 3 } \dfrac{ 1 }{ \mathrm{e}^x + \mathrm{e}^{-x} } \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int_{ 1 }^{ 3 } \dfrac{ 1 }{ u^2 + 1 } \text{d}u \cr &\quad = \left[ \arctan u \right]_{ 1 }^{ 3 } \cr &\quad = \arctan 3 - \arctan 1 \cr &\quad = \arctan 3 - \dfrac{ \pi }{ 4 } \end{aligned}

Final Answer: (a) $x(\ln x)^2 - 2x\ln x + 2x + C$
(b) $\arctan 3 - \dfrac{ \pi }{ 4 }$

pi_options.feedback: Your exact value in part (b) is correct. However, in part (a), this occurs if you make an error when integrating the remaining term $\int 2\ln x \text{d}x$, forgetting the $+2x$ term that arises from completing the integration by parts on $\ln x$.
Your part (a) integration is correct. In part (b), this error occurs if you make a sign error when subtracting the lower limit $\arctan(1) = \frac{\pi}{4}$, incorrectly adding it instead.

Your part (a) integration is correct. In part (b), this occurs if you completely neglect the lower boundary condition $x = 0 \implies u = 1$, evaluating the integral only at the upper boundary as $\arctan(3)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Inverse Trigonometric Integrals
bradley_insight.content: Recognizing that $\int \dfrac{ 1 }{ u^2 + 1 } \text{d}u = \arctan u$ is a highly valuable synoptic connection at A2 level. Always look out for algebraic substitutions that simplify complicated exponential or trigonometric fractions into standard rational forms that match inverse trigonometric patterns.

question:
The diagram shows a sketch of the curves $y = \sin 3x$ and $y = \cos 3x$ for $0 \le x \le \dfrac{ \pi }{ 2 }$. The curves intersect at the points $A$ and $B$, enclosing a region $R$.

(i) Show that the x-coordinates of the points $A$ and $B$ are $\dfrac{ \pi }{ 12 }$ and $\dfrac{ 5\pi }{ 12 }$.

(ii) Calculate the exact area of the region $R$.

(iii) A company is designing a trophy base. The base can be modelled as the solid formed when the area bounded by the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 9$, the y-axis, and the vertical line $x = 2$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the x-axis. Find the exact volume of this trophy base.
steps: Part (i): To find the points of intersection of the curves $y = \sin 3x$ and $y = \cos 3x$, equate them:\begin{aligned} &\sin 3x = \cos 3x \cr &\dfrac{ \sin 3x }{ \cos 3x } = 1 \cr &\tan 3x = 1 \end{aligned}Solve for $3x$ in the interval $0 \le 3x \le \dfrac{ 3\pi }{ 2 }$, which gives:\begin{aligned} &3x = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 4 }, \ \dfrac{ 5\pi }{ 4 } \cr &x = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 12 }, \ \dfrac{ 5\pi }{ 12 } \end{aligned}Thus, the x-coordinates of $A$ and $B$ are $\dfrac{ \pi }{ 12 }$ and $\dfrac{ 5\pi }{ 12 }$.

Part (ii): Over the interval $\left[ \dfrac{ \pi }{ 12 }, \dfrac{ 5\pi }{ 12 } \right]$, the curve $y = \sin 3x$ lies above $y = \cos 3x$.

The area of region $R$ is given by:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \int_{ \pi/12 }^{ 5\pi/12 } (\sin 3x - \cos 3x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \left[ -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } \cos 3x - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } \sin 3x \right]_{ \pi/12 }^{ 5\pi/12 } \end{aligned}

Substitute the limits of integration:

• At the upper limit $x = \dfrac{ 5\pi }{ 12 }$:\begin{aligned} &-\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } \cos\left( \dfrac{ 5\pi }{ 4 } \right) - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } \sin\left( \dfrac{ 5\pi }{ 4 } \right) \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }\left( -\dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 2 } \right) - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }\left( -\dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 2 } \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 6 } + \dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 6 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 3 } \end{aligned}
• At the lower limit $x = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 12 }$:\begin{aligned} &-\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } \cos\left( \dfrac{ \pi }{ 4 } \right) - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } \sin\left( \dfrac{ \pi }{ 4 } \right) \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }\left( \dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 2 } \right) - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }\left( \dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 2 } \right) \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 6 } - \dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 6 } \cr &\quad = -\dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 3 } \end{aligned}Subtract the lower limit from the upper limit:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 3 } - \left( -\dfrac{ \sqrt{2} }{ 3 } \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 2\sqrt{2} }{ 3 } \end{aligned}

Part (iii): Rearrange the circle equation to express $y^2$ in terms of $x$:$$y^2 = 9 - x^2$$Rotate this region from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$ about the x-axis:\begin{aligned} &V \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ 2 } y^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ 2 } (9 - x^2) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \left[ 9x - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } x^3 \right]_{ 0 }^{ 2 } \cr &\quad = \pi \left( 9(2) - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }(2)^3 - 0 \right) \cr &\quad = \pi \left( 18 - \dfrac{ 8 }{ 3 } \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 46\pi }{ 3 } \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (ii) $\dfrac{ 2\sqrt{2} }{ 3 }$, (iii) $\dfrac{ 46\pi }{ 3 }$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (ii) if you make a calculation slip when adding the upper and lower limit evaluations, such as evaluating $\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3} - \left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3} \right)$ as $\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3}$ by failing to distribute the double negative.
Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this error occurs if you forgot to integrate the $x^2/3$ term, evaluating the integral as $9(2) - 0 = 18$ and multiplying by $\pi$.

Your volume in part (iii) is correct. In part (ii), this occurs if you integrated $\sin 3x$ and $\cos 3x$ incorrectly without dividing by $3$ (forgetting the reverse chain rule factor), which doubles your final area.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Shading Trig Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating areas between trigonometric curves, sketching the graphs is essential to identify which curve is upper ($y_{\text{upper}}$) and which is lower ($y_{\text{lower}}$) over the interval. Substituting a midpoint value (like $x = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 4 }$) into both equations is a fast, bulletproof way to confirm which curve lies on top.

question:
The diagram shows the region $R$ bounded by the curves $y = x^2$ and $y = 8 - x^2$.

(i) Find the coordinates of the points of intersection of the two curves.

(ii) Calculate the exact area of the region $R$.

(iii) The base of a stone pillar can be modelled as the solid formed when the region bounded by the curve $y = \mathrm{e}^x$, the x-axis, the y-axis, and the vertical line $x = \ln 3$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the x-axis. Find the exact volume of this pillar base.
steps: Part (i): To find the points of intersection of the curves $y = x^2$ and $y = 8 - x^2$, equate them:\begin{aligned} &x^2 = 8 - x^2 \cr &2x^2 = 8 \cr &x^2 = 4 \cr &x = \pm 2 \end{aligned}Substitute $x = \pm 2$ into $y = x^2$:\begin{aligned} &y = (\pm 2)^2 \cr &y = 4 \end{aligned}Thus, the coordinates of the points of intersection are $(-2, 4)$ and $(2, 4)$.

Part (ii): The area of region $R$ is bounded by the upper curve $y = 8 - x^2$ and the lower curve $y = x^2$ from $x = -2$ to $x = 2$:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \int_{ -2 }^{ 2 } ((8 - x^2) - x^2) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int_{ -2 }^{ 2 } (8 - 2x^2) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \left[ 8x - \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 } x^3 \right]_{ -2 }^{ 2 } \end{aligned}

Substitute the upper and lower limits of integration:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \left( 8(2) - \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 }(2)^3 \right) \cr &\qquad - \left( 8(-2) - \dfrac{ 2 }{ 3 }(-2)^3 \right) \cr &\quad = \left( 16 - \dfrac{ 16 }{ 3 } \right) - \left( -16 + \dfrac{ 16 }{ 3 } \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 32 }{ 3 } - \left( -\dfrac{ 32 }{ 3 } \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 64 }{ 3 } \end{aligned}

Part (iii): Rotate the region bounded by $y = \mathrm{e}^x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = \ln 3$ about the x-axis:\begin{aligned} &V \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ \ln 3 } y^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ \ln 3 } (\mathrm{e}^x)^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ \ln 3 } \mathrm{e}^{ 2x } \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \left[ \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \mathrm{e}^{ 2x } \right]_{ 0 }^{ \ln 3 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 2 } \left( \mathrm{e}^{ 2\ln 3 } - \mathrm{e}^0 \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 2 }(9 - 1) \cr &\quad = 4\pi \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (ii) $\dfrac{ 64 }{ 3 }$, (iii) $4\pi$

pi_options.feedback: Your volume in part (iii) is correct. In part (ii), this error occurs if you only evaluate the integral on the positive interval $[0, 2]$ and forget to double it (or add the negative interval $[-2, 0]$), neglecting the symmetric nature of the shaded region.

Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this error occurs if you forgot to divide by $2$ when integrating $\mathrm{e}^{ 2x }$, evaluating the integral as $\pi [ \mathrm{e}^{ 2x } ]_0^{\ln 3}$, which gives $8\pi$.
Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this error occurs if you completely forgot to include the factor of $\pi$ in the Volume of Revolution formula.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Symmetry in Integration
bradley_insight.content: For symmetric boundaries (like $[-2, 2]$) of an even function, you can double the integral over the positive half: $2 \int_{ 0 }^{ 2 } f(x) \text{d}x$. This is an excellent pro-tip because substituting $0$ as a lower limit is far less prone to arithmetic and sign errors than substituting $-2$.

question:
The diagram shows the region $R$ bounded by the straight line $y = x$ and the curve $y = 4x - x^2$.

(i) Find the coordinates of the points of intersection of the line and the curve.

(ii) Calculate the exact area of the region $R$.

(iii) A plastic container lid can be modelled as the solid formed when the region bounded by the curve $y = \sqrt{x}$, the x-axis, and the vertical line $x = 4$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the x-axis. Find the exact volume of the lid.
steps:
Part (i): To find the points of intersection of $y = x$ and $y = 4x - x^2$, equate them:\begin{aligned} &x = 4x - x^2 \cr &x^2 - 3x = 0 \cr &x(x - 3) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives $x = 0$ and $x = 3$.

Substitute these into $y = x$:

• When $x = 0$, $y = 0$.
• When $x = 3$, $y = 3$.

Thus, the coordinates of the points of intersection are $(0, 0)$ and $(3, 3)$.

Part (ii): Over the interval $[0, 3]$, the curve $y = 4x - x^2$ lies above the straight line $y = x$.

The area of the region $R$ is given by:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \int_{ 0 }^{ 3 } ((4x - x^2) - x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int_{ 0 }^{ 3 } (3x - x^2) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \left[ \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 } x^2 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } x^3 \right]_{ 0 }^{ 3 } \end{aligned}

Substitute the upper and lower limits of integration:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \left( \dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 }(3)^2 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }(3)^3 \right) - 0 \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 27 }{ 2 } - 9 \cr &\quad = 4.5 \end{aligned}Thus, the exact area of the region $R$ is $4.5$ (or $\dfrac{ 9 }{ 2 }$).

Part (iii): Rotate the region bounded by $y = \sqrt{x}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 4$ about the x-axis:\begin{aligned} &V \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ 4 } y^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ 4 } (\sqrt{x})^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ 4 } x \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \left[ \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } x^2 \right]_{ 0 }^{ 4 } \cr &\quad = \pi \left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }(4)^2 - 0 \right) \cr &\quad = 8\pi \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (ii) $4.5$, (iii) $8\pi$

pi_options.feedback: Your volume in part (iii) is correct. In part (ii), this error occurs if you forgot to divide the $3x^2$ term by $2$, evaluating the integral as $3(9) - 9 = 18$ or forgetting to divide the entire sum by $2$, yielding double the actual area.
Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this error occurs if you forgot to divide by $2$ when integrating $x$, writing $\pi [ x^2 ]_0^4 = 16\pi$.
Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this occurs if you forgot to multiply the integrated value by $\pi$ in the Volume of Revolution formula.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Squaring the Integrand
bradley_insight.content: In the Volume of Revolution formula $V = \pi \int y^2 \text{d}x$, always square the function $y$ before you integrate. For a function like $y = \sqrt{x}$, squaring simplifies the integrand directly to $x$, making the integration exceptionally straightforward. Don't forget the factor of $\pi$!

question:
The curves $y = \mathrm{e}^x$ and $y = 4\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ intersect at a single point in the first quadrant.

(i) Show that the x-coordinate of the point of intersection of the two curves is $\ln 2$.

(ii) Calculate the exact area of the region bounded by the curve $y = \mathrm{e}^x$, the curve $y = 4\mathrm{e}^{-x}$, and the y-axis.

(iii) The base of a glass funnel can be modelled as the solid formed when the region bounded by the curve $y = \dfrac{ 1 }{ x }$, the x-axis, and the vertical lines $x = 1$ and $x = 3$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the x-axis. Find the exact volume of the funnel base.
steps: Part (i): Equate the curves $y = \mathrm{e}^x$ and $y = 4\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ to find their intersection:\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{e}^x = 4\mathrm{e}^{ -x } \cr &\mathrm{e}^{ 2x } = 4 \cr &2x = \ln 4 \cr &2x = \ln(2^2) \cr &2x = 2\ln 2 \cr &x = \ln 2 \end{aligned}Thus, the x-coordinate of the point of intersection is $\ln 2$.

Part (ii): Integrate between the y-axis ($x = 0$) and the point of intersection ($x = \ln 2$).

Over this interval, $y = 4\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ lies above $y = \mathrm{e}^x$. The area of the region is:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \int_{ 0 }^{ \ln 2 } (4\mathrm{e}^{ -x } - \mathrm{e}^x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \left[ -4\mathrm{e}^{ -x } - \mathrm{e}^x \right]_{ 0 }^{ \ln 2 } \end{aligned}

Substitute the upper and lower limits of integration:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \left( -4\mathrm{e}^{ -\ln 2 } - \mathrm{e}^{ \ln 2 } \right) - (-4\mathrm{e}^0 - \mathrm{e}^0) \cr &\quad = \left( -4\left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \right) - 2 \right) - (-4 - 1) \cr &\quad = (-2 - 2) - (-5) \cr &\quad = -4 + 5 \cr &\quad = 1 \end{aligned}Thus, the exact area of the region is $1$.

Part (iii): Rotate the region bounded by $y = \dfrac{ 1 }{ x }$ from $x = 1$ to $x = 3$ about the x-axis:\begin{aligned} &V \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 1 }^{ 3 } y^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 1 }^{ 3 } \left( \dfrac{ 1 }{ x } \right)^2 \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \int_{ 1 }^{ 3 } x^{ -2 } \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \pi \left[ -\dfrac{ 1 }{ x } \right]_{ 1 }^{ 3 } \cr &\quad = \pi \left( -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } - (-1) \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 2\pi }{ 3 } \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (ii) $1$, (iii) $\dfrac{ 2\pi }{ 3 }$

pi_options.feedback: Your volume in part (iii) is correct. This error in part (ii) occurs if you make sign errors when substituting $\mathrm{e}^{ -\ln 2 } = 0.5$ and $\mathrm{e}^{ \ln 2 } = 2$, or if you evaluated $-4(0.5) - 2$ incorrectly as $0$ instead of $-4$.
Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this error occurs if you integrated $x^{ -2 }$ as $\dfrac{x^{ -1 }}{ 2 }$ by mistake, or made an arithmetic slip when evaluating $-1/3 - (-1)$.
Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this occurs if you forgot to include the factor of $\pi$ in the Volume of Revolution formula.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Laws of Logarithms in Substitution
bradley_insight.content: When substituting logarithmic limits into exponential functions, remember that $\mathrm{e}^{ \ln a } = a$ and $\mathrm{e}^{ -\ln a } = \dfrac{ 1 }{ a }$. Using these algebraic identities immediately transforms complicated-looking exponential limits into simple, clean rational numbers.

question:
The curve $y = \dfrac{ 4 }{ x }$ and the straight line $y = 5 - x$ intersect at two points.

(i) Find the x-coordinates of the points of intersection.

(ii) Calculate the exact area of the region bounded by the curve and the straight line.

(iii) A decorative glass paperweight can be modelled as the solid formed when the region bounded by the curve $y = \sin x$, the x-axis, and the vertical lines $x = 0$ and $x = \pi$ is rotated through $360^\circ$ about the x-axis. Find the exact volume of the paperweight.
steps: Part (i): To find the points of intersection, equate the curve $y = \dfrac{ 4 }{ x }$ and the straight line $y = 5 - x$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 4 }{ x } = 5 - x \cr &4 = 5x - x^2 \cr &x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0 \cr &(x - 1)(x - 4) = 0 \end{aligned}Thus, the x-coordinates of the points of intersection are $x = 1$ and $x = 4$.

Part (ii): Over the interval $[1, 4]$, the line $y = 5 - x$ lies above the curve $y = \dfrac{ 4 }{ x }$.

The area of the region is given by:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \int_{ 1 }^{ 4 } \left( 5 - x - \dfrac{ 4 }{ x } \right) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \left[ 5x - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } x^2 - 4\ln x \right]_{ 1 }^{ 4 } \end{aligned}

Substitute the upper and lower limits of integration:\begin{aligned} &\text{Area} \cr &\quad = \left( 5(4) - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }(4)^2 - 4\ln 4 \right) \cr &\qquad - \left( 5(1) - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }(1)^2 - 4\ln 1 \right) \cr &\quad = (20 - 8 - 4\ln 4) - (5 - 0.5 - 0) \cr &\quad = (12 - 4\ln 4) - 4.5 \cr &\quad = 7.5 - 4\ln 4 \end{aligned}Note that this can also be expressed as $7.5 - 8\ln 2$.

Part (iii): The volume of revolution $V$ is formed by rotating $y = \sin x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = \pi$ about the x-axis:\begin{aligned} &V = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ \pi } y^2 \text{d}x \cr &\phantom{V} = \pi \int_{ 0 }^{ \pi } \sin^2 x \text{d}x \end{aligned}Apply the double-angle identity:$$\sin^2 x = \dfrac{ 1 - \cos 2x }{ 2 }$$Evaluate the integral:\begin{aligned} &V \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 2 } \int_{ 0 }^{ \pi } (1 - \cos 2x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 2 } \left[ x - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \sin 2x \right]_{ 0 }^{ \pi } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 2 } \left( \left( \pi - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 } \sin(2\pi) \right) - 0 \right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \pi }{ 2 }(\pi - 0) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ \pi^2 }{ 2 } \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (ii) $7.5 - 4\ln 4$, (iii) $\dfrac{ \pi^2 }{ 2 }$

pi_options.feedback: Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this error occurs if you forgot to divide by $2$ when using the double-angle identity $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$, leading to an integrated value of $\pi^2$ instead of $\dfrac{\pi^2}{2}$.

Your volume in part (iii) is correct. In part (ii), this occurs if you forgot to subtract the evaluation at the lower limit $x = 1$ ($5 - 0.5 = 4.5$), incorrectly reporting the upper limit's value of $12 - 4\ln 4$ as the final area.

Your area in part (ii) is correct. In part (iii), this error occurs if you forgot to square the integrand (integrating $\sin x$ instead of $\sin^2 x$), which yields $\pi [ -\cos x ]_0^\pi = 2\pi$, or if you made a power-of-$\pi$ omission.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Double Angle Identity for $\sin^2 x$
bradley_insight.content:
To integrate $\sin^2 x$ or $\cos^2 x$, you must use the double-angle trigonometric identities:

• $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{ 1 - \cos 2x }{ 2 }$
• $\cos^2 x = \dfrac{ 1 + \cos 2x }{ 2 }$

Integrating these squared terms directly without this linear conversion is a fatal algebraic error.

question:
Section (a)

(i) Prove that the sum of $n$ terms of an arithmetic progression with first term $a$ and last term $l$ is:$$S_n = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }n(a + l)$$(ii) The first term of an arithmetic progression is $5$ and the last term is $85$. The sum of the progression is $945$. Find the number of terms, $n$.

(iii) Find the common difference, $d$.

Section (b)

A woman decides to invest her annual savings in a savings account. At the end of Year 1 she invests £500. At the end of Year 2 she invests a further £500 and receives 3% interest on the first year's £500. At the end of Year 3 she invests a further £500 and 3% interest is added to the total sum of money which she has accumulated during the first two years.

(i) Show that she has £1,545.45 in her account at the end of Year 3.

(ii) Assuming that the woman continues to invest in this way, form and sum a series to prove that she will have $\dfrac{ 50000 }{ 3 }(1.03^n - 1)$ in her account at the end of $n$ years.

(iii) Hence, find the least number of years until her investment exceeds £9,000.
steps:
Section (a)

Part (i): Represent the sum of the arithmetic progression as:\begin{aligned} &S_n = a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) \cr &\qquad + \dots + (l - d) + l \end{aligned}Reversing the order of the terms gives:\begin{aligned} &S_n = l + (l - d) + (l - 2d) \cr &\qquad + \dots + (a + d) + a \end{aligned}Add these two equations together term-by-term:\begin{aligned} &2S_n = (a + l) + (a + l) \cr &\qquad + \dots + (a + l) \cr &2S_n = n(a + l) \cr &S_n = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }n(a + l) \end{aligned}

Part (ii): We are given first term $a = 5$, last term $l = 85$, and sum $S_n = 945$. Substitute these values into the sum formula:\begin{aligned} &945 = \dfrac{ n }{ 2 }(5 + 85) \cr &945 = 45n \cr &n = 21 \end{aligned}Thus, the number of terms is $21$.

Part (iii): Use the formula for the $n$-th term of an arithmetic progression to find $d$:\begin{aligned} &l = a + (n - 1)d \cr &85 = 5 + (21 - 1)d \cr &80 = 20d \cr &d = 4 \end{aligned}Thus, the common difference is $4$.

Section (b)

Part (i): Trace the accumulated balance at the end of each year:

• End of Year 1: £$500$

• End of Year 2: The previous £$500$ earns 3% interest, and a further £$500$ is added:\begin{aligned} &\text{Value} \cr &\quad = 500(1.03) + 500 \cr &\quad = 515 + 500 \cr &\quad = 1015 \end{aligned}
• End of Year 3: The previous £$1015$ earns 3% interest, and a further £$500$ is added:\begin{aligned} &\text{Value} \cr &\quad = 1015(1.03) + 500 \cr &\quad = 1045.45 + 500 \cr &\quad = 1545.45 \end{aligned}Thus, the accumulated balance at the end of Year 3 is £1,545.45.

Part (ii): The total value of the investment at the end of $n$ years forms a geometric series:\begin{aligned} &S_n = 500 + 500(1.03) \cr &\qquad + 500(1.03)^2 + \dots \cr &\qquad + 500(1.03)^{ n-1 } \end{aligned}This is a geometric progression with first term $a = 500$ and common ratio $r = 1.03$. Sum the series using the geometric sum formula:\begin{aligned} &S_n \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ a(r^n - 1) }{ r - 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 500(1.03^n - 1) }{ 1.03 - 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 500(1.03^n - 1) }{ 0.03 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 50000 }{ 3 }(1.03^n - 1) \end{aligned}

Part (iii): Set up the inequality to find when the investment exceeds £9,000:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 50000 }{ 3 }(1.03^n - 1) > 9000 \cr &1.03^n - 1 > \dfrac{ 27000 }{ 50000 } \cr &1.03^n - 1 > 0.54 \cr &1.03^n > 1.54 \end{aligned}Taking natural logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} &n \ln(1.03) > \ln(1.54) \cr &n > \dfrac{ \ln(1.54) }{ \ln(1.03) } \cr &n > 14.61 \end{aligned}Since $n$ must be an integer, the least number of years required is $15\text{ years}$.

Final Answer: Section (a) (ii) $n = 21$, (iii) $d = 4$
Section (b) (iii) $15\text{ years}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b)(iii) if you incorrectly round down your decimal value of $n > 14.61$ to $14$. At $14$ years, the accumulated investment is only £$8,543.14$, which does not exceed £9,000. You must round up to the next integer, which is $15$.
Your part (b) calculation is correct. However, this error occurs in Section (a) if you made an arithmetic slip when calculating $n$, such as using an incorrect sum formula or dividing incorrectly.

Your Section (a) calculations are correct. In Section (b)(iii), this error occurs if you set up the series sum incorrectly, such as using $a = 500(1.03) = 515$ instead of $500$ as the first term of the series, which shifts the powers of your geometric progression.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Deposit Timing in Financial Series
bradley_insight.content: When modeling savings schemes, look closely at when deposits are made. If deposits are made at the end of each year, the first year's deposit only accumulates interest for $n-1$ years. This shifts the power of the first term and changes the structure of your geometric series.

question:
Section (a)

(i) Prove that the sum of $n$ terms of a geometric progression with first term $a$ and common ratio $r$ is:$$S_n = \dfrac{ a(1 - r^n) }{ 1 - r }$$(ii) An infinite geometric progression has first term $12$ and third term $3$. Given that the common ratio $r$ is positive, find the value of $r$.

(iii) Find the sum to infinity, $S_\infty$, of this progression.

Section (b)

A graduate starts a new job with an initial salary of £24,000 in Year 1. Each year, their salary increases by 4% of the previous year's salary.

(i) Show that their salary in Year 4 is £26,996.74.

(ii) Form and sum a geometric series to prove that their total cumulative earnings over a career of $n$ years is given by $600000(1.04^n - 1)$.

(iii) Hence, find the least number of years of work required for their total cumulative earnings to exceed £350,000.
steps:
Section (a)

Part (i): Let the sum of the first $n$ terms of the geometric progression be:\begin{aligned} &S_n = a + ar + ar^2 \cr &\qquad + \dots + ar^{ n-1 } \end{aligned}Multiply both sides of this equation by $r$:\begin{aligned} &rS_n = ar + ar^2 + ar^3 \cr &\qquad + \dots + ar^n \end{aligned}Subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate middle terms:\begin{aligned} &S_n - rS_n = a - ar^n \cr &S_n(1 - r) = a(1 - r^n) \cr &S_n = \dfrac{ a(1 - r^n) }{ 1 - r } \end{aligned}

Part (ii): We are given the first term $a = 12$ and third term $u_3 = 3$.

The formula for the $n$-th term is $u_n = a r^{ n-1 }$. Substitute our values:\begin{aligned} &3 = 12r^2 \cr &r^2 = 0.25 \cr &r = 0.5 \end{aligned}Since $r$ is specified as positive, we reject the negative root.
Part (iii): Find the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ using the formula:\begin{aligned} &S_\infty \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ a }{ 1 - r } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 12 }{ 1 - 0.5 } \cr &\quad = 24 \end{aligned}

Section (b)

Part (i): The salary receives a 4% increase each year, representing a multiplier of $1.04$.

Since the initial salary in Year 1 is £$24000$, the salary in Year 4 is:\begin{aligned} &\text{Salary} \cr &\quad = 24000(1.04)^3 \cr &\quad = 24000(1.124864) \cr &\quad \approx 26996.74 \end{aligned}Thus, the salary in Year 4 is £26,996.74.

Part (ii): The total cumulative earnings over $n$ years is the sum of the annual salaries:\begin{aligned} &S_n = 24000 + 24000(1.04) \cr &\qquad + 24000(1.04)^2 + \dots \cr &\qquad + 24000(1.04)^{ n-1 } \end{aligned}This is a geometric series with first term $a = 24000$ and common ratio $r = 1.04$. Using the sum formula:\begin{aligned} &S_n \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ a(r^n - 1) }{ r - 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 24000(1.04^n - 1) }{ 1.04 - 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 24000(1.04^n - 1) }{ 0.04 } \cr &\quad = 600000(1.04^n - 1) \end{aligned}

Part (iii): Set up the inequality to find when the cumulative earnings exceed £350,000:\begin{aligned} &600000(1.04^n - 1) > 350000 \cr &1.04^n - 1 > \dfrac{ 350000 }{ 600000 } \cr &1.04^n - 1 > \dfrac{ 7 }{ 12 } \cr &1.04^n > \dfrac{ 19 }{ 12 } \end{aligned}Taking natural logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} &n \ln(1.04) > \ln\left( \dfrac{ 19 }{ 12 } \right) \cr &n > \dfrac{ \ln(1.5833) }{ \ln(1.04) } \cr &n > 11.72 \end{aligned}Since $n$ must be an integer, the least number of years required is $12\text{ years}$.

Final Answer: Section (a) (ii) $r = 0.5$, (iii) $S_\infty = 24$
Section (b) (iii) $12\text{ years}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b)(iii) if you incorrectly round down your decimal value of $n > 11.72$ to $11$. At $11$ years, the total cumulative earnings are only £$323,674.31$, which does not exceed £350,000. You must round up to the next integer, which is $12$.

Your part (b) calculation is correct. However, this error occurs in Section (a) if you forgot to take the square root of $r^2 = 0.25$ when solving for $r$ in part (ii), incorrectly setting $r = 0.25$ instead of $0.5$.

Your Section (a) calculations are correct. In Section (b)(iii), this error occurs if you set up the series sum incorrectly, such as using $a = 24000(1.04) = 24960$ instead of $24000$ as the first term of the series, which shifts the powers of your geometric progression.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Identifying Year $n$ Terms
bradley_insight.content: In exponential growth or salary models, remember that the salary in Year $n$ is represented by $a r^{ n-1 }$, not $a r^n$, because the salary in Year 1 does not receive an increase. Forgetting to subtract $1$ from the power is a very common exam error.

question:
Section (a)

(i) Prove that the sum of $n$ terms of an arithmetic progression with first term $a$ and common difference $d$ is:$$S_n = \dfrac{ n }{ 2 }[2a + (n - 1)d]$$(ii) An arithmetic progression has first term $11$ and common difference $6$. The sum of the first $k$ terms of this progression is $1220$. Show that:$$3k^2 + 8k - 1220 = 0$$(iii) Hence, find the value of $k$.

Section (b)

A student starts a savings scheme. In Month 1, they save £50. Each subsequent month, they increase the amount they save by £5.

(i) Show that the amount saved in Month 12 is £105.

(ii) Find the total amount saved by the student over a period of $n$ months, expressing your answer in the form $An^2 + Bn$, where $A$ and $B$ are constants to be found.

(iii) Hence, find the least number of months required for the student's total savings to exceed £2,000.
steps:
Section (a)

Part (i): We start with the sum formula $S_n = \dfrac{ n }{ 2 }(a + l)$.

The formula for the last term of an arithmetic progression is $l = a + (n - 1)d$. Substitute this into our sum formula:\begin{aligned} &S_n = \dfrac{ n }{ 2 }(a + [a + (n - 1)d]) \cr &S_n = \dfrac{ n }{ 2 }[2a + (n - 1)d] \end{aligned}

Part (ii): We are given the first term $a = 11$, common difference $d = 6$, and sum $S_k = 1220$. Substitute these into our sum formula:\begin{aligned} &1220 = \dfrac{ k }{ 2 }[2(11) + (k - 1)6] \cr &1220 = \dfrac{ k }{ 2 }[22 + 6k - 6] \cr &1220 = \dfrac{ k }{ 2 }[6k + 16] \cr &1220 = k(3k + 8) \cr &1220 = 3k^2 + 8k \cr &3k^2 + 8k - 1220 = 0 \end{aligned}

Part (iii): Solve the quadratic equation by factoring:\begin{aligned} &(3k + 61)(k - 20) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives $k = -\dfrac{ 61 }{ 3 }$ or $k = 20$. Since the number of terms $k$ must be a positive integer, we reject the negative root. Thus:$$k = 20$$

Section (b)

Part (i): The monthly savings form an arithmetic progression with first term $a = 50$ and common difference $d = 5$.

The savings in Month 12 is:\begin{aligned} &u_{12} \cr &\quad = a + (12 - 1)d \cr &\quad = 50 + 11(5) \cr &\quad = 50 + 55 \cr &\quad = 105 \end{aligned}Thus, the amount saved in Month 12 is £105.

Part (ii): The total savings over a period of $n$ months is the sum of our arithmetic series:\begin{aligned} &S_n \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ n }{ 2 }[2(50) + (n - 1)5] \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ n }{ 2 }[100 + 5n - 5] \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ n }{ 2 }[5n + 95] \cr &\quad = 2.5n^2 + 47.5n \end{aligned}Thus, our constants are $A = 2.5$ and $B = 47.5$.

Part (iii): Set up the quadratic inequality to find when the total savings exceed £2,000:\begin{aligned} &2.5n^2 + 47.5n > 2000 \cr &n^2 + 19n - 800 > 0 \end{aligned}Solve $n^2 + 19n - 800 = 0$ using the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} &n = \dfrac{ -19 \pm \sqrt{ 19^2 - 4(1)(-800) } }{ 2 } \cr &\phantom{n} = \dfrac{ -19 \pm \sqrt{ 361 + 3200 } }{ 2 } \cr &\phantom{n} = \dfrac{ -19 \pm \sqrt{ 3561 } }{ 2 } \end{aligned}Taking the positive root:\begin{aligned} &n \approx \dfrac{ -19 + 59.67 }{ 2 } \cr &n \approx 20.33 \end{aligned}Since $n$ must be an integer, the least number of months required for total savings to exceed £2,000 is $21\text{ months}$.

Final Answer: Section (a) (iii) $k = 20$
Section (b) (iii) $21\text{ months}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b)(iii) if you incorrectly round down your decimal value of $n > 20.33$ to $20$. At $20$ months, the total amount saved is only £$1,950$, which does not exceed £2,000. You must round up to the next integer, which is $21$.

Your part (b) calculation is correct. However, this error occurs in Section (a) if you solved the quadratic equation incorrectly or failed to reject the negative root, reporting a negative or decimal value for the number of terms.

Your Section (a) calculations are correct. In Section (b)(iii), this error occurs if you set up the series sum incorrectly, such as using $A = 5$ and $B = 50$ from a misinterpretation of the first term and common difference.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Rejecting Extraneous Roots
bradley_insight.content: When solving quadratic equations derived from real-world models (like finding the number of months $k$), you will often get a positive and a negative root. Since a number of terms must be positive, you must explicitly state that you are rejecting the negative root ($k > 0$).

question:
Section (a)

(i) The first three terms of an arithmetic progression are $x$, $3x + 1$, and $3x^2$, where $x > 0$. Show that $x = 2$.

(ii) Find the common difference, $d$, of this progression.

(iii) Find the sum of the first $15$ terms of this arithmetic progression.

Section (b)

An investor deposits £1,000 into a fund at the beginning of each year. The fund pays 5% compound interest per annum, which is calculated and added to the total accumulated value of the fund at the end of each year.

(i) Show that at the end of Year 3, the total value of the fund is £3,310.13.

(ii) Form and sum a geometric series to prove that the total value of the fund at the end of $n$ years is given by $21000(1.05^n - 1)$.

(iii) Hence, find the minimum number of years required for the total value of the fund to exceed £50,000.
steps:
Section (a)

Part (i): Since the terms $x$, $3x + 1$, and $3x^2$ form an arithmetic progression, the difference between consecutive terms must be constant:\begin{aligned} &(3x + 1) - x = 3x^2 - (3x + 1) \cr &2x + 1 = 3x^2 - 3x - 1 \cr &3x^2 - 5x - 2 = 0 \end{aligned}Solve this quadratic equation by factoring:\begin{aligned} &(3x + 1)(x - 2) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives $x = -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }$ or $x = 2$. Since $x > 0$, we reject the negative root. Thus, $x = 2$.
Part (ii): Substitute $x = 2$ back into the term differences to find the common difference $d$:\begin{aligned} &d = 2x + 1 \cr &d = 2(2) + 1 \cr &d = 5 \end{aligned}

Part (iii): Our arithmetic progression has first term $a = x = 2$ and common difference $d = 5$.

Calculate the sum of the first 15 terms using the sum formula:\begin{aligned} &S_{15} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 15 }{ 2 }[2(2) + (15 - 1)5] \cr &\quad = 7.5[4 + 14(5)] \cr &\quad = 7.5[4 + 70] \cr &\quad = 7.5(74) \cr &\quad = 555 \end{aligned}

Section (b)

Part (i): Deposits are made at the beginning of each year, and interest is calculated at the end of each year:

• End of Year 1: £$1000$ deposit earns 5% interest:$$\text{Value} = 1000(1.05) = 1050$$• End of Year 2: A further £$1000$ is added at the start of the year, and the total earns 5% interest:\begin{aligned} &\text{Value} \cr &\quad = (1050 + 1000)(1.05) \cr &\quad = 2050(1.05) \cr &\quad = 2152.50 \end{aligned}
• End of Year 3: A further £$1000$ is added at the start of the year, and the total earns 5% interest:\begin{aligned} &\text{Value} \cr &\quad = (2152.50 + 1000)(1.05) \cr &\quad = 3152.50(1.05) \cr &\quad = 3310.125 \cr &\quad \approx 3310.13 \end{aligned}Thus, the total value at the end of Year 3 is £3,310.13.

Part (ii): At the end of $n$ years, the total accumulated savings forms a geometric series:\begin{aligned} &S_n = 1000(1.05) + 1000(1.05)^2 \cr &\qquad + 1000(1.05)^3 + \dots \cr &\qquad + 1000(1.05)^n \end{aligned}This is a geometric progression with first term $a = 1000(1.05) = 1050$ and common ratio $r = 1.05$.

Using the sum formula:\begin{aligned} &S_n \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ a(r^n - 1) }{ r - 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1050(1.05^n - 1) }{ 1.05 - 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1050(1.05^n - 1) }{ 0.05 } \cr &\quad = 21000(1.05^n - 1) \end{aligned}

Part (iii): Set up the inequality to find when the total value exceeds £50,000:\begin{aligned} &21000(1.05^n - 1) > 50000 \cr &1.05^n - 1 > \dfrac{ 50000 }{ 21000 } \cr &1.05^n - 1 > \dfrac{ 50 }{ 21 } \cr &1.05^n > \dfrac{ 71 }{ 21 } \cr &1.05^n > 3.3810 \end{aligned}Taking natural logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} &n \ln(1.05) > \ln(3.3810) \cr &n > \dfrac{ \ln(3.3810) }{ \ln(1.05) } \cr &n > 24.97 \end{aligned}Since $n$ must be an integer, the minimum number of years required is $25\text{ years}$.

Final Answer: Section (a) (ii) $d = 5$, (iii) $S_{15} = 555$
Section (b) (iii) $25\text{ years}$

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Shifting the Sum to Infinity
bradley_insight.content: When deposits are made at the beginning of each year, every deposit receives interest at the end of that year.
