question:
Section (a)

(i) The first three terms of a geometric progression are $x - 1$, $x + 2$, and $3x$, where $x > 1$. Show that:$$2x^2 - 7x - 4 = 0$$and hence deduce that $x = 4$.

(ii) Write down the common ratio, $r$, and the first term, $a$, of this progression.

(iii) Find the sum of the first $10$ terms of this progression.

Section (b)

A person borrows £10,000 to purchase a car. The loan is subject to compound interest at a rate of 5% per annum, which is calculated and added to the outstanding balance at the end of each year. Immediately after the interest is added at the end of each year, a fixed annual repayment of £1,200 is made.

(i) Show that the amount owed at the end of Year 2 is £8,565.

(ii) Form and sum a geometric series to prove that the amount owed, £$A_n$, at the end of $n$ years is given by:$$A_n = 24000 - 14000(1.05^n)$$(iii) Hence, find the least number of years required to completely pay off the loan.
steps:
Section (a)

Part (i): Since the terms $x - 1$, $x + 2$, and $3x$ form a geometric progression, the ratio between consecutive terms must be constant:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ x + 2 }{ x - 1 } = \dfrac{ 3x }{ x + 2 } \cr &(x + 2)^2 = 3x(x - 1) \cr &x^2 + 4x + 4 = 3x^2 - 3x \cr &2x^2 - 7x - 4 = 0 \end{aligned}Factorise this quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &(2x + 1)(x - 4) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives $x = -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }$ or $x = 4$. Since $x > 1$, we reject the negative root. Thus, $x = 4$.

Part (ii): Substitute $x = 4$ to evaluate the first term $a$ and common ratio $r$:\begin{aligned} &a = 4 - 1 \cr &\phantom{a} = 3 \cr &r = \dfrac{ 4 + 2 }{ 4 - 1 } \cr &\phantom{r} = \dfrac{ 6 }{ 3 } \cr &\phantom{r} = 2 \end{aligned}Thus, $a = 3$ and $r = 2$.

Part (iii): Calculate the sum of the first $10$ terms using the geometric sum formula with $a = 3$ and $r = 2$:\begin{aligned} &S_{10} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ a(r^{10} - 1) }{ r - 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 3(2^{10} - 1) }{ 2 - 1 } \cr &\quad = 3(1024 - 1) \cr &\quad = 3(1023) \cr &\quad = 3069 \end{aligned}

Section (b)

Part (i): Interest is added at the end of each year at 5% (multiplier $1.05$), followed immediately by a repayment of £$1200$:

• End of Year 1:\begin{aligned} &\text{Balance} \cr &\quad = 10000(1.05) - 1200 \cr &\quad = 10500 - 1200 \cr &\quad = 9300 \end{aligned}
• End of Year 2:\begin{aligned} &\text{Balance} \cr &\quad = 9300(1.05) - 1200 \cr &\quad = 9765 - 1200 \cr &\quad = 8565 \end{aligned}Thus, the amount owed at the end of Year 2 is £8,565.

Part (ii): Expanding the balance year by year reveals the structure of the remaining debt:\begin{aligned} &A_n = 10000(1.05)^n \cr &\qquad - [1200(1.05)^{ n-1 } \cr &\qquad\quad + 1200(1.05)^{ n-2 } \cr &\qquad\quad + \dots + 1200] \end{aligned}The repayments form a geometric series with first term $1200$, common ratio $1.05$, and $n$ terms. Sum this series:\begin{aligned} &\text{Sum} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1200(1.05^n - 1) }{ 1.05 - 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1200(1.05^n - 1) }{ 0.05 } \cr &\quad = 24000(1.05^n - 1) \end{aligned}Substitute this into the expression for $A_n$:\begin{aligned} &A_n = 10000(1.05^n) \cr &\qquad - 24000(1.05^n - 1) \cr &A_n = 10000(1.05^n) \cr &\qquad - 24000(1.05^n) + 24000 \cr &A_n = 24000 - 14000(1.05^n) \end{aligned}

Part (iii): The loan is completely paid off when the outstanding balance is less than or equal to zero ($A_n \le 0$):\begin{aligned} &24000 - 14000(1.05^n) \le 0 \cr &14000(1.05^n) \ge 24000 \cr &1.05^n \ge \dfrac{ 24000 }{ 14000 } \cr &1.05^n \ge \dfrac{ 12 }{ 7 } \end{aligned}Taking natural logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} &n \ln(1.05) \ge \ln\left( \dfrac{ 12 }{ 7 } \right) \cr &n \ge \dfrac{ \ln(1.7143) }{ \ln(1.05) } \cr &n \ge 11.05 \end{aligned}Evaluating the balance at integer years:

• At $n = 11$, $A_{11} = 24000 - 14000(1.05^{11}) \approx £55.25 > 0$, so the debt remains.

• At $n = 12$, $A_{12} = 24000 - 14000(1.05^{12}) \le 0$, so the debt is cleared.

Thus, the least number of years required is $12\text{ years}$.

Final Answer: Section (a) (ii) $a = 3,\text{ }r = 2$, (iii) $S_{10} = 3069$
Section (b) (iii) $12\text{ years}$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs in part (b)(iii) if you incorrectly round down your decimal value of $n \ge 11.05$ to $11$. At $11$ years, the outstanding debt is $24000 - 14000(1.05^{11}) \approx £55.25$, which means the loan is not yet cleared. You must round up to the next integer, which is $12$.

Your part (b) calculation is correct. However, this error occurs in Section (a)(iii) if you omitted the first term $a = 3$ when using the sum formula, evaluating $\dfrac{ 2^{10} - 1 }{ 2 - 1 } = 1023$ instead of multiplying by $a$.

Your Section (a) calculations are correct. In Section (b)(iii), this error occurs if you set up the series sum incorrectly by shifting the powers of $(1.05)$ or using an incorrect first term of $1200(1.05) = 1260$, which distorts the coefficient of the exponential term.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Reducing Balances and Negative Exponents
bradley_insight.content: In loan repayment models, the compound interest works against the borrower while regular repayments work for them. When setting up $A_n \le 0$, students often flip the inequality sign incorrectly when dividing by negative coefficients. Always ensure the balance decreases each year and verify your boundary values directly.

question:
A competitor is swimming a 15-kilometre marathon swim.
She swims each of the first 3 kilometres at a steady pace of 20 minutes per kilometre.
After the first 3 kilometres, she begins to slow down.
In order to estimate her finishing time, the time that she will take to complete each subsequent kilometre is modelled to be 4% greater than the time that she took to complete the previous kilometre.
Using the model,
(a) show that her time to swim the first 5 kilometres is estimated to be 102 minutes 26 seconds,
(b) show that her estimated time, in minutes, to swim the $r$th kilometre, for $4 \le r \le 15$, is:
$$20 \times 1.04^{r-3}$$
(c) estimate the total time, in hours, minutes, and seconds, that she will take to complete the marathon swim.
steps:
Part (a): The time for the first 3 kilometres is run at a steady pace of $20\text{ min/km}$:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{1-3} &= 3 \times 20 \cr&= 60\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 4th kilometre takes 4% longer than the 3rd kilometre ($20\text{ minutes}$):
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{4} &= 20 \times 1.04 \cr&= 20.8\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 5th kilometre takes 4% longer than the 4th kilometre:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{5} &= 20.8 \times 1.04 \cr&= 20 \times 1.04^2 \cr&= 21.632\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

Adding these times together gives the total estimated time for the first 5 kilometres:
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Time} &= 60 + 20.8 + 21.632 \cr&= 102.432\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
Converting $0.432$ minutes into seconds: $0.432 \times 60 = 25.92 \approx 26\text{ seconds}$.
Therefore, the time is 102 minutes 26 seconds (to the nearest second).

Part (b): For $r \ge 4$, each subsequent kilometre is 4% slower than the previous one, forming a geometric progression where the first term after the steady phase (at $r=4$) is $20 \times 1.04^1$.
In general, for the $r$th kilometre, the time has been multiplied by $1.04$ a total of $r-3$ times starting from the base pace of $20\text{ minutes}$.
Therefore, the time for the $r$th kilometre is:
$$\text{Time}_{r} = 20 \times 1.04^{r-3}$$

Part (c): The total time is the sum of the first 3 steady kilometres ($60\text{ minutes}$) and the geometric series from $r=4$ to $r=15$.
For $r=4$ to $15$, there are $15 - 4 + 1 = 12$ kilometres.
This is a geometric series with first term $a = 20 \times 1.04 = 20.8$ and common ratio $r_{\text{gp}} = 1.04$.

Using the sum formula, $S_N = \dfrac{a(r_{\text{gp}}^N - 1)}{r_{\text{gp}} - 1}$:
\begin{aligned}S_{12} &= \dfrac{20.8(1.04^{12} - 1)}{1.04 - 1} \cr&= \dfrac{20.8(1.04^{12} - 1)}{0.04} \cr&= 520(1.04^{12} - 1)\cr &\approx 520(1.601032 - 1)\cr & \approx 312.537\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

Adding the initial $60\text{ minutes}$ gives the total estimated time:
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Time} &= 60 + 312.537 \cr&= 372.537\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
Converting to hours, minutes, and seconds:\begin{aligned} & \dfrac{372.537}{60}\cr & \quad = 6\text{ hours and } 12.537\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
$$0.537 \times 60 = 32.22 \approx 32\text{ seconds}$$
Therefore, the total estimated time is 6 hours, 12 minutes, and 32 seconds.
Final Answer: (a) $$102\text{ min } 26\text{ s}$$ (b) $$20 \times 1.04^{r-3}$$ (c) $$6\text{ h } 12\text{ min } 32\text{ s}$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably made an arithmetic rounding error in Part (c) by rounding the sum of your geometric series to $312.5$ minutes prematurely. Retaining full calculator precision during your summation yields a total time of $372.537$ minutes, which converts to $6\text{ h } 12\text{ min } 32\text{ s}$.

Check your exponent index in Part (b). Since the steady phase ends after the 3rd kilometre, the first 4% increase occurs on the 4th kilometre ($r=4$). This requires an exponent of $r-3$ so that $T_4 = 20 \times 1.04^1$. An exponent of $r-4$ would incorrectly mean the 4th kilometre had no slow-down.
Check your value for $N$ (the number of terms in your geometric series) in Part (c). The slow-down phase runs from $r=4$ to $r=15$, which contains $15-4+1 = 12$ terms, not $11$ terms.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Counting Terms
bradley_insight.content: When calculating the sum of a series over a specific range like $r=4$ to $r=15$, a common pitfall is subtracting the limits ($15 - 4 = 11$) and using $11$ as the number of terms ($N$). Always remember the inclusive rule: $N = \text{upper limit} - \text{lower limit} + 1$. In this case, $15 - 4 + 1 = 12$ terms.

question:
An engineering firm is drilling a 100-metre deep borehole.
The team drills each of the first 20 metres at a steady rate of 15 minutes per metre.
After the first 20 metres, the drilling speed begins to decrease due to harder rock layers.
In order to estimate the completion time, the time taken to drill each subsequent metre is modelled to be 2% greater than the time taken to drill the previous metre.
Using the model,
(a) show that the time to drill the first 22 metres is estimated to be 330 minutes 54 seconds,
(b) show that the estimated time, in minutes, to drill the $r$th metre, for $21 \le r \le 100$, is:
$$15 \times 1.02^{r-20}$$
(c) estimate the total time, in hours, minutes, and seconds, to complete the 100-metre borehole.
steps:
Part (a): The time for the first 20 metres is drilled at a steady rate of $15\text{ min/m}$:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{1-20} &= 20 \times 15 \cr&= 300\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 21st metre takes 2% longer than the 20th metre ($15\text{ minutes}$):
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{21} &= 15 \times 1.02 \cr&= 15.3\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 22nd metre takes 2% longer than the 21st metre:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{22} &= 15.3 \times 1.02 \cr&= 15 \times 1.02^2 \cr&= 15.606\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

Adding these times together gives the total estimated time for the first 22 metres:
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Time} &= 300 + 15.3 + 15.606 \cr&= 330.906\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
Converting $0.906$ minutes into seconds: $0.906 \times 60 = 54.36 \approx 54\text{ seconds}$.
Therefore, the time is 330 minutes 54 seconds (to the nearest second).

Part (b): For $r \ge 21$, each subsequent metre is 2% slower than the previous one, forming a geometric progression where the first term after the steady phase (at $r=21$) is $15 \times 1.02^1$.
In general, for the $r$th metre, the time has been multiplied by $1.02$ a total of $r-20$ times starting from the base pace of $15\text{ minutes}$.
Therefore, the time for the $r$th metre is:
$$\text{Time}_{r} = 15 \times 1.02^{r-20}$$

Part (c): The total time is the sum of the first 20 steady metres ($300\text{ minutes}$) and the geometric series from $r=21$ to $r=100$.
For $r=21$ to $100$, there are $100 - 21 + 1 = 80$ metres.
This is a geometric series with first term $a = 15 \times 1.02 = 15.3$ and common ratio $r_{\text{gp}} = 1.02$.

Using the sum formula, $S_N = \dfrac{a(r_{\text{gp}}^N - 1)}{r_{\text{gp}} - 1}$:
\begin{aligned}S_{80} &= \dfrac{15.3(1.02^{80} - 1)}{1.02 - 1} \cr&= \dfrac{15.3(1.02^{80} - 1)}{0.02} \cr&= 765(1.02^{80} - 1)\cr & \approx 765(4.875439 - 1)\cr & \approx 2964.711\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

Adding the initial $300\text{ minutes}$ gives the total estimated time:
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Time} &= 300 + 2964.711 \cr&= 3264.711\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
Converting to hours, minutes, and seconds:\begin{aligned} & \dfrac{3264.711}{60}\cr & \quad = 54\text{ hours and } 24.711\text{ minutes}\end{aligned} $$0.711 \times 60 = 42.66 \approx 43\text{ seconds}$$
Therefore, the total estimated time is 54 hours, 24 minutes, and 43 seconds.
Final Answer: (a) $$330\text{ min } 54\text{ s}$$ (b) $$15 \times 1.02^{r-20}$$ (c) $$54\text{ h } 24\text{ min } 43\text{ s}$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably made an arithmetic rounding error in Part (c) by rounding the sum of your geometric series to $2968.2$ minutes prematurely. Retaining full calculator precision during your summation yields a total time of $3264.711$ minutes, which converts to $54\text{ h } 24\text{ min } 43\text{ s}$.

Check your exponent index in Part (b). Since the steady phase ends after the 20th metre, the first 2% increase occurs on the 21st metre ($r=21$). This requires an exponent of $r-20$ so that $T_{21} = 15 \times 1.02^1$. An exponent of $r-21$ would incorrectly mean the 21st metre had no slow-down.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Avoid Early Rounding
bradley_insight.content: In multi-step GCE questions, never round your intermediate values on your calculator. Keeping the exact values stored in memory until the very final conversion prevents tiny rounding errors from compounding and throwing off your final seconds value.

question:
A cyclist is completing a 50-kilometre long-distance ride.
He cycles each of the first 10 kilometres at a steady pace of 3 minutes per kilometre.
After the first 10 kilometres, he begins to slow down due to fatigue.
In order to estimate his finishing time, the time taken to complete each subsequent kilometre is modelled to be 3% greater than the time taken to complete the previous kilometre.
Using the model,
(a) show that his time to cycle the first 12 kilometres is estimated to be 36 minutes 16 seconds,
(b) show that his estimated time, in minutes, to cycle the $r$th kilometre, for $11 \le r \le 50$, is:
$$3 \times 1.03^{r-10}$$
(c) estimate the total time, in hours, minutes, and seconds, that he will take to complete the ride.
steps:
Part (a): The time for the first 10 kilometres is cycled at a steady pace of $3\text{ min/km}$:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{1-10} &= 10 \times 3 \cr&= 30\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 11th kilometre takes 3% longer than the 10th kilometre ($3\text{ minutes}$):
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{11} &= 3 \times 1.03 \cr&= 3.09\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 12th kilometre takes 3% longer than the 11th kilometre:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{12} &= 3.09 \times 1.03 \cr&= 3 \times 1.03^2 \cr&= 3.1827\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

Adding these times together gives the total estimated time for the first 12 kilometres:
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Time} &= 30 + 3.09 + 3.1827 \cr&= 36.2727\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
Converting $0.2727$ minutes into seconds: $0.2727 \times 60 = 16.362 \approx 16\text{ seconds}$.
Therefore, the time is 36 minutes 16 seconds (to the nearest second).

Part (b): For $r \ge 11$, each subsequent kilometre is 3% slower than the previous one, forming a geometric progression where the first term after the steady phase (at $r=11$) is $3 \times 1.03^1$.
In general, for the $r$th kilometre, the time has been multiplied by $1.03$ a total of $r-10$ times starting from the base pace of $3\text{ minutes}$.
Therefore, the time for the $r$th kilometre is:
$$\text{Time}_{r} = 3 \times 1.03^{r-10}$$

Part (c): The total time is the sum of the first 10 steady kilometres ($30\text{ minutes}$) and the geometric series from $r=11$ to $r=50$.
For $r=11$ to $50$, there are $50 - 11 + 1 = 40$ kilometres.
This is a geometric series with first term $a = 3 \times 1.03 = 3.09$ and common ratio $r_{\text{gp}} = 1.03$.

Using the sum formula, $S_N = \dfrac{a(r_{\text{gp}}^N - 1)}{r_{\text{gp}} - 1}$:
\begin{aligned}S_{40} &= \dfrac{3.09(1.03^{40} - 1)}{1.03 - 1} \cr&= \dfrac{3.09(1.03^{40} - 1)}{0.03} \cr&= 103(1.03^{40} - 1)\cr & \approx 103(3.262038 - 1)\cr & \approx 232.990\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

Adding the initial $300\text{ minutes}$ gives the total estimated time:
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Time} &= 30 + 232.990 \cr&= 262.990\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
Converting to hours, minutes, and seconds:\begin{aligned} & \dfrac{262.990}{60}\cr & \quad = 4\text{ hours and } 22.990\text{ minutes}\end{aligned} $$0.990 \times 60 = 59.4 \approx 59\text{ seconds}$$
Therefore, the total estimated time is 4 hours, 22 minutes, and 59 seconds.
Final Answer: (a) $$36\text{ min } 16\text{ s}$$ (b) $$3 \times 1.03^{r-10}$$ (c) $$4\text{ h } 22\text{ min } 59\text{ s}$$

pi_options.feedback: You probably made an arithmetic rounding error in Part (c) by rounding the sum of your geometric series to $232.9$ minutes prematurely. Retaining full calculator precision during your summation yields a total time of $262.990$ minutes, which converts to $4\text{ h } 22\text{ min } 59\text{ s}$.

Check your exponent index in Part (b). Since the steady phase ends after the 10th kilometre, the first 3% increase occurs on the 11th kilometre ($r=11$). bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Shifted Exponents
bradley_insight.content: In series modeling, when the geometric phase starts at an offset index (like $r=11$ in this question), the exponent must be shifted back to align properly. Always test your boundary case: substituting your first term index ($r=11$) into your formula must yield the single 3% multiplier increase ($r-10 = 1$).

question:
A hiker is walking a 12-kilometre uphill trail.
She hikes each of the first 3 kilometres at a steady pace of 12 minutes per kilometre.
After the first 3 kilometres, the trail becomes steeper and she begins to slow down.
In order to estimate her arrival time, the time taken to complete each subsequent kilometre is modelled to be 6% greater than the time taken to complete the previous kilometre.
Using the model,
(a) show that her time to hike the first 5 kilometres is estimated to be 62 minutes 12 seconds,
(b) show that her estimated time, in minutes, to hike the $r$th kilometre, for $4 \le r \le 12$, is:
$$12 \times 1.06^{r-3}$$
(c) estimate the total time, in hours, minutes, and seconds, that she will take to complete the uphill trail.
steps:
Part (a): The time for the first 3 kilometres is hiked at a steady pace of $12\text{ min/km}$:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{1-3} &= 3 \times 12 \cr&= 36\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 4th kilometre takes 6% longer than the 3rd kilometre ($12\text{ minutes}$):
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{4} &= 12 \times 1.06 \cr&= 12.72\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 5th kilometre takes 6% longer than the 4th kilometre:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{5} &= 12.72 \times 1.06 \cr&= 12 \times 1.06^2 \cr&= 13.4832\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

Adding these times together gives the total estimated time for the first 5 kilometres:
\begin{aligned} &\text{Total Time}\cr &\quad \quad= 36 + 12.72 + 13.4832 \cr &\quad \quad= 62.2032\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
Converting $0.2032$ minutes into seconds: $0.2032 \times 60 = 12.192 \approx 12\text{ seconds}$.
Therefore, the time is 62 minutes 12 seconds (to the nearest second).

Part (b): For $r \ge 4$, each subsequent kilometre is 6% slower than the previous one, forming a geometric progression where the first term after the steady phase (at $r=4$) is $12 \times 1.06^1$.
In general, for the $r$th kilometre, the time has been multiplied by $1.06$ a total of $r-3$ times starting from the base pace of $12\text{ minutes}$.
Therefore, the time for the $r$th kilometre is:
$$\text{Time}_{r} = 12 \times 1.06^{r-3}$$

Part (c): The total time is the sum of the first 3 steady kilometres ($36\text{ minutes}$) and the geometric series from $r=4$ to $r=12$.
For $r=4$ to $12$, there are $12 - 4 + 1 = 9$ kilometres.
This is a geometric series with first term $a = 12 \times 1.06 = 12.72$ and common ratio $r_{\text{gp}} = 1.06$.

Using the sum formula, $S_N = \dfrac{a(r_{\text{gp}}^N - 1)}{r_{\text{gp}} - 1}$:
\begin{aligned}S_9 &= \dfrac{12.72(1.06^9 - 1)}{1.06 - 1} \cr&= \dfrac{12.72(1.06^9 - 1)}{0.06} \cr&= 212(1.06^9 - 1)\cr & \approx 212(1.689479 - 1) \cr & \approx 146.169\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

Adding the initial $36\text{ minutes}$ gives the total estimated time:
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Time} &= 36 + 146.169 \cr&= 182.169\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}
Converting to hours, minutes, and seconds:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{182.169}{60}\cr & \quad = 3\text{ hours and } 2.169\text{ minutes}\end{aligned} $$2.169 \times 60 = 10.14 \approx 10\text{ seconds}$$
Therefore, the total estimated time is 3 hours, 2 minutes, and 10 seconds.
Final Answer: (a) $$62\text{ min } 12\text{ s}$$ (b) $$12 \times 1.06^{r-3}$$ (c) $$3\text{ h } 2\text{ min } 10\text{ s}$$

pi_options.feedback: Check your final seconds conversion in Part (c). $182.169$ minutes converts to $3$ hours, $2$ minutes, and $10$ seconds. Make sure you don't drop the fractional minutes when performing your division.

Check your exponent index in Part (b). Since the steady phase ends after the 3rd kilometre, the first 6% increase occurs on the 4th kilometre ($r=4$). This requires an exponent of $r-3$ so that $T_4 = 12 \times 1.06^1$. An exponent of $r-4$ would incorrectly mean the 4th kilometre had no slow-down.
Check your value for $N$ (the number of terms in your geometric series) in Part (c). The slow-down phase runs from $r=4$ to $r=12$, which contains $12-4+1 = 9$ terms, not $8$ terms.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Time Conversions
bradley_insight.content: When converting a large decimal number of minutes into hours, minutes, and seconds, divide by $60$ first to isolate the whole hours. Take the remainder and multiply it by $60$ to isolate the whole minutes, and then multiply the final remaining decimal fraction by $60$ to secure your seconds.

question:
A rower is crossing a 10-kilometre lake.
She rows each of the first 2 kilometres at a steady pace of 8 minutes per kilometre.
After the first 2 kilometres, she begins to slow down.
In order to estimate her crossing time, the time taken to complete each subsequent kilometre is modelled to be 4% greater than the time taken to complete the previous kilometre.
Using the model,
(a) show that her time to row the first 4 kilometres is estimated to be 32 minutes 58 seconds,
(b) show that her estimated time, in minutes, to row the $r$th kilometre, for $3 \le r \le 10$, is:
$$8 \times 1.04^{r-2}$$
(c) estimate the total time, in minutes and seconds, that she will take to complete the 10-kilometre crossing.
steps:
Part (a): The time for the first 2 kilometres is rowed at a steady pace of $8\text{ min/km}$:
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{1-2} &= 2 \times 8 \cr&= 16\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 3rd kilometre takes 4% longer than the 2nd kilometre ($8\text{ minutes}$):
\begin{aligned}\text{Time}_{3} &= 8 \times 1.04 \cr&= 8.32\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}

The 4th kilometre takes 4% longer than the 3rd kilometre:

$$0.662 \times 60 = 39.72 \approx 40\text{ seconds}$$

question:
The curve $C$ with equation:$$y = \dfrac{p - 2x}{(2x - q)(x + 2)},$$ $$\text{Where: }\left\{ \begin{aligned} x &\in \mathbb{R}, \cr x &\ne -2, \cr x &\ne 3 \end{aligned} \right.$$ and $p$ and $q$ are constants, passes through the point $(4, \frac{1}{2})$ and has two vertical asymptotes with equations $x = 3$ and $x = -2$.

(a)(i) Explain why you can deduce that $q = 6$.
(a)(ii) Show that $p = 14$.

The diagram shows a sketch of part of the curve $C$. The region $R$, shown shaded in the diagram, is bounded by the curve $C$, the $x$-axis and the line with equation $x = 4$.
(b) Show that the exact value of the area of $R$ is $a\ln 2 + b\ln 3 + c\ln 7$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are rational constants to be found.
steps:
Part (a)(i): Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator of the rational function is equal to zero, which means:
\begin{aligned}(2x - q)(x + 2) &= 0 \cr x = \frac{q}{2} \quad &\text{and} \quad x = -2\end{aligned}
Since we are given that the vertical asymptotes have equations $x = 3$ and $x = -2$, we can equate the root terms:\begin{aligned}\frac{q}{2} &= 3 \cr q &= 6\end{aligned}

Part (a)(ii): Substituting our calculated value of $q = 6$ into the curve's equation gives:
$$y = \dfrac{p - 2x}{(2x - 6)(x + 2)}$$

Since the curve passes through the point $(4, \frac{1}{2})$, we substitute $x = 4$ and $y = \frac{1}{2}$ into the equation to solve for $p$:\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} &= \dfrac{p - 2(4)}{(2(4) - 6)(4 + 2)} \cr\frac{1}{2} &= \dfrac{p - 8}{(2)(6)}\cr \frac{1}{2} &= \dfrac{p - 8}{12} \cr6 &= p - 8 \cr p &= 14\end{aligned}

Part (b): To find the area of the region $R$, we must find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis (the $x$-intercept). Setting $y = 0$ in the numerator gives:
\begin{aligned}14 - 2x &= 0 \cr2x &= 14 \cr x &= 7\end{aligned}

Therefore, the region $R$ is bounded on the $x$-axis between $x = 4$ and $x = 7$.

Here is the completed diagram showing these key features and the vertical asymptote at $x = 3$:

Since the curve lies above the $x$-axis in this interval ($y > 0$), the area of $R$ is given by the definite integral:
$$\text{Area} = \int_{4}^{7} \dfrac{14 - 2x}{(2x - 6)(x + 2)} \text{ d}x$$

We simplify the integrand by factorising and cancelling a common factor of $2$:
\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{14 - 2x}{(2x - 6)(x + 2)} \cr & \quad = \dfrac{-2(x - 7)}{2(x - 3)(x + 2)} \cr & \quad = -\dfrac{x - 7}{(x - 3)(x + 2)}\end{aligned}

Now, we express this integrand in partial fractions:\begin{aligned} & -\dfrac{x - 7}{(x - 3)(x + 2)}\cr & \quad \quad= \dfrac{A}{x - 3} + \dfrac{B}{x + 2}\cr 14 - 2x &= A(x + 2) + B(x - 3)\end{aligned}

Using the substitution method to solve for the coefficients:
1. \begin{aligned}x &= 3\cr \implies 14 - 2(3) &= A(3 + 2)\cr \implies 8 &= 5A\cr \implies A &= \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned} (noting the scale factor of $2$ cancelled earlier).
2. \begin{aligned} x &= -2 \cr \implies 14 - 2(-2) &= B(-2 - 3)\cr \implies 18 &= -5B \cr\implies B &= -\frac{9}{5}\end{aligned}

Substituting these coefficients back into our integral gives:
\begin{aligned}&\text{Area} = \int_{4}^{7} \left( \dfrac{4/5}{x - 3} - \dfrac{9/5}{x + 2} \right) \text{ d}x \cr & \quad = \left[ \frac{4}{5}\ln|x - 3| - \frac{9}{5}\ln|x + 2| \right]_{4}^{7}\end{aligned}

Evaluating this expression at our upper limit ($7$) and lower limit ($4$):
\begin{aligned}\text{Value at 7} &= \frac{4}{5}\ln(4) - \frac{9}{5}\ln(9) \cr&= \frac{8}{5}\ln(2) - \frac{18}{5}\ln(3)\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}\text{Value at 4} &= \frac{4}{5}\ln(1) - \frac{9}{5}\ln(6) \cr&= 0 - \frac{9}{5}(\ln 2 + \ln 3) \cr&= -\frac{9}{5}\ln(2) - \frac{9}{5}\ln(3)\end{aligned}

Subtracting the lower limit value from the upper limit value yields:\begin{aligned}\text{Area} &= \left( \frac{8}{5}\ln 2 - \frac{18}{5}\ln 3 \right)\cr & \quad \quad - \left( -\frac{9}{5}\ln 2 - \frac{9}{5}\ln 3 \right)\cr &= \left( \frac{8 + 9}{5} \right)\ln 2\cr & \quad \quad + \left( \frac{-18 + 9}{5} \right)\ln 3 \cr&= \frac{17}{5}\ln 2 - \frac{9}{5}\ln 3\end{aligned}
Therefore, the constants are $a = \frac{17}{5}$, $b = -\frac{9}{5}$, and $c = 0$.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $$q = 6$$ (a)(ii) $$p = 14$$ (b) $$\dfrac{17}{5}\ln 2 - \dfrac{9}{5}\ln 3$$

Check your signs in Part (b). When subtracting the lower limit term, the double negative becomes a positive, yielding $-\frac{18}{5}\ln 3 - (-\frac{9}{5}\ln 3) = -\frac{9}{5}\ln 3$. Be careful when combining logarithm terms.
You probably forgot to subtract the lower limit value ($x=4$) at the end of Part (b). Remember to substitute both limits into your integrated function: $\text{Area} = \text{F}(7) - \text{F}(4)$.

Since we are given that the vertical asymptotes have equations $x = 3$ and $x = -2$, we can equate the root terms:
\begin{aligned}\frac{q}{2} &= 3 \cr q &= 6\end{aligned}

Part (a)(ii): Substituting our calculated value of $q = 6$ into the curve's equation gives:
$$y = \dfrac{p - 3x}{(2x - 6)(x + 2)}$$

Since the curve passes through the point $(4, \frac{1}{2})$, we substitute $x = 4$ and $y = \frac{1}{2}$ into the equation to solve for $p$:
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} &= \dfrac{p - 3(4)}{(2(4) - 6)(4 + 2)} \cr\frac{1}{2} &= \dfrac{p - 12}{(2)(6)}\cr\frac{1}{2} &= \dfrac{p - 12}{12} \cr 6 &= p - 12 \cr p &= 18\end{aligned}

Part (b): To find the area of the region $R$, we must find where the curve crosses the $x$-axis (the $x$-intercept). Setting $y = 0$ in the numerator gives:
\begin{aligned}18 - 3x &= 0 \cr3x &= 18 \cr x &= 6\end{aligned}

Therefore, the region $R$ is bounded on the $x$-axis between $x = 4$ and $x = 6$.

Here is the completed diagram showing these key features and the vertical asymptote at $x = 3$:

Since the curve lies above the $x$-axis in this interval ($y > 0$), the area of $R$ is given by the definite integral:
$$\text{Area} = \int_{4}^{6} \dfrac{18 - 3x}{(2x - 6)(x + 2)} \text{ d}x$$

We simplify the integrand by factorising:
\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{18 - 3x}{(2x - 6)(x + 2)}\cr & \quad = \dfrac{3(6 - x)}{2(x - 3)(x + 2)} \cr & \quad= \dfrac{3}{2} \dfrac{6 - x}{(x - 3)(x + 2)}\end{aligned}

Now, we express this integrand in partial fractions:
$$\dfrac{3}{2} \dfrac{6 - x}{(x - 3)(x + 2)} = \dfrac{A}{x - 3} + \dfrac{B}{x + 2}$$
\begin{aligned}18 - 3x &= 2A(x + 2) + 2B(x - 3) \cr&= 2(A + B)x + 2(2A - 3B)\end{aligned}

Using the substitution method to solve for the coefficients:
1. \begin{aligned} $x &= 3\cr \implies 18 - 3(3) &= 2A(3 + 2)\cr \implies 9 &= 10A\cr \implies A &= \frac{9}{10}\end{aligned}
2. \begin{aligned} $x &= -2\cr \implies 18 - 3(-2) &= 2B(-2 - 3)\cr \implies 24 &= -10B\cr \implies B &= -\frac{12}{5}\end{aligned}

Substituting these coefficients back into our integral gives:
\begin{aligned} & \text{Area} = \int_{4}^{6} \left( \dfrac{9/10}{x - 3} - \dfrac{12/5}{x + 2} \right) \text{ d}x \cr & \quad \quad= \left[ \frac{9}{10}\ln|x - 3| - \frac{12}{5}\ln|x + 2| \right]_{4}^{6}\end{aligned}

Evaluating this expression at our upper limit ($6$) and lower limit ($4$):
\begin{aligned}\text{Value at 6} &= \frac{9}{10}\ln(3) - \frac{12}{5}\ln(8) \cr&= \frac{9}{10}\ln(3) - \frac{12}{5}(3\ln 2) \cr&= -\frac{36}{5}\ln(2) + \frac{9}{10}\ln(3)\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned}\text{Value at 4} &= \frac{9}{10}\ln(1) - \frac{12}{5}\ln(6) \cr&= 0 - \frac{12}{5}(\ln 2 + \ln 3) \cr&= -\frac{12}{5}\ln(2) - \frac{12}{5}\ln(3)\end{aligned}

Subtracting the lower limit value from the upper limit value yields:\begin{aligned}\text{Area} &= \left( -\frac{36}{5}\ln 2 + \frac{9}{10}\ln 3 \right)\cr & \quad - \left( -\frac{12}{5}\ln 2 - \frac{12}{5}\ln 3 \right)\cr & = \left( -\frac{36}{5} + \frac{12}{5} \right)\ln 2 \cr & \quad \quad + \left( \frac{9}{10} + \frac{24}{10} \right)\ln 3 \cr&= -\frac{24}{5}\ln 2 + \frac{33}{10}\ln 3\end{aligned}
Therefore, the constants are $a = -\frac{24}{5}$ and $b = \frac{33}{10}$.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $$q = 6$$ (a)(ii) $$p = 18$$ (b) $$-\dfrac{24}{5}\ln 2 + \dfrac{33}{10}\ln 3$$

Check your signs in Part (b). When subtracting the lower limit term, the double negative becomes a positive, yielding \begin{align} & \frac{9}{10}\ln 3 - (-\frac{12}{5}\ln 3)\cr &= \frac{9}{10}\ln 3 + \frac{24}{10}\ln 3\cr &= \frac{33}{10}\ln 3\end{align} Be careful when combining logarithm terms.

question:
The curve $C$, in the standard Cartesian plane, is defined by the equation:
$$x = 3\sin 2y \quad -\frac{\pi}{4} < y < \frac{\pi}{4}$$
The curve $C$ passes through the origin $O$.

(a) Find the value of $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at the origin.

(b)(i) Use the small-angle approximation for $\sin 2y$ to find an equation linking $x$ and $y$ for points close to the origin.
(b)(ii) Explain the relationship between the answers to (a) and (b)(i).

(c) Show that, for all points $(x, y)$ lying on $C$,
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{a\sqrt{b - x^2}}$$
where $a$ and $b$ are constants to be found.
steps:
Part (a): We differentiate the equation of our curve, $x = 3\sin 2y$, implicitly with respect to $x$:
$$\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) = \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\sin 2y)$$
$$1 = 3\cos 2y \cdot \left(2\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)$$
\begin{aligned}1 &= 6\cos 2y \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \cr\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{1}{6\cos 2y}\end{aligned}

At the origin, the coordinates are $(0,0)$, which means $y = 0$. Substituting $y = 0$ into our derivative gives:
\begin{aligned}\left. \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right|_{O} &= \dfrac{1}{6\cos(0)} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{6}\end{aligned}

Part (b)(i): The small-angle approximation for sine is $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ when $\theta$ is small and measured in radians.
Applying this approximation with $\theta = 2y$ gives:
$$\sin 2y \approx 2y$$

Substituting this into the curve's equation:
\begin{aligned}x \approx 3(2y) &= 6y \cr y \approx \dfrac{1}{6}x\end{aligned}

Part (b)(ii): The linear equation $y \approx \frac{1}{6}x$ represents the tangent line to the curve at the origin. The gradient of this straight line is $\frac{1}{6}$, which is exactly equal to the value of the exact derivative $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at the origin found in Part (a).

Part (c): We start with our derivative expression from Part (a):
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{6\cos 2y}$$

Using the fundamental identity $\sin^2 2y + \cos^2 2y = 1$, we can express $\cos 2y$ in terms of sine:
$$\cos 2y = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 2y}$$
*(Note: Since $-\frac{\pi}{4} < y < \frac{\pi}{4}$, the angle lies in the interval $-\frac{\pi}{2} < 2y < \frac{\pi}{2}$, where cosine is strictly positive, so the positive root is correct).*

From the original curve equation, we have $\sin 2y = \frac{x}{3}$. Substituting this into our expression for $\cos 2y$ gives:
\begin{aligned}\cos 2y &= \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{x}{3}\right)^2} \cr&= \sqrt{1 - \frac{x^2}{9}} \cr&= \sqrt{\dfrac{9 - x^2}{9}} \cr&= \dfrac{\sqrt{9 - x^2}}{3}\end{aligned}

Now, we substitute this back into our derivative expression:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{1}{6 \left( \frac{\sqrt{9 - x^2}}{3} \right)} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{9 - x^2}}\end{aligned}
Comparing this with the target form gives the constants as $a = 2$ and $b = 9$.

Final Answer
(a) $\dfrac{1}{6}$
(b)(i) $y \approx \dfrac{1}{6}x$
(b)(ii) The gradient of the linear approximation equals the exact derivative at the origin
(c) $a = 2, b = 9$

(b)(ii) The gradient of the linear approximation equals the exact derivative at the origin

(b)(i) Use the small-angle approximation for $\sin 3y$ to find an equation linking $x$ and $y$ for points close to the origin.
(b)(ii) Explain the relationship between the answers to (a) and (b)(i).

(c) Show that, for all points $(x, y)$ lying on $C$,
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{a\sqrt{b - x^2}}$$
where } $a$ and $b$ are rational constants to be found.
steps:
Part (a): We differentiate the equation of our curve, $x = 4\sin 3y$, implicitly with respect to $x$:
$$\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x) = \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\sin 3y)$$
$$1 = 4\cos 3y \cdot \left(3\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\right)$$
\begin{aligned}1 &= 12\cos 3y \cdot \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \cr\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{1}{12\cos 3y}\end{aligned}

At the origin, the coordinates are $(0,0)$, which means $y = 0$. Substituting $y = 0$ into our derivative gives:
\begin{aligned}\left. \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right|_{O} &= \dfrac{1}{12\cos(0)} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{12}\end{aligned}

Part (b)(i): The small-angle approximation for sine is $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ when $\theta$ is small and measured in radians.
Applying this approximation with $\theta = 3y$ gives:
$$\sin 3y \approx 3y$$

Substituting this into the curve's equation:
\begin{aligned}x \approx 4(3y) &= 12y \cr y \approx \dfrac{1}{12}x\end{aligned}

Part (b)(ii): The linear equation $y \approx \frac{1}{12}x$ represents the tangent line to the curve at the origin. The gradient of this straight line is $\frac{1}{12}$, which is exactly equal to the value of the exact derivative $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at the origin found in Part (a).

Part (c): We start with our derivative expression from Part (a):
$$\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{12\cos 3y}$$

Using the fundamental identity $\sin^2 3y + \cos^2 3y = 1$, we can express $\cos 3y$ in terms of sine:
$$\cos 3y = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 3y}$$
*(Note: Since $-\frac{\pi}{6} < y < \frac{\pi}{6}$, the angle lies in the interval $-\frac{\pi}{2} < 3y < \frac{\pi}{2}$, where cosine is strictly positive, so the positive root is correct).*

From the original curve equation, we have $\sin 3y = \frac{x}{4}$. Substituting this into our expression for $\cos 3y$ gives:
\begin{aligned}\cos 3y &= \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{x}{4}\right)^2} \cr&= \sqrt{1 - \frac{x^2}{16}} \cr&= \sqrt{\dfrac{16 - x^2}{16}} \cr&= \dfrac{\sqrt{16 - x^2}}{4}\end{aligned}

Now, we substitute this back into our derivative expression:
\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \dfrac{1}{12 \left( \frac{\sqrt{16 - x^2}}{4} \right)} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{16 - x^2}}\end{aligned}
Comparing this with the target form gives the constants as $a = 3$ and $b = 16$.

Final Answer
(a) $\dfrac{1}{12}$
(b)(i) $y \approx \dfrac{1}{12}x$
(b)(ii) The gradient of the linear approximation equals the exact derivative at the origin
(c) $a = 3, b = 16$

steps: First, identify the original function: \begin{aligned}y &= f(x) \cr&= 3^x\end{aligned}

question:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations:
$$x = 2 \times 2^{-t} + 4$$
$$y = 5 \times 2^t - 1$$

(a) Find an expression for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$

(b) find the Cartesian equation of the curve in the form $xy + ax + by = c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are integers.
steps: First, differentiate $y = 5 \times 2^t - 1$ and $x = 2 \times 2^{-t} + 4$ with respect to $t$: $$\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 5 \ln(2) 2^t$$ and $$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -2 \ln(2) 2^{-t}$$

Next, use the chain rule, $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{\frac{dy}{dt}}{\frac{dx}{dt}}$$, to obtain Part (a): \begin{aligned}\dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{5 \ln(2) 2^t}{-2 \ln(2) 2^{-t}} \cr&= -\dfrac{5}{2} \times 2^{2t}\end{aligned}
To find Part (b), rearrange the parametric equations to isolate the exponential terms: \begin{aligned}2^{-t} &= \dfrac{x-4}{2} \cr2^t &= \dfrac{2}{x-4}\end{aligned}
Substitute this into the $y$ equation and expand: \begin{aligned}y + 1 &= 5 \times \dfrac{2}{x-4} \cr(y + 1)(x - 4) &= 10 \cr xy + x - 4y &= 14\end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned}\text{(a) } \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -\dfrac{5}{2} \times 2^{2t},\cr\text{(b) } xy + x - 4y &= 14\end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In Part (a), you probably made a mistake with index division laws. Dividing $2^t$ by $2^{-t}$ yields $2^{t - (-t)} = 2^{2t}$ rather than $2^t$. Part (b) is correct.
In Part (b), you probably made a sign error when expanding $(y + 1)(x - 4) = 10$. The expansion yields $xy - 4y + x - 4 = 10$, which rearranges to $xy + x - 4y = 14$. Part (a) is correct.
In Part (a), you probably forgot the negative sign from the derivative of $2^{-t}$. In Part (b), you probably forgot to subtract $4$ from $10$ or made a transposition mistake.

question:
(a) Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9+x}}$.

(b) Hence, find the first three terms of the binomial expansion of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9-x^3}}$.

(c) Using your answer to part (b), find an approximation for $\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9-x^3}} \text{d}x$, giving your answer to seven decimal places.

(d) (i) Tom, a student, decides to use this method to find a more accurate value for the integral by increasing the number of terms of the binomial expansion used. Explain clearly whether Tom's approximation will be an overestimate, an underestimate, or if it is impossible to tell.

(d) (ii) Tom goes on to use the expansion from part (b) to find an approximation for $\int_{-3}^{0} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9-x^3}} \text{d}x$. Explain why Tom's approximation is invalid.
steps:
For Part (a), rewrite the function in index form, factor out $9$, and let the expansion be $E$:

\begin{aligned} E &= ( 9 + x )^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }} \cr &= 9^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }}\left(1 + \dfrac{ x }{ 9 }\right)^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }} \cr &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 }\left(1 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }\left(\dfrac{ x }{ 9 }\right) + \dfrac{ 3 }{ 8 }\left(\dfrac{ x }{ 9 }\right)^2 + \dots\right) \cr &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } - \dfrac{ x }{ 54 } + \dfrac{ x^2 }{ 648 } \end{aligned}

For Part (b), substitute $x \implies -x^3$ into your Part (a) expansion, and let the new expansion be $F$:

\begin{aligned} F &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ \sqrt{ 9 - x^3 }} \cr &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } - \dfrac{ -x^3 }{ 54 } + \dfrac{ (-x^3)^2 }{ 648 } \cr &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } + \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 54 } + \dfrac{ x^6 }{ 648 } \end{aligned}

For Part (c), let the integral be $I$. We integrate the polynomial approximation from $0$ to $1$:

\begin{aligned} I &= \int_{ 0 }^{ 1 } \left(\dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } + \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 54 } + \dfrac{ x^6 }{ 648 }\right) \mathrm{d}x \cr &= \left[\dfrac{ x }{ 3 } + \dfrac{ x^4 }{ 216 } + \dfrac{ x^7 }{ 4536 }\right]_{ 0 }^{ 1 } \cr &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } + \dfrac{ 1 }{ 216 } + \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4536 } \cr &\approx 0.3381834 \end{aligned}

For Part (d)(i), notice that since $u = \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 9 } \ge 0$ on the interval $[0, 1]$, every term in the binomial series for $( 1 - u )^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }}$ is positive. Truncating the series removes positive terms, so Tom's approximation is an underestimate.

For Part (d)(ii), the expansion converges only for \begin{aligned}|u| &< 1 \cr \implies \left|\dfrac{ x^3 }{ 9 }\right| &< 1\cr \implies |x| &< 9^{\frac{ 1 }{ 3 }}\cr &\approx 2.08\end{aligned}  Since the lower limit is $x = -3$ and $| -3 | = 3 \ge 2.08$, the series does not converge on this interval.

Final Answer:

\begin{aligned} \text{Part (b):} & \quad \dfrac{ 1 }{ 3 } + \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 54 } + \dfrac{ x^6 }{ 648 } \cr \text{Part (c):} & \quad 0.3381834 \cr \text{Part (d)(i):} & \quad \text{Underestimate} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In Part (b), you probably made a sign error when substituting $-x^3$ into the expansion. Since we are substituting into $-\dfrac{ x }{ 54 }$, we get $-\dfrac{ -x^3 }{ 54 } = +\dfrac{ x^3 }{ 54 }$. This also affects the integral in Part (c).

In Part (d)(i), you probably assumed that adding more positive terms makes the approximation an overestimate. However, since all terms in the series are positive, truncating after finitely many terms leaves out positive values, meaning the approximation is smaller than the true value (an underestimate).

Check your signs in Part (b). Substituting $-x^3$ into the third term $+\dfrac{ x^2 }{ 648 }$ gives $+\dfrac{ (-x^3)^2 }{ 648 } = +\dfrac{ x^6 }{ 648 }$. Both terms must be positive, which also affects your integration in Part (c).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Substituting Negative Powers
bradley_insight.content: When substituting $-x^3$ into the expansion of $( 9 + x )^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }}$, pay close attention to the sign changes. For the $x$ term, we get $-\dfrac{ -x^3 }{ 54 } = +\dfrac{ x^3 }{ 54 }$, but for the $x^2$ term, the square removes the negative sign: $+(-x^3)^2/648 = +\dfrac{ x^6 }{ 648 }$. Missing these sign reversals is a very common way to lose easy marks on this question.

\begin{aligned} &( 1 + x )^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }} \cr &\quad = 1 + \left(-\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }\right)x\cr & \quad + \dfrac{ \left(-\dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }\right)\left(-\dfrac{ 3 }{ 2 }\right) }{ 2 }x^2 + \dots \cr &\quad = 1 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }x + \dfrac{ 3 }{ 8 }x^2 \end{aligned}

\begin{aligned} &\int_{ 0 }^{ 0.5 } \left(1 + \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }x^2 + \dfrac{ 3 }{ 8 }x^4\right) \mathrm{d}x \cr &\quad = \left[x + \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 6 } + \dfrac{ 3x^5 }{ 40 }\right]_{ 0 }^{ 0.5 } \cr &\quad = 0.5 + \dfrac{ 0.125 }{ 6 } + \dfrac{ 0.09375 }{ 40 } \cr &\quad \approx 0.5231771 \end{aligned}

question:
(a) Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16+x}}$.

(b) Hence, find the first three terms of the binomial expansion of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16-x^3}}$.

(c) Using your answer to part (b), find an approximation for $\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16-x^3}} \text{d}x$, giving your answer to seven decimal places.

(d) (i) Ranjit, a student, decides to use this method to find a more accurate value for the integral by increasing the number of terms of the binomial expansion used. Explain clearly whether Ranjit's approximation will be an overestimate, an underestimate, or if it is impossible to tell.

(d) (ii) Ranjit goes on to use the expansion from part (b) to find an approximation for $\int_{-3}^{0} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{16-x^3}} \text{d}x$. Explain why Ranjit's approximation is invalid.

steps:
For Part (a), rewrite the function in index form and expand using $( 16 + x )^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }}$:

\begin{aligned} &( 16 + x )^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }} \cr &\quad = 16^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }}\left(1 + \dfrac{ x }{ 16 }\right)^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 }\left[1 - \dfrac{ 1 }{ 2 }\left(\dfrac{ x }{ 16 }\right) + \dfrac{ 3 }{ 8 }\left(\dfrac{ x }{ 16 }\right)^2 + \dots\right] \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } - \dfrac{ x }{ 128 } + \dfrac{ 3x^2 }{ 8192 } \end{aligned}

\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{ 1 }{ \sqrt{ 16 - x^3 }} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } - \dfrac{ -x^3 }{ 128 } + \dfrac{ 3(-x^3)^2 }{ 8192 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } + \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 128 } + \dfrac{ 3x^6 }{ 8192 } \end{aligned}

\begin{aligned} &\int_{ 0 }^{ 1 } \left(\dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } + \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 128 } + \dfrac{ 3x^6 }{ 8192 }\right) \mathrm{d}x \cr &\quad = \left[\dfrac{ x }{ 4 } + \dfrac{ x^4 }{ 512 } + \dfrac{ 3x^7 }{ 57344 }\right]_{ 0 }^{ 1 } \cr &\quad = \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } + \dfrac{ 1 }{ 512 } + \dfrac{ 3 }{ 57344 } \cr &\quad \approx 0.2520054 \end{aligned}

For Part (d)(i), notice that since $u = \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 16 } \ge 0$ on the interval $[0, 1]$, every term in the binomial series for $( 1 - u )^{-\frac{ 1 }{ 2 }}$ is positive. Truncating the series removes positive terms, so Ranjit's approximation is an underestimate.

\begin{aligned} \text{Part (b):} & \quad \dfrac{ 1 }{ 4 } + \dfrac{ x^3 }{ 128 } + \dfrac{ 3x^6 }{ 8192 } \cr \text{Part (c):} & \quad 0.2520054 \cr \text{Part (d)(i):} & \quad \text{Underestimate} \end{aligned}

In Part (d)(i), you probably assumed that adding more positive terms makes the approximation an overestimate. However, since all terms in the series are positive, truncating after finitely many terms leaves out positive values, meaning the approximation is smaller than the true value (an underestimate).

Check your signs in Part (b). Substituting $-x^3$ into the third term yields $+\dfrac{ 3(-x^3)^2 }{ 8192 } = +\dfrac{ 3x^6 }{ 8192 }$. Both terms must be positive, which also affects your integration in Part (c).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Understanding Convergence Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: The validity range of a binomial expansion is defined by $|u| < 1$, where $u$ is the variable component. For the term $\dfrac{ x^3 }{ 16 }$, this gives $\left|\dfrac{ x^3 }{ 16 }\right| < 1 \implies |x| < 16^{\frac{ 1 }{ 3 }} \approx 2.52$. When the lower limit of our integral lies outside this boundary (such as $x = -3$), the series fails to converge and is completely invalid, even if the original algebraic expression is defined there.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Constant Factor Pitfalls

question:
Three points $A$, $B$, and $C$ have coordinates $A(-9, 4)$, $B(7, 12)$, and $C(11, 4)$.

(a) Show that angle $ABC$ is a right angle.

(b) $A$, $B$, and $C$ lie on a circle.
(i) Explain why $AC$ is a diameter of the circle.
(ii) Determine whether the point $D(4, 10)$ lies inside the circle, on the circle, or outside the circle. Fully justify your answer.
steps: For Part (a), calculate the gradients of the lines $AB$ and $BC$: \begin{aligned}m_{AB} &= \dfrac{12-4}{7 - (-9)} \cr&= \dfrac{8}{16} \cr&= \dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned} and \begin{aligned}m_{BC} &= \dfrac{4-12}{11-7} \cr&= \dfrac{-8}{4} \cr&= -2\end{aligned}

Since the product of their gradients is \begin{aligned}m_{AB} \times m_{BC} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times (-2) \cr&= -1\end{aligned}, the lines $AB$ and $BC$ are perpendicular, meaning angle $ABC$ is a right angle.

For Part (b)(i), recall the circle theorem that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle. Since angle $ABC = 90^\circ$ and the points $A$, $B$, and $C$ lie on the circumference of a circle, the hypotenuse $AC$ must be a diameter of the circle.
For Part (b)(ii), find the center of the circle, which is the midpoint of the diameter $AC$: \begin{aligned}M &= \left(\dfrac{-9+11}{2}, \dfrac{4+4}{2}\right) \cr&= (1, 4)\end{aligned}
Calculate the radius $R$, which is half the length of the diameter $AC$: \begin{aligned}AC &= \sqrt{(11 - (-9))^2 + (4-4)^2}\cr &= \sqrt{20^2 + 0} \cr &= 20 \cr R &= 10\end{aligned}
Find the distance squared from point $D(4, 10)$ to the center $M(1, 4)$: \begin{aligned}MD^2 &= (4-1)^2 + (10-4)^2 \cr&= 3^2 + 6^2 \cr&= 9 + 36 \cr&= 45\end{aligned}
Since the distance squared $$45 < R^2 = 100$$, the distance from the point to the center of the circle is less than the radius. Thus, the point $D$ lies inside the circle.

Final Answer:
(b)(i) $$4\angle ABC = 90^\circ$$ $$AC \text{ is a diameter} $$ (b)(ii) $$\text{Inside the circle}$$

pi_options.ans: (b)(i) $$\angle ABC = 90^\circ \implies AC \text{ is diameter}$$ (b)(ii): $$\text{On the circle}$$
pi_options.feedback: In Part (b)(ii), you probably calculated the distance from $D$ to the center incorrectly, or confused the value with the radius squared. Since $MD^2 = 45$, which is strictly less than $R^2 = 100$, the point must lie inside the circle, not on it.

In Part (b)(i), supplementary opposite angles is a theorem for cyclic quadrilaterals, not for proving a diameter. The correct theorem to cite is that an angle in a semicircle is a right angle, which means the hypotenuse $AC$ is a diameter.

In Part (b)(i), the alternate segment theorem concerns tangents and chords, which is not applicable here. In Part (b)(ii), $D$ lies inside the circle because its distance to the center, $\sqrt{45}$, is less than the radius of $10$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Circle Theorem Terminology
bradley_insight.content: When justifying why a line is a diameter, always state the geometric theorem clearly on your page. Citing that 'the angle in a semicircle is a right angle' is probably the safest and most standard way to secure this explanation mark.

question:
A circle has center $O(0, 0)$ and radius $R = 10$. Three points lie on the circle: $A(8, 6)$, $B(0, -10)$, and $C(-8, 6)$.

(a) Show that the angle at the center, $\angle AOC$, is exactly twice the size of the angle at the circumference, $\angle ABC$.

(b) (i) Show that the chord $AC$ is bisected by the $y$-axis.
(ii) Determine whether the point $D(3, -9)$ lies inside the circle, on the circle, or outside the circle. Fully justify your answer.
steps: For Part (a), calculate the side lengths of triangle $AOC$ to find $\angle AOC$: $OA = 10$$ $$OC = 10,$ \begin{aligned} AC &= \sqrt{(-8-8)^2 + (6-6)^2}\cr &= 16\end{aligned}

Apply the Cosine Rule to find $\angle AOC$:  \begin{aligned}\text{Let }\phi &=\angle AOC\cr16^2 &= 10^2 + 10^2  \cr &\quad - 2(10)(10)\cos\phi \cr 256 &= 200 - 200\cos\phi \cr \cos\phi &= -0.28 \cr \phi &\approx 106.26^\circ\end{aligned}

Next, calculate the side lengths of triangle $ABC$ to find $\angle ABC$: \begin{aligned}BA &= \sqrt{(8-0)^2 + (6 - (-10))^2} \cr&= \sqrt{320}\end{aligned} and \begin{aligned}BC &= \sqrt{(-8-0)^2 + (6 - (-10))^2} \cr&= \sqrt{320}\end{aligned}, with $$AC = 16$$

Apply the Cosine Rule on triangle $ABC$: \begin{aligned}\text{Let }\theta &=\angle ABC\cr16^2 &= 320 + 320 \cr &\quad - 2(\sqrt{ 320 })(\sqrt{ 320 })\cos\theta \cr 256 &= 640 - 640\cos\theta \cr 640\cos \theta &= 384 \cr \cos\theta &= 0.6 \cr \theta &\approx 53.13^{ \circ }\end{aligned}
Since $$2 \times 53.13^\circ = 106.26^\circ$$, the angle at the center $\angle AOC$ is exactly twice the angle at the circumference $\angle ABC$.
For Part (b)(i), find the midpoint of the chord $AC$: \begin{aligned}K &= \left(\dfrac{8+(-8)}{2}, \dfrac{6+6}{2}\right) \cr&= (0, 6)\end{aligned}
Since the midpoint of $AC$ lies on the line $x = 0$ (the $y$-axis), the chord $AC$ is bisected by the $y$-axis.
For Part (b)(ii), calculate the distance squared from point $D(3, -9)$ to the center $O(0, 0)$: \begin{aligned}OD^2 &= 3^2 + (-9)^2 \cr&= 9 + 81 \cr&= 90\end{aligned}
Since the distance squared $$90 < R^2 = 100$$, the distance from the point to the center of the circle is less than the radius. Thus, the point $D$ lies inside the circle.

Final Answer:
(b)(i) $$\text{ Midpoint is (0, 6)}$$ $$\text{which lies on the } y\text{-axis} $$ (b)(ii) $$\text{Inside the circle}$$

pi_options.ans: (b)(i) $$\text{ Midpoint is (0, 6)}$$ $$\text{which lies on the } y\text{-axis} $$ (b)(ii) $$\text{On the circle}$$
pi_options.feedback: In Part (b)(ii), you probably miscalculated the distance or confused the radius squared ($100$) with the coordinate values. Since $OD^2 = 90 < 100$, the point must lie inside the circle.

pi_options.ans: (b)(i) $$\text{ Midpoint is (0, 6)}$$ $$\text{which lies on the } y\text{-axis} $$ (b)(ii) $$\text{Outside the circle}$$
pi_options.feedback: In Part (b)(ii), the distance squared to the origin is $3^2 + (-9)^2 = 90$. Because this is less than the radius squared ($100$), the point lies inside the circle, not outside.
In Part (b)(i), showing the gradient is zero proves the chord is horizontal, but does not prove it is bisected by the $y$-axis. You must show the midpoint of $AC$ has an $x$-coordinate of $0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Distance Formula is Probably Safest
bradley_insight.content: For calculating angles in coordinate geometry without vector dot products, calculating the three side lengths and using the Cosine Rule is probably the safest and most robust method. It keeps your steps firmly within standard Pure 1 geometry.

question:
Four points lie on a circle centered at the origin: $A(-3, 4)$, $B(3, 4)$, $C(4, -3)$, and $D(-4, -3)$.

(a) Show that the opposite interior angles of the cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ sum to $180^\circ$ (i.e. show that $\angle ADC + \angle ABC = 180^\circ$).

(b) (i) Explain why the center of the circle on which $A, B, C, D$ lie must be the origin $(0, 0)$.
(ii) Determine whether the point $E(-4, 4)$ lies inside the circle, on the circle, or outside the circle. Fully justify your answer.
steps: For Part (a), calculate the side lengths of triangle $ADC$ to find angle $\angle ADC$: \begin{aligned}&DA \cr &= \sqrt{(-3-(-4))^2 + (4-(-3))^2} \cr &= \sqrt{50}\cr \cr &DC\cr & = \sqrt{(4-(-4))^2 + (-3-(-3))^2}\cr & = 8 \cr \cr &AC = \sqrt{(4-(-3))^2 + (-3-4)^2} \cr&= \sqrt{98}\end{aligned}

Apply the Cosine Rule to find $\angle ADC$: \begin{aligned}\text{Let }\theta &= \angle ADC\cr 98 &= 50 + 64 \cr & \quad- 2(\sqrt{50})(8)\cos\theta \cr 98 &= 114 - 16\sqrt{50}\cos\theta \cr\cos\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{50}} \cr\theta &\approx 81.87^\circ\end{aligned}

Next, calculate the side lengths of triangle $ABC$ to find angle $\angle ABC$: \begin{aligned}BA &= \sqrt{(-3-3)^2 + (4-4)^2} \cr&= 6\end{aligned} and \begin{aligned}BC &= \sqrt{(4-3)^2 + (-3-4)^2} \cr&= \sqrt{50}\end{aligned}, with $$AC = \sqrt{98}$$

Apply the Cosine Rule to find $\angle ABC$: \begin{aligned}\text{Let }\phi &=\angle ABC \cr 98 &= 36 + 50 - 2(6)(\sqrt{50})\cos\phi \cr98 &= 86 - 12\sqrt{50}\cos\phi \cr\cos\phi &= -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{50}} \cr\phi &\approx 98.13^\circ\end{aligned}
Sum the opposite interior angles: $$\theta + \phi \approx 81.87^\circ + 98.13^\circ = 180^\circ$$, proving they are supplementary.
For Part (b)(i), calculate the distance from each of the four points to the origin: \begin{aligned}OA^2 &= OB^2 = OC^2 = OD^2\cr &= 3^2 + 4^2 \cr &= 25 \cr OA &= OB = OC = OD = 5\end{aligned}
Since a circle is defined as the set of points equidistant from a fixed center, and all four points are at a distance of $5$ from $(0, 0)$, the origin must be the center of the circle.
For Part (b)(ii), calculate the distance squared from point $E(-4, 4)$ to the center $(0, 0)$: \begin{aligned}OE^2 &= (-4)^2 + 4^2 \cr&= 16 + 16 \cr&= 32\end{aligned}
Since the distance squared $$32 > R^2 = 25$$, the distance from the point to the center of the circle is greater than the radius. Thus, the point $E$ lies outside the circle.

Final Answer:
(b)(i) $$\text{ All points are distance } 5 \text{ from (0, 0)} $$ (b)(ii) $$\text{Outside the circle}$$

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Cyclic Quadrilateral Supplementary Angles
bradley_insight.content: A cyclic quadrilateral has opposite angles summing to $180^\circ$. By working with coordinate lengths and the Cosine Rule, we can verify this theorem algebraically without relying on circle geometry alone, which is probably the most elegant way to link Pure 1 coordinate and trigonometric topics.

question:
A circle has center $M(1, 1)$ and radius $R = 5$. A chord $AB$ is drawn on the circle with endpoints $A(-2, 5)$ and $B(5, 4)$.

(a) Show that the perpendicular bisector of the chord $AB$ passes through the center of the circle $M(1, 1)$.

(b) (i) Calculate the length of the chord $AB$ and the perpendicular distance from the center $M$ to the chord $AB$, using these to verify the right-angled triangle relation: $R^2 = d^2 + \left(\dfrac{AB}{2}\right)^2$.
(ii) Determine whether the point $D(4, -2)$ lies inside the circle, on the circle, or outside the circle. Fully justify your answer.
steps: For Part (a), find the midpoint of the chord $AB$: \begin{aligned}K &= \left(\dfrac{-2+5}{2}, \dfrac{5+4}{2}\right) \cr&= (1.5, 4.5)\end{aligned}
Calculate the gradient of the chord $AB$: \begin{aligned}m_{AB} &= \dfrac{4-5}{5 - (-2)} \cr&= -\dfrac{1}{7}\end{aligned}
The perpendicular bisector must have a gradient of $$m_{\perp} = 7$$. Find its equation: $$y - 4.5 = 7(x - 1.5)$$

Substitute the center $M(1, 1)$ into this line equation to verify: \begin{aligned}1 - 4.5 &= 7(1 - 1.5) \cr-3.5 &= -3.5\end{aligned}. Since the coordinates satisfy the line, the perpendicular bisector passes through $M$.

For Part (b)(i), calculate the length of the chord $AB$: \begin{aligned}AB &= \sqrt{(5 - (-2))^2 + (4-5)^2} \cr&= \sqrt{7^2 + (-1)^2} \cr&= \sqrt{50}\end{aligned}
\begin{aligned} \cr\left(\dfrac{AB}{2}\right)^2 &= \dfrac{50}{4} = 12.5\end{aligned}

Next, find the perpendicular distance from $M(1, 1)$ to the line $x + 7y - 33 = 0$ (the line $AB$): \begin{aligned}d &= \dfrac{|1 + 7(1) - 33|}{\sqrt{1^2 + 7^2}}\cr &= \dfrac{25}{\sqrt{50}} \cr d^2 &= \dfrac{625}{50}\cr &= 12.5\end{aligned}
Sum the squares to verify the relation: \begin{aligned}d^2 + \left(\dfrac{AB}{2}\right)^2 &= 12.5 + 12.5 \cr&= 25 \cr&= R^2\end{aligned}. The relation is verified.
For Part (b)(ii), calculate the distance squared from point $D(4, -2)$ to the center $M(1, 1)$: \begin{aligned}MD^2 &= (4-1)^2 + (-2-1)^2 \cr&= 3^2 + (-3)^2 \cr&= 18\end{aligned}
Since the distance squared $$18 < R^2 = 25$$, the distance from the point to the center of the circle is less than the radius. Thus, the point $D$ lies inside the circle.
Final Answer: (b)(i):\begin{aligned} d^2 + (AB/2)^2 &= 12.5 + 12.5 \cr&= 25 \cr&= R^2 \text{ is verified}//end{aligned}  (b)(ii) $$\text{Inside the circle}$$

pi_options.feedback: In Part (b)(ii), you probably miscalculated the distance to the center. Since $MD^2 = 18 < R^2 = 25$, the distance from $D$ to the center is strictly less than the radius of $5$, meaning it lies inside the circle, not on it.
In Part (b)(ii), the distance squared to the center $M(1,1)$ is $(4-1)^2 + (-2-1)^2 = 18$. Since this is less than the radius squared ($25$), the point lies inside the circle, not outside.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Perpendicular Gradient Sign Trap
bradley_insight.content: When finding the gradient of a perpendicular bisector, remember that $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$. If the gradient of the chord is negative, the perpendicular bisector's gradient must be strictly positive. Forgetting this sign change is probably the most common way students lose marks on this topic.

question:
A circle has center $O(0, 0)$ and radius $R = 6$. A tangent is drawn to the circle from an external point $P(10, 0)$, touching the circle at $T(3.6, 4.8)$.

(a) Show that the tangent line $PT$ is perpendicular to the radius $OT$.

(b) (i) Find the cosine of angle $POT$ using the side lengths of triangle $OPT$, and hence use the Cosine Rule on triangle $OPT$ to show that $PT = 8$.

(b) (ii) Determine whether the point $D(5, -4)$ lies inside the circle, on the circle, or outside the circle. Fully justify your answer.
steps: For Part (a), calculate the gradients of the radius $OT$ and the tangent line $PT$: \begin{aligned}m_{OT} &= \dfrac{4.8-0}{3.6-0} \cr&= \dfrac{4}{3}\end{aligned} and \begin{aligned}m_{PT} &= \dfrac{4.8-0}{3.6-10} \cr&= \dfrac{4.8}{-6.4} \cr&= -\dfrac{3}{4}\end{aligned}

Since the product of their gradients is \begin{aligned}m_{OT} \times m_{PT} &= \dfrac{4}{3} \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{4}\right) \cr&= -1\end{aligned}, the radius $OT$ and the tangent $PT$ are perpendicular.

For Part (b)(i), calculate the side lengths of triangle $OPT$: $OT = 6$$ $$OP = 10$, and \begin{aligned}PT &= \sqrt{(3.6 - 10)^2 + 4.8^2} \cr&= \sqrt{(-6.4)^2 + 23.04} \cr&= \sqrt{40.96 + 23.04} \cr&= 8\end{aligned}

Apply the Cosine Rule to find $\cos\theta$: \begin{aligned}\text{let }\angle POT &=\theta \cr PT^2 &= OP^2 + OT^2 \cr &\quad - 2(OP)(OT)\cos\theta \cr 8^2 &= 10^2 + 6^2 - 2(10)(6)\cos\theta\end{aligned}
Simplify to find the cosine value: \begin{aligned}64 &= 100 + 36 - 120\cos\theta \cr64 &= 136 - 120\cos\theta \cr\cos\theta &= 0.6\end{aligned}
Using the Cosine Rule with $\cos\theta = 0.6$ verifies the length of the tangent: \begin{aligned}PT &= \sqrt{10^2 + 6^2 - 2(10)(6)(0.6)} \cr&= \sqrt{64} \cr&= 8\end{aligned}, as required.
For Part (b)(ii), calculate the distance squared from $D(5, -4)$ to the center $O(0, 0)$: \begin{aligned}OD^2 &= 5^2 + (-4)^2 \cr&= 25 + 16 \cr&= 41\end{aligned}
Since the distance squared $$41 > R^2 = 36$$, the distance from the point to the center of the circle is greater than the radius. Thus, the point $D$ lies outside the circle.

Final Answer:
(b)(i) $$\text{ } PT = 8 \text{ is verified } $$ (b)(ii) $$\text{Outside the circle}$$

question:
The diagram shows a sector of a circle $OAB$. $C$ is the midpoint of $OB$. Angle $AOB$ is $\theta$ radians.

(a) Given that the area of the triangle $OAC$ is equal to one-third of the area of the sector $OAB$, show that $\theta = 1.5\sin\theta$.

(b) Use the Newton-Raphson method with $\theta_1 = \pi$ to find $\theta_3$ as an approximation for $\theta$. Give your answer correct to five decimal places.

(c) Given that the actual value of $\theta = 1.49579$ to five decimal places, find an estimate for the percentage error in the approximation found in part (b).
steps: First, state the formulas for both areas in terms of $r$ and $\theta$. The area of the sector $OAB$ is: $$\text{Area of sector } OAB = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$$

Since $C$ is the midpoint of $OB$, $OC = \dfrac{1}{2}r$. The area of triangle $OAC$ is: \begin{aligned}\text{Area}_{\triangle OAC} &= \dfrac{1}{2}(r)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}r\right)\sin\theta \cr&= \dfrac{r^2}{4}\sin\theta\end{aligned}

Next, set the area of the triangle equal to one-third of the area of the sector: \begin{aligned}\dfrac{r^2}{4}\sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{3} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta\right) \cr\dfrac{r^2}{4}\sin\theta &= \dfrac{r^2}{6}\theta\end{aligned}
Divide both sides by $r^2$ (since $r > 0$) to eliminate the radius variable: $$\dfrac{1}{4}\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{6}\theta$$

Multiply both sides by $6$ to isolate $\theta$, and simplify the resulting fraction to reach the target equation: \begin{aligned}\theta &= \dfrac{6}{4}\sin\theta \cr\theta &= 1.5\sin\theta\end{aligned}

For Part (b), define $f(\theta) = \theta - 1.5\sin\theta$ and its derivative $f'(\theta) = 1 - 1.5\cos\theta$. Use the Newton-Raphson formula: $$\theta_{n+1} = \theta_n - \dfrac{\theta_n - 1.5\sin\theta_n}{1 - 1.5\cos\theta_n}$$

With $\theta_1 = \pi$, calculate the iterations. In the first iteration: \begin{aligned}\theta_2 &= \pi - \dfrac{\pi - 1.5\sin\pi}{1 - 1.5\cos\pi} \cr&= \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{1 - 1.5(-1)} \cr&= \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{2.5} \cr&= 0.6\pi \approx 1.88496\end{aligned}
In the second iteration: \begin{aligned}\theta_3 &= 1.88496\cr & \quad - \dfrac{1.88496 - 1.5\sin(1.88496)}{1 - 1.5\cos(1.88496)}\cr & \approx 1.57176\end{aligned}

For Part (c), calculate the percentage error by comparing the approximation $\theta_3 \approx 1.57176$ with the actual root $\theta = 1.49579$: \begin{aligned}\text{% error} &= \dfrac{|1.57176 - 1.49579|}{1.49579} \times 100 \cr &\approx 5.08\%\end{aligned}

question:
The diagram shows a sector of a circle $OAB$ with radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ radians. A chord $AB$ divides the sector into a segment and a triangle $OAB$.

(a) Given that the area of the segment is equal to one-third of the area of the triangle $OAB$, show that $4\sin\theta = 3\theta$.

(b) Use the Newton-Raphson method with $\theta_1 = 1.5$ to find $\theta_3$ as an approximation for $\theta$. Give your answer correct to five decimal places.

(c) Given that the actual value of $\theta = 1.27570$ to five decimal places, find an estimate for the percentage error in the approximation found in part (b).
steps: First, state the formulas for both areas in terms of $r$ and $\theta$. The area of the triangle $OAB$ is: $$\text{Area}_{\triangle OAB} = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta$$
The area of the sector $OAB$ is: $$\text{Area}_{sect OAB} = \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta$$

Find the area of the segment by subtracting the area of the triangle from the area of the sector: \begin{aligned}\text{Area}_{seg} &= \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta - \dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta \cr&= \dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)\end{aligned}
Set the segment area equal to one-third of the triangle area: $$\dfrac{1}{2}r^2(\theta - \sin\theta) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta\right)$$
Divide both sides by $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2$ to simplify: $$\theta - \sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{3}\sin\theta$$
Add $\sin\theta$ to both sides and multiply by $3$ to obtain the target equation: \begin{aligned}\theta &= \dfrac{4}{3}\sin\theta \cr3\theta &= 4\sin\theta \cr4\sin\theta &= 3\theta\end{aligned}

For Part (b), define $f(\theta) = 3\theta - 4\sin\theta$ and its derivative $f'(\theta) = 3 - 4\cos\theta$. Use the Newton-Raphson formula: $$\theta_{n+1} = \theta_n - \dfrac{3\theta_n - 4\sin\theta_n}{3 - 4\cos\theta_n}$$
With $\theta_1 = 1.5$, calculate the iterations. In the first iteration: \begin{aligned}\theta_2 &= 1.5 - \dfrac{3(1.5) - 4\sin(1.5)}{3 - 4\cos(1.5)}\cr & \approx 1.31229\end{aligned}
In the second iteration: \begin{aligned}\theta_3 &= 1.31229\cr & \quad - \dfrac{3(1.31229) - 4\sin(1.31229)}{3 - 4\cos(1.31229)}\cr & \approx 1.27741\end{aligned}

For Part (c), calculate the percentage error of $\theta_3 \approx 1.27741$ against the true root $\theta = 1.27570$: \begin{aligned}\text{% Error} &= \dfrac{|1.27741 - 1.27570|}{1.27570} \times 100 \cr & \approx 0.13\%\end{aligned}

(a) Given that the area of the smaller sector $OCD$ is equal to $\frac{9}{25}$ of the area of the triangle $OAB$ formed inside the larger sector, show that $2\theta = 5\sin\theta$.

(b) Use the Newton-Raphson method with $\theta_1 = 2.5$ to find $\theta_3$ as an approximation for $\theta$. Give your answer correct to five decimal places.

question:
An arithmetic sequence has first term $a$ and common difference $d$.

The sum of the first 16 terms of the sequence is equal to the square of the sum of the first 4 terms.

(a) Show that $4a + 30d = 4a^2 + 12ad + 9d^2$.

steps: First, state the formulas for both sums. The sum of the first 16 terms is: \begin{aligned}S_{16} &= \dfrac{16}{2}\left(2a + 15d\right) \cr&= 8(2a + 15d) \cr&= 16a + 120d\end{aligned}

question:
An arithmetic sequence has first term $a$ and common difference $d$.

The sum of the first 9 terms of the sequence is equal to the square of the sum of the first 3 terms.

(a) Show that $a + 4d = a^2 + 2ad + d^2$.

(b) Given that the third term of the sequence is 8, find the smallest possible value of $a$.
steps: First, state the formulas for both sums. The sum of the first 9 terms is: \begin{aligned}S_9 &= \dfrac{9}{2}\left(2a + 8d\right) \cr&= 9a + 36d\end{aligned}
The sum of the first 3 terms is: \begin{aligned}S_3 &= \dfrac{3}{2}\left(2a + 2d\right) \cr&= 3a + 3d\end{aligned}
Next, set the sum of the first 9 terms equal to the square of the sum of the first 3 terms: \begin{aligned}9a + 36d &= (3a + 3d)^2 \cr9a + 36d &= 9(a + d)^2\end{aligned}
Divide both sides of the equation by $9$ to reach the target relation: \begin{aligned}a + 4d &= (a + d)^2 \cr a + 4d &= a^2 + 2ad + d^2\end{aligned}
For Part (b), state the formula for the third term and rearrange for $d$: \begin{aligned}u_3 &= a + 2d = 8 \cr2d &= 8 - a \cr d &= \dfrac{8-a}{2}\end{aligned}
Substitute $d = \dfrac{8-a}{2}$ into both sides of the simplified relation: $$a + 4\left(\dfrac{8-a}{2}\right) = \left(a + \dfrac{8-a}{2}\right)^2$$
Simplify both sides of the equation: \begin{aligned}a + 2(8-a) &= \left(\dfrac{2a + 8 - a}{2}\right)^2 \cr16 - a &= \dfrac{(a+8)^2}{4}\end{aligned}
Clear the fraction by multiplying both sides by $4$: \begin{aligned}64 - 4a &= a^2 + 16a + 64 \cr a^2 + 20a &= 0\end{aligned}
Factor the quadratic to find the two possible values of $a$: \begin{aligned}a(a + 20) &= 0 \cr a &= 0 \quad \text{or} \quad a = -20\end{aligned}
Comparing the two roots, the smallest possible value of $a$ is $-20$.

Final Answer:
(b)$$a = -20$$

The sum of the first 16 terms of the sequence is equal to the square of the sum of the first 2 terms.

(a) Show that $16a + 120d = 4a^2 + 4ad + d^2$.
