pi_options.feedback: You may have made an integration error on the exponential term. The integral of $\dfrac{1}{300}e^{-0.5t}$ is $-\dfrac{1}{150}e^{-0.5t}$, not $-\dfrac{1}{300}e^{-0.5t}$.
Check the sign of your constant of integration. Substituting $P = 100$ at $t = 0$ gives $\dfrac{1}{100} = \dfrac{1}{150} + A'$, which yields $A' = +\dfrac{1}{300}$, not $-\dfrac{1}{300}$.
Don't forget to take the square root of both sides at the end of the first model. Since the solved equation is $P^2 = 6250t + 10000$, taking the square root yields $P(t) = \sqrt{6250t + 10000}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Proportionality Integration Steps
bradley_insight.content: For standard separable differential equations of inverse proportionality (like $P \text{d}P = k \text{d}t$), always group the numeric multipliers with the linear constant $2k$ first. This avoids dragging fractions of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ through the algebra and eliminates minor arithmetic slips when applying the boundary conditions.

subtopic: Exponential and Logarithmic Functions and Graphs
question:
A clinical researcher is studying the concentration of a newly administered drug in a patient's bloodstream. Let $x$ represent the concentration of the drug (in units/L) at time $t$ hours. Initially, when $t = 0$, the concentration is $x = 0$. After $1$ hour, the concentration is $2$ units/L.

1. The researcher first assumes that the rate of increase of the drug concentration is proportional to the difference between a maximum saturation level of $10$ units/L and the current concentration $x$.
(a) Write down a differential equation to model this situation.
(b) Solve this differential equation to find $x$ in terms of $t$.

2. In a revised model, it is assumed that:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} = \dfrac{3(10 - x)^2}{100(t + 1)} \end{aligned}Solve this differential equation to find $x$ in terms of $t$, using the same initial condition of $x = 0$ at $t = 0$.

3. Compare the long-term behaviour of the two models as $t \to \infty$.
steps: Write the rate of increase for the first model as a differential equation:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} = k(10 - x) \end{aligned}where $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.

Solve the differential equation by separating the variables and integrating both sides:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{10 - x} \text{d}x &= k \text{d}t \cr \int \dfrac{1}{10 - x} \text{d}x &= \int k \text{d}t \cr -\ln(10 - x) &= kt + C \cr \ln(10 - x) &= -kt - C \cr 10 - x &= Ae^{-kt} \end{aligned}where $A = e^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

Apply the boundary conditions to find the values of $A$ and $k$:

Substitute $t = 0, x = 0$ into the equation:\begin{aligned} 10 - 0 &= Ae^{0} \cr A &= 10 \end{aligned}This gives $x(t) = 10(1 - e^{-kt})$. Now substitute $t = 1, x = 2$ to find $k$:\begin{aligned} 2 &= 10(1 - e^{-k}) \cr 0.2 &= 1 - e^{-k} \cr e^{-k} &= 0.8 \cr -k &= \ln 0.8 \cr k &= -\ln 0.8 \end{aligned}Substituting $e^{-kt} = (e^{-k})^t = 0.8^t$ yields:\begin{aligned} x(t) = 10(1 - 0.8^t) \end{aligned}

For the revised model, separate the variables and integrate both sides:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &= \dfrac{3(10 - x)^2}{100(t + 1)} \cr \dfrac{1}{(10 - x)^2} \text{d}x &= \dfrac{3}{100(t + 1)} \text{d}t \cr \int (10 - x)^{-2} \text{d}x &= \int \dfrac{3}{100(t + 1)} \text{d}t \cr \dfrac{1}{10 - x} &= \dfrac{3}{100}\ln(t + 1) + C' \end{aligned}

Apply the initial condition $t = 0,  x = 0$ to find $C'$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{10 - 0} &= \dfrac{3}{100}\ln(1) + C' \cr \dfrac{1}{10} &= 0 + C' \cr C' &= \dfrac{1}{10} \end{aligned}Now substitute $C' = \dfrac{1}{10}$ back and isolate $x$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{10 - x} &= \dfrac{3}{100}\ln(t + 1) + \dfrac{1}{10} \cr \dfrac{1}{10 - x} &= \dfrac{3\ln(t + 1) + 10}{100} \cr 10 - x &= \dfrac{100}{3\ln(t + 1) + 10} \cr x(t) &= 10 - \dfrac{100}{3\ln(t + 1) + 10} \end{aligned}

Analyze the long-term behaviour as $t \to \infty$:

For the first model:\begin{aligned} \text{As } t &\to \infty: \cr 0.8^t &\to 0 \cr x(t) &\to 10(1 - 0) \cr &= 10 \end{aligned}For the revised model:\begin{aligned} \text{As } t &\to \infty: \cr \ln(t + 1) &\to \infty \cr \dfrac{100}{3\ln(t + 1) + 10} &\to 0 \cr x(t) &\to 10 \end{aligned}Both models predict that the concentration will saturate at a limit of $10$ units/L. However, the first model approaches this limit much faster (exponential decay of the remaining concentration gap) compared to the slow logarithmic decay of the revised model.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} x(t) &= 10(1 - 0.8^t) \cr x(t) &= 10 - \dfrac{100}{3\ln(t + 1) + 10} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check the sign of your constant of integration $C'$. Substituting the boundary condition $t = 0,  x = 0$ into the expression \dfrac{1}{10 - x} = \dfrac{3}{100}\ln(t + 1) + C' yields $C' = +\dfrac{1}{10}$, not $-\dfrac{1}{10}$.

Double check your algebraic rearrangements when isolating $x$. Since $10 - x = \dfrac{100}{3\ln(t + 1) + 10}$, subtracting $10$ and multiplying by $-1$ results in subtracting the fraction from $10$, not adding it.
Check your exponential growth base in the first model. Since $e^{-k} = 0.8$, the function should contain $0.8^t$. It seems you may have mistakenly written $1 - e^{-k} = 0.2$ as the base itself.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Watch Your Signs in Log Integrals
bradley_insight.content: A very common error in GCE examinations is forgetting to apply the chain rule when integrating reciprocal linear functions. Integrating $\int \dfrac{1}{10 - x} \,\text{d}x$ must result in $-\ln(10 - x) + C$. Forgetting this negative sign completely skews the exponential growth behaviour of the concentration.

question:
A liquid is cooling in a temperature-controlled laboratory. Let $\theta$ be the temperature of the liquid in $^\circ\text{C}$ at time $t$ minutes. The ambient room temperature is kept constant at $20^\circ\text{C}$. At $t = 0$, the liquid is at $84^\circ\text{C}$, and at $t = 10$ minutes, it has cooled to $52^\circ\text{C}$.

1. A classic model assumes that the rate of decrease of the liquid's temperature is proportional to the difference between its current temperature $\theta$ and the ambient room temperature.
(a) Write down a differential equation to model this situation.
(b) Solve this differential equation to find $\theta$ in terms of $t$.

2. In a revised model, the rate of cooling is assumed to be governed by:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}\theta}{\text{d}t} = -\dfrac{(\theta - 20)^{3/2}}{30\sqrt{t + 4}} \end{aligned}Solve this differential equation to find $\theta$ in terms of $t$, using the same initial temperature of $84^\circ\text{C}$ at $t = 0$.

3. State, with a brief reason, what both models predict about the temperature of the liquid in the long term.
steps: Represent Newton's Law of Cooling as a differential equation, writing the rate of decrease as a negative rate of change:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}\theta}{\text{d}t} = -k(\theta - 20) \end{aligned}where $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.

Separate the variables and integrate to solve the equation:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\theta - 20} \text{d}\theta &= -k \text{d}t \cr \int \dfrac{1}{\theta - 20} \text{d}\theta &= \int -k \text{d}t \cr \ln(\theta - 20) &= -kt + C \cr \theta - 20 &= Ae^{-kt} \cr \theta(t) &= 20 + Ae^{-kt} \end{aligned}

Apply the initial conditions to find the constants $A$ and $k$:

Substitute $t = 0, \theta = 84$:\begin{aligned} 84 &= 20 + Ae^{0} \cr A &= 64 \end{aligned}This gives $\theta(t) = 20 + 64e^{-kt}$. Substitute $t = 10, \theta = 52$:\begin{aligned} 52 &= 20 + 64e^{-10k} \cr 32 &= 64e^{-10k} \cr e^{-10k} &= 0.5 \cr -10k &= \ln 0.5 \cr k &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{10} \end{aligned}Substituting $e^{-kt} = (e^{-10k})^{t/10} = 0.5^{t/10} = 2^{-t/10}$ yields:\begin{aligned} \theta(t) = 20 + 64\cdot 2^{-t/10} \end{aligned}

For the revised model, separate variables and integrate:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}\theta}{\text{d}t} = -\dfrac{(\theta - 20)^{3/2}}{30\sqrt{t + 4}} \cr & (\theta - 20)^{-3/2} \text{d}\theta\cr & \quad = -\dfrac{1}{30}(t + 4)^{-1/2} \text{d}t \cr &\int (\theta - 20)^{-3/2} \text{d}\theta \cr & \quad= -\dfrac{1}{30}\int (t + 4)^{-1/2} \text{d}t \cr &-2(\theta - 20)^{-1/2} \cr & \quad = -\dfrac{1}{30}\big(2\sqrt{t + 4}\big) + C \cr &2(\theta - 20)^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{15}\sqrt{t + 4} - C \end{aligned}

Multiply both sides by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ to simplify:\begin{aligned} (\theta - 20)^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{30}\sqrt{t + 4} + C' \end{aligned}where $C' = -\dfrac{1}{2}C$. Use the initial condition $t = 0,  \theta = 84$ to find $C'$:\begin{aligned} (84 - 20)^{-1/2} &= \dfrac{1}{30}\sqrt{0 + 4} + C' \cr 64^{-1/2} &= \dfrac{1}{30}(2) + C' \cr \dfrac{1}{8} &= \dfrac{1}{15} + C' \cr C' &= \dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{1}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{7}{120} \end{aligned}

Substitute $C'$ and isolate $\theta$:\begin{aligned} &(\theta - 20)^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{30}\sqrt{t + 4} + \dfrac{7}{120} \cr &\theta(t) - 20 = \big( \dfrac{1}{30}\sqrt{t + 4} + \dfrac{7}{120} \big)^{-2} \cr & \theta(t) = 20 + \big( \dfrac{1}{30}\sqrt{t + 4} + \dfrac{7}{120} \big)^{-2} \end{aligned}

Examine the long-term behaviour as $t \to \infty$:

For the first model:\begin{aligned} \text{As } t &\to \infty: \cr 2^{-t/10} &\to 0 \cr \theta(t) &\to 20 \end{aligned}For the revised model:\begin{aligned} \text{As } t &\to \infty: \cr \sqrt{t + 4} &\to \infty \cr \big( \dfrac{1}{30}\sqrt{t + 4} + \dfrac{7}{120} \big)^{-2} &\to 0 \cr \theta(t) &\to 20 \end{aligned}Both models predict that the liquid will cool down to approach the room temperature of $20^\circ\text{C}$ in the long term, and neither model projects that the temperature will fall below this ambient level.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \theta(t) &= 20 + 64\cdot 2^{-t/10} \cr \theta(t) &= 20 + \big( \dfrac{1}{30}\sqrt{t + 4} + \dfrac{7}{120} \big)^{-2} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your calculation for $C'$. When substituting $t = 0,  \theta = 84$, the equation is \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{1}{15} + C'. This yields $C' = \dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{7}{120}$, not \dfrac{1}{15}.
Note the sign of your power when isolating the expression. Since (\theta - 20)^{-1/2} = X, taking the reciprocal of the square of both sides gives \theta - 20 = X^{-2}, not $X^2$.
Make sure you subtract the ambient temperature of $20$ before solving for the multiplier $A$. At $t = 0$, $84 = 20 + A \implies A = 64$, not $84$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Fractional Integration Tricks
bradley_insight.content: When integrating powers of functions like $\int (\theta - 20)^{-3/2} \,\text{d}\theta$, be very precise with the fractional arithmetic. Increasing the power by $1$ gives a new power of $-1/2$. Dividing by this new power introduces a multiplier of $-2$, which must be handled cleanly before applying any substitutions.

question:
An investor establishes a retirement fund. Let $V$ represent the value of the fund (in thousands of pounds) at time $t$ years. Initially, when $t = 0$, the fund has a value of $V = 10$. After $5$ years, the value of the fund is $V = 20$.

1. A simple model assumes that the rate of increase of the fund's value is directly proportional to its current value.
(a) Write down a differential equation to model this situation.
(b) Solve this differential equation to find $V$ in terms of $t$.

2. In a revised model, the investor makes continuous annual withdrawals, and the rate of change of the fund's value is given by:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = 0.1V - 2 \end{aligned}Solve this differential equation to find $V$ in terms of $t$, using the same initial value of $V = 10$ at $t = 0$.

3. Compare the long-term behaviour predicted by the two models. Determine the exact time at which the fund is projected to run out under the revised model.
steps: Represent the rate of change for direct proportionality as a differential equation:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = kV \end{aligned}where $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.

Integrate the separable differential equation:\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{1}{V} \text{d}V &= \int k \text{d}t \cr \ln V &= kt + C \cr V(t) &= Ae^{kt} \end{aligned}where $A = e^C$. Substitute the boundary conditions:

Substitute $t = 0, V = 10 \implies A = 10$.

Now substitute $t = 5, V = 20$ into $V(t) = 10e^{kt}$:\begin{aligned} 20 &= 10e^{5k} \cr 2 &= e^{5k} \cr 5k &= \ln 2 \cr k &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{5} \end{aligned}Substituting $k$ back into the model gives:\begin{aligned} V(t) &= 10e^{\frac{\ln 2}{5}t} \cr &= 10\cdot 2^{t/5} \end{aligned}

For the revised model, separate variables and integrate:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} &= 0.1V - 2 \cr \dfrac{1}{0.1V - 2} \text{d}V &= \text{d}t \cr \int \dfrac{1}{0.1V - 2} \text{d}V &= \int \text{d}t \cr 10\ln|0.1V - 2| &= t + C' \end{aligned}

Solve for $V(t)$:\begin{aligned} \ln|0.1V - 2| &= 0.1t + 0.1C' \cr 0.1V - 2 &= Be^{0.1t} \cr 0.1V &= 2 + Be^{0.1t} \cr V(t) &= 20 + A'e^{0.1t} \end{aligned}where $A' = 10B$. Substitute the initial condition $t = 0,  V = 10$ to find $A'$:\begin{aligned} 10 &= 20 + A'e^{0} \cr A' &= -10 \end{aligned}So the value of the fund under the revised model is:\begin{aligned} V(t) = 20 - 10e^{0.1t} \end{aligned}

Compare the long-term behaviour and find the depletion point:

For the first model, $V(t) = 10\cdot 2^{t/5} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$, representing unbounded compound growth.

For the revised model, $V(t) = 20 - 10e^{0.1t}$ eventually decreases because the withdrawal term exceeds the growth term. The fund is exhausted when $V(t) = 0$:\begin{aligned} 20 - 10e^{0.1t} &= 0 \cr 10e^{0.1t} &= 20 \cr e^{0.1t} &= 2 \cr 0.1t &= \ln 2 \cr t &= 10\ln 2 \end{aligned}The fund runs out after exactly $10\ln 2$ years (approximately $6.93$ years).
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} V(t) &= 10\cdot 2^{t/5} \cr V(t) &= 20 - 10e^{0.1t} \cr t &= 10\ln 2 \text{ years} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check the final coefficient when solving for depletion time. The equation is $0.1t = \ln 2$, which means $t = 10\ln 2$ years, not $5\ln 2$ years.
Check the sign of your constant of integration. Since the initial value is $V = 10$ and $V(t) = 20 + A'e^{0.1t}$, substituting $t = 0$ gives $10 = 20 + A' \implies A' = -10$, not $+10$.

Be careful when integrating \int \dfrac{1}{0.1V - 2} \text{d}V. Because of the linear coefficient of $0.1$, the integral is $10\ln|0.1V - 2|$, which introduces the $0.1$ exponent factor in the exponential, not $1$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Watch Linear coefficients
bradley_insight.content: When integrating reciprocal linear expressions of the form $\int \dfrac{1}{aV - b} \,\text{d}V$, always remember the factor of $\dfrac{1}{a}$ that arises from reversing the chain rule. Omitting this multiplier leads to incorrect scale factors in the exponential exponent during subsequent rearrangements.

question:
An environmental scientist is monitoring a bird population, $B$, on an isolated island. When monitoring begins at $t = 0$, there are $100$ birds, and at $t = 1$ year, there are $150$ birds.

1. A simple geometric model assumes that the rate of increase of the bird population is directly proportional to the number of birds present.
(a) Write down a differential equation to model this situation.
(b) Solve this differential equation to find $B$ in terms of $t$.

2. A more realistic logistic model assumes that the island has a maximum carrying capacity of $500$ birds, and that the rate of growth is modeled by the differential equation:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}B}{\text{d}t} = \dfrac{B(500 - B)}{2000} \end{aligned}Solve this differential equation to find $B$ in terms of $t$, using the same initial population of $100$ birds at $t = 0$.

3. Compare the long-term behaviour predicted by the two models as $t \to \infty$.
steps: Represent exponential growth as a differential equation:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}B}{\text{d}t} = kB \end{aligned}where $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.

Solve by separating the variables and integrating both sides:\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{1}{B} \text{d}B &= \int k \text{d}t \cr \ln B &= kt + C \cr B(t) &= Ae^{kt} \end{aligned}where $A = e^C$. Substitute $t = 0, B = 100 \implies A = 100$.

Substitute $t = 1, B = 150$ into $B(t) = 100e^{kt}$:\begin{aligned} 150 &= 100e^{k} \cr e^k &= 1.5 \cr k &= \ln 1.5 \end{aligned}So the first model is:\begin{aligned} B(t) &= 100e^{(\ln 1.5)t} \cr &= 100\cdot 1.5^t \end{aligned}

For the logistic model, separate the variables:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{B(500 - B)} \text{d}B \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2000} \text{d}t \end{aligned}Decompose the left-hand fraction using partial fractions:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{B(500 - B)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{X}{B} + \dfrac{Y}{500 - B} \cr &1 = X(500 - B) + YB \end{aligned}By substituting $B = 0 \implies X = \dfrac{1}{500}$, and $B = 500 \implies Y = \dfrac{1}{500}$.

So the decomposed expression is:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{B(500 - B)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{500}\big( \dfrac{1}{B} + \dfrac{1}{500 - B} \big) \end{aligned}

Integrate both sides using the partial fraction decomposition:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{1}{500} \int \big( \dfrac{1}{B} + \dfrac{1}{500 - B} \big) \text{d}B \cr &\quad = \int \dfrac{1}{2000} \text{d}t \cr &\dfrac{1}{500}\big( \ln|B| - \ln|500 - B| \big) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{t}{2000} + C_1 \cr &\ln\big( \dfrac{B}{500 - B} \big) = \dfrac{t}{4} + C' \cr &\dfrac{B}{500 - B} = Ke^{t/4} \end{aligned}where $C' = 500C_1$.

Substitute the initial condition $t = 0,  B = 100$ to find $K$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{100}{500 - 100} = Ke^{0} \cr &\dfrac{100}{400} = K \cr &K = \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}This gives:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{B}{500 - B} = \dfrac{1}{4}e^{t/4} \end{aligned}

Rearrange to isolate $B(t)$:\begin{aligned} &B = (500 - B)\big(\dfrac{1}{4}e^{t/4}\big) \cr &B = 125e^{t/4} - \dfrac{1}{4}Be^{t/4} \cr &B\big(1 + \dfrac{1}{4}e^{t/4}\big) = 125e^{t/4} \cr &B(t) = \dfrac{125e^{t/4}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{4}e^{t/4}} \cr &B(t) = \dfrac{500e^{t/4}}{4 + e^{t/4}} \end{aligned}

Examine the long-term behaviour as $t \to \infty$:

For the simple geometric model, $B(t) = 100\cdot 1.5^t \to \infty$, which predicts unbounded population expansion.

For the logistic model, divide numerator and denominator by $e^{t/4}$:\begin{aligned} &B(t) = \dfrac{500}{4e^{-t/4} + 1} \cr &B(t) \to \dfrac{500}{0 + 1} = 500 \end{aligned}The simple model assumes infinite growth, whereas the logistic model predicts the population is bounded and will level off at the carrying capacity of $500$ birds.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} B(t) &= 100\cdot 1.5^t \cr B(t) &= \dfrac{500e^{t/4}}{4 + e^{t/4}} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Be careful with signs during your algebraic isolation steps. Rearranging $B\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{4}e^{t/4}\right) = 125e^{t/4}$ leads to addition in the denominator: $B(t) = \dfrac{500e^{t/4}}{4 + e^{t/4}}$, not subtraction.
Check your scaling factor when multiplying numerator and denominator by $4$. The numerator $125e^{t/4}$ multiplied by $4$ becomes $500e^{t/4}$, not $125e^{t/4}$.

Check your division steps when evaluating limits. Dividing the numerator and denominator of \dfrac{500e^{t/4}}{4 + e^{t/4}} by e^{t/4} yields \dfrac{500}{4e^{-t/4} + 1}, not \dfrac{500}{e^{-t/4} + 4}.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Master Partial Fractions in ODEs
bradley_insight.content: For logistic growth differential equations, decomposing the expression using partial fractions is a staple GCE topic. Always remember to divide by the carrying capacity multiplier (such as $500$) outside of the logarithmic brackets. Forgetting this coefficient causes incorrect constant values when applying initial conditions.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Show that $(x - 3)$ is a factor of:\begin{aligned} 2x^3 - 5x^2 - 4x + 3 \end{aligned}
steps: Define the polynomial as a function $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} f(x) = 2x^3 - 5x^2 - 4x + 3 \end{aligned}According to the Factor Theorem, a linear term $(x - a)$ is a factor of a polynomial $f(x)$ if and only if $f(a) = 0$. Therefore, $(x - 3)$ is a factor if $f(3) = 0$.

Substitute $x = 3$ into the polynomial and evaluate step-by-step:\begin{aligned} f(3) &= 2(3)^3 - 5(3)^2 - 4(3) + 3 \cr &= 2(27) - 5(9) - 12 + 3 \cr &= 54 - 45 - 12 + 3 \cr &= 9 - 12 + 3 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}

Conclude the proof based on the result:

Since $f(3) = 0$, by the Factor Theorem, $(x - 3)$ is indeed a factor of $2x^3 - 5x^2 - 4x + 3$.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} f(3) &= 0 \cr (x - 3) &\text{ is a factor} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Be careful with the sign when using the Factor Theorem. For a factor of $(x - a)$, you must test the root $x = a$, which means evaluating $f(3)$, not $f(-3)$.
For $(x - 3)$ to be a factor, evaluating the polynomial at $x = 3$ must result in exactly $0$. Any non-zero remainder means it is not a factor.
The root $x = 3$ corresponds to the factor $(x - 3)$, not $(x + 3)$. If $f(-3) = 0$, then $(x + 3)$ would be a factor.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Root Signs in the Factor Theorem
bradley_insight.content: A frequent error under pressure is substituting the wrong sign into the polynomial. Remember that the linear factor $(x - a)$ corresponds to the root $x = a$. For $(x - 3)$, always evaluate $f(3)$, whereas for $(x + 3)$, you would evaluate $f(-3)$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The polynomial $f(x)$ is defined by:\begin{aligned} f(x) = 3x^3 + kx^2 - 4x + 12 \end{aligned}where $k$ is a constant.

Given that $(x + 2)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, find the value of $k$.
steps: According to the Factor Theorem, since $(x + 2)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, the polynomial evaluated at the root $x = -2$ must equal $0$. That is:\begin{aligned} f(-2) = 0 \end{aligned}
Substitute $x = -2$ into the expression for $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} f(-2) &= 3(-2)^3 + k(-2)^2 \cr &\quad - 4(-2) + 12 \cr &= 3(-8) + 4k + 8 + 12 \cr &= -24 + 4k + 20 \cr &= 4k - 4 \end{aligned}
Set $f(-2)$ equal to $0$ and solve for the constant $k$:\begin{aligned} 4k - 4 &= 0 \cr 4k &= 4 \cr k &= 1 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} k = 1 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your evaluation of $(-2)^3$. It is $-8$, not $+8$. Using $+8$ gives \begin{aligned} 24 + 4k + 20 &= 0 \cr 4k &= -44 \cr k &= -11 \end{aligned.
Check your signs during the final solving steps. When setting $4k - 4 = 0$, adding $4$ to both sides gives $4k = 4$, which leads to $k = 1$, not $k = -1$.
You may have evaluated $f(2) = 0$ instead of $f(-2) = 0$. Remember that for a factor of $(x + 2)$, the root to substitute is $x = -2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Power of Negative Numbers
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating cubic powers of negative numbers like $(-2)^3$, ensure you preserve the negative sign, giving $-8$. It is highly common to accidentally write positive values when substituting, leading to completely incorrect algebraic systems.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Find the remainder when the polynomial:\begin{aligned} 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 5x + 8 \end{aligned}is divided by $(x - 2)$ using algebraic division.
steps:
To find the remainder, we perform polynomial division on $2x^3 - 3x^2 - 5x + 8$ using the divisor $(x - 2)$.

First, divide the leading term $2x^3$ by $x$ to get $2x^2$. Multiply $2x^2$ by the divisor $(x - 2)$:\begin{aligned} 2x^2(x - 2) = 2x^3 - 4x^2 \end{aligned}Subtract this from the original polynomial to find the first partial remainder:\begin{aligned} &(2x^3 - 3x^2 - 5x + 8) \cr &\quad - (2x^3 - 4x^2) \cr &\quad = x^2 - 5x + 8 \end{aligned}

Next, divide the leading term of the partial remainder, $x^2$, by $x$ to get $x$. Multiply $x$ by the divisor $(x - 2)$:\begin{aligned} x(x - 2) = x^2 - 2x \end{aligned}Subtract this from the current partial remainder:\begin{aligned} &(x^2 - 5x + 8) \cr &\quad - (x^2 - 2x) \cr &\quad = -3x + 8 \end{aligned}

Finally, divide the leading term of the new partial remainder, $-3x$, by $x$ to get $-3$. Multiply $-3$ by the divisor $(x - 2)$:\begin{aligned} -3(x - 2) = -3x + 6 \end{aligned}Subtract this to find the final numerical remainder:\begin{aligned}(-3x + 8) - (-3x + 6) = 2 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \text{Remainder} = 2 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Be very careful with your signs during subtraction at each step. For example, during the first subtraction, we compute $-3x^2 - (-4x^2)$, which is $-3x^2 + 4x^2 = x^2$. A sign error here will propagate through the remaining steps and yield an incorrect remainder.
Check your final subtraction step. We have $(-3x + 8) - (-3x + 6)$. This evaluates to $8 - 6 = 2$, not $8 + 6 = 14$ or any other addition error.
A remainder of $0$ would mean that $(x - 2)$ is a perfect factor of the polynomial. Double-check your subtraction steps; after dividing all terms, we are left with a constant remainder of $2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Subtraction of Negatives
bradley_insight.content: When performing algebraic long division, the single most common error is a sign slip during subtraction. Always write out the subtraction of negative terms explicitly (such as $-3x^2 - (-4x^2) = x^2$) to avoid making easy mental arithmetic mistakes.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The cubic polynomial $f(x)$ is given by:\begin{aligned} f(x) = 2x^3 - x^2 - 13x - 6 \end{aligned}1. Use the Factor Theorem to show that $(x - 3)$ is a linear factor of $f(x)$.

2. Hence, express $f(x)$ as the product of three linear factors.
steps: To prove that $(x - 3)$ is a factor of $f(x) = 2x^3 - x^2 - 13x - 6$, apply the Factor Theorem and evaluate $f(3)$:\begin{aligned} f(3) &= 2(3)^3 - (3)^2 - 13(3) - 6 \cr &= 2(27) - 9 - 39 - 6 \cr &= 54 - 9 - 39 - 6 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(3) = 0$, by the Factor Theorem, $(x - 3)$ is a linear factor of $f(x)$.

Perform polynomial division or equate coefficients to divide $f(x)$ by $(x - 3)$ and find the quadratic quotient:\begin{aligned} &2x^3 - x^2 - 13x - 6 \cr &\quad = (x - 3)(2x^2 + ax + 2) \end{aligned}Compare the $x^2$ coefficient on both sides:\begin{aligned} -1 &= -3(2) + a \cr -1 &= -6 + a \cr a &= 5 \end{aligned}So, the quadratic quotient is $2x^2 + 5x + 2$.

Fully factorise the quadratic quotient $2x^2 + 5x + 2$ into two linear factors:\begin{aligned} 2x^2 + 5x + 2 = (2x + 1)(x + 2) \end{aligned}Combine all three factors to express $f(x)$ in its fully factorised form:\begin{aligned} &f(x) \cr &\quad = (x - 3)(2x + 1)(x + 2) \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &f(x) \cr &\quad = (x - 3)(2x + 1)(x + 2) \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your quadratic factorization. Factoring the positive terms of $2x^2 + 5x + 2$ must yield $(2x + 1)(x + 2)$, not $(2x - 1)(x - 2)$.
The question asks you to express $f(x)$ as the product of 'three linear factors'. You must fully factorise the quadratic quotient $2x^2 + 5x + 2$ to complete the problem.
Be careful with your signs. Since $f(3) = 0$, the corresponding factor is $(x - 3)$, not $(x + 3)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Equating Coefficients over Long Division
bradley_insight.content: For factorising cubic polynomials once a root is known, equating coefficients is much faster than running a full synthetic or polynomial division. Since $2x^3$ requires the lead quadratic term to be $2x^2$, and $-6$ requires the constant term to be $+2$ when divided by $-3$, you only need a single comparison to find the middle coefficient $a$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The polynomial $f(x)$ is defined by:\begin{aligned} f(x) = ax^3 + bx^2 - 11x - 6 \end{aligned}where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

Given that both $(x - 2)$ and $(x + 3)$ are factors of $f(x)$, find the values of $a$ and $b$.
steps: According to the Factor Theorem, because $(x - 2)$ and $(x + 3)$ are factors, evaluating $f(x)$ at their roots $x = 2$ and $x = -3$ must result in $0$:\begin{aligned} f(2) &= 0 \cr f(-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}

Evaluate $f(2) = 0$ to set up the first equation:\begin{aligned} f(2) &= a(2)^3 + b(2)^2 - 11(2) - 6 \cr &= 8a + 4b - 22 - 6 \cr &= 8a + 4b - 28 \end{aligned}Setting this to $0$ and dividing by $4$ gives:\begin{aligned} 2a + b &= 7 \cr b &= 7 - 2a \quad \text{--- (1)} \end{aligned}

Evaluate $f(-3) = 0$ to set up the second equation:\begin{aligned} f(-3) &= a(-3)^3 + b(-3)^2 \cr &\quad - 11(-3) - 6 \cr &= -27a + 9b + 33 - 6 \cr &= -27a + 9b + 27 \end{aligned}Setting this to $0$ and dividing by $9$ gives:\begin{aligned} -3a + b &= -3 \cr b &= 3a - 3 \quad \text{--- (2)} \end{aligned}
Solve the simultaneous equations by equating the two expressions for $b$:\begin{aligned} 7 - 2a &= 3a - 3 \cr 10 &= 5a \cr a &= 2 \end{aligned}
Substitute $a = 2$ back into Equation 1 to find $b$:\begin{aligned} b &= 7 - 2(2) \cr b &= 3 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} a &= 2 \cr b &= 3 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You may have made a sign error when expanding $(-3)^3$. $(-3)^3 = -27$, not $+27$. This changes your second equation and leads to incorrect values for $a$ and $b$.
Double check your final substitution. Make sure you solve for $a$ first and substitute its value back to find $b$. It seems you may have reversed the values of $a$ and $b$.
Check your signs in Equation 1. Since $b = 7 - 2a$, substituting $a = 2$ yields $b = 7 - 4 = 3$, not $-3$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Simplifying Simultaneous Coefficients
bradley_insight.content: When solving simultaneous equations from factor evaluations, always search for common factors to simplify the linear equations before equating or using elimination. Reducing $8a + 4b = 28$ directly to $2a + b = 7$ keeps the mental arithmetic simple and highly resistant to minor division errors.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

By considering a change of sign, show that the equation:\begin{aligned} e^x - 4x^3 = 0 \end{aligned}has a root, $\alpha$, in the interval $[0.5, 1.0]$.
steps: Define the equation as a function $f(x)$:\begin{aligned} f(x) = e^x - 4x^3 \end{aligned}According to the Change of Sign rule, if a continuous function $f(x)$ changes sign over an interval $[a, b]$, then there must be at least one root of the equation $f(x) = 0$ in the interval $a < x < b$.

Evaluate the function at the lower boundary $x = 0.5$:\begin{aligned} f(0.5) &= e^{0.5} - 4(0.5)^3 \cr &\approx 1.6487 - 4(0.125) \cr &\approx 1.6487 - 0.5 \cr &= 1.1487 \end{aligned}Since $1.1487 > 0$, the function is positive at $x = 0.5$.

Evaluate the function at the upper boundary $x = 1.0$:\begin{aligned} f(1.0) &= e^{1.0} - 4(1.0)^3 \cr &\approx 2.7183 - 4 \cr &= -1.2817 \end{aligned}Since $-1.2817 < 0$, the function is negative at $x = 1.0$.

Conclude based on the change of sign:

Since $f(x)$ is continuous on the interval $[0.5, 1.0]$, and there is a change of sign between $x = 0.5$ ($f(0.5) > 0$) and $x = 1.0$ ($f(1.0) < 0$), there must be a root $\alpha$ in the interval $0.5 < \alpha < 1.0$.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} f(0.5) &= 1.1487 > 0 \cr f(1.0) &= -1.2817 < 0 \cr 0.5 &< \alpha < 1.0 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your signs during the evaluation steps. Since $e^{0.5} \approx 1.6487$ and $4(0.5)^3 = 0.5$, the value is $1.6487 - 0.5 = 1.1487$, which is positive. At $x = 1.0$, $e^{1.0} \approx 2.7183 < 4$, which yields a negative result.
The change of sign rule only shows that a root lies between the boundaries of the interval, $0.5 < \alpha < 1.0$. It does not mean the root itself is equal to one of the boundaries.

While evaluating $f(0) = 1$ is mathematically correct, the question specifically asks to show that the root lies in the interval $[0.5, 1.0]$. You must use $x = 0.5$ as your lower bound rather than $x = 0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Intermediate Value Theorem
bradley_insight.content: To secure full marks in root-locating questions, you must explicitly state two criteria: first, that there is a change of sign between the boundary values, and second, that the function $f(x)$ is continuous over that interval.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The equation $x^3 - 5x + 3 = 0$ has a real root, $\alpha$, in the interval $[0.5, 1.0]$.

1. Show that $\alpha$ lies in the interval $[0.6, 0.7]$.

2. By considering the sign of the function at a suitable boundary, show that the value of $\alpha$ is $0.66$ correct to $2$ decimal places.
steps: Define the function $f(x) = x^3 - 5x + 3$. To show that the root $\alpha$ lies in the interval $[0.6, 0.7]$, evaluate $f(x)$ at the boundaries $x = 0.6$ and $x = 0.7$:\begin{aligned} f(0.6) &= 0.6^3 - 5(0.6) + 3 \cr &= 0.216 - 3 + 3 \cr &= 0.216 > 0 \cr f(0.7) &= 0.7^3 - 5(0.7) + 3 \cr &= 0.343 - 3.5 + 3 \cr &= -0.157 < 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(0.6) > 0$ and $f(0.7) < 0$, the change of sign confirms that $0.6 < \alpha < 0.7$.

To prove that the root is $0.66$ correct to $2$ decimal places, we must establish that it lies within the rounding boundary interval $[0.655, 0.665]$. Let's test the lower rounding boundary $x = 0.655$:\begin{aligned} f(0.655) &= 0.655^3 - 5(0.655) + 3 \cr &\approx 0.2809 - 3.2750 + 3 \cr &= 0.0059 > 0 \end{aligned}
Now evaluate the function at the target value $x = 0.66$:\begin{aligned} f(0.66) &= 0.66^3 - 5(0.66) + 3 \cr &\approx 0.2875 - 3.3000 + 3 \cr &= -0.0125 < 0 \end{aligned}

Conclude based on the sign change:

Since $f(0.655) > 0$ and $f(0.66) < 0$, the root $\alpha$ must lie in the interval $0.655 < \alpha < 0.66$. Because any value within this narrow interval rounds directly to $0.66$ to $2$ decimal places, the proof is complete.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &0.655 < \alpha < 0.66 \cr &\implies \alpha \approx 0.66 \text{ (to 2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Testing $0.65$ is not sufficient to guarantee that the root rounds to $0.66$. Values between $0.65$ and $0.655$ round down to $0.65$. You must test the exact rounding boundary of $0.655$ to complete the proof.
Check your evaluations. Since $0.6^3 = 0.216$ and $-5(0.6) + 3 = 0$, $f(0.6) = 0.216$, which is positive. At $x = 0.7$, $f(0.7) = -0.157$, which is negative.
While values in this interval do round to $0.66$, your evaluation showed $f(0.66) < 0$ and $f(0.655) > 0$. This confirms the root is in the interval $0.655 < \alpha < 0.66$, not above $0.66$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Root Rounding Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: When an exam asks you to show a root is equal to a value to $d$ decimal places, do not just evaluate the rounded values. You must always test the midpoints of the rounding boundaries (i.e., ending in $5$ at the next decimal place) to prove the root is trapped within the correct rounding region.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The equation $x^3 - 3x - 1 = 0$ has a root, $\alpha$, in the interval $[1.5, 2.0]$.

1. Show that the equation can be rearranged into the iterative formula:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} = \sqrt{3 + \dfrac{1}{x_n}} \end{aligned}2. Using this iterative formula with a starting value of $x_1 = 1.8$, find the values of $x_2$, $x_3$, and $x_4$, giving your answers to $4$ decimal places.
steps: Rearrange the equation $x^3 - 3x - 1 = 0$ to isolate $x$ on one side (dividing by $x \ne 0$):\begin{aligned} x^3 &= 3x + 1 \cr x^2 &= 3 + \dfrac{1}{x} \cr x &= \sqrt{3 + \dfrac{1}{x}} \end{aligned}Writing this in iterative form yields the required formula:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} = \sqrt{3 + \dfrac{1}{x_n}} \end{aligned}
Calculate $x_2$ by substituting $x_1 = 1.8$ into the formula:\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \sqrt{3 + \dfrac{1}{1.8}} \cr &= \sqrt{3 + 0.5556} \cr &= \sqrt{3.5556} \cr &\approx 1.8856 \end{aligned}

Calculate $x_3$ by substituting $x_2 \approx 1.885618$ (using full calculator precision to prevent intermediate rounding errors):\begin{aligned} x_3 &= \sqrt{3 + \dfrac{1}{1.885618}} \cr &\approx \sqrt{3 + 0.5303} \cr &= \sqrt{3.5303} \cr &\approx 1.8789 \end{aligned}
Calculate $x_4$ by substituting $x_3 \approx 1.878916$:\begin{aligned} x_4 &= \sqrt{3 + \dfrac{1}{1.878917}} \cr &\approx \sqrt{3 + 0.5322} \cr &= \sqrt{3.5322} \cr &\approx 1.8794 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} x_2 &\approx 1.8856 \cr x_3 &\approx 1.8789 \cr x_4 &\approx 1.8794 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You may have made an arithmetic slip when evaluating $x_2 = \sqrt{3.5556}$. $\sqrt{3.5555...} \approx 1.8856$, not $1.8878$. This initial rounding slip cascaded into your calculations for $x_3$ and $x_4$.
Check your calculations for $x_4$. Substituting $x_3 \approx 1.8789$ back into the formula yields $\sqrt{3.5322} \approx 1.8794$, not $1.8812$.
Check your calculation steps for $x_3$. Substituting $x_2 \approx 1.8856$ yields $\sqrt{3 + 1/1.8856} \approx 1.8789$. Make sure you divide $1$ by $x_n$ before adding $3$ and taking the square root.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Avoid Intermediate Rounding
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating iterative formulas, never clear your calculator screen or use rounded 4 d.p. values for subsequent steps. Always store the full value in your calculator memory and run the formula on the exact decimal to ensure your final rounded answers are precise.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A curve has the equation $y = e^{-x} + x^2 - 3$.

1. Show that the equation $e^{-x} + x^2 - 3 = 0$ can be rearranged into the iterative form:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} = \sqrt{3 - e^{-x_n}} \end{aligned}2. Using this iterative form with $x_1 = 1.5$, find the values of $x_2$, $x_3$, and $x_4$, giving your answers to $4$ decimal places.
steps: Set $y = 0$ to find the $x$-intercept root of the equation:\begin{aligned} e^{-x} + x^2 - 3 &= 0 \cr x^2 &= 3 - e^{-x} \cr x &= \sqrt{3 - e^{-x}} \end{aligned}Writing this in iterative form yields the required equation:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} = \sqrt{3 - e^{-x_n}} \end{aligned}
Calculate $x_2$ by substituting $x_1 = 1.5$ into the formula:\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \sqrt{3 - e^{-1.5}} \cr &\approx \sqrt{3 - 0.2231} \cr &= \sqrt{2.7769} \cr &\approx 1.6664 \end{aligned}

Calculate $x_3$ by substituting $x_2 \approx 1.666394$ (using full calculator precision):\begin{aligned} x_3 &= \sqrt{3 - e^{-1.666394}} \cr &\approx \sqrt{3 - 0.1889} \cr &= \sqrt{2.8111} \cr &\approx 1.6766 \end{aligned}
Calculate $x_4$ by substituting $x_3 \approx 1.676626$:\begin{aligned} x_4 &= \sqrt{3 - e^{-1.676626}} \cr &\approx \sqrt{3 - 0.1870} \cr &= \sqrt{2.8130} \cr &\approx 1.6772 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} x_2 &\approx 1.6664 \cr x_3 &\approx 1.6766 \cr x_4 &\approx 1.6772 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You may have made a rounding error in $x_3$. $e^{-1.6664} \approx 0.1889$, which yields $x_3 = \sqrt{3 - 0.1889} \approx 1.6766$, not $1.6772$. Be careful not to skip an iteration step.
Check your calculations for $x_4$. Substituting $x_3 \approx 1.6766$ into the formula yields $\sqrt{2.8130} \approx 1.6772$, not $1.6912$.
Check your exponent sign in $x_3$. Remember that the term is $e^{-x_n}$. A positive exponent $e^{x_n}$ will yield a completely incorrect series of iterative approximations.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Exponential Sign Care
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating terms of the form $e^{-x_n}$ on a calculator, always be careful with the negative sign in the exponent. Dropping this sign changes the decay term into an exponential growth term, causing the iteration to rapidly diverge.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The equation $f(x) = 0$ is to be solved, where $f(x) = e^x - 5x^3$.

1. Show that the Newton-Raphson formula for this equation can be written in the form:\begin{aligned} &x_{n+1} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{e^{x_n}(x_n - 1) - 10x_n^3}{e^{x_n} - 15x_n^2} \end{aligned}2. Using the starting value $x_1 = 0.8$, find the values of $x_2$ and $x_3$ correct to $4$ decimal places.
steps: Find the derivative of $f(x) = e^x - 5x^3$:\begin{aligned} f'(x) = e^x - 15x^2 \end{aligned}The general Newton-Raphson formula is:\begin{aligned} x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} \end{aligned}

Substitute $f(x_n)$ and $f'(x_n)$ into the formula:\begin{aligned} &x_{n+1} \cr &\quad = x_n - \dfrac{e^{x_n} - 5x_n^3}{e^{x_n} - 15x_n^2} \end{aligned}Combining over a common denominator, the numerator simplifies to:\begin{aligned} &x_n(e^{x_n} - 15x_n^2) - (e^{x_n} - 5x_n^3) \cr &\quad = x_n e^{x_n} - 15x_n^3 - e^{x_n} + 5x_n^3 \cr &\quad = e^{x_n}(x_n - 1) - 10x_n^3 \end{aligned}Thus, the formula becomes:\begin{aligned} &x_{n+1} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{e^{x_n}(x_n - 1) - 10x_n^3}{e^{x_n} - 15x_n^2} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} x_2 &\approx 0.7546 \cr x_3 &\approx 0.7515 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your division sign when computing $x_3$. Since both $f(x_2)$ and $f'(x_2)$ are negative, their division yields a positive value: $\dfrac{-0.0198}{-6.4143} \approx +0.0031$. Subtracting this positive value gives $0.7546 - 0.0031 = 0.7515$, not $0.7546 + 0.0031 = 0.7577$.

Be careful with signs during division in the step for $x_2$. We have $0.8 - \dfrac{-0.3345}{-7.3745}$. Since the fraction evaluates to positive $+0.0454$, we are subtracting a positive number, yielding $0.8 - 0.0454 = 0.7546$, not $0.8 + 0.0454 = 0.8454$.

This value of $x_3$ is extremely close and corresponds to keeping full calculator precision ($x_3 \approx 0.7512$). However, if using the standard classroom method of substituting the rounded 4 d.p. value $x_2 = 0.7546$ back into the formula, the result resolves to $0.7515$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Newton-Raphson Sign Clashes
bradley_insight.content: The Newton-Raphson method is a major, high-yield A-Level topic, but it is highly prone to sign errors. Since the formula is $x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$, you must track three separate negative signs: the minus in the formula, the sign of $f(x_n)$, and the sign of $f'(x_n)$. Writing each evaluation step out clearly is key to preventing mistakes.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Solve the equation:\begin{aligned} \sec^2 \theta + 3\tan \theta = 5 \end{aligned}for $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$, giving your answers correct to $1$ decimal place where appropriate.
steps: Use the fundamental trigonometric identity $\sec^2 \theta = 1 + \tan^2 \theta$ to write the entire equation in terms of $\tan \theta$:\begin{aligned} (1 + \tan^2 \theta) + 3\tan \theta = 5 \end{aligned}
Rearrange the equation to form a standard quadratic equation in $\tan \theta$:\begin{aligned} \tan^2 \theta + 3\tan \theta - 4 = 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} (\tan \theta + 4)(\tan \theta - 1) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives two possible values for $\tan \theta$:\begin{aligned} \tan \theta &= 1 \cr \tan \theta &= -4 \end{aligned}
Solve for the first case, $\tan \theta = 1$, in the domain $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:\begin{aligned} \theta &= \tan^{-1}(1) \cr &= 45.0^\circ, \, 225.0^\circ \end{aligned}

Solve for the second case, $\tan \theta = -4$, in the domain $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:

The principal value is $\theta \approx -75.96^\circ$. Find the positive solutions within the required domain:\begin{aligned} \theta &= 180^\circ - 75.96^\circ \cr &= 104.0^\circ \cr \theta &= 360^\circ - 75.96^\circ \cr &= 284.0^\circ \end{aligned}Combining all solutions gives the final set of answers.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \theta &= 45.0^\circ, \, 104.0^\circ, \cr &\quad 225.0^\circ, \, 284.0^\circ \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You may have missed one of the negative tangent solutions. Since $\tan \theta = -4$, there are two solutions in the $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$ range: one in the second quadrant ($180^\circ - 76.0^\circ = 104.0^\circ$) and one in the fourth quadrant ($360^\circ - 76.0^\circ = 284.0^\circ$).

Be careful when translating negative tangent values. The root $x = -4$ corresponds to angles in the second and fourth quadrants, which are $104.0^\circ$ and $284.0^\circ$, not $76.0^\circ$ and $256.0^\circ$.
You found the solutions for the factor $(\tan \theta - 1) = 0$, but you must also solve for $(\tan \theta + 4) = 0$ to get the complete set of four solutions.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Quadrant Analysis of Negatives
bradley_insight.content: When solving trig equations yielding negative values (like $\tan \theta = -4$), always sketch a CAST diagram or tangent curve to help locate the correct quadrants. Tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants, which dictates performing $180^\circ - |\theta_{PV}|$ and $360^\circ - |\theta_{PV}|$ to find the correct angles within the positive domain.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Solve the equation:\begin{aligned} 2\text{cosec}^2 \theta + 5\cot \theta = 5 \end{aligned}for $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$, giving your answers correct to $1$ decimal place where appropriate.
steps: Use the cosecant-cotangent identity $\csc^2 \theta = 1 + \cot^2 \theta$ to rewrite the equation in terms of $\cot \theta$:\begin{aligned} 2(1 + \cot^2 \theta) + 5\cot \theta = 5 \end{aligned}
Expand and rearrange to form a standard quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} 2 + 2\cot^2 \theta + 5\cot \theta &= 5 \cr 2\cot^2 \theta + 5\cot \theta - 3 &= 0 \end{aligned}
Factorise the quadratic expression:\begin{aligned} (2\cot \theta - 1)(\cot \theta + 3) &= 0 \cr \cot \theta &= 0.5 \cr \cot \theta &= -3 \end{aligned}
Solve the first branch, $\cot \theta = 0.5$, which is equivalent to $\tan \theta = 2$:\begin{aligned} \theta &= \tan^{-1}(2) \cr &\approx 63.4^\circ, \, 243.4^\circ \end{aligned}

Solve the second branch, $\cot \theta = -3$, which is equivalent to $\tan \theta = -\dfrac{1}{3}$:

The principal value is $\theta \approx -18.4^\circ$. Finding the positive solutions in the domain:\begin{aligned} \theta &= 180^\circ - 18.4^\circ \cr &= 161.6^\circ \cr \theta &= 360^\circ - 18.4^\circ \cr &= 341.6^\circ \end{aligned}Combining all solutions yields the final set of answers.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \theta &= 63.4^\circ, \, 161.6^\circ, \cr &\quad 243.4^\circ, \, 341.6^\circ \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Make sure you completely evaluate both branches of the quadratic equation. The branch $\cot \theta = -3 \implies \tan \theta = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ yields two solutions in the domain: $161.6^\circ$ and $341.6^\circ$.
When taking the reciprocal of $\cot \theta = 0.5$, you must solve $\tan \theta = 2$. It seems you may have mistakenly solved $\tan \theta = 0.5$, which yields $\theta \approx 26.6^\circ$.
Make sure you fully solve the quadratic equation. Both positive and negative trigonometric branches should yield exactly two distinct solutions within the $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$ interval.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Reciprocating Trig Equations
bradley_insight.content: When solving equations written in terms of reciprocal functions like $\cot \theta = y$, always convert them to primary functions immediately using $\tan \theta = \dfrac{1}{y}$ before using your calculator's inverse functions. This completely avoids simple input mistakes.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Solve the equation:\begin{aligned} 3\cos 2\theta - \sin \theta = 2 \end{aligned}for $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$, giving your answers correct to $1$ decimal place where appropriate.
steps: Use the double-angle cosine identity $\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2 \theta$ to write the equation in terms of $\sin \theta$:\begin{aligned} 3(1 - 2\sin^2 \theta) - \sin \theta = 2 \end{aligned}

Expand, simplify, and rearrange the terms into a standard quadratic form:\begin{aligned} 3 - 6\sin^2 \theta - \sin \theta &= 2 \cr -6\sin^2 \theta - \sin \theta + 1 &= 0 \cr 6\sin^2 \theta + \sin \theta - 1 &= 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} (3\sin \theta - 1)(2\sin \theta + 1) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives two possible values for $\sin \theta$:\begin{aligned} \sin \theta &= \dfrac{1}{3} \cr \sin \theta &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}

Solve the first case, $\sin \theta = \dfrac{1}{3}$, in the domain $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:\begin{aligned} \theta &= \sin^{-1}\big(\dfrac{1}{3}\big) \cr &\approx 19.5^\circ, \, 160.5^\circ \end{aligned}

Solve the second case, $\sin \theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, in the domain $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:

The principal value is $\theta = -30.0^\circ$. The positive angles within the domain are:\begin{aligned} \theta &= 180^\circ - (-30.0^\circ) \cr &= 210.0^\circ \cr \theta &= 360^\circ + (-30.0^\circ) \cr &= 330.0^\circ \end{aligned}Combining all solutions gives the final set of answers.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \theta &= 19.5^\circ, \, 160.5^\circ, \cr &\quad 210.0^\circ, \, 330.0^\circ \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your quadrant adjustments for $\sin \theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. Sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants. The third quadrant solution is $180^\circ - (-30.0^\circ) = 210.0^\circ$, not $150.0^\circ$ (which is in the second quadrant where sine is positive).
Remember to solve completely for both roots of your factorised quadratic. The branch $\sin \theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ must produce two positive angles in the interval: $210.0^\circ$ and $330.0^\circ$.

For the positive branch $\sin \theta = \dfrac{1}{3}$, sine is positive in the first and second quadrants. This yields two solutions in the domain: $19.5^\circ$ and $180^\circ - 19.5^\circ = 160.5^\circ$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Choosing Double Angle Identities
bradley_insight.content: When dealing with $\cos 2\theta$, always look at the other trigonometric term in the equation to decide which identity to use. Since the other term is $-\sin \theta$, using $\cos 2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2 \theta$ immediately yields a solvable quadratic in sine.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Solve the equation:\begin{aligned} 4\sin^2 \theta - 8\cos \theta = 1 \end{aligned}for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, giving your answers in terms of $\arccos$.
steps: Use the fundamental identity $\sin^2 \theta = 1 - \cos^2 \theta$ to write the entire equation in terms of $\cos \theta$:\begin{aligned} 4(1 - \cos^2 \theta) - 8\cos \theta = 1 \end{aligned}

Expand, simplify, and rearrange the quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} 4 - 4\cos^2 \theta - 8\cos \theta - 1 &= 0 \cr -4\cos^2 \theta - 8\cos \theta + 3 &= 0 \cr 4\cos^2 \theta + 8\cos \theta - 3 &= 0 \end{aligned}

Since the quadratic expression does not factorise cleanly, apply the quadratic formula to solve for $\cos \theta$:\begin{aligned} &\cos \theta \cr &\quad = \dfrac{-8 \pm \sqrt{8^2 - 4(4)(-3)}}{2(4)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{-8 \pm \sqrt{112}}{8} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{-8 \pm 4\sqrt{7}}{8} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{7}}{2} \end{aligned}

Determine the valid branch of solutions by checking the range constraint of cosine, $-1 \le \cos \theta \le 1$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{-2 - \sqrt{7}}{2} &\approx -2.32 \quad \text{(outside range)} \cr \dfrac{-2 + \sqrt{7}}{2} &\approx 0.32 \quad \text{(within range)} \end{aligned}Therefore, we only solve the equation for the valid branch: $\cos \theta = \dfrac{-2 + \sqrt{7}}{2}$.

Find the solutions in radians within the domain $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$:\begin{aligned} \theta &= \arccos\big(\dfrac{-2 + \sqrt{7}}{2}\big) \cr \theta &= 2\pi - \arccos\big(\dfrac{-2 + \sqrt{7}}{2}\big) \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \theta &= \arccos\big(\dfrac{-2 + \sqrt{7}}{2}\big), \cr &\quad 2\pi - \arccos\big(\dfrac{-2 + \sqrt{7}}{2}\big) \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Remember to evaluate the validity of both branches of your quadratic formula result. The branch $\cos \theta = \dfrac{-2 - \sqrt{7}}{2} \approx -2.32$ is strictly outside the defined range of cosine, $-1 \le \cos \theta \le 1$, and produces no real solutions.

Check your quadrant adjustments for a positive cosine value. Cosine is positive in the first and fourth quadrants. The fourth quadrant solution is $2\pi - \theta_{PV}$, not $\pi - \theta_{PV}$ (which is in the second quadrant).

You found the principal value in the first quadrant, but remember that cosine is also positive in the fourth quadrant. You must include the corresponding fourth-quadrant solution $2\pi - \theta_{PV}$ to complete the set.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Range Boundaries of Cosine
bradley_insight.content: Whenever you solve a quadratic equation in sine or cosine, always check the validity of your roots. Since $-1 \le \cos \theta \le 1$, any roots outside this range are invalid. Discarding the incorrect branch immediately is essential to avoid writing down phantom solutions.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Solve the equation:\begin{aligned} 3\sin 2\theta = 4\cos \theta \end{aligned}for $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$, giving your answers correct to $1$ decimal place where appropriate.
steps: Use the double-angle sine identity $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin \theta \cos \theta$ to expand the left-hand side:\begin{aligned} 3(2\sin \theta \cos \theta) = 4\cos \theta \end{aligned}
Bring all terms to one side of the equation:\begin{aligned} 6\sin \theta \cos \theta - 4\cos \theta = 0 \end{aligned}

Factorise out the common term $2\cos \theta$:\begin{aligned} 2\cos \theta(3\sin \theta - 2) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives two branches to solve:\begin{aligned} \cos \theta &= 0 \cr \sin \theta &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}
Solve the first branch, $\cos \theta = 0$, in the domain $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:\begin{aligned} \theta = 90.0^\circ, \, 270.0^\circ \end{aligned}

Solve the second branch, $\sin \theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$, in the domain $0^\circ \le \theta \le 360^\circ$:\begin{aligned} \theta &= \sin^{-1}\big(\dfrac{2}{3}\big) \cr &\approx 41.8^\circ \cr \theta &= 180^\circ - 41.8^\circ \cr &= 138.2^\circ \end{aligned}Combining all solutions yields the final set of answers.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \theta &= 41.8^\circ, \, 90.0^\circ, \cr &\quad 138.2^\circ, \, 270.0^\circ \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You may have made the classic mistake of dividing both sides by $\cos \theta$ in the first step. Dividing by a variable term that can equal zero loses the valid solutions where $\cos \theta = 0 \implies \theta = 90.0^\circ, 270.0^\circ$. Always bring terms to one side and factorise.

Check your second quadrant calculation for $\sin \theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$. Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants. The second quadrant solution is $180^\circ - 41.8^\circ = 138.2^\circ$, not $180^\circ + 41.8^\circ = 221.8^\circ$.
You found the solutions for the $\cos \theta = 0$ branch, but you must also solve for $3\sin \theta - 2 = 0 \implies \sin \theta = \dfrac{2}{3}$ to find the complete set of four solutions.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Never Divide by Variable Trig Terms
bradley_insight.content: A very common error in A-Level exams is dividing both sides of an equation by a function like $\cos \theta$. This is algebraically illegal because it assumes $\cos \theta \ne 0$, resulting in the loss of major valid branches of solutions. Always bring all terms to one side and factorise.

subtopic: Sum of an AP or GP
question:
Clara and Dan are saving up for a holiday. Clara saves £80 in the first month, and increases the amount she saves by £15 each month.

1. Calculate how much Clara saves in total over 2 years (24 months).

Dan also saves £80 in the first month. The amount he saves each month is 8% more than the amount he saved in the previous month.

2. Explain why the amounts Dan saves each month form a geometric progression.

3. Calculate how much Dan saves in total over 2 years (24 months), giving your answer to the nearest pound.

4. Determine the month in which Dan's monthly savings first exceed Clara's monthly savings.
steps: Clara's monthly savings form an arithmetic progression with first term $a = 80$, common difference $d = 15$, and number of terms $n = 24$ months. Use the arithmetic sum formula:\begin{aligned} S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a + (n-1)d\big) \end{aligned}Substitute the values to find the total sum:\begin{aligned} S_{24} &= \dfrac{24}{2}\big(2(80) + (24 - 1)15\big) \cr &= 12(160 + 345) \cr &= 12(505) \cr &= 6060 \end{aligned}Clara saves £6060 in total.

Dan's monthly savings increase by a constant percentage of $8\%$ each month. This means each month's savings is a constant multiplier of $1.08$ times the previous month's savings:\begin{aligned} \text{Month}_{n+1} = 1.08 \times \text{Month}_n \end{aligned}Because there is a constant common ratio of $r = 1.08$, the savings form a geometric progression.

Dan's savings form a geometric progression with first term $a = 80$, common ratio $r = 1.08$, and $n = 24$ months. Use the geometric sum formula:\begin{aligned} S_n = \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1} \end{aligned}Substitute the values to calculate the total sum:\begin{aligned} S_{24} &= \dfrac{80(1.08^{24} - 1)}{1.08 - 1} \cr &\approx \dfrac{80(6.3412 - 1)}{0.08} \cr &= 1000(5.3412) \cr &\approx 5341 \end{aligned}Dan saves £5341 to the nearest pound.

Write the expressions for the savings in month $n$ for both Clara ($C_n$) and Dan ($D_n$):\begin{aligned} C_n &= 80 + 15(n - 1) \cr D_n &= 80(1.08)^{n-1} \end{aligned}We seek the smallest integer $n$ such that $D_n > C_n$. Let's test values near $n = 21$ and $n = 22$:\begin{aligned} \text{For } n &= 21: \cr C_{21} &= 80 + 15(20) \cr &= 380 \cr D_{21} &= 80(1.08)^{20} \cr &\approx 372.88 \cr \text{For } n &= 22: \cr C_{22} &= 80 + 15(21) \cr &= 395 \cr D_{22} &= 80(1.08)^{21} \cr &\approx 402.71 \end{aligned}Therefore, Dan's monthly savings first exceed Clara's monthly savings in month 22.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} S_{\text{Clara}} &= 6060 \cr S_{\text{Dan}} &= 5341 \cr \text{Month } &22 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your calculations for month 21. In month 21, Clara saves $80 + 15(20) = 380$, while Dan saves $80(1.08)^{20} \approx 372.88$, which is still less than Clara. Dan first exceeds Clara in month 22.
Check your term index in the arithmetic sum formula. The formula uses $(n-1)d$. For $n = 24$, this is $23d$, which is $345$. Using $24d = 360$ gives an incorrect sum of $5820$ or $6120$.

Check your calculation for Dan's geometric sum. The formula is $\dfrac{80(1.08^{24} - 1)}{0.08} = 1000(1.08^{24} - 1)$. Make sure you evaluate the exponent power first before subtracting $1$ and multiplying.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Track Term Indices Carefully
bradley_insight.content: When working with series word problems, be extremely careful with indices. The sum formula uses $(n-1)d$ and the $n$-th term formula uses $a r^{n-1}$. It is very common under pressure to use $nd$ or $a r^n$, which will shift all your calculations by a month and result in lost marks.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

An athlete is training for a marathon. On day 1, they run $5$ km. Each day they increase their distance by $d$ km.

1. Write down an expression in terms of $d$ for the distance run on day $20$.

2. Given that the total distance run over the first $20$ days is $195$ km, find the value of $d$.

3. Hence, calculate the distance the athlete runs on day $30$.
steps: Use the standard $n$-th term formula for an arithmetic progression, $u_n = a + (n-1)d$, with first term $a = 5$:\begin{aligned} u_{20} &= 5 + (20 - 1)d \cr &= 5 + 19d \end{aligned}

Set up the sum equation over the first $20$ days using $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a + (n-1)d\big)$:\begin{aligned} S_{20} &= \dfrac{20}{2}\big(2(5) + (20 - 1)d\big) \cr 195 &= 10(10 + 19d) \end{aligned}
Solve for the common difference $d$:\begin{aligned} 19.5 &= 10 + 19d \cr 19d &= 9.5 \cr d &= 0.5 \end{aligned}So the common daily increase is $0.5$ km.

Calculate the distance run on day $30$ using $a = 5$ and $d = 0.5$:\begin{aligned} u_{30} &= a + 29d \cr &= 5 + 29(0.5) \cr &= 5 + 14.5 \cr &= 19.5 \end{aligned}The athlete runs $19.5$ km on day $30$.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} u_{20} &= 5 + 19d \cr d &= 0.5 \cr u_{30} &= 19.5 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Remember that the $n$-th term formula is $u_n = a + (n-1)d$. The distance on day 20 must be $5 + 19d$, not $5 + 20d$.

Check your expansion of the sum formula. $S_{20} = 10(2a + 19d)$. Since $a = 5$, $2a = 10$, giving $10(10 + 19d) = 195$. If you used $a = 5$ instead of $2a = 10$, you would get an incorrect value of $d$.
Check your calculation for day 30. The distance is $a + 29d$. Since $d = 0.5$, this evaluates to $5 + 14.5 = 19.5$ km, not $20.0$ km.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: AS Level Foundations
bradley_insight.content: Arithmetic sequences are classified as AS-Level material, meaning they form the foundation of series questions. Always ensure you distinguish between the $n$-th term formula $a+(n-1)d$ and the sum formula $\dfrac{n}{2}(2a+(n-1)d)$; mixing these up is a very common source of lost marks.

subtopic: Sum to infinity of a GP
question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A geometric series has a first term $a$ and a common ratio $r$.

1. Given that the second term of the series is $6$ and the sum to infinity is $25$, show that:\begin{aligned} 25r^2 - 25r + 6 = 0 \end{aligned}2. Find the two possible values of $r$, and the corresponding values of $a$.
steps: Write down expressions for the second term and the sum to infinity:\begin{aligned} ar &= 6 \cr \dfrac{a}{1 - r} &= 25 \end{aligned}
Isolate $a$ in both equations and equate them to eliminate $a$:\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{6}{r} \cr a &= 25(1 - r) \cr \dfrac{6}{r} &= 25(1 - r) \end{aligned}
Rearrange the equation into the required quadratic form:\begin{aligned} 6 &= 25r(1 - r) \cr 6 &= 25r - 25r^2 \cr 25r^2 - 25r + 6 &= 0 \end{aligned}

Solve the quadratic equation using factorisation:\begin{aligned} (5r - 2)(5r - 3) &= 0 \cr r &= \dfrac{2}{5} \cr r &= \dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}Both ratios are valid because they satisfy the convergence condition $|r| < 1$.

Find the corresponding values of $a$ for each value of $r$:\begin{aligned} \text{For } r &= \dfrac{2}{5}: \cr a &= \dfrac{6}{2/5} \cr &= 15 \cr \text{For } r &= \dfrac{3}{5}: \cr a &= \dfrac{6}{3/5} \cr &= 10 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{2}{5}, \, a = 15 \cr r &= \dfrac{3}{5}, \, a = 10 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your signs when factorising the quadratic equation $25r^2 - 25r + 6 = 0$. Since the middle term is negative and the constant term is positive, both roots must be positive: $(5r - 2)(5r - 3) = 0 \implies r = 0.4, 0.6$.
When calculating the first term $a$, remember that $a = \dfrac{6}{r}$. Dividing $6$ by a fraction $\dfrac{2}{5}$ is equivalent to $6 \times \dfrac{5}{2} = 15$, not $6 \times 0.4 = 2.4$.
The quadratic equation yields two distinct positive roots, both of which are strictly less than $1$ (convergent). You must evaluate and write down both valid coordinate pairs of $(a, r)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Convergence Restrictions on Infinity
bradley_insight.content: Whenever a question refers to the 'sum to infinity', keep the convergence condition $|r| < 1$ in mind. If your quadratic equation produces any root $|r| \ge 1$, you must reject it immediately because a geometric series only converges when the common ratio lies strictly between $-1$ and $1$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Evaluate the following sums:

1. \begin{aligned} \sum_{r=1}^{50} (3r + 2) \end{aligned}2. \begin{aligned} \sum_{k=1}^{10} (5\cdot 2^k) \end{aligned}
steps: Identify the first sum $\sum_{r=1}^{50} (3r + 2)$ as an arithmetic series with $n = 50$ terms. Calculate the first term $a$ and last term $L$:\begin{aligned} a &= 3(1) + 2 \cr &= 5 \cr L &= 3(50) + 2 \cr &= 152 \end{aligned}
Use the arithmetic sum formula $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + L)$ to find the total:\begin{aligned} S_{50} &= \dfrac{50}{2}(5 + 152) \cr &= 25(157) \cr &= 3925 \end{aligned}

Identify the second sum $\sum_{k=1}^{10} (5\cdot 2^k)$ as a geometric series. Write out the first two terms to find $a$ and $r$:\begin{aligned} u_1 &= 5\cdot 2^1 \cr &= 10 \cr u_2 &= 5\cdot 2^2 \cr &= 20 \end{aligned}This gives a first term of $a = 10$, a common ratio of $r = 2$, and $n = 10$ terms.

Use the geometric sum formula $S_n = \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$ to calculate the total sum:\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10(2^{10} - 1)}{2 - 1} \cr &= 10(1024 - 1) \cr &= 10(1023) \cr &= 10230 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \sum_{r=1}^{50} (3r + 2) &= 3925 \cr \sum_{k=1}^{10} (5\cdot 2^k) &= 10230 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Be careful when identifying the first term $a$ of the geometric series. Since the lower limit is $k = 1$, the first term is $5 \cdot 2^1 = 10$, not $5$. Using $a = 5$ yields an incorrect sum of $5115$.

Check your arithmetic on Clara's sum. Make sure you add the constant $2$ to the first and last term calculation: $a = 5$ and $L = 152$. Forgetting to add $2$ to the terms will lead to an incorrect sum.
Check your geometric sum power index. The series has exactly $10$ terms ($k=1$ to $10$). Using $n=9$ instead of $10$ in the formula will produce an incorrect total.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Identifying First Terms in Sigma
bradley_insight.content: Never assume the coefficient of a term is the first term $a$ in sigma notation. Always substitute the lower limit of the sum (such as $k=1$ or $r=1$) directly into the expression to find the true first term of the series.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A sequence is defined by the recurrence relation:\begin{aligned} u_{n+1} = p u_n + q, \quad \text{for } n \ge 1 \end{aligned}where $p$ and $q$ are constants.

Given that $u_1 = 4$, $u_2 = 14$, and $u_3 = 44$:

1. Find the values of $p$ and $q$.

2. Calculate the value of $u_4$.
steps: Use the recurrence relation to set up a linear equation for $u_2$ in terms of $u_1$:\begin{aligned} u_2 &= p u_1 + q \cr 14 &= 4p + q \quad \text{--- (1)} \end{aligned}
Set up a second linear equation for $u_3$ in terms of $u_2$:\begin{aligned} u_3 &= p u_2 + q \cr 44 &= 14p + q \quad \text{--- (2)} \end{aligned}
Solve the simultaneous equations by subtracting Equation 1 from Equation 2:\begin{aligned} (14p + q) - (4p + q) &= 44 - 14 \cr 10p &= 30 \cr p &= 3 \end{aligned}
Substitute $p = 3$ back into Equation 1 to find $q$:\begin{aligned} 4(3) + q &= 14 \cr 12 + q &= 14 \cr q &= 2 \end{aligned}
Use the solved relation $u_{n+1} = 3u_n + 2$ with $u_3 = 44$ to calculate the value of $u_4$:\begin{aligned} u_4 &= 3u_3 + 2 \cr &= 3(44) + 2 \cr &= 132 + 2 \cr &= 134 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} p &= 3 \cr q &= 2 \cr u_4 &= 134 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Don't forget to add the constant term $q = 2$ in the final step. $u_4 = 3(44) + 2 = 134$, not $132$.
Check your signs during subtraction. Subtracting $(4p+q)$ from $(14p+q)$ yields $+10p$, not $-10p$. Similarly, $44-14 = +30$, which gives $p = 3$.
You wrote down the value of $u_3$ instead of calculating the next term $u_4$. Make sure to run the recurrence relation once more using $u_3 = 44$ to find $u_4$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Recurrence Linear Systems
bradley_insight.content: Recurrence relation problems are highly structured. Subtracting adjacent terms (such as $u_3 - u_2$) directly eliminates the additive constant $q$, immediately yielding a single-variable equation in the common multiplier $p$. This is always the most efficient path to solve these systems.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

1. Show that the expression:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} \end{aligned}can be written as $\csc^2 x - \sec^2 x$.

2. Hence find:\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} \text{d}x \end{aligned}
steps: To prove the identity, split the algebraic fraction into two separate terms over the common denominator:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} - \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x} - \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} \end{aligned}

Apply the reciprocal identities $\csc x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ and $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$ to complete the proof:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x} - \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \csc^2 x - \sec^2 x \end{aligned}

Use the simplified identity to rewrite the integral in terms of standard integrable functions:\begin{aligned} &\int \dfrac{\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x}{\sin^2 x \cos^2 x} \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int (\csc^2 x - \sec^2 x) \text{d}x \end{aligned}

Integrate each term individually using standard trigonometric integrals, remembering to add the constant of integration $C$:\begin{aligned} &\int \csc^2 x \text{d}x = -\cot x \cr &\int \sec^2 x \text{d}x = \tan x \cr &\int (\csc^2 x - \sec^2 x) \text{d}x \cr &\quad = -\cot x - \tan x + C \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} -\cot x - \tan x + C \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your standard integrals carefully. The integral of $\csc^2 x \text{d}x$ is $-\cot x + C$, not positive $\cot x + C$.
Be careful with your signs during integration. The integral of $-\sec^2 x \text{d}x$ is $-\tan x + C$. It seems you may have mistakenly integrated it as a positive tangent.
This is algebraically correct, but do not forget to include the arbitrary constant of integration, $+ C$, for an indefinite integral.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Splitting Complex Fractions
bradley_insight.content: When simplifying trigonometric quotients with a single term in the denominator, split the fraction into individual terms immediately. This frequently reduces the expression to basic reciprocal functions like $\sec^2 x$ or $\csc^2 x$, which have standard, easily integrable forms.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

1. Show that:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x \sin^2 x} \end{aligned}can be written as $\csc^2 x$.

2. Hence find:\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x \sin^2 x} \text{d}x \end{aligned}
steps: Substitute the Pythagorean identity $1 - \sin^2 x = \cos^2 x$ into the numerator of the expression:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x \sin^2 x} = \dfrac{\cos^2 x}{\cos^2 x \sin^2 x} \end{aligned}

Cancel the common term $\cos^2 x$ from both the numerator and the denominator, and apply the reciprocal identity $\csc x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\sin^2 x} = \csc^2 x \end{aligned}
Rewrite the integral using the proven identity:\begin{aligned} &\int \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x \sin^2 x} \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int \csc^2 x \text{d}x \end{aligned}
Perform the integration using the standard trigonometric derivative rule, where the derivative of $\cot x$ is $-\csc^2 x$:\begin{aligned} \int \csc^2 x \text{d}x = -\cot x + C \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} -\cot x + C \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Remember that the derivative of $\cot x$ is $-\csc^2 x$. Therefore, the indefinite integral of $\csc^2 x \text{d}x$ must be $-\cot x + C$, not positive $\cot x + C$.

Double check your reciprocal identities. Since $\csc x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}$, the integral simplifies to $\int \csc^2 x \text{d}x$, which integrates to $-\cot x + C$. It seems you may have integrated as if it simplified to $\sec^2 x$.
Your integration is correct, but always remember to add the arbitrary constant of integration, $+ C$, to complete any indefinite integration problem.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Spotting Pythagorean Identities
bradley_insight.content: Always look out for the standard identity $1 - \sin^2 x = \cos^2 x$ in algebraic fractions. Substituting this identity simplifies the quotient instantly, leaving a single reciprocal function that can be integrated using basic standard formulas.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

1. Show that:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin^2 2x} \end{aligned}can be written as $\csc 2x \cot 2x$.

2. Hence find:\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin^2 2x} \text{d}x \end{aligned}
steps: Separate the fraction into a product of two distinct trigonometric ratios:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin^2 2x} &= \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin 2x \cdot \sin 2x} \cr &= \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin 2x} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sin 2x} \end{aligned}

Use the standard definitions $\cot 2x = \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin 2x}$ and $\csc 2x = \dfrac{1}{\sin 2x}$ to complete the proof:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin 2x} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sin 2x} &= \cot 2x \csc 2x \cr &= \csc 2x \cot 2x \end{aligned}
Rewrite the integral using the simplified identity:\begin{aligned} &\int \dfrac{\cos 2x}{\sin^2 2x} \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int \csc 2x \cot 2x \text{d}x \end{aligned}

Apply the standard integral $\int \csc u \cot u \text{d}u = -\csc u + C$. Since $u = 2x$, use the reverse chain rule and divide the result by the linear coefficient $2$:\begin{aligned} \int \csc 2x \cot 2x \text{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\csc 2x + C \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} -\dfrac{1}{2}\csc 2x + C \end{aligned}

question:

1. Show that the expression:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sec^2 x - 1}{\sin^2 x} \end{aligned}can be written as $\sec^2 x$.

2. Hence find:\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{\sec^2 x - 1}{\sin^2 x} \text{d}x \end{aligned}
steps: Substitute the standard Pythagorean identity $\sec^2 x - 1 = \tan^2 x$ into the numerator of the expression:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sec^2 x - 1}{\sin^2 x} = \dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\sin^2 x} \end{aligned}

Use the definition $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ to rewrite $\tan^2 x$, and expand the compound fraction:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\tan^2 x}{\sin^2 x} &= \dfrac{\sin^2 x / \cos^2 x}{\sin^2 x} \cr &= \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\cos^2 x \cdot \sin^2 x} \end{aligned}
Cancel the common term $\sin^2 x$ from both the numerator and the denominator, and apply the definition of secant to complete the proof:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{\cos^2 x} = \sec^2 x \end{aligned}
Rewrite the integral using the simplified identity:\begin{aligned} &\int \dfrac{\sec^2 x - 1}{\sin^2 x} \text{d}x \cr &\quad = \int \sec^2 x \text{d}x \end{aligned}
Integrate using the standard trigonometric derivative rule, where the derivative of $\tan x$ is exactly $\sec^2 x$:\begin{aligned} \int \sec^2 x \text{d}x = \tan x + C \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \tan x + C \end{aligned}

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The curve $C$ has equation:\begin{aligned} &y = (c - x)\ln x \cr &\text{where } c \text{ is a constant } (c > 1) \end{aligned}The curve intersects the $x$-axis at the points $(1,0)$ and $(c,0)$.

Find, in terms of $c$, the exact area of the finite region bounded by the curve $C$ and the $x$-axis.
steps: The curve intersects the $x$-axis at the boundaries $x = 1$ and $x = c$. To find the exact area, set up the definite integral of the function over this interval:\begin{aligned} A = \int_{1}^{c} (c - x)\ln x \text{d}x \end{aligned}We can split this into two separate integrals to simplify the integration by parts:\begin{aligned} A &= c \int_{1}^{c} \ln x \text{d}x - \int_{1}^{c} x\ln x \text{d}x \cr &= c I_1 - I_2 \end{aligned}

Evaluate the first integral $I_1 = \int_{1}^{c} \ln x \text{d}x$ using integration by parts, where $u = \ln x$ and $v' = 1$:\begin{aligned} u &= \ln x \implies u' = \dfrac{1}{x} \cr v' &= 1 \implies v = x \cr \int \ln x \text{d}x &= x\ln x - \int 1 \text{d}x \cr &= x\ln x - x + C \end{aligned}
Evaluate the definite limits for $I_1$ from $1$ to $c$:\begin{aligned} I_1 &= \Big[ x\ln x - x \Big]_{1}^{c} \cr &= (c\ln c - c) - (1\ln 1 - 1) \cr &= c\ln c - c + 1 \end{aligned}

Evaluate the second integral $I_2 = \int_{1}^{c} x\ln x \text{d}x$ using integration by parts, where $u = \ln x$ and $v' = x$:\begin{aligned} u &= \ln x \implies u' = \dfrac{1}{x} \cr v' &= x \implies v = \dfrac{x^2}{2} \cr \int x\ln x \text{d}x &= \dfrac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int \dfrac{x}{2} \text{d}x \cr &= \dfrac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \dfrac{x^2}{4} + C \end{aligned}

Evaluate the definite limits for $I_2$ from $1$ to $c$:\begin{aligned} I_2 &= \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \dfrac{x^2}{4} \right]_{1}^{c} \cr &= \big( \dfrac{c^2}{2}\ln c - \dfrac{c^2}{4} \big) - \big( \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} \big) \cr &= \dfrac{c^2}{2}\ln c - \dfrac{c^2}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}

Assemble and simplify the terms to find the total area $A = c I_1 - I_2$:\begin{aligned} A &= c(c\ln c - c + 1) \cr &\quad - \big( \dfrac{c^2}{2}\ln c - \dfrac{c^2}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \big) \cr &= c^2\ln c - c^2 + c \cr &\quad - \dfrac{c^2}{2}\ln c + \dfrac{c^2}{4} - \dfrac{1}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{c^2}{2}\ln c - \dfrac{3c^2}{4} + c - \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \dfrac{c^2}{2}\ln c - \dfrac{3c^2}{4} + c - \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your collection of the $-c^2$ terms. Combining $-c^2 + \dfrac{c^2}{4}$ yields $-\dfrac{3c^2}{4}$, not $-\dfrac{c^2}{4}$.

Be very careful with your signs when subtracting $I_2$. The lower limit of $I_2$ evaluates to $-\dfrac{1}{4}$. Since we are subtracting $I_2$, we have $-\left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = +\dfrac{1}{4}$ inside the brackets, which becomes $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ when the negative sign is distributed.
Don't forget to combine the $\ln c$ terms. We have $c^2\ln c - \dfrac{c^2}{2}\ln c$, which simplifies to $\dfrac{c^2}{2}\ln c$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Tracking Constants in Integration

Carefully track the constant $c$ during subtraction of the upper and lower limits to avoid sign errors.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The curve has equation $y = 3x^2 \ln x$. The finite region $R$ is bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis, and the vertical lines $x = 1$ and $x = e$.

Find the exact area of the region $R$.
steps: Set up the definite integral for the area bounded by the curve, $x = 1$, and $x = e$:\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{1}^{e} 3x^2 \ln x \text{d}x \cr &= 3 \int_{1}^{e} x^2 \ln x \text{d}x \end{aligned}

Evaluate the indefinite integral $\int x^2 \ln x \text{d}x$ using integration by parts, where $u = \ln x$ and $v' = x^2$:\begin{aligned} u &= \ln x \implies u' = \dfrac{1}{x} \cr v' &= x^2 \implies v = \dfrac{x^3}{3} \cr \int x^2 \ln x \text{d}x &= \dfrac{x^3}{3}\ln x - \int \dfrac{x^2}{3} \text{d}x \cr &= \dfrac{x^3}{3}\ln x - \dfrac{x^3}{9} + C \end{aligned}

Multiply the indefinite integral by the coefficient $3$ before substituting the limits:\begin{aligned} 3 \int x^2 \ln x \text{d}x &= 3\big( \dfrac{x^3}{3}\ln x - \dfrac{x^3}{9} \big) \cr &= x^3\ln x - \dfrac{x^3}{3} \end{aligned}

Evaluate the definite integral using the upper limit $x = e$ and the lower limit $x = 1$:\begin{aligned} A &= \left[ x^3\ln x - \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right]_{1}^{e} \cr &= \big( e^3\ln e - \dfrac{e^3}{3} \big) - \big( 1^3\ln 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} \big) \cr &= \big( e^3 - \dfrac{e^3}{3} \big) - \big( 0 - \dfrac{1}{3} \big) \cr &= \dfrac{2e^3}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} \cr &= \dfrac{2e^3 + 1}{3} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} \dfrac{2e^3 + 1}{3} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your evaluation of the lower limit. The lower limit is $x = 1$, which gives $-\dfrac{1}{3}$. Since we subtract the lower limit, this becomes $-\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right) = +\dfrac{1}{3}$. This results in addition, not subtraction.
You may have forgotten to multiply by the coefficient $3$ from the original equation. The integral of $x^2 \ln x$ is indeed $\dfrac{2e^3 + 1}{9}$, but multiplying by $3$ yields $\dfrac{2e^3 + 1}{3}$.
This is only the evaluation at the upper limit $x = e$. You must also subtract the evaluation at the lower limit $x = 1$ to find the complete area of the region.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Limits of Integration with e
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating definite integrals with limits containing $e$, use the standard properties $\ln e = 1$ and $\ln 1 = 0$ to simplify your calculations early. This prevents cluttered algebraic terms and makes it easier to combine fractions.
