bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Factoring in Trigonometry
bradley_insight.content: The difference of two squares algebraic rule $a^4 - b^4 = (a^2 - b^2)(a^2 + b^2)$ is exceptionally useful when working with trigonometric functions. Because $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, any quartic difference $\cos^4\theta - \sin^4\theta$ simplifies instantly to a much simpler quadratic difference $\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Prove the identity:\begin{align}\dfrac{1}{1 - \sin\theta} &+ \dfrac{1}{1 + \sin\theta} \cr & \quad \equiv \dfrac{2}{\cos^2\theta}\end{align}
steps: Start with the left-hand side (LHS) of the identity:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{1 - \sin\theta} + \dfrac{1}{1 + \sin\theta} \end{aligned}

Combine the two fractions by finding a common denominator, which is the product of the two denominators: $(1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)$:\begin{aligned} &\text{LHS} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta) + (1 - \sin\theta)}{(1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)} \end{aligned}
Simplify the numerator by combining like terms and expand the denominator using the difference of two squares:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{2}{1 - \sin^2\theta} \end{aligned}

Apply the fundamental Pythagorean identity $1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta$ to substitute for the denominator:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{2}{\cos^2\theta} \cr &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}Since the left-hand side simplifies to the right-hand side, the identity is proven.
Final Answer: Identity proven: $\text{LHS} \equiv \text{RHS}$

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Trigonometric Denominators

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Prove the identity:$$\dfrac{\tan\theta}{\sin\theta} - \sin\theta\tan\theta \equiv \cos\theta$$
steps: Start with the left-hand side (LHS) of the identity:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\sin\theta} - \sin\theta\tan\theta \end{aligned}

Substitute $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ into both terms of the expression:\begin{aligned} \text{First Term} &= \dfrac{\sin\theta/\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} \cr \text{Second Term} &= \sin\theta\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \end{aligned}

Combine the two terms over their common denominator $\cos\theta$:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} - \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \cr &= \dfrac{1 - \sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \end{aligned}

Apply the fundamental Pythagorean identity $1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta$ to substitute for the numerator:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \cr &= \cos\theta \cr &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}Since the left-hand side simplifies to the right-hand side, the identity is proven.
Final Answer: Identity proven: $\text{LHS} \equiv \text{RHS}$

pi_options.feedback: Check your tangent identity substitution. Since $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, dividing this by $\sin\theta$ cancels out the $\sin\theta$, leaving $\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ rather than $\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$.
Check your algebra. Multiplying $\sin\theta$ by $\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ yields $\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta}$. The term $\cos\theta$ remains in the denominator.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Converting to Basic Functions
bradley_insight.content: A reliable, standard strategy for proving any trigonometric identity is to convert all non-basic functions (like tangent) into terms of sine and cosine: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$. Once everything is expressed using sines and cosines, standard algebraic fraction rules will lead you to the proof.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Show, by means of a counterexample, that the statement:$$\cos(A + B) \equiv \cos A + \cos B$$is not generally true for all angles $A$ and $B$.
steps: To disprove a universal mathematical statement, find a single specific counterexample (a set of angles $A$ and $B$) where the left-hand side (LHS) is not equal to the right-hand side (RHS). Let $A = 60^\circ$ and $B = 60^\circ$.
Evaluate the left-hand side (LHS) of the statement using these chosen angles:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \cos(60^\circ + 60^\circ) \cr &= \cos(120^\circ) \cr &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}
Evaluate the right-hand side (RHS) of the statement using the same angles:\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \cos(60^\circ) + \cos(60^\circ) \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} \cr &= 1 \end{aligned}

Compare the results of both sides. Since the LHS is not equal to the RHS:\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &\neq \text{RHS} \cr -\dfrac{1}{2} &\neq 1 \end{aligned}Because a case has been shown where the equation does not hold, the statement has been disproved by counterexample.
Final Answer: Disproved by counterexample: \begin{aligned} &\cos(60^\circ + 60^\circ) \cr & \qquad\neq \cos(60^\circ) + \cos(60^\circ)\end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your choice of angles. If you choose $A = 0^\circ$ and $B = 0^\circ$, then $\text{LHS} = 1$ and $\text{RHS} = 2$. While this is a valid counterexample because $1 \neq 2$, choosing non-zero angles is much safer and more illustrative for trigonometric functions.

Check your basic trigonometric values. The value of $\cos(120^\circ)$ is equal to $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ (or $-0.5$), not $1$. Use your calculator or the quadrant rules to verify your exact values.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Disproving Universal Claims
bradley_insight.content: In mathematics, proving a statement requires showing that it holds true for all possible cases, which requires general algebraic reasoning. However, disproving a statement (showing it is not generally true) only requires finding a single specific instance—a counterexample—where the statement fails.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Given that $(x - 1)$ and $(x + 1)$ are factors of the polynomial $3x^3 + px^2 + qx - 10$:

1. Find the values of the constants $p$ and $q$.

2. Determine the third linear factor of the polynomial.
steps: According to the factor theorem, if $(x - 1)$ is a factor of the polynomial $f(x) = 3x^3 + px^2 + qx - 10$, then $f(1) = 0$. Substitute $x = 1$ into the polynomial:\begin{aligned} 3(1)^3 + p(1)^2 + q(1) - 10 &= 0 \cr 3 + p + q - 10 &= 0 \cr p + q &= 7 \end{aligned}

Similarly, if $(x + 1)$ is a factor, then $f(-1) = 0$. Substitute $x = -1$ into the polynomial:\begin{aligned} 3(-1)^3 + p(-1)^2 &+ q(-1) - 10 = 0 \cr -3 + p &- q - 10 = 0 \cr p - q &= 13 \end{aligned}

Solve the system of equations by adding Equation 1 and Equation 2:\begin{aligned} (p + q) + (p - q) &= 7 + 13 \cr 2p &= 20 \cr p &= 10 \end{aligned}Substitute $p = 10$ back into Equation 1 to find $q$:\begin{aligned} 10 + q &= 7 \cr q &= -3 \end{aligned}Thus, the constants are $p = 10$ and $q = -3$.

Substitute the constants back to write the full polynomial:\begin{aligned} f(x) &= 3x^3 + 10x^2 - 3x - 10 \end{aligned}Since $(x - 1)$ and $(x + 1)$ are factors, their quadratic product $(x - 1)(x + 1) = x^2 - 1$ must also be a factor of the polynomial.

Write the cubic polynomial as the product of the quadratic factor and the unknown third linear factor $(ax + b)$:\begin{aligned} &3x^3 + 10x^2 - 3x - 10 \cr &\quad = (x^2 - 1)(ax + b) \cr &\quad = ax^3 + bx^2 - ax - b \end{aligned}

Equate the coefficients of the terms on both sides of the identity to find $a$ and $b$:

  • For the $x^3$ term: $a = 3$
  • For the constant term: $-b = -10 \implies b = 10$

Thus, the third linear factor is $3x + 10$.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &p = 10, \; q = -3 \cr &\text{Third factor: } 3x + 10 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your leading coefficient. The cubic term of the polynomial is $3x^3$. Since the quadratic factor starts with $x^2$, the third linear factor must start with $3x$ to produce $3x^3$, not just $x$.
Check your algebraic addition when solving the system of equations. Substituting $p = 10$ into $p + q = 7$ yields $10 + q = 7 \implies q = -3$, not $q = 3$.

Check your initial equations. Differentiating between $(x-1)$ and $(x+1)$ factors is critical. For $(x-1)$ we set $f(1)=0$, and for $(x+1)$ we set $f(-1)=0$. It seems you may have swapped the signs during substitution.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Equating Coefficients
bradley_insight.content: To find the third factor of a cubic when you already know two factors, multiply the two known factors to get a quadratic (here, $x^2 - 1$). You can then write the cubic as $(x^2 - 1)(ax + b)$. This inspection method is extremely fast and much less prone to sign errors than formal polynomial division.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Given that $(x - 2)$ and $(x + 3)$ are factors of the polynomial $f(x) = 2x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 12$:

Find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$.
steps: According to the factor theorem, if $(x - 2)$ is a factor of the polynomial $f(x)$, then $f(2) = 0$. Substitute $x = 2$ into the polynomial expression:\begin{aligned} 2(2)^3 + a(2)^2 + b(2) - 12 &= 0 \cr 16 + 4a + 2b - 12 &= 0 \cr 4a + 2b + 4 &= 0 \cr 2a + b &= -2 \end{aligned}

Similarly, if $(x + 3)$ is a factor of the polynomial $f(x)$, then $f(-3) = 0$. Substitute $x = -3$ into the polynomial expression:\begin{aligned} 2(-3)^3 + a(-3)^2 + b(-3) - 12 &= 0 \cr -54 + 9a - 3b - 12 &= 0 \cr 9a - 3b - 66 &= 0 \cr 3a - b &= 22 \end{aligned}
Solve the system of equations by adding Equation 1 and Equation 2:\begin{aligned} (2a + b) + (3a - b) &= -2 + 22 \cr 5a &= 20 \cr a &= 4 \end{aligned}
Substitute $a = 4$ back into Equation 1 to find $b$:\begin{aligned} 2(4) + b &= -2 \cr 8 + b &= -2 \cr b &= -10 \end{aligned}Thus, the constants are $a = 4$ and $b = -10$.
Final Answer: $$a = 4, \quad b = -10$$

Check your addition step when combining the equations. Adding $-2$ and $22$ yields $20$. Therefore, $5a = 20 \implies a = 4$. It seems you may have made a sign error, resulting in $a = -4$.
Check your simplification of Equation 1. Substituting $x = 2$ yields $4a + 2b = -4$, so $2a + b = -2$. It seems you may have made an arithmetic slip in dividing the constants.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dual Factor Theorem Solving
bradley_insight.content: When a polynomial has two unknown constants, you will always be given two factors to create two separate equations. Remember to write both in terms of $f(a) = 0$ using the Factor Theorem, and then solve them systematically using standard simultaneous elimination.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Let $f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6$.

1. Show that $(x - 3)$ is a factor of the polynomial $f(x)$.

2. Hence, factorise the polynomial $f(x)$ completely.
steps: According to the factor theorem, $(x - 3)$ is a factor of $f(x)$ if and only if $f(3) = 0$. Substitute $x = 3$ into the polynomial:\begin{aligned} f(3) &= 3^3 - 2(3^2) - 5(3) + 6 \cr &= 27 - 18 - 15 + 6 \cr &= 33 - 33 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(3) = 0$, the linear term $(x - 3)$ is verified to be a factor.

Since $(x - 3)$ is a factor, the cubic polynomial can be written as the product of $(x - 3)$ and a quadratic quotient $(ax^2 + bx + c)$:\begin{aligned} &x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6 \cr &\quad = (x - 3)(ax^2 + bx + c) \cr &\quad = ax^3 + bx^2 + cx \cr &\qquad - 3ax^2 - 3bx - 3c \cr &\quad = ax^3 + (b - 3a)x^2 \cr &\qquad + (c - 3b)x - 3c \end{aligned}

Equate the coefficients on both sides of the identity to find the values of $a$, $b$, and $c$:

  • For the $x^3$ term: $a = 1$
  • For the constant term: $-3c = 6 \implies c = -2$
  • For the $x^2$ term: $b - 3(1) = -2 \implies b = 1$

Substitute these values to write the quadratic quotient:\begin{aligned} \text{Quotient} &= x^2 + x - 2 \end{aligned}Verify by checking the $x$ term: $c - 3b = -5$, which matches the $-5x$ term perfectly.
Factorise this quadratic expression into two linear factors:\begin{aligned} x^2 + x - 2 &= (x + 2)(x - 1) \end{aligned}
Combine all the linear factors to write the completely factorised form of the cubic polynomial:\begin{aligned} f(x) &= (x - 3)(x + 2)(x - 1) \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$f(x) = (x - 3)(x + 2)(x - 1)$$

pi_options.feedback: Check your factorisation of the quadratic quotient $x^2 + x - 2$. The factors must multiply to $-2$ and add to $+1$. This gives $(x + 2)(x - 1) = 0$, not $(x - 2)(x + 1)$.
Check your coefficient matching for the $x^2$ term. From $b - 3a = -2$ with $a = 1$, we get $b - 3 = -2 \implies b = 1$. It seems you made a sign error, resulting in $b = -1$.
Check your verified factor. The question states that $(x - 3)$ is a factor since $f(3) = 0$. You cannot replace it with $(x + 3)$, which would correspond to $f(-3) = 0$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Spotting Quadratic Roots
bradley_insight.content: Using algebraic coefficient matching is an excellent alternative to long division. By setting $x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x - 3)(ax^2 + bx + c)$, you can easily identify $a$ from the leading term and $c$ from the constant term. This leaves only a simple subtraction to find the middle coefficient $b$.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Use the factor theorem to find an integer root of the cubic equation:$$2x^3 - 5x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0$$Hence, solve the equation completely.
steps: Use the factor theorem to find an integer root. Test small integer factors of the constant term $3$, starting with $x = 1$:\begin{aligned} f(1) &= 2(1)^3 - 5(1)^2 - 4(1) + 3 \cr &= 2 - 5 - 4 + 3 \cr &= -4 \neq 0 \end{aligned}

Next, test $x = -1$:\begin{aligned} f(-1) &= 2(-1)^3 - 5(-1)^2 \cr & \qquad- 4(-1) + 3 \cr &= -2 - 5 + 4 + 3 \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}Since $f(-1) = 0$, $x = -1$ is verified to be an integer root, and $(x + 1)$ is a factor of the polynomial.

Write the cubic expression as the product of $(x + 1)$ and a quadratic quotient $(ax^2 + bx + c)$:\begin{aligned} &2x^3 - 5x^2 - 4x + 3 \cr &\quad = (x + 1)(ax^2 + bx + c) \cr &\quad = ax^3 + (b + a)x^2 \cr &\qquad + (c + b)x + c \end{aligned}

Equate the coefficients on both sides of the identity to find the values of $a$, $b$, and $c$:

  • For the $x^3$ term: $a = 2$
  • For the constant term: $c = 3$
  • For the $x^2$ term: $b + 2 = -5 \implies b = -7$

Substitute these values to write the quadratic quotient expression:\begin{aligned} \text{Quotient} &= 2x^2 - 7x + 3 \end{aligned}Verify by checking the $x$ term: $b + c = -4$, which matches the $-4x$ term perfectly.

Set the quadratic quotient to $0$ and factorise to find the remaining roots of the equation:\begin{aligned} 2x^2 - 7x + 3 &= 0 \cr (2x - 1)(x - 3) &= 0 \end{aligned}This yields two remaining roots: $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = 3$.

Combining these with $x = -1$, the complete set of roots is $x = -1, \; \dfrac{1}{2}, \; 3$.
Final Answer: $$x = -1, \quad \dfrac{1}{2}, \quad 3$$

Check your factorisation of the quadratic quotient $2x^2 - 7x + 3 = 0$. The factors are $(2x - 1)(x - 3) = 0$. Solving these for $x$ yields positive roots $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = 3$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Root Hunting Strategy
bradley_insight.content: When hunting for an initial integer root of a polynomial, always search systematically among the integer factors of the constant term (here, the factors of $3$ are $\pm 1, \pm 3$). Starting with $1$ and $-1$ is the most efficient exam strategy.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Find the range of values of the constant $k$ for which the quadratic equation:$$3x^2 - 6x + k = 0$$has no real roots.
steps: Write down the coefficients of the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$:\begin{aligned} a &= 3 \cr b &= -6 \cr c &= k \end{aligned}
Write the algebraic formula for the discriminant $\Delta$:\begin{aligned} \Delta &= b^2 - 4ac \end{aligned}
Substitute the coefficients into the discriminant formula:\begin{aligned} \Delta &= (-6)^2 - 4(3)(k) \cr &= 36 - 12k \end{aligned}
According to the properties of quadratic equations, the equation has no real roots when the discriminant is strictly negative ($\Delta < 0$):\begin{aligned} 36 - 12k &< 0 \end{aligned}
Solve the linear inequality for the range of the parameter $k$:\begin{aligned} -12k &< -36 \cr k &> 3 \end{aligned}Thus, the quadratic equation has no real roots when $k > 3$.
Final Answer: $$k > 3$$

Check your boundary condition. For an equation to have 'no real roots', the discriminant must be strictly less than zero ($\Delta < 0$). The boundary condition $\Delta \le 0$ would include $\Delta = 0$, which corresponds to real, repeated roots.
Check your multiplication steps inside the discriminant. The term is $4ac = 12k$. It seems you may have squared the coefficient $a = 3$ or made an arithmetic slip.

bradley_insight.content: A very frequent slip in AS-level exam papers is forgetting to reverse the inequality sign when dividing by a negative number (such as dividing $-12k < -36$ by $-12$ to get $k > 3$). Always double-check this step to prevent losing easy marks.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

The triangle $ABC$ is such that $AC = 12\text{ cm}$, $AB = 18\text{ cm}$, and angle $ABC = 35^\circ$.

Find the two possible values for the area of triangle $ABC$. Give your answers to $1$ decimal place.
steps: First, sketch a diagram representing the given information. Because side $AC = 12\text{ cm}$ is shorter than the adjacent side $AB = 18\text{ cm}$, the side $AC$ can swing into two possible locations, creating an acute triangle ($ABC_2$) and an obtuse triangle ($ABC_1$):

Use the Sine Rule to find the two possible values for the angle $C = \angle ACB$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin C}{c} &= \dfrac{\sin B}{b} \cr \dfrac{\sin C}{18} &= \dfrac{\sin 35^\circ}{12} \cr \sin C &= 1.5\sin 35^\circ \cr \sin C &\approx 0.860364 \end{aligned}

Find the acute angle $C_1$ and the obtuse angle $C_2$ (where $C_2 = 180^\circ - C_1$):\begin{aligned} C_1 &= \arcsin(0.860364) \cr C_1 &\approx 59.4^\circ \cr C_2 &= 180^\circ - 59.4^\circ \cr C_2 &= 120.6^\circ \end{aligned}

For each case, calculate the corresponding third angle $A = \angle BAC$:\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 59.4^\circ \cr &= 85.6^\circ \cr A_2 &= 180^\circ - 35^\circ - 120.6^\circ \cr &= 24.4^\circ \end{aligned}

Calculate the area for Case 1 using the area formula $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}bc\sin A$ with $b = 12$ and $c = 18$:\begin{aligned} \text{Area}_1 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(12)(18)\sin(85.6^\circ) \cr &= 108\sin(85.6^\circ) \cr &\approx 107.7\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}
Calculate the area for Case 2:\begin{aligned} \text{Area}_2 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(12)(18)\sin(24.4^\circ) \cr &= 108\sin(24.4^\circ) \cr &\approx 44.5\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\text{Area}_1 = 107.7\text{ cm}^2 \cr &\text{Area}_2 = 44.5\text{ cm}^2 \end{aligned}

Remember that the Sine Rule is ambiguous when the side opposite the given angle is shorter than the adjacent side. This allows two valid, different triangles to be constructed, meaning you must calculate two possible areas.
Check your area calculations. Make sure you use the correct formula $\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}bc\sin A$. It seems you may have missed multiplying by the constant $108$ in the second case.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Ambiguous Case
bradley_insight.content: The ambiguous case of the Sine Rule (SSA) occurs when you are given two sides and a non-included acute angle, and the side opposite the angle is shorter than the other given side. This allows the opposite side to swing, creating an acute triangle and an obtuse triangle.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

A ship sails from port $P$ on a bearing of $045^\circ$ for $12\text{ km}$ to point $A$. It then changes course and sails on a bearing of $130^\circ$ for $15\text{ km}$ to point $B$.

Calculate the direct distance of $B$ from $P$, giving your answer in kilometres to $1$ decimal place.
steps: First, sketch a diagram with North-pointing lines at each vertex to help determine the internal angles of the triangle formed by $P$, $A$, and $B$:

Calculate the interior angle $\angle PAB$ using parallel North lines. The line $PA$ pointing South-West from $A$ makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the South line (alternate interior angles with the bearing at $P$). Since the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $130^\circ$:\begin{aligned} \angle PAB &= (180^\circ + 45^\circ) - 130^\circ \cr &= 225^\circ - 130^\circ \cr &= 95^\circ \end{aligned}

A triangle has sides of length $x\text{ cm}$, $(x + 2)\text{ cm}$, and $10\text{ cm}$. The angle between the sides of length $x\text{ cm}$ and $(x + 2)\text{ cm}$ is $60^\circ$.

Use the Cosine Rule to find the value of $x$. Give your answer to $1$ decimal place.

Apply the Cosine Rule, using the opposite side $a = 10$, and the adjacent sides $b = x$ and $c = x + 2$:\begin{aligned} &a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A \cr &10^2 = x^2 + (x + 2)^2 \cr &\qquad - 2x(x + 2)\cos(60^\circ) \end{aligned}

Substitute $\cos(60^\circ) = 0.5$ and expand the algebraic terms:\begin{aligned} &100 = x^2 + (x^2 + 4x + 4) \cr &\qquad - 2x(x + 2)(0.5) \cr &100 = 2x^2 + 4x + 4 \cr &\qquad - (x^2 + 2x) \cr &100 = x^2 + 2x + 4 \end{aligned}
Rearrange the terms into a standard quadratic equation of the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$:\begin{aligned} x^2 + 2x - 96 &= 0 \end{aligned}

Solve the quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} x &= \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{2^2 - 4(1)(-96)}}{2(1)} \cr &= \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 384}}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{388}}{2} \end{aligned}

Find the positive root since a side length must be positive, noting that $\sqrt{388} \approx 19.6977$:\begin{aligned} x &\approx \dfrac{-2 + 19.6977}{2} \cr &\approx \dfrac{17.6977}{2} \cr &\approx 8.8\text{ cm} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$8.8\text{ cm}$$

Substitute $r = 8$ back into Equation 1 to find the central angle $\theta$ in radians:\begin{aligned} 8\theta &= 10 \cr \theta &= \dfrac{10}{8} \cr &= 1.25\text{ radians} \end{aligned}

1. Use the Binomial Theorem to expand:$$\left(x + \sqrt{y}\right)^4$$2. Hence, write down the expansion of $(x - \sqrt{y})^4$ and find a simplified expression for:$$(x + \sqrt{y})^4 + (x - \sqrt{y})^4$$giving your answer in terms of $x$ and $y$.
steps: Use the Binomial Theorem to expand $(x + \sqrt{y})^4$ term by term using the binomial coefficients $1, 4, 6, 4, 1$:\begin{aligned} &(x + \sqrt{y})^4 \cr &\quad = \binom{4}{0}x^4(\sqrt{y})^0 + \binom{4}{1}x^3(\sqrt{y})^1 \cr &\qquad + \binom{4}{2}x^2(\sqrt{y})^2 + \binom{4}{3}x(\sqrt{y})^3 \cr &\qquad + \binom{4}{4}x^0(\sqrt{y})^4 \end{aligned}

Simplify each term of the expansion individually, noting that $(\sqrt{y})^3 = y\sqrt{y}$:\begin{aligned} &(x + \sqrt{y})^4 \cr &\quad = 1(x^4)(1) + 4(x^3)(\sqrt{y}) \cr &\qquad + 6(x^2)(y) + 4(x)(y\sqrt{y}) \cr &\qquad + 1(1)(y^2) \cr &\quad = x^4 + 4x^3\sqrt{y} + 6x^2y \cr &\qquad + 4xy\sqrt{y} + y^2 \end{aligned}

To write down the expansion of the conjugate term $(x - \sqrt{y})^4$, simply negate the odd powers of $\sqrt{y}$ from the previous expansion:\begin{aligned} &(x - \sqrt{y})^4 \cr &\quad = x^4 - 4x^3\sqrt{y} + 6x^2y \cr &\qquad - 4xy\sqrt{y} + y^2 \end{aligned}

Add the two expansions together. Notice that the irrational terms containing $\sqrt{y}$ have opposite signs and cancel out completely:\begin{aligned} &(x + \sqrt{y})^4 + (x - \sqrt{y})^4 \cr &\quad = (x^4 + 4x^3\sqrt{y} + 6x^2y \cr &\qquad + 4xy\sqrt{y} + y^2) \cr &\qquad + (x^4 - 4x^3\sqrt{y} + 6x^2y \cr &\qquad - 4xy\sqrt{y} + y^2) \cr &\quad = 2x^4 + 12x^2y + 2y^2 \cr &\quad = 2(x^4 + 6x^2y + y^2) \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\text{1. } x^4 + 4x^3\sqrt{y} + 6x^2y \cr &\qquad + 4xy\sqrt{y} + y^2 \cr &\text{2. } 2(x^4 + 6x^2y + y^2) \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your addition step. When combining the two expansions, only the odd-powered irrational terms containing $\sqrt{y}$ cancel out. The even-powered algebraic term $6x^2y$ exists in both expansions with positive signs, so adding them yields $12x^2y$, not $0$.
Check your fourth term in the first expansion. The term is $\binom{4}{3}x(\sqrt{y})^3$. Since $(\sqrt{y})^3 = y\sqrt{y}$, this term simplifies to $4xy\sqrt{y}$, not $4xy^2$.

Check your addition step. The question asks you to find the sum of $(x + \sqrt{y})^4 + (x - \sqrt{y})^4$. It seems you may have subtracted them instead, which would have cancelled the rational terms and doubled the irrational terms.

This conjugate structure is a highly useful algebraic shortcut.

steps: Write down the general term formula $T_{r+1}$ for the binomial expansion of $(a + b)^n$:\begin{aligned} T_{r+1} &= \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r \end{aligned}

Substitute the given parameters $a = 2$, $b = -3x$, and $n = 6$ into the general term formula:\begin{aligned} T_{r+1} &= \binom{6}{r} (2)^{6-r} (-3x)^r \cr &= \binom{6}{r} (2)^{6-r} (-3)^r x^r \end{aligned}

To find the coefficient of the term in $x^3$, we require the exponent of $x$ to be $3$, which means setting $r = 3$:\begin{aligned} T_4 &= \binom{6}{3} (2)^{6-3} (-3)^3 x^3 \cr &= \binom{6}{3} (2)^3 (-3)^3 x^3 \end{aligned}

Evaluate the constant components of the term individually, taking extreme care with the negative base raised to an odd power:\begin{aligned} \binom{6}{3} &= 20 \cr 2^3 &= 8 \cr (-3)^3 &= -27 \end{aligned}

Multiply these evaluated constants together to find the final coefficient of $x^3$:\begin{aligned} T_4 &= 20 \times 8 \times (-27)x^3 \cr &= 160 \times (-27)x^3 \cr &= -4320x^3 \end{aligned}Thus, the coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion is $-4320$.
Final Answer: $$-4320$$

question:
Part (a)
The vectors u and v are defined by $\mathbf{u} = 8\mathbf{i} - 15\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{v} = 3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$. Determine the range of values for $\mu$ such that:$$\mu|\mathbf{v}| > |\mathbf{u}|$$
Part (b)
The point $A$ has position vector $5\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j}$ and the point $B$ has position vector $17\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}$. Determine the position vector of the point $C$, which lies between $A$ and $B$, such that $AC : CB$ is $1 : 2$.
steps:
Part (a): Find the magnitude of each vector
To start, compute the magnitudes of u and v using the Pythagorean formula $|x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{u}| &= \sqrt{8^2 + (-15)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{64 + 225} \cr &= \sqrt{289} \cr &= 17 \end{aligned}Now find the magnitude of v:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{v}| &= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} \cr &= \sqrt{9 + 16} \cr &= \sqrt{25} \cr &= 5 \end{aligned}

Part (a): Solve the inequality
Substitute the computed magnitudes into the inequality $\mu|\mathbf{v}| > |\mathbf{u}|$:\begin{aligned} 5\mu &> 17 \cr \mu &> \dfrac{17}{5} \cr \mu &> 3.4 \end{aligned}

Part (b): Calculate vector $\vec{AB}$ and find $\vec{AC}$
Find the displacement vector $\vec{AB}$ by subtracting the position vector of $A$ from $B$:\begin{aligned} \vec{AB} &= \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \cr &= (17\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}) - (5\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 12\mathbf{i} + 18\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Now multiply this displacement vector by $\dfrac{1}{3}$ to find $\vec{AC}$:\begin{aligned} \vec{AC} &= \dfrac{1}{3}\vec{AB} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{3}(12\mathbf{i} + 18\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Part (b): Determine the position vector of point $C$
Add the displacement $\vec{AC}$ to the starting position vector $\mathbf{a}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{c} &= \mathbf{a} + \vec{AC} \cr &= (5\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j}) + (4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 9\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\mu > 3.4 \cr &\mathbf{c} = 9\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Given that $\mathbf{p} = 4\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}$, find the position vector of a point $X$ that lies in the direction of p such that the distance of $X$ from the origin is $35$ units.
steps:
Part (a): Find the magnitude of w
The magnitude $|\mathbf{w}|$ is computed as:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{w}| &= \sqrt{(-12)^2 + 5^2} \cr &= \sqrt{144 + 25} \cr &= \sqrt{169} \cr &= 13 \end{aligned}

Part (a): Construct the unit vector
To find the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ in the direction of w, divide w by its magnitude $|\mathbf{w}|$:\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{w}} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{w}}{|\mathbf{w}|} \cr &= \dfrac{-12\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j}}{13} \cr &= -\dfrac{12}{13}\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{5}{13}\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Part (b): Find the magnitude and unit vector of p
First find the magnitude $|\mathbf{p}|$:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{p}| &= \sqrt{4^2 + (-3)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{16 + 9} \cr &= \sqrt{25} \cr &= 5 \end{aligned}Now find the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{p}}$:\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{p}} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{p}}{|\mathbf{p}|} \cr &= \dfrac{4}{5}\mathbf{i} - \dfrac{3}{5}\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Part (b): Scale to the required distance
Since $X$ is at a distance of $35$ units from the origin in the direction of p, scale the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{p}}$ by a factor of $35$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x} &= 35\hat{\mathbf{p}} \cr &= 35\left( \dfrac{4}{5}\mathbf{i} - \dfrac{3}{5}\mathbf{j} \right) \cr &= 7(4\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 28\mathbf{i} - 21\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\hat{\mathbf{w}} = -\dfrac{12}{13}\mathbf{i} + \dfrac{5}{13}\mathbf{j} \cr &\mathbf{x} = 28\mathbf{i} - 21\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Your unit vector is correct, but you scaled p directly by $35$. Since p already has a magnitude of $5$, multiplying it directly by $35$ yields a vector with a magnitude of $175$. You must first find the unit vector of p before multiplying by $35$.

This prevents accidental double-scaling.

question:
Part (a)
Points $P$ and $Q$ have position vectors $\mathbf{p} = -3\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{q} = 7\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}$ respectively. Find the position vector of the midpoint of $PQ$.

Part (b)
The point $R$ lies on the line $PQ$ extended such that $Q$ lies between $P$ and $R$, and $PQ : QR$ is $2 : 1$. Find the position vector of $R$.
steps:
Part (a): Find the midpoint of $PQ$
The position vector of the midpoint $\mathbf{m}$ is the average of the position vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{m} &= \dfrac{\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{(-3 + 7)\mathbf{i} + (10 - 4)\mathbf{j}}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j}}{2} \cr &= 2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Part (b): Compute the vector $\vec{PQ}$
Find the vector $\vec{PQ}$ by subtracting the position vector of $P$ from $Q$:\begin{aligned} \vec{PQ} &= \mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p} \cr &= (7\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}) - (-3\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 10\mathbf{i} - 14\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Part (b): Find vector $\vec{QR}$ and position vector $\mathbf{r}$
Now find $\vec{QR}$:\begin{aligned} \vec{QR} &= \dfrac{1}{2}\vec{PQ} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2}(10\mathbf{i} - 14\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 5\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Add this displacement to the position vector of $Q$ to find the position vector of $R$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r} &= \mathbf{q} + \vec{QR} \cr &= (7\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}) + (5\mathbf{i} - 7\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 12\mathbf{i} - 11\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\mathbf{m} = 2\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} \cr &\mathbf{r} = 12\mathbf{i} - 11\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Your midpoint is correct, but check how you interpreted the ratio for $R$. It looks like you calculated $\vec{QR} = 2\vec{PQ}$ instead of $\dfrac{1}{2}\vec{PQ}$. The ratio $PQ : QR = 2 : 1$ means $PQ$ is twice the length of $QR$.
Your midpoint calculation is correct, but the position vector of $R$ cannot be identical to the midpoint of $PQ$. Re-read the definition of $R$, noting that $Q$ lies between $P$ and $R$.

question:
Part (a)
Relative to a fixed origin $O$, the points $D$, $E$, and $F$ have position vectors $\mathbf{d} = \mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}$, $\mathbf{e} = 5\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}$, and $\mathbf{f} = k\mathbf{i} + 13\mathbf{j}$ respectively, where $k$ is a constant.

• (i) Express $\vec{DE}$ and $\vec{EF}$ in terms of $\mathbf{i}$, $\mathbf{j}$, and $k$.
• (ii) Given that the points $D$, $E$, and $F$ are collinear, determine the value of $k$.

Part (b)
Using the value of $k$ found in part (a), find the ratio $DE : EF$.
steps:
Part (a)(i): Express the displacement vectors
Find $\vec{DE}$ and $\vec{EF}$ by subtracting the respective position vectors:\begin{aligned} \vec{DE} &= \mathbf{e} - \mathbf{d} \cr &= (5\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}) - (\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Now find $\vec{EF}$:\begin{aligned} \vec{EF} &= \mathbf{f} - \mathbf{e} \cr &= (k\mathbf{i} + 13\mathbf{j}) - (5\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (k - 5)\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Part (a)(ii): Solve for $k$ using collinearity
Since $D$, $E$, and $F$ are collinear, the vectors $\vec{DE}$ and $\vec{EF}$ must be parallel. Therefore, $\vec{EF} = \lambda \vec{DE}$ for some scalar multiplier $\lambda$:
$$(k - 5)\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j} = \lambda (4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j})$$

Part (a)(ii): Equate the components
Equate the $\mathbf{j}$ components to find $\lambda$:\begin{aligned} 9 &= 6\lambda \cr \lambda &= 1.5 \end{aligned}Now equate the $\mathbf{i}$ components and substitute $\lambda = 1.5$:\begin{aligned} k - 5 &= 4\lambda \cr k - 5 &= 4(1.5) \cr k - 5 &= 6 \cr k &= 11 \end{aligned}

Part (b): Determine the ratio $DE : EF$
From the relation $\vec{EF} = 1.5 \vec{DE}$ (since $\lambda = 1.5$), we know that the length of segment $EF$ is $1.5$ times the length of segment $DE$:\begin{aligned} DE : EF &= 1 : 1.5 \cr &= 2 : 3 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\vec{DE} = 4\mathbf{i} + 6\mathbf{j} \cr &\vec{EF} = (k - 5)\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j} \cr &k = 11 \cr &DE : EF = 2 : 3 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Your value for $k$ is correct, but check your ratio order. Since $\vec{EF} = 1.5\vec{DE}$, segment $EF$ is longer than $DE$. This means the ratio $DE : EF$ must be $1 : 1.5$, which simplifies to $2 : 3$, not $3 : 2$.

Your ratio is correct, but check your equation for $k$. Since $k - 5 = 6$, you need to add $5$ to both sides to solve for $k$. It looks like you may have subtracted $5$ or made another arithmetic slip.

Check your collinearity components. Equating the $\mathbf{j}$ components should yield $9 = 6\lambda \implies \lambda = 1.5$. It looks like you may have miscalculated $\lambda$, leading to errors in both $k$ and the final ratio.

question:
Part (a)
Two vectors a and b are defined by $\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{i} + \lambda\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = -6\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j}$. Given that a and b are parallel, find the value of the constant $\lambda$.

Part (b)
Using the value of $\lambda$ found in part (a), find the magnitude of the resultant vector $\mathbf{r} = 4\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$.
steps:
Part (a): Set up the parallel relation
If a and b are parallel, then $\mathbf{b} = k\mathbf{a}$ for some scalar constant $k$:
$$-6\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j} = k(2\mathbf{i} + \lambda\mathbf{j})$$

Part (a): Equate components to find $\lambda$
Equate the $\mathbf{i}$ components:\begin{aligned} -6 &= 2k \cr k &= -3 \end{aligned}Now equate the $\mathbf{j}$ components and substitute $k = -3$:\begin{aligned} 9 &= k\lambda \cr 9 &= -3\lambda \cr \lambda &= -3 \end{aligned}

Part (b): Find the resultant vector $\mathbf{r}$
Substitute $\lambda = -3$ into a to get $\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}$. Then calculate the linear combination $\mathbf{r} = 4\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}$:\begin{aligned} \mathbf{r} &= 4(2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j}) + (-6\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (8\mathbf{i} - 12\mathbf{j}) + (-6\mathbf{i} + 9\mathbf{j}) \cr &= 2\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Part (b): Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{r}$
Compute the magnitude using the Pythagorean formula:\begin{aligned} |\mathbf{r}| &= \sqrt{2^2 + (-3)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{4 + 9} \cr &= \sqrt{13} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\lambda = -3 \cr &|\mathbf{r}| = \sqrt{13} \end{aligned}

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Find the range of values of $k$ for which the quadratic equation $x^2 + 2kx + 12k = 0$ has no real roots.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the coefficients of the quadratic equation

The standard form of a quadratic equation is $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$. For the given equation $x^2 + 2kx + 12k = 0$, the coefficients are:\begin{aligned} a &= 1 \cr b &= 2k \cr c &= 12k \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the discriminant condition

For a quadratic equation to have no real roots, the discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ must be strictly less than zero ($\Delta < 0$):\begin{aligned} b^2 - 4ac &< 0 \cr (2k)^2 - 4(1)(12k) &< 0 \cr 4k^2 - 48k &< 0 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve the quadratic inequality

First, divide the entire inequality by $4$ to simplify, and then factorise:\begin{aligned} k^2 - 12k &< 0 \cr k(k - 12) &< 0 \end{aligned}The critical values where the expression equals zero are $k = 0$ and $k = 12$. Since we are looking for the range where the product is less than zero (negative), the solution lies strictly between the critical values:$$0 < k < 12$$
Final Answer: $$0 < k < 12$$

pi_options.feedback: You identified the correct critical values of $0$ and $12$, but you chose the region where the quadratic is positive. Since we require no real roots, we need $\Delta < 0$, which corresponds to the region between the critical values.
Check your simplification in the factorisation step. It looks like you forgot to square the $2k$ term as $(2k)^2 = 4k^2$, or you made an arithmetic slip while dividing by the common factor.
Be careful with signs. Setting the factor $k - 12 = 0$ yields a positive critical value $k = 12$, not $k = -12$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Quadratic Inequality Regions
bradley_insight.content: For a quadratic inequality of the form $k(k - c) < 0$ where $c > 0$, the solution region always lies between the critical values: $0 < k < c$. If the inequality were $> 0$, the solution would lie outside the critical values ($k < 0$ or $k > c$).

question:

Find the range of values of $k$ for which the quadratic equation $x^2 + 2kx + (3k + 4) = 0$ has two distinct real roots.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the coefficients

For the quadratic equation $x^2 + 2kx + (3k + 4) = 0$, the coefficients are:\begin{aligned} a &= 1 \cr b &= 2k \cr c &= 3k + 4 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the discriminant condition

For the quadratic equation to have two distinct real roots, the discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ must be strictly greater than zero ($\Delta > 0$):\begin{aligned} b^2 - 4ac &> 0 \cr (2k)^2 - 4(1)(3k + 4) &> 0 \cr 4k^2 - 12k - 16 &> 0 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve the quadratic inequality

Divide the entire inequality by $4$ and factorise the quadratic expression:\begin{aligned} k^2 - 3k - 4 &> 0 \cr (k - 4)(k + 1) &> 0 \end{aligned}The critical values are $k = -1$ and $k = 4$. Since we require the product to be strictly positive ($> 0$), the solution lies outside the interval between the critical values:\begin{aligned} &k < -1 \cr &\text{or } k > 4 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &k < -1 \cr &\text{or } k > 4 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: You found the correct critical values of $-1$ and $4$, but you chose the region between them. Since we require two distinct real roots, we need $\Delta > 0$, which corresponds to the outside regions: $k < -1$ or $k > 4$.

Check your factorisation of the quadratic $k^2 - 3k - 4$. Ensure the signs are correct: we need a product of $-4$ and a sum of $-3$, which gives $(k - 4)(k + 1) = 0$, leading to critical values $4$ and $-1$.
You correctly identified the upper region, but do not forget the negative region. Multiplying two negative factors also yields a positive result, so $k < -1$ is also a valid part of the solution.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Distinct Roots vs Repeated Roots
bradley_insight.content: For distinct real roots, always use a strict inequality $\Delta > 0$. Only use $\Delta \ge 0$ if the question asks for 'real roots' without specifying that they must be distinct.

question:
In this question you must show detailed reasoning.

Find the range of values of $k$ for which the quadratic equation $kx^2 + 6x + (k - 8) = 0$ has no real roots.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the coefficients

Identify the coefficients of the quadratic equation $kx^2 + 6x + (k - 8) = 0$:\begin{aligned} a &= k \cr b &= 6 \cr c &= k - 8 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the discriminant condition

For the equation to have no real roots, we require the discriminant to be strictly less than zero ($\Delta < 0$):\begin{aligned} b^2 - 4ac &< 0 \cr 6^2 - 4(k)(k - 8) &< 0 \cr 36 - 4k^2 + 32k &< 0 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve the quadratic inequality

Divide the entire inequality by $-4$. Remember that dividing by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality sign:\begin{aligned} k^2 - 8k - 9 &> 0 \cr (k - 9)(k + 1) &> 0 \end{aligned}The critical values are $k = -1$ and $k = 9$. Since the inequality is now greater than zero ($> 0$), the solution lies outside the critical values:\begin{aligned} &k < -1 \cr &\text{or } k > 9 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &k < -1 \cr &\text{or } k > 9 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Be careful when dividing an inequality by a negative number. When you divided $36 - 4k^2 + 32k < 0$ by $-4$, you must reverse the inequality sign to $> 0$. This makes the solution region outside the critical values, rather than between them.
Check your factorisation of $k^2 - 8k - 9$. We need two numbers that multiply to $-9$ and add to $-8$. These are $-9$ and $+1$, giving $(k-9)(k+1) > 0$, which yields critical values $9$ and $-1$.

While $k = 0$ is indeed the value for which the equation is no longer quadratic, the solved range $k < -1$ or $k > 9$ already completely excludes $0$. Thus, stating the exclusion is mathematically redundant.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Inequality Sign Reversal
bradley_insight.content: The most common source of lost marks in quadratic inequalities is forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. Always double-check this step carefully.

question:

The quadratic equation $(k + 1)x^2 + 4kx + (2k + 3) = 0$ has equal roots. Find the possible values of $k$.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the coefficients

For $(k + 1)x^2 + 4kx + (2k + 3) = 0$, the coefficients are:\begin{aligned} a &= k + 1 \cr b &= 4k \cr c &= 2k + 3 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Set up the equal roots condition

For a quadratic equation to have equal (repeated) roots, its discriminant must be exactly equal to zero ($\Delta = 0$):\begin{aligned} &b^2 - 4ac = 0 \cr &(4k)^2 - 4(k + 1)(2k + 3) = 0 \cr &16k^2 - 4(2k^2 + 5k + 3) = 0 \cr &16k^2 - 8k^2 - 20k - 12 = 0 \cr &8k^2 - 20k - 12 = 0 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve for $k$

Divide the entire equation by $4$ to simplify, and then factorise:\begin{aligned} 2k^2 - 5k - 3 &= 0 \cr (2k + 1)(k - 3) &= 0 \end{aligned}Solving this equation gives the possible values of $k$:\begin{aligned} k &= -0.5 \cr k &= 3 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &k = -0.5 \cr &k = 3 \end{aligned}

While the original coefficient $a = k+1$ cannot be $0$ (which would make $k = -1$), neither of your solved values is $-1$, so explicitly adding this exclusion is redundant.
Check your expansion and simplification. Ensure you expanded $4(k+1)(2k+3)$ correctly as $4(2k^2 + 5k + 3) = 8k^2 + 20k + 12$ before subtracting.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Checking the Quadratic Assumption

question:

Find the range of values of $k$ for which the line $y = kx - 1$ does not intersect the curve $y = x^2 + 4x + 8$.
steps:

To find the points of intersection, set the linear and quadratic equations equal to each other:\begin{aligned} kx - 1 &= x^2 + 4x + 8 \end{aligned}Rearrange all terms to one side to form a standard quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$:\begin{aligned} x^2 + (4 - k)x + 9 &= 0 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Identify the coefficients and set up the discriminant

For the quadratic equation $x^2 + (4 - k)x + 9 = 0$, the coefficients are:\begin{aligned} a &= 1 \cr b &= 4 - k \cr c &= 9 \end{aligned}Since the line and the curve do not intersect, the equation has no real solutions. Therefore, the discriminant must be strictly less than zero ($\Delta < 0$):\begin{aligned} b^2 - 4ac &< 0 \cr (4 - k)^2 - 4(1)(9) &< 0 \cr (4 - k)^2 - 36 &< 0 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve the quadratic inequality

Solve the inequality $(4 - k)^2 < 36$ directly:\begin{aligned} &-6 < 4 - k < 6 \cr &-10 < -k < 2 \cr &-2 < k < 10 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $$-2 < k < 10$$

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Line-Curve Intersections

question:
A curve $C$ has equation $y = f(x)$ where $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2$.

Part (a) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $C$ and determine their nature.

Part (b) Sketch the curve $C$, clearly indicating the coordinates of the stationary points and the points where the curve crosses the coordinate axes.

Part (c) Without performing the integration, state whether the integral below is positive or negative, giving a clear reason for your answer:$$\int_{2}^{6} (x^3 - 6x^2) \text{d}x$$
steps:
Step 1: Find the first derivative of the function
To find the stationary points, we first differentiate $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2$ with respect to $x$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= 3x^2 - 12x \end{aligned}

Step 2: Solve for the stationary points
Set the first derivative equal to zero to find the critical values of $x$:\begin{aligned} 3x^2 - 12x &= 0 \cr 3x(x - 4) &= 0 \cr x &= 0 \cr x &= 4 \end{aligned}
Substitute these values of $x$ back into the original equation to find their corresponding $y$-coordinates:

For $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} y &= 0^3 - 6(0)^2 \cr &= 0 \implies (0, 0) \end{aligned}
For $x = 4$:\begin{aligned} y &= 4^3 - 6(4)^2 \cr &= 64 - 96 \cr &= -32 \implies (4, -32) \end{aligned}

Step 3: Determine the nature of the stationary points
Find the second derivative of the function:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= 6x - 12 \end{aligned}Evaluate the second derivative at each critical point:

At $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= 6(0) - 12 \cr &= -12 < 0 \cr &\implies (0, 0) \text{ local max} \end{aligned}
At $x = 4$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= 6(4) - 12 \cr &= 12 > 0 \cr &\implies (4, -32) \text{ local min} \end{aligned}

Step 4: Find the coordinate intercepts and sketch the curve
Find where the curve crosses the axes:

To find the $y$-intercept, set $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} y &= 0^3 - 6(0)^2 \cr &= 0 \implies (0, 0) \end{aligned}
To find the $x$-intercepts, set $y = 0$:\begin{aligned} x^3 - 6x^2 &= 0 \cr x^2(x - 6) &= 0 \end{aligned}This gives the intercepts $x = 0$ (touching point) and $x = 6$ (crossing point) at:$$(0, 0) \quad \text{and} \quad (6, 0)$$Using these key features, the sketch of the curve $C$ is shown below:

Step 5: Determine the sign of the definite integral
Over the interval $[2, 6]$, the curve lies entirely on or below the $x$-axis (since the intercepts are at $0$ and $6$, and the local minimum is at $(4, -32)$). Since the area is located entirely beneath the $x$-axis, the value of the integral must be negative.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &(0, 0) \text{ (local maximum)} \cr &(4, -32) \text{ (local minimum)} \cr &\text{Intercepts: } (0, 0), \; (6, 0) \cr &\text{Integral is negative} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your second derivative test. At $x = 0$, $\dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} = -12 < 0$, which means $(0, 0)$ must be a local maximum, not a minimum. At $x = 4$, $\dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} = 12 > 0$, making $(4, -32)$ a local minimum, not a maximum.

Your stationary points are correct, but look closely at the graph between $x = 2$ and $x = 6$. The curve lies entirely below the $x$-axis in this interval. Since definite integration calculates the signed area, any area below the $x$-axis evaluates to a negative value.
Check your calculation of the $y$-coordinate for the stationary point at $x = 4$. Substituting $x = 4$ into $y = x^3 - 6x^2$ gives $64 - 96 = -32$, not $-16$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Qualitative Integration
bradley_insight.content: To determine the sign of a definite integral qualitatively, always look at your sketch. If the curve lies entirely below the $x$-axis over the boundaries of integration, the integral evaluates to a negative value. There is no need to calculate the actual integral.

question:
A curve $C$ has equation $y = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 8$.

Part (a) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $C$ and determine their nature.

Part (b) Sketch the curve $C$, clearly indicating the coordinates of the stationary points and the $y$-intercept.

Part (c) Using your sketch, state the number of distinct real roots of the equation $2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 8 = 0$, giving a clear reason for your answer.
steps:
Step 1: Differentiate the function
Find the first derivative of $y = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 8$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= 6x^2 - 6x - 12 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Solve for the stationary points
Set the derivative equal to zero and factorise to find the critical values of $x$:\begin{aligned} 6(x^2 - x - 2) &= 0 \cr 6(x - 2)(x + 1) &= 0 \cr x &= 2 \cr x &= -1 \end{aligned}
Substitute these values of $x$ back into the original equation to find their corresponding $y$-coordinates:

For $x = -1$:\begin{aligned} y &= 2(-1)^3 - 3(-1)^2 - 12(-1) + 8 \cr &= -2 - 3 + 12 + 8 \cr &= 15 \implies (-1, 15) \end{aligned}
For $x = 2$:\begin{aligned} y &= 2(2)^3 - 3(2)^2 - 12(2) + 8 \cr &= 16 - 12 - 24 + 8 \cr &= -12 \implies (2, -12) \end{aligned}

Step 3: Determine the nature of the stationary points
Find the second derivative:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= 12x - 6 \end{aligned}Evaluate the second derivative at each critical value:

At $x = -1$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= 12(-1) - 6 \cr &= -18 < 0 \cr &\implies (-1, 15) \text{ local max} \end{aligned}
At $x = 2$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= 12(2) - 6 \cr &= 18 > 0 \cr &\implies (2, -12) \text{ local min} \end{aligned}

Step 4: Sketch the curve
Find the $y$-intercept by setting $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} y &= 2(0)^3 - 3(0)^2 - 12(0) + 8 \cr &= 8 \implies (0, 8) \end{aligned}Sketch the positive cubic shape passing through the maximum $(-1, 15)$, the intercept $(0, 8)$, and the minimum $(2, -12)$:

Step 5: Determine the number of real roots
From the sketch, we observe that the local maximum $y$-value is positive ($15$) and the local minimum $y$-value is negative ($-12$). Since the curve must cross the $x$-axis between these values, it intersects the $x$-axis exactly **three** times. Therefore, there are exactly three distinct real roots.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &(-1, 15) \text{ (local maximum)} \cr &(2, -12) \text{ (local minimum)} \cr &y\text{-intercept: } (0, 8) \cr &\text{3 distinct real roots} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Your stationary points and intercept are correct, but think about the shape. Since the local maximum lies above the $x$-axis ($y = 15$) and the local minimum lies below the $x$-axis ($y = -12$), the curve must transition from positive to negative, crossing the $x$-axis 3 times in total.
Check your calculation of the $y$-coordinate for $x = -1$. Evaluating $y = 2(-1)^3 - 3(-1)^2 - 12(-1) + 8$ gives $-2 - 3 + 12 + 8 = 15$, not $9$.
Check your second derivative test. Since $\dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} = 12x - 6$, at $x = -1$ we get $-18 < 0$, making it a local maximum. At $x = 2$ we get $18 > 0$, making it a local minimum.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Stationary Points and Roots
bradley_insight.content: The coordinates of the local turning points of a cubic equation are a powerful tool for determining the number of roots. If $y_{\text{max}} \cdot y_{\text{min}} < 0$, the cubic must cross the $x$-axis three times (3 real roots). If $y_{\text{max}} \cdot y_{\text{min}} > 0$, it only crosses once (1 real root).

question:
A curve $C$ has equation $y = 12x - x^3$.

Part (b) Sketch the curve $C$, clearly indicating the coordinates of the stationary points and the points where the curve crosses the coordinate axes.

Part (c) Without performing the integration, state whether the integral below is positive or negative, giving a clear reason for your answer:$$\int_{0}^{\sqrt{12}} (12x - x^3) \text{d}x$$
steps:
Step 1: Differentiate the function
Differentiate $y = 12x - x^3$ with respect to $x$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= 12 - 3x^2 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Find the stationary points
Set the derivative equal to zero to find the critical values of $x$:\begin{aligned} 12 - 3x^2 &= 0 \cr 3(4 - x^2) &= 0 \cr x &= 2 \cr x &= -2 \end{aligned}
Substitute these back into the original equation to find their $y$-coordinates:

For $x = 2$:\begin{aligned} y &= 12(2) - 2^3 \cr &= 24 - 8 \cr &= 16 \implies (2, 16) \end{aligned}
For $x = -2$:\begin{aligned} y &= 12(-2) - (-2)^3 \cr &= -24 - (-8) \cr &= -16 \implies (-2, -16) \end{aligned}

Step 3: Determine the nature of the stationary points
Find the second derivative of the curve:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= -6x \end{aligned}Evaluate the second derivative at each critical point:

At $x = 2$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= -6(2) \cr &= -12 < 0 \cr &\implies (2, 16) \text{ local max} \end{aligned}
At $x = -2$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} &= -6(-2) \cr &= 12 > 0 \cr &\implies (-2, -16) \text{ local min} \end{aligned}

Step 4: Determine coordinate intercepts and sketch
Find where the curve crosses the axes:

To find the $y$-intercept, set $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} y &= 12(0) - 0^3 \cr &= 0 \implies (0, 0) \end{aligned}
To find the $x$-intercepts, set $y = 0$:\begin{aligned} 12x - x^3 &= 0 \cr x(12 - x^2) &= 0 \end{aligned}This gives the intercepts $x = 0$ or $x = \pm\sqrt{12} \approx \pm 3.46$.

Using these features, the sketch of the curve $C$ is shown below:

Step 5: Determine the sign of the definite integral
Over the interval $[0, \sqrt{12}]$, the curve lies entirely on or above the $x$-axis (since the boundary roots are at $0$ and $\sqrt{12}$, and the local maximum at $x = 2$ is positive). Since the area is located entirely above the $x$-axis, the integral must be positive.

Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &(2, 16) \text{ (local maximum)} \cr &(-2, -16) \text{ (local minimum)} \cr &\text{Intercepts: } (0, 0), \; (\pm\sqrt{12}, 0) \cr &\text{Integral is positive} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Be very careful with sign evaluation. Substituting $x = -2$ into $y = 12x - x^3$ gives $-24 - (-8) = -16$, not $-32$. This is a very common sign error when cubing negative bases.

Your stationary points are correct, but check the sign of the integral over the interval $[0, \sqrt{12}]$. Within this domain, the function lies above the $x$-axis, meaning the signed area must be positive.
Check your second derivative test. Since $\dfrac{\text{d}^2y}{\text{d}x^2} = -6x$, at $x = 2$ we get $-12 < 0 \implies$ local maximum, and at $x = -2$ we get $12 > 0 \implies$ local minimum.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Cubing Negative Numbers
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating terms like $-x^3$ with a negative value of $x$, always write out the expansion step-by-step: $-(-2)^3 = -(-8) = +8$. Forgetting that cubing a negative base maintains the negative sign is one of the most common ways to lose marks.

question:
A curve $C$ has equation $y = 2 + \dfrac{1}{x - 1}$.

Part (a) State the equations of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of $C$.

Part (b) Find the coordinates of the points where $C$ crosses the coordinate axes.

Part (c) Sketch the curve $C$, clearly indicating the asymptotes and the coordinates of the intersection points with the coordinate axes.
steps:
Step 1: Identify the asymptotes
The vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator of the fraction is equal to zero, causing the function to be undefined:\begin{aligned} x - 1 &= 0 \cr x &= 1 \end{aligned}The horizontal asymptote is found by observing the behavior of $y$ as $x \to \pm\infty$. As $x$ becomes extremely large, $\dfrac{1}{x - 1} \to 0$:\begin{aligned} y \to 2 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Find the axis intercepts
To find the $y$-intercept, set $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} y &= 2 + \dfrac{1}{0 - 1} \cr &= 2 - 1 \cr &= 1 \implies (0, 1) \end{aligned}
To find the $x$-intercept, set $y = 0$:\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2 + \dfrac{1}{x - 1} \cr \dfrac{1}{x - 1} &= -2 \cr x - 1 &= -0.5 \cr x &= 0.5 \implies (0.5, 0) \end{aligned}

Step 3: Sketch the curve
This is a translated reciprocal curve of $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$. Draw the asymptotes $x = 1$ and $y = 2$ as dashed lines, and sketch the branches passing through $(0, 1)$ and $(0.5, 0)$:
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\text{Asymptotes: } x = 1, \; y = 2 \cr &y\text{-intercept: } (0, 1) \cr &x\text{-intercept: } (0.5, 0) \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Check your $y$-intercept calculation. When $x = 0$, $y = 2 - 1 = 1$, not $-1$.
Check your vertical asymptote. The denominator is $x - 1$, which is undefined when $x = 1$, so the vertical asymptote is $x = 1$, not $x = -1$.
Check your algebra when solving for the $x$-intercept. Setting $y = 0$ gives $\dfrac{1}{x - 1} = -2$, so $x - 1 = -0.5$, which yields $x = 0.5$, not $2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Asymptote Anchors
bradley_insight.content: When sketching reciprocal functions, always draw the asymptotes first as dashed lines and label them with their equations. These act as boundaries that anchor your curve branches, ensuring your sketch is neat and mathematically accurate.

question:
A curve $C$ has equation $y = f(x)$, where $f(x) = 9 - x^2$.

Part (a) Sketch the graph of $y = f(x)$, indicating the coordinates of the turning point and the intercepts with the axes.

showing clearly the coordinates of the new turning points in each case.
steps:

The curve is an inverted parabola with its maximum turning point on the $y$-axis at $(0, 9)$.

$y$-intercept:
Setting $x = 0 \implies y = 9 \implies (0, 9)$.

$x$-intercepts:
To find the $x$-intercepts, set $y = 0$:\begin{aligned} 9 - x^2 &= 0 \cr x^2 &= 9 \cr x &= \pm 3 \implies (3, 0), \; (-3, 0) \end{aligned}

Step 2: Understand the transformations
We apply standard function transformation rules:
  • (i) $y = f(x) - 4$: This represents a vertical translation downwards by $4$ units. The turning point shifts from $(0, 9)$ down to $(0, 5)$.
  • (ii) $y = f(x + 2)$: This represents a horizontal translation to the left by $2$ units. The turning point shifts from $(0, 9)$ left to $(-2, 9)$.

Step 3: Sketch the transformed curves
The separate sets of axes for the original function and its two transformations are shown side-by-side below:

Check your transformation directions. The graph of $f(x) - a$ is a vertical shift downwards, which modifies the $y$-coordinate of the turning point to $(0, 5)$, not the $x$-coordinate.
Check the sign of your vertical translation. Subtracting $4$ from $f(x)$ shifts the curve down, so the $y$-coordinate should be $9 - 4 = 5$, not $9 + 4 = 13$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Horizontal Shifting
bradley_insight.content: Horizontal translations often confuse students because they seem counter-intuitive: $f(x + a)$ shifts the graph $a$ units to the left (negative direction), while $f(x - a)$ shifts the graph $a$ units to the right (positive direction). Always double-check your horizontal shift direction.

question:
In each of the two statements below, $c$ and $d$ are real numbers. One of the statements is true, while the other is false.\begin{aligned} &\text{A: } (3c + d)^2 = 9c^2 + d^2 \cr &\quad \text{for all real } c \text{ and } d \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} &\text{B: } 27c^3 + d^3 \cr &\quad = (3c + d)(9c^2 - 3cd + d^2) \cr &\quad \text{for all real } c \text{ and } d \end{aligned}(a) Identify the statement which is false. Show, by counterexample, that this statement is in fact false.

(b) Identify the statement which is true. Give a proof to show that this statement is in fact true.
steps:
To begin, we examine the two statements and determine which is false and which is true.

Statement A claims that $(3c + d)^2 = 9c^2 + d^2$ for all real $c$ and $d$. This is false because the expansion of a squared binomial always contains a middle term: $(3c + d)^2 = 9c^2 + 6cd + d^2$.

Statement B claims that $27c^3 + d^3 = (3c + d)(9c^2 - 3cd + d^2)$. This is a standard algebraic identity (the sum of cubes), so it is true.

Part (a): Disproving Statement A

To prove Statement A is false, we must provide a single counterexample where the left-hand side does not equal the right-hand side.

Let $c = 1$ and $d = 1$.

The left-hand side (LHS) of Statement A is:\begin{aligned} (3c + d)^2 &= (3(1) + 1)^2 \cr &= 4^2 \cr &= 16 \end{aligned}The right-hand side (RHS) of Statement A is:\begin{aligned} 9c^2 + d^2 &= 9(1)^2 + 1^2 \cr &= 9 + 1 \cr &= 10 \end{aligned}Since $16 \ne 10$, the identity does not hold for all real numbers $c$ and $d$, confirming Statement A is false.

Part (b): Proving Statement B

To prove Statement B is true for all real numbers $c$ and $d$, we expand the right-hand side of the equation and show that it simplifies to the left-hand side:\begin{aligned} &(3c + d)(9c^2 - 3cd + d^2) \cr &\quad = 3c(9c^2 - 3cd + d^2) \cr &\qquad + d(9c^2 - 3cd + d^2) \cr &\quad = 27c^3 - 9c^2d + 3cd^2 \cr &\qquad + 9c^2d - 3cd^2 + d^3 \cr &\quad = 27c^3 + d^3 \end{aligned}Since expanding the right-hand side results in the exact expression on the left-hand side, Statement B is proved to be true for all real values of $c$ and $d$.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } c = 1, \; d = 1 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true (proved)} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement B is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } c = 1, \; d = 1 \cr &\text{(b) Statement A is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: This distractor incorrectly identifies the truth values. Statement A is false because squaring a binomial $(3c+d)^2$ produces a middle term $6cd$, which is missing on the right-hand side.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } c = 0, \; d = 0 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: While Statement A is false, $c=0, d=0$ is not a valid counterexample because $0=0$ is true. A counterexample must show a case where the equation fails, such as $c=1, d=1$.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Neither statement is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: None} \cr &\text{(b) Both A and B are true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: Statement A is not an identity; it only holds if $c$ or $d$ is zero. In general, $(3c+d)^2 = 9c^2 + 6cd + d^2$, so it is false for all real $c$ and $d$.

bradley_insight.title: The Freshman's Dream and Difference of Cubes
bradley_insight.content: Always remember that squaring a binomial is not the same as squaring the individual terms: $(x + y)^2 \ne x^2 + y^2$. This common algebraic trap is known as the 'Freshman's Dream'. In contrast, the sum and difference of cubes are strict algebraic identities: $a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)$.

question:
In each of the two statements below, $a$ and $b$ are real numbers. One of the statements is true, while the other is false.\begin{aligned} &\text{A: } \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = a + b \cr &\quad \text{for all positive real } a, \; b \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} &\text{B: } a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab \cr &\quad \text{for all real } a, \; b \end{aligned}(a) Identify the statement which is false. Show, by counterexample, that this statement is in fact false.

(b) Identify the statement which is true. Give a proof to show that this statement is in fact true.
steps:
First, we analyze both statements.

Statement A claims that $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = a + b$ for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$. This is false because the square root does not distribute over addition.

Statement B claims that $a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$ for all real numbers $a$ and $b$. This is a well-known inequality (related to the AM-GM inequality) and is true.

Part (a): Disproving Statement A

To prove Statement A is false, we find a counterexample with positive real numbers $a$ and $b$.

Let $a = 3$ and $b = 4$.

The left-hand side (LHS) of Statement A is:\begin{aligned} \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} &= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} \cr &= \sqrt{9 + 16} \cr &= \sqrt{25} \cr &= 5 \end{aligned}The right-hand side (RHS) of Statement A is:\begin{aligned} a + b &= 3 + 4 \cr &= 7 \end{aligned}Since $5 \ne 7$, Statement A is false.

Part (b): Proving Statement B

To prove that $a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$ for all real numbers $a$ and $b$, we start from the fundamental property that the square of any real number is always non-negative:\begin{aligned} (a - b)^2 &\ge 0 \cr a^2 - 2ab + b^2 &\ge 0 \cr a^2 + b^2 &\ge 2ab \end{aligned}Since $(a - b)^2 \ge 0$ is true for all real numbers $a$ and $b$, the derived inequality $a^2 + b^2 \ge 2ab$ is also true for all real numbers $a$ and $b$.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } a = 3, \; b = 4 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true (proved)} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement B is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } a = -1, \; b = 1 \cr &\text{(b) Statement A is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: This distractor incorrectly identifies Statement B as false. However, even for negative numbers, $a^2+b^2 \ge 2ab$ holds because $(a-b)^2$ is never negative.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } a = 0, \; b = 0 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: The question specifies $a$ and $b$ must be positive real numbers ($a, b > 0$). $a=0, b=0$ is not a valid counterexample under those constraints, and it actually results in $0=0$, which is a true case.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } a = 1, \; b = 1 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is false} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: While Statement A is false ($ \sqrt{2} \ne 2$), Statement B is a fundamental truth in algebra derived from $(a-b)^2 \ge 0$. It cannot be false for any real numbers $a$ and $b$.

bradley_insight.title: Square Roots and Binomial Addition
bradley_insight.content: A very common error is assuming that the square root distributes over addition, i.e., $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = a + b$. Remember that $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} < a + b$ for all positive real numbers $a$ and $b$ because squaring both sides shows $a^2 + b^2 < a^2 + 2ab + b^2$ since $2ab > 0$.

question:
In each of the two statements below, $n$ represents a positive integer. One of the statements is true, while the other is false.\begin{aligned} &\text{A: } n^2 + n + 11 \text{ is prime} \cr &\quad \text{for all positive integers } n \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} &\text{B: } n^3 - n \text{ is a multiple of } 6 \cr &\quad \text{for all positive integers } n \end{aligned}(a) Identify the statement which is false. Show, by counterexample, that this statement is in fact false.

(b) Identify the statement which is true. Give a proof to show that this statement is in fact true.
steps:
First, we analyze both statements.

Statement A claims that $n^2 + n + 11$ is prime for all positive integers $n$. This is false because we can find values of $n$ that make the expression composite.

Statement B claims that $n^3 - n$ is a multiple of 6 for all positive integers $n$. This is a true statement of number theory.

Part (a): Disproving Statement A

To show Statement A is false, we search for a positive integer $n$ that results in a composite number.

Let $n = 10$.

Substituting $n = 10$ into the expression:\begin{aligned} n^2 + n + 11 &= 10^2 + 10 + 11 \cr &= 100 + 10 + 11 \cr &= 121 \end{aligned}Since $121 = 11 \times 11$, it is a composite number (not prime). Therefore, Statement A is false.

Part (b): Proving Statement B

To prove that $n^3 - n$ is always a multiple of 6 for any positive integer $n$, we begin by factoring the expression:\begin{aligned} n^3 - n &= n(n^2 - 1) \cr &= (n - 1)n(n + 1) \end{aligned}The factored expression is the product of three consecutive integers: $(n - 1)$, $n$, and $(n + 1)$.

We must show this product is divisible by both 2 and 3:

Divisibility by 2: In any set of three consecutive integers, at least one of them must be an even number. Therefore, the product must be divisible by 2.

Divisibility by 3: In any set of three consecutive integers, exactly one of them must be a multiple of 3. Therefore, the product must be divisible by 3.

Since 2 and 3 are prime numbers with no common factors, any number that is divisible by both 2 and 3 must also be divisible by their product, which is $2 \times 3 = 6$. Thus, $n^3 - n$ is always a multiple of 6.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } n = 10 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true (proved)} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement B is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } n = 1 \cr &\text{(b) Statement A is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: When $n=1$, $n^3-n = 0$. Since 0 is a multiple of 6 ($6 \times 0 = 0$), $n=1$ is not a counterexample. Statement A fails for larger $n$, such as $n=10$ or $n=11$.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } n = 1 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: Substituting $n=1$ into $n^2+n+11$ gives $13$, which is prime. A counterexample must result in a composite number to show the statement is false.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } n = 10 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true, multiple of 3 only} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: Statement B is a multiple of 6, not just 3. Because $(n-1)n(n+1)$ is a product of three consecutive integers, it must contain at least one even number (multiple of 2) and one multiple of 3.

bradley_insight.title: Consecutive Integers and Divisibility
bradley_insight.content: A product of $k$ consecutive integers is always divisible by $k!$. For $k = 3$ consecutive integers, $(n-1)n(n+1)$ must be divisible by $3! = 6$. This is because at least one of the integers must be even (divisible by 2) and exactly one must be a multiple of 3.

question:
In each of the two statements below, we are considering numbers under specific definitions. One of the statements is true, while the other is false.\begin{aligned} &\text{A: The sum of any two irrational} \cr &\quad \text{numbers is always irrational} \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} &\text{B: If } n \text{ is odd, then } n^2 - 1 \cr &\quad \text{is always a multiple of } 8 \end{aligned}(a) Identify the statement which is false. Show, by counterexample, that this statement is in fact false.

(b) Identify the statement which is true. Give a proof to show that this statement is in fact true.
steps:
First, we analyze both statements.

Statement A claims that the sum of any two irrational numbers is always irrational. This is false because we can construct two irrational numbers whose irrational parts cancel out upon addition.

Statement B claims that if $n$ is an odd integer, then $n^2 - 1$ is always a multiple of 8. This is a true statement.

Part (a): Disproving Statement A

To prove Statement A is false, we find two irrational numbers, $x$ and $y$, whose sum $x + y$ is rational.

Let $x = \sqrt{2}$ and $y = 2 - \sqrt{2}$.

Both $x$ and $y$ are irrational numbers because they cannot be expressed as a fraction of two integers.

Adding them together:\begin{aligned} x + y &= \sqrt{2} + (2 - \sqrt{2}) \cr &= 2 \end{aligned}Since 2 is a rational number, we have found two irrational numbers whose sum is rational. This proves Statement A is false.

Part (b): Proving Statement B

To prove Statement B is true, let $n$ be any odd integer. By definition, we can express $n$ as:\begin{aligned} n = 2k + 1 \end{aligned}where $k$ is an integer.

Now, substitute this expression into $n^2 - 1$:\begin{aligned} n^2 - 1 &= (2k + 1)^2 - 1 \cr &= (4k^2 + 4k + 1) - 1 \cr &= 4k^2 + 4k \cr &= 4k(k + 1) \end{aligned}We now analyze the term $k(k + 1)$, which is the product of two consecutive integers $k$ and $k + 1$. Since one of any two consecutive integers must be even, the product $k(k + 1)$ must be divisible by 2. Thus, we can write:\begin{aligned} k(k + 1) = 2m \end{aligned}for some integer $m$.

Substituting this back into our expression for $n^2 - 1$:\begin{aligned} n^2 - 1 &= 4(2m) \cr &= 8m \end{aligned}Since $8m$ is clearly a multiple of 8, Statement B is proved to be true for all odd integers $n$.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } \sqrt{2} + (2 - \sqrt{2}) = 2 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true (proved)} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement B is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } n = 1 \cr &\text{(b) Statement A is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: For $n=1$, $n^2-1=0$, which is a multiple of 8 ($8 \times 0$). Statement A is false because adding $\sqrt{2}$ and $-\sqrt{2}$ (both irrational) results in 0 (rational).

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: The sum $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}$ is irrational, so it does not serve as a counterexample. To disprove Statement A, you must find a sum of irrationals that results in a rational number.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } \sqrt{2} + (2 - \sqrt{2}) = 2 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is false} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: Statement B is a provable identity for odd integers. By expressing an odd number as $2k+1$, you can show the expression always contains a factor of $4 \times 2 = 8$.

bradley_insight.title: Defining Odd Integers in Proofs
bradley_insight.content: When proving statements about odd integers, always write $n = 2k + 1$ for some integer $k$. This allows you to expand and factor expressions algebraically. In this case, $4k(k+1)$ contains the product of two consecutive integers $k(k+1)$, which is always even, yielding an extra factor of 2.

question:
In each of the two statements below, $x$ is a real number. One of the statements is true, while the other is false.\begin{aligned} &\text{A: } x^2 > x \text{ for all real } x \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{B: }&x^2 - 6x + 10 > 0\cr & \text{ for all real } x \end{aligned}(a) Identify the statement which is false. Show, by counterexample, that this statement is in fact false.

(b) Identify the statement which is true. Give a proof to show that this statement is in fact true.
steps:
First, we analyze both statements.

Statement A claims that $x^2 > x$ for all real numbers $x$. This is false because squaring real numbers between 0 and 1 (inclusive) does not make them strictly larger.

Statement B claims that $x^2 - 6x + 10 > 0$ for all real numbers $x$. This is a true quadratic inequality.

Part (a): Disproving Statement A

To prove Statement A is false, we need to find a single real number $x$ for which $x^2$ is not strictly greater than $x$.

Let $x = 0$.

Substituting $x = 0$ into the inequality $x^2 > x$:\begin{aligned} 0^2 &> 0 \cr 0 &> 0 \end{aligned}Since $0 > 0$ is a false statement, $x = 0$ is a valid counterexample. (Alternatively, choosing $x = 1$ yields $1 > 1$, which is also false, and choosing $x = 0.5$ yields $0.25 > 0.5$, which is false). Thus, Statement A is false.

Part (b): Proving Statement B

To prove Statement B is true for all real numbers $x$, we complete the square for the quadratic expression $x^2 - 6x + 10$:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 6x + 10 &= (x^2 - 6x + 9) + 1 \cr &= (x - 3)^2 + 1 \end{aligned}We now analyze the components of this rewritten expression:

1. Since the square of any real number is always non-negative, we have:\begin{aligned} (x - 3)^2 \ge 0 \end{aligned}for all real numbers $x$.

2. Adding 1 to both sides of this inequality:\begin{aligned} (x - 3)^2 + 1 \ge 1 \end{aligned}Since $(x - 3)^2 + 1 \ge 1$ and $1 > 0$, we have:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 6x + 10 &> 0 \end{aligned}Therefore, $x^2 - 6x + 10 > 0$ for all real numbers $x$, which proves Statement B is true.
Final Answer: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } x = 0 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true (proved)} \end{aligned}

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement B is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } x = 3 \cr &\text{(b) Statement A is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: For $x=3$, the quadratic $x^2-6x+10$ equals 1, which is $>0$, so this is not a counterexample. Statement A is false because $0^2$ is not strictly greater than 0.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } x = 2 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is true} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: If $x=2$, then $x^2=4$. Since $4>2$, $x=2$ is not a counterexample for Statement A. You must choose a value in the range $[0, 1]$ to disprove Statement A.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) Statement A is false} \cr &\quad \text{Counterexample: } x = 0 \cr &\text{(b) Statement B is false} \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: Statement B is true for all real $x$ because it can be rewritten as $(x-3)^2+1$. Since a square is always $\ge 0$, adding 1 ensures the expression is always positive.

bradley_insight.title: The Power of Completing the Square
bradley_insight.content: Completing the square is one of the most powerful tools for proving quadratic inequalities. By writing a quadratic in the form $(x - p)^2 + q$, you instantly establish its minimum value. Since any real square $(x - p)^2 \ge 0$, the expression $(x - p)^2 + q$ is guaranteed to be at least $q$.

question:
The value of a motorcycle, £$V$, may be modeled as a continuous variable. At time $t$ years, the value of the motorcycle is given by:
$$V = Ae^{kt}$$
where $A$ and $k$ are constants.

When the motorcycle is new, it is worth £16,000. When the motorcycle is three years old, it is worth £12,000.

Determine the predicted value of the motorcycle when it is nine years old.
steps:
To find the value of the constants, we first use the initial condition. When the motorcycle is new, $t = 0$ and $V = 16000$.

Substitute these values into the model equation:
\begin{aligned} 16000 &= Ae^{k(0)} \cr 16000 &= A(1) \cr A &= 16000 \end{aligned}

So, the model becomes $V = 16000e^{kt}$.

Next, we use the second condition. When the motorcycle is three years old, $t = 3$ and $V = 12000$.

Substitute these values into our updated equation:
\begin{aligned} 12000 &= 16000e^{3k} \cr e^{3k} &= \dfrac{ 12000 }{ 16000 } \cr e^{3k} &= \dfrac{ 3 }{ 4 } \end{aligned}

We can leave the expression in this form instead of solving for $k$ as a decimal, which avoids rounding errors in the next step.

We want to find the value of the motorcycle when it is nine years old, so we set $t = 9$:
$$V = 16000e^{9k}$$
$$V = 16000\left( e^{3k} \right)^3$$

Substitute $e^{3k} = \dfrac{ 3 }{ 4 }$ into this equation:
\begin{aligned} V &= 16000\left( \dfrac{ 3 }{ 4 } \right)^3 \cr V &= 16000\left( \dfrac{ 27 }{ 64 } \right) \cr V &= 250 \times 27 \cr V &= 6750 \end{aligned}

Thus, the predicted value of the motorcycle after nine years is £6,750.
Final Answer: £$6{}750$

pi_options.feedback: This is the result of using a linear depreciation model rather than an exponential model. A linear model assumes the motorcycle loses a constant amount of value each year (linear depreciation of £1,333.33 per year), whereas an exponential model assumes it loses a constant percentage of its value.
