This error occurs if you incorrectly calculate the value at $t=9$ as $V = 16000 \times \left( \dfrac{ 3 }{ 4 } \right)^2$ instead of $16000 \times \left( \dfrac{ 3 }{ 4 } \right)^3$. A power of 2 represents the value after 6 years, not 9 years.
This can occur from a combination of algebraic errors in index laws or if you solve for $k$ as a rounded decimal too early, causing a significant loss of precision in the final calculation.

bradley_insight.title: Using Powers of the Base Instead of Solving for k
bradley_insight.content: When the target time ($t = 9$) is an exact multiple of the given time interval ($t = 3$), you do not need to find the numerical decimal value of $k$. Since $V = A(e^{3k})^3$, you can simply substitute the fraction representing $e^{3k}$ directly. This avoids rounding errors and keeps the calculations exact.

question:
The mass, $M$ grams, of a radioactive substance remaining at time $t$ years is modeled by:
$$M = M_0 e^{-kt}$$
where $M_0$ and $k$ are positive constants.

Initially, the mass of the substance is $80\text{ grams}$. After $5$ years, the mass has decayed to $50\text{ grams}$.

(a) Find the value of $M_0$ and show that $k \approx 0.0940$.

(b) Find the time taken, to the nearest tenth of a year, for the mass of the substance to decay to $20\text{ grams}$.
steps:
Part (a): Finding $M_0$ and $k$

The initial mass is $80\text{ grams}$, which means $M = 80$ when $t = 0$.
\begin{aligned} 80 &= M_0 e^{-k(0)} \cr M_0 &= 80 \end{aligned}

Now we use the second condition: $M = 50$ when $t = 5$.
\begin{aligned} 50 &= 80e^{-5k} \cr e^{-5k} &= \dfrac{ 50 }{ 80 } \cr e^{-5k} &= 0.625 \end{aligned}

Take the natural logarithm of both sides to solve for $k$:
\begin{aligned} -5k &= \ln(0.625) \cr k &= -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 5 }\ln(0.625) \cr k &\approx 0.0940007 \cr k &\approx 0.0940 \text{ (to 4 d.p.)} \end{aligned}

Part (b): Finding the time to decay to $20\text{ grams}$

Set $M = 20$ and solve for $t$ using our model $M = 80e^{-0.0940t}$:
\begin{aligned} 20 &= 80e^{-0.0940t} \cr e^{-0.0940t} &= \dfrac{ 20 }{ 80 } \cr e^{-0.0940t} &= 0.25 \end{aligned}

Take the natural logarithm of both sides:
\begin{aligned} -0.0940t &= \ln(0.25) \cr t &= \dfrac{ \ln(0.25) }{ -0.0940 } \cr t &\approx 14.74787 \end{aligned}

Rounding $14.74787$ to the nearest tenth of a year gives $14.7$ years.
Final Answer: $14.7$ years

pi_options.feedback: This is a rounding error. Dividing $-\ln(0.25)$ by $0.0940$ yields approximately $14.748$ years. Since the digit in the hundredths place is 4, this rounds down to $14.7$ years, not up to $14.8$ years.
This error occurs if you round the decay constant $k$ too severely to $0.09$ in intermediate steps, leading to $t = \dfrac{ \ln(0.25) }{ -0.09 } \approx 15.4$ years.

This error occurs if you use common logarithms (base 10) instead of natural logarithms (base $e$) when solving the exponential equation, or if you make an error in changing the sign during algebraic rearrangement.

bradley_insight.title: Rounding of Intermediate Constants
bradley_insight.content: Be very careful when using rounded intermediate values (like $k \approx 0.0940$) in subsequent calculations. To ensure maximum accuracy, always store the exact value of $k$ in your calculator's memory and use it for the final calculation before rounding the final answer.

question:
The temperature, $\theta^\circ\text{C}$, of a hot drink in a room at time $t$ minutes after being poured is modeled by:
$$\theta = 20 + Ae^{-kt}$$
where $A$ and $k$ are constants.

The initial temperature of the drink is $85^\circ\text{C}$. After $10$ minutes, the temperature has cooled to $50^\circ\text{C}$.

(a) Find the value of $A$.

(b) Find the value of $k$, giving your answer correct to 4 decimal places.

(c) Determine the temperature of the drink, to the nearest degree, after $25$ minutes.
steps:
Part (a): Finding $A$

The initial temperature is $85^\circ\text{C}$, so $\theta = 85$ when $t = 0$.
\begin{aligned} 85 &= 20 + Ae^{-k(0)} \cr 85 &= 20 + A \cr A &= 65 \end{aligned}

Part (b): Finding $k$

We are given that $\theta = 50$ when $t = 10$. Substitute $A = 65$ and these values into the model:
\begin{aligned} 50 &= 20 + 65e^{-10k} \cr 30 &= 65e^{-10k} \cr e^{-10k} &= \dfrac{ 30 }{ 65 } \cr e^{-10k} &= \dfrac{ 6 }{ 13 } \end{aligned}

Take the natural logarithm of both sides:
\begin{aligned} -10k &= \ln\left( \dfrac{ 6 }{ 13 } \right) \cr k &= -\dfrac{ 1 }{ 10 }\ln\left( \dfrac{ 6 }{ 13 } \right) \cr k &\approx 0.0773189 \cr k &\approx 0.0773 \text{ (to 4 d.p.)} \end{aligned}

Part (c): Finding the temperature after $25$ minutes

Substitute $t = 25$, $A = 65$, and $k = 0.0773$ into the model:
\begin{aligned} \theta &= 20 + 65e^{-0.0773(25)} \cr \theta &= 20 + 65e^{-1.9325} \cr \theta &\approx 20 + 65(0.144783) \cr \theta &\approx 20 + 9.4109 \cr \theta &\approx 29.4109 \end{aligned}

Rounding to the nearest degree gives $29^\circ\text{C}$.
Final Answer: $29^\circ\text{C}

pi_options.feedback: This is a minor calculation error. Ensure you do not round the exponent or value of $e^{-1.9325}$ too early. The unrounded calculation yields $29.41^\circ\text{C}$, which rounds down to $29^\circ\text{C}$.

This represents the limit as $t \to \infty$ (the ambient room temperature). While the drink will eventually cool to $20^\circ\text{C}$, after only 25 minutes it will still be slightly above room temperature.
This error can occur if you forget the negative sign in the exponent (evaluating $e^{1.9325}$), or if you make an error in subtracting the constant offset of 20.

bradley_insight.title: Understanding the Room Temperature Offset
bradley_insight.content: In the model $\theta = 20 + Ae^{-kt}$, as $t \to \infty$, the term $Ae^{-kt} \to 0$. This means that the temperature $\theta$ approaches $20^\circ\text{C}$ (the ambient room temperature). The constant offset represents this physical lower bound.

question:
The number of bacteria, $N$, in a laboratory culture at time $t$ hours is modeled by:
$$N = Ae^{kt}$$
where $A$ and $k$ are positive constants.

The initial population of bacteria is $500$. After $4$ hours, the population has grown to $1500$.

(a) State the value of $A$.

(b) Show that $e^{4k} = 3$, and hence find the exact value of $k$.

(c) Determine the population of bacteria in the culture after $12$ hours.
steps:
Part (a): Finding $A$

The initial population of bacteria is $500$, which means $N = 500$ when $t = 0$.
\begin{aligned} 500 &= Ae^{k(0)} \cr A &= 500 \end{aligned}

Part (b): Finding $k$

We are given that $N = 1500$ when $t = 4$. Substitute $A = 500$ into the equation:
\begin{aligned} 1500 &= 500e^{4k} \cr e^{4k} &= \dfrac{ 1500 }{ 500 } \cr e^{4k} &= 3 \end{aligned}

Taking the natural logarithm of both sides to find the exact value of $k$:
\begin{aligned} 4k &= \ln(3) \cr k &= \dfrac{ \ln(3) }{ 4 } \end{aligned}

Part (c): Finding the population after $12$ hours

We want to evaluate $N$ when $t = 12$. Substitute $A = 500$ and $t = 12$ into our model equation:
\begin{aligned} N &= 500e^{12k} \cr N &= 500\left( e^{4k} \right)^3 \end{aligned}

Since we know from Part (b) that $e^{4k} = 3$, we can substitute this directly:
\begin{aligned} N &= 500(3)^3 \cr N &= 500(27) \cr N &= 13500 \end{aligned}

Thus, the population of bacteria after 12 hours is $13,500$.
Final Answer: $13{}500$

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you multiply the population by 3 (calculating $1500 \times 3$) instead of recognizing that the population triples every 4 hours, which requires cubing the factor of 3 over 12 hours ($3^3 = 27$).
This is simply the population at $t = 4$ hours. After 12 hours, the population will have undergone two further tripling cycles.
This error occurs if you apply the tripling factor of 27 directly to the $t = 4$ population of 1500 (calculating $1500 \times 27$) instead of multiplying it by the initial population $A = 500$.

bradley_insight.title: Recognizing Tripling Times
bradley_insight.content: Since the population triples every 4 hours ($e^{4k} = 3$), the population after 12 hours (which is exactly three 4-hour intervals) must triple three times: $500 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 13500$. Recognizing this scaling factor is a fast way to verify your answers.

question:
The population of Town $X$, $P$, is modeled by $P = 15000e^{0.02t}$, and the population of Town $Y$, $Q$, is modeled by $Q = 22000e^{-0.01t}$, where $t$ is the number of years after the year 2020.

(a) State which town's population is predicted to grow and which is predicted to decay, justifying your answer.

(b) Find the number of years, to the nearest tenth of a year, after 2020 when the populations of the two towns are predicted to be equal.
steps:
Part (a): Growth vs Decay

The behavior of an exponential model $y = Ae^{kt}$ depends on the sign of the constant exponent coefficient, $k$:
1. For Town $X$, $k = 0.02 > 0$. Since the exponent is positive, the population is predicted to **grow**.
2. For Town $Y$, $k = -0.01 < 0$. Since the exponent is negative, the population is predicted to **decay**.

Part (b): Finding when populations are equal

To find when the populations are equal, set $P = Q$ and solve for $t$:
\begin{aligned} 15000e^{0.02t} &= 22000e^{-0.01t} \end{aligned}

Divide both sides by $15000$:
\begin{aligned} e^{0.02t} &= \dfrac{ 22000 }{ 15000 }e^{-0.01t} \cr e^{0.02t} &= \dfrac{ 22 }{ 15 }e^{-0.01t} \end{aligned}

To combine the exponential terms, divide both sides by $e^{-0.01t}$ (which is equivalent to multiplying both sides by $e^{0.01t}$):
\begin{aligned} \dfrac{ e^{0.02t} }{ e^{-0.01t} } &= \dfrac{ 22 }{ 15 } \cr e^{0.02t - (-0.01t)} &= \dfrac{ 22 }{ 15 } \cr e^{0.03t} &= \dfrac{ 22 }{ 15 } \end{aligned}

Take the natural logarithm of both sides:
\begin{aligned} 0.03t &= \ln\left( \dfrac{ 22 }{ 15 } \right) \cr t &= \dfrac{ 1 }{ 0.03 }\ln\left( \dfrac{ 22 }{ 15 } \right) \cr t &\approx 12.729 \end{aligned}

Rounding to the nearest tenth of a year gives $12.7$ years.
Final Answer: $12.7$ years

pi_options.feedback: This is a rounding error. The value $t \approx 12.729$ rounds down to $12.7$ because the digit in the hundredths place is 2.
This error occurs if you fail to divide by the combined exponent coefficient of $0.03$, leaving the calculation as $t = \ln\left( \dfrac{ 22 }{ 15 } \right) / 0.01 \approx 38.2$ years.

This error can occur if you incorrectly subtract the exponents when dividing (calculating $0.02 - 0.01 = 0.01$) instead of correctly adding them when dividing by a negative exponent ($0.02 - (-0.01) = 0.03$).

bradley_insight.title: Combining Exponentials with Different Bases
bradley_insight.content: When solving $Ae^{at} = Be^{-bt}$, always divide both sides by $e^{-bt}$ to get $e^{(a+b)t} = \dfrac{ B }{ A }$. This cleanly combines the exponents into a single positive exponential term, making it simple to take the natural logarithm of both sides.

question:
A curve $C$ has the equation:$$y = 3x^2 - 14x - 8$$The point $P$ lies on $C$ and is such that the tangent to $C$ at $P$ has the equation:$$y = -2x + c$$where $c$ is a constant.

Find the coordinates of $P$ and the value of $c$.
steps: First, we find the gradient function of the curve by differentiating the equation with respect to $x$:\begin{aligned} y &= 3x^2 - 14x - 8 \cr \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= 6x - 14 \end{aligned}

We are given that the tangent to the curve at $P$ is $y = -2x + c$. The gradient of this tangent line is $-2$.

Since the gradient of the curve at the point of tangency $P$ must equal the gradient of the tangent line, we set our derivative equal to $-2$ and solve for $x$:\begin{aligned} 6x - 14 &= -2 \cr 6x &= 12 \cr x &= 2 \end{aligned}Thus, the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $2$.

Next, we find the $y$-coordinate of $P$ by substituting $x = 2$ back into the curve's original equation:\begin{aligned} y &= 3(2)^2 - 14(2) - 8 \cr y &= 3(4) - 28 - 8 \cr y &= 12 - 36 \cr y &= -24 \end{aligned}So, the coordinates of the point of tangency are $P(2, -24)$.

Finally, since the tangent line passes through $P(2, -24)$, we substitute these coordinates into the tangent line equation $y = -2x + c$ to solve for $c$:\begin{aligned} -24 &= -2(2) + c \cr -24 &= -4 + c \cr c &= -20 \end{aligned}Thus, the coordinates of $P$ are $(2, -24)$ and the constant value is $c = -20$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &P(2, -24) \cr &c = -20 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you make a sign error when substituting the coordinates of $P(2, -24)$ into $y = -2x + c$, mistakenly calculating $-24 = -4 + c$ as $c = -28$ instead of $c = -20$.
This represents a common misconception where the constant $c$ is assumed to be the $y$-coordinate of the point of tangency. This is only true if the tangent line is horizontal (gradient is 0).

This is a calculation slip where the $y$-coordinate of $P$ is evaluated incorrectly (for example, by calculating $12 - 28 - 8$ as positive $12$), which consequently leads to an incorrect value for $c$.

bradley_insight.title: Finding Tangent Constants From Derivatives
bradley_insight.content: A tangent line $y = mx + c$ shares both the gradient and the coordinates of the tangency point $P$ with the curve. First, solve $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = m$ to find the $x$-coordinate, evaluate the curve's equation to find the $y$-coordinate, and then substitute both into the tangent equation to find $c$.

question:
A curve $C$ has the equation:$$y = 2x^2 - 8x + 9$$(a) Find the equation of the tangent to $C$ at the point $A$ where $x = 3$.

(b) This tangent intersects the $x$-axis at the point $P$ and the $y$-axis at the point $Q$. Find the area of the triangle $OPQ$, where $O$ is the origin.
steps:
Part (a): Finding the equation of the tangent

First, find the $y$-coordinate of point $A$ by substituting $x = 3$ into the curve's equation:\begin{aligned} y &= 2(3)^2 - 8(3) + 9 \cr y &= 18 - 24 + 9 \cr y &= 3 \end{aligned}So, the point of tangency is $A(3, 3)$.

Next, find the gradient function of the curve by differentiating:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 4x - 8 \end{aligned}Now, evaluate the derivative at $x = 3$ to find the gradient of the tangent, $m$:\begin{aligned} m &= 4(3) - 8 \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}

Using the point-slope formula $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ with $A(3, 3)$ and $m = 4$, we find the equation of the tangent line:\begin{aligned} y - 3 &= 4(x - 3) \cr y - 3 &= 4x - 12 \cr y &= 4x - 9 \end{aligned}

Part (b): Finding the area of triangle $OPQ$

Find the coordinate intercepts of the tangent line $y = 4x - 9$:

1. For the $x$-axis intercept (point $P$), set $y = 0$:\begin{aligned} 0 &= 4x - 9 \cr 4x &= 9 \cr x &= \dfrac{9}{4} \end{aligned}So, $P\left(\dfrac{9}{4}, 0\right)$.

2. For the $y$-axis intercept (point $Q$), set $x = 0$:\begin{aligned} y = -9 \end{aligned}So, $Q(0, -9)$.

The triangle $OPQ$ is a right-angled triangle at the origin $O(0, 0)$.

The base along the $x$-axis has a positive length of $\dfrac{9}{4}$ units, and the height along the $y$-axis has a positive length of $9$ units.

Calculate the area:\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{9}{4} \times 9 \cr &= \dfrac{81}{8} \cr &= 10.125 \end{aligned}Thus, the area of triangle $OPQ$ is $\dfrac{81}{8}$ square units.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &\text{Tangent: } y = 4x - 9 \cr &\text{Area} = \dfrac{81}{8} \text{ (or } 10.125\text{)} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is double the correct area. Remember that the area of a right-angled triangle is calculated using $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$, not just $\text{base} \times \text{height}$.

This error occurs if you make an algebraic mistake when simplifying the tangent equation, calculating $y - 3 = 4(x - 3)$ as $y = 4x - 3$. This leads to incorrect intercepts and an incorrect area calculation.
This error occurs if you evaluate the base intercept incorrectly as $x = 9$ (confusing it with the value of the $y$-intercept) rather than the correct value of $x = \dfrac{9}{4}$.

bradley_insight.title: Handling Negative Intercept Coordinates in Area Calculations
bradley_insight.content: When finding the area of a triangle formed by coordinate axes, the base and height must always be positive lengths. If an intercept coordinate is negative (such as $y = -9$), the corresponding physical length is $+9$. Never multiply by negative values for geometric areas.

question:
A curve $C$ has the equation:$$y = 3x^2 - 5x + 2$$(a) Find the equation of the normal to $C$ at the point $P(1, 0)$.

(b) Find the coordinates of the point $Q$ where this normal intersects the curve $C$ again.
steps:
Part (a): Finding the equation of the normal

First, find the gradient function of the curve by differentiating:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 6x - 5 \end{aligned}Evaluate the derivative at $x = 1$ to find the gradient of the tangent, $m_t$:\begin{aligned} m_t &= 6(1) - 5 \cr &= 1 \end{aligned}

The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient ($m_n$) is the negative reciprocal of $m_t$:\begin{aligned} m_n &= -\dfrac{1}{m_t} \cr &= -\dfrac{1}{1} \cr &= -1 \end{aligned}Use the point-slope formula with $P(1, 0)$ and gradient $m_n = -1$ to write the equation of the normal line:\begin{aligned} y - 0 &= -1(x - 1) \cr y &= -x + 1 \end{aligned}

Part (b): Finding the second intersection point $Q$

To find where the normal intersects the curve again, solve the equations simultaneously:\begin{aligned} 3x^2 - 5x + 2 &= -x + 1 \cr 3x^2 - 4x + 1 &= 0 \end{aligned}

Since we already know that $x = 1$ is a point of intersection (the point $P$), $(x - 1)$ must be a factor of the quadratic expression. We factor the quadratic:\begin{aligned} (3x - 1)(x - 1) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives $x = 1$ (which is $P$) or $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$ (which is $Q$).

Substitute $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$ back into the normal equation $y = -x + 1$ to find the $y$-coordinate of $Q$:\begin{aligned} y &= -\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) + 1 \cr &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}Thus, the coordinates of the point $Q$ are $Q\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &\text{Normal: } y = -x + 1 \cr &Q\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{2}{3}\right) \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs from a factoring mistake when solving the simultaneous quadratic equation $3x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0$, incorrectly identifying the factors as $(2x - 1)(x - 1) = 0$ instead of the correct $(3x - 1)(x - 1) = 0$.
This error stems from using the gradient of the tangent ($m_t = 1$) as the gradient of the normal, or forgetting to apply the negative reciprocal sign ($m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m_t}$).

This is a basic calculation slip when evaluating the $y$-coordinate of the point $Q$. Substituting $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$ into the line equation $y = -x + 1$ yields $y = \dfrac{2}{3}$, not $\dfrac{1}{3}$.

bradley_insight.title: Using Known Roots to Factor Simultaneous Quadratics
bradley_insight.content: When finding where a normal (or tangent) intersects a curve again, you already know one intersection point: the point of tangency, $P$. This means $(x - x_P)$ is guaranteed to be a factor of the resulting simultaneous equation. In this case, since $P$ is at $x = 1$, $(x - 1)$ must be a factor of $3x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0$, making the factorization $(3x - 1)(x - 1) = 0$ much easier to spot.

question:
A curve $C$ has the equation:$$y = \dfrac{8}{x} + 2x$$(a) Find an expression for $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$.

(b) The tangent to $C$ at a point $P$ in the first quadrant has a gradient of $0$. Find the coordinates of $P$.

(c) Find the equation of the normal to $C$ at the point where $x = 4$.
steps:
Part (a): Differentiating the expression

Rewrite the curve's equation using negative indices:\begin{aligned} y = 8x^{-1} + 2x \end{aligned}Now, apply the power rule of differentiation:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= -8x^{-2} + 2 \cr &= -\dfrac{8}{x^2} + 2 \end{aligned}

Part (b): Finding the point $P$

Since the gradient of the tangent at $P$ is $0$, we set our derivative equal to $0$:\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{8}{x^2} + 2 &= 0 \cr \dfrac{8}{x^2} &= 2 \cr 2x^2 &= 8 \cr x^2 &= 4 \cr x &= \pm 2 \end{aligned}Since $P$ is in the first quadrant, the $x$-coordinate must be positive, so we take $x = 2$.

Substitute $x = 2$ back into the curve's original equation to find the $y$-coordinate of $P$:\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{8}{2} + 2(2) \cr &= 4 + 4 \cr &= 8 \end{aligned}Thus, the coordinates of $P$ are $P(2, 8)$.

Part (c): Finding the equation of the normal at $x = 4$

First, find the point on the curve when $x = 4$:\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{8}{4} + 2(4) \cr &= 2 + 8 \cr &= 10 \end{aligned}So, the point on the curve is $(4, 10)$.
Next, find the gradient of the tangent at $x = 4$ by evaluating the derivative:\begin{aligned} m_t &= -\dfrac{8}{4^2} + 2 \cr &= -\dfrac{8}{16} + 2 \cr &= -0.5 + 2 \cr &= \dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}

The gradient of the normal is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient:\begin{aligned} m_n &= -\dfrac{1}{m_t} \cr &= -\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}Use the point-slope formula with point $(4, 10)$ and gradient $m_n = -\dfrac{2}{3}$ to write the normal equation:\begin{aligned} y - 10 &= -\dfrac{2}{3}(x - 4) \cr 3(y - 10) &= -2(x - 4) \cr 3y - 30 &= -2x + 8 \cr 2x + 3y - 38 &= 0 \end{aligned}
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = -\dfrac{8}{x^2} + 2 \cr &P(2, 8) \cr &2x + 3y - 38 = 0 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you ignore the restriction that $P$ must lie in the first quadrant. In the first quadrant, both coordinates must be positive, which means you must choose $x = 2$ instead of $x = -2$.
This error occurs if you use the gradient of the tangent ($m_t = 1.5$) instead of the perpendicular gradient of the normal ($m_n = -\dfrac{2}{3}$) to find the equation of the normal.

This is the result of using the correct normal gradient but mistakenly using the coordinates of point $P(2, 8)$ instead of the coordinates at $x = 4$ (which are $(4, 10)$) to write the normal equation.

bradley_insight.title: Understanding Perpendicular Gradients
bradley_insight.content: Always distinguish carefully between the tangent and the normal. The tangent gradient is given by the derivative $m_t = \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$. The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal: $m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m_t}$. Verify that $m_t \times m_n = -1$.

question:
A curve $C$ has the equation $y = x^2 - 4x + 7$ and a family of lines $L$ has the equation $y = mx + 3$, where $m$ is a constant.

(a) Show that if the line $L$ is a tangent to the curve $C$, then $m$ must satisfy the equation:$$(m+4)^2 - 16 = 0$$(b) Hence, find the two possible values of the gradient $m$.

(c) For each value of $m$, find the coordinates of the point of tangency.
steps:
Part (a): Setting up the tangency condition

To find the intersection of the curve and the line, set their equations equal to each other:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 4x + 7 &= mx + 3 \cr x^2 - 4x - mx + 7 - 3 &= 0 \cr x^2 - (m+4)x + 4 &= 0 \end{aligned}

For the line to be a tangent to the curve, they must intersect at exactly one point. This means the quadratic equation must have exactly one real root, so its discriminant must equal zero ($b^2 - 4ac = 0$):\begin{aligned} a &= 1 \cr b &= -(m + 4) \cr c &= 4 \end{aligned}Substitute these values into the discriminant formula:\begin{aligned} [-(m + 4)]^2 - 4(1)(4) &= 0 \cr (m + 4)^2 - 16 &= 0 \end{aligned}This is the required equation.

Part (b): Solving for $m$

We solve the equation by rearranging and taking square roots:\begin{aligned} (m+4)^2 &= 16 \cr m+4 &= \pm 4 \end{aligned}This gives two possible equations:

1. $m+4 = 4$, which gives $m = 0$

2. $m+4 = -4$, which gives $m = -8$

Thus, the two possible gradients are $m = 0$ and $m = -8$.

Part (c): Finding the points of tangency

We find the points of tangency by substituting each value of $m$ back into our simultaneous quadratic $x^2 - (m+4)x + 4 = 0$:

Case 1: $m = 0$\begin{aligned} x^2 - (0+4)x + 4 &= 0 \cr x^2 - 4x + 4 &= 0 \cr (x - 2)^2 &= 0 \cr x &= 2 \end{aligned}Substitute $x = 2$ into the line equation $y = 0x + 3$ to get $y = 3$.

So, the first point of tangency is $(2, 3)$.

Case 2: $m = -8$\begin{aligned} x^2 - (-8+4)x + 4 &= 0 \cr x^2 + 4x + 4 &= 0 \cr (x + 2)^2 &= 0 \cr x &= -2 \end{aligned}Substitute $x = -2$ into the line equation $y = -8x + 3$:\begin{aligned} y &= -8(-2) + 3 \cr &= 19 \end{aligned}So, the second point of tangency is $(-2, 19)$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &m = 0 \text{ with } (2, 3) \cr &m = -8 \text{ with } (-2, 19) \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs when solving the quadratic $(m+4)^2 = 16$ as $m + 4 = 4$ giving $m = 0$, but incorrectly carrying out the arithmetic for the negative root to get $m = \pm 4$ instead of $m = 0$ and $m = -8$.
This is a slip in finding the points of tangency. Remember that each gradient $m$ yields a distinct repeated root quadratic, resulting in different $x$-coordinates ($x = 2$ and $x = -2$).
This error stems from a coordinate calculation slip when substituting the $x$-coordinates back into the equations to find the corresponding $y$-coordinates.

bradley_insight.title: The Dual Approaches of Calculus and the Discriminant
bradley_insight.content: A line $y = mx + c$ is tangent to a quadratic curve $y = ax^2 + bx + d$ if and only if they intersect at exactly one point. This can be solved in two ways: by setting the discriminant of their simultaneous quadratic to zero (algebraic), or by setting $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = m$ (calculus). Both methods lead to the exact same results, showing the deep connection between algebra and calculus.

question:
(a) Solve the logarithmic equation:\begin{aligned} &2\log_{10} x \cr &\quad = 1 + \log_{10} 8 - \log_{10} 5 \end{aligned}(b) Solve the exponential equation:$$5^x = 3e^{0.2x}$$giving your answer correct to 3 decimal places.

(c) Express $9^x - 12 \times 3^x$ in terms of $y$, where $y = 3^x$.

Hence, solve the equation:$$9^x - 12 \times 3^x = -27$$
steps:
Part (a): Solving the logarithmic equation

To solve the equation, we rewrite the constant 1 as a logarithm in base 10: $1 = \log_{10} 10$.

Substitute this into the equation and use the laws of logarithms:\begin{aligned} &2\log_{10} x \cr &\quad = \log_{10} 10 + \log_{10} 8 - \log_{10} 5 \cr &\log_{10}(x^2) \cr &\quad = \log_{10} \left( \dfrac{10 \times 8}{5} \right) \cr &\log_{10}(x^2) = \log_{10} 16 \end{aligned}

Now, equate the arguments of the logarithms:\begin{aligned} x^2 &= 16 \cr x &= \pm 4 \end{aligned}Since the argument of a logarithm must be strictly positive ($x > 0$), we reject $x = -4$.

Thus, the only valid solution is $x = 4$.

Part (b): Solving the exponential equation

Take the natural logarithm ($\ln$) of both sides of $5^x = 3e^{0.2x}$:\begin{aligned} \ln(5^x) &= \ln(3e^{0.2x}) \cr x\ln(5) &= \ln(3) + 0.2x \end{aligned}

Rearrange to group the $x$ terms on one side and solve:\begin{aligned} x\ln(5) - 0.2x &= \ln(3) \cr x(\ln(5) - 0.2) &= \ln(3) \cr x &= \dfrac{\ln(3)}{\ln(5) - 0.2} \end{aligned}Evaluate this expression numerically:\begin{aligned} x &\approx \dfrac{1.098612}{1.609438 - 0.2} \cr &\approx \dfrac{1.098612}{1.409438} \cr &\approx 0.779468 \end{aligned}Rounding to 3 decimal places gives $x \approx 0.779$.

Part (c): Solving the quadratic in exponential form

Let $y = 3^x$. We can express $9^x$ as $(3^2)^x = (3^x)^2$, which gives $y^2$.

Substituting these into $9^x - 12 \times 3^x$, our expression in terms of $y$ is $y^2 - 12y$.

We now solve the equation $y^2 - 12y = -27$:\begin{aligned} y^2 - 12y + 27 &= 0 \cr (y - 3)(y - 9) &= 0 \end{aligned}This yields $y = 3$ or $y = 9$.

Now substitute back $y = 3^x$ and solve for $x$:

1. For $y = 3$:\begin{aligned} 3^x &= 3 \cr x &= 1 \end{aligned}

2. For $y = 9$:\begin{aligned} 3^x &= 9 \cr x &= 2 \end{aligned}Thus, the solutions are $x = 1$ or $x = 2$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } x = 4 \cr &\text{(b) } x \approx 0.779 \cr &\text{(c) } x = 1 \text{ or } x = 2 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a rounding slip in part (b). Evaluating $\dfrac{\ln(3)}{\ln(5) - 0.2}$ yields $0.779468\dots$ Since the digit in the ten-thousandths place is 4, this must round down to $0.779$ instead of up to $0.780$.

In part (c), $y = 3$ and $y = 9$ are the intermediate solutions for $y$, where $y = 3^x$. You must complete the final step of solving for $x$ by writing $3^x = 3$, giving $x = 1$, and $3^x = 9$, giving $x = 2$.

pi_options.ans: \begin{aligned} &\text{(a) } x = 4 \text{ or } x = -4 \cr &\text{(b) } x = 0.779 \cr &\text{(c) } x = 1 \text{ or } x = 2 \end{aligned}
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), the quadratic equation $x^2 = 16$ mathematically yields $x = \pm 4$. However, you must reject $x = -4$ because the original equation contains $\log_{10} x$, and the argument of a logarithm must be strictly positive.

bradley_insight.title: Logarithmic Domain Constraints
bradley_insight.content: Always check your final answers against the domain constraints of the original logarithmic equations. Since $\log_b(f(x))$ is only defined when $f(x) > 0$, any algebraic solution that causes an argument to be negative or zero must be strictly rejected.

question: Solve the following equation for $x$:\begin{aligned} &\log_2 (2x + 1) \cr &\quad - \log_2 (x - 1) = 3 \end{aligned}Show all of your working clearly.
steps: Apply the subtraction law of logarithms ($\log_b A - \log_b B = \log_b \left( \dfrac{A}{B} \right)$) to combine the left-hand side into a single logarithmic term:\begin{aligned} \log_2 \left( \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 1} \right) = 3 \end{aligned}
To remove the logarithm, rewrite the equation in its equivalent exponential form:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 1} &= 2^3 \cr &= 8 \end{aligned}
Solve the resulting linear equation for $x$:\begin{aligned} 2x + 1 &= 8(x - 1) \cr 2x + 1 &= 8x - 8 \cr -6x &= -9 \cr x &= \dfrac{-9}{-6} \cr x &= 1.5 \end{aligned}

We must verify that $x = 1.5$ satisfies the domain of the original logs:

1. For $\log_2 (2x + 1)$: $2(1.5) + 1 = 4$, which is $> 0$ (valid).

2. For $\log_2 (x - 1)$: $1.5 - 1 = 0.5$, which is $> 0$ (valid).

Thus, the solution is $x = 1.5$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} x = 1.5 \text{ (or } \dfrac{3}{2}\text{)} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a sign error during algebraic rearrangement. Moving terms across the equals sign correctly gives $-6x = -9$, which yields $x = 1.5$.
This error occurs if you incorrectly expand $8(x-1)$ as $8x-1$ or $8x-2$, failing to distribute the multiplication to the constant term inside the parentheses.
This error can occur if you mistake the base of the exponent as $3^2 = 9$ or $2 \times 3 = 6$ instead of $2^3 = 8$ when converting the logarithmic equation to exponential form.

bradley_insight.title: Verifying Logarithmic Arguments
bradley_insight.content: Even if your algebraic steps are perfectly correct, you should always check your final values against the original logs. If any solution results in a negative argument, such as $\log_b(-5)$, it must be discarded immediately.

question: Solve the exponential equation:$$4^{2x - 1} = 5^{x + 2}$$giving your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
steps: Take the natural logarithm ($\ln$) of both sides of the equation:\begin{aligned} \ln\left( 4^{2x - 1} \right) = \ln\left( 5^{x + 2} \right) \end{aligned}
Use the power law of logarithms to bring the exponents down as multipliers:\begin{aligned} (2x - 1)\ln(4) = (x + 2)\ln(5) \end{aligned}

Expand the brackets and group all terms containing $x$ on one side of the equation:\begin{aligned} &2x\ln(4) - \ln(4) \cr &\quad = x\ln(5) + 2\ln(5) \cr &2x\ln(4) - x\ln(5) \cr &\quad = \ln(4) + 2\ln(5) \end{aligned}
Factor out $x$ on the left-hand side and solve:\begin{aligned} &x\big(2\ln(4) - \ln(5)\big) \cr &\quad = \ln(4) + 2\ln(5) \cr &x = \dfrac{\ln(4) + 2\ln(5)}{2\ln(4) - \ln(5)} \end{aligned}

Evaluate this expression numerically using a calculator:\begin{aligned} x &\approx \dfrac{1.386294 + 3.218876}{2.772588 - 1.609438} \cr &\approx \dfrac{4.605170}{1.163150} \cr &\approx 3.959220 \end{aligned}Rounding to 3 decimal places gives $x \approx 3.959$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} x \approx 3.959 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a minor calculation/rounding slip that occurs if you use rounded intermediate values for $\ln(4) \approx 1.3863$ and $\ln(5) \approx 1.6094$ and make a rounding error during division. Always use full calculator precision before rounding at the very end.
This error occurs if you attempt to simplify the exponents directly without taking logarithms, such as incorrectly writing $2x - 1 = x + 2$ which ignores the differing base values.

This error is typically caused by a sign error when grouping the terms, such as subtracting $\ln(4)$ on the right-hand side instead of adding it, leading to $x = \dfrac{2\ln(5) - \ln(4)}{2\ln(4) - \ln(5)}$, which evaluates to approximately $2.454$.

bradley_insight.title: Exact Algebraic Rearrangements
bradley_insight.content: To avoid early rounding errors, do not convert logs to decimals in the intermediate steps. Keep them in their exact form (like $\ln(4)$ and $\ln(5)$) as coefficients, factor out $x$ algebraically, and only compute the final fraction at the very end.

question: Solve the equation:$$2^{2x} - 2^{x + 2} - 32 = 0$$giving your answer in its simplest exact form.
steps:
Use the laws of indices to split and rewrite the exponential terms in terms of a single base $2^x$:

1. $2^{2x} = (2^x)^2$

2. $2^{x + 2} = 2^x \times 2^2$, which simplifies to $4(2^x)$.

Substitute these into our equation:\begin{aligned} (2^x)^2 - 4(2^x) - 32 = 0 \end{aligned}
Introduce a substitution variable. Let $y = 2^x$. This transforms the exponential equation into a standard quadratic equation in terms of $y$:\begin{aligned} y^2 - 4y - 32 = 0 \end{aligned}
Solve the quadratic equation by factoring:\begin{aligned} (y - 8)(y + 4) = 0 \end{aligned}This gives $y = 8$ or $y = -4$.

Now substitute $y = 2^x$ back to solve for $x$:

1. For $y = 8$:\begin{aligned} 2^x &= 8 \cr 2^x &= 2^3 \cr x &= 3 \end{aligned}

2. For $y = -4$:\begin{aligned} 2^x = -4 \end{aligned}Since $2^x$ must be strictly positive for all real values of $x$ (the range of $a^x$ is $y > 0$), this equation has no real solutions.

Thus, the only valid solution is $x = 3$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} x = 3 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a very common error where a student attempts to solve $2^x = -4$ by writing $x = -2$. However, $2^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$, which is positive. An exponential term with a positive base can never equal a negative number.
These are the values for the substitution variable $y$, where $y = 2^x$. You must complete the final step of the problem by substituting $2^x$ back in and solving for $x$.
This error occurs if you misinterpret the laws of indices, for example, incorrectly expanding $2^{x+2}$ as $2^x + 2$, which changes the quadratic coefficients and leads to incorrect roots.

bradley_insight.title: Exponential Range Limitations
bradley_insight.content: Always remember that $a^x > 0$ for any real $x$ and any positive base $a$. When solving equations in quadratic form, any negative roots for the substitution variable (such as $y = -4$) must be discarded immediately as they cannot yield any real solutions for $x$.

question: Solve the simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} \log_3 x + \log_3 y &= 2 \cr \log_3 (2x - y) &= 1 \end{aligned}Show all of your algebraic working clearly, explaining why any solutions must be rejected.
steps: Apply the addition law of logarithms to combine the left-hand side of the first equation:\begin{aligned} \log_3(xy) = 2 \end{aligned}Convert this to its equivalent exponential form:\begin{aligned} xy &= 3^2 \cr xy &= 9 \end{aligned}
Now convert the second equation to its equivalent exponential form:\begin{aligned} 2x - y &= 3^1 \cr 2x - y &= 3 \end{aligned}

We now have a system of simultaneous equations:

1. $xy = 9$

2. $2x - y = 3$, which gives $y = 2x - 3$.

Substitute the expression for $y$ from the second equation into the first equation:\begin{aligned} x(2x - 3) &= 9 \cr 2x^2 - 3x - 9 &= 0 \end{aligned}

Solve the quadratic equation by factoring:\begin{aligned} 2x^2 - 6x + 3x - 9 &= 0 \cr 2x(x - 3) + 3(x - 3) &= 0 \cr (2x + 3)(x - 3) &= 0 \end{aligned}This gives $x = 3$ or $x = -1.5$ (or $-\dfrac{3}{2}$).

Now, calculate the corresponding $y$-values using $y = 2x - 3$:

1. If $x = 3$:\begin{aligned} y &= 2(3) - 3 \cr &= 3 \end{aligned}

2. If $x = -1.5$:\begin{aligned} y &= 2(-1.5) - 3 \cr &= -6 \end{aligned}

Verify both coordinate pairs against the domains of the original logarithmic equations:

1. For $(3, 3)$: the log arguments $x = 3$ and $y = 3$ are positive, and $2x - y = 6 - 3 = 3$, which is $> 0$. All are positive, so $(3, 3)$ is a valid solution.

2. For $(-1.5, -6)$: the log arguments are $x = -1.5 < 0$ and $y = -6 < 0$. Since logarithms of negative numbers are undefined, this coordinate pair must be rejected.

Thus, the only valid solution is $x = 3, y = 3$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &x = 3 \cr &y = 3 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a failure to apply domain restrictions. You must reject the coordinate pair $(-1.5, -6)$ because substituting negative values into $\log_3 x$ and $\log_3 y$ results in undefined real values.
This error occurs from a sign mistake during the factoring step, incorrectly factoring $2x^2 - 3x - 9 = 0$ as $(2x - 3)(x + 3) = 0$, leading to incorrect $x$-coordinates.
This is a basic algebraic slip when substituting $x = 3$ into $y = 2x - 3$, incorrectly performing the subtraction as $6 - 3 = -3$ instead of $+3$.

bradley_insight.title: Mandatory Domain Checks in Systems of Equations
bradley_insight.content: When solving simultaneous logarithmic systems, algebraic manipulations can introduce extraneous solutions. Always check each candidate solution pair $(x, y)$ in every original logarithmic term. If any term has a non-positive argument, that entire coordinate pair must be rejected.

question:
The coordinates of three points $A$, $B$, and $C$ are $(2, 6)$, $(4, 10)$, and $(6, 4)$ respectively.

(a) Show that $BAC$ is a right angle.

(b) A circle passes through all three points $A$, $B$, and $C$. Determine the equation of the circle.
steps:
Part (a): Showing $BAC$ is a right angle

To show that angle $BAC$ is a right angle, we calculate the gradients of the line segments $AB$ and $AC$ and show that they are perpendicular:

1. Gradient of $AB$ ($m_{AB}$):\begin{aligned} m_{AB} &= \dfrac{10 - 6}{4 - 2} \cr &= \dfrac{4}{2} \cr &= 2 \end{aligned}

2. Gradient of $AC$ ($m_{AC}$):\begin{aligned} m_{AC} &= \dfrac{4 - 6}{6 - 2} \cr &= \dfrac{-2}{4} \cr &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}

Multiply the two gradients to check for perpendicularity:\begin{aligned} m_{AB} \times m_{AC} &= 2 \times \left( -\dfrac{1}{2} \right) \cr &= -1 \end{aligned}Since the product of the gradients is $-1$, the lines $AB$ and $AC$ are perpendicular, which proves that $BAC$ is a right angle.

Part (b): Determining the equation of the circle

By Thales's Theorem, since $BAC$ is a right angle on the circumference of a circle, the line segment connecting $B(4, 10)$ and $C(6, 4)$ must be a diameter of the circle.

The centre of the circle is the midpoint of the diameter $BC$:\begin{aligned} \text{Centre } (h, k) &= \left( \dfrac{4 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{10 + 4}{2} \right) \cr &= (5, 7) \end{aligned}

The radius squared ($r^2$) is the distance from the centre $(5, 7)$ to any point on the circle, such as $C(6, 4)$:\begin{aligned} r^2 &= (6 - 5)^2 + (4 - 7)^2 \cr &= 1^2 + (-3)^2 \cr &= 1 + 9 \cr &= 10 \end{aligned}Now, write the equation of the circle in standard form $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$:\begin{aligned} (x - 5)^2 + (y - 7)^2 = 10 \end{aligned}
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} (x - 5)^2 + (y - 7)^2 = 10 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you use the diameter squared (or $2r$ squared) instead of the radius squared ($r^2$) in the equation of the circle, incorrectly calculating $r^2 = 100$ instead of $r^2 = 10$.
This is a calculation error in finding the radius squared. Make sure you calculate the distance from the centre $(5, 7)$ to one of the points correctly: $r^2 = 1 + 9 = 10$, not $40$.
This error occurs if you forget to flip the signs of the coordinates when writing the equation of the circle. A centre of $(h, k) = (5, 7)$ results in $(x - 5)^2 + (y - 7)^2 = r^2$.

bradley_insight.title: Thales's Theorem in Circle Coordinate Geometry
bradley_insight.content: According to Thales's Theorem, the angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the circle is a right angle. Conversely, if three points $A$, $B$, and $C$ on a circle form a right angle at $A$, then the line segment $BC$ must be a diameter of the circle. This lets you immediately find the centre of the circle (midpoint of $BC$) and its radius without solving simultaneous equations.

question:
A circle $C$ has the equation:$$x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 8y - 9 = 0$$(a) Find the coordinates of the centre of $C$ and the exact radius of $C$.

(b) Show that the point $P(6, 1)$ lies on the circle.

(c) Find the equation of the tangent to $C$ at the point $P$, giving your answer in the form $ax + by + c = 0$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are integers.
steps:
Part (a): Finding the centre and radius

Complete the square for both $x$ and $y$ variables in the equation:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 6x &= (x - 3)^2 - 9 \cr y^2 + 8y &= (y + 4)^2 - 16 \end{aligned}Substitute these back into the original equation:\begin{aligned} &(x - 3)^2 - 9 + (y + 4)^2 \cr &\qquad - 16 - 9 = 0 \cr &(x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 - 34 = 0 \cr &(x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 34 \end{aligned}Thus, the centre of $C$ is $(3, -4)$ and the exact radius is $r = \sqrt{34}$.

Part (b): Showing $P(6, 1)$ lies on the circle

Substitute the coordinates $x = 6, y = 1$ into our completed square equation:\begin{aligned} (6 - 3)^2 + (1 + 4)^2 &= 3^2 + 5^2 \cr &= 9 + 25 \cr &= 34 \end{aligned}Since the substitution satisfies the circle's equation, the point $P(6, 1)$ lies on the circle.

Part (c): Finding the equation of the tangent at $P$

First, find the gradient of the radius connecting the centre $C(3, -4)$ to $P(6, 1)$:\begin{aligned} m_r &= \dfrac{1 - (-4)}{6 - 3} \cr &= \dfrac{5}{3} \end{aligned}Since the tangent is perpendicular to the radius, its gradient ($m_t$) is the negative reciprocal:\begin{aligned} m_t &= -\dfrac{1}{m_r} \cr &= -\dfrac{3}{5} \end{aligned}

Use the point-slope formula with $P(6, 1)$ and $m_t = -\dfrac{3}{5}$:\begin{aligned} y - 1 &= -\dfrac{3}{5}(x - 6) \cr 5(y - 1) &= -3(x - 6) \cr 5y - 5 &= -3x + 18 \cr 3x + 5y - 23 &= 0 \end{aligned}Thus, the equation of the tangent is $3x + 5y - 23 = 0$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &\text{Centre: } (3, -4) \cr &\text{Radius} = \sqrt{34} \cr &3x + 5y - 23 = 0 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Remember that when completing the square, the constant on the right-hand side is $r^2$. Thus, the radius is $\sqrt{34}$, not $34$.
Be careful with signs when completing the square: $x^2 - 6x = (x-3)^2 - 9$ and $y^2 + 8y = (y+4)^2 - 16$. This gives a centre of $(3, -4)$, not $(-3, 4)$.
This is the result of using the gradient of the radius ($m_r = \dfrac{5}{3}$) instead of the perpendicular gradient of the tangent ($m_t = -\dfrac{3}{5}$) to write the tangent equation.

bradley_insight.title: Finding Tangents via the Radius Gradient
bradley_insight.content: A tangent to a circle at point $P$ is always perpendicular to the radius connecting the centre to $P$. Therefore, first find the gradient of the radius, $m_r = \dfrac{y_P - y_C}{x_P - x_C}$, and then use the negative reciprocal $m_t = -\dfrac{1}{m_r}$ for the tangent's gradient.

question:
A circle $C$ has the equation:$$(x - 2)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = 25$$The line $L$ has the equation:$$y = x - 2$$(a) Show that the line $L$ intersects the circle $C$ at the points $P(6, 4)$ and $Q(-1, -3)$.

(b) Calculate the exact length of the chord $PQ$, giving your answer in its simplest surd form.
steps:
Part (a): Showing the intersection points

Substitute the equation of the line $y = x - 2$ into the equation of the circle:\begin{aligned} (x - 2)^2 + (x - 2 - 1)^2 &= 25 \cr (x - 2)^2 + (x - 3)^2 &= 25 \end{aligned}Expand both brackets and simplify:\begin{aligned} &(x^2 - 4x + 4) \cr &\qquad + (x^2 - 6x + 9) = 25 \cr &2x^2 - 10x + 13 = 25 \cr &2x^2 - 10x - 12 = 0 \end{aligned}
Divide the entire equation by 2 and factor the resulting quadratic:\begin{aligned} x^2 - 5x - 6 &= 0 \cr (x - 6)(x + 1) &= 0 \end{aligned}This gives $x = 6$ or $x = -1$.

Now substitute these $x$-values back into $y = x - 2$ to find the corresponding $y$-coordinates:

1. For $x = 6$:\begin{aligned} y &= 6 - 2 \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}This gives $P(6, 4)$.

2. For $x = -1$:\begin{aligned} y &= -1 - 2 \cr &= -3 \end{aligned}This gives $Q(-1, -3)$.

This confirms that the line intersects the circle at $P(6, 4)$ and $Q(-1, -3)$.

Part (b): Calculating the chord length $PQ$

Use the distance formula between the points $P(6, 4)$ and $Q(-1, -3)$:\begin{aligned} PQ &= \sqrt{(6 - (-1))^2 + (4 - (-3))^2} \cr &= \sqrt{7^2 + 7^2} \cr &= \sqrt{49 + 49} \cr &= \sqrt{98} \cr &= 7\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}Thus, the exact length of the chord $PQ$ is $7\sqrt{2}$ units.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &\text{Points: } P(6, 4) \text{ and } Q(-1, -3) \cr &PQ = 7\sqrt{2} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs if you subtract the coordinates incorrectly or forget to square the differences before adding, calculating $PQ = \sqrt{(6 - (-1)) + (4 - (-3))}$, which gives $\sqrt{14}$.
This error occurs if you assume $PQ = 7 + 7 = 14$. You must use the Pythagorean distance formula $PQ = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}$, which evaluates to $7\sqrt{2}$.
Double check your factorization of the simultaneous quadratic $x^2 - 5x - 6 = 0$. This factors to $(x-6)(x+1) = 0$, giving $x = 6$ and $x = -1$, not $x = 1$.

bradley_insight.title: Symmetric Surds in Diagonal Chords
bradley_insight.content: When a line has a gradient of $1$ (like $y = x - 2$), the change in $x$ and $y$ between any two points is identical: $\Delta x = \Delta y$. Therefore, the chord length will always be in the form $\sqrt{d^2 + d^2} = d\sqrt{2}$, where $d$ is the difference in $x$-coordinates. This is a quick way to double-check surd calculations.

question:
The points $A(-2, 5)$ and $B(6, 11)$ are the endpoints of a diameter of a circle $C$.

(a) Find the coordinates of the centre of $C$.

(b) Find the radius of $C$, giving your answer in its simplest surd form.

(c) Write down the equation of the circle in the form $x^2 + y^2 + ax + by + c = 0$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are integers.
steps:
Part (a): Finding the centre of $C$

Since $A$ and $B$ are the endpoints of a diameter, the centre of the circle is the midpoint of the line segment $AB$:\begin{aligned} \text{Centre } (h, k) &= \left( \dfrac{-2 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{5 + 11}{2} \right) \cr &= \left( \dfrac{4}{2}, \dfrac{16}{2} \right) \cr &= (2, 8) \end{aligned}

Part (b): Finding the radius of $C$

First, calculate the length of the diameter $AB$ using the distance formula:\begin{aligned} AB &= \sqrt{(6 - (-2))^2 + (11 - 5)^2} \cr &= \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} \cr &= \sqrt{64 + 36} \cr &= \sqrt{100} \cr &= 10 \end{aligned}The radius $r$ is half the length of the diameter:\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{AB}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{10}{2} \cr &= 5 \end{aligned}

Part (c): Determining the expanded equation of the circle

First, write the equation of the circle in standard centre-radius form:\begin{aligned} (x - 2)^2 + (y - 8)^2 &= 5^2 \cr (x - 2)^2 + (y - 8)^2 &= 25 \end{aligned}

Now, fully expand the brackets and group the terms:\begin{aligned} &(x^2 - 4x + 4) \cr &\qquad + (y^2 - 16y + 64) = 25 \cr &x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 16y \cr &\qquad + 68 = 25 \cr &x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 16y \cr &\qquad + 43 = 0 \end{aligned}
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &\text{Centre: } (2, 8) \cr &r = 5 \cr &x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 16y \cr &\qquad + 43 = 0 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error occurs when expanding $(x-2)^2 + (y-8)^2 = 25$ if you add the constants $+4$ and $+64$ to get $+68$, but fail to subtract the $r^2 = 25$ term correctly (calculating $68 + 25 = 93$ instead of $68 - 25 = 43$).
This is a sign error in the expanded form, which happens if you use a centre of $(-2, -8)$ instead of $(2, 8)$.
This error occurs if you forget to equate the equation of the circle to $r^2 = 25$ on the right-hand side before expanding and grouping terms.

bradley_insight.title: From Centre-Radius to Expanded Standard Form
bradley_insight.content: When asked to express a circle equation in the expanded form $x^2 + y^2 + ax + by + c = 0$, start by writing it in the standard centre-radius form $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$. Fully expand the brackets, collect the constant terms on the left-hand side, and set the equation equal to zero.

question:
A circle $C$ has the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 20$ and a line $L$ has the equation $y = 2x + k$, where $k$ is a constant.

(a) Show that if the line $L$ is a tangent to the circle $C$, then $k$ must satisfy the equation:$$k^2 - 100 = 0$$(b) Hence, find the two possible values of the constant $k$.
steps:
Part (a): Setting up the simultaneous equation and discriminant

Substitute the line equation $y = 2x + k$ into the circle equation:\begin{aligned} x^2 + (2x + k)^2 &= 20 \cr x^2 + (4x^2 + 4kx + k^2) &= 20 \cr 5x^2 + 4kx + k^2 - 20 &= 0 \end{aligned}

This is a quadratic equation of the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, where:\begin{aligned} a &= 5 \cr b &= 4k \cr c &= k^2 - 20 \end{aligned}For the line to be tangent to the circle, they must intersect at exactly one point. This means our quadratic equation must have exactly one real root, so its discriminant must equal zero ($b^2 - 4ac = 0$):\begin{aligned} (4k)^2 - 4(5)(k^2 - 20) &= 0 \cr 16k^2 - 20(k^2 - 20) &= 0 \cr 16k^2 - 20k^2 + 400 &= 0 \cr -4k^2 + 400 &= 0 \end{aligned}
Divide the entire equation by $-4$ to simplify:\begin{aligned} k^2 - 100 = 0 \end{aligned}This is the required equation.

Part (b): Solving for $k$

Solve the equation by taking square roots:\begin{aligned} k^2 &= 100 \cr k &= \pm 10 \end{aligned}Thus, the two possible values of $k$ are $k = 10$ or $k = -10$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} k = 10 \text{ or } k = -10 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a basic algebraic error where taking the square root is omitted: taking the square root of $k^2 = 100$ gives $k = \pm 10$, not $\pm 100$.
This error occurs if you make a calculation slip in evaluating the discriminant, such as calculating $16k^2 - 20(k^2 - 20) = 0$ as $-4k^2 + 80 = 0$, giving $k^2 = 20$.
Remember that the equation $k^2 = 100$ has two real roots: a positive root $k = 10$ and a negative root $k = -10$. Both are valid and represent parallel tangent lines.

bradley_insight.title: Geometric Interpretation of Parallel Tangents
bradley_insight.content: Since the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 20$ is centred at the origin, a line of fixed gradient $m = 2$ can be tangent to the circle at two distinct, opposite points. This is why we get two symmetric values of $k$ ($k = 10$ and $k = -10$), representing the upper and lower parallel tangents.

question: Solve the following simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} 2x + y - z &= 5 \cr x - 2y + 3z &= -6 \cr 3x + y + 2z &= 3 \end{aligned}Show all of your algebraic working clearly.
steps:
We label our three equations to keep our working organized:

1. $2x + y - z = 5$

2. $x - 2y + 3z = -6$

3. $3x + y + 2z = 3$

Step 1: Eliminate $y$ using Equations 1 and 3

Rearrange Equation 1 to express $y$ in terms of $x$ and $z$:\begin{aligned} y = 5 - 2x + z \end{aligned}Substitute this expression into Equation 3:\begin{aligned} &3x + (5 - 2x + z) \cr &\qquad + 2z = 3 \cr &3x + 5 - 2x + z \cr &\qquad + 2z = 3 \cr &x + 3z + 5 = 3 \cr &x + 3z = -2 \end{aligned}We call this Equation 4: $x + 3z = -2$. Rearranging gives:\begin{aligned} x = -2 - 3z \end{aligned}

Step 2: Substitute our expressions into Equation 2

First, substitute $x = -2 - 3z$ into our expression for $y$:\begin{aligned} y &= 5 - 2(-2 - 3z) + z \cr &= 5 + 4 + 6z + z \cr &= 9 + 7z \end{aligned}Substitute $y = 9 + 7z$ and $x = -2 - 3z$ directly into Equation 2:\begin{aligned} &(-2 - 3z) - 2(9 + 7z) \cr &\qquad + 3z = -6 \cr &-2 - 3z - 18 \cr &\qquad - 14z + 3z = -6 \cr &-20 - 14z = -6 \cr &-14z = 14 \cr &z = -1 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve for $x$ and $y$

Substitute $z = -1$ back into our expression for $x$:\begin{aligned} x &= -2 - 3(-1) \cr &= -2 + 3 \cr &= 1 \end{aligned}Substitute $x = 1$ and $z = -1$ back into our expression for $y$ (Equation 1):\begin{aligned} y &= 5 - 2(1) + (-1) \cr &= 5 - 2 - 1 \cr &= 2 \end{aligned}Thus, the solutions are $x = 1, y = 2, z = -1$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &x = 1 \cr &y = 2 \cr &z = -1 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This error typically arises if you make a sign error when rearranging the first equation (e.g., writing $y = 5 + 2x - z$ instead of $y = 5 - 2x + z$) and then carry this mistake through the rest of the elimination steps.
This error is typically caused by a sign slip when substituting intermediate expressions, which leads to an incorrect value for $z$ (such as positive $1$ instead of $-1$).
This error occurs if you make a calculation slip when evaluating the linear equation $x + 3z = -2$. Double-check that substituting $z = -1$ yields $x - 3 = -2$, which gives $x = 1$.

bradley_insight.title: Systematic Variable Substitution
bradley_insight.content: When solving simultaneous equations in three variables, choose the variable that is easiest to isolate (usually one with a coefficient of $1$ or $-1$). Isolate it, substitute it into the other two equations, and you will reduce the problem to a standard two-variable simultaneous system.

question: Solve the simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} x + 3y + z &= 1 \cr 2x - y &= 8 \cr x - 2y - z &= 3 \end{aligned}
steps:
We label our three equations to analyze the system:

1. $x + 3y + z = 1$

2. $2x - y = 8$

3. $x - 2y - z = 3$

Step 1: Eliminate $z$ using Equations 1 and 3

Notice that Equation 2 does not contain the variable $z$. We can easily eliminate $z$ from the other two equations by adding Equation 1 and Equation 3 directly:\begin{aligned} &(x + 3y + z) \cr &\qquad + (x - 2y - z) = 1 + 3 \cr &2x + y = 4 \end{aligned}We call this Equation 4: $2x + y = 4$.

Step 2: Solve the two-variable system

We now have a simple system of two simultaneous equations in terms of $x$ and $y$:\begin{aligned} 2x - y &= 8 \cr 2x + y &= 4 \end{aligned}Add Equation 2 and Equation 4 to eliminate $y$:\begin{aligned} (2x - y) + (2x + y) &= 8 + 4 \cr 4x &= 12 \cr x &= 3 \end{aligned}
Substitute $x = 3$ back into Equation 4 to solve for $y$:\begin{aligned} 2(3) + y &= 4 \cr 6 + y &= 4 \cr y &= -2 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve for $z$

Substitute $x = 3$ and $y = -2$ into Equation 1 to find $z$:\begin{aligned} x + 3y + z &= 1 \cr 3 + 3(-2) + z &= 1 \cr 3 - 6 + z &= 1 \cr -3 + z &= 1 \cr z &= 4 \end{aligned}Thus, the solutions are $x = 3, y = -2, z = 4$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &x = 3 \cr &y = -2 \cr &z = 4 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a calculation slip in the final step. Substituting $x = 3$ and $y = -2$ back into the first equation yields $3 - 6 + z = 1$, which gives $z = 4$, not $z = 1$.
This represents a systemic sign error, which typically occurs if you subtract the simultaneous equations incorrectly or make a sign mistake during the initial algebraic rearrangement.
This error occurs if you make a sign error when solving the final linear equation $-3 + z = 1$, mistakenly calculating $z = -4$ instead of $z = 4$.

bradley_insight.title: Exploiting Missing Variables
bradley_insight.content: If one of the equations in a three-variable system is already missing a variable (such as $z$ in $2x - y = 8$), do not use substitution. Instead, eliminate that exact same variable from the other two equations. This immediately creates a standard two-variable simultaneous system.

question:
At a local cinema, ticket prices are £$x$ for children, £$y$ for students, and £$z$ for adults.

* The cost of $1$ child ticket, $2$ student tickets, and $1$ adult ticket is £$26$.

* The cost of $2$ child tickets, $1$ student ticket, and $3$ adult tickets is £$44$.

* The cost of $3$ child tickets and $2$ adult tickets is £$32$.

(a) Write down three equations in terms of $x$, $y$, and $z$ to represent this information.

(b) Solve your equations algebraically to find the price of each type of ticket.
steps:
Part (a): Writing the equations

Translate each bullet point into an algebraic equation:

1. $x + 2y + z = 26$

2. $2x + y + 3z = 44$

3. $3x + 2z = 32$

Part (b): Solving the system

We notice that Equation 3 does not contain $y$. Let's express $z$ in terms of $x$ from Equation 3:\begin{aligned} 2z &= 32 - 3x \cr z &= 16 - 1.5x \end{aligned}

Now, eliminate $y$ from Equations 1 and 2. Rearrange Equation 1 to express $y$:\begin{aligned} 2y &= 26 - x - z \cr y &= 13 - 0.5x - 0.5z \end{aligned}Substitute this expression for $y$ into Equation 2:\begin{aligned} &2x + y + 3z = 44 \cr &2x + (13 - 0.5x - 0.5z) \cr &\qquad + 3z = 44 \cr &1.5x + 13 + 2.5z = 44 \cr &1.5x + 2.5z = 31 \end{aligned}

Multiply this simplified equation by 2 to clear the decimals, forming Equation 4:\begin{aligned} 3x + 5z = 62 \end{aligned}Substitute our expression for $z$ ($z = 16 - 1.5x$) into Equation 4:\begin{aligned} 3x + 5(16 - 1.5x) &= 62 \cr 3x + 80 - 7.5x &= 62 \cr -4.5x + 80 &= 62 \cr -4.5x &= -18 \cr x &= 4 \end{aligned}

Now, find $y$ and $z$ by substituting $x = 4$ back into our expressions:

1. For $z$:\begin{aligned} z &= 16 - 1.5(4) \cr &= 16 - 6 \cr &= 10 \end{aligned}

2. For $y$ (substituting $x = 4, z = 10$ into Equation 1):\begin{aligned} 4 + 2y + 10 &= 26 \cr 14 + 2y &= 26 \cr 2y &= 12 \cr y &= 6 \end{aligned}Thus, the ticket prices are £$4$ for children, £$6$ for students, and £$10$ for adults.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &\text{Child: } £4 \cr &\text{Student: } £6 \cr &\text{Adult: } £10 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a calculation error that typically occurs if you use early decimal rounding on fractions in intermediate steps or make an algebraic slip when combining the ticket cost equations.
This is a substitution error when solving for the adult ticket price $z$. Substituting $x = 4$ into the third equation yields $12 + 2z = 32$, which gives $2z = 20$, so $z = 10$, not $8$.
This error occurs if you mix up the pricing variables $x$ (child tickets) and $y$ (student tickets) during the algebraic elimination process.

bradley_insight.title: Contextual Reality Checks
bradley_insight.content: In real-world modeling questions, the solutions represent physical quantities (such as currency values, ages, or dimensions). Therefore, the answers are almost guaranteed to be positive, clean integers or simple fractions. If you calculate negative or highly complex decimal values, review your initial equations immediately.

question:
A quadratic curve has the equation:$$y = ax^2 + bx + c$$The curve passes through the three coordinates $(1, 2)$, $(2, 9)$, and $(-1, 0)$.

(a) Show that these coordinates lead to the following system of linear equations:\begin{aligned} a + b + c &= 2 \cr 4a + 2b + c &= 9 \cr a - b + c &= 0 \end{aligned}(b) Solve the system of equations algebraically to determine the values of $a$, $b$, and $c$.
steps:
Part (a): Setting up the equations

Substitute each coordinate $(x, y)$ into the quadratic curve equation $y = ax^2 + bx + c$:

1. For $(1, 2)$:\begin{aligned} a(1)^2 + b(1) + c &= 2 \cr a + b + c &= 2 \end{aligned}

2. For $(2, 9)$:\begin{aligned} a(2)^2 + b(2) + c &= 9 \cr 4a + 2b + c &= 9 \end{aligned}

3. For $(-1, 0)$:\begin{aligned} a(-1)^2 + b(-1) + c &= 0 \cr a - b + c &= 0 \end{aligned}This confirms the system of equations.

Part (b): Solving the system

Label the three equations:

1. $a + b + c = 2$

2. $4a + 2b + c = 9$

3. $a - b + c = 0$
Subtract Equation 3 from Equation 1 to eliminate $a$ and $c$ directly:\begin{aligned} &(a + b + c) \cr &\qquad - (a - b + c) = 2 - 0 \cr &2b = 2 \cr &b = 1 \end{aligned}

Substitute $b = 1$ back into Equation 1 and Equation 2:

1. From Equation 1:\begin{aligned} a + 1 + c &= 2 \cr a + c &= 1 \cr c &= 1 - a \end{aligned}

2. From Equation 2:\begin{aligned} 4a + 2(1) + c &= 9 \cr 4a + c &= 7 \end{aligned}

Substitute $c = 1 - a$ into our simplified Equation 2:\begin{aligned} 4a + (1 - a) &= 7 \cr 3a + 1 &= 7 \cr 3a &= 6 \cr a &= 2 \end{aligned}Finally, solve for $c$:\begin{aligned} c &= 1 - a \cr &= 1 - 2 \cr &= -1 \end{aligned}Thus, the values are $a = 2, b = 1, c = -1$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &a = 2 \cr &b = 1 \cr &c = -1 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This is a sign slip. Subtracting the third equation from the first equation yields $2b = 2$, giving $b = 1$. Substituting this back yields $a = 2$ and $c = -1$.
This error arises from an addition or subtraction error when simplifying the simultaneous equations (such as miscalculating the difference between the first and second equations).
This is a calculation error in evaluating $c$. Since $a - b + c = 0$, substituting $a=2, b=1$ yields $2 - 1 + c = 0$, giving $c = -1$, not $1$.

bradley_insight.title: Curve Fitting and Simultaneous Linear Systems
bradley_insight.content: Any polynomial curve of degree $n$ is uniquely determined by $n+1$ distinct points. For a quadratic curve (degree 2), we require exactly 3 points. Substituting these points yields a system of three linear equations, showing the direct link between coordinate geometry and linear algebra.

question: Solve the simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} x + 2y - z &= 3 \cr 3x - y + 2z &= -7 \cr 2x + 3y + 3z &= 8 \end{aligned}
steps:
We label our three equations to begin the algebraic elimination process:

1. $x + 2y - z = 3$

2. $3x - y + 2z = -7$

3. $2x + 3y + 3z = 8$

Step 1: Express $z$ from Equation 1

Equation 1 has a coefficient of $-1$ for $z$. Rearrange it to express $z$ in terms of $x$ and $y$:\begin{aligned} z = x + 2y - 3 \end{aligned}

Step 2: Substitute $z$ into Equations 2 and 3

1. Substitute into Equation 2:\begin{aligned} &3x - y + 2(x + 2y - 3) = -7 \cr &3x - y + 2x \cr &\qquad + 4y - 6 = -7 \cr &5x + 3y = -1 \end{aligned}

2. Substitute into Equation 3:\begin{aligned} &2x + 3y + 3(x + 2y - 3) = 8 \cr &2x + 3y + 3x \cr &\qquad + 6y - 9 = 8 \cr &5x + 9y = 17 \end{aligned}

Step 3: Solve the two-variable system

We now have a simplified system of two equations:\begin{aligned} 5x + 3y &= -1 \cr 5x + 9y &= 17 \end{aligned}Subtract Equation 4 from Equation 5 to eliminate the $x$ terms:\begin{aligned} &(5x + 9y) - (5x + 3y) \cr &\qquad = 17 - (-1) \cr &6y = 18 \cr &y = 3 \end{aligned}

Substitute $y = 3$ back into Equation 4 to solve for $x$:\begin{aligned} 5x + 3(3) &= -1 \cr 5x + 9 &= -1 \cr 5x &= -10 \cr x &= -2 \end{aligned}Substitute $x = -2$ and $y = 3$ back into our expression for $z$:\begin{aligned} z &= x + 2y - 3 \cr &= -2 + 2(3) - 3 \cr &= 1 \end{aligned}Thus, the solutions are $x = -2, y = 3, z = 1$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &x = -2 \cr &y = 3 \cr &z = 1 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: This represents a sign error in the final step. Evaluating $z = x + 2y - 3$ with $x = -2$ and $y = 3$ yields $z = -2 + 2(3) - 3$, which evaluates to $1$, not $-1$.
This is a global sign error. This can happen if you multiply equations by negative factors but fail to distribute the negative sign to all terms, or if you subtract the equations in the wrong order.
This is a calculation slip when solving the two-variable simultaneous system $5x + 3y = -1$ and $5x + 9y = 17$, leading to incorrect values for $y$ and subsequently $z$.

bradley_insight.title: Sign Distribution with Negative Values
bradley_insight.content: When substituting expressions with negative values or subtracting simultaneous equations, always use parentheses: e.g., $17 - (-1) = 18$. Forgetting to distribute negative signs is the single most common cause of error in algebraic elimination.

question:
The position vectors of the points $A$ and $B$ relative to an origin $O$ are given by:\begin{aligned} \vec{OA} &= 3\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} \cr \vec{OB} &= 7\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} \end{aligned}Find:

(a) the magnitude of the vector $\vec{AB}$,

(b) the angle $\vec{AB}$ makes with the positive $x$-axis.
steps:
Part (a): Finding the magnitude of $\vec{AB}$

First, we find the vector $\vec{AB}$ by subtracting the position vector of $A$ from the position vector of $B$:\begin{aligned} \vec{AB} &= \vec{OB} - \vec{OA} \cr &= (7\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}) - (3\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j}) \cr &= (7 - 3)\mathbf{i} + (1 - (-2))\mathbf{j} \cr &= 4\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} \end{aligned}

Next, calculate the magnitude of the vector $\vec{AB}$ using Pythagoras' theorem:\begin{aligned} |\vec{AB}| &= \sqrt{4^2 + 3^2} \cr &= \sqrt{16 + 9} \cr &= \sqrt{25} \cr &= 5 \end{aligned}Thus, the magnitude of the vector $\vec{AB}$ is $5$ units.

Part (b): Finding the angle with the positive $x$-axis

The vector $\vec{AB} = 4\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j}$ lies in the first quadrant because both the $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ components are positive.

We find the angle $\theta$ that the vector makes with the positive $x$-axis using trigonometry:\begin{aligned} \tan\theta &= \dfrac{3}{4} \cr \theta &= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right) \cr &\approx 36.9^\circ \end{aligned}Thus, the angle the vector makes with the positive $x$-axis is approximately $36.9^\circ$.
Final Answer:\begin{aligned} &|\vec{AB}| = 5 \cr &\theta \approx 36.9^\circ \end{aligned}
