Therefore:\begin{aligned} &\text{Mean} > \text{Median} \implies \text{Positive skew} \cr &\text{Mean} < \text{Median} \implies \text{Negative skew} \end{aligned}Always state this explicit comparison when justifying skewness.

question:
An estate agency compiles a five-number summary of the selling prices of a sample of $40$ houses in a market town. The values (in thousands of pounds, $£1000\text{s}$) are:

$$\text{Minimum} = 180$$
$$Q_1 = 240$$
$$\text{Median} = 285$$
$$Q_3 = 340$$
$$\text{Maximum} = 580$$

The mean house price for this sample of $40$ houses is $£305\,000$.

(a) Show that the maximum price of $£580\,000$ is an outlier using the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ criterion.

(b) Show that the minimum price of $£180\,000$ is not an outlier.

(c) If the outlier of $£580\,000$ is removed from the data set, describe the effect this removal will have on:
(i) the median;
(ii) the mean;
(iii) the standard deviation.
steps:
(a) Upper Outlier Test on £580,000:

Calculate the interquartile range:\begin{aligned} &\text{IQR} \cr &\quad = Q_3 - Q_1 \cr &\quad = 340 - 240 \cr &\quad = 100 \end{aligned}
Calculate the upper outlier boundary:\begin{aligned} &\text{Upper Bound} \cr &\quad = Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &\quad = 340 + 1.5(100) \cr &\quad = 340 + 150 \cr &\quad = 490 \end{aligned}
Because $580 > 490$, the maximum price of $£580\,000$ is confirmed as an outlier.

(b) Lower Outlier Test on £180,000:

Calculate the lower outlier boundary:\begin{aligned} &\text{Lower Bound} \cr &\quad = Q_1 - 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &\quad = 240 - 1.5(100) \cr &\quad = 240 - 150 \cr &\quad = 90 \end{aligned}
Because $180 > 90$, the minimum price of $£180\,000$ is not an outlier.

(c)(i) Effect on the Median:

The median is a resistant measure of location. Removing a single extreme high value will have negligible effect (it may stay the same or decrease slightly to the new central value).

(c)(ii) Effect on the Mean:

The mean will decrease, because removing an unusually high value reduces the overall total sum of the data.

(c)(iii) Effect on the Standard Deviation:

The standard deviation will decrease, because removing the most extreme value reduces the overall spread and dispersion around the mean.
Final Answer: (a) $580 > 490$, outlier, (b) $180 > 90$, not an outlier, (c)(i) Negligible effect, (ii) Decreases, (iii) Decreases

pi_options.ans: (a) $580 > 490$, outlier, (b) $180 > 90$, not an outlier, (c)(i) Decreases significantly, (ii) Decreases, (iii) Decreases
pi_options.feedback: The median is resistant to outliers; removing a single extreme value causes negligible or no change, not a significant drop.

pi_options.ans: (a) $580 > 490$, outlier, (b) $180 > 90$, not an outlier, (c)(i) Negligible effect, (ii) Increases, (iii) Decreases
pi_options.feedback: Removing an extremely high score removes mass from the upper end, causing the mean to decrease, not increase.

pi_options.ans: (a) $580 > 490$, outlier, (b) $180 < 90$, outlier, (c)(i) Negligible effect, (ii) Decreases, (iii) Decreases
pi_options.feedback: A value of $180$ is strictly greater than the lower boundary of $90$, so the minimum price is not an outlier.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Resistance of Median vs Sensitivity of Mean
bradley_insight.content: The mean and standard deviation are non-resistant statistics: removing a single high outlier causes both to drop sharply. In contrast, the median and IQR are resistant statistics that remain virtually unchanged.

question:
The screenshot in the diagram shows the probability distribution for the continuous random variable $X$, where $X \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

The area of each of the unshaded regions under the curve is $0.025$. The lower boundary of the shaded region is at $46.080$ and the upper boundary of the shaded region is at $53.920$.

(a) Calculate the value of $\mu$.

(b) Calculate the value of $\sigma^2$.

(c) The random variable $Y$ is given by $Y = 3X + 10$.

(i) State the distribution of $Y$.

(ii) Find $\text{P}(Y > 172)$.
steps:
(a) Mean $\mu$:

By symmetry of the normal distribution, the population mean $\mu$ is located at the exact midpoint of the central shaded region:\begin{aligned} \mu &= \dfrac{46.080 + 53.920}{2} \cr &= 50 \end{aligned}

(b) Variance $\sigma^2$:

The unshaded tails each have an area of $0.025$, meaning the central shaded area is $0.95$.

From standard normal percentage points tables, the upper critical value is $z = 1.960$.

Standardising the upper boundary $x = 53.920$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{53.920 - 50}{\sigma} = 1.960 \cr &3.920 = 1.960\sigma \cr &\sigma = 2 \end{aligned}
Squaring gives the population variance:\begin{aligned} \sigma^2 &= 2^2 \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Distribution of $Y$:

For the linear transformation $Y = 3X + 10$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(Y) &= 3\text{E}(X) + 10 \cr &= 3(50) + 10 \cr &= 160 \end{aligned}
The variance scales quadratically:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(Y) &= 3^2\text{Var}(X) \cr &= 9(4) \cr &= 36 \end{aligned}
Hence:\begin{aligned} Y \sim \text{N}(160, 36) \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Probability $\text{P}(Y > 172)$:

Standardising with mean $160$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{36} = 6$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y > 172) &= \text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{172 - 160}{6}\right) \cr &= \text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{12}{6}\right) \cr &= \text{P}(Z > 2) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(2) \cr &= 1 - 0.9772 \cr &= 0.0228 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\mu = 50$, (b) $\sigma^2 = 4$, (c)(i) $Y \sim \text{N}(160, 36)$, (ii) $0.0228$

pi_options.feedback: Remember that for a linear transformation $Y = aX + b$, the variance scales quadratically: $\text{Var}(Y) = a^2\text{Var}(X) = 3^2(4) = 36$, rather than $3(4)$.
In part (b), solving the standardized equation yields the standard deviation $\sigma = 2$. You must square this to find the population variance $\sigma^2 = 4$.
With $0.025$ in each unshaded tail, the critical $z$-value is $1.960$, not $1.645$ (which leaves $0.05$ in a single tail).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Symmetry and Scale
bradley_insight.content: Always exploit symmetry first: the mean of a symmetric normal distribution is strictly halfway between equal tail boundaries. When evaluating $Y = aX + b$, remember that adding a constant shifts the mean but does not affect spread, while multiplying scales the standard deviation by $|a|$ and the variance by $a^2$.

question:
A precision manufacturing process produces metal shafts whose lengths, $W\text{ cm}$, are modelled by the continuous random variable $W \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

The screenshot in the diagram shows the distribution with two rejection tails shaded. The lower shaded region has an area of $0.0228$ with an upper boundary at $42.0$. The upper shaded region has an area of $0.0668$ with a lower boundary at $63.0$.

(a) Write down two simultaneous equations connecting $\mu$ and $\sigma$.

(b) Hence determine the value of $\mu$ and the value of $\sigma$.

(c) A shaft is accepted if its length lies between $45.0\text{ cm}$ and $60.0\text{ cm}$. Find the probability that a randomly chosen shaft is accepted.
steps:
(a) Simultaneous Equations:

For the lower tail:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W < 42.0) = 0.0228 \cr &\Phi(-2.00) = 0.0228 \cr &\dfrac{42.0 - \mu}{\sigma} = -2.00 \cr &42.0 = \mu - 2\sigma \end{aligned}
For the upper tail:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(W > 63.0) = 0.0668 \cr &\text{P}(W < 63.0) = 0.9332 \cr &\Phi(1.50) = 0.9332 \cr &\dfrac{63.0 - \mu}{\sigma} = 1.50 \cr &63.0 = \mu + 1.5\sigma \end{aligned}

(b) Values of $\mu$ and $\sigma$:

Subtracting the first equation from the second:\begin{aligned} &63.0 - 42.0 = 1.5\sigma - (-2\sigma) \cr &21.0 = 3.5\sigma \cr &\sigma = \dfrac{21.0}{3.5} \cr &\sigma = 6 \end{aligned}
Substituting $\sigma = 6$ into the first equation:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 42.0 + 2(6) \cr &= 42.0 + 12 \cr &= 54 \end{aligned}

(c) Acceptance Probability:

Standardising both limits for $W \sim \text{N}(54, 6^2)$:\begin{aligned} z_1 &= \dfrac{45.0 - 54}{6} \cr &= -1.5 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} z_2 &= \dfrac{60.0 - 54}{6} \cr &= 1.0 \end{aligned}
Calculating the probability between these values:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(45.0 < W < 60.0) \cr &\quad = \text{P}(-1.5 < Z < 1.0) \cr &\quad = \Phi(1.0) - \Phi(-1.5) \cr &\quad = 0.8413 - (1 - 0.9332) \cr &\quad = 0.8413 - 0.0668 \cr &\quad = 0.7745 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $42.0 = \mu - 2\sigma$ and $63.0 = \mu + 1.5\sigma$, (b) $\mu = 54, \sigma = 6$, (c) $0.7745$

pi_options.feedback: A boundary below the mean has a negative $z$-score. The standardized equation must be $z = -2.0$, producing $42.0 = \mu - 2\sigma$, not $\mu + 2\sigma$.
To calculate $\text{P}(-1.5 < Z < 1.0)$, compute \begin{aligned}\Phi(1.0) - \Phi(-1.5) &= 0.8413 - 0.0668 \cr &= 0.7745\end{aligned} Do not subtract both cumulative values from 1.
When substituting $\sigma = 6$ into $42.0 = \mu - 2\sigma$, rearranging gives $\mu = 42.0 + 2(6) = 54$, not $42.0 - 12$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Beware the Negative Sign
bradley_insight.content: The most frequent mistake in inverse normal problems is forgetting the negative sign on lower-tail $z$-scores. Because the tail area ($0.0228$) is well below $0.5$, the observation lies to the left of the mean, meaning $z = -2.00$ must be strictly negative.

question:
The diagram shows the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\bar{X}$ for random samples of size $n = 25$ taken from a normal population $X \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ under the null hypothesis $H_0: \mu = 120$, where the population standard deviation is known to be $\sigma = 15$.

A one-tailed hypothesis test is conducted at the $5\%$ significance level with alternative hypothesis $H_1: \mu > 120$.

(a) State the sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ under $H_0$, giving its mean and standard error.

(b) Show that the critical value for this test, rounded to two decimal places, is $c = 124.94$.

(c) A quality assurance manager draws a sample of $25$ items and observes a sample mean of $\bar{x} = 126.2$, as indicated by the arrow in the diagram.

(i) State the conclusion of the test in context.

(ii) Calculate the $p$-value for this test, giving your answer to four decimal places.
steps:
(a) Sampling Distribution of $\bar{X}$:

Under $H_0$, the sample mean is distributed as:\begin{aligned} \bar{X} &\sim \text{N}\left(\mu, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right) \cr &\sim \text{N}\left(120, \dfrac{15^2}{25}\right) \cr &\sim \text{N}(120, 9) \end{aligned}
The mean is $120$ and the standard error is:\begin{aligned} \text{SE} &= \dfrac{15}{\sqrt{25}} \cr &= 3 \end{aligned}

(b) Critical Value $c$:

For a one-tailed test at the $5\%$ significance level, the upper percentage point of the standard normal distribution is:\begin{aligned} z_{0.95} = 1.6449 \end{aligned}
Calculating the critical value on the scale of $\bar{X}$:\begin{aligned} c &= 120 + 1.6449(3) \cr &= 120 + 4.9347 \cr &= 124.9347... \cr &\approx 124.94 \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Test Conclusion:

The critical region is $\bar{X} \ge 124.94$.

Since the observed sample mean $\bar{x} = 126.2 > 124.94$, it lies inside the critical region.

Reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the $5\%$ level to suggest that the population mean is greater than $120$.

(c)(ii) Calculation of $p$-value:

Standardising the observed sample mean:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{126.2 - 120}{3} \cr &= \dfrac{6.2}{3} \cr &\approx 2.0667 \end{aligned}
Finding the upper tail probability:\begin{aligned} p\text{-value} &= \text{P}(\bar{X} \ge 126.2) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(2.067) \cr &= 1 - 0.9806 \cr &= 0.0194 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\bar{X} \sim \text{N}(120, 9)$, mean $120$, $\text{SE} = 3$, (b) $c = 124.94$, (c)(i) Reject $H_0$, (ii) $p = 0.0194$

pi_options.feedback: When evaluating the distribution of a sample mean, the standard error is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{15}{\sqrt{25}} = 3$, not the individual population standard deviation $15$.
The test is one-tailed at the $5\%$ level, so the critical value is $z = 1.6449$. The value $z = 1.960$ applies to a two-tailed test at the $5\%$ level.
Because the observed sample mean $\bar{x} = 126.2$ is greater than the critical value $124.94$, it falls inside the rejection region, so $H_0$ must be rejected.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dual Routes to Decision
bradley_insight.content: Notice how the critical value approach and the $p$-value approach arrive at the identical conclusion: $\bar{x} = 126.2 > 124.94$ (inside the critical region), which matches the fact that the $p$-value ($0.0194$) is strictly less than $\alpha = 0.05$. Both methods will always be entirely consistent.

question:
The diagram shows the probability density functions of two normally distributed random variables plotted on the same horizontal axis. Curve $A$ represents the population variable $X \sim \text{N}(\mu_A, \sigma_A^2)$ and Curve $B$ represents the sample mean $\bar{X}$ of a random sample of size $n$ drawn from the same population.

Curve $A$ is given by $X \sim \text{N}(50, 16)$.

(a) State the mean of each distribution, $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$.

(b) The standard deviation of the distribution shown by Curve $B$ is $\sigma_B = 2$.

(i) Calculate the sample size $n$.

(ii) Explain why the peak of Curve $B$ is higher than the peak of Curve $A$.

(c) Using the properties of the normal distribution, determine whether $\text{P}(46 \le X \le 54)$ is greater than, equal to, or less than $\text{P}(46 \le \bar{X} \le 54)$, justifying your answer clearly.
steps:
(a) Means of the Distributions:

The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean, so both curves are centered at the same value:\begin{aligned} \mu_A &= 50 \cr \mu_B &= 50 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Sample Size $n$:

For Curve $A$, the population standard deviation is $\sigma_A = \sqrt{16} = 4$.

Using the standard error formula for Curve $B$:\begin{aligned} \sigma_B &= \dfrac{\sigma_A}{\sqrt{n}} \cr 2 &= \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{n}} \cr \sqrt{n} &= 2 \cr n &= 4 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Explanation of Peak Height:

The total area under any probability density function must equal $1$.

Because Curve $B$ has a smaller standard deviation ($\\sigma_B = 2$ compared to $\sigma_A = 4$), its values are less spread out.

To preserve a total area of $1$, the curve must be taller around the mean.

(c) Probability Comparison:

Both intervals are centered on $\mu = 50$:\begin{aligned} &\text{For } X: \cr &[46, 54] = [\mu - \sigma, \mu + \sigma] \cr &\text{P}(46 \le X \le 54) \approx 0.6827 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} &\text{For } \bar{X}: \cr &[46, 54] = [\mu - 2\sigma_B, \mu + 2\sigma_B] \cr &\text{P}(46 \le \bar{X} \le 54) \approx 0.9545 \end{aligned}
Since $0.6827 < 0.9545$, $\text{P}(46 \le X \le 54)$ is less than $\text{P}(46 \le \bar{X} \le 54)$.
Final Answer: (a) $\mu_A = 50, \mu_B = 50$, (b)(i) $n = 4$, (ii) Total area is $1$, (c) Less than

pi_options.feedback: The standard error formula is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. If $\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{n}} = 2$, then $\sqrt{n} = 2$, which gives $n = 2^2 = 4$, not $n = 2$.
Because the distribution of $\bar{X}$ is more tightly clustered around the mean, a greater proportion of its area lies within $\pm 4$ units of the mean ($95.4\%$ compared to $68.3\%$).
The expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean: $\text{E}(\bar{X}) = \mu = 50$. The sample size $n$ divides the variance, never the mean.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Preserving Unit Area
bradley_insight.content: The maximum height of a normal density curve is given by $\dfrac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$. Because $\sigma$ appears in the denominator, halving the standard deviation from $4$ to $2$ doubles the peak height. This inverse relationship ensures the area under the curve remains strictly equal to $1$.

question:
A fair coin is spun $24$ times. The discrete random variable $X$ represents the number of heads obtained, so that $X \sim \text{B}(24, 0.5)$.

The diagram shows the discrete probability bars for $X$ overlaid with the continuous curve of the approximating normal distribution $Y \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

(a) State the mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$ of the approximating normal distribution $Y$.

(b) Explain why a continuity correction is required when approximating a discrete distribution using a continuous curve.

(c) With reference to the dashed boundary line at $x = 14.5$ shown in the diagram, write down the probability statement in terms of $Y$ that approximates $\text{P}(X \ge 15)$.

(d) Hence calculate an approximation for $\text{P}(X \ge 15)$, giving your answer to four decimal places.
steps:
(a) Mean and Variance:

For $X \sim \text{B}(n, p)$ with $n = 24$ and $p = 0.5$:\begin{aligned} \mu &= np \cr &= 24(0.5) \cr &= 12 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \sigma^2 &= np(1 - p) \cr &= 24(0.5)(0.5) \cr &= 6 \end{aligned}

(b) Explanation of Continuity Correction:

A discrete distribution concentrates probability at individual integer values, with each outcome $k$ represented by a bar of width $1$ over the interval $[k - 0.5, k + 0.5]$.

For a continuous distribution, the probability at any single point is zero:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y = k) = 0 \end{aligned}
A continuity correction shifts the boundary by $0.5$ so that the area under the continuous curve covers the corresponding discrete bar.

(c) Approximating Probability Statement:

The discrete event $X \ge 15$ includes the bars for $X = 15, 16, \dots, 24$.

The bar for $15$ starts at the lower boundary $14.5$.

Therefore, the approximating statement is:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y \ge 14.5) \end{aligned}

(d) Calculation of $\text{P}(X \ge 15)$:

Standardising $Y \sim \text{N}(12, 6)$ with standard deviation $\sqrt{6} \approx 2.4495$:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{14.5 - 12}{\sqrt{6}} \cr &= \dfrac{2.5}{2.4495} \cr &\approx 1.0206 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y \ge 14.5) &= \text{P}(Z \ge 1.0206) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(1.0206) \cr &= 1 - 0.8463 \cr &= 0.1537 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\mu = 12, \sigma^2 = 6$, (b) Adjusts width of discrete bars, (c) $\text{P}(Y \ge 14.5)$, (d) $0.1537$

pi_options.feedback: For $\text{P}(X \ge 15)$, the discrete bar for $15$ must be included. Its bar starts at $14.5$, so the integration boundary must be $14.5$, not $15.5$.
Omitting the continuity correction evaluates $\text{P}(Y \ge 15.0)$, which cuts through the centre of the bar for $15$ and understates the probability.
When standardising, the denominator is the standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{6} \approx 2.4495$, not the variance $\sigma^2 = 6$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Continuity Correction Rule of Thumb
bradley_insight.content: Always picture the discrete bar. For $X = 15$, the bar extends from $14.5$ to $15.5$. If the discrete inequality includes $15$ ($X \ge 15$), your continuous region must include that entire bar, starting at $14.5$. If the inequality is strict ($X > 15$), the bar for $15$ is excluded, meaning the region begins at $15.5$.

question:
The discrete random variable $X$ takes the values $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ and $5$ with probabilities given by the formula

$$\text{P}(X = x) = c(x + 2)(6 - x)$$
where $c$ is a constant.

(a) Show that $c = \dfrac{1}{77}$.

(b) Over a work placement, an apprentice technician attends a workshop on $77$ shifts. The random variable $X$ is used to model the number of faulty circuit boards repaired by the technician on a given shift. Assuming shifts are independent:

(i) Find the probability that the technician repairs no faulty boards on each of the first $2$ shifts of the placement and repairs exactly $2$ faulty boards on each of the next $2$ shifts. Give your answer in exact fractional form.

(ii) Find the expected number of shifts during the placement on which the technician repairs no faulty boards.
steps:
(a) Value of $c$:

Summing all probabilities to $1$ over $x \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$:\begin{aligned} &\sum_{x=0}^{5} \text{P}(X = x) = 1 \cr &c[(2)(6) + (3)(5) + (4)(4) \cr &\quad + (5)(3) + (6)(2) + (7)(1)] = 1 \cr &c(12 + 15 + 16 + 15 + 12 + 7) = 1 \cr &77c = 1 \cr &c = \dfrac{1}{77} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Combined Probability:

Calculating individual shift probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 0) &= \dfrac{(2)(6)}{77} \cr &= \dfrac{12}{77} \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 2) &= \dfrac{(4)(4)}{77} \cr &= \dfrac{16}{77} \end{aligned}
For independent shifts, the required combined probability is:\begin{aligned} \text{P} &= [\text{P}(X = 0)]^2 \times [\text{P}(X = 2)]^2 \cr &= \left(\dfrac{12}{77}\right)^2 \times \left(\dfrac{16}{77}\right)^2 \cr &= \dfrac{144}{5929} \times \dfrac{256}{5929} \cr &= \dfrac{36864}{35153041} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Expected Number of Shifts:

With $N = 77$ shifts and $p = \text{P}(X = 0) = \dfrac{12}{77}$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(\text{shifts}) &= Np \cr &= 77 \times \dfrac{12}{77} \cr &= 12 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: The question requires no repairs on each of the first 2 shifts and 2 repairs on each of the next 2 shifts. Each probability must be squared rather than multiplied once.
The total number of shifts in this placement is 77. Evaluating the expected frequency gives $77 \times \frac{12}{77} = 12$.
Carefully sum each term: $12 + 15 + 16 + 15 + 12 + 7 = 77$. An addition slip results in an incorrect constant $c$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Symmetry Simplifies the Sum
bradley_insight.content: Notice the symmetry in the terms: $(2)(6) = (6)(2) = 12$, and $(3)(5) = (5)(3) = 15$. Pairing these equal terms cuts your calculation time in half and minimizes mental arithmetic slips.

question:
The discrete random variable $X$ takes the values $1, 2, 3, 4$ and $5$ with probabilities given by

$$\text{P}(X = x) = k(6 - x)$$
where $k$ is a positive constant.

(a) Determine the value of $k$.

(b) Calculate:
(i) $\text{E}(X)$
(ii) $\text{Var}(X)$

(c) Find $\text{P}(X > \text{E}(X))$.

(d) In a quality audit, $60$ independent observations of $X$ are recorded. Find the expected number of observations in which $X$ exceeds its mean.
steps:
(a) Value of $k$:

Summing all probabilities over $x \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$:\begin{aligned} &\sum_{x=1}^{5} k(6 - x) = 1 \cr &k(5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1) = 1 \cr &15k = 1 \cr &k = \dfrac{1}{15} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Expectation $\text{E}(X)$:

Using $\text{E}(X) = \sum x \text{P}(X = x)$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(X) &= \dfrac{1(5) + 2(4) + 3(3)}{15} \cr &\quad + \dfrac{4(2) + 5(1)}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{5 + 8 + 9 + 8 + 5}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{35}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{7}{3} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Variance $\text{Var}(X)$:

First calculating $\text{E}(X^2)$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(X^2) &= \dfrac{1^2(5) + 2^2(4) + 3^2(3)}{15} \cr &\quad + \dfrac{4^2(2) + 5^2(1)}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{5 + 16 + 27 + 32 + 25}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{105}{15} \cr &= 7 \end{aligned}
Now applying $\text{Var}(X) = \text{E}(X^2) - [\text{E}(X)]^2$:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= 7 - \left(\dfrac{7}{3}\right)^2 \cr &= 7 - \dfrac{49}{9} \cr &= \dfrac{63 - 49}{9} \cr &= \dfrac{14}{9} \end{aligned}

(c) Probability $\text{P}(X > \text{E}(X))$:

Since $\text{E}(X) = \dfrac{7}{3} \approx 2.33$, the values of $X$ greater than the mean are $3, 4, 5$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}\left(X > \dfrac{7}{3}\right) &= \text{P}(X = 3)\cr &\quad + \text{P}(X = 4) \cr &\quad + \text{P}(X = 5) \cr &= \dfrac{3}{15} + \dfrac{2}{15} + \dfrac{1}{15} \cr &= \dfrac{6}{15} \cr &= 0.4 \end{aligned}

(d) Expected Frequency:

Over $N = 60$ independent observations:\begin{aligned} \text{Expected} &= 60 \times 0.4 \cr &= 24 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In the variance formula, remember to subtract the square of the mean: subtracting $(\frac{7}{3})^2 = \frac{49}{9}$ yields $\frac{14}{9}$, not $\frac{14}{3}$.
Because the mean is approximately $2.33$, the condition $X > \text{E}(X)$ requires $X \ge 3$. Including $X = 2$ overstates the probability.
The probabilities are strictly decreasing across the domain rather than symmetric, which pulls the expected value down to $\frac{7}{3}$ rather than $3$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Strict Inequalities on Integers
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating probabilities for discrete distributions, list the integers explicitly. Since $\text{E}(X) \approx 2.33$, the inequality $X > 2.33$ translates to $X \in \{3, 4, 5\}$. Never round the mean before interpreting the inequality.

question:
The discrete random variable $X$ has probability distribution defined by: $$\text{P}(X = x) = kx^2 $$ $$\text{for } x \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$$ where $k$ is a constant.

(a) Show that $k = \dfrac{1}{30}$.

(b) Find $\text{P}(2 \le X \le 3)$.

(c) Two independent observations of $X$, denoted by $X_1$ and $X_2$, are recorded. Find $\text{P}(X_1 + X_2 = 5)$.

(d) In an experiment, $90$ independent trials of $X$ are performed. Let $Y$ be the number of trials in which $X = 4$. Calculate the mean and variance of $Y$.
steps:
(a) Value of $k$:

Summing probabilities over the domain:\begin{aligned} &\sum_{x=1}^{4} kx^2 = 1 \cr &k(1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2) = 1 \cr &k(1 + 4 + 9 + 16) = 1 \cr &30k = 1 \cr &k = \dfrac{1}{30} \end{aligned}

(b) Probability $\text{P}(2 \le X \le 3)$:

Summing the probabilities for $x = 2$ and $x = 3$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(2 \le X \le 3) &= \text{P}(X = 2) \cr & \quad + \text{P}(X = 3) \cr &= \dfrac{2^2}{30} + \dfrac{3^2}{30} \cr &= \dfrac{4}{30} + \dfrac{9}{30} \cr &= \dfrac{13}{30} \end{aligned}

(c) Sum $X_1 + X_2 = 5$:

The mutually exclusive pairs $(X_1, X_2)$ summing to $5$ are $(1, 4)$, $(4, 1)$, $(2, 3)$, and $(3, 2)$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(1, 4) = \dfrac{1}{30} \times \dfrac{16}{30} = \dfrac{16}{900} \cr &\text{P}(2, 3) = \dfrac{4}{30} \times \dfrac{9}{30} = \dfrac{36}{900} \end{aligned}
Summing all ordered pairs:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X_1 + X_2 = 5) &= 2\left(\dfrac{16}{900}\right)\cr & \quad + 2\left(\dfrac{36}{900}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{32 + 72}{900} \cr &= \dfrac{104}{900} \cr &= \dfrac{26}{225} \end{aligned}

(d) Mean and Variance of $Y$:

The probability of observing $X = 4$ is:\begin{aligned} p &= \dfrac{4^2}{30} \cr &= \dfrac{16}{30} \cr &= \dfrac{8}{15} \end{aligned}
Thus $Y \sim \text{B}\left(90, \dfrac{8}{15}\right)$.

Mean:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(Y) &= 90 \times \dfrac{8}{15} \cr &= 48 \end{aligned}
Variance:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(Y) &= 90 \times \dfrac{8}{15} \times \left(1 - \dfrac{8}{15}\right) \cr &= 48 \times \dfrac{7}{15} \cr &= 22.4 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $k = \dfrac{1}{30}$, (b) $\dfrac{13}{30}$, (c) $\dfrac{26}{225}$, (d) $\text{E}(Y) = 48, \text{Var}(Y) = 22.4$

pi_options.feedback: The sum $X_1 + X_2 = 5$ can occur via the distinct ordered pairs $(1, 4)$, $(4, 1)$, $(2, 3)$, and $(3, 2)$. Omitting the reversed pairs halves the probability.
For a binomial distribution, the variance is given by $np(1 - p)$. Remember to multiply by $(1 - p) = \frac{7}{15}$ rather than stopping at $np$.
The domain includes $x = 4$, so the sum of squares is $1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30$, which gives $k = \frac{1}{30}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Ordered Pairs for Independent Sums
bradley_insight.content: When calculating the distribution of the sum of two independent variables, always list the outcomes as ordered coordinate pairs $(x_1, x_2)$. Because the observations are distinct, $(1, 4)$ and $(4, 1)$ are distinct mutually exclusive outcomes.

question:
The discrete random variable $X$ takes values in $\{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}$. Its probability distribution is shown in the table below, where $a$ and $b$ are probabilities:

$x$$-1$$0$$1$$2$$3$
$\text{P}(X = x)$$0.1$$a$$0.3$$b$$0.1$

The expected value of $X$ is $\text{E}(X) = 1.1$.

(a) Write down two simultaneous equations in $a$ and $b$, and hence show that $a = 0.2$ and $b = 0.3$.

(b) Calculate $\text{Var}(X)$.

(c) The random variable $W$ is defined by $W = 4X - 3$. Find $\text{E}(W)$ and $\text{Var}(W)$.
steps:
(a) Simultaneous Equations:

Total probability equals $1$:\begin{aligned} &0.1 + a + 0.3 + b + 0.1 = 1 \cr &a + b + 0.5 = 1 \cr &a + b = 0.5 \end{aligned}
Using the definition of expectation $\text{E}(X) = 1.1$:\begin{aligned} &(-1)(0.1) + 0(a) + 1(0.3) \cr &\quad + 2(b) + 3(0.1) = 1.1 \cr &-0.1 + 0.3 + 2b + 0.3 = 1.1 \cr &2b + 0.5 = 1.1 \cr &2b = 0.6 \cr &b = 0.3 \end{aligned}
Substituting into $a + b = 0.5$ gives:\begin{aligned} a &= 0.5 - 0.3 \cr &= 0.2 \end{aligned}

(b) Variance $\text{Var}(X)$:

First calculating $\text{E}(X^2)$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(X^2) &= (-1)^2(0.1) + 0^2(0.2) \cr &\quad + 1^2(0.3) + 2^2(0.3)\cr & \qquad + 3^2(0.1) \cr &= 0.1 + 0 + 0.3 + 1.2 + 0.9 \cr &= 2.5 \end{aligned}
Applying the variance formula:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= \text{E}(X^2) - [\text{E}(X)]^2 \cr &= 2.5 - 1.1^2 \cr &= 2.5 - 1.21 \cr &= 1.29 \end{aligned}

(c) Expectation and Variance of $W = 4X - 3$:

Expected value:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(W) &= 4\text{E}(X) - 3 \cr &= 4(1.1) - 3 \cr &= 4.4 - 3 \cr &= 1.4 \end{aligned}
Variance scales quadratically:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(W) &= 4^2\text{Var}(X) \cr &= 16(1.29) \cr &= 20.64 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $a = 0.2, b = 0.3$, (b) $\text{Var}(X) = 1.29$, (c) $\text{E}(W) = 1.4, \text{Var}(W) = 20.64$

pi_options.feedback: For a linear transformation $W = aX + b$, variance scales by $a^2$. Multiply by $4^2 = 16$ to obtain $16(1.29) = 20.64$ rather than $4(1.29)$.
Subtracting a constant shifts the distribution without affecting spread. The constant term $-3$ must not be subtracted from the variance.
Squaring a negative value gives a positive result: $(-1)^2(0.1) = +0.1$. A sign slip here reduces $\text{E}(X^2)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Shift Invariance of Spread
bradley_insight.content: Subtracting $3$ shifts the entire distribution along the number line, updating the expected value but leaving the spread completely unchanged. Hence $\text{Var}(4X - 3) = 16\text{Var}(X)$.

question:
The discrete random variable $X$ takes values in $\{1, 2, 3, 6\}$ with probabilities given by

$$\text{P}(X = x) = \dfrac{k}{x}$$
where $k$ is a constant.

(a) Find the value of $k$.

(b) The random variable $Y$ is defined by $Y = (X - 2)^2$.
(i) List the possible values that $Y$ can take.
(ii) Specify the probability distribution of $Y$ in a table.

(c) Calculate $\text{E}(Y)$.

(d) In a simulation of $48$ independent trials of $Y$, find the expected number of trials in which $Y = 1$.
steps:
(a) Value of $k$:

Summing probabilities over $x \in \{1, 2, 3, 6\}$:\begin{aligned} &\sum \text{P}(X = x) = 1 \cr &k\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6}\right) = 1 \cr &k\left(\dfrac{6 + 3 + 2 + 1}{6}\right) = 1 \cr &k\left(\dfrac{12}{6}\right) = 1 \cr &2k = 1 \cr &k = 0.5 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Distinct Values of $Y$:

Evaluating $Y = (X - 2)^2$ for each outcome:\begin{aligned} &x = 1 \implies y = (1 - 2)^2 = 1 \cr &x = 2 \implies y = (2 - 2)^2 = 0 \cr &x = 3 \implies y = (3 - 2)^2 = 1 \cr &x = 6 \implies y = (6 - 2)^2 = 16 \end{aligned}
Hence the distinct values that $Y$ can take are $0, 1, 16$.

(b)(ii) Probability Distribution Table:

Combining probabilities for duplicate outcomes:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y = 0) &= \text{P}(X = 2) \cr &= \dfrac{0.5}{2} \cr &= 0.25 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y = 1) &= \text{P}(X = 1) + \text{P}(X = 3) \cr &= \dfrac{0.5}{1} + \dfrac{0.5}{3} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{6} \cr &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y = 16) &= \text{P}(X = 6) \cr &= \dfrac{0.5}{6} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}
The distribution table is:

$y$$0$$1$$16$
$\text{P}(Y = y)$$0.25$$\dfrac{2}{3}$$\dfrac{1}{12}$

(c) Expectation $\text{E}(Y)$:

Using $\text{E}(Y) = \sum y \text{P}(Y = y)$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(Y) &= 0(0.25) + 1\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\cr & \qquad \quad + 16\left(\dfrac{1}{12}\right) \cr &= 0 + \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} \cr &= \dfrac{6}{3} \cr &= 2 \end{aligned}

(d) Expected Frequency:

For $N = 48$ independent trials and $\text{P}(Y = 1) = \dfrac{2}{3}$:\begin{aligned} \text{Expected} &= 48 \times \dfrac{2}{3} \cr &= 32 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Both $X = 1$ and $X = 3$ map to $Y = 1$. Add their probabilities together: $\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$, giving an expected frequency of $48 \times \frac{2}{3} = 32$.
For non-linear transformations, $\text{E}[g(X)] \neq g[\text{E}(X)]$. You cannot calculate $\text{E}(Y)$ by evaluating $(\text{E}(X) - 2)^2$.
Ensure all four reciprocals are included: $1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} = 2$. This leads to $k = 0.5$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Non-Linear Expectations
bradley_insight.content: A fundamental rule in probability is that expectation is linear but not non-linear: $\text{E}[g(X)] \neq g[\text{E}(X)]$. Always derive the probability distribution of $Y = g(X)$ first, combining duplicate values before evaluating $\sum y \text{P}(Y = y)$.

question:
A large cohort of trainee technicians took professional assessment tests in both Electrical Principles ($E$) and Mechanical Systems ($M$).

Of these candidates, $62\%$ passed Electrical Principles and $75\%$ passed Mechanical Systems. In addition, $18\%$ of the candidates did not pass either Electrical Principles or Mechanical Systems.

(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen candidate passed both Electrical Principles and Mechanical Systems.

(b) Determine, with detailed reasoning, whether passing Electrical Principles and passing Mechanical Systems are independent events.

(c) Find the probability that a randomly chosen candidate passed Electrical Principles given that they did not pass Mechanical Systems.
steps:
(a) Probability of Passing Both:

Let $E$ and $M$ denote passing Electrical Principles and Mechanical Systems respectively.

From the given data:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E) &= 0.62 \cr \text{P}(M) &= 0.75 \cr \text{P}(E' \cap M') &= 0.18 \end{aligned}
The union probability is:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cup M) &= 1 - 0.18 \cr &= 0.82 \end{aligned}
Using the addition rule of probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(E \cup M) = \text{P}(E) + \text{P}(M)\cr & \qquad \qquad - \text{P}(E \cap M) \cr &0.82 = 0.62 + 0.75 - \text{P}(E \cap M) \cr &0.82 = 1.37 - \text{P}(E \cap M) \cr &\text{P}(E \cap M) = 1.37 - 0.82 \cr &\text{P}(E \cap M) = 0.55 \end{aligned}

(b) Test for Independence:

For two events to be independent, the product of their individual probabilities must equal their intersection probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E) \times \text{P}(M) &= 0.62 \times 0.75 \cr &= 0.465 \end{aligned}
Comparing this product with the intersection:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cap M) = 0.55 \end{aligned}
Since $0.55 \neq 0.465$, passing Electrical Principles and passing Mechanical Systems are not independent.

(c) Conditional Probability:

Using the definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \mid M') = \dfrac{\text{P}(E \cap M')}{\text{P}(M')} \end{aligned}
Finding the required component probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cap M') &= \text{P}(E) - \text{P}(E \cap M) \cr &= 0.62 - 0.55 \cr &= 0.07 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(M') &= 1 - \text{P}(M) \cr &= 1 - 0.75 \cr &= 0.25 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the conditional probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \mid M') &= \dfrac{0.07}{0.25} \cr &= 0.28 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $0.55$, (b) Not independent, (c) $0.28$

pi_options.feedback: Do not assume independence to find the intersection. The intersection must be deduced from the addition rule using the union probability $1 - 0.18 = 0.82$.
The value $0.07$ is the joint probability $\text{P}(E \cap M')$. To determine the conditional probability, you must divide by $\text{P}(M') = 0.25$.
Check your arithmetic when rearranging the addition formula: $\text{P}(E \cap M) = 0.62 + 0.75 - 0.82 = 0.55$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Never Assume Independence
bradley_insight.content: A classic exam trap is calculating $\text{P}(A \cap B) = \text{P}(A)\text{P}(B)$ and then using that very result to conclude the events are independent! Always calculate the intersection from the given data (such as the union or complement) and only then test whether the product equals the intersection.

question:
A quality control process inspects microchips for two defects: Surface Flaws ($S$) and Circuit Breaks ($C$).

From production records, the probability that a randomly chosen microchip has a surface flaw is $\text{P}(S) = 0.08$. The probability that a microchip has a circuit break given that it has a surface flaw is $\text{P}(C \mid S) = 0.25$, whereas the probability that it has a circuit break given that it has no surface flaw is $\text{P}(C \mid S') = 0.05$.

(a) Calculate $\text{P}(S \cap C)$.

(b) Show that $\text{P}(C) = 0.066$.

(c) Determine whether having a surface flaw and having a circuit break are independent events.

(d) Find $\text{P}(S \mid C)$, giving your answer to three significant figures.
steps:
(a) Intersection $\text{P}(S \cap C)$:

Using the multiplication rule:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(S \cap C) &= \text{P}(S) \times \text{P}(C \mid S) \cr &= 0.08 \times 0.25 \cr &= 0.02 \end{aligned}

(b) Total Probability $\text{P}(C)$:

Partitioning by surface flaws:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(S') &= 1 - \text{P}(S) \cr &= 1 - 0.08 \cr &= 0.92 \end{aligned}
Applying the law of total probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C) &= \text{P}(S \cap C) + \text{P}(S' \cap C) \cr &= 0.02 + [\text{P}(S') \times \text{P}(C \mid S')] \cr &= 0.02 + (0.92 \times 0.05) \cr &= 0.02 + 0.046 \cr &= 0.066 \end{aligned}

(c) Test for Independence:

Two events $S$ and $C$ are independent if and only if $\text{P}(C \mid S) = \text{P}(C)$.

Comparing the conditional and marginal probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C \mid S) &= 0.25 \cr \text{P}(C) &= 0.066 \end{aligned}
Since $0.25 \neq 0.066$, having a surface flaw and having a circuit break are not independent.

(d) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(S \mid C)$:

Using Bayes' theorem:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(S \mid C) &= \dfrac{\text{P}(S \cap C)}{\text{P}(C)} \cr &= \dfrac{0.02}{0.066} \cr &= \dfrac{2}{6.6} \cr &= \dfrac{10}{33} \cr &\approx 0.303 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $0.02$, (b) $\text{P}(C) = 0.066$, (c) Not independent, (d) $0.303$

pi_options.feedback: To evaluate $\text{P}(S \mid C)$, the denominator must be $\text{P}(C) = 0.066$, not $\text{P}(S) = 0.08$. Dividing by $\text{P}(S)$ simply recalculates $\text{P}(C \mid S)$.
Independence requires $\text{P}(C \mid S) = \text{P}(C)$. Here, $0.25 \neq 0.066$, so the occurrence of $S$ alters the probability of $C$.
Remember that \begin{aligned} \text{P}(S' \cap C) &= \text{P}(S')\text{P}(C \mid S') \cr &= 0.92 \times 0.05 \cr &= 0.046 \end{aligned} Do not forget to multiply by $\text{P}(S')$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Conditional Definition of Independence
bradley_insight.content: While the product rule $\text{P}(A \cap B) = \text{P}(A)\text{P}(B)$ is common, verifying whether $\text{P}(B \mid A) = \text{P}(B)$ is often much faster when conditional probabilities are already given in the question stem.

question:
A language academy offers evening courses in French ($F$), German ($G$), and Spanish ($S$). In a cohort of $100$ adult learners:

$\bullet$ $40$ study French
$\bullet$ $30$ study German
$\bullet$ $35$ study Spanish
$\bullet$ $12$ study both French and German
$\bullet$ $14$ study both French and Spanish
$\bullet$ No student studies both German and Spanish

(a) Find the probability that a randomly selected learner studies none of these three languages.

(b) Determine whether studying French and studying German are independent events.

(c) State, with a clear reason, whether studying German and studying Spanish are mutually exclusive events.

(d) Find the probability that a learner studies French, given that they study Spanish.
steps:
(a) Probability of Studying None:

Since no student studies both German and Spanish, $\text{P}(G \cap S) = 0$ and the triple intersection is zero: $\text{P}(F \cap G \cap S) = 0$.

Using the addition principle for three events:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(F \cup G \cup S) \cr &\quad = \text{P}(F) + \text{P}(G) + \text{P}(S) \cr &\qquad - \text{P}(F \cap G) - \text{P}(F \cap S) \cr &\qquad - \text{P}(G \cap S) \cr &\quad = 0.40 + 0.30 + 0.35 \cr &\qquad - 0.12 - 0.14 - 0 \cr &\quad = 1.05 - 0.26 \cr &\quad = 0.79 \end{aligned}
The probability of studying none is:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(\text{None}) &= 1 - \text{P}(F \cup G \cup S) \cr &= 1 - 0.79 \cr &= 0.21 \end{aligned}

(b) Test for Independence of $F$ and $G$:

Evaluating the product of individual probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(F) \times \text{P}(G) &= 0.40 \times 0.30 \cr &= 0.12 \end{aligned}
Comparing with the intersection probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(F \cap G) = 0.12 \end{aligned}
Since $\text{P}(F \cap G) = \text{P}(F) \times \text{P}(G) = 0.12$, studying French and studying German are independent.

(c) Mutually Exclusive Test for $G$ and $S$:

Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur at the same time, meaning their intersection is empty.

Because no student studies both languages:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(G \cap S) = 0 \end{aligned}
Therefore, studying German and studying Spanish are mutually exclusive.

(d) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(F \mid S)$:

Using the conditional probability definition:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(F \mid S) &= \dfrac{\text{P}(F \cap S)}{\text{P}(S)} \cr &= \dfrac{0.14}{0.35} \cr &= \dfrac{14}{35} \cr &= \dfrac{2}{5} \cr &= 0.4 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $0.21$, (b) Independent, (c) Mutually exclusive, (d) $0.4$

pi_options.feedback: Check the product carefully: $0.40 \times 0.30 = 0.12$, which exactly equals $\text{P}(F \cap G) = 0.12$. Because the product equals the intersection, they are strictly independent.
The condition is that the student studies Spanish, so divide by $\text{P}(S) = 0.35$, yielding $\frac{0.14}{0.35} = 0.4$. Dividing by $\text{P}(F) = 0.40$ incorrectly computes $\text{P}(S \mid F)$.

When calculating the union, ensure you subtract both two-way intersections:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(\text{Union}) \cr &\quad = 0.40 + 0.30 \cr &\qquad + 0.35 - 0.12 \cr &\qquad - 0.14 \cr &\quad = 0.79 \cr &\text{P}(\text{None}) \cr &\quad = 1 - 0.79 \cr &\quad = 0.21 \end{aligned}

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Exact Independence Can Occur
bradley_insight.content: Students often assume exam questions will always conclude events are not independent. Here, $0.40 \times 0.30 = 0.12$ exactly matches the intersection. Always trust the arithmetic rather than guessing.

question:
Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that$$\text{P}(A) = p$$$$\text{P}(B) = 2p$$$$\text{P}(A \cup B) = 0.72$$where $p$ is a positive constant.

(a) Given that $A$ and $B$ are independent events, show that$$2p^2 - 3p + 0.72 = 0$$(b) Hence determine the value of $p$, stating why the alternative root must be rejected.

(c) Find $\text{P}(A' \cap B)$.

(d) Find $\text{P}(A \mid A \cup B)$, giving your answer as an exact fraction in simplest form.
steps:
(a) Deriving the Quadratic Equation:

Since $A$ and $B$ are independent:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A \cap B) &= \text{P}(A) \times \text{P}(B) \cr &= p(2p) \cr &= 2p^2 \end{aligned}
Substituting into the addition rule:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A \cup B) &= \text{P}(A) + \text{P}(B) \cr &\quad - \text{P}(A \cap B)\cr &0.72 = p + 2p - 2p^2 \cr &0.72 = 3p - 2p^2 \cr &2p^2 - 3p + 0.72 = 0 \end{aligned}

(b) Solving for $p$:

Using the quadratic formula:\begin{aligned} p &= \dfrac{-(-3) \pm \sqrt{(-3)^2 - 4(2)(0.72)}}{2(2)} \cr &= \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{9 - 5.76}}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{3.24}}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{3 \pm 1.8}{4} \end{aligned}
Evaluating the two roots:\begin{aligned} p_1 &= \dfrac{4.8}{4} = 1.2 \cr p_2 &= \dfrac{1.2}{4} = 0.3 \end{aligned}
If $p = 1.2$, then $\text{P}(B) = 2(1.2) = 2.4 > 1$, which is impossible because probabilities cannot exceed $1$.

Therefore, $p = 0.3$.

(c) Probability $\text{P}(A' \cap B)$:

With $p = 0.3$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A) &= 0.3 \cr \text{P}(B) &= 0.6 \cr \text{P}(A \cap B) &= 2(0.3)^2 \cr &= 0.18 \end{aligned}
Finding the required probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A' \cap B) &= \text{P}(B) - \text{P}(A \cap B) \cr &= 0.6 - 0.18 \cr &= 0.42 \end{aligned}

(d) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(A \mid A \cup B)$:

Since $A$ is a subset of $A \cup B$, their intersection is simply $A$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A \cap (A \cup B)) = \text{P}(A) = 0.3 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the conditional probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A \mid A \cup B) &= \dfrac{\text{P}(A)}{\text{P}(A \cup B)} \cr &= \dfrac{0.3}{0.72} \cr &= \dfrac{30}{72} \cr &= \dfrac{5}{12} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Probabilities must lie in the interval $[0, 1]$. If $p = 1.2$, then $\text{P}(B) = 2p = 2.4$, which violates probability axioms. You must reject $p = 1.2$.
The reduced sample space is $A \cup B$, so the denominator is $\text{P}(A \cup B) = 0.72$. Simplifying $\frac{0.3}{0.72}$ gives $\frac{5}{12}$.
Evaluating the discriminant gives $(-3)^2 - 4(2)(0.72) = 9 - 5.76 = 3.24$. Since $\sqrt{3.24} = 1.8$, the quadratic yields exact rational roots $1.2$ and $0.3$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Boundary Conditions on Probabilities
bradley_insight.content: Whenever an algebraic equation produces multiple solutions for a probability parameter, verify all defined events: $\text{P}(A) \in [0, 1]$, $\text{P}(B) \in [0, 1]$, and $\text{P}(A \cap B) \in [0, 1]$. While $p = 1.2$ might seem reasonable alone, it makes $\text{P}(B) = 2p = 2.4 > 1$, which is invalid.

question:
The events $E$ and $F$ have non-zero probabilities$$\text{P}(E) = 0.4$$$$\text{P}(F) = 0.5$$(a) Suppose first that $E$ and $F$ are mutually exclusive events:
(i) State the value of $\text{P}(E \cap F)$.
(ii) Explain why two events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.

(b) Suppose instead that $E$ and $F$ are independent events:
(i) Calculate $\text{P}(E \cap F)$.
(ii) Calculate $\text{P}(E \cup F)$.
(iii) State the value of $\text{P}(E \mid F')$.

(c) In a different scenario where $\text{P}(E) = 0.4$ and $\text{P}(F) = 0.5$, it is observed that $\text{P}(E \cup F) = 0.7$. Determine whether $E$ and $F$ are independent in this scenario.
steps:
(a)(i) Mutually Exclusive Intersection:

By definition, mutually exclusive events cannot occur simultaneously:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cap F) = 0 \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Mutually Exclusive vs Independent:

For independent events with non-zero probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cap F) &= \text{P}(E) \times \text{P}(F) \cr &> 0 \end{aligned}
However, for mutually exclusive events, $\text{P}(E \cap F) = 0$.

Since $\text{P}(E) \times \text{P}(F) \neq 0$, the two conditions contradict each other. Thus, events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.

(b) Independent Scenario:

(i) Intersection:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cap F) &= \text{P}(E) \times \text{P}(F) \cr &= 0.4 \times 0.5 \cr &= 0.2 \end{aligned}
(ii) Union:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cup F) &= \text{P}(E) + \text{P}(F) \cr &\quad - \text{P}(E \cap F)\cr &= 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.2 \cr &= 0.7 \end{aligned}
(iii) Conditional: If $E$ and $F$ are independent, the non-occurrence of $F$ does not affect the probability of $E$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \mid F') &= \text{P}(E) \cr &= 0.4 \end{aligned}

(c) Independence in Alternate Scenario:

Using the addition rule to find the intersection:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cap F) &= \text{P}(E) + \text{P}(F) \cr &\quad - \text{P}(E \cup F) \cr &= 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.7 \cr &= 0.2 \end{aligned}
Testing the independence product:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E) \times \text{P}(F) &= 0.4 \times 0.5 \cr &= 0.2 \end{aligned}
Since $\text{P}(E \cap F) = \text{P}(E) \times \text{P}(F) = 0.2$, the events $E$ and $F$ are independent.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $0$, (ii) $\text{P}(E)\text{P}(F) \neq 0$, (b)(i) $0.2$, (ii) $0.7$, (iii) $0.4$, (c) Independent

pi_options.feedback: If $E$ and $F$ are independent, knowledge that $F$ did not occur gives zero information about $E$. Therefore, $\text{P}(E \mid F') = \text{P}(E) = 0.4$, not $0$.
For independent events, $\text{P}(E \cap F) = 0.2 > 0$. You must subtract this intersection from the sum of the probabilities, giving $\text{P}(E \cup F) = 0.4 + 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.7$.

The rule $\text{P}(E \cup F) = \text{P}(E) + \text{P}(F)$ tests for mutually exclusive events, not independence. For independence, verify whether $\text{P}(E \cap F) = \text{P}(E)\text{P}(F)$, which holds here ($0.2 = 0.2$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Difference Between ME and Independent
bradley_insight.content: Mutually exclusive means the events cannot happen together (disjoint sets with $\text{P}(A \cap B) = 0$). Independent means one event happening provides zero information about the other. If two events are mutually exclusive and one happens, you know with $100\%$ certainty that the other did not—so they are maximally dependent!

question:
An engineer models the operational cycle time, $X\text{ minutes}$, of an industrial compressor using the distribution$$X \sim \text{N}(30, 16)$$Over an extended trial period, the engineer observes that the cycle time is less than $26\text{ minutes}$ on $6.7\%$ of cycles, and exceeds $34\text{ minutes}$ on $30.9\%$ of cycles.

(a) Investigate whether the engineer's initial model is a good fit for the data.

(b) The plant manager believes the variance $\sigma^2 = 16$ is accurate, but that the true mean $\mu$ has shifted. Calculate, correct to two significant figures, the refined value of $\mu$ that fits the trial data.

(c) Following a system overhaul, the engineer selects a random sample of $n$ operational cycles. The mean cycle time for these $n$ cycles is found to be $30.0\text{ minutes}$. Using the refined model parameters ($\mu = 32$, $\sigma = 4$), the engineer conducts a two-tailed hypothesis test at the $5\%$ significance level to determine whether the population mean cycle time has changed.

Given that the test result is statistically significant, determine the smallest possible sample size $n$.
steps:
(a) Model Evaluation:

Under the initial model $X \sim \text{N}(30, 16)$, $\sigma = 4$.

Evaluating the lower tail probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X < 26) &= \text{P}\left(Z < \dfrac{26 - 30}{4}\right) \cr &= \text{P}(Z < -1) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(1) \cr &= 1 - 0.8413 \cr &= 0.1587 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the upper tail probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X > 34) &= \text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{34 - 30}{4}\right) \cr &= \text{P}(Z > 1) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(1) \cr &= 0.1587 \end{aligned}
The model predicts $15.9\%$ in both tails, which does not match the observed $6.7\%$ and $30.9\%$. The model is a poor fit.

(b) Refined Mean $\mu$:

For the lower tail proportion of $0.067$:\begin{aligned} \Phi(-1.50) \approx 0.0668 \end{aligned}
Standardising with $\sigma = 4$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{26 - \mu}{4} &= -1.50 \cr 26 - \mu &= -6 \cr \mu &= 32 \end{aligned}
Checking with the upper tail proportion of $0.309$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{34 - 32}{4} &= 0.50 \cr \text{P}(Z > 0.50) &= 1 - 0.6915 \cr &= 0.3085 \end{aligned}
Both tails confirm $\mu = 32$.

(c) Smallest Sample Size $n$:

Under $H_0: \mu = 32$, the sampling distribution is:\begin{aligned} \bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(32, \dfrac{16}{n}\right) \end{aligned}
For a two-tailed test at the $5\%$ level, the critical $z$-value is $1.960$.

Since $\bar{x} = 30.0 < 32$, the test statistic must lie in the lower rejection tail:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{30 - 32}{4/\sqrt{n}} \le -1.960 \cr &-0.5\sqrt{n} \le -1.960 \cr &0.5\sqrt{n} \ge 1.960 \cr &\sqrt{n} \ge 3.920 \cr &n \ge 3.920^2 \cr &n \ge 15.37 \end{aligned}
Since $n$ must be an integer, the smallest possible sample size is $n = 16$.
Final Answer: (a) Poor fit, (b) $\mu = 32$, (c) $n = 16$

pi_options.feedback: The test is two-tailed because it investigates whether the mean has changed. The critical value is $1.960$ rather than the one-tailed value $1.645$.
Because $n \ge 15.37$, selecting $n = 15$ yields a test statistic below the critical magnitude, failing to achieve significance. You must round up to $16$.
In the lower tail equation, $26 - \mu = -6$ rearranges to $\mu = 32$. A sign error yields $20$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Always Round Up for Sample Sizes
bradley_insight.content: When determining the minimum sample size required to achieve significance, always round up to the next integer. If $n \ge 15.37$, selecting $n = 15$ leaves the test statistic just outside the rejection region, while $n = 16$ guarantees significance.

question:
A quality analyst models the weight, $W\text{ grams}$, of cereal boxes using the distribution$$W \sim \text{N}(505, 25)$$Records show that $2.3\%$ of boxes weigh less than $495\text{ grams}$ and $15.9\%$ of boxes weigh more than $512\text{ grams}$.

(a) Show that the current model does not fit these observed proportions.

(b) Assuming a normal distribution remains appropriate, determine refined values for both the mean $\mu$ and the standard deviation $\sigma$ that match the observed proportions.

(c) The packing machinery is adjusted to reduce overweight boxes. A sample of $n$ boxes yields a mean weight of $\bar{w} = 502.5\text{ grams}$. A one-tailed hypothesis test is conducted at the $1\%$ significance level with hypotheses$$H_0: \mu = 505$$$$H_1: \mu < 505$$assuming $\sigma = 5$. Determine the minimum sample size $n$ required for this sample mean to lead to the rejection of $H_0$.
steps:
(a) Model Evaluation:

Under $W \sim \text{N}(505, 25)$, $\sigma = 5$.

Evaluating the lower tail:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(W < 495) &= \text{P}\left(Z < \dfrac{495 - 505}{5}\right) \cr &= \text{P}(Z < -2) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(2) \cr &= 0.0228 \cr &\approx 2.3\% \end{aligned}
Evaluating the upper tail:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(W > 512) &= \text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{512 - 505}{5}\right) \cr &= \text{P}(Z > 1.4) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(1.4) \cr &= 1 - 0.9192 \cr &= 0.0808 \cr &\approx 8.1\% \end{aligned}
The model predicts $8.1\%$ above $512\text{ g}$, which contradicts the observed $15.9\%$. Thus the model is invalid.

(b) Refined Parameters:

From normal percentage tables:\begin{aligned} \Phi(-2.00) &= 0.0228 \cr \Phi(1.00) &= 0.8413 \end{aligned}
Setting up simultaneous equations:\begin{aligned} 495 &= \mu - 2\sigma \cr 512 &= \mu + \sigma \end{aligned}
Subtracting the equations:\begin{aligned} 512 - 495 &= \sigma - (-2\sigma) \cr 17 &= 3\sigma \cr \sigma &= \dfrac{17}{3} \cr &\approx 5.67 \end{aligned}
Substituting back to find $\mu$:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 512 - \dfrac{17}{3} \cr &= \dfrac{1519}{3} \cr &\approx 506.3 \end{aligned}

(c) Sample Size for Hypothesis Test:

Under $H_0: \mu = 505$, the test statistic is:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{\bar{w} - 505}{5/\sqrt{n}} \cr &= \dfrac{502.5 - 505}{5/\sqrt{n}} \cr &= \dfrac{-2.5}{5/\sqrt{n}} \cr &= -0.5\sqrt{n} \end{aligned}
For a one-tailed test at the $1\%$ level, the critical $z$-value is $-2.326$.

Setting up the rejection inequality:\begin{aligned} -0.5\sqrt{n} &\le -2.326 \cr 0.5\sqrt{n} &\ge 2.326 \cr \sqrt{n} &\ge 4.652 \cr n &\ge 4.652^2 \cr n &\ge 21.64 \end{aligned}
Hence the minimum sample size is $n = 22$.
Final Answer: (a) Model invalid, (b) $\mu = 506.3, \sigma = 5.67$, (c) $n = 22$

pi_options.feedback: For a $1\%$ one-tailed test, the critical value is $2.326$. The value $1.645$ corresponds to a $5\%$ significance level.
Because $n \ge 21.64$, taking $n = 21$ yields a test statistic of $-2.291$, which does not fall in the critical region. You must round up to $22$.
A weight below the mean has a negative $z$-score ($z = -2$). Setting $495 = \mu + 2\sigma$ inverts the direction of the lower tail.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Stringent Significance Levels
bradley_insight.content: Notice how moving from a $5\%$ test ($z = 1.645$) to a $1\%$ test ($z = 2.326$) substantially increases the required sample size from $11$ to $22$. Higher confidence requires greater sample evidence.

question:
The tensile strength of steel cables, $S\text{ kN}$, is known to follow a normal distribution with mean $\mu = 450\text{ kN}$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 24\text{ kN}$.

A metallurgy team tests a new manufacturing process and takes a random sample of size $n$. They test the hypotheses$$H_0: \mu = 450$$$$H_1: \mu > 450$$at the $2.5\%$ significance level.

(a) State the sampling distribution of the sample mean $\bar{S}$ under $H_0$ in terms of $n$.

(b) Write down an expression in terms of $n$ for the critical value $c$ of the test.

(c) The team requires that if the true population mean has increased to $460\text{ kN}$, the probability of rejecting $H_0$ (the statistical power) should be at least $0.975$.

Determine the smallest integer sample size $n$ that satisfies this requirement.
steps:
(a) Sampling Distribution:

Under $H_0$, the sample mean has distribution:\begin{aligned} \bar{S} &\sim \text{N}\left(450, \dfrac{24^2}{n}\right) \cr &\sim \text{N}\left(450, \dfrac{576}{n}\right) \end{aligned}

(b) Critical Value $c$:

For an upper one-tailed test at the $2.5\%$ level, the critical $z$-value is $1.960$.

The critical value expression is:\begin{aligned} c &= 450 + 1.960\left(\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \cr &= 450 + \dfrac{47.04}{\sqrt{n}} \end{aligned}

(c) Determining Sample Size $n$:

Under the alternative distribution where $\mu = 460$:\begin{aligned} \bar{S} \sim \text{N}\left(460, \dfrac{576}{n}\right) \end{aligned}
We require the power to satisfy:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(\bar{S} > c \mid \mu = 460) \ge 0.975 \end{aligned}
Standardising under $\mu = 460$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}\left(Z > \dfrac{c - 460}{24/\sqrt{n}}\right) \ge 0.975 \end{aligned}
Since $\text{P}(Z > -1.960) = 0.975$, the standardised threshold requires:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{c - 460}{24/\sqrt{n}} \le -1.960 \cr &c - 460 \le -1.960\left(\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \end{aligned}
Substituting $c = 450 + 1.960\left(\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{n}}\right)$:\begin{aligned} &-10 + 1.960\left(\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \cr &\quad \le -1.960\left(\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \cr &3.920\left(\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \ge 10 \cr &\dfrac{94.08}{\sqrt{n}} \ge 10 \cr &\sqrt{n} \ge 9.408 \cr &n \ge 9.408^2 \cr &n \ge 88.51 \end{aligned}
Hence the smallest integer sample size is $n = 89$.
Final Answer: (a) $\bar{S} \sim \text{N}\left(450, \dfrac{576}{n}\right)$, (b) $c = 450 + \dfrac{47.04}{\sqrt{n}}$, (c) $n = 89$

pi_options.feedback: Guaranteeing $97.5\%$ power requires setting the threshold at $-1.960$ on the alternative distribution, which combines both distances: $1.960 + 1.960 = 3.920$.
Since $n \ge 88.51$, taking $n = 88$ results in a statistical power strictly below $0.975$. The minimum integer sample size is $89$.
The significance level is $2.5\%$, so the critical value is $1.960$ rather than $1.645$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Sample Size and Statistical Power
bradley_insight.content: To determine sample size for a target power, the shift in mean must span the distance between the two critical thresholds. Here, $10 = (1.960 + 1.960)\dfrac{24}{\sqrt{n}}$, directly giving $\sqrt{n} = 9.408$ and $n = 89$.

question:
The concentration of an active compound in a chemical solution is modelled by a normal distribution with unknown mean $\mu\text{ mg/l}$ and known standard deviation $\sigma = 1.8\text{ mg/l}$.

(a) Find the minimum sample size $n$ required to construct a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ with a total width of at most $0.80\text{ mg/l}$.

(b) A chemist takes a random sample of the size found in part (a) and calculates a sample mean of $\bar{x} = 24.35\text{ mg/l}$.
(i) Construct the $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$.
(ii) Using your confidence interval, state the conclusion of a two-tailed hypothesis test at the $5\%$ significance level for$$H_0: \mu = 25.0$$$$H_1: \mu \neq 25.0$$
steps:
(a) Sample Size for Interval Width:

A $95\%$ confidence interval has half-width:\begin{aligned} E &= 1.960\left(\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \cr &= 1.960\left(\dfrac{1.8}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{3.528}{\sqrt{n}} \end{aligned}
The total width is $2E$:\begin{aligned} \text{Width} &= 2\left(\dfrac{3.528}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{7.056}{\sqrt{n}} \end{aligned}
Setting $\text{Width} \le 0.80$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{7.056}{\sqrt{n}} \le 0.80 \cr &\sqrt{n} \ge \dfrac{7.056}{0.80} \cr &\sqrt{n} \ge 8.82 \cr &n \ge 8.82^2 \cr &n \ge 77.79 \end{aligned}
Hence the minimum sample size is $n = 78$.

(b)(i) Constructing the $95\%$ Interval:

With $n = 78$ and $\bar{x} = 24.35$:\begin{aligned} E &= 1.960\left(\dfrac{1.8}{\sqrt{78}}\right) \cr &= \dfrac{3.528}{8.8318} \cr &\approx 0.3995 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the interval limits:\begin{aligned} \text{Lower} &= 24.35 - 0.3995 \cr &= 23.95 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{Upper} &= 24.35 + 0.3995 \cr &= 24.75 \end{aligned}
The $95\%$ confidence interval is $[23.95, 24.75]$.

(b)(ii) Hypothesis Test Conclusion:

Under $H_0$, the hypothesised population mean is $\mu = 25.0$.

Because $25.0$ lies entirely outside the $95\%$ confidence interval $[23.95, 24.75]$, we reject $H_0$.

There is sufficient evidence at the $5\%$ significance level to conclude that the mean concentration is not $25.0\text{ mg/l}$.
Final Answer: (a) $n = 78$, (b)(i) $[23.95, 24.75]$, (ii) Reject $H_0$

pi_options.feedback: The total width of a confidence interval is $2E$. Setting the half-width $E \le 0.80$ produces an interval twice as wide as required.
Because $n \ge 77.79$, choosing $n = 77$ results in an interval width exceeding $0.80$. You must round up to $78$.
Since the hypothesised value $25.0$ lies outside the $95\%$ confidence interval, it is an implausible value for $\mu$ at the $5\%$ level, so $H_0$ must be rejected.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Confidence Intervals as Hypothesis Tests
bradley_insight.content: A two-tailed hypothesis test at significance level $\alpha$ is exactly dual to a $(1 - \alpha)$ confidence interval: if the null value lies outside the interval, reject $H_0$; if it lies inside, do not reject $H_0$.

question:
Two automated assembly lines, Line $A$ and Line $B$, produce identical metal bolts. The lengths of bolts from Line $A$ are distributed as $X_A \sim \text{N}(60.0, 1.44)$ and from Line $B$ as $X_B \sim \text{N}(\mu_B, 1.44)$, with lengths independent between lines.

An engineer collects equal-sized samples of $n$ bolts from each line to test whether Line $B$ produces longer bolts on average:$$H_0: \mu_B - \mu_A = 0$$$$H_1: \mu_B - \mu_A > 0$$at the $5\%$ significance level.

(a) State the distribution of the difference in sample means $\bar{X}_B - \bar{X}_A$ under $H_0$.

(b) In a sample with observed difference $\bar{x}_B - \bar{x}_A = 0.65\text{ mm}$, the test result is statistically significant. Find the smallest possible integer value of $n$.
steps:
(a) Distribution of Difference in Sample Means:

For independent samples of size $n$, the variances add:\begin{aligned} &\text{Var}(\bar{X}_B - \bar{X}_A) \cr &\quad = \text{Var}(\bar{X}_B) \cr &\qquad + \text{Var}(\bar{X}_A) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1.44}{n} + \dfrac{1.44}{n} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2.88}{n} \end{aligned}Under $H_0$, the expected value is zero:\begin{aligned} &(\bar{X}_B - \bar{X}_A) \cr &\quad \sim \text{N}\left(0, \dfrac{2.88}{n}\right) \end{aligned}

(b) Minimum Sample Size $n$:

For an upper one-tailed test at the $5\%$ level, the critical $z$-value is $1.645$.

The standard error of the difference is:\begin{aligned} \text{SE} &= \sqrt{\dfrac{2.88}{n}} \cr &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2.88}}{\sqrt{n}} \end{aligned}
The test statistic must satisfy:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{0.65 - 0}{\sqrt{2.88/n}} \ge 1.645 \cr &\dfrac{0.65\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{2.88}} \ge 1.645 \end{aligned}
Evaluating the numerical terms:\begin{aligned} \sqrt{2.88} &\approx 1.6971 \cr 0.65\sqrt{n} &\ge 1.645(1.6971) \cr 0.65\sqrt{n} &\ge 2.7917 \cr \sqrt{n} &\ge \dfrac{2.7917}{0.65} \cr \sqrt{n} &\ge 4.2949 \cr n &\ge 4.2949^2 \cr n &\ge 18.45 \end{aligned}
Since $n$ must be an integer, the smallest possible sample size is $n = 19$.
Final Answer: (a) $(\bar{X}_B - \bar{X}_A) \sim \text{N}\left(0, \dfrac{2.88}{n}\right)$, (b) $n = 19$

pi_options.feedback: Variances of independent random variables always add: $\text{Var}(X - Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)$. Never subtract variances.
The test is one-tailed at the $5\%$ level, so the critical value is $1.645$, not the two-tailed value $1.960$.
Since $n \ge 18.45$, a sample size of $18$ produces a test statistic of $1.625$, which fails to reach the critical threshold of $1.645$. You must round up to $19$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Independent Variances Always Add
bradley_insight.content: Even though you are taking the difference between two sample means, the variability increases. The variance of the difference is the sum of the individual variances: $\dfrac{1.44}{n} + \dfrac{1.44}{n} = \dfrac{2.88}{n}$.

question:
An environmental health agency investigates airborne pollution across $40$ regional districts. The particulate concentration, measured as $\text{PM}_{10}$ in $\mu\text{g/m}^3$, has been grouped as shown in the table below:

$\text{PM}_{10}$Frequency
$0\text{–}$$12$
$10\text{–}$$16$
$20\text{–}$$6$
$30\text{–}$$4$
$40\text{–}$$1$
$60\text{–}80$$1$

A cumulative frequency curve was generated from these data using spreadsheet software, as shown in Diagram A.


An analyst uses Diagram A to estimate the median $\text{PM}_{10}$ concentration and obtains the estimate $10.0\,\mu\text{g/m}^3$. The true median calculated directly from the raw sample data is $14.5\,\mu\text{g/m}^3$.

(a)
(i) A systematic error was made in generating Diagram A. Identify this error.
(ii) State how this systematic error affects the analyst's estimate of the median.
(iii) State another factor inherent to grouped data that affects the accuracy of this median estimate, explaining its effect.

The agency also records the childhood respiratory clinic admission rate (admissions per $1000$ residents) for the $38$ districts where full medical records were available. The scatter diagram shown in Diagram B displays admission rate plotted against $\text{PM}_{10}$ concentration.


The product moment correlation coefficient (PMCC) for these $38$ districts is $r = 0.324$, with an associated $p$-value of $0.047$.

(b)
(i) Does this information suggest that there is a positive association between particulate concentration and respiratory clinic admissions? Justify your conclusion.
(ii) The analyst uses the spreadsheet to fit a linear regression line to these data. A heavily industrialised port district has a recorded $\text{PM}_{10}$ concentration of $68.0\,\mu\text{g/m}^3$, but no respiratory admission data are available. Is it reliable to use this regression line to estimate the admission rate for this district? Explain your reasoning.
steps:
(a)(i) Systematic Error in Diagram A:

The cumulative frequencies have been plotted at the midpoints of each class interval rather than at the upper class boundaries.

(a)(ii) Effect on Median Estimate:

Because the points are plotted at midpoints instead of upper boundaries, the entire cumulative frequency curve is shifted to the left.

This causes the estimated median to be underestimated (lower than its true value).

(a)(iii) Effect of Grouping:

Linear interpolation assumes that data values are distributed uniformly across each class interval.

If values within the median class are clustered rather than evenly spread, the interpolated estimate will differ from the true median.

(b)(i) Evidence of Association:

We test $H_0: \rho = 0$ against $H_1: \rho > 0$ at the $5\%$ significance level.

Since the $p$-value ($0.047$) is less than $0.05$, we reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $5\%$ level to suggest a positive association between particulate concentration and respiratory admissions.

(b)(ii) Reliability of Regression Line:

A value of $\text{PM}_{10} = 68.0\,\mu\text{g/m}^3$ lies substantially beyond the range of the observed sample data (where nearly all values are below $40\,\mu\text{g/m}^3$).

Using the regression line for this district involves extrapolation, which is unreliable as the linear relationship may not hold at extreme levels.
Final Answer: (a)(i) Plotted at midpoints, (ii) Underestimated, (iii) Linear interpolation assumption, (b)(i) Significant positive association, (ii) Unreliable due to extrapolation

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) Plotted at lower boundaries, (ii) Overestimated, (iii) Linear interpolation assumption, (b)(i) Significant positive association, (ii) Unreliable due to extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: Points were plotted at midpoints ($5, 15, 25\dots$) rather than lower boundaries ($0, 10, 20\dots$). Plotting to the left of upper boundaries underestimates the median.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) Plotted at midpoints, (ii) Underestimated, (iii) Linear interpolation assumption, (b)(i) No significant association, (ii) Unreliable due to extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: Because the $p$-value ($0.047$) is strictly less than the $0.05$ significance threshold, the null hypothesis is rejected, providing significant evidence of positive association.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) Plotted at midpoints, (ii) Underestimated, (iii) Linear interpolation assumption, (b)(i) Significant positive association, (ii) Reliable because line fits all data
pi_options.feedback: Predicting for a value far outside the observed explanatory range ($68$ compared to values under $40$) is extrapolation, which is inherently unreliable.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Midpoints vs Upper Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: Plotting cumulative frequency at class midpoints is a frequent spreadsheet error because software often defaults to category centres. Always ensure cumulative frequency is plotted at the upper class boundary, since cumulative totals count values up to that upper limit.

question:
The diagram shows a histogram representing the distribution of particulate concentration ($\mu\text{g/m}^3$) across a sample of $70$ industrial monitoring stations.

The recorded frequencies for each interval are:
$\bullet$ $0 \le x < 10$: $12$ stations
$\bullet$ $10 \le x < 20$: $24$ stations
$\bullet$ $20 \le x < 30$: $18$ stations
$\bullet$ $30 \le x < 50$: $10$ stations
$\bullet$ $50 \le x < 70$: $6$ stations

(a) Identify the error that has been made in drawing the bar for the class $30 \le x < 50$.

(b) Using the correct frequencies, estimate the median particulate concentration using linear interpolation. Give your answer to three significant figures.

(c) For these $70$ stations, the correlation coefficient between particulate concentration and sulphur dioxide concentration is $r = 0.428$ ($p$-value $< 0.001$). An environmental officer claims: "Higher particulate emissions cause higher sulphur dioxide emissions." Explain why this claim is not statistically justified.
steps:
(a) Error in Histogram:

For a histogram with unequal class widths, bar height must represent frequency density:\begin{aligned} \text{FD} &= \dfrac{\text{Frequency}}{\text{Class Width}} \end{aligned}For the class $30 \le x < 50$, the class width is $20$ and frequency is $10$:\begin{aligned} \text{FD} &= \dfrac{10}{20} \cr &= 0.5 \end{aligned}The bar has been drawn with height equal to $1.5$ rather than the correct frequency density of $0.5$.

(b) Estimating the Median:

Total frequency is $n = 70$. The median position is:\begin{aligned} \text{Position} &= \dfrac{70}{2} \cr &= 35 \end{aligned}Cumulative frequencies up to class boundaries are:\begin{aligned} &0 \le x < 10: 12 \cr &10 \le x < 20: 12 + 24 = 36 \end{aligned}Since $35$ lies between $12$ and $36$, the median lies in $10 \le x < 20$.

Applying linear interpolation:\begin{aligned} \text{Median} &= 10 + \left(\dfrac{35 - 12}{24}\right) \times 10 \cr &= 10 + \left(\dfrac{23}{24}\right) \times 10 \cr &= 10 + 9.583 \cr &\approx 19.6 \end{aligned}

(c) Correlation vs Causation:

A statistically significant correlation does not imply a causal relationship.

A confounding third variable (such as overall volume of industrial activity or weather conditions) could simultaneously cause increases in both pollutants.
Final Answer: (a) Plotted frequency instead of density, (b) $19.6$, (c) Correlation does not imply causation

pi_options.ans: (a) Plotted frequency instead of density, (b) $20.4$, (c) Correlation does not imply causation
pi_options.feedback: Check the interpolation formula. The class runs from $10$ to $20$ with $24$ observations. Adding $\frac{23}{24} \times 10$ to the lower bound of $10$ gives $19.6$, not $20.4$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Plotted frequency instead of density, (b) $19.6$, (c) Claim is valid due to low p-value
pi_options.feedback: Even with an extremely low $p$-value, observational correlation cannot establish a direct causal mechanism between two variables.

pi_options.ans: (a) Incorrect class width used, (b) $17.5$, (c) Correlation does not imply causation
pi_options.feedback: The error is that the bar height was miscalculated. The class width of $20$ is correct, but dividing $10$ by $20$ gives $0.5$ rather than the plotted height.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Area Represents Frequency
bradley_insight.content: In a histogram with unequal class widths, area represents frequency. Never plot raw frequencies on the vertical axis, as wider classes will appear artificially inflated.

question:
The diagram displays parallel box plots comparing broadband download speeds ($\text{Mbps}$) across random samples of residential connections in Urban and Rural districts.

The summary values extracted from the box plots are:
$\bullet$ Urban: Minimum $= 30$, $Q_1 = 52$, Median $= 68$, $Q_3 = 84$, Maximum $= 115$
$\bullet$ Rural: Minimum $= 8$, $Q_1 = 18$, Median $= 28$, $Q_3 = 42$, Whisker end $= 74$, with one point plotted at $108\text{ Mbps}$

(a) Show that the value $108\text{ Mbps}$ in the Rural sample is an outlier according to the standard $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule.

(b) Compare the distributions of broadband speeds in Urban and Rural districts, referring to central tendency, spread, and skewness.

(c) A technician suggests removing the data point at $108\text{ Mbps}$ from the Rural dataset before calculating the mean.
(i) Give one valid reason why this data point should be removed.
(ii) Give one valid reason why this data point should be retained.
steps:
(a) Outlier Verification:

For the Rural distribution, the interquartile range is:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= Q_3 - Q_1 \cr &= 42 - 18 \cr &= 24 \end{aligned}Calculating the upper outlier boundary:\begin{aligned} \text{Boundary} &= Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &= 42 + 1.5(24) \cr &= 42 + 36 \cr &= 78 \end{aligned}Since $108 > 78$, the speed of $108\text{ Mbps}$ is an outlier.

(b) Comparison of Distributions:

Central Tendency: Urban speeds have a substantially higher median ($68\text{ Mbps}$) than Rural speeds ($28\text{ Mbps}$).

Spread: Urban speeds have greater spread, with an $\text{IQR}$ of $32\text{ Mbps}$ compared to $24\text{ Mbps}$ for Rural.

Skewness: Both distributions are approximately symmetrical within the interquartile box, though the Rural distribution exhibits positive skewness due to the extreme upper outlier.

(c) Treatment of Outlier:

(i) Reason to remove: It may represent a data entry error or an unrepresentative commercial fibre connection that distorts the sample mean.

(ii) Reason to retain: It may be a genuine residential high-speed fibre connection that accurately reflects the full population range.
Final Answer: (a) $108 > 78$, (b) Urban has higher median and IQR, (c)(i) May distort mean, (ii) May be a genuine reading

pi_options.ans: (a) $108 > 88$, (b) Urban has higher median and IQR, (c)(i) May distort mean, (ii) May be a genuine reading
pi_options.feedback: Calculating the upper limit requires $Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) = 42 + 1.5(24) = 78$, not $88$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $108 > 78$, (b) Rural has higher median and IQR, (c)(i) May distort mean, (ii) May be a genuine reading
pi_options.feedback: Urban has a higher median ($68$ vs $28$) and a higher interquartile range ($32$ vs $24$).

pi_options.ans: (a) $108 > 78$, (b) Urban has higher median and IQR, (c)(i) Always remove outliers, (ii) Never remove outliers
pi_options.feedback: Outlier removal requires pedagogical justification (such as identifying measurement error or preserving legitimate extreme values), not rigid blanket rules.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Three Strands of Comparison
bradley_insight.content: Whenever asked to compare two distributions, always structure your answer into three distinct strands: location (median), spread (IQR), and shape (skewness). Always cite figures in context with appropriate units.

question:
A retail marketing director collects data on weekly advertising expenditure ($x$, in $£1000\text{s}$) and weekly sales revenue ($y$, in $£1000\text{s}$) for $22$ regional stores.

The scatter diagram shows the data along with a fitted line of best fit. One distinct store is labelled as Point $P$ at $(46, 32)$.

(a) Describe the nature of the correlation shown by the main cluster of stores (excluding Point $P$).

(b) Point $P$ corresponds to a store that suffered extended power disruptions during the promotional campaign. State the effect that removing Point $P$ would have on:
(i) the value of the product moment correlation coefficient $r$,
(ii) the gradient of the regression line of $y$ on $x$.

(c) The equation of the regression line using all $22$ stores is$$y = 1.62x + 16.5$$The director uses this equation to predict the sales revenue for a new flagship store with an advertising budget of $£60,000$ ($x = 60$). Comment on the validity of this prediction.
steps:
(a) Correlation of Main Cluster:

Excluding Point $P$, the points lie tightly around an upward-sloping line, demonstrating strong positive linear correlation.

(b)(i) Effect on Correlation Coefficient $r$:

Point $P$ at $(46, 32)$ lies far below the linear trend established by the main cluster.

Removing Point $P$ reduces residual scatter, causing $r$ to increase (become closer to $+1$).

(b)(ii) Effect on Regression Gradient:

Point $P$ has a high $x$-value and a low $y$-value, exerting downward leverage on the right-hand end of the regression line.

Removing Point $P$ allows the line to tilt steeper, causing the gradient to increase.

(c) Validity of Prediction at $x = 60$:

The observed advertising values range from $x = 4$ to $x = 46$.

Predicting at $x = 60$ requires extrapolation beyond the range of the data. Furthermore, sales revenue may experience diminishing returns at high advertising spend, making the linear model unreliable.
Final Answer: (a) Strong positive, (b)(i) Increases, (ii) Increases, (c) Unreliable due to extrapolation

pi_options.ans: (a) Weak positive, (b)(i) Increases, (ii) Increases, (c) Unreliable due to extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: The points in the main cluster follow a very narrow linear band, which indicates strong rather than weak positive correlation.

pi_options.ans: (a) Strong positive, (b)(i) Decreases, (ii) Decreases, (c) Unreliable due to extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: Because Point $P$ contradicts the positive trend and pulls the line downward, removing it strengthens the correlation and steepens the slope.

pi_options.ans: (a) Strong positive, (b)(i) Increases, (ii) Increases, (c) Reliable because equation is linear
pi_options.feedback: Even with a strong linear fit, predicting outside the domain of explanatory data ($x = 60$) is extrapolation and is statistically unreliable.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: High Leverage Outliers
bradley_insight.content: An outlier with an extreme $x$-value exerts disproportionate leverage on a regression line. Point $P$ acts like a weight on a seesaw, pulling the right side of the line down. Removing it immediately increases both $r$ and the slope.

question:
The cumulative frequency curve in the diagram models the examination completion times (in minutes) for a large cohort of $400$ candidates.
