The dashed reference lines indicate that:
$\bullet$ The $10\text{th}$ percentile is $P_{10} = 45\text{ minutes}$
$\bullet$ The median ($50\text{th}$ percentile) is $Q_2 = 60\text{ minutes}$
$\bullet$ The $90\text{th}$ percentile is $P_{90} = 75\text{ minutes}$

(a) Calculate the $10\text{th}$ to $90\text{th}$ interdecile range for this examination.

(b) An examiner suggests that completion times $T$ can be modelled by a normal distribution:$$T \sim \text{N}(60, 11.7^2)$$(i) Explain how the symmetry of $P_{10}$ and $P_{90}$ about the median supports this suggestion.
(ii) Show that for a normal distribution with $\sigma = 11.7$, the theoretical $10\text{th}$ to $90\text{th}$ interdecile range is approximately $30.0\text{ minutes}$, and comment on the quality of the model.

(c) The examination had a strict time limit of $90\text{ minutes}$. Candidates who did not finish within the time limit were recorded as completing at $90\text{ minutes}$. State how this data collection constraint affects the upper tail of the distribution.
steps:
(a) Interdecile Range:

Evaluating the difference between the $90\text{th}$ and $10\text{th}$ percentiles:\begin{aligned} \text{IDR} &= P_{90} - P_{10} \cr &= 75 - 45 \cr &= 30\text{ minutes} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Symmetry Supporting Normal Model:

Evaluating the distances from the median ($Q_2 = 60$):\begin{aligned} Q_2 - P_{10} &= 60 - 45 \cr &= 15 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} P_{90} - Q_2 &= 75 - 60 \cr &= 15 \end{aligned}Because both percentiles are equidistant ($15\text{ minutes}$) from the median, the distribution is symmetrical, supporting a normal model.

(b)(ii) Theoretical Interdecile Range:

From standard normal tables, $\Phi(1.2816) = 0.90$.

Under $T \sim \text{N}(60, 11.7^2)$:\begin{aligned} P_{90} &= 60 + 1.2816(11.7) \cr &= 60 + 14.995 \cr &= 74.995 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} P_{10} &= 60 - 1.2816(11.7) \cr &= 60 - 14.995 \cr &= 45.005 \end{aligned}The theoretical range is:\begin{aligned} \text{Range} &= 74.995 - 45.005 \cr &= 29.99 \cr &\approx 30.0\text{ minutes} \end{aligned}This matches the observed value ($30\text{ minutes}$) almost exactly, indicating the normal model provides an excellent fit.

(c) Effect of Upper Limit:

Recording unfinished candidates at exactly $90\text{ minutes}$ creates an artificial accumulation of values (right-censoring) at the upper boundary.

This truncates the upper tail, preventing the smooth, tapering tail characteristic of a true normal distribution.
Final Answer: (a) $30\text{ minutes}$, (b)(i) Equidistant from median, (ii) $30.0\text{ minutes}$ matches observed, (c) Right-censoring truncates tail

pi_options.ans: (a) $15\text{ minutes}$, (b)(i) Equidistant from median, (ii) $30.0\text{ minutes}$ matches observed, (c) Right-censoring truncates tail
pi_options.feedback: The interdecile range is the distance from $P_{10}$ to $P_{90}$, which is $75 - 45 = 30\text{ minutes}$, rather than the distance from the median to a single decile.

pi_options.ans: (a) $30\text{ minutes}$, (b)(i) Equidistant from median, (ii) $37.5\text{ minutes}$ does not match, (c) Right-censoring truncates tail
pi_options.feedback: For the $90\text{th}$ percentile, $z = 1.282$, giving $1.282 \times 11.7 \approx 15.0\text{ minutes}$ each side, which totals $30.0\text{ minutes}$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $30\text{ minutes}$, (b)(i) Equidistant from median, (ii) $30.0\text{ minutes}$ matches observed, (c) Extends tail infinitely
pi_options.feedback: Capping unfinished candidates at $90\text{ minutes}$ truncates the tail and creates an artificial spike at $90$, rather than extending the tail.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Right-Censoring in Practice
bradley_insight.content: In real-world data collection, time limits cause right-censoring: we know a candidate took at least $90\text{ minutes}$, but not their true completion time. A normal distribution assumes tails extend indefinitely, so any capped dataset will diverge from normality at the boundary.

question:
The random variable $X$ has the binomial distribution $\text{B}(15, 0.4)$.

Showing your calculation in full, find $\text{P}(X = 6)$. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.
steps:
Binomial Probability Formula:

For $X \sim \text{B}(n, p)$, the probability of obtaining exactly $x$ successes is given by:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = x) &= \dbinom{n}{x}p^x(1 - p)^{n - x} \end{aligned}Here $n = 15$, $p = 0.4$, $1 - p = 0.6$, and $x = 6$.

Calculation:

Substituting the values into the formula:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 6) &= \dbinom{15}{6}(0.4)^6(0.6)^9 \cr &= 5005(0.004096) \cr &\qquad \times 0.010078 \cr &= 0.2066 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: $0.2066$

pi_options.feedback: Do not forget the binomial coefficient. Multiplying $(0.4)^6(0.6)^9$ without $\dbinom{15}{6} = 5005$ gives only a single combination of trials.
Check the indices in your formula. The power for failure must be $15 - 6 = 9$, rather than using $6$ for both powers.
Ensure you use the specified success probability of $0.4$. Using $0.5$ assumes a symmetric distribution.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Evaluating the Binomial Coefficient
bradley_insight.content: Always calculate the combination $\dbinom{n}{x}$ first. Here $\dbinom{15}{6} = 5005$. Because probabilities of powers like $(0.4)^6$ and $(0.6)^9$ become very small, keep full precision on your calculator before multiplying by the coefficient.

question:
The random variable $Y$ has the binomial distribution $\text{B}(20, 0.35)$.

(a) Showing your calculation, find $\text{P}(Y = 8)$.

(b) Using cumulative binomial tables or statistical calculator functions, find:
(i) $\text{P}(Y \le 6)$
(ii) $\text{P}(Y > 9)$
(iii) $\text{P}(5 \le Y \le 10)$
steps:
(a) Exact Probability $\text{P}(Y = 8)$:

Using the binomial probability formula with $n = 20$ and $p = 0.35$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y = 8) &= \dbinom{20}{8}(0.35)^8(0.65)^{12} \cr &= 125970(0.0002252) \cr &\qquad \times 0.005688 \cr &= 0.1614 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Cumulative Probability $\text{P}(Y \le 6)$:

Evaluating directly from the cumulative binomial distribution function:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y \le 6) = 0.4166 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Upper Tail $\text{P}(Y > 9)$:

Rewriting in terms of the cumulative probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y > 9) &= 1 - \text{P}(Y \le 9) \cr &= 1 - 0.8782 \cr &= 0.1218 \end{aligned}

(b)(iii) Interval $\text{P}(5 \le Y \le 10)$:

Subtracting the cumulative tail below $5$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(5 \le Y \le 10) \cr &\quad = \text{P}(Y \le 10) \cr &\qquad - \text{P}(Y \le 4) \cr &\quad = 0.9468 - 0.1182 \cr &\quad = 0.8286 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: To include $Y = 5$, subtract $\text{P}(Y \le 4)$. Subtracting $\text{P}(Y \le 5)$ incorrectly removes the outcome $Y = 5$ from the interval.
Because the inequality is strict, $\text{P}(Y > 9)$ is equivalent to $1 - \text{P}(Y \le 9)$. Subtracting $\text{P}(Y \le 8)$ incorrectly includes $9$ in the upper tail.
In part (a), do not omit the combination term $\dbinom{20}{8} = 125970$. Without it, you obtain only the probability of one specific sequence.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Inclusion in Binomial Intervals
bradley_insight.content: For a discrete variable, always note which values are included. To find $\text{P}(5 \le Y \le 10)$, we want the sum from $5$ to $10$. We take all values up to $10$, which is $\text{P}(Y \le 10)$, and remove values up to $4$, which is $\text{P}(Y \le 4)$.

question:
A manufacturing firm produces precision sensors. Historically, $8\%$ of the sensors produced have a calibration defect. A quality assurance inspector selects a random sample of $25$ sensors from a day's production run.

Let $X$ denote the number of defective sensors in the sample.

(a) State two assumptions necessary for $X$ to be modelled by a binomial distribution.

(b) Showing your calculation in full, find the probability that exactly $2$ sensors in the sample are defective.

(c) Find the probability that at least $3$ sensors in the sample are defective.
steps:
(a) Modelling Assumptions:

Any two of the following conditions:

The probability of a sensor being defective is constant $(p = 0.08)$.

Whether one sensor is defective is independent of any other sensor.

There is a fixed number of trials $(n = 25)$.

(b) Probability of Exactly $2$ Defective Sensors:

Under $X \sim \text{B}(25, 0.08)$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 2) &= \dbinom{25}{2}(0.08)^2(0.92)^{23} \cr &= 300(0.0064) \cr &\qquad \times 0.14697 \cr &= 0.2822 \end{aligned}

(c) Probability of At Least $3$ Defective Sensors:

Using the complement rule:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 3) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 2) \end{aligned}From the cumulative binomial distribution for $n = 25$ and $p = 0.08$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \le 2) = 0.6768 \end{aligned}Evaluating the upper tail:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 3) &= 1 - 0.6768 \cr &= 0.3232 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Constant probability and independent trials, (b) $0.2822$, (c) $0.3232$

pi_options.feedback: The question asks for at least 3 defective sensors, which is $\text{P}(X \ge 3)$. The value $0.6768$ is $\text{P}(X \le 2)$; you must subtract this from 1.
For at least 3, the complement is at most 2. Subtracting $\text{P}(X \le 3)$ mistakenly excludes the outcome $X = 3$.
The binomial model requires independent trials and a constant probability of success. In part (b), remember to multiply by the combination $\dbinom{25}{2} = 300$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Binomial Modelling Conditions
bradley_insight.content: Exam questions frequently ask for the four conditions of a binomial model: Fixed number of trials ($n$), two possible outcomes (success/failure), constant probability of success ($p$), and independent trials. Stating any two clearly secures full credit.

question:
The discrete random variable $W$ follows a binomial distribution $\text{B}(n, p)$.

The mean and variance of $W$ are given by$$\text{E}(W) = 7.2$$$$\text{Var}(W) = 4.32$$(a) Determine the value of $n$ and the value of $p$.

(b) Showing your calculation, find $\text{P}(W = 8)$. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.
steps:
(a) Determining $n$ and $p$:

For $W \sim \text{B}(n, p)$, the mean and variance are given by:\begin{aligned} &\text{E}(W) = np = 7.2 \cr &\text{Var}(W) = np(1 - p) = 4.32 \end{aligned}Dividing the variance by the mean:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{np(1 - p)}{np} = \dfrac{4.32}{7.2} \cr &1 - p = 0.6 \cr &p = 0.4 \end{aligned}Substituting $p = 0.4$ back into the mean equation:\begin{aligned} n(0.4) &= 7.2 \cr n &= \dfrac{7.2}{0.4} \cr n &= 18 \end{aligned}

(b) Calculating $\text{P}(W = 8)$:

Using $W \sim \text{B}(18, 0.4)$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(W = 8) &= \dbinom{18}{8}(0.4)^8(0.6)^{10} \cr &= 43758(0.0006554) \cr &\qquad \times 0.006047 \cr &= 0.1734 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Dividing variance by mean gives $1 - p = 0.6$, which means $p = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4$. Taking $p = 0.6$ confuses failure with success.
Remember to include the binomial coefficient $\dbinom{18}{8} = 43758$ in your probability calculation.
Ensure the power of failure is $18 - 8 = 10$. A power slip alters the resulting probability.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Variance to Mean Ratio
bradley_insight.content: For any binomial distribution, $\dfrac{\text{Var}(W)}{\text{E}(W)} = \dfrac{np(1 - p)}{np} = 1 - p$. This ratio immediately yields the probability of failure $q = 1 - p$ in one step.

question:
A specialist nursery sells sunflower seeds with a germination probability of $0.80$. Seeds are planted in planting cells arranged in trays of $10$.

(a) Showing your calculation in full, find the probability that exactly $8$ seeds germinate in a randomly selected tray of $10$ seeds.

(b) A gardener purchases $5$ independent trays of $10$ seeds. Find the probability that exactly $8$ seeds germinate in at least $4$ of the $5$ trays. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.
steps:
(a) Single Tray Probability:

Let $X$ denote the number of germinating seeds in a tray of $10$, so $X \sim \text{B}(10, 0.80)$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 8) &= \dbinom{10}{8}(0.80)^8(0.20)^2 \cr &= 45(0.16777)(0.04) \cr &= 0.3020 \end{aligned}

(b) Two-Stage Binomial Model:

Let $Y$ denote the number of trays in which exactly $8$ seeds germinate.

Since there are $5$ independent trays, $Y$ follows a new binomial distribution:\begin{aligned} Y \sim \text{B}(5, 0.3020) \end{aligned}We require the probability that at least $4$ trays have this outcome:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y \ge 4) &= \text{P}(Y = 4) + \text{P}(Y = 5) \end{aligned}

Evaluating the Component Probabilities:

For $Y = 4$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y = 4) &= \dbinom{5}{4}(0.3020)^4(0.6980)^1 \cr &= 5(0.008318)(0.6980) \cr &= 0.0290 \end{aligned}For $Y = 5$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y = 5) &= (0.3020)^5 \cr &= 0.0025 \end{aligned}Adding the probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y \ge 4) &= 0.0290 + 0.0025 \cr &= 0.0315 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: The event at least 4 includes both $Y = 4$ and $Y = 5$. Do not forget to add $\text{P}(Y = 5) = (0.3020)^5 = 0.0025$.
In the second-stage calculation for $\text{P}(Y = 4)$, remember to multiply by the combination $\dbinom{5}{4} = 5$.
In part (a), evaluate $\dbinom{10}{8}(0.8)^8(0.2)^2$. Using an index of 8 for both terms alters the probability.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Two-Stage Binomial Distributions
bradley_insight.content: A classic exam technique is the two-stage binomial: the probability calculated in part (a) becomes the success parameter $p$ for a new binomial distribution in part (b). Always define the new variable explicitly (e.g. $Y \sim \text{B}(5, 0.3020)$).

question:
The Venn diagram shows the extracurricular clubs attended by $50$ sixth form students. $B$ represents the set of students who attend Badminton club, $C$ represents the set of students who attend Chess club, and $R$ represents the set of students who attend Robotics club.

The diagram shows the number of students in each set.

(a) Explain what $C \cap R'$ means in this context.

(b) One of these students is chosen at random. Find the probability that this student attends:
(i) exactly two of these clubs,
(ii) Chess or Badminton or both.

(c) Determine whether attending Chess club and attending Robotics club are statistically independent for these students.
steps:
(a) Contextual Meaning:

$C \cap R'$ represents the students who attend Chess club but do not attend Robotics club.

(b)(i) Exactly Two Clubs:

Because Badminton and Robotics do not overlap, the students attending exactly two clubs are in $(B \cap C)$ and $(C \cap R)$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(\text{Exactly 2}) &= \dfrac{5 + 6}{50} \cr &= \dfrac{11}{50} \cr &= 0.22 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Chess or Badminton or Both:

Summing all regions in $C \cup B$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C \cup B) &= \dfrac{15 + 5 + 14 + 6}{50} \cr &= \dfrac{40}{50} \cr &= 0.8 \end{aligned}

(c) Test for Independence:

Finding the individual probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C) &= \dfrac{5 + 14 + 6}{50} \cr &= \dfrac{25}{50} \cr &= 0.5 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(R) &= \dfrac{6 + 6}{50} \cr &= \dfrac{12}{50} \cr &= 0.24 \end{aligned}Calculating the product of probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C) \times \text{P}(R) &= 0.5 \times 0.24 \cr &= 0.12 \end{aligned}From the diagram, the intersection probability is:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C \cap R) &= \dfrac{6}{50} \cr &= 0.12 \end{aligned}Since $\text{P}(C \cap R) = \text{P}(C) \times \text{P}(R)$, attending Chess club and attending Robotics club are statistically independent.
Final Answer: (a) Attend Chess but not Robotics, (b)(i) $0.22$, (ii) $0.8$, (c) Independent

pi_options.ans: (a) Attend Chess but not Robotics, (b)(i) $0.22$, (ii) $0.8$, (c) Not independent
pi_options.feedback: Evaluate the product test:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C) \times \text{P}(R) &= 0.5 \times 0.24 \cr &= 0.12 \end{aligned}Because this matches $\text{P}(C \cap R) = 0.12$, the events are independent.

pi_options.ans: (a) Attend Chess but not Robotics, (b)(i) $0.10$, (ii) $0.8$, (c) Independent
pi_options.feedback: There are two separate overlap regions: $5$ students attend Badminton and Chess, and $6$ students attend Chess and Robotics, giving $11$ students in total.

pi_options.ans: (a) Attend Chess but not Robotics, (b)(i) $0.22$, (ii) $0.68$, (c) Independent
pi_options.feedback: The union $C \cup B$ includes all students in Chess, including the $6$ students who also attend Robotics: $15 + 5 + 14 + 6 = 40$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Independence in Venn Diagrams
bradley_insight.content: Never assume that overlapping sets in a Venn diagram cannot be independent! While mutually exclusive sets with non-zero probability can never be independent, overlapping sets can satisfy $\text{P}(A \cap B) = \text{P}(A)\text{P}(B)$ perfectly.

question:
The Venn diagram shows the subject choices of $60$ students in a college. $A$ represents Art, $B$ represents Biology, and $C$ represents Chemistry.

(a) Describe in words the group of students represented by the set $(A \cup B) \cap C'$.

(b) A student is selected at random from the cohort. Calculate the probability that this student studies:
(i) at least two of these subjects,
(ii) Chemistry, given that they study Biology.

(c) Determine, with detailed reasoning, whether studying Art and studying Biology are statistically independent.
steps:
(a) Set Description:

$(A \cup B) \cap C'$ represents students who study Art or Biology (or both), but do not study Chemistry.

(b)(i) At Least Two Subjects:

Summing the four intersection regions:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(\text{At least 2}) &= \dfrac{5 + 4 + 6 + 3}{60} \cr &= \dfrac{18}{60} \cr &= 0.3 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(C \mid B)$:

Total students studying Biology:\begin{aligned} n(B) &= 14 + 5 + 6 + 3 \cr &= 28 \end{aligned}Students studying both Chemistry and Biology:\begin{aligned} n(C \cap B) &= 6 + 3 \cr &= 9 \end{aligned}Calculating the conditional probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C \mid B) &= \dfrac{n(C \cap B)}{n(B)} \cr &= \dfrac{9}{28} \end{aligned}

(c) Independence of $A$ and $B$:

Finding the individual probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A) &= \dfrac{11 + 5 + 4 + 3}{60} \cr &= \dfrac{23}{60} \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(B) &= \dfrac{28}{60} \end{aligned}Calculating the product of probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A) \times \text{P}(B) &= \dfrac{23}{60} \times \dfrac{28}{60} \cr &= \dfrac{644}{3600} \cr &\approx 0.1789 \end{aligned}From the diagram:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(A \cap B) &= \dfrac{5 + 3}{60} \cr &= \dfrac{8}{60} \cr &\approx 0.1333 \end{aligned}Since $0.1333 \neq 0.1789$, studying Art and studying Biology are not independent.
Final Answer: (a) Study Art or Biology but not Chemistry, (b)(i) $0.3$, (ii) $\dfrac{9}{28}$, (c) Not independent

pi_options.ans: (a) Study Art or Biology but not Chemistry, (b)(i) $0.3$, (ii) $\dfrac{3}{20}$, (c) Not independent
pi_options.feedback: For $\text{P}(C \mid B)$, the reduced sample space is set $B$, which has $28$ students. Dividing by $60$ evaluates the joint probability $\text{P}(C \cap B)$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Study Art or Biology but not Chemistry, (b)(i) $0.3$, (ii) $\dfrac{9}{28}$, (c) Independent

pi_options.ans: (a) Study Art or Biology but not Chemistry, (b)(i) $0.25$, (ii) $\dfrac{9}{28}$, (c) Not independent
pi_options.feedback: The condition at least two includes students taking all three subjects ($3$ students), giving $5 + 4 + 6 + 3 = 18$ students.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Conditional Denominators
bradley_insight.content: When computing a conditional probability $\text{P}(X \mid Y)$ directly from a Venn diagram, always restrict your attention entirely to the circle for $Y$. Its total frequency becomes your new denominator.

question:
A survey of $80$ local residents investigates ownership of alternative fuel vehicles. $E$ represents the set of residents who own a fully Electric car, and $H$ represents the set of residents who own a Hybrid car.

The number of residents in each region of the Venn diagram is shown in terms of an unknown integer $x$.

(a) Form an equation in $x$ and hence show that $x = 12$.

(b) A resident from the survey is chosen at random. Find the probability that this resident owns:
(i) an Electric car,
(ii) a Hybrid car, given that they own an Electric car.

(c) Determine whether owning an Electric car and owning a Hybrid car are statistically independent events for this group of residents.
steps:
(a) Forming and Solving the Equation:

The sum of all four regions equals the total surveyed population ($80$):\begin{aligned} &22 + x + (2x + 6) + 16 = 80 \cr &3x + 44 = 80 \cr &3x = 36 \cr &x = 12 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Electric Car Ownership:

Total residents owning an Electric car:\begin{aligned} n(E) &= 22 + 12 \cr &= 34 \end{aligned}Calculating the probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E) &= \dfrac{34}{80} \cr &= \dfrac{17}{40} \cr &= 0.425 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Hybrid Given Electric:

Using the conditional probability definition:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(H \mid E) &= \dfrac{n(E \cap H)}{n(E)} \cr &= \dfrac{12}{34} \cr &= \dfrac{6}{17} \end{aligned}

(c) Test for Independence:

Total residents owning a Hybrid car with $x = 12$:\begin{aligned} n(H) &= 12 + [2(12) + 6] \cr &= 12 + 30 \cr &= 42 \end{aligned}Calculating marginal and joint probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(H) &= \dfrac{42}{80} \cr &= 0.525 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E) \times \text{P}(H) &= 0.425 \times 0.525 \cr &= 0.2231 \end{aligned}From the diagram:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(E \cap H) &= \dfrac{12}{80} \cr &= 0.15 \end{aligned}Since $0.15 \neq 0.2231$, owning an Electric car and owning a Hybrid car are not independent.
Final Answer: (a) $x = 12$, (b)(i) $0.425$, (ii) $\dfrac{6}{17}$, (c) Not independent

pi_options.feedback: The condition is owning an Electric car, so divide by $n(E) = 34$, giving $\dfrac{12}{34} = \dfrac{6}{17}$. Dividing by $42$ calculates $\text{P}(E \mid H)$.
Notice that $\text{P}(H \mid E) = \dfrac{6}{17} \approx 0.353$, whereas $\text{P}(H) = 0.525$. Because knowledge of $E$ changes the probability of $H$, they are not independent.
The set $E$ includes both residents who own only an Electric car ($22$) and residents who own both ($12$), giving $34$ in total.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Algebraic Regions
bradley_insight.content: When Venn diagrams contain algebraic terms like $2x + 6$, always write out the total equation first. Once $x$ is found, immediately write down the evaluated numbers for all regions to avoid substitution errors later.

question:
The Venn diagram shows the probabilities associated with three events $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ defined on the sample space $S$.

(a) State, with a clear mathematical reason, whether events $X$ and $Z$ are mutually exclusive.

(b) Calculate:
(i) $\text{P}(X \cup Y)$
(ii) $\text{P}(X \mid Y')$
(iii) $\text{P}(Y \mid X \cup Z)$

(c) Determine whether events $X$ and $Y$ are statistically independent.
steps:
(a) Mutually Exclusive Test for $X$ and $Z$:

Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen together.

From the diagram, circles $X$ and $Z$ do not intersect:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \cap Z) = 0 \end{aligned}Therefore, $X$ and $Z$ are mutually exclusive.

(b)(i) Union $\text{P}(X \cup Y)$:

Summing all regions in $X$ and $Y$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \cup Y) &= 0.20 + 0.10 + 0.15 \cr &= 0.45 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(X \mid Y')$:

Total probability for $Y$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y) &= 0.10 + 0.15 + 0.05 \cr &= 0.30 \end{aligned}Finding the complement:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y') &= 1 - 0.30 \cr &= 0.70 \end{aligned}Evaluating the conditional probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \mid Y') &= \dfrac{\text{P}(X \cap Y')}{\text{P}(Y')} \cr &= \dfrac{0.20}{0.70} \cr &= \dfrac{2}{7} \end{aligned}

(b)(iii) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(Y \mid X \cup Z)$:

Finding the intersection of $Y$ with $X \cup Z$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y \cap (X \cup Z)) &= 0.10 + 0.05 \cr &= 0.15 \end{aligned}Finding the union probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \cup Z) \cr &\quad = (0.20 + 0.10) \cr &\qquad + (0.05 + 0.30) \cr &\quad = 0.30 + 0.35 \cr &\quad = 0.65 \end{aligned}Evaluating the conditional probability:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y \mid X \cup Z) &= \dfrac{0.15}{0.65} \cr &= \dfrac{15}{65} \cr &= \dfrac{3}{13} \end{aligned}

(c) Test for Independence of $X$ and $Y$:

Calculating individual probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X) &= 0.20 + 0.10 \cr &= 0.30 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y) &= 0.10 + 0.15 + 0.05 \cr &= 0.30 \end{aligned}Multiplying the probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X) \times \text{P}(Y) &= 0.30 \times 0.30 \cr &= 0.09 \end{aligned}From the diagram:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \cap Y) = 0.10 \end{aligned}Since $0.10 \neq 0.09$, events $X$ and $Y$ are not independent.
Final Answer: (a) Mutually exclusive because $\text{P}(X \cap Z) = 0$, (b)(i) $0.45$, (ii) $\dfrac{2}{7}$, (iii) $\dfrac{3}{13}$, (c) Not independent

Notice that $\text{P}(X \cap Y) = 0.10$, whereas $\text{P}(X)\text{P}(Y) = 0.09$. Because these values are not equal, the events are not independent.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Probabilities Directly on Regions
bradley_insight.content: When region labels are already given as decimals, they represent probabilities directly rather than frequencies. Verify that all regions (including the outside region) sum to strictly $1.00$ before calculating.

question:
The Venn diagram shows the module enrolments of $50$ computing students. $A$ represents Advanced Algorithms, $B$ represents Computer Science, and $C$ represents Cybersecurity. The circle representing set $A$ lies entirely inside the circle representing set $B$.

(a) State what the subset relationship $A \subset B$ means in the context of these course enrolments.

(b) A student is chosen at random. Find the probability that this student studies:
(i) Computer Science, given that they study Advanced Algorithms ($\text{P}(B \mid A)$),
(ii) exactly one of these three modules.

(c) Determine whether enrolling in Computer Science ($B$) and enrolling in Cybersecurity ($C$) are statistically independent events.
steps:
(a) Subset Meaning in Context:

The relation $A \subset B$ means that every student who enrols in Advanced Algorithms is also enrolled in Computer Science.

(b)(i) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(B \mid A)$:

Because set $A$ is completely contained within set $B$:\begin{aligned} A \cap B = A \end{aligned}Applying the conditional probability formula:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(B \mid A) &= \dfrac{\text{P}(B \cap A)}{\text{P}(A)} \cr &= \dfrac{\text{P}(A)}{\text{P}(A)} \cr &= 1 \end{aligned}If a student studies Advanced Algorithms, it is certain ($100\%$ probability) that they study Computer Science.

(b)(ii) Exactly One Module:

Because $A \subset B$, any student taking $A$ is automatically taking at least two modules ($A$ and $B$).

Students taking exactly one module are those in $B$ only and in $C$ only:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(\text{Exactly 1}) &= \dfrac{14 + 15}{50} \cr &= \dfrac{29}{50} \cr &= 0.58 \end{aligned}

(c) Independence of $B$ and $C$:

Total students enrolled in Computer Science ($B$):\begin{aligned} n(B) &= 8 + 14 + 6 \cr &= 28 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(B) &= \dfrac{28}{50} \cr &= 0.56 \end{aligned}Total students enrolled in Cybersecurity ($C$):\begin{aligned} n(C) &= 6 + 15 \cr &= 21 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(C) &= \dfrac{21}{50} \cr &= 0.42 \end{aligned}Calculating the product of probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(B) \times \text{P}(C) &= 0.56 \times 0.42 \cr &= 0.2352 \end{aligned}From the diagram, the intersection probability is:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(B \cap C) &= \dfrac{6}{50} \cr &= 0.12 \end{aligned}Since $0.12 \neq 0.2352$, studying Computer Science and studying Cybersecurity are not independent.
Final Answer: (a) Every Advanced Algorithms student studies Computer Science, (b)(i) $1$, (ii) $0.58$, (c) Not independent

pi_options.ans: (a) Every Advanced Algorithms student studies Computer Science, (b)(i) $1$, (ii) $0.74$, (c) Not independent

pi_options.ans: (a) Every Advanced Algorithms student studies Computer Science, (b)(i) $\dfrac{2}{7}$, (ii) $0.58$, (c) Not independent
pi_options.feedback: The condition is studying $A$, so the denominator is $n(A) = 8$. Since all $8$ students also study $B$, the conditional probability is $\dfrac{8}{8} = 1$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Every Advanced Algorithms student studies Computer Science, (b)(i) $1$, (ii) $0.58$, (c) Independent
