bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Subsets and Conditional Certainty
bradley_insight.content: When one set is entirely contained within another ($A \subset B$), knowing that event $A$ occurred guarantees that event $B$ has occurred. Hence $\text{P}(B \mid A) = 1$ always holds for any subset relationship.

question:
An artisan manufacturer produces hand-glazed ceramic floor tiles, each of area $2.5\text{ m}^2$. Surface blemishes on the tiles occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate of $0.6\text{ per m}^2$.

(a) Find the probability that a randomly chosen tile contains at most $2$ blemishes. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.

(b) Find the probability that, in a random sample of $6$ tiles, exactly $4$ tiles will contain at most $2$ blemishes each. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.
steps:
(a) Probability for a Single Tile:

First scaling the mean rate for a tile of area $2.5\text{ m}^2$:\begin{aligned} \lambda &= 0.6 \times 2.5 \cr &= 1.5 \end{aligned}Let $X$ denote the number of blemishes on a single tile, so $X \sim \text{Po}(1.5)$.

Evaluating the probability of at most $2$ blemishes:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \le 2) \cr &\quad = \text{P}(X = 0) + \text{P}(X = 1) \cr &\qquad + \text{P}(X = 2) \cr &\quad = \text{e}^{-1.5}\left(1 + 1.5 + \dfrac{1.5^2}{2}\right) \cr &\quad = \text{e}^{-1.5}(1 + 1.5 + 1.125) \cr &\quad = \text{e}^{-1.5}(3.625) \cr &\quad = 0.8088 \end{aligned}

(b) Sample of $6$ Tiles:

Let $Y$ denote the number of tiles out of $6$ that contain at most $2$ blemishes.

Since the tiles are independent, $Y$ follows a binomial distribution:\begin{aligned} Y \sim \text{B}(6, 0.8088) \end{aligned}Calculating the probability that exactly $4$ tiles meet this criterion:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(Y = 4) &= \dbinom{6}{4}(0.8088)^4 \cr &\qquad \times (0.1912)^2 \cr &= 15(0.42788) \cr &\qquad \times (0.03656) \cr &= 0.2346 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: Remember to include the binomial coefficient $\dbinom{6}{4} = 15$. Multiplying only the powers gives the probability of a single ordered sequence.
Ensure you scale the rate by the area of the tile: multiplying $0.6$ by $2.5$ gives $\lambda = 1.5$. Using $\lambda = 0.6$ evaluates the probability for only $1\text{ m}^2$.
Check the power of failure in the binomial formula. For $n = 6$ and $y = 4$, the power of $(1 - p)$ must be $6 - 4 = 2$, not $4$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Two-Stage Modelling
bradley_insight.content: This is a classic exam structure: stage one uses a Poisson distribution to evaluate the probability of an outcome on a single item, and stage two feeds that probability directly into a Binomial distribution to model a sample of items.

question:
Flaws in rolls of woven silk fabric occur at a constant average rate of $1.6\text{ flaws per 10 metres}$.

(a) State two assumptions necessary for the number of flaws in a length of fabric to be modelled by a Poisson distribution.

(b) A standard roll has a length of $25\text{ metres}$. Find the probability that a randomly chosen standard roll contains:
(i) exactly $3$ flaws,
(ii) at least $2$ flaws.

(c) A tailor inspects $5$ independent $25\text{ metre}$ rolls. Find the probability that none of these $5$ rolls contains more than $4$ flaws.
steps:
(a) Modelling Assumptions:

Any two of the following conditions:

Flaws occur independently of one another.

Flaws occur at a constant average rate per unit length.

Flaws occur singly (cannot occur simultaneously at the exact same point).

(b)(i) Exactly $3$ Flaws in $25\text{ Metres}$:

Scaling the mean rate for a $25\text{ metre}$ roll:\begin{aligned} \lambda &= 1.6 \times \dfrac{25}{10} \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}Let $X$ denote the number of flaws in a $25\text{ metre}$ roll, so $X \sim \text{Po}(4)$.

Evaluating $\text{P}(X = 3)$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 3) &= \dfrac{\text{e}^{-4}(4^3)}{3!} \cr &= \dfrac{\text{e}^{-4}(64)}{6} \cr &= 0.1954 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) At Least $2$ Flaws:

Using the complement rule:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 2) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 1) \cr &= 1 - [\text{P}(X = 0)\cr & + \quad\text{P}(X = 1)] \cr &= 1 - \text{e}^{-4}(1 + 4) \cr &= 1 - 5\text{e}^{-4} \cr &= 1 - 0.09158 \cr &= 0.9084 \end{aligned}

(c) Inspection of $5$ Independent Rolls:

For a single roll, the condition of not more than $4$ flaws is $\text{P}(X \le 4)$.

From Poisson tables or calculation for $\lambda = 4$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \le 4) = 0.6288 \end{aligned}For all $5$ rolls to independently satisfy this condition:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(\text{All } 5) &= (0.6288)^5 \cr &= 0.0977 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Independent flaws and constant rate, (b)(i) $0.1954$, (ii) $0.9084$, (c) $0.0977$

pi_options.feedback: For at least 2 flaws, the complement is at most 1. Subtracting $\text{P}(X \le 2)$ removes the outcome $X = 2$ from the desired probability.
Remember to scale the rate to 25 metres: $1.6 \times 2.5 = 4$. Using $\lambda = 1.6$ evaluates the probability for only 10 metres of fabric.

pi_options.ans: (a) Fixed number of trials and two outcomes, (b)(i) $0.1954$, (ii) $0.9084$, (c) $0.0977$
pi_options.feedback: A fixed number of trials and binary outcomes are conditions for a Binomial distribution, not a Poisson model.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Rate Scaling Proportionality
bradley_insight.content: A defining property of the Poisson process is that the mean rate $\lambda$ scales strictly in direct proportion to the size of the interval (length, area, or time). Always calculate the new rate $\lambda$ before writing down probability formulas.

question:
At an environmental research station, acoustic sensors monitor nocturnal bird calls from two species:
$\bullet$ Calls from Species $A$ occur randomly at an average rate of $1.8\text{ per hour}$.
$\bullet$ Calls from Species $B$ occur randomly at an average rate of $2.2\text{ per hour}$, independently of Species $A$.

(a) State the distribution of the total number of bird calls recorded in a $2\text{ hour}$ observation window.

(b) Find the probability that exactly $7$ calls in total are recorded during a $2\text{ hour}$ window.

(c) Find the probability that more than $10$ calls in total are recorded during a $2\text{ hour}$ window.
steps:
(a) Combined Distribution:

The sum of two independent Poisson variables is also a Poisson variable whose mean rate is the sum of the individual rates.

For a $2\text{ hour}$ window:\begin{aligned} \lambda_A &= 1.8 \times 2 \cr &= 3.6 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \lambda_B &= 2.2 \times 2 \cr &= 4.4 \end{aligned}Let $X$ denote the total number of calls in $2\text{ hours}$:\begin{aligned} \lambda &= 3.6 + 4.4 \cr &= 8 \end{aligned}Hence:\begin{aligned} X \sim \text{Po}(8) \end{aligned}

(b) Probability of Exactly $7$ Calls:

Using $X \sim \text{Po}(8)$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 7) &= \dfrac{\text{e}^{-8}(8^7)}{7!} \cr &= \dfrac{\text{e}^{-8}(2097152)}{5040} \cr &= 0.1396 \end{aligned}

(c) Probability of More Than $10$ Calls:

Using the complement rule:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X > 10) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 10) \end{aligned}From cumulative Poisson tables for $\lambda = 8$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \le 10) = 0.8159 \end{aligned}Evaluating the upper tail:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X > 10) &= 1 - 0.8159 \cr &= 0.1841 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $X \sim \text{Po}(8)$, (b) $0.1396$, (c) $0.1841$

pi_options.feedback: Remember to scale the rates for a 2-hour window: multiplying the combined rate of 4.0 by 2 gives $\lambda = 8$. Using $\lambda = 4$ models only a single hour.
Because the inequality is strict, $\text{P}(X > 10)$ equals $1 - \text{P}(X \le 10)$. Subtracting $\text{P}(X \le 9)$ incorrectly includes 10 in the upper tail.
Ensure you divide $8^7$ by $7! = 5040$. A factorial slip will distort the evaluated probability.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Additivity of Poisson Variables
bradley_insight.content: If $X \sim \text{Po}(\lambda_1)$ and $Y \sim \text{Po}(\lambda_2)$ are independent, then their sum is strictly Poisson: $X + Y \sim \text{Po}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)$. This additive property holds exclusively when the processes are mutually independent.

question:
The discrete random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda$, where $\lambda > 0$.

(a) Given that$$\text{P}(X = 2) = 3\,\text{P}(X = 3)$$show that $\lambda = 1$.

(b) Using $\lambda = 1$, find $\text{P}(X \ge 1)$.

(c) Find the conditional probability $\text{P}(X = 1 \mid X \le 2)$, giving your answer in exact fractional form in terms of $\text{e}$.
steps:
(a) Showing that $\lambda = 1$:

Writing the given condition using the Poisson formula:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X = 2) = 3\,\text{P}(X = 3) \cr &\dfrac{\text{e}^{-\lambda}\lambda^2}{2!} = 3\left(\dfrac{\text{e}^{-\lambda}\lambda^3}{3!}\right) \cr &\dfrac{\lambda^2}{2} = \dfrac{3\lambda^3}{6} \cr &\dfrac{\lambda^2}{2} = \dfrac{\lambda^3}{2} \cr &\lambda^2 = \lambda^3 \end{aligned}Since $\lambda > 0$, dividing both sides by $\lambda^2$ gives:\begin{aligned} \lambda = 1 \end{aligned}

(b) Probability $\text{P}(X \ge 1)$:

Using the complement rule with $\lambda = 1$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 1) &= 1 - \text{P}(X = 0) \cr &= 1 - \text{e}^{-1} \cr &= 1 - 0.3679 \cr &= 0.6321 \end{aligned}

(c) Conditional Probability $\text{P}(X = 1 \mid X \le 2)$:

Using the definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X = 1 \mid X \le 2) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\text{P}(X = 1)}{\text{P}(X \le 2)} \end{aligned}Evaluating the individual probabilities in terms of $\text{e}$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 1) &= \dfrac{\text{e}^{-1}(1^1)}{1!} \cr &= \text{e}^{-1} \end{aligned}Evaluating the denominator:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(X \le 2) \cr &\quad = \text{e}^{-1}\left(1 + 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right) \cr &\quad = 2.5\text{e}^{-1} \end{aligned}Evaluating the ratio:\begin{aligned} \text{Ratio} &= \dfrac{\text{e}^{-1}}{2.5\text{e}^{-1}} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{2.5} \cr &= \dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\lambda = 1$, (b) $0.6321$, (c) $\dfrac{2}{5}$

pi_options.feedback: Ensure you include the zero term in the denominator. The outcome $X = 0$ contributes $1\text{e}^{-1}$, making the denominator $2.5\text{e}^{-1}$ rather than $2\text{e}^{-1}$.
The value $0.3679$ is $\text{P}(X = 0)$. To find $\text{P}(X \ge 1)$, subtract this value from 1.
Check the evaluation of the ratio: dividing $\text{e}^{-1}$ by $2.5\text{e}^{-1}$ simplifies to $\dfrac{1}{2.5} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Cancelling Powers and Factorials
bradley_insight.content: In algebraic Poisson equations, the exponential factor $\text{e}^{-\lambda}$ never equals zero and cancels immediately from both sides. Dividing consecutive powers of $\lambda$ simplifies the expression directly to a linear equation in $\lambda$.

question:
A rare genetic trait occurs in $0.4\%$ of a specific breed of sheep. A farmer has a flock of $600$ sheep.

Let $X$ denote the number of sheep in the flock that carry this genetic trait.

(a) Explain why a Poisson distribution is a suitable model to approximate the distribution of $X$.

(b) State the parameter $\lambda$ of the approximating Poisson distribution.

(c) Using the Poisson approximation, calculate the probability that:
(i) exactly $3$ sheep in the flock carry the trait,
(ii) between $2$ and $5$ sheep (inclusive) carry the trait.
steps:
(a) Justification of Poisson Approximation:

The original distribution is binomial with $n = 600$ and $p = 0.004$.

The Poisson approximation is appropriate because:

The number of trials } $n$ is large $(n > 50)$.

The probability of success $p$ is small $(p < 0.1)$.

The product $np$ is moderate $(np < 10)$.

(b) Parameter $\lambda$:

Setting the Poisson mean equal to the binomial mean:\begin{aligned} \lambda &= np \cr &= 600 \times 0.004 \cr &= 2.4 \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Exactly $3$ Sheep Carrying the Trait:

Using $X \sim \text{Po}(2.4)$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 3) &= \dfrac{\text{e}^{-2.4}(2.4^3)}{3!} \cr &= \dfrac{\text{e}^{-2.4}(13.824)}{6} \cr &= 0.2090 \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Between $2$ and $5$ Sheep (Inclusive):

Expressing the interval in terms of cumulative probabilities:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(2 \le X \le 5) \cr &\quad = \text{P}(X \le 5) \cr &\qquad - \text{P}(X \le 1) \end{aligned}Evaluating the lower cumulative term:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \le 1) &= \text{P}(X = 0) + \text{P}(X = 1) \cr &= \text{e}^{-2.4}(1 + 2.4) \cr &= 3.4\text{e}^{-2.4} \cr &= 0.3084 \end{aligned}From Poisson cumulative tables for $\lambda = 2.4$, $\text{P}(X \le 5) = 0.9643$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(2 \le X \le 5) \cr &\quad = 0.9643 - 0.3084 \cr &\quad = 0.6559 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Large $n$ and small $p$, (b) $\lambda = 2.4$, (c)(i) $0.2090$, (ii) $0.6559$

pi_options.feedback: To include $X = 2$, subtract $\text{P}(X \le 1)$. Subtracting $\text{P}(X \le 2)$ removes the outcome $X = 2$ from the probability interval.
Convert the percentage correctly: $0.4\% = 0.004$. Multiplying by 600 yields $\lambda = 2.4$, rather than 24.
Symmetry with known variance describes conditions for a Normal approximation, not a Poisson approximation to a Binomial.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: When to Use Poisson Approximation
bradley_insight.content: Remember the criteria for approximating $\text{B}(n, p)$ by $\text{Po}(\lambda)$: $n$ must be large ($n > 50$) and $p$ must be small ($p < 0.1$), giving a manageable mean $\lambda = np \le 10$. If $np$ exceeds $10$, a Normal approximation is generally preferred.

subtopic: Critical Region and Type I Error
question:
A trainee archer can historically hit the bullseye on $20\%$ of her attempts. After completing a specialised training course, she wishes to test whether her accuracy has improved. She takes a random sample of $12$ independent shots.

(a)
(i) Write down suitable null and alternative hypotheses to test whether her accuracy has improved.
(ii) State a suitable test statistic that she could use.

(b) Using a $5\%$ significance level, find the critical region for this test.

(c)
(i) State the probability of a Type I error for this test.
(ii) Explain what a Type I error means in this context.

(d) In her test sample of $12$ shots, the archer hits the bullseye on $5$ occasions. What conclusion should she reach? Justify your answer.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses and Test Statistic:

Let $p$ denote the probability that the archer hits the bullseye on any given attempt.\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.2 \cr &H_1: p > 0.2 \end{aligned}The test statistic is $X$, the number of successful bullseye hits achieved in $12$ attempts.

(b) Critical Region:

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(12, 0.2)$.

Evaluating probabilities in the upper tail for a $5\%$ test:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 5) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 4) \cr &= 1 - 0.9274 \cr &= 0.0726 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 6) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 5) \cr &= 1 - 0.9806 \cr &= 0.0194 \end{aligned}Since $0.0194 \le 0.05$ and $0.0726 > 0.05$, the critical region is $X \ge 6$.

(c) Type I Error:

(i) Probability: The probability of a Type I error equals the actual significance level:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(\text{Type I Error}) &= \text{P}(X \ge 6 \mid H_0) \cr &= 0.0194 \end{aligned}(ii) Contextual meaning: Concluding that the archer's accuracy has improved when in reality her underlying success probability has remained unchanged at $0.2$.

(d) Test Conclusion:

The observed test statistic is $x = 5$.

Since $5$ does not lie in the critical region ($5 < 6$), we fail to reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ significance level to suggest that the archer's accuracy has improved.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $H_0: p = 0.2, H_1: p > 0.2$, (ii) Number of hits in $12$, (b) $X \ge 6$, (c)(i) $0.0194$, (ii) Concluding improved when unchanged, (d) Insufficient evidence of improvement

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $H_0: p = 0.2, H_1: p > 0.2$, (ii) Number of hits in $12$, (b) $X \ge 5$, (c)(i) $0.0726$, (ii) Concluding improved when unchanged, (d) Sufficient evidence of improvement
pi_options.feedback: The critical region probability must strictly not exceed the nominal significance level ($0.05$). Because $\text{P}(X \ge 5) = 0.0726 > 0.05$, the boundary must be $X \ge 6$.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $H_0: p = 0.2, H_1: p \neq 0.2$, (ii) Number of hits in $12$, (b) $X \ge 6$, (c)(i) $0.0194$, (ii) Concluding improved when unchanged, (d) Insufficient evidence of improvement
pi_options.feedback: The question investigates whether accuracy has improved, requiring an upper one-tailed alternative hypothesis ($H_1: p > 0.2$) rather than a two-tailed test.

pi_options.ans: (a)(i) $H_0: p = 0.2, H_1: p > 0.2$, (ii) Number of hits in $12$, (b) $X \ge 6$, (c)(i) $0.0194$, (ii) Concluding unchanged when improved, (d) Insufficient evidence of improvement
pi_options.feedback: A Type I error is rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is true (concluding an improvement occurred when skill remained unchanged).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Actual vs Nominal Significance Level
bradley_insight.content: For a discrete distribution like the Binomial, you cannot usually achieve an exact $5\%$ tail. The nominal level is $5\%$, but the critical region must contain probability $\le 0.05$. The actual significance level (here $0.0194$) is the true probability of committing a Type I error.

question:
A manufacturing process historically produces defective micro-switches at a rate of $25\%$. Following the installation of new precision tooling, a production engineer claims that the proportion of defective switches has decreased. A random sample of $16$ micro-switches is selected and tested.

Let $p$ denote the probability that a randomly chosen micro-switch is defective.

(a) State the null and alternative hypotheses for this test.

(b) Using a $5\%$ significance level, determine the critical region for this test.

(c) Calculate the actual significance level (the probability of a Type I error) of the test.

(d) In the sample of $16$ switches, exactly $1$ switch is found to be defective. State the conclusion of the test in context.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

Testing for a reduction in the defect rate:\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.25 \cr &H_1: p < 0.25 \end{aligned}

(b) Critical Region:

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(16, 0.25)$.

Evaluating lower tail probabilities:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \le 1) &= \text{P}(X = 0) + \text{P}(X = 1) \cr &= 0.0100 + 0.0535 \cr &= 0.0635 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 0) &= (0.75)^{16} \cr &= 0.0100 \end{aligned}Since $0.0635 > 0.05$ and $0.0100 \le 0.05$, the critical region is $X = 0$.

(c) Actual Significance Level:

The probability of rejecting $H_0$ given that $H_0$ is true is:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X = 0 \mid H_0) = 0.0100 \end{aligned}The actual significance level is $0.0100$ (or $1.00\%$).

(d) Test Conclusion:

The observed test statistic is $x = 1$.

Since $1$ is not in the critical region ($1 > 0$), we fail to reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to support the claim that the proportion of defective micro-switches has decreased.
Final Answer: (a) $H_0: p = 0.25, H_1: p < 0.25$, (b) $X = 0$, (c) $0.0100$, (d) Insufficient evidence defect rate decreased

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.25, H_1: p < 0.25$, (b) $X \le 1$, (c) $0.0635$, (d) Sufficient evidence defect rate decreased
pi_options.feedback: Because $\text{P}(X \le 1) = 0.0635$ exceeds the $0.05$ significance threshold, the outcome $X = 1$ cannot be in the critical region.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.25, H_1: p > 0.25$, (b) $X = 0$, (c) $0.0100$, (d) Insufficient evidence defect rate decreased
pi_options.feedback: The claim is that the defect rate has decreased, requiring a lower-tail alternative hypothesis ($H_1: p < 0.25$).

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.25, H_1: p < 0.25$, (b) $X = 0$, (c) $0.0500$, (d) Insufficient evidence defect rate decreased
pi_options.feedback: The actual significance level is the exact probability of the critical region under $H_0$, which is $0.0100$, rather than the nominal $0.05$ target.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Strict Upper Limits on Tail Probabilities
bradley_insight.content: In a discrete test, never choose a critical value whose cumulative probability exceeds the nominal significance level. Even though $0.0635$ is close to $0.05$, adopting $X \le 1$ would inflate the Type I error rate beyond the agreed $5\%$ risk.

question:
A board game uses a four-sided spinner. A player suspects that the spinner is biased towards or against the colour blue, which should theoretically have a probability of $0.25$ of occurring on any spin.

To investigate this suspicion, the player spins the spinner $20$ times in independent trials.

(a) State suitable hypotheses for a two-tailed test.

(b) Using a $5\%$ level of significance ($2.5\%$ in each tail), find the critical region for this test.

(c) Calculate the probability of a Type I error for this test.

(d) The spinner lands on blue on $9$ of the $20$ spins. State the conclusion of the test in context.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

Testing for any bias (two-tailed):\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.25 \cr &H_1: p \neq 0.25 \end{aligned}

(b) Critical Region:

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(20, 0.25)$. The target significance level is $0.025$ in each tail.

Lower tail:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \le 1) &= 0.0243 \cr \text{P}(X \le 2) &= 0.0913 \end{aligned}Since $0.0243 \le 0.025$ and $0.0913 > 0.025$, the lower critical region is $X \le 1$.

Upper tail:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 9) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 8) \cr &= 1 - 0.9591 \cr &= 0.0409 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 10) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 9) \cr &= 1 - 0.9861 \cr &= 0.0139 \end{aligned}Since $0.0139 \le 0.025$ and $0.0409 > 0.025$, the upper critical region is $X \ge 10$.

The critical region is $X \le 1$ or $X \ge 10$.

(c) Probability of Type I Error:

Summing the probabilities of both rejection tails:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(\text{Type I Error}) \cr & \qquad= \text{P}(X \le 1) + \text{P}(X \ge 10) \cr &\qquad= 0.0243 + 0.0139 \cr & \qquad= 0.0382 \end{aligned}

(d) Test Conclusion:

The observed value is $x = 9$.

Since $9$ does not lie in either tail ($1 < 9 < 10$), we fail to reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to suggest that the spinner is biased.
Final Answer: (a) $H_0: p = 0.25, H_1: p \neq 0.25$, (b) $X \le 1\text{ or }X \ge 10$, (c) $0.0382$, (d) Insufficient evidence of bias

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.25, H_1: p \neq 0.25$, (b) $X \le 1\text{ or }X \ge 9$, (c) $0.0652$, (d) Sufficient evidence of bias
pi_options.feedback: Because $\text{P}(X \ge 9) = 0.0409$ exceeds the half-level target of $0.025$, the upper critical boundary must begin at $X = 10$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.25, H_1: p > 0.25$, (b) $X \le 1\text{ or }X \ge 10$, (c) $0.0382$, (d) Insufficient evidence of bias
pi_options.feedback: The player suspects bias in either direction (towards or against blue), which requires a two-tailed alternative hypothesis ($H_1: p \neq 0.25$).

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.25, H_1: p \neq 0.25$, (b) $X \le 1\text{ or }X \ge 10$, (c) $0.0500$, (d) Insufficient evidence of bias
pi_options.feedback: The actual significance level is the sum of the two tail probabilities: $0.0243 + 0.0139 = 0.0382$, rather than the nominal $0.05$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Splitting Two-Tailed Significance
bradley_insight.content: For a two-tailed test at significance level $\alpha$, evaluate each tail independently against $\alpha / 2$. The total probability of a Type I error is then the sum of the actual probabilities in the two separate tails.

question:
A digital marketing team knows that their current promotional email has a baseline click-through rate of $12\%$. They redesign the email layout and send it to a random sample of $30$ prospective subscribers to investigate whether the click-through rate has increased.

Let $X$ denote the number of subscribers in the sample who click the link.

(a) State suitable hypotheses to test the marketing team's claim.

(b) In the sample of $30$ subscribers, $7$ click the link.
(i) Calculate the $p$-value corresponding to this result.
(ii) Stating your conclusion in context, determine whether the team should adopt the new layout at the $5\%$ significance level.

(c) Explain what a Type I error would represent in this business context, and state whether a Type I error could have occurred based on your conclusion in part (b)(ii).
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

Testing for an increase in the click-through rate:\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.12 \cr &H_1: p > 0.12 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Calculation of $p$-value:

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(30, 0.12)$.

The $p$-value is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as $x = 7$:\begin{aligned} p\text{-value} &= \text{P}(X \ge 7) \cr &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 6) \end{aligned}From the cumulative binomial distribution for $n = 30$ and $p = 0.12$:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \le 6) = 0.9416 \end{aligned}Evaluating the tail probability:\begin{aligned} p\text{-value} &= 1 - 0.9416 \cr &= 0.0584 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Decision:

Comparing the $p$-value to the $0.05$ significance level:\begin{aligned} 0.0584 > 0.05 \end{aligned}Since the $p$-value is greater than $0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to show that the new layout improves the click-through rate. The team should not adopt the new layout.

(c) Type I Error Analysis:

A Type I error would occur if the team concluded that the new layout increased click-through rate when it actually had no effect.

Because the team did not reject $H_0$, a Type I error could not have occurred (only a Type II error was possible).
Final Answer: (a) $H_0: p = 0.12, H_1: p > 0.12$, (b)(i) $0.0584$, (ii) Do not adopt new layout, (c) Adopting when unchanged; could not occur

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.12, H_1: p > 0.12$, (b)(i) $0.0584$, (ii) Adopt new layout, (c) Adopting when unchanged; could have occurred
pi_options.feedback: Because the $p$-value ($0.0584$) is greater than $0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$. Since $H_0$ was not rejected, a Type I error is impossible.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.12, H_1: p > 0.12$, (b)(i) $0.0218$, (ii) Adopt new layout, (c) Adopting when unchanged; could have occurred
pi_options.feedback: Remember to evaluate $\text{P}(X \ge 7) = 1 - \text{P}(X \le 6)$. Subtracting $\text{P}(X \le 7)$ excludes the observed outcome $X = 7$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: p = 0.12, H_1: p \neq 0.12$, (b)(i) $0.0584$, (ii) Do not adopt new layout, (c) Keeping old when improved; could not occur
pi_options.feedback: The team specifically suspects an increase in click-through rate, which requires an upper one-tailed alternative hypothesis ($H_1: p > 0.12$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Which Error Could Have Occurred?
bradley_insight.content: A classic exam conceptual check asks: Which type of error could have been made? If you fail to reject $H_0$, you could only have made a Type II error (failing to detect a real change). A Type I error can only happen when $H_0$ is rejected.

subtopic: Type I and Type II Errors
question:
A clinical diagnostic kit has a known sensitivity of $p = 0.70$ (it correctly detects an antibody in $70\%$ of infected patients). A biotechnology laboratory develops an enhanced reagent and tests it on a random sample of $20$ verified patient blood samples to see if sensitivity has improved.

The test is conducted at the $5\%$ significance level.

(a) State suitable hypotheses for this test.

(b) Find the critical region for the test.

(c) Calculate the probability of a Type I error.

(d) Given that the true sensitivity of the enhanced reagent has actually increased to $p = 0.90$, calculate the probability of a Type II error for this test. Give your answer correct to four decimal places.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

Testing for an increase in sensitivity:\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.70 \cr &H_1: p > 0.70 \end{aligned}

(b) Critical Region:

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(20, 0.70)$.

Evaluating upper tail probabilities for a $5\%$ test:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 17) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 16) \cr &= 1 - 0.8929 \cr &= 0.1071 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \ge 18) &= 1 - \text{P}(X \le 17) \cr &= 1 - 0.9645 \cr &= 0.0355 \end{aligned}Since $0.0355 \le 0.05$ and $0.1071 > 0.05$, the critical region is $X \ge 18$.

(c) Probability of Type I Error:

The probability of rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is true is:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(\text{Type I Error})\cr & \qquad= \text{P}(X \ge 18 \mid p = 0.70) \cr & \qquad= 0.0355 \end{aligned}

(d) Probability of Type II Error:

A Type II error occurs when we fail to reject $H_0$ even though $H_1$ is true ($p = 0.90$).

The non-rejection region is $X \le 17$. Under the true distribution $X \sim \text{B}(20, 0.90)$:\begin{aligned} &\text{P}(\text{Type II Error})\cr & \qquad= \text{P}(X \le 17 \mid p = 0.90) \end{aligned}Let $Y = 20 - X \sim \text{B}(20, 0.10)$ denote failures:\begin{aligned} \text{P}(X \le 17) &= \text{P}(Y \ge 3) \cr &= 1 - \text{P}(Y \le 2) \cr &= 1 - 0.6769 \cr &= 0.3231 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: The value $0.6769$ is the statistical power (the probability of rejecting $H_0$ when $p = 0.90$). The Type II error probability is $1 - 0.6769 = 0.3231$.
Because $\text{P}(X \ge 17) = 0.1071 > 0.05$, adopting $X \ge 17$ exceeds the allowed significance level. The critical region must be $X \ge 18$.
The research specifically tests whether sensitivity has improved, requiring a one-tailed alternative hypothesis ($H_1: p > 0.70$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Balance Between Type I and Type II Errors
bradley_insight.content: Type I error is the probability of false alarm ($H_0$ rejected when true). Type II error is the probability of missing an effect ($H_0$ accepted when false). Notice how statistical power is strictly $$1 - \text{P}(\text{Type II Error})$$ $$= 1 - 0.3231$$ $$= 0.6769$$.

question:
A civil engineer conducts quality-control tests on concrete mixes. She investigates how the water-to-cement ratio, $x$ (measured as a percentage, $\%$), affects the $28\text{-day}$ compressive strength of the concrete, $y$ (measured in megapascals, $\text{MPa}$).

The results of her test batches are shown in the scatter diagram below.

(a) Describe the relationship between compressive strength and water-to-cement ratio shown in the diagram.

(b) The equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for these data is$$y = 86.0 - 0.95x$$(i) Interpret the gradient and the vertical intercept of the regression line in this context.
(ii) Estimate the compressive strength of concrete when the water-to-cement ratio is $18\%$. Comment on the reliability of this estimate.
steps:
(a) Description of Relationship:

The scatter diagram shows a strong negative linear correlation (as the water-to-cement ratio increases, the compressive strength decreases).

(b)(i) Interpretation of Gradient and Intercept:

Gradient ($-0.95$): For every $1\%$ increase in the water-to-cement ratio, the $28\text{-day}$ compressive strength is estimated to decrease by $0.95\text{ MPa}$.

Vertical Intercept ($86.0$): The theoretical compressive strength of concrete with a water-to-cement ratio of $0\%$ is $86.0\text{ MPa}$ (though this is physically unrealistic as concrete requires water to hydrate and set).

(b)(ii) Estimation and Reliability:

Substituting $x = 18$ into the regression equation:\begin{aligned} y &= 86.0 - 0.95(18) \cr &= 86.0 - 17.1 \cr &= 68.9\text{ MPa} \end{aligned}Reliability: This estimate is unreliable because $x = 18\%$ lies well outside the range of the experimental data ($36.5\%$ to $67.5\%$)—making this an extrapolation.
Final Answer: (a) Strong negative linear correlation, (b)(i) $-0.95\text{ MPa per }1\%$ and $86.0\text{ MPa}$ at $0\%$, (ii) $68.9\text{ MPa}$, unreliable extrapolation

pi_options.ans: (a) Strong negative linear correlation, (b)(i) $-0.95\text{ MPa per }1\%$ and $86.0\text{ MPa}$ at $0\%$, (ii) $68.9\text{ MPa}$, reliable interpolation
pi_options.feedback: Because $x = 18\%$ lies far below the lowest observed water-to-cement ratio of $36.5\%$, this prediction is an extrapolation and is statistically unreliable.

pi_options.ans: (a) Strong negative linear correlation, (b)(i) $+0.95\text{ MPa per }1\%$ and $86.0\text{ MPa}$ at $0\%$, (ii) $103.1\text{ MPa}$, unreliable extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: The gradient is negative ($-0.95$), meaning compressive strength decreases as water content increases. Adding $0.95(18)$ inverts the physical relationship.

pi_options.ans: (a) Weak positive linear correlation, (b)(i) $-0.95\text{ MPa per }1\%$ and $86.0\text{ MPa}$ at $0\%$, (ii) $68.9\text{ MPa}$, unreliable extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: The points in the scatter diagram slope downwards from top-left to bottom-right, demonstrating negative correlation rather than positive.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Interpreting Contextual Gradients
bradley_insight.content: When asked to interpret the gradient of a regression line $y = a + bx$, always state three components: the direction of change (increase or decrease), the numerical amount ($b$), and the specific contextual units for both variables ($y\text{ per unit }x$).

question:
An automotive engineer evaluates a diesel engine on a dynamometer. He measures the engine torque output, $x$ (in $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$), and the corresponding fuel flow rate, $y$ (in litres per hour, $\text{L/h}$).

The scatter diagram shows his test results along with the fitted line of best fit.

The equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is$$y = 2.5 + 0.07x$$(a) State the type of correlation shown in the diagram.

(b) Give an interpretation in context for:
(i) the gradient value of $0.07$,
(ii) the intercept value of $2.5$.

(c) Estimate the fuel flow rate when the engine torque is $210\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. Comment on the reliability of this estimate.
steps:
(a) Correlation:

The scatter diagram shows a strong positive linear correlation (as engine torque increases, fuel flow rate increases).

(b)(i) Gradient ($0.07$):

For each $1\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ increase in engine torque output, the fuel flow rate is estimated to increase by $0.07\text{ L/h}$.

(b)(ii) Intercept ($2.5$):

When the engine produces zero torque (for example, while idling), the baseline fuel flow rate is estimated to be $2.5\text{ L/h}$.

(c) Estimation and Reliability:

Substituting $x = 210$ into the regression equation:\begin{aligned} y &= 2.5 + 0.07(210) \cr &= 2.5 + 14.7 \cr &= 17.2\text{ L/h} \end{aligned}Reliability: This estimate is reliable because $x = 210\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ lies comfortably within the range of the observed test data ($110$ to $290\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$)—making this an interpolation.
Final Answer: (a) Positive linear correlation, (b)(i) $0.07\text{ L/h per N}\cdot\text{m}$, (ii) Idle rate $2.5\text{ L/h}$, (c) $17.2\text{ L/h}$, reliable interpolation

pi_options.ans: (a) Positive linear correlation, (b)(i) $0.07\text{ L/h per N}\cdot\text{m}$, (ii) Idle rate $2.5\text{ L/h}$, (c) $17.2\text{ L/h}$, unreliable extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: Because $x = 210\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ lies within the range of measured torque values ($110$ to $290\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$), this is interpolation, making the estimate reliable.

pi_options.ans: (a) Positive linear correlation, (b)(i) $2.5\text{ L/h per N}\cdot\text{m}$, (ii) Idle rate $0.07\text{ L/h}$, (c) $17.2\text{ L/h}$, reliable interpolation
pi_options.feedback: The gradient is $0.07$ (the coefficient of $x$), while $2.5$ is the constant vertical intercept. Do not confuse the gradient with the intercept.

pi_options.ans: (a) Negative linear correlation, (b)(i) $0.07\text{ L/h per N}\cdot\text{m}$, (ii) Idle rate $2.5\text{ L/h}$, (c) $17.2\text{ L/h}$, reliable interpolation
pi_options.feedback: The slope of the line is positive and points rise from left to right, indicating positive correlation.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Interpolation vs Extrapolation
bradley_insight.content: Estimating within the domain of the explanatory variable is interpolation and is generally reliable. Estimating outside that domain is extrapolation and carries substantial risk because the linear trend may not continue.

question:
A battery technology company monitors the degradation of lithium-ion cells. For a sample of cells, engineers record the number of complete discharge cycles, $x$ (measured in hundreds of cycles), and the internal electrical resistance, $y$ (in milliohms, $\text{m}\Omega$).

The results are plotted in the scatter diagram below. One anomalous cell is identified and labelled as Point $Q$ at $(8.5, 18)$.

(a) Describe the correlation shown by the main cluster of cells (excluding Point $Q$).

(b) Point $Q$ was found to have a faulty internal sensor that under-reported resistance. State the effect that removing Point $Q$ from the dataset would have on:
(i) the product moment correlation coefficient $r$,
(ii) the gradient of the regression line of $y$ on $x$.

(c) The equation of the regression line calculated using all data points is$$y = 11.2 + 3.9x$$Explain why it is not appropriate to use this equation to predict the internal resistance of a cell after $1500$ discharge cycles ($x = 15$).
steps:
(a) Correlation of Main Cluster:

The main cluster exhibits a strong positive linear correlation (as discharge cycles increase, internal resistance increases).

(b)(i) Effect on Correlation Coefficient $r$:

Point $Q$ at $(8.5, 18)$ lies well below the positive linear trend established by the other cells.

Removing Point $Q$ reduces residual scatter around the line, so $r$ will increase (become closer to $+1$).

(b)(ii) Effect on Regression Gradient:

Point $Q$ is located at a high $x$-value ($8.5$) and a low $y$-value ($18$), exerting downward leverage on the right-hand end of the regression line.

Removing Point $Q$ will allow the line to tilt steeper, meaning the gradient will increase.

(c) Inappropriateness of Prediction at $x = 15$:

The observed data only extend up to approximately $x = 9.2$ ($920$ cycles).

Predicting at $x = 15$ ($1500$ cycles) is an extrapolation beyond the experimental domain. The linear degradation rate may alter or the battery may fail entirely, making the estimate unreliable.
Final Answer: (a) Strong positive linear correlation, (b)(i) Increases, (ii) Increases, (c) Unreliable due to extrapolation

pi_options.ans: (a) Strong positive linear correlation, (b)(i) Decreases, (ii) Increases, (c) Unreliable due to extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: Because Point $Q$ contradicts the strong positive linear trend, removing it reduces unexplained variation, which increases $r$ towards $+1$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Strong positive linear correlation, (b)(i) Increases, (ii) Decreases, (c) Unreliable due to extrapolation
pi_options.feedback: Point $Q$ pulls the right-hand end of the line downwards. Removing it allows the line to rotate upwards, increasing the gradient.

pi_options.ans: (a) Weak negative linear correlation, (b)(i) Increases, (ii) Increases, (c) Reliable because regression equation is known
pi_options.feedback: The main cluster clearly rises from left to right, showing positive correlation. Predictions beyond $x = 9.2$ are extrapolations regardless of the equation.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: High-Leverage Outliers
bradley_insight.content: An outlier near the extremes of the horizontal axis acts like a weight on a seesaw, exerting high leverage on both the slope and the correlation coefficient. Removing an outlier below the line at high $x$ pulls the gradient up and tightens the fit.

question:
An education researcher investigates the relationship between weekly study time, $x$ (in hours), and performance in a modular test, $y$ (scored as a percentage, $\%$).

The scatter diagram shows the data for $10$ students. The line of best fit of $y$ on $x$ is plotted, with vertical dashed lines indicating the residual deviations for three selected students.

The equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is$$y = 26 + 2x$$(a) Explain why the method of least squares minimizes the sum of squares of the vertical deviations rather than the horizontal deviations.

(b) A student achieves a score of $80\%$ in the test. Explain why it is statistically inappropriate to rearrange the equation $y = 26 + 2x$ to estimate this student's weekly study time.

(c) Calculate the residual for the student who studied for $12\text{ hours}$ and scored $58\%$.
steps:
(a) Vertical Deviations in Least Squares:

In the regression model of $y$ on $x$, $y$ is the dependent (response) variable and $x$ is the independent (explanatory) variable.

The model assumes that values of $x$ are known or measured with minimal error, while random variation occurs in $y$. Therefore, the line is chosen to minimize the sum of squared vertical errors in the predicted response $y$.

(b) Inappropriateness of Rearranging the Equation:

The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is calculated specifically to minimize vertical errors for predicting $y$ from $x$.

Rearranging this equation does not minimize horizontal errors. To predict $x$ given $y$, a separate regression line of $x$ on $y$ must be calculated.

(c) Calculating the Residual:

For $x = 12\text{ hours}$, the predicted test score $\hat{y}$ is:\begin{aligned} \hat{y} &= 26 + 2(12) \cr &= 26 + 24 \cr &= 50 \end{aligned}The residual is the actual value minus the predicted value:\begin{aligned} \text{Residual} &= y - \hat{y} \cr &= 58 - 50 \cr &= +8 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $y$ is response variable containing error, (b) Requires regression of $x$ on $y$, (c) $+8$

pi_options.ans: (a) $x$ is response variable containing error, (b) Requires regression of $x$ on $y$, (c) $+8$
pi_options.feedback: The response variable plotted on the vertical axis is $y$ (the test score), not $x$. Least squares minimizes vertical errors in the response variable.

pi_options.ans: (a) $y$ is response variable containing error, (b) Valid to rearrange the equation, (c) $+8$
pi_options.feedback: Rearranging the regression line of $y$ on $x$ to predict $x$ produces biased estimates because it minimizes vertical deviations rather than horizontal deviations.

pi_options.ans: (a) $y$ is response variable containing error, (b) Requires regression of $x$ on $y$, (c) $-8$
pi_options.feedback: Residual is defined as $\text{Actual } y - \text{Predicted } \hat{y}$. Because $58 - 50 = +8$, the point lies above the line, giving a positive residual.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Residual Sign Convention
bradley_insight.content: Always remember the order: $\text{Residual} = y - \hat{y}$ (Actual minus Predicted). A point lying above the regression line has a positive residual, while a point below the line has a negative residual.

question:
A transport safety agency records the stopping distance, $y$ (in metres), of a test vehicle travelling at various speeds, $x$ (in miles per hour, $\text{mph}$).

A technician fits a linear regression line to the data:$$y = 1.74x - 26.3$$The data points and the fitted regression line are displayed in the scatter diagram below.

(a) With reference to the distribution of points relative to the line in the diagram, explain why a linear regression model is not suitable for these data.

(b) Using the technician's equation, estimate the stopping distance of a vehicle travelling at $15\text{ mph}$. Explain what this result demonstrates regarding the validity of the linear model.

(c) Based on physical principles (such as kinetic energy), suggest a more appropriate mathematical relationship between stopping distance $y$ and vehicle speed $x$.
steps:
(a) Unsuitability of Linear Model:

The points form a distinct curved (non-linear) pattern rather than a straight line.

The data points lie above the line at both ends and below the line in the middle, indicating a systematic pattern in the residuals that violates the assumption of linearity.

(b) Estimate at $15\text{ mph}$ and Model Validity:

Substituting $x = 15$ into the linear equation:\begin{aligned} y &= 1.74(15) - 26.3 \cr &= 26.1 - 26.3 \cr &= -0.2\text{ m} \end{aligned}A negative stopping distance is physically impossible, which demonstrates that the linear model breaks down and is invalid at low speeds.

(c) Appropriate Physical Model:

Because kinetic energy is proportional to the square of velocity, the work required to stop a vehicle scales with $v^2$.

A quadratic model of the form $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ (or $y = kx^2$) would be much more appropriate.
Final Answer: (a) Distinct curved pattern in residuals, (b) $-0.2\text{ m}$, physically impossible distance, (c) Quadratic model $y = ax^2 + bx + c$

pi_options.ans: (a) Points are randomly scattered around line, (b) $-0.2\text{ m}$, physically impossible distance, (c) Quadratic model $y = ax^2 + bx + c$
pi_options.feedback: The points are not randomly scattered; they follow a clear upward curve, which demonstrates that the linear assumption is incorrect.

pi_options.ans: (a) Distinct curved pattern in residuals, (b) $+0.2\text{ m}$, acceptable prediction, (c) Quadratic model $y = ax^2 + bx + c$
pi_options.feedback: Evaluating: \begin{aligned}1.74(15) - 26.3 &= 26.1 - 26.3\cr & = -0.2\text{ m}\end{aligned} A negative stopping distance is impossible in reality.

pi_options.ans: (a) Distinct curved pattern in residuals, (b) $-0.2\text{ m}$, physically impossible distance, (c) Exponential model $y = a\text{e}^{bx}$
pi_options.feedback: Stopping distance physically relates to kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, which indicates a quadratic relationship with velocity squared rather than exponential growth.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Residual Patterns Indicate Model Form
bradley_insight.content: A good linear fit produces residuals that are randomly scattered above and below the line. If residuals show a U-shape (positive at ends, negative in the middle), it is definitive visual proof that the underlying relationship is non-linear.

topic: Measures of Location, Spread, and Box Plots
question:
Rowan investigates the hourly fees charged by private driving instructors in County A. He collects a random sample of hourly rates, in pounds (£), and computes the following summary statistics:$$\begin{aligned} &\text{Min.} &&: 22.0 \cr &\text{1st Qu.} &&: 28.0 \cr &\text{Median} &&: 31.0 \cr &\text{Mean} &&: 33.5 \cr &\text{3rd Qu.} &&: 36.0 \cr &\text{Max.} &&: 58.0 \end{aligned}$$(a) Showing all calculations, comment on any outliers for the hourly fees in Rowan's sample.

(b) Describe the skewness of the data and explain what it means in this context.

Cerys also investigates driving instructor fees. She collects an independent random sample of hourly fees in County B and produces the box plot shown in the diagram below.

(c)
(i) What will happen to the mean of Cerys's sample if the outlier is removed?
(ii) What will happen to the median of Cerys's sample if the outlier is removed?

(d) Compare and contrast the distributions of driving instructor hourly fees for Cerys's sample and Rowan's sample.
steps:
(a) Outlier Calculations for Rowan's Sample:

Finding the interquartile range:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= Q_3 - Q_1 \cr &= 36.0 - 28.0 \cr &= 8.0 \end{aligned}Calculating the outlier boundaries:\begin{aligned} \text{Lower} &= Q_1 - 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &= 28.0 - 1.5(8.0) \cr &= 28.0 - 12.0 \cr &= 16.0 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \text{Upper} &= Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &= 36.0 + 1.5(8.0) \cr &= 36.0 + 12.0 \cr &= 48.0 \end{aligned}Since the minimum fee ($£22.0$) is greater than $16.0$, there are no lower outliers.

Since the maximum fee ($£58.0$) is greater than $48.0$, there is at least one outlier at the upper end.

(b) Skewness of Rowan's Data:

The mean ($£33.5$) is greater than the median ($£31.0$), and $Q_3 - Q_2 = 5.0$ is greater than $Q_2 - Q_1 = 3.0$.

This indicates positive skewness.

In context, this means that most driving instructors charge between $£28$ and $£36$, while a small number of instructors charge substantially higher fees.

(c) Effect of Removing Outlier in Cerys's Sample:

(i) Mean: Removing the extreme high outlier at $£55$ will cause the mean to decrease.

(ii) Median: Because the median is resistant to extreme values, it will stay the same (or change very little).

(d) Comparing Distributions:

Location: The median fee in County A ($£31.0$) is higher than in County B ($£29.0$).

Spread: The interquartile range in County B ($34 - 25 = 9.0$) is slightly higher than in County A ($8.0$), indicating slightly more varied fees in County B.

Shape: Both distributions exhibit positive skewness with high outliers.
Final Answer: (a) Outlier at $£58.0$, (b) Positive skew; majority lower with few high fees, (c)(i) Decreases, (ii) Little to no change, (d) County A has higher median, County B has higher IQR

pi_options.ans: (a) Outlier at $£58.0$, (b) Positive skew; majority lower with few high fees, (c)(i) Increases, (ii) Decreases, (d) County A has higher median, County B has higher IQR
pi_options.feedback: Removing an extremely high outlier removes a large value from the total sum, which causes the mean to decrease, while the median remains resistant.

pi_options.ans: (a) No outliers present, (b) Positive skew; majority lower with few high fees, (c)(i) Decreases, (ii) Little to no change, (d) County A has higher median, County B has higher IQR
pi_options.feedback: The upper boundary is $Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) = 36.0 + 12.0 = 48.0$. Because the maximum value of $58.0$ exceeds $48.0$, it is an outlier.

pi_options.ans: (a) Outlier at $£58.0$, (b) Negative skew; majority higher with few low fees, (c)(i) Decreases, (ii) Little to no change, (d) County A has higher median, County B has higher IQR
pi_options.feedback: Because the mean ($33.5$) is greater than the median ($31.0$), the tail extends towards higher values, which indicates positive skewness.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Comparing Summary Distributions
bradley_insight.content: When comparing two distributions from summary data, always provide context and state three specific elements: a measure of central tendency (median), a measure of dispersion (IQR), and the presence of skewness or outliers.

topic: Measures of Location, Spread, and Box Plots
question:
A logistics manager monitors the delivery times (in minutes) for urgent packages dispatched by two rival courier firms, Courier A and Courier B. Random samples of delivery times are displayed in the parallel box plots below.

(a) Using the summary values from the box plot for Courier B, show that the delivery time of $58\text{ minutes}$ is an outlier according to the standard $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule.

(b) A medical laboratory requires predictable, consistent delivery times for blood samples. Advise the laboratory on which courier to select, justifying your choice using appropriate statistical measures of location and spread.

(c) Describe the skewness of the delivery times for Courier A, justifying your answer using the quartiles.
steps:
(a) Outlier Calculation for Courier B:

From the box plot for Courier B, $Q_1 = 28$ and $Q_3 = 38$:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= 38 - 28 \cr &= 10 \end{aligned}Calculating the upper outlier boundary:\begin{aligned} \text{Upper} &= Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &= 38 + 1.5(10) \cr &= 38 + 15 \cr &= 53 \end{aligned}Since $58 > 53$, the delivery time of $58\text{ minutes}$ is an outlier.

(b) Courier Recommendation:

The laboratory should choose Courier A.

Although Courier A has a slightly higher median ($30\text{ minutes}$ compared to $28\text{ minutes}$ for Courier B), Courier A has a smaller interquartile range ($34 - 26 = 8\text{ minutes}$ compared to $10\text{ minutes}$ for Courier B) and no extreme outliers, indicating more consistent and predictable delivery times.

(c) Skewness of Courier A:

Evaluating quartile distances:\begin{aligned} Q_2 - Q_1 &= 30 - 26 \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} Q_3 - Q_2 &= 34 - 30 \cr &= 4 \end{aligned}Since $Q_3 - Q_2 = Q_2 - Q_1 = 4$, the distribution of delivery times for Courier A is approximately symmetrical.
Final Answer: (a) $58 > 53$, (b) Courier A due to lower IQR and no outliers, (c) Symmetrical as $Q_3 - Q_2 = Q_2 - Q_1 = 4$

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Consistency Means Smaller Spread
bradley_insight.content: In examination questions, the words 'consistent', 'reliable', or 'predictable' always direct you to compare a measure of spread (the IQR or standard deviation). The distribution with the smaller spread is the more consistent one.

topic: Measures of Location, Spread, and Box Plots
question:
The box plot in the diagram displays the daily wait times (in minutes) for a random sample of patients attending an urgent care walk-in clinic.

(a) Showing your working, calculate the lower and upper outlier boundaries for these wait times.

(b) Confirm that both the recorded values of $4\text{ minutes}$ and $68\text{ minutes}$ are outliers.

(c) A late audit record reveals another patient who waited $12\text{ minutes}$. State, with a clear reason, whether this wait time would be classified as an outlier.

(d) Explain why the median and interquartile range are more appropriate measures for summarising these data than the mean and standard deviation.
steps:
(a) Outlier Boundaries:

From the box plot, $Q_1 = 24$ and $Q_3 = 36$:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= 36 - 24 \cr &= 12 \end{aligned}Calculating the lower boundary:\begin{aligned} \text{Lower} &= Q_1 - 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &= 24 - 1.5(12) \cr &= 24 - 18 \cr &= 6 \end{aligned}Calculating the upper boundary:\begin{aligned} \text{Upper} &= Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &= 36 + 1.5(12) \cr &= 36 + 18 \cr &= 54 \end{aligned}

(b) Confirming Outliers:

Comparing the recorded wait times against the boundaries:\begin{aligned} 4 &< 6 \cr 68 &> 54 \end{aligned}Because $4\text{ minutes}$ is below the lower boundary and $68\text{ minutes}$ is above the upper boundary, both values are outliers.

(c) Classification of $12\text{ Minutes}$:

A wait time of $12\text{ minutes}$ lies comfortably within the non-outlier interval ($6 \le 12 \le 54$). Therefore, it is not an outlier.

(d) Justification of Measures:

The median and interquartile range are more appropriate because the dataset contains extreme outliers and exhibits skewness.

The mean and standard deviation are heavily influenced by extreme values, whereas the median and $\text{IQR}$ are robust measures of location and spread.
Final Answer: (a) Lower $= 6$, Upper $= 54$, (b) Both outside boundaries, (c) Not an outlier as $6 \le 12 \le 54$, (d) Median and IQR are robust to outliers

pi_options.ans: (a) Lower $= 12$, Upper $= 48$, (b) Both outside boundaries, (c) Not an outlier as $6 \le 12 \le 54$, (d) Median and IQR are robust to outliers
pi_options.feedback: Remember to multiply the IQR by $1.5$: $1.5 \times 12 = 18$. Subtracting $12$ directly without multiplying by $1.5$ gives incorrect boundaries.

pi_options.feedback: A value is an outlier only if it falls beyond the calculated boundaries ($< 6$ or $> 54$). Since $12 \ge 6$, it is not an outlier.

pi_options.feedback: When data contain outliers or skewness, the mean and standard deviation are distorted, making the median and IQR far more representative.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Non-Symmetric Outlier Boundaries
bradley_insight.content: Notice that lower and upper boundaries are calculated relative to their respective quartiles ($Q_1 - 1.5\text{IQR}$ and $Q_3 + 1.5\text{IQR}$), not the median. Always calculate both boundaries independently.

topic: Measures of Location, Spread, and Box Plots
question:
A national examining body displays the distribution of scores achieved by candidates in a qualifying examination using both a cumulative frequency curve and a directly aligned box plot, as shown in the diagram.

(a) Using the box plot, state the median score and calculate the interquartile range.

(b) Determine whether the examination scores exhibit positive skewness, negative skewness, or are approximately symmetrical. Justify your answer using quartile differences.

(c) A teacher claims that at least $75\%$ of candidates scored $38$ marks or more. Explain, with reference to the box plot, whether this claim is correct.

(d) A certificate of distinction is awarded to the top $10\%$ of candidates. Use the cumulative frequency curve to estimate the minimum score required to achieve a distinction.
steps:
(a) Median and Interquartile Range:

From the box plot and aligned cumulative frequency curve:\begin{aligned} \text{Median} = 50 \end{aligned}Finding the interquartile range with $Q_1 = 38$ and $Q_3 = 64$:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= Q_3 - Q_1 \cr &= 64 - 38 \cr &= 26 \end{aligned}

(b) Skewness:

Comparing quartile differences:\begin{aligned} Q_2 - Q_1 &= 50 - 38 \cr &= 12 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} Q_3 - Q_2 &= 64 - 50 \cr &= 14 \end{aligned}Since $Q_3 - Q_2 > Q_2 - Q_1$ ($14 > 12$), the distribution exhibits slight positive skewness.

(c) Evaluating the Teacher's Claim:

The claim is correct.

The lower quartile $Q_1 = 38$ marks represents the $25\text{th}$ percentile, meaning exactly $75\%$ of candidates achieved a score greater than or equal to $38$.

(d) Distinction Score (Top $10\%$):

The top $10\%$ corresponds to the $90\text{th}$ percentile ($90\%$ cumulative frequency).

Reading horizontally from $90\%$ on the cumulative frequency curve and down to the horizontal axis gives an estimated minimum score of approximately $73$ marks.
Final Answer: (a) Median $= 50, \text{IQR} = 26$, (b) Slight positive skew as $14 > 12$, (c) Correct as $Q_1 = 38$ leaves $75\%$ above, (d) $73$

pi_options.ans: (a) Median $= 50, \text{IQR} = 26$, (b) Symmetrical as $14 \approx 12$, (c) Correct as $Q_1 = 38$ leaves $75\%$ above, (d) $73$
pi_options.feedback: Because $Q_3 - Q_2 = 14$ is strictly greater than $Q_2 - Q_1 = 12$, the upper half of the interquartile box is more stretched, indicating positive skewness.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dual Representation Alignment
bradley_insight.content: Notice how the key landmarks on a box plot align with the cumulative frequency curve: $Q_1$ is at $25\%$, the median is at $50\%$, and $Q_3$ is at $75\%$. Projecting vertically between the two plots provides immediate cross-verification.

topic: Measures of Location, Spread, and Box Plots
question:
The weekly overtime hours worked by a random sample of factory technicians are summarised in the box plot shown in the diagram.

(a) Show that the value of $35\text{ hours}$ is an outlier.

(b) Factory management introduces a revised overtime pay formula. Each technician receives weekly overtime pay, $P$ (in pounds, £), calculated from their overtime hours, $x$, according to the linear formula:$$P = 25x + 50$$(i) Find the median weekly overtime pay.
(ii) Calculate the interquartile range of weekly overtime pay.

(c) State, with mathematical justification, whether the technician who worked $35\text{ hours}$ of overtime will remain an outlier in the distribution of overtime pay $P$.
steps:
(a) Outlier Verification:

From the box plot, $Q_1 = 4$ and $Q_3 = 16$:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= 16 - 4 \cr &= 12 \end{aligned}Calculating the upper outlier boundary:\begin{aligned} \text{Upper} &= Q_3 + 1.5(\text{IQR}) \cr &= 16 + 1.5(12) \cr &= 16 + 18 \cr &= 34 \end{aligned}Since $35 > 34$, the value of $35\text{ hours}$ is an outlier.

(b)(i) Median Overtime Pay:

The median of the original hours is $x = 10$. Applying the linear transformation $P = 25x + 50$:\begin{aligned} \text{Median}(P) &= 25(10) + 50 \cr &= 250 + 50 \cr &= £300 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Interquartile Range of Pay:

The constant addition ($+50$) shifts the position but does not affect spread. The interquartile range scales solely by $25$:\begin{aligned} \text{IQR}(P) &= 25 \times \text{IQR}(x) \cr &= 25 \times 12 \cr &= £300 \end{aligned}

(c) Outlier Status Under Linear Transformation:

Yes, it remains an outlier.

Evaluating the pay for $35\text{ hours}$:\begin{aligned} P(35) &= 25(35) + 50 \cr &= 875 + 50 \cr &= £925 \end{aligned}Evaluating the transformed upper boundary:\begin{aligned} \text{Upper}(P) &= 25(34) + 50 \cr &= 850 + 50 \cr &= £900 \end{aligned}Since $£925 > £900$, the value remains an outlier.

In general, linear coding ($ax + b$ with $a > 0$) scales all data points and boundaries by the exact same factors, preserving outlier classification.
Final Answer: (a) $35 > 34$, (b)(i) $£300$, (ii) $£300$, (c) Yes, linear coding preserves outlier boundaries

pi_options.ans: (a) $35 > 34$, (b)(i) $£300$, (ii) $£350$, (c) Yes, linear coding preserves outlier boundaries
pi_options.feedback: Adding a constant shifts the distribution without affecting spread. The IQR is simply $25 \times 12 = £300$. Do not add 50 to the IQR.

pi_options.ans: (a) $35 \le 34$, (b)(i) $£300$, (ii) $£300$, (c) Yes, linear coding preserves outlier boundaries
pi_options.feedback: Calculating the boundary gives $16 + 1.5(12) = 34$. Because $35$ exceeds $34$, it is an outlier.

pi_options.ans: (a) $35 > 34$, (b)(i) $£300$, (ii) $£300$, (c) No, adding base pay eliminates outlier status
pi_options.feedback: Linear coding scales and shifts every observation and boundary identically, so relative outlier status is strictly preserved.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Invariance Under Linear Coding
bradley_insight.content: For any linear coding $y = ax + b$ with $a > 0$, the interquartile range scales by $a$, while the constant $b$ cancels out: $\text{IQR}(y) = a\text{IQR}(x)$. Because both the data points and the boundary thresholds shift and scale together, outlier status is invariant under linear transformations.

question:
A logistics firm tenders for two separate transport contracts: Contract $R$ (regional) and Contract $N$ (national). The managing director estimates that the probability of winning Contract $R$ is $0.60$, the probability of winning Contract $N$ is $0.45$, and the probability of winning both contracts is $0.25$.

(a) Show that the probability that the firm wins neither contract is $0.20$.

(b) Find the probability that the firm wins exactly one contract.

(c) Given that the firm does not win Contract $R$, find the probability that it wins Contract $N$.
steps:
(a) Probability of neither contract:

We first find the probability of winning at least one contract using the addition rule of probability:\begin{aligned} &P(R \cup N) \cr &\quad = P(R) + P(N) - P(R \cap N) \cr &\quad = 0.60 + 0.45 - 0.25 \cr &\quad = 0.80 \end{aligned}The probability of winning neither contract is the complement of the union:\begin{aligned} P(R' \cap N') &= 1 - P(R \cup N) \cr &= 1 - 0.80 \cr &= 0.20 \end{aligned}

(b) Probability of exactly one contract:

Winning exactly one contract corresponds to the union minus the intersection:\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly one}) &= P(R \cup N) \cr & \quad - P(R \cap N) \cr &= 0.80 - 0.25 \cr &= 0.55 \end{aligned}Alternatively, we can sum the two mutually exclusive exclusive regions directly:\begin{aligned} &P(R \cap N') + P(R' \cap N) \cr &\quad = (0.60 - 0.25) + (0.45 - 0.25) \cr &\quad = 0.35 + 0.20 \cr &\quad = 0.55 \end{aligned}

(c) Conditional probability:

Using the definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} P(N \mid R') &= \dfrac{P(N \cap R')}{P(R')} \end{aligned}We determine the numerator and denominator separately:\begin{aligned} P(N \cap R') &= P(N) - P(R \cap N) \cr &= 0.45 - 0.25 \cr &= 0.20 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} P(R') &= 1 - P(R) \cr &= 1 - 0.60 \cr &= 0.40 \end{aligned}Substituting these values into the ratio gives:\begin{aligned} P(N \mid R') &= \dfrac{0.20}{0.40} \cr &= 0.5 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you evaluated the unconditioned probability $P(N) = 0.45$ rather than the conditional probability $P(N \mid R') = \dfrac{P(N \cap R')}{P(R')}$. The given condition that Contract $R$ is not won restricts the sample space to $R'$, which has probability $0.40$.

In part (b), $0.80$ is the probability of winning at least one contract, $P(R \cup N)$, which includes winning both contracts. To find the probability of winning exactly one contract, you must subtract the intersection $P(R \cap N) = 0.25$.
In part (c), you evaluated the intersection $P(R \cap N)$ or divided by an incorrect total instead of dividing $P(N \cap R') = 0.20$ by $P(R') = 0.40$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Restricted Sample Space
bradley_insight.content: When calculating a conditional probability such as $P(N \mid R')$, students often mistakenly divide by the entire sample space or divide by $P(N)$ rather than $P(R')$. Always identify the given condition first—here, the firm has failed to win Contract $R$, which immediately shrinks the total possible outcomes to $R'$ with total probability $1 - 0.60 = 0.40$.

question:
A quality-assurance system inspects precision components for two types of defect: electrical defect ($E$) and mechanical defect ($M$). For a randomly selected component from Batch 1, $P(E) = 0.15$ and $P(M) = 0.20$.

(a) Given that for Batch 1 the two defects occur independently, find the probability that a randomly selected component:
 (i) has both defects,
 (ii) has at least one defect,
 (iii) has an electrical defect, given that it has at least one defect.

(b) For a second batch, Batch 2, the probability of an electrical defect remains $0.15$, but the defects are no longer independent. It is found that $P(E \cup M) = 0.28$ and $P(E \mid M) = 0.35$. Find $P(M)$ for Batch 2.
steps:
(a)(i) Probability of both defects (independent):

Since defects $E$ and $M$ occur independently in Batch 1, the multiplication rule applies directly:\begin{aligned} P(E \cap M) &= P(E) \times P(M) \cr &= 0.15 \times 0.20 \cr &= 0.03 \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Probability of at least one defect:

Applying the addition rule of probability:\begin{aligned} P(E \cup M) &= P(E) + P(M)\cr & \quad - P(E \cap M) \cr &= 0.15 + 0.20 - 0.03 \cr &= 0.32 \end{aligned}

(a)(iii) Conditional probability:

Applying the conditional probability definition:\begin{aligned} P(E \mid E \cup M) &= \dfrac{P(E \cap (E \cup M))}{P(E \cup M)} \end{aligned}Because $E \subseteq (E \cup M)$, the intersection simplifies to $E$:\begin{aligned} P(E \mid E \cup M) &= \dfrac{P(E)}{P(E \cup M)} \cr &= \dfrac{0.15}{0.32} \cr &= \dfrac{15}{32} \quad (0.46875) \end{aligned}

(b) Finding $P(M)$ for Batch 2:

From the definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} P(E \cap M) &= P(E \mid M) P(M) \cr &= 0.35 P(M) \end{aligned}Substituting into the general addition rule:\begin{aligned} &P(E \cup M) = P(E) + P(M) \cr & \qquad \qquad \quad- P(E \cap M) \cr &0.28 = 0.15 + P(M) - 0.35 P(M) \cr &0.28 - 0.15 = 0.65 P(M) \cr &0.13 = 0.65 P(M) \cr &P(M) = \dfrac{0.13}{0.65} \cr &P(M) = 0.2 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (a)(ii), you computed $P(E) + P(M) = 0.15 + 0.20 = 0.35$ without subtracting the intersection $P(E \cap M) = 0.03$. The events are independent, not mutually exclusive.
In part (a)(iii), you stated $P(E) = 0.15$ without conditioning on the restricted sample space $E \cup M$. The denominator must be $P(E \cup M) = 0.32$.
In part (b), you substituted $0.35$ directly for $P(E \cap M)$ instead of $0.35 P(M)$. Remember that $P(E \cap M) = P(E \mid M) P(M)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Subsets in Conditional Probability
bradley_insight.content: Notice in part (a)(iii) that event $E$ is entirely contained within the union $E \cup M$. Therefore, $E \cap (E \cup M) = E$. Whenever event $A$ is a subset of event $B$, the conditional probability simplifies neatly to $P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A)}{P(B)}$.

question:
A survey of $120$ college students investigated membership in three enrichment societies: Chess ($C$), Debate ($D$), and Robotics ($R$). The findings were as follows:
• $15$ students belong to none of the three societies.
• $65$ students belong to Chess.
• $55$ students belong to Debate.
• $48$ students belong to Robotics.
• $28$ students belong to both Chess and Debate.
• $22$ students belong to both Debate and Robotics.
• $25$ students belong to both Chess and Robotics.
• $x$ students belong to all three societies.

A student is chosen at random from the survey.

(a) Show that $x = 12$.

(b) Find the probability that the student belongs to:
 (i) exactly two societies,
 (ii) Robotics, given that the student does not belong to Chess.

(c) Determine, with mathematical justification, whether the events "belongs to Chess" and "belongs to Robotics" are statistically independent.
steps:
(a) Determining $x$:

The number of students belonging to at least one society is:\begin{aligned} n(C \cup D \cup R) &= 120 - 15 \cr &= 105 \end{aligned}Applying the principle of inclusion-exclusion for three sets:\begin{aligned} &n(C \cup D \cup R) \cr &= n(C) + n(D) + n(R) \cr &\quad - n(C \cap D) - n(D \cap R)\cr &\quad - n(C \cap R) + n(C \cap D \cap R) \end{aligned}Substituting the known counts:\begin{aligned} &105 = 65 + 55 + 48 \cr &\qquad - (28 + 22 + 25) + x \cr &105 = 168 - 75 + x \cr &105 = 93 + x \cr &x = 105 - 93 \cr &x = 12 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Probability of exactly two societies:

We determine the counts belonging to exactly two societies by removing the central intersection $x = 12$ from each two-set overlap:\begin{aligned} &n(C \cap D \text{ only}) = 28 - 12 = 16 \cr &n(D \cap R \text{ only}) = 22 - 12 = 10 \cr &n(C \cap R \text{ only}) = 25 - 12 = 13 \end{aligned}Summing these counts:\begin{aligned} n(\text{exactly two}) &= 16 + 10 + 13 \cr &= 39 \end{aligned}Thus the probability is:\begin{aligned} P(\text{exactly two}) &= \dfrac{39}{120} \cr &= \dfrac{13}{40} \quad (0.325) \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Conditional probability $P(R \mid C')$:

The total number of students not belonging to Chess is:\begin{aligned} n(C') &= 120 - 65 \cr &= 55 \end{aligned}The number of students in Robotics who do not belong to Chess is:\begin{aligned} n(R \cap C') &= n(R) - n(C \cap R) \cr &= 48 - 25 \cr &= 23 \end{aligned}Hence:\begin{aligned} P(R \mid C') &= \dfrac{n(R \cap C')}{n(C')} \cr &= \dfrac{23}{55} \end{aligned}

(c) Testing statistical independence of $C$ and $R$:

For $C$ and $R$ to be independent, we require $P(C \cap R) = P(C) \times P(R)$.

Evaluating each probability:\begin{aligned} P(C \cap R) &= \dfrac{25}{120} = \dfrac{5}{24} \approx 0.2083 \cr P(C) &= \dfrac{65}{120} = \dfrac{13}{24} \cr P(R) &= \dfrac{48}{120} = \dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}Evaluating the product:\begin{aligned} P(C) \times P(R) &= \dfrac{13}{24} \times \dfrac{2}{5} \cr &= \dfrac{26}{120}\cr & = \dfrac{13}{60}\cr & \approx 0.2167 \end{aligned}Since $\dfrac{5}{24} \neq \dfrac{13}{60}$, the events are not independent.
Final Answer: (a) $x = 12$, (b)(i) $\dfrac{13}{40}$, (ii) $\dfrac{23}{55}$, (c) Not independent as $P(C \cap R) \neq P(C) \times P(R)$

pi_options.ans: (a) $x = 12$, (b)(i) $\dfrac{5}{8}$, (ii) $\dfrac{23}{55}$, (c) Not independent as $P(C \cap R) \neq P(C) \times P(R)$
pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(i), you summed the full overlaps $28 + 22 + 25 = 75$ and divided by $120$. This includes the $12$ students belonging to all three societies three times. You must subtract $12$ from each overlap before adding.

pi_options.ans: (a) $x = 12$, (b)(i) $\dfrac{13}{40}$, (ii) $\dfrac{23}{120}$, (c) Not independent as $P(C \cap R) \neq P(C) \times P(R)$
pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(ii), you computed the joint probability $P(R \cap C') = \dfrac{23}{120}$ over all $120$ students instead of conditioning on $n(C') = 55$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $x = 12$, (b)(i) $\dfrac{13}{40}$, (ii) $\dfrac{23}{55}$, (c) Independent as both probabilities are close to $0.21$
pi_options.feedback: In part (c), statistical independence requires exact algebraic equality: $P(C \cap R) = P(C) \times P(R)$. Since $\dfrac{25}{120} \neq \dfrac{26}{120}$, they cannot be claimed as independent.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Pairwise Overlaps in 3-Set Venns
bradley_insight.content: A frequent mistake in three-set Venn problems is assuming that 'belongs to Chess and Debate' means only those two. In examination questions, stated intersections include the central three-way region $x$ unless the word 'only' is explicitly included.

question:
An aerospace manufacturing facility sources microchips from three suppliers: $A$, $B$, and $C$.
• Supplier $A$ supplies $50\%$ of the microchips, and $2\%$ of these are defective.
• Supplier $B$ supplies $30\%$ of the microchips, and $3\%$ of these are defective.
• Supplier $C$ supplies $20\%$ of the microchips, and $5\%$ of these are defective.

(a) A microchip is selected at random from the total supply.
 (i) Show that the probability that the microchip is defective is $0.029$.
 (ii) Given that the microchip is defective, find the probability that it was supplied by Supplier $B$. Give your answer as an exact fraction in simplest form.

(b) Two microchips are chosen at random from the total supply, independently of each other. Find the probability that exactly one of the two microchips is defective and that this defective microchip came from Supplier $A$.
steps:
(a)(i) Overall probability of a defective chip:

By the law of total probability:\begin{aligned} &P(D) \cr &= P(A)P(D \mid A) + P(B)P(D \mid B) \cr &\quad + P(C)P(D \mid C) \end{aligned}Substituting the given values:\begin{aligned} P(D) &= (0.50)(0.02) + (0.30)(0.03) \cr &\quad + (0.20)(0.05) \cr &= 0.010 + 0.009 + 0.010 \cr &= 0.029 \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Conditional probability of Supplier $B$:

Applying Bayes' theorem:\begin{aligned} P(B \mid D) &= \dfrac{P(B \cap D)}{P(D)} \cr &= \dfrac{P(B)P(D \mid B)}{P(D)} \cr &= \dfrac{0.30 \times 0.03}{0.029} \cr &= \dfrac{0.009}{0.029} \cr &= \dfrac{9}{29} \end{aligned}

(b) Multi-stage probability with two chips:

Let $D_A$ denote the event that a chip is defective and from Supplier $A$:\begin{aligned} P(D_A) &= P(A \cap D) \cr &= 0.50 \times 0.02 \cr &= 0.010 \end{aligned}Let $D'$ denote the event that a chip is not defective (from any supplier):\begin{aligned} P(D') &= 1 - P(D) \cr &= 1 - 0.029 \cr &= 0.971 \end{aligned}The event that exactly one chip is defective and comes from Supplier $A$ can happen in two mutually exclusive orders: $(D_A, D')$ or $(D', D_A)$:\begin{aligned} P &= 2 \times P(D_A) \times P(D') \cr &= 2 \times 0.010 \times 0.971 \cr &= 0.01942 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you evaluated only a single sequence $(D_A, D')$. Because either the first chip or the second chip could be the defective one from Supplier $A$, you must multiply by $2$ to account for both orders.

In part (a)(ii), you stated $P(D \mid B) = 0.03$ instead of reversing the condition to find $P(B \mid D)$. The condition restricts the sample space to defective chips, giving denominator $P(D) = 0.029$.
In part (b), you paired the defective chip from $A$ with a non-defective chip restricted to Supplier $A$ ($0.49$) rather than any non-defective chip across all suppliers ($0.971$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Order in Independent Pair Selections
bradley_insight.content: In multi-stage independent trials, students often calculate the probability of one specific sequence (e.g. chip 1 is defective from $A$, chip 2 is non-defective) and forget the factor of $2$. Unless the question specifies a particular draw order, always account for both permutations.

question:
Two events $A$ and $B$ are such that $P(A) = 0.60$, $P(B) = p$, and $P(A \cup B) = 0.85$.

(a) Find an expression for $P(A \cap B)$ in terms of $p$.

(b) Determine the range of possible values of $p$.

(c) Given that $A$ and $B$ are independent:
 (i) show that $p = 0.625$,
 (ii) find the value of $P(A' \mid B)$.

(d) Given instead that $P(A \mid B) = 0.50$, find the value of $p$.
steps:
(a) Expression for $P(A \cap B)$:

Applying the addition rule of probability:\begin{aligned} &P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\cr & \qquad- P(A \cap B) \cr &0.85 = 0.60 + p - P(A \cap B) \cr &P(A \cap B) = p + 0.60 - 0.85 \cr &P(A \cap B) = p - 0.25 \end{aligned}

(b) Range of possible values of $p$:

Every probability must lie between $0$ and $1$.

Since the intersection cannot be negative:\begin{aligned} P(A \cap B) \ge 0 &\implies p - 0.25 \ge 0 \cr &\implies p \ge 0.25 \end{aligned}Furthermore, since $B \subseteq (A \cup B)$:\begin{aligned} P(B) \le P(A \cup B) &\implies p \le 0.85 \end{aligned}Therefore, the allowable range for $p$ is:\begin{aligned} 0.25 \le p \le 0.85 \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Showing $p = 0.625$ under independence:

If $A$ and $B$ are independent, $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \times P(B)$:\begin{aligned} &p - 0.25 = 0.60p \cr &p - 0.60p = 0.25 \cr &0.40p = 0.25 \cr &p = \dfrac{0.25}{0.40} \cr &p = 0.625 \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Value of $P(A' \mid B)$:

Because $A$ and $B$ are independent, knowing that $B$ has occurred does not affect the probability of $A$ or its complement $A'$:\begin{aligned} P(A' \mid B) &= P(A') \cr &= 1 - P(A) \cr &= 1 - 0.60 \cr &= 0.4 \end{aligned}

(d) Finding $p$ when $P(A \mid B) = 0.50$:

Using the definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} P(A \mid B) &= \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \cr 0.50 &= \dfrac{p - 0.25}{p} \end{aligned}Solving for $p$:\begin{aligned} &0.50p = p - 0.25 \cr &0.25 = p - 0.50p \cr &0.25 = 0.50p \cr &p = \dfrac{0.25}{0.50} \cr &p = 0.5 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), stating $0 \le p \le 1$ ignores the constraints given by $P(A) = 0.60$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.85$. If $p < 0.25$, the intersection $p - 0.25$ would be negative; if $p > 0.85$, $P(B)$ would exceed the union $P(A \cup B)$.
In part (c)(ii), $0.6$ is $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$, but the question asks for the complement $P(A' \mid B) = 1 - P(A) = 0.4$.
In part (d), you solved $p - 0.25 = 0$ instead of $p - 0.25 = 0.50p$. Make sure to multiply through by the denominator $P(B) = p$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Independence Simplifies Conditionals
bradley_insight.content: In part (c)(ii), do not waste time setting up Bayes' formula: if $A$ and $B$ are independent, knowing that $B$ has occurred provides zero information about $A$ (or $A'$). Hence \begin{aligned}P(A' \mid B) & = P(A')\cr &= 1 - P(A) \cr &= 0.40\end{aligned} immediately.

question:
(a) An autonomous exploration rover is programmed to cross a difficult terrain ditch. In a trial run, it is allowed up to two attempts to cross the ditch, but if it succeeds on its first attempt, it does not attempt the crossing again. The probability that the rover is successful on its first attempt is $p$. If it fails the first attempt, the probability that it is successful on its second attempt is also $p$. The overall probability that the rover successfully clears the ditch within the two attempts is $0.51$.
Find the value of $p$.

(b) The following table shows the numbers of research officers employed by a wildlife conservation trust, classified by base region and scientific department:
RegionEcologyGenetics
North146
South78
Two research officers are chosen at random without replacement to attend an international symposium. Given that the first officer chosen is based in the North region, find the probability that both chosen officers are from the Ecology department.
steps:
(a) Setting up the probability equation for $p$:

The rover clears the ditch if it succeeds on attempt 1, or fails attempt 1 and succeeds on attempt 2:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{clears}) \cr &\quad = P(\text{1st}) + P(\text{fails 1st})P(\text{2nd}) \cr &\quad = p + (1 - p)p \cr &\quad = 2p - p^2 \end{aligned}Equating this to $0.51$ gives a quadratic equation:\begin{aligned} &2p - p^2 = 0.51 \cr &p^2 - 2p + 0.51 = 0 \cr &(p - 0.3)(p - 1.7) = 0 \end{aligned}Since $p$ represents a probability, $0 \le p \le 1$, we reject $p = 1.7$:\begin{aligned} p = 0.3 \end{aligned}
