(b) Conditional probability without replacement:

First, determine the totals from the table:
• Total officers: $14 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 35$
• North officers: $14 + 6 = 20$
• Ecology officers: $14 + 7 = 21$

We require $P(\text{both Ecology} \mid \text{1st North})$. Using the conditional definition:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{both Eco} \mid \text{1st North}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{P(\text{1st North Eco} \cap \text{2nd Eco})}{P(\text{1st North})} \end{aligned}Calculating the joint and marginal probabilities:\begin{aligned} P(\text{1st North}) &= \dfrac{20}{35} \end{aligned}For the numerator, the first officer must be North Ecology and the second must be any remaining Ecology officer:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{1st North Eco} \cap \text{2nd Eco}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{14}{35} \times \dfrac{20}{34} \end{aligned}Substituting these into the conditional probability expression:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{both Eco} \mid \text{1st North}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{\frac{14}{35} \times \frac{20}{34}}{\frac{20}{35}} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{14}{20} \times \dfrac{20}{34} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{14}{34} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{7}{17} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $p = 0.3$, (b) $\dfrac{7}{17}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you evaluated the probability of picking a single North Ecology officer out of the total staff, rather than finding the conditional probability that both chosen officers belong to Ecology given that the first is from the North.
In part (a), you solved the quadratic equation correctly but failed to reject the root $p = 1.7$. Probabilities must strictly satisfy $0 \le p \le 1$.
In part (b), you used with-replacement probabilities or incorrectly reduced the remaining pool of Ecology officers to $19$ instead of $20$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Cancelling the First Pick
bradley_insight.content: Notice how the fraction simplifies directly when applying conditional probability. The condition that the first officer is from the North immediately restricts the first selection to the $20$ North officers, of which $14$ are Ecology: $\dfrac{14}{20}$. Then, for the second pick, $20$ Ecology officers remain out of $34$ total staff: $\dfrac{14}{20} \times \dfrac{20}{34} = \dfrac{14}{34} = \dfrac{7}{17}$.

question:
(a) A candidate takes a professional certification test. She is permitted up to two attempts. The probability that she passes on her first attempt is $p$. If she fails the first attempt, she attends an intensive revision workshop, and the probability that she passes on her second attempt increases to $p + 0.20$. If she passes on her first attempt, she does not take the test again. The probability that she passes the test within the two attempts is $0.76$.
Find the value of $p$.

(b) A healthcare audit classifies $40$ medical consultants by employment status and specialty:
StatusSurgicalMedical
Full-time168
Part-time610
Two consultants are chosen at random without replacement to serve on an advisory panel. Given that the first consultant chosen is employed Full-time, find the probability that both chosen consultants belong to the Surgical specialty.
steps:
(a) Setting up and solving the quadratic equation for $p$:

The candidate passes if she succeeds on attempt 1, or fails attempt 1 and succeeds on attempt 2:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{passes}) \cr &\quad = p + (1 - p)(p + 0.20) \cr &\quad = p + p + 0.20 - p^2 - 0.20p \cr &\quad = 1.8p - p^2 + 0.20 \end{aligned}Equating this expression to $0.76$:\begin{aligned} &1.8p - p^2 + 0.20 = 0.76 \cr &p^2 - 1.8p + 0.56 = 0 \cr &(p - 0.4)(p - 1.4) = 0 \end{aligned}Since $p$ is a probability, $0 \le p \le 1$, we reject $p = 1.4$:\begin{aligned} p = 0.4 \end{aligned}

(b) Calculating the conditional probability:

Find the group totals from the table:
• Total consultants: $16 + 8 + 6 + 10 = 40$
• Full-time consultants: $16 + 8 = 24$
• Surgical consultants: $16 + 6 = 22$

For both consultants to be Surgical given that the first is Full-time, the first must be a Full-time Surgical consultant and the second must be any remaining Surgical consultant:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{1st FT Surg} \mid \text{1st FT}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{16}{24} = \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}Given that the first consultant was Surgical, $21$ Surgical consultants remain out of $39$ total remaining consultants:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{2nd Surg} \mid \text{1st FT Surg}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{21}{39} = \dfrac{7}{13} \end{aligned}Multiplying these dependent probabilities:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{both Surg} \mid \text{1st FT}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{7}{13} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{14}{39} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $p = 0.4$, (b) $\dfrac{14}{39}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you forgot to reduce the number of Surgical consultants by $1$ for the second pick, using $\dfrac{22}{39}$ instead of $\dfrac{21}{39}$.
In part (a), you accepted the extraneous root $p = 1.4$. A probability cannot exceed $1$.
In part (b), you calculated the unconditional joint probability of selecting two Surgical consultants without conditioning on the first consultant being Full-time.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Check the Boundary Range
bradley_insight.content: Whenever solving quadratic equations in probability problems, always check the physical feasibility of both algebraic solutions. Since any probability must satisfy $0 \le p \le 1$, an extraneous root like $p = 1.4$ must be explicitly rejected.

question:
(a) A trainee technician attempts a complex precision calibration task. The probability that he completes the calibration successfully on any single attempt is a constant probability $p$, where $0 < p < 1$. Once he succeeds, no further attempts are made. The probability that he succeeds on his second attempt is $0.24$.
Given that $p < 0.50$:
 (i) find the value of $p$,
 (ii) find the probability that he requires all three attempts and succeeds on the third attempt.

(b) A technology firm employs $60$ software engineers classified by primary programming language and working arrangement:
LanguageRemoteOffice
Python1810
Java128
C++66
Two software engineers are selected at random without replacement to lead a pilot project. Given that the first engineer selected works Remotely, find the probability that both selected engineers specialise in Python.
steps:
(a)(i) Finding the value of $p$:

Success on the second attempt requires failing the first attempt and succeeding on the second:\begin{aligned} P(\text{success on 2nd}) &= (1 - p)p \cr 0.24 &= p - p^2 \cr p^2 - p + 0.24 &= 0 \cr (p - 0.4)(p - 0.6) &= 0 \end{aligned}Since we are given that $p < 0.50$:\begin{aligned} p = 0.4 \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Probability of succeeding on the third attempt:

This corresponds to failing the first two attempts and succeeding on the third:\begin{aligned} P(\text{fail, fail, pass}) &= (1 - p)^2 p \cr &= (1 - 0.4)^2 \times 0.4 \cr &= (0.6)^2 \times 0.4 \cr &= 0.36 \times 0.4 \cr &= 0.144 \end{aligned}

(b) Conditional probability without replacement:

Determine the totals from the transposed table:
• Total engineers: $60$
• Remote engineers: $18 + 12 + 6 = 36$
• Python engineers: $18 + 10 = 28$

Given that the first engineer works Remotely, the probability that this engineer specialises in Python is:\begin{aligned} P(\text{1st Python} \mid \text{1st Remote}) &= \dfrac{18}{36}\cr & = \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}For the second selection, $27$ Python engineers remain out of $59$ total remaining engineers:\begin{aligned} P(\text{2nd Python} \mid \text{1st Python}) &= \dfrac{27}{59} \end{aligned}Multiplying these probabilities:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{both Python} \mid \text{1st Remote}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{27}{59} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{27}{118} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (a)(i), you chose the root $p = 0.6$, violating the given condition that $p < 0.50$.
In part (a)(ii), you computed $(1 - p)^3 = (0.6)^3 = 0.216$, which is the probability of failing all three attempts rather than succeeding on the third attempt.
In part (b), you used $\dfrac{18}{60}$ as the initial probability instead of conditioning on the first engineer being Remote ($\dfrac{18}{36}$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Transposed Contingency Tables
bradley_insight.content: When reading tables where categories are arranged by row rather than column, always sum along the relevant row or column carefully before setting up conditional fractions. Here, summing the Remote column gives $18 + 12 + 6 = 36$, which forms the reduced sample space for the first pick.

question:
(a) In a tennis tournament, a player is allowed up to two serves on each point. The probability that her first serve is in is $0.65$. If her first serve is in, the probability that she wins the point is $0.70$. If her first serve is out (a fault), she takes a second serve. The probability that her second serve is in is $0.80$. If her second serve is in, the probability that she wins the point is $0.45$. If her second serve is out (a double fault), she loses the point immediately.
 (i) Find the probability that the player wins the point on her serve.
 (ii) Given that the player won the point, find the probability that she won it on her second serve.

(b) A Sixth Form college records the science subject chosen by $80$ students across two year groups:
SubjectYear 12Year 13
Physics1510
Chemistry1214
Biology1811
Two students are chosen at random without replacement to represent the college at a science fair. Given that the first student chosen is from Year 13, find the probability that both chosen students study Physics.
steps:
(a)(i) Overall probability of winning the point:

The player can win the point via two mutually exclusive sequences:
• First serve in and win: $0.65 \times 0.70 = 0.455$
• First serve out, second serve in and win: $$(1 - 0.65) \times 0.80 \times 0.45$$ $$= 0.35 \times 0.80 \times 0.45$$ $$= 0.126$$ Summing these probabilities:\begin{aligned} P(\text{win}) &= 0.455 + 0.126 \cr &= 0.581 \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Conditional probability of winning on second serve:

Applying Bayes' theorem:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{2nd serve win} \mid \text{win}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{P(\text{2nd serve win})}{P(\text{win})} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{0.126}{0.581} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{126}{581} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{18}{83} \end{aligned}

(b) Two selections without replacement:

Total students: $80$.
• Total Year 13: $10 + 14 + 11 = 35$
• Total Physics: $15 + 10 = 25$

Given that the first student is from Year 13, the probability that this student studies Physics is:\begin{aligned} P(\text{1st Physics} \mid \text{1st Y13}) &= \dfrac{10}{35} = \dfrac{2}{7} \end{aligned}For the second selection, $24$ Physics students remain out of $79$ total remaining students:\begin{aligned} P(\text{2nd Physics} \mid \text{1st Physics}) &= \dfrac{24}{79} \end{aligned}Multiplying these probabilities:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{both Physics} \mid \text{1st Y13}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2}{7} \times \dfrac{24}{79} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{48}{553} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (a)(ii), you stated the joint probability $0.126$ rather than dividing by $P(\text{win}) = 0.581$ to obtain the conditional probability.
In part (a)(i), you did not account for the probability of faulting the first serve ($0.35$), erroneously adding $(0.65 \times 0.70) + (0.80 \times 0.45)$.
In part (b), you sampled with replacement or calculated the joint unconditional probability over the full $80$ students instead of conditioning on Year 13.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Don't Forget the First Fault
bradley_insight.content: In multi-stage service models, a very common error in part (a)(i) is multiplying $0.80 \times 0.45$ without the preceding factor of $0.35$. The second serve is only taken when the first serve is a fault, so the branch probability must begin with $1 - 0.65 = 0.35$.

question:
(a) A board game requires a player to roll a double six with two dice to begin play. With a pair of weighted dice, the probability of rolling a double six on any single throw is $p$. A player is allowed up to two throws to roll a double six, stopping immediately if successful on the first throw. The probability that the player begins play within the two throws is $\frac{7}{16}$.
 (i) Show that $p = \frac{1}{4}$.
 (ii) If the player is instead allowed up to three throws, find the probability that they roll their first double six on the third throw.

(b) A veterinary clinic treats $50$ animals over a weekend, categorized by appointment type and species:
AppointmentDogCat
Routine1614
Emergency812
Two animal records are chosen at random without replacement.
 (i) Given that the first record chosen is an Emergency appointment, find the probability that both records chosen are for Dogs.
 (ii) Given that both records chosen are for Cats, find the probability that at least one of the two appointments was an Emergency appointment.
steps:
(a)(i) Showing $p = \frac{1}{4}$:

The probability of rolling a double six within two throws is:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{success}) \cr &\quad = p + (1 - p)p \cr &\quad = 2p - p^2 \end{aligned}Setting this equal to $\frac{7}{16}$:\begin{aligned} &2p - p^2 = \dfrac{7}{16} \cr &32p - 16p^2 = 7 \cr &16p^2 - 32p + 7 = 0 \cr &(4p - 1)(4p - 7) = 0 \end{aligned}Since $p$ is a probability, $p \le 1$, rejecting $p = \frac{7}{4}$ gives:\begin{aligned} p = \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Probability of success on the third throw:

This requires two initial failures followed by a success:\begin{aligned} P(\text{fail, fail, pass}) &= (1 - p)^2 p \cr &= \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)^2 \times \dfrac{1}{4} \cr &= \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 \times \dfrac{1}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{9}{16} \times \dfrac{1}{4} \cr &= \dfrac{9}{64} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Finding $P(\text{both Dogs} \mid \text{1st Emergency})$:

From the table:
• Emergency appointments: $8 + 12 = 20$
• Total Dogs: $16 + 8 = 24$

The first appointment is an Emergency Dog with conditional probability:\begin{aligned} P(\text{1st Dog} \mid \text{1st Emer}) &= \dfrac{8}{20} = \dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}For the second selection, $23$ Dogs remain out of $49$ total remaining records:\begin{aligned} P(\text{2nd Dog} \mid \text{1st Dog}) &= \dfrac{23}{49} \end{aligned}Multiplying these probabilities:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{both Dogs} \mid \text{1st Emer}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{23}{49} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{46}{245} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Finding $P(\ge 1\text{ Emer} \mid \text{both Cats})$:

There are $14 + 12 = 26$ Cats in total, of which $14$ are Routine and $12$ are Emergency.

We use the complementary probability of selecting two Routine appointments given both are Cats:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{both Rout} \mid \text{both Cats}) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{14}{26} \times \dfrac{13}{25} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{7}{13} \times \dfrac{13}{25} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{7}{25} \end{aligned}Subtracting from $1$:\begin{aligned} &P(\ge 1\text{ Emer} \mid \text{both Cats}) \cr &\quad = 1 - \dfrac{7}{25} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{18}{25} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a)(i) $p = \dfrac{1}{4}$, (ii) $\dfrac{9}{64}$, (b)(i) $\dfrac{46}{245}$, (ii) $\dfrac{18}{25}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (a)(ii), you calculated $(1 - p)^3 = \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^3 = \dfrac{27}{64}$, which is the probability of failing all three throws rather than succeeding on the third throw.
In part (a)(i), you selected the root $p = \dfrac{7}{4} = 1.75$. Probabilities cannot be greater than $1$.
In part (b)(ii), $\dfrac{7}{25}$ is the probability that both Cat appointments were Routine. To find the probability of at least one Emergency appointment, you must subtract this from $1$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Complementary Shortcut with Two Cats
bradley_insight.content: For 'at least one' conditions within a restricted subpopulation, it is almost always faster to use $1 - P(\text{none})$. In part (b)(ii), once we restrict to the $26$ Cats, the probability that neither is an Emergency appointment is simply the probability that both are Routine: $\dfrac{14}{26} \times \dfrac{13}{25} = \dfrac{7}{25}$. Subtracting from $1$ gives $\dfrac{18}{25}$ immediately.

question:
Elena arrives at a harbour terminal at a random point in time to catch a passenger ferry across an estuary. The ferries are scheduled to depart at regular $15$-minute intervals.

(a) Assume that Elena boards the next available ferry.
 (i) Suggest an appropriate distribution to model her waiting time, in minutes, and state its parameters.
 (ii) State the mean and the variance of this distribution.
 (iii) State an assumption you have made in proposing this model.

(b) Now assume that the probability that Elena misses the next available ferry because she is purchasing a refreshment is $0.20$. If she misses the next ferry, she is certain to board the one after that.
 (i) Find the probability that her total waiting time is between $10$ and $22$ minutes.
 (ii) Given that she waits between $10$ and $22$ minutes, find the probability that she boards the first available ferry.
steps:
(a)(i) Suggesting the distribution:

Since Elena arrives at a random point in time throughout the $15$-minute cycle, her waiting time $X$ is uniformly spread over the interval $[0, 15]$:

Continuous Uniform (Rectangular) distribution, $X \sim U(0, 15)$, with lower parameter $a = 0$ and upper parameter $b = 15$.

(a)(ii) Mean and variance:

Using the standard formulas for $U(a, b)$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(X) &= \dfrac{a + b}{2} \cr &= \dfrac{0 + 15}{2} \cr &= 7.5 \end{aligned}For the variance:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= \dfrac{(b - a)^2}{12} \cr &= \dfrac{(15 - 0)^2}{12} \cr &= \dfrac{225}{12} \cr &= 18.75 \end{aligned}

(a)(iii) Stating an assumption:

Ferries depart strictly on schedule and Elena's arrival time is completely independent of the timetable (uniformly distributed over the interval).

(b)(i) Probability total waiting time is between $10$ and $22$ minutes:

Let $W \sim U(0, 15)$ be the initial arrival wait.

Let $M'$ be the event that she boards the first ferry, with $P(M') = 0.80$, so her waiting time is $T = W$.

Let $M$ be the event that she misses the first ferry, with $P(M) = 0.20$, so her waiting time is $T = W + 15$.

Using the law of total probability:\begin{aligned} &P(10 < T < 22) \cr &\quad = P(M') P(10 < W < 15) \cr &\qquad + P(M) P(10 < W + 15 < 22) \cr &\quad = 0.80 P(10 < W < 15) \cr &\qquad + 0.20 P(0 < W < 7) \end{aligned}Evaluating the uniform probabilities with $f(w) = \dfrac{1}{15}$:\begin{aligned} &P(10 < T < 22) \cr &\quad = 0.80\left(\dfrac{5}{15}\right) \cr &\qquad + 0.20\left(\dfrac{7}{15}\right) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4}{15} + \dfrac{1.4}{15} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{5.4}{15} \cr &\quad = 0.36 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Conditional probability of boarding the first ferry:

Applying the definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{1st ferry} \mid 10 < T < 22) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{P(M' \cap 10 < T < 22)}{P(10 < T < 22)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4 / 15}{5.4 / 15} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4}{5.4} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{40}{54} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{20}{27} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(i), you evaluated $P(10 < W < 22)$ directly using a single uniform interval rather than conditioning on whether the first ferry was caught or missed.
In part (b)(ii), you gave the joint probability $\dfrac{4}{15} \approx 0.267$ instead of dividing by the total probability $P(10 < T < 22) = 0.36$.
In part (a)(ii), you computed the variance as $\dfrac{15^2}{15} = 15$ instead of dividing by $12$: $\text{Var}(X) = \dfrac{15^2}{12} = 18.75$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Partitioning Waiting Times
bradley_insight.content: Notice how the missing-ferry event creates two disjoint intervals for $T$: if Elena catches the first ferry, her wait is $W \in [0, 15]$; if she misses it, her wait is $W + 15 \in [15, 30]$. To find $P(10 < T < 22)$, split the interval into $[10, 15]$ for the first ferry and $[15, 22]$ for the second, weighting each by its respective probability.

question:
The duration of a specialised chemical curing process, $T$ minutes, is modelled by a continuous uniform distribution over the interval $[12, 30]$.

(a) Write down the probability density function, $f(t)$, for all values of $t$.

(b) Find:
 (i) $\text{E}(T)$ and $\text{Var}(T)$,
 (ii) $\text{P}(T > 24)$,
 (iii) the conditional probability $\text{P}(T > 24 \mid T > 18)$.

(c) The operational cost of monitoring the curing process is given by $C = 4T + 15$ pounds.
Find the expected cost and the standard deviation of the cost.
steps:
(a) Probability density function $f(t)$:

The width of the interval is $b - a = 30 - 12 = 18$. The constant density is $\dfrac{1}{18}$:\begin{aligned} f(t) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{18} & 12 \le t \le 30 \cr 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Finding $\text{E}(T)$ and $\text{Var}(T)$:

Using the standard formulas for $U(a, b)$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(T) &= \dfrac{12 + 30}{2} \cr &= 21 \end{aligned}For the variance:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(T) &= \dfrac{(30 - 12)^2}{12} \cr &= \dfrac{18^2}{12} \cr &= \dfrac{324}{12} \cr &= 27 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Finding $\text{P}(T > 24)$:

Using the uniform probability formula:\begin{aligned} P(T > 24) &= \dfrac{30 - 24}{18} \cr &= \dfrac{6}{18} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}

(b)(iii) Finding $\text{P}(T > 24 \mid T > 18)$:

Using the definition of conditional probability:\begin{aligned} &P(T > 24 \mid T > 18) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{P(T > 24)}{P(T > 18)} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{(30 - 24) / 18}{(30 - 18) / 18} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{6 / 18}{12 / 18} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{6}{12} \cr &\quad = 0.5 \end{aligned}

(c) Finding $\text{E}(C)$ and $\text{SD}(C)$:

For expectation, applying linear properties:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(C) &= 4\text{E}(T) + 15 \cr &= 4(21) + 15 \cr &= 84 + 15 \cr &= 99 \end{aligned}For the standard deviation:\begin{aligned} \text{SD}(C) &= 4\sqrt{\text{Var}(T)} \cr &= 4\sqrt{27} \cr &= 4(3\sqrt{3}) \cr &= 12\sqrt{3} \cr &\approx 20.78 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $f(t) = \dfrac{1}{18}$, (b)(i) $21$ and $27$, (ii) $\dfrac{1}{3}$, (iii) $0.5$, (c) $\text{E}(C) = 99$, $\text{SD}(C) = 12\sqrt{3}$

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), $432$ is the variance $\text{Var}(C) = 16 \times 27$. The question asks for the standard deviation, so you must take the square root: $\sqrt{432} = 12\sqrt{3}$.
In part (b)(iii), you assumed that the continuous uniform distribution is memoryless. It is not; the condition $T > 18$ truncates the domain to $[18, 30]$, giving $\dfrac{30 - 24}{30 - 18} = 0.5$.
In part (b)(i), you divided $18^2$ by $18$ instead of by $12$. The variance formula for a continuous uniform distribution has a fixed denominator of $12$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Uniform Distributions Have Memory
bradley_insight.content: Unlike the exponential distribution, the continuous uniform distribution is not memoryless. When given $T > 18$, the remaining time is uniformly distributed over the shortened interval $[18, 30]$ of width $12$. Hence \begin{aligned}P(T > 24 \mid T > 18) &= \dfrac{30 - 24}{30 - 18}\cr & = \dfrac{6}{12} \cr & = 0.5\end{aligned}

question:
In a precision engineering workshop, components are cut to nominal lengths. The measurement error, $X\text{ mm}$, is modelled by a continuous uniform distribution on the interval $[-0.5, 0.5]$.

(a) State:
 (i) $\text{E}(X)$,
 (ii) $\text{Var}(X)$.

(b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen component has a measurement error:
 (i) greater than $0.2\text{ mm}$,
 (ii) with a magnitude (absolute value) greater than $0.35\text{ mm}$.

(c) A square metal plate is designed to have a side length of $20\text{ mm}$. Due to measurement error, the actual side length is $Y = 20 + X\text{ mm}$. The recorded area of the plate is $A = Y^2\text{ mm}^2$.
 (i) Expand $(20 + X)^2$ and hence determine the expected area, $\text{E}(A)$.
 (ii) Explain why the expected area is strictly greater than the nominal area of $400\text{ mm}^2$.
steps:
(a)(i) Finding $\text{E}(X)$:

By symmetry about zero:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(X) &= \dfrac{-0.5 + 0.5}{2} \cr &= 0 \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Finding $\text{Var}(X)$:

The width of the interval is $0.5 - (-0.5) = 1$:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= \dfrac{1^2}{12} \cr &= \dfrac{1}{12} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Probability error is greater than $0.2$:

Since the total width is $1$:\begin{aligned} P(X > 0.2) &= \dfrac{0.5 - 0.2}{1} \cr &= 0.3 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Probability magnitude is greater than $0.35$:

The event $|X| > 0.35$ means $X > 0.35$ or $X < -0.35$:\begin{aligned} &P(|X| > 0.35) \cr &\quad = P(X > 0.35) \cr &\qquad + P(X < -0.35) \cr &\quad = (0.5 - 0.35) \cr &\qquad + (-0.35 - (-0.5)) \cr &\quad = 0.15 + 0.15 \cr &\quad = 0.3 \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Expanding and finding $\text{E}(A)$:

Expanding the area expression:\begin{aligned} A &= (20 + X)^2 \cr &= 400 + 40X + X^2 \end{aligned}Taking expectations:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(A) &= \text{E}(400 + 40X + X^2) \cr &= 400 + 40\text{E}(X) + \text{E}(X^2) \end{aligned}Since $\text{E}(X) = 0$, we have $\text{E}(X^2) = \text{Var}(X) + [\text{E}(X)]^2 = \dfrac{1}{12}$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(A) &= 400 + 0 + \dfrac{1}{12} \cr &= 400\dfrac{1}{12} \quad (\approx 400.083) \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Explanation of positive bias:

Because $\text{Var}(X) > 0$, the squared error term $X^2$ is strictly positive for all non-zero errors. Therefore, its expectation $\text{E}(X^2) = \dfrac{1}{12}$ systematically increases the expected area above the nominal area.

pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(ii), $0.15$ accounts for only the upper tail $X > 0.35$. Because the condition involves magnitude $|X| > 0.35$, you must also include the symmetric lower tail $X < -0.35$.

In part (c)(i), you assumed $\text{E}(Y^2) = [\text{E}(Y)]^2 = 20^2 = 400$. In general, $\text{E}(Y^2) = [\text{E}(Y)]^2 + \text{Var}(Y)$, so the non-zero variance adds $\dfrac{1}{12}$ to the expected area.
In part (a)(ii), you computed the variance with a denominator of $6$ instead of $12$. The variance of $U(-0.5, 0.5)$ is $\dfrac{1^2}{12} = \dfrac{1}{12}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Jensen's Inequality in Area Models
bradley_insight.content: A classic theoretical question asks why $\text{E}(Y^2) > [\text{E}(Y)]^2$. Because squaring is a strictly convex function, $\text{E}(Y^2) = [\text{E}(Y)]^2 + \text{Var}(Y)$. Any uncertainty in measuring the side length introduces a positive bias into the expected area.

question:
The duration of customer technical support calls, $T$ minutes, is modelled by a continuous uniform distribution over the interval $[0, 8]$.

(a) Write down the probability density function of $T$.

(b) Find the probability that a randomly chosen call lasts:
 (i) more than $6$ minutes,
 (ii) between $2$ and $5$ minutes.

(c) A quality auditor monitors a random sample of $10$ independent customer support calls.
Let $Y$ denote the number of calls in the sample that last more than $6$ minutes.
 (i) State the distribution of $Y$, including its parameters.
 (ii) Find the probability that exactly $3$ of the $10$ calls last more than $6$ minutes. Give your answer to four decimal places.
 (iii) Find the probability that at least $2$ of the $10$ calls last more than $6$ minutes. Give your answer to four decimal places.
steps:
(a) Probability density function:

The constant density on $[0, 8]$ is $\dfrac{1}{8 - 0} = 0.125$:\begin{aligned} f(t) = \begin{cases} 0.125 & 0 \le t \le 8 \cr 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Probability a call lasts more than $6$ minutes:

Using the uniform distribution:\begin{aligned} P(T > 6) &= \dfrac{8 - 6}{8} \cr &= \dfrac{2}{8} \cr &= 0.25 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Probability a call lasts between $2$ and $5$ minutes:

Evaluating the interval probability:\begin{aligned} P(2 < T < 5) &= \dfrac{5 - 2}{8} \cr &= \dfrac{3}{8} \cr &= 0.375 \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Distribution of $Y$:

Since there are $n = 10$ independent trials and the probability of success on each trial is $p = 0.25$:\begin{aligned} Y \sim B(10, 0.25) \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Probability of exactly $3$ calls:

Applying the binomial probability formula:\begin{aligned} P(Y = 3) &= \binom{10}{3} (0.25)^3 (0.75)^7 \cr &= 120 \times 0.015625 \cr &\qquad \times 0.133484 \cr &\approx 0.2503 \end{aligned}

(c)(iii) Probability of at least $2$ calls:

Using the complement rule:\begin{aligned} &P(Y \ge 2)\cr &= 1 - [P(Y = 0) + P(Y = 1)] \end{aligned}Calculating the individual probabilities:\begin{aligned} P(Y = 0) &= (0.75)^{10} \cr &\approx 0.05631 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} P(Y = 1) &= 10(0.25)(0.75)^9 \cr &\approx 0.18771 \end{aligned}Summing and subtracting from $1$:\begin{aligned} P(Y \ge 2) &= 1 - [0.05631 + 0.18771] \cr &= 1 - 0.24402 \cr &= 0.7560 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (c)(iii), $0.2440$ is $P(Y \le 1)$. To find the probability of at least $2$ calls, you must subtract this from $1$.
In part (c)(ii), you omitted the binomial coefficient $\binom{10}{3} = 120$, evaluating $(0.25)^3 (0.75)^7$ only.
In part (b)(i), you found $P(T < 6) = \dfrac{6}{8} = 0.75$ instead of $P(T > 6) = \dfrac{8 - 6}{8} = 0.25$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Bridging Continuous and Discrete Distributions
bradley_insight.content: Examination boards frequently connect continuous distributions with the Binomial distribution. The continuous uniform distribution provides the single-trial success probability $p = P(T > 6) = 0.25$, which then acts as the parameter for a discrete sample of size $n = 10$.

question:
An automated sorting facility processes parcel weights, $W\text{ kg}$, which are uniformly distributed over the interval $[2, 10]$.
• Parcels with $W \le 4$ are routed to Conveyor 1.
• Parcels with $4 < W \le 8$ are routed to Conveyor 2.
• Parcels with $W > 8$ are routed to the Heavy Goods Station.

(a) Find the probability that a randomly selected parcel:
 (i) is routed to Conveyor 1,
 (ii) is routed to Conveyor 2,
 (iii) is routed to the Heavy Goods Station.

(b) Parcels routed to Conveyor 2 undergo an automated scanning check. The time taken to scan a parcel, $S$ seconds, depends linearly on its weight: $S = 3W + 5$.
Given that a parcel is routed to Conveyor 2:
 (i) state the conditional distribution of its weight, $W$,
 (ii) find the expected scanning time, $\text{E}(S)$,
 (iii) find the variance of the scanning time, $\text{Var}(S)$.
steps:
(a) Routing probabilities:

The parcel weight is $W \sim U(2, 10)$ with interval width $10 - 2 = 8$.

(i) Conveyor 1:\begin{aligned} P(W \le 4) &= \dfrac{4 - 2}{8} \cr &= \dfrac{2}{8} \cr &= 0.25 \end{aligned}(ii) Conveyor 2:\begin{aligned} P(4 < W \le 8) &= \dfrac{8 - 4}{8} \cr &= \dfrac{4}{8} \cr &= 0.5 \end{aligned}(iii) Heavy Goods Station:\begin{aligned} P(W > 8) &= \dfrac{10 - 8}{8} \cr &= \dfrac{2}{8} \cr &= 0.25 \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Conditional distribution of $W$:

Given that the parcel is on Conveyor 2, its weight is restricted to the interval $[4, 8]$. Since the density was constant over $[2, 10]$, it remains constant over $[4, 8]$:

$W \mid \text{Conveyor 2} \sim U(4, 8)$.

(b)(ii) Expected scanning time $\text{E}(S)$:

For $W \sim U(4, 8)$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(W) &= \dfrac{4 + 8}{2} \cr &= 6 \end{aligned}Using linear properties of expectation:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(S) &= 3\text{E}(W) + 5 \cr &= 3(6) + 5 \cr &= 18 + 5 \cr &= 23 \end{aligned}

(b)(iii) Variance of the scanning time $\text{Var}(S)$:

For $W \sim U(4, 8)$, the variance is:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(W) &= \dfrac{(8 - 4)^2}{12} \cr &= \dfrac{16}{12} \cr &= \dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}Using the variance transformation rule $\text{Var}(aW + b) = a^2 \text{Var}(W)$:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(S) &= 3^2 \text{Var}(W) \cr &= 9 \times \dfrac{4}{3} \cr &= 12 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(iii), you multiplied $\text{Var}(W)$ by $3$ instead of $3^2 = 9$. Remember that $\text{Var}(aW + b) = a^2 \text{Var}(W)$.

In part (b)(i), you stated the unconditional distribution $U(2, 10)$. Given that the parcel is on Conveyor 2, its weight is restricted to the interval $[4, 8]$, so the conditional distribution is $U(4, 8)$.
In part (b)(iii), you added the constant $5$ to the variance. Adding a constant shifts the distribution but does not change its spread: $\text{Var}(aW + b) = a^2 \text{Var}(W)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Truncation Preserves Uniformity
bradley_insight.content: A crucial property of the continuous uniform distribution is that conditioning on a sub-interval simply creates a new continuous uniform distribution over that sub-interval. Truncating $W \sim U(2, 10)$ to $4 < W \le 8$ directly yields $W \sim U(4, 8)$.

question:
A transport planner investigates the daily commuting times of office workers in a metropolitan district. She records the daily commuting time, $t$ minutes, for $100$ randomly selected workers:
Commuting time, $t$ (min)Number of workers
$t < 20$6
$20 \le t < 30$14
$30 \le t < 40$22
$40 \le t < 50$26
$50 \le t < 60$18
$60 \le t < 70$10
$t \ge 70$4
(a) Explain why a normal distribution may be an appropriate model for the commuting times in this sample.

The planner uses the distribution $\text{N}(44, 14^2)$ to model the commuting times.

(b) Find the number of workers in the sample that this model would predict to have a daily commuting time in the range:
 (i) $40 \le t < 50$,
 (ii) $t \ge 70$.

(c) Use your answers to part (b):
 (i) to comment on the suitability of this model,
 (ii) to explain how the planner could improve the model by changing one of its parameters.

(d) A colleague wishes to use the improved model to predict the commuting times of workers in a remote rural district. Comment on this plan.
steps:
(a) Justifying the model choice:

The observed frequencies are unimodal and roughly symmetrical, peaking in the central modal interval $40 \le t < 50$ ($26$ workers) and decreasing smoothly into both tails.

(b)(i) Expected frequency for $40 \le t < 50$:

Standardising under $T \sim \text{N}(44, 14^2)$:\begin{aligned} &P(40 \le T < 50) \cr &\quad = P\left(\dfrac{40 - 44}{14} \le Z < \dfrac{50 - 44}{14}\right) \cr &\quad = P(-0.286 \le Z < 0.429) \cr &\quad = \Phi(0.429) - \Phi(-0.286) \cr &\quad = 0.6659 - (1 - 0.6124) \cr &\quad = 0.6659 - 0.3876 \cr &\quad = 0.2783 \end{aligned}Multiplying by the sample size $N = 100$:\begin{aligned} 100 \times 0.2783 &= 27.83 \cr &\approx 28 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Expected frequency for $t \ge 70$:

Standardising the upper tail:\begin{aligned} P(T \ge 70) &= P\left(Z \ge \dfrac{70 - 44}{14}\right) \cr &= P(Z \ge 1.857) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(1.857) \cr &= 1 - 0.9683 \cr &= 0.0317 \end{aligned}Multiplying by $N = 100$:\begin{aligned} 100 \times 0.0317 &= 3.17 \cr &\approx 3 \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Comment on model suitability:

The model is suitable because the predicted frequencies ($28$ and $3$) closely match the observed frequencies ($26$ and $4$).

(c)(ii) Improving the model:

The planner could calculate the sample mean and sample standard deviation directly from the grouped frequency table and update $\mu$ and $\sigma$ accordingly.

(d) Comment on transferring the model:

The model is unsuitable for a rural district because commuting distances, transport modes, and traffic conditions in rural areas differ substantially from metropolitan areas.
Final Answer: (b)(i) $28$, (ii) $3$

pi_options.feedback: These values are the observed frequencies from the table, not the predicted frequencies generated by the normal model $\text{N}(44, 14^2)$.
In part (b)(ii), you may have used $\Phi(1.857)$ or an incorrect tail probability calculation rather than $1 - \Phi(1.857) = 0.0317$.
In part (b)(i), you evaluated $\Phi(0.429) - 0.5 = 0.1659$ or omitted the lower tail below the mean, leading to an incorrect predicted count.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Transposing Wide Tables
bradley_insight.content: Notice how the original frequency table has been transposed so that categories run down rows rather than across columns. When auditing data tables on portrait screens, keeping categories vertical ensures that boundary signs and numbers remain fully legible without horizontal scrolling.

question:
A manufacturer of electric vehicle batteries models the full-charge driving range, $X\text{ km}$, as a normal distribution $\text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$. Quality control testing reveals that $10\%$ of the batteries achieve a range of less than $380\text{ km}$, whilst $5\%$ of the batteries achieve a range of more than $460\text{ km}$.

(a) Write down two simultaneous equations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$.

(b) Find the values of $\mu$ and $\sigma$, giving each value to three significant figures.

(c) Batteries with a range of less than $370\text{ km}$ are classed as sub-standard and must be recycled. Find the percentage of batteries that must be recycled.

(d) A random sample of $5$ batteries is selected independently from the production line. Find the probability that exactly one battery has a range greater than $450\text{ km}$.
steps:
(a) Setting up simultaneous equations:

For the lower tail $P(X < 380) = 0.10$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{380 - \mu}{\sigma} &= -1.2816 \cr 380 &= \mu - 1.2816\sigma \end{aligned}For the upper tail $P(X > 460) = 0.05$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{460 - \mu}{\sigma} &= 1.6449 \cr 460 &= \mu + 1.6449\sigma \end{aligned}

(b) Solving for $\mu$ and $\sigma$:

Subtracting the first equation from the second:\begin{aligned} 460 - 380 &= 2.9265\sigma \cr 80 &= 2.9265\sigma \cr \sigma &= \dfrac{80}{2.9265} \cr &\approx 27.336 \cr &\approx 27.3\text{ km} \end{aligned}Substituting $\sigma$ back to find $\mu$:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 460 - 1.6449(27.336) \cr &= 460 - 44.965 \cr &\approx 415.035 \cr &\approx 415\text{ km} \end{aligned}

(c) Percentage of batteries to be recycled:

Standardising for $X < 370$ using unrounded values:\begin{aligned} Z &= \dfrac{370 - 415.035}{27.336} \cr &\approx -1.648 \end{aligned}Evaluating the tail probability:\begin{aligned} P(Z < -1.648) &= 1 - \Phi(1.648) \cr &= 1 - 0.9503 \cr &= 0.0497 \cr &= 4.97\% \end{aligned}

(d) Binomial probability for a sample of $5$:

First, find the probability that a single battery exceeds $450\text{ km}$:\begin{aligned} Z &= \dfrac{450 - 415.035}{27.336} \cr &\approx 1.279 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} p &= 1 - \Phi(1.279) \cr &= 1 - 0.8995 \cr &= 0.1005 \end{aligned}Let $Y \sim B(5, 0.1005)$ denote the number of such batteries:\begin{aligned} P(Y = 1) &= \binom{5}{1} (0.1005)^1 (0.8995)^4 \cr &= 5 \times 0.1005 \times 0.6547 \cr &\approx 0.329 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (b) $\mu = 415\text{ km}$, $\sigma = 27.3\text{ km}$, (c) $4.97\%$, (d) $0.329$

pi_options.feedback: In part (d), $0.101$ is the single-battery probability $p = P(X > 450)$. You must evaluate the binomial probability for $1$ battery out of $5$: $\binom{5}{1} p (1 - p)^4$.
In part (a), you used positive $z$-scores for both tails, forgetting that a lower tail of $10\%$ requires a negative $z$-value: $z = -1.2816$.
In part (c), you doubled the tail probability, treating the condition as two-tailed rather than strictly $X < 370$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Signs in Inverse Normal Tail Values
bradley_insight.content: A frequent sign error occurs when writing the equation for a lower tail like $P(X < 380) = 0.10$. Because $380$ lies below the mean, the standardised value must be negative: $z = -1.2816$. Forgetting this negative sign will produce an impossible negative or inflated standard deviation.

question:
A commercial seed merchant claims that $65\%$ of its heirloom tomato seeds successfully germinate under standard nursery conditions. A grower sows a random sample of $200$ seeds. Let $X$ denote the number of seeds that successfully germinate.

(a) State why a normal approximation to the distribution of $X$ is appropriate in this case.

(b) Specify the mean and the variance of the approximating normal distribution.

(c) Using the normal approximation with a continuity correction, find the probability that:
 (i) at least $140$ seeds germinate,
 (ii) between $120$ and $135$ seeds germinate (inclusive).
steps:
(a) Justifying the normal approximation:

Here $X \sim B(200, 0.65)$. The sample size $n = 200$ is large, and neither $p = 0.65$ nor $q = 0.35$ is close to $0$ or $1$ ($np = 130 > 5$ and $nq = 70 > 5$).

(b) Specifying parameters:

Calculating the mean and variance:\begin{aligned} \mu &= np \cr &= 200 \times 0.65 \cr &= 130 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} \sigma^2 &= np(1 - p) \cr &= 200 \times 0.65 \times 0.35 \cr &= 45.5 \end{aligned}Hence $Y \sim \text{N}(130, 45.5)$, with $\sigma = \sqrt{45.5} \approx 6.745$.

(c)(i) Probability of at least $140$ seeds:

Applying the continuity correction for $X \ge 140$ gives $Y \ge 139.5$:\begin{aligned} P(X \ge &140)\cr &\approx P(Y \ge 139.5) \cr &= P\left(Z \ge \dfrac{139.5 - 130}{6.745}\right) \cr &= P(Z \ge 1.408) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(1.408) \cr &= 1 - 0.9205 \cr &= 0.0795 \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Probability between $120$ and $135$ seeds (inclusive):

Applying continuity corrections for $120 \le X \le 135$ gives $119.5 \le Y \le 135.5$:\begin{aligned} Z_1 &= \dfrac{119.5 - 130}{6.745} \cr &= -1.557 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} Z_2 &= \dfrac{135.5 - 130}{6.745} \cr &= 0.815 \end{aligned}Evaluating the interval probability:\begin{aligned} &P(-1.557 \le Z \le 0.815) \cr &\quad = \Phi(0.815) - \Phi(-1.557) \cr &\quad = 0.7925 - (1 - 0.9402) \cr &\quad = 0.7925 - 0.0598 \cr &\quad = 0.7328 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (c)(i), you used $140.5$ instead of $139.5$ for the continuity correction. 'At least $140$' includes $140$, so the continuous interval must start at $139.5$.
In part (c)(ii), you applied the continuity corrections in the wrong direction ($120.5$ and $134.5$), shrinking the interval rather than expanding it to cover the inclusive integer bounds.
In part (b), you gave the standard deviation $\sigma = 6.75$ as the variance. The variance is $\sigma^2 = npq = 45.5$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Direction of Continuity Corrections
bradley_insight.content: To avoid getting continuity corrections backwards, think of discrete integers as blocks of width $1$ centred on each integer. The integer $140$ occupies the interval $[139.5, 140.5]$. Therefore, 'at least $140$' must include the entire block for $140$, beginning at $139.5$.

question:
A bottling plant fills bottles of cold-pressed olive oil. The volume of oil dispensed, $X\text{ ml}$, is normally distributed with a known standard deviation of $\sigma = 4.5\text{ ml}$. The dispensing machine is calibrated to deliver a population mean volume of $\mu = 500\text{ ml}$.

Following routine maintenance, the quality assurance manager suspects that the machine is underfilling bottles. A random sample of $16$ bottles is inspected, yielding a sample mean volume of $\bar{x} = 497.8\text{ ml}$.

(a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses to test the manager's suspicion.

(b) State the distribution of the sample mean, $\bar{X}$, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

(c) Test, at the $5\%$ significance level, whether there is evidence that the machine is underfilling bottles. State your conclusion clearly in context.

(d) Determine the critical value of the sample mean, $\bar{x}$, for this test at the $5\%$ significance level.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

The test is one-tailed because the manager suspects underfilling:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \mu = 500 \cr &H_1: \mu < 500 \end{aligned}

(b) Distribution of the sample mean under $H_0$:

For a sample of size $n = 16$ from a normal population:\begin{aligned} \bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(500, \dfrac{4.5^2}{16}\right) \end{aligned}The standard error is:\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\bar{x}} &= \dfrac{4.5}{\sqrt{16}} \cr &= \dfrac{4.5}{4} \cr &= 1.125 \end{aligned}Hence $\bar{X} \sim \text{N}(500, 1.125^2)$.

(c) Calculating test statistic and conclusion:

Standardising the observed sample mean $\bar{x} = 497.8$:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{497.8 - 500}{1.125} \cr &= \dfrac{-2.2}{1.125} \cr &\approx -1.956 \end{aligned}At the $5\%$ significance level for a lower-tail test, the critical value is $z_{\text{crit}} = -1.645$.

Since $-1.956 < -1.645$, the test statistic falls into the critical region. We reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $5\%$ level that the dispensing machine is underfilling bottles.

(d) Determining the critical value of $\bar{x}$:

Using the critical $z$-value:\begin{aligned} \bar{x}_{\text{crit}} &= 500 - 1.645(1.125) \cr &= 500 - 1.851 \cr &= 498.15\text{ ml} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you stated a two-tailed alternative hypothesis $H_1: \mu \neq 500$. The question specifies that the manager suspects underfilling, which requires a one-tailed test $H_1: \mu < 500$.
In part (b), you used the population variance $\sigma^2 = 4.5^2$ for the sample mean. The variance of the sample mean is $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = \dfrac{4.5^2}{16} = 1.125^2$.
In part (c), you divided by $\sigma = 4.5$ instead of the standard error $1.125$, leading to an underestimated test statistic and an incorrect non-rejection decision.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Dividing by the Square Root of n
bradley_insight.content: The most common blunder in sample mean hypothesis testing is standardising with $\sigma$ instead of the standard error $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. Always remember that sample means have much less variability than individual observations: $\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}$.

question:
An airline imposes weight limits on passenger luggage. The weight of an empty hard-shell suitcase, $S\text{ kg}$, is modelled by $S \sim \text{N}(3.2, 0.4^2)$. The weight of the packed contents, $C\text{ kg}$, is modelled by $C \sim \text{N}(18.5, 2.5^2)$. The variables $S$ and $C$ are assumed to be independent.

(a) Let $T = S + C$ denote the total weight of a randomly chosen packed suitcase.
 (i) Find the mean and the standard deviation of $T$.
 (ii) The airline charges an excess baggage fee if $T > 23.0\text{ kg}$. Find the probability that a randomly chosen packed suitcase incurs this fee.

(b) Two independent packed suitcases, $T_1$ and $T_2$, are checked in by two travelling companions. Find the probability that the combined weight of the two suitcases exceeds $45.0\text{ kg}$.

(c) Find the probability that the magnitude of the difference in weight between the two suitcases, $|T_1 - T_2|$, is greater than $3.0\text{ kg}$.
steps:
(a)(i) Mean and standard deviation of $T$:

Using properties of linear combinations of independent normal variables:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(T) &= \text{E}(S) + \text{E}(C) \cr &= 3.2 + 18.5 \cr &= 21.7\text{ kg} \end{aligned}For the variance:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(T) &= \text{Var}(S) + \text{Var}(C) \cr &= 0.4^2 + 2.5^2 \cr &= 0.16 + 6.25 \cr &= 6.41 \end{aligned}The standard deviation is:\begin{aligned} \text{SD}(T) &= \sqrt{6.41} \cr &\approx 2.532 \cr &\approx 2.53\text{ kg} \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Probability of excess baggage fee:

Standardising for $T > 23.0$:\begin{aligned} P(T > &23.0)\cr &= P\left(Z > \dfrac{23.0 - 21.7}{2.532}\right) \cr &= P(Z > 0.513) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(0.513) \cr &= 1 - 0.6960 \cr &= 0.304 \end{aligned}

(b) Combined weight of two suitcases:

Let $W = T_1 + T_2$. Since $T_1$ and $T_2$ are independent:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(W) &= 21.7 + 21.7 = 43.4\text{ kg} \cr \text{Var}(W) &= 6.41 + 6.41 = 12.82 \end{aligned}So $W \sim \text{N}(43.4, 12.82)$ with $\text{SD}(W) = \sqrt{12.82} \approx 3.581$. Standardising for $W > 45.0$:\begin{aligned} P(W > &45.0)\cr &= P\left(Z > \dfrac{45.0 - 43.4}{3.581}\right) \cr &= P(Z > 0.447) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(0.447) \cr &= 1 - 0.6726 \cr &= 0.3274 \end{aligned}

(c) Difference in weight between two suitcases:

Let $D = T_1 - T_2$. The parameters are:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(D) &= 21.7 - 21.7 = 0 \cr \text{Var}(D) &= \text{Var}(T_1) + \text{Var}(T_2) \cr &= 6.41 + 6.41 = 12.82 \end{aligned}So $D \sim \text{N}(0, 12.82)$. Because the distribution is symmetric about $0$:\begin{aligned} P(|D| > 3.0) &= 2P(D > 3.0) \cr &= 2P\left(Z > \dfrac{3.0 - 0}{3.581}\right) \cr &= 2P(Z > 0.838) \cr &= 2(1 - 0.7990) \cr &= 2(0.2010) \cr &= 0.402 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (a)(i), you added the standard deviations directly ($0.4 + 2.5 = 2.9$) rather than adding variances. For independent variables, $\text{Var}(S + C) = \text{Var}(S) + \text{Var}(C)$.
In part (c), you calculated a single tail $P(D > 3.0) = 0.2010$. The condition asks for the magnitude $|T_1 - T_2| > 3.0$, so you must double this to account for both tails.
In part (c), you subtracted the variances, setting $\text{Var}(T_1 - T_2) = 0$. Variances always add for independent random variables: $\text{Var}(T_1 - T_2) = \text{Var}(T_1) + \text{Var}(T_2)$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Variances Always Add
bradley_insight.content: A perennial trap in A Level Statistics is subtracting variances when finding the distribution of a difference, such as $T_1 - T_2$. Because $\text{Var}(-X) = (-1)^2 \text{Var}(X) = \text{Var}(X)$, uncertainties always compound: $\text{Var}(T_1 - T_2) = \text{Var}(T_1) + \text{Var}(T_2)$.

question:
Marcus is an energy commodities analyst monitoring wholesale energy prices. He records the monthly prices of two energy commodities derived from different extraction sources, Crude Oil and Natural Gas, across $12$ randomly selected months, to investigate whether there is any correlation.
The product moment correlation coefficient for this first dataset is $r = 0.238$. There are $12$ data points, and the corresponding $p$-value for a two-tailed test is $0.456$.

(a) Comment on the correlation between the prices of Crude Oil and Natural Gas in this sample.

Marcus also records the monthly prices of two refined petroleum products, Crude Oil and Heating Oil, across $12$ randomly selected months, to investigate whether there is any correlation.
The product moment correlation coefficient for this second dataset is $r = 0.672$. There are $12$ data points.

(b) Stating your hypotheses clearly, test at the $5\%$ level of significance whether there is any evidence of correlation between the prices of these two products.

(c) Without referring to the positioning of the points on the scatter diagrams, suggest why the product moment correlation coefficient is higher for the second dataset than for the first.
steps:
(a) Commenting on the first dataset:

There is a weak positive linear correlation in the sample ($r = 0.238$). However, because the $p$-value ($0.456$) is much greater than $0.05$, there is no statistically significant evidence of correlation in the population.

(b) Hypothesis test for Crude Oil vs Heating Oil:

State the null and alternative hypotheses, where $\rho$ denotes the population correlation coefficient:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \rho = 0 \cr &H_1: \rho \neq 0 \end{aligned}For a two-tailed test with sample size $n = 12$ at the $5\%$ significance level (degrees of freedom $\nu = 12 - 2 = 10$), the critical value from statistical tables is:\begin{aligned} r_{\text{crit}} = \pm 0.5760 \end{aligned}Comparing the sample correlation coefficient $r = 0.672$:\begin{aligned} |0.672| > 0.5760 \end{aligned}Since the test statistic exceeds the critical value, we reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $5\%$ level of a correlation between the prices of Crude Oil and Heating Oil.

(c) Contextual reason for higher correlation:

Heating oil is directly refined from crude oil (crude oil is its raw material feedstock), meaning their production and refining costs are inextricably linked, whereas natural gas has different extraction and market dynamics.
Final Answer: (b) Reject $H_0$ as $|0.672| > 0.5760$

pi_options.feedback: You used the critical value for $n = 8$ or applied a $1\%$ two-tailed significance level instead of the $5\%$ level for $n = 12$ ($0.5760$).
You used the one-tailed critical value ($0.4973$). The question asks whether there is 'any evidence of correlation', which requires a two-tailed test with critical value $0.5760$.
The sample value is $r = 0.672$, which is strictly greater than the critical value $0.5760$, so $H_0$ must be rejected, not accepted.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed Phrasing
bradley_insight.content: Look carefully at the wording in correlation hypothesis tests: 'is there any evidence of correlation' mandates a two-tailed test ($H_1: \rho \neq 0$), whereas 'is there evidence of positive correlation' specifies a one-tailed test ($H_1: \rho > 0$). Using the wrong tail cuts or doubles your critical significance threshold.

question:
A teacher records the weekly independent study hours, $h$, and the subsequent assessment scores, $s\%$, for a sample of $11$ students.
For the full sample of $11$ students, the product moment correlation coefficient is $r = 0.384$. A particular student, labelled as Point $P$ on the scatter diagram, logged $8.5$ study hours but achieved an anomalous score of $18\%$.

(a) Stating your hypotheses clearly, test at the $5\%$ level of significance whether there is evidence of positive correlation between study hours and assessment scores for the full sample of $11$ students.

(b) If Point $P$ is removed from the dataset, explain what effect this will have on:
 (i) the value of the product moment correlation coefficient, $r$,
 (ii) the gradient of the least-squares regression line of $s$ on $h$.

(c) State an assumption required about the underlying bivariate population when carrying out a hypothesis test for the product moment correlation coefficient.
steps:
(a) One-tailed hypothesis test for positive correlation:

Set up the hypotheses:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \rho = 0 \cr &H_1: \rho > 0 \end{aligned}For a one-tailed test with sample size $n = 11$ at the $5\%$ significance level, the critical value from tables is:\begin{aligned} r_{\text{crit}} = 0.5214 \end{aligned}Comparing the test statistic:\begin{aligned} 0.384 < 0.5214 \end{aligned}Since $r < r_{\text{crit}}$, we do not reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to conclude that there is a positive correlation between study hours and scores for the full sample.

(b)(i) Effect of removing Point $P$ on $r$:

Point $P$ is a severe outlier that contradicts the overall strong positive trend (high study hours with a very low score). Removing Point $P$ will cause $r$ to increase significantly closer to $+1$.

(b)(ii) Effect of removing Point $P$ on the regression gradient:

Point $P$ acts as an influential point that pulls down the right end of the line. Removing Point $P$ will cause the gradient of the regression line of $s$ on $h$ to increase.

(c) Underlying distributional assumption:

The bivariate data $(H, S)$ must follow a bivariate normal distribution.
Final Answer: (a) Do not reject $H_0$ as $0.384 < 0.5214$, (b)(i) $r$ increases, (ii) Gradient increases, (c) Bivariate normality

pi_options.ans: (a) Reject $H_0$ as $0.384 > 0.300$, (b)(i) $r$ increases, (ii) Gradient increases, (c) Bivariate normality
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you used an arbitrary threshold or an incorrect critical value. For $n = 11$ at the $5\%$ one-tailed level, the critical value is $0.5214$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Do not reject $H_0$ as $0.384 < 0.5214$, (b)(i) $r$ decreases, (ii) Gradient increases, (c) Bivariate normality
pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(i), removing an outlier that contradicts the positive trend tightens the remaining points along a straight line, which increases $r$, not decreases it.

pi_options.ans: (a) Do not reject $H_0$ as $0.384 < 0.5214$, (b)(i) $r$ increases, (ii) Gradient decreases, (c) Independent normal errors only
pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(ii), Point $P$ pulls the right-hand tail of the regression line downward. Removing it pivots the line upward at high $h$, meaning the gradient increases.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: PMCC Requires Bivariate Normality
bradley_insight.content: A standard A Level bookwork question asks for the assumption behind PMCC hypothesis testing. Students often write 'the data is normally distributed'. The precise requirement is that the variables follow a *bivariate normal distribution* (both variables are individually normal, and their joint distribution forms a 3D bell shape).

question:
A microbiologist measures the incubation time, $t$ hours, and the bacterial colony population, $N$ (in thousands), for $10$ laboratory cultures.
The scatter diagram illustrates a non-linear relationship between $t$ and $N$. The product moment correlation coefficient between $t$ and $N$ is calculated as $r = 0.885$.

The microbiologist suspects that the population growth follows an exponential model of the form:$$N = a b^t$$where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

(a) Show that this model can be expressed in the linear form $\log_{10} N = \alpha + \beta t$, stating expressions for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.

(b) When the transformed variable $y = \log_{10} N$ is plotted against $t$, the product moment correlation coefficient between $t$ and $y$ is found to be $r' = 0.994$.
 (i) Explain why $r'$ is substantially higher than $r$.
 (ii) Stating your hypotheses clearly, test at the $1\%$ level of significance whether there is evidence of positive linear correlation between $t$ and $y$.
steps:
(a) Linearising the exponential model:

Taking base-$10$ logarithms of both sides:\begin{aligned} N &= a b^t \cr \log_{10} N &= \log_{10}(a b^t) \cr &= \log_{10} a + \log_{10}(b^t) \cr &= \log_{10} a + t \log_{10} b \end{aligned}Comparing this with $\log_{10} N = \alpha + \beta t$:\begin{aligned} \alpha &= \log_{10} a \cr \beta &= \log_{10} b \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Explaining why $r'$ is higher:

The PMCC $r$ measures the strength of a *linear* relationship. Because the original data is non-linear (exponential growth), $r = 0.885$ underestimates the strength of the association. The logarithmic transformation linearises the relationship, so the transformed points lie almost exactly on a straight line, yielding $r' = 0.994$.

(b)(ii) Testing for positive linear correlation at $1\%$ level:

State the hypotheses for the transformed variables:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \rho = 0 \cr &H_1: \rho > 0 \end{aligned}For a one-tailed test with sample size $n = 10$ at the $1\%$ level, the critical value from statistical tables is:\begin{aligned} r_{\text{crit}} = 0.7155 \end{aligned}Comparing the transformed correlation coefficient:\begin{aligned} 0.994 > 0.7155 \end{aligned}Since $r' > r_{\text{crit}}$, we reject $H_0$.

There is overwhelming evidence at the $1\%$ significance level of a positive linear correlation between $t$ and $\log_{10} N$.
Final Answer: (a) $\alpha = \log_{10} a$, $\beta = \log_{10} b$, (b)(ii) Reject $H_0$ as $0.994 > 0.7155$

pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you did not take logarithms of the parameters $a$ and $b$. Comparing $\log_{10} N = \log_{10} a + t \log_{10} b$ shows $\alpha = \log_{10} a$ and $\beta = \log_{10} b$.
In part (b)(ii), $0.995$ is not a critical value from statistical tables. For $n = 10$ at the $1\%$ one-tailed level, $r_{\text{crit}} = 0.7155$.
In part (b)(ii), $0.5494$ is the critical value at the $5\%$ level. The question specifically asked for a test at the $1\%$ level ($r_{\text{crit}} = 0.7155$).

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: PMCC Measures Linearity Only
bradley_insight.content: A high correlation of $r = 0.885$ does not mean the relationship is linear! As this problem illustrates, a curved exponential curve can produce a misleadingly depressed PMCC. Transforming variables to achieve linearity is the proper mathematical tool for modelling power and exponential laws.

question:
A materials engineer investigates the effect of curing temperature, $x\text{ }^\circ\text{C}$, on the tensile strength, $y\text{ MPa}$, of a new composite polymer. The experiment is conducted at $10$ temperatures between $12^\circ\text{C}$ and $50^\circ\text{C}$.
The equation of the least-squares regression line of $y$ on $x$ is:$$y = 10.5 + 0.710x$$(a) Give an interpretation of:
 (i) the gradient ($0.710$), in the context of the experiment,
 (ii) the intercept ($10.5$), commenting on whether it has a sensible physical interpretation.

(b) The engineer uses the regression equation to estimate the tensile strength for a curing temperature of:
 (i) $30^\circ\text{C}$,
 (ii) $65^\circ\text{C}$.

(c) Comment on the reliability of each of your estimates in part (b).

(d) A technician claims that increasing the curing temperature causes the increase in tensile strength. Explain why a strong statistical correlation does not necessarily prove causality.
steps:
(a)(i) Interpretation of the gradient:

For every $1^\circ\text{C}$ increase in curing temperature, the model predicts an increase of $0.710\text{ MPa}$ in the tensile strength of the polymer.

(a)(ii) Interpretation of the intercept:

The intercept $10.5\text{ MPa}$ represents the predicted tensile strength at a curing temperature of $0^\circ\text{C}$. However, this may not be physically meaningful because the polymer resin might not cure or set at $0^\circ\text{C}$, and $0^\circ\text{C}$ lies well outside the experimental range $[12, 50]$.

(b)(i) Estimate for $x = 30^\circ\text{C}$:

Substituting $x = 30$ into the regression line:\begin{aligned} y &= 10.5 + 0.710(30) \cr &= 10.5 + 21.3 \cr &= 31.8\text{ MPa} \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Estimate for $x = 65^\circ\text{C}$:

Substituting $x = 65$ into the regression line:\begin{aligned} y &= 10.5 + 0.710(65) \cr &= 10.5 + 46.15 \cr &= 56.65\text{ MPa} \end{aligned}

(c) Reliability of estimates:

• The estimate at $30^\circ\text{C}$ is reliable because it is an interpolation within the experimental range $[12, 50]$.
• The estimate at $65^\circ\text{C}$ is unreliable because it is an extrapolation far beyond the experimental range, where the polymer may degrade or change state.

(d) Correlation versus causality:

Correlation indicates an association between two variables, but it does not prove cause and effect. The observed relationship could be driven by a confounding third variable (e.g. chemical reaction rate or pressure), or the material structure could alter at higher temperatures.
Final Answer: (b)(i) $31.8\text{ MPa}$, (ii) $56.65\text{ MPa}$, (c) (i) Reliable, (ii) Unreliable

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), predicting at $65^\circ\text{C}$ is an extrapolation outside the range of observed data $[12, 50]$. We cannot assume the linear relationship continues beyond the measured bounds, making it unreliable.
In part (b)(i), you computed $0.710 \times 30 = 21.3$ and added an incorrect constant instead of $10.5 + 21.3 = 31.8\text{ MPa}$.
In part (c), you reversed the definitions of interpolation and extrapolation. Interpolation within the domain is reliable; extrapolation beyond it is unreliable.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: The Danger of Extrapolation
bradley_insight.content: Examiners love testing extrapolation. Even if a linear regression model has an $r$ value close to $1$, extending the line beyond the observed range of explanatory values ($x > 50$) assumes without justification that physical properties do not alter. Always state that extrapolation is unreliable.

question:
A meteorologist investigates the relationship between altitude, $h$ (in hundreds of metres above sea level), and atmospheric temperature, $T\text{ (}^\circ\text{C)}$, on a mountain range. Measurements are recorded simultaneously at $12$ weather stations:
The summary statistics for the $12$ pairs of observations are:\begin{aligned} \sum h &= 156 \cr \sum T &= 87.5 \cr \sum h^2 &= 2608 \cr \sum T^2 &= 1118.75 \cr \sum hT &= 761.5 \end{aligned}(a) Calculate:
 (i) $S_{hh}$, $S_{TT}$, and $S_{hT}$,
 (ii) the product moment correlation coefficient, $r$, between $h$ and $T$.

(b) Stating your hypotheses clearly, test at the $1\%$ significance level whether there is evidence of negative correlation between altitude and temperature.

(c) State the effect on the value of $r$ if the temperature had been recorded in degrees Fahrenheit ($F = 1.8T + 32$) instead of degrees Celsius.
steps:
(a)(i) Calculating summary sums of squares:

Using the standard formulas with $n = 12$:\begin{aligned} S_{hh} &= \sum h^2 - \dfrac{(\sum h)^2}{n} \cr &= 2608 - \dfrac{156^2}{12} \cr &= 2608 - 2028 \cr &= 580 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} S_{TT} &= \sum T^2 - \dfrac{(\sum T)^2}{n} \cr &= 1118.75 - \dfrac{87.5^2}{12} \cr &= 1118.75 - 638.02 \cr &= 480.73 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} S_{hT} &= \sum hT - \dfrac{(\sum h)(\sum T)}{n} \cr &= 761.5 - \dfrac{156 \times 87.5}{12} \cr &= 761.5 - 1137.5 \cr &= -376 \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Calculating the PMCC $r$:

Applying the correlation formula:\begin{aligned} r &= \dfrac{S_{hT}}{\sqrt{S_{hh} S_{TT}}} \cr &= \dfrac{-376}{\sqrt{580 \times 480.73}} \cr &= \dfrac{-376}{\sqrt{278823.4}} \cr &= \dfrac{-376}{528.04} \cr &\approx -0.712 \end{aligned}

(b) One-tailed hypothesis test for negative correlation:

State the hypotheses:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \rho = 0 \cr &H_1: \rho < 0 \end{aligned}For a one-tailed test with sample size $n = 12$ at the $1\%$ significance level, the critical value from statistical tables is:\begin{aligned} r_{\text{crit}} = -0.6581 \end{aligned}Comparing the test statistic:\begin{aligned} -0.712 < -0.6581 \end{aligned}Since $r < r_{\text{crit}}$, the test statistic lies in the critical region. We reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $1\%$ level that there is a negative correlation between altitude and temperature.

(c) Effect of linear coding on $r$:

The linear transformation $F = 1.8T + 32$ is a positive linear scaling ($1.8 > 0$). The product moment correlation coefficient is invariant under positive linear transformations, so the value of $r$ remains completely unchanged ($r = -0.712$).

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), $-0.7079$ is the two-tailed $1\%$ critical value. The question asks whether there is evidence of negative correlation, which is a one-tailed test with critical value $-0.6581$.
In part (a)(ii), you omitted the negative sign on $S_{hT} = -376$. Since temperature decreases as altitude increases, the correlation coefficient must be negative ($r = -0.712$).
In part (c), linear coding does not scale the PMCC. The product moment correlation coefficient is dimensionless and completely invariant under positive linear transformations.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Coding Invariance of Correlation
bradley_insight.content: A classic revision test: if $Y' = aY + b$ with $a > 0$, the correlation coefficient $r$ remains identical! The units cancel completely in the fraction $\dfrac{S_{xY'}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} S_{Y'Y'}}}$. Only if you multiply by a negative scale factor ($a < 0$) would the sign of $r$ flip.

question:
(a) Explain the difference between a census and a sample.

(b) A local council transport officer wishes to investigate the commuting habits of secondary school teachers working across a county.

To obtain a sample, she interviews adults dressed in professional attire entering St Jude’s High School on a Wednesday morning at 8:45 am.

Give two reasons to explain why this sampling procedure is not satisfactory.
steps:
(a) Difference between a census and a sample:

• A census gathers data from every single member of the target population.
• A sample gathers data from a selected subset or part of the population to draw inferences about the whole.

(b) Evaluating the sampling procedure:

The procedure is unsatisfactory for several reasons:

1. Geographical / institutional bias: Surveying only one specific school (St Jude’s High School) is not representative of teachers across the entire county, whose commuting patterns (such as rural vs urban transit) may differ substantially.

2. Selection / observational bias: Selecting individuals based on 'professional attire' is subjective and unreliable. It may exclude teachers wearing practical or casual dress (e.g. PE, science, or art teachers) while mistakenly interviewing non-teaching staff (e.g. administrative staff, governors, or visiting parents).

3. Time / opportunity bias: Surveying only at 8:45 am on a single weekday excludes teachers arriving earlier (e.g. 7:30–8:00 am), part-time staff arriving later, or staff who are already inside the building.
Final Answer: (a) Census observes every member; sample observes a subset, (b) Non-representative of county and subjective attire filter

pi_options.ans: (a) Census is an estimate; sample is exact, (b) Non-representative of county and subjective attire filter
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you reversed the definitions. A census collects data from the entire population and gives an exact picture (free from sampling error), whereas a sample provides an estimate.

pi_options.ans: (a) Census observes every member; sample observes a subset, (b) Sample size is too large and teachers are difficult to interview
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), the flaw is not the sample size or difficulty of interviewing, but the severe bias introduced by opportunity sampling at a single school location using visual clothing criteria.

pi_options.ans: (a) Census observes every member; sample observes a subset, (b) A census should always be carried out instead of a sample
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), taking a sample is completely acceptable; the issue lies in the flawed, non-random sampling methodology used by the officer.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Identifying Sampling Bias
bradley_insight.content: When exam boards ask why a sampling method is flawed, look for three classic traps: location bias (only one site surveyed), time bias (only one restrictive time slot), and inclusion criteria (an arbitrary visual filter like 'professional attire' that does not map directly to the target population).

question:
(a) State one advantage and one disadvantage of carrying out a census rather than taking a sample.

(b) Define what is meant by a sampling frame.

(c) A logistics firm employs $480$ warehouse operatives, each assigned a payroll number from $1$ to $480$. The operations director wishes to select a systematic sample of $30$ operatives to inspect safety equipment.
 (i) Describe how this systematic sample should be selected.
 (ii) Given that the second operative selected has payroll number $23$, determine the payroll numbers of the first and third operatives selected.
steps:
(a) Advantage and disadvantage of a census:

• Advantage: It provides completely accurate information about the population with zero sampling error.
• Disadvantage: It is time-consuming, expensive, and impractical if testing destroys the items.

(b) Definition of a sampling frame:

A sampling frame is an exhaustive, uniquely identifiable list of all members or sampling units in the population from which a sample is drawn.

(c)(i) Procedure for systematic sampling:

1. Calculate the sampling interval $k$:\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{N}{n} \cr &= \dfrac{480}{30} \cr &= 16 \end{aligned}2. Generate a random integer $r$ between $1$ and $16$ inclusive to serve as the starting point.
3. Select the operative numbered $r$, and then select every $16^{\text{th}}$ operative thereafter: $r, r + 16, r + 32, \dots$

(c)(ii) Finding the first and third operative numbers:

Since the second operative is numbered $23$ and the constant interval is $k = 16$:\begin{aligned} \text{First} &= 23 - 16 \cr &= 7 \end{aligned}For the third operative:\begin{aligned} \text{Third} &= 23 + 16 \cr &= 39 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Advantage: Completely accurate; Disadvantage: Expensive/time-consuming, (b) List of all population members, (c)(i) Interval $k = 16$, (ii) First: $7$; Third: $39$

pi_options.ans: (a) Advantage: Completely accurate; Disadvantage: Expensive/time-consuming, (b) The size of the sample, (c)(i) Interval $k = 16$, (ii) First: $7$; Third: $39$
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), a sampling frame is not the sample size; it is the physical or electronic list of all population units (e.g. an electoral register or staff payroll list) from which the sample is drawn.

pi_options.ans: (a) Advantage: Completely accurate; Disadvantage: Expensive/time-consuming, (b) List of all population members, (c)(i) Interval $k = 16$, (ii) First: $15$; Third: $31$
pi_options.feedback: In part (c)(ii), you used an incorrect interval of $8$ instead of $k = 16$. With $k = 16$, the first number is $23 - 16 = 7$ and the third is $23 + 16 = 39$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Advantage: Cheap to carry out; Disadvantage: Introduces bias, (b) List of all population members, (c)(i) Interval $k = 16$, (ii) First: $7$; Third: $39$
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), a census is typically very expensive and time-consuming, not cheap. Its primary strength is complete accuracy and the absence of sampling error.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Describing Systematic Sampling
bradley_insight.content: To earn full marks when describing systematic sampling, you must explicitly state three steps: (1) calculating the interval $k = \dfrac{N}{n}$, (2) choosing a random starting number between $1$ and $k$, and (3) taking every $k^{\text{th}}$ member thereafter.

question:
A Sixth Form college has $600$ students enrolled across Year 12 and Year 13. The distribution of students by year group and study pathway is shown in the table below:
Year GroupAcademicVocational
Year 1221090
Year 13180120
A researcher wishes to take a sample of $60$ students, stratified by Year Group and Study Pathway.

(a) Calculate the number of students that should be selected from each of the four categories.

(b) State one advantage of using stratified sampling rather than simple random sampling in this scenario.

(c) Describe how quota sampling differs from stratified sampling, and state one disadvantage of quota sampling.
steps:
(a) Calculating stratified sample sizes:

The overall population size is $N = 600$, and the sample size is $n = 60$. The constant sampling fraction is:\begin{aligned} \text{Fraction} &= \dfrac{60}{600} \cr &= 0.1 \end{aligned}Multiplying each stratum frequency by $0.1$:\begin{aligned} \text{Year 12 Academic} &= 210 \times 0.1 \cr &= 21 \cr \text{Year 12 Vocational} &= 90 \times 0.1\cr & = 9 \cr \text{Year 13 Academic} &= 180 \times 0.1\cr & = 18 \cr \text{Year 13 Vocational} &= 120 \times 0.1\cr & = 12 \end{aligned}Checking the sum: $21 + 9 + 18 + 12 = 60$.

(b) Advantage of stratified sampling:

It guarantees that every year group and pathway is represented in the exact proportion in which it exists in the population, eliminating the risk of under-representing smaller subsets.

(c) Quota sampling vs stratified sampling:

• Difference: In stratified sampling, participants within each stratum are chosen using a random sampling method from an existing sampling frame. In quota sampling, participants are chosen non-randomly (often via opportunity sampling by an interviewer) until the predetermined quota for each stratum is filled.
• Disadvantage of quota sampling: It introduces interviewer bias, non-response cannot be measured, and it is non-random.
Final Answer: (a) Y12 Acad: $21$, Y12 Voc: $9$, Y13 Acad: $18$, Y13 Voc: $12$, (b) Preserves exact population proportions, (c) Quota is non-random; introduces interviewer bias

pi_options.ans: (a) Y12 Acad: $15$, Y12 Voc: $15$, Y13 Acad: $15$, Y13 Voc: $15$, (b) Preserves exact population proportions, (c) Quota is non-random; introduces interviewer bias
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), you took equal sample sizes of $15$ from each category. Stratified sampling requires proportional allocation according to the size of each subgroup in the population.

pi_options.ans: (a) Y12 Acad: $21$, Y12 Voc: $9$, Y13 Acad: $18$, Y13 Voc: $12$, (b) It is faster and requires no sampling frame, (c) Quota is non-random; introduces interviewer bias
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), stratified sampling requires an exhaustive sampling frame and is often slower and more complex than simple random sampling. Its main advantage is proportional representation.

pi_options.ans: (a) Y12 Acad: $21$, Y12 Voc: $9$, Y13 Acad: $18$, Y13 Voc: $12$, (b) Preserves exact population proportions, (c) Quota sampling is always completely random
pi_options.feedback: In part (c), quota sampling is strictly a non-random sampling technique because the interviewer decides whom to question until each category quota is filled.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Stratified vs Quota Distinction
bradley_insight.content: Examiners frequently test the contrast between stratified and quota sampling. Both divide the population into mutually exclusive subgroups, but stratified sampling uses a random selection method from an existing list (sampling frame), whereas quota sampling uses non-random selection and requires no sampling frame.

question:
A dental practice has $1200$ registered patients listed in alphabetical order on its electronic database. The practice manager wishes to conduct a patient satisfaction survey using a simple random sample of $50$ patients.

(a) Describe how the practice manager could select this simple random sample using a random number generator.

(b) The practice posts satisfaction questionnaires to the $50$ selected patients, but only $18$ completed questionnaires are returned.
 (i) State the statistical term used to describe this problem.
 (ii) Explain why this low response rate may introduce bias into the survey results.

(c) Suggest an alternative sampling method that could be used if no sampling frame was available.
steps:
(a) Selecting a simple random sample:

1. Allocate a unique integer from $1$ to $1200$ to each patient on the database.
2. Use a computer random number generator (or calculator) to generate integers between $1$ and $1200$.
3. Discard any duplicate numbers until $50$ distinct numbers are obtained.
4. Select the patients whose assigned numbers correspond to these $50$ generated numbers.

(b)(i) Statistical term for unreturned surveys:

Non-response (or non-response bias).

(b)(ii) Why non-response introduces bias:

Those patients who take the time to complete and return the survey may not be representative of the typical patient population. For example, individuals with extreme views (very dissatisfied or exceptionally pleased patients) are far more motivated to respond, distorting the satisfaction score.

(c) Alternative method without a sampling frame:

Quota sampling (or opportunity / convenience sampling).
Final Answer: (a) Number $1$ to $1200$, generate $50$ unique numbers, (b)(i) Non-response, (ii) Extreme views over-represented, (c) Quota or opportunity sampling

pi_options.ans: (a) Number $1$ to $1200$, pick first $50$, (b)(i) Non-response, (ii) Extreme views over-represented, (c) Quota or opportunity sampling
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), taking the first $50$ patients is an opportunity/convenience sample from an alphabetical list, which gives patients with later surnames zero chance of selection.

pi_options.ans: (a) Number $1$ to $1200$, generate $50$ unique numbers, (b)(i) Measurement error, (ii) Extreme views over-represented, (c) Quota or opportunity sampling
pi_options.feedback: In part (b)(i), failure to return postal surveys is termed 'non-response', not measurement error. Measurement error refers to inaccuracies in recording data values.

pi_options.ans: (a) Number $1$ to $1200$, generate $50$ unique numbers, (b)(i) Non-response, (ii) Extreme views over-represented, (c) Stratified sampling
pi_options.feedback: In part (c), stratified sampling strictly requires an existing sampling frame so that participants can be randomly chosen from each stratum.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Remember to Ignore Duplicates
bradley_insight.content: Whenever you describe selecting a random sample using random numbers, you must explicitly write that repeat numbers (duplicates) must be ignored or discarded. Without that phrase, you risk losing a method mark under strict mark schemes.

question:
