Sampling without replacement:\begin{aligned} P(RR) &= \dfrac{4}{n} \times \dfrac{3}{n - 1} \cr &= \dfrac{12}{n(n - 1)} \end{aligned}

(b)(i) Forming the quadratic equation:

Setting the probability equal to $\dfrac{2}{15}$:\begin{aligned} &\dfrac{12}{n^2 - n} = \dfrac{2}{15} \cr &12 \times 15 = 2(n^2 - n) \cr &180 = 2n^2 - 2n \cr &2n^2 - 2n - 180 = 0 \cr &n^2 - n - 90 = 0 \end{aligned}

(b)(ii) Finding $n$ and yellow counters:

Factorising the quadratic:\begin{aligned} (n - 10)(n + 9) = 0 \end{aligned}Since $n > 0$, we reject $n = -9$:\begin{aligned} n = 10 \end{aligned}The number of yellow counters is:\begin{aligned} 10 - 4 = 6 \end{aligned}

(c)(i) Conditional probability for third counter:

Given that the first two counters drawn were yellow, $4$ red and $4$ yellow counters remain out of $8$ counters:\begin{aligned} &P(R_3 \mid Y_1 \cap Y_2) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4}{8} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2} \cr &\quad = 0.5 \end{aligned}

(c)(ii) Exactly one red counter in three draws:

The single red counter can be drawn in three mutually exclusive positions ($RYY$, $YRY$, or $YYR$):\begin{aligned} &P(RYY) \cr &\quad = \dfrac{4}{10} \times \dfrac{6}{9} \times \dfrac{5}{8} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{120}{720} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}Since all three orders have equal probability:\begin{aligned} &P(\text{exactly } 1R) \cr &\quad = 3 \times \dfrac{1}{6} \cr &\quad = \dfrac{1}{2} \cr &\quad = 0.5 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $\dfrac{12}{n(n - 1)}$, (b)(i) $n^2 - n - 90 = 0$, (ii) $10$ counters ($6$ yellow), (c)(i) $0.5$, (ii) $0.5$

pi_options.feedback: In part (c)(ii), $\dfrac{1}{6}$ accounts for only one specific sequence ($RYY$). The red counter can be first, second, or third, so you must multiply by $3$ to give $\dfrac{3}{6} = 0.5$.
In part (b)(ii), solving $(n - 10)(n + 9) = 0$ gives $n = 10$. The total number of counters must be positive, so $n = 10$, leaving $6$ yellow counters.
In part (c)(i), knowing that two yellow counters were removed leaves $8$ counters in total, of which $4$ are red: $\dfrac{4}{8} = 0.5$, not $\dfrac{4}{10} = 0.4$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Direct Sub-population Conditioning
bradley_insight.content: For part (c)(i), never set up a complicated Bayes formula when the history is already completely known. If the first two draws were yellow, simply remove two yellow counters from the bag. You are left with $4$ red and $4$ yellow, making the probability $\dfrac{4}{8} = 0.5$ immediately.

question:
(a) A precision manufacturing firm produces structural steel rods. The length of a rod, $X\text{ cm}$, is modelled by a normal distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$.

Quality control testing reveals that $10\%$ of the rods exceed $25.4\text{ cm}$ in length and that $20\%$ of the rods are shorter than $24.2\text{ cm}$.

 (i) Find the values of $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$.

A specialised modular assembly requires rods that are less than $25.0\text{ cm}$ in length.

 (ii) Calculate the percentage of steel rods that will be too long for this assembly.

(b) Give one reason why the normal distribution is widely used in statistical modelling.
steps:
(a)(i) Finding $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$:

For the upper tail where $10\%$ exceed $25.4\text{ cm}$:\begin{aligned} P(X > 25.4) &= 0.10 \cr \dfrac{25.4 - \mu}{\sigma} &= 1.2816 \cr 25.4 &= \mu + 1.2816\sigma \end{aligned}For the lower tail where $20\%$ are below $24.2\text{ cm}$:\begin{aligned} P(X < 24.2) &= 0.20 \cr \dfrac{24.2 - \mu}{\sigma} &= -0.8416 \cr 24.2 &= \mu - 0.8416\sigma \end{aligned}Subtracting the two equations:\begin{aligned} 1.2 &= 2.1232\sigma \cr \sigma &= \dfrac{1.2}{2.1232} \cr &\approx 0.5652 \cr \sigma^2 &\approx 0.319 \end{aligned}Substituting $\sigma$ to find $\mu$:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 24.2 \cr &\quad + 0.8416(0.5652) \cr &\approx 24.676 \cr &\approx 24.7\text{ cm} \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Percentage too long for assembly:

Too long means length $X > 25.0\text{ cm}$:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{25.0 - 24.676}{0.5652} \cr &\approx 0.573 \end{aligned}Evaluating the upper-tail probability:\begin{aligned} P(X > 25.0) &= 1 - \Phi(0.573) \cr &= 1 - 0.7167 \cr &= 0.2833 \cr &= 28.3\% \end{aligned}

(b) Importance of the normal distribution:

By the Central Limit Theorem, the distribution of the sample mean (or the sum of many independent random effects) tends towards a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the underlying population shape.
Final Answer: (a)(i) $\mu = 24.7\text{ cm}$, $\sigma^2 = 0.319$, (ii) $28.3\%$, (b) Central Limit Theorem

pi_options.feedback: In part (a)(i), $0.565$ is the standard deviation $\sigma$. The question asks for the variance $\sigma^2$, which is $0.5652^2 \approx 0.319$.
In part (a)(ii), $71.7\%$ is the percentage that are acceptable ($X < 25.0$). The question asks for the percentage that are too long ($X > 25.0$), which is $100\% - 71.7\% = 28.3\%$.
In part (a)(i), you used a positive $z$-value for the lower tail ($20\%$). Because $24.2$ lies below the mean, $z = -0.8416$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: State Variance When Asked for Variance
bradley_insight.content: A frequent lost mark in part (a)(i) is providing $\sigma = 0.565$ and forgetting to square it. When an exam question specifies $\sigma^2$, always compute both: $\sigma = 0.565\text{ cm}$ and $\sigma^2 = 0.319\text{ cm}^2$.

question:
An engineering factory manufactures steel bolts and matching nuts.
The mass of a bolt, $B\text{ g}$, is modelled by $B \sim \text{N}(45.0, 1.8^2)$.
The mass of a nut, $N\text{ g}$, is modelled by $N \sim \text{N}(22.0, 1.2^2)$.
Bolts and nuts are manufactured independently.

(a) A single bolt and a single nut are fastened together. Find the probability that their combined mass exceeds $70.0\text{ g}$.

(b) A standard trade pack contains $10$ bolts and $10$ nuts packed into an empty container. The mass of the empty container, $C\text{ g}$, is modelled by $C \sim \text{N}(60.0, 4.0^2)$ independently of the contents.
Find the probability that the total mass of a randomly chosen trade pack exceeds $740\text{ g}$.

(c) Find the probability that the mass of a randomly chosen bolt is more than twice the mass of a randomly chosen nut.
steps:
(a) Combined mass of one bolt and one nut:

Let $T = B + N$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(T) &= 45.0 + 22.0 \cr &= 67.0\text{ g} \end{aligned}Since $B$ and $N$ are independent, add their variances:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(T) &= 1.8^2 + 1.2^2 \cr &= 3.24 + 1.44 \cr &= 4.68 \end{aligned}So $T \sim \text{N}(67.0, 4.68)$. Standardising for $T > 70.0$:\begin{aligned} P(T > 70.0) &= 1 - \Phi\left(\dfrac{70 - 67}{\sqrt{4.68}}\right) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(1.387) \cr &= 1 - 0.9173 \cr &= 0.0827 \end{aligned}

(b) Total mass of a trade pack:

Let $W = \sum_{i=1}^{10} B_i + \sum_{i=1}^{10} N_i + C$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(W) &= 10(45) + 10(22) \cr &\quad + 60 \cr &= 730\text{ g} \end{aligned}For the variance, sum the individual variances:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(W) &= 10(1.8^2) \cr &\quad + 10(1.2^2) \cr &\quad + 4.0^2 \cr &= 32.4 + 14.4 \cr &\quad + 16.0 \cr &= 62.8 \end{aligned}Standardising for $W > 740$:\begin{aligned} P(W > 740) &= 1 - \Phi\left(\dfrac{740 - 730}{\sqrt{62.8}}\right) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(1.262) \cr &= 1 - 0.8965 \cr &= 0.1035 \end{aligned}

(c) Bolt mass more than twice nut mass:

We require $P(B > 2N)$, which rearranges to $P(B - 2N > 0)$.

Let $D = B - 2N$:\begin{aligned} \text{E}(D) &= 45 - 2(22) \cr &= 1\text{ g} \end{aligned}Applying the linear variance rule $$\text{Var}(aX + bY)$$ $$= a^2\text{Var}(X) + b^2\text{Var}(Y)$$:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(D) &= 1.8^2 + (-2)^2(1.2^2) \cr &= 3.24 + 4(1.44) \cr &= 3.24 + 5.76 \cr &= 9.0 \end{aligned}So $\sigma_D = \sqrt{9.0} = 3.0$. Standardising for $D > 0$:\begin{aligned} P(D > 0) &= P\left(Z > \dfrac{0 - 1}{3.0}\right) \cr &= P(Z > -0.333) \cr &= \Phi(0.333) \cr &= 0.6305 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you calculated $1 - \Phi(0.333) = 0.3695$. Because $z = -0.333$ is negative, $P(Z > -0.333) = \Phi(0.333) = 0.6305$.
In part (b), you evaluated $\text{Var}(10B) = 10^2(1.8^2) = 324$. Because the pack contains $10$ independent bolts, you must add $10$ separate variances: $10 \times 1.8^2 = 32.4$.
In part (a), you added the standard deviations directly ($1.8 + 1.2 = 3.0$). For independent variables, variances add: $\sigma^2 = 1.8^2 + 1.2^2 = 4.68$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Sum of 10 Items vs 10 Times One Item
bradley_insight.content: A classic trap is confusing the sum of $10$ independent items with scaling one item by $10$. When packing $10$ independent bolts, $\text{Var}(B_1 + \dots + B_{10}) = 10\text{Var}(B) = 32.4$. In contrast, multiplying a single bolt by $10$ gives $\text{Var}(10B) = 10^2\text{Var}(B) = 324$.

question:
A regional dairy fills cartons of fresh milk. The volume dispensed, $X\text{ ml}$, is normally distributed with a known population standard deviation of $\sigma = 12.0\text{ ml}$ and a nominal target mean of $\mu = 1000\text{ ml}$.

Following maintenance work, the production manager suspects that the machine is underfilling cartons. A random sample of $25$ cartons is taken, yielding a sample mean volume of $\bar{x} = 995.2\text{ ml}$.

(a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses to test the manager's suspicion.

(b) State the distribution of the sample mean, $\bar{X}$, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

(c) Test, at the $2.5\%$ level of significance, whether there is evidence that the machine is underfilling cartons.

(d) Determine the critical value of the sample mean, $\bar{x}$, for this test at the $2.5\%$ level of significance.

(e) State the probability of making a Type I error in this test.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

The manager specifically suspects underfilling, so the test is one-tailed:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \mu = 1000 \cr &H_1: \mu < 1000 \end{aligned}

(b) Distribution of $\bar{X}$ under $H_0$:

For sample size $n = 25$:\begin{aligned} \bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(1000, \dfrac{12.0^2}{25}\right) \end{aligned}The standard error is:\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\bar{x}} &= \dfrac{12.0}{\sqrt{25}} \cr &= \dfrac{12.0}{5} \cr &= 2.4\text{ ml} \end{aligned}So $\bar{X} \sim \text{N}(1000, 2.4^2)$.

(c) Test statistic and conclusion:

Standardising the observed sample mean:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{995.2 - 1000}{2.4} \cr &= \dfrac{-4.8}{2.4} \cr &= -2.0 \end{aligned}For a lower-tail test at the $2.5\%$ significance level, the critical value is:\begin{aligned} z_{\text{crit}} = -1.96 \end{aligned}Comparing the test statistic:\begin{aligned} -2.0 < -1.96 \end{aligned}Because $-2.0$ falls inside the critical region, we reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $2.5\%$ level that the machine is underfilling cartons.

(d) Critical value of $\bar{x}$:

Using the critical $z$-value:\begin{aligned} \bar{x}_{\text{crit}} &= 1000 - 1.96(2.4) \cr &= 1000 - 4.704 \cr &= 995.3\text{ ml} \end{aligned}

(e) Probability of a Type I error:

The probability of a Type I error (rejecting $H_0$ when it is actually true) is precisely the significance level of the test: $0.025$ (or $2.5\%$).

pi_options.feedback: In part (a), the manager suspects underfilling, requiring a one-tailed test $H_1: \mu < 1000$. A two-tailed test $H_1: \mu \neq 1000$ would only be used if testing for any change in fill volume.
In part (b), you used the population variance $\sigma^2 = 12^2$ instead of the sample mean variance $\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n} = \dfrac{12^2}{25} = 2.4^2$.
In part (c), $-2.0$ is more extreme than $-1.96$, so $H_0$ must be rejected. In part (e), the probability of a Type I error equals the chosen significance level of $0.025$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Type I Error Equals Significance Level
bradley_insight.content: A Type I error is defined as rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true. The probability of this happening is simply the size of the critical region, which is always equal to the significance level $\alpha$ (here, $0.025$).

question:
The number of incoming emergency calls received per hour by an emergency dispatch switchboard follows a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda = 36$.

Let $Y$ denote the total number of emergency calls received during a $2$-hour shift.

(a) State the exact distribution of $Y$, including its parameter.

(b) Explain why a normal distribution provides an appropriate approximation for the distribution of $Y$.

(c) State the mean and the variance of the approximating normal distribution.

(d) Using the normal approximation with a continuity correction, find the probability that the dispatch switchboard receives:
 (i) at least $80$ calls during a $2$-hour shift,
 (ii) between $65$ and $75$ calls inclusive during a $2$-hour shift.
steps:
(a) Exact distribution of $Y$:

For a $2$-hour interval, the mean scales proportionally: $\lambda = 36 \times 2 = 72$:\begin{aligned} Y \sim \text{Po}(72) \end{aligned}

(b) Justifying normal approximation:

A normal approximation is appropriate because the Poisson parameter $\lambda = 72$ is large (typically $\lambda > 15$).

(c) Parameters of approximating distribution:

For a Poisson distribution, the mean and variance are both equal to $\lambda$:\begin{aligned} \mu &= 72 \cr \sigma^2 &= 72 \end{aligned}So the approximating distribution is $X \sim \text{N}(72, 72)$, with $\sigma = \sqrt{72} \approx 8.485$.

(d)(i) Probability of at least $80$ calls:

Applying the continuity correction for $Y \ge 80$ gives $X > 79.5$:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{79.5 - 72}{\sqrt{72}} \cr &= \dfrac{7.5}{8.485} \cr &\approx 0.884 \end{aligned}Evaluating the upper-tail probability:\begin{aligned} P(Y \ge 80) &\approx 1 - \Phi(0.884) \cr &= 1 - 0.8117 \cr &= 0.1883 \cr &\approx 0.188 \end{aligned}

(d)(ii) Probability between $65$ and $75$ calls inclusive:

Applying continuity corrections for $65 \le Y \le 75$ gives $64.5 < X < 75.5$:\begin{aligned} z_1 &= \dfrac{64.5 - 72}{8.485} \cr &= \dfrac{-7.5}{8.485} \cr &\approx -0.884 \cr z_2 &= \dfrac{75.5 - 72}{8.485} \cr &= \dfrac{3.5}{8.485} \cr &\approx 0.412 \end{aligned}Evaluating the interval probability:\begin{aligned} &P(-0.884 < Z < 0.412) \cr &\quad = \Phi(0.412) - \Phi(-0.884) \cr &\quad = 0.6599 - (1 - 0.8117) \cr &\quad = 0.6599 - 0.1883 \cr &\quad = 0.4716 \cr &\quad \approx 0.472 \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (d)(i), you used $80.5$ for the continuity correction. 'At least $80$' includes $80$, so the continuous interval starts at $79.5$, giving $z = 0.884$ and probability $0.188$.
In part (d)(ii), you shrunk the interval to $[65.5, 74.5]$. Because the bounds are inclusive, the continuous region expands to $[64.5, 75.5]$.
In part (a), you did not adjust the rate parameter for a $2$-hour period. The hourly rate is $36$, so for $2$ hours the parameter is $\lambda = 36 \times 2 = 72$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Poisson Mean and Variance Equality
bradley_insight.content: A key feature of the Poisson distribution is that its mean and variance are identical: $\text{E}(Y) = \text{Var}(Y) = \lambda$. When approximating $\text{Po}(72)$ with a normal distribution, the standard deviation is always $\sqrt{\lambda} = \sqrt{72}$.

question:
The external diameter, $D\text{ mm}$, of precision ball bearings produced by an automated lathe is modelled by a normal distribution with mean $\mu = 15.00\text{ mm}$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 0.08\text{ mm}$.

(a) Find the probability that a randomly selected ball bearing has a diameter within $0.10\text{ mm}$ of the target mean.

(b) Bearings are considered acceptable for aerospace use if their diameter lies within the symmetric tolerance interval $[15.00 - k, 15.00 + k]$. Given that $98\%$ of the manufactured bearings are acceptable, determine the value of $k$ to three significant figures.

(c) A random sample of $n$ ball bearings is selected from the production line. Find the minimum sample size, $n$, required such that the probability that the sample mean diameter $\bar{D}$ lies within $0.02\text{ mm}$ of the true population mean is at least $0.95$.
steps:
(a) Probability within $0.10\text{ mm}$ of the mean:

We require $P(14.90 < D < 15.10)$:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{0.10}{0.08} \cr &= 1.25 \end{aligned}Using the symmetry of the standard normal distribution:\begin{aligned} & P(-1.25 < Z < 1.25) \cr & \qquad= 2\Phi(1.25) - 1 \cr & \qquad= 2(0.8944) - 1 \cr & \qquad= 1.7888 - 1 \cr & \qquad= 0.7888 \end{aligned}

(b) Finding tolerance limit $k$ for $98\%$ acceptability:

A central area of $0.98$ leaves $0.01$ in each tail, so $\Phi(z) = 0.99$:\begin{aligned} z = 2.326 \end{aligned}Relating $z$ to $k$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{k}{0.08} &= 2.326 \cr k &= 2.326 \times 0.08 \cr &= 0.18608 \cr &\approx 0.186\text{ mm} \end{aligned}

(c) Determining minimum sample size $n$:

The sample mean follows $\bar{D} \sim \text{N}\left(15.00, \dfrac{0.08^2}{n}\right)$. We require:\begin{aligned} P(|\bar{D} - 15.00| < 0.02) \ge 0.95 \end{aligned}Standardising the boundary:\begin{aligned} z = \dfrac{0.02}{0.08 / \sqrt{n}} \end{aligned}For a central probability of $0.95$, the critical $z$-value is $1.96$:\begin{aligned} \dfrac{0.02}{0.08 / \sqrt{n}} &\ge 1.96 \cr 0.25\sqrt{n} &\ge 1.96 \cr \sqrt{n} &\ge \dfrac{1.96}{0.25} \cr \sqrt{n} &\ge 7.84 \cr n &\ge 7.84^2 \cr n &\ge 61.4656 \end{aligned}Since $n$ must be an integer, the minimum sample size is:\begin{aligned} n = 62 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $0.7888$, (b) $k = 0.186\text{ mm}$, (c) $n = 62$

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you used $z = 2.054$ (from a one-tailed $98\%$ value). For a symmetric central interval of $98\%$, the upper tail contains $1\%$, which gives $z = 2.326$ and $k = 0.186\text{ mm}$.
In part (c), rounding down to $61$ gives a probability strictly below $0.95$. Because $n \ge 61.47$, you must round up to the next integer: $n = 62$.
In part (a), $0.8944$ is $\Phi(1.25)$. For the interval between $-1.25$ and $1.25$, you must calculate $2\Phi(1.25) - 1 = 0.7888$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Always Round Sample Sizes Up
bradley_insight.content: Whenever solving an inequality for sample size ($n \ge 61.47$), you must always round up to the next integer, regardless of decimal size. Choosing $n = 61$ would fail the specification, making $n = 62$ the true minimum required sample.

question:
A software company has established that $30\%$ of users who register for a free trial of an application upgrade to a paid subscription within their first month.

A random sample of $12$ new trial users is selected.

(a) Calculate the probability that at least one of these $12$ users upgrades to a paid subscription within their first month.

Following the introduction of an interactive onboarding tutorial, the head of product believes that the proportion of users upgrading to a paid subscription has increased.

A random sample of $12$ new trial users who completed the interactive tutorial is selected. It is found that $7$ of them upgraded to a paid subscription within their first month.

(b) Stating your hypotheses clearly, carry out a hypothesis test at the $5\%$ level of significance to determine whether there is evidence to support the head of product's belief.

(c) Suggest one way in which the design of this statistical test could be improved.
steps:
(a) Probability of at least one upgrade:

Let $X \sim \text{B}(12, 0.30)$ denote the number of users upgrading. Using the complement of zero upgrades:\begin{aligned} P(X \ge 1) &= 1 - P(X = 0) \cr &= 1 - (1 - 0.30)^{12} \cr &= 1 - (0.70)^{12} \cr &= 1 - 0.01384 \cr &= 0.9862 \end{aligned}

(b) Hypothesis test:

State the null and alternative hypotheses, where $p$ is the true population upgrade proportion:\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.30 \cr &H_1: p > 0.30 \end{aligned}Under $H_0$, the test distribution is $X \sim \text{B}(12, 0.30)$.

Calculate the probability of observing $7$ or more upgrades (the upper tail):\begin{aligned} P(X \ge 7) &= 1 - P(X \le 6) \cr &= 1 - 0.9614 \cr &= 0.0386 \end{aligned}Comparing to the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$:\begin{aligned} 0.0386 < 0.05 \end{aligned}Because the $p$-value is less than $0.05$, we reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $5\%$ level to support the head of product's belief that the upgrade proportion has increased.

(c) Improving the test design:

Use a larger sample size ($n > 12$). A larger sample increases the statistical power of the test, reduces the probability of a Type II error, and decreases the granularity of the discrete binomial distribution.
Final Answer: (a) $0.9862$, (b) Reject $H_0$ as $0.0386 < 0.05$, (c) Increase sample size

pi_options.ans: (a) $0.9862$, (b) Do not reject $H_0$ as $0.0386 < 0.05$, (c) Increase sample size
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), when the $p$-value ($0.0386$) is less than the significance level ($0.05$), the decision rule is to reject $H_0$, not accept it.
In part (a), $0.0138$ is $P(X = 0)$. To find the probability of at least one upgrade, you must subtract this from $1$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $0.9862$, (b) Do not reject $H_0$ as $0.0792 > 0.05$, (c) Decrease sample size
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), $P(X \ge 7) = 1 - P(X \le 6) = 0.0386$. In part (c), decreasing the sample size would increase error rates rather than improving the test.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: P-Value vs Critical Region Decision
bradley_insight.content: In a one-tailed upper test, you reject $H_0$ if $P(X \ge x) \le \alpha$. Here, $P(X \ge 7) = 0.0386$, which is strictly less than $0.05$, placing the observation $7$ firmly inside the critical region.

question:
A manufacturing process produces microchips, of which historically $15\%$ have minor cosmetic defects.

An engineering team introduces an upgraded laser-cutting tool intended to reduce the proportion of defective microchips. A random sample of $20$ microchips produced using the new tool is inspected, and exactly $1$ microchip is found to have a defect.

(a) Stating your hypotheses clearly, test at the $5\%$ significance level whether there is evidence that the new tool has reduced the defect rate.

(b) Determine the critical region for this test at the $5\%$ level of significance.

(c) State the probability of committing a Type I error in this test.
steps:
(a) Lower-tail hypothesis test:

State the hypotheses, where $p$ represents the true defect rate:\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.15 \cr &H_1: p < 0.15 \end{aligned}Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(20, 0.15)$, where $X$ is the number of defective microchips.

Calculate the probability of observing $1$ or fewer defects:\begin{aligned} P(X = 0) &= (0.85)^{20} \cr &\approx 0.0388 \end{aligned}\begin{aligned} P(X = 1) &= 20(0.15)(0.85)^{19} \cr &\approx 0.1368 \end{aligned}Summing these probabilities:\begin{aligned} P(X \le 1) &= 0.0388 + 0.1368 \cr &= 0.1756 \end{aligned}Comparing to the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$:\begin{aligned} 0.1756 > 0.05 \end{aligned}Because $0.1756 > 0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to conclude that the new tool has reduced the defect rate.

(b) Determining the critical region:

We find the values in the lower tail where the cumulative probability is less than or equal to $0.05$:\begin{aligned} P(X = 0) &= 0.0388 \le 0.05 \cr P(X \le 1) &= 0.1756 > 0.05 \end{aligned}Therefore, the critical region is:\begin{aligned} X = 0 \end{aligned}

(c) Probability of a Type I error:

A Type I error occurs when $H_0$ is rejected despite being true. This equals the probability of falling into the critical region under $H_0$:\begin{aligned} P(X = 0) = 0.0388 \quad (3.88\%) \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) Do not reject $H_0$ as $0.1756 > 0.05$, (b) $X = 0$, (c) $0.0388$

pi_options.feedback: In part (a), when the $p$-value ($0.1756$) is greater than the significance level ($0.05$), the evidence is not strong enough to reject $H_0$.
In part (b), $P(X \le 1) = 0.1756$, which is greater than $0.05$. Therefore, $X = 1$ cannot be part of the critical region at the $5\%$ level.
In part (c), for a discrete distribution the probability of a Type I error is the actual significance level ($P(X = 0) = 0.0388$), not the nominal $0.05$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Critical Regions in Small Discrete Samples
bradley_insight.content: Notice how strict the critical region becomes with $n = 20$ and $p = 0.15$. Only $X = 0$ achieves a cumulative probability below $0.05$. Observing even a single defect ($X = 1$) pushes the cumulative probability to $0.1756$, falling well outside the rejection zone.

question:
A plant geneticist investigates the inheritance of flower colour in a hybrid cross of sweet peas. Under standard genetic theory, the expected proportion of plants bearing purple flowers is $0.75$.

The geneticist suspects that environmental factors in a new greenhouse may be altering this inheritance ratio. A random sample of $20$ plants is grown in the greenhouse, and $11$ of them produce purple flowers.

(a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses to test whether the true proportion of plants producing purple flowers differs from $0.75$.

(b) Test, at the $5\%$ level of significance, whether there is evidence that the proportion of purple-flowered plants differs from $0.75$.

(c) Determine the critical region for this two-tailed test, allocating as close to $2.5\%$ as possible to each tail, and state the actual significance level of the test.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

Where $p$ is the true proportion of plants with purple flowers:\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.75 \cr &H_1: p \neq 0.75 \end{aligned}

(b) Two-tailed hypothesis test:

Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(20, 0.75)$, where $X$ is the number of purple-flowered plants.

Because the observed value $x = 11$ is less than the expected mean $\text{E}(X) = 20(0.75) = 15$, we evaluate the lower tail:\begin{aligned} P(X \le 11) \end{aligned}Letting $Y = 20 - X \sim \text{B}(20, 0.25)$ denote non-purple plants:\begin{aligned} P(X \le 11) &= P(Y \ge 9) \cr &= 1 - P(Y \le 8) \cr &= 1 - 0.9591 \cr &= 0.0409 \end{aligned}For a two-tailed test, double the one-tailed probability to find the $p$-value:\begin{aligned} p\text{-value} &= 2 \times 0.0409 \cr &= 0.0818 \end{aligned}Comparing to $\alpha = 0.05$:\begin{aligned} 0.0818 > 0.05 \end{aligned}Because the $p$-value exceeds $0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to suggest that the proportion differs from $0.75$.

(c) Determining the critical region:

We allocate up to $0.025$ to each tail.

For the lower tail:\begin{aligned} P(X \le 10) &= P(Y \ge 10) \cr &= 1 - 0.9861 \cr &= 0.0139 \le 0.025 \cr P(X \le 11) &= 0.0409 > 0.025 \end{aligned}So the lower critical region is $X \le 10$.

For the upper tail:\begin{aligned} P(X \ge 19) &= P(Y \le 1) \cr &= 0.0243 \le 0.025 \cr P(X \ge 18) &= P(Y \le 2) \cr &= 0.0913 > 0.025 \end{aligned}So the upper critical region is $X \ge 19$.

The combined critical region is:\begin{aligned} X \le 10 \quad \text{or} \quad X \ge 19 \end{aligned}Summing the two tails gives the actual significance level:\begin{aligned} \text{Actual level} &= 0.0139 + 0.0243 \cr &= 0.0382 \quad (3.82\%) \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) $H_0: p = 0.75$, $H_1: p \neq 0.75$, (b) Do not reject $H_0$, (c) $X \le 10$ or $X \ge 19$, and $0.0382$

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), you compared the single-tail probability $0.0409$ to $0.05$ instead of doubling it for a two-tailed test ($2 \times 0.0409 = 0.0818 > 0.05$).
In part (a), the question asks whether the proportion *differs* from $0.75$, which specifies a two-tailed alternative hypothesis $H_1: p \neq 0.75$.
In part (c), $P(X \le 11) = 0.0409 > 0.025$, so $11$ cannot be in the lower critical region. The actual significance level is $0.0139 + 0.0243 = 0.0382$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Doubling P-Values for Two-Tailed Tests
bradley_insight.content: When evaluating a two-tailed binomial hypothesis using the $p$-value method, you must double the single tail probability: $$p\text{-value}$$ &&= 2 \times P(X \le 11)$$ $$= 0.0818$$ Alternatively, compare the single-tail probability directly to half the significance level: $0.0409 > 0.025$.

question:
The probability that an automated smoke detector triggers an audible alarm during a fire incident is $0.85$.

(a) Find the minimum number of independent detectors, $n$, that must be installed in an auditorium to ensure that the probability that at least one detector triggers an alarm during an incident is greater than $0.999$.

(b) A safety equipment manufacturer claims that an upgraded optical sensor has an alarm activation rate greater than $0.85$. In a trial of $25$ simulated fire incidents, the upgraded sensor successfully triggers an alarm on $24$ occasions.

Stating your hypotheses clearly, test the manufacturer's claim at the $1\%$ level of significance.
steps:
(a) Finding minimum number of detectors $n$:

Let $X \sim \text{B}(n, 0.85)$ denote the number of sounding detectors:\begin{aligned} P(X \ge 1) &> 0.999 \cr 1 - P(X = 0) &> 0.999 \cr 1 - (0.15)^n &> 0.999 \cr (0.15)^n &< 0.001 \end{aligned}Taking logarithms of both sides (reversing the inequality as $\log(0.15) < 0$):\begin{aligned} n\log(0.15) &< \log(0.001) \cr n &> \dfrac{\log(0.001)}{\log(0.15)} \cr n &> \dfrac{-3}{-0.8239} \cr n &> 3.64 \end{aligned}Since $n$ must be an integer, the minimum number is:\begin{aligned} n = 4 \end{aligned}

(b) Testing the manufacturer's claim:

State the hypotheses, where $p$ is the true activation probability:\begin{aligned} &H_0: p = 0.85 \cr &H_1: p > 0.85 \end{aligned}Under $H_0$, $X \sim \text{B}(25, 0.85)$.

Calculate the upper tail probability for $x \ge 24$:\begin{aligned} &P(X \ge 24)\cr&= P(X = 24) + P(X = 25) \end{aligned}Evaluating each term:\begin{aligned} P(X = 24) &= 25(0.85)^{24}(0.15) \cr &\approx 0.0759 \cr P(X = 25) &= (0.85)^{25} \cr &\approx 0.0172 \end{aligned}Summing these values:\begin{aligned} P(X \ge 24) &= 0.0759 + 0.0172 \cr &= 0.0931 \end{aligned}Comparing to the significance level $\alpha = 0.01$:\begin{aligned} 0.0931 > 0.01 \end{aligned}Because $0.0931 > 0.01$, we do not reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $1\%$ level to support the manufacturer's claim that the activation rate exceeds $0.85$.
Final Answer: (a) $n = 4$, (b) Do not reject $H_0$ as $0.0931 > 0.01$

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), because the $p$-value ($0.0931$) is greater than the significance level ($0.01$), the null hypothesis must not be rejected.
In part (b), you evaluated $P(X = 25)$ only. The test statistic requires the cumulative tail $$P(X \ge 24)$$ $$ = 0.0759 + 0.0172$$ $$ = 0.0931$$

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Inequality Reversal with Logarithms
bradley_insight.content: When solving $(0.15)^n < 0.001$, remember that the logarithm of any number strictly between $0$ and $1$ is negative. Dividing by $\log(0.15)$ flips the inequality sign from $<$ to $>$, giving $n > 3.64$, so $n = 4$.

subtopic: Type I and Type II Errors
question:
A component manufacturer supplies batches of precision resistors. A client applies an acceptance sampling plan to decide whether to accept or reject a large consignment:
• A random sample of $15$ resistors is tested from the consignment.
• The consignment is accepted if at most $1$ resistor is defective ($X \le 1$).
• The consignment is rejected if $2$ or more resistors are defective ($X \ge 2$).

The client tests the null hypothesis $H_0: p = 0.05$ against the alternative hypothesis $H_1: p > 0.05$, where $p$ is the true proportion of defective resistors in the consignment.

(a) State the critical region for rejecting the consignment.

(b) Calculate the probability of a Type I error (the producer's risk of having an acceptable consignment rejected).

(c) If a substandard consignment with a true defect rate of $p = 0.20$ is delivered, calculate the probability of a Type II error (the consumer's risk of accepting a substandard consignment).

(d) Calculate the statistical power of the test against the specific alternative $p = 0.20$.
steps:
(a) Critical region:

The consignment is rejected when $2$ or more defective resistors are found:\begin{aligned} X \ge 2 \end{aligned}

(b) Probability of a Type I error:

A Type I error is rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is true ($p = 0.05$):\begin{aligned} &P(\text{Type I})\cr &= P(X \ge 2 \mid p = 0.05) \cr &= 1 - P(X \le 1 \mid p = 0.05) \end{aligned}Under $X \sim \text{B}(15, 0.05)$:\begin{aligned} P(X = 0) &= (0.95)^{15} \cr &\approx 0.4633 \cr P(X = 1) &= 15(0.05)(0.95)^{14} \cr &\approx 0.3658 \end{aligned}Summing these values:\begin{aligned} P(X \le 1) &= 0.4633 + 0.3658 \cr &= 0.8291 \end{aligned}Subtracting from $1$:\begin{aligned} P(\text{Type I}) &= 1 - 0.8291 \cr &= 0.1709 \quad (17.09\%) \end{aligned}

(c) Probability of a Type II error:

A Type II error is accepting $H_0$ when $H_1$ is true ($p = 0.20$):\begin{aligned} P(\text{Type II}) &= P(X \le 1 \mid p = 0.20) \end{aligned}Under $X \sim \text{B}(15, 0.20)$:\begin{aligned} P(X = 0) &= (0.80)^{15} \cr &\approx 0.0352 \cr P(X = 1) &= 15(0.20)(0.80)^{14} \cr &\approx 0.1319 \end{aligned}Adding these values:\begin{aligned} P(\text{Type II}) &= 0.0352 + 0.1319 \cr &= 0.1671 \quad (16.71\%) \end{aligned}

(d) Statistical power of the test:

The power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis:\begin{aligned} \text{Power} &= 1 - P(\text{Type II}) \cr &= 1 - 0.1671 \cr &= 0.8329 \quad (83.29\%) \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (b), $0.8291$ is the probability of accepting $H_0$. A Type I error is rejecting $H_0$ when it is true, which equals $1 - 0.8291 = 0.1709$.
In parts (c) and (d), you reversed the Type II error and the power. The Type II error is accepting $H_0$ ($0.1671$), and the power is rejecting $H_0$ ($1 - 0.1671 = 0.8329$).
In part (a), the critical region is the set of values that lead to the *rejection* of $H_0$, which is $X \ge 2$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Power and Error Duality
bradley_insight.content: Always remember the relationship $\text{Power} = 1 - \beta$, where $\beta$ is the probability of a Type II error. Power measures the test's ability to detect a defect when one actually exists—here, an $83.29\%$ chance of intercepting a substandard consignment.

question:
A long-serving fleet operations manager at a logistics company informs the newly appointed manager that the daily delivery mileage of company vans is normally distributed with a mean of $145.0\text{ km}$ and a standard deviation of $18.0\text{ km}$.

The new manager believes that the daily delivery mileage during the peak holiday season will have a different mean. Subsequently, she randomly selects $36$ daily delivery mileage records from the holiday season. The sample mean for this sample is $150.8\text{ km}$.

(a) Stating your hypotheses clearly, carry out a hypothesis test to show that the new manager's belief can be supported at the $10\%$ level of significance.

(b) In this context, give one practical reason why the new manager's belief could be true.
steps:
(a) Hypothesis test for a difference in mean mileage:

State the null and alternative hypotheses, where $\mu$ is the population mean daily mileage during the holiday season:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \mu = 145.0 \cr &H_1: \mu \neq 145.0 \end{aligned}Under $H_0$, the sample mean follows:\begin{aligned} \bar{X} \sim \text{N}\left(145.0, \dfrac{18.0^2}{36}\right) \end{aligned}Calculate the standard error:\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\bar{x}} &= \dfrac{18.0}{\sqrt{36}} \cr &= \dfrac{18.0}{6} \cr &= 3.0\text{ km} \end{aligned}Calculate the test statistic:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{150.8 - 145.0}{3.0} \cr &= \dfrac{5.8}{3.0} \cr &\approx 1.933 \end{aligned}For a two-tailed test at the $10\%$ significance level, the critical values are:\begin{aligned} z_{\text{crit}} = \pm 1.645 \end{aligned}Comparing the test statistic:\begin{aligned} 1.933 > 1.645 \end{aligned}Because the test statistic exceeds the critical value, we reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $10\%$ level to support the new manager's belief that the mean daily mileage differs during the peak holiday season.

(b) Practical context:

During the peak holiday season, increased consumer demand requires vans to make more deliveries and complete longer routes, leading to a higher average daily mileage.
Final Answer: (a) Reject $H_0$ as $1.933 > 1.645$, (b) Increased seasonal delivery volume

pi_options.ans: (a) Do not reject $H_0$ as $1.933 < 1.960$, (b) Increased seasonal delivery volume
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), $1.960$ is the critical value for a $5\%$ two-tailed test. The question specifies a $10\%$ significance level, which has critical values $z = \pm 1.645$, leading to the rejection of $H_0$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Reject $H_0$ as $1.933 > 1.282$, (b) Increased seasonal delivery volume
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), $1.282$ is the critical value for a $10\%$ one-tailed test. The belief states that the mean is 'different', requiring a two-tailed test with critical values $\pm 1.645$.

pi_options.ans: (a) Reject $H_0$ as $1.933 > 1.645$, (b) Vans require more frequent servicing
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), more frequent servicing does not explain why delivery mileage changes; the change in mileage is driven by higher delivery volume and extended delivery routes.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Matching Alpha to Tail Structure
bradley_insight.content: Notice that at the $5\%$ two-tailed level ($z_{\text{crit}} = 1.960$), we would fail to reject $H_0$ because $1.933 < 1.960$. Specifying a $10\%$ two-tailed level puts $5\%$ into each tail ($z_{\text{crit}} = 1.645$), allowing the manager's claim to be accepted.

question:
A bottling plant fills bottles of sparkling mineral water. The volume of water dispensed per bottle, $V\text{ ml}$, is normally distributed with mean $750.0\text{ ml}$ and standard deviation $8.0\text{ ml}$.

Following the installation of a new dispensing valve, the quality assurance manager suspects that the machine is overfilling the bottles.

A random sample of $16$ bottles is tested, yielding a sample mean volume of $754.2\text{ ml}$.

(a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses to test the manager's suspicion.

(b) Stating the distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis, test the manager's suspicion at the $5\%$ level of significance.

(c) Calculate the $p$-value for this test.

(d) Determine the critical value of the sample mean, $\bar{v}$, for this test at the $5\%$ level of significance.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

The manager suspects overfilling, which specifies an upper-tail test:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \mu = 750.0 \cr &H_1: \mu > 750.0 \end{aligned}

(b) Test of the manager's suspicion:

Under $H_0$, the sample mean follows:\begin{aligned} \bar{V} \sim \text{N}\left(750.0, \dfrac{8.0^2}{16}\right) \end{aligned}The standard error is:\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\bar{v}} &= \dfrac{8.0}{\sqrt{16}} \cr &= \dfrac{8.0}{4} \cr &= 2.0\text{ ml} \end{aligned}Calculate the test statistic:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{754.2 - 750.0}{2.0} \cr &= \dfrac{4.2}{2.0} \cr &= 2.10 \end{aligned}For an upper-tail test at the $5\%$ significance level, the critical value is:\begin{aligned} z_{\text{crit}} = 1.645 \end{aligned}Comparing the test statistic:\begin{aligned} 2.10 > 1.645 \end{aligned}Because $z > z_{\text{crit}}$, we reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $5\%$ level that the machine is overfilling bottles.

(c) Calculating the $p$-value:

Evaluating the upper-tail probability for $z = 2.10$:\begin{aligned} p\text{-value} &= P(Z > 2.10) \cr &= 1 - \Phi(2.10) \cr &= 1 - 0.9821 \cr &= 0.0179 \end{aligned}

(d) Critical value of $\bar{v}$:

Using the critical value $z_{\text{crit}} = 1.645$:\begin{aligned} \bar{v}_{\text{crit}} &= 750.0 + 1.645(2.0) \cr &= 750.0 + 3.29 \cr &= 753.29 \cr &\approx 753.3\text{ ml} \end{aligned}

pi_options.feedback: In part (a), the manager specifically suspects overfilling, which requires a one-tailed test $H_1: \mu > 750$, not a two-tailed test.
In part (c), you doubled the tail probability ($2 \times 0.0179 = 0.0358$). For a one-tailed test, the $p$-value is simply the single tail probability $P(Z > 2.10) = 0.0179$.
In part (b), you standardised using $\sigma = 8.0$ instead of the standard error $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = 2.0$, producing an incorrect $z$-score of $0.525$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Critical Value vs Test Statistic Equivalence
bradley_insight.content: Notice how parts (b) and (d) confirm each other: the observed sample mean of $754.2\text{ ml}$ exceeds the critical boundary of $753.3\text{ ml}$, which corresponds directly to the test statistic $z = 2.10$ exceeding $z_{\text{crit}} = 1.645$.

question:
The duration of service transactions, $T$ seconds, at an automated banking kiosk has an unknown distribution with mean $\mu = 85.0\text{ seconds}$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 24.0\text{ seconds}$.

A branch manager suspects that the introduction of a redesigned touch-screen interface has altered the population mean transaction time.

She records the transaction times for a random sample of $64$ customers using the redesigned interface, obtaining a sample mean of $\bar{t} = 79.5\text{ seconds}$.

(a) Explain how the Central Limit Theorem enables a hypothesis test to be carried out even though the population distribution of $T$ is unknown.

(b) Stating your hypotheses clearly, test at the $5\%$ level of significance whether there is evidence that the mean transaction time has changed.

(c) Calculate a $95\%$ confidence interval for the new population mean transaction time, $\mu$.
steps:
(a) Application of the Central Limit Theorem:

The Central Limit Theorem states that for a large sample size ($n \ge 30$), the distribution of the sample mean $\bar{T}$ is approximately normal regardless of the underlying population distribution. Because $n = 64$ is large, we can model $\bar{T}$ as normally distributed.

(b) Hypothesis test:

State the hypotheses for a two-tailed test:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \mu = 85.0 \cr &H_1: \mu \neq 85.0 \end{aligned}Calculate the standard error:\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\bar{t}} &= \dfrac{24.0}{\sqrt{64}} \cr &= \dfrac{24.0}{8} \cr &= 3.0\text{ s} \end{aligned}Calculate the test statistic:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{79.5 - 85.0}{3.0} \cr &= \dfrac{-5.5}{3.0} \cr &\approx -1.833 \end{aligned}For a two-tailed test at the $5\%$ significance level, the critical values are:\begin{aligned} z_{\text{crit}} = \pm 1.960 \end{aligned}Comparing the test statistic:\begin{aligned} -1.833 > -1.960 \end{aligned}Because $-1.833$ does not fall into the critical region, we do not reject $H_0$.

There is insufficient evidence at the $5\%$ level to suggest that the mean transaction time has changed.

(c) $95\%$ confidence interval:

Using the formula $\bar{t} \pm 1.960\sigma_{\bar{t}}$:\begin{aligned} \bar{t} \pm 1.960(3.0) &= 79.5 \pm 5.88 \end{aligned}Evaluating the limits:\begin{aligned} [79.5 - 5.88, 79.5 + 5.88] &= [73.62, 85.38] \cr &\approx [73.6, 85.4]\text{ s} \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a) CLT guarantees normal sample mean for large $n$, (b) Do not reject $H_0$, (c) $[73.6, 85.4]\text{ s}$

pi_options.ans: (a) CLT guarantees normal sample mean for large $n$, (b) Reject $H_0$, (c) $[73.6, 85.4]\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), $|-1.833| = 1.833 < 1.960$, so the test statistic falls outside the critical region. $H_0$ must not be rejected.

pi_options.ans: (a) CLT guarantees the population is normal, (b) Do not reject $H_0$, (c) $[73.6, 85.4]\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: In part (a), the Central Limit Theorem applies to the distribution of the *sample mean*, not the population itself. The population distribution remains non-normal.

pi_options.ans: (a) CLT guarantees normal sample mean for large $n$, (b) Do not reject $H_0$, (c) $[76.5, 82.5]\text{ s}$
pi_options.feedback: In part (c), you used a critical value of $1.0$ instead of $1.960$. The margin of error is $1.960 \times 3.0 = 5.88\text{ s}$.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Duality of Tests and Confidence Intervals
bradley_insight.content: Notice how the $95\%$ confidence interval $[73.6, 85.4]\text{ s}$ contains the baseline value $85.0\text{ s}$. When a $95\%$ confidence interval contains the hypothesized null parameter, a two-tailed test at the $5\%$ level will always fail to reject $H_0$.

question:
A food packaging facility produces packets of breakfast cereal with a stated nominal net mass of $500.0\text{ g}$. The mass of a packet, $W\text{ g}$, is normally distributed with standard deviation $\sigma = 15.0\text{ g}$.

The quality control team tests the null hypothesis $H_0: \mu = 500.0\text{ g}$ against the alternative hypothesis $H_1: \mu < 500.0\text{ g}$ at the $2.5\%$ level of significance using a random sample of size $n$.

(a) If a sample of size $n = 25$ packets is taken:
 (i) find the critical region for the sample mean $\bar{w}$,
 (ii) find the probability of committing a Type II error if the true population mean mass has slipped to $\mu = 490.0\text{ g}$.

(b) The quality control team wishes to adjust the sample size so that the lower boundary of the critical region is exactly $\bar{w} = 494.0\text{ g}$ at the $2.5\%$ significance level ($z = -1.960$). Determine the required sample size, $n$.
steps:
(a)(i) Finding the critical region for $n = 25$:

Calculate the standard error:\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\bar{w}} &= \dfrac{15.0}{\sqrt{25}} \cr &= \dfrac{15.0}{5} \cr &= 3.0\text{ g} \end{aligned}For a lower-tail test at the $2.5\%$ significance level, $z_{\text{crit}} = -1.960$:\begin{aligned} \bar{w}_{\text{crit}} &= 500.0 - 1.960(3.0) \cr &= 500.0 - 5.88 \cr &= 494.12\text{ g} \end{aligned}The critical region is:\begin{aligned} \bar{w} \le 494.12\text{ g} \end{aligned}

(a)(ii) Probability of a Type II error when $\mu = 490.0$:

A Type II error occurs when $H_0$ is accepted despite being false. We accept $H_0$ when $\bar{w} > 494.12\text{ g}$:\begin{aligned}& P(\text{Type II})\cr &= P(\bar{W} > 494.12 \mid \mu = 490.0) \end{aligned}Standardising under the true mean $\mu = 490.0\text{ g}$:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{494.12 - 490.0}{3.0} \cr &= \dfrac{4.12}{3.0} \cr &\approx 1.373 \end{aligned}Evaluating the upper-tail probability:\begin{aligned} P(Z > 1.373) &= 1 - \Phi(1.373) \cr &= 1 - 0.9151 \cr &= 0.0849 \quad (8.49\%) \end{aligned}

(b) Finding required sample size $n$:

Setting the critical boundary equal to $494.0\text{ g}$:\begin{aligned} 500.0 - 1.960\left(\dfrac{15.0}{\sqrt{n}}\right) &= 494.0 \cr 6.0 &= \dfrac{29.4}{\sqrt{n}} \cr \sqrt{n} &= \dfrac{29.4}{6.0} \cr &= 4.9 \cr n &= 4.9^2 \cr &= 24.01 \end{aligned}Rounding to the nearest integer gives:\begin{aligned} n = 24 \end{aligned}
Final Answer: (a)(i) $\bar{w} \le 494.12\text{ g}$, (ii) $0.0849$, (b) $n = 24$

pi_options.feedback: In part (a)(ii), $0.9151$ is $\Phi(1.373)$, the probability of rejecting $H_0$. A Type II error is accepting $H_0$, which is the upper tail: $1 - 0.9151 = 0.0849$.
In part (a)(i), the test is for underfilling ($H_1: \mu < 500$), so the critical region lies in the lower tail: $\bar{w} \le 494.12\text{ g}$.
In part (b), $\sqrt{n} = 4.9$, so $n = 4.9^2 = 24.01 \approx 24$. You must square $4.9$ rather than leaving it unsquared.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Shifting Distributions for Type II Error
bradley_insight.content: To calculate the probability of a Type II error, keep the acceptance boundary fixed from the original test ($\bar{w} > 494.12$) and re-standardise using the new, true mean ($\mu = 490.0$). The standard error $\sigma_{\bar{w}} = 3.0$ remains unchanged.

question:
An agricultural research station investigates the efficacy of two distinct soil conditioning treatments, Treatment A and Treatment B, on the yield of commercial tomato crops.

• The yield per plot using Treatment A follows a normal distribution with mean $\mu_A$ and standard deviation $\sigma_A = 4.2\text{ kg}$.
• The yield per plot using Treatment B follows a normal distribution with mean $\mu_B$ and standard deviation $\sigma_B = 3.6\text{ kg}$.

A random sample of $36$ plots given Treatment A produces a sample mean yield of $\bar{x}_A = 48.5\text{ kg}$.
An independent random sample of $49$ plots given Treatment B produces a sample mean yield of $\bar{x}_B = 46.2\text{ kg}$.

(a) State suitable null and alternative hypotheses to test whether Treatment A produces a higher mean yield than Treatment B.

(b) State the distribution of the difference in sample means, $\bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B$, assuming the null hypothesis is true.

(c) Test, at the $1\%$ level of significance, whether there is evidence that Treatment A produces a higher mean yield than Treatment B.

(d) State an essential statistical assumption regarding the two samples required for this test to be valid.
steps:
(a) Hypotheses:

Testing whether Treatment A produces a higher mean yield than Treatment B:\begin{aligned} &H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B \cr &H_1: \mu_A > \mu_B \end{aligned}(Equivalently, $H_0: \mu_A - \mu_B = 0$ versus $H_1: \mu_A - \mu_B > 0$).

(b) Distribution of $\bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B$ under $H_0$:

Under $H_0$, the mean difference is $0$. Summing the independent variances of the sample means:\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(\bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B) &= \dfrac{\sigma_A^2}{n_A} + \dfrac{\sigma_B^2}{n_B} \cr &= \dfrac{4.2^2}{36} + \dfrac{3.6^2}{49} \cr &= \dfrac{17.64}{36} + \dfrac{12.96}{49} \cr &= 0.49 + 0.2645 \cr &= 0.7545 \end{aligned}Therefore:\begin{aligned} \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B \sim \text{N}(0, 0.7545) \end{aligned}

(c) Hypothesis test at $1\%$ significance level:

Calculate the standard error:\begin{aligned} \text{SE} &= \sqrt{0.7545} \cr &\approx 0.8686\text{ kg} \end{aligned}Observed difference in sample means:\begin{aligned} \bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B &= 48.5 - 46.2 \cr &= 2.3\text{ kg} \end{aligned}Calculate the test statistic:\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{2.3 - 0}{0.8686} \cr &\approx 2.648 \end{aligned}For an upper-tail test at the $1\%$ level, the critical value is:\begin{aligned} z_{\text{crit}} = 2.326 \end{aligned}Comparing the test statistic:\begin{aligned} 2.648 > 2.326 \end{aligned}Because $z > z_{\text{crit}}$, we reject $H_0$.

There is significant evidence at the $1\%$ level that Treatment A produces a higher mean yield than Treatment B.

(d) Essential statistical assumption:

The two samples must be completely independent of each other.
Final Answer: (a) $H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B$, $H_1: \mu_A > \mu_B$, (b) $N(0, 0.7545)$, (c) Reject $H_0$, (d) Independent samples

pi_options.feedback: In part (c), because the test statistic $z = 2.648$ is strictly greater than the critical value $2.326$, $H_0$ must be rejected.
In part (a), the research question asks whether Treatment A produces a *higher* yield, which requires a one-tailed test $H_1: \mu_A > \mu_B$.

pi_options.ans: (a) $H_0: \mu_A = \mu_B$, $H_1: \mu_A > \mu_B$, (b) $N(0, 0.2255)$, (c) Reject $H_0$, (d) Samples must have equal variance
pi_options.feedback: In part (b), variances always add: $$\text{Var}(\bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B)$$ $$= 0.49 + 0.2645 = 0.7545$$ You must never subtract the variances.

bradley_insight.title: The Head Teacher's Eye: Variances Always Add in Differences
bradley_insight.content: A perennial error in two-sample normal tests is subtracting the variances because of the minus sign in $\bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B$. Differences in independent random variables always increase total uncertainty, so variances must always be added: $\dfrac{\sigma_A^2}{n_A} + \dfrac{\sigma_B^2}{n_B}$.
